1953-iran-coup.title: Mohammad Reza Pahlavi
1953-iran-coup.summary: The last Shah of Iran, whom John Kiriakou describes as an absolute monarch and dictator who ran a bloodthirsty intelligence service against his own citizens, held formal diplomatic relations with Israel, and sent Iran's oil to the United States and the United Kingdom. Restored to the throne after the 1953 overthrow of Mohammad Mosaddegh, he left the country on a ski vacation in February 1979 and never returned.

1953-iran-coup.title: SAVAK
1953-iran-coup.summary: The intelligence service of the Shah of Iran, which John Kiriakou describes as bloodthirsty and as having spent far more effort investigating and murdering Iranian citizens than operating abroad. He credits its record — torture, executions of tens of thousands, and bodies dismembered and left in the street — with the durability of Iranian hostility to the Pahlavi family half a century later.

1953-iran-coup.title: Haroon Yenor trial
1953-iran-coup.summary: Federal terrorism prosecution in which John Kiriakou testified as a defense expert witness; Yenor, arrested in November 2024 on charges tied to an alleged plot to bomb the New York Stock Exchange and a synagogue, was acquitted on all six charges on June 30; Kiriakou's expert testimony argued the FBI supplied the idea, the bomb, the explosives, the timer, the detonation cord, and the getaway car.

1953-iran-coup.title: Myanmar's civil war, per Kiriakou
1953-iran-coup.summary: John Kiriakou's account of Myanmar as the only country in the world continuously at war without a single day of peace since World War II, its Buddhist-majority persecution of Muslims, Christians, and Hindus, his view that Aung San Suu Kyi should have her Nobel Peace Prize stripped, and his argument that the world ignores the country's atrocities because it has gems rather than oil.

1953-iran-coup.title: Sofia, Bulgaria Dead Drop
1953-iran-coup.summary: John Kiriakou's account of a CIA trip to Sofia, Bulgaria, in which he tracked down and debriefed a retired Bulgarian general — a Cold War-era trainee at Fort Polk, Louisiana — about his proximity to the 1975 assassination of CIA station chief Richard Welch in Athens.

1953-iran-coup.title: The Kashgar execution
1953-iran-coup.summary: The 1999 street execution John Kiriakou has said he witnessed in Kashgar in China''s Xinjiang region, at the height of what he calls the East Turkestan Independence Movement, a flatbed truck with loudspeakers pulling into the old Silk Road quarter of the city, an announcement in Mandarin, and the shooting of a handcuffed man on the back of the truck. Kiriakou pairs the anecdote with his broader assessment: China is not running a genocide of the Uyghurs, but it is running a cultural erasure, supplanting them with Han Chinese, tearing down the traditional Silk Road city, and enforcing Beijing time all the way to the western border.

1993-bush-assassination-plot.title: Office of Leadership Analysis
1993-bush-assassination-plot.summary: CIA analytic office — internally called LDA, for Leadership Development Analysis — founded by CIA psychiatrist Jerome Post, where John Kiriakou was hired at the start of his CIA career and spent his first seven and a half years as Saddam Hussein's classified psychological profiler. His first assignment, given on his first day, was covering Iraq and Kuwait, a portfolio his boss described as so quiet the office sometimes went days without a single incoming cable.

1993-bush-assassination-plot.title: Asel al-Ghabandi
1993-bush-assassination-plot.summary: Kuwaiti resistance figure during the 1990–91 Iraqi occupation; per John Kiriakou, a "bona fide hero" whose telephone reporting on Iraqi troop movements, roadblocks, atrocities, and the location of inspections reached the CIA every single day via NSA [call interception](/wiki/the-intercept) — Kiriakou's account of the resistance figure who best understood how to weaponize the certainty that the Americans were listening to everything.

1993-bush-assassination-plot.title: The Kashgar execution
1993-bush-assassination-plot.summary: The 1999 street execution John Kiriakou has said he witnessed in Kashgar in China''s Xinjiang region, at the height of what he calls the East Turkestan Independence Movement, a flatbed truck with loudspeakers pulling into the old Silk Road quarter of the city, an announcement in Mandarin, and the shooting of a handcuffed man on the back of the truck. Kiriakou pairs the anecdote with his broader assessment: China is not running a genocide of the Uyghurs, but it is running a cultural erasure, supplanting them with Han Chinese, tearing down the traditional Silk Road city, and enforcing Beijing time all the way to the western border.

1993-bush-assassination-plot.title: The USS Abraham Lincoln crisis
1993-bush-assassination-plot.summary: The September 2026 reporting John Kiriakou aired on his own show describing sailor mental-health collapse aboard the U.S. Navy aircraft carrier USS Abraham Lincoln, sailors attempting to jump overboard, socks stuffed into toilets to force a return home, food indistinguishable from federal prison food, and messages scrawled on the wing of a parked aircraft including *"All this for the Holy Land"* and *"Be a good boy and do what Israel tells you to"*. Kiriakou reads the crisis as the point at which the American military begins to notice, and reject, the wars its civilian leadership is picking.

1993-bush-assassination-plot.title: The Frank Kendall Air Force One case
1993-bush-assassination-plot.summary: The 2026 Espionage Act investigation of former Secretary of the Air Force Frank Kendall, an acknowledged MAGA Republican expert whom John Kiriakou describes as having publicly warned that the Boeing 747 the government of Qatar gifted the United States for use as Air Force One was not up to the security standards a presidential aircraft requires. Kiriakou reads the resulting grand-jury proceeding as embarrassment prosecution, and expects Kendall not to be indicted, but the case illustrates the reach of Espionage Act charges Kiriakou himself faced.

1993-bush-assassination-plot.title: William Webster
1993-bush-assassination-plot.summary: Director of Central Intelligence during the 1990 invasion of Kuwait, and before that a federal judge and Director of the FBI; per John Kiriakou, "a lovely man … just a very kind, nice man" and "a giant in my mind" — the director Kiriakou first briefed at four in the morning, on fifteen minutes' notice, during the Kuwait task force, and who sat two seats away from him in the Oval Office on the morning of the invasion.

2023-classified-documents-scandal.title: Barack Obama
2023-classified-documents-scandal.summary: 44th U.S. president; in John Kiriakou's account, Obama publicly recounted refusing Benjamin Netanyahu's demand to bomb Iran and calling Israel's threat to use nuclear weapons a bluff — a bluff Kiriakou says Donald Trump later believed.

2023-classified-documents-scandal.title: Carrying classified material out of a SCIF
2023-classified-documents-scandal.summary: The two lawful procedures John Kiriakou describes for removing classified documents from a secure facility — a double-enveloped, double-marked package addressed to your home agency, or a leather bag with a double lock — and his flat statement that nothing about either allows a document to be forgotten in a garage for twelve years.

2023-classified-documents-scandal.title: The pillow-talk disclosure case
2023-classified-documents-scandal.summary: A case John Kiriakou witnessed from the next desk: a CIA officer told a classified fact to a former senior officer turned CNN commentator during an affair, he repeated it on air, and the agency identified her within days. Her punishment was four weeks'' suspension without pay and a memo in her file. Kiriakou uses it as the benchmark for how far the handling of disclosures has moved — today, he says, it would be an Espionage Act prosecution and about five years in prison.

2023-classified-documents-scandal.title: The Kashgar execution
2023-classified-documents-scandal.summary: The 1999 street execution John Kiriakou has said he witnessed in Kashgar in China''s Xinjiang region, at the height of what he calls the East Turkestan Independence Movement, a flatbed truck with loudspeakers pulling into the old Silk Road quarter of the city, an announcement in Mandarin, and the shooting of a handcuffed man on the back of the truck. Kiriakou reads the crisis as the point at which the American military begins to notice, and reject, the wars its civilian leadership is picking.

2023-classified-documents-scandal.summary: The 2026 Espionage Act investigation of former Secretary of the Air Force Frank Kendall, an acknowledged MAGA Republican expert whom John Kiriakou describes as having publicly warned that the Boeing 747 the government of Qatar gifted the United States for use as Air Force One was not up to the security standards a presidential aircraft requires. Kiriakou reads the resulting grand-jury proceeding as embarrassment prosecution, and expects Kendall not to be indicted, but the case illustrates the reach of Espionage Act charges Kiriakou himself faced.

2026-iran-war-economic-shock.title: The two hundred billion dollar war request
2026-iran-war-economic-shock.summary: The Defense Department''s supplemental request for the 2026 Iran war, made without consulting Congress. John Kiriakou''s contribution is his verdict on the Republicans who dropped their objections on the grounds that wartime is no time for questions: a bunch of cowards.

2026-iran-war-economic-shock.title: The USS Abraham Lincoln crisis
2026-iran-war-economic-shock.summary: The September 2026 reporting John Kiriakou aired on his own show describing sailor mental-health collapse aboard the U.S. Navy aircraft carrier USS Abraham Lincoln, sailors attempting to jump overboard, socks stuffed into toilets to force a return home, food indistinguishable from federal prison food, and messages scrawled on the wing of a parked aircraft including *"All this for the Holy Land"* and *"Be a good boy and do what Israel tells you to"*. Kiriakou reads the crisis as the point at which the American military begins to notice, and reject, the wars its civilian leadership is picking.

2026-iran-war-economic-shock.title: Greater and Lesser Tunb Islands
2026-iran-war-economic-shock.summary: Two small, largely uninhabited islands in the Persian Gulf, belonging to the emirate of Sharjah in the UAE, occupied by Iran in a 1990s incident John Kiriakou recounts as CIA analyst; Kiriakou correctly predicted the UAE would not go to war over them given Sharjah's heavy trade dependence on Iran, and has since used the case against 2026 speculation that the United States would seize them back.

2026-iran-war-economic-shock.title: The Danish Greenland demolition plan
2026-iran-war-economic-shock.summary: Denmark's preparations to destroy its own airstrips in Greenland rather than let an American invasion use them, including blood supplies moved into place. John Kiriakou confirms the preparations were real and made because the Danes took Donald Trump at his word.

2026-iran-war-economic-shock.title: The Hajj ban as leverage
2026-iran-war-economic-shock.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer to what a Saudi retaliation against Iran would look like: not a military strike but a ban on Iranians making the pilgrimage to Mecca. He notes it was done at the turn of the 1980s, that it produced a crisis, and that Iranian terrorist attacks against Saudis followed.

2026-iran-war-economic-shock.title: The Netanyahu death rumour
2026-iran-war-economic-shock.summary: A theory advanced by well-regarded podcasters during the 2026 Iran war that Benjamin Netanyahu had been killed and the fact concealed — his son's seven-day silence read as sitting shiva. John Kiriakou recounts it collapsing when Netanyahu gave a press conference, and sets it against the real decapitation campaign against the IRGC.

2026-iran-war.title: Decapitation strikes
2026-iran-war.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that killing an adversary's leadership does not defeat the adversary — grounded in a standing joke from his own service that the CIA had killed twenty-seven separate "number three" figures in al-Qaeda, and applied to the 2026 Iran war, where the entire political, military and scientific leadership was killed in the opening days and the fighting continued regardless.

2026-iran-war.title: Erbil and the Kurdish autonomy question
2026-iran-war.summary: Reading reports that Erbil airport in Iraqi Kurdistan had been targeted twice on the first night of the 2026 war, John Kiriakou drew out the implication: Baghdad had said repeatedly it would take no part in an American attack on Iran, but the Kurds hold autonomy in the north, and the strikes on Erbil suggest they may be supporting the attack independently of the Iraqi government.

2026-iran-war.title: Population decline as a national-security question
2026-iran-war.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that demographic collapse — an emigrated Greek middle class, a shrinking Russia, and a Chinese population he believes is far smaller than claimed — is a strategic variable rather than a social one, and that some countries may not remain viable as countries without large population changes.

2026-iran-war.title: Prison pedophile accounts
2026-iran-war.summary: John Kiriakou's account of encountering convicted pedophiles for the first time in federal prison, drawing on advice from a psychiatrist friend and his own work running the chapel library — one of only two safe spaces in prison for inmates convicted of child sex crimes.

2026-iran-war.title: The "Soylent Green is people" cable easter egg
2026-iran-war.summary: A long-running CIA case-officer in-joke in which the line "Soylent Green is people" is hidden inside classified operational cables as a sequence of incongruously lowercase letters

2026-iran-war.title: The BBC and the sanctions coverage
2026-iran-war.summary: John Kiriakou's assessment of the BBC — that it has a long history of offering both sides, which American broadcasters do not — set against his memory of watching it from inside the CIA in the run-up to the liberation of Kuwait, when its reporting on starving Iraqi children under sanctions drove him mad, because food was not sanctioned and Saddam Hussein was refusing to distribute it.

2026-strike-wave.title: 2026 Iran war economic shock
2026-strike-wave.summary: John Kiriakou''s running assessment of the economic damage from the 2026 Iran war — an oil shock he says already exceeds both 1970s shocks combined, a natural-gas shock worse than the Nord Stream destruction, and a chokepoint problem that runs through fertilizer as much as fuel, since 65% of the world''s supply must transit the Strait of Hormuz. His summary: "This is an economic slowdown of choice."

2026-strike-wave.title: Richard D. Wolff
2026-strike-wave.summary: American Marxian economist, professor emeritus at the University of Massachusetts Amherst and a recurring guest of John Kiriakou, who calls him one of his favourite people and says he feels smarter after every conversation; Wolff's appearances supply Kiriakou's audience with a class analysis of tariffs, federal debt and the periodic crashes of capitalism.

2026-strike-wave.title: Trump tariffs
2026-strike-wave.summary: The across-the-board tariffs imposed by Donald Trump on United States trading partners, which John Kiriakou describes as having shaken up the economy faster than any president in generations — causing chaos in global stock markets, laying the groundwork for inflation and economic contraction, and producing political upheaval at home.

2026-strike-wave.title: Europe's 2026 jet fuel crisis
2026-strike-wave.summary: The Associated Press report, which John Kiriakou opened his programme with on 16 April 2026, that Europe would run out of jet fuel within six weeks — a shortage he called an economic calamity that would ripple across the entire planet, and which the economist Richard D. Wolff traced not to any shortage of crude but to the closure of the Strait of Hormuz starving the refineries that convert petroleum into jet fuel.

2026-strike-wave.title: 2026 Iran war
2026-strike-wave.summary: The open-ended American and Israeli war against Iran that John Kiriakou tracked week by week on his own show — a conflict he says was sold as three weeks, ran into its fifth month, achieved every decapitation objective it set, and continued anyway. His grade for it is a D, and his forecast is a Truth Social post declaring victory while nothing changes.

2026-strike-wave.title: Europe and the 2026 Iran war
2026-strike-wave.summary: The rupture between the United States and its European allies over the 2026 Iran war, as the economist Richard D. Wolff described it on John Kiriakou''s programme: Europe was not told the attack was coming, refused Donald Trump''s request for help halfway through it, and was then publicly attacked by him for refusing. Wolff''s verdict was that the alliance did not survive it — ''NATO is dead, the alliance is dead, and the blame for it is 100% on the US.''

2028-presidential-field.title: JD Vance
2028-presidential-field.summary: Vice president and 2028 Republican front-runner, whose Joe Rogan interview admitting the administration "mishandled the Epstein files" John Kiriakou reads not as candour but as an authorised manoeuvre — and whose passing remark that any documents tying Epstein to intelligence "wouldn't exist in 2026" Kiriakou treats as a matter-of-fact accusation that the CIA destroyed evidence.

2028-presidential-field.title: International Spy Museum
2028-presidential-field.summary: The Washington museum of espionage. John Kiriakou, who gives private tours of it, describes its room on the CIA torture program as a video loop in which only the torturers are given a voice — and in which he, the officer who exposed the program, is never mentioned.

2028-presidential-field.title: Oman
2028-presidential-field.summary: The Gulf sultanate John Kiriakou singles out as America's most durable friend in the region and its most useful channel to Iran — a country that has acted as go-between for Washington and Tehran many times, and which he argues should be approached again in place of carrier deployments and public threats.

2028-presidential-field.title: Sharia law
2028-presidential-field.summary: Islamic jurisprudence. Challenged by a viewer who equated it with executions of gay people, forced child marriage and the criminalisation of apostasy, John Kiriakou answers that those acts are largely the work of ISIS rather than of any government, and that Sharia is in substance a body of civil law covering inheritance, insurance, education, property ownership and commercial disputes.

2028-presidential-field.title: Wealth concentration
2028-presidential-field.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that the present distribution of wealth is historically unprecedented and politically unsustainable — that trillionaires have never existed before, that five men hold as much as the bottom eighty per cent of the world, and that a defence budget approaching $1.5 trillion cannot be reconciled with the social spending it would have to displace.

2028-presidential-field.title: CIA intelligence failures
2028-presidential-field.summary: John Kiriakou's standing position that the CIA has missed every major world event since its founding in 1947 — the building and the fall of the Berlin Wall, the collapse of the Soviet Union, the Iran hostage crisis, 9/11 — and that the remedy is therefore not more money but fewer overseas bases and actual accountability, of which he says there has been none.

9-11-commission.title: Omar al-Bayoumi
9-11-commission.summary: The Saudi national who housed and funded two of the 9/11 hijackers in California; John Kiriakou describes him as a Saudi intelligence officer working under a ghost job, places him at President Bush's Crawford ranch before the attacks, and says the CIA blocked the 9/11 Commission from investigating him.

9-11-commission.title: CIA–FBI interagency rivalry and 9/11
9-11-commission.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the historical CIA–FBI rivalry, dating to J. Edgar Hoover's opposition to the 1947 National Security Act, and how it manifested before September 11 when Cofer Black's Counterterrorism Center withheld from the FBI that hijackers Nawaf al-Hazmi and Khalid al-Mihdhar had been granted U.S. visas.

9-11-commission.title: Code Pink
9-11-commission.summary: The women-led peace group co-founded by Medea Benjamin. John Kiriakou first met them as a Senate staffer — he was the man who threw them out of a hearing he had produced, and got a lecture from Senator Shaheen for it. When he was arrested they were "right there next to me"; they threw his going-away party on the roof of the Hay-Adams, commissioned a folk group to sing a song rewritten about him, and quietly arranged for Roger Waters to pay off the second mortgage so his family could keep the house. He calls them his angels, and the one institution in American life he still trusts.

9-11-commission.title: National Security Act of 1947
9-11-commission.summary: The law that created the CIA and the National Security Council — passed, in John Kiriakou's telling, only because Harry Truman lied to J. Edgar Hoover. Hoover lobbied Capitol Hill to kill the bill until Truman promised the CIA would be a division of the FBI; the bill passed, Hoover realized he'd been duped, and ordered the FBI not to cooperate with the new agency — a freeze that lasted, incredibly, until after 9/11. Kiriakou's account of how the agency was designed at all runs through a room in New York where MI6 officers sat down with Bill Donovan, Prescott Bush and some pads of paper.

9-11-commission.title: Israeli foreknowledge of 9/11
9-11-commission.summary: John Kiriakou's stated belief that Israeli intelligence had penetrated al-Qaeda and knew an attack was coming but withheld the warning as a policy decision, offered as his explanation for the dozens of Israelis arrested in New York in the days after the attacks.

9-11-commission.title: Kiki Camarena case
9-11-commission.summary: 1985 abduction and murder of U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration agent Enrique "Kiki" Camarena in Mexico; cited by John Kiriakou as the trigger for the 1985 U.S. statute authorizing the extraterritorial seizure of foreign nationals — the legal authority underpinning the 2026 U.S. operation that seized President Nicolás Maduro of Venezuela.

9-11-plea-agreements.title: Guantánamo Bay detention camp
9-11-plea-agreements.summary: Per John Kiriakou — as chief of counterterrorism operations in Pakistan after September 11, 2001 — the Guantanamo detention facility began as a temporary holding measure intended to last two to three weeks while the CIA and Justice Department determined which federal district court should try each prisoner, not as a long-term detention infrastructure. The Rawalpindi jail had reached capacity, Pakistani intelligence demanded the prisoners be removed, and CIA headquarters directed Kiriakou to load them onto a C-12 cargo plane and fly them to Cuba.

9-11-plea-agreements.title: Khalid Sheikh Mohammed
9-11-plea-agreements.summary: Mastermind of the September 11, 2001 attacks; identified to the CIA by Abu Zubaydah, in the course of FBI interrogator Ali Soufan's rapport-based debriefing at the black site, as the man behind the kunya "Mukhtar" the agency had been hunting since at least 1996 for the Bojinka plot; per Kiriakou's relay of his self-account, radicalized by news video of an Israeli soldier with his boot on the neck of a Palestinian woman.

9-11-plea-agreements.title: Guantanamo Bay
9-11-plea-agreements.summary: U.S. naval base in Cuba; site of CIA detention operations during the post-9/11 enhanced interrogation program; briefly served by John Kiriakou as interim Chief during the summer of 2002.

9-11-plea-agreements.title: Yalta conference
9-11-plea-agreements.summary: The February 1945 Allied conference, which John Kiriakou uses as his teaching example of what a well-placed spy is worth: Stalin, told by a source inside the White House that Roosevelt was ill, insisted on a venue requiring a punishing multi-leg journey, then refused to delay the talks — and an exhausted Roosevelt, Kiriakou says, conceded Poland in order to go to bed.

9-11-plea-agreements.title: Superdelegates
9-11-plea-agreements.summary: The Democratic Party's automatic-delegate system, which John Kiriakou describes as created after George McGovern's 1972 landslide loss to return nominating power to party insiders. He cites West Virginia and Wyoming in 2016, where Bernie Sanders won the vote and Hillary Clinton took every delegate, and notes the Republican Party has no equivalent — which is why an insurgent like Donald Trump could win its nomination.

9-11-plea-agreements.title: Truck and Cat in the Hat
9-11-plea-agreements.summary: An incident at FCI Loretto in which John Kiriakou, told by one prisoner that another had called him a rat, invented a slur he knew would enrage a convicted serial killer — who beat the accuser badly enough to require a helicopter medevac. Kiriakou presents it as a live application of two rules he says he learned at the CIA: let others do your dirty work, and admit nothing, deny everything, make counter-accusations.

911-attribution-of-responsibility.title: The ballot-name-confusion tactic
911-attribution-of-responsibility.summary: John Kiriakou's historical tour of the ballot-splitting tactic, running a second candidate with the same name as the incumbent to peel off votes from voters who cannot tell the two apart. He anchors the account with the 2026 Alaska Senate race in which two men named Dan Sullivan appeared on the same ballot, then works back through John F. Kennedy's own 1946 use of the trick, a Florida 2020 race decided by 32 votes, and Russian and Indian variants that push the mechanic to comic extremes.

911-attribution-of-responsibility.title: Elizabeth Rouser
911-attribution-of-responsibility.summary: Named only in a producer/narrator voiceover on a Kiriakou interview episode, not in Kiriakou's own words; not attributable to Kiriakou in the corpus.

911-attribution-of-responsibility.title: Katherine Gun
911-attribution-of-responsibility.summary: UK whistleblower named once in an unlabeled multi-speaker panel transcript; not safely attributable to Kiriakou in the corpus.

911-attribution-of-responsibility.title: Mir Aimal Kansi CIA headquarters attack
911-attribution-of-responsibility.summary: The 1993 shooting outside CIA headquarters by Pakistani gunman Mir Aimal Kansi, who killed two and wounded seven CIA-bound commuters before fleeing to Pakistan; per John Kiriakou, the CIA located Kansi months later but had to hand the arrest to the FBI, and the resulting "how the FBI got their man" Time magazine cover so enraged senior CIA officers that it shaped the agency's insistence on going it alone against al-Qaeda after 9/11.

911-attribution-of-responsibility.title: Pete Hoekstra
911-attribution-of-responsibility.summary: Named once in an unlabeled multi-speaker panel transcript; not safely attributable to Kiriakou in the corpus.

911-attribution-of-responsibility.title: Restraint Camp
911-attribution-of-responsibility.summary: A term for foreign-policy conservatives who favor ending forever wars and regime-change interventions; not attributable to Kiriakou in the corpus.

a-dangerous-neighborhood.title: The Bahraini fire brigade
a-dangerous-neighborhood.summary: A report John Kiriakou says he found credible during the 2026 Iran war — that a Bahraini fire brigade refused to fight the fire at Manama airport after an Iranian strike. His explanation is the kingdom''s sectarian arrangement: a Shia-majority population under a Sunni royal family, which he says ''can be a problem at times.''

a-dangerous-neighborhood.title: 2026 Iran war
a-dangerous-neighborhood.summary: The open-ended American and Israeli war against Iran that John Kiriakou tracked week by week on his own show — a conflict he says was sold as three weeks, ran into its fifth month, achieved every decapitation objective it set, and continued anyway. His grade for it is a D, and his forecast is a Truth Social post declaring victory while nothing changes.

a-dangerous-neighborhood.title: Iranian strikes on Gulf hotels
a-dangerous-neighborhood.summary: John Kiriakou''s reading of the Iranian drone and missile attacks on hotels in Abu Dhabi, Dubai and Muscat during the 2026 war: not targeted killings, but deliberate strikes at the tourist economies of the Gulf states, aimed at hotels famous enough to empty the country of visitors.

a-dangerous-neighborhood.title: Qat in Yemen
a-dangerous-neighborhood.summary: The afternoon shrub-chewing habit of Yemen, and the special dispensation the CIA had to issue so that its officers could take part in it. John Kiriakou explains that no source could be developed in a qat-chewing country by an officer who would not chew.

a-dangerous-neighborhood.title: Bombing the Omanis
a-dangerous-neighborhood.summary: John Kiriakou's judgement that Iran's strikes on the Gulf states — and above all on Oman, which had been trying to broker peace — made enemies Iran did not need to make, of governments that would otherwise have sat the war out.

a-middle-east-reading-list.summary: John Kiriakou's historical tour of the ballot-splitting tactic, running a second candidate with the same name as the incumbent to peel off votes from voters who cannot tell the two apart. a-middle-east-reading-list.title: The CIA close-and-continuing-contact rule
a-middle-east-reading-list.summary: The CIA policy John Kiriakou has described as *"written in stone"*, every officer must report to headquarters any close and continuing contact with a foreign national, defined explicitly to include sexual relationships, so that a name trace can identify hostile intelligence approaches. Kiriakou frames the rule as the operational counter to honey-trap recruitment, and offers the case of the woman officer who slept with her own recruited source, was demoted to analyst rather than fired, and finally lost her job for hiding under her desk on 9/11.

a-policy-support-organization.title: The indicator he'd be watching
a-policy-support-organization.summary: Asked what single sign would most alarm him if he were still inside the CIA on the first day of the 2026 Iran war, John Kiriakou named the movement of ground forces: about fifty thousand American troops are in the region, which cannot invade a country of ninety-two million, and it is the arrival of hundreds of thousands more — plus the last uncommitted carrier battle group — that would frighten him.

a-policy-support-organization.summary: John Kiriakou's historical tour of the ballot-splitting tactic, running a second candidate with the same name as the incumbent to peel off votes from voters who cannot tell the two apart. He anchors the account with the 2026 Alaska Senate race in which two men named Dan Sullivan appeared on the same ballot, then works back through John F. Kennedy's own 1946 use of the trick, a Florida 2020 race decided by 32 votes, and Russian and Indian variants that push the mechanic to comic extremes.

a-policy-support-organization.title: Elizabeth Rouser
a-policy-support-organization.summary: Named only in a producer/narrator voiceover on a Kiriakou interview episode, not in Kiriakou's own words; not attributable to Kiriakou in the corpus.

a-policy-support-organization.title: Erbil and the Kurdish autonomy question
a-policy-support-organization.summary: Reading reports that Erbil airport in Iraqi Kurdistan had been targeted twice on the first night of the 2026 war, John Kiriakou drew out the implication: Baghdad had said repeatedly it would take no part in an American attack on Iran, but the Kurds hold autonomy in the north, and the strikes on Erbil suggest they may be supporting the attack independently of the Iraqi government.

a-policy-support-organization.title: Katherine Gun
a-policy-support-organization.summary: UK whistleblower named once in an unlabeled multi-speaker panel transcript; not safely attributable to Kiriakou in the corpus.

a-policy-support-organization.title: Pete Hoekstra
a-policy-support-organization.summary: Named once in an unlabeled multi-speaker panel transcript; not safely attributable to Kiriakou in the corpus.

a-virtual-state-of-war-with-venezuela.title: Hope is not a strategy
a-virtual-state-of-war-with-venezuela.summary: Opening a February 2025 commentary with a maxim he attributes to business school — that hope is not a strategy — John Kiriakou nonetheless set out four things he was hoping the second Trump administration meant, on the grounds that if they did not come from Trump he did not expect them from anyone else in American politics.

a-virtual-state-of-war-with-venezuela.title: Donald Trump
a-virtual-state-of-war-with-venezuela.summary: 45th and 47th U.S. president. Per John Kiriakou, a man genuinely convinced he was doing right by bombing Iran, "duped" by the same Netanyahu nuclear bluff Obama once rejected — and, at the same time, the most blindly pro-Israel president in history, an admirer of autocrats who has never once criticized Vladimir Putin, and prone to gestures — from the Gulf of America to a since-abandoned "Department of War" rename — that test the edges of his actual authority.

a-virtual-state-of-war-with-venezuela.title: Kiriakou's Cuba trip
a-virtual-state-of-war-with-venezuela.summary: John Kiriakou's account of his first visit to Cuba, where his books sit in the national library and officials treated him warmly — and a Cuban vice president told him every U.S. president is 'the same,' blaming Cuba while it cannot keep the lights on. He was invited as a guest of the Havana international book fair after his first two books were translated into Spanish, and later wrote about how the U.S. embargo shapes daily life there, from a dengue-fever hospital bill he had to pay in euros to a diet dominated by squash.

a-virtual-state-of-war-with-venezuela.title: Marco Rubio
a-virtual-state-of-war-with-venezuela.summary: U.S. official whom John Kiriakou identifies as the real motivator behind pressure on Venezuela; Kiriakou argues Venezuela is not a meaningful drug threat to the U.S. and that Rubio simply wants Maduro gone.

a-virtual-state-of-war-with-venezuela.title: 2028 presidential field
a-virtual-state-of-war-with-venezuela.summary: John Kiriakou's assessment of the wide-open 2028 presidential race — the first in his life, he says, where he has no idea who either party will nominate. Predictive markets were listing 44 Democrats and 26 Republicans as possible candidates. His own preferred candidate is Tucker Carlson, whom he says he has repeatedly begged to run; his working assumption about anyone who does want the job is that they are "a narcissist and probably a sociopath on top of it."

a-virtual-state-of-war-with-venezuela.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
a-virtual-state-of-war-with-venezuela.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

aafia-siddiqui.title: Kiriakou's grandmother arrested for espionage
aafia-siddiqui.summary: The 1934 arrest of John Kiriakou's maternal grandmother in fascist-era Greece — married at fourteen to an eighteen-year-old man who had by then become an American citizen, she was picked up by the authorities on a bare espionage charge Kiriakou attributes to her being married to *"I Amerikanida"* — the American woman. Kiriakou's grandfather bought her way out by bribing the prison guard with American magazines, and the couple then boarded a ship to the United States, arriving as immigrants in 1934.

aafia-siddiqui.title: The War Department renaming
aafia-siddiqui.summary: John Kiriakou's support for restoring the name Department of War — because Truman changed it in 1947 to avoid the United States looking like an aggressor, and the record since does not support the euphemism — together with his point that a president cannot rename a federal department by executive order.

aafia-siddiqui.title: Venezuelan embassy occupation (2019)
aafia-siddiqui.summary: A 2019 sit-in at the Venezuelan embassy in Washington, D.C., which John Kiriakou says he joined at the Venezuelan government's request the night the United States broke relations with Venezuela; he says he still keeps Venezuelan government property from that night at his house.

aafia-siddiqui.title: Kiriakou's Iran trips
aafia-siddiqui.summary: John Kiriakou's account of his own visits to Iran and his Iranian-American partner's regular travel there — noting Tehran's status as the cosmetic-surgery capital of the Middle East, a warning to Iranian state TV viewers about American fast food rather than American generals, and his own repeated but unfulfilled invitations to visit.

aafia-siddiqui.title: Trump cartel terrorist designation
aafia-siddiqui.summary: Donald Trump's early second-term State Department designation of drug cartels as terrorist organizations, which John Kiriakou says was understood at the time mainly as a paperwork exercise to free up agencies like the NSA and DIA to spend money on intercepting communications and training foreign nationals — but which Kiriakou says Trump has since treated as license to attack any vessel he personally deems cartel-linked.

aafia-siddiqui.title: Khaled Mashal
aafia-siddiqui.summary: Senior Hamas political leader; survived a 1997 Mossad poisoning attempt in Amman, Jordan; the operation's failure and the political fallout in Jordan are the canonical example, in John Kiriakou's account, of Israeli operational hostility carried out in friendly third-country territory without regard for the diplomatic consequences.

abbas-and-the-three-state-problem.title: The CIA close-and-continuing-contact rule
abbas-and-the-three-state-problem.summary: The CIA policy John Kiriakou has described as *"written in stone"*, every officer must report to headquarters any close and continuing contact with a foreign national, defined explicitly to include sexual relationships, so that a name trace can identify hostile intelligence approaches. Kiriakou frames the rule as the operational counter to honey-trap recruitment, and offers the case of the woman officer who slept with her own recruited source, was demoted to analyst rather than fired, and finally lost her job for hiding under her desk on 9/11.

abbas-and-the-three-state-problem.title: The Hellenic Axis
abbas-and-the-three-state-problem.summary: The Greece-Cyprus-Israel bloc that Israeli officials framed in August 2026 as their strategic counterpoint to the Saudi-Pakistan-Turkey defense pact, an alignment John Kiriakou reads as Greek elites accepting an Israeli presence they can no longer control, while the Greek street pushes the other way. Kiriakou treats the Greek state's fear of Turkey as real, and the Israeli offer as a bargain Greeks will refuse in the 2027 elections.

abbas-and-the-three-state-problem.title: Trump's need for glorification
abbas-and-the-three-state-problem.summary: John Kiriakou''s psychological reading of why the 2026 Iran war happened — that Donald Trump "craves glorification," has pursued it by attaching his name to public landmarks, and concluded that "real glory can only come with war": becoming the president who succeeded in overthrowing the Iranian government where every predecessor since Carter had failed. Kiriakou attributes the false expectation of quick collapse to wealthy Iranian-American exiles.

abbas-and-the-three-state-problem.title: Afghan War Logs
abbas-and-the-three-state-problem.summary: A 2010 WikiLeaks publication discussed on a panel Kiriakou joined; the specific lines about it in the corpus belong to other panelists, not Kiriakou.

abbas-and-the-three-state-problem.title: *The human rights guy*
abbas-and-the-three-state-problem.summary: The nickname John Kiriakou says colleagues at the CIA used for him behind his back after he refused to be trained in the enhanced interrogation program and reported another officer for hooding prisoners at the Abu Zubaydah takedown safe house. He learned it from a friend, an Army Reserve brigadier general and psychiatrist named Steve, who framed it as a warning, and Kiriakou answered *"I'm not afraid of them. I'm right and they're wrong."*

abbas-and-the-three-state-problem.title: The New Castle News
abbas-and-the-three-state-problem.summary: The Pennsylvania local paper John Kiriakou says he tries to scan every day and can no longer afford — $250 a year for a sixteen-page paper with no Wednesday or Sunday edition, edited by a 28-year-old, in a region he describes as a news desert.

abbottabad.title: Agent payment mechanics
abbottabad.summary: How the CIA physically pays a recruited agent — cash every month, a receipt signed with any alias the agent chooses, and a polygraph regime built around the assumption that the officer handling the money is the person most likely to steal it.

abbottabad.title: Abu Zubaydah
abbottabad.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

abbottabad.title: Brian Ross
abbottabad.summary: American investigative journalist and seven-time Emmy Award winner who was a prominent reporter at ABC News when, in December 2007, he conducted the on-camera interview with John Kiriakou that produced the first public confirmation by a U.S. official that the CIA waterboarded prisoners. Per Kiriakou, Ross called him out of the blue with the assertion that a source said Kiriakou had personally tortured Abu Zubaydah; Kiriakou's decision to give the interview anyway — driven by the conclusion that 'Brian Ross's source is at the White House and they're going to pin this on me' — became the pivot point of his entire post-CIA life.

abbottabad.title: Jennifer Matthews
abbottabad.summary: CIA analyst who was made chief of base at Khost, Afghanistan without operational or security training in order to complete the tour requirement for promotion, and who was killed there with six other officers by a Jordanian double agent she had gone outside the fortified perimeter to greet with a birthday cake.

abbottabad.title: Jose Rodriguez
abbottabad.summary: Senior CIA officer of the post-9/11 era; identified by John Kiriakou as among those responsible for crimes committed in the name of national security; described as believing himself to be a good guy.

abbottabad.title: Khalid Sheikh Mohammed
abbottabad.summary: Mastermind of the September 11, 2001 attacks; identified to the CIA by Abu Zubaydah, in the course of FBI interrogator Ali Soufan's rapport-based debriefing at the black site, as the man behind the kunya "Mukhtar" the agency had been hunting since at least 1996 for the Bojinka plot; per Kiriakou's relay of his self-account, radicalized by news video of an Israeli soldier with his boot on the neck of a Palestinian woman.

abdul-amir-al-jamri.title: The Dilmun burial mounds
abdul-amir-al-jamri.summary: The ancient grave mounds standing in the Shia villages of Bahrain — ordinary ones ten or twenty feet high, royal ones fifty — which John Kiriakou took visiting friends and family to see, and which sat in the same villages the government was raiding at night during the uprising.

abdul-amir-al-jamri.title: The Gulf Daily News
abdul-amir-al-jamri.summary: Bahrain's English-language newspaper, and the source John Kiriakou turned to when a bomb went off at the Ministry of Labour two months into his posting — its Indian reporter, whose telephone was bugged like his own, told him a civil uprising was about to explode.

abdul-amir-al-jamri.title: Kiriakou's grandmother arrested for espionage
abdul-amir-al-jamri.summary: The 1934 arrest of John Kiriakou's maternal grandmother in fascist-era Greece — married at fourteen to an eighteen-year-old man who had by then become an American citizen, she was picked up by the authorities on a bare espionage charge Kiriakou attributes to her being married to *"I Amerikanida"* — the American woman. Kiriakou's grandfather bought her way out by bribing the prison guard with American magazines, and the couple then boarded a ship to the United States, arriving as immigrants in 1934.

abdul-amir-al-jamri.title: Salman bin Hamad
abdul-amir-al-jamri.summary: The Bahraini heir presumptive who became John Kiriakou's friend during his 1994–96 posting — president of the Bahrain Center for Studies and Research and patron of the environmental association, both of which fell in Kiriakou's economic brief, and a companion on nights out at a nightclub by the naval base.

abdul-amir-al-jamri.title: The declared officer
abdul-amir-al-jamri.summary: The CIA officer whose identity is formally disclosed to the host country's intelligence service — as John Kiriakou was in Athens, taken by his chief within days of arrival to be introduced to the head of the Greek service.

abdul-amir-al-jamri.title: Mahmoud al-Mabhouh
abdul-amir-al-jamri.summary: Senior Hamas figure assassinated by Mossad in a Dubai hotel room in January 2010; the operation has been studied by intelligence services worldwide for its tradecraft, in particular the unsolved question of how the assassination team locked the hotel-room door from the inside after killing him.

abdul-el-sayed.title: Michigan 2026 Democratic Senate primary
abdul-el-sayed.summary: The contest between the AIPAC-backed Haley Stevens and the DSA-backed Abdul El-Sayed, which John Kiriakou calls one of the most fascinating races he has seen and reads as the first real failure of the electability argument establishment Democrats have relied on.

abdul-el-sayed.title: Mike Rogers
abdul-el-sayed.summary: Former Republican congressman from Michigan and repeat Senate candidate, who lost narrowly in 2024 and ran again in 2026. John Kiriakou singles out his campaign advertisement calling Abdul El-Sayed a communist Trojan horse as an insult to the intelligence of Michigan voters.

abdul-el-sayed.title: John Fetterman
abdul-el-sayed.summary: The Pennsylvania senator whose fall from progressive Democratic hero to reliable AIPAC vote John Kiriakou has been tracking week by week on his own show, including the September 2026 Wall Street Journal investigation, based on more than a dozen former staffers and leaked internal texts, that reported Fetterman had lost interest in the job of a senator, skipped a June meeting with three paralysed veterans from his own state to appear on Fox News less than an hour later, and dismissed a Children's Hospital of Philadelphia request as *"they just want free trips to DC."*

abdul-el-sayed.title: Kiriakou's grandmother arrested for espionage
abdul-el-sayed.summary: The 1934 arrest of John Kiriakou's maternal grandmother in fascist-era Greece — married at fourteen to an eighteen-year-old man who had by then become an American citizen, she was picked up by the authorities on a bare espionage charge Kiriakou attributes to her being married to *"I Amerikanida"* — the American woman. Kiriakou's grandfather bought her way out by bribing the prison guard with American magazines, and the couple then boarded a ship to the United States, arriving as immigrants in 1934.

abdul-el-sayed.title: Cori Bush
abdul-el-sayed.summary: Former U.S. Representative from St. Louis (Missouri's 1st congressional district); cited by John Kiriakou as one of the two named cases of AIPAC successfully primarying an incumbent for delivering a House floor speech describing the Gaza war as a "wholesale massacre of Palestinian civilians."

abdul-el-sayed.title: Jamaal Bowman
abdul-el-sayed.summary: Former U.S. Representative from New York; cited by John Kiriakou alongside Cori Bush as the second documented case of AIPAC successfully primarying an incumbent House member for criticizing Israeli conduct in the Gaza war.

abigail-spanberger.title: The Jay Jones texts
abigail-spanberger.summary: The leaked 2022 text messages in which Virginia''s Democratic candidate for attorney general joked about shooting Republicans — which John Kiriakou called shameful on reflex, before landing on the position he now holds: that everyone talks that way privately, that Republicans do it constantly, and that he no longer cares.

abigail-spanberger.title: Winsome Earle-Sears and the machine gun
abigail-spanberger.summary: John Kiriakou's verdict on the lieutenant governor of Virginia who ran for the top job in 2025 — that she is a nut, that her earlier campaign photographs showed her smiling and holding a machine gun, and that at the gubernatorial debate she had to be repeatedly slapped down for talking over her opponent.

abigail-spanberger.title: The pardoned January 6th defendants
abigail-spanberger.summary: John Kiriakou's observation that a striking number of the January 6th defendants pardoned by Donald Trump have got into trouble since their release — one arrested for threatening to kill the House minority leader, another shot dead in a gunfight with a police officer in Indiana — and his agreement that the base rate may explain all of it.

abigail-spanberger.title: The Tomahawk red line
abigail-spanberger.summary: John Kiriakou's judgement that giving Ukraine Tomahawk cruise missiles would be a very bad idea — because it would risk drawing NATO in and risk a tactical nuclear strike on Ukrainian positions — set against Peter Kuznick's assessment that Ukraine is losing and is now snatching old men off the street.

abigail-spanberger.title: The George Mason confrontation
abigail-spanberger.summary: The videotaped encounter at George Mason University in which former CIA director John Brennan poked a questioner in the chest — an incident John Kiriakou says at least a dozen friends sent him, and which showed him, for the first time in thirty-five years of knowing the man, a frightened John Brennan.

abigail-spanberger.title: The manager's ranking
abigail-spanberger.summary: John Kiriakou's answer to a viewer who asked whether he would ever appear on Joe Rogan's show alongside Mike Baker — that his new manager, who represents some very senior people, told him he is more highly sought after than Baker is, so there is no reason to legitimise him.

abolish-the-cia.title: Defense HUMINT Service
abolish-the-cia.summary: The Pentagon's human collection outfit, which John Kiriakou names as one of the three agencies that already do everything the CIA does — alongside the State Department's Bureau of Intelligence and Research for analysis and the NSA for interception — and which is therefore the core of his argument that Langley is redundant rather than merely badly run.

abolish-the-cia.title: Kiriakou's serial-killer letters
abolish-the-cia.summary: John Kiriakou's account of writing letters, as research for a planned book, to several well-known serial killers — including David Berkowitz ("Son of Sam"), Gary Leon Ridgway (the Green River Killer), the BTK killer, the "co-ed killer," and Manson family member Tex Watson — and the uniformly evangelical, Jesus-focused responses he received instead of the interviews he wanted.

abolish-the-cia.title: Kiriakou's Pakistan-Islam economic critique
abolish-the-cia.summary: John Kiriakou's controversial view that Islam has held Pakistan back economically, contrasting Pakistan's stalled development since the 1960s with South Korea's — which had the same GDP as Pakistan in 1964 — and citing lost productivity from prayer breaks and holy days, resentment over partition, and spending on nuclear weapons instead of infrastructure and education.

abolish-the-cia.title: Prison pedophile accounts
abolish-the-cia.summary: John Kiriakou's account of encountering convicted pedophiles for the first time in federal prison, drawing on advice from a psychiatrist friend and his own work running the chapel library — one of only two safe spaces in prison for inmates convicted of child sex crimes.

abolish-the-cia.title: The Hellenic Axis
abolish-the-cia.summary: The Greece-Cyprus-Israel bloc that Israeli officials framed in August 2026 as their strategic counterpoint to the Saudi-Pakistan-Turkey defense pact, an alignment John Kiriakou reads as Greek elites accepting an Israeli presence they can no longer control, while the Greek street pushes the other way. Kiriakou treats the Greek state's fear of Turkey as real, and the Israeli offer as a bargain Greeks will refuse in the 2027 elections.

abolish-the-cia.title: Trump's need for glorification
abolish-the-cia.summary: John Kiriakou''s psychological reading of why the 2026 Iran war happened — that Donald Trump "craves glorification," has pursued it by attaching his name to public landmarks, and concluded that "real glory can only come with war": becoming the president who succeeded in overthrowing the Iranian government where every predecessor since Carter had failed. Kiriakou attributes the false expectation of quick collapse to wealthy Iranian-American exiles.

abraham-accords.title: Nobel Peace Prize
abraham-accords.summary: The prize a Swedish parliamentarian nominated John Kiriakou for in 2016 — a marker of how far world opinion had swung his way after prison. Kiriakou once believed Obama deserved his; he came to see it as unearned, and he treats Trump's foreign policy as substantially organized around wanting one too — "never underestimate Donald Trump's desire to win a Nobel Peace Prize," a White House friend told him. Netanyahu's nomination of Trump he summarized in a single unprintable phrase.

abraham-accords.title: King Abdullah II of Jordan
abraham-accords.summary: The Jordanian monarch whom John Kiriakou rates as knowing more about the Middle East than anyone else who leads or studies it, and as almost never wrong across twenty-five years of foreign-policy predictions. Kiriakou recounts the deathbed succession that made him king against his own expectations, and his refusal after October 7 to accept Palestinian refugees on the grounds that doing so would deliver Israel the ethnic cleansing it wanted.

abraham-accords.title: Kiriakou prison manipulation tactics
abraham-accords.summary: John Kiriakou's account of applying CIA tradecraft — including deliberate deception, forged paperwork, and manipulating other inmates into violence — to protect himself and control his environment during his federal prison sentence.

abraham-accords.title: Mount Weather
abraham-accords.summary: U.S. government continuity-of-government underground facility on the Virginia–West Virginia line

abraham-accords.title: NewsGuard
abraham-accords.summary: A media-rating organization, founded by the former head of Court TV and a former Wall Street Journal publisher, that scores news outlets 0-100 for reliability. Per John Kiriakou, NewsGuard docks any outlet that takes a position on Ukraine or Syria contrary to its preferred line, is subscribed to mostly by government entities (chiefly the Pentagon), and singled out Consortium News, the Grayzone, Antiwar.com, and ScheerPost over their criticism of U.S. policy — prompting a First Amendment lawsuit.

abraham-accords.title: The Cyprus fruit relabel
abraham-accords.summary: The 1970s workaround John Kiriakou has described for the Arab boycott of Israeli produce, Israeli fruit shipped to Cyprus, repacked in *"Produce of Cyprus"* boxes, then sold on into the Gulf. Kiriakou uses it as the specific answer to why the Abraham Accords look, in his account, less like a diplomatic breakthrough than the final removal of a fig leaf on a trade that had already been happening for half a century.

abraham-bolden.title: Alan Dershowitz
abraham-bolden.summary: American attorney and Harvard Law professor; John Kiriakou describes debating him on Piers Morgan's show over Jeffrey Epstein, telling Dershowitz he would have wanted to see him "hanging from a tree" had he sought leniency for Epstein as an Israeli spy — and cites attorney David Boies's on-air statement that Dershowitz was far more than Epstein's lawyer, also serving as his publicist, friend, and a guest on Epstein's island.

abraham-bolden.title: Dick Cheney
abraham-bolden.summary: U.S. Vice President under George W. Bush. Per John Kiriakou — recounting CIA Director George Tenet's memoir — Cheney intercepted the presidential finding authorizing the CIA's enhanced interrogation program in the Oval Office anteroom and took it from Tenet before Bush could sign it. Tenet later concluded the president probably never actually signed the finding and probably told the truth when he said he had no idea the program was taking place. Kiriakou characterizes Cheney as the one who actually ran foreign policy, intelligence policy, and defense policy during the Bush years.

abraham-bolden.title: Donald Trump
abraham-bolden.summary: 45th and 47th U.S. president. Per John Kiriakou, a man genuinely convinced he was doing right by bombing Iran, "duped" by the same Netanyahu nuclear bluff Obama once rejected — and, at the same time, the most blindly pro-Israel president in history, an admirer of autocrats who has never once criticized Vladimir Putin, and prone to gestures — from the Gulf of America to a since-abandoned "Department of War" rename — that test the edges of his actual authority.

abraham-bolden.title: Kill the Messenger (Gary Webb)
abraham-bolden.summary: The 2014 film about journalist Gary Webb, on which John Kiriakou served as script advisor; when Kiriakou was arrested in January 2012, the FBI seized his electronics, including a draft of the unclassified Hollywood script, and stamped every page "top secret" despite Kiriakou having no role in writing it.

abraham-bolden.title: Ghislaine Maxwell
abraham-bolden.summary: British socialite and convicted sex offender; per John Kiriakou, her father Robert Maxwell was a prolific Mossad spy, and she is the likely conduit through whom Jeffrey Epstein was introduced to and recruited by Mossad.

abraham-bolden.title: Ross Ulbricht
abraham-bolden.summary: Founder of the online marketplace Silk Road, sentenced to life plus 75 years before being pardoned by President Trump; John Kiriakou met Ulbricht's mother and sister two weeks before the pardon and calls the length of the original sentence a sickening miscarriage of justice.

abraham-lincoln-collection.title: Lincoln's last turd
abraham-lincoln-collection.summary: A purported piece of human waste attributed by a Pennsylvania circus-freak-show museum to Abraham Lincoln on the night of his assassination; auctioned for $5,000; subsequent DNA analysis disproved the attribution. John Kiriakou's failed bid for the artifact is the anecdote that, recirculated in early 2026, made him an internet meme figure.

abraham-lincoln-collection.title: Kiriakou's money-laundering tip
abraham-lincoln-collection.summary: John Kiriakou's account of taking a chief operating officer job at a boutique investment firm early in the COVID pandemic that he came to believe was an international money-laundering operation possibly backed by Iran — downloading 15,000 pages of supporting documents before an FBI agent told him the bureau would only take interest if the case involved Russia, China, terrorism, or January 6th.

abraham-lincoln-collection.title: Kiriakou on Christmas
abraham-lincoln-collection.summary: John Kiriakou's account of finding Christmas so depressing since his two divorces that he does not decorate or mark it at all — and of the year he replaced it by taking his children to every station on the New York City subway system in a single day.

abraham-lincoln-collection.title: Joby Warrick's Washington Post resignation
abraham-lincoln-collection.summary: John Kiriakou's account of his friend Joby Warrick, a multiple Pulitzer Prize-winning investigative journalist, resigning from the Washington Post because investigative journalism at the paper was dead — amid an 80% staff reduction since Jeff Bezos bought the paper.

abraham-lincoln-collection.title: Aldrich Ames
abraham-lincoln-collection.summary: Senior CIA officer — a GS-15 who rose to chief of counterintelligence for the Soviet branch — who spied for the KGB for nine years. Per John Kiriakou, Ames walked into the Soviet embassy in Washington in April 1985 and sold the identities of two CIA-recruited double agents for $50,000 to clear a debt run up by his second marriage; both were executed. He went on to identify more than thirty agents, compromise over a hundred clandestine operations, cause at least twelve deaths and take more than $2 million, while being known throughout the agency as a daily drunk and promoted at every turn. The KGB protected him with a decoy mole hunt; analyst Sandy Grimes caught him by matching his handler meetings to his bank deposits.

abraham-lincoln-collection.title: Amaryllis Fox Kennedy
abraham-lincoln-collection.summary: Former CIA non-official-cover officer who worked under commercial cover as an international art consultant, later a Trump campaign manager and nominee for deputy CIA director. Per John Kiriakou, Senator Tom Cotton threatened to filibuster her appointment; the president responded by naming her deputy national security adviser instead — a job Kiriakou considers more powerful, since the CIA director reports to the national security adviser.

abraxas-corporation.title: Meeting Elon Musk in 2009
abraxas-corporation.summary: The evening in 2009 when John Kiriakou, waiting to pitch a television idea to an incoming NBC president in a Washington bar, was introduced to a friend the executive had brought along — asked him what he did for a living, and listened to him talk about Mars all night.

abraxas-corporation.title: Ted Rall
abraxas-corporation.summary: American editorial cartoonist and two-time Pulitzer Prize finalist; co-host with John Kiriakou of the daily news-commentary podcast "Deprogram," launched in September 2025 and by late 2025 running every weekday morning.

abraxas-corporation.title: The Jordanian intelligence service
abraxas-corporation.summary: The service John Kiriakou calls one of the best in the world and arguably the best in the Middle East — good, in his account, out of necessity: half of Jordan''s population is Palestinian, Black September once fought on the steps of the palace, and the survival of the monarchy depends on having infiltrated every faction in the country.

abraxas-corporation.title: Private Intelligence
abraxas-corporation.summary: Post-CIA commercial intelligence work performed by John Kiriakou — both operational (surveillance, bribery, dossier-building for private clients) and analytical (paid forecasts for hedge funds, mutual funds, and a global mining company). Per Kiriakou, his clients ranged from a Cypriot billionaire investigating his daughter's fiancé to the ninth-largest hedge fund in the world.

abraxas-corporation.title: Hamilton 68
abraxas-corporation.summary: A company founded by former CIA, FBI, NSA and Director of National Intelligence officials that rates news sites as reliable or unreliable, contracting mainly with the Pentagon to flag articles on government computers with green or red check marks; John Kiriakou says it threatened Consortium News with a "Kremlin apologist" red-check designation, after which PayPal permanently suspended the outlet's account and confiscated its funds.

abraxas-corporation.title: The Romanian silver mine
abraxas-corporation.summary: The private-intelligence assignment John Kiriakou uses to explain what commercial analysis actually buys: a mining client wanted to know who would win a Romanian municipal election, because a silver deposit lay under a village that would have to be destroyed to reach it.

abu-nidal-disruption.title: John Kiriakou
abu-nidal-disruption.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

abu-nidal-disruption.title: Saddam Hussein
abu-nidal-disruption.summary: President of Iraq from 1979 until the 2003 U.S. invasion; subject of John Kiriakou's CIA portfolio from January 1990 onward, in which capacity Kiriakou became, at age 25, "Saddam Hussein's intelligence community biographer" and the analyst who briefed President George H. W. Bush in the Oval Office on the morning of the 1990 invasion of Kuwait.

abu-nidal-disruption.title: Iraqi invasion of Kuwait
abu-nidal-disruption.summary: John Kiriakou''s most detailed account of the intelligence process around the 1990 Iraqi invasion of Kuwait and its 1991 liberation. As a first-year CIA analyst on a ''training account'' covering Iraq, Kiriakou produced the June 30, 1990 warning paper for the White House; suggested calling the US Defense Attaché in Baghdad to drive to the border and report what he saw (the answer: ''Literally the entire Iraqi military is heading south''); briefed the August 2 Oval Office meeting with Bush; and later took a single phone call from General Colin Powell that led, eight hours later, to 47 cruise missiles striking the Iraqi Intelligence Service headquarters in Baghdad.

abu-nidal-disruption.title: Principals Committee Meeting (February 2003)
abu-nidal-disruption.summary: Senior-most interagency forum of the U.S. national security apparatus, normally chaired by the president. Per John Kiriakou — who served as notetaker for CIA Director George Tenet at the eve-of-Iraq-invasion meeting on February 19–20, 2003 — Vice President Dick Cheney chaired in place of Bush, General Tommy Franks ended his order-of-battle briefing with 'If all goes as planned, we can be in Tehran by August,' and an NSC senior director said 'When we cross that border tomorrow morning, they're going to throw flowers at us.'

abu-nidal-disruption.title: British Bases in Cyprus
abu-nidal-disruption.summary: British sovereign bases in Cyprus host a large American contingent. Kiriakou, a quarter Cypriot, on the bases as evacuation hub, missile target, and suspected nuclear site — and on the 46-year US weapons embargo almost no American knows about.

abu-nidal-disruption.title: Marty Gottesfeld
abu-nidal-disruption.summary: American hacktivist and computer security engineer, convicted for a 2014 denial-of-service attack on Boston Children's Hospital in protest of the treatment of patient Justina Pelletier; a fellow federal prisoner of John Kiriakou who has publicly taken up the case of Donnie Reynolds Jr.

abu-omar-rendition.title: Alec Baldwin
abu-omar-rendition.summary: Actor with whom John Kiriakou recounts a bitter falling-out — Baldwin calling him a liar over lunch at a meeting about a play in which Baldwin was to play him, later attaching to a Kiriakou TV pitch that AMC bought the next day, then quitting for HBO and killing the deal without a word.

abu-omar-rendition.title: Jennings Randolph
abu-omar-rendition.summary: Longtime U.S. Senator from West Virginia who, in a phone call John Kiriakou made to thank him as a college student, gave him the advice he says shaped his life: always do the right thing, not the expedient one.

abu-omar-rendition.title: Kiriakou's Omega Seamaster
abu-omar-rendition.summary: The wristwatch John Kiriakou bought himself in the Athens duty-free the day after Christmas 1999, on his way to recruit an asset in another European country, at the end of a Christmas that had gone badly in a failing first marriage.

abu-omar-rendition.title: The Jerusalem bluff
abu-omar-rendition.summary: An interrogation in Pakistan in 2002 in which John Kiriakou, faced with a senior al-Qaeda prisoner working through the organisation's own resistance training, threatened to send him to Jerusalem rather than Guantánamo. Kiriakou supplied the account to explain a clip of the exchange circulating without its context.

abu-omar-rendition.title: The Los Angeles Times Iran op-ed
abu-omar-rendition.summary: An op-ed on Iranian foreign policy in Latin America that John Kiriakou was commissioned to write about six months after blowing the whistle on the torture programme. He had barely begun when the CIA general counsel's office telephoned to warn him off the subject — a call he could not explain for fourteen years, and which he now attributes to his own wife rather than to a source inside the newspaper.

abu-omar-rendition.title: Afghanistan 2011 Kerry Trip
abu-omar-rendition.summary: John Kiriakou's 2011 trip to Afghanistan as senior investigator for the Senate Foreign Relations Committee under Chairman John Kerry, where the pair sat through a briefing with 11 one-to-four-star generals presenting an optimistic account of the war — after which Kerry mused the U.S. might win, only for Kiriakou to tell him the U.S. controlled only Kabul, and that the same rosy briefing had been given every year since 2002.

abu-zubaydah-as-a-sounding-board.title: The German POW chess analogy
abu-zubaydah-as-a-sounding-board.summary: The reasoning John Kiriakou gave ABC News in December 2007 for why he had believed at the time that waterboarding was necessary: he had heard of Second World War German prisoners who, over months of playing chess with their interrogators, built enough rapport to talk, and he judged that al-Qaeda prisoners were a different order of adversary who would never be seduced into cooperating.

abu-zubaydah-as-a-sounding-board.title: The slap approval cable
abu-zubaydah-as-a-sounding-board.summary: The cable-by-cable approval chain that governed each escalation of the CIA''s enhanced interrogation techniques, described by John Kiriakou in his December 2007 ABC News interview: permission for even a single open-handed slap of Abu Zubaydah came from Washington after a discussion, was granted by the deputy director for operations, and had to be reported back by cable afterwards.

abu-zubaydah-as-a-sounding-board.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
abu-zubaydah-as-a-sounding-board.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

abu-zubaydah-as-a-sounding-board.title: Abu Zubaydah
abu-zubaydah-as-a-sounding-board.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

abu-zubaydah-as-a-sounding-board.title: Waterboarding
abu-zubaydah-as-a-sounding-board.summary: Torture technique in which a prisoner is restrained on an inclined board with the head lower than the feet, a cloth placed over the face, and water poured continuously over it to simulate drowning. Per John Kiriakou, waterboarding was treated as a criminal act under U.S. and international law for decades before 2002 — including a post–World War II execution of Japanese soldiers who waterboarded American POWs, and a 1968 court-martial of a U.S. soldier photographed waterboarding a North Vietnamese prisoner — before the CIA reauthorized it after September 11. Abu Zubaydah was waterboarded 83 times; Khalid Sheikh Mohammed 187 times.

abu-zubaydah-as-a-sounding-board.title: Corkscrew landings in Afghanistan
abu-zubaydah-as-a-sounding-board.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the tight spiralling helicopter approaches used to evade rocket and Stinger fire on landings in Afghanistan after 9/11, with the side doors open, and of the passengers around him being sick while he found it exhilarating.

abu-zubaydah-cremation-footnote.title: Abu Zubaydah
abu-zubaydah-cremation-footnote.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

abu-zubaydah-cremation-footnote.title: Senate Torture Report
abu-zubaydah-cremation-footnote.summary: The December 2014 executive summary of the U.S. Senate Select Committee on Intelligence's study of the CIA's post-9/11 detention and interrogation program; the first public disclosure of techniques including rectal feeding with hummus, sexual assault with broomsticks, and prolonged sleep deprivation.

abu-zubaydah-cremation-footnote.title: Ali Soufan
abu-zubaydah-cremation-footnote.summary: FBI special agent who handled Abu Zubaydah immediately after his March 2002 capture; through patient, respectful interrogation produced the only actionable intelligence ever obtained from the detainee, including the first identification of "Mukhtar" as Khalid Sheikh Mohammed.

abu-zubaydah-cremation-footnote.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
abu-zubaydah-cremation-footnote.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

abu-zubaydah-cremation-footnote.title: Espionage Act
abu-zubaydah-cremation-footnote.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

abu-zubaydah-cremation-footnote.title: Federal plea coercion
abu-zubaydah-cremation-footnote.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that the federal justice system coerces guilty pleas by stacking charges and winning 98.2% of its cases — so that even innocent defendants take deals, as he did, told by his own attorney that the system is 'not about justice; it's about mitigating damage.'

abu-zubaydah-diary.title: The two Abu Zubaydahs
abu-zubaydah-diary.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the first cousin who shared Abu Zubaydah's name, whose activities were folded into a single intelligence picture of a man Kiriakou called a terrorist Superman — and who vanished as soon as the capture reached the newspapers.

abu-zubaydah-diary.title: The SpongeBob shirt
abu-zubaydah-diary.summary: The bright red SpongeBob SquarePants shirt, a Christmas present from his children, that John Kiriakou happened to be wearing when Abu Zubaydah opened his one good eye and realised the Americans had him.

abu-zubaydah-diary.title: Abu Zubaydah
abu-zubaydah-diary.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

abu-zubaydah-diary.title: CIA and NSA exotic programs
abu-zubaydah-diary.summary: Two obscure U.S. intelligence programs John Kiriakou has discussed — a late-1980s FBI/Defense Department investigation into a senior NSA officer who came out as a member of the Church of Satan and was accused of ritual sacrifice (which found no evidence), and a 1990s CIA battlefield laser weapon designed to blind rather than kill enemy soldiers, shelved after lawyers determined it violated international law.

abu-zubaydah-diary.title: Buzzy Krongard
abu-zubaydah-diary.summary: The executive director of the CIA — the agency's third-ranking officer — who sat on the board of Johns Hopkins Medical Center and, on learning that Abu Zubaydah had been captured wounded, had the hospital's top trauma surgeon flown to Pakistan on a CIA jet.

abu-zubaydah-diary.title: Rhodes Jewish deportation and family rescue story
abu-zubaydah-diary.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the 1944 Nazi roundup and deportation of roughly 2,000 Jewish residents of the island of Rhodes to Auschwitz, of whom only 14 survived — and of his own great-grandfather, a chauffeur, hiding his Jewish employer from the Nazis until the war's end.

abu-zubaydah.title: The cremation footnote
abu-zubaydah.summary: A footnote John Kiriakou cites from the declassified executive summary of the Senate torture report, stating that Abu Zubaydah will never be permitted to leave Guantanamo — despite never having joined al-Qaeda, never having pledged fealty to Osama bin Laden and never having been charged — and that on his death the CIA will cremate his body and scatter the ashes at sea.

abu-zubaydah.title: CIA versus FBI at a raid
abu-zubaydah.summary: John Kiriakou''s two-sentence account of the institutional difference between the two agencies, drawn from joint raids in Pakistan in 2002: the FBI numbers the four walls with sticky notes, photographs the inside of every drawer and collects every piece of paper, because it is building a case. The CIA breaks down the door, grabs all the men and sends them to Guantánamo.

abu-zubaydah.title: Galls.com sponsor story
abu-zubaydah.summary: John Kiriakou's account of outfitting the CIA's post-9/11 Islamabad station for terrorist-safe-house raids by ordering roughly $50,000 of tactical gear from the law-enforcement retailer galls.com on his CIA credit card, shipped to Pakistan via State Department diplomatic pouch in under a week — a story he now retells as an ad-read for the retailer, which sponsors one of his podcast appearances.

abu-zubaydah.title: Jane Harman
abu-zubaydah.summary: Former U.S. Representative from California who served as ranking member and later chair of the House Intelligence Committee. Per John Kiriakou, Harman was present in the room when congressional leadership was briefed on the CIA's enhanced interrogation program; when reporters later asked her about the program, she denied knowing about it. Kiriakou told the New York Times she had been in the room, after which Harman revised her account to say she had left early and that an aide remained as a notetaker.

abu-zubaydah.title: Jennings Randolph
abu-zubaydah.summary: Longtime U.S. Senator from West Virginia who, in a phone call John Kiriakou made to thank him as a college student, gave him the advice he says shaped his life: always do the right thing, not the expedient one.

abu-zubaydah.title: Kiki Camarena case
abu-zubaydah.summary: 1985 abduction and murder of U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration agent Enrique "Kiki" Camarena in Mexico; cited by John Kiriakou as the trigger for the 1985 U.S. statute authorizing the extraterritorial seizure of foreign nationals — the legal authority underpinning the 2026 U.S. operation that seized President Nicolás Maduro of Venezuela.

access-agent.title: Jeffrey Epstein
access-agent.summary: Convicted sex offender; per John Kiriakou, was "an Israeli access agent" rather than a CIA asset, because the CIA collects foreign intelligence and Epstein's targets — Bill Clinton, Bill Gates, Prince Andrew — were not foreign. Kiriakou further holds that Epstein did die by suicide in federal custody, because in the Bureau of Prisons the cameras never work and the guards are always asleep.

access-agent.title: Mount Weather
access-agent.summary: U.S. government continuity-of-government underground facility on the Virginia–West Virginia line

access-agent.title: CIA record deniability
