access-agent.summary: John Kiriakou's account of how senior CIA officers occasionally decide to keep an event out of the written record — illustrated by a recruited asset who committed a public murder, after which the Deputy Director for Operations told Kiriakou, on second thought, 'let's not put that in writing.'

access-agent.title: Marble Framework
access-agent.summary: A CIA obfuscation tool revealed in the Vault 7 leaks; per John Kiriakou, the agency embedded snippets of Farsi and Cyrillic in the code of domestic hacking operations so that any discovery could be falsely attributed to Iran or Russia.

access-agent.title: "One dead pedophile"
access-agent.summary: John Kiriakou's explanation of why he believes the American intelligence community will not examine whether Jeffrey Epstein worked for a foreign service — that the accusation points at Israel, that the relationship with Israel is uniquely valuable, and that nobody in Washington will upset it over one dead pedophile when covering it up is easier.

access-agent.title: Signal and the parking lot
access-agent.summary: John Kiriakou's account of how a clandestine source is actually contacted — an innocuous telephone question with a pre-agreed answer standing for a time and a place fixed in advance, and a physical signal such as the flowerpot on Bob Woodward's balcony — offered as the reason investigators looking for an email trail between a service and its agent will not find one.

active-measures.title: CIA political action group
active-measures.summary: The CIA's most secretive clandestine propaganda arm — successor to the Cold War 'active measures group' — which John Kiriakou says places and funds propagandists worldwide; no officer of it has been publicly identified since 1982, and he encountered its work funding the DNC's and RNC's international arms in post-war Kuwait.

active-measures.title: Italian election covert action
active-measures.summary: What John Kiriakou calls the CIA''s very first covert action: bribing Italian journalists in the 1949 election to write in favor of the Christian Democrats, who narrowly beat the Communists — a operation he says amounted to stealing the election.

active-measures.title: Trump's need for glorification
active-measures.summary: John Kiriakou''s psychological reading of why the 2026 Iran war happened — that Donald Trump "craves glorification," has pursued it by attaching his name to public landmarks, and concluded that "real glory can only come with war": becoming the president who succeeded in overthrowing the Iranian government where every predecessor since Carter had failed. Kiriakou attributes the false expectation of quick collapse to wealthy Iranian-American exiles.

active-measures.title: Jordanian al-Qaeda detainee
active-measures.summary: The subject of John Kiriakou's first-ever interrogation in Pakistan — a Jordanian who had gone to Afghanistan to run an orphanage, joined al-Qaeda for its funding, and told the truth about his escape route because 'I'm your prisoner; what good would it do to lie?'

active-measures.title: *The human rights guy*
active-measures.summary: The nickname John Kiriakou says colleagues at the CIA used for him behind his back after he refused to be trained in the enhanced interrogation program and reported another officer for hooding prisoners at the Abu Zubaydah takedown safe house. He learned it from a friend, an Army Reserve brigadier general and psychiatrist named Steve, who framed it as a warning, and Kiriakou answered *"I'm not afraid of them. I'm right and they're wrong."*

active-measures.title: The University of Salamanca professorship
active-measures.summary: John Kiriakou's teaching post in the graduate intelligence studies programme at the University of Salamanca, where he lectures on introductory intelligence studies and the history of terrorism, at an institution he describes as older than Spain itself.

acts-of-service.title: Kiriakou on soccer
acts-of-service.summary: John Kiriakou's public reversal on football, a sport he had dismissed since his teens on the strength of a Saturday Night Live joke about a match between Yemen and Saudi Arabia being decided early by an insurmountable one-nil lead. Watching the 2026 World Cup, he concluded he had been wrong.

acts-of-service.title: The 2026 World Cup final
acts-of-service.summary: Spain''s victory over Argentina in a final John Kiriakou described as dirty on the losers'' part and notable for a red card, and the awkwardness that followed: Donald Trump, who had exerted considerable influence over FIFA and whose country was hosting, had to present the trophy to a nation whose leadership he had spent weeks publicly attacking. The Spanish press cropped him out of the celebration photographs.

acts-of-service.title: 2026 Iran war
acts-of-service.summary: The open-ended American and Israeli war against Iran that John Kiriakou tracked week by week on his own show — a conflict he says was sold as three weeks, ran into its fifth month, achieved every decapitation objective it set, and continued anyway. His grade for it is a D, and his forecast is a Truth Social post declaring victory while nothing changes.

acts-of-service.title: Brian Ross
acts-of-service.summary: American investigative journalist and seven-time Emmy Award winner who was a prominent reporter at ABC News when, in December 2007, he conducted the on-camera interview with John Kiriakou that produced the first public confirmation by a U.S. official that the CIA waterboarded prisoners. Per Kiriakou, Ross called him out of the blue with the assertion that a source said Kiriakou had personally tortured Abu Zubaydah; Kiriakou's decision to give the interview anyway — driven by the conclusion that 'Brian Ross's source is at the White House and they're going to pin this on me' — became the pivot point of his entire post-CIA life.

acts-of-service.title: The Knight Ridder panel
acts-of-service.summary: At an April 2022 Assange benefit in Washington, John Kiriakou described a Zoom panel on which two former Knight Ridder reporters spoke for ninety minutes without once mentioning Julian Assange, and one of them, asked why, said he saw Assange as an activist rather than a journalist.

acts-of-service.title: Zohran Mamdani
acts-of-service.summary: John Kiriakou's assessment of the New York mayoral candidate in September 2025 — a smart young man running a very good campaign, surrounding himself with older seasoned New Yorkers rather than going in like a bull in a china shop, and gaining rather than losing ground the more the establishment attacked him.

administrative-remedy-process.title: Bureau of Prisons
administrative-remedy-process.summary: The federal agency that ran John Kiriakou's incarceration — and one of his most persistent post-prison targets. The BOP overrode his judge's camp recommendation by deeming him "a threat to the public safety," threatened him with "diesel therapy" until 1,600 logged phone calls and letters from a dozen House members and two senators backed it off, and, per Kiriakou, functions as "an employment agency for unemployable semi-literate rural white men" and "a dumping ground for failed medical professionals" — an agency for which a prisoner's death is cheaper than his treatment.

administrative-remedy-process.title: Charles Samuels
administrative-remedy-process.summary: Director of the Bureau of Prisons during Kiriakou's incarceration, and the official to whom Kiriakou publicly appealed over the heads of the Loretto staff in a letter from Loretto.

administrative-remedy-process.title: Prison Legal News
administrative-remedy-process.summary: The longest-running publication produced by and for current and former prisoners in American history, co-founded by former prisoner Paul Wright, and a recurring source in Kiriakou's account of Bureau of Prisons practice.

administrative-remedy-process.title: Education at FCI Loretto
administrative-remedy-process.summary: The classes, drug programme and good-conduct rules at FCI Loretto, which Kiriakou described in a letter from Loretto as correcting nothing — and which taught him, he wrote, how to cook methamphetamine and defraud a mortgage company.

administrative-remedy-process.title: Five per cent of the population, twenty-five per cent of the prisoners
administrative-remedy-process.summary: The statistic John Kiriakou returns to from inside prison — that the United States holds five per cent of the world''s people and a quarter of its prisoners, more per head than Russia, China or Iran — and the causes he assigns: the war on drugs, election-year lawmaking, and a Congress creating some fifty new crimes a year.

administrative-remedy-process.title: Karl Rove
administrative-remedy-process.summary: U.S. political strategist; manager of George W. Bush's 2000 and 2004 presidential campaigns; in 2008 he and John Kiriakou were hired by John Rendon to rehabilitate the reputation of an Indonesian general banned from the United States on human-rights grounds — a job Kiriakou says produced four unpublishable op-eds and nothing else.

admiral-crowe.title: The Fifth Fleet in Bahrain
admiral-crowe.summary: The United States naval presence based in Bahrain since 1976 — the naval component of Central Command, headquartered at Manama. For John Kiriakou as a young diplomat it was mainly a social resource: the officers'' club for its salad bar, the enlisted club for football and cheap beer. It was also, he came to understand, the reason his reporting on Bahraini extrajudicial killings went nowhere. The ambassador''s summary of the alliance was four words long. In 2026 the headquarters was itself hit by Iranian missiles — an outcome that, in Kiriakou''s reading, inverts the entire purpose of the Gulf basing architecture.

admiral-crowe.title: Bahrain Posting (1994–1996)
admiral-crowe.summary: John Kiriakou's 1994–1996 assignment to Bahrain under U.S. State Department cover as second secretary for economic affairs — arriving with his wife Joanne and infant son Chris on August 1, 1994, into a tiny Gulf monarchy whose sectarian tensions erupted, two months later, into the first Intifada.

admiral-crowe.title: Bahrain Prime Minister "Mr. 10 Percent"
admiral-crowe.summary: John Kiriakou's account of Bahrain's long-serving prime minister, the Amir's uncle, universally nicknamed "Mr. 10 Percent" for allegedly requiring a 10 percent cash cut on business deals — a cold, calculating figure Kiriakou calls "the definition of corruption," pointedly excluded from the national motto, yet credited with turning Bahrain into the Gulf's banking hub.

admiral-crowe.title: Isa bin Salman Al Khalifa
admiral-crowe.summary: Amir of Bahrain from 1961 until his death in 1999; per John Kiriakou, who was posted to Bahrain 1994–1996, a short, "roly poly," sweet-natured ruler who kept an open beach palace for Westerners, disliked Jordan's King Hussein, and was heartbroken by the Columbine shooting even as he privately could not grasp why he should extend more support to his own Shia majority.

admiral-crowe.title: Hawala system
admiral-crowe.summary: Informal, ledger-based money-transfer network used across the Middle East, South Asia, and their diasporas to move funds without involving banks; per John Kiriakou's first-person account of testing one in the UAE — handing $50 to a grocer for a 16-digit number to redeem at an Arabic bakery in Bethesda, Maryland — completely untraceable; identified by Kiriakou (later, as Chief Investigator on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee) as one of the principal channels through which al-Qaeda moved operational money in the post-9/11 period, along with DHL.

admiral-crowe.title: Kiriakou's public-speaking training
admiral-crowe.summary: The origin John Kiriakou gives for his manner as a speaker: a tenth-grade speech and debate class taught by Dr. Scarvel, his father''s childhood best friend, who drilled his students out of verbal fillers and pushed Kiriakou into competitive extemporaneous debate. Kiriakou credits the class with teaching him to let silence do the work of ''um''.

admit-nothing-deny-everything.title: Espionage Act
admit-nothing-deny-everything.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

admit-nothing-deny-everything.title: Arabic and Greek
admit-nothing-deny-everything.summary: The qualification John Kiriakou says opened the door to his transfer from CIA analysis to operations: a post in Athens wanted Greek or Arabic, and he had both — by most of his tellings the only officer in the agency who did. The chief who hired him gave the reason in one sentence: it is easier and cheaper to take a linguist and teach him operations than the other way round. The pairing also became a detection tool, since the language nobody speaks in Pakistan is Arabic.

admit-nothing-deny-everything.title: Bahrain Posting (1994–1996)
admit-nothing-deny-everything.summary: John Kiriakou's 1994–1996 assignment to Bahrain under U.S. State Department cover as second secretary for economic affairs — arriving with his wife Joanne and infant son Chris on August 1, 1994, into a tiny Gulf monarchy whose sectarian tensions erupted, two months later, into the first Intifada.

admit-nothing-deny-everything.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
admit-nothing-deny-everything.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

admit-nothing-deny-everything.title: The Department of Education SWAT raid
admit-nothing-deny-everything.summary: John Kiriakou's account of a pre-dawn armed raid on the home of a Washington Times journalist and her husband, an official at the Department of Education — carried out, he says, by the Department of Education's own armed SWAT team, which seized the reporter's notes and refused to return them. He uses the episode to point out that several civilian federal departments maintain armed tactical units, and that no other journalist covered it.

admit-nothing-deny-everything.title: Lenín Moreno
admit-nothing-deny-everything.summary: President of Ecuador during the final year of Julian Assange's asylum in the country's London embassy. John Kiriakou, speaking four days before Assange's removal, called Moreno a two-faced traitor who was trading Assange for American money, tariffs and debt relief, and dismissed the INA Papers accusations against Assange as factually untrue.

adnan-khashoggi.title: Beef jerky anomaly in the Epstein files
adnan-khashoggi.summary: A pattern John Kiriakou has flagged in the released Epstein correspondence: on the order of 1,300 to 1,500 emails discuss beef jerky — making it, teaching others to make it, freezing and storing it — and none discuss eating it. Kiriakou treats it as an unexplained code and declines to speculate about what it stands for.

adnan-khashoggi.title: Gerald Bull
adnan-khashoggi.summary: British inventor of the "big gun" — a barrel so large it had to be leaned against a mountain — first offered to Israel and rejected, then sold to Iraq under Saddam Hussein; assassinated by Mossad in Brussels once Iraqi engineers solved the cracking problem with a barrel-smoothing sleeve nicknamed "the condom," after which the Israelis also bombed the gun itself.

adnan-khashoggi.title: Population decline as a national-security question
adnan-khashoggi.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that demographic collapse — an emigrated Greek middle class, a shrinking Russia, and a Chinese population he believes is far smaller than claimed — is a strategic variable rather than a social one, and that some countries may not remain viable as countries without large population changes.

adnan-khashoggi.title: Prison pedophile accounts
adnan-khashoggi.summary: John Kiriakou's account of encountering convicted pedophiles for the first time in federal prison, drawing on advice from a psychiatrist friend and his own work running the chapel library — one of only two safe spaces in prison for inmates convicted of child sex crimes.

adnan-khashoggi.title: Roy Cohn
adnan-khashoggi.summary: Closeted McCarthy-era prosecutor and fixer, later a mentor, advisor and attorney to Donald Trump from the 1970s onward; per John Kiriakou, one of the darkest, ugliest figures in modern American history, who — while closely allied with a similarly closeted J. Edgar Hoover — was central to ruining the lives of gay men, and who died of AIDS in the 1980s alone and unloved.

adnan-khashoggi.title: The "Soylent Green is people" cable easter egg
adnan-khashoggi.summary: A long-running CIA case-officer in-joke in which the line "Soylent Green is people" is hidden inside classified operational cables as a sequence of incongruously lowercase letters

advanced-counterterrorism-operations-cou.title: The bomb course
advanced-counterterrorism-operations-cou.summary: The week-long CIA explosives course at a facility in another state, where John Kiriakou learned to build a Molotov cocktail, then a detonator rig, then an ammonium nitrate bomb — his final exam, which put a van's transmission three hundred yards into the woods.

advanced-counterterrorism-operations-cou.title: Counterterrorist driving
advanced-counterterrorism-operations-cou.summary: The vehicle training at the Farm — the PIT manoeuvre and how to avoid one, when to ram a roadblock and where to hit it, reversing at sixty miles an hour — conducted in a fleet of junkyard beaters the CIA bought expressly to be wrecked.

advanced-counterterrorism-operations-cou.title: The Farm
advanced-counterterrorism-operations-cou.summary: The CIA's clandestine training facility in Virginia; site of approximately 80% of all CIA operational training

advanced-counterterrorism-operations-cou.title: Kiriakou's titanium knee
advanced-counterterrorism-operations-cou.summary: The injury John Kiriakou took crashing a junkyard car through a roadblock in CIA training — his seat tore free of the floor and his knees hit the dashboard — which sixteen years later was diagnosed as spontaneous osteonecrosis and cost him the joint.

advanced-counterterrorism-operations-cou.title: The operations course graduation
advanced-counterterrorism-operations-cou.summary: The end of CIA field training: a graduation ceremony at which the whole class wore full disguises for the photograph, and a certificate that is itself classified and therefore cannot be displayed — it stays in the officer''s personnel file.

advanced-counterterrorism-operations-cou.title: The operational cable
advanced-counterterrorism-operations-cou.summary: The written product of every CIA field meeting — drafted the same day, printed and handed to the instructors at the Farm, who critiqued the prose, the conduct of the meeting and what the officer had been wearing.

advanced-counterterrorism-operations.title: Mort Halperin
advanced-counterterrorism-operations.summary: Former Assistant Secretary of State, Assistant Secretary of Defense, and senior director of the National Security Council; author of the law John Kiriakou was convicted of violating (the Intelligence Identities Protection Act); wrote to President Obama stating that this is not why he wrote the law and that Kiriakou should be pardoned.

advanced-counterterrorism-operations.title: Washington political culture
advanced-counterterrorism-operations.summary: John Kiriakou's account of how Washington changed across the forty-four years he has lived in it — from a city where members of opposing parties shared houses, churches and Friday-night poker games to one he calls hideous, angry and backstabbing, in which the polarisation is itself the reason nothing gets done and political violence keeps being waved past.

advanced-counterterrorism-operations.title: Counterterrorism Center deaths in the line of duty
advanced-counterterrorism-operations.summary: The colleagues John Kiriakou names as having been killed doing the work he did — Helge Boes and Mike Spann of the Counterterrorism Center, and the officer who sat beside him when he was chief of the counterintelligence branch of the Osama bin Laden group, killed with six colleagues by a suicide bomber in Afghanistan. He pairs the physical risk with a second cost he states as near-certain: that a marriage will not survive an operational tour.

advanced-counterterrorism-operations.title: The TikTok fan edits
advanced-counterterrorism-operations.summary: The short-form videos made by a University of Texas sophomore, giving John Kiriakou a chipmunk voice and laser eyes, which reached Gen Z at scale and led within weeks to representation by a major talent agency and meetings about film and television.

advanced-counterterrorism-operations.title: Trump cartel terrorist designation
advanced-counterterrorism-operations.summary: Donald Trump's early second-term State Department designation of drug cartels as terrorist organizations, which John Kiriakou says was understood at the time mainly as a paperwork exercise to free up agencies like the NSA and DIA to spend money on intercepting communications and training foreign nationals — but which Kiriakou says Trump has since treated as license to attack any vessel he personally deems cartel-linked.

advanced-counterterrorism-operations.title: Expanding the definition of terrorism
advanced-counterterrorism-operations.summary: John Kiriakou's objection to the widening of the U.S. terrorism designation beyond groups that use violence for political ends — covering the addition of organisations loosely associated with Antifa, which he argues is not a group at all, and the designation of Latin American narco organisations, which he says should be answered with criminal charges rather than drone strikes.

advice-to-an-aspiring-intelligence-analy.title: The two hundred billion dollar war request
advice-to-an-aspiring-intelligence-analy.summary: The Defense Department''s supplemental request for the 2026 Iran war, made without consulting Congress. John Kiriakou''s contribution is his verdict on the Republicans who dropped their objections on the grounds that wartime is no time for questions: a bunch of cowards.

advice-to-an-aspiring-intelligence-analy.title: The Danish Greenland demolition plan
advice-to-an-aspiring-intelligence-analy.summary: Denmark's preparations to destroy its own airstrips in Greenland rather than let an American invasion use them, including blood supplies moved into place. John Kiriakou confirms the preparations were real and made because the Danes took Donald Trump at his word.

advice-to-an-aspiring-intelligence-analy.title: The Hajj ban as leverage
advice-to-an-aspiring-intelligence-analy.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer to what a Saudi retaliation against Iran would look like: not a military strike but a ban on Iranians making the pilgrimage to Mecca. He notes it was done at the turn of the 1980s, that it produced a crisis, and that Iranian terrorist attacks against Saudis followed.

advice-to-an-aspiring-intelligence-analy.title: "The Spy Who Talked Too Much"
advice-to-an-aspiring-intelligence-analy.summary: Steve Coll's New Yorker profile of John Kiriakou, written after Coll had been welcomed into his home, and which Kiriakou telephoned him from prison to complain about. Coll's defence was that authors do not write their own headlines — a defence Kiriakou concedes, while still rating Coll among the country's great investigative journalists.

advice-to-an-aspiring-intelligence-analy.title: "Only two and a half more years"
advice-to-an-aspiring-intelligence-analy.summary: The consolation John Kiriakou says he takes from the second Trump term's remaining span, and his reasons for doubting that a Democratic successor would undo any of it. He points to Joe Biden's failure to reverse the first term, including the never-restored relationship with Cuba.

advice-to-an-aspiring-intelligence-analy.title: The empire on the ropes
advice-to-an-aspiring-intelligence-analy.summary: John Kiriakou's answer to whether the American empire is finished — that it is on the ropes but certainly not over — and, in the same exchange, his first unqualified statement that Israeli tactics were inspired by Nazi Germany, a comparison he says he hesitated for years to make.

advice-to-the-next-generation.title: The death of investigative journalism
advice-to-the-next-generation.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the collapse of investigative reporting inside the American mainstream press — Joby Warrick's resignation from the *Washington Post*, the paper that brought down a president, and the 80 per cent of its staff Kiriakou says have gone since Jeff Bezos bought it — together with the outlets he says are doing the work instead, and his advice to a student who wants to do it anyway.

advice-to-the-next-generation.title: Kent State shooting
advice-to-the-next-generation.summary: The 1970 shooting of unarmed student protesters by the Ohio National Guard; John Kiriakou says a family friend's daughter was among those killed — the closing event of a 1968–69 upheaval he treats both as the formation of his own politics and as the historical measure against which he judges the present.

advice-to-the-next-generation.title: 2026 Iran war
advice-to-the-next-generation.summary: The open-ended American and Israeli war against Iran that John Kiriakou tracked week by week on his own show — a conflict he says was sold as three weeks, ran into its fifth month, achieved every decapitation objective it set, and continued anyway. His grade for it is a D, and his forecast is a Truth Social post declaring victory while nothing changes.

advice-to-the-next-generation.title: Al-Qaeda training manual interrogation-resistance tactics
advice-to-the-next-generation.summary: A captured al-Qaeda training manual instructing operatives on how to resist interrogation, including feigning illness — a technique John Kiriakou says he saw a detainee use, and recognized, during a capture and interrogation in Pakistan.

advice-to-the-next-generation.title: Kiriakou's 2026 viral wave
advice-to-the-next-generation.summary: The sudden surge in John Kiriakou''s public recognition in the spring of 2026 — five hundred selfies in three and a half hours in Dublin, a documentary shoot in Berlin interrupted thirty-five times, strangers stopping him in Poland who spoke no English — which he attributes to an algorithm he does not understand and an audience he had not expected: men between fifteen and thirty.

advice-to-the-next-generation.title: Small-country intelligence services
advice-to-the-next-generation.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of dealing with the intelligence services of very small states — Djibouti, whose entire service he says occupied less space than his rented townhouse, and whose director''s office was half the size of his living room. His operating rule is that respect is the whole of the tradecraft: address the director as Your Excellency, and doors open that money cannot.

afghan-heroin-policy.title: Haqqani White House meeting
afghan-heroin-policy.summary: A mid-to-late-1980s White House meeting between President Ronald Reagan and a Taliban delegation, per John Kiriakou — a former boss of his served as translator. One member of that delegation, a man named Haqqani, went on to found the Haqqani network, later responsible for the capture of Bowe Bergdahl and the kidnapping, rape, and torture of a Canadian couple.

afghan-heroin-policy.title: Prepublication review
afghan-heroin-policy.summary: The CIA clearance process every former officer's writing must pass through, and John Kiriakou's account of what it did to his eighth book — five weeks instead of two, a missed publisher's deadline, six pages redacted as classified that he says the agency had itself declassified a decade earlier, and an appeal route requiring another ninety days.

afghan-heroin-policy.title: Ai Weiwei
afghan-heroin-policy.summary: Chinese contemporary artist and pro-democracy activist; designer of the Beijing Olympic Stadium; per John Kiriakou, produced a Lego portrait of him as one of 178 political prisoners in the series, with Kiriakou's panel positioned next to Martin Luther King Jr.; the work is now in the permanent collection of the Smithsonian Institution.

afghan-heroin-policy.title: The Eastern Mediterranean gas field
afghan-heroin-policy.summary: The natural gas discovered off the south-eastern coast of Cyprus and running toward Lebanon, Israel and Palestine, which John Kiriakou identifies as the real source of Greek–Turkish tension. Turkey feels excluded although none of the gas lies in its waters; and although the founding agreement acknowledged a Palestinian share, Israel decides its size — an amount Kiriakou predicts will be zero.

afghan-heroin-policy.title: The Imia crisis
afghan-heroin-policy.summary: The 1996 confrontation between Greece and Turkey over an uninhabited Aegean islet, which John Kiriakou cites as the last time the two came close to exchanging fire — a flag raised, a flag taken down, warships dispatched, and Bill Clinton telephoning both capitals to tell them to stop.

afghan-heroin-policy.title: Prisoner disposition from Pakistan
afghan-heroin-policy.summary: How captured prisoners were routed out of Pakistan in John Kiriakou's account — cooperation recorded in his reporting, headquarters consulted by telephone, most men flown to Guantanamo on a C-12, and the ones judged important enough sent, as he puts it, a different way.

afghan-languages.title: Edward Snowden
afghan-languages.summary: Former NSA contractor who in 2013 disclosed the scope of U.S. [mass surveillance](/wiki/mass-surveillance), including the Section 702 collection program. Per John Kiriakou — who counts Snowden among the small group of national-security whistleblowers prosecuted under the Espionage Act — Snowden was ''stuck between two awful slippery slopes'': breaking his oath and chain of command on one side, and on the other catching something ''cut and dry against the Constitution'' that no one would act on. Kiriakou notes Snowden could not use his chain of command (as Kiriakou could not, his own chain being Jose Rodriguez), and that Judge Leonie Brinkema had reserved the Snowden case for herself before he fled the country.

afghan-languages.title: FBI Arrest Strategies
afghan-languages.summary: Per John Kiriakou, the FBI deliberately times arrests for Thursdays or Friday evenings because no federal arraignments happen on Fridays, forcing detainees to spend the weekend in jail before facing a judge on Monday — a tactic he says he saw applied to January 6 defendants as well as to himself.

afghan-languages.title: Fort Gordon
afghan-languages.summary: The U.S. Army installation in Georgia where NSA whistleblower Reality Winner, interviewed on Kiriakou's show, worked as a contractor linguist before her arrest.

afghan-languages.title: Government Accountability Project
afghan-languages.summary: The Washington whistleblower-advocacy law firm and NGO, known as GAP, whose attorney Jesselyn Radack took John Kiriakou's case after his 2012 arrest and told him he was a whistleblower whether he thought so or not.

afghan-languages.title: Miranda Rights
afghan-languages.summary: Reality Winner, interviewed on Kiriakou's show, says she was never read her Miranda rights during her 2017 arrest by the FBI.

afghan-languages.title: Terry Aubry
afghan-languages.summary: Named by Kiriakou both as an FBI whistleblower who exposed racism at the bureau and as one of two Intercept journalists who sent him to prison.

afghan-national-police-poisoning.title: The Afghan police tribal rotation
afghan-national-police-poisoning.summary: An American anti-corruption scheme in Afghanistan that John Kiriakou describes as achieving the reverse of its purpose: someone in the Pentagon decided that regional chiefs of police should come from other tribes in other parts of the country, so a man from Herat would head the police in Kandahar — which only deepened hatred between tribes and did nothing at all about corruption.

afghan-national-police-poisoning.title: The Taliban truck escort origin
afghan-national-police-poisoning.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of how the Taliban began: as a Pakistani government scheme under Benazir Bhutto to take madrasa students — talib, plural taliban — out of the religious schools and put them with Kalashnikovs aboard Pakistani trucks crossing Afghanistan to Iran, to stop mujahideen fighters from pirating the cargo.

afghan-national-police-poisoning.title: The Hazara leader's judo belts
afghan-national-police-poisoning.summary: An encounter John Kiriakou describes from Afghanistan in about 2007: a very senior Hazara leader displayed every judo belt he had ever earned, white through black, in a large shadow box on his living room wall — and explained that he had gone to fifth dan not for sport but because Hazaras were forbidden to own weapons and he needed some way to protect himself.

afghan-national-police-poisoning.title: Afghan rare earth minerals
afghan-national-police-poisoning.summary: John Kiriakou's argument, made days after the fall of Kabul in August 2021, that the country with real leverage in Afghanistan was China — which holds an exclusive contract to mine rare earth metals valued in a Defense Department report at one trillion dollars, and therefore has a stake in a stable long-term Afghan government even a Taliban one.

afghan-national-police-poisoning.title: Kandahar
afghan-national-police-poisoning.summary: The southern Afghan city and province that recurs across John Kiriakou's Afghanistan material — site of one of the two al-Qaeda training camps Abu Zubaydah founded, whose commanders were captured in the same March 2002 raids; the town Bill Clinton said he would have had to destroy, killing 300 innocents, to kill bin Laden in the 1990s; and a stop on Kiriakou's Senate-era heroin-poppy investigation, when the military helicoptered him down before refusing to let him walk the poppy fields.

afghan-national-police-poisoning.title: Kiriakou's speaking tours
afghan-national-police-poisoning.summary: The lecture circuit John Kiriakou described in December 2025: a tour of England, Wales, Scotland, Ireland and Northern Ireland in January and February of that year, and a nationwide American tour due to begin the following February — one strand of a workload he said he was not sure he could keep up.

afghan-police-tribal-rotation.title: The Afghan National Police poisoning
afghan-police-tribal-rotation.summary: An incident John Kiriakou recalls from a 2012 New York Times report and treats as the clearest single illustration of why the American project in Afghanistan failed: at a DynCorp-run training facility that had deliberately mixed recruits from every tribe and region, one recruit poisoned the evening stew and then let four Taliban fighters into the dormitory to stab the survivors in their beds.

afghan-police-tribal-rotation.summary: An encounter John Kiriakou describes from Afghanistan in about 2007: a very senior Hazara leader displayed every judo belt he had ever earned, white through black, in a large shadow box on his living room wall — and explained that he had gone to fifth dan not for sport but because Hazaras were forbidden to own weapons and he needed some way to protect himself.

afghan-police-tribal-rotation.summary: The lecture circuit John Kiriakou described in December 2025: a tour of England, Wales, Scotland, Ireland and Northern Ireland in January and February of that year, and a nationwide American tour due to begin the following February — one strand of a workload he said he was not sure he could keep up.

afghan-rare-earth-minerals.title: The rare earth calculation
afghan-rare-earth-minerals.summary: John Kiriakou's explanation of how China came to control the world market in rare earth metals — not by holding the only deposits, which exist everywhere including under California's Salton Sea, but by being willing to absorb the economic loss of mining ore that is mostly waste, at a fraction of American defence spending.

afghan-rare-earth-minerals.title: Afghan heroin policy
afghan-rare-earth-minerals.summary: The post-2001 U.S. policy in Afghanistan of protecting, and per John Kiriakou actively encouraging, the cultivation of heroin poppy. Under the Taliban in 2000 Afghanistan produced 0% of the world's heroin; by 2009 under American occupation it produced 93%. Per a DEA officer Kiriakou consulted with on the policy paper he was preparing for Senator Kerry, the strategic rationale was that nearly all of the heroin flowed to Iran and Russia, addiction in those countries was considered desirable as a long-run societal weakener, and the same logic now operates in reverse with Chinese fentanyl flowing into the United States.

afghan-war-logs.title: Collateral Murder Video
afghan-war-logs.summary: The 2010 WikiLeaks release of gun-camera footage from a 2007 U.S. Apache helicopter attack in Baghdad; part of the trove of Iraq and Afghan war logs, Guantanamo files, and State Department cables leaked by Chelsea Manning, which John Kiriakou credits with corroborating major abuses and helping to touch off the Arab Spring.

afghan-war-logs.title: Ethan Mccord Collateral Murder
afghan-war-logs.summary: The US soldier who carried wounded children out of the street in the Collateral Murder video released by WikiLeaks.

afghanistan-2011-kerry-trip.title: Abu Omar rendition
afghanistan-2011-kerry-trip.summary: The CIA's kidnapping of a Milan cleric, Abu Omar, who was sent to Egypt to be tortured; John Kiriakou calls it a case that ought to be taught at the CIA as how not to run a rendition, and it is what ultimately sent him to prison, after he confirmed a former colleague's surname to a journalist claiming to be writing a book about it.

afghanistan-2011-kerry-trip.title: CIA/FBI Budget Fearmongering
afghanistan-2011-kerry-trip.summary: John Kiriakou's account of how the FBI, under J. Edgar Hoover, pioneered the tactic of citing a shifting parade of enemies before Congress to justify annual budget increases — communists, anarchists, gangsters, beatniks, anti-war protesters — a tactic the CIA later adopted wholesale, citing "communism" until 2001 and "terrorism" since, without needing further explanation to win budget increases.

afghanistan-2011-kerry-trip.title: Dick Cheney
afghanistan-2011-kerry-trip.summary: U.S. Vice President under George W. Bush. Per John Kiriakou — recounting CIA Director George Tenet's memoir — Cheney intercepted the presidential finding authorizing the CIA's enhanced interrogation program in the Oval Office anteroom and took it from Tenet before Bush could sign it. Tenet later concluded the president probably never actually signed the finding and probably told the truth when he said he had no idea the program was taking place. Kiriakou characterizes Cheney as the one who actually ran foreign policy, intelligence policy, and defense policy during the Bush years.

afghanistan-2011-kerry-trip.title: The Directorate of Operations
afghanistan-2011-kerry-trip.summary: The CIA's clandestine service, which John Kiriakou joined from analysis because he spoke both Greek and Arabic — a culture he describes as wildly different from the analytic side, short on institutional memory and organised around the race to become a station chief.

afghanistan-2011-kerry-trip.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
afghanistan-2011-kerry-trip.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

afghanistan-2011-kerry-trip.title: Espionage Act
afghanistan-2011-kerry-trip.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

agent-inducements.title: Agent payment mechanics
agent-inducements.summary: How the CIA physically pays a recruited agent — cash every month, a receipt signed with any alias the agent chooses, and a polygraph regime built around the assumption that the officer handling the money is the person most likely to steal it.

agent-inducements.title: Asset acquisition cycle
agent-inducements.summary: The four-step process — spot, assess, develop, recruit — taught as the first lesson of CIA case officer training

agent-inducements.title: CIA cash room
agent-inducements.summary: John Kiriakou's description of the rooms at large CIA stations stacked floor-to-ceiling with cash — tens or hundreds of millions of dollars — from which an officer can sign out whatever an operation needs, as when he took $2 million to buy safe houses for the Abu Zubaydah capture.

agent-inducements.title: The polygraph
agent-inducements.summary: The lie-detector examination that gates entry to the CIA, described by John Kiriakou from the inside: the twenty-minute wiring-up, the psychiatrist''s advice to stare at a speck on the wall, the deliberately planted false accusation used to test a candidate''s reaction, and his contention that the machine screens out exactly the wrong people.

agent-inducements.title: Scholar-in-Residence program
agent-inducements.summary: The current CIA recruitment program, in operation as of the late 2020s, under which the agency places retiring senior officers as 'CIA Scholar in Residence' professors at major American universities. Per John Kiriakou, the program serves as the agency's principal university-recruitment channel since the 1993 Equal Employment Opportunity Act forbade the older practice of having professors covertly recruit students into the CIA. Officers identified as scholars in residence are openly disclosed; the recruitment work continues, just no longer in secret.

agent-inducements.title: The restaurants in witness protection
agent-inducements.summary: What became of the foreign intelligence officer John Kiriakou recruited in Athens — resettled in the United States under a made-up name, given citizenship for his family and seed money to start again, and last heard of owning seven restaurants — and the resettlement package Kiriakou says the CIA offers a burned agent.

agent-payment-mechanics.title: Agent inducements
agent-payment-mechanics.summary: The non-cash things the CIA can offer a recruited agent — a child's university place anywhere in America, treatment at a top hospital for a sick spouse, or a carefully staged personal gift — and the standing arrangements with universities and large corporations that make them possible.

agent-payment-mechanics.title: CIA cash room
agent-payment-mechanics.summary: John Kiriakou's description of the rooms at large CIA stations stacked floor-to-ceiling with cash — tens or hundreds of millions of dollars — from which an officer can sign out whatever an operation needs, as when he took $2 million to buy safe houses for the Abu Zubaydah capture.

agent-payment-mechanics.title: "He''s been ours since the ''70s"
agent-payment-mechanics.summary: An episode John Kiriakou uses to convey the scale of CIA penetration of foreign political classes: spotting a former prime minister at a diplomatic cocktail party, rushing back to the embassy to file for a name trace and vulnerability assessment before anyone else could approach him, and receiving a same-day instruction to cease and desist because the man had already been an agency asset for decades.

agent-payment-mechanics.title: The four-question torture exam
agent-payment-mechanics.summary: A final examination set by a former CIA officer teaching alongside John Kiriakou at Liberty University, consisting of four escalating questions about whether the student would torture — the terrorist, then his wife in front of him, then their children — with the last question asking the student to justify the previous three answers to God. Kiriakou describes it as the most powerful exam he has ever seen.

agent-payment-mechanics.title: Abbottabad
agent-payment-mechanics.summary: The Pakistani garrison city where Osama bin Laden was found and killed — named for a British major who was Pakistan's first military trainer, home to the Pakistani military's leadership, and in John Kiriakou's judgement the last place bin Laden could have lived unnoticed by the Pakistani state.

agent-payment-mechanics.title: Liberty University
agent-payment-mechanics.summary: Evangelical university in Lynchburg, Virginia — the largest in the world — where John Kiriakou taught for several years as an adjunct professor of intelligence studies in the Jesse Helms School of Government. He says he warned the school he disagreed with it on 95% of the issues and was hired anyway, on the dean's reasoning that "torture's not Christian"; he enjoyed the post while clashing constantly with the institution over the treatment of Middle Eastern Christians.

agnes-von-kurowsky-grave-story.title: Kiriakou's personal anecdotes
agnes-von-kurowsky-grave-story.summary: Three personal stories John Kiriakou has told in interviews — tracking down and meeting Andy Warhol as a college senior, a Congolese vice president's remark that Americans promise democracy while the Chinese provide food, and Kiriakou's own Zelle account being suspended over Cuba-sanctions compliance after a paid article about his Cuba trip.

agnes-von-kurowsky-grave-story.title: Spies of Arlington National Cemetery
agnes-von-kurowsky-grave-story.summary: On the Walk With History podcast, John Kiriakou — author of Remains of the Day: A Definitive Guide to Washington D.C.''s Historic Cemeteries — toured Arlington National Cemetery and told personal and historical stories about the intelligence figures buried there, including OSS founder William Donovan, deputy CIA director Vernon Walters, codebreakers William and Elizabeth Friedman, slain station chiefs Richard Welch and William Buckley, U-2 pilot Francis Gary Powers, and Mike Spann, the first CIA officer killed after 9/11.

agnes-von-kurowsky-grave-story.title: Bashar al-Assad
agnes-von-kurowsky-grave-story.summary: President of Syria; John Kiriakou recounts warning Senator John Kerry to stop publicly calling Assad 'my dear friend' after a speech enraged Washington's Lebanese community, with Kerry citing motorcycle rides they had taken together to the Golan Heights.

agnes-von-kurowsky-grave-story.title: Jack Murphy NATO Sabotage Story
agnes-von-kurowsky-grave-story.summary: John Kiriakou's account of a story reported by podcaster Jack Murphy — over a year in the making, drawing on CIA and Army intelligence sources — alleging the CIA worked through a NATO partner to conduct sabotage inside Russia, including munitions-warehouse fires and rail explosions; killed before publication after the CIA deputy director denied it on a call with the editor and blamed "rogue Ukrainians."

agnes-von-kurowsky-grave-story.title: Remains of the Day Treasury Clerk Story
agnes-von-kurowsky-grave-story.summary: John Kiriakou's account of finding the grave of an obscure Treasury Department clerk who, during the 1814 British burning of Washington, rescued the Declaration of Independence, Constitution, Bill of Rights, and Washington's military commission from the National Archives — and who, after later being deemed too difficult, was quietly transferred to the National Lighthouse Service, where out of boredom he invented the refractor light still used in American lighthouses today.

agnes-von-kurowsky-grave-story.title: U.S. foreign policy process
agnes-von-kurowsky-grave-story.summary: Three foreign-policy observations from John Kiriakou — the narrow legal basis for U.S. military presence abroad, which he says does not cover American special forces in Syria; the formal congressional travel-clearance process that undercuts Pentagon and White House claims of no advance knowledge of Nancy Pelosi's Taiwan trip; and the depth of U.S.-China economic interdependence that Kiriakou says makes antagonizing Beijing strategically unwise.

ahmed-chalabi.title: Dick Cheney
ahmed-chalabi.summary: U.S. Vice President under George W. Bush. Per John Kiriakou — recounting CIA Director George Tenet's memoir — Cheney intercepted the presidential finding authorizing the CIA's enhanced interrogation program in the Oval Office anteroom and took it from Tenet before Bush could sign it. Tenet later concluded the president probably never actually signed the finding and probably told the truth when he said he had no idea the program was taking place. Kiriakou characterizes Cheney as the one who actually ran foreign policy, intelligence policy, and defense policy during the Bush years.

ahmed-chalabi.title: Iraq WMD intelligence
ahmed-chalabi.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of how the case for Iraqi weapons of mass destruction was fabricated: the intelligence community''s consensus was that Iraq had no WMD, but the White House had already decided to invade and sought analysis to fit the policy.

ahmed-chalabi.title: Asel al-Ghabandi
ahmed-chalabi.summary: Kuwaiti resistance figure during the 1990–91 Iraqi occupation; per John Kiriakou, a "bona fide hero" whose telephone reporting on Iraqi troop movements, roadblocks, atrocities, and the location of inspections reached the CIA every single day via NSA [call interception](/wiki/the-intercept) — Kiriakou's account of the resistance figure who best understood how to weaponize the certainty that the Americans were listening to everything.

ahmed-chalabi.title: Yellowcake Niger forgery
ahmed-chalabi.summary: The fabricated intelligence document claiming Iraq had attempted to buy yellowcake uranium from Niger; passed to the U.S. via the British (originally from the Italians); identified by CIA analysts including John Kiriakou as a forgery on sight ("it's not even in the right font"); pulled from President George W. Bush's State of the Union draft by Colin Powell; reinserted by Vice President Dick Cheney; pulled out by the CIA again; delivered in the 2003 State of the Union address anyway.

ahmed-chalabi.title: Leadership profiling
ahmed-chalabi.summary: The CIA practice of producing classified psychological profiles of foreign leaders for the president, vice president, national security advisor and the secretaries of state and defense before any meeting. It was John Kiriakou's first job at the agency, where he served as Saddam Hussein's classified psychological biographer working alongside psychiatrists, psychologists and anthropologists.

ahmed-chalabi.title: Robert Maxwell
ahmed-chalabi.summary: British media proprietor and father of Ghislaine Maxwell; described by John Kiriakou as "a prolific Mossad spy — that's a historic fact," and as the family channel through which the Epstein operation, in Kiriakou's phrase, was "kept all in the family."

ahmed-khatib.title: George Habash
ahmed-khatib.summary: Co-founder of the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine; as a young Lebanese medical student he was the college roommate at the American University of Beirut of Ahmed Khatib, the doctor whom Iraq installed as occupation governor of Kuwait on August 2, 1990 — a connection John Kiriakou carried into the Oval Office that day.

ahmed-khatib.title: PFLP
ahmed-khatib.summary: Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine; Palestinian armed group co-founded by George Habash and Ahmed Khatib, college roommates at the American University of Beirut. It is one of the Arab organizations John Kiriakou worked against during his Athens tour, where a semi-secret 1980s deal let the Arab groups transit Greece unmolested so long as they did not kill Greeks. Kiriakou's chance paper on Khatib made him the White House expert on the occupation governor of Kuwait in August 1990, and two of the Front's retired cadres later sat across a table from him in Jordan for a Sacha Baron Cohen shoot.

ahmed-khatib.title: Iraqi invasion of Kuwait
ahmed-khatib.summary: John Kiriakou''s most detailed account of the intelligence process around the 1990 Iraqi invasion of Kuwait and its 1991 liberation. As a first-year CIA analyst on a ''training account'' covering Iraq, Kiriakou produced the June 30, 1990 warning paper for the White House; suggested calling the US Defense Attaché in Baghdad to drive to the border and report what he saw (the answer: ''Literally the entire Iraqi military is heading south''); briefed the August 2 Oval Office meeting with Bush; and later took a single phone call from General Colin Powell that led, eight hours later, to 47 cruise missiles striking the Iraqi Intelligence Service headquarters in Baghdad.

ahmed-khatib.title: Saddam Hussein
ahmed-khatib.summary: President of Iraq from 1979 until the 2003 U.S. invasion; subject of John Kiriakou's CIA portfolio from January 1990 onward, in which capacity Kiriakou became, at age 25, "Saddam Hussein's intelligence community biographer" and the analyst who briefed President George H. W. Bush in the Oval Office on the morning of the 1990 invasion of Kuwait.

ahmed-khatib.title: Central Intelligence Agency
ahmed-khatib.summary: U.S. foreign intelligence service; John Kiriakou's employer from 1990 to 2004 and the central institution of KiriPedia

ahmed-khatib.title: Kuwait Liberation Day
ahmed-khatib.summary: February 1991 expulsion of Iraqi forces from Kuwait by the U.S.-led coalition; John Kiriakou entered the country with U.S. Marines on the day of liberation; the small American flags waved by the crowds — and the post-liberation arrival of Democratic and Republican National Committee personnel ostensibly to assist the country's transition to democracy — were, per Kiriakou, the work of professional propagandist John Rendon.

ai-weiwei.title: Andres Serrano
ai-weiwei.summary: American artist; in the 1980s the creator of Piss Christ — a beaker of urine containing an inverted crucifix — which so enraged President Ronald Reagan that he cut off funding to the National Endowment for the Arts. Per John Kiriakou, also the photographer of a torture-chamber series at Tate Modern, London, in which one panel is a photograph of Kiriakou next to a panel of a U.S. military torturer.

ai-weiwei.title: Afghan heroin policy
ai-weiwei.summary: The post-2001 U.S. policy in Afghanistan of protecting, and per John Kiriakou actively encouraging, the cultivation of heroin poppy. Under the Taliban in 2000 Afghanistan produced 0% of the world's heroin; by 2009 under American occupation it produced 93%. Per a DEA officer Kiriakou consulted with on the policy paper he was preparing for Senator Kerry, the strategic rationale was that nearly all of the heroin flowed to Iran and Russia, addiction in those countries was considered desirable as a long-run societal weakener, and the same logic now operates in reverse with Chinese fentanyl flowing into the United States.

ai-weiwei.title: Bahrain Posting (1994–1996)
ai-weiwei.summary: John Kiriakou's 1994–1996 assignment to Bahrain under U.S. State Department cover as second secretary for economic affairs — arriving with his wife Joanne and infant son Chris on August 1, 1994, into a tiny Gulf monarchy whose sectarian tensions erupted, two months later, into the first Intifada.

ai-weiwei.title: Brian Kelley
ai-weiwei.summary: Chief of counterintelligence at the CIA; framed by FBI counterintelligence chief Robert Hanssen — the actual Soviet/Russian mole — as the source of executed agents; spent a year and a half on leave without pay, surrounded around the clock by FBI agents, while his daughter was approached and told her father would face the death penalty if he did not confess.

ai-weiwei.title: Cuban double agents
ai-weiwei.summary: John Kiriakou's assessment of Cuban intelligence as one of the best services on the planet, defensive in nature and trained by the KGB, and his flat claim — repeated across several tellings — that the CIA has never recruited a Cuban who did not turn out to be working for Havana all along.

ai-weiwei.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
ai-weiwei.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

ai-whistleblower-initiative.title: Plus 972
ai-whistleblower-initiative.summary: The Israeli platform that, per a 2026 Berlin panel, has published a striking number of IDF whistleblowers as AI enters modern warfare.

ai-whistleblower-initiative.title: Whistleblower Protection Act
ai-whistleblower-initiative.summary: United States statute protecting federal employees who disclose government wrongdoing from retaliation; per John Kiriakou, national security employees — including those at the CIA, Pentagon, FBI, NSA, DEA, White House, and Homeland Security — are explicitly exempt from its protections, leaving them with no legally safe avenue to report illegal activity within their agencies.

ai-whistleblower-initiative.title: US Military Venture Capital
ai-whistleblower-initiative.summary: Per John Kiriakou, the U.S. military now purchases technology using a venture-capital investment model, a shift he cites as a warning sign about how national-security institutions acquire emerging tech.

ai-whistleblower-initiative.title: Der Spiegel
ai-whistleblower-initiative.summary: At a 2026 Berlin panel, a former Der Spiegel journalist said it took him years before he could call Julian Assange a publisher rather than an activist.

ai-whistleblower-initiative.title: Ethan Mccord Collateral Murder
ai-whistleblower-initiative.summary: The US soldier who carried wounded children out of the street in the Collateral Murder video released by WikiLeaks.

ai-whistleblower-initiative.title: Meredith Whittaker
ai-whistleblower-initiative.summary: Per John Kiriakou, Meredith Whittaker is developing a new, and by his account successful, business model for the encrypted-messaging app Signal, an alternative he cites alongside ProtonMail's compromised attempt at the same thing.

aipac-foreign-agent-registration.title: Israeli integration into U.S. agencies
aipac-foreign-agent-registration.summary: John Kiriakou''s objection to the formal embedding of Israeli personnel inside American defense and intelligence institutions — a National Defense Authorization Act provision collocating them with the Pentagon and opening Five Eyes-style liaison with the CIA, arriving in the same weeks as a DIA all-hands warning that Israeli services were unusually aggressive in recruiting inside DIA. His argument is that the two cannot both be true: either Israel is a critical counterintelligence threat or it is a partner.

aipac-foreign-agent-registration.title: John Fetterman
aipac-foreign-agent-registration.summary: The Pennsylvania senator whose fall from progressive Democratic hero to reliable AIPAC vote John Kiriakou has been tracking week by week on his own show, including the September 2026 Wall Street Journal investigation, based on more than a dozen former staffers and leaked internal texts, that reported Fetterman had lost interest in the job of a senator, skipped a June meeting with three paralysed veterans from his own state to appear on Fox News less than an hour later, and dismissed a Children's Hospital of Philadelphia request as *"they just want free trips to DC."*

aipac-foreign-agent-registration.title: Yalta conference
aipac-foreign-agent-registration.summary: The February 1945 Allied conference, which John Kiriakou uses as his teaching example of what a well-placed spy is worth: Stalin, told by a source inside the White House that Roosevelt was ill, insisted on a venue requiring a punishing multi-leg journey, then refused to delay the talks — and an exhausted Roosevelt, Kiriakou says, conceded Poland in order to go to bed.

aipac-foreign-agent-registration.title: Jamaal Bowman
aipac-foreign-agent-registration.summary: Former U.S. Representative from New York; cited by John Kiriakou alongside Cori Bush as the second documented case of AIPAC successfully primarying an incumbent House member for criticizing Israeli conduct in the Gaza war.

aipac-foreign-agent-registration.title: The Armenian podcasters
aipac-foreign-agent-registration.summary: Three naturalised Armenian-American podcasters who, independently of one another, told John Kiriakou during a week in Los Angeles that the Turks were outspending and out-lobbying Armenia in Washington — and his reply as a dual Greek citizen.

aipac-foreign-agent-registration.title: The October 2025 poll of American Jews
aipac-foreign-agent-registration.summary: The Washington Post poll John Kiriakou cited, released on 5 October 2025, which he said found for the first time that a majority of American Jews believed Israel was committing genocide in Gaza — and the question he built on it.

aipac.title: Alec Baldwin
aipac.summary: Actor with whom John Kiriakou recounts a bitter falling-out — Baldwin calling him a liar over lunch at a meeting about a play in which Baldwin was to play him, later attaching to a Kiriakou TV pitch that AMC bought the next day, then quitting for HBO and killing the deal without a word.

aipac.title: Alex Padilla
aipac.summary: U.S. Senator from California who was forced to the ground and handcuffed at a June 2025 press event after identifying himself as a sitting senator; per John Kiriakou, DHS Secretary Kristi Noem's claim that he failed to identify himself was false, and the White House's stated interest in prosecuting him was legally baseless because sitting senators have congressional immunity while acting in the course of their duties.

aipac.title: Glenn-Symington Act
aipac.summary: U.S. federal statute, co-authored by Senators John Glenn and Stuart Symington, that prohibits the U.S. government from providing foreign aid of any kind to any country possessing a nuclear weapons program that has not signed the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty; per John Kiriakou, Israel is the only country in the world meeting both criteria, making the law the principal reason the U.S. government officially declines to acknowledge the Israeli nuclear program.

aipac.title: James Fishback
aipac.summary: Florida gubernatorial candidate whom Kiriakou says he never personally endorsed, despite viral claims and a since-deleted tweet posted by his assistant; Kiriakou calls Fishback's stance on Israel well-considered but distances himself from Fishback's other stated positions, including a proposed sin tax on OnlyFans creators, an immigration moratorium, and comments Kiriakou calls racist.

aipac.title: John Fetterman
aipac.summary: The Pennsylvania senator whose fall from progressive Democratic hero to reliable AIPAC vote John Kiriakou has been tracking week by week on his own show, including the September 2026 Wall Street Journal investigation, based on more than a dozen former staffers and leaked internal texts, that reported Fetterman had lost interest in the job of a senator, skipped a June meeting with three paralysed veterans from his own state to appear on Fox News less than an hour later, and dismissed a Children's Hospital of Philadelphia request as *"they just want free trips to DC."*

aipac.title: Kiriakou and Cenk Uygur
aipac.summary: A grievance John Kiriakou carried for a decade — that Cenk Uygur had spent thirty minutes attacking him over his first letter from prison — resolved live on air in July 2026 when Uygur produced his archive, found no such segment, and both men concluded it had been mistaken identity.

air-india-flight-182.title: Muslim Brotherhood terrorist designation
air-india-flight-182.summary: John Kiriakou''s objection to the designation of the Muslim Brotherhood, or elements of it, as a terrorist organisation: that the group is more than a century old, has never carried out an anti-American terrorist operation, and had never been so designated by any previous administration. He distinguishes fundamentalism and hostility from terrorism, has made the same argument to a former IDF spokesman''s face, and traces the American quarrel with the Brotherhood back to its winning an Egyptian election.

air-india-flight-182.title: The Hannity Lockerbie exchange
air-india-flight-182.summary: A televised argument in which John Kiriakou says he embarrassed Sean Hannity by pointing out that the 1986 American bombing that killed Muammar Gaddafi's daughter came three years before the Lockerbie bombing, and so could not have been revenge for it.

air-india-flight-182.title: Islamofascism
air-india-flight-182.summary: A term John Kiriakou says was introduced into American media around 2004 and 2005, was created by a public relations firm working for the Republican National Committee, was pushed hard into everyday usage, failed to catch on, and was quietly abandoned. He offers it as his clearest example of manufactured vocabulary intended as domestic propaganda.

air-wars-are-overrated.title: Hamas
air-wars-are-overrated.summary: The Palestinian movement behind the October 7, 2023 attack; John Kiriakou argues that a case could be made for calling it a freedom-fighting organization dedicated to the liberation of its people rather than simply a terrorist group, notes it is labeled a terrorist organization by only a small minority of UN member states, and has ruled Gaza since Israel's 2005 withdrawal.

air-wars-are-overrated.title: The F-35 shootdown
air-wars-are-overrated.summary: Footage from the 2026 Iran war showing an F-35 hit by Iranian ground fire, initially dismissed as artificial. John Kiriakou notes the Pentagon confirmed the pilot reached a Middle East airbase wounded, and that nobody explained how a supposedly obliterated adversary had hit an invisible aircraft.

air-wars-are-overrated.title: The house of cards theory
air-wars-are-overrated.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the strategic premise behind the 2026 Iran war — that decapitating the Iranian government would bring the whole state down — and of why it fails. To win, he argues, the United States would have to destroy the entire Iranian government and military and install a puppet; Iran wins simply by surviving.

air-wars-are-overrated.title: Hezbollah
air-wars-are-overrated.summary: Lebanese Shia militant organization and political party. Per John Kiriakou, Israel''s strategic goal regarding Hezbollah is not to defeat it outright but to keep Lebanon in a state of chaos that serves Israeli interests. He cites two Israeli operations: the simultaneous pager-detonation attack that decapitated Hezbollah''s leadership, which he called ''the most incredible operation I''ve ever seen,'' and the strike that killed former leader Hassan Nasrallah by leveling an entire complex and killing roughly 300 people — which he characterized as a war crime.

air-wars-are-overrated.title: The two hundred billion dollar war request
air-wars-are-overrated.summary: The Defense Department''s supplemental request for the 2026 Iran war, made without consulting Congress. John Kiriakou''s contribution is his verdict on the Republicans who dropped their objections on the grounds that wartime is no time for questions: a bunch of cowards.

air-wars-are-overrated.title: The Netanyahu death rumour
air-wars-are-overrated.summary: A theory advanced by well-regarded podcasters during the 2026 Iran war that Benjamin Netanyahu had been killed and the fact concealed — his son's seven-day silence read as sitting shiva. John Kiriakou recounts it collapsing when Netanyahu gave a press conference, and sets it against the real decapitation campaign against the IRGC.

akrotiri-village-evacuation.title: British Bases in Cyprus
akrotiri-village-evacuation.summary: British sovereign bases in Cyprus host a large American contingent. Kiriakou, a quarter Cypriot, on the bases as evacuation hub, missile target, and suspected nuclear site — and on the 46-year US weapons embargo almost no American knows about.

akrotiri-village-evacuation.title: Iranian suicide drones
akrotiri-village-evacuation.summary: John Kiriakou''s description of the weapon he expected to define Iran''s side of the 2026 war: one-way drones built inside Iran from Iranian parts, in large numbers, costing five to ten thousand dollars each, with explosives strapped on and flown remotely into a target. He treats them as the reason an aircraft carrier can no longer defend itself, the reason air defence fails on arithmetic rather than on technology, and the reason the Gulf states are reassessing the value of American bases.

akrotiri-village-evacuation.title: Erbil and the Kurdish autonomy question
akrotiri-village-evacuation.summary: Reading reports that Erbil airport in Iraqi Kurdistan had been targeted twice on the first night of the 2026 war, John Kiriakou drew out the implication: Baghdad had said repeatedly it would take no part in an American attack on Iran, but the Kurds hold autonomy in the north, and the strikes on Erbil suggest they may be supporting the attack independently of the Iraqi government.

akrotiri-village-evacuation.title: The AI he uses
akrotiri-village-evacuation.summary: Asked which AI tool he uses and why, John Kiriakou named Perplexity over ChatGPT, on two grounds: ChatGPT invents things about him, and Perplexity — for reasons he says he does not fully understand — returns much deeper analysis when he asks it to look at something.

akrotiri-village-evacuation.title: The Al Mayadeen debate
akrotiri-village-evacuation.summary: Two days before the 2026 attack on Iran, John Kiriakou went on the Lebanese network Al Mayadeen expecting the usual point-counterpoint with an academic and found himself opposite Iran's lead nuclear negotiator. His argument to the negotiator — that what the two sides were then negotiating was the JCPOA under another name — was rejected outright before being accepted.

akrotiri-village-evacuation.title: The strike on Ahmadinejad's house
akrotiri-village-evacuation.summary: On the first day of the 2026 war, reports placed one of the targets in Tehran at Narmak, believed to be the residence of former Iranian president Mahmoud Ahmadinejad. John Kiriakou broke into the broadcast to call it gratuitous and an act of murder: Ahmadinejad is retired, holds no authority, and — in Kiriakou''s description — was a moderate.

al-jazeera-blocked-in-the-united-states.title: 2026 Iran war
al-jazeera-blocked-in-the-united-states.summary: The open-ended American and Israeli war against Iran that John Kiriakou tracked week by week on his own show — a conflict he says was sold as three weeks, ran into its fifth month, achieved every decapitation objective it set, and continued anyway. His grade for it is a D, and his forecast is a Truth Social post declaring victory while nothing changes.

al-jazeera-blocked-in-the-united-states.title: The Iranian elementary school strike
al-jazeera-blocked-in-the-united-states.summary: A Tomahawk cruise missile strike at the start of the 2026 war that killed more than 175 people at an Iranian elementary school. The United States denied responsibility until its own investigation confirmed it; John Kiriakou traces the failure to targeting data a decade out of date and expects no one to be punished for it.

al-jazeera-blocked-in-the-united-states.title: The AI he uses
al-jazeera-blocked-in-the-united-states.summary: Asked which AI tool he uses and why, John Kiriakou named Perplexity over ChatGPT, on two grounds: ChatGPT invents things about him, and Perplexity — for reasons he says he does not fully understand — returns much deeper analysis when he asks it to look at something.

al-jazeera-blocked-in-the-united-states.title: The strike on Ahmadinejad's house
al-jazeera-blocked-in-the-united-states.summary: On the first day of the 2026 war, reports placed one of the targets in Tehran at Narmak, believed to be the residence of former Iranian president Mahmoud Ahmadinejad. John Kiriakou broke into the broadcast to call it gratuitous and an act of murder: Ahmadinejad is retired, holds no authority, and — in Kiriakou''s description — was a moderate.

al-jazeera-blocked-in-the-united-states.title: "A policy support organization"
al-jazeera-blocked-in-the-united-states.summary: Asked how the CIA workforce would be reacting to the war on Iran, John Kiriakou answered from the Iraq war: people put their heads down and did as they were told, after a boss told an assembled group — all of whom opposed the invasion — that the agency is not a policy organization but a policy support organization, and would do what the White House told it to do.

al-jazeera-blocked-in-the-united-states.title: Akrotiri Village Evacuation
al-jazeera-blocked-in-the-united-states.summary: Kiriakou says the drone that hit Britain's Akrotiri base in Cyprus was likely an Israeli operation, staged and then falsely blamed on Iran.

al-julani.title: ISIS
al-julani.summary: The Islamic State, in John Kiriakou''s account, is an American policy failure made flesh — created because a faction decided al-Qaeda was not radical or violent enough, founded by Baghdadi while he sat in a U.S. military prison in Iraq, armed with hardware captured from the U.S.-supplied Iraqi army, and — per an email he cites from Hillary Clinton to John Podesta — funded by the governments of Saudi Arabia and Qatar. Kiriakou repeatedly punctured the anti-ISIS coalition''s logic: ISIS operated in seven countries while the U.S. bombed two, and Turkey had no real quarrel with ISIS at all — their common enemy was the Kurds.

al-julani.title: Barbara Leaf
al-julani.summary: American diplomat, assistant secretary of state for the Near East, and — in John Kiriakou's description — an old friend of his. He cites her trip to Damascus, made within days of al-Julani taking power and alongside the special envoy for hostage affairs, as the moment American recognition was traded for the lifting of the ten-million-dollar bounty on the new Syrian leader.

al-julani.title: Daniel Pearl
al-julani.summary: The Wall Street Journal correspondent murdered in Pakistan in 2002, whom John Kiriakou met at the American embassy in Islamabad on the day he disappeared and tried to talk out of the meeting — and whose killing was later confessed to twice, by two different men.

al-julani.title: Greater and Lesser Tunb Islands
al-julani.summary: Two small, largely uninhabited islands in the Persian Gulf, belonging to the emirate of Sharjah in the UAE, occupied by Iran in a 1990s incident John Kiriakou recounts as CIA analyst; Kiriakou correctly predicted the UAE would not go to war over them given Sharjah's heavy trade dependence on Iran, and has since used the case against 2026 speculation that the United States would seize them back.

al-julani.title: The Stinger buyback
al-julani.summary: The standing reward programme John Kiriakou administered at the American embassy in Islamabad — a hundred thousand dollars in cash, paid over the counter, for each Stinger missile the United States had given the mujahideen from 1986 and now wanted back before its forty-year shelf life ran out.

al-julani.title: Kashmir
al-julani.summary: The disputed territory John Kiriakou says is front and centre for every Pakistani and largely absent from Indian minds, and on which his own sympathies lie with Pakistan — a promised 1940s referendum that never happened. He also describes the appearance that ended his participation in South Asian media: an Indian programme cut his pro-Pakistani answer, aired only his prediction that India would win a conventional war, and the death threats resumed.

al-qaeda-foot-soldier-profile.title: Foreign aid
al-qaeda-foot-soldier-profile.summary: John Kiriakou's advocacy of a hundredfold increase in the American foreign-aid budget — a position he concedes puts him in "a very minuscule minority" — argued on the grounds that every dollar spent saves five or ten in refugee crises, civil wars and attacks on the United States, and that development is the only thing that empties terrorist recruiting pools. His counter-example is the Sana'a water-treatment plant, built by the European Union and rendered pointless by American and Saudi politics.

al-qaeda-foot-soldier-profile.title: Agent payment mechanics
al-qaeda-foot-soldier-profile.summary: How the CIA physically pays a recruited agent — cash every month, a receipt signed with any alias the agent chooses, and a polygraph regime built around the assumption that the officer handling the money is the person most likely to steal it.

al-qaeda-foot-soldier-profile.title: Ali Soufan
al-qaeda-foot-soldier-profile.summary: FBI special agent who handled Abu Zubaydah immediately after his March 2002 capture; through patient, respectful interrogation produced the only actionable intelligence ever obtained from the detainee, including the first identification of "Mukhtar" as Khalid Sheikh Mohammed.

al-qaeda-foot-soldier-profile.title: Brian Ross
al-qaeda-foot-soldier-profile.summary: American investigative journalist and seven-time Emmy Award winner who was a prominent reporter at ABC News when, in December 2007, he conducted the on-camera interview with John Kiriakou that produced the first public confirmation by a U.S. official that the CIA waterboarded prisoners. Per Kiriakou, Ross called him out of the blue with the assertion that a source said Kiriakou had personally tortured Abu Zubaydah; Kiriakou's decision to give the interview anyway — driven by the conclusion that 'Brian Ross's source is at the White House and they're going to pin this on me' — became the pivot point of his entire post-CIA life.

al-qaeda-foot-soldier-profile.title: Counterterrorism Center
al-qaeda-foot-soldier-profile.summary: The CIA's Counterterrorism Center (CTC) — the unit where John Kiriakou spent the defining years of his operational career. He joined in the late 1990s as the only officer in the entire CIA fluent in both Greek and Arabic, served as chief of counterintelligence in the bin Laden unit, watched the Center swell from a few hundred employees to nearly 2,000 by September 12, 2001, and it was to CTC that he walked back down in May 2002 to refuse the torture program — the moment, he says, the CIA began to turn on him.

al-qaeda-foot-soldier-profile.title: Renting Afghan warlords
al-qaeda-foot-soldier-profile.summary: The CIA's opening strategy in Afghanistan after the September 11 attacks — paying the country's warlords in cash rather than trying to buy their loyalty outright, captured in an agency saying that you cannot buy an Afghan warlord but you can certainly rent one.

al-qaeda-software.title: Kiriakou's transfer to the Directorate of Operations
