al-qaeda-software.summary: John Kiriakou's roughly two-month internal campaign to transfer from the CIA's analytic Directorate of Intelligence to the operational Directorate of Operations, overcoming what he calls a "natural bias in operations against the eggheads on the analytic side," followed by an Athens posting secured because he was the only person in the entire CIA fluent in both Greek and Arabic. Covers his full CIA career arc from 1988/1990 recruitment through analyst years on Iraq, the switch to operations, 9/11, the enhanced-interrogation refusal, executive assistant to the deputy director for operations, and his eventual resignation and post-CIA career.

al-qaeda-software.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
al-qaeda-software.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

al-qaeda-software.title: Mitchell and Jessen
al-qaeda-software.summary: The two American psychologists who pitched the CIA's enhanced interrogation program to Director George Tenet at a cocktail party in late October 2001; designers of the program and its theoretical underpinning, "learned helplessness."

al-qaeda-software.title: "Admit nothing, deny everything, make counter-accusations"
al-qaeda-software.summary: One of the twenty life lessons John Kiriakou says the CIA taught him in training, and a slogan sold on coffee mugs and t-shirts in the headquarters gift shop — by far the most popular mug in the building. It was treated at Langley as a joke that was not quite a joke; in federal prison Kiriakou used it as an operating rule, and credits it with getting him out of an investigation into a prison-yard fight with nothing given up.

al-qaeda-software.title: Alex Station
al-qaeda-software.summary: CIA unit that tracked Osama bin Laden beginning in 1995; per John Kiriakou, who served as chief of its counterintelligence branch, the unit kept extremely tight security around its files, limited FBI investigators' access to information about future 9/11 hijackers Khaled al-Mihdhar and Nawaf al-Hazmi, and — under a deliberate policy of non-cooperation with the FBI — failed to watchlist participants in the Malaysia summit where al-Qaeda planned the attacks.

al-qaeda-software.title: Zawahiri assassination
al-qaeda-software.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the drone strike that killed al-Qaeda's Ayman al-Zawahiri — using a bladed, warhead-less missile fired as he stepped onto a balcony to smoke, deliberately chosen to avoid killing the women and children inside.

al-qaeda-training-manual-interrogation-t.title: China's base in Djibouti
al-qaeda-training-manual-interrogation-t.summary: Camp Lemonnier in Djibouti, the abandoned French base the Djiboutians offered to the Americans and the Chinese took a share of — split down the middle by a chain-link fence, the only Chinese military installation outside China, and the centrepiece of John Kiriakou's argument that China is not an expansionist power.

al-qaeda-training-manual-interrogation-t.title: Irish intelligence services
al-qaeda-training-manual-interrogation-t.summary: Ireland's intelligence and law-enforcement services, which John Kiriakou toured and met with during a speaking trip to Belfast, Cork, Dublin, and Waterford. Per Kiriakou, Irish intelligence and the Garda are especially strong at anti-money-laundering investigation and counterterrorism — the latter traced, he says, to the large number of Irish militants trained by Carlos the Jackal in Libya and Lebanon during the 1970s.

al-qaeda-training-manual-interrogation-t.title: Kent State shooting
al-qaeda-training-manual-interrogation-t.summary: The 1970 shooting of unarmed student protesters by the Ohio National Guard; John Kiriakou says a family friend's daughter was among those killed — the closing event of a 1968–69 upheaval he treats both as the formation of his own politics and as the historical measure against which he judges the present.

al-qaeda-training-manual-interrogation-t.title: 2026 Iran war
al-qaeda-training-manual-interrogation-t.summary: The open-ended American and Israeli war against Iran that John Kiriakou tracked week by week on his own show — a conflict he says was sold as three weeks, ran into its fifth month, achieved every decapitation objective it set, and continued anyway. His grade for it is a D, and his forecast is a Truth Social post declaring victory while nothing changes.

al-qaeda-training-manual-interrogation-t.title: Kiriakou's 2026 viral wave
al-qaeda-training-manual-interrogation-t.summary: The sudden surge in John Kiriakou''s public recognition in the spring of 2026 — five hundred selfies in three and a half hours in Dublin, a documentary shoot in Berlin interrupted thirty-five times, strangers stopping him in Poland who spoke no English — which he attributes to an algorithm he does not understand and an audience he had not expected: men between fifteen and thirty.

al-qaeda-training-manual-interrogation-t.title: Small-country intelligence services
al-qaeda-training-manual-interrogation-t.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of dealing with the intelligence services of very small states — Djibouti, whose entire service he says occupied less space than his rented townhouse, and whose director''s office was half the size of his living room. His operating rule is that respect is the whole of the tradecraft: address the director as Your Excellency, and doors open that money cannot.

alan-dershowitz.title: Jonathan Pollard
alan-dershowitz.summary: U.S. Navy civilian intelligence analyst convicted in 1985 of spying for Israel; the canonical proven case of Israeli espionage against the United States; cited by John Kiriakou in his 2024 Piers Morgan debate with a former Mossad director who denied any Israeli spying on the U.S.

alan-dershowitz.title: Jeffrey Epstein
alan-dershowitz.summary: Convicted sex offender; per John Kiriakou, was "an Israeli access agent" rather than a CIA asset, because the CIA collects foreign intelligence and Epstein's targets — Bill Clinton, Bill Gates, Prince Andrew — were not foreign. Kiriakou further holds that Epstein did die by suicide in federal custody, because in the Bureau of Prisons the cameras never work and the guards are always asleep.

alan-dershowitz.title: Peter Mandelson
alan-dershowitz.summary: British politician; described by John Kiriakou as the former British ambassador to Washington and as someone likely to be charged with serious crimes in connection with Jeffrey Epstein.

alan-dershowitz.title: Kiriakou prison manipulation tactics
alan-dershowitz.summary: John Kiriakou's account of applying CIA tradecraft — including deliberate deception, forged paperwork, and manipulating other inmates into violence — to protect himself and control his environment during his federal prison sentence.

alan-dershowitz.title: Ross Ulbricht
alan-dershowitz.summary: Founder of the online marketplace Silk Road, sentenced to life plus 75 years before being pardoned by President Trump; John Kiriakou met Ulbricht's mother and sister two weeks before the pardon and calls the length of the original sentence a sickening miscarriage of justice.

alan-dershowitz.title: Abraham Bolden
alan-dershowitz.summary: The first African-American Secret Service agent assigned to a presidential detail; per John Kiriakou, he quite literally saved John F. Kennedy's life in Chicago in October 1963 and was subjected to overt racism by fellow agents, who told him to his face they would not protect Kennedy from assassination because of his civil-rights sympathies.

albert-stubblebine.title: Lynn Buchanan
albert-stubblebine.summary: A Fort Meade-trained Army intelligence veteran of the CIA and NSA remote-viewing programs — a primary source, Kiriakou says, not a TV psychic.

albert-stubblebine.title: Russell Targ
albert-stubblebine.summary: Named in a post-produced narration segment appended to an interview featuring John Kiriakou, describing Targ as an original Stanford Research Institute scientist behind government remote-viewing protocols — not a claim made by Kiriakou himself, who elsewhere expresses skepticism that remote viewing ever worked.

albert-stubblebine.title: Project Stargate
albert-stubblebine.summary: The CIA's remote-viewing program, which Kiriakou says burned millions for decades and failed — and which he understands is being revisited.

albert-stubblebine.title: Bay Path University
albert-stubblebine.summary: Per John Kiriakou, he teaches in the graduate intelligence-studies program at Bay Path University in Massachusetts, covering introduction to intelligence, the history of terrorism, and intelligence and cybersecurity.

albert-stubblebine.title: Espionage Act
albert-stubblebine.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

albert-stubblebine.title: Sweat Lodge
albert-stubblebine.summary: Per John Kiriakou, the federal prison where he was incarcerated had a Native American sweat lodge that was shut down after it was misused for sex rather than religious ceremony; he says he has never personally been in a sweat lodge.

albright-in-pyongyang.title: Bill Clinton
albright-in-pyongyang.summary: 42nd U.S. president whom John Kiriakou describes as wholly disinterested in intelligence — briefed by the CIA only twice in eight years, with Vice President Al Gore taking the daily briefing instead and relaying anything important.

albright-in-pyongyang.title: Camp David Final Talks
albright-in-pyongyang.summary: Middle East peace negotiations held at Camp David in the final days of the Clinton administration. Per John Kiriakou — relaying an account from a senior NSC officer who was present — the talks came extraordinarily close to a comprehensive agreement: with President Clinton, Vice President Al Gore, Yasser Arafat, Mahmoud Abbas, and Israeli Foreign Minister Shimon Peres around an enormous Sharpie-marked map of Jerusalem, dividing the city block by block. When the division was complete, Gore said ''My God, we have peace'' — and Arafat replied ''I can never sell this to the Palestinian people'' and walked out.

albright-in-pyongyang.title: Failure to accept responsibility
albright-in-pyongyang.summary: The federal sentencing enhancement that John Kiriakou says explains why 98 per cent of federal criminal cases end in a plea bargain: a defendant who refuses a deal, goes to trial and loses has time added to the sentence for failing to accept responsibility.

albright-in-pyongyang.title: Nationalizing the midterms
albright-in-pyongyang.summary: John Kiriakou's recurring comparison between contemporary party messaging and Newt Gingrich's 1994 Contract with America, including his advice that Speaker Mike Johnson should keep Gingrich on his couch and ask him nightly how the 1994 midterms were nationalised.

albright-in-pyongyang.title: The French in the streets
albright-in-pyongyang.summary: John Kiriakou's stated admiration for how quickly the French take to the streets, offered while questioning Ted Rall about the chances of violence during the 2025 French political crisis, alongside his observation that he could not recall a French president ever resigning.

albright-in-pyongyang.title: The nine-dollar-eighty-three premium
albright-in-pyongyang.summary: John Kiriakou's own Affordable Care Act premium, which he gives as $9.83 a month, and the doctor who asked him why he carried the plan at all. Offered during a October 2025 discussion of the government shutdown and the expiring Obamacare subsidies.

aldrich-ames.title: John Kiriakou
aldrich-ames.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

aldrich-ames.title: Jennings Randolph
aldrich-ames.summary: Longtime U.S. Senator from West Virginia who, in a phone call John Kiriakou made to thank him as a college student, gave him the advice he says shaped his life: always do the right thing, not the expedient one.

aldrich-ames.title: Steven Lalas
aldrich-ames.summary: American with top-secret clearance recruited as a spy for Greece's National Intelligence Service (EYP) in a provocative mid-1990s operation run by the country's conservative government. Per John Kiriakou, who did not know Lawless personally, the case was so sensitive that his handler reported directly to the EYP director out of fear the CIA had planted a mole inside the service. Lawless was caught, served about seven years, and was given Greek citizenship on release.

aldrich-ames.title: How Can I Keep from Singing
aldrich-ames.summary: Biography of folk singer Pete Seeger and John Kiriakou's stated favorite book. Per Kiriakou, Seeger was the most important man in his life besides his father and grandfather; the two exchanged Christmas cards for years, and Seeger rallied publicly to Kiriakou's defense during his prosecution. Kiriakou identifies Seeger's 1958 defiance of HUAC — pleading the First Amendment rather than the Fifth and going to prison for it — as the model for how he wanted to live his own life.

aldrich-ames.title: Kiriakou's money-laundering tip
aldrich-ames.summary: John Kiriakou's account of taking a chief operating officer job at a boutique investment firm early in the COVID pandemic that he came to believe was an international money-laundering operation possibly backed by Iran — downloading 15,000 pages of supporting documents before an FBI agent told him the bureau would only take interest if the case involved Russia, China, terrorism, or January 6th.

aldrich-ames.title: The Russian illegals program
aldrich-ames.summary: The Russian practice, described by John Kiriakou, of recruiting people — sometimes as children — training them abroad and inserting them into Western countries as sleepers who live ordinary lives for decades until they are activated. Kiriakou says a group of illegals was broken up by the FBI in his own Arlington, Virginia neighbourhood and traded for American spies, and that he knows a former KGB sleeper in Brooklyn who refused activation after the birth of his daughter.

alec-baldwin.title: Abu Omar rendition
alec-baldwin.summary: The CIA's kidnapping of a Milan cleric, Abu Omar, who was sent to Egypt to be tortured; John Kiriakou calls it a case that ought to be taught at the CIA as how not to run a rendition, and it is what ultimately sent him to prison, after he confirmed a former colleague's surname to a journalist claiming to be writing a book about it.

alec-baldwin.title: AIPAC
alec-baldwin.summary: The American Israel Public Affairs Committee — the U.S. political organization that, in John Kiriakou's framing, ought to be registered as a foreign-lobbying entity but is not, and that wields decisive electoral power against U.S. elected officials who express support for Palestinian human rights.

alec-baldwin.title: CIA animal surveillance experiments
alec-baldwin.summary: Cold-War CIA efforts to turn animals into listening devices, which John Kiriakou describes as failures — including microphones and cameras mounted on pigeons trained to land on the Soviet embassy, which could reach the compound but never captured anything meaningful.

alec-baldwin.title: Citizens United
alec-baldwin.summary: The Supreme Court decision John Kiriakou blames for legalizing unlimited corporate political money and for corporations having "taken over" two of the three branches of government — and which he says lets AIPAC pour tens of millions into single congressional races to defeat candidates who cross Israel.

alec-baldwin.title: Havana Syndrome
alec-baldwin.summary: Cluster of neurological symptoms — including nausea, ringing in the ears, vertigo, and traumatic brain injury — reported by American diplomatic and intelligence personnel beginning in Havana, Cuba, and subsequently at posts around the world. Per John Kiriakou, his initial skepticism gave way when a friend developed Havana Syndrome with an MRI-confirmed traumatic brain injury after a meeting outside the Russian Foreign Ministry; Kiriakou attributes the syndrome to Russian or Chinese directed-energy weapons and acknowledges the United States used a similar weapon during the operation to capture Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro.

alec-baldwin.title: Mitchell and Jessen
alec-baldwin.summary: The two American psychologists who pitched the CIA's enhanced interrogation program to Director George Tenet at a cocktail party in late October 2001; designers of the program and its theoretical underpinning, "learned helplessness."

alex-karp.title: In-Q-Tel
alex-karp.summary: The CIA's openly acknowledged venture capital arm; provided Palantir Technologies its first $1.5 million in seed funding; in John Kiriakou's account the principal vehicle by which the agency finances private-sector development of technologies it intends to use.

alex-karp.title: Palantir Technologies
alex-karp.summary: U.S. data-analytics and intelligence-software company; received its first $1.5 million in seed funding from the CIA's In-Q-Tel venture-capital arm around 2002; characterized by John Kiriakou as functionally inseparable from the CIA in 2025, drawing the majority of its revenue from agency contracts and operating across DARPA, NSA, and the broader U.S. national-security apparatus.

alex-karp.title: Peter Thiel
alex-karp.summary: U.S. venture capitalist; co-founder of Palantir Technologies; subject of a biographical assessment commissioned from John Kiriakou by an unnamed interest group alongside Palantir CEO Alex Karp.

alex-karp.title: Arrais Corporation
alex-karp.summary: Private intelligence firm; companion entity to The Analysis Corporation; originally an LLC pass-through for retired Senior Intelligence Service personnel from the CIA's operations side; subsequently acquired by IBM for over $1 billion.

alex-karp.title: CIA National Resources Division
alex-karp.summary: The Central Intelligence Agency's domestic intelligence-collection arm, created in the 1980s by Director William J. Casey

alex-karp.title: Balochistan drone base
alex-karp.summary: Secret CIA drone surveillance base in southwestern Pakistan's Balochistan region; its location was inadvertently disclosed when investigative journalist Jason Leopold filed a Freedom of Information Act request for Pentagon aviation-fuel-delivery records and identified an outsized fuel flow to the otherwise-undocumented base.

alex-padilla.title: AIPAC
alex-padilla.summary: The American Israel Public Affairs Committee — the U.S. political organization that, in John Kiriakou's framing, ought to be registered as a foreign-lobbying entity but is not, and that wields decisive electoral power against U.S. elected officials who express support for Palestinian human rights.

alex-padilla.title: Donald Trump
alex-padilla.summary: 45th and 47th U.S. president. Per John Kiriakou, a man genuinely convinced he was doing right by bombing Iran, "duped" by the same Netanyahu nuclear bluff Obama once rejected — and, at the same time, the most blindly pro-Israel president in history, an admirer of autocrats who has never once criticized Vladimir Putin, and prone to gestures — from the Gulf of America to a since-abandoned "Department of War" rename — that test the edges of his actual authority.

alex-padilla.title: Giuliani Pardon Solicitation
alex-padilla.summary: Per John Kiriakou, a meeting at the Trump International Hotel in Washington in which Rudy Giuliani's associate solicited $2 million in exchange for a presidential pardon — a story that subsequently appeared as a front-page New York Times article. Giuliani publicly denied ever meeting Kiriakou; Kiriakou sent the Times the photograph taken at the meeting that morning, and the paper published the story with the note that it had seen documentary proof.

alex-padilla.title: Henry Kissinger
alex-padilla.summary: The former secretary of state John Kiriakou calls the biggest living war criminal — "the butcher of Cyprus, the butcher of Chile" — and blames, via the declassified record, for keeping the Greek junta in power. Kiriakou met him once as a new CIA officer, jokes that your natural impulse on meeting him "should be to become involuntarily violent," and marvels that both parties treat him as a foreign policy god. Yet he concedes the dark craftsman his due: Kissinger had goals, realpolitik was real, and it was Kissinger who got Nixon to China.

alex-padilla.title: Iran 12-Day War
alex-padilla.summary: 2025 Israeli air campaign against Iran during which Israel killed at least fourteen Iranian nuclear scientists by destroying the apartment buildings they lived in; preceded for each scientist by Farsi-language telephone calls from Iranian-Jewish Mossad and Shin Bet officers offering defection in lieu of certain death; characterized by John Kiriakou as a categorical departure from CIA targeting doctrine in its acceptable-civilian-casualty calculus.

alex-padilla.title: Iran Nuclear Assessment
alex-padilla.summary: Per John Kiriakou's assessment, the US–Israeli military campaign against Iran was a war of choice driven by Israeli political pressure rather than genuine intelligence indicating an Iranian nuclear weapons threat. The CIA produced two National Intelligence Estimates concluding Iran had no nuclear weapons program; Supreme Leader Ayatollah Khamenei issued a fatwa in the 1980s forbidding such a program. The U.S. went to war anyway, in Kiriakou's view, after President Trump replaced the Joint Chiefs of Staff with officers willing to accept Israeli intelligence and proceed.

alex-station.title: Galls.com sponsor story
alex-station.summary: John Kiriakou's account of outfitting the CIA's post-9/11 Islamabad station for terrorist-safe-house raids by ordering roughly $50,000 of tactical gear from the law-enforcement retailer galls.com on his CIA credit card, shipped to Pakistan via State Department diplomatic pouch in under a week — a story he now retells as an ad-read for the retailer, which sponsors one of his podcast appearances.

alex-station.title: Khobar Towers bombing
alex-station.summary: June 25, 1996 truck bombing of a U.S. military housing complex in Khobar, Saudi Arabia, that killed 19 U.S. Air Force personnel. John Kiriakou, then a CIA officer living across the water in Bahrain, felt the blast shatter his own windows and drove to the scene the next morning. He says the U.S. government worked hard to blame Iran and a small Saudi Hezbollah cell with no evidence, when the attack was in fact carried out by a radical Saudi group — a predecessor of al-Qaeda, which took credit for it.

alex-station.title: Mir Aimal Kansi CIA headquarters attack
alex-station.summary: The 1993 shooting outside CIA headquarters by Pakistani gunman Mir Aimal Kansi, who killed two and wounded seven CIA-bound commuters before fleeing to Pakistan; per John Kiriakou, the CIA located Kansi months later but had to hand the arrest to the FBI, and the resulting "how the FBI got their man" Time magazine cover so enraged senior CIA officers that it shaped the agency's insistence on going it alone against al-Qaeda after 9/11.

alex-station.title: "Kill them all"
alex-station.summary: The one-line departure hug John Kiriakou says he got from his own CIA boss, an elegant, thousand-dollar-suit man he calls John, whom he had joked belonged in the State Department, on the day Kiriakou left Washington to become chief of counterterrorism operations in Pakistan after 9/11. Kiriakou uses it as the compressed summary of the mood inside the building he was leaving behind.

alex-station.title: Ruby Ridge
alex-station.summary: 1992 federal standoff in Idaho involving Randy Weaver, triggered by an allegation that Weaver had sold a shotgun with a barrel two inches shorter than the legal minimum; per John Kiriakou, FBI sniper Lon Horiuchi shot and killed Weaver's wife while she was holding her baby, and Horiuchi was never punished. Kiriakou describes Ruby Ridge as one of the events that, after his own imprisonment, caused him to fundamentally reassess his earlier acceptance of the official government account.

alex-station.title: Waco Siege
alex-station.summary: 1993 federal operation against the Branch Davidian compound near Waco, Texas, led by David Koresh, resulting in the deaths of more than twenty-seven people — more than half of them children. Per John Kiriakou, a CIA colleague's reaction upon hearing the news was 'It's about time.' Kiriakou describes this as the kind of response he once might have shared, but which his later experiences with government abuse of power caused him to revisit.

alexa.title: Brett McGurk
alexa.summary: Senior U.S. diplomat; John Kiriakou cites reporting that McGurk was caught in a sexual encounter atop a U.S. embassy while overseeing the campaign against ISIS, offering it as an example of the adultery culture he considers a security risk.

alexa.title: LSD Mind Manipulation
alexa.summary: Kiriakou on the CIA dosing unwitting men with LSD in safe houses, using sex workers as bait, to find out whether the drug could unlock secrets.

alexa.title: OnlyFans
alexa.summary: Per John Kiriakou, the man who owned OnlyFans — whom he describes as Ukrainian-American rather than Israeli — was a major donor and strong supporter of Israel, part of a broader claim Kiriakou makes about Israeli involvement in the porn industry.

alexa.title: Trump Dni Replacement
alexa.summary: Trump privately asked cabinet members about replacing his Director of National Intelligence, frustrated that the DNI had protected Joe Kent.

alexa.title: FBI manufactured terrorism cases
alexa.summary: John Kiriakou's account of terrorism prosecutions in which the FBI supplies the plot, the target, the explosives and the transport, then arrests the person it recruited. His central case is the 2026 Miami trial of a mentally ill homeless man facing six counts each carrying life without parole, in which Kiriakou testified for the defence and told the court that the FBI was "clearly the criminal in this case." The defendant was acquitted on every count.

alexa.title: Podcast Bros
alexa.summary: Per Sohrab Ahmari, speaking on the same Megyn Kelly panel as Kiriakou, podcast bros.

alexander-acosta.title: Prince Andrew
alexander-acosta.summary: British royal, now Andrew Mountbatten Windsor, named repeatedly by John Kiriakou as one of the un-recruitable principals whose access made Jeffrey Epstein valuable to a foreign intelligence service. Kiriakou has asked why Andrew was never charged over conduct with minors, reads his alleged provision of classified Ministry of Defence documents to Epstein as evidence of espionage rather than vanity — and expects him to face no criminal consequence at all, because the statute of limitations has run.

alexander-acosta.title: David Boies
alexander-acosta.summary: The American litigator John Kiriakou has appeared alongside on Piers Morgan's programme, and whose observation about Alan Dershowitz — that he was not merely Epstein's attorney but his publicist — Kiriakou treats as the key distinction in the case.

alexander-acosta.title: The Epstein statute of limitations
alexander-acosta.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that nobody in the United States will be prosecuted over the Jeffrey Epstein case because the limitation period on the sex offences has run — a lapse he says may itself have been part of the plan, which leaves victims with civil suits against the estate, leaves the men named to social ruin rather than trial, and leaves only an improbable continuing-conspiracy theory as a route to criminal charges.

alexander-acosta.title: Jeffrey Epstein
alexander-acosta.summary: Convicted sex offender; per John Kiriakou, was "an Israeli access agent" rather than a CIA asset, because the CIA collects foreign intelligence and Epstein's targets — Bill Clinton, Bill Gates, Prince Andrew — were not foreign. Kiriakou further holds that Epstein did die by suicide in federal custody, because in the Bureau of Prisons the cameras never work and the guards are always asleep.

alexander-acosta.title: Alan Dershowitz
alexander-acosta.summary: American attorney and Harvard Law professor; John Kiriakou describes debating him on Piers Morgan's show over Jeffrey Epstein, telling Dershowitz he would have wanted to see him "hanging from a tree" had he sought leniency for Epstein as an Israeli spy — and cites attorney David Boies's on-air statement that Dershowitz was far more than Epstein's lawyer, also serving as his publicist, friend, and a guest on Epstein's island.

alexander-acosta.title: Epstein Files Transparency Act
alexander-acosta.summary: The law compelling the Justice Department to release the Epstein files by a fixed deadline, passed 419 to 1 in the House and 99 to nothing in the Senate and then, in John Kiriakou's account, simply not complied with.

alfreda-bikowsky.title: Cofer Black's warning to the liaison class
alfreda-bikowsky.summary: The briefing Cofer Black gave to a class of visiting foreign liaison officers weeks before 11 September 2001 — code words about a honey salesman, a great football match and an enormous wedding — and the private exchange afterwards in which he told John Kiriakou he had been deadly serious.

alfreda-bikowsky.title: Jennifer Matthews
alfreda-bikowsky.summary: CIA analyst who was made chief of base at Khost, Afghanistan without operational or security training in order to complete the tour requirement for promotion, and who was killed there with six other officers by a Jordanian double agent she had gone outside the fortified perimeter to greet with a birthday cake.

alfreda-bikowsky.title: Kiriakou's transfer to the Directorate of Operations
alfreda-bikowsky.summary: John Kiriakou's roughly two-month internal campaign to transfer from the CIA's analytic Directorate of Intelligence to the operational Directorate of Operations, overcoming what he calls a "natural bias in operations against the eggheads on the analytic side," followed by an Athens posting secured because he was the only person in the entire CIA fluent in both Greek and Arabic. Covers his full CIA career arc from 1988/1990 recruitment through analyst years on Iraq, the switch to operations, 9/11, the enhanced-interrogation refusal, executive assistant to the deputy director for operations, and his eventual resignation and post-CIA career.

alfreda-bikowsky.title: Alex Station
alfreda-bikowsky.summary: CIA unit that tracked Osama bin Laden beginning in 1995; per John Kiriakou, who served as chief of its counterintelligence branch, the unit kept extremely tight security around its files, limited FBI investigators' access to information about future 9/11 hijackers Khaled al-Mihdhar and Nawaf al-Hazmi, and — under a deliberate policy of non-cooperation with the FBI — failed to watchlist participants in the Malaysia summit where al-Qaeda planned the attacks.

alfreda-bikowsky.title: Mike Scheuer
alfreda-bikowsky.summary: Founder and chief of "Alec Station", the CIA unit dedicated to tracking Osama bin Laden in the years before September 11, 2001; per John Kiriakou — alongside his New York FBI counterpart John O'Neill — "100 percent correct" about bin Laden, and uniformly hated for it inside the agency.

alfreda-bikowsky.title: Zawahiri assassination
alfreda-bikowsky.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the drone strike that killed al-Qaeda's Ayman al-Zawahiri — using a bladed, warhead-less missile fired as he stepped onto a balcony to smoke, deliberately chosen to avoid killing the women and children inside.

ali-abdullah-saleh.title: Houthis
ali-abdullah-saleh.summary: The Iran-aligned movement that controls the most important parts of Yemen, described by John Kiriakou as fierce fighters who beat the Saudi military over a decade of war and who in July 2026 declared a naval blockade of Saudi shipping.

ali-abdullah-saleh.title: Yemen
ali-abdullah-saleh.summary: Country on the southern Arabian Peninsula; setting of five John Kiriakou trips between 1990 and approximately 2010, spanning the country's brief unification, its civil war, and its present condition as a high-threat operating environment for U.S. and allied diplomatic personnel.

ali-abdullah-saleh.title: Bab al-Mandab
ali-abdullah-saleh.summary: The strait where the Horn of Africa nearly meets the south-western tip of the Arabian Peninsula, which John Kiriakou identifies as one of the few American national interests in Yemen and as a chokepoint whose closure would push the global economy into recession.

ali-abdullah-saleh.title: John Kiriakou
ali-abdullah-saleh.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

ali-abdullah-saleh.title: Dead Drop (podcast)
ali-abdullah-saleh.summary: John Kiriakou''s narrative podcast, launched in late 2025 — a season-long, memoir-style retelling of his life in intelligence, from recruitment ("The New Recruit") through Athens ("Golden Boy") to the post-9/11 hunt ("The Hunt Begins"), with mini-episodes like "A Spy''s Guide to Sofia." Written by Kiriakou with Alan Katz, produced by Costard & Touchstone Productions, with Kiriakou, Katz, and Nick Mechanic as executive producers. Its stated goal: "the deepest possible perspective on the world of spying and what makes any spy tick."

ali-abdullah-saleh.title: John Kerry
ali-abdullah-saleh.summary: U.S. Senator from Massachusetts; chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee during John Kiriakou's 2009 service as the committee's senior investigator; subsequently U.S. Secretary of State; characterized by Kiriakou as a coward who buckled under CIA pressure on the Dasht-i-Leili reopening and as personally fixated on his perceived theft of the Secretary of State position by Hillary Clinton; the famously thrown medals were duplicates purchased at the post exchange.

ali-from-newark.title: Kiriakou on animated television
ali-from-newark.summary: John Kiriakou's stated taste in television cartoons — South Park, Family Guy, The Simpsons and Bob's Burgers — his judgement that South Park is by far the most cutting edge of them, and the episodes he thought worth buying outright.

ali-from-newark.title: The Brennan felony referral
ali-from-newark.summary: John Kiriakou's July 2025 report, sourced to Matt Taibbe, that the Justice Department was moving beyond referred misdemeanour charges against John Brennan and James Comey for allegedly lying to Congress and was actively pursuing felony conspiracy charges against at least Brennan — a prospect Kiriakou said he would attend the trial of every single day.

ali-from-newark.title: The homelessness executive order
ali-from-newark.summary: Donald Trump's July 2025 executive order on homelessness, which John Kiriakou criticised on the ground that it understates the population by two thirds and proposes forcible commitment to facilities that do not exist — while conceding that Trump diagnoses the problem better than his predecessors did.

ali-from-newark.title: The Macron defamation suit
ali-from-newark.summary: The Macrons' libel action against Candace Owens over her claim that Brigitte Macron was born male, which John Kiriakou discussed as a question of venue — and which prompted him to say he wished he had sued the Los Angeles Times in England when he had the chance.

ali-from-newark.title: The mental health parity gap
ali-from-newark.summary: John Kiriakou's account of American mental health provision — parity written into the Affordable Care Act and entirely unenforced, more mentally ill people in most county jails than in the mental hospitals, and his condition that nobody should be forced into treatment until the treatment is worth being forced into.

ali-from-newark.title: The Bureau of Prisons polos
ali-from-newark.summary: What John Kiriakou says he saw on the morning of 6 January 2021 while parking on Capitol Hill for a meeting with his attorney Bruce Fein — a group of men stripping off Bureau of Prisons logo polo shirts and pulling on black ones — and the sentence he says he shouted at them.

ali-hassan-al-majid.title: Saddam Hussein
ali-hassan-al-majid.summary: President of Iraq from 1979 until the 2003 U.S. invasion; subject of John Kiriakou's CIA portfolio from January 1990 onward, in which capacity Kiriakou became, at age 25, "Saddam Hussein's intelligence community biographer" and the analyst who briefed President George H. W. Bush in the Oval Office on the morning of the 1990 invasion of Kuwait.

ali-hassan-al-majid.title: Ahmed Chalabi
ali-hassan-al-majid.summary: Iraqi exile and founder of the Iraqi National Congress; per John Kiriakou, a Shia-Kurdish con man who looted Petra Bank in Jordan of $36 million in the 1980s, was sentenced to death in absentia, was pardoned at CIA request, then pocketed $6 million in CIA seed funding for the INC and bought a Mayfair house in cash; later resurrected by Dick Cheney to feed the Pentagon fabricated WMD intelligence used to justify the 2003 invasion of Iraq.

ali-hassan-al-majid.title: Iraqi invasion of Kuwait
ali-hassan-al-majid.summary: John Kiriakou''s most detailed account of the intelligence process around the 1990 Iraqi invasion of Kuwait and its 1991 liberation. As a first-year CIA analyst on a ''training account'' covering Iraq, Kiriakou produced the June 30, 1990 warning paper for the White House; suggested calling the US Defense Attaché in Baghdad to drive to the border and report what he saw (the answer: ''Literally the entire Iraqi military is heading south''); briefed the August 2 Oval Office meeting with Bush; and later took a single phone call from General Colin Powell that led, eight hours later, to 47 cruise missiles striking the Iraqi Intelligence Service headquarters in Baghdad.

ali-hassan-al-majid.title: Uday Hussein
ali-hassan-al-majid.summary: Eldest son of Saddam Hussein; described by John Kiriakou as so dangerous a successor-in-waiting that Saddam's two sons-in-law — Hussein Kamel and Saddam Kamel — defected to Jordan in January 1993 specifically out of fear of him.

ali-hassan-al-majid.title: CIA cable priority levels
ali-hassan-al-majid.summary: The five levels of immediacy assigned to U.S. government cable traffic, as described by John Kiriakou. From lowest to highest: Routine, Priority, Immediate, Flash, CRITIC. Most career officers will never see a CRITIC; during the Gulf War, Kiriakou''s desk was receiving multiple CRITICs a day, each one announcing a hostile missile launch.

ali-hassan-al-majid.title: George Habash
ali-hassan-al-majid.summary: Co-founder of the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine; as a young Lebanese medical student he was the college roommate at the American University of Beirut of Ahmed Khatib, the doctor whom Iraq installed as occupation governor of Kuwait on August 2, 1990 — a connection John Kiriakou carried into the Oval Office that day.

ali-mohamed.title: Alex Station
ali-mohamed.summary: CIA unit that tracked Osama bin Laden beginning in 1995; per John Kiriakou, who served as chief of its counterintelligence branch, the unit kept extremely tight security around its files, limited FBI investigators' access to information about future 9/11 hijackers Khaled al-Mihdhar and Nawaf al-Hazmi, and — under a deliberate policy of non-cooperation with the FBI — failed to watchlist participants in the Malaysia summit where al-Qaeda planned the attacks.

ali-mohamed.title: 9/11 attribution of responsibility
ali-mohamed.summary: John Kiriakou's evolving view of who bears ultimate responsibility for the September 11 attacks — that al-Qaeda carried them out but was, in his current view, "allowed" to, amid a distracted Bush administration, an uninvestigated Saudi government, and an Israeli government he believes had a vested interest in the attacks proceeding.

ali-mohamed.title: Mir Aimal Kansi CIA headquarters attack
ali-mohamed.summary: The 1993 shooting outside CIA headquarters by Pakistani gunman Mir Aimal Kansi, who killed two and wounded seven CIA-bound commuters before fleeing to Pakistan; per John Kiriakou, the CIA located Kansi months later but had to hand the arrest to the FBI, and the resulting "how the FBI got their man" Time magazine cover so enraged senior CIA officers that it shaped the agency's insistence on going it alone against al-Qaeda after 9/11.

ali-mohamed.title: Israeli art student spy ring
ali-mohamed.summary: A spring 2001 U.S. counterintelligence report on so-called "Israeli art students" who used counterfeit visas to try to access federal buildings and military sites, some living on the same Hollywood, Florida block as 9/11 hijacker Mohamed Atta; per John Kiriakou, the "dancing Israelis" stopped by NYPD in a white panel van on 9/11 were part of the same espionage effort and were released back to Israel rather than prosecuted.

ali-mohamed.title: Office of Special Plans Israeli leak
ali-mohamed.summary: A major Israeli spy operation John Kiriakou says was uncovered in the 2000s involving a leak from the Pentagon's Office of Special Plans, headed by Paul Wolfowitz and Douglas Feith — both authors, with Richard Perle, of the "Clean Break" report advocating a dual-containment strategy against Iraq and Iran on behalf of Benjamin Netanyahu. Per Kiriakou, Wolfowitz and Feith did not merely fail to take Israeli counterintelligence seriously; he believes they actively helped abet it.

ali-mohamed.title: Operation Mega
ali-mohamed.summary: A 1997 FBI investigation into a senior U.S. government official believed to be passing highly sensitive information to Israel, opened after the NSA intercepted an Israeli intelligence communication referring to a source code-named "Mega." Per John Kiriakou, unlike similar investigations into other countries, the case never resulted in an indictment or public disclosure, and the identity of the American official was never revealed.

ali-soufan.title: Abu Zubaydah
ali-soufan.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

ali-soufan.title: The cremation footnote
ali-soufan.summary: A footnote John Kiriakou cites from the declassified executive summary of the Senate torture report, stating that Abu Zubaydah will never be permitted to leave Guantanamo — despite never having joined al-Qaeda, never having pledged fealty to Osama bin Laden and never having been charged — and that on his death the CIA will cremate his body and scatter the ashes at sea.

ali-soufan.title: Khobar Towers bombing
ali-soufan.summary: June 25, 1996 truck bombing of a U.S. military housing complex in Khobar, Saudi Arabia, that killed 19 U.S. Air Force personnel. John Kiriakou, then a CIA officer living across the water in Bahrain, felt the blast shatter his own windows and drove to the scene the next morning. He says the U.S. government worked hard to blame Iran and a small Saudi Hezbollah cell with no evidence, when the attack was in fact carried out by a radical Saudi group — a predecessor of al-Qaeda, which took credit for it.

ali-soufan.title: "I''m a non-person"
ali-soufan.summary: The phrase John Kiriakou uses for his standing after prison: a former colleague was sent to deliver congratulations from a mutual friend who had risen to a senior administration post, together with the message that he could never speak to Kiriakou again. Kiriakou pairs it with the loss of his federal pension after nineteen and a half years of service, and with the fact that in eight years no other CIA officer joined him in speaking publicly.

ali-soufan.title: Eric Holder
ali-soufan.summary: Attorney General of the United States under Barack Obama, and the head of the Justice Department that reopened and then brought the 2012 prosecution of John Kiriakou. In Kiriakou's account Holder personally doubted that the espionage charge was sound, told John Brennan so in writing, and signed off on it anyway.

ali-soufan.title: John O'Neill
ali-soufan.summary: Special Agent in Charge of the FBI's New York field office for counterterrorism; "brash, flawed" but, per John Kiriakou, "spot-on about Osama bin Laden — 100 percent correct." Mentored FBI Arabic translator Ali Soufan. The principal subject of Lawrence Wright's book The Looming Tower.

all-it-takes-is-a-signature.title: The Epstein statute of limitations
all-it-takes-is-a-signature.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that nobody in the United States will be prosecuted over the Jeffrey Epstein case because the limitation period on the sex offences has run — a lapse he says may itself have been part of the plan, which leaves victims with civil suits against the estate, leaves the men named to social ruin rather than trial, and leaves only an improbable continuing-conspiracy theory as a route to criminal charges.

all-it-takes-is-a-signature.title: Prince Andrew
all-it-takes-is-a-signature.summary: British royal, now Andrew Mountbatten Windsor, named repeatedly by John Kiriakou as one of the un-recruitable principals whose access made Jeffrey Epstein valuable to a foreign intelligence service. Kiriakou has asked why Andrew was never charged over conduct with minors, reads his alleged provision of classified Ministry of Defence documents to Epstein as evidence of espionage rather than vanity — and expects him to face no criminal consequence at all, because the statute of limitations has run.

all-it-takes-is-a-signature.title: Freedom of Information Act
all-it-takes-is-a-signature.summary: The U.S. transparency law that runs through John Kiriakou's story from every direction — his plea agreement banned him from ever filing a FOIA request on himself, so he filed one with the Bureau of Prisons anyway and got back pages stamped "FOIA EXEMPT — DO NOT RELEASE TO INMATE"; a FOIA request exposed the prison commissary skim; Jason Leopold's requests revealed that a detainee's eye was removed under sedation without his knowledge and that NBC's Ken Dilanian sent his stories to the CIA before his own editor; and a FOIA request is how Kiriakou learned Gary Johnson had quietly lobbied for his early release.

all-it-takes-is-a-signature.title: Jeffrey Epstein
all-it-takes-is-a-signature.summary: Convicted sex offender; per John Kiriakou, was "an Israeli access agent" rather than a CIA asset, because the CIA collects foreign intelligence and Epstein's targets — Bill Clinton, Bill Gates, Prince Andrew — were not foreign. Kiriakou further holds that Epstein did die by suicide in federal custody, because in the Bureau of Prisons the cameras never work and the guards are always asleep.

all-it-takes-is-a-signature.title: Senate Foreign Relations Committee
all-it-takes-is-a-signature.summary: Kiriakou was senior investigator under John Kerry — and still held the post when his own federal prosecution came to a head in January 2012.

all-it-takes-is-a-signature.title: The North Korea SEAL Team Six operation
all-it-takes-is-a-signature.summary: The 2018 mission in which American special forces attempted to plant an eavesdropping device on North Korean soil, killed a boatload of fishermen and withdrew without planting it — which John Kiriakou uses to call Donald Trump a liar, because such an operation requires the president's signature on a finding, and to note that Congress was never told.

allen-dulles.title: Presidents and the CIA
allen-dulles.summary: John Kiriakou's observation that some presidents actively lead the CIA while others are led around by it — citing George H.W. Bush's ongoing "love affair" with the agency after his 11-month stint as director, and Richard Nixon's close relationship with the CIA, which Kiriakou says was one of the things that brought down his presidency.

allen-dulles.title: Ruby Ridge
allen-dulles.summary: 1992 federal standoff in Idaho involving Randy Weaver, triggered by an allegation that Weaver had sold a shotgun with a barrel two inches shorter than the legal minimum; per John Kiriakou, FBI sniper Lon Horiuchi shot and killed Weaver's wife while she was holding her baby, and Horiuchi was never punished. Kiriakou describes Ruby Ridge as one of the events that, after his own imprisonment, caused him to fundamentally reassess his earlier acceptance of the official government account.

allen-dulles.title: The four-question torture exam
allen-dulles.summary: A final examination set by a former CIA officer teaching alongside John Kiriakou at Liberty University, consisting of four escalating questions about whether the student would torture — the terrorist, then his wife in front of him, then their children — with the last question asking the student to justify the previous three answers to God. Kiriakou describes it as the most powerful exam he has ever seen.

allen-dulles.title: Waco Siege
allen-dulles.summary: 1993 federal operation against the Branch Davidian compound near Waco, Texas, led by David Koresh, resulting in the deaths of more than twenty-seven people — more than half of them children. Per John Kiriakou, a CIA colleague's reaction upon hearing the news was 'It's about time.' Kiriakou describes this as the kind of response he once might have shared, but which his later experiences with government abuse of power caused him to revisit.

allen-dulles.title: Kiriakou's volunteer trip to Guatemala
allen-dulles.summary: A visit John Kiriakou made to Guatemala to volunteer for a couple of weeks at an orphanage, which he recounts as the closing evidence in his argument about the 1954 coup: the orphanage was ringed by a twenty-foot concrete wall, and he could barely sleep for the gunfire outside.

allen-dulles.title: Operation Paperclip
allen-dulles.summary: The program by which the CIA's predecessor brought Nazi scientists to the United States after World War II; John Kiriakou notes the FBI opposed it, that the Nazis surrendered to the U.S. fearing the Soviets, and that V-2 rocket father Wernher von Braun is buried near his home in Virginia.

amaryllis-fox-kennedy.title: Oman
amaryllis-fox-kennedy.summary: The Gulf sultanate John Kiriakou singles out as America's most durable friend in the region and its most useful channel to Iran — a country that has acted as go-between for Washington and Tehran many times, and which he argues should be approached again in place of carrier deployments and public threats.

amaryllis-fox-kennedy.title: Sharia law
amaryllis-fox-kennedy.summary: Islamic jurisprudence. Challenged by a viewer who equated it with executions of gay people, forced child marriage and the criminalisation of apostasy, John Kiriakou answers that those acts are largely the work of ISIS rather than of any government, and that Sharia is in substance a body of civil law covering inheritance, insurance, education, property ownership and commercial disputes.

amaryllis-fox-kennedy.title: The botched pitch
amaryllis-fox-kennedy.summary: The one operation John Kiriakou describes as a failure of his career: a two-year development of a terrorist working under journalist cover, brought to the point of a recruitment pitch and destroyed at the table when his station chief seized the meeting and threatened the target instead of pitching him. The target fled screaming for police, the host government''s deputy prime minister complained to the American ambassador, and the man later described the encounter to a third intelligence service as an approach by "two caricatures of CIA men."

amaryllis-fox-kennedy.title: Wealth concentration
amaryllis-fox-kennedy.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that the present distribution of wealth is historically unprecedented and politically unsustainable — that trillionaires have never existed before, that five men hold as much as the bottom eighty per cent of the world, and that a defence budget approaching $1.5 trillion cannot be reconciled with the social spending it would have to displace.

amaryllis-fox-kennedy.title: Flock cameras
amaryllis-fox-kennedy.summary: Automated licence-plate reading cameras mounted on police vehicles and on poles disguised as utility poles. John Kiriakou describes them as blanket, constant surveillance and a direct assault on civil liberties, more dangerous than the public realises, and says they are the point at which Edward Snowden's predictions have already come true.

amaryllis-fox-kennedy.title: Seyyed Hossein Nasr
amaryllis-fox-kennedy.summary: The scholar of Islamic philosophy under whom John Kiriakou studied Shiism as an undergraduate. Kiriakou calls him probably the most important Shia Muslim scholar in the world, notes that he is the father of Vali Nasr, and remarks that at ninety-eight he is still teaching.

american-media-consolidation.title: The CIA and Hollywood
american-media-consolidation.summary: The CIA''s standing arrangement with the film industry, as John Kiriakou describes it: a branch inside the Office of Public Affairs whose only job is to cooperate with Hollywood studios, on the model the FBI has run since the 1950s, so that what comes out of Hollywood carries a pro-agency message. Kiriakou notes it is technically illegal for the CIA to propagandise the American public and says that is exactly what happens every time an agency-linked film is released.

american-media-consolidation.title: CIA media relations
american-media-consolidation.summary: John Kiriakou's account of how the CIA shapes press coverage in the 2020s without needing an Operation Mockingbird-style infiltration program — because corporate media now recites CIA messaging willingly, most journalists simply rewrite emailed statements from the agency's Office of Public Affairs, and the CIA allegedly manipulates algorithms and backs podcasts to spread its point of view.

american-media-consolidation.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
american-media-consolidation.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

american-media-consolidation.title: Jeffrey Epstein
american-media-consolidation.summary: Convicted sex offender; per John Kiriakou, was "an Israeli access agent" rather than a CIA asset, because the CIA collects foreign intelligence and Epstein's targets — Bill Clinton, Bill Gates, Prince Andrew — were not foreign. Kiriakou further holds that Epstein did die by suicide in federal custody, because in the Bureau of Prisons the cameras never work and the guards are always asleep.

american-media-consolidation.title: John Brennan
american-media-consolidation.summary: Former Director of the CIA; characterized in KiriPedia's source corpus as the principal architect of the agency's enhanced interrogation program and as having plotted against an elected President

american-media-consolidation.title: The KGB denial cables
american-media-consolidation.summary: Two occasions on which, according to John Kiriakou, the first message the CIA received after an American killing came from the KGB and said the same thing: we promise it wasn''t us. One followed the assassination of Athens station chief Richard Welch in December 1975, the other the killing of President Kennedy in November 1963. Kiriakou treats them as evidence of a standing gentleman''s agreement between the two services not to touch each other''s people — one he expects to hold even where Russian troops overrun CIA bases.

american-missile-stockpiles.title: The Iron Dome
american-missile-stockpiles.summary: Israel's air-defence system as John Kiriakou reads it — impressive against a wave of slow Iranian drones, but shown by the handful that got through, and later by Iranian ballistic missiles, to be not all it is cracked up to be; each exchange, in his account, buying Iran intelligence about the gaps.

american-missile-stockpiles.title: Strategic patience
american-missile-stockpiles.summary: The doctrine John Kiriakou uses to describe a state that absorbs an attack and answers with a response calibrated to be smaller than the provocation — Iran's telegraphed drone waves against Israel, and India's refusal to escalate against Pakistan, which he says kept a war from becoming a nuclear one.

american-missile-stockpiles.title: The Pentagon's congressional district strategy
american-missile-stockpiles.summary: The practice John Kiriakou describes of placing defence manufacturing orders in effectively all 435 congressional districts, so that every member of Congress has constituents dependent on the defence budget — and nobody has an incentive to vote against it.

american-missile-stockpiles.title: The Litani River
american-missile-stockpiles.summary: The largest natural water source in the Middle East, which John Kiriakou says makes southern Lebanon more valuable than oil — and the northern edge of the depopulated strip he describes Israel creating there.

american-missile-stockpiles.title: The AI he uses
american-missile-stockpiles.summary: Asked which AI tool he uses and why, John Kiriakou named Perplexity over ChatGPT, on two grounds: ChatGPT invents things about him, and Perplexity — for reasons he says he does not fully understand — returns much deeper analysis when he asks it to look at something.

american-missile-stockpiles.title: U.S. diplomatic vacancies
american-missile-stockpiles.summary: John Kiriakou's account of how the mass dismissal of career U.S. ambassadors — never replaced — left the Gulf without American envoys as war with Iran loomed, so allied royals had to ask him personally whether the U.S. would attack.

american-psychological-association.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
american-psychological-association.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

american-psychological-association.title: Cold cell
american-psychological-association.summary: A CIA interrogation technique in which a stripped detainee is chained to a ceiling eyebolt in a cell chilled to 50°F, then doused with a bucket of ice water at hourly intervals; never authorized; documented to have killed at least two prisoners.

american-psychological-association.title: Waterboarding
american-psychological-association.summary: Torture technique in which a prisoner is restrained on an inclined board with the head lower than the feet, a cloth placed over the face, and water poured continuously over it to simulate drowning. Per John Kiriakou, waterboarding was treated as a criminal act under U.S. and international law for decades before 2002 — including a post–World War II execution of Japanese soldiers who waterboarded American POWs, and a 1968 court-martial of a U.S. soldier photographed waterboarding a North Vietnamese prisoner — before the CIA reauthorized it after September 11. Abu Zubaydah was waterboarded 83 times; Khalid Sheikh Mohammed 187 times.

american-psychological-association.title: PTSD
american-psychological-association.summary: Post-traumatic stress disorder runs through John Kiriakou''s life and worldview — he had it coming out of Greece after an assassination attempt, brought it home from Pakistan alongside his shock at colleagues'' willingness to kill, and was blindsided by a delayed post-prison version that helped end his marriage. For six months after release he dreamed the same dream nightly: that he was out by mistake and had to get back inside before midnight count. He still takes a repurposed blood-pressure drug that stops the dreams, and he extends the diagnosis outward — to secret-site interrogators who came back crying, to drone pilots, and to prisoners released angry and untreated.

american-psychological-association.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
american-psychological-association.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

american-psychological-association.title: Abu Zubaydah
american-psychological-association.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

american-shoes.title: The declared officer
american-shoes.summary: The CIA officer whose identity is formally disclosed to the host country's intelligence service — as John Kiriakou was in Athens, taken by his chief within days of arrival to be introduced to the head of the Greek service.

american-shoes.title: Kiriakou's first recruitment
american-shoes.summary: How John Kiriakou made his first CIA recruitment in Athens: by combing 25-year-old Greek police files not for people who had talked but for people who had answered back, finding one such man in a communist neighbourhood coffee shop, and buying his telephone number from a waiter for the price of a fifty.

american-shoes.title: There is no such thing as bad food in Athens
american-shoes.summary: The lesson John Kiriakou says he learned at a lorry drivers' stop outside Corinth, where the food was as good as his grandmother's — reached on the three-and-a-half-hour drives he made to meet a source too sensitive to be met in Athens, with a vineyard tour as his cover story.

american-shoes.title: Kiriakou's Athens house
american-shoes.summary: The five-storey house in the northern Athens suburb of Kifissia that John Kiriakou found for himself after refusing the embassy's offer — no square rooms, a balcony off every one of them facing a different way, and a garden with a 200-year-old olive tree whose oil the family cooked with for two years.

american-shoes.title: The Snickers bar
american-shoes.summary: The ritual in John Kiriakou''s Athens station: when an officer made a recruitment, the boss announced it in the staff meeting, everyone applauded, and he threw the officer a Snickers bar.

american-shoes.title: The Athens carjacking
american-shoes.summary: The motorcyclist who followed John Kiriakou''s car through Athens two months into his posting — leading to a gun drawn on a ten-lane intersection, a shot fired, a disabled motorcycle, and a question asked back in Washington: *is John a hothead?*

americans-and-the-word-socialism.title: Mike Rogers
americans-and-the-word-socialism.summary: Former Republican congressman from Michigan and repeat Senate candidate, who lost narrowly in 2024 and ran again in 2026. John Kiriakou singles out his campaign advertisement calling Abdul El-Sayed a communist Trojan horse as an insult to the intelligence of Michigan voters.

americans-and-the-word-socialism.title: Michigan 2026 Democratic Senate primary
americans-and-the-word-socialism.summary: The contest between the AIPAC-backed Haley Stevens and the DSA-backed Abdul El-Sayed, which John Kiriakou calls one of the most fascinating races he has seen and reads as the first real failure of the electability argument establishment Democrats have relied on.

americans-and-the-word-socialism.title: The Greek health care system
americans-and-the-word-socialism.summary: John Kiriakou's description of Greek health care as a two-tier system in which the private sector buys nothing but position in the queue — a procedure that takes eleven or twelve months on the public system takes one or two privately, and the care itself is the same.

americans-and-the-word-socialism.title: Islamofascism
americans-and-the-word-socialism.summary: A term John Kiriakou says was introduced into American media around 2004 and 2005, was created by a public relations firm working for the Republican National Committee, was pushed hard into everyday usage, failed to catch on, and was quietly abandoned. He offers it as his clearest example of manufactured vocabulary intended as domestic propaganda.

americans-and-the-word-socialism.title: Kiriakou and third parties
americans-and-the-word-socialism.summary: John Kiriakou's advocacy for viable third parties, and his 2016 experience touring the West with Libertarian candidate Gary Johnson — including the disorganization that convinced him the party would never break through, epitomized by a colleague who ignored an airport page thinking it was 'NSA tracking my movements.'

americans-and-the-word-socialism.title: CIA Arabic hiring practices
americans-and-the-word-socialism.summary: John Kiriakou's account of how few CIA officers historically spoke Arabic — he was one of only two people in the entire agency fluent in both Greek and Arabic — and of how the agency's more recent pool of Arabic speakers, dominated by Arab Christian hires who clear background checks easily, often carries an innate anti-Muslim bias that limits their operational usefulness.

americans-who-tell-the-truth-portrait.title: Ralph Nader
americans-who-tell-the-truth-portrait.summary: American consumer advocate and perennial third-party presidential candidate. In January 2013 Nader co-signed a letter to the president asking for John Kiriakou to be pardoned; weeks later Kiriakou thanked him by name at his portrait unveiling as a steadfast supporter whose backing he described as humbling. Nader's 2000 independent run also anchors Kiriakou's account of how third-party candidates were shut out of the presidential debates.

americans-who-tell-the-truth-portrait.title: Heather Kiriakou
americans-who-tell-the-truth-portrait.summary: John Kiriakou's wife, a senior CIA analyst who — in his account — was one of the best analysts in the entire intelligence community and who lost her job at the agency for no reason other than being married to him. She sat off camera at his December 2007 ABC News interview and told him afterwards that he had said nothing classified.

americans-who-tell-the-truth-portrait.title: Government Accountability Project
americans-who-tell-the-truth-portrait.summary: The Washington whistleblower-advocacy law firm and NGO, known as GAP, whose attorney Jesselyn Radack took John Kiriakou's case after his 2012 arrest and told him he was a whistleblower whether he thought so or not.

americans-who-tell-the-truth-portrait.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
americans-who-tell-the-truth-portrait.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

americans-who-tell-the-truth-portrait.title: FCI Loretto
americans-who-tell-the-truth-portrait.summary: U.S. Federal Correctional Institution in Loretto, Pennsylvania; the low-medium-security prison at which John Kiriakou served 23 months of a 30-month sentence following his 2013 Espionage Act–era plea deal; the originally ordered "minimum security work camp" placement was countermanded — per Kiriakou, on Brennan's direct intervention — to place him in the actual prison alongside the general population.

americans-who-tell-the-truth-portrait.title: Jesselyn Radack
americans-who-tell-the-truth-portrait.summary: American national-security attorney and former Justice Department ethics official who directs the whistleblower-defense practice at the Government Accountability Project. Per John Kiriakou, Radack was herself driven out of the Justice Department, had her law license threatened, and was placed on the no-fly list after blowing the whistle in the John Walker Lindh case; she went on to represent Kiriakou after his 2012 arrest and, separately, helped connect him to a path to reach Edward Snowden in 2013.

amir.title: Faisalabad
amir.summary: The Pakistani textile city of some seven or eight million people where Abu Zubaydah was captured in March 2002 — concrete, mud and corrugated tin in John Kiriakou's description, with a brand-new glass-and-steel McDonald's standing in the middle of it.

amir.title: The Lahore safe house
amir.summary: The ten-bedroom house in the best neighbourhood of Lahore that the CIA bought outright for two million dollars in cash in March 2002, on a cover story invented on the spot — that its buyers were textile barons — and from whose roof the team could catch seven satellites.

amir.title: Navigating Pakistan without maps
amir.summary: The logistical problem John Kiriakou says nearly undid the Abu Zubaydah operation: in 2002 Pakistan had no maps to buy, no street signs and no addresses, so the CIA team navigated a city of twelve million by shoe advertisement, traffic policeman, British school and McDonald''s — rehearsing the route twice in the small hours before the raids.

amir.title: Site 13
amir.summary: The house in Faisalabad, nearest of the thirteen targets to the CIA safe house, where Abu Zubaydah was shot at two o'clock in the morning on the night of the raids — announced to John Kiriakou on the roof a mile away by the sound of a battering ram failing against a steel-reinforced door.

amir.title: Colonel Khaled
amir.summary: The ISI chief in Lahore who worked alongside John Kiriakou through the Abu Zubaydah operation — a man who had never wanted to be a soldier, who spent their first meeting drawing Kiriakou's portrait instead of taking notes, and who explained the spliced telephone wires that nearly derailed the hunt.

amir.title: Faisalabad Hospital
amir.summary: The hospital where a dying Abu Zubaydah was taken after the raid of March 2002 — open windows, animals in the corridors, mosquitoes on open wounds, and a bar of Irish Spring soap used as a pincushion for reusable syringes — which came under fire from the street while he was on the operating table.

amnesty-international.title: Salt Typhoon
amnesty-international.summary: The Chinese intelligence operation John Kiriakou describes as having hit the jackpot — collecting data on effectively every American through the telephone companies — and his blunt assessment that the Chinese cyber unit is good and American defences are not.

amnesty-international.title: The Ai Weiwei Lego portrait
amnesty-international.summary: The Alcatraz installation for which Ai Weiwei built 178 portraits of political prisoners out of Lego, and John Kiriakou's account of how his own inclusion was nearly blocked — Amnesty International told the artist it did not regard Kiriakou as a political prisoner, and only relented the week he left prison.

amnesty-international.title: The Bolton raid
amnesty-international.summary: John Kiriakou's reading of the August 2025 FBI search of John Bolton's home and office — that emailing national defense information to family members is the Espionage Act's definition of espionage, on a precedent set in Kiriakou's own case — together with the FBI evidence sticker he says is still on the back of his own computer.

amnesty-international.title: The disappearance of Daniel Hale
amnesty-international.summary: John Kiriakou's account of losing touch with the drone whistleblower Daniel Hale after his release from prison — a brief reappearance on social media, a shut-down account a week later, and a circle of friends none of whom has heard from him since.

amnesty-international.title: Thin Thread
amnesty-international.summary: Competing NSA programs at the center of the post-9/11 mass-surveillance turn. Per John Kiriakou, on September 11, 2001 NSA Director Michael Hayden implemented Operation Thin Thread — which 'vacuums up every phone call, every text message, every email, every bit of metadata from every American' — and reportedly called 9/11 'the greatest possible gift to NSA.' Three NSA officers (Bill Binney, Kirk Wiebe, and Ed Loomis) had built a competing program, Stellar Wind, that could collect the same data while protecting Americans' identities; Hayden chose to grab everything instead. Kiriakou says it was Tom Drake's effort to report the illegality that destroyed Drake.

amnesty-international.title: 2026 congressional landscape
amnesty-international.summary: John Kiriakou's read on two developments affecting the 2026 midterm landscape — the Supreme Court's disallowance of Virginia's redistricting, which he says makes a Democratic House win less certain given widespread Republican-favoring gerrymandering, and Marjorie Taylor Greene's resignation despite winning her last race with 77.5% of the vote, because she knew she could not survive another Republican primary.

an-actual-summit.title: The Sue Mi Terry case
an-actual-summit.summary: John Kiriakou's reading of the prosecution of analyst Sue Mi Terry — charged not under the Espionage Act but under the Foreign Agents Registration Act, an offence he reduces to failing to fill out a form on the internet, and one whose nominal sentencing range he says means nothing in practice.

an-actual-summit.title: Sergey Lavrov
an-actual-summit.summary: Russian foreign minister, and previously Russian ambassador to the United Nations during John Kiriakou's assignment there, where the two worked the same Security Council. Kiriakou describes him as the most admired diplomat in the building — the most powerful, important and strategic ambassador there despite operating with far smaller resources than his American, British, French and Chinese counterparts, and better than most of the American diplomats Kiriakou worked for. When Lavrov was abruptly sidelined in late 2025, Kiriakou's reading was retirement rather than disgrace.

an-actual-summit.title: The search for a country to take Gaza
an-actual-summit.summary: John Kiriakou's account of Israel approaching one country after another — Albania, Indonesia, Egypt, Saudi Arabia and finally South Sudan — to accept expelled Gazans, a project he calls the literal definition of ethnic cleansing and says cannot be done because it is illegal.

an-actual-summit.title: The seat-belt roadblocks
an-actual-summit.summary: What John Kiriakou reported the federalised National Guard, police, FBI, ATF and DEA were actually doing at roadblocks on Washington's main thoroughfares in August 2025 — writing tickets for unworn seat belts and broken brake lights, in neighbourhoods he says have no street crime to speak of.

an-actual-summit.title: The thrown sandwich
an-actual-summit.summary: The arrest of a man who threw a sandwich at a National Guardsman at 14th and U Street in Washington in August 2025, charged with felony assault on a police officer with a stated demand for ten years — an overcharge John Kiriakou said no Washington jury would ever convict on.

an-actual-summit.title: Walking Robert Morgenthau to the hearing room
an-actual-summit.summary: John Kiriakou's recollection of taking the arm of a very elderly Robert Morgenthau in a Senate corridor and walking him to a Foreign Relations Committee hearing — and of telling him he had just read a book about Smyrna, and had not known his father coined the word genocide.

analysis-corporation.title: John Brennan
analysis-corporation.summary: Former Director of the CIA; characterized in KiriPedia's source corpus as the principal architect of the agency's enhanced interrogation program and as having plotted against an elected President

analysis-corporation.title: Arrais Corporation
analysis-corporation.summary: Private intelligence firm; companion entity to The Analysis Corporation; originally an LLC pass-through for retired Senior Intelligence Service personnel from the CIA's operations side; subsequently acquired by IBM for over $1 billion.

analysis-corporation.title: Al Qaeda Software
analysis-corporation.summary: A claim raised on a Kiriakou-appearance podcast that "Al-Qaeda" is also the name of a terrorist-tracking software, alongside its use as the name of the terrorist organization.

analysis-corporation.title: Central Intelligence Agency
analysis-corporation.summary: U.S. foreign intelligence service; John Kiriakou's employer from 1990 to 2004 and the central institution of KiriPedia

analysis-corporation.title: Hamilton 68
analysis-corporation.summary: A company founded by former CIA, FBI, NSA and Director of National Intelligence officials that rates news sites as reliable or unreliable, contracting mainly with the Pentagon to flag articles on government computers with green or red check marks; John Kiriakou says it threatened Consortium News with a "Kremlin apologist" red-check designation, after which PayPal permanently suspended the outlet's account and confiscated its funds.

analysis-corporation.title: Private Intelligence
analysis-corporation.summary: Post-CIA commercial intelligence work performed by John Kiriakou — both operational (surveillance, bribery, dossier-building for private clients) and analytical (paid forecasts for hedge funds, mutual funds, and a global mining company). Per Kiriakou, his clients ranged from a Cypriot billionaire investigating his daughter's fiancé to the ninth-largest hedge fund in the world.

andres-serrano.title: Ai Weiwei
andres-serrano.summary: Chinese contemporary artist and pro-democracy activist; designer of the Beijing Olympic Stadium; per John Kiriakou, produced a Lego portrait of him as one of 178 political prisoners in the series, with Kiriakou's panel positioned next to Martin Luther King Jr.; the work is now in the permanent collection of the Smithsonian Institution.

andres-serrano.title: Cuban double agents
andres-serrano.summary: John Kiriakou's assessment of Cuban intelligence as one of the best services on the planet, defensive in nature and trained by the KGB, and his flat claim — repeated across several tellings — that the CIA has never recruited a Cuban who did not turn out to be working for Havana all along.

andres-serrano.title: Robert Hanssen
andres-serrano.summary: FBI counterintelligence chief and Soviet/Russian mole; framed CIA counterintelligence chief Brian Kelley as the source of compromised assets — leading the FBI to surveil Kelly for a year and a half and threaten his family with the death penalty — before Hanssen himself was identified as the actual traitor.

andres-serrano.title: Scholar-in-Residence program
andres-serrano.summary: The current CIA recruitment program, in operation as of the late 2020s, under which the agency places retiring senior officers as 'CIA Scholar in Residence' professors at major American universities. Per John Kiriakou, the program serves as the agency's principal university-recruitment channel since the 1993 Equal Employment Opportunity Act forbade the older practice of having professors covertly recruit students into the CIA. Officers identified as scholars in residence are openly disclosed; the recruitment work continues, just no longer in secret.
