andres-serrano.title: Wesley Clark
andres-serrano.summary: Retired U.S. Army four-star general and former Clinton administration adviser; per John Kiriakou, "a very good guy", "one of the very, very few people at that level", and the public source of the account that in the weeks after 9/11 the Pentagon was working to a memo listing seven governments to be overthrown. Kiriakou treats Clark's story as corroborated by his own — on 6 May 2002 a CIA security officer told him, in the course of signing him onto the agency's most sensitive programmes, that the United States would invade Iraq the following year.

andres-serrano.title: Access Agent
andres-serrano.summary: CIA (and foreign intelligence service) term for a recruited asset whose value lies not in the secrets they hold directly but in their regular social access to high-value targets — politicians, executives, heads of state — who cannot themselves be recruited. Per John Kiriakou, the access agent is funded generously to maintain an environment in which the targets feel comfortable and return repeatedly; kompromat — compromising photographs or recordings — may be collected as a secondary tool. Kiriakou identifies Jeffrey Epstein as a textbook access agent, in his assessment working for Israeli intelligence.

andrew-bustamante.title: John Kiriakou
andrew-bustamante.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

andrew-bustamante.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
andrew-bustamante.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

andrew-bustamante.title: Presidents and the CIA
andrew-bustamante.summary: John Kiriakou's observation that some presidents actively lead the CIA while others are led around by it — citing George H.W. Bush's ongoing "love affair" with the agency after his 11-month stint as director, and Richard Nixon's close relationship with the CIA, which Kiriakou says was one of the things that brought down his presidency.

andrew-bustamante.title: Sarah Adams
andrew-bustamante.summary: A former CIA open-source analyst and frequent television commentator on terrorist threats, whom John Kiriakou dismisses in unusually direct terms: that she never held access to classified information, that she analysed press rather than intelligence, and that she has built a living out of predicting imminent disaster.

andrew-bustamante.title: The botched pitch
andrew-bustamante.summary: The one operation John Kiriakou describes as a failure of his career: a two-year development of a terrorist working under journalist cover, brought to the point of a recruitment pitch and destroyed at the table when his station chief seized the meeting and threatened the target instead of pitching him. The target fled screaming for police, the host government''s deputy prime minister complained to the American ambassador, and the man later described the encounter to a third intelligence service as an approach by "two caricatures of CIA men."

andrew-bustamante.title: UK secrecy laws
andrew-bustamante.summary: John Kiriakou's view that Britain is even harsher on whistleblowers and dissent than the United States, using the Official Secrets Act and Terrorism Act to stop people at airports and threaten arrest merely for supporting Palestinian rights.

andrew-feinstein.title: Meredith Whittaker
andrew-feinstein.summary: Per John Kiriakou, Meredith Whittaker is developing a new, and by his account successful, business model for the encrypted-messaging app Signal, an alternative he cites alongside ProtonMail's compromised attempt at the same thing.

andrew-feinstein.title: Ai Whistleblower Initiative
andrew-feinstein.summary: The AI Whistleblower Initiative, working on legal protections for the wave of whistleblowers now coming out of the artificial-intelligence industry.

andrew-feinstein.title: Belmarsh Prison
andrew-feinstein.summary: The maximum-security London prison where Julian Assange was held for years on a bail-jumping sentence John Kiriakou calls a fabrication — kept in solitary confinement alongside the worst offenders in the United Kingdom, and held past the expiry of his sentence at the request of the United States. Kiriakou corresponded with Assange there and watched the letters change.

andrew-feinstein.title: Der Spiegel
andrew-feinstein.summary: At a 2026 Berlin panel, a former Der Spiegel journalist said it took him years before he could call Julian Assange a publisher rather than an activist.

andrew-feinstein.title: Ethan Mccord Collateral Murder
andrew-feinstein.summary: The US soldier who carried wounded children out of the street in the Collateral Murder video released by WikiLeaks.

andrew-feinstein.title: Plus 972
andrew-feinstein.summary: The Israeli platform that, per a 2026 Berlin panel, has published a striking number of IDF whistleblowers as AI enters modern warfare.

andrew-warren.title: Mary Margaret Graham
andrew-warren.summary: CIA Senior Intelligence Service officer and later Deputy Director of National Intelligence for Collection under John Negroponte — described by John Kiriakou as a career "reports officer" who had never personally recruited a source, and as his difficult chief of station in a later domestic assignment.

andrew-warren.title: Cover stop
andrew-warren.summary: A routine, innocuous errand run in the middle of a surveillance detection route so that an intelligence officer has a plausible reason to be where he is — the 7-Eleven, the dry cleaner, the wine shop — and, in John Kiriakou's account, also a petty-expense line item that has ended CIA careers.

andrew-warren.title: Deloitte Consulting Career
andrew-warren.summary: John Kiriakou's post-CIA career at Deloitte Consulting (2004–2008), covering two corporate acquisitions he says he drove — India Tiger Analysis and, in effect, Bering Point — and ending in his effective firing weeks before his ABC News whistleblower interview aired.

andrew-warren.title: John Kiriakou
andrew-warren.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

andrew-warren.title: Central Intelligence Agency
andrew-warren.summary: U.S. foreign intelligence service; John Kiriakou's employer from 1990 to 2004 and the central institution of KiriPedia

andrew-warren.title: Concealment of the CIA budget
andrew-warren.summary: John Kiriakou''s description of how the CIA hides its spending: there is no publicly available written CIA budget, and individual line items are distributed across unrelated federal departments under invented cover programmes — a practice he says persists unchanged, and which once repeatedly exposed the agency to Senator William Proxmire''s Golden Fleece Award.

andy-warhol-encounter.title: Agnes von Kurowsky grave story
andy-warhol-encounter.summary: John Kiriakou's account of discovering the Washington, D.C. grave of Agnes von Kurowsky, the World War I Red Cross nurse whose four-month wartime romance with a young ambulance driver, Ernest Hemingway, made her the model for the lead female character in six of his books, including A Farewell to Arms.

andy-warhol-encounter.title: Spies of Arlington National Cemetery
andy-warhol-encounter.summary: On the Walk With History podcast, John Kiriakou — author of Remains of the Day: A Definitive Guide to Washington D.C.''s Historic Cemeteries — toured Arlington National Cemetery and told personal and historical stories about the intelligence figures buried there, including OSS founder William Donovan, deputy CIA director Vernon Walters, codebreakers William and Elizabeth Friedman, slain station chiefs Richard Welch and William Buckley, U-2 pilot Francis Gary Powers, and Mike Spann, the first CIA officer killed after 9/11.

andy-warhol-encounter.title: Bashar al-Assad
andy-warhol-encounter.summary: President of Syria; John Kiriakou recounts warning Senator John Kerry to stop publicly calling Assad 'my dear friend' after a speech enraged Washington's Lebanese community, with Kerry citing motorcycle rides they had taken together to the Golan Heights.

andy-warhol-encounter.title: Jack Murphy NATO Sabotage Story
andy-warhol-encounter.summary: John Kiriakou's account of a story reported by podcaster Jack Murphy — over a year in the making, drawing on CIA and Army intelligence sources — alleging the CIA worked through a NATO partner to conduct sabotage inside Russia, including munitions-warehouse fires and rail explosions; killed before publication after the CIA deputy director denied it on a call with the editor and blamed "rogue Ukrainians."

andy-warhol-encounter.title: Remains of the Day Treasury Clerk Story
andy-warhol-encounter.summary: John Kiriakou's account of finding the grave of an obscure Treasury Department clerk who, during the 1814 British burning of Washington, rescued the Declaration of Independence, Constitution, Bill of Rights, and Washington's military commission from the National Archives — and who, after later being deemed too difficult, was quietly transferred to the National Lighthouse Service, where out of boredom he invented the refractor light still used in American lighthouses today.

andy-warhol-encounter.title: U.S. foreign policy process
andy-warhol-encounter.summary: Three foreign-policy observations from John Kiriakou — the narrow legal basis for U.S. military presence abroad, which he says does not cover American special forces in Syria; the formal congressional travel-clearance process that undercuts Pentagon and White House claims of no advance knowledge of Nancy Pelosi's Taiwan trip; and the depth of U.S.-China economic interdependence that Kiriakou says makes antagonizing Beijing strategically unwise.

angela-merkel.title: Edward Snowden
angela-merkel.summary: Former NSA contractor who in 2013 disclosed the scope of U.S. [mass surveillance](/wiki/mass-surveillance), including the Section 702 collection program. Per John Kiriakou — who counts Snowden among the small group of national-security whistleblowers prosecuted under the Espionage Act — Snowden was ''stuck between two awful slippery slopes'': breaking his oath and chain of command on one side, and on the other catching something ''cut and dry against the Constitution'' that no one would act on. Kiriakou notes Snowden could not use his chain of command (as Kiriakou could not, his own chain being Jose Rodriguez), and that Judge Leonie Brinkema had reserved the Snowden case for herself before he fled the country.

angela-merkel.title: Hillary Clinton
angela-merkel.summary: Former U.S. Secretary of State and 2016 presidential candidate; John Kiriakou describes her as arguably the most neoconservative candidate Democrats could have nominated, more militarist even than her husband, and credits her — separately — with correctly describing Iran as a military dictatorship run by the IRGC rather than a genuine theocracy.

angela-merkel.title: NSA
angela-merkel.summary: Kiriakou on the agency whose Utah facility boasts room to store every American's calls, texts and emails for the next 500 years.

angela-merkel.title: Espionage Act
angela-merkel.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

angela-merkel.title: Jack Teixeira
angela-merkel.summary: Massachusetts Air National Guard reservist arrested in April 2023 for leaking classified Pentagon documents to a small Discord server. John Kiriakou, discussing the case the day after Teixeira's arrest, initially suspected a covert action program rather than a genuine leak, ultimately concluded Teixeira was not a whistleblower, and predicted — correctly — that he would be charged under the Espionage Act and take a plea bargain.

angela-merkel.title: Terry Aubry
angela-merkel.summary: Named by Kiriakou both as an FBI whistleblower who exposed racism at the bureau and as one of two Intercept journalists who sent him to prison.

angry-birds.title: John Kiriakou's Briefing Room
angry-birds.summary: A twice-weekly news and commentary programme launched by John Kiriakou in July 2026, presented as analysis rather than partisan opinion, and distinct from his storytelling podcast Dead Drop.

angry-birds.title: 2026 Iran war
angry-birds.summary: The open-ended American and Israeli war against Iran that John Kiriakou tracked week by week on his own show — a conflict he says was sold as three weeks, ran into its fifth month, achieved every decapitation objective it set, and continued anyway. His grade for it is a D, and his forecast is a Truth Social post declaring victory while nothing changes.

angry-birds.title: 2028 presidential field
angry-birds.summary: John Kiriakou's assessment of the wide-open 2028 presidential race — the first in his life, he says, where he has no idea who either party will nominate. Predictive markets were listing 44 Democrats and 26 Republicans as possible candidates. His own preferred candidate is Tucker Carlson, whom he says he has repeatedly begged to run; his working assumption about anyone who does want the job is that they are "a narcissist and probably a sociopath on top of it."

angry-birds.title: Abraham Accords
angry-birds.summary: The Trump-brokered normalization deals between Israel and Gulf Arab states — in John Kiriakou's judgment "a terrible idea in the first place," a great victory for Israel and the Gulf Arabs that was "a punch in the throat to the Palestinians." He argues the Accords are how Trump meant to "solve the Middle East in a day" — by screwing the Palestinians — that Hamas read the abandonment correctly, that October 7 shattered the project, and that reviving the Accords (Saudis in, victory declared, Nobel collected) remains the organizing goal of Trump's regional policy.

angry-birds.title: Amaryllis Fox Kennedy
angry-birds.summary: Former CIA non-official-cover officer who worked under commercial cover as an international art consultant, later a Trump campaign manager and nominee for deputy CIA director. Per John Kiriakou, Senator Tom Cotton threatened to filibuster her appointment; the president responded by naming her deputy national security adviser instead — a job Kiriakou considers more powerful, since the CIA director reports to the national security adviser.

angry-birds.title: Andrew Bustamante
angry-birds.summary: Former CIA officer who sells CIA-style training online; John Kiriakou identifies him as the lone critic of his work hosting a show on a Russian network, and argues Bustamante's training business — open to anyone who pays — is the more problematic of the two.

another-bentley.title: The Imran Khan request
another-bentley.summary: John Kiriakou's account of Imran Khan's dealings with the United States — that while still prime minister Khan warned the Americans he would start blaming them for everything, drawing the reply that they were blamed for everything anyway; and that after his arrest he got word out asking for help, which produced an approach to his former wife Jemima Goldsmith and a refusal from Pakistan.

another-bentley.title: The Pentagon and the Pakistani arsenal
another-bentley.summary: What John Kiriakou says he was told unofficially while stationed in Pakistan in 2002 — that Pervez Musharraf had turned control of the Pakistani nuclear arsenal over to the United States, and that the Pentagon controlled it — and Pakistan's insistence in the years since that this was never true, which Kiriakou says would be the more worrying answer.

another-bentley.title: Imran Khan
another-bentley.summary: Former Prime Minister of Pakistan; subsequently deposed and imprisoned; his political party, the PTI (Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf), sent John Kiriakou a formal demand for apology after a November 2025 Indian-media interview in which Kiriakou observed that India would prevail over Pakistan in a conventional conflict; Kiriakou's reply has not been transcribed in polite company.

another-bentley.title: Pakistani corruption and democracy
another-bentley.summary: John Kiriakou's assessment that corruption in Pakistan is so deep and so broad that a genuinely functioning democracy is almost impossible there — set against a long history of military coups, a habit of imprisoning former prime ministers, and his insistence that Imran Khan should not be in a cell.

another-bentley.title: Benazir Bhutto
another-bentley.summary: Pakistani politician; twice Prime Minister of Pakistan; characterized in KiriPedia's source corpus as personally corrupt and married to an even more corrupt husband

another-bentley.title: ISI
another-bentley.summary: Pakistan''s Inter-Services Intelligence agency, the CIA''s principal counterterrorism partner during John Kiriakou''s 2002 posting. Per Kiriakou, there were effectively ''two parallel ISIs'': one made up of Sandhurst-trained, FBI-schooled professionals he calls heroes who risked their lives on counterterrorism, and another — ''people with long beards who gave you a dirty look'' — who had created Kashmiri terrorist groups like Jaish-e-Mohammed and were attacking Shia mosques and Americans. Because of this, the CIA never told the ISI the identity of high-value targets, referring to Abu Zubaydah only as ''Mr. Fish.''

anthony-fauci.title: John Kiriakou
anthony-fauci.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

anthony-fauci.title: The chilling effect of whistleblower prosecutions
anthony-fauci.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that national-security prosecutions are not primarily about convictions but about deterrence — that the CIA cares about sending a message where the FBI cares about promotions, that his own case was meant to frighten anyone else considering disclosure, and that a New York Times reporter told him every national-security source the paper had went silent on the day of his arrest.

anthony-fauci.title: Church Committee
anthony-fauci.summary: U.S. Senate investigative committee operating in 1975–1976 that examined domestic intelligence abuses by the CIA, FBI, and NSA; per John Kiriakou, the Church Committee — alongside the concurrent Pike Committee in the House — was the last genuine moment of legislative oversight over the intelligence community, born of a national consensus that government had gone dangerously off course. Its work led to the creation of the permanent Senate Select Committee on Intelligence, which Kiriakou says ceased to function as real oversight roughly seven years after its founding.

anthony-fauci.title: CIA Gmail account felony case
anthony-fauci.summary: Per John Kiriakou, a CIA colleague working the counterterrorism fusion center night shift was ordered by cable to check a terrorist suspect's Gmail account and password, did so, and was later charged with a felony for illegally accessing a computer — despite having acted only on explicit written instructions from headquarters.

anthony-fauci.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
anthony-fauci.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

anthony-fauci.title: Congressional intelligence oversight
anthony-fauci.summary: John Kiriakou''s standing criticism of the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence and the House Permanent Select Committee — that unlike the armed services and foreign relations committees, they do not perform oversight at all: "They''re just cheerleaders." His illustration is a sitting committee chairman who summoned him privately, then asked whether Kiriakou would write the criticism publicly on his behalf.

antisemitism-and-anti-zionism.title: Germany and Israel
antisemitism-and-anti-zionism.summary: John Kiriakou's account of German support for Israeli policy as an overcorrection driven by shame over the Nazi past, and of the resulting cultural blacklisting of critics of Israel in Germany — a pattern he put to Roger Waters, who described being effectively unpublishable in the German press.

antisemitism-and-anti-zionism.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
antisemitism-and-anti-zionism.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

antisemitism-and-anti-zionism.title: Roger Waters
antisemitism-and-anti-zionism.summary: Founding member of the British rock band Pink Floyd; outspoken supporter of Palestinian human rights; anonymously paid off John Kiriakou's second mortgage during his federal prison sentence, sparing his wife and children the loss of the family home; only discovered to be the benefactor years later; subsequently a personal friend of Kiriakou and a recurring guest on his programme.

antisemitism-and-anti-zionism.title: The logic of radicalization
antisemitism-and-anti-zionism.summary: John Kiriakou''s explanation of why an isolated state escalates rather than moderates: it stops caring what anyone else thinks, concludes it can count on no one, and does things its own way. He applies it to Israel''s 2026 death penalty law and judges the law a serious mistake in Zionism''s own terms.

antisemitism-and-anti-zionism.title: Middle East Forum
antisemitism-and-anti-zionism.summary: The publication — 'clearly an Israeli publication,' in John Kiriakou's words, and one he had never heard of before a Google alert surfaced it — that ran a piece by the political adviser to the Israeli foreign minister calling Kiriakou antisemitic and describing his writing as evidence of 'the rot' in the American intellectual left. Kiriakou took the phrase as a compliment and says the episode shows how closely Israel monitors even small independent outlets.

antisemitism-and-anti-zionism.title: Israeli strike on Qatar
antisemitism-and-anti-zionism.summary: The Israeli bombing of Qatar that John Kiriakou treats as Benjamin Netanyahu's decisive overreach — an attack on a major non-NATO ally that hosts the largest air force base in the world, which Kiriakou says forced Donald Trump into a public falsehood about advance warning and then into the recognition that Israel acts in Israel's interests rather than America's.

anwar-al-awlaki.title: Falls Church mosque
anwar-al-awlaki.summary: Large mosque on Route 7 in Falls Church, Virginia; the site at which John Kiriakou, in 1993 as a CIA Arabic-language trainee, met then-imam Anwar al-Awlaki on a class field trip; the same mosque at which the September 11 hijackers prayed the night before the attacks.

anwar-al-awlaki.title: Haqqani White House meeting
anwar-al-awlaki.summary: A mid-to-late-1980s White House meeting between President Ronald Reagan and a Taliban delegation, per John Kiriakou — a former boss of his served as translator. One member of that delegation, a man named Haqqani, went on to found the Haqqani network, later responsible for the capture of Bowe Bergdahl and the kidnapping, rape, and torture of a Canadian couple.

anwar-al-awlaki.title: Kiriakou and Cenk Uygur
anwar-al-awlaki.summary: A grievance John Kiriakou carried for a decade — that Cenk Uygur had spent thirty minutes attacking him over his first letter from prison — resolved live on air in July 2026 when Uygur produced his archive, found no such segment, and both men concluded it had been mistaken identity.

anwar-al-awlaki.title: Leonard Peltier
anwar-al-awlaki.summary: The American Indian Movement prisoner John Kiriakou names when asked which cases deserve attention alongside Assange's — an old and ailing man whom he calls factually innocent, and whose continued imprisonment he offers as evidence that the system's incentives run only one way.

anwar-al-awlaki.title: OnlyFans
anwar-al-awlaki.summary: Per John Kiriakou, the man who owned OnlyFans — whom he describes as Ukrainian-American rather than Israeli — was a major donor and strong supporter of Israel, part of a broader claim Kiriakou makes about Israeli involvement in the porn industry.

anwar-al-awlaki.title: The MintPress prediction
anwar-al-awlaki.summary: The forecast John Kiriakou volunteers against himself — that asked in a post-election interview alongside Thomas Drake and Jesselyn Radack whether whistleblowers would fare better or worse under Donald Trump, he alone answered that nothing could be worse than Barack Obama, and was wrong.

april-glaspie.title: Iraqi invasion of Kuwait
april-glaspie.summary: John Kiriakou''s most detailed account of the intelligence process around the 1990 Iraqi invasion of Kuwait and its 1991 liberation. As a first-year CIA analyst on a ''training account'' covering Iraq, Kiriakou produced the June 30, 1990 warning paper for the White House; suggested calling the US Defense Attaché in Baghdad to drive to the border and report what he saw (the answer: ''Literally the entire Iraqi military is heading south''); briefed the August 2 Oval Office meeting with Bush; and later took a single phone call from General Colin Powell that led, eight hours later, to 47 cruise missiles striking the Iraqi Intelligence Service headquarters in Baghdad.

april-glaspie.title: Saddam Hussein
april-glaspie.summary: President of Iraq from 1979 until the 2003 U.S. invasion; subject of John Kiriakou's CIA portfolio from January 1990 onward, in which capacity Kiriakou became, at age 25, "Saddam Hussein's intelligence community biographer" and the analyst who briefed President George H. W. Bush in the Oval Office on the morning of the 1990 invasion of Kuwait.

april-glaspie.title: United Food and Commercial Workers
april-glaspie.summary: The huge K Street labor union where a young John Kiriakou — from a family with a long labor history — was working when Dr. Jerrold Post''s class assignment changed his life: shadow your boss for a week and write his psychological profile. Kiriakou''s boss was a mean old-school organizer whose back had been broken by scabs; halfway through the week Kiriakou called him a racist ("which he was"), and the resulting paper diagnosed the man as a sociopath and potentially dangerous. The paper is what put Kiriakou on the CIA''s radar.

april-glaspie.title: 1993 Bush Kuwait assassination plot
april-glaspie.summary: Iraqi intelligence plot, foiled by Kuwaiti authorities, to assassinate former President George H. W. Bush during his post-liberation "victory lap" visit to Kuwait; the U.S. response, per John Kiriakou's first-person account of his telephone call with Chairman of the Joint Chiefs Colin Powell, was 47 cruise missiles fired into the Iraqi Intelligence Service headquarters in Baghdad eight hours later.

april-glaspie.title: Mort Halperin
april-glaspie.summary: Former Assistant Secretary of State, Assistant Secretary of Defense, and senior director of the National Security Council; author of the law John Kiriakou was convicted of violating (the Intelligence Identities Protection Act); wrote to President Obama stating that this is not why he wrote the law and that Kiriakou should be pardoned.

april-glaspie.title: Norman Schwarzkopf
april-glaspie.summary: U.S. Army general and commander of CENTCOM during the 1991 Gulf War; per John Kiriakou, the architect of the "visionary" flanking maneuver that bypassed Iraq's fortified Kuwait–Saudi border, struck from the north, and produced the Highway of Death.

aq-khan.title: ISI
aq-khan.summary: Pakistan''s Inter-Services Intelligence agency, the CIA''s principal counterterrorism partner during John Kiriakou''s 2002 posting. Per Kiriakou, there were effectively ''two parallel ISIs'': one made up of Sandhurst-trained, FBI-schooled professionals he calls heroes who risked their lives on counterterrorism, and another — ''people with long beards who gave you a dirty look'' — who had created Kashmiri terrorist groups like Jaish-e-Mohammed and were attacking Shia mosques and Americans. Because of this, the CIA never told the ISI the identity of high-value targets, referring to Abu Zubaydah only as ''Mr. Fish.''

aq-khan.title: Pervez Musharraf
aq-khan.summary: Pakistani general and military dictator who ruled during John Kiriakou's 2002 posting as CIA chief of counterterrorism operations in Pakistan. Per Kiriakou, the United States 'essentially just purchased Musharraf,' paying tens of millions in cash to the ISI and meeting him several times a week — and in return 'he would let us do whatever we wanted.' Kiriakou says Musharraf, fearing the nuclear arsenal could fall into terrorist hands, unofficially turned control of Pakistan's nuclear weapons over to the Pentagon. Musharraf later pardoned proliferator A.Q. Khan.

aq-khan.title: The Pentagon and the Pakistani arsenal
aq-khan.summary: What John Kiriakou says he was told unofficially while stationed in Pakistan in 2002 — that Pervez Musharraf had turned control of the Pakistani nuclear arsenal over to the United States, and that the Pentagon controlled it — and Pakistan's insistence in the years since that this was never true, which Kiriakou says would be the more worrying answer.

aq-khan.title: Composition of the Saudi military
aq-khan.summary: John Kiriakou's long-standing claim that there are almost no Saudi nationals in the Saudi armed forces below the most senior ranks, and that the rank and file are Pakistanis hired from among Pakistan's poor. He treats it as a standing joke in the Gulf and as a limit on what Saudi Arabia can contribute to any war with Iran.

aq-khan.title: Mr. Fish
aq-khan.summary: The cover name the CIA used for Abu Zubaydah in Pakistan in 2002 — invented because the Americans would not tell their Pakistani partners who the target was, and derived from the only thing they would say about him: that he was a big fish.

aq-khan.title: Tora Bora
aq-khan.summary: Mountainous cave complex in eastern Afghanistan that served as an al-Qaeda redoubt after the September 11 attacks. Per John Kiriakou — chief of counterterrorism operations in Pakistan at the time — the CIA killed al-Qaeda military-affairs chief Mohammed Atef there in October 2001, and Tora Bora was the backdrop to the hunt for the senior al-Qaeda leadership that culminated in the capture of Abu Zubaydah. Kiriakou also recounts an Egyptian al-Qaeda fighter he later recruited who survived a cruise-missile strike on a Tora Bora cave — one of only two who came out alive, his ears bleeding, describing the explosion as the most hideous sound he had ever heard.

arab-states-and-the-gaza-war.title: The Damascus consulate strike
arab-states-and-the-gaza-war.summary: The April 2024 Israeli attack on Iran's consulate in Damascus, which John Kiriakou describes as an unambiguous violation of the Vienna Convention, and whose official Israeli explanation — that it had not occurred to anyone the world would read it as a provocation — he calls disingenuous and intended purely for domestic audiences.

arab-states-and-the-gaza-war.title: The Eastern Mediterranean gas field
arab-states-and-the-gaza-war.summary: The natural gas discovered off the south-eastern coast of Cyprus and running toward Lebanon, Israel and Palestine, which John Kiriakou identifies as the real source of Greek–Turkish tension. Turkey feels excluded although none of the gas lies in its waters; and although the founding agreement acknowledged a Palestinian share, Israel decides its size — an amount Kiriakou predicts will be zero.

arab-states-and-the-gaza-war.title: Iran's 2024 drone retaliation
arab-states-and-the-gaza-war.summary: John Kiriakou's account of Iran's telegraphed 2024 drone strike on Israel — hundreds of slow drones, launched with advance warning to the U.S. and Jordan, nearly all shot down, which he reads as a controlled show of force and an intelligence victory that exposed the Iron Dome.

arab-states-and-the-gaza-war.title: Afghan heroin policy
arab-states-and-the-gaza-war.summary: The post-2001 U.S. policy in Afghanistan of protecting, and per John Kiriakou actively encouraging, the cultivation of heroin poppy. Under the Taliban in 2000 Afghanistan produced 0% of the world's heroin; by 2009 under American occupation it produced 93%. Per a DEA officer Kiriakou consulted with on the policy paper he was preparing for Senator Kerry, the strategic rationale was that nearly all of the heroin flowed to Iran and Russia, addiction in those countries was considered desirable as a long-run societal weakener, and the same logic now operates in reverse with Chinese fentanyl flowing into the United States.

arab-states-and-the-gaza-war.title: Israeli strike on Qatar
arab-states-and-the-gaza-war.summary: The Israeli bombing of Qatar that John Kiriakou treats as Benjamin Netanyahu's decisive overreach — an attack on a major non-NATO ally that hosts the largest air force base in the world, which Kiriakou says forced Donald Trump into a public falsehood about advance warning and then into the recognition that Israel acts in Israel's interests rather than America's.

arab-states-and-the-gaza-war.title: The October 8 Gaza cars
arab-states-and-the-gaza-war.summary: The account John Kiriakou has passed on from a Greek journalist friend, an investigative reporter for a major Athens newspaper who reached the Gaza envelope on October 8, 2023, one day after the Hamas attack, and saw a line of Israeli cars with their occupants still dead inside and *"giant rocket holes in the roofs of the cars,"* damage inconsistent with the ground assault the Israeli government has said killed them. Kiriakou uses the anecdote as an example of a story he does not have to speculate about, his friend was on the ground with an IDF handler who refused to explain what had happened.

arabic-and-greek.title: The Communist Party of Greece
arabic-and-greek.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of Greek communism: a civil war from 1946 to 1949 whose bitterness still scars families, a party banned outright until Andreas Papandreou legalised it in 1980, and a present-day remnant polling between three and five per cent — enough for parliamentary representation and not enough to be a factor.

arabic-and-greek.title: The oath in the auditorium
arabic-and-greek.summary: The scene John Kiriakou returns to when asked what set him on the path to blowing the whistle: standing in the CIA''s auditorium on his first day with three hundred other new hires, right hand in the air, swearing to uphold the Constitution against all enemies foreign and domestic — and his later suspicion that he may have been the only person in the room who meant it.

arabic-and-greek.title: Witness K case
arabic-and-greek.summary: Australian intelligence scandal in which a former ASIS officer known as Witness K exposed Australia's bugging of the East Timorese cabinet during oil and gas revenue negotiations; his lawyer, Bernard Collaery, describes the ASIO raids on both their homes and offices as paralleling the FBI's raid on John Kiriakou.

arabic-and-greek.title: Zbigniew Brzezinski
arabic-and-greek.summary: National security adviser to Jimmy Carter, named in John Kiriakou's account of Afghanistan as an architect of the policy of luring the Soviet Union into a war there — a policy Kiriakou says literally destroyed the country and set the conditions for the Taliban.

arabic-and-greek.title: Arabists
arabic-and-greek.summary: The label applied inside the U.S. government to diplomats and analysts who knew Arabic and Middle Eastern history, and which John Kiriakou confirms functioned as a dismissal — the assumption being that anyone who understood the region was blindly prejudiced against Israel, or antisemitic.

arabic-and-greek.title: The concealed carry advertisements
arabic-and-greek.summary: The anecdote John Kiriakou offers about surveillance capitalism: a private telephone conversation in which a friend told him he needed a concealed carry permit, followed within the hour by a Facebook feed consisting entirely of advertisements for concealed carry classes.

arabists.title: The 189 undeclared officers
arabists.summary: A figure John Kiriakou attributes to the CIA''s director of security, given to his intake class on his first day at the agency in January 1990: against two declared Israeli intelligence officers at the embassy in Washington, the FBI counted at least 189 undeclared ones operating across the United States. He pairs it with the fact that Israeli liaison officers were barred from CIA headquarters.

arabists.title: Abraham Accords
arabists.summary: The Trump-brokered normalization deals between Israel and Gulf Arab states — in John Kiriakou's judgment "a terrible idea in the first place," a great victory for Israel and the Gulf Arabs that was "a punch in the throat to the Palestinians." He argues the Accords are how Trump meant to "solve the Middle East in a day" — by screwing the Palestinians — that Hamas read the abandonment correctly, that October 7 shattered the project, and that reviving the Accords (Saudis in, victory declared, Nobel collected) remains the organizing goal of Trump's regional policy.

arabists.title: Amnesty International
arabists.summary: The human rights organization whose torture report forms part of John Kiriakou's core defense — the CIA's crimes were already public knowledge before he confirmed them on ABC, and the Justice Department's own declination letter said so — and the organization whose silence during his prosecution he cannot forgive. He begged Amnesty for a one-sentence statement and got a New Yorker subscription instead; it took Ai Weiwei to change their minds, and by then he was walking out of prison.

arabists.title: Arabic and Greek
arabists.summary: The qualification John Kiriakou says opened the door to his transfer from CIA analysis to operations: a post in Athens wanted Greek or Arabic, and he had both — by most of his tellings the only officer in the agency who did. The chief who hired him gave the reason in one sentence: it is easier and cheaper to take a linguist and teach him operations than the other way round. The pairing also became a detection tool, since the language nobody speaks in Pakistan is Arabic.

arabists.title: Deuce Martinez
arabists.summary: The former CIA analyst whose business card was the basis of two of the three Espionage Act charges brought against John Kiriakou. Kiriakou scanned and emailed the card — which showed Martinez had gone to work for Mitchell and Jessen, the firm of the torture programme's architects — to a New York Times reporter and later to an ABC News reporter. The judge threw the espionage counts out.

arabists.title: Human Rights Watch
arabists.summary: The organization whose 2005 report that the CIA was torturing its prisoners — two years before John Kiriakou''s ABC interview — anchors his defense that he confirmed rather than revealed the program. It is also the middle link in the chain that ended in his arrest: working with the John Adams Project, Human Rights Watch employed the investigator who carried a classified name from journalist Matthew Cole to the Guantánamo defense attorneys, and when the FBI walked that chain backwards it arrived at Kiriakou''s door.

area-fifty-eight.title: Luis Elizondo
area-fifty-eight.summary: Why John Kiriakou never booked the best-known public advocate for unidentified aerial phenomena on his RT programme: viewers kept insisting Elizondo was an expert, so Kiriakou researched him and found chiefly Elizondo saying he was an expert. He says he does not know what the man is an expert on, and that it was not a fit for the show.

area-fifty-eight.title: The Australian pilot
area-fifty-eight.summary: The disappearance John Kiriakou recounts as an argument for declassification rather than as proof of anything: a pilot in his early twenties flying on 10 September 1978 who radioed that a silver cylinder was above his aircraft matching his speed exactly, said it was not an aircraft, was cut off by a loud sound of electronic interference, and was never seen again — along with the plane.

area-fifty-eight.title: Kiriakou's UFO sighting
area-fifty-eight.summary: The object John Kiriakou and his father watched from the side of Route 60 in Amish country, western Pennsylvania, on a Friday night in 1981 — three flashes of white light, then a silent orange trapezoid hanging a couple of thousand feet up, which left at a speed he had never seen before or since.

area-fifty-eight.title: Leaks come from the Pentagon
area-fifty-eight.summary: John Kiriakou''s rule of attribution for national security leaks, drawn from his own CIA experience: ninety-nine times out of a hundred the leak came from the Pentagon — which he says leaks constantly, is so gigantic that the source cannot be traced, and does not polygraph anybody. He adds the motive: somebody who opposed the operation and was overruled.

area-fifty-eight.title: Sixteen people knew
area-fifty-eight.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer to why deeply held secrets do not leak: at the outset only sixteen people in the entire federal government knew about the CIA torture programme, which is why it stayed hidden for years.

area-fifty-eight.title: The unswept roof
area-fifty-eight.summary: John Kiriakou''s two security observations after the killing of Charlie Kirk: that drone surveillance of outdoor events is cheap, easy and has no reason not to be used; and that the building the shooter is said to have fired from had been closed for renovation since April and supposedly locked up tight, yet nobody in the campus police department appears to have walked up to the roof to check.

arianna-huffington.title: Bureau of Prisons
arianna-huffington.summary: The federal agency that ran John Kiriakou's incarceration — and one of his most persistent post-prison targets. The BOP overrode his judge's camp recommendation by deeming him "a threat to the public safety," threatened him with "diesel therapy" until 1,600 logged phone calls and letters from a dozen House members and two senators backed it off, and, per Kiriakou, functions as "an employment agency for unemployable semi-literate rural white men" and "a dumping ground for failed medical professionals" — an agency for which a prisoner's death is cheaper than his treatment.

arianna-huffington.title: Letter from Loretto
arianna-huffington.summary: Prison newsletter written by John Kiriakou from FCI Loretto, modeled on Martin Luther King's "Letter from Birmingham Jail," which exposed two crimes committed against him by guards and went viral after being relayed to the Huffington Post, drawing national press to the prison.

arianna-huffington.title: Oliver Stone
arianna-huffington.summary: American film director with whom John Kiriakou struck up a friendship after his release from prison. Stone optioned the rights to one chapter of Kiriakou's first book, co-developed an unmade History Channel series with him, blurbed his book on Abu Zubaydah, and was among the public figures who campaigned against the Bureau of Prisons' attempt to shut down Kiriakou's prison blog. The two disagree sharply over whether the CIA killed John F. Kennedy.

arianna-huffington.title: FCI Loretto
arianna-huffington.summary: U.S. Federal Correctional Institution in Loretto, Pennsylvania; the low-medium-security prison at which John Kiriakou served 23 months of a 30-month sentence following his 2013 Espionage Act–era plea deal; the originally ordered "minimum security work camp" placement was countermanded — per Kiriakou, on Brennan's direct intervention — to place him in the actual prison alongside the general population.

arianna-huffington.title: Jake Tapper
arianna-huffington.summary: CNN anchor who drove to FCI Loretto to interview the imprisoned John Kiriakou — and who asked President Obama at a press conference why he had insisted on prosecuting a man who exposed a crime, a question Obama answered by walking away from the podium. Tapper's visit was the head of a media wave that began with a smuggled-out letter on the Huffington Post, and it became Kiriakou's protection inside; even a guard known as a psychopath left him alone rather than find CNN parked beside his car.

arianna-huffington.title: The open letter to Edward Snowden
arianna-huffington.summary: The letter John Kiriakou wrote from prison in 2013 to Edward Snowden, sent privately through a shared attorney and carrying three pieces of advice — hire the best national-security lawyers available, cultivate a base of support on Capitol Hill, and never under any circumstances talk to the FBI — which went viral and reached its addressee only because Arianna Huffington published it.

arkady-shevchenko.title: Gore Vidal
arkady-shevchenko.summary: American novelist and essayist; per John Kiriakou, a Sidwell Friends/St. Albans/Phillips Exeter alumnus who enlisted after Pearl Harbor rather than attend college, wrote the controversial 1948 novel The City and the Pillar, won a National Book Award in 1993, and was buried near his one lasting partner, Howard Austen, and his boyhood best friend, James Trimble, who was killed at Iwo Jima.

arkady-shevchenko.title: Joseph B. Chambers
arkady-shevchenko.summary: Civil War Medal of Honor recipient buried at Oak Park Cemetery in New Castle, Pennsylvania, whose grave John Kiriakou discovered as a child while looking for salamanders — sparking a lifelong interest in history.

arkady-shevchenko.title: New Castle, Pennsylvania
arkady-shevchenko.summary: John Kiriakou's home town, an hour north of Pittsburgh on the edge of Amish country — a rust-belt city of roughly 40,000 to 50,000 people when he was growing up and around 18,000 to 20,000 now, whose decline he measures by the arrival of DEA and ATF field offices. It is also where, aged eight or nine and hunting salamanders in Oak Park Cemetery, he found the grave of a Medal of Honor private and acquired the lifelong interest in cemeteries that became a book.

arkady-shevchenko.title: Remains of the Day (book)
arkady-shevchenko.summary: John Kiriakou's book, announced for publication by Simon and Schuster in March 2026, billed as a definitive guide to the historic cemeteries of Washington DC and the first in a planned series; the second installment will cover the Mafia graves of New York City.

arlington-cemetery-spies.title: Francis Gary Powers
arlington-cemetery-spies.summary: U-2 pilot whose 1960 shoot-down over the Soviet Union and subsequent capture the CIA initially denied any knowledge of, denying not only that he was CIA but that he was U.S. government at all, until trading him in a bridge-of-spies prisoner exchange. Buried at Arlington National Cemetery. Per John Kiriakou, after his U-2 career Powers ended up piloting a Los Angeles traffic helicopter, and was killed when it crashed.

arlington-cemetery-spies.title: Vernon Walters
arlington-cemetery-spies.summary: U.S. Army general who served as Deputy Director of the CIA, Ambassador to Germany, Ambassador to the United Nations, and as Nixon''s occasional secret envoy to foreign leaders. Per John Kiriakou — who met him at an early-career analysts'' dinner — Walters said the only time he was ever afraid for his safety was during a secret Nixon-ordered peace mission to Fidel Castro in Cuba, when it occurred to him that Castro could poison him and no one but Nixon would know he was there: ''I wouldn''t trust Nixon to call my wife.'' Then he looked at Castro and thought: ''I can take this scrawny son of a bitch.''

arlington-cemetery-spies.title: Remains of the Day Treasury Clerk Story
arlington-cemetery-spies.summary: John Kiriakou's account of finding the grave of an obscure Treasury Department clerk who, during the 1814 British burning of Washington, rescued the Declaration of Independence, Constitution, Bill of Rights, and Washington's military commission from the National Archives — and who, after later being deemed too difficult, was quietly transferred to the National Lighthouse Service, where out of boredom he invented the refractor light still used in American lighthouses today.

arlington-cemetery-spies.title: U.S. foreign policy process
arlington-cemetery-spies.summary: Three foreign-policy observations from John Kiriakou — the narrow legal basis for U.S. military presence abroad, which he says does not cover American special forces in Syria; the formal congressional travel-clearance process that undercuts Pentagon and White House claims of no advance knowledge of Nancy Pelosi's Taiwan trip; and the depth of U.S.-China economic interdependence that Kiriakou says makes antagonizing Beijing strategically unwise.

arlington-cemetery-spies.title: Torture as a recruiting tool
arlington-cemetery-spies.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that interrogations, drone strikes and targeted killings have generated more enemies than they removed — supported by the arithmetic he uses, from an al-Qaeda core of a few hundred in Afghanistan to an ISIS he numbered at some thirty-five thousand, by the fighters he personally captured who told him they had no quarrel with America until a drone killed their families, and by his answer to the charge that it was his disclosure rather than the programme that put Americans at risk.

arlington-cemetery-spies.title: CovertAction Magazine
arlington-cemetery-spies.summary: The muckraking outlet "exposing covert action since 1978" — and one of John Kiriakou's three long-running syndicated column homes, alongside Consortium News and ScheerPost. Kiriakou joined its podcast arm, the CovertAction Bulletin, appearing on panels with Peter Dale Scott and Pepe Escobar, and jokes that the Pentagon's browser-plugin credibility warnings — red check marks against outlets like CovertAction — are the surest sign it's worth reading.

arming-the-crazies.title: Chaos as the Israeli objective
arming-the-crazies.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer to whether Netanyahu''s government actually wanted an American invasion of Iran: what the Israelis want in Iran is what they got in Libya — chaos, civil war, and as many dead Iranians as possible.

arming-the-crazies.title: 2026 Iran war
arming-the-crazies.summary: The open-ended American and Israeli war against Iran that John Kiriakou tracked week by week on his own show — a conflict he says was sold as three weeks, ran into its fifth month, achieved every decapitation objective it set, and continued anyway. His grade for it is a D, and his forecast is a Truth Social post declaring victory while nothing changes.

arming-the-crazies.title: The Kenya mission
arming-the-crazies.summary: Asked in March 2026 whether he had ever run a mission in Africa, John Kiriakou answered that he had — one, in Kenya — and then declined to say anything further about it, adding that he was not certain he was permitted to confirm even that he had been in the country. It is one of the clearest instances in the corpus of him marking the edge of what he will disclose.

arming-the-crazies.title: United States–DRC relations
arming-the-crazies.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of why American policy toward the Democratic Republic of the Congo is quietly comfortable while the east of the country is in chaos: the United States buys as much Congolese rare earth metal as can be dug out of the ground, and the central government''s weakness against Rwanda is a problem Donald Trump claimed to have solved for the purposes of a Nobel Peace Prize case, with a peace Kiriakou says lasted a couple of weeks.

arming-the-crazies.title: Closing the Gulf embassies
arming-the-crazies.summary: John Kiriakou''s reading of the American decision, announced live on air on 3 March 2026, to close its embassies in Saudi Arabia and Kuwait: that in the whole of the first Gulf War no American embassy was closed except Kuwait''s own, whose diplomats were taken to Iraq as human shields, and that shutting two at once meant Washington had concluded the war was about to get very much worse.

arming-the-crazies.title: The east Mediterranean gas partnership
arming-the-crazies.summary: John Kiriakou''s explanation for why the Greek government is solidly pro-Israel while the Greek public is solidly anti-Israel: Cyprus sits on an ocean of natural gas, and the Greeks, Cypriots, Israelis and — to a lesser extent — Egyptians lift it together and share the money. The arrangement drives Turkey to distraction, and in his reading puts Greek–Turkish relations on track to get worse.

arnon-milchan.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
arnon-milchan.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

arnon-milchan.title: Israeli Nuclear Program
arnon-milchan.summary: Israel's widely assumed but officially unacknowledged nuclear arsenal; per John Kiriakou, the conventional wisdom within the CIA is that Israel possesses between 120 and 220 nuclear weapons, and the U.S. government's refusal to formally acknowledge this is driven by a specific legal obligation under the Glenn-Symington Act, which would require cutting off all foreign aid to any nuclear-armed country not party to the Non-Proliferation Treaty.

arnon-milchan.title: John Kerry
arnon-milchan.summary: U.S. Senator from Massachusetts; chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee during John Kiriakou's 2009 service as the committee's senior investigator; subsequently U.S. Secretary of State; characterized by Kiriakou as a coward who buckled under CIA pressure on the Dasht-i-Leili reopening and as personally fixated on his perceived theft of the Secretary of State position by Hillary Clinton; the famously thrown medals were duplicates purchased at the post exchange.

arnon-milchan.title: John Kiriakou
arnon-milchan.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

arnon-milchan.title: MOSSAD
arnon-milchan.summary: Israel's primary external intelligence service; characterized by John Kiriakou as universally hostile in his and his CIA colleagues' professional dealings with it ("never had a positive encounter with Mossad"); operates almost exclusively in the operational rather than analytical domain; the CIA is, per Kiriakou, categorically forbidden from spying on it.

arnon-milchan.title: Senate Foreign Relations Committee
arnon-milchan.summary: Kiriakou was senior investigator under John Kerry — and still held the post when his own federal prosecution came to a head in January 2012.

arrais-corporation.title: Denied areas
arrais-corporation.summary: The CIA term for countries so hostile and so heavily surveilled that ordinary operational movement is impossible — the Soviet Union, Cuba, Syria, and later Russia, China, North Korea and Iran — and the reason, in John Kiriakou's account, that officers heading to one get specialist briefings, eight-hour surveillance detection routes, and that the Agency has to fall back on liaison services instead of its own sources.

arrais-corporation.title: In-Q-Tel
arrais-corporation.summary: The CIA's openly acknowledged venture capital arm; provided Palantir Technologies its first $1.5 million in seed funding; in John Kiriakou's account the principal vehicle by which the agency finances private-sector development of technologies it intends to use.

arrais-corporation.title: John Brennan
arrais-corporation.summary: Former Director of the CIA; characterized in KiriPedia's source corpus as the principal architect of the agency's enhanced interrogation program and as having plotted against an elected President

arrais-corporation.title: Palantir Technologies
arrais-corporation.summary: U.S. data-analytics and intelligence-software company; received its first $1.5 million in seed funding from the CIA's In-Q-Tel venture-capital arm around 2002; characterized by John Kiriakou as functionally inseparable from the CIA in 2025, drawing the majority of its revenue from agency contracts and operating across DARPA, NSA, and the broader U.S. national-security apparatus.

arrais-corporation.title: Private Intelligence
arrais-corporation.summary: Post-CIA commercial intelligence work performed by John Kiriakou — both operational (surveillance, bribery, dossier-building for private clients) and analytical (paid forecasts for hedge funds, mutual funds, and a global mining company). Per Kiriakou, his clients ranged from a Cypriot billionaire investigating his daughter's fiancé to the ninth-largest hedge fund in the world.

arrais-corporation.title: The Analysis Corporation
arrais-corporation.summary: Arlington, Virginia–based [private intelligence firm](/wiki/private-intelligence); one of two companion entities (alongside Arrais Corporation) created as LLC pass-throughs for retired Senior Intelligence Service personnel; John Brennan was appointed its CEO in 2005.

aryan-brotherhood.title: The Italians at Loretto
aryan-brotherhood.summary: The mafia contingent at FCI Loretto — men with last names like Gambino, Bonanno, Lucchese, Genovese, DeCavalcante — who adopted John Kiriakou in his second year, largely because he hated the FBI as much as they did. The cast included the boss of the Gambino family (in on a dozen-plus murder counts, the man who replaced John Gotti), Pete the Bonanno captain across the hall who asked why he sat "with those Nazi retards," and a crooked guard on the payroll delivering pork loin and fresh mozzarella. When the FBI later came to Kiriakou's door asking him to inform on Pete, his answer was "get off my property."

aryan-brotherhood.title: The Nation of Islam at Loretto
aryan-brotherhood.summary: The largest Muslim faction at FCI Loretto — African American converts to the Nation of Islam — two of whom walked into John Kiriakou's cell in his first days holding their own newspaper, in which Louis Farrakhan had called him a hero of the Muslim people for opposing torture. They told him he would have no trouble with them; one declined the handshake he offered, on the ground that he does not shake hands with the white devil. The Aryans, meanwhile, had decided he was a CIA assassin who killed Muslims. Kiriakou kept his mouth shut and let both beliefs stand.

aryan-brotherhood.title: Bureau of Prisons
aryan-brotherhood.summary: The federal agency that ran John Kiriakou's incarceration — and one of his most persistent post-prison targets. The BOP overrode his judge's camp recommendation by deeming him "a threat to the public safety," threatened him with "diesel therapy" until 1,600 logged phone calls and letters from a dozen House members and two senators backed it off, and, per Kiriakou, functions as "an employment agency for unemployable semi-literate rural white men" and "a dumping ground for failed medical professionals" — an agency for which a prisoner's death is cheaper than his treatment.

aryan-brotherhood.title: Espionage Act
aryan-brotherhood.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

aryan-brotherhood.title: The rooftop double agent
aryan-brotherhood.summary: A 2001 operation in which John Kiriakou flew out monthly to impersonate a station chief in meetings with a recruited double agent, and, after the hostile service ordered the agent to kill him, frightened the man on a hotel roof rather than confronting him.

aryan-brotherhood.title: Prison tattoos
aryan-brotherhood.summary: Tattoos as John Kiriakou encountered them at FCI Loretto — the swastika-necked welcoming committee on his first day, the Lady Justice piece that made him laugh and then think, the constant pressure on him to get one, and his flat refusal to take a souvenir of the place.

asel-al-ghabandi.title: Iraqi invasion of Kuwait
asel-al-ghabandi.summary: John Kiriakou''s most detailed account of the intelligence process around the 1990 Iraqi invasion of Kuwait and its 1991 liberation. As a first-year CIA analyst on a ''training account'' covering Iraq, Kiriakou produced the June 30, 1990 warning paper for the White House; suggested calling the US Defense Attaché in Baghdad to drive to the border and report what he saw (the answer: ''Literally the entire Iraqi military is heading south''); briefed the August 2 Oval Office meeting with Bush; and later took a single phone call from General Colin Powell that led, eight hours later, to 47 cruise missiles striking the Iraqi Intelligence Service headquarters in Baghdad.

asel-al-ghabandi.title: 1993 Bush Kuwait assassination plot
asel-al-ghabandi.summary: Iraqi intelligence plot, foiled by Kuwaiti authorities, to assassinate former President George H. W. Bush during his post-liberation "victory lap" visit to Kuwait; the U.S. response, per John Kiriakou's first-person account of his telephone call with Chairman of the Joint Chiefs Colin Powell, was 47 cruise missiles fired into the Iraqi Intelligence Service headquarters in Baghdad eight hours later.

asel-al-ghabandi.title: Ahmed Chalabi
asel-al-ghabandi.summary: Iraqi exile and founder of the Iraqi National Congress; per John Kiriakou, a Shia-Kurdish con man who looted Petra Bank in Jordan of $36 million in the 1980s, was sentenced to death in absentia, was pardoned at CIA request, then pocketed $6 million in CIA seed funding for the INC and bought a Mayfair house in cash; later resurrected by Dick Cheney to feed the Pentagon fabricated WMD intelligence used to justify the 2003 invasion of Iraq.

asel-al-ghabandi.title: Ali Hassan al-Majid
asel-al-ghabandi.summary: Saddam Hussein cousin known as "Chemical Ali" and "the Butcher of Kurdistan"; per John Kiriakou, also briefly served as the Iraqi-installed governor of occupied Kuwait — "the Butcher of Kuwait" — and was engaged in the wholesale slaughter of Kurds in the north, Shia in the south, and Kuwaitis under occupation.

asel-al-ghabandi.title: April Glaspie
asel-al-ghabandi.summary: U.S. Ambassador to Iraq in the run-up to the 1990 invasion of Kuwait; per John Kiriakou, delivered to Saddam Hussein — on a NODIS cable from Secretary of State James Baker — the line that the United States took no position on Arab-Arab border disputes, which Saddam is widely held to have read as a green light to invade. Kiriakou, who was in the CIA operations center the night her reporting cable came back, holds that she got a bum rap.

asel-al-ghabandi.title: Gerald Bull
asel-al-ghabandi.summary: British inventor of the "big gun" — a barrel so large it had to be leaned against a mountain — first offered to Israel and rejected, then sold to Iraq under Saddam Hussein; assassinated by Mossad in Brussels once Iraqi engineers solved the cracking problem with a barrel-smoothing sleeve nicknamed "the condom," after which the Israelis also bombed the gun itself.

asian-fuel-reserves-2026.title: 2026 Iran war economic shock
asian-fuel-reserves-2026.summary: John Kiriakou''s running assessment of the economic damage from the 2026 Iran war — an oil shock he says already exceeds both 1970s shocks combined, a natural-gas shock worse than the Nord Stream destruction, and a chokepoint problem that runs through fertilizer as much as fuel, since 65% of the world''s supply must transit the Strait of Hormuz. His summary: "This is an economic slowdown of choice."

asian-fuel-reserves-2026.title: Iranian oil sanctions relief, 2026
asian-fuel-reserves-2026.summary: The American decision, during the war it was fighting against Iran, to lift sanctions on Iranian oil at sea in order to hold prices down. John Kiriakou pairs it with the moment an Indian ship paid Iran for oil in yuan and was waved through — after which, he says, the sanctions came off.

asian-fuel-reserves-2026.title: Strait of Hormuz
asian-fuel-reserves-2026.summary: The shipping chokepoint at the mouth of the Persian Gulf, and the centre of gravity of the 2026 Iran war in John Kiriakou''s account — a strait whose only navigable deep water lies on the Iranian side of the maritime border, closed not by Iran''s aggression but, as he insists, by the American and Israeli attack that provoked it: "The Strait of Hormuz was open. We''re the ones that forced the closure."

asian-fuel-reserves-2026.title: Air wars are overrated
asian-fuel-reserves-2026.summary: John Kiriakou''s summary judgement on the 2026 Iran and Lebanon campaigns, delivered as the meta-headline of the whole war: air power flattened Gaza without destroying Hamas, is bogging down against Hezbollah, and cannot produce the outcome the war requires.

asian-fuel-reserves-2026.title: The Ras Laffan strike
asian-fuel-reserves-2026.summary: The Iranian attack on Qatar's Ras Laffan liquefied natural gas facilities during the 2026 war, which John Kiriakou discussed as taking seventeen per cent of Qatari export capacity offline for an estimated three to five years — one of the strikes that drove oil past a hundred dollars a barrel.

asked-about-my-children.title: The bowl of dates
asked-about-my-children.summary: The detail John Kiriakou uses to compress his argument about interrogation: that the intelligence the CIA''s contractors reported as the fruit of waterboarding had in fact been obtained by an FBI agent who offered Abu Zubaydah a bowl of dates.

asked-about-my-children.title: College tuition as an inducement
asked-about-my-children.summary: The recruitment inducement John Kiriakou describes as among the CIA's most effective — enrolling a source's child at any American university and paying for it — and the arrangements with universities and corporations he says make it possible.

asked-about-my-children.title: The autographed basketball
asked-about-my-children.summary: A recruitment John Kiriakou has cited as proof that an agent''s price is not always money: a source who loved the Chicago Bulls, an ordinary basketball bought from the NBA online store with a forged provenance involving Michael Jordan, and an acrylic display box.

asked-about-my-children.title: Curtailment cables
asked-about-my-children.summary: The career-ending requests John Kiriakou says he read coming back from the CIA's black sites — officers, doctors, psychologists and nurses asking to end their tours early rather than continue to take part in the interrogation programme — and his conclusion that if that many people were objecting in classified channels, someone would surely go public.

asked-about-my-children.title: The Faisalabad cash run
asked-about-my-children.summary: The drive John Kiriakou made to Faisalabad, Pakistan roughly two weeks before the capture of Abu Zubaydah, with two million dollars in cash in two duffel bags in the van, and the exchange with his colleague about why anyone would cheat the CIA out of twenty dollars.

asked-about-my-children.title: The hooding dispute
asked-about-my-children.summary: The argument John Kiriakou says he had with a subordinate at a CIA safe house in Pakistan on the night of the Abu Zubaydah raid, over hoods placed on captured prisoners; both men reported each other to headquarters, and Kiriakou was the one reprimanded.

assange-and-solitary-confinement.title: "Ecuador is open for business"
assange-and-solitary-confinement.summary: The Wall Street Journal headline John Kiriakou says appeared the day after he hand-delivered a letter to Ecuador's ambassador in Washington asking that Julian Assange's internet access be restored, and which made him fear Assange was about to be used as a bargaining chip.

assange-and-solitary-confinement.title: The Guardian smear series
assange-and-solitary-confinement.summary: The run of articles about Julian Assange that John Kiriakou characterised in 2018 as a pile-on based on anonymous sources leaking intelligence-agency material, and which he read as a formal psychological operation intended to weaken Assange rather than as journalism.

assange-and-solitary-confinement.title: "Embrace it and keep telling it"
assange-and-solitary-confinement.summary: The advice John Kiriakou says he was given days after his arrest — that he could not hide from the prosecution but had to embrace it, and had to keep telling his side of the story until it became the side of record, because the government would eventually move on to its next target.

assange-and-solitary-confinement.title: Whistleblowers and suicide
assange-and-solitary-confinement.summary: John Kiriakou's claim, drawn from conversations with some fifty whistleblowers, that every one of them considered suicide in the early stage of their case — and his own account of the family vigil that kept him from the garage.

assange-and-solitary-confinement.title: Julian Assange
assange-and-solitary-confinement.summary: Kiriakou — a 15-year friend and former WikiLeaks board member — on why Assange is a publisher owed a journalist's immunity, and a political prisoner.

assange-and-solitary-confinement.title: Seventy-two denied motions
assange-and-solitary-confinement.summary: The count John Kiriakou gives of the pretrial motions filed in his case and denied by Judge Leonie Brinkema — seventy-two denied and none granted — which he offers as the mechanism by which a national security defendant in the Eastern District of Virginia is prevented from mounting a defence at all.

assange-and-the-european-court-of-human-.title: Sealing the courtroom
assange-and-the-european-court-of-human-.summary: The physical measures John Kiriakou describes as accompanying a classified-information trial: plastic sheeting and duct tape over the windows so lasers cannot read the vibrations, white noise in the vestibule, and the clearing of everyone but the judge, jury, bailiff, clerk, lawyers and defendant.

assange-and-the-european-court-of-human-.title: The jury consultant's advice
assange-and-the-european-court-of-human-.summary: What John Kiriakou''s jury consultant told him about a national security trial in the Eastern District of Virginia: that in any other district in America he would say fight and win, but in that one, "buddy, you don''t have a prayer. Take the deal."

assange-and-the-european-court-of-human-.title: The swimming pool substitution
assange-and-the-european-court-of-human-.summary: John Kiriakou''s illustration of how classified words are handled at trial: prosecutors and judge agree in advance to replace them with harmless unclassified substitutes, so that "Vault 7" becomes "swimming pool" — and the jury, told the real words are too secret for their ears, concludes the defendant must be guilty.

assange-and-the-european-court-of-human-.title: Pan Quake
assange-and-the-european-court-of-human-.summary: An open-source, nonprofit, advertising-free social media platform hosted in Iceland on geothermal power and built on a content blockchain, conceived by Suzie Dawson and promoted by John Kiriakou as a brand ambassador from 2021. Kiriakou described its offshore incorporation and subscription model as deliberate defences against the attacks he expected from the CIA and NSA, and later said its Icelandic bank account was frozen at the FBI's request over the platform's association with Julian Assange supporters.

assange-and-the-european-court-of-human-.title: The Istanbul peace talks
assange-and-the-european-court-of-human-.summary: The early Russia–Ukraine negotiations in Istanbul that John Kiriakou says lasted three days and were never revived — talks the United States neither attended nor encouraged the Ukrainians to attend, and after which, he notes, the words "peace talks" disappeared from American discourse.

assange-and-the-european-court-of-human-.title: The solitary confinement precedents
assange-and-the-european-court-of-human-.summary: The legal argument John Kiriakou made repeatedly between 2020 and 2022 in defence of Julian Assange, and revived in 2025 for the Australian pilot Daniel Duggan — that no extradition to the United States can succeed once a court is asked to find that American solitary confinement is not torture, a proposition already contradicted by the United Nations, by the United States' own federal torture statute, and by a line of British and European rulings blocking extraditions on exactly that ground.

assange-plea-deal.title: Barry Pollock
assange-plea-deal.summary: Washington defense attorney who represented Julian Assange; John Kiriakou credits Pollock with negotiating the deal that let Assange be processed in Saipan — the U.S. district closest to Australia — rather than be brought to Virginia.

assange-plea-deal.title: Espionage Act
assange-plea-deal.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

assange-plea-deal.title: Julian Assange
assange-plea-deal.summary: Kiriakou — a 15-year friend and former WikiLeaks board member — on why Assange is a publisher owed a journalist's immunity, and a political prisoner.

assange-plea-deal.title: Abu Zubaydah
assange-plea-deal.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

assange-plea-deal.title: Edward Snowden
assange-plea-deal.summary: Former NSA contractor who in 2013 disclosed the scope of U.S. [mass surveillance](/wiki/mass-surveillance), including the Section 702 collection program. Per John Kiriakou — who counts Snowden among the small group of national-security whistleblowers prosecuted under the Espionage Act — Snowden was ''stuck between two awful slippery slopes'': breaking his oath and chain of command on one side, and on the other catching something ''cut and dry against the Constitution'' that no one would act on. Kiriakou notes Snowden could not use his chain of command (as Kiriakou could not, his own chain being Jose Rodriguez), and that Judge Leonie Brinkema had reserved the Snowden case for herself before he fled the country.

assange-plea-deal.title: George Tenet
assange-plea-deal.summary: Director of Central Intelligence from 1997 to 2004, spanning the September 11 attacks and the early enhanced-interrogation program; identified by John Kiriakou as John Brennan's institutional patron at the agency; the figure who ordered the Five Eyes intelligence services to "open the files" to each other in the early 2000s.

assassination-approval-process.title: Maduro Capture
assassination-approval-process.summary: CIA-driven nighttime operation in which a team of Delta Force commandos entered Venezuela and removed Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro and his wife from their beds. Per John Kiriakou, the key enabling intelligence — per a New York Times account he cited — came from a CIA asset inside Maduro''s presidential palace who called when Maduro went to sleep: ''He''s sound asleep. If you''re going to do it, do it now.'' At least eighty people were killed in the operation, including approximately thirty-five Cubans. Kiriakou compares it to the 1989 capture of Manuel Noriega, in which US forces blasted death metal at the Vatican Embassy until Noriega was asked to leave.

assassination-approval-process.title: The four requirements of a coup
assassination-approval-process.summary: The checklist John Kiriakou says is taught at West Point for overthrowing a government — the presidential palace and the leader, the broadcast stations, the capital's major intersections, and the support of the military — which he uses to argue that regime change in Venezuela cannot work, because the fourth item belongs to the incumbent.

assassination-approval-process.title: Venezuela regime change (2026)
assassination-approval-process.summary: John Kiriakou''s assessment of the American operation that removed Venezuela''s president — a clear violation of international law, since none of the three recognised grounds for one state attacking another applied, but not a violation of US law, which since 1985 has expressly permitted special forces to cross borders and seize people for trial. His reluctant conclusion at the time: "as much as I hate admitting it, this regime change seems to be working right now."

assassination-approval-process.title: Hamid Karzai
assassination-approval-process.summary: The president installed in Afghanistan after the American invasion, whom John Kiriakou uses as the standing illustration of what occupation actually buys: after twenty years and more than a trillion dollars, Karzai was ''little more than the mayor of Kabul'' — and did not control all of Kabul either. The line began as a joke among Senate Foreign Relations Committee staff, and Kiriakou used it to Senator John Kerry''s face ten years into the war.

assassination-approval-process.title: Venezuela Boat Strikes
assassination-approval-process.summary: September 2025 U.S. military strike on a boat in the Caribbean that killed 11 people the White House called drug traffickers; John Kiriakou calls it piracy on the high seas followed by mass murder, arguing the victims were never charged with a crime and that the boat's unusual passenger count undercuts the drug-trafficking story.

assassination-approval-process.title: The regime change approval process
assassination-approval-process.summary: John Kiriakou's step-by-step account of how a proposal to overthrow a foreign government travels through the United States government — beginning as a memo written at an officer's own desk, cleared by lawyers at the Justice Department and the National Security Council, signed by the president as an executive order, and ending in a safe on the seventh floor at CIA headquarters while the order itself goes to the Pentagon.

asset-acquisition-cycle.title: Brett McGurk
