brad-birkenfeld.summary: The Swedish programmer and friend of Julian Assange arrested in Ecuador in 2019 on the order of President Lenín Moreno, whose open-ended detention John Kiriakou treats as the collateral consequence of the same government's decision to hand Assange to the British.

brad-birkenfeld.title: Sentencing enhancements
brad-birkenfeld.summary: John Kiriakou''s explanation of how a nine-year federal offence becomes a forty-year sentence: the sentencing table''s forty offence levels and seven criminal-history columns, and the enhancements stacked on top of a base level — for terrorism, for hacking, and, in the case he considers most perverse, for having pleaded not guilty and lost.

brad-birkenfeld.title: The open letter to Edward Snowden
brad-birkenfeld.summary: The letter John Kiriakou wrote from prison in 2013 to Edward Snowden, sent privately through a shared attorney and carrying three pieces of advice — hire the best national-security lawyers available, cultivate a base of support on Capitol Hill, and never under any circumstances talk to the FBI — which went viral and reached its addressee only because Arianna Huffington published it.

brad-birkenfeld.title: The Senate WikiLeaks ban
brad-birkenfeld.summary: The instruction John Kiriakou watched the Senate security officer deliver in person to all one hundred senators and every committee after the WikiLeaks cables were published — that opening the material on a Senate computer would be the crime of unauthorized access to classified information, and that anyone who did so would be prosecuted.

breaking-the-nuclear-taboo.title: Netanyahu's nuclear threat to Trump
breaking-the-nuclear-taboo.summary: John Kiriakou's account, sourced to friends in the White House and the administration, that Donald Trump agreed to bomb Iran because Benjamin Netanyahu threatened to use nuclear weapons against Iran if the United States did not act. Kiriakou presents it as the reason a request every previous president refused was finally granted.

breaking-the-nuclear-taboo.title: Central Intelligence Agency
breaking-the-nuclear-taboo.summary: U.S. foreign intelligence service; John Kiriakou's employer from 1990 to 2004 and the central institution of KiriPedia

breaking-the-nuclear-taboo.title: John Kiriakou
breaking-the-nuclear-taboo.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

breaking-the-nuclear-taboo.title: AIPAC
breaking-the-nuclear-taboo.summary: The American Israel Public Affairs Committee — the U.S. political organization that, in John Kiriakou's framing, ought to be registered as a foreign-lobbying entity but is not, and that wields decisive electoral power against U.S. elected officials who express support for Palestinian human rights.

breaking-the-nuclear-taboo.title: Bill Richardson
breaking-the-nuclear-taboo.summary: U.S. Congressman, Ambassador to the United Nations, Secretary of Energy, and Governor of New Mexico; became friends with John Kiriakou at McClarty Associates; promised Secretary of State in exchange for endorsing Barack Obama in the 2008 Democratic primary; ultimately offered Commerce instead, then CIA director informally, before withdrawing his Commerce nomination.

breaking-the-nuclear-taboo.title: Brian Ross
breaking-the-nuclear-taboo.summary: American investigative journalist and seven-time Emmy Award winner who was a prominent reporter at ABC News when, in December 2007, he conducted the on-camera interview with John Kiriakou that produced the first public confirmation by a U.S. official that the CIA waterboarded prisoners. Per Kiriakou, Ross called him out of the blue with the assertion that a source said Kiriakou had personally tortured Abu Zubaydah; Kiriakou's decision to give the interview anyway — driven by the conclusion that 'Brian Ross's source is at the White House and they're going to pin this on me' — became the pivot point of his entire post-CIA life.

brett-mcgurk.title: CIA adultery culture
brett-mcgurk.summary: John Kiriakou's recurring characterization of the CIA officer corps as riddled with adultery and casual sex — which he frames not as gossip but as a systemic counterintelligence vulnerability that makes officers easy to recruit.

brett-mcgurk.title: Alexa
brett-mcgurk.summary: Per John Kiriakou, Amazon''s Alexa smart speaker reports directly to the NSA — and he owns one anyway. The device recurs across his interviews as the standing example of the surveillance trade-off in modern smart-home technology, and of his own negotiated exception to it: one speaker, in one room, against the advice of every intelligence officer he has ever known.

brett-mcgurk.title: Asset acquisition cycle
brett-mcgurk.summary: The four-step process — spot, assess, develop, recruit — taught as the first lesson of CIA case officer training

brett-mcgurk.title: Barack Obama
brett-mcgurk.summary: 44th U.S. president; in John Kiriakou's account, Obama publicly recounted refusing Benjamin Netanyahu's demand to bomb Iran and calling Israel's threat to use nuclear weapons a bluff — a bluff Kiriakou says Donald Trump later believed.

brett-mcgurk.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
brett-mcgurk.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

brett-mcgurk.title: Caspar Weinberger
brett-mcgurk.summary: U.S. Secretary of Defense under Ronald Reagan; John Kiriakou cites Weinberger's assessment that Jonathan Pollard's espionage caused "grave damage" — the highest category of harm — to U.S. national security.

brian-kelley.title: Robert Hanssen
brian-kelley.summary: FBI counterintelligence chief and Soviet/Russian mole; framed CIA counterintelligence chief Brian Kelley as the source of compromised assets — leading the FBI to surveil Kelly for a year and a half and threaten his family with the death penalty — before Hanssen himself was identified as the actual traitor.

brian-kelley.title: Eric O'Neill
brian-kelley.summary: Former FBI analyst placed as Robert Hanssen's nominal assistant in the final months of the FBI's mole investigation; his role was to observe Hanssen and detect tradecraft slip-ups that would confirm Hanssen as the mole. After Hanssen's arrest, O'Neill resigned from the FBI, citing the stress of the operation. Subject of the 2007 film Breach.

brian-kelley.title: Harold James Nicholson
brian-kelley.summary: Former CIA Station Chief, Singapore; the third major modern CIA mole for the Russians after Aldrich Ames and Robert Hanssen. Per John Kiriakou, Nicholson was a senior officer at the CIA Counterterrorism Center during Kiriakou's tenure there. Sentenced to 31 years and seven months in 1997. While in prison, attempted to recruit his own son to act as a courier between him and the Russian intelligence service so his espionage payments could continue to compound for his eventual release — and was caught when his son walked up to the Russian embassy in Washington under FBI surveillance.

brian-kelley.title: Cuban double agents
brian-kelley.summary: John Kiriakou's assessment of Cuban intelligence as one of the best services on the planet, defensive in nature and trained by the KGB, and his flat claim — repeated across several tellings — that the CIA has never recruited a Cuban who did not turn out to be working for Havana all along.

brian-kelley.title: Afghan heroin policy
brian-kelley.summary: The post-2001 U.S. policy in Afghanistan of protecting, and per John Kiriakou actively encouraging, the cultivation of heroin poppy. Under the Taliban in 2000 Afghanistan produced 0% of the world's heroin; by 2009 under American occupation it produced 93%. Per a DEA officer Kiriakou consulted with on the policy paper he was preparing for Senator Kerry, the strategic rationale was that nearly all of the heroin flowed to Iran and Russia, addiction in those countries was considered desirable as a long-run societal weakener, and the same logic now operates in reverse with Chinese fentanyl flowing into the United States.

brian-kelley.title: Ahmed Khatib
brian-kelley.summary: Iraqi-installed occupation governor of Kuwait announced on August 2, 1990, hours after the invasion; medical doctor trained at the American University of Beirut whose mother had been a Sudanese slave in the Kuwaiti royal household; college roommate of George Habash and co-founder of the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine.

brian-ross.title: Kiriakou's Omega Seamaster
brian-ross.summary: The wristwatch John Kiriakou bought himself in the Athens duty-free the day after Christmas 1999, on his way to recruit an asset in another European country, at the end of a Christmas that had gone badly in a failing first marriage.

brian-ross.title: The CIA–State Department cover agreement
brian-ross.summary: The standing arrangement under which CIA officers serve abroad under State Department cover. As a senior investigator for the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, John Kiriakou was told the agency was misusing the agreement to place officers from the torture program under diplomatic cover so that publishing their names would expose journalists to the Intelligence Identities Protection Act. His written query, sent over Senator John Kerry''s signature, came back classified above his own clearance.

brian-ross.title: The Jerusalem bluff
brian-ross.summary: An interrogation in Pakistan in 2002 in which John Kiriakou, faced with a senior al-Qaeda prisoner working through the organisation's own resistance training, threatened to send him to Jerusalem rather than Guantánamo. Kiriakou supplied the account to explain a clip of the exchange circulating without its context.

brian-ross.title: The Bolivian visa line
brian-ross.summary: The CIA's interrogation of John Kiriakou's wife, then a serving senior officer, over a single sentence in a Los Angeles Times op-ed her husband had written and had already cleared through the agency's own publications review board. Told the piece was cleared, the security officer replied that one line in it was top secret — the statement that Iranians no longer needed visas to travel to Bolivia. Kiriakou had taken it off the Bolivian foreign ministry's website.

brian-ross.title: The woman escorted from the White House
brian-ross.summary: Before John Kiriakou spoke to ABC News, someone else had already blown the whistle on the CIA's secret prisons — a woman at the White House whom he respected deeply, who was escorted out of the building, stripped of her badge and told never to come back, and who has always insisted it was not her.

brian-ross.title: Corporate competitive intelligence
brian-ross.summary: The private-sector discipline John Kiriakou entered on leaving the CIA in 2004: collecting human-source intelligence on rival firms for a big-four accountancy. He was the fourth CIA officer Deloitte had hired into a group that paired former intelligence collectors with corporate research analysts, and his requirements were a rival''s pricing models, its discount structure, and which of its top-producing partners were unhappy enough to be poached. All the major firms, he says, run the same operation against each other.

british-bases-in-cyprus.title: Akrotiri Village Evacuation
british-bases-in-cyprus.summary: Kiriakou says the drone that hit Britain's Akrotiri base in Cyprus was likely an Israeli operation, staged and then falsely blamed on Iran.

british-bases-in-cyprus.title: Aldrich Ames
british-bases-in-cyprus.summary: Senior CIA officer — a GS-15 who rose to chief of counterintelligence for the Soviet branch — who spied for the KGB for nine years. Per John Kiriakou, Ames walked into the Soviet embassy in Washington in April 1985 and sold the identities of two CIA-recruited double agents for $50,000 to clear a debt run up by his second marriage; both were executed. He went on to identify more than thirty agents, compromise over a hundred clandestine operations, cause at least twelve deaths and take more than $2 million, while being known throughout the agency as a daily drunk and promoted at every turn. The KGB protected him with a decoy mole hunt; analyst Sandy Grimes caught him by matching his handler meetings to his bank deposits.

british-bases-in-cyprus.title: John Kiriakou
british-bases-in-cyprus.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

british-bases-in-cyprus.title: The Green Line in Nicosia
british-bases-in-cyprus.summary: The division of Nicosia between the Republic of Cyprus and the Turkish-occupied north, which John Kiriakou toured in July 2026 and described as maintained through deliberate humiliation rather than any interest in settlement.

british-bases-in-cyprus.title: Abu Nidal Organization
british-bases-in-cyprus.summary: Per John Kiriakou, the CIA destroyed the Abu Nidal Organization from within by exploiting Abu Nidal''s pathological paranoia: rather than recruiting members (impossible given the group''s extreme anti-American orientation), the agency planted false signals that various members were already cooperating with US intelligence. Members began killing each other one by one. Kiriakou: ''Next thing you know, they''ve all killed each other and the only one left is Abu Nidal.'' He also disbelieves the official heart-attack cause of Abu Nidal''s death, attributing it to a Saddam Hussein ''control'' decision.

british-bases-in-cyprus.title: Bojinka plot
british-bases-in-cyprus.summary: 1996 Khalid Sheikh Mohammed–planned operation, prepared in a Manila, Philippines apartment, to hijack as many as fourteen Boeing 747s and crash them into buildings along the U.S. West Coast; disrupted only by accident, when a cleaning lady let herself into the apartment while the planner was out, recognized the materials laid out as a terrorist plot, and called the police — who alerted Filipino intelligence and, in turn, the CIA. The plot's architect was known to U.S. intelligence for the next six years only by the alias "Mukhtar," his true identity as Khalid Sheikh Mohammed surfacing only when Abu Zubaydah named him to FBI agent Ali Soufan in 2002.

bruce-fein.title: Jared Kushner
bruce-fein.summary: Donald Trump's son-in-law and senior adviser during the first Trump administration, and the first person inside the White House to open a channel on John Kiriakou's pardon. After Trump saw Kiriakou on Tucker Carlson's show, Kushner's attorney called Kiriakou's attorney Bruce Fein; the meeting that followed produced a request for a one-page paper — three-quarters of it Kiriakou's story, the last quarter an argument for how pardoning him would help Trump get re-elected — after which Kiriakou never heard back.

bruce-fein.title: Rudy Giuliani
bruce-fein.summary: Former U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of New York and Mayor of New York City; in 2018 attempted to extort $2 million from John Kiriakou in exchange for arranging a presidential pardon from President Trump; the attempt was reported to the New York Times by Kiriakou himself and corroborated by Giuliani's then-aide Noelle Dunphy after Giuliani sexually harassed her.

bruce-fein.title: John Kiriakou
bruce-fein.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

bruce-fein.title: Bureau of Prisons
bruce-fein.summary: The federal agency that ran John Kiriakou's incarceration — and one of his most persistent post-prison targets. The BOP overrode his judge's camp recommendation by deeming him "a threat to the public safety," threatened him with "diesel therapy" until 1,600 logged phone calls and letters from a dozen House members and two senators backed it off, and, per Kiriakou, functions as "an employment agency for unemployable semi-literate rural white men" and "a dumping ground for failed medical professionals" — an agency for which a prisoner's death is cheaper than his treatment.

bruce-fein.title: Central Intelligence Agency
bruce-fein.summary: U.S. foreign intelligence service; John Kiriakou's employer from 1990 to 2004 and the central institution of KiriPedia

bruce-fein.title: Groupthink at the CIA
bruce-fein.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the institutional conformity he says has made the CIA wrong about nearly every major international development since its creation — a failure he attributes to analysts agreeing with one another around a conference table while invoking red-team and outside-the-box vocabulary that changes nothing. He and his attorney Bruce Fein discussed writing a book about it.

bruno-jordan-operation.title: The Jordanian intelligence service
bruno-jordan-operation.summary: The service John Kiriakou calls one of the best in the world and arguably the best in the Middle East — good, in his account, out of necessity: half of Jordan''s population is Palestinian, Black September once fought on the steps of the palace, and the survival of the monarchy depends on having infiltrated every faction in the country.

bruno-jordan-operation.title: Central Intelligence Agency
bruno-jordan-operation.summary: U.S. foreign intelligence service; John Kiriakou's employer from 1990 to 2004 and the central institution of KiriPedia

bruno-jordan-operation.title: The Directorate of Science and Technology
bruno-jordan-operation.summary: One of the CIA's four directorates, which in John Kiriakou's time was an afterthought responsible for disguises and briefcases with hidden compartments, and which he says now works with Palantir, Amazon, Nvidia and Elon Musk's companies on work closer to DARPA's than to anything the agency did in the past.

bruno-jordan-operation.title: Executive Order 12333
bruno-jordan-operation.summary: The U.S. presidential directive — in its post-9/11 amended form — that grants the CIA the legal authority to kill any individual anywhere in the world deemed by the agency to pose a "clear and present danger" to the United States; the legal foundation underlying both CIA paramilitary operations and the agency's contractor relationships including with Blackwater.

bruno-jordan-operation.title: Kiriakou's acting career
bruno-jordan-operation.summary: The film role John Kiriakou took in 2025 after Tyrel Ventura wrote a part for him — a former CIA officer running a billionaire's security detail — which he shot in Mexico for a month and which made him, at sixty-odd, a member of the Screen Actors Guild.

bruno-jordan-operation.title: MOSSAD
bruno-jordan-operation.summary: Israel's primary external intelligence service; characterized by John Kiriakou as universally hostile in his and his CIA colleagues' professional dealings with it ("never had a positive encounter with Mossad"); operates almost exclusively in the operational rather than analytical domain; the CIA is, per Kiriakou, categorically forbidden from spying on it.

bulldozing-the-olive-orchards.title: The coffee with the Jordanian intern
bulldozing-the-olive-orchards.summary: A morning meeting John Kiriakou took with a young intern from the Jordanian embassy who had found him on LinkedIn — and which he credits with reminding him that Palestinians are not a monolith, a point he says pro-Palestinian Westerners in particular tend to get wrong.

bulldozing-the-olive-orchards.title: The three pro-Israel countries
bulldozing-the-olive-orchards.summary: A global opinion poll John Kiriakou reported in August 2025 which, on his account, found only three countries with majority pro-Israel populations — Israel, the United States, and, to his own bafflement, Nigeria — with Turkey the most anti-Israel country outside the Middle East and Greece at 74 per cent against.

bulldozing-the-olive-orchards.title: The New Castle News
bulldozing-the-olive-orchards.summary: The Pennsylvania local paper John Kiriakou says he tries to scan every day and can no longer afford — $250 a year for a sixteen-page paper with no Wednesday or Sunday edition, edited by a 28-year-old, in a region he describes as a news desert.

bulldozing-the-olive-orchards.title: The twenty-thousand-dollar tweet
bulldozing-the-olive-orchards.summary: John Kiriakou's account of asking Jeanine Pirro for help with a pardon and being quoted $20,000 by her assistant — for a tweet. He refused, and says he was never invited back on her programme.

bulldozing-the-olive-orchards.title: The witness letter
bulldozing-the-olive-orchards.summary: A letter John Kiriakou received in August 2025 informing him that he would be called as a witness in Noelle Dunphy's defamation case against Rudy Giuliani — a consequence, he says, of having told the New York Times that Giuliani's people tried to squeeze $2 million out of him for a pardon.

bulldozing-the-olive-orchards.title: The Las Vegas case
bulldozing-the-olive-orchards.summary: John Kiriakou's scepticism about the Justice Department's claim that it played no role in a Las Vegas child-exploitation case involving an Israeli suspect who left the country — on the ground that electronic images and electronic communications would have made the matter federal.

bureau-of-prisons-advisory-board.title: Abu Zubaydah
bureau-of-prisons-advisory-board.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

bureau-of-prisons-advisory-board.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
bureau-of-prisons-advisory-board.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

bureau-of-prisons-advisory-board.title: The false volunteer
bureau-of-prisons-advisory-board.summary: A walk-in at an American embassy who claimed access to a high-priority target, was placed under surveillance and found to be a restaurant dishwasher, and whom John Kiriakou deliberately intimidated into never approaching an American embassy again.

bureau-of-prisons-advisory-board.title: Kiriakou's podcast breakthrough
bureau-of-prisons-advisory-board.summary: The sequence by which John Kiriakou went from saying yes to every podcast request, including from teenagers, to appearances with the largest hosts in the world — a rise he attributes to three friends' shows triggering an algorithm in October 2024.

bureau-of-prisons-advisory-board.title: Spy films John Kiriakou considers accurate
bureau-of-prisons-advisory-board.summary: Kiriakou's assessment of which espionage films get it right — Argo, The Recruit and Bridge of Spies — and his flat rejection of the action genre's premises, including the hidden weapons stash.

bureau-of-prisons-advisory-board.title: Origin of the Kiriakou name
bureau-of-prisons-advisory-board.summary: The Kiriakou surname originates in a clerical error at a Rhodes courthouse, where John Kiriakou's great-great-grandfather, arrested for stealing a potato while starving, gave a patronymic that was written down as his family name and never corrected.

bureau-of-prisons.title: Nick Bryant
bureau-of-prisons.summary: Investigative journalist, activist and co-founder of Epstein Justice, author of The Franklin Scandal, and a repeat guest on John Kiriakou's programme, where Kiriakou describes him as knowing the Epstein case better than anybody else in America.

bureau-of-prisons.title: Public safety factor
bureau-of-prisons.summary: The Bureau of Prisons classification that barred Kiriakou from a minimum-security camp by rating him as dangerous as a murderer, applied over the objections of both his sentencing judge and the prosecutor who convicted him.

bureau-of-prisons.title: The Taliban spokesman setup
bureau-of-prisons.summary: Kiriakou's account of a prisoner transferred into FCI Loretto for five days who presented himself as the Taliban's American spokesman, while a guard photographed the encounter from the treeline — an attempt, in his telling, to manufacture a second case against him.

bureau-of-prisons.title: Witness K case
bureau-of-prisons.summary: Australian intelligence scandal in which a former ASIS officer known as Witness K exposed Australia's bugging of the East Timorese cabinet during oil and gas revenue negotiations; his lawyer, Bernard Collaery, describes the ASIO raids on both their homes and offices as paralleling the FBI's raid on John Kiriakou.

bureau-of-prisons.title: Four deaths at Loretto
bureau-of-prisons.summary: John Kiriakou's tally of the prisoners who died during his twenty-three months at FCI Loretto — four, all of preventable illness, two of heart attacks and two of cancer — and his account of one of them, a man he ate with daily who was given Tylenol for months before an outside x-ray found stage four spinal cancer.

bureau-of-prisons.title: Jim Moran
bureau-of-prisons.summary: Twelve-term Democratic congressman from Northern Virginia and John Kiriakou's own representative, who took the floor of the House to call for his release and a presidential pardon, and wrote twice to the director of the Bureau of Prisons asking that his constituent receive halfway-house time. In Kiriakou's account he was one of only a handful of elected officials willing to help at all.

burn-notice.title: Petra Bank
burn-notice.summary: Jordan-based bank founded by Ahmed Chalabi and used by the entire Iraqi refugee community in Jordan; per John Kiriakou, looted of $36 million in a single night when Chalabi transferred every dollar to secret accounts abroad and fled to Syria in the trunk of his secretary's car — bankrupting every Iraqi in the country, driving some to suicide, and earning a death sentence the CIA later had lifted so he could front the Iraqi opposition.

burn-notice.title: Spy films and television on screen
burn-notice.summary: John Kiriakou's scene-by-scene verdicts on how spy films and television handle real tradecraft — what they get right (static surveillance from upper floors, hostile operational meetings, exchanges of bona fides, breaking into offices), what they invent (silent helicopters, high-speed submersibles, Batcaves, gadgets that cannot be bought), and the shows he says commit felonies on screen. He opens with why CIA officers watch them at all — *"not because they love the CIA movies, but because they love to criticize them."*

burn-notice.title: Zero Dark Thirty
burn-notice.summary: 2012 film dramatizing the CIA hunt for Osama bin Laden, criticized on release for suggesting torture produced the intelligence that led to his capture. John Kiriakou surveys the mixed critical reception — praise from Time and the New Yorker for its craft, condemnation from journalist Michael Wolff and director Kathryn Bigelow's critics for what they called pro-torture propaganda — and notes his friend Senator John McCain said the film left him "sick... because it is wrong."

burn-notice.title: ''Once CIA, always CIA''
burn-notice.summary: The comment-section accusation John Kiriakou says angers him more than any other — that no one who has served in the CIA ever really leaves it, and that whistleblowers are therefore still working for the agency. He calls it "the most intellectually lazy, stupid, thoughtless position that anybody could take", says the agency actively benefits from it because it splits the anti-CIA public, and answers the version aimed at himself by pointing at his prison sentence.

burn-notice.title: Afghan heroin policy
burn-notice.summary: The post-2001 U.S. policy in Afghanistan of protecting, and per John Kiriakou actively encouraging, the cultivation of heroin poppy. Under the Taliban in 2000 Afghanistan produced 0% of the world's heroin; by 2009 under American occupation it produced 93%. Per a DEA officer Kiriakou consulted with on the policy paper he was preparing for Senator Kerry, the strategic rationale was that nearly all of the heroin flowed to Iran and Russia, addiction in those countries was considered desirable as a long-run societal weakener, and the same logic now operates in reverse with Chinese fentanyl flowing into the United States.

burn-notice.title: Ahmed Chalabi
burn-notice.summary: Iraqi exile and founder of the Iraqi National Congress; per John Kiriakou, a Shia-Kurdish con man who looted Petra Bank in Jordan of $36 million in the 1980s, was sentenced to death in absentia, was pardoned at CIA request, then pocketed $6 million in CIA seed funding for the INC and bought a Mayfair house in cash; later resurrected by Dick Cheney to feed the Pentagon fabricated WMD intelligence used to justify the 2003 invasion of Iraq.

business-class-after-9-11.title: ''Don''t try to save the government money''
business-class-after-9-11.summary: The instruction John Kiriakou says a CIA supervisor gave him for parking in the nine-dollar economy lot at Dulles instead of the twenty-five-dollar daily lot, and the two trips it produced: a Pittsburgh approach funded entirely by a five-dollar bill, and a $195 fattoush salad in a Dubai nightclub.

business-class-after-9-11.title: Security, medical and finance
business-class-after-9-11.summary: The warning John Kiriakou says his first station chief gave him and that he passed on in turn to a first-tour case officer in Pakistan: there are only three offices at the CIA that can wreck your career — security, medical and finance — and only finance can send you to prison.

business-class-after-9-11.title: Post-9/11 supplemental appropriations
business-class-after-9-11.summary: The emergency money Congress pushed into the CIA after the September 11 attacks — a supplemental appropriation of roughly 160 per cent the day after, another at the end of the year, and a counterterrorism directorate that could not spend what it had been given.

business-class-after-9-11.title: Counterterrorism Center
business-class-after-9-11.summary: The CIA's Counterterrorism Center (CTC) — the unit where John Kiriakou spent the defining years of his operational career. He joined in the late 1990s as the only officer in the entire CIA fluent in both Greek and Arabic, served as chief of counterintelligence in the bin Laden unit, watched the Center swell from a few hundred employees to nearly 2,000 by September 12, 2001, and it was to CTC that he walked back down in May 2002 to refuse the torture program — the moment, he says, the CIA began to turn on him.

business-class-after-9-11.title: The General Muhammad equipment gift
business-class-after-9-11.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the end of the Abu Zubaydah operation in Pakistan, when headquarters told him to throw away or hand over the truckloads of equipment his station had bought — and of learning weeks later from his day-to-day Pakistani contact that the brigadier general who accepted the gift had simply taken it all himself.

business-class-after-9-11.title: The suicide watch protocol
business-class-after-9-11.summary: The federal suicide watch procedure as John Kiriakou describes it from inside — a room with windows on four sides, volunteer prisoners watching in four-hour shifts around the clock, and paper sheets that cannot be knotted — which he uses to enumerate, step by step, everything that failed in the case of Jeffrey Epstein.

butler-rally-shooting.title: Charlie Kirk shooting
butler-rally-shooting.summary: Kiriakou questions the official account: a court filing says the ATF could not match the autopsy bullet to the rifle tied to the suspect.

butler-rally-shooting.title: Secret Service
butler-rally-shooting.summary: The U.S. agency protecting the president. John Kiriakou, who worked alongside it for 35 years, describes a culture of complacency and poor follow-up — great with guns, weak on training and follow-through — and calls the 2024 Butler rally shooting a colossal historic screw-up in which coverage of the surrounding buildings was outsourced to a county sheriff's department. He has also encountered the Service as an adversary, outside the Venezuelan embassy in Washington in 2019.

butler-rally-shooting.title: Cofer Black
butler-rally-shooting.summary: Former head of the CIA Counterterrorism Center during and immediately after the September 11 attacks; principal architect of the agency's paramilitary turn on September 12, 2001; later Vice President of Blackwater under Erik Prince.

butler-rally-shooting.title: Washington political culture
butler-rally-shooting.summary: John Kiriakou's account of how Washington changed across the forty-four years he has lived in it — from a city where members of opposing parties shared houses, churches and Friday-night poker games to one he calls hideous, angry and backstabbing, in which the polarisation is itself the reason nothing gets done and political violence keeps being waved past.

butler-rally-shooting.title: The denials after Dallas
butler-rally-shooting.summary: John Kiriakou''s account, drawn from CIA historical files he read as a junior analyst, of how fast foreign governments moved to clear themselves after the assassination of John F. Kennedy: the Soviets came to the Americans within minutes, the Chinese did the same, and the Cubans asked the Mexicans to pass on that it was not them.

butler-rally-shooting.title: The unsearched car at Mar-a-Lago
butler-rally-shooting.summary: An episode John Kiriakou related in July 2024 as evidence that the Secret Service''s problem is systemic rather than confined to the Butler rally: a retired Army colonel and Republican fundraiser was asked at the Mar-a-Lago gate whether he had weapons in the car, said yes, went back to his hotel to lock them up — and later realised nobody had ever searched the vehicle.

buzzy-krongard.title: Abu Zubaydah
buzzy-krongard.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

buzzy-krongard.title: The SpongeBob shirt
buzzy-krongard.summary: The bright red SpongeBob SquarePants shirt, a Christmas present from his children, that John Kiriakou happened to be wearing when Abu Zubaydah opened his one good eye and realised the Americans had him.

buzzy-krongard.title: The Syrian bodyguard
buzzy-krongard.summary: The 330-pound guard captured alongside Abu Zubaydah, whose gunshot wound John Kiriakou examined and found ringed by a dinner-plate powder burn — evidence that contradicted the official account and left Kiriakou with a question about Pakistani intentions he says he will never be able to answer.

buzzy-krongard.title: Abu Zubaydah's diary
buzzy-krongard.summary: The notebook captured with Abu Zubaydah, containing drawings and poetry, over which the CIA and the FBI came to deep disagreement — an FBI psychologist calling it the rantings of a crazy person and John Kiriakou insisting it showed creativity in a man who was not crazy at all.

buzzy-krongard.title: The two Abu Zubaydahs
buzzy-krongard.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the first cousin who shared Abu Zubaydah's name, whose activities were folded into a single intelligence picture of a man Kiriakou called a terrorist Superman — and who vanished as soon as the capture reached the newspapers.

buzzy-krongard.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
buzzy-krongard.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

caleb-maupin.title: The Backstory
caleb-maupin.summary: The daily Radio Sputnik programme John Kiriakou co-hosted with Lee Stranahan, carried on terrestrial radio in the Washington area as well as online. It was the successor to his earlier show Loud and Clear with Brian Becker, and he described its format as two men with a beer talking about the day.

caleb-maupin.title: Haiti
caleb-maupin.summary: A country John Kiriakou studied for the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, where he found that the seven largest merchant families — the families that run the entire Haitian economy — are white. He treats Haiti's poverty as manufactured rather than accidental, and its unrest as a story the American press declines to cover.

caleb-maupin.title: The 2021 Cuba protests
caleb-maupin.summary: The July 2021 demonstrations in Cuba, which John Kiriakou declined to read as the beginning of a revolution. He called them a test run to gauge the government's reaction, objected that a New York Times line about Democrats treading lightly in Florida meant nothing anyone could act on, and noted that everything touching Cuba is too politically loaded in the United States to be discussed plainly.

caleb-maupin.title: Sanctions Effectiveness
caleb-maupin.summary: John Kiriakou's assessment that U.S. sanctions have been so overused against disfavored countries that nations like China now route around them entirely, and that sanctions work only when reserved for the worst actors and imposed in concert with other countries — citing apartheid South Africa as a success and Cuba/Venezuela as failures that instead entrench nationalist narratives.

caleb-maupin.title: Daniel Ortega
caleb-maupin.summary: The president of Nicaragua, and the case John Kiriakou contrasts with Cuba: where he read the 2021 Cuban protests as a test run, he said Nicaragua''s circumstances — a social security shortfall, a rise in the price of bread, and eight opposition party leaders arrested and imprisoned before an election — amounted to grounds for a real uprising.

caleb-maupin.title: The Peace and Friendship Bridge
caleb-maupin.summary: A bridge across the narrow Pakistan–China frontier that John Kiriakou saw advertised on billboards across Pakistan while serving there, and the exchange it produced with a Pakistani general: asked why so much was being made of it, the general said the Chinese were the only friends Pakistan had who had never turned on them — and then looked at Kiriakou.

cameo.title: Alexa
cameo.summary: Per John Kiriakou, Amazon''s Alexa smart speaker reports directly to the NSA — and he owns one anyway. The device recurs across his interviews as the standing example of the surveillance trade-off in modern smart-home technology, and of his own negotiated exception to it: one speaker, in one room, against the advice of every intelligence officer he has ever known.

cameo.title: The CIA divorce rate
cameo.summary: John Kiriakou's account of why marriages fail at the CIA at a rate he says exceeds that of any other part of the U.S. government — the impossibility of explaining a midnight departure to a spouse without a clearance, and the difficulty officers have switching off a professional habit of deception. He gives the figure variously as over 75 percent and upwards of 80 percent, says he was determined not to become a statistic and became one anyway, and dates the end of his first marriage to a sentence spoken in an armoured car on the way to Athens airport. Both his divorces have been costly; of the second he says the agency played an active role he is barred by court order from explaining.

cameo.title: Cold cell
cameo.summary: A CIA interrogation technique in which a stripped detainee is chained to a ceiling eyebolt in a cell chilled to 50°F, then doused with a bucket of ice water at hourly intervals; never authorized; documented to have killed at least two prisoners.

cameo.title: Death threats against Kiriakou
cameo.summary: The threats John Kiriakou has received across two decades — first after going public about the CIA torture program, when FBI advice that at least two were credible sent his family out of the country, and later in waves tied to his opposition to Gina Haspel, his remarks about Pakistan, and his advocacy on Palestine and the Epstein case.

cameo.title: FBI manufactured terrorism cases
cameo.summary: John Kiriakou's account of terrorism prosecutions in which the FBI supplies the plot, the target, the explosives and the transport, then arrests the person it recruited. His central case is the 2026 Miami trial of a mentally ill homeless man facing six counts each carrying life without parole, in which Kiriakou testified for the defence and told the court that the FBI was "clearly the criminal in this case." The defendant was acquitted on every count.

cameo.title: Justice Department self-immolation attempt
cameo.summary: An attempted self-immolation at a Washington rally in support of Julian Assange and WikiLeaks, held outside the Department of Justice, at which John Kiriakou was speaking. Kiriakou and another demonstrator physically stopped a naked man who had doused himself in lighter fluid; an attorney present intervened with the arresting officers and the man was taken to a hospital rather than a jail.

camp-david-final-talks.title: Bill Clinton
camp-david-final-talks.summary: 42nd U.S. president whom John Kiriakou describes as wholly disinterested in intelligence — briefed by the CIA only twice in eight years, with Vice President Al Gore taking the daily briefing instead and relaying anything important.

camp-david-final-talks.title: MOSSAD
camp-david-final-talks.summary: Israel's primary external intelligence service; characterized by John Kiriakou as universally hostile in his and his CIA colleagues' professional dealings with it ("never had a positive encounter with Mossad"); operates almost exclusively in the operational rather than analytical domain; the CIA is, per Kiriakou, categorically forbidden from spying on it.

camp-david-final-talks.title: Prince Andrew
camp-david-final-talks.summary: British royal, now Andrew Mountbatten Windsor, named repeatedly by John Kiriakou as one of the un-recruitable principals whose access made Jeffrey Epstein valuable to a foreign intelligence service. Kiriakou has asked why Andrew was never charged over conduct with minors, reads his alleged provision of classified Ministry of Defence documents to Epstein as evidence of espionage rather than vanity — and expects him to face no criminal consequence at all, because the statute of limitations has run.

camp-david-final-talks.title: Albright in Pyongyang
camp-david-final-talks.summary: John Kiriakou's account of Bill Clinton's stated regret over the final week of his presidency — that he wished he had pursued diplomatic relations with North Korea instead of Israeli-Palestinian peace — and of Madeleine Albright being in Pyongyang rather than at the talks.

camp-david-final-talks.title: Brian Ross
camp-david-final-talks.summary: American investigative journalist and seven-time Emmy Award winner who was a prominent reporter at ABC News when, in December 2007, he conducted the on-camera interview with John Kiriakou that produced the first public confirmation by a U.S. official that the CIA waterboarded prisoners. Per Kiriakou, Ross called him out of the blue with the assertion that a source said Kiriakou had personally tortured Abu Zubaydah; Kiriakou's decision to give the interview anyway — driven by the conclusion that 'Brian Ross's source is at the White House and they're going to pin this on me' — became the pivot point of his entire post-CIA life.

camp-david-final-talks.title: Central Intelligence Agency
camp-david-final-talks.summary: U.S. foreign intelligence service; John Kiriakou's employer from 1990 to 2004 and the central institution of KiriPedia

canada-as-a-bargaining-chip.title: China's generals without combat experience
canada-as-a-bargaining-chip.summary: Presented with the observation that China's purged and reshuffled top brass are now too young to have fought in any war, John Kiriakou agreed it mattered little in the near term and a great deal in the long term — because American military planning will have to account for an adversary whose senior commanders have never been in combat.

canada-as-a-bargaining-chip.title: China as mediator
canada-as-a-bargaining-chip.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that China is the plausible mediator of Middle Eastern and Ukrainian conflicts, grounded in his claim that — Tibet and its border wars aside — China has no history of invading other countries, and his observation of how quickly Beijing accepted an offhand suggestion that it might mediate between Israel and Iran.

canada-as-a-bargaining-chip.title: China as economic threat
canada-as-a-bargaining-chip.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that China is the real threat to the West not militarily — it has one aircraft carrier to America's two dozen and rarely invades — but economically, buying friends worldwide while the U.S. spends a trillion dollars a year on weapons.

canada-as-a-bargaining-chip.title: Ilhan Omar
canada-as-a-bargaining-chip.summary: U.S. Representative whom John Kiriakou credits with sponsoring a rewrite of the Espionage Act in two consecutive Congresses — legislation he says is dead on arrival with a Republican House because of who she is. Kiriakou has also sat at her table — in January 2026 he was one of about twenty guests at a dinner where Omar described the federal operation in Minneapolis and the budget manoeuvre that funded every part of the government except Homeland Security.

canada-as-a-bargaining-chip.title: Macron and the airplane steps
canada-as-a-bargaining-chip.summary: Asked what he thought was behind the French president's bruised appearance at Davos, John Kiriakou gave the blunt answer — "honestly, I think she hits him" — and dated his own change of mind to the footage at the top of the airplane steps.

canada-as-a-bargaining-chip.title: The killing of Alex Pretty
canada-as-a-bargaining-chip.summary: John Kiriakou''s verdict on the shooting of a man by immigration agents in Minneapolis in January 2026: a Kent State moment for the administration, a cover-up in progress, and — because there is no statute of limitations on murder — a case that will outlive the presidency and put people in prison.

cancelling-the-2026-midterms.title: The filibuster and Harry Reid's lesson
cancelling-the-2026-midterms.summary: John Kiriakou's defence of the Senate filibuster, offered as praise for John Thune's refusal to abolish it under pressure from the White House, and grounded in what he regards as Harry Reid's costly mistake over judicial nominations.

cancelling-the-2026-midterms.title: CIA liaison relationships
cancelling-the-2026-midterms.summary: John Kiriakou's critique of CIA intelligence-liaison relationships with foreign governments — sharply expanded after 9/11 — arguing that officers do not consider the long-term risk that disclosing sensitive operations to foreign services hands those governments leverage, including potential blackmail material, over the United States, and that no one left in Congress has the will to provide real oversight of the practice.

cancelling-the-2026-midterms.title: Civilian ships and piracy
cancelling-the-2026-midterms.summary: Why merchant crews cannot defend themselves: by international treaty no civilian ship may carry a weapon. John Kiriakou handled international piracy as a Senate Foreign Relations Committee staffer and brought Captain Richard Phillips to testify.

cancelling-the-2026-midterms.title: Jon Stewart
cancelling-the-2026-midterms.summary: American broadcaster, on whom John Kiriakou publicly accepted a correction from a viewer, and about whom he tells a single unflattering story from their one meeting.

cancelling-the-2026-midterms.title: Gangstalking claims
cancelling-the-2026-midterms.summary: The belief, put to John Kiriakou almost daily, that the CIA subjects private individuals to permanent multi-person surveillance and electromagnetic attack. He rejects it as untrue and as a matter for psychiatry, while conceding that one element of the folklore has a real basis.

cancelling-the-2026-midterms.title: The car pickup meeting
cancelling-the-2026-midterms.summary: A clandestine meeting technique in which an agent is collected from a street corner and ducks out of sight — and the occasion when a French intelligence officer used it on John Kiriakou, a colleague rather than an asset, and was refused.

candace-owens.title: French intelligence (DGSE)
candace-owens.summary: The French foreign intelligence service; characterized as exceptionally talented, exceptionally aggressive, and routinely lethal in the conduct of its operations

candace-owens.title: The Macron defamation suit
candace-owens.summary: The Macrons' libel action against Candace Owens over her claim that Brigitte Macron was born male, which John Kiriakou discussed as a question of venue — and which prompted him to say he wished he had sued the Los Angeles Times in England when he had the chance.

candace-owens.title: Kiriakou on animated television
candace-owens.summary: John Kiriakou's stated taste in television cartoons — South Park, Family Guy, The Simpsons and Bob's Burgers — his judgement that South Park is by far the most cutting edge of them, and the episodes he thought worth buying outright.

candace-owens.title: The Brennan felony referral
candace-owens.summary: John Kiriakou's July 2025 report, sourced to Matt Taibbe, that the Justice Department was moving beyond referred misdemeanour charges against John Brennan and James Comey for allegedly lying to Congress and was actively pursuing felony conspiracy charges against at least Brennan — a prospect Kiriakou said he would attend the trial of every single day.

candace-owens.title: The homelessness executive order
candace-owens.summary: Donald Trump's July 2025 executive order on homelessness, which John Kiriakou criticised on the ground that it understates the population by two thirds and proposes forcible commitment to facilities that do not exist — while conceding that Trump diagnoses the problem better than his predecessors did.

candace-owens.title: The mental health parity gap
candace-owens.summary: John Kiriakou's account of American mental health provision — parity written into the Affordable Care Act and entirely unenforced, more mentally ill people in most county jails than in the mental hospitals, and his condition that nobody should be forced into treatment until the treatment is worth being forced into.

carlos-the-jackal.title: Revolutionary Organization 17 November
carlos-the-jackal.summary: Greek far-left urban guerrilla group active 1975–2002; the deadliest terrorist organization in Greek history

carlos-the-jackal.title: Richard Welch
carlos-the-jackal.summary: CIA Athens station chief assassinated December 23, 1975; the first victim of [Revolutionary Organization 17 November](/wiki/revolutionary-organization-17-november)

carlos-the-jackal.title: Abu Zubaydah
carlos-the-jackal.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

carlos-the-jackal.title: Billy Waugh
carlos-the-jackal.summary: Long-serving CIA paramilitary contractor; U.S. Army Special Forces ("Green Beret") veteran of World War II, Korea, and Vietnam; holder of approximately seventeen Purple Hearts (license plate "17 HITS"); resident of Niceville, Florida; died in his nineties.

carlos-the-jackal.title: Mike Mastrovito
carlos-the-jackal.summary: Twenty-five-year Secret Service veteran; founder and first director of the Secret Service Intelligence Division; later, after a forced retirement, a CIA contractor specializing in Greek terrorism; close colleague of John Kiriakou in Athens. Started his career at the end of the Eisenhower administration, was in Dallas with President Kennedy, and was effectively removed from the Secret Service after Sara Jane Moore's 1975 attempt on President Ford — having interviewed Moore two weeks earlier on a threatening letter she had sent.

carrying-classified-out-of-a-scif.title: Espionage Act
carrying-classified-out-of-a-scif.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

carrying-classified-out-of-a-scif.title: The 2023 classified documents scandal
carrying-classified-out-of-a-scif.summary: The run of discoveries of classified material in the private possession of Donald Trump, Joe Biden and Mike Pence, which John Kiriakou treats not as a scandal about any of them but as proof that the Espionage Act as currently applied makes almost everyone technically guilty. He rates Pence's briefing books as more highly classified than anything Julian Assange published, and says Biden's Senate-era documents are the ones that cannot be explained away.

carrying-classified-out-of-a-scif.title: Barack Obama
carrying-classified-out-of-a-scif.summary: 44th U.S. president; in John Kiriakou's account, Obama publicly recounted refusing Benjamin Netanyahu's demand to bomb Iran and calling Israel's threat to use nuclear weapons a bluff — a bluff Kiriakou says Donald Trump later believed.

carrying-classified-out-of-a-scif.title: Classified email
carrying-classified-out-of-a-scif.summary: John Kiriakou was serving overseas the day classified email was introduced at the CIA, and remembers his station chief saying there was no way to control it. His own illustration of what followed is a lunch invitation to his wife — a fellow senior CIA officer — marked Secret HUM 4-82, and her reply naming a deli and a time, marked the same way.

carrying-classified-out-of-a-scif.title: The mosaic concept
carrying-classified-out-of-a-scif.summary: The intelligence method John Kiriakou names for assembling a complete operational picture out of individually trivial fragments — one tile at a time, worthless alone, decisive together. He attributes the idea to Soviet thinking of the 1960s, cites Mossad's Iranian networks as the clearest modern demonstration, and warns that the same logic is what would let an American prosecutor charge a scholar with espionage for reading declassified documents.

carrying-classified-out-of-a-scif.title: Over-classification
carrying-classified-out-of-a-scif.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of why the American government classifies far more than it can ever review: not conspiracy but incentive. At lesser agencies a classification stamp is a status marker — it puts you in the in-crowd and above the colleague who lacks access — and at the CIA everything carries a stamp by default. His complaint about press coverage of classified-document scandals is that it never reaches the underlying question of why the documents were secret at all.

carrying-passports-in-washington.title: Astrology at the CIA
carrying-passports-in-washington.summary: John Kiriakou''s confirmation that astrology played a role in CIA work in the 1950s and early 1960s as part of MK-ULTRA, alongside time travel and teleportation — and his explanation for why: officials with unlimited budgets and no obligation to report to the public reasoned that there was probably nothing to it, but that if there were, it would make them a star.

carrying-passports-in-washington.title: "Christians are suckers"
carrying-passports-in-washington.summary: John Kiriakou's explanation for how a president who does not go to church, has no spiritual adviser and could not name a line of scripture can push school prayer without cost — that he thinks most Christians are suckers, an assessment Kiriakou says he hates to make and believes anyway.

carrying-passports-in-washington.title: E. Jean Carroll
carrying-passports-in-washington.summary: The plaintiff whose persistence John Kiriakou singled out for deep respect — she kept suing after the political tide turned against her, and won an award he put at eighty-three or eighty-five million dollars on a day when Donald Trump won almost everything else in the federal courts.

carrying-passports-in-washington.title: Find a Grave
carrying-passports-in-washington.summary: The cemetery database John Kiriakou calls literally his favourite website on the internet, which he opens during the ten-minute countdown before broadcasts and uses to decide who goes into his cemetery books — and which supplied him the story of Greta Zimmer Friedman.

carrying-passports-in-washington.title: CIA backdoor banking
carrying-passports-in-washington.summary: John Kiriakou's answer to a question about the intelligence community opening Western capital markets to sanctioned groups — that the CIA's interests frequently diverge from the national interest, that its friends are often hostile to the State Department and the White House, and that it will arrange backdoor banking, investment and loans to keep those outlaws going.

carrying-passports-in-washington.title: The Ramot Junction shooting
carrying-passports-in-washington.summary: The September 2025 bus stop attack in an East Jerusalem settlement in which two Palestinians from the West Bank killed six Israelis, and John Kiriakou's divided answer — that opposition to attacks on civilians has to be unconditional, and that he does not know what he would do if strangers took his house.

carter-page.title: FISA court
carter-page.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the secret Foreign Intelligence Surveillance court — created under Carter, sitting atop the Justice Department, issuing warrants that are never public — which he says was abused against Carter Page as part of what he believes was John Brennan's plan to deny Trump the presidency.

carter-page.title: James Comey
carter-page.summary: Former FBI director indicted under the second Trump administration, whose prosecution John Kiriakou reads as a search for charges to fit a man rather than evidence of a crime — and which he expects to collapse, unlike the parallel case against John Brennan.

carter-page.title: John Brennan
carter-page.summary: Former Director of the CIA; characterized in KiriPedia's source corpus as the principal architect of the agency's enhanced interrogation program and as having plotted against an elected President

carter-page.title: John Durham
carter-page.summary: United States attorney for Connecticut appointed to investigate the origins of the Russia inquiry. Speaking in December 2019, John Kiriakou described Durham as having obtained John Brennan''s call logs, his emails from his time as CIA director, and the contemporaneous notes Brennan took in meetings with other agency heads — and read Durham''s own insistence that this was a criminal investigation rather than an inquiry as pointing at process crimes: false statements and perjury.

carter-page.title: Tucker Carlson
carter-page.summary: American broadcaster and former Fox News host; a personal friend of John Kiriakou's for years, appearing on Kiriakou's radio and podcast work and hosting him roughly a dozen times on his own Fox show. Kiriakou calls him possibly the most brilliant and best-informed person he has ever encountered, and relays Glenn Greenwald's belief that Carlson could win the presidency — an idea Carlson privately dismisses.

carter-page.title: John Kiriakou
carter-page.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

carving-up-iran.title: "Iran posed no threat"
carving-up-iran.summary: John Kiriakou''s core objection to the 2026 war, stated as a chain of negatives: Iran had no nuclear weapon, no nuclear weapons programme, no wish for one, a religious ruling against one, and no delivery system if it had had one — findings he says were confirmed twice by the CIA and by the IAEA.

carving-up-iran.title: Killing Khamenei
carving-up-iran.summary: John Kiriakou's assessment that the killing of Ayatollah Khamenei during the 2026 war would change nothing, because the West had seriously overestimated his authority — an argument he extends to the American habit of expecting a war to end when a leader is removed.

carving-up-iran.title: "Beyond Your Dreams"
carving-up-iran.summary: The gloss a host gave John Kiriakou on his first trip to China when he asked what the beautiful car with the BYD badge was — and the answer he got when he asked why he had never heard of it, which was that the United States is the only country where they are not sold.

carving-up-iran.title: Chaos as the Israeli objective
carving-up-iran.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer to whether Netanyahu''s government actually wanted an American invasion of Iran: what the Israelis want in Iran is what they got in Libya — chaos, civil war, and as many dead Iranians as possible.

carving-up-iran.title: Dumping the treasury bonds
carving-up-iran.summary: The second economic weapon John Kiriakou says China holds against the United States — its position as the second or third largest holder of long-term government treasury bonds, which it could simply dump, and which he says would crash the entire American economy.

carving-up-iran.title: Lavrov on sanctions
carving-up-iran.summary: The two remarks by Russian foreign minister Sergey Lavrov that John Kiriakou pairs to summarise the failure of the sanctions weapon — that Russia was surprised by how swiftly the Americans imposed sanctions, and, a year or two later, surprised by how quickly Russia got around them.

caspar-weinberger.title: Jonathan Pollard
caspar-weinberger.summary: U.S. Navy civilian intelligence analyst convicted in 1985 of spying for Israel; the canonical proven case of Israeli espionage against the United States; cited by John Kiriakou in his 2024 Piers Morgan debate with a former Mossad director who denied any Israeli spying on the U.S.

caspar-weinberger.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
caspar-weinberger.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

caspar-weinberger.title: MOSSAD
caspar-weinberger.summary: Israel's primary external intelligence service; characterized by John Kiriakou as universally hostile in his and his CIA colleagues' professional dealings with it ("never had a positive encounter with Mossad"); operates almost exclusively in the operational rather than analytical domain; the CIA is, per Kiriakou, categorically forbidden from spying on it.

caspar-weinberger.title: Sheldon Adelson
caspar-weinberger.summary: American casino magnate and Republican megadonor. In John Kiriakou's account Adelson sent his private jet to fly Jonathan Pollard from prison to Israel, paid out of his own pocket to move the American embassy to Jerusalem, and functions as Kiriakou's standing unit of measurement for what political money can buy — including in the negative, as the patron the Libertarian Party never had.

caspar-weinberger.title: Alexa
caspar-weinberger.summary: Per John Kiriakou, Amazon''s Alexa smart speaker reports directly to the NSA — and he owns one anyway. The device recurs across his interviews as the standing example of the surveillance trade-off in modern smart-home technology, and of his own negotiated exception to it: one speaker, in one room, against the advice of every intelligence officer he has ever known.

caspar-weinberger.title: Asset acquisition cycle
caspar-weinberger.summary: The four-step process — spot, assess, develop, recruit — taught as the first lesson of CIA case officer training

censorship-on-the-left.title: The Washington Post under Bezos
censorship-on-the-left.summary: John Kiriakou''s running account of the decline of a newspaper he subscribes to and no longer recognises — an editorial board he says has gone wholly right-wing and obsequious to its owner, foreign bureaus and sports and local coverage cut back, a comment of his own rejected for criticising Jeff Bezos, and his own short list of what he would want the paper to be instead.

censorship-on-the-left.title: The Communist Party of Greece
censorship-on-the-left.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of Greek communism: a civil war from 1946 to 1949 whose bitterness still scars families, a party banned outright until Andreas Papandreou legalised it in 1980, and a present-day remnant polling between three and five per cent — enough for parliamentary representation and not enough to be a factor.

censorship-on-the-left.title: The Ann Coulter dinner
censorship-on-the-left.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of an unplanned dinner in Los Angeles around 2016 at which a college friend arrived with Ann Coulter, and of finding her interesting, well-informed and lovely — from which he concludes that the public hatred she trades in is an act, and one he says she has seriously cashed in on.

censorship-on-the-left.title: The ATF funding rider
censorship-on-the-left.summary: The provision John Kiriakou describes as the reason no American felon has had firearm rights restored since the 1990s: a Clinton-era law permitting non-violent, non-drug felons to apply to the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco and Firearms, paired in the same statute with a bar on any federal money being spent to investigate the applications.

censorship-on-the-left.title: The calls not to attack Iran
censorship-on-the-left.summary: John Kiriakou''s report, given in late January 2026 and sourced to friendships he had recently formed in three Middle Eastern royal families, that the Saudis, Jordanians, Egyptians and Emiratis had all telephoned Donald Trump to ask him not to attack Iran — the Egyptians warning of an almost immediate region-wide war — and that the Israelis had asked the same thing, for the unsentimental reason that they had not replaced the interceptors spent in the last round.

censorship-on-the-left.title: The Guantanamo airfare catch
censorship-on-the-left.summary: The pair of legal traps John Kiriakou describes around the detainees at Guantanamo Bay who have been cleared for release: no country will take them and Congress defunded the ability to pay for their flights, while a separate 2009 statute forbids any of them from setting foot on United States soil — so that even a conviction could not be served in an American prison.

central-american-task-force.title: Iran-Contra
central-american-task-force.summary: The mid-1980s scandal in which the Reagan administration secretly sold weapons to Iran and diverted the proceeds — laundered through Cyprus — to fund the Contra rebels in Nicaragua. Per John Kiriakou, Iran-Contra marks the precise end of what he calls the ''golden age'' of congressional intelligence oversight: the roughly 1975–1982 window opened by the Church and Pike Committees, when ''serious people, heavyweights'' actually held the CIA accountable. After Iran-Contra, he says, the oversight committees reverted to being ''cheerleaders'' for the agency — a posture that has held ever since.

central-american-task-force.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
central-american-task-force.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

central-american-task-force.title: George W. Bush
central-american-task-force.summary: 43rd President of the United States. In John Kiriakou's telling, Bush signed the August 1, 2002 executive order that authorized the CIA torture program, spent years telling the public "we don't torture," and — days after Kiriakou's 2007 ABC interview — blamed torture on "a rogue CIA officer" while walking from the White House South Portico to Marine One, a moment Kiriakou instantly read as the White House preparing to pin the program on him. Bush also ordered the FBI removed from Abu Zubaydah's black site, flew the bin Laden family out of the country after 9/11, and loosened the assassination ban of Executive Order 12333.

central-american-task-force.title: The promotion panel
central-american-task-force.summary: The CIA board that reviews an officer for advancement, and the one that reviewed John Kiriakou weeks after the Abu Zubaydah capture — where his refusal to be trained in the enhanced interrogation techniques was recorded as *"a shocking lack of commitment to counterterrorism"*, and he was passed over.

central-american-task-force.title: 1953 Iran coup
central-american-task-force.summary: The U.S.- and UK-backed overthrow of Iran's democratically elected prime minister, Mohammad Mossadegh; per John Kiriakou, the coup served British national interests rather than American ones, and the subsequent outlawing of secular political opposition under the Shah forced dissent into the mosques — producing a religious rather than secular revolution in 1979.

central-american-task-force.title: Adnan Khashoggi
central-american-task-force.summary: Saudi arms dealer and Iran-Contra middleman whom John Kiriakou says was mentioned 'all the time' at the CIA — in pointed contrast to Jeffrey Epstein, whose name he never once heard there.

ceuta-migrant-crossings-2026.title: Spanish enclaves in North Africa
ceuta-migrant-crossings-2026.summary: Ceuta and the smaller Spanish territories on the Moroccan coast, held under treaties more than four centuries old. In John Kiriakou's account they are colonial remnants that Morocco resents, that Israel has used to needle Spain over its criticism of Israeli occupation, and that United States policy now formally describes as an occupation.

ceuta-migrant-crossings-2026.title: Morocco–Algeria rivalry
ceuta-migrant-crossings-2026.summary: The long enmity between Morocco and Algeria over primacy in North Africa, which John Kiriakou identifies as the actual cause of the 2026 mass crossing into Ceuta after Spain's prime minister paid an official visit to Algiers.

ceuta-migrant-crossings-2026.title: Thomas Massie
ceuta-migrant-crossings-2026.summary: Republican U.S. Representative from Kentucky known for a constitutionalist voting record and consistent opposition to foreign military intervention; per John Kiriakou, a principled America-First congressman who votes with the president on the vast majority of issues, and whose opposition to U.S. funding of Israel and foreign wars is the only plausible explanation for the roughly $30 million spent by the Israel lobby to unseat him in a primary.

ceuta-migrant-crossings-2026.title: Temporary protected status
ceuta-migrant-crossings-2026.summary: The American immigration category for people who cannot safely return home because of armed conflict, natural disaster or other temporary catastrophe. John Kiriakou treats it as a policy with no exit: when conditions in the home country never improve — often, he argues, because of American action — revoking the status amounts to a death sentence.

ceuta-migrant-crossings-2026.title: AIPAC
ceuta-migrant-crossings-2026.summary: The American Israel Public Affairs Committee — the U.S. political organization that, in John Kiriakou's framing, ought to be registered as a foreign-lobbying entity but is not, and that wields decisive electoral power against U.S. elected officials who express support for Palestinian human rights.

ceuta-migrant-crossings-2026.title: Haiti
ceuta-migrant-crossings-2026.summary: A country John Kiriakou studied for the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, where he found that the seven largest merchant families — the families that run the entire Haitian economy — are white. He treats Haiti's poverty as manufactured rather than accidental, and its unrest as a story the American press declines to cover.

chaos-as-the-israeli-objective.title: MBS and Netanyahu asked Trump to attack Iran
chaos-as-the-israeli-objective.summary: John Kiriakou's account that Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu jointly went to Donald Trump and asked him to attack Iran — a move Kiriakou finds hard to reconcile with MBS's own years of work to improve Saudi relations with Tehran.

chaos-as-the-israeli-objective.title: Marco Rubio and Iran policy
chaos-as-the-israeli-objective.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer to who was actually driving American policy toward Iran in 2026: with the Vice President, the Director of National Intelligence and the Chairman of the Joint Chiefs all reported as opposed, and with Marco Rubio holding both the State Department and the National Security Adviser''s job, the policy was Rubio''s.

chaos-as-the-israeli-objective.title: Killing Khamenei
chaos-as-the-israeli-objective.summary: John Kiriakou's assessment that the killing of Ayatollah Khamenei during the 2026 war would change nothing, because the West had seriously overestimated his authority — an argument he extends to the American habit of expecting a war to end when a leader is removed.

chaos-as-the-israeli-objective.title: Arming the crazies
chaos-as-the-israeli-objective.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the American habit of arming the most radical faction available — the Mujahideen over any other Afghan force, the White Russians over the Red — and his expectation, stated days into the 2026 war, that the United States and Israel would begin arming factions inside Iran and that the factions chosen would be the radical ones.

chaos-as-the-israeli-objective.title: "Iran posed no threat"
chaos-as-the-israeli-objective.summary: John Kiriakou''s core objection to the 2026 war, stated as a chain of negatives: Iran had no nuclear weapon, no nuclear weapons programme, no wish for one, a religious ruling against one, and no delivery system if it had had one — findings he says were confirmed twice by the CIA and by the IAEA.

chaos-as-the-israeli-objective.title: The difficulty of getting out
chaos-as-the-israeli-objective.summary: John Kiriakou''s standing formulation about regime change: it is easy to invade a country and easy to overthrow a government, and very difficult to leave. He measures it in the twenty years the United States spent in Afghanistan and the nineteen in Iraq.

chaos-computer-club-wikileaks.title: Daniel Domscheit-Berg
chaos-computer-club-wikileaks.summary: A WikiLeaks associate discussed on the same panel as John Kiriakou; the anecdote about meeting him via the Chaos Computer Club was told by fellow panelist John Goetz, a Der Spiegel journalist — not by Kiriakou himself.

chaos-computer-club-wikileaks.title: Ai Whistleblower Initiative
chaos-computer-club-wikileaks.summary: The AI Whistleblower Initiative, working on legal protections for the wave of whistleblowers now coming out of the artificial-intelligence industry.

chaos-computer-club-wikileaks.title: Andrew Feinstein
chaos-computer-club-wikileaks.summary: Referenced on the same WikiLeaks-conference panel as John Kiriakou; the description of Feinstein's talk on the multiple factors that ended apartheid was given by another panelist putting a question to Kiriakou, not by Kiriakou himself.

chaos-computer-club-wikileaks.title: Belmarsh Prison
chaos-computer-club-wikileaks.summary: The maximum-security London prison where Julian Assange was held for years on a bail-jumping sentence John Kiriakou calls a fabrication — kept in solitary confinement alongside the worst offenders in the United Kingdom, and held past the expiry of his sentence at the request of the United States. Kiriakou corresponded with Assange there and watched the letters change.

chaos-computer-club-wikileaks.title: Chelsea Manning
chaos-computer-club-wikileaks.summary: Former U.S. Army intelligence analyst who provided WikiLeaks its 2010 trove of military and diplomatic documents. Per John Kiriakou, Manning meets the legal definition of whistleblower for exposing war crimes, was a torture victim of prolonged solitary confinement with forced nudity, and was sentenced to 35 years in prison before Barack Obama commuted — not pardoned — her sentence. Kiriakou says Manning later refused a grand jury's offer of immunity and chose renewed jail time rather than testify against Julian Assange.

chaos-computer-club-wikileaks.title: Central Intelligence Agency
chaos-computer-club-wikileaks.summary: U.S. foreign intelligence service; John Kiriakou's employer from 1990 to 2004 and the central institution of KiriPedia

charles-littlejohn-prosecution.title: Leonie Brinkema
charles-littlejohn-prosecution.summary: U.S. federal judge in the Eastern District of Virginia — informally the 'Espionage Court' — a Reagan appointee John Kiriakou calls "a hanging judge." Per Kiriakou, Brinkema systematically reserved all major national security cases for herself rather than allowing them to be distributed randomly among judges, and ruled in Kiriakou's case that his reason for blowing the whistle was legally irrelevant and that classified documents could not be used in his defense — effectively making it impossible to mount one.

charles-littlejohn-prosecution.title: Chelsea Manning
charles-littlejohn-prosecution.summary: Former U.S. Army intelligence analyst who provided WikiLeaks its 2010 trove of military and diplomatic documents. Per John Kiriakou, Manning meets the legal definition of whistleblower for exposing war crimes, was a torture victim of prolonged solitary confinement with forced nudity, and was sentenced to 35 years in prison before Barack Obama commuted — not pardoned — her sentence. Kiriakou says Manning later refused a grand jury's offer of immunity and chose renewed jail time rather than testify against Julian Assange.

charles-littlejohn-prosecution.title: Espionage Act
charles-littlejohn-prosecution.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

charles-littlejohn-prosecution.title: Prosecutorial careerism
charles-littlejohn-prosecution.summary: John Kiriakou''s explanation for why senior federal prosecutors pursue high-profile national-security cases regardless of their merits: the conviction of a famous defendant is the entry ticket to a partnership at a large firm, a congressional candidacy, or a run for governor.

charles-littlejohn-prosecution.title: "Don''t charge Donald Trump with espionage"
charles-littlejohn-prosecution.summary: An opinion piece John Kiriakou wrote for Consortium News after the classified documents were found at Mar-a-Lago, arguing against an Espionage Act prosecution of Trump — and, in its subheading, against Espionage Act prosecutions of anyone else either. He uses it as the frame for his position that the statute should be scrapped and rewritten to reach only those who mean the country harm.

charles-littlejohn-prosecution.title: Sentencing enhancements
