Asked by Veteran Intelligence Professionals for Sanity to examine the science, Binney analyzed the speed of the upload and concluded the emails could only have been copied in person to a thumb drive, not taken remotely by Russia — an argument he later made to Donald Trump in the Oval Office. Kiriakou calls him a friend, the most brilliant person he has met on electronics, and a member of the whistleblower circle he belongs to.

cia-big-tech-revolving-door.title: Field loadout
cia-big-tech-revolving-door.summary: John Kiriakou''s itemised answer to a question he says no one had ever asked him — what a CIA operations officer actually carried in the field. In Athens: a 9mm in a tearaway fanny pack, a snub-nose .38 on his ankle, a Buck knife, and some 47 rounds. In Pakistan: one 9mm, and a daily prayer that he would not have to use it. Plus $2,000–$5,000 in cash on an ordinary day, because "intelligence is a cash business."

cia-budget-concealment.title: William Proxmire
cia-budget-concealment.summary: Democratic senator from Wisconsin, elected in the special election following Joseph McCarthy's death, whose monthly Golden Fleece Award targeted wasteful federal spending. John Kiriakou describes Proxmire as a recurring irritant to the CIA — which, he says, repeatedly saw its concealed budget line items exposed to ridicule because the cover stories invented to hide them looked exactly like waste.

cia-budget-concealment.title: Mary Margaret Graham
cia-budget-concealment.summary: CIA Senior Intelligence Service officer and later Deputy Director of National Intelligence for Collection under John Negroponte — described by John Kiriakou as a career "reports officer" who had never personally recruited a source, and as his difficult chief of station in a later domestic assignment.

cia-budget-concealment.title: USAID as a CIA cover vehicle
cia-budget-concealment.summary: John Kiriakou's account of USAID's use by the CIA as a channel for covert operations and money laundering rather than as an undercover posting for individual officers — including a declassified 1972 exchange in which Henry Kissinger confirmed the CIA had paid Laotian mercenaries through USAID payroll checks.

cia-budget-concealment.title: Julian Assange
cia-budget-concealment.summary: Kiriakou — a 15-year friend and former WikiLeaks board member — on why Assange is a publisher owed a journalist's immunity, and a political prisoner.

cia-budget-concealment.title: Tuesday morning kill list
cia-budget-concealment.summary: Weekly CIA targeting meeting instituted by John Brennan in 2009 during his service as Deputy National Security Advisor for Counterterrorism in the Obama administration; produced a written list of individuals to be killed in the following week; per John Kiriakou, the program was a source of pride within the Obama administration and was made operationally possible by the targeting-software sophistication of the period.

cia-budget-concealment.title: ZunZuneo
cia-budget-concealment.summary: Covert social-media platform built for Cuba through USAID during the George W. Bush administration, intended by John Kiriakou's account to instigate an Arab Spring-style uprising. He says Cubans were indifferent to it, the project died, and its existence became public only when it was leaked by accident to the Guardian.

cia-cable-priority-levels.title: Kiriakou's transfer to the Directorate of Operations
cia-cable-priority-levels.summary: John Kiriakou's roughly two-month internal campaign to transfer from the CIA's analytic Directorate of Intelligence to the operational Directorate of Operations, overcoming what he calls a "natural bias in operations against the eggheads on the analytic side," followed by an Athens posting secured because he was the only person in the entire CIA fluent in both Greek and Arabic. Covers his full CIA career arc from 1988/1990 recruitment through analyst years on Iraq, the switch to operations, 9/11, the enhanced-interrogation refusal, executive assistant to the deputy director for operations, and his eventual resignation and post-CIA career.

cia-cable-priority-levels.title: Iraqi invasion of Kuwait
cia-cable-priority-levels.summary: John Kiriakou''s most detailed account of the intelligence process around the 1990 Iraqi invasion of Kuwait and its 1991 liberation. As a first-year CIA analyst on a ''training account'' covering Iraq, Kiriakou produced the June 30, 1990 warning paper for the White House; suggested calling the US Defense Attaché in Baghdad to drive to the border and report what he saw (the answer: ''Literally the entire Iraqi military is heading south''); briefed the August 2 Oval Office meeting with Bush; and later took a single phone call from General Colin Powell that led, eight hours later, to 47 cruise missiles striking the Iraqi Intelligence Service headquarters in Baghdad.

cia-cable-priority-levels.title: 1993 Bush Kuwait assassination plot
cia-cable-priority-levels.summary: Iraqi intelligence plot, foiled by Kuwaiti authorities, to assassinate former President George H. W. Bush during his post-liberation "victory lap" visit to Kuwait; the U.S. response, per John Kiriakou's first-person account of his telephone call with Chairman of the Joint Chiefs Colin Powell, was 47 cruise missiles fired into the Iraqi Intelligence Service headquarters in Baghdad eight hours later.

cia-cable-priority-levels.title: Ahmed Chalabi
cia-cable-priority-levels.summary: Iraqi exile and founder of the Iraqi National Congress; per John Kiriakou, a Shia-Kurdish con man who looted Petra Bank in Jordan of $36 million in the 1980s, was sentenced to death in absentia, was pardoned at CIA request, then pocketed $6 million in CIA seed funding for the INC and bought a Mayfair house in cash; later resurrected by Dick Cheney to feed the Pentagon fabricated WMD intelligence used to justify the 2003 invasion of Iraq.

cia-cable-priority-levels.title: Ali Hassan al-Majid
cia-cable-priority-levels.summary: Saddam Hussein cousin known as "Chemical Ali" and "the Butcher of Kurdistan"; per John Kiriakou, also briefly served as the Iraqi-installed governor of occupied Kuwait — "the Butcher of Kuwait" — and was engaged in the wholesale slaughter of Kurds in the north, Shia in the south, and Kuwaitis under occupation.

cia-cable-priority-levels.title: Bahrain Posting (1994–1996)
cia-cable-priority-levels.summary: John Kiriakou's 1994–1996 assignment to Bahrain under U.S. State Department cover as second secretary for economic affairs — arriving with his wife Joanne and infant son Chris on August 1, 1994, into a tiny Gulf monarchy whose sectarian tensions erupted, two months later, into the first Intifada.

cia-car-hacking.title: Vault 7
cia-car-hacking.summary: The 2017 WikiLeaks disclosure of thousands of pages of CIA Directorate of Science and Technology documents — leaked by agency engineer Joshua Schulte — revealing CIA technical capabilities including remote takeover of internet-connected cars, conversion of smart-TV speakers into covert microphones, and the planting of Russian or Persian language fragments in foreign systems to mislead attribution.

cia-car-hacking.title: Julian Assange
cia-car-hacking.summary: Kiriakou — a 15-year friend and former WikiLeaks board member — on why Assange is a publisher owed a journalist's immunity, and a political prisoner.

cia-car-hacking.title: CIA Smart TV Surveillance
cia-car-hacking.summary: Per John Kiriakou, a CIA technical capability — disclosed publicly by the 2017 Vault 7 leaks — to convert a smart television's speaker system into a covert listening microphone even while the television appears to be switched off.

cia-car-hacking.title: Joshua Schulte
cia-car-hacking.summary: Former CIA Directorate of Science and Technology engineer; source of the 2017 Vault 7 WikiLeaks disclosure of the agency's offensive technical capabilities; currently serving a 40-year federal sentence for espionage; maintains his innocence.

cia-car-hacking.title: Palantir Technologies
cia-car-hacking.summary: U.S. data-analytics and intelligence-software company; received its first $1.5 million in seed funding from the CIA's In-Q-Tel venture-capital arm around 2002; characterized by John Kiriakou as functionally inseparable from the CIA in 2025, drawing the majority of its revenue from agency contracts and operating across DARPA, NSA, and the broader U.S. national-security apparatus.

cia-car-hacking.title: The Directorate of Science and Technology
cia-car-hacking.summary: One of the CIA's four directorates, which in John Kiriakou's time was an afterthought responsible for disguises and briefcases with hidden compartments, and which he says now works with Palantir, Amazon, Nvidia and Elon Musk's companies on work closer to DARPA's than to anything the agency did in the past.

cia-cash-room.title: Agent payment mechanics
cia-cash-room.summary: How the CIA physically pays a recruited agent — cash every month, a receipt signed with any alias the agent chooses, and a polygraph regime built around the assumption that the officer handling the money is the person most likely to steal it.

cia-cash-room.title: Abu Zubaydah
cia-cash-room.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

cia-cash-room.title: The Directorate of Science and Technology
cia-cash-room.summary: One of the CIA's four directorates, which in John Kiriakou's time was an afterthought responsible for disguises and briefcases with hidden compartments, and which he says now works with Palantir, Amazon, Nvidia and Elon Musk's companies on work closer to DARPA's than to anything the agency did in the past.

cia-cash-room.title: Executive Order 12333
cia-cash-room.summary: The U.S. presidential directive — in its post-9/11 amended form — that grants the CIA the legal authority to kill any individual anywhere in the world deemed by the agency to pose a "clear and present danger" to the United States; the legal foundation underlying both CIA paramilitary operations and the agency's contractor relationships including with Blackwater.

cia-cash-room.title: Julian Assange
cia-cash-room.summary: Kiriakou — a 15-year friend and former WikiLeaks board member — on why Assange is a publisher owed a journalist's immunity, and a political prisoner.

cia-cash-room.title: Post-9/11 supplemental appropriations
cia-cash-room.summary: The emergency money Congress pushed into the CIA after the September 11 attacks — a supplemental appropriation of roughly 160 per cent the day after, another at the end of the year, and a counterterrorism directorate that could not spend what it had been given.

cia-crimes-reports.title: Publications Review Board
cia-crimes-reports.summary: The CIA office that must clear anything a former officer publishes. John Kiriakou says everything he writes goes to it — books, articles, "even a letter to the editor of Home and Garden magazine" — and describes how the turnaround tracked his standing at the agency: his first book took 22 months to clear while the leadership hated him; his most recent six cleared in days.

cia-crimes-reports.title: Heather Kiriakou
cia-crimes-reports.summary: John Kiriakou's wife, a senior CIA analyst who — in his account — was one of the best analysts in the entire intelligence community and who lost her job at the agency for no reason other than being married to him. She sat off camera at his December 2007 ABC News interview and told him afterwards that he had said nothing classified.

cia-crimes-reports.title: The IRS audits of Kiriakou
cia-crimes-reports.summary: John Kiriakou says that within weeks of his December 2007 ABC News interview confirming CIA waterboarding he was audited by the Internal Revenue Service, and that he was audited again every single year thereafter. He places the audits alongside FBI surveillance and repeated CIA criminal referrals as part of a single pattern of retaliation that preceded his prosecution by five years.

cia-crimes-reports.title: Brian Ross
cia-crimes-reports.summary: American investigative journalist and seven-time Emmy Award winner who was a prominent reporter at ABC News when, in December 2007, he conducted the on-camera interview with John Kiriakou that produced the first public confirmation by a U.S. official that the CIA waterboarded prisoners. Per Kiriakou, Ross called him out of the blue with the assertion that a source said Kiriakou had personally tortured Abu Zubaydah; Kiriakou's decision to give the interview anyway — driven by the conclusion that 'Brian Ross's source is at the White House and they're going to pin this on me' — became the pivot point of his entire post-CIA life.

cia-crimes-reports.title: Prison as temporary duty
cia-crimes-reports.summary: The frame John Kiriakou and his wife adopted in the weeks between his sentencing and his surrender: that a thirty-month sentence was to be treated as a long overseas posting. He had spent much of his CIA career deployed for months at a time, once for two years, and says the family handled the separation the way it had handled those. The analogy borrowed a specific piece of agency vocabulary — TDY, the assignment nobody asks you about.

cia-crimes-reports.title: The Grand Mosque cover story
cia-crimes-reports.summary: A single fabricated account of innocent travel that John Kiriakou says he heard roughly twenty-five times from Arab men detained in Pakistan after the September 11 attacks — a trip to Karachi to study Arabic, a lost passport, and a ride to the Grand Mosque. Its details were wrong in ways that gave it away, and Kiriakou treats its uniformity as evidence of poor operational security rather than of innocence.

cia-culture-of-lying.title: Congressional intelligence oversight
cia-culture-of-lying.summary: John Kiriakou''s standing criticism of the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence and the House Permanent Select Committee — that unlike the armed services and foreign relations committees, they do not perform oversight at all: "They''re just cheerleaders." His illustration is a sitting committee chairman who summoned him privately, then asked whether Kiriakou would write the criticism publicly on his behalf.

cia-culture-of-lying.title: Jeffrey Sterling
cia-culture-of-lying.summary: Former CIA officer convicted of nine felonies, including seven counts of espionage, after giving a New York Times interview about a racial discrimination lawsuit he had filed against the CIA. Per John Kiriakou, Sterling was not accused of spying for a foreign country; his underlying case was that the CIA had passed him over for promotion and told him explicitly it was because of his race. Daniel Ellsberg asked Sterling to go to trial specifically so the constitutionality of the Espionage Act could be challenged; Sterling did, was convicted, and was sentenced by Judge Leonie Brinkema to what she described as 'Kiriakou plus 12 months.'

cia-culture-of-lying.title: Watergate
cia-culture-of-lying.summary: The scandal that ended Nixon''s presidency and the standing benchmark in John Kiriakou''s vocabulary — the CIA spying on the Senate committee investigating its torture program was, to him, "a Watergate-level kind of scandal," except that this time nothing came of it. He draws one lesson from it above all others: Nixon did not fall for the burglary but for the cover-up. Watergate touches his own story directly — his lead defense attorney had been John Mitchell''s lawyer — and its cast overlapped with the agency he joined, from E. Howard Hunt to the tradecraft by which Deep Throat summoned Bob Woodward.

cia-culture-of-lying.title: Mike Pompeo
cia-culture-of-lying.summary: CIA director and later Secretary of State under Trump. John Kiriakou read Pompeo's 2017 speech branding WikiLeaks a "hostile non-state intelligence service" as the groundwork for an Espionage Act case against Julian Assange in the Eastern District of Virginia — the "Espionage Court" where Kiriakou himself was prosecuted. Friends who briefed Pompeo told Kiriakou he was extraordinarily bright but wrong on Iran; Kiriakou's own verdict soured permanently when Pompeo named Gina Haspel deputy director, flirted publicly with reinstating torture, and called Chelsea Manning a traitor — a crime she was never convicted of.

cia-culture-of-lying.title: The Pentagon's congressional district strategy
cia-culture-of-lying.summary: The practice John Kiriakou describes of placing defence manufacturing orders in effectively all 435 congressional districts, so that every member of Congress has constituents dependent on the defence budget — and nobody has an incentive to vote against it.

cia-culture-of-lying.title: 2026 Iran war
cia-culture-of-lying.summary: The open-ended American and Israeli war against Iran that John Kiriakou tracked week by week on his own show — a conflict he says was sold as three weeks, ran into its fifth month, achieved every decapitation objective it set, and continued anyway. His grade for it is a D, and his forecast is a Truth Social post declaring victory while nothing changes.

cia-democrats-2016.title: Intelligence Agencies
cia-democrats-2016.summary: Kiriakou counts roughly 19 publicly known US intelligence agencies and calls the proliferation Pentagon empire-building on duplicative work.

cia-democrats-2016.title: 1953 Iran coup
cia-democrats-2016.summary: The U.S.- and UK-backed overthrow of Iran's democratically elected prime minister, Mohammad Mossadegh; per John Kiriakou, the coup served British national interests rather than American ones, and the subsequent outlawing of secular political opposition under the Shah forced dissent into the mosques — producing a religious rather than secular revolution in 1979.

cia-democrats-2016.title: AIPAC
cia-democrats-2016.summary: The American Israel Public Affairs Committee — the U.S. political organization that, in John Kiriakou's framing, ought to be registered as a foreign-lobbying entity but is not, and that wields decisive electoral power against U.S. elected officials who express support for Palestinian human rights.

cia-democrats-2016.title: Barack Obama
cia-democrats-2016.summary: 44th U.S. president; in John Kiriakou's account, Obama publicly recounted refusing Benjamin Netanyahu's demand to bomb Iran and calling Israel's threat to use nuclear weapons a bluff — a bluff Kiriakou says Donald Trump later believed.

cia-democrats-2016.title: CIA adultery culture
cia-democrats-2016.summary: John Kiriakou's recurring characterization of the CIA officer corps as riddled with adultery and casual sex — which he frames not as gossip but as a systemic counterintelligence vulnerability that makes officers easy to recruit.

cia-democrats-2016.title: CIA cable priority levels
cia-democrats-2016.summary: The five levels of immediacy assigned to U.S. government cable traffic, as described by John Kiriakou. From lowest to highest: Routine, Priority, Immediate, Flash, CRITIC. Most career officers will never see a CRITIC; during the Gulf War, Kiriakou''s desk was receiving multiple CRITICs a day, each one announcing a hostile missile launch.

cia-directorates.title: CIA Training Doctrine
cia-directorates.summary: ''Our job is to break the law'' — Kiriakou on what CIA training actually teaches, why it applies only overseas, and the ethics class that never comes.

cia-directorates.title: Advanced Counterterrorism Operations
cia-directorates.summary: The six-week specialist course John Kiriakou flew back from Athens to attend roughly eighteen months before 9/11 as one of fourteen officers selected worldwide — high-threat operations, technical collection, and a driving syllabus built around crashing through roadblocks that left the class with whiplash. By accident of timing it meant a trained cadre was ready to deploy the moment the attacks came.

cia-directorates.title: Anwar al-Awlaki
cia-directorates.summary: American-born al-Qaeda propagandist; in 1993 the imam of the Falls Church, Virginia mosque visited by John Kiriakou's CIA Arabic-language class on a field trip; in 2001 the cleric at whose mosque the 9/11 hijackers prayed the night before the attacks; killed by U.S. drone strike in Yemen in approximately 2011.

cia-directorates.title: Butler rally shooting
cia-directorates.summary: The July 2024 attempt on Donald Trump's life at a rally in Butler, Pennsylvania, on which John Kiriakou takes no position as to who was responsible but argues the published facts cannot be reconciled with a competent Secret Service — and that the questions it leaves open are owed an answer for the historical record whether or not anyone alive gets one.

cia-directorates.title: Charlie Kirk shooting
cia-directorates.summary: Kiriakou questions the official account: a court filing says the ATF could not match the autopsy bullet to the rifle tied to the suspect.

cia-directorates.title: CIA liaison relationships
cia-directorates.summary: John Kiriakou's critique of CIA intelligence-liaison relationships with foreign governments — sharply expanded after 9/11 — arguing that officers do not consider the long-term risk that disclosing sensitive operations to foreign services hands those governments leverage, including potential blackmail material, over the United States, and that no one left in Congress has the will to provide real oversight of the practice.

cia-disguise-program.title: The Farm
cia-disguise-program.summary: The CIA's clandestine training facility in Virginia; site of approximately 80% of all CIA operational training

cia-disguise-program.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
cia-disguise-program.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

cia-disguise-program.title: Jeffrey Epstein
cia-disguise-program.summary: Convicted sex offender; per John Kiriakou, was "an Israeli access agent" rather than a CIA asset, because the CIA collects foreign intelligence and Epstein's targets — Bill Clinton, Bill Gates, Prince Andrew — were not foreign. Kiriakou further holds that Epstein did die by suicide in federal custody, because in the Bureau of Prisons the cameras never work and the guards are always asleep.

cia-disguise-program.title: John Kiriakou
cia-disguise-program.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

cia-disguise-program.title: Surveillance detection route
cia-disguise-program.summary: Tradecraft technique used by intelligence officers and assets to determine whether they are being followed before, during, or after an operational meeting

cia-disguise-program.title: Cofer Black
cia-disguise-program.summary: Former head of the CIA Counterterrorism Center during and immediately after the September 11 attacks; principal architect of the agency's paramilitary turn on September 12, 2001; later Vice President of Blackwater under Erik Prince.

cia-divorce-rate.title: Phil Ochs
cia-divorce-rate.summary: 1960s–70s protest folk singer; John Kiriakou retells a story from Pete Seeger about the night Ochs — who had fallen into depression after being unable to sing following a mugging in Africa — called Seeger just before taking his own life.

cia-divorce-rate.title: The CIA entrance examinations
cia-divorce-rate.summary: The two rounds of testing John Kiriakou sat before joining the CIA in 1990: a current-affairs multiple choice he found trivially easy, a blank fold-out map of the world, and a psychological inventory of several thousand agree-or-disagree statements that repeated the same proposition hundreds of questions apart to catch inconsistency — followed by an interview panel of a psychologist, a psychiatrist and an anthropologist.

cia-divorce-rate.title: Venezuelan embassy occupation (2019)
cia-divorce-rate.summary: A 2019 sit-in at the Venezuelan embassy in Washington, D.C., which John Kiriakou says he joined at the Venezuelan government's request the night the United States broke relations with Venezuela; he says he still keeps Venezuelan government property from that night at his house.

cia-divorce-rate.title: FBI manufactured terrorism cases
cia-divorce-rate.summary: John Kiriakou's account of terrorism prosecutions in which the FBI supplies the plot, the target, the explosives and the transport, then arrests the person it recruited. His central case is the 2026 Miami trial of a mentally ill homeless man facing six counts each carrying life without parole, in which Kiriakou testified for the defence and told the court that the FBI was "clearly the criminal in this case." The defendant was acquitted on every count.

cia-divorce-rate.title: The Tiffany stationery letter
cia-divorce-rate.summary: The deliberately expensive note John Kiriakou wrote to his first wife on Tiffany & Co. stationery, telling her he was halving her child support on the advice of counsel — a tactic suggested by his divorce lawyer to force her to file, and which worked the next day.

cia-divorce-rate.title: They deserve an apology
cia-divorce-rate.summary: John Kiriakou's statement that he feels he owes the men his government tortured an apology, that they deserve compensation they will never receive, and that at the very least they are owed the apology.

cia-driving-training.title: Exchange of bona fides
cia-driving-training.summary: The challenge-and-response protocol taught on the first day of CIA operational training, by which two intelligence officers who have never met establish that they are on the same side — a fixed nonsense phrase answered by a fixed nonsense phrase. Per John Kiriakou it is drilled hard enough that forgetting it under pressure, a staple of spy films, does not happen; if one side does not have the bona fides, "anything goes."

cia-driving-training.title: Bill Buckley
cia-driving-training.summary: CIA station chief in Beirut kidnapped by Palestinian Islamic Jihad in March 1984; tortured at length over fifteen months; killed in captivity; the case from which the agency derived a generation of operational-security lessons including the abandonment of single-point tracking devices in CIA officers' personal kit.

cia-driving-training.title: Burn Notice
cia-driving-training.summary: Both a piece of real CIA tradecraft — a worldwide cable forbidding every officer from speaking to a named person — and the USA Network spy series named after it, which John Kiriakou watched as a fan before he became its script adviser — a job he obtained by sitting next to its creator, Matt Nix, on a flight from Washington to Los Angeles, having previously run the show's credits in slow motion to find out who was advising it. Nobody was. By the time the plane landed Kiriakou had the job for season six.

cia-driving-training.title: CIA psychological evaluations
cia-driving-training.summary: The two kinds of psychological work John Kiriakou describes inside the CIA — the recurring psychiatric screening every officer undergoes, before employment, again three years after hiring and every five years thereafter for life; and the long-distance evaluation of foreign leaders carried out by the analytic side. The agency's clinical psychologists are split between the two, with a third group in operations advising case officers on the sources they recruit.

cia-driving-training.title: Concealment devices
cia-driving-training.summary: Hollowed everyday objects — known inside the CIA as CDs — issued to officers to hide documents, equipment and, in the larger sizes, a gun. Per John Kiriakou every CIA officer has access to them, some are simply assigned with no instructions attached, and the way they are found in real life is the way they are found in *The Good Shepherd* — by an anomaly a hand can feel.

cia-driving-training.title: Congressional intelligence oversight
cia-driving-training.summary: John Kiriakou''s standing criticism of the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence and the House Permanent Select Committee — that unlike the armed services and foreign relations committees, they do not perform oversight at all: "They''re just cheerleaders." His illustration is a sitting committee chairman who summoned him privately, then asked whether Kiriakou would write the criticism publicly on his behalf.

cia-drug-facilitation.title: Contra rebels
cia-drug-facilitation.summary: The right-wing Nicaraguan insurgency armed by the Reagan administration against the Sandinista government. In John Kiriakou's account they were conservatives, right-wingers, in some cases fascists, and disgruntled military officers; they were split into a northern group the United States armed and a southern group that financed itself by selling cocaine — a distinction that became the pivot of the Gary Webb affair, and that Kiriakou uses to answer the CIA's standing denial that it had anything to do with the drug trade.

cia-drug-facilitation.title: Jack Devine
cia-drug-facilitation.summary: A former CIA officer John Kiriakou worked for briefly in 2001 or 2002, and describes with real warmth as a great officer and a true believer — while flatly rejecting his insistence that the agency was never involved with cocaine. Asked to choose between Devine and a thirty-year DEA veteran who agrees with him, Kiriakou picks the DEA man.

cia-drug-facilitation.title: Yemen Diplomatic Pouch Arrest
cia-drug-facilitation.summary: Per John Kiriakou, his most wholly negative experience with a foreign intelligence service: arrested at Sana''a Airport in Yemen in 1991, eighteen months into his CIA career, after his Riyadh station chief asked him to carry a diplomatic pouch on a long-weekend trip. Yemeni officials demanded the sealed pouch go through the X-ray machine. When the scan revealed a handheld walkie-talkie inside, someone shouted ''Jassus'' — spy — and Kiriakou was handcuffed and placed in an airport cell. The incident triggered a diplomatic chain reaction reaching the Yemeni Prime Minister before a Yemeni officer hacked open the diplomatic seal with a curved jambiya dagger to confirm the pouch contained only mail and the radio. Kiriakou spent the rest of the weekend under heavy surveillance; he later said each of his five trips to Yemen was worse than the last.

cia-drug-facilitation.title: Fentanyl as a weapon of mass destruction
cia-drug-facilitation.summary: John Kiriakou's objection to the designation of fentanyl as a weapon of mass destruction — that a WMD is by definition a single weapon that kills large numbers at once, that no drug can be that, and that stretching the term cheapens and disables it. He notes in passing that Venezuela does not make fentanyl and that what it does ship goes to Western Europe.

cia-drug-facilitation.title: Saudi nuclear program
cia-drug-facilitation.summary: Saudi Arabia's decades-long pursuit of uranium enrichment, nominally for nuclear power, which John Kiriakou notes was already old news when he arrived at the CIA in 1990 and which conventional wisdom has always read as a weapons programme.

cia-drug-facilitation.title: The CIA buyout offer
cia-drug-facilitation.summary: The deferred-resignation offer extended to CIA staff in early 2025 on the same terms given to other federal workers — six to eight months' pay, no requirement to come to work, and then the end of the contract — which John Kiriakou discussed as part of a broader reorientation of the agency towards the Western Hemisphere.

cia-entrance-exams.title: The CIA divorce rate
cia-entrance-exams.summary: John Kiriakou's account of why marriages fail at the CIA at a rate he says exceeds that of any other part of the U.S. government — the impossibility of explaining a midnight departure to a spouse without a clearance, and the difficulty officers have switching off a professional habit of deception. He gives the figure variously as over 75 percent and upwards of 80 percent, says he was determined not to become a statistic and became one anyway, and dates the end of his first marriage to a sentence spoken in an armoured car on the way to Athens airport. Both his divorces have been costly; of the second he says the agency played an active role he is barred by court order from explaining.

cia-entrance-exams.title: The polygraph
cia-entrance-exams.summary: The lie-detector examination that gates entry to the CIA, described by John Kiriakou from the inside: the twenty-minute wiring-up, the psychiatrist''s advice to stare at a speck on the wall, the deliberately planted false accusation used to test a candidate''s reaction, and his contention that the machine screens out exactly the wrong people.

cia-entrance-exams.title: Jerrold Post
cia-entrance-exams.summary: American political psychiatrist and CIA officer who recruited John Kiriakou into the agency in 1988 through the CIA's covert campus recruiting program, working undercover as a George Washington University professor; founder of the CIA's Political Psychology Division (also called the Office of Leadership Analysis). Held a bachelor's, master's, and PhD in psychology and a PhD in political science, all from Yale, plus an MD from Harvard, and authored a dozen books on the psychology of world leaders and terrorists. Per Kiriakou, Post identified in him not just writing talent but "sociopathic tendencies" — and, when Kiriakou later blew the whistle, called to congratulate him, telling him that reaction proved he was not a true sociopath. Died of COVID-19, approximately 2022.

cia-entrance-exams.title: United Food and Commercial Workers
cia-entrance-exams.summary: The huge K Street labor union where a young John Kiriakou — from a family with a long labor history — was working when Dr. Jerrold Post''s class assignment changed his life: shadow your boss for a week and write his psychological profile. Kiriakou''s boss was a mean old-school organizer whose back had been broken by scabs; halfway through the week Kiriakou called him a racist ("which he was"), and the resulting paper diagnosed the man as a sociopath and potentially dangerous. The paper is what put Kiriakou on the CIA''s radar.

cia-entrance-exams.title: Arabic and Greek
cia-entrance-exams.summary: The qualification John Kiriakou says opened the door to his transfer from CIA analysis to operations: a post in Athens wanted Greek or Arabic, and he had both — by most of his tellings the only officer in the agency who did. The chief who hired him gave the reason in one sentence: it is easier and cheaper to take a linguist and teach him operations than the other way round. The pairing also became a detection tool, since the language nobody speaks in Pakistan is Arabic.

cia-entrance-exams.title: Asset acquisition cycle
cia-entrance-exams.summary: The four-step process — spot, assess, develop, recruit — taught as the first lesson of CIA case officer training

cia-fbi-911-interagency-rivalry.title: National Security Act of 1947
cia-fbi-911-interagency-rivalry.summary: The law that created the CIA and the National Security Council — passed, in John Kiriakou's telling, only because Harry Truman lied to J. Edgar Hoover. Hoover lobbied Capitol Hill to kill the bill until Truman promised the CIA would be a division of the FBI; the bill passed, Hoover realized he'd been duped, and ordered the FBI not to cooperate with the new agency — a freeze that lasted, incredibly, until after 9/11. Kiriakou's account of how the agency was designed at all runs through a room in New York where MI6 officers sat down with Bill Donovan, Prescott Bush and some pads of paper.

cia-fbi-911-interagency-rivalry.title: Kiriakou's transfer to the Directorate of Operations
cia-fbi-911-interagency-rivalry.summary: John Kiriakou's roughly two-month internal campaign to transfer from the CIA's analytic Directorate of Intelligence to the operational Directorate of Operations, overcoming what he calls a "natural bias in operations against the eggheads on the analytic side," followed by an Athens posting secured because he was the only person in the entire CIA fluent in both Greek and Arabic. Covers his full CIA career arc from 1988/1990 recruitment through analyst years on Iraq, the switch to operations, 9/11, the enhanced-interrogation refusal, executive assistant to the deputy director for operations, and his eventual resignation and post-CIA career.

cia-fbi-911-interagency-rivalry.title: World Trade Center
cia-fbi-911-interagency-rivalry.summary: The twin towers whose burning image reached John Kiriakou on the little TV of Cofer Black's secretary — he compared it aloud to the 1930s Empire State Building accident, protested that the day was too clear not to see the tower, and watched the second plane hit as the words left his mouth. Kiriakou ties the towers' story back to the neglected files of the 1990 Kahane assassination and the 1993 bombing, whose captured plotters said they had meant to kill 200,000 by collapsing the buildings into each other — and to John O'Neill, the al-Qaeda-obsessed FBI man who became WTC security chief and died there on his first days at work.

cia-fbi-911-interagency-rivalry.title: CIA versus FBI at a raid
cia-fbi-911-interagency-rivalry.summary: John Kiriakou''s two-sentence account of the institutional difference between the two agencies, drawn from joint raids in Pakistan in 2002: the FBI numbers the four walls with sticky notes, photographs the inside of every drawer and collects every piece of paper, because it is building a case. The CIA breaks down the door, grabs all the men and sends them to Guantánamo.

cia-fbi-911-interagency-rivalry.title: The French human sources
cia-fbi-911-interagency-rivalry.summary: John Kiriakou''s confirmation of what Chris Hedges was told by French intelligence after 9/11 — that the CIA had no human assets inside al-Qaeda at all, while the French thwarted attacks by having recruited people next to the plotters — and the general principle he draws from it: that no amount of money spent on electronics substitutes for a human source.

cia-fbi-911-interagency-rivalry.title: Trump
cia-fbi-911-interagency-rivalry.summary: Kiriakou applied for a pardon on the last day of Trump's first term — and says Trump had agreed to it, until the last-minute reversal.

cia-fbi-budget-fearmongering.title: Abu Omar rendition
cia-fbi-budget-fearmongering.summary: The CIA's kidnapping of a Milan cleric, Abu Omar, who was sent to Egypt to be tortured; John Kiriakou calls it a case that ought to be taught at the CIA as how not to run a rendition, and it is what ultimately sent him to prison, after he confirmed a former colleague's surname to a journalist claiming to be writing a book about it.

cia-fbi-budget-fearmongering.title: Afghanistan 2011 Kerry Trip
cia-fbi-budget-fearmongering.summary: John Kiriakou's 2011 trip to Afghanistan as senior investigator for the Senate Foreign Relations Committee under Chairman John Kerry, where the pair sat through a briefing with 11 one-to-four-star generals presenting an optimistic account of the war — after which Kerry mused the U.S. might win, only for Kiriakou to tell him the U.S. controlled only Kabul, and that the same rosy briefing had been given every year since 2002.

cia-fbi-budget-fearmongering.title: Dick Cheney
cia-fbi-budget-fearmongering.summary: U.S. Vice President under George W. Bush. Per John Kiriakou — recounting CIA Director George Tenet's memoir — Cheney intercepted the presidential finding authorizing the CIA's enhanced interrogation program in the Oval Office anteroom and took it from Tenet before Bush could sign it. Tenet later concluded the president probably never actually signed the finding and probably told the truth when he said he had no idea the program was taking place. Kiriakou characterizes Cheney as the one who actually ran foreign policy, intelligence policy, and defense policy during the Bush years.

cia-fbi-budget-fearmongering.title: The Directorate of Operations
cia-fbi-budget-fearmongering.summary: The CIA's clandestine service, which John Kiriakou joined from analysis because he spoke both Greek and Arabic — a culture he describes as wildly different from the analytic side, short on institutional memory and organised around the race to become a station chief.

cia-fbi-budget-fearmongering.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
cia-fbi-budget-fearmongering.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

cia-fbi-budget-fearmongering.title: Espionage Act
cia-fbi-budget-fearmongering.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

cia-fbi-incompatible-computer-systems.title: Learned Helplessness
cia-fbi-incompatible-computer-systems.summary: Psychological concept adapted by the CIA as the theoretical basis for its post-9/11 enhanced interrogation program; per John Kiriakou, the goal of techniques including waterboarding was not primarily to elicit specific information but to render the prisoner so terrified of his captors that he would volunteer confessions on demand. In practice, applied to Abu Zubaydah, it meant a dog cage he would climb into on command, a coffin filled with cockroaches, and a towel whose mere appearance made him crumple — a programme Kiriakou says had far less to do with gathering intelligence than with ruining a man's life.

cia-fbi-incompatible-computer-systems.title: Defense HUMINT Service
cia-fbi-incompatible-computer-systems.summary: The Pentagon's human collection outfit, which John Kiriakou names as one of the three agencies that already do everything the CIA does — alongside the State Department's Bureau of Intelligence and Research for analysis and the NSA for interception — and which is therefore the core of his argument that Langley is redundant rather than merely badly run.

cia-fbi-incompatible-computer-systems.title: The lawfare template
cia-fbi-incompatible-computer-systems.summary: The assessment of John Kiriakou''s prosecution that he quotes most often and finds most alarming: a former United States attorney for Utah told him the Kiriakou case was the template for the Democratic Party''s policy of lawfare. Kiriakou''s gloss is that if they do not like you they can ruin your life, and there is nothing you can do to protect yourself.

cia-fbi-incompatible-computer-systems.title: The science fiction writer FOIA request
cia-fbi-incompatible-computer-systems.summary: The Freedom of Information Act request John Kiriakou filed with the CIA about a 1950s science fiction writer long rumoured to have been an undercover officer — answered only with a letter saying the agency lacked the manpower to meet its statutory ninety-day deadline. Fifteen years later, he says, he is still waiting.

cia-fbi-incompatible-computer-systems.title: The General Assembly workaround
cia-fbi-incompatible-computer-systems.summary: A proposal John Kiriakou says a Russian diplomat described to him: letting the United Nations General Assembly take implementable decisions without Security Council permission, so that a supermajority of states could override an American veto. Kiriakou, whose last CIA tour was at the United Nations and who found the institution paralysed, says he thinks it is a good idea.

cia-fbi-incompatible-computer-systems.title: The minister of Awqaf compliment
cia-fbi-incompatible-computer-systems.summary: The moment John Kiriakou calls the highlight of his Bahrain tour and freely describes as an ego booster: interpreting for Ambassador David Ransom''s first courtesy call on the only Bahraini cabinet member who did not speak fluent English, and being complimented on his Arabic on the way out — something he says he still thinks about thirty years later.

cia-fbi-organized-crime.title: Bilderberg and weapon sales
cia-fbi-organized-crime.summary: John Kiriakou's claim, sourced to someone he knew who attended, that elite gatherings like Bilderberg and the Shangri-La Dialogue are — beneath the talk of global issues — fundamentally 'all about weapon sales' and defense-contractor deals.

cia-fbi-organized-crime.title: CIA and the UFO question
cia-fbi-organized-crime.summary: John Kiriakou's consistent answer that UFOs and alien technology are a Pentagon matter, not a CIA one — though he says nearly every former fighter-pilot friend of his has seen something inexplicable, sometimes emerging from the ocean.

cia-fbi-organized-crime.title: Kissinger and the petrodollar
cia-fbi-organized-crime.summary: John Kiriakou's endorsement of the theory that Henry Kissinger deliberately structured the 1970s petrodollar to tie the U.S. to Middle Eastern oil — creating a standing rationale for policing the region, even as America exports its own fracked oil.

cia-fbi-organized-crime.title: Operation Gladio
cia-fbi-organized-crime.summary: A CIA, MI6, Vatican and NATO operation to leave 'stay-behind' sleeper networks across Western Europe after World War II in case of a Soviet invasion; John Kiriakou, who learned of it only after leaving the CIA, notes it was made public by Italian PM Andreotti in 1990.

cia-fbi-organized-crime.title: Carlos the Jackal
cia-fbi-organized-crime.summary: Venezuelan-born militant (Ilich Ramírez Sánchez) active in the 1970s and 1980s; per John Kiriakou, 'the Osama bin Laden of the 70s and 80s.' Kiriakou spent his Athens posting trying to identify the middleman linking Carlos to the Greek terrorist group 17 November, then six months working the lead with MI5 in London; Carlos was finally run down by CIA contractor Billy Waugh in a Khartoum vegetable market and captured in 1994.

cia-fbi-organized-crime.title: CIA National Resources Division
cia-fbi-organized-crime.summary: The Central Intelligence Agency's domestic intelligence-collection arm, created in the 1980s by Director William J. Casey

cia-fbi-social-media-embed.title: Central Intelligence Agency
cia-fbi-social-media-embed.summary: U.S. foreign intelligence service; John Kiriakou's employer from 1990 to 2004 and the central institution of KiriPedia

cia-fbi-social-media-embed.title: Israeli intelligence presence in the United States
cia-fbi-social-media-embed.summary: John Kiriakou's account of Israeli intelligence activity inside the United States — dozens of undeclared Mossad and Shin Bet officers identified by the FBI, a critical-threat counterintelligence classification alongside Russia, North Korea and Cuba, and a pattern of harassment and intimidation directed at declared CIA officers posted to Israel.

cia-fbi-social-media-embed.title: Operation Mockingbird
cia-fbi-social-media-embed.summary: The CIA's mid-twentieth-century program of recruiting and managing American journalists as influence assets; in John Kiriakou's account, no longer operationally necessary in the contemporary period because the U.S. media voluntarily reprints CIA-supplied material, and in at least one documented case sends articles to the agency for clearance before sending them to its own editor.

cia-fbi-social-media-embed.title: Truman's CIA op-ed
cia-fbi-social-media-embed.summary: A 1963 Washington Post op-ed in which former President Harry Truman — who signed the CIA into being in 1947 — called it a 'damn fool mistake' that should be disbanded; John Kiriakou notes the piece ran in the morning edition and vanished from the evening one.

cia-fbi-social-media-embed.title: CIA media revolving door
cia-fbi-social-media-embed.summary: John Kiriakou's proposed reform to bar CIA officers from becoming paid media personalities without a cooling-off period, and to strip the security clearances of retirees who go straight from the agency to cable-news punditry.

cia-fbi-social-media-embed.title: Edward Snowden
cia-fbi-social-media-embed.summary: Former NSA contractor who in 2013 disclosed the scope of U.S. [mass surveillance](/wiki/mass-surveillance), including the Section 702 collection program. Per John Kiriakou — who counts Snowden among the small group of national-security whistleblowers prosecuted under the Espionage Act — Snowden was ''stuck between two awful slippery slopes'': breaking his oath and chain of command on one side, and on the other catching something ''cut and dry against the Constitution'' that no one would act on. Kiriakou notes Snowden could not use his chain of command (as Kiriakou could not, his own chain being Jose Rodriguez), and that Judge Leonie Brinkema had reserved the Snowden case for herself before he fled the country.

cia-feeder-schools.title: CIA–Big Tech revolving door
cia-feeder-schools.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of the traffic between the CIA and the major technology companies — "they work hand in glove" — illustrated by a supervisor who resigned five years short of his thirty-year pension for a Microsoft job paying eight times his government salary. The exchange, he argues, benefits both sides and is for that reason dangerous: the agency gains access to the most advanced companies in the world, and the companies gain a direct channel into the intelligence community.

cia-feeder-schools.title: FCI Loretto
cia-feeder-schools.summary: U.S. Federal Correctional Institution in Loretto, Pennsylvania; the low-medium-security prison at which John Kiriakou served 23 months of a 30-month sentence following his 2013 Espionage Act–era plea deal; the originally ordered "minimum security work camp" placement was countermanded — per Kiriakou, on Brennan's direct intervention — to place him in the actual prison alongside the general population.

cia-feeder-schools.title: Field loadout
cia-feeder-schools.summary: John Kiriakou''s itemised answer to a question he says no one had ever asked him — what a CIA operations officer actually carried in the field. In Athens: a 9mm in a tearaway fanny pack, a snub-nose .38 on his ankle, a Buck knife, and some 47 rounds. In Pakistan: one 9mm, and a daily prayer that he would not have to use it. Plus $2,000–$5,000 in cash on an ordinary day, because "intelligence is a cash business."

cia-feeder-schools.title: Osama bin Laden
cia-feeder-schools.summary: Founder and leader of al-Qaeda and the central target of the manhunt that shaped John Kiriakou's counterterrorism career. Per Kiriakou, bin Laden came from a billionaire Saudi construction family, was never one of the CIA-funded Afghan mujahideen, overruled subordinates who wanted to attack Israel and insisted the 9/11 attacks hit the United States to crash its economy, escaped Tora Bora dressed as a woman, and spent his final years next to Pakistan's equivalent of West Point — where, Kiriakou says, you would have to be a "mental defective" not to know he was there. Kiriakou believes the United States never intended to capture him alive.

cia-feeder-schools.title: Freemasons and Opus Dei at the CIA
cia-feeder-schools.summary: John Kiriakou's characterisation of the affinity networks at the top of the CIA — a great many senior officers who are Freemasons, and periods in which most of the leadership belonged to Opus Dei and attended the same church in Great Falls, Virginia. He rejects the idea that these are plots, describing them instead as accidental clusters of men who look out for one another.

cia-feeder-schools.title: The CIA spotter professor
cia-feeder-schools.summary: How John Kiriakou entered the CIA: a graduate-school professor who liked his writing style asked him to stay after class, and turned out to be an undercover officer working as a talent spotter. Kiriakou, who had been planning on Capitol Hill or the foreign service, says he had given the agency no thought at all until it approached him.

cia-founding-1947.title: National Security Act of 1947
cia-founding-1947.summary: The law that created the CIA and the National Security Council — passed, in John Kiriakou's telling, only because Harry Truman lied to J. Edgar Hoover. Hoover lobbied Capitol Hill to kill the bill until Truman promised the CIA would be a division of the FBI; the bill passed, Hoover realized he'd been duped, and ordered the FBI not to cooperate with the new agency — a freeze that lasted, incredibly, until after 9/11. Kiriakou's account of how the agency was designed at all runs through a room in New York where MI6 officers sat down with Bill Donovan, Prescott Bush and some pads of paper.

cia-founding-1947.title: William Donovan
cia-founding-1947.summary: General William "Wild Bill" Donovan — Medal of Honor recipient, decorated World War I veteran, Wall Street figure, and founder of the wartime Office of Strategic Services (OSS). Per John Kiriakou, Donovan had President Truman's ear and insisted the new agency be independent rather than a division of the FBI; he was among the men who sat down with visiting MI6 officers in New York in 1946–47 and sketched out a centralized intelligence service on pads of paper, and he became — in Kiriakou's telling — the first director of the CIA, over the sustained opposition of J. Edgar Hoover.

cia-founding-1947.title: Church Committee
cia-founding-1947.summary: U.S. Senate investigative committee operating in 1975–1976 that examined domestic intelligence abuses by the CIA, FBI, and NSA; per John Kiriakou, the Church Committee — alongside the concurrent Pike Committee in the House — was the last genuine moment of legislative oversight over the intelligence community, born of a national consensus that government had gone dangerously off course. Its work led to the creation of the permanent Senate Select Committee on Intelligence, which Kiriakou says ceased to function as real oversight roughly seven years after its founding.

cia-founding-1947.title: CIA–FBI interagency rivalry and 9/11
cia-founding-1947.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the historical CIA–FBI rivalry, dating to J. Edgar Hoover's opposition to the 1947 National Security Act, and how it manifested before September 11 when Cofer Black's Counterterrorism Center withheld from the FBI that hijackers Nawaf al-Hazmi and Khalid al-Mihdhar had been granted U.S. visas.

cia-founding-1947.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
cia-founding-1947.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

cia-founding-1947.title: Kiriakou's transfer to the Directorate of Operations
cia-founding-1947.summary: John Kiriakou's roughly two-month internal campaign to transfer from the CIA's analytic Directorate of Intelligence to the operational Directorate of Operations, overcoming what he calls a "natural bias in operations against the eggheads on the analytic side," followed by an Athens posting secured because he was the only person in the entire CIA fluent in both Greek and Arabic. Covers his full CIA career arc from 1988/1990 recruitment through analyst years on Iraq, the switch to operations, 9/11, the enhanced-interrogation refusal, executive assistant to the deputy director for operations, and his eventual resignation and post-CIA career.

cia-gmail-account-felony-case.title: Three Felonies a Day
cia-gmail-account-felony-case.summary: Book by Harvard Law professor Harvey Silverglate, cited by John Kiriakou, arguing that the United States is so overcriminalized and so overregulated that the average American going about normal daily life inadvertently commits three felonies every day. Kiriakou cites the book in the context of warrantless government surveillance: if authorities decide they want a particular person, they can obtain that person''s metadata, sift it for technical violations, and destroy their life — without any genuine predicate offense.

cia-gmail-account-felony-case.title: Anthony Fauci
cia-gmail-account-felony-case.summary: American physician and public-health official whose pardon John Kiriakou condemned as "unacceptable" in a May 2026 Fox News appearance. Kiriakou''s objection is partly personal: his cousin George was, he says, the second person in Ohio to die of COVID, in very early 2020. Kiriakou confined himself to the pardon and to his own family''s loss, and made no claim of his own about the origin of the virus.

cia-gmail-account-felony-case.title: Church Committee
cia-gmail-account-felony-case.summary: U.S. Senate investigative committee operating in 1975–1976 that examined domestic intelligence abuses by the CIA, FBI, and NSA; per John Kiriakou, the Church Committee — alongside the concurrent Pike Committee in the House — was the last genuine moment of legislative oversight over the intelligence community, born of a national consensus that government had gone dangerously off course. Its work led to the creation of the permanent Senate Select Committee on Intelligence, which Kiriakou says ceased to function as real oversight roughly seven years after its founding.

cia-gmail-account-felony-case.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
cia-gmail-account-felony-case.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

cia-gmail-account-felony-case.title: The Greek Orthodox Church
cia-gmail-account-felony-case.summary: The church John Kiriakou was raised in and still belongs to — the institution behind his Greek fluency and his family''s immigrant history, a recurring thread in his accounts of Athens, Damascus, Bethlehem and Washington, and, in two cases, an actor in his own story: the church the FBI followed him into, and the priest who tried to get him a pardon.

cia-gmail-account-felony-case.title: John Kiriakou
cia-gmail-account-felony-case.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

cia-groupthink.title: Sociopathic Tendencies
cia-groupthink.summary: Per John Kiriakou, the CIA actively recruits for what its instructors call 'sociopathic tendencies' — not full clinical sociopathy, but the capacity to operate in legal, moral, and ethical gray areas without being paralyzed by regret. Kiriakou describes this as the trait that makes case officers effective at recruitment and adaptable in the field, and offers his own act of whistleblowing as evidence he does not possess the deeper sociopathy that, in his view, characterizes the most institutionally successful intelligence officers.

cia-groupthink.title: Bruce Fein
cia-groupthink.summary: John Kiriakou's longtime attorney and one of his closest friends; a Harvard Law-trained constitutional scholar, former Deputy Attorney General under President Reagan and former General Counsel of the Federal Communications Commission. Fein took the call from Jared Kushner's attorney that opened Kiriakou's first pardon track, sat beside him at the 2018 Trump International Hotel meeting at which Rudy Giuliani's aide solicited $2 million for a presidential pardon, and is his co-author on a long-planned book about the CIA's record of failure.

cia-groupthink.title: George Tenet
cia-groupthink.summary: Director of Central Intelligence from 1997 to 2004, spanning the September 11 attacks and the early enhanced-interrogation program; identified by John Kiriakou as John Brennan's institutional patron at the agency; the figure who ordered the Five Eyes intelligence services to "open the files" to each other in the early 2000s.

cia-groupthink.title: Jose Rodriguez
cia-groupthink.summary: Senior CIA officer of the post-9/11 era; identified by John Kiriakou as among those responsible for crimes committed in the name of national security; described as believing himself to be a good guy.

cia-groupthink.title: Barack Obama
cia-groupthink.summary: 44th U.S. president; in John Kiriakou's account, Obama publicly recounted refusing Benjamin Netanyahu's demand to bomb Iran and calling Israel's threat to use nuclear weapons a bluff — a bluff Kiriakou says Donald Trump later believed.

cia-groupthink.title: Bureau of Prisons
cia-groupthink.summary: The federal agency that ran John Kiriakou's incarceration — and one of his most persistent post-prison targets. The BOP overrode his judge's camp recommendation by deeming him "a threat to the public safety," threatened him with "diesel therapy" until 1,600 logged phone calls and letters from a dozen House members and two senators backed it off, and, per Kiriakou, functions as "an employment agency for unemployable semi-literate rural white men" and "a dumping ground for failed medical professionals" — an agency for which a prisoner's death is cheaper than his treatment.

cia-insiders-guide-to-surveillance.title: Kiriakou's serial-killer letters
cia-insiders-guide-to-surveillance.summary: John Kiriakou's account of writing letters, as research for a planned book, to several well-known serial killers — including David Berkowitz ("Son of Sam"), Gary Leon Ridgway (the Green River Killer), the BTK killer, the "co-ed killer," and Manson family member Tex Watson — and the uniformly evangelical, Jesus-focused responses he received instead of the interviews he wanted.

cia-insiders-guide-to-surveillance.title: Kiriakou's Pakistan-Islam economic critique
cia-insiders-guide-to-surveillance.summary: John Kiriakou's controversial view that Islam has held Pakistan back economically, contrasting Pakistan's stalled development since the 1960s with South Korea's — which had the same GDP as Pakistan in 1964 — and citing lost productivity from prayer breaks and holy days, resentment over partition, and spending on nuclear weapons instead of infrastructure and education.

cia-insiders-guide-to-surveillance.title: Yemen Diplomatic Pouch Arrest
cia-insiders-guide-to-surveillance.summary: Per John Kiriakou, his most wholly negative experience with a foreign intelligence service: arrested at Sana''a Airport in Yemen in 1991, eighteen months into his CIA career, after his Riyadh station chief asked him to carry a diplomatic pouch on a long-weekend trip. Yemeni officials demanded the sealed pouch go through the X-ray machine. When the scan revealed a handheld walkie-talkie inside, someone shouted ''Jassus'' — spy — and Kiriakou was handcuffed and placed in an airport cell. The incident triggered a diplomatic chain reaction reaching the Yemeni Prime Minister before a Yemeni officer hacked open the diplomatic seal with a curved jambiya dagger to confirm the pouch contained only mail and the radio. Kiriakou spent the rest of the weekend under heavy surveillance; he later said each of his five trips to Yemen was worse than the last.

cia-insiders-guide-to-surveillance.title: DARPA LifeLog
cia-insiders-guide-to-surveillance.summary: A Pentagon research program meant to track every email, photo, location and purchase of a person; John Kiriakou notes it was killed on February 4, 2004 — one day before Mark Zuckerberg filed the Facebook LLC.

cia-insiders-guide-to-surveillance.title: Non-Personal Communication
cia-insiders-guide-to-surveillance.summary: Per John Kiriakou, a category of espionage tradecraft encompassing all methods of passing information between an officer and an agent — or between two intelligence services — that do not require the parties to meet in person. Techniques include concealment devices (e.g. hollowed-out objects no passerby would willingly touch, such as a dead rat or a used condom), signal sites and dead drops coordinated by chalk marks, and burst transmissions sent through devices hidden in false-backed drawers.

cia-insiders-guide-to-surveillance.title: The CIA Insider's Guide omnibus
cia-insiders-guide-to-surveillance.summary: Skyhorse Publishing's plan to reissue John Kiriakou's three CIA Insider's Guides as a single updated volume of some 550 pages, with an introduction Tucker Carlson wrote in a day — part of what Kiriakou described in 2026 as a big book year.

cia-intelligence-failures.title: Wealth concentration
cia-intelligence-failures.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that the present distribution of wealth is historically unprecedented and politically unsustainable — that trillionaires have never existed before, that five men hold as much as the bottom eighty per cent of the world, and that a defence budget approaching $1.5 trillion cannot be reconciled with the social spending it would have to displace.

cia-intelligence-failures.title: 2028 presidential field
cia-intelligence-failures.summary: John Kiriakou's assessment of the wide-open 2028 presidential race — the first in his life, he says, where he has no idea who either party will nominate. Predictive markets were listing 44 Democrats and 26 Republicans as possible candidates. His own preferred candidate is Tucker Carlson, whom he says he has repeatedly begged to run; his working assumption about anyone who does want the job is that they are "a narcissist and probably a sociopath on top of it."

cia-intelligence-failures.title: Amaryllis Fox Kennedy
cia-intelligence-failures.summary: Former CIA non-official-cover officer who worked under commercial cover as an international art consultant, later a Trump campaign manager and nominee for deputy CIA director. Per John Kiriakou, Senator Tom Cotton threatened to filibuster her appointment; the president responded by naming her deputy national security adviser instead — a job Kiriakou considers more powerful, since the CIA director reports to the national security adviser.

cia-intelligence-failures.title: Andrew Bustamante
cia-intelligence-failures.summary: Former CIA officer who sells CIA-style training online; John Kiriakou identifies him as the lone critic of his work hosting a show on a Russian network, and argues Bustamante's training business — open to anyone who pays — is the more problematic of the two.

cia-intelligence-failures.title: Angry Birds
cia-intelligence-failures.summary: The mobile game John Kiriakou describes as his only vice besides buying art, played every morning for nine consecutive years and cited by his ex-wife as a grievance in their marriage.

cia-intelligence-failures.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
cia-intelligence-failures.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

cia-internal-social-culture.title: The CIA barber shop
cia-internal-social-culture.summary: The barber in the basement of CIA headquarters, which John Kiriakou visited once on the reasoning that it saved a trip across town and found stocked with Playboys and Penthouses — one of several amenities, alongside a dry cleaner and a post office substation, that made the building function as a self-contained town.

cia-internal-social-culture.title: The encounter at the Greek ambassador's residence
cia-internal-social-culture.summary: An exchange John Kiriakou describes from a dinner a few weeks after his 2015 release from prison, in which Senator Ron Wyden — then vice chairman of the Senate Intelligence Committee — welcomed him home, was told Kiriakou had expected him to speak up, and answered that it had taken everything he had simply to keep his own security clearance. Kiriakou offers it as evidence that the intelligence oversight committees are afraid of the agencies they oversee.

cia-internal-social-culture.title: ''Once CIA, always CIA''
cia-internal-social-culture.summary: The comment-section accusation John Kiriakou says angers him more than any other — that no one who has served in the CIA ever really leaves it, and that whistleblowers are therefore still working for the agency. He calls it "the most intellectually lazy, stupid, thoughtless position that anybody could take", says the agency actively benefits from it because it splits the anti-CIA public, and answers the version aimed at himself by pointing at his prison sentence.

cia-internal-social-culture.title: The move to Fort Myer
cia-internal-social-culture.summary: John Kiriakou's report that Stephen Miller, Pete Hegseth and Kristi Noem all moved with their families onto Fort Myer army base into housing reserved for one- to four-star generals — 'the mother of all gated communities' — after Miller sold his Arlington house to escape protesters chalking his public sidewalk.

cia-internal-social-culture.title: The filibuster and Harry Reid's lesson
cia-internal-social-culture.summary: John Kiriakou's defence of the Senate filibuster, offered as praise for John Thune's refusal to abolish it under pressure from the White House, and grounded in what he regards as Harry Reid's costly mistake over judicial nominations.

cia-internal-social-culture.title: The Sudan massacre
cia-internal-social-culture.summary: The killing of at least 624 civilians by a government-affiliated militia in Sudan in late October 2025, which John Kiriakou called a crime against humanity — and which he reads as a proxy war financed by the United Arab Emirates on one side and Saudi Arabia on the other, with a Wahhabi component traceable to Hassan al-Turabi.

cia-language-training.title: Arabic and Greek
cia-language-training.summary: The qualification John Kiriakou says opened the door to his transfer from CIA analysis to operations: a post in Athens wanted Greek or Arabic, and he had both — by most of his tellings the only officer in the agency who did. The chief who hired him gave the reason in one sentence: it is easier and cheaper to take a linguist and teach him operations than the other way round. The pairing also became a detection tool, since the language nobody speaks in Pakistan is Arabic.

cia-language-training.title: Kiriakou's transfer to the Directorate of Operations
cia-language-training.summary: John Kiriakou's roughly two-month internal campaign to transfer from the CIA's analytic Directorate of Intelligence to the operational Directorate of Operations, overcoming what he calls a "natural bias in operations against the eggheads on the analytic side," followed by an Athens posting secured because he was the only person in the entire CIA fluent in both Greek and Arabic. Covers his full CIA career arc from 1988/1990 recruitment through analyst years on Iraq, the switch to operations, 9/11, the enhanced-interrogation refusal, executive assistant to the deputy director for operations, and his eventual resignation and post-CIA career.

cia-language-training.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
cia-language-training.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

cia-language-training.title: The polygraph
cia-language-training.summary: The lie-detector examination that gates entry to the CIA, described by John Kiriakou from the inside: the twenty-minute wiring-up, the psychiatrist''s advice to stare at a speck on the wall, the deliberately planted false accusation used to test a candidate''s reaction, and his contention that the machine screens out exactly the wrong people.

cia-language-training.title: George Washington University
cia-language-training.summary: The Washington university where John Kiriakou took a bachelor's degree in Middle Eastern studies and began a master's in legislative affairs, and where a professor who was in fact a CIA spotter recruited him into the agency — an institution that recurs throughout his account as the place his intelligence career began, as the venue of his first CIA tests, and later as a classroom he taught in himself.

cia-language-training.title: Zbigniew Brzezinski
cia-language-training.summary: National security adviser to Jimmy Carter, named in John Kiriakou's account of Afghanistan as an architect of the policy of luring the Soviet Union into a war there — a policy Kiriakou says literally destroyed the country and set the conditions for the Taliban.

cia-liaison-relationships.title: Cofer Black
cia-liaison-relationships.summary: Former head of the CIA Counterterrorism Center during and immediately after the September 11 attacks; principal architect of the agency's paramilitary turn on September 12, 2001; later Vice President of Blackwater under Erik Prince.

cia-liaison-relationships.title: The car pickup meeting
cia-liaison-relationships.summary: A clandestine meeting technique in which an agent is collected from a street corner and ducks out of sight — and the occasion when a French intelligence officer used it on John Kiriakou, a colleague rather than an asset, and was refused.

cia-liaison-relationships.title: Charlie Kirk shooting
cia-liaison-relationships.summary: Kiriakou questions the official account: a court filing says the ATF could not match the autopsy bullet to the rifle tied to the suspect.

cia-liaison-relationships.title: Romania and US military positioning
cia-liaison-relationships.summary: John Kiriakou's assessment that Romania has become the United States' next staging option toward the Middle East, because Greece is full and Turkey is pursuing its own course.

cia-liaison-relationships.title: Jon Stewart
cia-liaison-relationships.summary: American broadcaster, on whom John Kiriakou publicly accepted a correction from a viewer, and about whom he tells a single unflattering story from their one meeting.

cia-liaison-relationships.title: Gangstalking claims
cia-liaison-relationships.summary: The belief, put to John Kiriakou almost daily, that the CIA subjects private individuals to permanent multi-person surveillance and electromagnetic attack. He rejects it as untrue and as a matter for psychiatry, while conceding that one element of the folklore has a real basis.

cia-media-relations.title: CIA media revolving door
cia-media-relations.summary: John Kiriakou's proposed reform to bar CIA officers from becoming paid media personalities without a cooling-off period, and to strip the security clearances of retirees who go straight from the agency to cable-news punditry.

cia-media-relations.title: Thomas Drake
cia-media-relations.summary: NSA whistleblower; per John Kiriakou, the source for the statement that on the morning of September 11, 2001, NSA Director Mike Hayden told agency personnel NSA had been 'waiting for a 9/11' to implement the mass-electronic-surveillance program that NSA's founding charter forbids.

cia-media-relations.title: Whistleblower psychology
cia-media-relations.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of what distinguishes people who come forward: psychological studies showing whistleblowers hold a much more sharply defined sense of right and wrong than the general population, weighed against his own claim that there is no whistleblower who has not contemplated suicide in the period after going public.

cia-media-relations.title: Sigurdur Thordarson
cia-media-relations.summary: The FBI's key witness against Julian Assange, described by John Kiriakou as a convicted paedophile, a convicted embezzler and a self-admitted liar — one of three facts he lists, alongside the bugging of the Ecuadorian embassy and the reported plot to kidnap or kill Assange, in asking whether judges can keep such things out of their heads.

cia-media-relations.title: Wolf Blitzer at CIA headquarters
cia-media-relations.summary: What John Kiriakou says he saw a couple of weeks into his CIA career in 1990: the CNN correspondent Wolf Blitzer walking the halls of headquarters with a camera crew and no security escort, filming a stand-up in front of an agency sign. Kiriakou offers it, alongside the Bob Woodward episode, as evidence that the supposed wall between the CIA and the American press does not exist.

cia-media-relations.title: The CIA and Hollywood
cia-media-relations.summary: The CIA''s standing arrangement with the film industry, as John Kiriakou describes it: a branch inside the Office of Public Affairs whose only job is to cooperate with Hollywood studios, on the model the FBI has run since the 1950s, so that what comes out of Hollywood carries a pro-agency message. Kiriakou notes it is technically illegal for the CIA to propagandise the American public and says that is exactly what happens every time an agency-linked film is released.

cia-media-revolving-door.title: Abolish the CIA
cia-media-revolving-door.summary: John Kiriakou's position that the CIA should be abolished because its functions are already duplicated by the other 17 U.S. intelligence agencies — analysis by the State Department, human spying by the Pentagon, technology by DARPA, NSA and the private sector.

cia-media-revolving-door.title: Church Committee
cia-media-revolving-door.summary: U.S. Senate investigative committee operating in 1975–1976 that examined domestic intelligence abuses by the CIA, FBI, and NSA; per John Kiriakou, the Church Committee — alongside the concurrent Pike Committee in the House — was the last genuine moment of legislative oversight over the intelligence community, born of a national consensus that government had gone dangerously off course. Its work led to the creation of the permanent Senate Select Committee on Intelligence, which Kiriakou says ceased to function as real oversight roughly seven years after its founding.

cia-media-revolving-door.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
cia-media-revolving-door.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

cia-media-revolving-door.title: McCain-Feinstein Amendment
cia-media-revolving-door.summary: 2015 amendment, sponsored by Senator John McCain, that formally and permanently banned torture by U.S. government personnel, codifying the Army Field Manual as the single interrogation standard for all agencies. Per John Kiriakou, it restored the original language of the 1946 Federal Torture Act after U.S. policy had drifted from it through post-9/11 reinterpretation — and passed, he says, in part because of his own 2007 whistleblowing.

cia-media-revolving-door.title: "Only Fox came to my defence"
