cia-media-revolving-door.summary: John Kiriakou's account of how the American networks labelled him — MSNBC never using the word whistleblower and calling him a CIA leaker, CNN taking a year to change, and Fox, he says, being the only outlet that defended him at the time — offered as evidence that the label a case receives is drawn along political lines rather than factual ones.

cia-media-revolving-door.title: Wolf Blitzer at CIA headquarters
cia-media-revolving-door.summary: What John Kiriakou says he saw a couple of weeks into his CIA career in 1990: the CNN correspondent Wolf Blitzer walking the halls of headquarters with a camera crew and no security escort, filming a stand-up in front of an agency sign. Kiriakou offers it, alongside the Bob Woodward episode, as evidence that the supposed wall between the CIA and the American press does not exist.

cia-national-resources-division.title: Palantir Technologies
cia-national-resources-division.summary: U.S. data-analytics and intelligence-software company; received its first $1.5 million in seed funding from the CIA's In-Q-Tel venture-capital arm around 2002; characterized by John Kiriakou as functionally inseparable from the CIA in 2025, drawing the majority of its revenue from agency contracts and operating across DARPA, NSA, and the broader U.S. national-security apparatus.

cia-national-resources-division.title: Denied areas
cia-national-resources-division.summary: The CIA term for countries so hostile and so heavily surveilled that ordinary operational movement is impossible — the Soviet Union, Cuba, Syria, and later Russia, China, North Korea and Iran — and the reason, in John Kiriakou's account, that officers heading to one get specialist briefings, eight-hour surveillance detection routes, and that the Agency has to fall back on liaison services instead of its own sources.

cia-national-resources-division.title: William J. Casey
cia-national-resources-division.summary: Director of Central Intelligence under Reagan; creator of the CIA's domestic collection arm, architect of the purge that installed a businessman with no intelligence experience as deputy director for operations, and — per John Kiriakou — the man whose campaign to cut Congress out ended the only period of real intelligence oversight the United States has ever had.

cia-national-resources-division.title: Central Intelligence Agency
cia-national-resources-division.summary: U.S. foreign intelligence service; John Kiriakou's employer from 1990 to 2004 and the central institution of KiriPedia

cia-national-resources-division.title: CIA Political Psychology Division
cia-national-resources-division.summary: The Central Intelligence Agency unit founded by Dr. Gerald Post in the 1970s to produce long-distance psychiatric evaluations of foreign leaders

cia-national-resources-division.title: Will Hurd
cia-national-resources-division.summary: Former CIA case officer, congressman and OpenAI board member whom John Kiriakou says he mentored at the agency; Kiriakou cites him as an example of the intelligence and tech worlds merging.

cia-operational-psychologists.title: CIA psychological evaluations
cia-operational-psychologists.summary: The two kinds of psychological work John Kiriakou describes inside the CIA — the recurring psychiatric screening every officer undergoes, before employment, again three years after hiring and every five years thereafter for life; and the long-distance evaluation of foreign leaders carried out by the analytic side. The agency's clinical psychologists are split between the two, with a third group in operations advising case officers on the sources they recruit.

cia-operational-psychologists.title: The CIA under a left-wing president
cia-operational-psychologists.summary: John Kiriakou's two-part answer to a hypothetical about a socialist administration — that most of the CIA would carry on as though nothing had happened, because officers serve at the pleasure of the president, while elements of the directorate of operations would actively seek to remove such a president. His supporting example is John F. Kennedy.

cia-operational-psychologists.title: The NYPD intelligence post
cia-operational-psychologists.summary: The New York Police Department position — deputy commissioner for intelligence — that John Kiriakou says traditionally goes to someone coming out of the CIA, and which he uses to explain why the agency is indifferent to who wins a New York mayoral election so long as the post and its liaison with the joint terrorism task force survive.

cia-operational-psychologists.title: The two officers who changed
cia-operational-psychologists.summary: John Kiriakou's account of two colleagues he liked as junior officers and watched become something else — one who rose to deputy director for counterterrorism at both the CIA and the FBI and whom he calls a war criminal, and one who took over the bin Laden unit and became, in his phrase, a stone cold killer.

cia-operational-psychologists.title: Torture and morale inside the CIA
cia-operational-psychologists.summary: John Kiriakou's account of what the torture programme did to morale at the CIA — a compartment so tight that nobody knew for six or eight months, a workforce that split between objectors and true believers who enjoyed the work, and a pullback by George Tenet around 2005 that ended active torture at the secret sites while leaving the prisons open and Guantanamo untouched.

cia-operational-psychologists.title: The forged award certificate
cia-operational-psychologists.summary: A recruited source John Kiriakou says he brought to tears twice — first by telling him his reporting had gone directly to the president of the United States, then by presenting him with an award certificate Kiriakou had made himself in Word with clip art, the agency seal, and a forged signature of the director, which he then took back for safekeeping on the grounds that being seen with it would get the man killed.

cia-pentagon-war-divide.title: 2026 Iran war
cia-pentagon-war-divide.summary: The open-ended American and Israeli war against Iran that John Kiriakou tracked week by week on his own show — a conflict he says was sold as three weeks, ran into its fifth month, achieved every decapitation objective it set, and continued anyway. His grade for it is a D, and his forecast is a Truth Social post declaring victory while nothing changes.

cia-pentagon-war-divide.title: Laura Loomer
cia-pentagon-war-divide.summary: The American activist who publicly called John Kiriakou a Russian spy, a Russian asset and a common criminal. Kiriakou consulted a lawyer as he had over an earlier attack, was advised that she carried too little weight to be worth suing, and let it go; he reads her later reversal on Russia and Ukraine as the calculation of someone who has accepted she will never be given a government job.

cia-pentagon-war-divide.title: National Security Council
cia-pentagon-war-divide.summary: The White House body that, in John Kiriakou's telling, sat on the pro-war side of every fight that defined his era — gung-ho for the Iraq invasion alongside Cheney's and Rumsfeld's offices while the CIA, State Department, and Joint Chiefs opposed it; the place where an official predicted Iraqis would "throw flowers at us"; a signature stop in the approval chain for both the torture program and covert action findings; and the perch from which John Brennan, as its number two, urged the Justice Department to secretly reopen the case against Kiriakou.

cia-pentagon-war-divide.title: The Palestinian expulsion from the Gulf
cia-pentagon-war-divide.summary: John Kiriakou's account of what happened to the roughly one million Palestinians who had made up the middle class of Kuwait, Bahrain, the United Arab Emirates and Saudi Arabia, expelled en masse after the 1991 liberation of Kuwait as retaliation for the Palestine Liberation Organization's support for Saddam Hussein's invasion, and replaced with Filipino, Indian and Pakistani labour. Kiriakou treats it as the structural reason the Palestinians *"have never recovered"* and as the precedent for the Arab silence he sees today.

cia-pentagon-war-divide.title: Russia and NATO membership
cia-pentagon-war-divide.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the opening that was available with Moscow in the early 2000s and was refused — deep cooperation on terrorism, narcotics and proliferation offered only on terms of junior partnership, and approaches from both Yeltsin and Putin about joining NATO that met, in his words, the cold shoulder.

cia-pentagon-war-divide.title: The Saudi-Pakistan-Turkey defense pact
cia-pentagon-war-divide.summary: The 2026 realignment John Kiriakou describes as a tectonic shift in Middle Eastern geopolitics, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan signing a mutual-defense treaty joined by Turkey and offered to Iran and Egypt, born of the perception that the United States can no longer defend its Gulf allies and that Israel's threat to strike NATO member Turkey has broken Article 5.

cia-political-action-group.title: Active measures
cia-political-action-group.summary: The in-house name John Kiriakou gives to the CIA branch responsible for propaganda and for countering hostile propaganda — a division he describes as running twenty-four hours a day, paired with an opposing anti-active-measures branch, and as the ancestor of the political action group that remains the agency's clandestine propaganda arm.

cia-political-action-group.title: James Clapper
cia-political-action-group.summary: Director of National Intelligence under Obama, and in John Kiriakou's account the standing example of two arguments at once — that lying to Congress carries no consequence at the top of the intelligence community, and that career military officers make poor intelligence chiefs because they cannot tell a president no.

cia-political-action-group.title: Abu Zubaydah
cia-political-action-group.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

cia-political-action-group.title: Bilderberg and weapon sales
cia-political-action-group.summary: John Kiriakou's claim, sourced to someone he knew who attended, that elite gatherings like Bilderberg and the Shangri-La Dialogue are — beneath the talk of global issues — fundamentally 'all about weapon sales' and defense-contractor deals.

cia-political-action-group.title: Carlos the Jackal
cia-political-action-group.summary: Venezuelan-born militant (Ilich Ramírez Sánchez) active in the 1970s and 1980s; per John Kiriakou, 'the Osama bin Laden of the 70s and 80s.' Kiriakou spent his Athens posting trying to identify the middleman linking Carlos to the Greek terrorist group 17 November, then six months working the lead with MI5 in London; Carlos was finally run down by CIA contractor Billy Waugh in a Khartoum vegetable market and captured in 1994.

cia-political-action-group.title: The regime change approval process
cia-political-action-group.summary: John Kiriakou's step-by-step account of how a proposal to overthrow a foreign government travels through the United States government — beginning as a memo written at an officer's own desk, cleared by lawyers at the Justice Department and the National Security Council, signed by the president as an executive order, and ending in a safe on the seventh floor at CIA headquarters while the order itself goes to the Pentagon.

cia-political-neutrality-tradition.title: John Brennan
cia-political-neutrality-tradition.summary: Former Director of the CIA; characterized in KiriPedia's source corpus as the principal architect of the agency's enhanced interrogation program and as having plotted against an elected President

cia-political-neutrality-tradition.title: Barack Obama
cia-political-neutrality-tradition.summary: 44th U.S. president; in John Kiriakou's account, Obama publicly recounted refusing Benjamin Netanyahu's demand to bomb Iran and calling Israel's threat to use nuclear weapons a bluff — a bluff Kiriakou says Donald Trump later believed.

cia-political-neutrality-tradition.title: Donald Trump
cia-political-neutrality-tradition.summary: 45th and 47th U.S. president. Per John Kiriakou, a man genuinely convinced he was doing right by bombing Iran, "duped" by the same Netanyahu nuclear bluff Obama once rejected — and, at the same time, the most blindly pro-Israel president in history, an admirer of autocrats who has never once criticized Vladimir Putin, and prone to gestures — from the Gulf of America to a since-abandoned "Department of War" rename — that test the edges of his actual authority.

cia-political-neutrality-tradition.title: Hillary Clinton
cia-political-neutrality-tradition.summary: Former U.S. Secretary of State and 2016 presidential candidate; John Kiriakou describes her as arguably the most neoconservative candidate Democrats could have nominated, more militarist even than her husband, and credits her — separately — with correctly describing Iran as a military dictatorship run by the IRGC rather than a genuine theocracy.

cia-political-neutrality-tradition.title: Bill Clinton
cia-political-neutrality-tradition.summary: 42nd U.S. president whom John Kiriakou describes as wholly disinterested in intelligence — briefed by the CIA only twice in eight years, with Vice President Al Gore taking the daily briefing instead and relaying anything important.

cia-political-neutrality-tradition.title: John Kerry
cia-political-neutrality-tradition.summary: U.S. Senator from Massachusetts; chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee during John Kiriakou's 2009 service as the committee's senior investigator; subsequently U.S. Secretary of State; characterized by Kiriakou as a coward who buckled under CIA pressure on the Dasht-i-Leili reopening and as personally fixated on his perceived theft of the Secretary of State position by Hillary Clinton; the famously thrown medals were duplicates purchased at the post exchange.

cia-political-psychology-division.title: Jerrold Post
cia-political-psychology-division.summary: American political psychiatrist and CIA officer who recruited John Kiriakou into the agency in 1988 through the CIA's covert campus recruiting program, working undercover as a George Washington University professor; founder of the CIA's Political Psychology Division (also called the Office of Leadership Analysis). Held a bachelor's, master's, and PhD in psychology and a PhD in political science, all from Yale, plus an MD from Harvard, and authored a dozen books on the psychology of world leaders and terrorists. Per Kiriakou, Post identified in him not just writing talent but "sociopathic tendencies" — and, when Kiriakou later blew the whistle, called to congratulate him, telling him that reaction proved he was not a true sociopath. Died of COVID-19, approximately 2022.

cia-political-psychology-division.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
cia-political-psychology-division.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

cia-political-psychology-division.title: CIA National Resources Division
cia-political-psychology-division.summary: The Central Intelligence Agency's domestic intelligence-collection arm, created in the 1980s by Director William J. Casey

cia-political-psychology-division.title: John Kiriakou
cia-political-psychology-division.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

cia-political-psychology-division.title: Bob (CIA HR)
cia-political-psychology-division.summary: Pseudonym for the CIA officer who served as director of human resources for the agency in the late 1980s and personally oversaw John Kiriakou's hiring

cia-political-psychology-division.title: Stansfield Turner
cia-political-psychology-division.summary: Admiral and Director of Central Intelligence under Jimmy Carter from 1977 to 1981; named by John Kiriakou as one of only two CIA directors he considers good, because he tried to rein the organization in, and remembered inside the agency for the October 1977 mass firing of Directorate of Operations officers that CIA officers call the Friday Night Massacre.

cia-psychological-evaluations.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
cia-psychological-evaluations.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

cia-psychological-evaluations.title: Iraqi invasion of Kuwait
cia-psychological-evaluations.summary: John Kiriakou''s most detailed account of the intelligence process around the 1990 Iraqi invasion of Kuwait and its 1991 liberation. As a first-year CIA analyst on a ''training account'' covering Iraq, Kiriakou produced the June 30, 1990 warning paper for the White House; suggested calling the US Defense Attaché in Baghdad to drive to the border and report what he saw (the answer: ''Literally the entire Iraqi military is heading south''); briefed the August 2 Oval Office meeting with Bush; and later took a single phone call from General Colin Powell that led, eight hours later, to 47 cruise missiles striking the Iraqi Intelligence Service headquarters in Baghdad.

cia-psychological-evaluations.title: Espionage Act
cia-psychological-evaluations.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

cia-psychological-evaluations.title: Kiriakou's Russian media work
cia-psychological-evaluations.summary: John Kiriakou's account of hosting a daily Sputnik radio show for seven and a half years with full contractual freedom to criticize anyone, including Putin — which he did on the morning of the Ukraine invasion — offered as a rebuttal to claims that Russian outlets are mere propaganda.

cia-psychological-evaluations.title: Private prison system
cia-psychological-evaluations.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the U.S. private prison industry as an incentive to keep beds filled and cut costs on food and medicine — illustrated by the 'sewer trout,' dog-food, and dead-rat-in-the-Kool-Aid stories from his own incarceration.

cia-psychological-evaluations.title: Thomas Drake
cia-psychological-evaluations.summary: NSA whistleblower; per John Kiriakou, the source for the statement that on the morning of September 11, 2001, NSA Director Mike Hayden told agency personnel NSA had been 'waiting for a 9/11' to implement the mass-electronic-surveillance program that NSA's founding charter forbids.

cia-record-deniability.title: Jeffrey Epstein
cia-record-deniability.summary: Convicted sex offender; per John Kiriakou, was "an Israeli access agent" rather than a CIA asset, because the CIA collects foreign intelligence and Epstein's targets — Bill Clinton, Bill Gates, Prince Andrew — were not foreign. Kiriakou further holds that Epstein did die by suicide in federal custody, because in the Bureau of Prisons the cameras never work and the guards are always asleep.

cia-record-deniability.title: Classification compartments
cia-record-deniability.summary: John Kiriakou's explanation of the U.S. secrecy tiers above 'top secret' — the TS/SCI/TK/gamma clearances everyone at the CIA gets, and the additional compartments that mean even senior officials can be barred from a single cable.

cia-record-deniability.title: Access Agent
cia-record-deniability.summary: CIA (and foreign intelligence service) term for a recruited asset whose value lies not in the secrets they hold directly but in their regular social access to high-value targets — politicians, executives, heads of state — who cannot themselves be recruited. Per John Kiriakou, the access agent is funded generously to maintain an environment in which the targets feel comfortable and return repeatedly; kompromat — compromising photographs or recordings — may be collected as a secondary tool. Kiriakou identifies Jeffrey Epstein as a textbook access agent, in his assessment working for Israeli intelligence.

cia-record-deniability.title: AIPAC
cia-record-deniability.summary: The American Israel Public Affairs Committee — the U.S. political organization that, in John Kiriakou's framing, ought to be registered as a foreign-lobbying entity but is not, and that wields decisive electoral power against U.S. elected officials who express support for Palestinian human rights.

cia-record-deniability.title: China as economic threat
cia-record-deniability.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that China is the real threat to the West not militarily — it has one aircraft carrier to America's two dozen and rarely invades — but economically, buying friends worldwide while the U.S. spends a trillion dollars a year on weapons.

cia-record-deniability.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
cia-record-deniability.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

cia-recruitment-through-academia.title: Recruiting foreign students
cia-recruitment-through-academia.summary: The long-horizon intelligence argument for admitting foreign students to American universities — that a doctoral student in the hard sciences recruited on campus goes home to a weapons programme as an asset already in place — and John Kiriakou's view that collapsing enrolment is an operational loss nobody at the top is thinking about.

cia-recruitment-through-academia.title: John le Carré
cia-recruitment-through-academia.summary: British novelist and former MI6 officer, the subject of a full episode of John Kiriakou's Dead Drop podcast. Kiriakou's argument is that le Carré is the only spy novelist to have changed the business of spying itself — supplying its working vocabulary, from 'Joes' and 'lamplighters' to 'honey trap', and shaping how officers understood their own world.

cia-recruitment-through-academia.title: Bernie Sanders
cia-recruitment-through-academia.summary: United States senator from Vermont. John Kiriakou, who watched him daily from the Senate Foreign Relations Committee staff, describes Sanders holding open breakfast in the Senate cafeteria for anyone who walked in — insisting only that they call him "Bernie" — and names him the one 2016 candidate willing to talk about shrinking the military.

cia-recruitment-through-academia.title: Europe without Russian gas
cia-recruitment-through-academia.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that Europe needs Russia more than Russia needs Europe, made from what he has physically encountered rather than from figures. Speaking in Nottingham in 2025 he found the concert hall so cold that the audience complained, and was told by the manager that the venue could not afford to heat itself without Russian gas. He reports the same of homes in Britain, Germany and Greece, where American gas is simply too expensive to substitute.

cia-recruitment-through-academia.title: The CIA spotter professor
cia-recruitment-through-academia.summary: How John Kiriakou entered the CIA: a graduate-school professor who liked his writing style asked him to stay after class, and turned out to be an undercover officer working as a talent spotter. Kiriakou, who had been planning on Capitol Hill or the foreign service, says he had given the agency no thought at all until it approached him.

cia-recruitment-through-academia.title: The Panda card
cia-recruitment-through-academia.summary: The Chinese national payment card John Kiriakou encountered in Hong Kong, where he found few places willing to take Mastercard or Visa. Asked why, he was given a one-sentence answer about routing: Visa and Mastercard transactions pass through New York, Panda card transactions pass through Shanghai, and so fall outside the reach of American sanctions. He treats it as both an instance of Chinese strategic competence and an argument that the American card duopoly is a racket.

cia-remote-vehicle-control.title: CIA Car Hacking
cia-remote-vehicle-control.summary: Kiriakou on the Vault 7 disclosure that the CIA can seize control of a moving car and stage the crash as a suicide or an accident — a capability he says is not limited to electric vehicles, whose only counter is the emergency brake, and which he treats as the clearest example of a leak that is a matter of life and death rather than embarrassment.

cia-remote-vehicle-control.title: Vault 7
cia-remote-vehicle-control.summary: The 2017 WikiLeaks disclosure of thousands of pages of CIA Directorate of Science and Technology documents — leaked by agency engineer Joshua Schulte — revealing CIA technical capabilities including remote takeover of internet-connected cars, conversion of smart-TV speakers into covert microphones, and the planting of Russian or Persian language fragments in foreign systems to mislead attribution.

cia-remote-vehicle-control.title: CIA Smart TV Surveillance
cia-remote-vehicle-control.summary: Per John Kiriakou, a CIA technical capability — disclosed publicly by the 2017 Vault 7 leaks — to convert a smart television's speaker system into a covert listening microphone even while the television appears to be switched off.

cia-remote-vehicle-control.title: Michael Hastings
cia-remote-vehicle-control.summary: American investigative journalist whose 2013 death in a single-vehicle Los Angeles car crash is invoked by John Kiriakou as the canonical real-world referent for the CIA car-remote-takeover capability disclosed in the 2017 Vault 7 documents.

cia-remote-vehicle-control.title: Matt DeHart
cia-remote-vehicle-control.summary: American Army veteran and whistleblower prosecuted on charges including child pornography that the Justice Department later admitted, in court, did not exist; per John Kiriakou, DeHart fled to Canada at the first sign of military trouble, was returned to the U.S., and was held without bond as a flight risk.

cia-remote-vehicle-control.title: Todd Blanch
cia-remote-vehicle-control.summary: Per Megyn Kelly, reading Trump's own statement live during her interview with Kiriakou, Todd Blanch was named the incoming acting Attorney General, replacing Pam Bondi.

cia-satan-church-nsa-investigation.title: MK-Ultra
cia-satan-church-nsa-investigation.summary: The CIA's mid-twentieth-century umbrella program of mind-control, behavioral-modification, and biological-warfare experimentation, encompassing subprojects such as MK-Chickwit and MK-Seesaw; active 1952–1975; documented practices included LSD dosing of unwitting American citizens in CIA-rented brothels and the aerosolized release of pathogens into the San Francisco fog; 80% of the program's documentation was destroyed by the CIA in defiance of a 1975 preservation order from Senator Frank Church.

cia-satan-church-nsa-investigation.title: Tuesday morning kill list
cia-satan-church-nsa-investigation.summary: Weekly CIA targeting meeting instituted by John Brennan in 2009 during his service as Deputy National Security Advisor for Counterterrorism in the Obama administration; produced a written list of individuals to be killed in the following week; per John Kiriakou, the program was a source of pride within the Obama administration and was made operationally possible by the targeting-software sophistication of the period.

cia-satan-church-nsa-investigation.title: Abu Zubaydah's diary
cia-satan-church-nsa-investigation.summary: The notebook captured with Abu Zubaydah, containing drawings and poetry, over which the CIA and the FBI came to deep disagreement — an FBI psychologist calling it the rantings of a crazy person and John Kiriakou insisting it showed creativity in a man who was not crazy at all.

cia-satan-church-nsa-investigation.title: Alfreda Bikowsky
cia-satan-church-nsa-investigation.summary: Senior CIA officer who headed Alec Station and, before that, served as its chief of operations, overseeing the CIA's torture program; per John Kiriakou, "bad news from the get-go," and part of a failed attempt with Rich Blee to turn a San Diego al-Qaeda cell into double agents.

cia-satan-church-nsa-investigation.title: BDS movement
cia-satan-church-nsa-investigation.summary: The Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions movement against Israel; John Kiriakou notes that some 40 U.S. states now have anti-BDS laws that can require a speaker at a publicly funded university to sign a pledge of support for Israel — which he refuses to do.

cia-satan-church-nsa-investigation.title: Butler rally shooting
cia-satan-church-nsa-investigation.summary: The July 2024 attempt on Donald Trump's life at a rally in Butler, Pennsylvania, on which John Kiriakou takes no position as to who was responsible but argues the published facts cannot be reconciled with a competent Secret Service — and that the questions it leaves open are owed an answer for the historical record whether or not anyone alive gets one.

cia-sexpionage.title: Gust Avrakotos
cia-sexpionage.summary: CIA case officer, John Kiriakou's operations mentor, and a central figure in Charlie Wilson's War — the prolific, divisive covert-war veteran Kiriakou credits as the greatest teacher of his adult life.

cia-sexpionage.title: Maduro Capture
cia-sexpionage.summary: CIA-driven nighttime operation in which a team of Delta Force commandos entered Venezuela and removed Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro and his wife from their beds. Per John Kiriakou, the key enabling intelligence — per a New York Times account he cited — came from a CIA asset inside Maduro''s presidential palace who called when Maduro went to sleep: ''He''s sound asleep. If you''re going to do it, do it now.'' At least eighty people were killed in the operation, including approximately thirty-five Cubans. Kiriakou compares it to the 1989 capture of Manuel Noriega, in which US forces blasted death metal at the Vatican Embassy until Noriega was asked to leave.

cia-sexpionage.title: Permanent wartime economy
cia-sexpionage.summary: John Kiriakou's thesis that since 9/11 the United States has run a permanent wartime economy so large that cutting the defense budget would trigger a depression — likening the dependency to crack addiction and warning it makes war almost inevitable.

cia-sexpionage.title: The CIA and honey-trapping
cia-sexpionage.summary: John Kiriakou's explanation of why the CIA, unlike the Russians, Chinese, Israelis and French, does not run honey-trap recruitment operations. He credits an instructor's story about a 1970s attempt against an Iranian mulla, who reacted to the incriminating photographs by asking for 8×10s and wallets, as the moment the agency concluded coercion produces resentment rather than sources.

cia-sexpionage.title: A spy's guide to a city
cia-sexpionage.summary: The premise of the third season of John Kiriakou''s Dead Drop podcast: that a CIA officer reads a city in a wholly different way from a tourist. The tourist looks for the Parthenon or the Eiffel Tower; the officer is thinking about surveillance, counter-surveillance and surveillance detection, and about not being shot from behind a building.

cia-sexpionage.title: The Texas Muslim development
cia-sexpionage.summary: A housing development planned by a group of wealthy Muslim professionals in Texas — twenty-five or thirty large houses on an empty tract with a mosque at the centre, marketed to other Muslim doctors, lawyers and engineers. John Kiriakou cites the alarm it caused, up to and including Governor Greg Abbott, as a case study in unnecessary panic.

cia-smart-tv-surveillance.title: Vault 7
cia-smart-tv-surveillance.summary: The 2017 WikiLeaks disclosure of thousands of pages of CIA Directorate of Science and Technology documents — leaked by agency engineer Joshua Schulte — revealing CIA technical capabilities including remote takeover of internet-connected cars, conversion of smart-TV speakers into covert microphones, and the planting of Russian or Persian language fragments in foreign systems to mislead attribution.

cia-smart-tv-surveillance.title: CIA Car Hacking
cia-smart-tv-surveillance.summary: Kiriakou on the Vault 7 disclosure that the CIA can seize control of a moving car and stage the crash as a suicide or an accident — a capability he says is not limited to electric vehicles, whose only counter is the emergency brake, and which he treats as the clearest example of a leak that is a matter of life and death rather than embarrassment.

cia-smart-tv-surveillance.title: Tulsi Gabbard
cia-smart-tv-surveillance.summary: U.S. Director of National Intelligence; a longtime family friend of John Kiriakou's, who has known her since she was 12; Kiriakou calls her appointment "an inspired choice" despite disagreeing with her decision to join the Republican Party, and says she appears to have given up her opposition to Section 702 surveillance to secure Senate confirmation.

cia-smart-tv-surveillance.title: Alexa
cia-smart-tv-surveillance.summary: Per John Kiriakou, Amazon''s Alexa smart speaker reports directly to the NSA — and he owns one anyway. The device recurs across his interviews as the standing example of the surveillance trade-off in modern smart-home technology, and of his own negotiated exception to it: one speaker, in one room, against the advice of every intelligence officer he has ever known.

cia-smart-tv-surveillance.title: CIA Remote Vehicle Control
cia-smart-tv-surveillance.summary: John Kiriakou's account, corroborated by Forbes' Andy Greenberg's real-world demonstration, that the CIA can remotely take over a car's systems and cause a fatal crash disguised as an accident.

cia-smart-tv-surveillance.title: Foreign aid
cia-smart-tv-surveillance.summary: John Kiriakou's advocacy of a hundredfold increase in the American foreign-aid budget — a position he concedes puts him in "a very minuscule minority" — argued on the grounds that every dollar spent saves five or ten in refugee crises, civil wars and attacks on the United States, and that development is the only thing that empties terrorist recruiting pools. His counter-example is the Sana'a water-treatment plant, built by the European Union and rendered pointless by American and Saudi politics.

cia-spy-tech-amazon.title: China's base in Djibouti
cia-spy-tech-amazon.summary: Camp Lemonnier in Djibouti, the abandoned French base the Djiboutians offered to the Americans and the Chinese took a share of — split down the middle by a chain-link fence, the only Chinese military installation outside China, and the centrepiece of John Kiriakou's argument that China is not an expansionist power.

cia-spy-tech-amazon.title: China as economic threat
cia-spy-tech-amazon.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that China is the real threat to the West not militarily — it has one aircraft carrier to America's two dozen and rarely invades — but economically, buying friends worldwide while the U.S. spends a trillion dollars a year on weapons.

cia-spy-tech-amazon.title: Djibouti
cia-spy-tech-amazon.summary: The small Horn of Africa state a few miles across the water from Yemen that hosts Camp Lemonnier — the American drone base for the Yemen and Somalia wars, inherited from the departing French, and shared with China's only overseas military base behind a fence down the middle, in what John Kiriakou calls the worst kept secret in the world.

cia-spy-tech-amazon.title: CIA disguise program
cia-spy-tech-amazon.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the CIA's disguise and forgery specialists — including a master disguise maker recruited from a beauty academy who built him a custom bald-head mask over six weeks, and a master forger recruited off his college newspaper cartoons.

cia-spy-tech-amazon.title: Abraham Accords
cia-spy-tech-amazon.summary: The Trump-brokered normalization deals between Israel and Gulf Arab states — in John Kiriakou's judgment "a terrible idea in the first place," a great victory for Israel and the Gulf Arabs that was "a punch in the throat to the Palestinians." He argues the Accords are how Trump meant to "solve the Middle East in a day" — by screwing the Palestinians — that Hamas read the abandonment correctly, that October 7 shattered the project, and that reviving the Accords (Saudis in, victory declared, Nobel collected) remains the organizing goal of Trump's regional policy.

cia-spy-tech-amazon.title: Access Agent
cia-spy-tech-amazon.summary: CIA (and foreign intelligence service) term for a recruited asset whose value lies not in the secrets they hold directly but in their regular social access to high-value targets — politicians, executives, heads of state — who cannot themselves be recruited. Per John Kiriakou, the access agent is funded generously to maintain an environment in which the targets feel comfortable and return repeatedly; kompromat — compromising photographs or recordings — may be collected as a secondary tool. Kiriakou identifies Jeffrey Epstein as a textbook access agent, in his assessment working for Israeli intelligence.

cia-torture-program-whistleblowing.title: FBI apologies to Kiriakou
cia-torture-program-whistleblowing.summary: John Kiriakou says three FBI agents who worked on his prosecution have written to apologize since his conviction — one saying the case was 'directed and driven by seniormost officials' while mid- and street-level personnel objected, but 'we just followed orders.'

cia-torture-program-whistleblowing.title: International Spy Museum
cia-torture-program-whistleblowing.summary: The Washington museum of espionage. John Kiriakou, who gives private tours of it, describes its room on the CIA torture program as a video loop in which only the torturers are given a voice — and in which he, the officer who exposed the program, is never mentioned.

cia-torture-program-whistleblowing.title: Ruining the whistleblower
cia-torture-program-whistleblowing.summary: John Kiriakou's account of what a prosecution of a whistleblower is actually for — not conviction but ruin, personally, professionally and financially — offered as the thing he did not think through before he spoke, and the thing he says then happened to him exactly as described.

cia-torture-program-whistleblowing.title: The inside-job refusal
cia-torture-program-whistleblowing.summary: Pressed on controlled-demolition theories about the World Trade Center, John Kiriakou refuses the premise while conceding the limits of his own expertise — he was inside the CIA''s Counterterrorism Center before the attacks, and says he has never seen any evidence that 9/11 was an inside job.

cia-torture-program-whistleblowing.title: The mosquito cloud
cia-torture-program-whistleblowing.summary: The night John Kiriakou waited beside Abu Zubaydah's hospital bed in Faisalabad in a room full of mosquitoes, having stopped taking his anti-malarial because of the nightmares — and turned the ceiling fan to full blast in a cold March room until an FBI agent asked what he was doing.

cia-torture-program-whistleblowing.title: The Sociopath Next Door
cia-torture-program-whistleblowing.summary: The book John Kiriakou reaches for when explaining why the CIA's leadership looks the way it does — sociopaths climbing over the people around them, as in any Fortune 500 company — and the source of his claim that 85 percent of American prisoners have a diagnosable mental illness.

cia-training-doctrine.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
cia-training-doctrine.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

cia-training-doctrine.title: Doing Time Like a Spy
cia-training-doctrine.summary: Prison memoir by John Kiriakou, full title Doing Time Like a Spy: How the CIA Taught Me to Survive and Thrive in Prison; winner of two literary awards and reissued in a second edition by Simon and Schuster.

cia-training-doctrine.title: FCI Loretto
cia-training-doctrine.summary: U.S. Federal Correctional Institution in Loretto, Pennsylvania; the low-medium-security prison at which John Kiriakou served 23 months of a 30-month sentence following his 2013 Espionage Act–era plea deal; the originally ordered "minimum security work camp" placement was countermanded — per Kiriakou, on Brennan's direct intervention — to place him in the actual prison alongside the general population.

cia-training-doctrine.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
cia-training-doctrine.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

cia-training-doctrine.title: The Italians at Loretto
cia-training-doctrine.summary: The mafia contingent at FCI Loretto — men with last names like Gambino, Bonanno, Lucchese, Genovese, DeCavalcante — who adopted John Kiriakou in his second year, largely because he hated the FBI as much as they did. The cast included the boss of the Gambino family (in on a dozen-plus murder counts, the man who replaced John Gotti), Pete the Bonanno captain across the hall who asked why he sat "with those Nazi retards," and a crooked guard on the payroll delivering pork loin and fresh mozzarella. When the FBI later came to Kiriakou's door asking him to inform on Pete, his answer was "get off my property."

cia-training-doctrine.title: CIA directorates
cia-training-doctrine.summary: The four-part internal division of the CIA as John Kiriakou describes it to lay audiences — the Directorate of Intelligence that analyses, the Directorate of Operations that recruits spies and steals secrets, the administrative arm that makes the trains run on time, and the Directorate of Science and Technology that supplies the scientists, forgers and disguise makers — the structure that determines which training a new officer receives.

cia-ufo-question.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
cia-ufo-question.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

cia-ufo-question.title: John Kiriakou
cia-ufo-question.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

cia-ufo-question.title: Bilderberg and weapon sales
cia-ufo-question.summary: John Kiriakou's claim, sourced to someone he knew who attended, that elite gatherings like Bilderberg and the Shangri-La Dialogue are — beneath the talk of global issues — fundamentally 'all about weapon sales' and defense-contractor deals.

cia-ufo-question.title: CIA and FBI ties to organized crime
cia-ufo-question.summary: John Kiriakou's survey of documented U.S. intelligence partnerships with organized crime — the FBI securing wartime ports with the Genovese family, the CIA's Castro plots with the Trafficantes, its work with the Escobar cartel against Colombian communists, and a mob hitman deployed against the Klan.

cia-ufo-question.title: Kissinger and the petrodollar
cia-ufo-question.summary: John Kiriakou's endorsement of the theory that Henry Kissinger deliberately structured the 1970s petrodollar to tie the U.S. to Middle Eastern oil — creating a standing rationale for policing the region, even as America exports its own fracked oil.

cia-ufo-question.title: Sixteen people knew
cia-ufo-question.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer to why deeply held secrets do not leak: at the outset only sixteen people in the entire federal government knew about the CIA torture programme, which is why it stayed hidden for years.

cia-versus-fbi-at-a-raid.title: Abu Zubaydah
cia-versus-fbi-at-a-raid.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

cia-versus-fbi-at-a-raid.title: Site 13
cia-versus-fbi-at-a-raid.summary: The house in Faisalabad, nearest of the thirteen targets to the CIA safe house, where Abu Zubaydah was shot at two o'clock in the morning on the night of the raids — announced to John Kiriakou on the roof a mile away by the sound of a battering ram failing against a steel-reinforced door.

cia-versus-fbi-at-a-raid.title: CIA–FBI interagency rivalry and 9/11
cia-versus-fbi-at-a-raid.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the historical CIA–FBI rivalry, dating to J. Edgar Hoover's opposition to the 1947 National Security Act, and how it manifested before September 11 when Cofer Black's Counterterrorism Center withheld from the FBI that hijackers Nawaf al-Hazmi and Khalid al-Mihdhar had been granted U.S. visas.

cia-versus-fbi-at-a-raid.title: 9/11 attribution of responsibility
cia-versus-fbi-at-a-raid.summary: John Kiriakou's evolving view of who bears ultimate responsibility for the September 11 attacks — that al-Qaeda carried them out but was, in his current view, "allowed" to, amid a distracted Bush administration, an uninvestigated Saudi government, and an Israeli government he believes had a vested interest in the attacks proceeding.

cia-versus-fbi-at-a-raid.title: Alex Station
cia-versus-fbi-at-a-raid.summary: CIA unit that tracked Osama bin Laden beginning in 1995; per John Kiriakou, who served as chief of its counterintelligence branch, the unit kept extremely tight security around its files, limited FBI investigators' access to information about future 9/11 hijackers Khaled al-Mihdhar and Nawaf al-Hazmi, and — under a deliberate policy of non-cooperation with the FBI — failed to watchlist participants in the Malaysia summit where al-Qaeda planned the attacks.

cia-versus-fbi-at-a-raid.title: Ali Mohamed
cia-versus-fbi-at-a-raid.summary: Egyptian-American former U.S. Army sergeant who trained at Fort Bragg while secretly working for Egyptian intelligence, later trained some of the 9/11 hijackers and other al-Qaeda operatives, and was arrested in connection with the 1998 U.S. embassy bombings before disappearing under the George W. Bush administration; John Kiriakou speculates he was actually a double agent working for al-Qaeda — or possibly Israeli intelligence — against his CIA handlers.

cia.title: Breaking the nuclear taboo
cia.summary: John Kiriakou's reporting that Donald Trump considered using a tactical nuclear weapon in Iran not for military necessity but to break what he regards as warfare's final taboo, freeing future presidents to use larger weapons — and the related account that the chairman of the Joint Chiefs refused him the nuclear codes.

cia.title: Eric Swallwell
cia.summary: Kiriakou names Swalwell once — a passing aside contrasting today's partisan Congress with the Church and Pike Committees of 1975.

cia.title: Haqqani White House meeting
cia.summary: A mid-to-late-1980s White House meeting between President Ronald Reagan and a Taliban delegation, per John Kiriakou — a former boss of his served as translator. One member of that delegation, a man named Haqqani, went on to found the Haqqani network, later responsible for the capture of Bowe Bergdahl and the kidnapping, rape, and torture of a Canadian couple.

cia.title: PricewaterhouseCoopers
cia.summary: The Big Four accounting firm that keeps intersecting John Kiriakou's story — as a target of the corporate human-source intelligence he collected after leaving the CIA, as the audience of 140 partners he told his Pakistan recruitment story to ("what I did and what you do really isn't that different"), as the auditor that spent three years trying to find the Pentagon's money before giving up, and as the Greek government's book-cooking auditor in the debt crisis, never prosecuted.

cia.title: Senior Executive Service
cia.summary: Highest tier of the U.S. federal civil service, above GS-1 through GS-15 pay grades; per John Kiriakou, members of the SES — and its agency-specific equivalents such as the CIA's Senior Intelligence Service — are the career officials who functionally operate the federal government across presidential administrations, serving thirty to forty years while presidents come and go every four or eight, and are protected from dismissal by the Civil Service Act.

cia.title: The "Soylent Green is people" cable easter egg
cia.summary: A long-running CIA case-officer in-joke in which the line "Soylent Green is people" is hidden inside classified operational cables as a sequence of incongruously lowercase letters

citizens-united.title: Thomas Massie
citizens-united.summary: Republican U.S. Representative from Kentucky known for a constitutionalist voting record and consistent opposition to foreign military intervention; per John Kiriakou, a principled America-First congressman who votes with the president on the vast majority of issues, and whose opposition to U.S. funding of Israel and foreign wars is the only plausible explanation for the roughly $30 million spent by the Israel lobby to unseat him in a primary.

citizens-united.title: Abu Omar rendition
citizens-united.summary: The CIA's kidnapping of a Milan cleric, Abu Omar, who was sent to Egypt to be tortured; John Kiriakou calls it a case that ought to be taught at the CIA as how not to run a rendition, and it is what ultimately sent him to prison, after he confirmed a former colleague's surname to a journalist claiming to be writing a book about it.

citizens-united.title: AIPAC
citizens-united.summary: The American Israel Public Affairs Committee — the U.S. political organization that, in John Kiriakou's framing, ought to be registered as a foreign-lobbying entity but is not, and that wields decisive electoral power against U.S. elected officials who express support for Palestinian human rights.

citizens-united.title: CIA animal surveillance experiments
citizens-united.summary: Cold-War CIA efforts to turn animals into listening devices, which John Kiriakou describes as failures — including microphones and cameras mounted on pigeons trained to land on the Soviet embassy, which could reach the compound but never captured anything meaningful.

citizens-united.title: Havana Syndrome
citizens-united.summary: Cluster of neurological symptoms — including nausea, ringing in the ears, vertigo, and traumatic brain injury — reported by American diplomatic and intelligence personnel beginning in Havana, Cuba, and subsequently at posts around the world. Per John Kiriakou, his initial skepticism gave way when a friend developed Havana Syndrome with an MRI-confirmed traumatic brain injury after a meeting outside the Russian Foreign Ministry; Kiriakou attributes the syndrome to Russian or Chinese directed-energy weapons and acknowledges the United States used a similar weapon during the operation to capture Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro.

citizens-united.title: MK-Ultra
citizens-united.summary: The CIA's mid-twentieth-century umbrella program of mind-control, behavioral-modification, and biological-warfare experimentation, encompassing subprojects such as MK-Chickwit and MK-Seesaw; active 1952–1975; documented practices included LSD dosing of unwitting American citizens in CIA-rented brothels and the aerosolized release of pathogens into the San Francisco fog; 80% of the program's documentation was destroyed by the CIA in defiance of a 1975 preservation order from Senator Frank Church.

civil-confinement.title: Cook
civil-confinement.summary: The elderly Kentucky prisoner who worked with John Kiriakou in the FCI Loretto chapel, finished a 20-year child pornography sentence, and was back inside within four months facing 60 more — the case Kiriakou uses to answer critics of civil confinement.

civil-confinement.title: FCI Loretto
civil-confinement.summary: U.S. Federal Correctional Institution in Loretto, Pennsylvania; the low-medium-security prison at which John Kiriakou served 23 months of a 30-month sentence following his 2013 Espionage Act–era plea deal; the originally ordered "minimum security work camp" placement was countermanded — per Kiriakou, on Brennan's direct intervention — to place him in the actual prison alongside the general population.

civil-confinement.title: Federal prison security levels
civil-confinement.summary: The ladder of federal custody as John Kiriakou describes it — penitentiary, medium, low and minimum-security camp — the transfer rules that let long-sentence prisoners descend it, and why that placed dangerous men inside the low-security prison where he served his sentence.

civil-confinement.title: The black box
civil-confinement.summary: The restraint apparatus in which John Kiriakou was moved from FCI Loretto to an outside medical appointment — handcuffs, leg irons, a waist chain and a steel box locked over the cuffs so the lock could not be picked — and the form he refused to sign because it required him to call everybody sir.

civil-confinement.title: Legal mail
civil-confinement.summary: The privileged correspondence category John Kiriakou used to smuggle the Letters from Loretto and the manuscript of his book out of prison — addressed to his attorney Jesselyn Radack and marked legal mail, which staff were forbidden to open.

civil-confinement.title: Depression in prison
civil-confinement.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the condition he says everybody inside has, and the three-part regime he set against it — eating right, exercising daily and finding a distraction — which in his own case meant more than a hundred books, 7,000 letters and a book written in longhand.

civilian-ships-and-piracy.title: Cancelling the 2026 midterms
civilian-ships-and-piracy.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that the 2026 war cannot win the midterm elections for the Republicans, and his flagged-as-paranoid worry that it may instead furnish the pretext for a national emergency and a cancelled election.

civilian-ships-and-piracy.title: CIA liaison relationships
civilian-ships-and-piracy.summary: John Kiriakou's critique of CIA intelligence-liaison relationships with foreign governments — sharply expanded after 9/11 — arguing that officers do not consider the long-term risk that disclosing sensitive operations to foreign services hands those governments leverage, including potential blackmail material, over the United States, and that no one left in Congress has the will to provide real oversight of the practice.

civilian-ships-and-piracy.title: Counterterrorism Center
civilian-ships-and-piracy.summary: The CIA's Counterterrorism Center (CTC) — the unit where John Kiriakou spent the defining years of his operational career. He joined in the late 1990s as the only officer in the entire CIA fluent in both Greek and Arabic, served as chief of counterintelligence in the bin Laden unit, watched the Center swell from a few hundred employees to nearly 2,000 by September 12, 2001, and it was to CTC that he walked back down in May 2002 to refuse the torture program — the moment, he says, the CIA began to turn on him.

civilian-ships-and-piracy.title: David Ransom
civilian-ships-and-piracy.summary: U.S. Ambassador to Bahrain during the period of John Kiriakou's posting there; characterized by Kiriakou as one of the finest people he worked for in his CIA career

civilian-ships-and-piracy.title: Defense Intelligence Agency
civilian-ships-and-piracy.summary: The Pentagon's intelligence arm, of which John Kiriakou holds a low opinion he states plainly and expects to be criticised for. He attributes the targeting data behind the 2026 Iranian elementary school strike to the agency.

civilian-ships-and-piracy.title: Gangstalking claims
civilian-ships-and-piracy.summary: The belief, put to John Kiriakou almost daily, that the CIA subjects private individuals to permanent multi-person surveillance and electromagnetic attack. He rejects it as untrue and as a matter for psychiatry, while conceding that one element of the folklore has a real basis.

classification-compartments.title: Kiriakou's transfer to the Directorate of Operations
classification-compartments.summary: John Kiriakou's roughly two-month internal campaign to transfer from the CIA's analytic Directorate of Intelligence to the operational Directorate of Operations, overcoming what he calls a "natural bias in operations against the eggheads on the analytic side," followed by an Athens posting secured because he was the only person in the entire CIA fluent in both Greek and Arabic. Covers his full CIA career arc from 1988/1990 recruitment through analyst years on Iraq, the switch to operations, 9/11, the enhanced-interrogation refusal, executive assistant to the deputy director for operations, and his eventual resignation and post-CIA career.

classification-compartments.title: Thomas Drake
classification-compartments.summary: NSA whistleblower; per John Kiriakou, the source for the statement that on the morning of September 11, 2001, NSA Director Mike Hayden told agency personnel NSA had been 'waiting for a 9/11' to implement the mass-electronic-surveillance program that NSA's founding charter forbids.

classification-compartments.title: Espionage Act
classification-compartments.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

classification-compartments.title: Julian Assange
classification-compartments.summary: Kiriakou — a 15-year friend and former WikiLeaks board member — on why Assange is a publisher owed a journalist's immunity, and a political prisoner.

classification-compartments.title: CIA record deniability
classification-compartments.summary: John Kiriakou's account of how senior CIA officers occasionally decide to keep an event out of the written record — illustrated by a recruited asset who committed a public murder, after which the Deputy Director for Operations told Kiriakou, on second thought, 'let's not put that in writing.'

classification-compartments.title: The pillow talk leak case
classification-compartments.summary: A 1990s CIA disclosure John Kiriakou witnessed from the next desk: a colleague passed classified information to a retired senior officer she was involved with, who repeated it on CNN as a terrorism consultant. The agency traced it to her within days and punished her administratively — a letter in her file, two weeks without pay, a year without promotion. Kiriakou holds it up as the correct way to handle mishandled classified information.

classified-email.title: Heather Kiriakou
classified-email.summary: John Kiriakou's wife, a senior CIA analyst who — in his account — was one of the best analysts in the entire intelligence community and who lost her job at the agency for no reason other than being married to him. She sat off camera at his December 2007 ABC News interview and told him afterwards that he had said nothing classified.

classified-email.title: Over-classification
classified-email.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of why the American government classifies far more than it can ever review: not conspiracy but incentive. At lesser agencies a classification stamp is a status marker — it puts you in the in-crowd and above the colleague who lacks access — and at the CIA everything carries a stamp by default. His complaint about press coverage of classified-document scandals is that it never reaches the underlying question of why the documents were secret at all.

classified-email.title: National Archives declassification
classified-email.summary: John Kiriakou''s exposé of why U.S. records go undeclassified: the National Archives runs a 20-year-old computer with no connectivity, its head has asked for a smaller budget, and Freedom of Information Act requests face what he calls a 500-year backlog.

classified-email.title: The mosaic concept
classified-email.summary: The intelligence method John Kiriakou names for assembling a complete operational picture out of individually trivial fragments — one tile at a time, worthless alone, decisive together. He attributes the idea to Soviet thinking of the 1960s, cites Mossad's Iranian networks as the clearest modern demonstration, and warns that the same logic is what would let an American prosecutor charge a scholar with espionage for reading declassified documents.

classified-email.title: Sensitive but unclassified
classified-email.summary: SBU — the intelligence community's name for what other agencies call controlled unclassified information. John Kiriakou stresses that it is a control and not a classification, gives gun-cleaning manuals and unreleased Commerce Department trade figures as examples, and warns that folding it under the Espionage Act would place an entire additional layer of federal employees — people with no clearances at all — inside the reach of the statute.

classified-email.title: The 2023 classified documents scandal
classified-email.summary: The run of discoveries of classified material in the private possession of Donald Trump, Joe Biden and Mike Pence, which John Kiriakou treats not as a scandal about any of them but as proof that the Espionage Act as currently applied makes almost everyone technically guilty. He rates Pence's briefing books as more highly classified than anything Julian Assange published, and says Biden's Senate-era documents are the ones that cannot be explained away.

cleaning-up-after-tora-bora.title: The lapis lazuli paperweight
cleaning-up-after-tora-bora.summary: The chunk of raw lapis lazuli John Kiriakou says he took from Osama bin Laden's house in Afghanistan and still keeps — described on air as magnificent, and agreed on air to have probably served as bin Laden's paperweight.

cleaning-up-after-tora-bora.title: The Kerry yacht tax
cleaning-up-after-tora-bora.summary: John Kiriakou's account, from his time on John Kerry's Senate staff, of the ocean-going boat Kerry docked in Rhode Island to avoid the Massachusetts yacht tax — the flood of angry calls it produced, and the advice Kiriakou gave the staff director about it.

cleaning-up-after-tora-bora.title: The O'Reilly exclusivity rule
cleaning-up-after-tora-bora.summary: The condition Bill O'Reilly's producer attached to booking John Kiriakou — that he appear on no other programme for three days either side — and Kiriakou's refusal to surrender a week of his diary, which meant he never appeared on the show at all.

cleaning-up-after-tora-bora.title: The porn on bin Laden's computers
cleaning-up-after-tora-bora.summary: The question a Pittsburgh newspaper editor put to John Kiriakou on live television hoping to embarrass him — about the pornography found on Osama bin Laden's computers — and the answer that left the programme's host saying he had been rendered speechless for the first time in twenty-five years.

cleaning-up-after-tora-bora.title: The Sputnik shutdown
cleaning-up-after-tora-bora.summary: The 2020 cancellation of the radio programme John Kiriakou co-hosted at Sputnik, and what he says followed — a five-thousand-dollar crowdfunder for a camera and a microphone that became one of the more successful independent political podcasts.

cleaning-up-after-tora-bora.title: The Trump weave
cleaning-up-after-tora-bora.summary: The name a speakers' bureau gave to John Kiriakou's platform manner — starting one story, turning off into another, and coming back to finish the first — a habit he attributes to never writing anything down before he walks to the podium.

clickers-and-touchers.title: The dorm as a reward
clickers-and-touchers.summary: John Kiriakou's explanation that moving a federal prisoner from a cell to a dormitory is a privilege earned over time, and why Ghislaine Maxwell's rapid promotion to dormitory living made no sense to him.

clickers-and-touchers.title: The guard booth rounds
clickers-and-touchers.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of federal prison staffing from the inside: rounds required every eight or fifteen minutes and performed once an hour or two, cameras that are down half the time, and a hiring standard he says amounts to a GED and no felony convictions.

clickers-and-touchers.title: Chomo
clickers-and-touchers.summary: The prison term for a child molester, which John Kiriakou first heard on his first day at FCI Loretto when two skinheads at the Aryan table put it to him as the last of three vetting questions before deciding whether he could eat with them.

clickers-and-touchers.title: Prince Andrew
clickers-and-touchers.summary: British royal, now Andrew Mountbatten Windsor, named repeatedly by John Kiriakou as one of the un-recruitable principals whose access made Jeffrey Epstein valuable to a foreign intelligence service. Kiriakou has asked why Andrew was never charged over conduct with minors, reads his alleged provision of classified Ministry of Defence documents to Epstein as evidence of espionage rather than vanity — and expects him to face no criminal consequence at all, because the statute of limitations has run.

clickers-and-touchers.title: The blacked-out grand jury minutes
clickers-and-touchers.summary: John Kiriakou on the 119 pages of grand jury minutes released in the Epstein document tranches with every single word blacked out, despite two federal judges having ordered their release.

clickers-and-touchers.title: The letter to Larry Nassar
clickers-and-touchers.summary: The letter from Jeffrey Epstein to the convicted USA Gymnastics doctor Larry Nassar that John Kiriakou singled out from the released documents, in which Epstein wrote that he would have gone home by the time it arrived and blamed everything on Donald Trump.

clint-goswick.title: FCI Loretto
clint-goswick.summary: U.S. Federal Correctional Institution in Loretto, Pennsylvania; the low-medium-security prison at which John Kiriakou served 23 months of a 30-month sentence following his 2013 Espionage Act–era plea deal; the originally ordered "minimum security work camp" placement was countermanded — per Kiriakou, on Brennan's direct intervention — to place him in the actual prison alongside the general population.

clint-goswick.title: The Second Chance Act
clint-goswick.summary: The resentencing law John Kiriakou read about in The New York Times inside FCI Loretto and used to win freedom for other prisoners — most notably Mark Lanzalotti, whose petition he wrote and who was released 17 years into a 30-year sentence.

clint-goswick.title: Chomo
clint-goswick.summary: The prison term for a child molester, which John Kiriakou first heard on his first day at FCI Loretto when two skinheads at the Aryan table put it to him as the last of three vetting questions before deciding whether he could eat with them.

clint-goswick.title: Doing Time Like a Spy
clint-goswick.summary: Prison memoir by John Kiriakou, full title Doing Time Like a Spy: How the CIA Taught Me to Survive and Thrive in Prison; winner of two literary awards and reissued in a second edition by Simon and Schuster.

clint-goswick.title: Larry Raviv
clint-goswick.summary: Fellow federal prisoner of John Kiriakou, convicted of murder-for-hire after taking out a life insurance policy on his business partner to pay off a $100,000 mob gambling debt and hiring a hitman to kill him. Raviv negotiated a 20-year sentence, down from what would normally be life without parole, by testifying against the hitman, who died of a heart attack while awaiting extradition trial. Kiriakou later engineered a violent beating against Raviv after Raviv called him a "rat" for being summoned to the lieutenant's office for a Jake Tapper interview.

clint-goswick.title: The Romanian twins
clint-goswick.summary: The adopted children John Kiriakou says his FCI Loretto roommate Robert the Australian abandoned at the gate of the Romanian embassy in Washington — one of the stories Kiriakou judged to be true, in a stream of claims he otherwise treated as invention.

clive-stafford-smith.title: Aafia Siddiqui
clive-stafford-smith.summary: Pakistani-American neuroscientist arrested in Afghanistan and convicted in the United States of attempting to shoot FBI agents; per John Kiriakou, who covered the arrest as a terrorism consultant for ABC News and has followed the case since, she never had a gun and never fired, the bullet holes offered as proof predated her capture, and the CIA took her three children — two later recovered, the youngest never found.

clive-stafford-smith.title: Hamid Karzai
clive-stafford-smith.summary: The president installed in Afghanistan after the American invasion, whom John Kiriakou uses as the standing illustration of what occupation actually buys: after twenty years and more than a trillion dollars, Karzai was ''little more than the mayor of Kabul'' — and did not control all of Kabul either. The line began as a joke among Senate Foreign Relations Committee staff, and Kiriakou used it to Senator John Kerry''s face ten years into the war.

clive-stafford-smith.title: The 1991 Saudi plan for Gaza
clive-stafford-smith.summary: A proposal John Kiriakou says he watched Ambassador Chas Freeman float to the Saudis during his first overseas tour in 1991 — that Saudi Arabia fund a port, an airport, a desalination plant and an electrical grid in Gaza. The Saudis agreed; Israel refused outright. Kiriakou raises it because the identical arrangement resurfaced in the Israeli press more than three decades later.

clive-stafford-smith.title: Kiriakou on travel
clive-stafford-smith.summary: John Kiriakou''s own ranking of the countries he has visited: Greece his favourite and, he insists, the best food anywhere; Oman the most beautiful landscape; Syria the most extraordinary civilisation; and Chile the cheapest, illustrated by a bottle of a vineyard''s locked-away reserve that cost $8.50 on his honeymoon.

clive-stafford-smith.title: Nigel Farage
clive-stafford-smith.summary: John Kiriakou's assessment that Nigel Farage was a fringe joke five years ago and is no less fascistic now, only accepted — and his prediction that if Farage becomes leader of the Conservative Party it will be the end of that party as a viable political force.

clive-stafford-smith.title: The War Department renaming
clive-stafford-smith.summary: John Kiriakou's support for restoring the name Department of War — because Truman changed it in 1947 to avoid the United States looking like an aggressor, and the record since does not support the euphemism — together with his point that a president cannot rename a federal department by executive order.

clock-tower-x.title: The October 2025 poll of American Jews
clock-tower-x.summary: The Washington Post poll John Kiriakou cited, released on 5 October 2025, which he said found for the first time that a majority of American Jews believed Israel was committing genocide in Gaza — and the question he built on it.

clock-tower-x.title: The Armenian podcasters
clock-tower-x.summary: Three naturalised Armenian-American podcasters who, independently of one another, told John Kiriakou during a week in Los Angeles that the Turks were outspending and out-lobbying Armenia in Washington — and his reply as a dual Greek citizen.

clock-tower-x.title: AIPAC
clock-tower-x.summary: The American Israel Public Affairs Committee — the U.S. political organization that, in John Kiriakou's framing, ought to be registered as a foreign-lobbying entity but is not, and that wields decisive electoral power against U.S. elected officials who express support for Palestinian human rights.

clock-tower-x.title: Kiriakou on artificial intelligence
clock-tower-x.summary: John Kiriakou's stated experience with and objections to large language models — a ChatGPT exchange in which the system stated his degrees incorrectly, refused his correction and then cut him off, and a test in which every scholarly citation it produced for his university syllabus turned out to be fabricated. He also describes AI as the flagging layer of contemporary surveillance.

clock-tower-x.title: Abdul El-Sayed
clock-tower-x.summary: Physician and Democratic Socialists of America-backed candidate in Michigan's 2026 Democratic Senate primary. John Kiriakou, who discloses a $100 donation to the campaign, presents him as the test case for whether the electability argument still works for establishment Democrats.

clock-tower-x.title: AIPAC and foreign-agent registration
clock-tower-x.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that AIPAC is the only organization of its kind exempt from registering under the Foreign Agents Registration Act — set against his own experience around 2008, when a contract worth five or six thousand dollars to write four op-eds praising the Abu Dhabi Chamber of Commerce obliged him to register as a foreign agent.

closing-the-gulf-embassies.title: THAAD stocks in the Gulf
closing-the-gulf-embassies.summary: John Kiriakou's report, during the 2026 war, that the United Arab Emirates were seven days from exhausting their THAAD interceptors and Qatar four days — with American resupply unable to keep pace.

closing-the-gulf-embassies.title: 2026 Iran war
closing-the-gulf-embassies.summary: The open-ended American and Israeli war against Iran that John Kiriakou tracked week by week on his own show — a conflict he says was sold as three weeks, ran into its fifth month, achieved every decapitation objective it set, and continued anyway. His grade for it is a D, and his forecast is a Truth Social post declaring victory while nothing changes.

closing-the-gulf-embassies.title: Arming the crazies
closing-the-gulf-embassies.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the American habit of arming the most radical faction available — the Mujahideen over any other Afghan force, the White Russians over the Red — and his expectation, stated days into the 2026 war, that the United States and Israel would begin arming factions inside Iran and that the factions chosen would be the radical ones.

closing-the-gulf-embassies.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
closing-the-gulf-embassies.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

closing-the-gulf-embassies.title: Chaos as the Israeli objective
closing-the-gulf-embassies.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer to whether Netanyahu''s government actually wanted an American invasion of Iran: what the Israelis want in Iran is what they got in Libya — chaos, civil war, and as many dead Iranians as possible.

closing-the-gulf-embassies.title: Iranian sleeper cells
closing-the-gulf-embassies.summary: John Kiriakou's assessment of Iran's clandestine reach abroad — that the IRGC and the Ministry of Intelligence and Security do run sleeper cells worldwide, but probably not in the United States, Canada or the UK, and that the greater danger is the unaffiliated lone attacker. He also argues Iranian operatives are consistently poor, and identifies the Gulf's real vulnerability as its tourist landmarks rather than its military bases.

club-fed-myth.title: Supervised release travel restrictions
club-fed-myth.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the years of court supervision that followed his prison term, in which a judge refused him permission to travel abroad to give paid speeches while he was expected to earn a living, and in which he had to surrender his passport on returning from every trip he was allowed to take.

club-fed-myth.title: The Oz analogy
club-fed-myth.summary: John Kiriakou's habit of explaining federal prison social structure through the HBO drama Oz, in which rival gangs are forced to share a single unit — and his identification with the show's unaffiliated Irish character, who belonged to no faction and survived by playing them off one another.

club-fed-myth.title: The Virginia pardon and voting rights
club-fed-myth.summary: John Kiriakou's account of applying to have his voting rights restored in Virginia after leaving prison and receiving, unasked, a full state pardon delivered by courier from the office of Governor Terry McAuliffe — followed by a courthouse clerk and a state employee who between them got him registered in time to vote.

club-fed-myth.title: Kiriakou's prison designation
club-fed-myth.summary: The discrepancy between the minimum-security work camp John Kiriakou was sentenced to and the low-security prison the Bureau of Prisons actually placed him in, which he cites whenever the subject of preferential designations arises.

club-fed-myth.title: The culling of friendships
club-fed-myth.summary: John Kiriakou''s description of what happened to his private life after he confirmed the CIA''s torture program: friends and even family members began walking away from him before any charge was filed, a process he came to regard, oddly, as a culling exercise that dispatched phonies and left the people who genuinely loved him.

club-fed-myth.title: The Cat in the Hat and Truck
