club-fed-myth.summary: The prison anecdote John Kiriakou uses to illustrate the CIA counter-accusation tradecraft he applied at FCI Loretto, a cellmate applicant called Cat in the Hat named him a rat to a serial killer named Truck within earshot; Kiriakou answered by remarking Cat in the Hat had earlier called Truck a pedophile; Truck beat Cat in the Hat almost to death and had to be lifelighted by helicopter to Pittsburgh.

clyde-hall.title: The body in the barrel
clyde-hall.summary: The exchange John Kiriakou reports having with a fellow prisoner who explained his conviction by saying the police had found a body in a barrel in his storage unit — and that a hundred people had access to the unit — to which Kiriakou's only reply was that he was not judging him.

clyde-hall.title: The Macron defamation suit
clyde-hall.summary: The Macrons' libel action against Candace Owens over her claim that Brigitte Macron was born male, which John Kiriakou discussed as a question of venue — and which prompted him to say he wished he had sued the Los Angeles Times in England when he had the chance.

clyde-hall.title: The FLETC badge
clyde-hall.summary: The shiny gold badge John Kiriakou carried before joining the CIA, issued after he trained at the Federal Law Enforcement Training Center — and which he insists never made him a law enforcement officer, a distinction he uses to deny the same status to ICE agents and federal prison guards.

clyde-hall.title: The hundred-drachma coins
clyde-hall.summary: How demonstrators in Athens broke the windows of the American embassy during John Kiriakou's posting there in 1999 — with hundred-drachma coins the size of an Eisenhower dollar, worth about a quarter, followed by paint-filled balloons fired from slingshots.

clyde-hall.title: The Mayflower Madam analogy
clyde-hall.summary: John Kiriakou's argument, borrowed from the 1980s Mayflower Madam case, that the Epstein 'list' will disappoint anyone expecting a schedule of clients — because address books contain the dry cleaner and the Chinese takeaway alongside everyone else, and nobody keeps a spreadsheet of their crimes.

clyde-hall.title: The Yugo factory argument
clyde-hall.summary: The dinner-table confrontation in which one of John Kiriakou's uncles in Greece demanded to know why the United States had bombed the Yugo factory — an accusation Kiriakou could answer only technically, because he thought the 1999 bombing of Yugoslavia was wrong in the first place.

code-pink.title: Bureau of Prisons
code-pink.summary: The federal agency that ran John Kiriakou's incarceration — and one of his most persistent post-prison targets. The BOP overrode his judge's camp recommendation by deeming him "a threat to the public safety," threatened him with "diesel therapy" until 1,600 logged phone calls and letters from a dozen House members and two senators backed it off, and, per Kiriakou, functions as "an employment agency for unemployable semi-literate rural white men" and "a dumping ground for failed medical professionals" — an agency for which a prisoner's death is cheaper than his treatment.

code-pink.title: Oliver Stone
code-pink.summary: American film director with whom John Kiriakou struck up a friendship after his release from prison. Stone optioned the rights to one chapter of Kiriakou's first book, co-developed an unmade History Channel series with him, blurbed his book on Abu Zubaydah, and was among the public figures who campaigned against the Bureau of Prisons' attempt to shut down Kiriakou's prison blog. The two disagree sharply over whether the CIA killed John F. Kennedy.

code-pink.title: Kiriakou's transfer to the Directorate of Operations
code-pink.summary: John Kiriakou's roughly two-month internal campaign to transfer from the CIA's analytic Directorate of Intelligence to the operational Directorate of Operations, overcoming what he calls a "natural bias in operations against the eggheads on the analytic side," followed by an Athens posting secured because he was the only person in the entire CIA fluent in both Greek and Arabic. Covers his full CIA career arc from 1988/1990 recruitment through analyst years on Iraq, the switch to operations, 9/11, the enhanced-interrogation refusal, executive assistant to the deputy director for operations, and his eventual resignation and post-CIA career.

code-pink.title: Espionage Act
code-pink.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

code-pink.title: Signature strikes
code-pink.summary: The drone-targeting doctrine, exposed by Daniel Hale's leak, under which the U.S. kills people not for who they are but for patterns of behavior or association; John Kiriakou says operators treat any male over 12 as a legitimate target on the theory that he 'could pick up a gun.'

code-pink.title: "Take our word for it"
code-pink.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the standing justification given after American strikes kill civilians — that there was a terrorist present, and that the public would agree if it could see the intelligence — set against his statement that he saw that intelligence and it was fabricated, and applied to the 2021 Kabul strike that killed seven children.

cofer-black-pre-9-11-warning.title: The Foreign Relations volume and the sources still alive
cofer-black-pre-9-11-warning.summary: The errand that put John Kiriakou and Cofer Black in a car to the White House on the morning of 11 September 2001: three declassified cables due to be printed in a State Department history volume named CIA sources who were still living — and an obscure law requiring the United States to resettle any source it outs.

cofer-black-pre-9-11-warning.title: Alfreda Bikowsky
cofer-black-pre-9-11-warning.summary: Senior CIA officer who headed Alec Station and, before that, served as its chief of operations, overseeing the CIA's torture program; per John Kiriakou, "bad news from the get-go," and part of a failed attempt with Rich Blee to turn a San Diego al-Qaeda cell into double agents.

cofer-black-pre-9-11-warning.title: Cofer Black
cofer-black-pre-9-11-warning.summary: Former head of the CIA Counterterrorism Center during and immediately after the September 11 attacks; principal architect of the agency's paramilitary turn on September 12, 2001; later Vice President of Blackwater under Erik Prince.

cofer-black-pre-9-11-warning.title: The liaison class
cofer-black-pre-9-11-warning.summary: The course John Kiriakou ran at the CIA for visiting officers of allied intelligence services — the setting for Cofer Black's warning weeks before 9/11, and the reason Kiriakou was in the counterterrorism chief's office to ask whether he had meant it.

cofer-black-pre-9-11-warning.title: Counterterrorism Center
cofer-black-pre-9-11-warning.summary: The CIA's Counterterrorism Center (CTC) — the unit where John Kiriakou spent the defining years of his operational career. He joined in the late 1990s as the only officer in the entire CIA fluent in both Greek and Arabic, served as chief of counterintelligence in the bin Laden unit, watched the Center swell from a few hundred employees to nearly 2,000 by September 12, 2001, and it was to CTC that he walked back down in May 2002 to refuse the torture program — the moment, he says, the CIA began to turn on him.

cofer-black-pre-9-11-warning.title: John Kiriakou
cofer-black-pre-9-11-warning.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

cofer-black.title: Dick Clarke
cofer-black.summary: The White House counterterrorism chief John Kiriakou describes as the most highly respected non-ideological counterterrorism professional in government — demoted by the incoming Bush administration, ignored when he warned Condoleezza Rice that a terrible attack was coming, and, on Kiriakou's account, lied to by CIA director George Tenet about al-Qaeda operatives already inside the United States.

cofer-black.title: The 2026 KSM confession ruling
cofer-black.summary: The Guantanamo military commission ruling, issued by Lieutenant Colonel Michael Shramma in late August 2026 and reported by John Kiriakou as breaking news on September 1, that threw out Khalid Sheikh Mohammed's confession as inadmissible because the CIA had waterboarded him 183 times, and further threw out his 2007 non-torture Guantanamo interrogations because FBI agents *"intentionally failed to explicitly tell KSM that he had a right to remain silent, that he had a right to consult an attorney, and that what he told them could be used against him at trial."* Kiriakou reads it as the moment the American torture programme made the trial of the man who murdered three thousand Americans impossible.

cofer-black.title: US Military Venture Capital
cofer-black.summary: Per John Kiriakou, the U.S. military now purchases technology using a venture-capital investment model, a shift he cites as a warning sign about how national-security institutions acquire emerging tech.

cofer-black.title: "Kill them all"
cofer-black.summary: The one-line departure hug John Kiriakou says he got from his own CIA boss, an elegant, thousand-dollar-suit man he calls John, whom he had joked belonged in the State Department, on the day Kiriakou left Washington to become chief of counterterrorism operations in Pakistan after 9/11. Kiriakou uses it as the compressed summary of the mood inside the building he was leaving behind.

cofer-black.title: Trump
cofer-black.summary: Kiriakou applied for a pardon on the last day of Trump's first term — and says Trump had agreed to it, until the last-minute reversal.

cofer-black.title: The custody standoff
cofer-black.summary: The week John Kiriakou used his CIA surveillance training to find his own sons after his ex-wife hid them in breach of a custody order — ending with him carrying his eight-year-old out of a Greek Orthodox church during the consecration, a felony charge that was dropped, and a hostage-style handover at a diner on the state line.

coffee-with-a-cabinet-member.title: The writ of coram nobis
coffee-with-a-cabinet-member.summary: The second route out of his conviction that John Kiriakou describes, besides a pardon: a writ of coram nobis, under which the Justice Department would go to the Eastern District of Virginia and state that it made a mistake in prosecuting him, admits the mistake, and asks that the conviction be overturned. He calls them exceedingly rare, citing one around 2001 and one in 1986.

coffee-with-a-cabinet-member.title: The multi-state permit
coffee-with-a-cabinet-member.summary: The warning John Kiriakou says he was given when he obtained his concealed carry permit: that the multi-state permit is not recognised in New York, New Jersey or Maryland, and that he should not carry a concealed weapon in any of them. He raised it while rejecting a friend''s theory that gun rights would decide a New York governor''s race.

coffee-with-a-cabinet-member.title: The Crenshaw text messages
coffee-with-a-cabinet-member.summary: John Kiriakou's account of taking his girlfriend's phone at midnight, finding a message from Dan Crenshaw asking what she was wearing, and texting back that he was her boyfriend and Crenshaw should ask his own wife — who had a ten-month-old baby at the time. Kiriakou says the woman showed him other messages that were filthy, and that she had saved them in case she needed to use them.

coffee-with-a-cabinet-member.title: The January 6 pipe bomber report
coffee-with-a-cabinet-member.summary: The story John Kiriakou says he posted to Facebook and nobody else picked up: a report that the FBI had identified the person who placed pipe bombs outside the RNC and DNC as a former Capitol Police officer who had been on rotation to the CIA doing physical security, recognised from a limp caused by a college sports injury, at a stated confidence of 94 per cent. She had not been charged, and Kiriakou lists the questions it would raise if true.

coffee-with-a-cabinet-member.title: The Red Fort bombing
coffee-with-a-cabinet-member.summary: John Kiriakou''s on-air attribution of a car bombing outside the Red Fort in New Delhi to Kashmiri separatist groups — offered with the acknowledgement that saying so brings him death threats from Pakistanis, and with a flat definition: groups that murder civilians for political purposes are terrorist groups, whatever their political point may be.

coffee-with-a-cabinet-member.title: Zaluzhny and the Nordstream prosecution
coffee-with-a-cabinet-member.summary: John Kiriakou''s reaction to German investigators drawing a bead on the former commander-in-chief of the Ukrainian armed forces over the Nordstream sabotage: that the CIA and the Pentagon now wish the case would go away, that the truth is not supposed to come out in such an operation, that Seymour Hersh probably had the kernel but not the details, and that it was very likely a joint operation. He expects somebody to go to prison.

cointelpro.title: Church Committee
cointelpro.summary: U.S. Senate investigative committee operating in 1975–1976 that examined domestic intelligence abuses by the CIA, FBI, and NSA; per John Kiriakou, the Church Committee — alongside the concurrent Pike Committee in the House — was the last genuine moment of legislative oversight over the intelligence community, born of a national consensus that government had gone dangerously off course. Its work led to the creation of the permanent Senate Select Committee on Intelligence, which Kiriakou says ceased to function as real oversight roughly seven years after its founding.

cointelpro.title: The Weaponization Subcommittee
cointelpro.summary: The Select Subcommittee on the Weaponization of the Federal Government, created in January 2023 and promoted as a second Church Committee. John Kiriakou says he is a thousand per cent in favour of a second Church Committee and that this is not one: it was created on a straight party-line vote, the Democrats refused to take their seats, and its remit is the FBI''s treatment of conservatives rather than the crimes the original committee exposed.

cointelpro.title: Jim Jordan
cointelpro.summary: Republican congressman from Ohio and chairman of the House Judiciary Committee. John Kiriakou describes a genuinely divided view of him: one of only four members of Congress he names as a friend of whistleblowers, and simultaneously the chairman whose Weaponization subcommittee he says is a partisan counterfeit of the Church Committee — with the whole question settled against Jordan by the Ohio State wrestlers who told him their team doctor was abusing them.

cointelpro.title: Martin Luther King Jr.
cointelpro.summary: The civil rights leader whose Letter from Birmingham Jail John Kiriakou explicitly honored in naming his own Letters from Loretto, and whose example — with Mandela and Gandhi — anchored Kiriakou''s decision to forgive his prosecutors: "I only lost two years of my life, not 35." Kiriakou''s parents marched for civil rights with King; he quotes King''s line about preaching nonviolence while his government is the world''s major purveyor of violence, and lists King''s assassination among the acts attributed to the unelected security state.

cointelpro.title: MLK assassination
cointelpro.summary: The April 1968 killing of Martin Luther King Jr. John Kiriakou, having set out to read everything he could find on it, concluded that if James Earl Ray fired the shot he was a patsy — citing the implausibility of a lifelong alcoholic making a perfect shot from a flophouse bathroom a block away, and the FBI's documented attempt two years earlier to push King into suicide.

cointelpro.title: Jim Bamford
cointelpro.summary: The author John Kiriakou credits with having written the definitive book on the NSA and with first making Americans aware of the surveillance state. Kiriakou highlights Bamford''s 2023 book Spy Fail for a claim he says should have been front-page news and was not: that the FBI lost ten of its Chinese sources because Peter Strzok''s counterintelligence unit had a Chinese mole inside it.

cold-cell.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
cold-cell.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

cold-cell.title: Sleep deprivation
cold-cell.summary: A CIA interrogation technique used against high-value detainees post-9/11; the agency was authorized to deny prisoners sleep for up to 12 days continuously; people died; at least one detainee was rendered permanently clinically insane.

cold-cell.title: Justice Department self-immolation attempt
cold-cell.summary: An attempted self-immolation at a Washington rally in support of Julian Assange and WikiLeaks, held outside the Department of Justice, at which John Kiriakou was speaking. Kiriakou and another demonstrator physically stopped a naked man who had doused himself in lighter fluid; an attorney present intervened with the arresting officers and the man was taken to a hospital rather than a jail.

cold-cell.title: Music as torture
cold-cell.summary: The use of recorded music played on indefinite loop as a coercive interrogation technique. Per John Kiriakou, the CIA's post-9/11 rotation ran to the Bee Gees and the SpongeBob SquarePants theme song, and the practice was not an invention of the war on terror — he places its use throughout the Vietnam War.

cold-cell.title: Walling
cold-cell.summary: A CIA interrogation technique in which a detainee is slammed against a wall; designed on paper to use a padded fiberboard surface and a rolled towel around the neck, but applied in practice against bare concrete-block walls without protective measures, producing in at least one case permanent brain damage.

cold-cell.title: Gul Rahman
cold-cell.summary: Prisoner who froze to death in a CIA cold cell at the Salt Pit black site in Afghanistan; the only death in the torture programme the agency acknowledges, and the third claim in the civil suit brought against James Mitchell and Bruce Jessen. John Kiriakou says nobody has ever been brought to justice for it.

cold-war.title: Soviet Union
cold-war.summary: The superpower whose collapse framed the start of John Kiriakou's CIA career — it was "literally in the process of collapsing" when he joined in January 1990, ushering in a brief "peace dividend" era when the agency's new threats were environmental degradation and AIDS. Kiriakou cites Brzezinski's "Afghan trap" that lured the Soviets into Afghanistan, argues the U.S. abandoned the radicalized mujahideen the moment the Soviets were beaten, notes America then took "a vacation from history," and recalls that Jonathan Pollard's stolen documents were traded by Israel to the Soviets in exchange for Russian Jews.

cold-war.title: Russia and NATO membership
cold-war.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the opening that was available with Moscow in the early 2000s and was refused — deep cooperation on terrorism, narcotics and proliferation offered only on terms of junior partnership, and approaches from both Yeltsin and Putin about joining NATO that met, in his words, the cold shoulder.

cold-war.title: Bilderberg and weapon sales
cold-war.summary: John Kiriakou's claim, sourced to someone he knew who attended, that elite gatherings like Bilderberg and the Shangri-La Dialogue are — beneath the talk of global issues — fundamentally 'all about weapon sales' and defense-contractor deals.

cold-war.title: Carlos the Jackal
cold-war.summary: Venezuelan-born militant (Ilich Ramírez Sánchez) active in the 1970s and 1980s; per John Kiriakou, 'the Osama bin Laden of the 70s and 80s.' Kiriakou spent his Athens posting trying to identify the middleman linking Carlos to the Greek terrorist group 17 November, then six months working the lead with MI5 in London; Carlos was finally run down by CIA contractor Billy Waugh in a Khartoum vegetable market and captured in 1994.

cold-war.title: CIA and FBI ties to organized crime
cold-war.summary: John Kiriakou's survey of documented U.S. intelligence partnerships with organized crime — the FBI securing wartime ports with the Genovese family, the CIA's Castro plots with the Trafficantes, its work with the Escobar cartel against Colombian communists, and a mob hitman deployed against the Klan.

cold-war.title: Russia was always the same enemy
cold-war.summary: John Kiriakou''s observation, from inside the CIA, that the collapse of the Soviet Union changed nothing about how the agency worked on Russia. The marching orders given to his colleagues on the Russia account were not to change policy at all: Russia was treated as the same enemy it had been as the Soviet Union, with a brief exception during the Yeltsin presidency.

colin-powell.title: Iraq WMD intelligence
colin-powell.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of how the case for Iraqi weapons of mass destruction was fabricated: the intelligence community''s consensus was that Iraq had no WMD, but the White House had already decided to invade and sought analysis to fit the policy.

colin-powell.title: MOSSAD
colin-powell.summary: Israel's primary external intelligence service; characterized by John Kiriakou as universally hostile in his and his CIA colleagues' professional dealings with it ("never had a positive encounter with Mossad"); operates almost exclusively in the operational rather than analytical domain; the CIA is, per Kiriakou, categorically forbidden from spying on it.

colin-powell.title: Lawrence Wilkerson
colin-powell.summary: Retired Army colonel, chief of staff and closest friend to Secretary of State Colin Powell; John Kiriakou counts him among the most consequential military whistleblowers, cites his count of 108 deaths in military custody, and says Wilkerson confirmed on air that Powell's UN case for the Iraq war was knowingly "sold."

colin-powell.title: Saddam Hussein
colin-powell.summary: President of Iraq from 1979 until the 2003 U.S. invasion; subject of John Kiriakou's CIA portfolio from January 1990 onward, in which capacity Kiriakou became, at age 25, "Saddam Hussein's intelligence community biographer" and the analyst who briefed President George H. W. Bush in the Oval Office on the morning of the 1990 invasion of Kuwait.

colin-powell.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
colin-powell.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

colin-powell.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
colin-powell.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

collateral-murder-video.title: Julian Assange
collateral-murder-video.summary: Kiriakou — a 15-year friend and former WikiLeaks board member — on why Assange is a publisher owed a journalist's immunity, and a political prisoner.

collateral-murder-video.title: Chelsea Manning
collateral-murder-video.summary: Former U.S. Army intelligence analyst who provided WikiLeaks its 2010 trove of military and diplomatic documents. Per John Kiriakou, Manning meets the legal definition of whistleblower for exposing war crimes, was a torture victim of prolonged solitary confinement with forced nudity, and was sentenced to 35 years in prison before Barack Obama commuted — not pardoned — her sentence. Kiriakou says Manning later refused a grand jury's offer of immunity and chose renewed jail time rather than testify against Julian Assange.

collateral-murder-video.title: Afghan War Logs
collateral-murder-video.summary: A 2010 WikiLeaks publication discussed on a panel Kiriakou joined; the specific lines about it in the corpus belong to other panelists, not Kiriakou.

collateral-murder-video.title: Iraqi invasion of Kuwait
collateral-murder-video.summary: John Kiriakou''s most detailed account of the intelligence process around the 1990 Iraqi invasion of Kuwait and its 1991 liberation. As a first-year CIA analyst on a ''training account'' covering Iraq, Kiriakou produced the June 30, 1990 warning paper for the White House; suggested calling the US Defense Attaché in Baghdad to drive to the border and report what he saw (the answer: ''Literally the entire Iraqi military is heading south''); briefed the August 2 Oval Office meeting with Bush; and later took a single phone call from General Colin Powell that led, eight hours later, to 47 cruise missiles striking the Iraqi Intelligence Service headquarters in Baghdad.

collateral-murder-video.title: The CIA Insider's Guide to Surveillance and Surveillance Detection
collateral-murder-video.summary: Book by John Kiriakou drawing on his experience as a surveillance detection instructor at the CIA and as a private surveillance training consultant. The book covers the techniques used by intelligence professionals to identify whether they are being followed — including the four-phase surveillance detection route, concealment device placement and retrieval, and counter-surveillance strategy — adapted for use by corporate executives, journalists, and others who want to confirm whether they are being followed.

collateral-murder-video.title: FISA court
collateral-murder-video.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the secret Foreign Intelligence Surveillance court — created under Carter, sitting atop the Justice Department, issuing warrants that are never public — which he says was abused against Carter Page as part of what he believes was John Brennan's plan to deny Trump the presidency.

college-tuition-as-an-inducement.title: The autographed basketball
college-tuition-as-an-inducement.summary: A recruitment John Kiriakou has cited as proof that an agent''s price is not always money: a source who loved the Chicago Bulls, an ordinary basketball bought from the NBA online store with a forged provenance involving Michael Jordan, and an acrylic display box.

college-tuition-as-an-inducement.title: "You were the first person that ever asked me about my children"
college-tuition-as-an-inducement.summary: The answer John Kiriakou says he received when he asked a mid-level al-Qaeda member he had recruited in Pakistan why he had allowed the recruitment to happen: that in five years of detention Kiriakou had been the first person to ask about his children.

college-tuition-as-an-inducement.title: The prostitute hypothetical
college-tuition-as-an-inducement.summary: The classroom exercise John Kiriakou uses in university lectures to demonstrate that the CIA gave its operations officers no ethical guidelines at all — a recruited terrorist source who demands a prostitute, and then the same demand for a child.

college-tuition-as-an-inducement.title: Arabic and Greek
college-tuition-as-an-inducement.summary: The qualification John Kiriakou says opened the door to his transfer from CIA analysis to operations: a post in Athens wanted Greek or Arabic, and he had both — by most of his tellings the only officer in the agency who did. The chief who hired him gave the reason in one sentence: it is easier and cheaper to take a linguist and teach him operations than the other way round. The pairing also became a detection tool, since the language nobody speaks in Pakistan is Arabic.

college-tuition-as-an-inducement.title: Bankruptcy and the dropped charges
college-tuition-as-an-inducement.summary: The sequence John Kiriakou places at the centre of his case: that the espionage counts against him were dropped only after his legal fees had bankrupted him, which he presents as evidence that the government''s aim was attrition rather than conviction.

college-tuition-as-an-inducement.title: Curtailment cables
college-tuition-as-an-inducement.summary: The career-ending requests John Kiriakou says he read coming back from the CIA's black sites — officers, doctors, psychologists and nurses asking to end their tours early rather than continue to take part in the interrogation programme — and his conclusion that if that many people were objecting in classified channels, someone would surely go public.

colonel-khaled.title: Faisalabad Hospital
colonel-khaled.summary: The hospital where a dying Abu Zubaydah was taken after the raid of March 2002 — open windows, animals in the corridors, mosquitoes on open wounds, and a bar of Irish Spring soap used as a pincushion for reusable syringes — which came under fire from the street while he was on the operating table.

colonel-khaled.title: The Lahore safe house
colonel-khaled.summary: The ten-bedroom house in the best neighbourhood of Lahore that the CIA bought outright for two million dollars in cash in March 2002, on a cover story invented on the spot — that its buyers were textile barons — and from whose roof the team could catch seven satellites.

colonel-khaled.title: Faisalabad
colonel-khaled.summary: The Pakistani textile city of some seven or eight million people where Abu Zubaydah was captured in March 2002 — concrete, mud and corrugated tin in John Kiriakou's description, with a brand-new glass-and-steel McDonald's standing in the middle of it.

colonel-khaled.title: Mr. Fish
colonel-khaled.summary: The cover name the CIA used for Abu Zubaydah in Pakistan in 2002 — invented because the Americans would not tell their Pakistani partners who the target was, and derived from the only thing they would say about him: that he was a big fish.

colonel-khaled.title: Navigating Pakistan without maps
colonel-khaled.summary: The logistical problem John Kiriakou says nearly undid the Abu Zubaydah operation: in 2002 Pakistan had no maps to buy, no street signs and no addresses, so the CIA team navigated a city of twelve million by shoe advertisement, traffic policeman, British school and McDonald''s — rehearsing the route twice in the small hours before the raids.

colonel-khaled.title: The Punjab Elite Force
colonel-khaled.summary: The Pakistani provincial counterterrorism unit that supplied part of the assault manpower for the Abu Zubaydah raids of March 2002 — black trousers, black t-shirts stencilled with a pistol, and, in John Kiriakou's telling, a refusal to wear body armour on the grounds that if God called them that night they would go.

commercial-off-the-shelf-tradecraft.title: Surveillance detection route
commercial-off-the-shelf-tradecraft.summary: Tradecraft technique used by intelligence officers and assets to determine whether they are being followed before, during, or after an operational meeting

commercial-off-the-shelf-tradecraft.title: The CIA Insider's Guide to Surveillance and Surveillance Detection
commercial-off-the-shelf-tradecraft.summary: Book by John Kiriakou drawing on his experience as a surveillance detection instructor at the CIA and as a private surveillance training consultant. The book covers the techniques used by intelligence professionals to identify whether they are being followed — including the four-phase surveillance detection route, concealment device placement and retrieval, and counter-surveillance strategy — adapted for use by corporate executives, journalists, and others who want to confirm whether they are being followed.

commercial-off-the-shelf-tradecraft.title: Cover position
commercial-off-the-shelf-tradecraft.summary: The occupational identity under which an intelligence officer operates abroad. John Kiriakou''s account collapses the popular idea that certain embassy jobs are tell-tale: because a diplomatic mission has to do its real work every day, every position in and out of an embassy is simultaneously a genuine job and a possible cover, which is precisely what makes cover work.

commercial-off-the-shelf-tradecraft.title: The Islamabad surveillance incident
commercial-off-the-shelf-tradecraft.summary: The episode in which John Kiriakou, then the CIA's chief of counterterrorism operations in Pakistan, detected a motorcyclist following him, resolved to kill the man, and discovered on a passing impulse that the surveillance was friendly.

commercial-off-the-shelf-tradecraft.title: Operational vehicles
commercial-off-the-shelf-tradecraft.summary: The cars John Kiriakou used in the field. In the Middle East they were whatever the rental company supplied — usually a Toyota — on the reasoning that anonymity was the point; in Athens, where the threat justified it, he was issued a factory-built, level-four armoured BMW 540 that broke down constantly.

commercial-off-the-shelf-tradecraft.title: 2028 presidential field
commercial-off-the-shelf-tradecraft.summary: John Kiriakou's assessment of the wide-open 2028 presidential race — the first in his life, he says, where he has no idea who either party will nominate. Predictive markets were listing 44 Democrats and 26 Republicans as possible candidates. His own preferred candidate is Tucker Carlson, whom he says he has repeatedly begged to run; his working assumption about anyone who does want the job is that they are "a narcissist and probably a sociopath on top of it."

communications-management-unit.title: Liam O'Grady
communications-management-unit.summary: The Eastern District of Virginia judge who sentenced Daniel Hale, and who in John Kiriakou''s account surprised the courtroom twice: with a sentence of 45 months rather than the far longer term expected, and with a recommendation that Hale serve it in a low-security prison where he could be treated for depression and addiction. The Bureau of Prisons ignored the recommendation and sent him to the communications management unit at Marion instead.

communications-management-unit.title: The roadblock strike
communications-management-unit.summary: The drone strike Daniel Hale described at his own sentencing and that John Kiriakou retells as the reason Hale became a whistleblower: a car approaching a U.S. roadblock in Afghanistan, two girls aged six and nine visible inside, an order to fire given twice over Hale''s objection, and a father who afterwards hid his daughters'' bodies in a village dumpster for fear that special forces would take them.

communications-management-unit.title: Sigurdur Thordarson
communications-management-unit.summary: The FBI's key witness against Julian Assange, described by John Kiriakou as a convicted paedophile, a convicted embezzler and a self-admitted liar — one of three facts he lists, alongside the bugging of the Ecuadorian embassy and the reported plot to kidnap or kill Assange, in asking whether judges can keep such things out of their heads.

communications-management-unit.title: The Walmart phone call
communications-management-unit.summary: John Kiriakou''s account, from a White House friend, that Jared Kushner personally telephoned the chief executive of Walmart to find a job for a woman whose life sentence Donald Trump had commuted, and rang back every six months to check on her.

communications-management-unit.title: Eastern State Penitentiary
communications-management-unit.summary: The Philadelphia prison where, per John Kiriakou, solitary confinement was invented in 1829 — a neo-Gothic stone penitentiary of tiny cells arranged as spokes around a central guard post, each containing a bed, a chair, a table, a chamber pot and a Bible, on the theory that a man left alone with scripture would emerge a law-abiding Christian. What happened instead, Kiriakou says, is that everybody went insane — and the practice was kept anyway, because it worked as punishment.

communications-management-unit.title: Operation Fast and Furious
communications-management-unit.summary: The ATF gun-walking operation John Kiriakou describes as the background to the Donnie Reynolds Jr case — in which agents let 2,000 weapons reach Mexican cartel buyers in the hope of tracing them upward, arrested nobody at the top, and then turned back on the small players when Congress demanded answers.

concealment-devices.title: The Directorate of Science and Technology
concealment-devices.summary: One of the CIA's four directorates, which in John Kiriakou's time was an afterthought responsible for disguises and briefcases with hidden compartments, and which he says now works with Palantir, Amazon, Nvidia and Elon Musk's companies on work closer to DARPA's than to anything the agency did in the past.

concealment-devices.title: Spy films and television on screen
concealment-devices.summary: John Kiriakou's scene-by-scene verdicts on how spy films and television handle real tradecraft — what they get right (static surveillance from upper floors, hostile operational meetings, exchanges of bona fides, breaking into offices), what they invent (silent helicopters, high-speed submersibles, Batcaves, gadgets that cannot be bought), and the shows he says commit felonies on screen. He opens with why CIA officers watch them at all — *"not because they love the CIA movies, but because they love to criticize them."*

concealment-devices.title: Meeting Elon Musk in 2009
concealment-devices.summary: The evening in 2009 when John Kiriakou, waiting to pitch a television idea to an incoming NBC president in a Washington bar, was introduced to a friend the executive had brought along — asked him what he did for a living, and listened to him talk about Mars all night.

concealment-devices.title: Abraxas Corporation
concealment-devices.summary: The private intelligence company founded in the 1990s by retired CIA operations officers as a tax pass-through and a place to smoke cigars and tell stories — which, after 9/11, made its founders, in John Kiriakou's phrase, Mega Millions rich.

concealment-devices.title: Bill Buckley
concealment-devices.summary: CIA station chief in Beirut kidnapped by Palestinian Islamic Jihad in March 1984; tortured at length over fifteen months; killed in captivity; the case from which the agency derived a generation of operational-security lessons including the abandonment of single-point tracking devices in CIA officers' personal kit.

concealment-devices.title: The Brüno shoot in Jordan
concealment-devices.summary: The scene John Kiriakou set up for Sacha Baron Cohen in Amman — four retired Palestinian militants, found in the Damascus telephone book at the Library of Congress, shown hardcore pornography by a character they believed to be an Austrian documentary journalist — which produced no reaction at all and was cut from the film entirely.

condoleezza-rice.title: Cofer Black
condoleezza-rice.summary: Former head of the CIA Counterterrorism Center during and immediately after the September 11 attacks; principal architect of the agency's paramilitary turn on September 12, 2001; later Vice President of Blackwater under Erik Prince.

condoleezza-rice.title: Principals Committee Meeting (February 2003)
condoleezza-rice.summary: Senior-most interagency forum of the U.S. national security apparatus, normally chaired by the president. Per John Kiriakou — who served as notetaker for CIA Director George Tenet at the eve-of-Iraq-invasion meeting on February 19–20, 2003 — Vice President Dick Cheney chaired in place of Bush, General Tommy Franks ended his order-of-battle briefing with 'If all goes as planned, we can be in Tehran by August,' and an NSC senior director said 'When we cross that border tomorrow morning, they're going to throw flowers at us.'

condoleezza-rice.title: The Condoleezza Rice meeting
condoleezza-rice.summary: The nine o'clock White House appointment John Kiriakou and Cofer Black never kept on the morning of 11 September 2001. The Government Printing Office was about to issue a volume of declassified Greece-Turkey-Cyprus cables in an edition of five or ten copies; three of them named CIA sources who were still alive, and an obscure statute obliges the government to offer citizenship and resettlement to any recruited source it outs. The two men were going to ask the National Security Advisor to quietly pull three cables nobody would miss. The car was at the East entrance at 8.15.

condoleezza-rice.title: George Tenet
condoleezza-rice.summary: Director of Central Intelligence from 1997 to 2004, spanning the September 11 attacks and the early enhanced-interrogation program; identified by John Kiriakou as John Brennan's institutional patron at the agency; the figure who ordered the Five Eyes intelligence services to "open the files" to each other in the early 2000s.

condoleezza-rice.title: Dick Clarke
condoleezza-rice.summary: The White House counterterrorism chief John Kiriakou describes as the most highly respected non-ideological counterterrorism professional in government — demoted by the incoming Bush administration, ignored when he warned Condoleezza Rice that a terrible attack was coming, and, on Kiriakou's account, lied to by CIA director George Tenet about al-Qaeda operatives already inside the United States.

condoleezza-rice.title: "When did you become a fascist?"
condoleezza-rice.summary: The exchange John Kiriakou recalls with a former intern of his, a Yale sophomore he had supervised in Bahrain in the mid-1990s who resurfaced ten years later as a Pentagon under-secretariat for intelligence hire, briefing the CIA on Iraq. Walking him to his car after the briefing, Kiriakou asked *"Michael, when did you become a fascist?"* and got the answer he uses to date the neoconservative capture of the Bush administration, *"We're in charge now. We're in charge and Saddam Hussein's going to die."*

congressional-intelligence-oversight.title: Church Committee
congressional-intelligence-oversight.summary: U.S. Senate investigative committee operating in 1975–1976 that examined domestic intelligence abuses by the CIA, FBI, and NSA; per John Kiriakou, the Church Committee — alongside the concurrent Pike Committee in the House — was the last genuine moment of legislative oversight over the intelligence community, born of a national consensus that government had gone dangerously off course. Its work led to the creation of the permanent Senate Select Committee on Intelligence, which Kiriakou says ceased to function as real oversight roughly seven years after its founding.

congressional-intelligence-oversight.title: The encounter at the Greek ambassador's residence
congressional-intelligence-oversight.summary: An exchange John Kiriakou describes from a dinner a few weeks after his 2015 release from prison, in which Senator Ron Wyden — then vice chairman of the Senate Intelligence Committee — welcomed him home, was told Kiriakou had expected him to speak up, and answered that it had taken everything he had simply to keep his own security clearance. Kiriakou offers it as evidence that the intelligence oversight committees are afraid of the agencies they oversee.

congressional-intelligence-oversight.title: Mujahedin-e Khalq (MEK)
congressional-intelligence-oversight.summary: Iranian opposition group that John Kiriakou describes as 'a quasi-communist cult' and a former U.S.-designated terrorist organization. Founded by a husband-and-wife team in the 1960s and based in northeastern Iraq, the MEK launched cross-border terrorist attacks into Iran and, per Kiriakou, attempted to murder the American ambassador and the senior U.S. general in Iran — carrying out anti-American attacks for decades. After Saddam Hussein expelled them they relocated to Paris; current leader Maryam Rajavi is widely believed to have killed or had killed her vanished husband to take over. In 2009 the MEK hired high-powered Washington lobbyists (from Howard Dean to Rudy Giuliani) to get off the terrorism list, and Kiriakou says it is now funded by Israel and used as assassins-for-hire in Tehran.

congressional-intelligence-oversight.title: The approvals required to kill Assange
congressional-intelligence-oversight.summary: John Kiriakou's reading of the 2021 Yahoo News report on CIA plans to abduct or assassinate Julian Assange — that an operation of that kind requires three separate approvals, from the Justice Department's Office of Legal Counsel, from the government of the target's own Five Eyes country, and from the congressional oversight committees — and his conclusion that if the planning went as far as reported, all three were given.

congressional-intelligence-oversight.title: The Capitol switchboard
congressional-intelligence-oversight.summary: John Kiriakou's advice, drawn from years as a congressional staffer, on how ordinary constituents actually move members of Congress — that the House will act on a single letter, that the Senate needs ten or twenty calls to put an issue on a senator's agenda, and that the Capitol operator will identify a caller's own representative for them.

congressional-intelligence-oversight.title: Anthony Fauci
congressional-intelligence-oversight.summary: American physician and public-health official whose pardon John Kiriakou condemned as "unacceptable" in a May 2026 Fox News appearance. Kiriakou''s objection is partly personal: his cousin George was, he says, the second person in Ohio to die of COVID, in very early 2020. Kiriakou confined himself to the pardon and to his own family''s loss, and made no claim of his own about the origin of the virus.

consortium-news.title: John Kiriakou
consortium-news.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

consortium-news.title: Julian Assange
consortium-news.summary: Kiriakou — a 15-year friend and former WikiLeaks board member — on why Assange is a publisher owed a journalist's immunity, and a political prisoner.

consortium-news.title: Ray McGovern
consortium-news.summary: Former senior CIA analyst turned antiwar dissident, and one of John Kiriakou's closest friends — "like a brother to me." Kiriakou began working at the CIA on the Monday after the Friday McGovern retired in January 1990, so the two never overlapped inside; they became comrades in the whistleblower world instead. McGovern coined the "MICIMATT" framing Kiriakou often borrows, went into Putin's office with Oliver Stone for a 40-minute meeting, and — per Kiriakou — believes 9/11 was a conspiracy, a view Kiriakou affectionately notes is far from his own.

consortium-news.title: CovertAction Magazine
consortium-news.summary: The muckraking outlet "exposing covert action since 1978" — and one of John Kiriakou's three long-running syndicated column homes, alongside Consortium News and ScheerPost. Kiriakou joined its podcast arm, the CovertAction Bulletin, appearing on panels with Peter Dale Scott and Pepe Escobar, and jokes that the Pentagon's browser-plugin credibility warnings — red check marks against outlets like CovertAction — are the surest sign it's worth reading.

consortium-news.title: Kiriakou on influencing Trump
consortium-news.summary: John Kiriakou's 2019 account of how to move Donald Trump on a policy question — that the president is malleable but needs to hear the same thing from three different people he respects, illustrated with an episode in which Rand Paul mentioned Kiriakou to Trump two weeks after an aide had, and Trump remembered the earlier mention. Kiriakou used the theory to argue that a pardon for Julian Assange was reachable.

consortium-news.title: Kiriakou's morning reading list
consortium-news.summary: The specific news diet John Kiriakou reads before he opens his mouth to speak, an ideologically deliberate spread across American mainstream, American right, British mainstream, Israeli press, Arab press, and independent alt-media, framed by him as the analyst's guard against believing the outlets you agree with.

consulting-for-royal-families.title: Signing with CAA
consulting-for-royal-families.summary: The representation John Kiriakou says followed the 2026 virality of his podcast clips: a contract with the Creative Artists Agency covering books, film, consulting and licensing, and a run of advertising approaches including one from the maker of the spectacle frames he already wore.

consulting-for-royal-families.title: Gulf security bargain
consulting-for-royal-families.summary: The decades-old arrangement — traced by John Kiriakou to FDR and the Saudi king, and originally British — under which Gulf Arab monarchies host U.S. bases and sell oil in dollars in exchange for American protection; a bargain Kiriakou says collapsed when those bases failed to shield them during the war on Iran.

consulting-for-royal-families.title: Iranian suicide drones
consulting-for-royal-families.summary: John Kiriakou''s description of the weapon he expected to define Iran''s side of the 2026 war: one-way drones built inside Iran from Iranian parts, in large numbers, costing five to ten thousand dollars each, with explosives strapped on and flown remotely into a target. He treats them as the reason an aircraft carrier can no longer defend itself, the reason air defence fails on arithmetic rather than on technology, and the reason the Gulf states are reassessing the value of American bases.

consulting-for-royal-families.title: Kiriakou cameo practice
consulting-for-royal-families.summary: John Kiriakou's post-2026 use of the Cameo personalised-video service — running at roughly 25 to 30 hours a week, some 900 messages in the month of March 2026 alone, nearly 2,000 messages in total by July 2026 — that he says has produced three cases in which the person receiving the video message afterwards told him he had talked them out of committing suicide, including a 15-year-old bulimic girl to whom Kiriakou gave his personal phone number.

consulting-for-royal-families.title: The underlying sadness
consulting-for-royal-families.summary: The change several people have independently reported to John Kiriakou about himself since his prosecution — an underlying sadness that was not there before — which he says he does not see in himself, considering himself a happy and well-adjusted person.

consulting-for-royal-families.title: The Tiffany stationery letter
consulting-for-royal-families.summary: The deliberately expensive note John Kiriakou wrote to his first wife on Tiffany & Co. stationery, telling her he was halving her child support on the advice of counsel — a tactic suggested by his divorce lawyer to force her to file, and which worked the next day.

consulting-job-entrapment-offers.title: Kiriakou's legal counteroffensive
consulting-job-entrapment-offers.summary: John Kiriakou's announcement in February 2021 that after thirteen years of being reactive and responsive to his detractors he intended to start going after people, having connected with Harvard and Georgetown law professors — a plan he described without giving detail, saying only that things were turning around.

consulting-job-entrapment-offers.title: Phone microphone ad targeting
consulting-job-entrapment-offers.summary: John Kiriakou's account of a spoken telephone conversation about concealed carry permits being followed, five minutes later, by a Facebook feed in which every single advertisement was for a concealed carry class — offered as evidence for his claim that the platforms go further than they admit and listen when the phone is turned off.

consulting-job-entrapment-offers.title: Generals in national security posts
consulting-job-entrapment-offers.summary: John Kiriakou''s blanket objection to putting retired generals in charge of the CIA, the Office of the Director of National Intelligence, the Defense Department or the National Security Council, resting on a single argument about how officers reach flag rank: generals became generals by saying ''yes sir'', and what a president needs is somebody who can tell him why an idea is terrible.

consulting-job-entrapment-offers.title: Heather Kiriakou
consulting-job-entrapment-offers.summary: John Kiriakou's wife, a senior CIA analyst who — in his account — was one of the best analysts in the entire intelligence community and who lost her job at the agency for no reason other than being married to him. She sat off camera at his December 2007 ABC News interview and told him afterwards that he had said nothing classified.

consulting-job-entrapment-offers.title: ''Joe Bidenopoulos''
consulting-job-entrapment-offers.summary: The nickname John Kiriakou says Joe Biden carries in the Greek-American community — a reputation for being so pro-Greek-American that he is called Joe Bidenopoulos — which Kiriakou hoped in 2023 might give him a connection worth trying in his pursuit of a presidential pardon.

consulting-job-entrapment-offers.title: The Pineapple Militia case
consulting-job-entrapment-offers.summary: The Miami FBI entrapment prosecution in which, per John Kiriakou's July 2026 testimony as a defense expert witness by video from Athens, federal agents recruited a homeless, mentally ill Muslim man living in an alley behind a restaurant into a fictitious militia they called the "pineapple militia," proposed targets he had never proposed, refused four of his refusals to join, wrote a plot to bomb the New York Stock Exchange, built the bomb themselves, and arrested him when they handed it to him. Kiriakou uses the case as the canonical example of what he says are the 99 per cent of FBI terrorism cases that are fabricated.

contra-rebels.title: CIA Drug Facilitation
contra-rebels.summary: Per John Kiriakou, the CIA''s reported involvement in facilitating the arrival of cocaine into the United States during the era that became the crack epidemic, and his own firsthand discovery — as a Senate Foreign Relations Committee investigator — that under American military control Afghanistan produced 93% of the world''s heroin. A DEA contact told him the report would never be published because ''we want Iran and Russia to be addicted to heroin. It weakens their societies.'' Kiriakou draws a direct parallel to the current fentanyl crisis: China is doing to the US what the US did to Iran and Russia.

contra-rebels.title: Adnan Khashoggi
contra-rebels.summary: Saudi arms dealer and Iran-Contra middleman whom John Kiriakou says was mentioned 'all the time' at the CIA — in pointed contrast to Jeffrey Epstein, whose name he never once heard there.

contra-rebels.title: Kill the Messenger (Gary Webb)
contra-rebels.summary: The 2014 film about journalist Gary Webb, on which John Kiriakou served as script advisor; when Kiriakou was arrested in January 2012, the FBI seized his electronics, including a draft of the unclassified Hollywood script, and stamped every page "top secret" despite Kiriakou having no role in writing it.

contra-rebels.title: Iran-Contra
contra-rebels.summary: The mid-1980s scandal in which the Reagan administration secretly sold weapons to Iran and diverted the proceeds — laundered through Cyprus — to fund the Contra rebels in Nicaragua. Per John Kiriakou, Iran-Contra marks the precise end of what he calls the ''golden age'' of congressional intelligence oversight: the roughly 1975–1982 window opened by the Church and Pike Committees, when ''serious people, heavyweights'' actually held the CIA accountable. After Iran-Contra, he says, the oversight committees reverted to being ''cheerleaders'' for the agency — a posture that has held ever since.

contra-rebels.title: Dark Alliance
contra-rebels.summary: Gary Webb's seven-part San Jose Mercury News investigation reporting that cocaine reaching Los Angeles and fuelling the crack epidemic had travelled through Nicaragua with the CIA's knowledge. John Kiriakou's account stresses what Webb did and did not claim — that the agency turned a blind eye rather than ran the operation — and that three separate federal investigations later found his reporting correct.

contra-rebels.title: Domino theory
contra-rebels.summary: The Cold War doctrine, described by John Kiriakou as Ronald Reagan's organising obsession in Central America, holding that if one country there fell to communism the rest would fall in sequence up to the American border — the stated rationale for backing the Contra rebels against the Sandinistas.

cook-the-recidivist.title: Civil confinement
cook-the-recidivist.summary: The policy John Kiriakou proposed from inside FCI Loretto — moving sex offenders to a secure location on prison grounds after their sentences end rather than releasing them — an argument that drew public criticism and which he defends with the case of a prisoner named Cook.

cook-the-recidivist.title: FCI Loretto
cook-the-recidivist.summary: U.S. Federal Correctional Institution in Loretto, Pennsylvania; the low-medium-security prison at which John Kiriakou served 23 months of a 30-month sentence following his 2013 Espionage Act–era plea deal; the originally ordered "minimum security work camp" placement was countermanded — per Kiriakou, on Brennan's direct intervention — to place him in the actual prison alongside the general population.

cook-the-recidivist.title: Federal prison security levels
cook-the-recidivist.summary: The ladder of federal custody as John Kiriakou describes it — penitentiary, medium, low and minimum-security camp — the transfer rules that let long-sentence prisoners descend it, and why that placed dangerous men inside the low-security prison where he served his sentence.

cook-the-recidivist.title: The black box
cook-the-recidivist.summary: The restraint apparatus in which John Kiriakou was moved from FCI Loretto to an outside medical appointment — handcuffs, leg irons, a waist chain and a steel box locked over the cuffs so the lock could not be picked — and the form he refused to sign because it required him to call everybody sir.

cook-the-recidivist.title: Legal mail
cook-the-recidivist.summary: The privileged correspondence category John Kiriakou used to smuggle the Letters from Loretto and the manuscript of his book out of prison — addressed to his attorney Jesselyn Radack and marked legal mail, which staff were forbidden to open.

cook-the-recidivist.title: Depression in prison
cook-the-recidivist.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the condition he says everybody inside has, and the three-part regime he set against it — eating right, exercising daily and finding a distraction — which in his own case meant more than a hundred books, 7,000 letters and a book written in longhand.

cori-bush.title: AIPAC
cori-bush.summary: The American Israel Public Affairs Committee — the U.S. political organization that, in John Kiriakou's framing, ought to be registered as a foreign-lobbying entity but is not, and that wields decisive electoral power against U.S. elected officials who express support for Palestinian human rights.

cori-bush.title: Jamaal Bowman
cori-bush.summary: Former U.S. Representative from New York; cited by John Kiriakou alongside Cori Bush as the second documented case of AIPAC successfully primarying an incumbent House member for criticizing Israeli conduct in the Gaza war.

cori-bush.title: Josh Shapiro
cori-bush.summary: Governor of Pennsylvania; veteran of the Israel Defense Forces, in which he served during his late-teen kibbutz year before returning to U.S. citizenship; cited by John Kiriakou as the principal example of the loyalty question raised by American elected officials who have served the Israeli state — a disqualification Kiriakou states in absolute terms, and one he judges to have ended Shapiro's national prospects.

cori-bush.title: Abdul El-Sayed
cori-bush.summary: Physician and Democratic Socialists of America-backed candidate in Michigan's 2026 Democratic Senate primary. John Kiriakou, who discloses a $100 donation to the campaign, presents him as the test case for whether the electability argument still works for establishment Democrats.

cori-bush.title: AIPAC and foreign-agent registration
cori-bush.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that AIPAC is the only organization of its kind exempt from registering under the Foreign Agents Registration Act — set against his own experience around 2008, when a contract worth five or six thousand dollars to write four op-eds praising the Abu Dhabi Chamber of Commerce obliged him to register as a foreign agent.

cori-bush.title: BDS movement
cori-bush.summary: The Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions movement against Israel; John Kiriakou notes that some 40 U.S. states now have anti-BDS laws that can require a speaker at a publicly funded university to sign a pledge of support for Israel — which he refuses to do.

corkscrew-landings-in-afghanistan.title: The booby-trapped Christmas cards
corkscrew-landings-in-afghanistan.summary: Among the devices al-Qaeda left behind in positions it was forced to evacuate in Afghanistan, John Kiriakou describes a detonator laid flat inside a Christmas card, so that opening the card would take the reader''s hands off.

corkscrew-landings-in-afghanistan.title: The Dublin compensation
corkscrew-landings-in-afghanistan.summary: The night John Kiriakou spent in Dublin at an airline's expense after a mechanical fault in Madrid cost him his connection — a four-star hotel, an expedited check-in, a shuttle bus and half his fare refunded into his checking account six weeks later — offered as the standard American passengers do not get.

corkscrew-landings-in-afghanistan.title: Abu Zubaydah as a sounding board
corkscrew-landings-in-afghanistan.summary: The second, longer phase of Abu Zubaydah''s usefulness to the CIA, described by John Kiriakou in his December 2007 ABC News interview: once the prisoner had given up what he knew about current operations, his value shifted from threat reporting to analysis, with case officers reading him the names of men arrested in European capitals and asking whether the operations attributed to them made sense.

corkscrew-landings-in-afghanistan.title: "You were the first person that ever asked me about my children"
corkscrew-landings-in-afghanistan.summary: The answer John Kiriakou says he received when he asked a mid-level al-Qaeda member he had recruited in Pakistan why he had allowed the recruitment to happen: that in five years of detention Kiriakou had been the first person to ask about his children.

corkscrew-landings-in-afghanistan.title: Bigger than the Russian embassy
corkscrew-landings-in-afghanistan.summary: Why American embassies in small, strategically unimportant countries are enormous: the answer John Kiriakou says he was given by a station chief on one of his first CIA trips — that the building had to be bigger than the Soviet one across town. He describes American embassies in Africa as "absolutely gigantic" for that reason alone, and calls the US embassy in Cairo an enormous facility matched by an equally enormous Russian one.

corkscrew-landings-in-afghanistan.title: CIA operational psychologists
corkscrew-landings-in-afghanistan.summary: The branch of the CIA's psychological staff that John Kiriakou says he worked with directly as a case officer — not the analysts who profile foreign leaders, but the clinicians who vet a prospective recruit for insanity or invention, and advise an officer on exactly how hard a source can be pushed before he breaks.

corporate-competitive-intelligence.title: Deloitte Consulting Career
corporate-competitive-intelligence.summary: John Kiriakou's post-CIA career at Deloitte Consulting (2004–2008), covering two corporate acquisitions he says he drove — India Tiger Analysis and, in effect, Bering Point — and ending in his effective firing weeks before his ABC News whistleblower interview aired.

corporate-competitive-intelligence.title: Brian Ross
corporate-competitive-intelligence.summary: American investigative journalist and seven-time Emmy Award winner who was a prominent reporter at ABC News when, in December 2007, he conducted the on-camera interview with John Kiriakou that produced the first public confirmation by a U.S. official that the CIA waterboarded prisoners. Per Kiriakou, Ross called him out of the blue with the assertion that a source said Kiriakou had personally tortured Abu Zubaydah; Kiriakou's decision to give the interview anyway — driven by the conclusion that 'Brian Ross's source is at the White House and they're going to pin this on me' — became the pivot point of his entire post-CIA life.

corporate-competitive-intelligence.title: Counterterrorism Center
corporate-competitive-intelligence.summary: The CIA's Counterterrorism Center (CTC) — the unit where John Kiriakou spent the defining years of his operational career. He joined in the late 1990s as the only officer in the entire CIA fluent in both Greek and Arabic, served as chief of counterintelligence in the bin Laden unit, watched the Center swell from a few hundred employees to nearly 2,000 by September 12, 2001, and it was to CTC that he walked back down in May 2002 to refuse the torture program — the moment, he says, the CIA began to turn on him.

corporate-competitive-intelligence.title: Abu Zubaydah
corporate-competitive-intelligence.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

corporate-competitive-intelligence.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
corporate-competitive-intelligence.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

corporate-competitive-intelligence.title: Dasht-i-Leili massacre
corporate-competitive-intelligence.summary: Late-November 2001 mass suffocation of approximately 2,000 surrendered Taliban prisoners in unventilated shipping containers in the Afghan desert; the prisoners' surrender was negotiated by the CIA via the Northern Alliance, the transport order was issued by the CIA, and the operation was overseen by Northern Alliance warlord Abdul Rashid Dostum; John Kiriakou in 2009 as Senate Foreign Relations Committee investigator attempted to reopen the case under a 2008 Obama campaign promise; the CIA's classified response was, per Kiriakou, "go fuck yourself."

corporate-whistleblower-protections.title: Mark MacGann
corporate-whistleblower-protections.summary: The Uber whistleblower whose case John Kiriakou presented on his own programme: a 52-year-old Irishman who ran the company''s lobbying across Europe, the Middle East and Africa from 2014 to 2016, and who later handed 124,000 pages of internal documents covering 2013 to 2017 to the Guardian. Kiriakou''s account turns on one point — that the opportunity Uber marketed to low-income drivers was never what it claimed, and that the company''s leadership knew it from the beginning.

corporate-whistleblower-protections.title: The UPMC whistleblower case
corporate-whistleblower-protections.summary: A False Claims Act suit against neurosurgeons at the University of Pittsburgh Medical Center, alleging inflated operation counts and needlessly complex procedures. John Kiriakou — a Pittsburgh native — argues the charge is not merely fraud but deliberate endangerment of patients for profit, calls the False Claims Act 'the RICO statute of health care', and says the story deserved national coverage it never got.

corporate-whistleblower-protections.title: The Ukraine call whistleblower
corporate-whistleblower-protections.summary: The intelligence officer whose complaint triggered Donald Trump's first impeachment, and whom John Kiriakou declines to accept as a whistleblower at all — not on partisan grounds but on procedural ones. The complaint went to the Justice Department rather than the oversight committees, and its prose, he says, is lawyers' prose rather than the uniform CIA analytic style every analyst is trained into. He is nonetheless emphatic that naming the man was indefensible.

corporate-whistleblower-protections.title: Chelsea Manning
corporate-whistleblower-protections.summary: Former U.S. Army intelligence analyst who provided WikiLeaks its 2010 trove of military and diplomatic documents. Per John Kiriakou, Manning meets the legal definition of whistleblower for exposing war crimes, was a torture victim of prolonged solitary confinement with forced nudity, and was sentenced to 35 years in prison before Barack Obama commuted — not pardoned — her sentence. Kiriakou says Manning later refused a grand jury's offer of immunity and chose renewed jail time rather than testify against Julian Assange.

corporate-whistleblower-protections.title: Daniel Hale
corporate-whistleblower-protections.summary: Per John Kiriakou, drone whistleblower Daniel Hale — an NSA contractor and drone targeting analyst who exposed an 80% civilian death rate in the U.S. drone program, was ordered to fire on two young girls his superior called "goats," and was sentenced to 45 months (of which Kiriakou says he actually served about 18) despite prosecutors seeking nine to eleven years.

corporate-whistleblower-protections.title: The OPCW Douma investigation
corporate-whistleblower-protections.summary: The chemical weapons inquiry into the alleged 2018 attack in Douma, Syria, which John Kiriakou describes as falsified rather than merely disputed: fifteen investigators objected that their analysis had been taken out of context or fabricated outright, and the false version was then used to reach a political conclusion. He credits WikiLeaks with being the only reason any of it is public — and notes that major American shows carried on repeating the original story anyway.

cory-booker.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
cory-booker.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

cory-booker.title: Democratic silence on the Iran war
cory-booker.summary: John Kiriakou's observation that the only front-facing critics of the 2026 Iran war came from the isolationist right, while Democrats said nothing. He attributes the silence to fear of an AIPAC-funded primary challenge, and singles out Senator Cory Booker as the illustration.

cory-booker.title: Jonathan Pollard
cory-booker.summary: U.S. Navy civilian intelligence analyst convicted in 1985 of spying for Israel; the canonical proven case of Israeli espionage against the United States; cited by John Kiriakou in his 2024 Piers Morgan debate with a former Mossad director who denied any Israeli spying on the U.S.

cory-booker.title: The AIPAC "Holy Land" trip offer
cory-booker.summary: An approach John Kiriakou says he received within days of becoming chief investigator of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee: two AIPAC representatives offered him an all-expenses-paid trip to what they called the Holy Land, never using the word Israel, and told him it was cleared by the Senate ethics committee. He declined; colleagues of his went. He pairs the story with his account of AIPAC staff stationed in congressional offices, while insisting the practice is not unique to them.

cory-booker.title: Restraint Camp
cory-booker.summary: A term for foreign-policy conservatives who favor ending forever wars and regime-change interventions; not attributable to Kiriakou in the corpus.

cory-booker.title: The 189 undeclared officers
cory-booker.summary: A figure John Kiriakou attributes to the CIA''s director of security, given to his intake class on his first day at the agency in January 1990: against two declared Israeli intelligence officers at the embassy in Washington, the FBI counted at least 189 undeclared ones operating across the United States. He pairs it with the fact that Israeli liaison officers were barred from CIA headquarters.

cost-of-the-2026-iran-war.title: Strikes on US bases in the 2026 Iran war
cost-of-the-2026-iran-war.summary: John Kiriakou's assessment of the damage Iranian retaliation did to the American basing network across the Middle East during the 2026 war — including the loss of Incirlik air base in Turkey — and of the resupply problem that followed, with matériel routed through European and Indian ports. His verdict is that none of it was unforeseeable; Iran had announced it in advance.

cost-of-the-2026-iran-war.title: The hundred-million-a-day briefing
cost-of-the-2026-iran-war.summary: A story John Kiriakou tells from his time as a CIA analyst during the Gulf War: the president''s morning briefer returned to the office and reported that the president had been shocked speechless on being told the United States was spending one hundred million dollars a day in the Gulf.

cost-of-the-2026-iran-war.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
cost-of-the-2026-iran-war.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

cost-of-the-2026-iran-war.title: Donald Trump
cost-of-the-2026-iran-war.summary: 45th and 47th U.S. president. Per John Kiriakou, a man genuinely convinced he was doing right by bombing Iran, "duped" by the same Netanyahu nuclear bluff Obama once rejected — and, at the same time, the most blindly pro-Israel president in history, an admirer of autocrats who has never once criticized Vladimir Putin, and prone to gestures — from the Gulf of America to a since-abandoned "Department of War" rename — that test the edges of his actual authority.

cost-of-the-2026-iran-war.title: The obliteration claim
cost-of-the-2026-iran-war.summary: Donald Trump's statement that the Iranian nuclear programme had been "obliterated", and John Kiriakou's reading of it. Kiriakou offers three possibilities — the president lied, was tricked, or did not understand what had been achieved — and notes the claim's incompatibility with the later justification that Iran was days away from a weapon.

cost-of-the-2026-iran-war.title: Russian refusal of US mediation
cost-of-the-2026-iran-war.summary: The Russian announcement during the 2026 Iran war that it would no longer take part in Ukraine settlement talks led by the United States, on the grounds that Washington had negotiated with Iran and attacked it mid-negotiation. John Kiriakou's assessment was that the reasoning was correct.

counterterrorism-center.title: Mort Halperin
counterterrorism-center.summary: Former Assistant Secretary of State, Assistant Secretary of Defense, and senior director of the National Security Council; author of the law John Kiriakou was convicted of violating (the Intelligence Identities Protection Act); wrote to President Obama stating that this is not why he wrote the law and that Kiriakou should be pardoned.

counterterrorism-center.title: Twenty-five al-Qaeda members
counterterrorism-center.summary: The Senate Foreign Relations Committee study John Kiriakou cites as finding that by the end of 2001 there were twenty-five active al-Qaeda members still in Afghanistan — the basis for his claim that the group was finished as a fighting force by Christmas.

counterterrorism-center.title: Joseph Wilson
counterterrorism-center.summary: Former U.S. Ambassador to Niger and former Deputy Chief of Mission in Baghdad; husband of covert CIA officer Valerie Plame; in 2003 traveled to Niger at CIA request to investigate the Bush administration's claim that Iraq had attempted to purchase yellowcake uranium for a nuclear weapon, found no such Iraqi approach had occurred, and published a New York Times op-ed debunking the claim — triggering the administration's retaliatory outing of his wife.

counterterrorism-center.title: Mohamedou Ould Slahi
counterterrorism-center.summary: Mauritanian citizen, medical student in Germany at the time of his 2001 detention; held at Guantánamo Bay for fourteen years on the basis of one phone call from his cousin asking him to relay news of a family death to a second cousin who was in al-Qaeda; identified by John Kiriakou as one of the most morally significant figures of the post-9/11 period; subject of the film The Mauritanian; became a personal friend of Kiriakou's after both men were released.

counterterrorism-center.title: National Intelligence Council
counterterrorism-center.summary: Body housed at the CIA comprising the most senior analysts drawn from across the entire intelligence community. Its officers — National Intelligence Officers (NIOs) — hold positions at the Senior Intelligence Service level and are responsible for long-range strategic analysis on specific portfolio areas, as well as the production of National Intelligence Estimates. Per John Kiriakou, learning that the NIO for Warning had held the same job for forty-two years and just received a waiver to stay until seventy was the moment he first believed in the existence of the deep state.

counterterrorism-center.title: Taliban embassy raid
counterterrorism-center.summary: John Kiriakou's account of raiding the last functioning Taliban embassy, in Peshawar, in the middle of the night after 9/11 — a raid that turned up phone bills showing dozens of calls to U.S. cities that stopped on September 10 and resumed on September 16, evidence of possible sleeper cells the FBI never translated.

counterterrorist-driving.title: The bomb course
counterterrorist-driving.summary: The week-long CIA explosives course at a facility in another state, where John Kiriakou learned to build a Molotov cocktail, then a detonator rig, then an ammonium nitrate bomb — his final exam, which put a van's transmission three hundred yards into the woods.

counterterrorist-driving.title: Kiriakou's titanium knee
counterterrorist-driving.summary: The injury John Kiriakou took crashing a junkyard car through a roadblock in CIA training — his seat tore free of the floor and his knees hit the dashboard — which sixteen years later was diagnosed as spontaneous osteonecrosis and cost him the joint.

counterterrorist-driving.title: The shooting house
counterterrorist-driving.summary: The live-fire decision course at the Farm where a trainee has about three quarters of a second to decide whether the figure at the window is a gunman or a woman holding a baby — and where John Kiriakou says he never missed, which he connects to his own account of the temperament the CIA selects for.

counterterrorist-driving.title: The Advanced Counterterrorism Operations course
