counterterrorist-driving.summary: The six-week CIA course for which John Kiriakou says he was one of only about a dozen officers in the entire agency selected — and which he finished, as he puts it, just in time for 9/11.

counterterrorist-driving.title: The operations course graduation
counterterrorist-driving.summary: The end of CIA field training: a graduation ceremony at which the whole class wore full disguises for the photograph, and a certificate that is itself classified and therefore cannot be displayed — it stays in the officer''s personnel file.

counterterrorist-driving.title: The El Salvador hotel drill
counterterrorist-driving.summary: A night exercise at the Farm in which trainees sat alone in a mock flea-bag hotel room in El Salvador, were visited by two men announcing housekeeping, and were shot with paint pellets. All eight failed, and the lesson John Kiriakou drew from it he says he never forgot.

cover-position.title: Amaryllis Fox Kennedy
cover-position.summary: Former CIA non-official-cover officer who worked under commercial cover as an international art consultant, later a Trump campaign manager and nominee for deputy CIA director. Per John Kiriakou, Senator Tom Cotton threatened to filibuster her appointment; the president responded by naming her deputy national security adviser instead — a job Kiriakou considers more powerful, since the CIA director reports to the national security adviser.

cover-position.title: Operational vehicles
cover-position.summary: The cars John Kiriakou used in the field. In the Middle East they were whatever the rental company supplied — usually a Toyota — on the reasoning that anonymity was the point; in Athens, where the threat justified it, he was issued a factory-built, level-four armoured BMW 540 that broke down constantly.

cover-position.title: Andrew Bustamante
cover-position.summary: Former CIA officer who sells CIA-style training online; John Kiriakou identifies him as the lone critic of his work hosting a show on a Russian network, and argues Bustamante's training business — open to anyone who pays — is the more problematic of the two.

cover-position.title: Surveillance detection route
cover-position.summary: Tradecraft technique used by intelligence officers and assets to determine whether they are being followed before, during, or after an operational meeting

cover-position.title: The botched pitch
cover-position.summary: The one operation John Kiriakou describes as a failure of his career: a two-year development of a terrorist working under journalist cover, brought to the point of a recruitment pitch and destroyed at the table when his station chief seized the meeting and threatened the target instead of pitching him. The target fled screaming for police, the host government''s deputy prime minister complained to the American ambassador, and the man later described the encounter to a third intelligence service as an approach by "two caricatures of CIA men."

cover-position.title: Commercial off-the-shelf tradecraft
cover-position.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of how much CIA field equipment is simply bought rather than built. He describes the pen recorder arriving while he was in Pakistan and early GPS units in Athens being repurposed to map surveillance detection routes, and states the underlying economics: buying existing technology is far cheaper than developing it from scratch.

cover-stop.title: John Kiriakou
cover-stop.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

cover-stop.title: Chief of station
cover-stop.summary: The CIA's senior officer in a foreign country — appointed by the CIA director alone, outranking the ambassador's intelligence equities in practice, and in John Kiriakou's account the figure who sets the moral temperature of a station, from the officer who handed him his first counterterrorism assignment to the one who walks into a minister's office fifteen minutes after the human rights officer has left.

cover-stop.title: Intelligence peddlers
cover-stop.summary: John Kiriakou''s breakdown of who actually walks into an American embassy offering information: the overwhelming majority are fabricators or probes, a few per cent are peddlers selling the same nugget to five embassies in a month, and about one per cent are the real thing.

cover-stop.title: Kiriakou on wine
cover-stop.summary: John Kiriakou's long-standing interest in wine — a subscription to Wine Spectator running a quarter of a century, a climate-controlled cellar built into his house, an eye that has twice caught a host passing off a cheap bottle as something better, and a professional life in which wine served in turn as cover story, surveillance-detection errand, recruitment currency and diplomatic catastrophe.

cover-stop.title: Andrew Warren
cover-stop.summary: Former CIA officer and station chief who, per John Kiriakou, was protected and lavishly funded by his supervisor "Mary Margaret," then convicted of raping 23 women — videotaping every attack — before a post-prison religious conversion and further sexual assault convictions.

cover-stop.title: Spies of Arlington National Cemetery
cover-stop.summary: On the Walk With History podcast, John Kiriakou — author of Remains of the Day: A Definitive Guide to Washington D.C.''s Historic Cemeteries — toured Arlington National Cemetery and told personal and historical stories about the intelligence figures buried there, including OSS founder William Donovan, deputy CIA director Vernon Walters, codebreakers William and Elizabeth Friedman, slain station chiefs Richard Welch and William Buckley, U-2 pilot Francis Gary Powers, and Mike Spann, the first CIA officer killed after 9/11.

covert-action-program.title: No plan for day two
covert-action-program.summary: The lesson John Kiriakou says he learned early at the CIA: the United States is very good at overthrowing governments and has no idea what to do afterwards. The planning is all about day one. He lists Iraq, Afghanistan, Libya, Syria, Sudan and Somalia as the record, and gives three reasons the same officials keep repeating the mistake.

covert-action-program.title: Maduro Capture
covert-action-program.summary: CIA-driven nighttime operation in which a team of Delta Force commandos entered Venezuela and removed Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro and his wife from their beds. Per John Kiriakou, the key enabling intelligence — per a New York Times account he cited — came from a CIA asset inside Maduro''s presidential palace who called when Maduro went to sleep: ''He''s sound asleep. If you''re going to do it, do it now.'' At least eighty people were killed in the operation, including approximately thirty-five Cubans. Kiriakou compares it to the 1989 capture of Manuel Noriega, in which US forces blasted death metal at the Vatican Embassy until Noriega was asked to leave.

covert-action-program.title: María Corina Machado
covert-action-program.summary: The Venezuelan opposition leader and Nobel Peace Prize laureate whom John Kiriakou rates no higher than Juan Guaidó: a figure in a permanently divided right-wing opposition who commands no armies and no troops. He reads the prize itself as part of the propaganda campaign against Maduro, and expects that if Maduro leaves the next leader of Venezuela will be a senior military officer rather than a civilian politician.

covert-action-program.title: Venezuela regime change (2026)
covert-action-program.summary: John Kiriakou''s assessment of the American operation that removed Venezuela''s president — a clear violation of international law, since none of the three recognised grounds for one state attacking another applied, but not a violation of US law, which since 1985 has expressly permitted special forces to cross borders and seize people for trial. His reluctant conclusion at the time: "as much as I hate admitting it, this regime change seems to be working right now."

covert-action-program.title: Manuel Noriega
covert-action-program.summary: Panamanian dictator and one of the most notorious drug traffickers in the Western Hemisphere who, John Kiriakou notes, was a paid CIA source for decades before being driven from the Vatican embassy in Panama City by U.S. forces blasting death metal and captured in the 1989 invasion.

covert-action-program.title: Watching naval movements
covert-action-program.summary: One of the first lessons John Kiriakou says he learned at the CIA: to read American military intentions, watch naval movements — one carrier strike group means business, two means war. He used it to correctly predict the 2026 strike on Iran days in advance.

covertaction-magazine.title: Julian Assange
covertaction-magazine.summary: Kiriakou — a 15-year friend and former WikiLeaks board member — on why Assange is a publisher owed a journalist's immunity, and a political prisoner.

covertaction-magazine.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
covertaction-magazine.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

covertaction-magazine.title: Consortium News
covertaction-magazine.summary: Independent investigative news outlet John Kiriakou has written for since at least 2017, founded by Polk Award-winning journalist Robert Parry, who broke major stories on Iran-Contra. Kiriakou's columns there have covered John Bolton's exit, the entrapment of Maria Butina, his own first tour in Saudi Arabia and the 2019 Ukraine-call whistleblower. He says PayPal permanently shuttered the outlet's account and briefly seized its funds before backing down under public pressure, while still refusing to reinstate it.

covertaction-magazine.title: Spies of Arlington National Cemetery
covertaction-magazine.summary: On the Walk With History podcast, John Kiriakou — author of Remains of the Day: A Definitive Guide to Washington D.C.''s Historic Cemeteries — toured Arlington National Cemetery and told personal and historical stories about the intelligence figures buried there, including OSS founder William Donovan, deputy CIA director Vernon Walters, codebreakers William and Elizabeth Friedman, slain station chiefs Richard Welch and William Buckley, U-2 pilot Francis Gary Powers, and Mike Spann, the first CIA officer killed after 9/11.

covertaction-magazine.title: Federal plea coercion
covertaction-magazine.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that the federal justice system coerces guilty pleas by stacking charges and winning 98.2% of its cases — so that even innocent defendants take deals, as he did, told by his own attorney that the system is 'not about justice; it's about mitigating damage.'

covertaction-magazine.title: Kiriakou's morning reading list
covertaction-magazine.summary: The specific news diet John Kiriakou reads before he opens his mouth to speak, an ideologically deliberate spread across American mainstream, American right, British mainstream, Israeli press, Arab press, and independent alt-media, framed by him as the analyst's guard against believing the outlets you agree with.

craig-murray.title: The voice vote on the Epstein files
craig-murray.summary: John Kiriakou's account of how the Senate passed the Epstein files release without a roll call — a voice vote he says Chuck Schumer requested to save the majority leader, leaving no written record of how anyone voted and allowing every senator but one House holdout to claim they had stood up to the pedophiles.

craig-murray.title: The can of ravioli
craig-murray.summary: John Kiriakou's confession that he eats tinned ravioli cold, straight from the can, and refuses on principle to pay more than ninety-nine cents for it — used, when the price reached $2.49, as his own answer to the polling finding that Americans care about prices more than anything else.

craig-murray.title: The colour-coded badges
craig-murray.summary: The CIA's badge system as John Kiriakou describes it — blue for the top secret compartments everyone in the building holds, green for contractors, yellow for the language instructors cleared only to secret, red for the man in the cafeteria doughnut shop and the woman who vacuums at night — and the lettered suffixes that were dropped once the letters themselves gave the game away.

craig-murray.title: The culture of secrecy and the truth
craig-murray.summary: Asked how he decided what counted as true inside an institution built on secrecy, and whether that changed after he left, John Kiriakou answered no twice — because in his account everyone knows the difference in their gut, and the job is to stop the culture of secrecy from bastardising what you already know.

craig-murray.title: The family that spans the spectrum
craig-murray.summary: John Kiriakou''s Greek relations, offered as a political cross-section: his grandmother''s first cousin sat on the politburo of the Communist Party of Greece, a close cousin was elected governor of the Dodecanese for the Conservatives, he has everybody in between — and all of them, to his bafflement, love the American ambassador.

craig-murray.title: The Scooter Libby deposition
craig-murray.summary: The 2006 or 2007 session at which John Kiriakou, appearing as a witness in the Scooter Libby case, mentioned that the only conversation he had witnessed between two senior CIA officers concerned a covert action programme — and the agency's general counsel jumped up and stopped him mid-sentence, because an officer may not say the words at all.

critical-analytic-thinking.title: Lie Detection
critical-analytic-thinking.summary: Per John Kiriakou, both a subject he addresses in his book The CIA Insider's Guide to Lying and Lie Detection and a practical skill he describes using throughout his career. Physical tells include gaze direction (down to conceal, up to construct), fidgeting, and throat-clearing; structural tells — losing the thread mid-conversation and self-contradiction — are more reliable, because the truth is stable while a lie requires maintenance and eventually collapses under its own complexity.

critical-analytic-thinking.title: Doing Time Like a Spy
critical-analytic-thinking.summary: Prison memoir by John Kiriakou, full title Doing Time Like a Spy: How the CIA Taught Me to Survive and Thrive in Prison; winner of two literary awards and reissued in a second edition by Simon and Schuster.

critical-analytic-thinking.title: Asset acquisition cycle
critical-analytic-thinking.summary: The four-step process — spot, assess, develop, recruit — taught as the first lesson of CIA case officer training

critical-analytic-thinking.title: Diesel Therapy
critical-analytic-thinking.summary: Per John Kiriakou, a punitive practice within the U.S. Federal Bureau of Prisons in which an inmate is placed into indefinite transit — moved continuously from facility to facility — for up to six months, with no access to phone, email, or pen and paper, and listed on the BOP website only as 'in transit' with no destination. Kiriakou described it as the one threat at FCI Loretto that actually frightened him.

critical-analytic-thinking.title: FCI Loretto
critical-analytic-thinking.summary: U.S. Federal Correctional Institution in Loretto, Pennsylvania; the low-medium-security prison at which John Kiriakou served 23 months of a 30-month sentence following his 2013 Espionage Act–era plea deal; the originally ordered "minimum security work camp" placement was countermanded — per Kiriakou, on Brennan's direct intervention — to place him in the actual prison alongside the general population.

critical-analytic-thinking.title: John Kiriakou
critical-analytic-thinking.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

crypto-ag.title: Over-classification
crypto-ag.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of why the American government classifies far more than it can ever review: not conspiracy but incentive. At lesser agencies a classification stamp is a status marker — it puts you in the in-crowd and above the colleague who lacks access — and at the CIA everything carries a stamp by default. His complaint about press coverage of classified-document scandals is that it never reaches the underlying question of why the documents were secret at all.

crypto-ag.title: Julian Assange
crypto-ag.summary: Kiriakou — a 15-year friend and former WikiLeaks board member — on why Assange is a publisher owed a journalist's immunity, and a political prisoner.

crypto-ag.title: Encryption before the key
crypto-ag.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of where encryption actually fails, offered against John McAfee''s claim that no communication can be private. Kiriakou defers to the technologists he knows — Edward Snowden, Bill Binney, Thomas Drake and Kirk Wiebe — who tell him sufficiently sophisticated encryption does work. The exposure is upstream of the cipher: if an agency can reach your machine as you type, before you hit the encryption key, the encryption never gets a chance. He nonetheless encrypts everything he sends, and rejects the argument that encryption is what lets attacks through.

crypto-ag.title: Hillary Clinton
crypto-ag.summary: Former U.S. Secretary of State and 2016 presidential candidate; John Kiriakou describes her as arguably the most neoconservative candidate Democrats could have nominated, more militarist even than her husband, and credits her — separately — with correctly describing Iran as a military dictatorship run by the IRGC rather than a genuine theocracy.

crypto-ag.title: Bernie Sanders
crypto-ag.summary: United States senator from Vermont. John Kiriakou, who watched him daily from the Senate Foreign Relations Committee staff, describes Sanders holding open breakfast in the Senate cafeteria for anyone who walked in — insisting only that they call him "Bernie" — and names him the one 2016 candidate willing to talk about shrinking the military.

crypto-ag.title: Bill Barr
crypto-ag.summary: Per Sean Davis, speaking on the same Megyn Kelly panel as Kiriakou, the attorney general under the first Trump administration, seen as competent but not fully loyal, whose relationship with Trump ended in a "breakup."

ctc-line-of-duty-deaths.title: Surveillance detection route
ctc-line-of-duty-deaths.summary: Tradecraft technique used by intelligence officers and assets to determine whether they are being followed before, during, or after an operational meeting

ctc-line-of-duty-deaths.title: Abu Zubaydah
ctc-line-of-duty-deaths.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

ctc-line-of-duty-deaths.title: Advanced Counterterrorism Operations
ctc-line-of-duty-deaths.summary: The six-week specialist course John Kiriakou flew back from Athens to attend roughly eighteen months before 9/11 as one of fourteen officers selected worldwide — high-threat operations, technical collection, and a driving syllabus built around crashing through roadblocks that left the class with whiplash. By accident of timing it meant a trained cadre was ready to deploy the moment the attacks came.

ctc-line-of-duty-deaths.title: Anwar al-Awlaki
ctc-line-of-duty-deaths.summary: American-born al-Qaeda propagandist; in 1993 the imam of the Falls Church, Virginia mosque visited by John Kiriakou's CIA Arabic-language class on a field trip; in 2001 the cleric at whose mosque the 9/11 hijackers prayed the night before the attacks; killed by U.S. drone strike in Yemen in approximately 2011.

ctc-line-of-duty-deaths.title: Asset acquisition cycle
ctc-line-of-duty-deaths.summary: The four-step process — spot, assess, develop, recruit — taught as the first lesson of CIA case officer training

ctc-line-of-duty-deaths.title: Double-Agent Capture
ctc-line-of-duty-deaths.summary: Clandestine operation in which an intelligence service, having identified a recruited agent as working simultaneously for a hostile service, arranges a controlled final meeting to apprehend the agent before the agent can carry out orders — which may include killing the handler. Per John Kiriakou, he ran one such operation in the Middle East in the early 2000s after an NSA analyst warned him that his agent had just been ordered to shoot him in the next meeting.

cu-chi-tunnels.title: Kiriakou's visit to Vietnam (2026)
cu-chi-tunnels.summary: A week in Vietnam in August 2026, taken around a paid speech to Australian investment bankers and shaped by four cousins who fought there. John Kiriakou broadcast an episode from Ho Chi Minh City and used the trip to argue that commerce, not force, is what turns a country pro-American.

cu-chi-tunnels.title: The Saigon CIA station photograph
cu-chi-tunnels.summary: The Pulitzer-winning image of evacuees climbing a ladder to a helicopter during the fall of Saigon in 1975. John Kiriakou, who talked his way onto the roof in 2026, points out that the building most Americans take for the embassy was in fact an apartment block that secretly housed the CIA's Saigon station.

cu-chi-tunnels.title: The McDonald's theory of regime change
cu-chi-tunnels.summary: John Kiriakou''s argument, drawn from Vietnam and Cuba, that commerce accomplishes what force cannot: to turn a country pro-Western, open a McDonald''s rather than bomb it.

cu-chi-tunnels.title: 2026 Iran war
cu-chi-tunnels.summary: The open-ended American and Israeli war against Iran that John Kiriakou tracked week by week on his own show — a conflict he says was sold as three weeks, ran into its fifth month, achieved every decapitation objective it set, and continued anyway. His grade for it is a D, and his forecast is a Truth Social post declaring victory while nothing changes.

cu-chi-tunnels.title: Abraham Accords
cu-chi-tunnels.summary: The Trump-brokered normalization deals between Israel and Gulf Arab states — in John Kiriakou's judgment "a terrible idea in the first place," a great victory for Israel and the Gulf Arabs that was "a punch in the throat to the Palestinians." He argues the Accords are how Trump meant to "solve the Middle East in a day" — by screwing the Palestinians — that Hamas read the abandonment correctly, that October 7 shattered the project, and that reviving the Accords (Saudis in, victory declared, Nobel collected) remains the organizing goal of Trump's regional policy.

cu-chi-tunnels.title: The rooftop double agent
cu-chi-tunnels.summary: A 2001 operation in which John Kiriakou flew out monthly to impersonate a station chief in meetings with a recruited double agent, and, after the hostile service ordered the agent to kill him, frightened the man on a hotel roof rather than confronting him.

cuba-protests-2021.title: Daniel Ortega
cuba-protests-2021.summary: The president of Nicaragua, and the case John Kiriakou contrasts with Cuba: where he read the 2021 Cuban protests as a test run, he said Nicaragua''s circumstances — a social security shortfall, a rise in the price of bread, and eight opposition party leaders arrested and imprisoned before an election — amounted to grounds for a real uprising.

cuba-protests-2021.title: Haiti
cuba-protests-2021.summary: A country John Kiriakou studied for the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, where he found that the seven largest merchant families — the families that run the entire Haitian economy — are white. He treats Haiti's poverty as manufactured rather than accidental, and its unrest as a story the American press declines to cover.

cuba-protests-2021.title: Caleb Maupin
cuba-protests-2021.summary: American journalist and Marxist commentator, a recurring guest on John Kiriakou's radio programme The Backstory, whom Kiriakou introduces as one of the best-informed people out there. Kiriakou endorses his analysis of automation and capitalism while noting he does not agree with all of it, and proposed putting him on air opposite a libertarian economist.

cuba-protests-2021.title: "Only two and a half more years"
cuba-protests-2021.summary: The consolation John Kiriakou says he takes from the second Trump term's remaining span, and his reasons for doubting that a Democratic successor would undo any of it. He points to Joe Biden's failure to reverse the first term, including the never-restored relationship with Cuba.

cuba-protests-2021.title: Sanctions Effectiveness
cuba-protests-2021.summary: John Kiriakou's assessment that U.S. sanctions have been so overused against disfavored countries that nations like China now route around them entirely, and that sanctions work only when reserved for the worst actors and imposed in concert with other countries — citing apartheid South Africa as a success and Cuba/Venezuela as failures that instead entrench nationalist narratives.

cuba-protests-2021.title: The Backstory
cuba-protests-2021.summary: The daily Radio Sputnik programme John Kiriakou co-hosted with Lee Stranahan, carried on terrestrial radio in the Washington area as well as online. It was the successor to his earlier show Loud and Clear with Brian Becker, and he described its format as two men with a beer talking about the day.

cuban-double-agents.title: F-35 avionics dispute with Israel
cuban-double-agents.summary: John Kiriakou's account of how Israel demanded F-35 fighters without the deliberately degraded avionics the U.S. installs on export models — and, refused, allegedly worked through American defense contractors to steal the technology instead.

cuban-double-agents.title: MK-Ultra
cuban-double-agents.summary: The CIA's mid-twentieth-century umbrella program of mind-control, behavioral-modification, and biological-warfare experimentation, encompassing subprojects such as MK-Chickwit and MK-Seesaw; active 1952–1975; documented practices included LSD dosing of unwitting American citizens in CIA-rented brothels and the aerosolized release of pathogens into the San Francisco fog; 80% of the program's documentation was destroyed by the CIA in defiance of a 1975 preservation order from Senator Frank Church.

cuban-double-agents.title: Robert Hanssen
cuban-double-agents.summary: FBI counterintelligence chief and Soviet/Russian mole; framed CIA counterintelligence chief Brian Kelley as the source of compromised assets — leading the FBI to surveil Kelly for a year and a half and threaten his family with the death penalty — before Hanssen himself was identified as the actual traitor.

cuban-double-agents.title: Israel's counterintelligence threat ranking
cuban-double-agents.summary: John Kiriakou's repeated point that the American intelligence community formally ranks Israel a critical counterintelligence threat — the same tier as North Korea, China, Russia, Iran and Cuba — specifically for spying on and infiltrating the US government, and that policy has responded by giving Israel more access rather than less.

cuban-double-agents.title: "He''s been ours since the ''70s"
cuban-double-agents.summary: An episode John Kiriakou uses to convey the scale of CIA penetration of foreign political classes: spotting a former prime minister at a diplomatic cocktail party, rushing back to the embassy to file for a name trace and vulnerability assessment before anyone else could approach him, and receiving a same-day instruction to cease and desist because the man had already been an agency asset for decades.

cuban-double-agents.title: Andres Serrano
cuban-double-agents.summary: American artist; in the 1980s the creator of Piss Christ — a beaker of urine containing an inverted crucifix — which so enraged President Ronald Reagan that he cut off funding to the National Endowment for the Arts. Per John Kiriakou, also the photographer of a torture-chamber series at Tate Modern, London, in which one panel is a photograph of Kiriakou next to a panel of a U.S. military torturer.

curtailment-cables.title: The bowl of dates
curtailment-cables.summary: The detail John Kiriakou uses to compress his argument about interrogation: that the intelligence the CIA''s contractors reported as the fruit of waterboarding had in fact been obtained by an FBI agent who offered Abu Zubaydah a bowl of dates.

curtailment-cables.title: The rogue officer remark
curtailment-cables.summary: The answer President George W. Bush shouted to a reporter on his way to the helicopter — that if there was torture, it was the work of a rogue CIA officer — which John Kiriakou has said convinced him he was about to be made the scapegoat, and which led him to accept Brian Ross's interview offer.

curtailment-cables.title: The declination letter
curtailment-cables.summary: The letter the Justice Department sent John Kiriakou's attorneys in December 2008 declining to prosecute him, on the grounds that the torture allegations were already public through human rights organizations and that it is illegal to classify a crime — and the celebration dinner that was followed three weeks later by Barack Obama's inauguration.

curtailment-cables.title: Arabic and Greek
curtailment-cables.summary: The qualification John Kiriakou says opened the door to his transfer from CIA analysis to operations: a post in Athens wanted Greek or Arabic, and he had both — by most of his tellings the only officer in the agency who did. The chief who hired him gave the reason in one sentence: it is easier and cheaper to take a linguist and teach him operations than the other way round. The pairing also became a detection tool, since the language nobody speaks in Pakistan is Arabic.

curtailment-cables.title: Five and a half years on the table
curtailment-cables.summary: John Kiriakou''s stated regret about his own whistleblowing — not that he did it, but that he waited: he learned of the torture programme in May 2002, it began on 2 August 2002, and he said nothing until 11 December 2007.

curtailment-cables.title: The oath in the auditorium
curtailment-cables.summary: The scene John Kiriakou returns to when asked what set him on the path to blowing the whistle: standing in the CIA''s auditorium on his first day with three hundred other new hires, right hand in the air, swearing to uphold the Constitution against all enemies foreign and domestic — and his later suspicion that he may have been the only person in the room who meant it.

curveball.title: Ahmed Chalabi
curveball.summary: Iraqi exile and founder of the Iraqi National Congress; per John Kiriakou, a Shia-Kurdish con man who looted Petra Bank in Jordan of $36 million in the 1980s, was sentenced to death in absentia, was pardoned at CIA request, then pocketed $6 million in CIA seed funding for the INC and bought a Mayfair house in cash; later resurrected by Dick Cheney to feed the Pentagon fabricated WMD intelligence used to justify the 2003 invasion of Iraq.

curveball.title: Valerie Plame
curveball.summary: Covert CIA case officer whose identity was publicly outed by the Bush administration in retaliation for her husband, former U.S. ambassador to Niger Joseph Wilson, publishing a New York Times op-ed debunking the administration's claim that Iraq had attempted to purchase yellowcake uranium from Niger. Per John Kiriakou, Plame's CIA career ended on the day her cover was blown — she could never travel overseas under cover again; no one was prosecuted for the leak.

curveball.title: Saddam Hussein
curveball.summary: President of Iraq from 1979 until the 2003 U.S. invasion; subject of John Kiriakou's CIA portfolio from January 1990 onward, in which capacity Kiriakou became, at age 25, "Saddam Hussein's intelligence community biographer" and the analyst who briefed President George H. W. Bush in the Oval Office on the morning of the 1990 invasion of Kuwait.

curveball.title: Joseph Wilson
curveball.summary: Former U.S. Ambassador to Niger and former Deputy Chief of Mission in Baghdad; husband of covert CIA officer Valerie Plame; in 2003 traveled to Niger at CIA request to investigate the Bush administration's claim that Iraq had attempted to purchase yellowcake uranium for a nuclear weapon, found no such Iraqi approach had occurred, and published a New York Times op-ed debunking the claim — triggering the administration's retaliatory outing of his wife.

curveball.title: George W. Bush
curveball.summary: 43rd President of the United States. In John Kiriakou's telling, Bush signed the August 1, 2002 executive order that authorized the CIA torture program, spent years telling the public "we don't torture," and — days after Kiriakou's 2007 ABC interview — blamed torture on "a rogue CIA officer" while walking from the White House South Portico to Marine One, a moment Kiriakou instantly read as the White House preparing to pin the program on him. Bush also ordered the FBI removed from Abu Zubaydah's black site, flew the bin Laden family out of the country after 9/11, and loosened the assassination ban of Executive Order 12333.

curveball.title: John Kiriakou
curveball.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

custody-standoff.title: Mary Jane Stevens
custody-standoff.summary: The lawyer who represented John Kiriakou through his custody dispute — who told him to wait for Monday and go to court, was ignored, and then got the assurance from a hostile police chief that let him walk into the hearing without being arrested.

custody-standoff.title: Cofer Black
custody-standoff.summary: Former head of the CIA Counterterrorism Center during and immediately after the September 11 attacks; principal architect of the agency's paramilitary turn on September 12, 2001; later Vice President of Blackwater under Erik Prince.

custody-standoff.title: Cofer Black's warning to the liaison class
custody-standoff.summary: The briefing Cofer Black gave to a class of visiting foreign liaison officers weeks before 11 September 2001 — code words about a honey salesman, a great football match and an enormous wedding — and the private exchange afterwards in which he told John Kiriakou he had been deadly serious.

custody-standoff.title: The Foreign Relations volume and the sources still alive
custody-standoff.summary: The errand that put John Kiriakou and Cofer Black in a car to the White House on the morning of 11 September 2001: three declassified cables due to be printed in a State Department history volume named CIA sources who were still living — and an obscure law requiring the United States to resettle any source it outs.

custody-standoff.title: John Kiriakou
custody-standoff.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

custody-standoff.title: The Condoleezza Rice meeting
custody-standoff.summary: The nine o'clock White House appointment John Kiriakou and Cofer Black never kept on the morning of 11 September 2001. The Government Printing Office was about to issue a volume of declassified Greece-Turkey-Cyprus cables in an edition of five or ten copies; three of them named CIA sources who were still alive, and an obscure statute obliges the government to offer citizenship and resettlement to any recruited source it outs. The two men were going to ask the National Security Advisor to quietly pull three cables nobody would miss. The car was at the East entrance at 8.15.

cypriot-billionaire-investigation.title: The Oman oil lease
cypriot-billionaire-investigation.summary: A private-intelligence assignment in which an oil company that had leased a field on Oman's border with Yemen for ninety-nine years discovered al-Qaeda controlled the ground, and sent John Kiriakou to Muscat to ask whether the Omani government would clear them out.

cypriot-billionaire-investigation.title: The Romanian silver mine
cypriot-billionaire-investigation.summary: The private-intelligence assignment John Kiriakou uses to explain what commercial analysis actually buys: a mining client wanted to know who would win a Romanian municipal election, because a silver deposit lay under a village that would have to be destroyed to reach it.

cypriot-billionaire-investigation.title: Abraxas Corporation
cypriot-billionaire-investigation.summary: The private intelligence company founded in the 1990s by retired CIA operations officers as a tax pass-through and a place to smoke cigars and tell stories — which, after 9/11, made its founders, in John Kiriakou's phrase, Mega Millions rich.

cypriot-billionaire-investigation.title: David Boies
cypriot-billionaire-investigation.summary: The American litigator John Kiriakou has appeared alongside on Piers Morgan's programme, and whose observation about Alan Dershowitz — that he was not merely Epstein's attorney but his publicist — Kiriakou treats as the key distinction in the case.

cypriot-billionaire-investigation.title: The Brüno shoot in Jordan
cypriot-billionaire-investigation.summary: The scene John Kiriakou set up for Sacha Baron Cohen in Amman — four retired Palestinian militants, found in the Damascus telephone book at the Library of Congress, shown hardcore pornography by a character they believed to be an Austrian documentary journalist — which produced no reaction at all and was cut from the film entirely.

cypriot-billionaire-investigation.title: Black Cube
cypriot-billionaire-investigation.summary: Israeli [private intelligence firm](/wiki/private-intelligence) staffed by former Mossad personnel; reportedly used by attorney David Boies in the Jeffrey Epstein litigation; named by John Kiriakou as a representative of the no-compunction operating posture characteristic of Israeli private and public intelligence.

cyprus-green-line.title: Kiriakou's Cypriot ancestry
cyprus-green-line.summary: The DNA result showing John Kiriakou to be 24 per cent Cypriot — his largest single ancestry — which corrected a family belief that the line came from Crete and coincided with an invitation to address a Cypriot diaspora conference.

cyprus-green-line.title: John Kerry
cyprus-green-line.summary: U.S. Senator from Massachusetts; chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee during John Kiriakou's 2009 service as the committee's senior investigator; subsequently U.S. Secretary of State; characterized by Kiriakou as a coward who buckled under CIA pressure on the Dasht-i-Leili reopening and as personally fixated on his perceived theft of the Secretary of State position by Hillary Clinton; the famously thrown medals were duplicates purchased at the post exchange.

cyprus-green-line.title: British Bases in Cyprus
cyprus-green-line.summary: British sovereign bases in Cyprus host a large American contingent. Kiriakou, a quarter Cypriot, on the bases as evacuation hub, missile target, and suspected nuclear site — and on the 46-year US weapons embargo almost no American knows about.

cyprus-green-line.title: Origin of the Kiriakou name
cyprus-green-line.summary: The Kiriakou surname originates in a clerical error at a Rhodes courthouse, where John Kiriakou's great-great-grandfather, arrested for stealing a potato while starving, gave a patronymic that was written down as his family name and never corrected.

cyprus-green-line.title: The false volunteer
cyprus-green-line.summary: A walk-in at an American embassy who claimed access to a high-priority target, was placed under surveillance and found to be a restaurant dishwasher, and whom John Kiriakou deliberately intimidated into never approaching an American embassy again.

cyprus-green-line.title: Kiriakou's podcast breakthrough
cyprus-green-line.summary: The sequence by which John Kiriakou went from saying yes to every podcast request, including from teenagers, to appearances with the largest hosts in the world — a rise he attributes to three friends' shows triggering an algorithm in October 2024.

damascus-consulate-strike.title: Iran's 2024 drone retaliation
damascus-consulate-strike.summary: John Kiriakou's account of Iran's telegraphed 2024 drone strike on Israel — hundreds of slow drones, launched with advance warning to the U.S. and Jordan, nearly all shot down, which he reads as a controlled show of force and an intelligence victory that exposed the Iron Dome.

damascus-consulate-strike.title: Iran Nuclear Assessment
damascus-consulate-strike.summary: Per John Kiriakou's assessment, the US–Israeli military campaign against Iran was a war of choice driven by Israeli political pressure rather than genuine intelligence indicating an Iranian nuclear weapons threat. The CIA produced two National Intelligence Estimates concluding Iran had no nuclear weapons program; Supreme Leader Ayatollah Khamenei issued a fatwa in the 1980s forbidding such a program. The U.S. went to war anyway, in Kiriakou's view, after President Trump replaced the Joint Chiefs of Staff with officers willing to accept Israeli intelligence and proceed.

damascus-consulate-strike.title: The Arab states and the Gaza war
damascus-consulate-strike.summary: John Kiriakou's country-by-country reading of how the Arab governments positioned themselves after October 2023 — the Gulf states ranked by their fear of Iran, Jordan caught between its border and its population, Egypt sealing Rafah to prevent a repeat of earlier refugee flows — and his conclusion that every one of them is calculating damage to itself first and the Palestinians second.

damascus-consulate-strike.title: China as economic threat
damascus-consulate-strike.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that China is the real threat to the West not militarily — it has one aircraft carrier to America's two dozen and rarely invades — but economically, buying friends worldwide while the U.S. spends a trillion dollars a year on weapons.

damascus-consulate-strike.title: The dispersal of the Iranian program
damascus-consulate-strike.summary: John Kiriakou's assessment that neither the Israeli nor the American strikes had any lasting effect on Iran's nuclear programme, because the facilities are spread across the country and mostly deep underground — and his reading of Iran's shrugging response as the best evidence that the bombing did not work.

damascus-consulate-strike.title: The Syria chemical attack correction
damascus-consulate-strike.summary: John Kiriakou's public retraction of what he wrote about the August 2013 chemical attack near Damascus. Asked about the passage in his book on Iran, he said he had written it before United Nations whistleblowers came forward to say they did not believe it was a Syrian government attack, and thanked the questioner for the chance to correct it.

daniel-domscheit-berg.title: Chaos Computer Club Wikileaks
daniel-domscheit-berg.summary: The Berlin hacker collective that shaped WikiLeaks' early years — and where a journalist first met Daniel Domscheit-Berg under a pseudonym.

daniel-domscheit-berg.title: Julian Assange
daniel-domscheit-berg.summary: Kiriakou — a 15-year friend and former WikiLeaks board member — on why Assange is a publisher owed a journalist's immunity, and a political prisoner.

daniel-domscheit-berg.title: Der Spiegel
daniel-domscheit-berg.summary: At a 2026 Berlin panel, a former Der Spiegel journalist said it took him years before he could call Julian Assange a publisher rather than an activist.

daniel-domscheit-berg.title: Wikileaks as a System
daniel-domscheit-berg.summary: Per John Kiriakou, WikiLeaks functions less as a single leader than as a durable system — one that protected whistleblowers, helped popularize the term "whistleblower" itself, was credited with contributing to the Arab Spring, weathered pressure to become a defanged NGO, and outlasted the political fallout of its 2010 cable releases (including, in Kiriakou's account, an unintended assist to Donald Trump's election).

daniel-domscheit-berg.title: CIA Car Hacking
daniel-domscheit-berg.summary: Kiriakou on the Vault 7 disclosure that the CIA can seize control of a moving car and stage the crash as a suicide or an accident — a capability he says is not limited to electric vehicles, whose only counter is the emergency brake, and which he treats as the clearest example of a leak that is a matter of life and death rather than embarrassment.

daniel-domscheit-berg.title: Ai Whistleblower Initiative
daniel-domscheit-berg.summary: The AI Whistleblower Initiative, working on legal protections for the wave of whistleblowers now coming out of the artificial-intelligence industry.

daniel-duggan.title: The solitary confinement precedents
daniel-duggan.summary: The legal argument John Kiriakou made repeatedly between 2020 and 2022 in defence of Julian Assange, and revived in 2025 for the Australian pilot Daniel Duggan — that no extradition to the United States can succeed once a court is asked to find that American solitary confinement is not torture, a proposition already contradicted by the United Nations, by the United States' own federal torture statute, and by a line of British and European rulings blocking extraditions on exactly that ground.

daniel-duggan.title: Eastern State Penitentiary
daniel-duggan.summary: The Philadelphia prison where, per John Kiriakou, solitary confinement was invented in 1829 — a neo-Gothic stone penitentiary of tiny cells arranged as spokes around a central guard post, each containing a bed, a chair, a table, a chamber pot and a Bible, on the theory that a man left alone with scripture would emerge a law-abiding Christian. What happened instead, Kiriakou says, is that everybody went insane — and the practice was kept anyway, because it worked as punishment.

daniel-duggan.title: Julian Assange
daniel-duggan.summary: Kiriakou — a 15-year friend and former WikiLeaks board member — on why Assange is a publisher owed a journalist's immunity, and a political prisoner.

daniel-duggan.title: Communications management unit
daniel-duggan.summary: The two restricted-contact units inside the American federal prison system, at Terre Haute and Marion; built for "the worst of the worst" but, in John Kiriakou's account, used to silence prisoners whose messages are inconvenient — and a practice he groups with solitary confinement as torture. He served part of his own sentence in a modified one.

daniel-duggan.title: Solitary confinement
daniel-duggan.summary: The prison isolation practice the United Nations calls a form of torture; John Kiriakou, drawing on his own ten days in a six-by-sixteen-foot cell, argues that jailing depressed prisoners like Daniel Hale in solitary 'for their own safety' is precisely what drives them to suicide.

daniel-duggan.title: FCI Loretto
daniel-duggan.summary: U.S. Federal Correctional Institution in Loretto, Pennsylvania; the low-medium-security prison at which John Kiriakou served 23 months of a 30-month sentence following his 2013 Espionage Act–era plea deal; the originally ordered "minimum security work camp" placement was countermanded — per Kiriakou, on Brennan's direct intervention — to place him in the actual prison alongside the general population.

daniel-ellsberg.title: Espionage Act
daniel-ellsberg.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

daniel-ellsberg.title: Julian Assange
daniel-ellsberg.summary: Kiriakou — a 15-year friend and former WikiLeaks board member — on why Assange is a publisher owed a journalist's immunity, and a political prisoner.

daniel-ellsberg.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
daniel-ellsberg.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

daniel-ellsberg.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
daniel-ellsberg.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

daniel-ellsberg.title: John Kiriakou
daniel-ellsberg.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

daniel-ellsberg.title: The twenty-seven cousins
daniel-ellsberg.summary: John Kiriakou has said Daniel Ellsberg was a hero in his family before he was six years old — because seven of his twenty-seven first cousins on his mother's side fought in Vietnam believing what they had been told, and it was Ellsberg who showed the family that all of it had been a lie.

daniel-hale.title: RDAP program
daniel-hale.summary: The Bureau of Prisons' Residential Drug and Alcohol Program, which can shave 12 to 18 months off a federal sentence; John Kiriakou repeatedly advises fellow whistleblowers that, combined with good behavior and a halfway house, it can turn a five-year sentence into as little as two and a half years.

daniel-hale.title: Leonard Peltier
daniel-hale.summary: The American Indian Movement prisoner John Kiriakou names when asked which cases deserve attention alongside Assange's — an old and ailing man whom he calls factually innocent, and whose continued imprisonment he offers as evidence that the system's incentives run only one way.

daniel-hale.title: The disappearance of Daniel Hale
daniel-hale.summary: John Kiriakou's account of losing touch with the drone whistleblower Daniel Hale after his release from prison — a brief reappearance on social media, a shut-down account a week later, and a circle of friends none of whom has heard from him since.

daniel-hale.title: The Intercept's exposed sources
daniel-hale.summary: John Kiriakou's charge that national security whistleblowers who take material to The Intercept end up in prison. He names Reality Winner and Terry Albury as sources whose identities the outlet exposed, says the same thing happened to Daniel Hale, and identifies the outlet's two national security reporters, Richard Esposito and Matthew Cole, as the journalists responsible for sending him to prison. His question is whether the pattern is incompetence or something worse.

daniel-hale.title: The MintPress prediction
daniel-hale.summary: The forecast John Kiriakou volunteers against himself — that asked in a post-election interview alongside Thomas Drake and Jesselyn Radack whether whistleblowers would fare better or worse under Donald Trump, he alone answered that nothing could be worse than Barack Obama, and was wrong.

daniel-hale.title: The roadblock strike
daniel-hale.summary: The drone strike Daniel Hale described at his own sentencing and that John Kiriakou retells as the reason Hale became a whistleblower: a car approaching a U.S. roadblock in Afghanistan, two girls aged six and nine visible inside, an order to fire given twice over Hale''s objection, and a father who afterwards hid his daughters'' bodies in a village dumpster for fear that special forces would take them.

daniel-ortega.title: The 2021 Cuba protests
daniel-ortega.summary: The July 2021 demonstrations in Cuba, which John Kiriakou declined to read as the beginning of a revolution. He called them a test run to gauge the government's reaction, objected that a New York Times line about Democrats treading lightly in Florida meant nothing anyone could act on, and noted that everything touching Cuba is too politically loaded in the United States to be discussed plainly.

daniel-ortega.title: Haiti
daniel-ortega.summary: A country John Kiriakou studied for the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, where he found that the seven largest merchant families — the families that run the entire Haitian economy — are white. He treats Haiti's poverty as manufactured rather than accidental, and its unrest as a story the American press declines to cover.

daniel-ortega.title: Caleb Maupin
daniel-ortega.summary: American journalist and Marxist commentator, a recurring guest on John Kiriakou's radio programme The Backstory, whom Kiriakou introduces as one of the best-informed people out there. Kiriakou endorses his analysis of automation and capitalism while noting he does not agree with all of it, and proposed putting him on air opposite a libertarian economist.

daniel-ortega.title: The Backstory
daniel-ortega.summary: The daily Radio Sputnik programme John Kiriakou co-hosted with Lee Stranahan, carried on terrestrial radio in the Washington area as well as online. It was the successor to his earlier show Loud and Clear with Brian Becker, and he described its format as two men with a beer talking about the day.

daniel-ortega.title: Sanctions Effectiveness
daniel-ortega.summary: John Kiriakou's assessment that U.S. sanctions have been so overused against disfavored countries that nations like China now route around them entirely, and that sanctions work only when reserved for the worst actors and imposed in concert with other countries — citing apartheid South Africa as a success and Cuba/Venezuela as failures that instead entrench nationalist narratives.

daniel-ortega.title: Iran under sanctions: daily life
daniel-ortega.summary: John Kiriakou's account of being talked out of his own assumptions about Iran by a close friend who travels there once or twice a year and eventually started filming ordinary life — leading him to conclude that a country with no American embassy, diplomatic presence or business presence since 1979 nonetheless lacks for nothing.

daniel-pearl.title: Khalid Sheikh Mohammed
daniel-pearl.summary: Mastermind of the September 11, 2001 attacks; identified to the CIA by Abu Zubaydah, in the course of FBI interrogator Ali Soufan's rapport-based debriefing at the black site, as the man behind the kunya "Mukhtar" the agency had been hunting since at least 1996 for the Bojinka plot; per Kiriakou's relay of his self-account, radicalized by news video of an Israeli soldier with his boot on the neck of a Palestinian woman.

daniel-pearl.title: Waterboarding
daniel-pearl.summary: Torture technique in which a prisoner is restrained on an inclined board with the head lower than the feet, a cloth placed over the face, and water poured continuously over it to simulate drowning. Per John Kiriakou, waterboarding was treated as a criminal act under U.S. and international law for decades before 2002 — including a post–World War II execution of Japanese soldiers who waterboarded American POWs, and a 1968 court-martial of a U.S. soldier photographed waterboarding a North Vietnamese prisoner — before the CIA reauthorized it after September 11. Abu Zubaydah was waterboarded 83 times; Khalid Sheikh Mohammed 187 times.

daniel-pearl.title: Tommy McHale
daniel-pearl.summary: Highly decorated Port Authority of New York and New Jersey detective who worked as a terrorist hunter alongside John Kiriakou in Islamabad, Pakistan after 9/11; a survivor of the 1993 World Trade Center bombing whose best friend died on 9/11.

daniel-pearl.title: Al-Julani
daniel-pearl.summary: The former al-Qaeda commander and, per John Kiriakou, co-founder of ISIS who was installed as president of Syria and received at the White House. Kiriakou''s initial reading was that no one moves from a ten-million-dollar American bounty to a state visit in months without being a long-term CIA asset — until a senior Turkish official told him over dinner that al-Julani was Turkey''s: ''We created him from nothing and we installed him in Syria.'' Kiriakou judged that version more plausible than his own.

daniel-pearl.title: The Stinger buyback
daniel-pearl.summary: The standing reward programme John Kiriakou administered at the American embassy in Islamabad — a hundred thousand dollars in cash, paid over the counter, for each Stinger missile the United States had given the mujahideen from 1986 and now wanted back before its forty-year shelf life ran out.

daniel-pearl.title: Bashar al-Assad
daniel-pearl.summary: President of Syria; John Kiriakou recounts warning Senator John Kerry to stop publicly calling Assad 'my dear friend' after a speech enraged Washington's Lebanese community, with Kerry citing motorcycle rides they had taken together to the Golan Heights.

dark-alliance.title: Contra rebels
dark-alliance.summary: The right-wing Nicaraguan insurgency armed by the Reagan administration against the Sandinista government. In John Kiriakou's account they were conservatives, right-wingers, in some cases fascists, and disgruntled military officers; they were split into a northern group the United States armed and a southern group that financed itself by selling cocaine — a distinction that became the pivot of the Gary Webb affair, and that Kiriakou uses to answer the CIA's standing denial that it had anything to do with the drug trade.

dark-alliance.title: Oscar Blandón
dark-alliance.summary: The senior Contra leader whom Gary Webb's reporting identified as running the cocaine operation that moved product from Nicaragua to Los Angeles, and one of two men named in the Dark Alliance series.

dark-alliance.title: Kill the Messenger (Gary Webb)
dark-alliance.summary: The 2014 film about journalist Gary Webb, on which John Kiriakou served as script advisor; when Kiriakou was arrested in January 2012, the FBI seized his electronics, including a draft of the unclassified Hollywood script, and stamped every page "top secret" despite Kiriakou having no role in writing it.

dark-alliance.title: CIA Drug Facilitation
dark-alliance.summary: Per John Kiriakou, the CIA''s reported involvement in facilitating the arrival of cocaine into the United States during the era that became the crack epidemic, and his own firsthand discovery — as a Senate Foreign Relations Committee investigator — that under American military control Afghanistan produced 93% of the world''s heroin. A DEA contact told him the report would never be published because ''we want Iran and Russia to be addicted to heroin. It weakens their societies.'' Kiriakou draws a direct parallel to the current fentanyl crisis: China is doing to the US what the US did to Iran and Russia.

dark-alliance.title: Domino theory
dark-alliance.summary: The Cold War doctrine, described by John Kiriakou as Ronald Reagan's organising obsession in Central America, holding that if one country there fell to communism the rest would fall in sequence up to the American border — the stated rationale for backing the Contra rebels against the Sandinistas.

dark-alliance.title: Walter Pincus
dark-alliance.summary: The Washington Post reporter who, in John Kiriakou's account of the Gary Webb affair, took the CIA's side of the cocaine story and put it on the paper's front page — wrong, and Kiriakou believes knowingly so.

darpa-lifelog.title: Abu Zubaydah
darpa-lifelog.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

darpa-lifelog.title: The CIA Insider's Guide to Surveillance and Surveillance Detection
darpa-lifelog.summary: Book by John Kiriakou drawing on his experience as a surveillance detection instructor at the CIA and as a private surveillance training consultant. The book covers the techniques used by intelligence professionals to identify whether they are being followed — including the four-phase surveillance detection route, concealment device placement and retrieval, and counter-surveillance strategy — adapted for use by corporate executives, journalists, and others who want to confirm whether they are being followed.

darpa-lifelog.title: Thomas Drake
darpa-lifelog.summary: NSA whistleblower; per John Kiriakou, the source for the statement that on the morning of September 11, 2001, NSA Director Mike Hayden told agency personnel NSA had been 'waiting for a 9/11' to implement the mass-electronic-surveillance program that NSA's founding charter forbids.

darpa-lifelog.title: Walk-in
darpa-lifelog.summary: In John Kiriakou's telling, someone who walks into an embassy offering information; 95% are lunatics or liars, some are 'intelligence peddlers' or hostile 'probes,' and about 1% are 'the real McCoy' — a framework he used to see through a supposed 'walk-in' tip during the Abu Zubaydah hunt. A genuine walk-in — a witness to a terrorist assassination — was later hypnotized by CIA psychologists in a London hotel room and read back a stolen van's license plate, verifying his account.

darpa-lifelog.title: Palantir Technologies
darpa-lifelog.summary: U.S. data-analytics and intelligence-software company; received its first $1.5 million in seed funding from the CIA's In-Q-Tel venture-capital arm around 2002; characterized by John Kiriakou as functionally inseparable from the CIA in 2025, drawing the majority of its revenue from agency contracts and operating across DARPA, NSA, and the broader U.S. national-security apparatus.

dasht-i-leili-massacre.title: General Abdul Rashid Dostum
dasht-i-leili-massacre.summary: Northern Alliance Afghan warlord; overseer of the November–December 2001 Dasht-i-Leili massacre; characterized by John Kiriakou as a serial defector between the Taliban and the Northern Alliance and as a psychopath.

dasht-i-leili-massacre.title: John Kiriakou
dasht-i-leili-massacre.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

dasht-i-leili-massacre.title: John Kerry
dasht-i-leili-massacre.summary: U.S. Senator from Massachusetts; chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee during John Kiriakou's 2009 service as the committee's senior investigator; subsequently U.S. Secretary of State; characterized by Kiriakou as a coward who buckled under CIA pressure on the Dasht-i-Leili reopening and as personally fixated on his perceived theft of the Secretary of State position by Hillary Clinton; the famously thrown medals were duplicates purchased at the post exchange.

dasht-i-leili-massacre.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
dasht-i-leili-massacre.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

dasht-i-leili-massacre.title: Qala-i-Jangi uprising
dasht-i-leili-massacre.summary: The late-November 2001 prisoner uprising at a fortress in northern Afghanistan during which CIA officer Mike Spann was killed; the event during which the American al-Qaeda figure John Walker Lindh was captured; among the first major firefights of the post-9/11 Afghan campaign.

dasht-i-leili-massacre.title: The State Department cover investigation
dasht-i-leili-massacre.summary: One of the inquiries John Kiriakou opened as senior investigator on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, on a reporter's tip that the CIA was placing some of its torturers under State Department cover in violation of the cover agreement between the two departments. He wrote to the State Department asking for clarification. Five or six weeks later a colleague told him a reply had come and had been classified above his clearance; asked what it said, the colleague summarised it as an obscenity. That was the end of the investigation.

dave-phillips.title: The shank planting incident
dave-phillips.summary: The episode at FCI Loretto in which Dave Phillips made two homemade weapons, planted them on a pedophile the group was feuding with and informed on him anonymously — a plan John Kiriakou refused to join, and which cost Phillips a transfer while leaving Kiriakou untouched.

dave-phillips.title: Seven thousand letters
dave-phillips.summary: The correspondence John Kiriakou conducted from FCI Loretto — 7,000 letters to 675 different people over 23 months, begun because of an unsolicited postcard of a rose that reached him four hours into his sentence.

dave-phillips.title: Spotting a CIA impostor
dave-phillips.summary: John Kiriakou's method for exposing people who falsely claim to have served in the CIA — a short sequence of questions about directorate, division and leadership whose correct answers, he says, cannot be guessed by anyone who was never inside.

dave-phillips.title: Sarge
dave-phillips.summary: The FCI Loretto correctional officer John Kiriakou named in a Letter from Loretto for swearing at him and trashing his cell — conduct he later learned was not merely a Bureau of Prisons infraction but a misdemeanour crime, and one of two offences he says the letter inadvertently exposed.

dave-phillips.title: Rule six: the body endures more than the brain says
dave-phillips.summary: The CIA maxim John Kiriakou carried into prison — that the human body can take much more punishment than the brain believes — which he applied first to being punched in the face and then, more importantly, to depression.

dave-phillips.title: The Second Chance Act
dave-phillips.summary: The resentencing law John Kiriakou read about in The New York Times inside FCI Loretto and used to win freedom for other prisoners — most notably Mark Lanzalotti, whose petition he wrote and who was released 17 years into a 30-year sentence.

david-boies.title: Jeffrey Epstein
david-boies.summary: Convicted sex offender; per John Kiriakou, was "an Israeli access agent" rather than a CIA asset, because the CIA collects foreign intelligence and Epstein's targets — Bill Clinton, Bill Gates, Prince Andrew — were not foreign. Kiriakou further holds that Epstein did die by suicide in federal custody, because in the Bureau of Prisons the cameras never work and the guards are always asleep.

david-boies.title: Alexander Acosta and the sweetheart deal
david-boies.summary: The US attorney who gave Jeffrey Epstein his 2006 non-prosecution agreement and later said he had been ordered to — a chain of command John Kiriakou traces upward to an attorney general famous for his powerlessness, and therefore to somebody above him whom nobody has ever named.

david-boies.title: Prince Andrew
david-boies.summary: British royal, now Andrew Mountbatten Windsor, named repeatedly by John Kiriakou as one of the un-recruitable principals whose access made Jeffrey Epstein valuable to a foreign intelligence service. Kiriakou has asked why Andrew was never charged over conduct with minors, reads his alleged provision of classified Ministry of Defence documents to Epstein as evidence of espionage rather than vanity — and expects him to face no criminal consequence at all, because the statute of limitations has run.

david-boies.title: The Epstein statute of limitations
david-boies.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that nobody in the United States will be prosecuted over the Jeffrey Epstein case because the limitation period on the sex offences has run — a lapse he says may itself have been part of the plan, which leaves victims with civil suits against the estate, leaves the men named to social ruin rather than trial, and leaves only an improbable continuing-conspiracy theory as a route to criminal charges.

david-boies.title: The Trilateral Commission
david-boies.summary: The body John Kiriakou says he used to dismiss as conspiracy-theory material until someone close to him attended one of its meetings and told him what was actually discussed there: arms deals — and at Davos, how to manage the global economy.

david-boies.title: Black Cube
david-boies.summary: Israeli [private intelligence firm](/wiki/private-intelligence) staffed by former Mossad personnel; reportedly used by attorney David Boies in the Jeffrey Epstein litigation; named by John Kiriakou as a representative of the no-compunction operating posture characteristic of Israeli private and public intelligence.

david-hicks.title: Julian Assange
david-hicks.summary: Kiriakou — a 15-year friend and former WikiLeaks board member — on why Assange is a publisher owed a journalist's immunity, and a political prisoner.

david-hicks.title: Kandahar
david-hicks.summary: The southern Afghan city and province that recurs across John Kiriakou's Afghanistan material — site of one of the two al-Qaeda training camps Abu Zubaydah founded, whose commanders were captured in the same March 2002 raids; the town Bill Clinton said he would have had to destroy, killing 300 innocents, to kill bin Laden in the 1990s; and a stop on Kiriakou's Senate-era heroin-poppy investigation, when the military helicoptered him down before refusing to let him walk the poppy fields.

david-hicks.title: Pakistan Station (2002)
david-hicks.summary: John Kiriakou's January 2002 arrival in Islamabad to become CIA chief of counterterrorism operations — a journey via London and Kuwait with lost luggage, a warning that steered him away from the soon-to-be-bombed Marriott, a skeleton counterterrorism branch of seven CIA retirees, and the raids that followed.

david-hicks.title: George Tenet
david-hicks.summary: Director of Central Intelligence from 1997 to 2004, spanning the September 11 attacks and the early enhanced-interrogation program; identified by John Kiriakou as John Brennan's institutional patron at the agency; the figure who ordered the Five Eyes intelligence services to "open the files" to each other in the early 2000s.

david-hicks.title: Guantánamo Bay detention camp
david-hicks.summary: Per John Kiriakou — as chief of counterterrorism operations in Pakistan after September 11, 2001 — the Guantanamo detention facility began as a temporary holding measure intended to last two to three weeks while the CIA and Justice Department determined which federal district court should try each prisoner, not as a long-term detention infrastructure. The Rawalpindi jail had reached capacity, Pakistani intelligence demanded the prisoners be removed, and CIA headquarters directed Kiriakou to load them onto a C-12 cargo plane and fly them to Cuba.

david-hicks.title: Senate Torture Report
david-hicks.summary: The December 2014 executive summary of the U.S. Senate Select Committee on Intelligence's study of the CIA's post-9/11 detention and interrogation program; the first public disclosure of techniques including rectal feeding with hummus, sexual assault with broomsticks, and prolonged sleep deprivation.

david-petraeus.title: Public safety factor
david-petraeus.summary: The Bureau of Prisons classification that barred Kiriakou from a minimum-security camp by rating him as dangerous as a murderer, applied over the objections of both his sentencing judge and the prosecutor who convicted him.

david-petraeus.title: The CIA–State Department cover agreement
david-petraeus.summary: The standing arrangement under which CIA officers serve abroad under State Department cover. As a senior investigator for the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, John Kiriakou was told the agency was misusing the agreement to place officers from the torture program under diplomatic cover so that publishing their names would expose journalists to the Intelligence Identities Protection Act. His written query, sent over Senator John Kerry''s signature, came back classified above his own clearance.

david-petraeus.title: The FBI raids on Kiriakou's home
david-petraeus.summary: Twenty-two agents, eight hours, a sledgehammer hole in the kitchen wall that is still there, potted plants emptied onto the floor and every piece of electronics removed — twice, and with no charge arising from either. John Kiriakou uses the raids as the ground for his flat description of the bureau as an outlaw organization.

david-petraeus.title: Slow-rolling the president
david-petraeus.summary: John Kiriakou's 2017 forecast that the CIA would not confront Donald Trump but outlast him — senior officers with twenty-five and thirty years in the building having already waited out several presidents — offered as the agency's characteristic response to a president it neither trusts nor is trusted by.

david-petraeus.title: The HardTalk interview
david-petraeus.summary: The first interview John Kiriakou gave after leaving prison, on the BBC programme he describes as hard-hitting and mean-spirited, in which a host pressing him to show remorse drew the formulation he has used ever since: it is not a crime to reveal a crime.

david-petraeus.title: The philosophy class
david-petraeus.summary: The introductory philosophy lecture at Miami University of Ohio in which John Kiriakou's own whistleblowing was set as the ethical dilemma, unknown to the professor with Kiriakou's son sitting in the room — the episode Kiriakou offers when asked how he survived losing his career, his pension and his marriage.

david-ransom.title: John Kiriakou
david-ransom.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

david-ransom.title: John Brennan
david-ransom.summary: Former Director of the CIA; characterized in KiriPedia's source corpus as the principal architect of the agency's enhanced interrogation program and as having plotted against an elected President

david-ransom.title: David Rockefeller in Bahrain
david-ransom.summary: Per John Kiriakou — economic officer at the American Embassy in Bahrain, 1994–1996, and control officer for a David Rockefeller visit — Rockefeller''s award from the US-Bahrain Banking Society was a cover stop. After three days of documented public appearances, Rockefeller flew on a military plane to Baghdad to deliver a secret message to Saddam Hussein: stop violating sanctions, or the United States would take military action. Kiriakou cites the trip as a textbook case of how public figures are used as deniable back-channel intermediaries.

david-ransom.title: Abu Zubaydah
david-ransom.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

david-ransom.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
david-ransom.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

david-ransom.title: Kiriakou on Christmas
david-ransom.summary: John Kiriakou's account of finding Christmas so depressing since his two divorces that he does not decorate or mark it at all — and of the year he replaced it by taking his children to every station on the New York City subway system in a single day.

david-rockefeller-bahrain.title: David Ransom
david-rockefeller-bahrain.summary: U.S. Ambassador to Bahrain during the period of John Kiriakou's posting there; characterized by Kiriakou as one of the finest people he worked for in his CIA career

david-rockefeller-bahrain.title: Thomas Drake
david-rockefeller-bahrain.summary: NSA whistleblower; per John Kiriakou, the source for the statement that on the morning of September 11, 2001, NSA Director Mike Hayden told agency personnel NSA had been 'waiting for a 9/11' to implement the mass-electronic-surveillance program that NSA's founding charter forbids.

david-rockefeller-bahrain.title: John Kiriakou
david-rockefeller-bahrain.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

david-rockefeller-bahrain.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
david-rockefeller-bahrain.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

david-rockefeller-bahrain.title: Gerald Bull
david-rockefeller-bahrain.summary: British inventor of the "big gun" — a barrel so large it had to be leaned against a mountain — first offered to Israel and rejected, then sold to Iraq under Saddam Hussein; assassinated by Mossad in Brussels once Iraqi engineers solved the cracking problem with a barrel-smoothing sleeve nicknamed "the condom," after which the Israelis also bombed the gun itself.

david-rockefeller-bahrain.title: Iran Nuclear Assessment
david-rockefeller-bahrain.summary: Per John Kiriakou's assessment, the US–Israeli military campaign against Iran was a war of choice driven by Israeli political pressure rather than genuine intelligence indicating an Iranian nuclear weapons threat. The CIA produced two National Intelligence Estimates concluding Iran had no nuclear weapons program; Supreme Leader Ayatollah Khamenei issued a fatwa in the 1980s forbidding such a program. The U.S. went to war anyway, in Kiriakou's view, after President Trump replaced the Joint Chiefs of Staff with officers willing to accept Israeli intelligence and proceed.

dead-drop-podcast.title: John Kiriakou's Briefing Room
dead-drop-podcast.summary: A twice-weekly news and commentary programme launched by John Kiriakou in July 2026, presented as analysis rather than partisan opinion, and distinct from his storytelling podcast Dead Drop.

dead-drop-podcast.title: President's Daily Brief
dead-drop-podcast.summary: Per John Kiriakou, the President's Daily Brief (PDB) is a roughly 16-page, top-secret intelligence document produced daily for the president, written in a uniform CIA house style, briefed each morning, and — in his account — used partly to gauge and flatter incoming presidents.

dead-drop-podcast.title: John Kiriakou
dead-drop-podcast.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

dead-drop-podcast.title: Death threats against Kiriakou
dead-drop-podcast.summary: The threats John Kiriakou has received across two decades — first after going public about the CIA torture program, when FBI advice that at least two were credible sent his family out of the country, and later in waves tied to his opposition to Gina Haspel, his remarks about Pakistan, and his advocacy on Palestine and the Epstein case.

dead-drop-podcast.title: Threats against John Kiriakou
