dead-drop-podcast.summary: The stalkers and death threats John Kiriakou has received since going public in 2007 — including a woman who believed he had proposed to her in code on C-SPAN and arrived at his office armed, and a caller who recited his son's home address.

dead-drop-podcast.title: Barry Eisler
dead-drop-podcast.summary: Former CIA officer turned bestselling novelist, and a recurring guest of John Kiriakou's, who describes him as one of the very few former intelligence officers to have succeeded at storytelling outside the secret world as thoroughly as he did inside it.

dead-drop.title: The oath to the Constitution
dead-drop.summary: The oath sworn with a raised right hand on the first day at the CIA, in an auditorium full of new hires, to protect the Constitution against all enemies foreign and domestic — and the secrecy agreement signed alongside it, which John Kiriakou and Ray McGovern both treat as merely a contract. Kiriakou uses the oath to answer the charge that he broke a promise, to explain why torture had to be disclosed, and to state a rule of precedence: when a law, a policy or a signed agreement conflicts with the Constitution, the Constitution wins every time. He suspects he was the only person in the room who meant it.

dead-drop.title: Aldrich Ames
dead-drop.summary: Senior CIA officer — a GS-15 who rose to chief of counterintelligence for the Soviet branch — who spied for the KGB for nine years. Per John Kiriakou, Ames walked into the Soviet embassy in Washington in April 1985 and sold the identities of two CIA-recruited double agents for $50,000 to clear a debt run up by his second marriage; both were executed. He went on to identify more than thirty agents, compromise over a hundred clandestine operations, cause at least twelve deaths and take more than $2 million, while being known throughout the agency as a daily drunk and promoted at every turn. The KGB protected him with a decoy mole hunt; analyst Sandy Grimes caught him by matching his handler meetings to his bank deposits.

dead-drop.title: Central Intelligence Agency
dead-drop.summary: U.S. foreign intelligence service; John Kiriakou's employer from 1990 to 2004 and the central institution of KiriPedia

dead-drop.title: John Kiriakou
dead-drop.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

dead-drop.title: Amnesty International
dead-drop.summary: The human rights organization whose torture report forms part of John Kiriakou's core defense — the CIA's crimes were already public knowledge before he confirmed them on ABC, and the Justice Department's own declination letter said so — and the organization whose silence during his prosecution he cannot forgive. He begged Amnesty for a one-sentence statement and got a New Yorker subscription instead; it took Ai Weiwei to change their minds, and by then he was walking out of prison.

dead-drop.title: Counterterrorism Center
dead-drop.summary: The CIA's Counterterrorism Center (CTC) — the unit where John Kiriakou spent the defining years of his operational career. He joined in the late 1990s as the only officer in the entire CIA fluent in both Greek and Arabic, served as chief of counterintelligence in the bin Laden unit, watched the Center swell from a few hundred employees to nearly 2,000 by September 12, 2001, and it was to CTC that he walked back down in May 2002 to refuse the torture program — the moment, he says, the CIA began to turn on him.

death-of-investigative-journalism.title: Advice to the next generation
death-of-investigative-journalism.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer to a Gen Z viewer who said he felt helpless — that helplessness is not new, that 1968 and 1969 were worse, and that the remedy is four concrete things: run for any office at all, starting with the local water board; demonstrate; ride your elected officials and vote them out if they will not do what they are told; and write.

death-of-investigative-journalism.title: 2026 Iran war
death-of-investigative-journalism.summary: The open-ended American and Israeli war against Iran that John Kiriakou tracked week by week on his own show — a conflict he says was sold as three weeks, ran into its fifth month, achieved every decapitation objective it set, and continued anyway. His grade for it is a D, and his forecast is a Truth Social post declaring victory while nothing changes.

death-of-investigative-journalism.title: Al-Qaeda training manual interrogation-resistance tactics
death-of-investigative-journalism.summary: A captured al-Qaeda training manual instructing operatives on how to resist interrogation, including feigning illness — a technique John Kiriakou says he saw a detainee use, and recognized, during a capture and interrogation in Pakistan.

death-of-investigative-journalism.title: China's base in Djibouti
death-of-investigative-journalism.summary: Camp Lemonnier in Djibouti, the abandoned French base the Djiboutians offered to the Americans and the Chinese took a share of — split down the middle by a chain-link fence, the only Chinese military installation outside China, and the centrepiece of John Kiriakou's argument that China is not an expansionist power.

death-of-investigative-journalism.title: Irish intelligence services
death-of-investigative-journalism.summary: Ireland's intelligence and law-enforcement services, which John Kiriakou toured and met with during a speaking trip to Belfast, Cork, Dublin, and Waterford. Per Kiriakou, Irish intelligence and the Garda are especially strong at anti-money-laundering investigation and counterterrorism — the latter traced, he says, to the large number of Irish militants trained by Carlos the Jackal in Libya and Lebanon during the 1970s.

death-of-investigative-journalism.title: Kent State shooting
death-of-investigative-journalism.summary: The 1970 shooting of unarmed student protesters by the Ohio National Guard; John Kiriakou says a family friend's daughter was among those killed — the closing event of a 1968–69 upheaval he treats both as the formation of his own politics and as the historical measure against which he judges the present.

death-threats-against-kiriakou.title: John Kiriakou
death-threats-against-kiriakou.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

death-threats-against-kiriakou.title: Jeffrey Epstein
death-threats-against-kiriakou.summary: Convicted sex offender; per John Kiriakou, was "an Israeli access agent" rather than a CIA asset, because the CIA collects foreign intelligence and Epstein's targets — Bill Clinton, Bill Gates, Prince Andrew — were not foreign. Kiriakou further holds that Epstein did die by suicide in federal custody, because in the Bureau of Prisons the cameras never work and the guards are always asleep.

death-threats-against-kiriakou.title: Justice Department self-immolation attempt
death-threats-against-kiriakou.summary: An attempted self-immolation at a Washington rally in support of Julian Assange and WikiLeaks, held outside the Department of Justice, at which John Kiriakou was speaking. Kiriakou and another demonstrator physically stopped a naked man who had doused himself in lighter fluid; an attorney present intervened with the arresting officers and the man was taken to a hospital rather than a jail.

death-threats-against-kiriakou.title: The move to Fort Myer
death-threats-against-kiriakou.summary: John Kiriakou's report that Stephen Miller, Pete Hegseth and Kristi Noem all moved with their families onto Fort Myer army base into housing reserved for one- to four-star generals — 'the mother of all gated communities' — after Miller sold his Arlington house to escape protesters chalking his public sidewalk.

death-threats-against-kiriakou.title: The CIA barber shop
death-threats-against-kiriakou.summary: The barber in the basement of CIA headquarters, which John Kiriakou visited once on the reasoning that it saved a trip across town and found stocked with Playboys and Penthouses — one of several amenities, alongside a dry cleaner and a post office substation, that made the building function as a self-contained town.

death-threats-against-kiriakou.title: The tax rates from Eisenhower to Nixon
death-threats-against-kiriakou.summary: John Kiriakou's explanation for the American wealth gap and the size of the deficit — that from Eisenhower through Nixon the top rate of tax ran upwards of seventy-five per cent and the wealthy whittled it down from there, whereas now they begin at almost nothing and whittle down from that.

decapitation-strikes.title: Tulsi Gabbard
decapitation-strikes.summary: U.S. Director of National Intelligence; a longtime family friend of John Kiriakou's, who has known her since she was 12; Kiriakou calls her appointment "an inspired choice" despite disagreeing with her decision to join the Republican Party, and says she appears to have given up her opposition to Section 702 surveillance to secure Senate confirmation.

decapitation-strikes.title: The Samson Option
decapitation-strikes.summary: John Kiriakou's assessment, given during the 2026 Iran war, that Israel would use nuclear weapons if it believed the state itself was about to collapse. He notes that a year earlier he would have called the idea ridiculous, and that analysts put the Israeli arsenal at between eighty and two hundred warheads.

decapitation-strikes.title: 2026 Iran war
decapitation-strikes.summary: The open-ended American and Israeli war against Iran that John Kiriakou tracked week by week on his own show — a conflict he says was sold as three weeks, ran into its fifth month, achieved every decapitation objective it set, and continued anyway. His grade for it is a D, and his forecast is a Truth Social post declaring victory while nothing changes.

decapitation-strikes.title: Bill Pulte
decapitation-strikes.summary: The housing developer serving as acting Director of National Intelligence after Tulsi Gabbard's resignation. John Kiriakou, relaying the assessment of people who know him, calls him smart, personally decent and completely loyal to Trump — while saying he could not find the ODNI with a map and a GPS unit, and predicting his sole function will be to fire the president's enemies.

decapitation-strikes.title: Congressional intelligence oversight
decapitation-strikes.summary: John Kiriakou''s standing criticism of the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence and the House Permanent Select Committee — that unlike the armed services and foreign relations committees, they do not perform oversight at all: "They''re just cheerleaders." His illustration is a sitting committee chairman who summoned him privately, then asked whether Kiriakou would write the criticism publicly on his behalf.

decapitation-strikes.title: Iran strike factions (2026)
decapitation-strikes.summary: John Kiriakou's reporting, sourced to a former colleague at the White House, that a 2026 decision to strike Iran pitted an anti-war camp of JD Vance and Tulsi Gabbard against a pro-war camp led by Marco Rubio — with the Joint Chiefs newly compliant because Trump had replaced them all.

declare-victory-and-go-home.title: The airbridge
declare-victory-and-go-home.summary: John Kiriakou''s definition of an airbridge, given when the term surfaced in reporting on German aid to Gaza: a direct path into another country''s airspace along which safety is guaranteed — his worked example being Cyprus to Gaza, with an undertaking that the Israeli Air Force will not shoot the aircraft down.

declare-victory-and-go-home.title: "Every Israeli I ever knew"
declare-victory-and-go-home.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the attitudes he encountered among Israelis he knew professionally and socially — that almost every one of them wanted the Palestinians killed or exiled — together with his description of a sensibility he says is palpable walking around Tel Aviv and Jerusalem, and his immediate self-correction when he overstated the claim.

declare-victory-and-go-home.title: Abraham Accords
declare-victory-and-go-home.summary: The Trump-brokered normalization deals between Israel and Gulf Arab states — in John Kiriakou's judgment "a terrible idea in the first place," a great victory for Israel and the Gulf Arabs that was "a punch in the throat to the Palestinians." He argues the Accords are how Trump meant to "solve the Middle East in a day" — by screwing the Palestinians — that Hamas read the abandonment correctly, that October 7 shattered the project, and that reviving the Accords (Saudis in, victory declared, Nobel collected) remains the organizing goal of Trump's regional policy.

declare-victory-and-go-home.title: Bigger than the Russian embassy
declare-victory-and-go-home.summary: Why American embassies in small, strategically unimportant countries are enormous: the answer John Kiriakou says he was given by a station chief on one of his first CIA trips — that the building had to be bigger than the Soviet one across town. He describes American embassies in Africa as "absolutely gigantic" for that reason alone, and calls the US embassy in Cairo an enormous facility matched by an equally enormous Russian one.

declare-victory-and-go-home.title: The Greek offer for the Bamiyan Buddhas
declare-victory-and-go-home.summary: John Kiriakou's account that the Greek government, in the depths of its own economic depression, tried to buy the Bamiyan Buddhas from the Taliban in order to save them — intending to donate the statues back to a post-Taliban Afghan government. The offer was refused and the fifteen-hundred-year-old figures were destroyed.

declare-victory-and-go-home.title: The Costa Rica model
declare-victory-and-go-home.summary: John Kiriakou's suggestion, raised while discussing Russian demands to demilitarise Ukraine, that a country can simply have no military at all — Costa Rica having a national police force, no army, no navy, and a coast guard of one boat in the Atlantic and one in the Pacific. He immediately noted why it would not be permitted in Ukraine's case.

declared-officer.title: John Kiriakou
declared-officer.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

declared-officer.title: American shoes
declared-officer.summary: The detail by which the chief of the Greek intelligence service identified John Kiriakou as an American within minutes of meeting him — not his Greek, which was fluent, but his footwear — and which sent Kiriakou straight to a shoe shop before working the anarchist quarters of Athens.

declared-officer.title: Bahrain Posting (1994–1996)
declared-officer.summary: John Kiriakou's 1994–1996 assignment to Bahrain under U.S. State Department cover as second secretary for economic affairs — arriving with his wife Joanne and infant son Chris on August 1, 1994, into a tiny Gulf monarchy whose sectarian tensions erupted, two months later, into the first Intifada.

declared-officer.title: There is no such thing as bad food in Athens
declared-officer.summary: The lesson John Kiriakou says he learned at a lorry drivers' stop outside Corinth, where the food was as good as his grandmother's — reached on the three-and-a-half-hour drives he made to meet a source too sensitive to be met in Athens, with a vineyard tour as his cover story.

declared-officer.title: Abdul Amir al-Jamri
declared-officer.summary: The Bahraini cleric who led the Shia opposition during the 1990s uprising, and whom John Kiriakou interviewed for a human rights report in 1991 — an interview that had the Bahraini prime minister demanding, within the hour, that both American officers be expelled from the country.

declared-officer.title: Admiral William Crowe
declared-officer.summary: Former Chairman of the U.S. Joint Chiefs of Staff and former CENTCOM commander who had lived in Bahrain, author of the "pound for pound" formula every Bahraini and every American ambassador quotes, and the visiting dignitary John Kiriakou was assigned to escort — a week that ended with the Bahraini Prime Minister refusing to let go of Kiriakou's hand.

declassifying-for-a-foreign-government.title: Donald Trump
declassifying-for-a-foreign-government.summary: 45th and 47th U.S. president. Per John Kiriakou, a man genuinely convinced he was doing right by bombing Iran, "duped" by the same Netanyahu nuclear bluff Obama once rejected — and, at the same time, the most blindly pro-Israel president in history, an admirer of autocrats who has never once criticized Vladimir Putin, and prone to gestures — from the Gulf of America to a since-abandoned "Department of War" rename — that test the edges of his actual authority.

declassifying-for-a-foreign-government.title: H. R. McMaster
declassifying-for-a-foreign-government.summary: National Security Adviser during the May 2017 controversy over Donald Trump's disclosure of intelligence to Russian officials, whose public defence — that the president had not been briefed on the source of the information — John Kiriakou treated as a fork in which either answer reflects badly on McMaster himself.

declassifying-for-a-foreign-government.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
declassifying-for-a-foreign-government.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

declassifying-for-a-foreign-government.title: David Petraeus
declassifying-for-a-foreign-government.summary: Retired U.S. Army general and director of the CIA who, per John Kiriakou, confirmed the names of ten covert CIA operatives to his biographer and girlfriend and was never criminally charged — a contrast Kiriakou cites repeatedly as proof that his own prosecution under the Intelligence Identities Protection Act was selective. Kiriakou''s explanation for the disparity: Petraeus had not blown the whistle on the torture program and embarrassed the agency.

declassifying-for-a-foreign-government.title: James Risen
declassifying-for-a-foreign-government.summary: The New York Times reporter whose refusal to testify in the Jeffrey Sterling prosecution — through the Fourth Circuit, the Supreme Court and a Justice Department climbdown — John Kiriakou treats as the precedent that a later administration would want to overturn by making an example of a journalist.

declassifying-for-a-foreign-government.title: Slow-rolling the president
declassifying-for-a-foreign-government.summary: John Kiriakou's 2017 forecast that the CIA would not confront Donald Trump but outlast him — senior officers with twenty-five and thirty years in the building having already waited out several presidents — offered as the agency's characteristic response to a president it neither trusts nor is trusted by.

decorum-in-the-reagan-years.title: Get thrown out spicily
decorum-in-the-reagan-years.summary: John Kiriakou''s criticism of Representative Al Green''s protest at the 2026 State of the Union address: that holding up a banned sign and then walking out quietly accomplished nothing, and that if you are going to be removed you should struggle and fight back.

decorum-in-the-reagan-years.title: Impeach him again
decorum-in-the-reagan-years.summary: John Kiriakou's warning that if the Democrats win a House majority in 2026 and immediately move to impeach Donald Trump again, they should never win another race — and his prediction that this is exactly what they will do.

decorum-in-the-reagan-years.title: Nationalizing the midterms
decorum-in-the-reagan-years.summary: John Kiriakou's recurring comparison between contemporary party messaging and Newt Gingrich's 1994 Contract with America, including his advice that Speaker Mike Johnson should keep Gingrich on his couch and ask him nightly how the 1994 midterms were nationalised.

decorum-in-the-reagan-years.title: The six-hour queue for seats
decorum-in-the-reagan-years.summary: John Kiriakou on learning that members of Congress arrive six hours early with packed meals to hold a seat for the State of the Union, and that in 2026 the absence of 112 Democrats freed those seats for the cabinet, the sub-cabinet and visitors.

decorum-in-the-reagan-years.title: The Trump appointees to the Court
decorum-in-the-reagan-years.summary: John Kiriakou's assessment that Donald Trump's Supreme Court appointees have been surprisingly good, and that the justices he regards as disasters — Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas — were appointed by more moderate presidents.

decorum-in-the-reagan-years.title: Donald Trump
decorum-in-the-reagan-years.summary: 45th and 47th U.S. president. Per John Kiriakou, a man genuinely convinced he was doing right by bombing Iran, "duped" by the same Netanyahu nuclear bluff Obama once rejected — and, at the same time, the most blindly pro-Israel president in history, an admirer of autocrats who has never once criticized Vladimir Putin, and prone to gestures — from the Gulf of America to a since-abandoned "Department of War" rename — that test the edges of his actual authority.

deep-state.title: National Intelligence Council
deep-state.summary: Body housed at the CIA comprising the most senior analysts drawn from across the entire intelligence community. Its officers — National Intelligence Officers (NIOs) — hold positions at the Senior Intelligence Service level and are responsible for long-range strategic analysis on specific portfolio areas, as well as the production of National Intelligence Estimates. Per John Kiriakou, learning that the NIO for Warning had held the same job for forty-two years and just received a waiver to stay until seventy was the moment he first believed in the existence of the deep state.

deep-state.title: No good guy
deep-state.summary: John Kiriakou's standing refusal to treat opposition to Donald Trump and defence of the intelligence agencies as a single position — that a citizen may dislike Trump's policies without throwing in with the CIA, the FBI and the likes of John Brennan — together with the electoral remedy he attaches to it.

deep-state.title: The Grenier counterinsurgency op-ed
deep-state.summary: The New York Times piece by former CIA officer Robert Grenier arguing that the storming of the Capitol should be treated as an insurgency, and John Kiriakou's published answer to it — that a colleague of thirty years using that word is asking for people to be killed, and that counterinsurgency describes a set of practices the Constitution forbids at home.

deep-state.title: UC Global and the state secrets privilege
deep-state.summary: The Spanish private security company that John Kiriakou says copied the electronic devices of everyone visiting Julian Assange at the Ecuadorian embassy in London and passed the contents to the CIA. When two journalists and two attorneys sued and the case survived dismissal, the agency moved to invoke the state secrets privilege — which Kiriakou treats as proof that a plain constitutional violation can be left without any remedy at all.

deep-state.title: Intelligence switching in the Iran–Iraq war
deep-state.summary: John Kiriakou''s account that during the Iran–Iraq war the United States supplied top-secret overhead imagery to whichever side was losing ground, switching as the front moved — giving the Iraqis imagery when Iran advanced, and the Iranians imagery when Iraq advanced. His summary: ''So it was hideous.''

deep-state.title: Phil Mudd
deep-state.summary: Former CIA and FBI official turned television commentator, whom John Kiriakou uses alongside John Brennan as an example of a pattern he says governs Washington: senior intelligence alumni making escalating on-air accusations against Donald Trump as a route to a network contract or a return to government.

defense-humint-service.title: Abolish the CIA
defense-humint-service.summary: John Kiriakou's position that the CIA should be abolished because its functions are already duplicated by the other 17 U.S. intelligence agencies — analysis by the State Department, human spying by the Pentagon, technology by DARPA, NSA and the private sector.

defense-humint-service.title: CIA–FBI incompatible computer systems
defense-humint-service.summary: John Kiriakou's claim that from the CIA's founding in 1947 until 2009 the computer systems of the CIA and the FBI were not compatible with one another — no message could be sent from one to the other and no intelligence shared — which he offers both as the material substrate of the interagency hatred that helped make September 11 possible, and as the gap through which James Mitchell and Bruce Jessen were able to pass Ali Soufan's FBI debriefings of Abu Zubaydah off as the fruits of torture.

defense-humint-service.title: Langley
defense-humint-service.summary: The Virginia location of CIA headquarters and, in John Kiriakou''s usage, shorthand for the agency''s permanent power. It''s where he worked as the CIA''s lone Iraq-Kuwait analyst — told to start on Iraq "because nothing ever happened there" — where a cafeteria conversation invited him into the torture program, where he walked past the Kryptos sculpture every day for fifteen years without solving it, and the place agencies return to after apologizing to Congress, "where of course nothing ever changes." When a host suggested the real government of America is out in Langley and Washington''s white marble is for show, Kiriakou''s answer was: "that''s about the shape of it."

defense-humint-service.title: National Security Agency
defense-humint-service.summary: The U.S. signals-intelligence agency. John Kiriakou notes it was never created by an act of Congress and that its own charter forbids collection on Americans — a rule that, when he entered government, meant heads rolled over accidental intercepts, and which he says has since been inverted into total collection stored in Utah for 500 years.

defense-humint-service.title: The SIGINT–HUMINT balance
defense-humint-service.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer to what he calls the most important question facing any incoming CIA director: how to divide investment between signals intelligence and human intelligence. His position is that signals collection cannot supply the one thing policy requires — a person in the room when a decision is taken — and that every new director says so on arrival and then drifts back toward the technology.

defense-humint-service.title: The nineteen intelligence agencies
defense-humint-service.summary: Asked how many American intelligence agencies there are, John Kiriakou put the number at about nineteen, said there are no genuinely secret ones left, and argued that the sprawl is empire-building by the Pentagon — before asking why the Department of Agriculture and the Department of Commerce need intelligence agencies at all.

defense-intelligence-agency.title: The Iranian elementary school strike
defense-intelligence-agency.summary: A Tomahawk cruise missile strike at the start of the 2026 war that killed more than 175 people at an Iranian elementary school. The United States denied responsibility until its own investigation confirmed it; John Kiriakou traces the failure to targeting data a decade out of date and expects no one to be punished for it.

defense-intelligence-agency.title: Targeting analyst
defense-intelligence-agency.summary: A specialized CIA analyst — distinct from an intelligence analyst — who sifts millions of pieces of data, much of it metadata, to physically locate a person for capture or killing; John Kiriakou credits one with finding Abu Zubaydah down to 14 sites.

defense-intelligence-agency.title: Hamas
defense-intelligence-agency.summary: The Palestinian movement behind the October 7, 2023 attack; John Kiriakou argues that a case could be made for calling it a freedom-fighting organization dedicated to the liberation of its people rather than simply a terrorist group, notes it is labeled a terrorist organization by only a small minority of UN member states, and has ruled Gaza since Israel's 2005 withdrawal.

defense-intelligence-agency.title: Cancelling the 2026 midterms
defense-intelligence-agency.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that the 2026 war cannot win the midterm elections for the Republicans, and his flagged-as-paranoid worry that it may instead furnish the pretext for a national emergency and a cancelled election.

defense-intelligence-agency.title: CIA liaison relationships
defense-intelligence-agency.summary: John Kiriakou's critique of CIA intelligence-liaison relationships with foreign governments — sharply expanded after 9/11 — arguing that officers do not consider the long-term risk that disclosing sensitive operations to foreign services hands those governments leverage, including potential blackmail material, over the United States, and that no one left in Congress has the will to provide real oversight of the practice.

defense-intelligence-agency.title: Civilian ships and piracy
defense-intelligence-agency.summary: Why merchant crews cannot defend themselves: by international treaty no civilian ship may carry a weapon. John Kiriakou handled international piracy as a Senate Foreign Relations Committee staffer and brought Captain Richard Phillips to testify.

deloitte-consulting-career.title: Plato Cacheris
deloitte-consulting-career.summary: Legendary Washington, D.C. defense attorney who served as John Kiriakou''s lead counsel in his 2012–2013 Espionage Act prosecution. Per Kiriakou, when discovery revealed the FBI had run a fake-diplomat sting against him, Cacheris explained the government''s posture bluntly: ''Because they have a shit case and they know it''s shit, and that''s why we''re going to trial.'' He spent most of the case urging trial, then drove to Kiriakou''s house on decision day and said ''You stupid son of a bitch — take the deal.'' Cacheris also represented FBI spy Robert Hanssen.

deloitte-consulting-career.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
deloitte-consulting-career.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

deloitte-consulting-career.title: Corporate competitive intelligence
deloitte-consulting-career.summary: The private-sector discipline John Kiriakou entered on leaving the CIA in 2004: collecting human-source intelligence on rival firms for a big-four accountancy. He was the fourth CIA officer Deloitte had hired into a group that paired former intelligence collectors with corporate research analysts, and his requirements were a rival''s pricing models, its discount structure, and which of its top-producing partners were unhappy enough to be poached. All the major firms, he says, run the same operation against each other.

deloitte-consulting-career.title: The Kite Runner rescue mission
deloitte-consulting-career.summary: 2007 covert operation in which John Kiriakou, newly departed from the CIA and working as a corporate-intelligence consultant, was hired by Paramount Studios to secretly evacuate the Afghan child actors of the film "The Kite Runner" and their extended families after real death threats over the film's content.

deloitte-consulting-career.title: 2026 congressional landscape
deloitte-consulting-career.summary: John Kiriakou's read on two developments affecting the 2026 midterm landscape — the Supreme Court's disallowance of Virginia's redistricting, which he says makes a Democratic House win less certain given widespread Republican-favoring gerrymandering, and Marjorie Taylor Greene's resignation despite winning her last race with 77.5% of the vote, because she knew she could not survive another Republican primary.

deloitte-consulting-career.title: Andrew Warren
deloitte-consulting-career.summary: Former CIA officer and station chief who, per John Kiriakou, was protected and lavishly funded by his supervisor "Mary Margaret," then convicted of raping 23 women — videotaping every attack — before a post-prison religious conversion and further sexual assault convictions.

democratic-change-in-the-middle-east.title: Saudi influence in Egypt
democratic-change-in-the-middle-east.summary: John Kiriakou's account of Saudi Arabia's role in Egypt — not merely supporting the government that displaced the Muslim Brotherhood but bankrolling it and ensuring its survival — which he places within a history of Saudi interference in Egyptian internal affairs reaching back to the nationalist revolution of 1958.

democratic-change-in-the-middle-east.title: Kuwait as a sectarian model
democratic-change-in-the-middle-east.summary: John Kiriakou's nomination of Kuwait as the one country in the Middle East to have managed a transition toward a workable form of democracy and sectarian coexistence — an argument he makes without concealing that it began with the royal family bulldozing an entire Shia neighbourhood in the early 1980s.

democratic-change-in-the-middle-east.title: The U.S.–Saudi relationship
democratic-change-in-the-middle-east.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the American alliance with Saudi Arabia as a straightforward trade — basing rights and oil in exchange for weapons sales and protection — and of the price the United States pays for it, which he describes as a demonstrated willingness to walk away from its own commitments to international law and human rights in order to protect the regime.

democratic-change-in-the-middle-east.title: The Saudi fear of an election
democratic-change-in-the-middle-east.summary: The explanation a Saudi diplomat gave John Kiriakou in the late 1990s for the royal family''s opposition to democracy in the kingdom: if there were an election in Saudi Arabia, Osama bin Laden would win it — a remark Kiriakou uses to argue that the regime''s problem was not that its princes loved al-Qaeda but that it feared its own population did.

democratic-change-in-the-middle-east.title: Saudi aid priorities
democratic-change-in-the-middle-east.summary: John Kiriakou''s characterisation of Saudi generosity abroad as real but consistently misdirected: instead of building schools they build mosques, instead of building hospitals they send planeloads of Qurans, and instead of water treatment plants or power plants they send money for weapons, ammunition and training.

democratic-change-in-the-middle-east.title: Saudi Arabia and radicalism
democratic-change-in-the-middle-east.summary: John Kiriakou's long-held position that Saudi Arabia is the primary generator of radical movements worldwide — a claim he locates not in the government alone but in the whole structure of Saudi government and society, in which a clerical establishment tells the rulers what to think while the rulers privately do as they please.

democratic-party-2025-approval-decline.title: Kamala Harris
democratic-party-2025-approval-decline.summary: Vice President under Joe Biden and 2024 Democratic presidential nominee; per John Kiriakou, installed as the party's nominee without a competitive primary despite having failed to reach the 2020 Iowa caucus, and closed out her 2024 campaign courting the Cheney family as a symbol of American values. Kiriakou, a lifelong progressive, says her pursuit of Dick Cheney's endorsement is what decided him against voting for her.

democratic-party-2025-approval-decline.title: MOSSAD
democratic-party-2025-approval-decline.summary: Israel's primary external intelligence service; characterized by John Kiriakou as universally hostile in his and his CIA colleagues' professional dealings with it ("never had a positive encounter with Mossad"); operates almost exclusively in the operational rather than analytical domain; the CIA is, per Kiriakou, categorically forbidden from spying on it.

democratic-party-2025-approval-decline.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
democratic-party-2025-approval-decline.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

democratic-party-2025-approval-decline.title: Joe Biden
democratic-party-2025-approval-decline.summary: 46th President of the United States; Vice President during the first Obama term; at John Kerry's December 2009 Christmas party, recognized John Kiriakou from a 15-year-prior conversation about a mutual hometown friend, and openly told a Kiriakou colleague within Kiriakou's hearing — and across the room from Kerry — that he disliked the colleague.

democratic-party-2025-approval-decline.title: The two-party system
democratic-party-2025-approval-decline.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of American party politics as a spent form — more Americans now call themselves independents than Democrats or Republicans, the two parties are ''two sides of the same coin,'' and ideology has displaced party as the organizing fact. He tells it partly as autobiography: a third-generation Democrat whose grandparents joined the party for Franklin Roosevelt and who left it himself.

democratic-party-2025-approval-decline.title: Donald Trump
democratic-party-2025-approval-decline.summary: 45th and 47th U.S. president. Per John Kiriakou, a man genuinely convinced he was doing right by bombing Iran, "duped" by the same Netanyahu nuclear bluff Obama once rejected — and, at the same time, the most blindly pro-Israel president in history, an admirer of autocrats who has never once criticized Vladimir Putin, and prone to gestures — from the Gulf of America to a since-abandoned "Department of War" rename — that test the edges of his actual authority.

democratic-redistricting-collapse.title: Mike Johnson
democratic-redistricting-collapse.summary: Speaker of the House during the fight over the Epstein files, whose procedural manoeuvres John Kiriakou reads as a sustained attempt to prevent his own party from ever having to vote — first by blocking the motion in the Rules Committee, then by adjourning the House until September so that nothing at all could be voted on — and whose midterm framing of Democrats as communists Kiriakou dismisses outright.

democratic-redistricting-collapse.title: James Woolsey
democratic-redistricting-collapse.summary: Director of Central Intelligence for twenty-three months at the start of the Clinton administration, forced out over his refusal to discipline anyone after the exposure of Aldrich Ames, and later chairman of Booz Allen Hamilton; John Kiriakou notes that his family attributed four years of illness before his death to Havana syndrome.

democratic-redistricting-collapse.title: President's Daily Brief
democratic-redistricting-collapse.summary: Per John Kiriakou, the President's Daily Brief (PDB) is a roughly 16-page, top-secret intelligence document produced daily for the president, written in a uniform CIA house style, briefed each morning, and — in his account — used partly to gauge and flatter incoming presidents.

democratic-redistricting-collapse.title: Aldrich Ames
democratic-redistricting-collapse.summary: Senior CIA officer — a GS-15 who rose to chief of counterintelligence for the Soviet branch — who spied for the KGB for nine years. Per John Kiriakou, Ames walked into the Soviet embassy in Washington in April 1985 and sold the identities of two CIA-recruited double agents for $50,000 to clear a debt run up by his second marriage; both were executed. He went on to identify more than thirty agents, compromise over a hundred clandestine operations, cause at least twelve deaths and take more than $2 million, while being known throughout the agency as a daily drunk and promoted at every turn. The KGB protected him with a decoy mole hunt; analyst Sandy Grimes caught him by matching his handler meetings to his bank deposits.

democratic-redistricting-collapse.title: Ali Abdullah Saleh
democratic-redistricting-collapse.summary: President of Yemen for decades, close to both Saudi Arabia and the United States until Yemen's 1990 Security Council vote on Kuwait, after which his country collapsed into civil war; he fled to Saudi Arabia and was killed by a bomb planted in the palace where he had taken refuge.

democratic-redistricting-collapse.title: Bab al-Mandab
democratic-redistricting-collapse.summary: The strait where the Horn of Africa nearly meets the south-western tip of the Arabian Peninsula, which John Kiriakou identifies as one of the few American national interests in Yemen and as a chokepoint whose closure would push the global economy into recession.

democratic-silence-on-the-iran-war.title: Cory Booker
democratic-silence-on-the-iran-war.summary: Per John Kiriakou, he was "especially furious" with Democratic senator Cory Booker for running through the halls of Congress to get to a photo op standing behind Benjamin Netanyahu, which Kiriakou cites as an example of Democratic silence in the face of AIPAC pressure.

democratic-silence-on-the-iran-war.title: The AIPAC "Holy Land" trip offer
democratic-silence-on-the-iran-war.summary: An approach John Kiriakou says he received within days of becoming chief investigator of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee: two AIPAC representatives offered him an all-expenses-paid trip to what they called the Holy Land, never using the word Israel, and told him it was cleared by the Senate ethics committee. He declined; colleagues of his went. He pairs the story with his account of AIPAC staff stationed in congressional offices, while insisting the practice is not unique to them.

democratic-silence-on-the-iran-war.title: AIPAC
democratic-silence-on-the-iran-war.summary: The American Israel Public Affairs Committee — the U.S. political organization that, in John Kiriakou's framing, ought to be registered as a foreign-lobbying entity but is not, and that wields decisive electoral power against U.S. elected officials who express support for Palestinian human rights.

democratic-silence-on-the-iran-war.title: Senate Foreign Relations Committee
democratic-silence-on-the-iran-war.summary: Kiriakou was senior investigator under John Kerry — and still held the post when his own federal prosecution came to a head in January 2012.

democratic-silence-on-the-iran-war.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
democratic-silence-on-the-iran-war.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

democratic-silence-on-the-iran-war.title: Jonathan Pollard
democratic-silence-on-the-iran-war.summary: U.S. Navy civilian intelligence analyst convicted in 1985 of spying for Israel; the canonical proven case of Israeli espionage against the United States; cited by John Kiriakou in his 2024 Piers Morgan debate with a former Mossad director who denied any Israeli spying on the U.S.

denied-areas.title: John Kiriakou
denied-areas.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

denied-areas.title: CIA National Resources Division
denied-areas.summary: The Central Intelligence Agency's domestic intelligence-collection arm, created in the 1980s by Director William J. Casey

denied-areas.title: Fabricated intelligence reporting
denied-areas.summary: The three things John Kiriakou says CIA case officers are caught doing — inventing intelligence outright, holding real reports back to smooth out a monthly quota, and padding cover-stop expenses — and his argument that the fabrication is driven by production targets set by bad managers.

denied-areas.title: Six different passports
denied-areas.summary: John Kiriakou's answer to what has changed for intelligence officers since his own service — that he carried six different passports, and that he does not know how officers cross borders now that AI and facial recognition mean everything is scanned and stored — coupled with his advice not to let the technology take over the job.

denied-areas.title: The Chinese embassy in London
denied-areas.summary: John Kiriakou's assessment of the Chinese mission planned for London — an embassy occupying an entire city block that would be the largest in the world, approved over street protests, and which he calls 'the mother of all spy dens.' He contrasts it with Washington's refusal of the same proposal, and predicts China will now build such embassies everywhere.

denied-areas.title: The hotel bar operation
denied-areas.summary: The night a visiting foreign delegation's security detail was expected in a boutique hotel bar and every seat in it turned out to be occupied by a CIA officer — an episode John Kiriakou offers as an example of bad leadership, and which left his colleagues personally out of pocket for their espresso martinis.

department-of-education-swat-raid.title: Espionage Act
department-of-education-swat-raid.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

department-of-education-swat-raid.title: Julian Assange
department-of-education-swat-raid.summary: Kiriakou — a 15-year friend and former WikiLeaks board member — on why Assange is a publisher owed a journalist's immunity, and a political prisoner.

department-of-education-swat-raid.title: "Admit nothing, deny everything, make counter-accusations"
department-of-education-swat-raid.summary: One of the twenty life lessons John Kiriakou says the CIA taught him in training, and a slogan sold on coffee mugs and t-shirts in the headquarters gift shop — by far the most popular mug in the building. It was treated at Langley as a joke that was not quite a joke; in federal prison Kiriakou used it as an operating rule, and credits it with getting him out of an investigation into a prison-yard fight with nothing given up.

department-of-education-swat-raid.title: The chilling effect of whistleblower prosecutions
department-of-education-swat-raid.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that national-security prosecutions are not primarily about convictions but about deterrence — that the CIA cares about sending a message where the FBI cares about promotions, that his own case was meant to frighten anyone else considering disclosure, and that a New York Times reporter told him every national-security source the paper had went silent on the day of his arrest.

department-of-education-swat-raid.title: Consortium News
department-of-education-swat-raid.summary: Independent investigative news outlet John Kiriakou has written for since at least 2017, founded by Polk Award-winning journalist Robert Parry, who broke major stories on Iran-Contra. Kiriakou's columns there have covered John Bolton's exit, the entrapment of Maria Butina, his own first tour in Saudi Arabia and the 2019 Ukraine-call whistleblower. He says PayPal permanently shuttered the outlet's account and briefly seized its funds before backing down under public pressure, while still refusing to reinstate it.

department-of-education-swat-raid.title: Eastern District of Virginia
department-of-education-swat-raid.summary: The U.S. federal district covering northern Virginia — home to Langley, the Pentagon, DHS and much of the intelligence-contractor industry — which John Kiriakou calls 'the espionage court' because the Justice Department files the great majority of its national security prosecutions there and because, in his telling, no national-security defendant has ever won a case in it; Kiriakou, Julian Assange, Edward Snowden and Jeffrey Sterling were all charged there.

der-spiegel.title: Daniel Domscheit-Berg
der-spiegel.summary: A WikiLeaks associate discussed on the same panel as John Kiriakou; the anecdote about meeting him via the Chaos Computer Club was told by fellow panelist John Goetz, a Der Spiegel journalist — not by Kiriakou himself.

der-spiegel.title: Julian Assange
der-spiegel.summary: Kiriakou — a 15-year friend and former WikiLeaks board member — on why Assange is a publisher owed a journalist's immunity, and a political prisoner.

der-spiegel.title: Ai Whistleblower Initiative
der-spiegel.summary: The AI Whistleblower Initiative, working on legal protections for the wave of whistleblowers now coming out of the artificial-intelligence industry.

der-spiegel.title: Andrew Feinstein
der-spiegel.summary: Referenced on the same WikiLeaks-conference panel as John Kiriakou; the description of Feinstein's talk on the multiple factors that ended apartheid was given by another panelist putting a question to Kiriakou, not by Kiriakou himself.

der-spiegel.title: Belmarsh Prison
der-spiegel.summary: The maximum-security London prison where Julian Assange was held for years on a bail-jumping sentence John Kiriakou calls a fabrication — kept in solitary confinement alongside the worst offenders in the United Kingdom, and held past the expiry of his sentence at the request of the United States. Kiriakou corresponded with Assange there and watched the letters change.

der-spiegel.title: Chaos Computer Club Wikileaks
der-spiegel.summary: The Berlin hacker collective that shaped WikiLeaks' early years — and where a journalist first met Daniel Domscheit-Berg under a pseudonym.

destroying-the-dome-of-the-rock.title: The pardoned January 6th defendants
destroying-the-dome-of-the-rock.summary: John Kiriakou's observation that a striking number of the January 6th defendants pardoned by Donald Trump have got into trouble since their release — one arrested for threatening to kill the House minority leader, another shot dead in a gunfight with a police officer in Indiana — and his agreement that the base rate may explain all of it.

destroying-the-dome-of-the-rock.title: The Tomahawk red line
destroying-the-dome-of-the-rock.summary: John Kiriakou's judgement that giving Ukraine Tomahawk cruise missiles would be a very bad idea — because it would risk drawing NATO in and risk a tactical nuclear strike on Ukrainian positions — set against Peter Kuznick's assessment that Ukraine is losing and is now snatching old men off the street.

destroying-the-dome-of-the-rock.title: The Scooter Libby deposition
destroying-the-dome-of-the-rock.summary: The 2006 or 2007 session at which John Kiriakou, appearing as a witness in the Scooter Libby case, mentioned that the only conversation he had witnessed between two senior CIA officers concerned a covert action programme — and the agency's general counsel jumped up and stopped him mid-sentence, because an officer may not say the words at all.

destroying-the-dome-of-the-rock.title: The $230 million claim
destroying-the-dome-of-the-rock.summary: John Kiriakou's reaction to a sitting president demanding a quarter of a billion dollars in compensation from his own Justice Department — he telephoned his friend and former attorney Bruce Fein, expecting to be told it was impossible, and was told instead that an obscure nineteenth-century law makes it perfectly legal.

destroying-the-dome-of-the-rock.title: Trading informants to El Salvador
destroying-the-dome-of-the-rock.summary: John Kiriakou's reaction to reports that the secretary of state had agreed to hand over American informants in El Salvador in exchange for the use of Salvadoran prisons — that it is, in plain terms, a death sentence, and that the surprise is not that people will stop cooperating but that they never seem to.

destroying-the-dome-of-the-rock.title: The thirty-year-old nominee
destroying-the-dome-of-the-rock.summary: The nominee to head the Office of Special Counsel who withdrew in October 2025 after text messages surfaced in which he acknowledged a Nazi streak — and John Kiriakou's separate objection, which was that a man six years out of school has no business running an office at the Justice Department in the first place.

deuce-martinez.title: Espionage Act
deuce-martinez.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

deuce-martinez.title: Abu Zubaydah
deuce-martinez.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

deuce-martinez.title: Human Rights Watch
deuce-martinez.summary: The organization whose 2005 report that the CIA was torturing its prisoners — two years before John Kiriakou''s ABC interview — anchors his defense that he confirmed rather than revealed the program. It is also the middle link in the chain that ended in his arrest: working with the John Adams Project, Human Rights Watch employed the investigator who carried a classified name from journalist Matthew Cole to the Guantánamo defense attorneys, and when the FBI walked that chain backwards it arrived at Kiriakou''s door.

deuce-martinez.title: Abraham Accords
deuce-martinez.summary: The Trump-brokered normalization deals between Israel and Gulf Arab states — in John Kiriakou's judgment "a terrible idea in the first place," a great victory for Israel and the Gulf Arabs that was "a punch in the throat to the Palestinians." He argues the Accords are how Trump meant to "solve the Middle East in a day" — by screwing the Palestinians — that Hamas read the abandonment correctly, that October 7 shattered the project, and that reviving the Accords (Saudis in, victory declared, Nobel collected) remains the organizing goal of Trump's regional policy.

deuce-martinez.title: Ali Soufan
deuce-martinez.summary: FBI special agent who handled Abu Zubaydah immediately after his March 2002 capture; through patient, respectful interrogation produced the only actionable intelligence ever obtained from the detainee, including the first identification of "Mukhtar" as Khalid Sheikh Mohammed.

deuce-martinez.title: Arabists
deuce-martinez.summary: The label applied inside the U.S. government to diplomats and analysts who knew Arabic and Middle Eastern history, and which John Kiriakou confirms functioned as a dismissal — the assumption being that anyone who understood the region was blindly prejudiced against Israel, or antisemitic.

dewey-clarridge.title: CIA Drug Facilitation
dewey-clarridge.summary: Per John Kiriakou, the CIA''s reported involvement in facilitating the arrival of cocaine into the United States during the era that became the crack epidemic, and his own firsthand discovery — as a Senate Foreign Relations Committee investigator — that under American military control Afghanistan produced 93% of the world''s heroin. A DEA contact told him the report would never be published because ''we want Iran and Russia to be addicted to heroin. It weakens their societies.'' Kiriakou draws a direct parallel to the current fentanyl crisis: China is doing to the US what the US did to Iran and Russia.

dewey-clarridge.title: Mecca Agreement
dewey-clarridge.summary: A trilateral mutual-defence pact between Pakistan, Turkey and Saudi Arabia signed in Mecca in August 2026. John Kiriakou treats it as the most consequential development in the region and one the American media largely ignored, because it makes three separate bilateral enmities collectively enforceable and leaves the United States out of the arrangement entirely.

dewey-clarridge.title: Saudi nuclear program
dewey-clarridge.summary: Saudi Arabia's decades-long pursuit of uranium enrichment, nominally for nuclear power, which John Kiriakou notes was already old news when he arrived at the CIA in 1990 and which conventional wisdom has always read as a weapons programme.

dewey-clarridge.title: Contra rebels
dewey-clarridge.summary: The right-wing Nicaraguan insurgency armed by the Reagan administration against the Sandinista government. In John Kiriakou's account they were conservatives, right-wingers, in some cases fascists, and disgruntled military officers; they were split into a northern group the United States armed and a southern group that financed itself by selling cocaine — a distinction that became the pivot of the Gary Webb affair, and that Kiriakou uses to answer the CIA's standing denial that it had anything to do with the drug trade.

dewey-clarridge.title: Jack Devine
dewey-clarridge.summary: A former CIA officer John Kiriakou worked for briefly in 2001 or 2002, and describes with real warmth as a great officer and a true believer — while flatly rejecting his insistence that the agency was never involved with cocaine. Asked to choose between Devine and a thirty-year DEA veteran who agrees with him, Kiriakou picks the DEA man.

dewey-clarridge.title: The rooftop double agent
dewey-clarridge.summary: A 2001 operation in which John Kiriakou flew out monthly to impersonate a station chief in meetings with a recruited double agent, and, after the hostile service ordered the agent to kill him, frightened the man on a hotel roof rather than confronting him.

dgse.title: Candace Owens
dgse.summary: The commentator whose claims about the killing of Charlie Kirk John Kiriakou has publicly declined to accept. He credits her reach and her intelligence and rejects her method, citing an earlier occasion — a conference call he says he was on — at which she claimed irrefutable proof that the Italian government had stolen the 2020 election and that its release would return Donald Trump to office.

dgse.title: Five Eyes
dgse.summary: The intelligence-sharing partnership of the United States, United Kingdom, Canada, Australia, and New Zealand

dgse.title: Central Intelligence Agency
dgse.summary: U.S. foreign intelligence service; John Kiriakou's employer from 1990 to 2004 and the central institution of KiriPedia

dgse.title: Death threats against Kiriakou
dgse.summary: The threats John Kiriakou has received across two decades — first after going public about the CIA torture program, when FBI advice that at least two were credible sent his family out of the country, and later in waves tied to his opposition to Gina Haspel, his remarks about Pakistan, and his advocacy on Palestine and the Epstein case.

dgse.title: JFK assassination
dgse.summary: November 22, 1963 killing of President John F. Kennedy in Dallas, Texas. John Kiriakou's position, drawn from a Pakistan-station encounter with Bay of Pigs commander Jean Gately, an RFK Jr. account of CIA Director John McCone's same-day exchange with Bobby Kennedy Sr., and a White House contact's confirmation that the remaining classified Kennedy documents all contain the word "Israel," is that elements of the CIA were probably involved and that Israeli intelligence was involved as well.

dgse.title: John Ratcliffe
dgse.summary: CIA director under Trump's second term; per John Kiriakou, a "bombthrower" he mostly disagrees with politically but supported as a needed disruptor for the agency — "a good guy, expert in what he does," though "not a visionary thinker" and, on Kiriakou's later assessment, a neocon who has outmanoeuvred Tulsi Gabbard for primacy over U.S. intelligence. Ratcliffe told the White House the CIA had no objection to pardoning Kiriakou.

dianne-feinstein.title: Senate Torture Report
dianne-feinstein.summary: The December 2014 executive summary of the U.S. Senate Select Committee on Intelligence's study of the CIA's post-9/11 detention and interrogation program; the first public disclosure of techniques including rectal feeding with hummus, sexual assault with broomsticks, and prolonged sleep deprivation.

dianne-feinstein.title: Bureau of Prisons
dianne-feinstein.summary: The federal agency that ran John Kiriakou's incarceration — and one of his most persistent post-prison targets. The BOP overrode his judge's camp recommendation by deeming him "a threat to the public safety," threatened him with "diesel therapy" until 1,600 logged phone calls and letters from a dozen House members and two senators backed it off, and, per Kiriakou, functions as "an employment agency for unemployable semi-literate rural white men" and "a dumping ground for failed medical professionals" — an agency for which a prisoner's death is cheaper than his treatment.

dianne-feinstein.title: Senate Intelligence Committee
dianne-feinstein.summary: The Senate Select Committee on Intelligence — the CIA's designated overseer, which John Kiriakou credits with the torture report's unimpeachable method (6 million contemporaneous CIA field cables) and simultaneously dismisses, along with its House counterpart, as "little more than cheerleaders for the CIA" since the mid-1980s. It sits in the official whistleblower channel he calls a proven dead end, and its own investigation was famously spied on by the very agency it oversees.

dianne-feinstein.title: John Kiriakou
dianne-feinstein.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

dianne-feinstein.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
dianne-feinstein.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

dianne-feinstein.title: The counterintelligence report that stopped
dianne-feinstein.summary: John Kiriakou's account of an annual FBI assessment of the worst counterintelligence threats to the United States that named Russia, China and Israel every year, reported each time by Newsweek's Jeff Stein — until, he says, Dianne Feinstein changed the rules so that the report no longer had to be issued.

diary-of-a-ceo-january-2026.title: John Kiriakou
diary-of-a-ceo-january-2026.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

diary-of-a-ceo-january-2026.title: Kent State shooting
diary-of-a-ceo-january-2026.summary: The 1970 shooting of unarmed student protesters by the Ohio National Guard; John Kiriakou says a family friend's daughter was among those killed — the closing event of a 1968–69 upheaval he treats both as the formation of his own politics and as the historical measure against which he judges the present.

diary-of-a-ceo-january-2026.title: Kiriakou cameo practice
diary-of-a-ceo-january-2026.summary: John Kiriakou's post-2026 use of the Cameo personalised-video service — running at roughly 25 to 30 hours a week, some 900 messages in the month of March 2026 alone, nearly 2,000 messages in total by July 2026 — that he says has produced three cases in which the person receiving the video message afterwards told him he had talked them out of committing suicide, including a 15-year-old bulimic girl to whom Kiriakou gave his personal phone number.

diary-of-a-ceo-january-2026.title: Alexa
diary-of-a-ceo-january-2026.summary: Per John Kiriakou, Amazon''s Alexa smart speaker reports directly to the NSA — and he owns one anyway. The device recurs across his interviews as the standing example of the surveillance trade-off in modern smart-home technology, and of his own negotiated exception to it: one speaker, in one room, against the advice of every intelligence officer he has ever known.

diary-of-a-ceo-january-2026.title: Carlos the Jackal
diary-of-a-ceo-january-2026.summary: Venezuelan-born militant (Ilich Ramírez Sánchez) active in the 1970s and 1980s; per John Kiriakou, 'the Osama bin Laden of the 70s and 80s.' Kiriakou spent his Athens posting trying to identify the middleman linking Carlos to the Greek terrorist group 17 November, then six months working the lead with MI5 in London; Carlos was finally run down by CIA contractor Billy Waugh in a Khartoum vegetable market and captured in 1994.

diary-of-a-ceo-january-2026.title: The CIA divorce rate
diary-of-a-ceo-january-2026.summary: John Kiriakou's account of why marriages fail at the CIA at a rate he says exceeds that of any other part of the U.S. government — the impossibility of explaining a midnight departure to a spouse without a clearance, and the difficulty officers have switching off a professional habit of deception. He gives the figure variously as over 75 percent and upwards of 80 percent, says he was determined not to become a statistic and became one anyway, and dates the end of his first marriage to a sentence spoken in an armoured car on the way to Athens airport. Both his divorces have been costly; of the second he says the agency played an active role he is barred by court order from explaining.

dick-cheney.title: Ross Ulbricht
dick-cheney.summary: Founder of the online marketplace Silk Road, sentenced to life plus 75 years before being pardoned by President Trump; John Kiriakou met Ulbricht's mother and sister two weeks before the pardon and calls the length of the original sentence a sickening miscarriage of justice.

dick-cheney.title: The Taft joke
dick-cheney.summary: The moment at a White House briefing that John Kiriakou offers as the whole difference between the two men at the top of the Bush administration — a self-deprecating crack about William Howard Taft that left the president helpless with laughter and the vice president standing like a statue.

dick-cheney.title: "When did you become a fascist?"
dick-cheney.summary: The exchange John Kiriakou recalls with a former intern of his, a Yale sophomore he had supervised in Bahrain in the mid-1990s who resurfaced ten years later as a Pentagon under-secretariat for intelligence hire, briefing the CIA on Iraq. Walking him to his car after the briefing, Kiriakou asked *"Michael, when did you become a fascist?"* and got the answer he uses to date the neoconservative capture of the Bush administration, *"We're in charge now. We're in charge and Saddam Hussein's going to die."*

dick-cheney.title: Abraham Bolden
dick-cheney.summary: The first African-American Secret Service agent assigned to a presidential detail; per John Kiriakou, he quite literally saved John F. Kennedy's life in Chicago in October 1963 and was subjected to overt racism by fellow agents, who told him to his face they would not protect Kennedy from assassination because of his civil-rights sympathies.

dick-cheney.title: CIA/FBI Budget Fearmongering
dick-cheney.summary: John Kiriakou's account of how the FBI, under J. Edgar Hoover, pioneered the tactic of citing a shifting parade of enemies before Congress to justify annual budget increases — communists, anarchists, gangsters, beatniks, anti-war protesters — a tactic the CIA later adopted wholesale, citing "communism" until 2001 and "terrorism" since, without needing further explanation to win budget increases.

dick-cheney.title: Richard Perle
dick-cheney.summary: Prominent neoconservative adviser to the George W. Bush White House whom John Kiriakou credits with planting the idea of invading Iraq in Dick Cheney's mind the day after 9/11.

dick-clarke.title: The Condoleezza Rice meeting
dick-clarke.summary: The nine o'clock White House appointment John Kiriakou and Cofer Black never kept on the morning of 11 September 2001. The Government Printing Office was about to issue a volume of declassified Greece-Turkey-Cyprus cables in an edition of five or ten copies; three of them named CIA sources who were still alive, and an obscure statute obliges the government to offer citizenship and resettlement to any recruited source it outs. The two men were going to ask the National Security Advisor to quietly pull three cables nobody would miss. The car was at the East entrance at 8.15.

dick-clarke.title: Cofer Black
dick-clarke.summary: Former head of the CIA Counterterrorism Center during and immediately after the September 11 attacks; principal architect of the agency's paramilitary turn on September 12, 2001; later Vice President of Blackwater under Erik Prince.

dick-clarke.title: Condoleezza Rice
dick-clarke.summary: U.S. National Security Advisor on 9/11; John Kiriakou had a meeting booked with her that morning, watched her tell George Tenet to "take one for the team" rather than correct the record on Abu Zubaydah, and offers her failure to act on the CIA's warnings as his alternative to any theory that the attacks were allowed to happen.

dick-clarke.title: Langley
dick-clarke.summary: The Virginia location of CIA headquarters and, in John Kiriakou''s usage, shorthand for the agency''s permanent power. It''s where he worked as the CIA''s lone Iraq-Kuwait analyst — told to start on Iraq "because nothing ever happened there" — where a cafeteria conversation invited him into the torture program, where he walked past the Kryptos sculpture every day for fifteen years without solving it, and the place agencies return to after apologizing to Congress, "where of course nothing ever changes." When a host suggested the real government of America is out in Langley and Washington''s white marble is for show, Kiriakou''s answer was: "that''s about the shape of it."

dick-clarke.title: Osama bin Laden
dick-clarke.summary: Founder and leader of al-Qaeda and the central target of the manhunt that shaped John Kiriakou's counterterrorism career. Per Kiriakou, bin Laden came from a billionaire Saudi construction family, was never one of the CIA-funded Afghan mujahideen, overruled subordinates who wanted to attack Israel and insisted the 9/11 attacks hit the United States to crash its economy, escaped Tora Bora dressed as a woman, and spent his final years next to Pakistan's equivalent of West Point — where, Kiriakou says, you would have to be a "mental defective" not to know he was there. Kiriakou believes the United States never intended to capture him alive.

dick-clarke.title: Alex Station
dick-clarke.summary: CIA unit that tracked Osama bin Laden beginning in 1995; per John Kiriakou, who served as chief of its counterintelligence branch, the unit kept extremely tight security around its files, limited FBI investigators' access to information about future 9/11 hijackers Khaled al-Mihdhar and Nawaf al-Hazmi, and — under a deliberate policy of non-cooperation with the FBI — failed to watchlist participants in the Malaysia summit where al-Qaeda planned the attacks.

diesel-therapy.title: FCI Loretto
diesel-therapy.summary: U.S. Federal Correctional Institution in Loretto, Pennsylvania; the low-medium-security prison at which John Kiriakou served 23 months of a 30-month sentence following his 2013 Espionage Act–era plea deal; the originally ordered "minimum security work camp" placement was countermanded — per Kiriakou, on Brennan's direct intervention — to place him in the actual prison alongside the general population.

diesel-therapy.title: Bureau of Prisons
diesel-therapy.summary: The federal agency that ran John Kiriakou's incarceration — and one of his most persistent post-prison targets. The BOP overrode his judge's camp recommendation by deeming him "a threat to the public safety," threatened him with "diesel therapy" until 1,600 logged phone calls and letters from a dozen House members and two senators backed it off, and, per Kiriakou, functions as "an employment agency for unemployable semi-literate rural white men" and "a dumping ground for failed medical professionals" — an agency for which a prisoner's death is cheaper than his treatment.

diesel-therapy.title: John Kiriakou
diesel-therapy.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

diesel-therapy.title: Letter from Loretto
diesel-therapy.summary: Prison newsletter written by John Kiriakou from FCI Loretto, modeled on Martin Luther King's "Letter from Birmingham Jail," which exposed two crimes committed against him by guards and went viral after being relayed to the Huffington Post, drawing national press to the prison.

diesel-therapy.title: This desk kills fascism
diesel-therapy.summary: The sign Kiriakou taped to the cell desk on which he wrote the letters from Loretto, borrowed from Woody Guthrie's guitar, torn down by a guard within hours and kept by Kiriakou ever since.

diesel-therapy.title: Critical Analytic Thinking
diesel-therapy.summary: Per John Kiriakou, the foundational discipline of CIA analyst training and the most practically valuable skill he carried into civilian life: questioning all incoming information — including, especially, sources whose ideological positions align with one''s own — and arriving at conclusions from evidence rather than prior belief. Kiriakou cites his own COVID lab-leak conclusion, reached against his initial instinct, as an example of the method in practice.

dig-a-hole-and-put-him-in-the-hole.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
dig-a-hole-and-put-him-in-the-hole.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

dig-a-hole-and-put-him-in-the-hole.title: Jose Rodriguez
dig-a-hole-and-put-him-in-the-hole.summary: Senior CIA officer of the post-9/11 era; identified by John Kiriakou as among those responsible for crimes committed in the name of national security; described as believing himself to be a good guy.

dig-a-hole-and-put-him-in-the-hole.title: Mitchell and Jessen
dig-a-hole-and-put-him-in-the-hole.summary: The two American psychologists who pitched the CIA's enhanced interrogation program to Director George Tenet at a cocktail party in late October 2001; designers of the program and its theoretical underpinning, "learned helplessness."

dig-a-hole-and-put-him-in-the-hole.title: The Pineapple Militia case
dig-a-hole-and-put-him-in-the-hole.summary: The Miami FBI entrapment prosecution in which, per John Kiriakou's July 2026 testimony as a defense expert witness by video from Athens, federal agents recruited a homeless, mentally ill Muslim man living in an alley behind a restaurant into a fictitious militia they called the "pineapple militia," proposed targets he had never proposed, refused four of his refusals to join, wrote a plot to bomb the New York Stock Exchange, built the bomb themselves, and arrested him when they handed it to him. Kiriakou uses the case as the canonical example of what he says are the 99 per cent of FBI terrorism cases that are fabricated.

dig-a-hole-and-put-him-in-the-hole.title: George Tenet
dig-a-hole-and-put-him-in-the-hole.summary: Director of Central Intelligence from 1997 to 2004, spanning the September 11 attacks and the early enhanced-interrogation program; identified by John Kiriakou as John Brennan's institutional patron at the agency; the figure who ordered the Five Eyes intelligence services to "open the files" to each other in the early 2000s.

dig-a-hole-and-put-him-in-the-hole.title: Gina Haspel
dig-a-hole-and-put-him-in-the-hole.summary: Director of the Central Intelligence Agency under President Trump's first term; known to John Kiriakou and others at the CIA as "Bloody Gina"; per Kiriakou, flew out to the secret black site to sit in on one of the enhanced-interrogation torture sessions "just because she could," personally supervised the torture of USS Cole bombing suspect Rahim al-Nashiri, and later fed the CIA's torture tapes into an industrial document grinder after being explicitly told by White House Counsel not to destroy them.

dilmun-burial-mounds.title: Abdul Amir al-Jamri
dilmun-burial-mounds.summary: The Bahraini cleric who led the Shia opposition during the 1990s uprising, and whom John Kiriakou interviewed for a human rights report in 1991 — an interview that had the Bahraini prime minister demanding, within the hour, that both American officers be expelled from the country.

dilmun-burial-mounds.title: The Bahrain water table
dilmun-burial-mounds.summary: The prehistoric aquifer that surfaces in Bahrain — running, in John Kiriakou's telling, from the Atlantic beneath the whole of Africa — which until the 1970s gushed out of the ground in natural springs and made the island an oasis, and which overdevelopment has since dropped some thirty-five feet.

dilmun-burial-mounds.title: Bahrain Posting (1994–1996)
dilmun-burial-mounds.summary: John Kiriakou's 1994–1996 assignment to Bahrain under U.S. State Department cover as second secretary for economic affairs — arriving with his wife Joanne and infant son Chris on August 1, 1994, into a tiny Gulf monarchy whose sectarian tensions erupted, two months later, into the first Intifada.

dilmun-burial-mounds.title: Bahrain Intifada (1994)
dilmun-burial-mounds.summary: The first Bahraini Intifada, a Shia uprising against the Sunni Al Khalifa monarchy that began roughly two months into John Kiriakou's 1994 Bahrain posting with a bombing at the Ministry of Labor, led by Abdul Amir Al-Jamri, and met by the government first with police, then armored personnel carriers and tanks, and executions.

dilmun-burial-mounds.title: The Gulf Daily News
dilmun-burial-mounds.summary: Bahrain's English-language newspaper, and the source John Kiriakou turned to when a bomb went off at the Ministry of Labour two months into his posting — its Indian reporter, whose telephone was bugged like his own, told him a civil uprising was about to explode.

dilmun-burial-mounds.title: Bahrain Prime Minister "Mr. 10 Percent"
dilmun-burial-mounds.summary: John Kiriakou's account of Bahrain's long-serving prime minister, the Amir's uncle, universally nicknamed "Mr. 10 Percent" for allegedly requiring a 10 percent cash cut on business deals — a cold, calculating figure Kiriakou calls "the definition of corruption," pointedly excluded from the national motto, yet credited with turning Bahrain into the Gulf's banking hub.

dimitris-koufodinas.title: Revolutionary Organization 17 November
dimitris-koufodinas.summary: Greek far-left urban guerrilla group active 1975–2002; the deadliest terrorist organization in Greek history

dimitris-koufodinas.title: Stephen Saunders
dimitris-koufodinas.summary: British defense attaché in Athens assassinated by Revolutionary Organization 17 November in March 2000

dimitris-koufodinas.title: The Welch .45
dimitris-koufodinas.summary: The single .45 caliber pistol used by Revolutionary Organization 17 November in every confirmed assassination over the group's twenty-seven-year operational life
