epstein-statute-of-limitations.title: Les Wexner
epstein-statute-of-limitations.summary: Ohio billionaire retail magnate; John Kiriakou cites Vanity Fair allegations that Wexner funneled millions to Jeffrey Epstein as his 'tax advisor,' offering it as evidence for his own view that Epstein's money and access served the Israelis.

epstein-statute-of-limitations.title: "All it takes is a signature"
epstein-statute-of-limitations.summary: John Kiriakou's answer, drawn from his years as a Senate investigator, to the claim that Congress had run out of time to obtain the Epstein flight logs — that a committee's investigative power is exercised by one senator signing a piece of paper, which can be done at any hour, and that the excuse is therefore not a sensible one.

epstein-statute-of-limitations.title: The Epstein files and the Starmer government
epstein-statute-of-limitations.summary: John Kiriakou's prediction that the Epstein disclosures could bring down Keir Starmer's government, on the strength of evidence that Prince Andrew and Peter Mandelson gave Epstein classified British Ministry of Defence documents — an Official Secrets Act matter that in America would fall under the Espionage Act.

epstein-statute-of-limitations.title: The Trilateral Commission
epstein-statute-of-limitations.summary: The body John Kiriakou says he used to dismiss as conspiracy-theory material until someone close to him attended one of its meetings and told him what was actually discussed there: arms deals — and at Davos, how to manage the global economy.

erbil-and-the-kurdish-autonomy-question.title: 2026 Iran war
erbil-and-the-kurdish-autonomy-question.summary: The open-ended American and Israeli war against Iran that John Kiriakou tracked week by week on his own show — a conflict he says was sold as three weeks, ran into its fifth month, achieved every decapitation objective it set, and continued anyway. His grade for it is a D, and his forecast is a Truth Social post declaring victory while nothing changes.

erbil-and-the-kurdish-autonomy-question.title: "A policy support organization"
erbil-and-the-kurdish-autonomy-question.summary: Asked how the CIA workforce would be reacting to the war on Iran, John Kiriakou answered from the Iraq war: people put their heads down and did as they were told, after a boss told an assembled group — all of whom opposed the invasion — that the agency is not a policy organization but a policy support organization, and would do what the White House told it to do.

erbil-and-the-kurdish-autonomy-question.title: Akrotiri Village Evacuation
erbil-and-the-kurdish-autonomy-question.summary: Kiriakou says the drone that hit Britain's Akrotiri base in Cyprus was likely an Israeli operation, staged and then falsely blamed on Iran.

erbil-and-the-kurdish-autonomy-question.title: Al Jazeera blocked in the United States
erbil-and-the-kurdish-autonomy-question.summary: Within hours of the first strikes on Iran, John Kiriakou reported that American cable carriers had pulled Al Jazeera — a friend in Florida texted him that Dish Network had blocked it, and viewers reported the same of Comcast Xfinity in Boston. His reading was blunt: they do not want Americans to see what is happening in the Middle East.

erbil-and-the-kurdish-autonomy-question.title: American missile stockpiles
erbil-and-the-kurdish-autonomy-question.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that the United States has run its interceptor stocks down to the point of strategic vulnerability — that the conventional wisdom in Washington was that a round of the Iran war ended because the Patriots ran out, and that a country which cannot fight a two-front war certainly cannot do it below maximum production.

erbil-and-the-kurdish-autonomy-question.title: Andrew Bustamante
erbil-and-the-kurdish-autonomy-question.summary: Former CIA officer who sells CIA-style training online; John Kiriakou identifies him as the lone critic of his work hosting a show on a Russian network, and argues Bustamante's training business — open to anyone who pays — is the more problematic of the two.

eric-holder.title: John Brennan
eric-holder.summary: Former Director of the CIA; characterized in KiriPedia's source corpus as the principal architect of the agency's enhanced interrogation program and as having plotted against an elected President

eric-holder.title: Brian Ross
eric-holder.summary: American investigative journalist and seven-time Emmy Award winner who was a prominent reporter at ABC News when, in December 2007, he conducted the on-camera interview with John Kiriakou that produced the first public confirmation by a U.S. official that the CIA waterboarded prisoners. Per Kiriakou, Ross called him out of the blue with the assertion that a source said Kiriakou had personally tortured Abu Zubaydah; Kiriakou's decision to give the interview anyway — driven by the conclusion that 'Brian Ross's source is at the White House and they're going to pin this on me' — became the pivot point of his entire post-CIA life.

eric-holder.title: Ali Soufan
eric-holder.summary: FBI special agent who handled Abu Zubaydah immediately after his March 2002 capture; through patient, respectful interrogation produced the only actionable intelligence ever obtained from the detainee, including the first identification of "Mukhtar" as Khalid Sheikh Mohammed.

eric-holder.title: Espionage Act
eric-holder.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

eric-holder.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
eric-holder.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

eric-holder.title: David Petraeus
eric-holder.summary: Retired U.S. Army general and director of the CIA who, per John Kiriakou, confirmed the names of ten covert CIA operatives to his biographer and girlfriend and was never criminally charged — a contrast Kiriakou cites repeatedly as proof that his own prosecution under the Intelligence Identities Protection Act was selective. Kiriakou''s explanation for the disparity: Petraeus had not blown the whistle on the torture program and embarrassed the agency.

eric-oneill.title: Harold James Nicholson
eric-oneill.summary: Former CIA Station Chief, Singapore; the third major modern CIA mole for the Russians after Aldrich Ames and Robert Hanssen. Per John Kiriakou, Nicholson was a senior officer at the CIA Counterterrorism Center during Kiriakou's tenure there. Sentenced to 31 years and seven months in 1997. While in prison, attempted to recruit his own son to act as a courier between him and the Russian intelligence service so his espionage payments could continue to compound for his eventual release — and was caught when his son walked up to the Russian embassy in Washington under FBI surveillance.

eric-oneill.title: Robert Hanssen
eric-oneill.summary: FBI counterintelligence chief and Soviet/Russian mole; framed CIA counterintelligence chief Brian Kelley as the source of compromised assets — leading the FBI to surveil Kelly for a year and a half and threaten his family with the death penalty — before Hanssen himself was identified as the actual traitor.

eric-oneill.title: Brian Kelley
eric-oneill.summary: Chief of counterintelligence at the CIA; framed by FBI counterintelligence chief Robert Hanssen — the actual Soviet/Russian mole — as the source of executed agents; spent a year and a half on leave without pay, surrounded around the clock by FBI agents, while his daughter was approached and told her father would face the death penalty if he did not confess.

eric-oneill.title: Cuban double agents
eric-oneill.summary: John Kiriakou's assessment of Cuban intelligence as one of the best services on the planet, defensive in nature and trained by the KGB, and his flat claim — repeated across several tellings — that the CIA has never recruited a Cuban who did not turn out to be working for Havana all along.

eric-oneill.title: Afghan heroin policy
eric-oneill.summary: The post-2001 U.S. policy in Afghanistan of protecting, and per John Kiriakou actively encouraging, the cultivation of heroin poppy. Under the Taliban in 2000 Afghanistan produced 0% of the world's heroin; by 2009 under American occupation it produced 93%. Per a DEA officer Kiriakou consulted with on the policy paper he was preparing for Senator Kerry, the strategic rationale was that nearly all of the heroin flowed to Iran and Russia, addiction in those countries was considered desirable as a long-run societal weakener, and the same logic now operates in reverse with Chinese fentanyl flowing into the United States.

eric-oneill.title: Ai Weiwei
eric-oneill.summary: Chinese contemporary artist and pro-democracy activist; designer of the Beijing Olympic Stadium; per John Kiriakou, produced a Lego portrait of him as one of 178 political prisoners in the series, with Kiriakou's panel positioned next to Martin Luther King Jr.; the work is now in the permanent collection of the Smithsonian Institution.

eric-swallwell.title: Church Committee
eric-swallwell.summary: U.S. Senate investigative committee operating in 1975–1976 that examined domestic intelligence abuses by the CIA, FBI, and NSA; per John Kiriakou, the Church Committee — alongside the concurrent Pike Committee in the House — was the last genuine moment of legislative oversight over the intelligence community, born of a national consensus that government had gone dangerously off course. Its work led to the creation of the permanent Senate Select Committee on Intelligence, which Kiriakou says ceased to function as real oversight roughly seven years after its founding.

eric-swallwell.title: Mexican 9 Month Work Visas
eric-swallwell.summary: A George W. Bush-administration proposal, negotiated with Mexico in the six to eight months before 9/11, to give undocumented Mexican workers renewable nine-month U.S. work visas requiring federal income tax payment — killed by the September 11 attacks before it could be ratified.

eric-swallwell.title: Central Intelligence Agency
eric-swallwell.summary: U.S. foreign intelligence service; John Kiriakou's employer from 1990 to 2004 and the central institution of KiriPedia

eric-swallwell.title: Jose Rodriguez
eric-swallwell.summary: Senior CIA officer of the post-9/11 era; identified by John Kiriakou as among those responsible for crimes committed in the name of national security; described as believing himself to be a good guy.

eric-swallwell.title: Trump
eric-swallwell.summary: Kiriakou applied for a pardon on the last day of Trump's first term — and says Trump had agreed to it, until the last-minute reversal.

eric-swallwell.title: Mexico City as an espionage hub
eric-swallwell.summary: John Kiriakou''s assessment of Mexico City as one of the world''s principal centres of international espionage, alongside Vienna, London, Paris and Washington — driven by a gargantuan American embassy that Russian services target from next door — and his reading of why Mexico simply ignored a dossier of suspected Russian officers handed over by the Biden administration.

erik-prince.title: Blackwater
erik-prince.summary: The private military contractor founded by Erik Prince that ran the CIA's Global Response Staff and, until shut down by Leon Panetta, a global assassination program; staffed at the board level with former CIA officers including Cofer Black as Vice President.

erik-prince.title: Cofer Black
erik-prince.summary: Former head of the CIA Counterterrorism Center during and immediately after the September 11 attacks; principal architect of the agency's paramilitary turn on September 12, 2001; later Vice President of Blackwater under Erik Prince.

erik-prince.title: Leon Panetta
erik-prince.summary: CIA Director under President Obama (2009–2011) and subsequent Secretary of Defense; per John Kiriakou, the official who on arrival as Director shut down the Blackwater-operated CIA worldwide assassination program — and in the course of explaining the decision to the House Intelligence Committee publicly outed Erik Prince. Also one of Kiriakou's two go-to examples (with David Petraeus) of senior intelligence figures who disclosed the identities of covert CIA officers without consequence while Kiriakou himself was prosecuted for the same statute.

erik-prince.title: Tyrell Vanto
erik-prince.summary: Hollywood screenwriter and director; son of Jesse Vanto; friend of John Kiriakou; wrote and directed the late-2025 film in which Kiriakou made his acting debut.

erik-prince.title: John Kiriakou
erik-prince.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

erik-prince.title: Jeff Fahey
erik-prince.summary: American actor; star of the Tyrell Vanto film in which John Kiriakou made his acting debut in late 2025; characterized by Kiriakou as generous with his time and on-set advice.

espionage-act.title: The Department of Education SWAT raid
espionage-act.summary: John Kiriakou's account of a pre-dawn armed raid on the home of a Washington Times journalist and her husband, an official at the Department of Education — carried out, he says, by the Department of Education's own armed SWAT team, which seized the reporter's notes and refused to return them. He uses the episode to point out that several civilian federal departments maintain armed tactical units, and that no other journalist covered it.

espionage-act.title: Jack Teixeira
espionage-act.summary: Massachusetts Air National Guard reservist arrested in April 2023 for leaking classified Pentagon documents to a small Discord server. John Kiriakou, discussing the case the day after Teixeira's arrest, initially suspected a covert action program rather than a genuine leak, ultimately concluded Teixeira was not a whistleblower, and predicted — correctly — that he would be charged under the Espionage Act and take a plea bargain.

espionage-act.title: "I''m a non-person"
espionage-act.summary: The phrase John Kiriakou uses for his standing after prison: a former colleague was sent to deliver congratulations from a mutual friend who had risen to a senior administration post, together with the message that he could never speak to Kiriakou again. Kiriakou pairs it with the loss of his federal pension after nineteen and a half years of service, and with the fact that in eight years no other CIA officer joined him in speaking publicly.

espionage-act.title: Obama's drone escalation
espionage-act.summary: The pair of figures John Kiriakou uses to measure what changed between the Bush and Obama administrations — twenty-four people killed by drones in George W. Bush's last month in office against four hundred and forty in Barack Obama's — offered as the answer to anyone who treats the drone programme as an inherited policy rather than an expanded one.

espionage-act.title: The pillow-talk disclosure case
espionage-act.summary: A case John Kiriakou witnessed from the next desk: a CIA officer told a classified fact to a former senior officer turned CNN commentator during an affair, he repeated it on air, and the agency identified her within days. Her punishment was four weeks'' suspension without pay and a memo in her file. Kiriakou uses it as the benchmark for how far the handling of disclosures has moved — today, he says, it would be an Espionage Act prosecution and about five years in prison.

espionage-act.title: The Bolton raid
espionage-act.summary: John Kiriakou's reading of the August 2025 FBI search of John Bolton's home and office — that emailing national defense information to family members is the Espionage Act's definition of espionage, on a precedent set in Kiriakou's own case — together with the FBI evidence sticker he says is still on the back of his own computer.

ethan-mccord-collateral-murder.title: Ai Whistleblower Initiative
ethan-mccord-collateral-murder.summary: The AI Whistleblower Initiative, working on legal protections for the wave of whistleblowers now coming out of the artificial-intelligence industry.

ethan-mccord-collateral-murder.title: Andrew Feinstein
ethan-mccord-collateral-murder.summary: Referenced on the same WikiLeaks-conference panel as John Kiriakou; the description of Feinstein's talk on the multiple factors that ended apartheid was given by another panelist putting a question to Kiriakou, not by Kiriakou himself.

ethan-mccord-collateral-murder.title: Belmarsh Prison
ethan-mccord-collateral-murder.summary: The maximum-security London prison where Julian Assange was held for years on a bail-jumping sentence John Kiriakou calls a fabrication — kept in solitary confinement alongside the worst offenders in the United Kingdom, and held past the expiry of his sentence at the request of the United States. Kiriakou corresponded with Assange there and watched the letters change.

ethan-mccord-collateral-murder.title: Chaos Computer Club Wikileaks
ethan-mccord-collateral-murder.summary: The Berlin hacker collective that shaped WikiLeaks' early years — and where a journalist first met Daniel Domscheit-Berg under a pseudonym.

ethan-mccord-collateral-murder.title: Chelsea Manning
ethan-mccord-collateral-murder.summary: Former U.S. Army intelligence analyst who provided WikiLeaks its 2010 trove of military and diplomatic documents. Per John Kiriakou, Manning meets the legal definition of whistleblower for exposing war crimes, was a torture victim of prolonged solitary confinement with forced nudity, and was sentenced to 35 years in prison before Barack Obama commuted — not pardoned — her sentence. Kiriakou says Manning later refused a grand jury's offer of immunity and chose renewed jail time rather than testify against Julian Assange.

ethan-mccord-collateral-murder.title: Afghan War Logs
ethan-mccord-collateral-murder.summary: A 2010 WikiLeaks publication discussed on a panel Kiriakou joined; the specific lines about it in the corpus belong to other panelists, not Kiriakou.

europe-and-the-2026-iran-war.title: Europe's 2026 jet fuel crisis
europe-and-the-2026-iran-war.summary: The Associated Press report, which John Kiriakou opened his programme with on 16 April 2026, that Europe would run out of jet fuel within six weeks — a shortage he called an economic calamity that would ripple across the entire planet, and which the economist Richard D. Wolff traced not to any shortage of crude but to the closure of the Strait of Hormuz starving the refineries that convert petroleum into jet fuel.

europe-and-the-2026-iran-war.title: 2026 Iran war
europe-and-the-2026-iran-war.summary: The open-ended American and Israeli war against Iran that John Kiriakou tracked week by week on his own show — a conflict he says was sold as three weeks, ran into its fifth month, achieved every decapitation objective it set, and continued anyway. His grade for it is a D, and his forecast is a Truth Social post declaring victory while nothing changes.

europe-and-the-2026-iran-war.title: Richard D. Wolff
europe-and-the-2026-iran-war.summary: American Marxian economist, professor emeritus at the University of Massachusetts Amherst and a recurring guest of John Kiriakou, who calls him one of his favourite people and says he feels smarter after every conversation; Wolff's appearances supply Kiriakou's audience with a class analysis of tariffs, federal debt and the periodic crashes of capitalism.

europe-and-the-2026-iran-war.title: 2026 Iran war economic shock
europe-and-the-2026-iran-war.summary: John Kiriakou''s running assessment of the economic damage from the 2026 Iran war — an oil shock he says already exceeds both 1970s shocks combined, a natural-gas shock worse than the Nord Stream destruction, and a chokepoint problem that runs through fertilizer as much as fuel, since 65% of the world''s supply must transit the Strait of Hormuz. His summary: "This is an economic slowdown of choice."

europe-and-the-2026-iran-war.title: The 2026 strike wave
europe-and-the-2026-iran-war.summary: The proliferation of American strikes in early 2026, from Minneapolis to the Southern California ports, which John Kiriakou raised alongside a February reversal in the job market and the question of whether union membership was rising after years of decline. The economist Richard D. Wolff's answer placed it in the ordinary rhythm of capitalist downturns and ended on employers squeezing workers who were, he said, beginning to really fight back.

europe-and-the-2026-iran-war.title: China as economic threat
europe-and-the-2026-iran-war.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that China is the real threat to the West not militarily — it has one aircraft carrier to America's two dozen and rarely invades — but economically, buying friends worldwide while the U.S. spends a trillion dollars a year on weapons.

europe-jet-fuel-crisis-2026.title: Europe and the 2026 Iran war
europe-jet-fuel-crisis-2026.summary: The rupture between the United States and its European allies over the 2026 Iran war, as the economist Richard D. Wolff described it on John Kiriakou''s programme: Europe was not told the attack was coming, refused Donald Trump''s request for help halfway through it, and was then publicly attacked by him for refusing. Wolff''s verdict was that the alliance did not survive it — ''NATO is dead, the alliance is dead, and the blame for it is 100% on the US.''

europe-jet-fuel-crisis-2026.title: Richard D. Wolff
europe-jet-fuel-crisis-2026.summary: American Marxian economist, professor emeritus at the University of Massachusetts Amherst and a recurring guest of John Kiriakou, who calls him one of his favourite people and says he feels smarter after every conversation; Wolff's appearances supply Kiriakou's audience with a class analysis of tariffs, federal debt and the periodic crashes of capitalism.

europe-jet-fuel-crisis-2026.title: 2026 Iran war economic shock
europe-jet-fuel-crisis-2026.summary: John Kiriakou''s running assessment of the economic damage from the 2026 Iran war — an oil shock he says already exceeds both 1970s shocks combined, a natural-gas shock worse than the Nord Stream destruction, and a chokepoint problem that runs through fertilizer as much as fuel, since 65% of the world''s supply must transit the Strait of Hormuz. His summary: "This is an economic slowdown of choice."

europe-jet-fuel-crisis-2026.title: Strait of Hormuz
europe-jet-fuel-crisis-2026.summary: The shipping chokepoint at the mouth of the Persian Gulf, and the centre of gravity of the 2026 Iran war in John Kiriakou''s account — a strait whose only navigable deep water lies on the Iranian side of the maritime border, closed not by Iran''s aggression but, as he insists, by the American and Israeli attack that provoked it: "The Strait of Hormuz was open. We''re the ones that forced the closure."

europe-jet-fuel-crisis-2026.title: 2026 Iran war
europe-jet-fuel-crisis-2026.summary: The open-ended American and Israeli war against Iran that John Kiriakou tracked week by week on his own show — a conflict he says was sold as three weeks, ran into its fifth month, achieved every decapitation objective it set, and continued anyway. His grade for it is a D, and his forecast is a Truth Social post declaring victory while nothing changes.

europe-jet-fuel-crisis-2026.title: The 2026 strike wave
europe-jet-fuel-crisis-2026.summary: The proliferation of American strikes in early 2026, from Minneapolis to the Southern California ports, which John Kiriakou raised alongside a February reversal in the job market and the question of whether union membership was rising after years of decline. The economist Richard D. Wolff's answer placed it in the ordinary rhythm of capitalist downturns and ended on employers squeezing workers who were, he said, beginning to really fight back.

europe-without-russian-gas.title: Nuclear war is winnable
europe-without-russian-gas.summary: The belief John Kiriakou says is held by a real faction in both Ukraine and the United States: that a nuclear exchange can be survived and won. He traces the American version to Pat Buchanan''s 1992 presidential campaign — we come out from our caves and continue the fight — and reconstructs the Ukrainian version as a bet that if Russia went nuclear, the American, British and French arsenals would answer. He calls the reasoning insanity and thinks it is nonetheless being done.

europe-without-russian-gas.title: Kiriakou's Ukraine settlement prediction
europe-without-russian-gas.summary: The endgame John Kiriakou forecast in June 2025 and calls deliberately unbold: Russia keeps the disputed eastern territories and Crimea, Ukraine never joins NATO but probably joins the European Union, and Moscow gets ninety per cent of what it wanted. The one demand he expects Russia to trade away is denazification, which he reads as propaganda rather than policy.

europe-without-russian-gas.title: The Panda card
europe-without-russian-gas.summary: The Chinese national payment card John Kiriakou encountered in Hong Kong, where he found few places willing to take Mastercard or Visa. Asked why, he was given a one-sentence answer about routing: Visa and Mastercard transactions pass through New York, Panda card transactions pass through Shanghai, and so fall outside the reach of American sanctions. He treats it as both an instance of Chinese strategic competence and an argument that the American card duopoly is a racket.

europe-without-russian-gas.title: Ukraine as a proxy war
europe-without-russian-gas.summary: John Kiriakou's assessment, given two months into the 2022 Russian invasion, that the United States was funding a proxy war it knew Ukraine could not win in order to bog Russia down — and that the outcome was already fixed, so peace talks should happen at once.

europe-without-russian-gas.title: Operation Spiderweb
europe-without-russian-gas.summary: The Ukrainian drone attack on Russia's strategic bomber fleet in June 2025, which John Kiriakou calls a brilliant operation and — against Volodymyr Zelensky's account — one Ukraine could not have run alone. Eighteen months of preparation, drones smuggled across eleven time zones by human couriers, and command from Kyiv all required outside help, he argues; and Donald Trump's uncharacteristic public silence afterwards is his evidence that Washington was in on it.

europe-without-russian-gas.title: The scholar-in-residence pipeline
europe-without-russian-gas.summary: John Kiriakou's description of retired CIA operations officers taking scholar-in-residence posts at universities and teaching literature courses that function, by their own account, as a recruitment funnel — students enrol knowing the instructor is a former officer and hoping for help getting in.

evangelical-zionism.title: The Iron Dome
evangelical-zionism.summary: Israel's air-defence system as John Kiriakou reads it — impressive against a wave of slow Iranian drones, but shown by the handful that got through, and later by Iranian ballistic missiles, to be not all it is cracked up to be; each exchange, in his account, buying Iran intelligence about the gaps.

evangelical-zionism.title: The Greek Orthodox Church
evangelical-zionism.summary: The church John Kiriakou was raised in and still belongs to — the institution behind his Greek fluency and his family''s immigrant history, a recurring thread in his accounts of Athens, Damascus, Bethlehem and Washington, and, in two cases, an actor in his own story: the church the FBI followed him into, and the priest who tried to get him a pardon.

evangelical-zionism.title: The Litani River
evangelical-zionism.summary: The largest natural water source in the Middle East, which John Kiriakou says makes southern Lebanon more valuable than oil — and the northern edge of the depopulated strip he describes Israel creating there.

evangelical-zionism.title: Abraham Accords
evangelical-zionism.summary: The Trump-brokered normalization deals between Israel and Gulf Arab states — in John Kiriakou's judgment "a terrible idea in the first place," a great victory for Israel and the Gulf Arabs that was "a punch in the throat to the Palestinians." He argues the Accords are how Trump meant to "solve the Middle East in a day" — by screwing the Palestinians — that Hamas read the abandonment correctly, that October 7 shattered the project, and that reviving the Accords (Saudis in, victory declared, Nobel collected) remains the organizing goal of Trump's regional policy.

evangelical-zionism.title: American missile stockpiles
evangelical-zionism.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that the United States has run its interceptor stocks down to the point of strategic vulnerability — that the conventional wisdom in Washington was that a round of the Iran war ended because the Patriots ran out, and that a country which cannot fight a two-front war certainly cannot do it below maximum production.

evangelical-zionism.title: Arnon Milchan
evangelical-zionism.summary: Israeli-American Hollywood producer and, per John Kiriakou, an Israeli super-spy and arms dealer for LAKAM; central to a Netanyahu corruption charge, and named in FBI documents alongside Netanyahu in the smuggling of U.S. nuclear secrets.

every-israeli-i-ever-knew.title: Declare victory and go home
every-israeli-i-ever-knew.summary: The exit John Kiriakou prescribed for Israel in Gaza: turn the territory back to the United Nations, declare Hamas destroyed, declare victory, then engage the Saudis on the Abraham Accords and negotiate a deal later. His reasoning was that nothing remained to destroy, that killing as many people as possible is not a viable policy, and that Israel had no other way out.

every-israeli-i-ever-knew.title: The other five percent
every-israeli-i-ever-knew.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of Israeli intelligence operations inside the United States: that for decades Israeli officers have been spread across the country trying to penetrate American defence contractors and steal defence secrets — because, in his formulation, Washington gives Israel ninety-five per cent of what it has, and Israel wants the remaining five.

every-israeli-i-ever-knew.title: Palestine House
every-israeli-i-ever-knew.summary: The Washington, DC meeting space and gallery for pro-Palestinian human rights groups, artists and musicians that John Kiriakou describes as newly opened on Capitol Hill — housed in a building donated by a Lebanese-American property developer, running programming several nights a week, and headed by Miko Peled.

every-israeli-i-ever-knew.title: The airbridge
every-israeli-i-ever-knew.summary: John Kiriakou''s definition of an airbridge, given when the term surfaced in reporting on German aid to Gaza: a direct path into another country''s airspace along which safety is guaranteed — his worked example being Cyprus to Gaza, with an undertaking that the Israeli Air Force will not shoot the aircraft down.

every-israeli-i-ever-knew.title: Bigger than the Russian embassy
every-israeli-i-ever-knew.summary: Why American embassies in small, strategically unimportant countries are enormous: the answer John Kiriakou says he was given by a station chief on one of his first CIA trips — that the building had to be bigger than the Soviet one across town. He describes American embassies in Africa as "absolutely gigantic" for that reason alone, and calls the US embassy in Cairo an enormous facility matched by an equally enormous Russian one.

every-israeli-i-ever-knew.title: "Do not ever attempt to contact me again"
every-israeli-i-ever-knew.summary: The reply John Kiriakou says he received from John Kerry, then Secretary of State, after emailing him privately in the days before reporting to prison to beg that his sentence be commuted. Kiriakou had worked closely with Kerry for two and a half years; the one-line answer, sent after two or three days, was the last he ever heard from him.

evidence-of-previous-heroism.title: The 11(c)(1)(C) plea
evidence-of-previous-heroism.summary: The unusual plea structure John Kiriakou's lawyers negotiated in 2012, in which the sentence is written into the agreement and the judge may accept or reject it but cannot change it. Judge Leonie Brinkema told the court she had never seen one in her career, said she did not like it, and told Kiriakou that if she could she would have given him ten years.

evidence-of-previous-heroism.title: Plato Cacheris
evidence-of-previous-heroism.summary: Legendary Washington, D.C. defense attorney who served as John Kiriakou''s lead counsel in his 2012–2013 Espionage Act prosecution. Per Kiriakou, when discovery revealed the FBI had run a fake-diplomat sting against him, Cacheris explained the government''s posture bluntly: ''Because they have a shit case and they know it''s shit, and that''s why we''re going to trial.'' He spent most of the case urging trial, then drove to Kiriakou''s house on decision day and said ''You stupid son of a bitch — take the deal.'' Cacheris also represented FBI spy Robert Hanssen.

evidence-of-previous-heroism.title: From the Alien and Sedition Acts to the Espionage Act
evidence-of-previous-heroism.summary: A lineage John Kiriakou endorsed on the In Limine podcast: that language was lifted from the Alien and Sedition Acts into the Espionage Act of 1917 during the anti-radical hysteria of that period, making a straight line from the earliest American political prosecutions to the statute used against modern whistleblowers.

evidence-of-previous-heroism.title: Kermit Roosevelt and Mosaddegh
evidence-of-previous-heroism.summary: The CIA officer John Kiriakou names as the man who ran the 1953 overthrow of Iran's Prime Minister Mosaddegh on behalf of British Petroleum — who called it the gravest mistake of his life in the only interview he ever gave, and who, according to the documents Kiriakou has since read in the archives, did not actually run it at all.

evidence-of-previous-heroism.title: Prosecutorial careerism
evidence-of-previous-heroism.summary: John Kiriakou''s explanation for why senior federal prosecutors pursue high-profile national-security cases regardless of their merits: the conviction of a famous defendant is the entry ticket to a partnership at a large firm, a congressional candidacy, or a run for governor.

evidence-of-previous-heroism.title: The Laura Ingraham exchange
evidence-of-previous-heroism.summary: John Kiriakou's account of an on-air exchange with Fox News host Laura Ingraham about torture, in which she told him she hated his position and he replied that anyone who wants torture as an instrument of policy should have the courage to go to Capitol Hill and change the law rather than pretend the existing law does not apply.

exchange-of-bona-fides.title: Spy films and television on screen
exchange-of-bona-fides.summary: John Kiriakou's scene-by-scene verdicts on how spy films and television handle real tradecraft — what they get right (static surveillance from upper floors, hostile operational meetings, exchanges of bona fides, breaking into offices), what they invent (silent helicopters, high-speed submersibles, Batcaves, gadgets that cannot be bought), and the shows he says commit felonies on screen. He opens with why CIA officers watch them at all — *"not because they love the CIA movies, but because they love to criticize them."*

exchange-of-bona-fides.title: CIA driving training
exchange-of-bona-fides.summary: The counterterrorism-driving component of CIA training, in which officers are ambushed in a simulated third-country no-man's-land and must "get off the X" — get out of the kill zone. John Kiriakou's own run ended with the instructors killing his engine by remote, a robot in a van firing paintballs at him, and Kiriakou shooting out his own car windows to get an angle on the robot. "Damn it, Kiriakou. That was the last decent car we had."

exchange-of-bona-fides.title: CIA psychological evaluations
exchange-of-bona-fides.summary: The two kinds of psychological work John Kiriakou describes inside the CIA — the recurring psychiatric screening every officer undergoes, before employment, again three years after hiring and every five years thereafter for life; and the long-distance evaluation of foreign leaders carried out by the analytic side. The agency's clinical psychologists are split between the two, with a third group in operations advising case officers on the sources they recruit.

exchange-of-bona-fides.title: Bill Buckley
exchange-of-bona-fides.summary: CIA station chief in Beirut kidnapped by Palestinian Islamic Jihad in March 1984; tortured at length over fifteen months; killed in captivity; the case from which the agency derived a generation of operational-security lessons including the abandonment of single-point tracking devices in CIA officers' personal kit.

exchange-of-bona-fides.title: Burn Notice
exchange-of-bona-fides.summary: Both a piece of real CIA tradecraft — a worldwide cable forbidding every officer from speaking to a named person — and the USA Network spy series named after it, which John Kiriakou watched as a fan before he became its script adviser — a job he obtained by sitting next to its creator, Matt Nix, on a flight from Washington to Los Angeles, having previously run the show's credits in slow motion to find out who was advising it. Nobody was. By the time the plane landed Kiriakou had the job for season six.

exchange-of-bona-fides.title: The Grasshopper
exchange-of-bona-fides.summary: A recruited terrorist source John Kiriakou ran under a cryptonym, who called him after midnight on a dedicated burner, met him behind a church with a paper bag of his wife's gold jewellery, and was given five thousand dollars from station funds as what the chief of station called an early Christmas bonus.

executive-assistant-to-the-deputy-direct.title: Cheney's airstrip question
executive-assistant-to-the-deputy-direct.summary: A one-line request from Vice President Dick Cheney — what is the longest airstrip in northern Iraq made of? — that nobody in the CIA's operations directorate could answer, and that John Kiriakou eventually resolved by asking the agency librarian. The answer came back within a day, with the exact mix. The purpose was to work out whether the runway would take a transport aircraft carrying two tanks.

executive-assistant-to-the-deputy-direct.title: AIPAC
executive-assistant-to-the-deputy-direct.summary: The American Israel Public Affairs Committee — the U.S. political organization that, in John Kiriakou's framing, ought to be registered as a foreign-lobbying entity but is not, and that wields decisive electoral power against U.S. elected officials who express support for Palestinian human rights.

executive-assistant-to-the-deputy-direct.title: Bill Clinton
executive-assistant-to-the-deputy-direct.summary: 42nd U.S. president whom John Kiriakou describes as wholly disinterested in intelligence — briefed by the CIA only twice in eight years, with Vice President Al Gore taking the daily briefing instead and relaying anything important.

executive-assistant-to-the-deputy-direct.title: The CIA as a policy support agency
executive-assistant-to-the-deputy-direct.summary: John Kiriakou''s standing correction to the idea that the CIA has a foreign policy of its own: it is not a policy agency but a policy support agency, it serves at the pleasure of the president, and its officers have no civil service protections at all. Career staff can slow-roll an order they dislike until an administration ends — but in a hot war, he says, they do as they are told.

executive-assistant-to-the-deputy-direct.title: Greater Israel
executive-assistant-to-the-deputy-direct.summary: The territorial project John Kiriakou believes the Israeli government genuinely holds: the expulsion of every Palestinian, beginning in Gaza and continuing into the West Bank, pursued on a hundred- or two-hundred-year horizon in the confidence that the United States will never push back.

executive-assistant-to-the-deputy-direct.title: Iran Nuclear Assessment
executive-assistant-to-the-deputy-direct.summary: Per John Kiriakou's assessment, the US–Israeli military campaign against Iran was a war of choice driven by Israeli political pressure rather than genuine intelligence indicating an Iranian nuclear weapons threat. The CIA produced two National Intelligence Estimates concluding Iran had no nuclear weapons program; Supreme Leader Ayatollah Khamenei issued a fatwa in the 1980s forbidding such a program. The U.S. went to war anyway, in Kiriakou's view, after President Trump replaced the Joint Chiefs of Staff with officers willing to accept Israeli intelligence and proceed.

executive-order-12333.title: Falls Church mosque
executive-order-12333.summary: Large mosque on Route 7 in Falls Church, Virginia; the site at which John Kiriakou, in 1993 as a CIA Arabic-language trainee, met then-imam Anwar al-Awlaki on a class field trip; the same mosque at which the September 11 hijackers prayed the night before the attacks.

executive-order-12333.title: Ninth Circuit contractor ruling (2025)
executive-order-12333.summary: Approximately July 2025 U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit ruling, in a case brought by Abu Zubaydah against CIA contractors who had tortured him, holding that contractors operating under a written CIA contract are legally protected as agents of the agency; extends Executive Order 12333 authority to contractor operations including the Blackwater assassination program; received almost no U.S. media coverage.

executive-order-12333.title: Project Gateway
executive-order-12333.summary: A CIA astral-projection and remote-viewing effort that John Kiriakou describes as a sub-program of MK-Ultra, launched after a fabricated source claimed the Soviets were experimenting with ESP.

executive-order-12333.title: Global Response Staff
executive-order-12333.summary: The CIA's protective-security program for case officers operating in high-threat environments; run for the agency by Blackwater; especially active in Baghdad's Green Zone during the Iraq War, where movement between fixed locations was treated as life-threatening.

executive-order-12333.title: Recruiting from the bottom
executive-order-12333.summary: The targeting method John Kiriakou believes produced the killings of Iran''s leadership: not agents at the top of the state but destitute refugees at street level, paid a hundred dollars a month to write down when a general leaves his building and by which route. He contrasts it with the CIA''s own record in Iran, where it spent his career trying and failing to recruit inside the Ayatollah''s office, the foreign ministry and the IRGC.

executive-order-12333.title: Title 10 vs Title 50
executive-order-12333.summary: The U.S. legal-code distinction governing which kinds of armed action fall under military authority (Title 10) and which fall under intelligence authority (Title 50); the operative legal frame for the post-9/11 question of whether CIA contractors can lawfully kill in the agency's name, addressed in the 2025 Ninth Circuit ruling in the Abu Zubaydah contractor case.

expanding-the-definition-of-terrorism.title: Trump cartel terrorist designation
expanding-the-definition-of-terrorism.summary: Donald Trump's early second-term State Department designation of drug cartels as terrorist organizations, which John Kiriakou says was understood at the time mainly as a paperwork exercise to free up agencies like the NSA and DIA to spend money on intercepting communications and training foreign nationals — but which Kiriakou says Trump has since treated as license to attack any vessel he personally deems cartel-linked.

expanding-the-definition-of-terrorism.title: Anwar al-Awlaki
expanding-the-definition-of-terrorism.summary: American-born al-Qaeda propagandist; in 1993 the imam of the Falls Church, Virginia mosque visited by John Kiriakou's CIA Arabic-language class on a field trip; in 2001 the cleric at whose mosque the 9/11 hijackers prayed the night before the attacks; killed by U.S. drone strike in Yemen in approximately 2011.

expanding-the-definition-of-terrorism.title: Abu Zubaydah
expanding-the-definition-of-terrorism.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

expanding-the-definition-of-terrorism.title: Advanced Counterterrorism Operations
expanding-the-definition-of-terrorism.summary: The six-week specialist course John Kiriakou flew back from Athens to attend roughly eighteen months before 9/11 as one of fourteen officers selected worldwide — high-threat operations, technical collection, and a driving syllabus built around crashing through roadblocks that left the class with whiplash. By accident of timing it meant a trained cadre was ready to deploy the moment the attacks came.

expanding-the-definition-of-terrorism.title: Asset acquisition cycle
expanding-the-definition-of-terrorism.summary: The four-step process — spot, assess, develop, recruit — taught as the first lesson of CIA case officer training

expanding-the-definition-of-terrorism.title: Counterterrorism Center deaths in the line of duty
expanding-the-definition-of-terrorism.summary: The colleagues John Kiriakou names as having been killed doing the work he did — Helge Boes and Mike Spann of the Counterterrorism Center, and the officer who sat beside him when he was chief of the counterintelligence branch of the Osama bin Laden group, killed with six colleagues by a suicide bomber in Afghanistan. He pairs the physical risk with a second cost he states as near-certain: that a marriage will not survive an operational tour.

expanding-your-realm.title: Bob Grenier
expanding-your-realm.summary: Career CIA officer who served as station chief in Islamabad before, during, and after 9/11; later associate deputy director of operations for policy support and Iraq Mission Manager; John Kiriakou's boss and, for one year, his supervisor as executive assistant.

expanding-your-realm.title: Jim Pavitt
expanding-your-realm.summary: Long-serving CIA Deputy Director for Operations during the early post-9/11 period; characterized by John Kiriakou as "a legendary officer and a really great guy"; mocked John Brennan openly within the agency for Brennan's recurring stated ambition to head his own intelligence agency.

expanding-your-realm.title: John Brennan
expanding-your-realm.summary: Former Director of the CIA; characterized in KiriPedia's source corpus as the principal architect of the agency's enhanced interrogation program and as having plotted against an elected President

expanding-your-realm.title: The MI5 model for America
expanding-your-realm.summary: The discussions John Kiriakou says he took part in on his first trip to London as a CIA officer in 1992 or 1993, about creating an American equivalent of Britain’s MI5 — a domestic intelligence service, without arrest powers, that would spy on citizens and hand what it found to the FBI — and his observation thirty years later that it looked to be coming to pass.

expanding-your-realm.title: Deep state
expanding-your-realm.summary: John Kiriakou''s position on the deep state — that it is not a right-wing trope but an accurate description of something he served inside for fifteen years at the CIA and two more on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee staff. He is indifferent to the label ("call it the state, call it the federal bureaucracy") and insists on the substance: "It''s there to stay. It''s not going anywhere."

expanding-your-realm.title: George Tenet
expanding-your-realm.summary: Director of Central Intelligence from 1997 to 2004, spanning the September 11 attacks and the early enhanced-interrogation program; identified by John Kiriakou as John Brennan's institutional patron at the agency; the figure who ordered the Five Eyes intelligence services to "open the files" to each other in the early 2000s.

extraordinary-rendition.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
extraordinary-rendition.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

extraordinary-rendition.title: Abu Zubaydah
extraordinary-rendition.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

extraordinary-rendition.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
extraordinary-rendition.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

extraordinary-rendition.title: Intelligence Identities Protection Act
extraordinary-rendition.summary: U.S. law enacted in 1982 that makes it a crime to knowingly disclose the identity of a covert intelligence officer; per John Kiriakou, his 2012 prosecution under the act arose from confirming a single surname of a former CIA colleague to a journalist — a confirmation that was never published. The name passed through a chain from journalist to Human Rights Watch to Guantanamo defense attorneys before reaching a judge and ultimately the FBI, which traced it back to Kiriakou.

extraordinary-rendition.title: The secret prisons the heads of state did not know about
extraordinary-rendition.summary: John Kiriakou's account of how the CIA's black sites were established — as arrangements struck directly between the director of the CIA and the head of the host country's intelligence service, in some cases without the knowledge of that country's own head of state — and his statement that he learned the extent of the system only years after leaving, by reading the press.

extraordinary-rendition.title: Maher Arar
extraordinary-rendition.summary: Canadian-Syrian political-science professor at the University of Toronto; in 2002, returning from a family visit in Tunis, was seized by the FBI at JFK at CIA request, secretly rendered to Damascus, and tortured by Syrian intelligence for eight to nine months until they concluded he was the wrong man. The U.S. denied any involvement to the Canadian government until Arar's wife produced a credit-card receipt from his return flight. He sued the U.S. and lost on national-security grounds, then sued the Canadian government and won six million dollars. Per John Kiriakou, his case is the canonical illustration of the CIA rendition program rendering the wrong person.

f-35-israel-avionics.title: MOSSAD
f-35-israel-avionics.summary: Israel's primary external intelligence service; characterized by John Kiriakou as universally hostile in his and his CIA colleagues' professional dealings with it ("never had a positive encounter with Mossad"); operates almost exclusively in the operational rather than analytical domain; the CIA is, per Kiriakou, categorically forbidden from spying on it.

f-35-israel-avionics.title: Israeli training of American police
f-35-israel-avionics.summary: The practice, which John Kiriakou opposes, of Israeli police and IDF personnel training American local police departments, including at the Atlanta facility known as Cop City.

f-35-israel-avionics.title: The F-35 shootdown
f-35-israel-avionics.summary: Footage from the 2026 Iran war showing an F-35 hit by Iranian ground fire, initially dismissed as artificial. John Kiriakou notes the Pentagon confirmed the pilot reached a Middle East airbase wounded, and that nobody explained how a supposedly obliterated adversary had hit an invisible aircraft.

f-35-israel-avionics.title: Israeli integration into U.S. agencies
f-35-israel-avionics.summary: John Kiriakou''s objection to the formal embedding of Israeli personnel inside American defense and intelligence institutions — a National Defense Authorization Act provision collocating them with the Pentagon and opening Five Eyes-style liaison with the CIA, arriving in the same weeks as a DIA all-hands warning that Israeli services were unusually aggressive in recruiting inside DIA. His argument is that the two cannot both be true: either Israel is a critical counterintelligence threat or it is a partner.

f-35-israel-avionics.title: NDAA 2027 US–Israel fusion provisions
f-35-israel-avionics.summary: Provisions in the proposed National Defense Authorization Act for 2027 and the companion intelligence authorization bill that would create a permanent Pentagon executive agent for US–Israeli military fusion and lock in permanent intelligence sharing tied to Israel's qualitative military edge. John Kiriakou describes the effect as handing over voluntarily the technology Israel previously ran spies to steal.

f-35-israel-avionics.title: Veterans' benefits for IDF service
f-35-israel-avionics.summary: A bill sponsored by a Republican congressman from Pennsylvania and one from Ohio that would extend US veterans' benefits to any American who joins the Israel Defense Forces. John Kiriakou calls it an outrage and, as an American, treason.

f-35-sale-to-turkey.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
f-35-sale-to-turkey.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

f-35-sale-to-turkey.title: Donald Trump
f-35-sale-to-turkey.summary: 45th and 47th U.S. president. Per John Kiriakou, a man genuinely convinced he was doing right by bombing Iran, "duped" by the same Netanyahu nuclear bluff Obama once rejected — and, at the same time, the most blindly pro-Israel president in history, an admirer of autocrats who has never once criticized Vladimir Putin, and prone to gestures — from the Gulf of America to a since-abandoned "Department of War" rename — that test the edges of his actual authority.

f-35-sale-to-turkey.title: Major non-NATO ally status for Ukraine
f-35-sale-to-turkey.summary: John Kiriakou''s forecast of how the Russian demand that Ukraine never join NATO can be met without leaving Ukraine unprotected: the designation of major non-NATO ally, already held by Australia, Japan, South Korea, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates, which he says confers essentially the same rights without the membership.

f-35-sale-to-turkey.title: Ahmed Chalabi
f-35-sale-to-turkey.summary: Iraqi exile and founder of the Iraqi National Congress; per John Kiriakou, a Shia-Kurdish con man who looted Petra Bank in Jordan of $36 million in the 1980s, was sentenced to death in absentia, was pardoned at CIA request, then pocketed $6 million in CIA seed funding for the INC and bought a Mayfair house in cash; later resurrected by Dick Cheney to feed the Pentagon fabricated WMD intelligence used to justify the 2003 invasion of Iraq.

f-35-sale-to-turkey.title: Espionage Act
f-35-sale-to-turkey.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

f-35-sale-to-turkey.title: Pickaxe Mountain
f-35-sale-to-turkey.summary: The Iranian site whose ongoing excavation Benjamin Netanyahu publicised in July 2026 and which Donald Trump, in response, said he already knew about — using the exchange to tell an ally publicly not to brief the press ahead of him. John Kiriakou reads the episode as Netanyahu attempting to move American public opinion and Trump refusing to be moved.

failure-to-accept-responsibility.title: Albright in Pyongyang
failure-to-accept-responsibility.summary: John Kiriakou's account of Bill Clinton's stated regret over the final week of his presidency — that he wished he had pursued diplomatic relations with North Korea instead of Israeli-Palestinian peace — and of Madeleine Albright being in Pyongyang rather than at the talks.

failure-to-accept-responsibility.title: Nationalizing the midterms
failure-to-accept-responsibility.summary: John Kiriakou's recurring comparison between contemporary party messaging and Newt Gingrich's 1994 Contract with America, including his advice that Speaker Mike Johnson should keep Gingrich on his couch and ask him nightly how the 1994 midterms were nationalised.

failure-to-accept-responsibility.title: The French in the streets
failure-to-accept-responsibility.summary: John Kiriakou's stated admiration for how quickly the French take to the streets, offered while questioning Ted Rall about the chances of violence during the 2025 French political crisis, alongside his observation that he could not recall a French president ever resigning.

failure-to-accept-responsibility.title: The nine-dollar-eighty-three premium
failure-to-accept-responsibility.summary: John Kiriakou's own Affordable Care Act premium, which he gives as $9.83 a month, and the doctor who asked him why he carried the plan at all. Offered during a October 2025 discussion of the government shutdown and the expiring Obamacare subsidies.

failure-to-accept-responsibility.title: Eastern District of Virginia
failure-to-accept-responsibility.summary: The U.S. federal district covering northern Virginia — home to Langley, the Pentagon, DHS and much of the intelligence-contractor industry — which John Kiriakou calls 'the espionage court' because the Justice Department files the great majority of its national security prosecutions there and because, in his telling, no national-security defendant has ever won a case in it; Kiriakou, Julian Assange, Edward Snowden and Jeffrey Sterling were all charged there.

failure-to-accept-responsibility.title: Federal plea coercion
failure-to-accept-responsibility.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that the federal justice system coerces guilty pleas by stacking charges and winning 98.2% of its cases — so that even innocent defendants take deals, as he did, told by his own attorney that the system is 'not about justice; it's about mitigating damage.'

faisalabad-hospital.title: Colonel Khaled
faisalabad-hospital.summary: The ISI chief in Lahore who worked alongside John Kiriakou through the Abu Zubaydah operation — a man who had never wanted to be a soldier, who spent their first meeting drawing Kiriakou's portrait instead of taking notes, and who explained the spliced telephone wires that nearly derailed the hunt.

faisalabad-hospital.title: Site 13
faisalabad-hospital.summary: The house in Faisalabad, nearest of the thirteen targets to the CIA safe house, where Abu Zubaydah was shot at two o'clock in the morning on the night of the raids — announced to John Kiriakou on the roof a mile away by the sound of a battering ram failing against a steel-reinforced door.

faisalabad-hospital.title: Faisalabad
faisalabad-hospital.summary: The Pakistani textile city of some seven or eight million people where Abu Zubaydah was captured in March 2002 — concrete, mud and corrugated tin in John Kiriakou's description, with a brand-new glass-and-steel McDonald's standing in the middle of it.

faisalabad-hospital.title: Mr. Fish
faisalabad-hospital.summary: The cover name the CIA used for Abu Zubaydah in Pakistan in 2002 — invented because the Americans would not tell their Pakistani partners who the target was, and derived from the only thing they would say about him: that he was a big fish.

faisalabad-hospital.title: The toll booth plan
faisalabad-hospital.summary: John Kiriakou's first idea for catching Abu Zubaydah in 2002 — to put CIA officers dressed as Pakistanis in the toll booths of the Lahore–Faisalabad motorway and grab him as he came through — drawn from his own summer job as a toll collector on the Pennsylvania Turnpike, and abandoned as, in his own words, a terrible idea.

faisalabad-hospital.title: Amir
faisalabad-hospital.summary: The pseudonym John Kiriakou gives the Muslim, ethnically Arab domestic officer sent on temporary duty to Pakistan to help with the Abu Zubaydah hunt — the colleague who drove them into India by GPS, drank the roadside tea and had diarrhoea for six weeks, and invented the textile-baron cover story on the spot.

faisalabad.title: Site 13
faisalabad.summary: The house in Faisalabad, nearest of the thirteen targets to the CIA safe house, where Abu Zubaydah was shot at two o'clock in the morning on the night of the raids — announced to John Kiriakou on the roof a mile away by the sound of a battering ram failing against a steel-reinforced door.

faisalabad.title: Abu Zubaydah
faisalabad.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

faisalabad.title: Amir
faisalabad.summary: The pseudonym John Kiriakou gives the Muslim, ethnically Arab domestic officer sent on temporary duty to Pakistan to help with the Abu Zubaydah hunt — the colleague who drove them into India by GPS, drank the roadside tea and had diarrhoea for six weeks, and invented the textile-baron cover story on the spot.
