faisalabad.summary: The ISI chief in Lahore who worked alongside John Kiriakou through the Abu Zubaydah operation — a man who had never wanted to be a soldier, who spent their first meeting drawing Kiriakou's portrait instead of taking notes, and who explained the spliced telephone wires that nearly derailed the hunt.

faisalabad.title: The toll booth plan
faisalabad.summary: John Kiriakou's first idea for catching Abu Zubaydah in 2002 — to put CIA officers dressed as Pakistanis in the toll booths of the Lahore–Faisalabad motorway and grab him as he came through — drawn from his own summer job as a toll collector on the Pennsylvania Turnpike, and abandoned as, in his own words, a terrible idea.

faisalabad.title: Faisalabad Hospital
faisalabad.summary: The hospital where a dying Abu Zubaydah was taken after the raid of March 2002 — open windows, animals in the corridors, mosquitoes on open wounds, and a bar of Irish Spring soap used as a pincushion for reusable syringes — which came under fire from the street while he was on the operating table.

fake-cia-resumes.title: Hugh Francis Redmond
fake-cia-resumes.summary: The first CIA officer to die in the line of duty, per John Kiriakou — a Special Activities Division officer sent to Shanghai in 1946 under cover as an ice cream machine salesman, arrested by the Chinese communists in 1951, held and tortured for nineteen years, and declared a suicide by Beijing in 1970. The CIA denied he had ever worked for it until his name was declassified and added to the Wall of Honor.

fake-cia-resumes.title: Robert David Steele
fake-cia-resumes.summary: The former intelligence officer and podcaster whose death during the COVID-19 pandemic John Kiriakou was asked to explain. Kiriakou, who had appeared on his show, calls him a sweet man who died of the disease, and offers a blunt assessment of his work: he did not believe most of the conspiracy theories he promoted, but they brought him an audience.

fake-cia-resumes.title: The lawfare template
fake-cia-resumes.summary: The assessment of John Kiriakou''s prosecution that he quotes most often and finds most alarming: a former United States attorney for Utah told him the Kiriakou case was the template for the Democratic Party''s policy of lawfare. Kiriakou''s gloss is that if they do not like you they can ruin your life, and there is nothing you can do to protect yourself.

fake-cia-resumes.title: The science fiction writer FOIA request
fake-cia-resumes.summary: The Freedom of Information Act request John Kiriakou filed with the CIA about a 1950s science fiction writer long rumoured to have been an undercover officer — answered only with a letter saying the agency lacked the manpower to meet its statutory ninety-day deadline. Fifteen years later, he says, he is still waiting.

fake-cia-resumes.title: The CIA as a paramilitary organization
fake-cia-resumes.summary: John Kiriakou''s periodisation of the CIA''s mission — spying and analysis until Vietnam, restored after the Church and Pike hearings of 1975, and converted immediately after September 11 into a paramilitary body that he says it has remained ever since. His objection is stated without hedging: drawing up a kill list every Tuesday and dispatching officers to carry it out is not intelligence, it is murder.

fake-cia-resumes.title: The Greek turn toward Israel
fake-cia-resumes.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of why Athens abandoned its traditional pro-Arab alignment and embraced Israel — a 180-degree flip he attributes to the collapse of Turkey''s relationship with Israel and, above all, to money: Israeli property buying that he says has tripled Greek house prices, and Cypriot gas fields Greece hopes to develop with Israeli partners.

falls-church-mosque.title: Anwar al-Awlaki
falls-church-mosque.summary: American-born al-Qaeda propagandist; in 1993 the imam of the Falls Church, Virginia mosque visited by John Kiriakou's CIA Arabic-language class on a field trip; in 2001 the cleric at whose mosque the 9/11 hijackers prayed the night before the attacks; killed by U.S. drone strike in Yemen in approximately 2011.

falls-church-mosque.title: Avril Haines
falls-church-mosque.summary: Per John Kiriakou, the National Security Council lawyer who decided whether names could lawfully go on John Brennan's kill list — and said yes in almost every case — before becoming CIA deputy director during the agency's hacking of the Senate Intelligence Committee, and then Director of National Intelligence. Kiriakou calls her appointment the disastrous half of a week in which Biden also named Bill Burns, and says she has never had to answer for any of it.

falls-church-mosque.title: Executive Order 12333
falls-church-mosque.summary: The U.S. presidential directive — in its post-9/11 amended form — that grants the CIA the legal authority to kill any individual anywhere in the world deemed by the agency to pose a "clear and present danger" to the United States; the legal foundation underlying both CIA paramilitary operations and the agency's contractor relationships including with Blackwater.

falls-church-mosque.title: Expanding the definition of terrorism
falls-church-mosque.summary: John Kiriakou's objection to the widening of the U.S. terrorism designation beyond groups that use violence for political ends — covering the addition of organisations loosely associated with Antifa, which he argues is not a group at all, and the designation of Latin American narco organisations, which he says should be answered with criminal charges rather than drone strikes.

falls-church-mosque.title: James Clapper
falls-church-mosque.summary: Director of National Intelligence under Obama, and in John Kiriakou's account the standing example of two arguments at once — that lying to Congress carries no consequence at the top of the intelligence community, and that career military officers make poor intelligence chiefs because they cannot tell a president no.

falls-church-mosque.title: Prince Muhammad bin Naif
falls-church-mosque.summary: Saudi prince, former head of Saudi intelligence and briefly crown prince, described by John Kiriakou as the golden boy of the royal family and the West's preferred successor. He survived an al-Qaeda assassin who detonated a bomb concealed inside his own body at an open house in Riyadh, was decorated at CIA headquarters for surviving it, and was then overthrown and placed under arrest by Muhammad bin Salman.

false-flags-are-too-hard.title: SEAL Team Six attrition
false-flags-are-too-hard.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer to the claim that the Navy SEALs who killed Osama bin Laden have since been killed off: the dead came from the broader unit rather than the raid party, SEAL Team Six numbers several hundred men rather than the dozen or so people imagine, and losing a high number of them to accidents and combat is, in his phrase, very sadly common.

false-flags-are-too-hard.title: Robert David Steele
false-flags-are-too-hard.summary: The former intelligence officer and podcaster whose death during the COVID-19 pandemic John Kiriakou was asked to explain. Kiriakou, who had appeared on his show, calls him a sweet man who died of the disease, and offers a blunt assessment of his work: he did not believe most of the conspiracy theories he promoted, but they brought him an audience.

false-flags-are-too-hard.title: The Obama recruitment thesis
false-flags-are-too-hard.summary: John Kiriakou''s public explanation of what happened to Barack Obama: not that the CIA created him, but that a first-term senator with no national security experience is exactly the kind of president the agency wants, and that the first briefing several levels above top secret is enough to hook him. Kiriakou supports the reading with two quotations Obama gave to reporters, including that he never had any idea he would be so good at killing people.

false-flags-are-too-hard.title: Bin Laden health rumors
false-flags-are-too-hard.summary: John Kiriakou's dismissal of the claim that Osama bin Laden died years before the 2011 raid. He says the CIA received a steady stream of medical rumours about him — kidney failure, dialysis in a cave, a spinal disorder — none of which turned out to be true, and that bin Laden was in fine health apart from arthritis and a hip problem until the day he died.

false-flags-are-too-hard.title: Chuck Grassley
false-flags-are-too-hard.summary: The senior senator from Iowa, and in John Kiriakou's assessment the one member of Congress who has taken whistleblower protection seriously as a legislative project — a count he has variously put at one finger, at two names, and at four out of 535. Grassley wrote the whistleblower protection statutes, speaks every year at the National Whistleblower Day luncheon, and is the name Kiriakou gives prospective whistleblowers as the single friendly ear on Capitol Hill. Kiriakou's personal verdict is colder — Grassley, he has said, never did anything for him.

false-flags-are-too-hard.title: The Grand Mosque cover story
false-flags-are-too-hard.summary: A single fabricated account of innocent travel that John Kiriakou says he heard roughly twenty-five times from Arab men detained in Pakistan after the September 11 attacks — a trip to Karachi to study Arabic, a lost passport, and a ride to the Grand Mosque. Its details were wrong in ways that gave it away, and Kiriakou treats its uniformity as evidence of poor operational security rather than of innocence.

family-jewels.title: Church Committee
family-jewels.summary: U.S. Senate investigative committee operating in 1975–1976 that examined domestic intelligence abuses by the CIA, FBI, and NSA; per John Kiriakou, the Church Committee — alongside the concurrent Pike Committee in the House — was the last genuine moment of legislative oversight over the intelligence community, born of a national consensus that government had gone dangerously off course. Its work led to the creation of the permanent Senate Select Committee on Intelligence, which Kiriakou says ceased to function as real oversight roughly seven years after its founding.

family-jewels.title: MK-Ultra
family-jewels.summary: The CIA's mid-twentieth-century umbrella program of mind-control, behavioral-modification, and biological-warfare experimentation, encompassing subprojects such as MK-Chickwit and MK-Seesaw; active 1952–1975; documented practices included LSD dosing of unwitting American citizens in CIA-rented brothels and the aerosolized release of pathogens into the San Francisco fog; 80% of the program's documentation was destroyed by the CIA in defiance of a 1975 preservation order from Senator Frank Church.

family-jewels.title: French village LSD bread experiment
family-jewels.summary: John Kiriakou's account of a compartmented MK-Ultra experiment in which the CIA dosed the only bakery of a small French village he does not name with LSD — in some tellings by breaking in at night and spiking the yeast, in others by contaminating the flour supplied to it — so that the hapless baker sold the whole village an unwitting trip. Kiriakou places it as the sequel to the San Francisco bacterium release and calls it, in the agency's own terms, a successful operation.

family-jewels.title: Pike Committee
family-jewels.summary: U.S. House investigative committee operating in 1975–1976 in parallel with the Senate's Church Committee; per John Kiriakou, the two committees together were the apex — and the last genuine exercise — of congressional oversight of the CIA, staffed by heavyweights and followed by a golden age that lasted only until Iran-Contra. Their work created the permanent House and Senate intelligence committees, which Kiriakou says degraded within a decade into cheerleaders for the agency.

family-jewels.title: Project Gateway
family-jewels.summary: A CIA astral-projection and remote-viewing effort that John Kiriakou describes as a sub-program of MK-Ultra, launched after a fabricated source claimed the Soviets were experimenting with ESP.

family-jewels.title: Executive Order 12333
family-jewels.summary: The U.S. presidential directive — in its post-9/11 amended form — that grants the CIA the legal authority to kill any individual anywhere in the world deemed by the agency to pose a "clear and present danger" to the United States; the legal foundation underlying both CIA paramilitary operations and the agency's contractor relationships including with Blackwater.

fbi-apologies-to-kiriakou.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
fbi-apologies-to-kiriakou.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

fbi-apologies-to-kiriakou.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
fbi-apologies-to-kiriakou.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

fbi-apologies-to-kiriakou.title: Kiriakou's transfer to the Directorate of Operations
fbi-apologies-to-kiriakou.summary: John Kiriakou's roughly two-month internal campaign to transfer from the CIA's analytic Directorate of Intelligence to the operational Directorate of Operations, overcoming what he calls a "natural bias in operations against the eggheads on the analytic side," followed by an Athens posting secured because he was the only person in the entire CIA fluent in both Greek and Arabic. Covers his full CIA career arc from 1988/1990 recruitment through analyst years on Iraq, the switch to operations, 9/11, the enhanced-interrogation refusal, executive assistant to the deputy director for operations, and his eventual resignation and post-CIA career.

fbi-apologies-to-kiriakou.title: John Kiriakou
fbi-apologies-to-kiriakou.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

fbi-apologies-to-kiriakou.title: Central Intelligence Agency
fbi-apologies-to-kiriakou.summary: U.S. foreign intelligence service; John Kiriakou's employer from 1990 to 2004 and the central institution of KiriPedia

fbi-apologies-to-kiriakou.title: John Kerry
fbi-apologies-to-kiriakou.summary: U.S. Senator from Massachusetts; chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee during John Kiriakou's 2009 service as the committee's senior investigator; subsequently U.S. Secretary of State; characterized by Kiriakou as a coward who buckled under CIA pressure on the Dasht-i-Leili reopening and as personally fixated on his perceived theft of the Secretary of State position by Hillary Clinton; the famously thrown medals were duplicates purchased at the post exchange.

fbi-arrest-strategies.title: FCI Loretto
fbi-arrest-strategies.summary: U.S. Federal Correctional Institution in Loretto, Pennsylvania; the low-medium-security prison at which John Kiriakou served 23 months of a 30-month sentence following his 2013 Espionage Act–era plea deal; the originally ordered "minimum security work camp" placement was countermanded — per Kiriakou, on Brennan's direct intervention — to place him in the actual prison alongside the general population.

fbi-arrest-strategies.title: Edward Snowden
fbi-arrest-strategies.summary: Former NSA contractor who in 2013 disclosed the scope of U.S. [mass surveillance](/wiki/mass-surveillance), including the Section 702 collection program. Per John Kiriakou — who counts Snowden among the small group of national-security whistleblowers prosecuted under the Espionage Act — Snowden was ''stuck between two awful slippery slopes'': breaking his oath and chain of command on one side, and on the other catching something ''cut and dry against the Constitution'' that no one would act on. Kiriakou notes Snowden could not use his chain of command (as Kiriakou could not, his own chain being Jose Rodriguez), and that Judge Leonie Brinkema had reserved the Snowden case for herself before he fled the country.

fbi-arrest-strategies.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
fbi-arrest-strategies.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

fbi-arrest-strategies.title: Amnesty International
fbi-arrest-strategies.summary: The human rights organization whose torture report forms part of John Kiriakou's core defense — the CIA's crimes were already public knowledge before he confirmed them on ABC, and the Justice Department's own declination letter said so — and the organization whose silence during his prosecution he cannot forgive. He begged Amnesty for a one-sentence statement and got a New Yorker subscription instead; it took Ai Weiwei to change their minds, and by then he was walking out of prison.

fbi-arrest-strategies.title: Barack Obama
fbi-arrest-strategies.summary: 44th U.S. president; in John Kiriakou's account, Obama publicly recounted refusing Benjamin Netanyahu's demand to bomb Iran and calling Israel's threat to use nuclear weapons a bluff — a bluff Kiriakou says Donald Trump later believed.

fbi-arrest-strategies.title: Bureau of Prisons
fbi-arrest-strategies.summary: The federal agency that ran John Kiriakou's incarceration — and one of his most persistent post-prison targets. The BOP overrode his judge's camp recommendation by deeming him "a threat to the public safety," threatened him with "diesel therapy" until 1,600 logged phone calls and letters from a dozen House members and two senators backed it off, and, per Kiriakou, functions as "an employment agency for unemployable semi-literate rural white men" and "a dumping ground for failed medical professionals" — an agency for which a prisoner's death is cheaper than his treatment.

fbi-manufactured-terrorism-cases.title: The CIA divorce rate
fbi-manufactured-terrorism-cases.summary: John Kiriakou's account of why marriages fail at the CIA at a rate he says exceeds that of any other part of the U.S. government — the impossibility of explaining a midnight departure to a spouse without a clearance, and the difficulty officers have switching off a professional habit of deception. He gives the figure variously as over 75 percent and upwards of 80 percent, says he was determined not to become a statistic and became one anyway, and dates the end of his first marriage to a sentence spoken in an armoured car on the way to Athens airport. Both his divorces have been costly; of the second he says the agency played an active role he is barred by court order from explaining.

fbi-manufactured-terrorism-cases.title: Alexa
fbi-manufactured-terrorism-cases.summary: Per John Kiriakou, Amazon''s Alexa smart speaker reports directly to the NSA — and he owns one anyway. The device recurs across his interviews as the standing example of the surveillance trade-off in modern smart-home technology, and of his own negotiated exception to it: one speaker, in one room, against the advice of every intelligence officer he has ever known.

fbi-manufactured-terrorism-cases.title: Cameo
fbi-manufactured-terrorism-cases.summary: The personalised-video app John Kiriakou joined in February 2026 and turned into an unexpected second career — around 2,600 videos, roughly 900 of them in his first month alone. Half are birthday messages and most of the rest are requests for CIA stories, but about two hundred have been appeals for advice or a pep talk, and three of those people later told him he had talked them out of suicide.

fbi-manufactured-terrorism-cases.title: CIA culture of lying
fbi-manufactured-terrorism-cases.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of deception as an occupational condition at the CIA — the tradecraft of detecting it, the training that instils it, and the institutional rot he says follows when officers cannot switch it off: a deputy director who married five successive secretaries, promotion panels that traded advancement for sex, and staff psychiatrists overheard planning how to push a colleague toward resignation or suicide.

fbi-manufactured-terrorism-cases.title: Congressional intelligence oversight
fbi-manufactured-terrorism-cases.summary: John Kiriakou''s standing criticism of the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence and the House Permanent Select Committee — that unlike the armed services and foreign relations committees, they do not perform oversight at all: "They''re just cheerleaders." His illustration is a sitting committee chairman who summoned him privately, then asked whether Kiriakou would write the criticism publicly on his behalf.

fbi-manufactured-terrorism-cases.title: Muslim Brotherhood terrorist designation
fbi-manufactured-terrorism-cases.summary: John Kiriakou''s objection to the designation of the Muslim Brotherhood, or elements of it, as a terrorist organisation: that the group is more than a century old, has never carried out an anti-American terrorist operation, and had never been so designated by any previous administration. He distinguishes fundamentalism and hostility from terrorism, has made the same argument to a former IDF spokesman''s face, and traces the American quarrel with the Brotherhood back to its winning an Egyptian election.

fbi-raid-on-kiriakou-s-home.title: Peter Strzok
fbi-raid-on-kiriakou-s-home.summary: Senior FBI counterintelligence officer who, per John Kiriakou, oversaw the FBI operation that included a fake Japanese-diplomat sting designed to induce Kiriakou to commit espionage, and who personally placed Kiriakou in handcuffs when he was arrested on January 12, 2012. Kiriakou did not learn Strzok's identity until 2017, when a Washington Post reporter called to ask for comment on Strzok's firing.

fbi-raid-on-kiriakou-s-home.title: David Petraeus
fbi-raid-on-kiriakou-s-home.summary: Retired U.S. Army general and director of the CIA who, per John Kiriakou, confirmed the names of ten covert CIA operatives to his biographer and girlfriend and was never criminally charged — a contrast Kiriakou cites repeatedly as proof that his own prosecution under the Intelligence Identities Protection Act was selective. Kiriakou''s explanation for the disparity: Petraeus had not blown the whistle on the torture program and embarrassed the agency.

fbi-raid-on-kiriakou-s-home.title: Jim Bamford
fbi-raid-on-kiriakou-s-home.summary: The author John Kiriakou credits with having written the definitive book on the NSA and with first making Americans aware of the surveillance state. Kiriakou highlights Bamford''s 2023 book Spy Fail for a claim he says should have been front-page news and was not: that the FBI lost ten of its Chinese sources because Peter Strzok''s counterintelligence unit had a Chinese mole inside it.

fbi-raid-on-kiriakou-s-home.title: Leon Panetta
fbi-raid-on-kiriakou-s-home.summary: CIA Director under President Obama (2009–2011) and subsequent Secretary of Defense; per John Kiriakou, the official who on arrival as Director shut down the Blackwater-operated CIA worldwide assassination program — and in the course of explaining the decision to the House Intelligence Committee publicly outed Erik Prince. Also one of Kiriakou's two go-to examples (with David Petraeus) of senior intelligence figures who disclosed the identities of covert CIA officers without consequence while Kiriakou himself was prosecuted for the same statute.

fbi-raid-on-kiriakou-s-home.title: Church Committee
fbi-raid-on-kiriakou-s-home.summary: U.S. Senate investigative committee operating in 1975–1976 that examined domestic intelligence abuses by the CIA, FBI, and NSA; per John Kiriakou, the Church Committee — alongside the concurrent Pike Committee in the House — was the last genuine moment of legislative oversight over the intelligence community, born of a national consensus that government had gone dangerously off course. Its work led to the creation of the permanent Senate Select Committee on Intelligence, which Kiriakou says ceased to function as real oversight roughly seven years after its founding.

fbi-raid-on-kiriakou-s-home.title: COINTELPRO
fbi-raid-on-kiriakou-s-home.summary: The FBI programme of warrantless surveillance and disruption directed at Americans, and one of the four abuses John Kiriakou names when explaining what the Church Committee actually investigated. He treats it as the historical benchmark for what a real congressional inquiry into the security agencies looks like — and, through the campaign against Martin Luther King, as proof that the state will destroy a citizen it considers a threat.

fbi.title: Central Intelligence Agency
fbi.summary: U.S. foreign intelligence service; John Kiriakou's employer from 1990 to 2004 and the central institution of KiriPedia

fbi.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
fbi.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

fbi.title: John Brennan
fbi.summary: Former Director of the CIA; characterized in KiriPedia's source corpus as the principal architect of the agency's enhanced interrogation program and as having plotted against an elected President

fbi.title: The Taliban spokesman setup
fbi.summary: Kiriakou's account of a prisoner transferred into FCI Loretto for five days who presented himself as the Taliban's American spokesman, while a guard photographed the encounter from the treeline — an attempt, in his telling, to manufacture a second case against him.

fbi.title: Intelligence Agencies
fbi.summary: Kiriakou counts roughly 19 publicly known US intelligence agencies and calls the proliferation Pentagon empire-building on duplicative work.

fbi.title: The Pineapple Militia case
fbi.summary: The Miami FBI entrapment prosecution in which, per John Kiriakou's July 2026 testimony as a defense expert witness by video from Athens, federal agents recruited a homeless, mentally ill Muslim man living in an alley behind a restaurant into a fictitious militia they called the "pineapple militia," proposed targets he had never proposed, refused four of his refusals to join, wrote a plot to bomb the New York Stock Exchange, built the bomb themselves, and arrested him when they handed it to him. Kiriakou uses the case as the canonical example of what he says are the 99 per cent of FBI terrorism cases that are fabricated.

fci-loretto.title: Kiriakou's serial-killer letters
fci-loretto.summary: John Kiriakou's account of writing letters, as research for a planned book, to several well-known serial killers — including David Berkowitz ("Son of Sam"), Gary Leon Ridgway (the Green River Killer), the BTK killer, the "co-ed killer," and Manson family member Tex Watson — and the uniformly evangelical, Jesus-focused responses he received instead of the interviews he wanted.

fci-loretto.title: Kiriakou's Pakistan-Islam economic critique
fci-loretto.summary: John Kiriakou's controversial view that Islam has held Pakistan back economically, contrasting Pakistan's stalled development since the 1960s with South Korea's — which had the same GDP as Pakistan in 1964 — and citing lost productivity from prayer breaks and holy days, resentment over partition, and spending on nuclear weapons instead of infrastructure and education.

fci-loretto.title: The prison food economy
fci-loretto.summary: The underground kitchen at FCI Loretto, where meals were cooked in bin liners heated by improvised immersion elements, guards stole and resold the food they were meant to be guarding, and Kiriakou stopped going to the cafeteria for the last six to eight months of his sentence.

fci-loretto.title: The Romanian twins
fci-loretto.summary: The adopted children John Kiriakou says his FCI Loretto roommate Robert the Australian abandoned at the gate of the Romanian embassy in Washington — one of the stories Kiriakou judged to be true, in a stream of claims he otherwise treated as invention.

fci-loretto.title: Sharon Scranage
fci-loretto.summary: CIA secretary stationed in Ghana in the 1980s; the only other American besides John Kiriakou to have been charged under the Intelligence Identities Protection Act of 1982; revealed the names of CIA officers and sources in Ghana to a Ghanaian intelligence-service lover during pillow talk, leading to the execution of the named sources by Ghanaian authorities; sentenced to nine months in prison.

fci-loretto.title: The Taliban spokesman setup
fci-loretto.summary: Kiriakou's account of a prisoner transferred into FCI Loretto for five days who presented himself as the Taliban's American spokesman, while a guard photographed the encounter from the treeline — an attempt, in his telling, to manufacture a second case against him.

federal-plea-coercion.title: Espionage Act
federal-plea-coercion.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

federal-plea-coercion.title: Edward Snowden
federal-plea-coercion.summary: Former NSA contractor who in 2013 disclosed the scope of U.S. [mass surveillance](/wiki/mass-surveillance), including the Section 702 collection program. Per John Kiriakou — who counts Snowden among the small group of national-security whistleblowers prosecuted under the Espionage Act — Snowden was ''stuck between two awful slippery slopes'': breaking his oath and chain of command on one side, and on the other catching something ''cut and dry against the Constitution'' that no one would act on. Kiriakou notes Snowden could not use his chain of command (as Kiriakou could not, his own chain being Jose Rodriguez), and that Judge Leonie Brinkema had reserved the Snowden case for herself before he fled the country.

federal-plea-coercion.title: Mark Lanzotti
federal-plea-coercion.summary: John Kiriakou's best friend in prison — an Italian sentenced to triple life without parole for a first-time nonviolent meth conspiracy he was the only man to voluntarily leave; Kiriakou wrote the appeal that won his release, and he is now the top-selling realtor on the Jersey Shore.

federal-plea-coercion.title: The contrition requirement
federal-plea-coercion.summary: The rule John Kiriakou says defeats his own pardon applications before they begin — that an applicant must show proof of contrition — and his refusal to meet it. Asked whether he is sorry for the crime he committed, his answer is no, and that he would do it again.

federal-plea-coercion.title: The plea-hearing objection
federal-plea-coercion.summary: John Kiriakou's account of standing up at his own plea hearing, over his lawyer's objection, to tell the judge that the statement of facts the prosecutors had written into his plea agreement was untrue — and of her reply that it was just window dressing.

federal-plea-coercion.title: The threat to testify
federal-plea-coercion.summary: How John Kiriakou says he turned down the government''s "best and final" offer of ten years: by warning that he would have to take the stand in his own defence and might let slip the war crimes he had witnessed in fifteen years at the CIA.

federal-prison-security-levels.title: FCI Loretto
federal-prison-security-levels.summary: U.S. Federal Correctional Institution in Loretto, Pennsylvania; the low-medium-security prison at which John Kiriakou served 23 months of a 30-month sentence following his 2013 Espionage Act–era plea deal; the originally ordered "minimum security work camp" placement was countermanded — per Kiriakou, on Brennan's direct intervention — to place him in the actual prison alongside the general population.

federal-prison-security-levels.title: Chomo
federal-prison-security-levels.summary: The prison term for a child molester, which John Kiriakou first heard on his first day at FCI Loretto when two skinheads at the Aryan table put it to him as the last of three vetting questions before deciding whether he could eat with them.

federal-prison-security-levels.title: The black box
federal-prison-security-levels.summary: The restraint apparatus in which John Kiriakou was moved from FCI Loretto to an outside medical appointment — handcuffs, leg irons, a waist chain and a steel box locked over the cuffs so the lock could not be picked — and the form he refused to sign because it required him to call everybody sir.

federal-prison-security-levels.title: Civil confinement
federal-prison-security-levels.summary: The policy John Kiriakou proposed from inside FCI Loretto — moving sex offenders to a secure location on prison grounds after their sentences end rather than releasing them — an argument that drew public criticism and which he defends with the case of a prisoner named Cook.

federal-prison-security-levels.title: Cook
federal-prison-security-levels.summary: The elderly Kentucky prisoner who worked with John Kiriakou in the FCI Loretto chapel, finished a 20-year child pornography sentence, and was back inside within four months facing 60 more — the case Kiriakou uses to answer critics of civil confinement.

federal-prison-security-levels.title: Truck
federal-prison-security-levels.summary: The convicted serial killer at FCI Loretto who sought John Kiriakou's approval, claimed to have run guns to Angolan rebels in a shrimp boat, and beat a prisoner unconscious after Kiriakou told him the man had called him a pedophile.

federal-torture-act.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
federal-torture-act.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

federal-torture-act.title: Espionage Act
federal-torture-act.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

federal-torture-act.title: Waterboarding
federal-torture-act.summary: Torture technique in which a prisoner is restrained on an inclined board with the head lower than the feet, a cloth placed over the face, and water poured continuously over it to simulate drowning. Per John Kiriakou, waterboarding was treated as a criminal act under U.S. and international law for decades before 2002 — including a post–World War II execution of Japanese soldiers who waterboarded American POWs, and a 1968 court-martial of a U.S. soldier photographed waterboarding a North Vietnamese prisoner — before the CIA reauthorized it after September 11. Abu Zubaydah was waterboarded 83 times; Khalid Sheikh Mohammed 187 times.

federal-torture-act.title: Mitchell and Jessen
federal-torture-act.summary: The two American psychologists who pitched the CIA's enhanced interrogation program to Director George Tenet at a cocktail party in late October 2001; designers of the program and its theoretical underpinning, "learned helplessness."

federal-torture-act.title: Five and a half years on the table
federal-torture-act.summary: John Kiriakou''s stated regret about his own whistleblowing — not that he did it, but that he waited: he learned of the torture programme in May 2002, it began on 2 August 2002, and he said nothing until 11 December 2007.

federal-torture-act.title: The Salim lawsuit
federal-torture-act.summary: The civil action brought against James Mitchell and Bruce Jessen by two survivors of the torture programme and the family of a prisoner who froze to death at a CIA site in Afghanistan — and the defence John Kiriakou found sickening, that the inventors of Zyklon B had not been prosecuted at Nuremberg.

felix-rodriguez.title: Donald Trump
felix-rodriguez.summary: 45th and 47th U.S. president. Per John Kiriakou, a man genuinely convinced he was doing right by bombing Iran, "duped" by the same Netanyahu nuclear bluff Obama once rejected — and, at the same time, the most blindly pro-Israel president in history, an admirer of autocrats who has never once criticized Vladimir Putin, and prone to gestures — from the Gulf of America to a since-abandoned "Department of War" rename — that test the edges of his actual authority.

felix-rodriguez.title: Jeffrey Epstein
felix-rodriguez.summary: Convicted sex offender; per John Kiriakou, was "an Israeli access agent" rather than a CIA asset, because the CIA collects foreign intelligence and Epstein's targets — Bill Clinton, Bill Gates, Prince Andrew — were not foreign. Kiriakou further holds that Epstein did die by suicide in federal custody, because in the Bureau of Prisons the cameras never work and the guards are always asleep.

felix-rodriguez.title: JFK assassination
felix-rodriguez.summary: November 22, 1963 killing of President John F. Kennedy in Dallas, Texas. John Kiriakou's position, drawn from a Pakistan-station encounter with Bay of Pigs commander Jean Gately, an RFK Jr. account of CIA Director John McCone's same-day exchange with Bobby Kennedy Sr., and a White House contact's confirmation that the remaining classified Kennedy documents all contain the word "Israel," is that elements of the CIA were probably involved and that Israeli intelligence was involved as well.

felix-rodriguez.title: Bill Clinton
felix-rodriguez.summary: 42nd U.S. president whom John Kiriakou describes as wholly disinterested in intelligence — briefed by the CIA only twice in eight years, with Vice President Al Gore taking the daily briefing instead and relaying anything important.

felix-rodriguez.title: Charlie Kirk shooting
felix-rodriguez.summary: Kiriakou questions the official account: a court filing says the ATF could not match the autopsy bullet to the rifle tied to the suspect.

felix-rodriguez.title: Iran Nuclear Assessment
felix-rodriguez.summary: Per John Kiriakou's assessment, the US–Israeli military campaign against Iran was a war of choice driven by Israeli political pressure rather than genuine intelligence indicating an Iranian nuclear weapons threat. The CIA produced two National Intelligence Estimates concluding Iran had no nuclear weapons program; Supreme Leader Ayatollah Khamenei issued a fatwa in the 1980s forbidding such a program. The U.S. went to war anyway, in Kiriakou's view, after President Trump replaced the Joint Chiefs of Staff with officers willing to accept Israeli intelligence and proceed.

fentanyl-and-china.title: Afghan heroin policy
fentanyl-and-china.summary: The post-2001 U.S. policy in Afghanistan of protecting, and per John Kiriakou actively encouraging, the cultivation of heroin poppy. Under the Taliban in 2000 Afghanistan produced 0% of the world's heroin; by 2009 under American occupation it produced 93%. Per a DEA officer Kiriakou consulted with on the policy paper he was preparing for Senator Kerry, the strategic rationale was that nearly all of the heroin flowed to Iran and Russia, addiction in those countries was considered desirable as a long-run societal weakener, and the same logic now operates in reverse with Chinese fentanyl flowing into the United States.

fentanyl-and-china.title: CIA Drug Facilitation
fentanyl-and-china.summary: Per John Kiriakou, the CIA''s reported involvement in facilitating the arrival of cocaine into the United States during the era that became the crack epidemic, and his own firsthand discovery — as a Senate Foreign Relations Committee investigator — that under American military control Afghanistan produced 93% of the world''s heroin. A DEA contact told him the report would never be published because ''we want Iran and Russia to be addicted to heroin. It weakens their societies.'' Kiriakou draws a direct parallel to the current fentanyl crisis: China is doing to the US what the US did to Iran and Russia.

fentanyl-and-china.title: John Kerry
fentanyl-and-china.summary: U.S. Senator from Massachusetts; chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee during John Kiriakou's 2009 service as the committee's senior investigator; subsequently U.S. Secretary of State; characterized by Kiriakou as a coward who buckled under CIA pressure on the Dasht-i-Leili reopening and as personally fixated on his perceived theft of the Secretary of State position by Hillary Clinton; the famously thrown medals were duplicates purchased at the post exchange.

fentanyl-and-china.title: The West Africa cocaine route
fentanyl-and-china.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of where cocaine transiting Venezuela actually goes: not north to the United States but east to West Africa, onto camels along an old Tuareg track to Morocco, and by boat to Spain. The drugs, he says, are meant for Western Europe — and are not Venezuelan to begin with, but Colombian and Ecuadorian.

fentanyl-and-china.title: Contra rebels
fentanyl-and-china.summary: The right-wing Nicaraguan insurgency armed by the Reagan administration against the Sandinista government. In John Kiriakou's account they were conservatives, right-wingers, in some cases fascists, and disgruntled military officers; they were split into a northern group the United States armed and a southern group that financed itself by selling cocaine — a distinction that became the pivot of the Gary Webb affair, and that Kiriakou uses to answer the CIA's standing denial that it had anything to do with the drug trade.

fentanyl-and-china.title: Kill the Messenger (Gary Webb)
fentanyl-and-china.summary: The 2014 film about journalist Gary Webb, on which John Kiriakou served as script advisor; when Kiriakou was arrested in January 2012, the FBI seized his electronics, including a draft of the unclassified Hollywood script, and stamped every page "top secret" despite Kiriakou having no role in writing it.

fentanyl-as-a-weapon-of-mass-destruction.title: The Caracas checklist
fentanyl-as-a-weapon-of-mass-destruction.summary: The sequence of steps John Kiriakou says an operation to overthrow the Venezuelan government would run through — pressure Maduro into flight, secure the presidential palace, co-opt or bombard the military, take the television and radio stations, hold the main intersections of the capital — and his insistence that none of it is the hard part.

fentanyl-as-a-weapon-of-mass-destruction.title: CIA Drug Facilitation
fentanyl-as-a-weapon-of-mass-destruction.summary: Per John Kiriakou, the CIA''s reported involvement in facilitating the arrival of cocaine into the United States during the era that became the crack epidemic, and his own firsthand discovery — as a Senate Foreign Relations Committee investigator — that under American military control Afghanistan produced 93% of the world''s heroin. A DEA contact told him the report would never be published because ''we want Iran and Russia to be addicted to heroin. It weakens their societies.'' Kiriakou draws a direct parallel to the current fentanyl crisis: China is doing to the US what the US did to Iran and Russia.

fentanyl-as-a-weapon-of-mass-destruction.title: Fentanyl and China
fentanyl-as-a-weapon-of-mass-destruction.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that China declines to stop the flow of fentanyl into the United States for the same reason he says the United States tolerated Afghan heroin reaching Iran and Russia — because an addicted society is a weaker one. He distinguishes Chinese-made illicit fentanyl, largely produced in Mexico, from the medical fentanyl that created the addiction pathway.

fentanyl-as-a-weapon-of-mass-destruction.title: Russia is not the gravest threat
fentanyl-as-a-weapon-of-mass-destruction.summary: John Kiriakou's rejection of the first policy speech by MI6's first woman chief, Blaise Metreweli, which named Russia and the Russo-Ukrainian war as the greatest danger to Britain and Europe. His counter-case is demographic and fiscal — Russia is practically bankrupt with a birth rate that would empty it in a century — and his own candidate for the real threat is not a state at all.

fentanyl-as-a-weapon-of-mass-destruction.title: The fentanyl-from-cocaine claim
fentanyl-as-a-weapon-of-mass-destruction.summary: The assertion that seventy per cent of American overdoses trace to fentanyl processed from Venezuelan cocaine, which John Kiriakou refuted on air by reading the DEA's own fact sheet — fentanyl is not made from cocaine, it is mixed into it, along with almost everything else on the market.

fentanyl-as-a-weapon-of-mass-destruction.title: The West Africa cocaine route
fentanyl-as-a-weapon-of-mass-destruction.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of where cocaine transiting Venezuela actually goes: not north to the United States but east to West Africa, onto camels along an old Tuareg track to Morocco, and by boat to Spain. Its work led to the creation of the permanent Senate Select Committee on Intelligence, which Kiriakou says ceased to function as real oversight roughly seven years after its founding.

fidel-castro.title: Syria as a regime-change template
fidel-castro.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that the fall of Bashar al-Assad shows organic regime change is faster, cheaper and less destructive than the enforced kind — and should be studied as a model. He allows aid to local forces as legitimate policy, and notes without prompting that in Syria the CIA was supplying al-Qaeda while the Pentagon supplied a group at war with it.

fidel-castro.title: The catering truck transfer
fidel-castro.summary: The covert removal of Donald Trump from Air Force One at the end of a NATO summit in Turkey — boarded in front of the television cameras, driven across the tarmac inside an airport catering truck, and flown on to Britain aboard a smaller jet while the White House press corps travelled on the aircraft everyone believed he was on.

fidel-castro.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
fidel-castro.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

fidel-castro.title: ISIS
fidel-castro.summary: The Islamic State, in John Kiriakou''s account, is an American policy failure made flesh — created because a faction decided al-Qaeda was not radical or violent enough, founded by Baghdadi while he sat in a U.S. military prison in Iraq, armed with hardware captured from the U.S.-supplied Iraqi army, and — per an email he cites from Hillary Clinton to John Podesta — funded by the governments of Saudi Arabia and Qatar. Kiriakou repeatedly punctured the anti-ISIS coalition''s logic: ISIS operated in seven countries while the U.S. bombed two, and Turkey had no real quarrel with ISIS at all — their common enemy was the Kurds.

fidel-castro.title: Syrian sanctions relief
fidel-castro.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that lifting sanctions on Syria was the most effective counter-terrorism measure available — because the recruits he interrogated joined for money, and an economy that offers roads, a working port and wages removes the recruiting pool rather than the recruiters.

field-loadout.title: CIA–Big Tech revolving door
field-loadout.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of the traffic between the CIA and the major technology companies — "they work hand in glove" — illustrated by a supervisor who resigned five years short of his thirty-year pension for a Microsoft job paying eight times his government salary. The exchange, he argues, benefits both sides and is for that reason dangerous: the agency gains access to the most advanced companies in the world, and the companies gain a direct channel into the intelligence community.

field-loadout.title: CIA feeder schools
field-loadout.summary: John Kiriakou's correction to the assumption that Georgetown is the CIA's principal university pipeline — George Washington University, he says, sends more people to the agency than Georgetown does, the first applied intelligence master's programme in the country was at Mercyhurst College in Erie, Pennsylvania, and he himself teaches intelligence studies to a largely American cohort at the University of Salamanca in Spain, many of whom end up at the CIA.

field-loadout.title: FCI Loretto
field-loadout.summary: U.S. Federal Correctional Institution in Loretto, Pennsylvania; the low-medium-security prison at which John Kiriakou served 23 months of a 30-month sentence following his 2013 Espionage Act–era plea deal; the originally ordered "minimum security work camp" placement was countermanded — per Kiriakou, on Brennan's direct intervention — to place him in the actual prison alongside the general population.

field-loadout.title: Osama bin Laden
field-loadout.summary: Founder and leader of al-Qaeda and the central target of the manhunt that shaped John Kiriakou's counterterrorism career. Per Kiriakou, bin Laden came from a billionaire Saudi construction family, was never one of the CIA-funded Afghan mujahideen, overruled subordinates who wanted to attack Israel and insisted the 9/11 attacks hit the United States to crash its economy, escaped Tora Bora dressed as a woman, and spent his final years next to Pakistan's equivalent of West Point — where, Kiriakou says, you would have to be a "mental defective" not to know he was there. Kiriakou believes the United States never intended to capture him alive.

fifth-fleet.title: Admiral William Crowe
fifth-fleet.summary: Former Chairman of the U.S. Joint Chiefs of Staff and former CENTCOM commander who had lived in Bahrain, author of the "pound for pound" formula every Bahraini and every American ambassador quotes, and the visiting dignitary John Kiriakou was assigned to escort — a week that ended with the Bahraini Prime Minister refusing to let go of Kiriakou's hand.

fifth-fleet.title: Hezbollah
fifth-fleet.summary: Lebanese Shia militant organization and political party. Per John Kiriakou, Israel''s strategic goal regarding Hezbollah is not to defeat it outright but to keep Lebanon in a state of chaos that serves Israeli interests. He cites two Israeli operations: the simultaneous pager-detonation attack that decapitated Hezbollah''s leadership, which he called ''the most incredible operation I''ve ever seen,'' and the strike that killed former leader Hassan Nasrallah by leveling an entire complex and killing roughly 300 people — which he characterized as a war crime.

fifth-fleet.title: John Kiriakou
fifth-fleet.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

fifth-fleet.title: Donald Trump
fifth-fleet.summary: 45th and 47th U.S. president. Per John Kiriakou, a man genuinely convinced he was doing right by bombing Iran, "duped" by the same Netanyahu nuclear bluff Obama once rejected — and, at the same time, the most blindly pro-Israel president in history, an admirer of autocrats who has never once criticized Vladimir Putin, and prone to gestures — from the Gulf of America to a since-abandoned "Department of War" rename — that test the edges of his actual authority.

fifth-fleet.title: Marco Rubio
fifth-fleet.summary: U.S. official whom John Kiriakou identifies as the real motivator behind pressure on Venezuela; Kiriakou argues Venezuela is not a meaningful drug threat to the U.S. and that Rubio simply wants Maduro gone.

fifth-fleet.title: Kiriakou''s recommended reading
fifth-fleet.summary: Asked in March 2026 what to read about the CIA, John Kiriakou named his own first two books and, beyond them, a 1980s history called The Rise and Fall of the CIA, which he says was his own first real introduction to covert action and its failures.

fifty-new-crimes-a-year.title: Bill Clinton
fifty-new-crimes-a-year.summary: 42nd U.S. president whom John Kiriakou describes as wholly disinterested in intelligence — briefed by the CIA only twice in eight years, with Vice President Al Gore taking the daily briefing instead and relaying anything important.

fifty-new-crimes-a-year.title: Church Committee
fifty-new-crimes-a-year.summary: U.S. Senate investigative committee operating in 1975–1976 that examined domestic intelligence abuses by the CIA, FBI, and NSA; per John Kiriakou, the Church Committee — alongside the concurrent Pike Committee in the House — was the last genuine moment of legislative oversight over the intelligence community, born of a national consensus that government had gone dangerously off course. Its work led to the creation of the permanent Senate Select Committee on Intelligence, which Kiriakou says ceased to function as real oversight roughly seven years after its founding.

fifty-new-crimes-a-year.title: Presidential appetite for intelligence
fifty-new-crimes-a-year.summary: John Kiriakou''s ranking of the presidents he served under by how much intelligence they actually wanted — from George H. W. Bush, who asked for special analytic products constantly, to Bill Clinton, who he says was briefed twice in eight years.

fifty-new-crimes-a-year.title: The Al Udeid strike
fifty-new-crimes-a-year.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of Iran''s face-saving retaliation for the American bombing of its nuclear sites in June 2025 — a single missile fired at Al Udeid air base in Qatar, announced two hours in advance, which he says hit a geodesic dome housing top secret communications.

fifty-new-crimes-a-year.title: The Clinton asset purge
fifty-new-crimes-a-year.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of the human-rights screening ordered in the first days of the Clinton administration, under which the CIA fired fully one third of its recruited assets — the informants whose reporting depended on their proximity to right-wing death squads in Latin America.

fifty-new-crimes-a-year.title: The Penn State textbooks
fifty-new-crimes-a-year.summary: How a week-long high-school scholarship to Penn State sent the teenage John Kiriakou into the university bookstore to buy the textbooks for Middle East courses he was not enrolled in — the purchase he credits with turning a childhood fascination into a field of study.

find-a-grave.title: Greta Zimmer Friedman
find-a-grave.summary: The Austrian-born dental assistant John Kiriakou found listed on Find a Grave as a "pop culture icon" — the woman a sailor grabbed and kissed in Times Square on V-J Day 1945, misidentified for years as a nurse, buried at Arlington, and whose story Kiriakou tells as the reason he writes cemetery books.

find-a-grave.title: Astrology at the CIA
find-a-grave.summary: John Kiriakou''s confirmation that astrology played a role in CIA work in the 1950s and early 1960s as part of MK-ULTRA, alongside time travel and teleportation — and his explanation for why: officials with unlimited budgets and no obligation to report to the public reasoned that there was probably nothing to it, but that if there were, it would make them a star.

find-a-grave.title: Carrying passports in Washington
find-a-grave.summary: John Kiriakou's report in September 2025 that people in Washington had begun carrying their passports for fear of being scooped up by immigration enforcement — alongside the case of an American symphony violinist held for three weeks, and his own belief that ethnic profiling violates the Fourth Amendment.

find-a-grave.title: "Christians are suckers"
find-a-grave.summary: John Kiriakou's explanation for how a president who does not go to church, has no spiritual adviser and could not name a line of scripture can push school prayer without cost — that he thinks most Christians are suckers, an assessment Kiriakou says he hates to make and believes anyway.

find-a-grave.title: E. Jean Carroll
find-a-grave.summary: The plaintiff whose persistence John Kiriakou singled out for deep respect — she kept suing after the political tide turned against her, and won an award he put at eighty-three or eighty-five million dollars on a day when Donald Trump won almost everything else in the federal courts.

find-a-grave.title: Special operations officer
find-a-grave.summary: The CIA staff category John Kiriakou describes as an assistant to the operations people — abbreviated SOO and pronounced "Sue" — most of whose members, he says, could not get through operational training, and whose duties included assembling surveillance teams for a case officer's dangerous meetings and filing his accounting paperwork at the end of a long night.

first-recruitment-in-athens.title: The Snickers bar
first-recruitment-in-athens.summary: The ritual in John Kiriakou''s Athens station: when an officer made a recruitment, the boss announced it in the staff meeting, everyone applauded, and he threw the officer a Snickers bar.

first-recruitment-in-athens.title: American shoes
first-recruitment-in-athens.summary: The detail by which the chief of the Greek intelligence service identified John Kiriakou as an American within minutes of meeting him — not his Greek, which was fluent, but his footwear — and which sent Kiriakou straight to a shoe shop before working the anarchist quarters of Athens.

first-recruitment-in-athens.title: There is no such thing as bad food in Athens
first-recruitment-in-athens.summary: The lesson John Kiriakou says he learned at a lorry drivers' stop outside Corinth, where the food was as good as his grandmother's — reached on the three-and-a-half-hour drives he made to meet a source too sensitive to be met in Athens, with a vineyard tour as his cover story.

first-recruitment-in-athens.title: Intelligence peddlers
first-recruitment-in-athens.summary: John Kiriakou''s breakdown of who actually walks into an American embassy offering information: the overwhelming majority are fabricators or probes, a few per cent are peddlers selling the same nugget to five embassies in a month, and about one per cent are the real thing.

first-recruitment-in-athens.title: John Kiriakou
first-recruitment-in-athens.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

first-recruitment-in-athens.title: The Athens carjacking
first-recruitment-in-athens.summary: The motorcyclist who followed John Kiriakou''s car through Athens two months into his posting — leading to a gun drawn on a ten-lane intersection, a shot fired, a disabled motorcycle, and a question asked back in Washington: *is John a hothead?*

fisa-court.title: James Comey
fisa-court.summary: Former FBI director indicted under the second Trump administration, whose prosecution John Kiriakou reads as a search for charges to fit a man rather than evidence of a crime — and which he expects to collapse, unlike the parallel case against John Brennan.

fisa-court.title: Julian Assange
fisa-court.summary: Kiriakou — a 15-year friend and former WikiLeaks board member — on why Assange is a publisher owed a journalist's immunity, and a political prisoner.

fisa-court.title: Eastern District of Virginia
fisa-court.summary: The U.S. federal district covering northern Virginia — home to Langley, the Pentagon, DHS and much of the intelligence-contractor industry — which John Kiriakou calls 'the espionage court' because the Justice Department files the great majority of its national security prosecutions there and because, in his telling, no national-security defendant has ever won a case in it; Kiriakou, Julian Assange, Edward Snowden and Jeffrey Sterling were all charged there.

fisa-court.title: Carter Page
fisa-court.summary: Trump campaign adviser against whom, per John Kiriakou, the FBI lied to the FISA court multiple times in order to obtain surveillance warrants. Kiriakou offers the episode as evidence less of a conspiracy than of an assumption — that at that level, with everything classified, officials believe the truth will simply never come out.

fisa-court.title: John Durham
fisa-court.summary: United States attorney for Connecticut appointed to investigate the origins of the Russia inquiry. Speaking in December 2019, John Kiriakou described Durham as having obtained John Brennan''s call logs, his emails from his time as CIA director, and the contemporaneous notes Brennan took in meetings with other agency heads — and read Durham''s own insistence that this was a criminal investigation rather than an inquiry as pointing at process crimes: false statements and perjury.

fisa.title: John Brennan
fisa.summary: Former Director of the CIA; characterized in KiriPedia's source corpus as the principal architect of the agency's enhanced interrogation program and as having plotted against an elected President

fisa.title: Central Intelligence Agency
fisa.summary: U.S. foreign intelligence service; John Kiriakou's employer from 1990 to 2004 and the central institution of KiriPedia

fisa.title: John Kiriakou
fisa.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

fisa.title: Patriot Act
fisa.summary: U.S. law passed after the September 11 attacks that vastly expanded domestic surveillance authority. Per John Kiriakou, the Patriot Act ''opened up everything'' — and he disputes the common belief that 9/11 was required to pass it: ''You underestimate Congress. They didn''t need a catastrophe — they would just pass it because they can.'' He ties it to NSA bulk-collection programs that vacuum up every phone call, text, email, and piece of metadata from Americans, in violation of the NSA''s own charter.

fisa.title: Bill Clinton
fisa.summary: 42nd U.S. president whom John Kiriakou describes as wholly disinterested in intelligence — briefed by the CIA only twice in eight years, with Vice President Al Gore taking the daily briefing instead and relaying anything important.

fisa.title: The Gabbard confirmation fight
fisa.summary: John Kiriakou's February 2025 assessment that Tulsi Gabbard was in real danger of not being confirmed as Director of National Intelligence — not because the Democrats opposed her, which they did, but because she was losing Republicans over Section 702, and had been telling them privately that she supported a renewal he knows she opposes.

five-and-a-half-years-on-the-table.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
five-and-a-half-years-on-the-table.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

five-and-a-half-years-on-the-table.title: Curtailment cables
five-and-a-half-years-on-the-table.summary: The career-ending requests John Kiriakou says he read coming back from the CIA's black sites — officers, doctors, psychologists and nurses asking to end their tours early rather than continue to take part in the interrogation programme — and his conclusion that if that many people were objecting in classified channels, someone would surely go public.

five-and-a-half-years-on-the-table.title: Federal Torture Act
five-and-a-half-years-on-the-table.summary: United States statute criminalizing torture; per John Kiriakou, on the books since at least 1946, with concrete enforcement history — after World War II the United States executed Japanese soldiers convicted of waterboarding American prisoners of war, meaning waterboarding was at that time a capital offense under U.S. law. The act was effectively set aside for the CIA's enhanced interrogation program after 2002.

five-and-a-half-years-on-the-table.title: The 1968 waterboarding conviction
five-and-a-half-years-on-the-table.summary: The precedent John Kiriakou uses to dispose of the argument that waterboarding was legally uncertain after 2002: a January 1968 Washington Post front page showing an American soldier waterboarding a North Vietnamese prisoner, an investigation ordered by Defense Secretary Robert McNamara, and the soldier''s arrest, conviction for torture and imprisonment. The law, Kiriakou points out, never changed in between.

five-and-a-half-years-on-the-table.title: Geneva Conventions
five-and-a-half-years-on-the-table.summary: The laws of war at the center of John Kiriakou''s most-told confrontation story: finding hooded prisoners in Pakistan, he demanded of the officer in charge — "Are you seriously telling me that you have never read the Geneva Convention? It is a war crime to put hoods on them. Take the hoods off." The two reported each other to headquarters; Kiriakou got in trouble — "they didn''t give two shits about the Geneva Convention." He indicts the Bush administration''s twin dodges: that al-Qaeda fighters, as non-state actors, fell outside the Conventions'' protections, and that the techniques weren''t torture at all.

five-and-a-half-years-on-the-table.title: Leaking versus whistleblowing
five-and-a-half-years-on-the-table.summary: The distinction John Kiriakou insists is legal rather than rhetorical — whistleblowing being the disclosure of waste, fraud, abuse, illegality or threats to public health and safety, and leaking being everything else. He applies the same statutory test to Edward Snowden, to Chelsea Manning and to his own case, holds that motive is irrelevant to whether the test is met, and had to have the definition explained to him by his own attorney, because no whistleblower thinks he is one.

five-eyes.title: Mount Weather
five-eyes.summary: U.S. government continuity-of-government underground facility on the Virginia–West Virginia line

five-eyes.title: The approvals required to kill Assange
five-eyes.summary: John Kiriakou's reading of the 2021 Yahoo News report on CIA plans to abduct or assassinate Julian Assange — that an operation of that kind requires three separate approvals, from the Justice Department's Office of Legal Counsel, from the government of the target's own Five Eyes country, and from the congressional oversight committees — and his conclusion that if the planning went as far as reported, all three were given.

five-eyes.title: The Greenland prediction he got wrong
five-eyes.summary: John Kiriakou's account of dismissing the idea that the United States would seize Greenland on a podcast one afternoon, and hearing Stephen Miller say the opposite on CNN an hour later — after which he treated the threat to a NATO member as a legitimate problem, and looked to Emmanuel Macron rather than Keir Starmer to stop it.

five-eyes.title: "One dead pedophile"
five-eyes.summary: John Kiriakou's explanation of why he believes the American intelligence community will not examine whether Jeffrey Epstein worked for a foreign service — that the accusation points at Israel, that the relationship with Israel is uniquely valuable, and that nobody in Washington will upset it over one dead pedophile when covering it up is easier.

five-eyes.title: The debate with the Mossad director
five-eyes.summary: John Kiriakou's account of his first appearance on Piers Morgan's programme, where he debated a former director of the Mossad who he says could not stop chuckling, and the exchange about Israeli espionage that ended in "no comment".

five-eyes.title: French intelligence (DGSE)
five-eyes.summary: The French foreign intelligence service; characterized as exceptionally talented, exceptionally aggressive, and routinely lethal in the conduct of its operations

flock-cameras.title: Mass Surveillance
flock-cameras.summary: Kiriakou says the NSA has dropped any pretext of protecting civil liberties, warehousing every call, text and email in the Utah desert.

flock-cameras.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
flock-cameras.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

flock-cameras.title: John Kiriakou
flock-cameras.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

flock-cameras.title: 2028 presidential field
flock-cameras.summary: John Kiriakou's assessment of the wide-open 2028 presidential race — the first in his life, he says, where he has no idea who either party will nominate. Predictive markets were listing 44 Democrats and 26 Republicans as possible candidates. His own preferred candidate is Tucker Carlson, whom he says he has repeatedly begged to run; his working assumption about anyone who does want the job is that they are "a narcissist and probably a sociopath on top of it."

flock-cameras.title: Amaryllis Fox Kennedy
flock-cameras.summary: Former CIA non-official-cover officer who worked under commercial cover as an international art consultant, later a Trump campaign manager and nominee for deputy CIA director. Per John Kiriakou, Senator Tom Cotton threatened to filibuster her appointment; the president responded by naming her deputy national security adviser instead — a job Kiriakou considers more powerful, since the CIA director reports to the national security adviser.

flock-cameras.title: Andrew Bustamante
flock-cameras.summary: Former CIA officer who sells CIA-style training online; John Kiriakou identifies him as the lone critic of his work hosting a show on a Russian network, and argues Bustamante's training business — open to anyone who pays — is the more problematic of the two.

forcing-iran-toward-a-bomb.title: The Iran–Israel exchange assessment
forcing-iran-toward-a-bomb.summary: John Kiriakou''s judgement — which he expects to be unpopular — that Iran came out ahead of Israel in their direct missile exchange: the Iron Dome proved fallible, Iranian targeting was selective where Israel''s was not, and the ceasefire came, in his reading, because Israel had run out of missiles.

forcing-iran-toward-a-bomb.title: The Syria chemical attack correction
forcing-iran-toward-a-bomb.summary: John Kiriakou's public retraction of what he wrote about the August 2013 chemical attack near Damascus. Asked about the passage in his book on Iran, he said he had written it before United Nations whistleblowers came forward to say they did not believe it was a Syrian government attack, and thanked the questioner for the chance to correct it.

forcing-iran-toward-a-bomb.title: CIA attention to West Africa
forcing-iran-toward-a-bomb.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer on whether the CIA is likely to be operating in Burkina Faso: for all the years he was at the agency it cared very little about Africa and especially West Africa, but the presence of al-Qaeda and Islamic State affiliates plus the drug trade makes CIA and special forces involvement probable — and, he adds, the American public will not hear about it.

forcing-iran-toward-a-bomb.title: CIA–FBI incompatible computer systems
forcing-iran-toward-a-bomb.summary: John Kiriakou's claim that from the CIA's founding in 1947 until 2009 the computer systems of the CIA and the FBI were not compatible with one another — no message could be sent from one to the other and no intelligence shared — which he offers both as the material substrate of the interagency hatred that helped make September 11 possible, and as the gap through which James Mitchell and Bruce Jessen were able to pass Ali Soufan's FBI debriefings of Abu Zubaydah off as the fruits of torture.

forcing-iran-toward-a-bomb.title: Fake CIA résumés
forcing-iran-toward-a-bomb.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of being used as a human authenticator in the private sector: at the consulting firm he joined after leaving the CIA, every job applicant claiming agency service was sent to dinner with him, and by his count fully half of them had never set foot inside the CIA.

forcing-iran-toward-a-bomb.title: Hugh Francis Redmond
forcing-iran-toward-a-bomb.summary: The first CIA officer to die in the line of duty, per John Kiriakou — a Special Activities Division officer sent to Shanghai in 1946 under cover as an ice cream machine salesman, arrested by the Chinese communists in 1951, held and tortured for nineteen years, and declared a suicide by Beijing in 1970. The CIA denied he had ever worked for it until his name was declassified and added to the Wall of Honor.

foreign-aid.title: The al-Qaeda foot soldier
foreign-aid.summary: What John Kiriakou says he learned from interviewing captured al-Qaeda fighters — not the leaders but the eighteen-, nineteen- and twenty-year-olds, who told essentially the same story: an isolated village, illiteracy, no job skills, a poor relationship with their father, an age at which they wanted to marry, and no father willing to give them a daughter. The local imam offered $300 a month to go to Afghanistan, and $500 to their parents if they were martyred.

foreign-aid.title: The Sanaa sewer project
foreign-aid.summary: The example John Kiriakou uses for what patient foreign assistance looks like: on a visit to Yemen around 2000 he called on the Dutch ambassador and the Italian defence attaché, who were proud because their governments had just finished building a sewer system and water treatment facility for the capital — a project that had taken about fifteen years.

foreign-aid.title: CIA Smart TV Surveillance
foreign-aid.summary: Per John Kiriakou, a CIA technical capability — disclosed publicly by the 2017 Vault 7 leaks — to convert a smart television's speaker system into a covert listening microphone even while the television appears to be switched off.

foreign-aid.title: Israeli foreknowledge of 9/11
foreign-aid.summary: John Kiriakou's stated belief that Israeli intelligence had penetrated al-Qaeda and knew an attack was coming but withheld the warning as a policy decision, offered as his explanation for the dozens of Israelis arrested in New York in the days after the attacks.

foreign-aid.title: Marjorie Taylor Greene
foreign-aid.summary: American congresswoman whom John Kiriakou, despite deep political disagreement, has repeatedly credited for breaking with her party on the Epstein files, on military aid to Israel, and on Gaza. He describes her as courageous for pressing Donald Trump to release the files unredacted, and says the pressure ultimately forced her out of Washington.

foreign-aid.title: Nixon's guarantee of Israeli national security
foreign-aid.summary: John Kiriakou's account that AIPAC, having begun to focus on election fundraising in the late 1960s, succeeded in getting President Nixon to guarantee Israeli national security in 1969 — a commitment he says no American president had made before.

fort-chapman.title: Jennifer Matthews
fort-chapman.summary: CIA analyst who was made chief of base at Khost, Afghanistan without operational or security training in order to complete the tour requirement for promotion, and who was killed there with six other officers by a Jordanian double agent she had gone outside the fortified perimeter to greet with a birthday cake.

fort-chapman.title: Senior Intelligence Service
fort-chapman.summary: The CIA's executive rank above the General Schedule, entry to which requires a tour outside an officer's own directorate and a tour in the policy community — a box-checking requirement John Kiriakou identifies as the reason an untrained analyst was sent to run a base in Afghanistan. Its officers are career staff rather than political appointees, some with thirty or forty years in place, which is why Kiriakou describes the service as capable of simply waiting a president out — or slow-rolling him. Its officers in the Counterterrorism Center were also the authors of the torture techniques.

fort-chapman.title: Abu Zubaydah
fort-chapman.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

fort-chapman.title: Maduro Capture
fort-chapman.summary: CIA-driven nighttime operation in which a team of Delta Force commandos entered Venezuela and removed Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro and his wife from their beds. Per John Kiriakou, the key enabling intelligence — per a New York Times account he cited — came from a CIA asset inside Maduro''s presidential palace who called when Maduro went to sleep: ''He''s sound asleep. If you''re going to do it, do it now.'' At least eighty people were killed in the operation, including approximately thirty-five Cubans. Kiriakou compares it to the 1989 capture of Manuel Noriega, in which US forces blasted death metal at the Vatican Embassy until Noriega was asked to leave.

fort-chapman.title: Alfreda Bikowsky
fort-chapman.summary: Senior CIA officer who headed Alec Station and, before that, served as its chief of operations, overseeing the CIA's torture program; per John Kiriakou, "bad news from the get-go," and part of a failed attempt with Rich Blee to turn a San Diego al-Qaeda cell into double agents.

fort-chapman.title: 9/11 plea agreements
fort-chapman.summary: The Biden-era plea deals under which Khalid Sheikh Mohammed and co-defendants agreed to plead guilty to murdering 2,976 people in exchange for life without parole and a guarantee against transfer to the Colorado supermax — vacated by the Secretary of Defense after public backlash. Per John Kiriakou, the deals existed because torture had rendered every confession inadmissible, leaving no usable evidence.

fort-gordon.title: Miranda Rights
fort-gordon.summary: Reality Winner, interviewed on Kiriakou's show, says she was never read her Miranda rights during her 2017 arrest by the FBI.

fort-gordon.title: Watermark
fort-gordon.summary: Reality Winner, on Kiriakou's show, describes the printer watermark that let the NSA trace her leaked document to a specific office.

fort-gordon.title: Afghan Languages
fort-gordon.summary: The three major languages of Afghanistan — Pashto, Dari (a form of Persian), and Arabic — as discussed on John Kiriakou's show with NSA whistleblower and former military linguist Reality Winner.

fort-gordon.title: Edward Snowden
