fort-gordon.summary: Former NSA contractor who in 2013 disclosed the scope of U.S. [mass surveillance](/wiki/mass-surveillance), including the Section 702 collection program. Per John Kiriakou — who counts Snowden among the small group of national-security whistleblowers prosecuted under the Espionage Act — Snowden was ''stuck between two awful slippery slopes'': breaking his oath and chain of command on one side, and on the other catching something ''cut and dry against the Constitution'' that no one would act on. Kiriakou notes Snowden could not use his chain of command (as Kiriakou could not, his own chain being Jose Rodriguez), and that Judge Leonie Brinkema had reserved the Snowden case for herself before he fled the country.

fort-gordon.title: FBI Arrest Strategies
fort-gordon.summary: Per John Kiriakou, the FBI deliberately times arrests for Thursdays or Friday evenings because no federal arraignments happen on Fridays, forcing detainees to spend the weekend in jail before facing a judge on Monday — a tactic he says he saw applied to January 6 defendants as well as to himself.

fort-gordon.title: Government Accountability Project
fort-gordon.summary: The Washington whistleblower-advocacy law firm and NGO, known as GAP, whose attorney Jesselyn Radack took John Kiriakou's case after his 2012 arrest and told him he was a whistleblower whether he thought so or not.

four-deaths-at-loretto.title: Bureau of Prisons
four-deaths-at-loretto.summary: The federal agency that ran John Kiriakou's incarceration — and one of his most persistent post-prison targets. The BOP overrode his judge's camp recommendation by deeming him "a threat to the public safety," threatened him with "diesel therapy" until 1,600 logged phone calls and letters from a dozen House members and two senators backed it off, and, per Kiriakou, functions as "an employment agency for unemployable semi-literate rural white men" and "a dumping ground for failed medical professionals" — an agency for which a prisoner's death is cheaper than his treatment.

four-deaths-at-loretto.title: The Public Health Service in the prisons
four-deaths-at-loretto.summary: John Kiriakou's contrast between the United States Public Health Service officers he worked with during fifteen years at the CIA, whom he found excellent, and the Public Health Service physician assistants he encountered as a prisoner at FCI Loretto, whom he describes as the dregs of the service — people dumped into the Bureau of Prisons because they could not work anywhere else in government.

four-deaths-at-loretto.title: Larry
four-deaths-at-loretto.summary: The prisoner at FCI Loretto who complained of back pain for more than a year, was given Tylenol, and progressed from a cane to a walker to a wheelchair before a chaplain forced an outside hospital referral — which found stage four cancer of the spine. He died in his bunk two weeks later.

four-deaths-at-loretto.title: Medical care in federal prison
four-deaths-at-loretto.summary: Kiriakou's account of health care at FCI Loretto, where a bunkmate's months of reported chest pain ended in a heart attack, a prisoner with untreated back pain was diagnosed with terminal cancer weeks before he died, and Kiriakou himself collapsed after being handed a drug nobody had explained to him.

four-deaths-at-loretto.title: FCI Loretto
four-deaths-at-loretto.summary: U.S. Federal Correctional Institution in Loretto, Pennsylvania; the low-medium-security prison at which John Kiriakou served 23 months of a 30-month sentence following his 2013 Espionage Act–era plea deal; the originally ordered "minimum security work camp" placement was countermanded — per Kiriakou, on Brennan's direct intervention — to place him in the actual prison alongside the general population.

four-deaths-at-loretto.title: The black box
four-deaths-at-loretto.summary: The restraint apparatus in which John Kiriakou was moved from FCI Loretto to an outside medical appointment — handcuffs, leg irons, a waist chain and a steel box locked over the cuffs so the lock could not be picked — and the form he refused to sign because it required him to call everybody sir.

france-recognizes-palestine.title: Proposals to relocate the Palestinians
france-recognizes-palestine.summary: John Kiriakou's account of recurring schemes to solve the Palestinian question by moving the population somewhere else — including a 1980s proposal to rename a barren diamond of land on the Saudi–Iraqi border "Palestine" and resettle everyone there — and his verdict that picking up an entire people and moving them is unprecedented and untenable.

france-recognizes-palestine.title: Ireland recognizes Palestine
france-recognizes-palestine.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of the American reaction to Ireland''s recognition of Palestine, which he says he witnessed the aftermath of while in the country: the CIA was indifferent, but the State Department was apoplectic — not about Ireland itself, but about the precedent, which Kiriakou says other European states promptly began to follow.

france-recognizes-palestine.title: Famine in Gaza
france-recognizes-palestine.summary: The starvation of the civilian population of the Gaza Strip, which John Kiriakou describes as a United Nations-declared famine caused not by an absence of food but by an Israeli refusal to let food reach the people who need it; Kiriakou characterises it as a war crime, a crime against humanity and a form of genocide, attributing that characterisation to the United Nations and the International Court of Justice rather than to himself.

france-recognizes-palestine.title: The Egyptian berm
france-recognizes-palestine.summary: The earthwork Egypt built along its Gaza frontier more than a year before July 2025, which John Kiriakou describes as a defence not against Palestinians but against Israel — built because Cairo feared the border being thrown open from the other side, and because Egyptian troops would not fire on two million people.

france-recognizes-palestine.title: Hostages and prisoners
france-recognizes-palestine.summary: John Kiriakou's objection to the vocabulary of the Gaza war — that Israelis held by Hamas are called hostages while Palestinians held by Israel without charge are called prisoners — which he treats as one instance of a wider pattern in which allies have governments and adversaries have regimes.

france-recognizes-palestine.title: Trump's NATO reversal
france-recognizes-palestine.summary: John Kiriakou's explanation for Donald Trump's turn from hostility to enthusiasm for NATO — that he genuinely expected Vladimir Putin to do as he was told, and embraced the alliance out of anger when Putin would not settle the war in Ukraine, because the alternative was standing alone.

frances-haugen.title: Elliott Abrams
frances-haugen.summary: The Reagan-era assistant secretary of state whose 2023 appointment to a Biden administration advisory board John Kiriakou treated as proof that neoliberal and neoconservative foreign policy are the same policy with interchangeable players — a man who pleaded guilty over Iran-Contra, was pardoned, helped sell the Iraqi weapons of mass destruction case, and then served Donald Trump on Iran and Venezuela.

frances-haugen.title: The Baltimore tunnel
frances-haugen.summary: The rail tunnel built in 1850 just north of Baltimore that John Kiriakou names as the physical reason the American northeast has no high-speed rail — it is too narrow to admit a high-speed train, so every train on the corridor must be built to fit through it.

frances-haugen.title: The Capitol Hill cocaine ring
frances-haugen.summary: The 1983 congressional drug scandal John Kiriakou stumbled into at eighteen, when an FBI agent called at his father's house and then asked him whether he had ever seen his congressman trade stamps for cocaine — a question he answered no to, and which turned out to be exactly what the congressman was doing.

frances-haugen.title: The cocaine in the West Wing
frances-haugen.summary: John Kiriakou's explanation of how a bag of cocaine came to be found in a White House cubby in July 2023 — the phone cubbies outside every vaulted area, the fingerprints that every cleared visitor has already surrendered, and his prediction that despite an investigation requiring only a couple of hours of work, the public would never be told whose it was.

frances-haugen.title: The nuclear testing legacy
frances-haugen.summary: John Kiriakou's observation that the United States waited seventy years after the Second World War before offering money and relocation to the South Pacific communities contaminated by its own atmospheric nuclear tests — a delay he called ridiculous, and a measure of how casually the era's tens of thousands of test detonations were treated.

frances-haugen.title: The legal definition of whistleblowing
frances-haugen.summary: John Kiriakou''s insistence that whistleblowing is a legally defined act rather than a figure of speech: bringing to light evidence of waste, fraud, abuse, illegality, or threats to public health or public safety — at any level of government.

francis-gary-powers.title: Spies of Arlington National Cemetery
francis-gary-powers.summary: On the Walk With History podcast, John Kiriakou — author of Remains of the Day: A Definitive Guide to Washington D.C.''s Historic Cemeteries — toured Arlington National Cemetery and told personal and historical stories about the intelligence figures buried there, including OSS founder William Donovan, deputy CIA director Vernon Walters, codebreakers William and Elizabeth Friedman, slain station chiefs Richard Welch and William Buckley, U-2 pilot Francis Gary Powers, and Mike Spann, the first CIA officer killed after 9/11.

francis-gary-powers.title: Mike Spann
francis-gary-powers.summary: CIA officer; first American killed in combat in Afghanistan after the September 11 attacks and, in John Kiriakou's telling, the first of his own colleagues to die in the line of duty in the war that followed; killed during the November 2001 Qala-i-Jangi prison uprising; worked ten feet from Kiriakou in the Counterterrorism Center bullpen. Kiriakou, who lives within walking distance of Arlington National Cemetery, still visits his grave.

francis-gary-powers.title: Vernon Walters
francis-gary-powers.summary: U.S. Army general who served as Deputy Director of the CIA, Ambassador to Germany, Ambassador to the United Nations, and as Nixon''s occasional secret envoy to foreign leaders. Per John Kiriakou — who met him at an early-career analysts'' dinner — Walters said the only time he was ever afraid for his safety was during a secret Nixon-ordered peace mission to Fidel Castro in Cuba, when it occurred to him that Castro could poison him and no one but Nixon would know he was there: ''I wouldn''t trust Nixon to call my wife.'' Then he looked at Castro and thought: ''I can take this scrawny son of a bitch.''

francis-gary-powers.title: William Donovan
francis-gary-powers.summary: General William "Wild Bill" Donovan — Medal of Honor recipient, decorated World War I veteran, Wall Street figure, and founder of the wartime Office of Strategic Services (OSS). Per John Kiriakou, Donovan had President Truman's ear and insisted the new agency be independent rather than a division of the FBI; he was among the men who sat down with visiting MI6 officers in New York in 1946–47 and sketched out a centralized intelligence service on pads of paper, and he became — in Kiriakou's telling — the first director of the CIA, over the sustained opposition of J. Edgar Hoover.

francis-gary-powers.title: William and Elizabeth Friedman
francis-gary-powers.summary: American cryptologists who, per John Kiriakou, broke the Nazi Enigma encryption largely by exploiting a single known fact: every German communication ended with ''Heil Hitler'' — sometimes spelled out, sometimes abbreviated ''HH.'' Working outward from the letters H, E, I, L, T, R, they cracked the code one letter at a time. Their work led directly to the founding of the National Security Agency. Both are buried at Arlington National Cemetery.

francis-gary-powers.title: Bill Buckley
francis-gary-powers.summary: CIA station chief in Beirut kidnapped by Palestinian Islamic Jihad in March 1984; tortured at length over fifteen months; killed in captivity; the case from which the agency derived a generation of operational-security lessons including the abandonment of single-point tracking devices in CIA officers' personal kit.

frank-heart-attack.title: The glyburide incident
frank-heart-attack.summary: The episode John Kiriakou described in a Letter from Loretto of 12 September 2014: handed a bottle of glyburide by the prison pharmacy without explanation, he crashed twice and passed out on the floor — and his physician father-in-law told him the drug could have put him into heart failure.

frank-heart-attack.title: Larry
frank-heart-attack.summary: The prisoner at FCI Loretto who complained of back pain for more than a year, was given Tylenol, and progressed from a cane to a walker to a wheelchair before a chaplain forced an outside hospital referral — which found stage four cancer of the spine. He died in his bunk two weeks later.

frank-heart-attack.title: Medical care in federal prison
frank-heart-attack.summary: Kiriakou's account of health care at FCI Loretto, where a bunkmate's months of reported chest pain ended in a heart attack, a prisoner with untreated back pain was diagnosed with terminal cancer weeks before he died, and Kiriakou himself collapsed after being handed a drug nobody had explained to him.

frank-heart-attack.title: Kiriakou on mass incarceration
frank-heart-attack.summary: The argument Kiriakou developed in the letters from Loretto and has repeated since: that the United States holds a quarter of the world''s prisoners with five per cent of its people, that the cause is the drug war and election-year legislating, and that reform died in the Senate without a vote.

frank-heart-attack.title: Paul Wright
frank-heart-attack.summary: The former prisoner who founded the Human Rights Defense Center and co-created Prison Legal News — the longest-running publication produced by and for current and former prisoners in American history — and whose reporting John Kiriakou draws on for the finding that the Bureau of Prisons' own grievance system increases prison violence.

frank-heart-attack.title: The chapel job
frank-heart-attack.summary: The work assignment John Kiriakou was given at FCI Loretto after he volunteered to teach a class — *"if I want you to teach a class I'll ask you to teach a class"* — and was made a janitor in the chapel instead, at $1.08 a month.

frank-russo.title: Pete Calabrese
frank-russo.summary: The senior Bonanno family member at FCI Loretto, known as Peter the Rabbit, who challenged John Kiriakou over his friendship with the cooperating witness Frank Russo and told him Russo brought dishonour to the Italians.

frank-russo.title: The rat and pedophile table
frank-russo.summary: The cafeteria table at FCI Loretto reserved for cooperating witnesses and sex offenders — a placement that also carried a ban from the television room, and which John Kiriakou describes as an outcome cooperators knew to expect before they agreed to testify.

frank-russo.title: FCI Loretto
frank-russo.summary: U.S. Federal Correctional Institution in Loretto, Pennsylvania; the low-medium-security prison at which John Kiriakou served 23 months of a 30-month sentence following his 2013 Espionage Act–era plea deal; the originally ordered "minimum security work camp" placement was countermanded — per Kiriakou, on Brennan's direct intervention — to place him in the actual prison alongside the general population.

frank-russo.title: Jimmy Dimora
frank-russo.summary: The Cuyahoga County official convicted in the corruption case that also sent John Kiriakou's FCI Loretto bunkmate Frank Russo to prison — the man Russo testified against, and who in Kiriakou's account received a draconian sentence and will die in prison.

frank-russo.title: Mark Lanzalotti
frank-russo.summary: The prisoner John Kiriakou describes as his closest friend at FCI Loretto and one of the finest human beings he has known — a first-time non-violent drug defendant sentenced to triple life without parole for refusing to inform, the prison's foremost cook and bookie, and the man whose release Kiriakou secured by writing his Second Chance Act petition.

frank-russo.title: The stinger
frank-russo.summary: The improvised prison cooking rig John Kiriakou describes at FCI Loretto — a wall-plug faceplate wired to live current and dropped into a bucket of water — which produced restaurant-quality Italian food daily and, on one occasion, killed a correctional officer.

frank-serpico.title: "There is almost no upside"
frank-serpico.summary: John Kiriakou''s accounting of what blowing the whistle cost him — pension, friends, freedom and finally family — set against the single thing he says is left: knowing he did the right thing. And his timeline, from the whistle in 2007 to a vindication he says took eleven years.

frank-serpico.title: The legal definition of whistleblowing
frank-serpico.summary: John Kiriakou''s insistence that whistleblowing is a legally defined act rather than a figure of speech: bringing to light evidence of waste, fraud, abuse, illegality, or threats to public health or public safety — at any level of government.

frank-serpico.title: Whistleblower psychology
frank-serpico.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of what distinguishes people who come forward: psychological studies showing whistleblowers hold a much more sharply defined sense of right and wrong than the general population, weighed against his own claim that there is no whistleblower who has not contemplated suicide in the period after going public.

frank-serpico.title: Edward Snowden
frank-serpico.summary: Former NSA contractor who in 2013 disclosed the scope of U.S. [mass surveillance](/wiki/mass-surveillance), including the Section 702 collection program. Per John Kiriakou — who counts Snowden among the small group of national-security whistleblowers prosecuted under the Espionage Act — Snowden was ''stuck between two awful slippery slopes'': breaking his oath and chain of command on one side, and on the other catching something ''cut and dry against the Constitution'' that no one would act on. Kiriakou notes Snowden could not use his chain of command (as Kiriakou could not, his own chain being Jose Rodriguez), and that Judge Leonie Brinkema had reserved the Snowden case for herself before he fled the country.

frank-serpico.title: The NYPD intelligence post
frank-serpico.summary: The New York Police Department position — deputy commissioner for intelligence — that John Kiriakou says traditionally goes to someone coming out of the CIA, and which he uses to explain why the agency is indifferent to who wins a New York mayoral election so long as the post and its liaison with the joint terrorism task force survive.

frank-serpico.title: Angela Merkel
frank-serpico.summary: German chancellor whose mobile phone the NSA was intercepting, in what John Kiriakou treats as the cleanest illustration of the two-tier American attitude to surveillance: the interception of one of Washington''s closest allies was big news, Hillary Clinton flew to Germany to apologise, and — per Kiriakou — the United States then did it again. Asked about it in Berlin, his answer was that intercepting her phone is exactly what he wants the CIA to be doing.

frank-snepp.title: The Vietnam speech
frank-snepp.summary: A paid speaking engagement John Kiriakou described in February 2026 — booked by a New York speakers bureau for the morning of 10 August, addressing three hundred Australian investment bankers at their annual convention in a country he had never visited and had always wanted to.

frank-snepp.title: John Kiriakou
frank-snepp.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

frank-snepp.title: Kyriakos Mitsotakis
frank-snepp.summary: The Greek prime minister John Kiriakou names when asked which world leader he would put in Donald Trump's place — a choice he qualifies by admitting he did not vote for the man the first time and has since been pleasantly surprised.

frank-snepp.title: Sports and the Steelers bar
frank-snepp.summary: Asked whether he enjoys any sport, John Kiriakou named baseball and football, and described walking to a Steelers bar in Clarendon, Arlington, to watch a game he could have watched at home — for the five hundred screaming Pittsburgh fans.

frank-snepp.title: Trump's Supreme Court appointees
frank-snepp.summary: An assessment John Kiriakou volunteered in February 2026 and that runs against his politics elsewhere: that Donald Trump''s appointees to the Supreme Court have been surprisingly good, and that the justices he regards as disasters — Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas — were put there by moderate presidents.

frank-snepp.title: The USS Gerald Ford plumbing failure
frank-snepp.summary: Days before the 2026 war, John Kiriakou raised the possibility that a sewage failure severe enough to send the carrier USS Gerald R. Ford back to Norfolk was sabotage by a crew that did not want to go to war with Iran.

freedom-of-information-act.title: Jake Tapper
freedom-of-information-act.summary: CNN anchor who drove to FCI Loretto to interview the imprisoned John Kiriakou — and who asked President Obama at a press conference why he had insisted on prosecuting a man who exposed a crime, a question Obama answered by walking away from the podium. Tapper's visit was the head of a media wave that began with a smuggled-out letter on the Huffington Post, and it became Kiriakou's protection inside; even a guard known as a psychopath left him alone rather than find CNN parked beside his car.

freedom-of-information-act.title: George H.W. Bush
freedom-of-information-act.summary: The 41st president — and the one John Kiriakou briefed a number of times, finding him "far more worldly" than the others, as befits a former CIA director. Kiriakou credits him with throwing away his presidency by keeping his word and stopping short of Baghdad, faults the ceasefire's helicopter loophole that let Saddam slaughter the Shia, calls him the last president to give the Arabs a fair shake — cutting off loan guarantees until Israel stopped building settlements — and traces the second Iraq war's personal edge to Saddam's 1993 attempt to assassinate him.

freedom-of-information-act.title: George W. Bush
freedom-of-information-act.summary: 43rd President of the United States. In John Kiriakou's telling, Bush signed the August 1, 2002 executive order that authorized the CIA torture program, spent years telling the public "we don't torture," and — days after Kiriakou's 2007 ABC interview — blamed torture on "a rogue CIA officer" while walking from the White House South Portico to Marine One, a moment Kiriakou instantly read as the White House preparing to pin the program on him. Bush also ordered the FBI removed from Abu Zubaydah's black site, flew the bin Laden family out of the country after 9/11, and loosened the assassination ban of Executive Order 12333.

freedom-of-information-act.title: Oliver Stone
freedom-of-information-act.summary: American film director with whom John Kiriakou struck up a friendship after his release from prison. Stone optioned the rights to one chapter of Kiriakou's first book, co-developed an unmade History Channel series with him, blurbed his book on Abu Zubaydah, and was among the public figures who campaigned against the Bureau of Prisons' attempt to shut down Kiriakou's prison blog. The two disagree sharply over whether the CIA killed John F. Kennedy.

freedom-of-information-act.title: The buried Senate documents
freedom-of-information-act.summary: John Kiriakou's account of a sitting senator who could not obtain a set of documents classified in the 1970s. Long past the point where mandatory declassification should have applied, the CIA disclaimed them as not its own; they turned out to be Senate documents, which no disclosure law reaches, and no authority existed to compel their release.

freedom-of-information-act.title: Thirty-year mandatory declassification
freedom-of-information-act.summary: The statutory requirement, described by John Kiriakou, that classified American documents be released after thirty years — a law he says virtually nobody knows about, and which he raises against the continued withholding of Kennedy assassination records more than sixty years on. He also describes the redaction practice that operates alongside it.

freemasons-and-opus-dei-at-the-cia.title: The tier one walk-up
freemasons-and-opus-dei-at-the-cia.summary: The recruitment John Kiriakou calls one of the best operations of his career and credits entirely to his mentor Gust Avrakotos: an approach to an official of a tier one country — one of America''s greatest enemies — made by the simple expedient of walking right up to the man''s house, a technique Avrakotos had used himself in the 1970s.

freemasons-and-opus-dei-at-the-cia.title: CIA attention to West Africa
freemasons-and-opus-dei-at-the-cia.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer on whether the CIA is likely to be operating in Burkina Faso: for all the years he was at the agency it cared very little about Africa and especially West Africa, but the presence of al-Qaeda and Islamic State affiliates plus the drug trade makes CIA and special forces involvement probable — and, he adds, the American public will not hear about it.

freemasons-and-opus-dei-at-the-cia.title: CIA–FBI incompatible computer systems
freemasons-and-opus-dei-at-the-cia.summary: John Kiriakou's claim that from the CIA's founding in 1947 until 2009 the computer systems of the CIA and the FBI were not compatible with one another — no message could be sent from one to the other and no intelligence shared — which he offers both as the material substrate of the interagency hatred that helped make September 11 possible, and as the gap through which James Mitchell and Bruce Jessen were able to pass Ali Soufan's FBI debriefings of Abu Zubaydah off as the fruits of torture.

freemasons-and-opus-dei-at-the-cia.title: Fake CIA résumés
freemasons-and-opus-dei-at-the-cia.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of being used as a human authenticator in the private sector: at the consulting firm he joined after leaving the CIA, every job applicant claiming agency service was sent to dinner with him, and by his count fully half of them had never set foot inside the CIA.

freemasons-and-opus-dei-at-the-cia.title: Forcing Iran toward a bomb
freemasons-and-opus-dei-at-the-cia.summary: John Kiriakou''s argument that Western pressure risks producing the very outcome it claims to prevent: repeated Israeli assassinations of Iranian scientists and generals and strikes on Iranian sites may eventually leave Ayatollah Khamenei with no choice but to permit a defensive weapon — despite the religious prohibition Kiriakou credits him with maintaining, and despite successive American estimates that Iran is not seeking one.

freemasons-and-opus-dei-at-the-cia.title: GeoRisk Solutions
freemasons-and-opus-dei-at-the-cia.summary: The political risk consultancy John Kiriakou founded with the dean of the University of Salamanca's intelligence studies programme, staffed with academics and a former assistant secretary of state, with offices in Salamanca and Washington and a stated business of selling cost-effective country and regional risk analysis to banks, funds and companies.

french-village-lsd-bread-experiment.title: MK-Ultra
french-village-lsd-bread-experiment.summary: The CIA's mid-twentieth-century umbrella program of mind-control, behavioral-modification, and biological-warfare experimentation, encompassing subprojects such as MK-Chickwit and MK-Seesaw; active 1952–1975; documented practices included LSD dosing of unwitting American citizens in CIA-rented brothels and the aerosolized release of pathogens into the San Francisco fog; 80% of the program's documentation was destroyed by the CIA in defiance of a 1975 preservation order from Senator Frank Church.

french-village-lsd-bread-experiment.title: Operation Midnight Climax
french-village-lsd-bread-experiment.summary: Sub-project of the CIA's MK-Ultra program, conducted in San Francisco. Per John Kiriakou, the CIA rented a safe house and paid sex workers to bring men back to it, where agents dosed the men with LSD without their knowledge or consent, then observed their behavior through one-way mirrors. The operation followed an earlier phase in which the CIA had dosed its own employees; when that produced suicides, it moved to using unconsenting members of the public.

french-village-lsd-bread-experiment.title: LSD Mind Manipulation
french-village-lsd-bread-experiment.summary: Kiriakou on the CIA dosing unwitting men with LSD in safe houses, using sex workers as bait, to find out whether the drug could unlock secrets.

french-village-lsd-bread-experiment.title: Family Jewels
french-village-lsd-bread-experiment.summary: The CIA's internal catalogue of its own abuses, demanded in full by the Church and Pike Committees in 1975; per John Kiriakou, MK-Ultra and its assassination programs surfaced first, 85 percent of the MK-Ultra files were shredded in defiance of a direct order, and new officers were taught that everything in the file belonged to the era before 1975.

french-village-lsd-bread-experiment.title: "Our job is to break the law"
french-village-lsd-bread-experiment.summary: The line John Kiriakou says CIA instructors repeated in training, and the qualification he attached to it at the time: the job is to break the law over there, not here. He describes participating willingly in break-ins abroad while insisting a warrant is required at home.

french-village-lsd-bread-experiment.title: The San Francisco bacterium release
french-village-lsd-bread-experiment.summary: The MK-ULTRA experiment John Kiriakou describes in which the CIA waited for an unusually foggy day, released a bacterium across San Francisco and its public transit system to see how many people it could infect, and gave eight people a rare upper respiratory infection.

fridays-at-the-agency.title: The CIA's internal social culture
fridays-at-the-agency.summary: John Kiriakou's one-word characterisation of the agency's internal culture — "incestuous" — describing a club for every conceivable interest, actively encouraged officer-to-officer romances, and a design intent that officers should have no need of friends or activities outside the building.

fridays-at-the-agency.title: The CIA barber shop
fridays-at-the-agency.summary: The barber in the basement of CIA headquarters, which John Kiriakou visited once on the reasoning that it saved a trip across town and found stocked with Playboys and Penthouses — one of several amenities, alongside a dry cleaner and a post office substation, that made the building function as a self-contained town.

fridays-at-the-agency.title: Abraham Accords
fridays-at-the-agency.summary: The Trump-brokered normalization deals between Israel and Gulf Arab states — in John Kiriakou's judgment "a terrible idea in the first place," a great victory for Israel and the Gulf Arabs that was "a punch in the throat to the Palestinians." He argues the Accords are how Trump meant to "solve the Middle East in a day" — by screwing the Palestinians — that Hamas read the abandonment correctly, that October 7 shattered the project, and that reviving the Accords (Saudis in, victory declared, Nobel collected) remains the organizing goal of Trump's regional policy.

fridays-at-the-agency.title: Death threats against Kiriakou
fridays-at-the-agency.summary: The threats John Kiriakou has received across two decades — first after going public about the CIA torture program, when FBI advice that at least two were credible sent his family out of the country, and later in waves tied to his opposition to Gina Haspel, his remarks about Pakistan, and his advocacy on Palestine and the Epstein case.

fridays-at-the-agency.title: Hamid Karzai
fridays-at-the-agency.summary: The president installed in Afghanistan after the American invasion, whom John Kiriakou uses as the standing illustration of what occupation actually buys: after twenty years and more than a trillion dollars, Karzai was ''little more than the mayor of Kabul'' — and did not control all of Kabul either. The line began as a joke among Senate Foreign Relations Committee staff, and Kiriakou used it to Senator John Kerry''s face ten years into the war.

fridays-at-the-agency.title: The move to Fort Myer
fridays-at-the-agency.summary: John Kiriakou's report that Stephen Miller, Pete Hegseth and Kristi Noem all moved with their families onto Fort Myer army base into housing reserved for one- to four-star generals — 'the mother of all gated communities' — after Miller sold his Arlington house to escape protesters chalking his public sidewalk.

from-alien-and-sedition-to-espionage.title: Kermit Roosevelt and Mosaddegh
from-alien-and-sedition-to-espionage.summary: The CIA officer John Kiriakou names as the man who ran the 1953 overthrow of Iran's Prime Minister Mosaddegh on behalf of British Petroleum — who called it the gravest mistake of his life in the only interview he ever gave, and who, according to the documents Kiriakou has since read in the archives, did not actually run it at all.

from-alien-and-sedition-to-espionage.title: The 11(c)(1)(C) plea
from-alien-and-sedition-to-espionage.summary: The unusual plea structure John Kiriakou's lawyers negotiated in 2012, in which the sentence is written into the agreement and the judge may accept or reject it but cannot change it. Judge Leonie Brinkema told the court she had never seen one in her career, said she did not like it, and told Kiriakou that if she could she would have given him ten years.

from-alien-and-sedition-to-espionage.title: Evidence of previous heroism
from-alien-and-sedition-to-espionage.summary: A phrase John Kiriakou attributes to Judge Leonie Brinkema at his 2013 sentencing. When his service in Pakistan and his role in the capture of Abu Zubaydah were raised in mitigation, the judge ruled — in what Kiriakou gives as her exact words — that any evidence of previous heroism is irrelevant.

from-alien-and-sedition-to-espionage.title: Plato Cacheris
from-alien-and-sedition-to-espionage.summary: Legendary Washington, D.C. defense attorney who served as John Kiriakou''s lead counsel in his 2012–2013 Espionage Act prosecution. Per Kiriakou, when discovery revealed the FBI had run a fake-diplomat sting against him, Cacheris explained the government''s posture bluntly: ''Because they have a shit case and they know it''s shit, and that''s why we''re going to trial.'' He spent most of the case urging trial, then drove to Kiriakou''s house on decision day and said ''You stupid son of a bitch — take the deal.'' Cacheris also represented FBI spy Robert Hanssen.

from-alien-and-sedition-to-espionage.title: Prosecutorial careerism
from-alien-and-sedition-to-espionage.summary: John Kiriakou''s explanation for why senior federal prosecutors pursue high-profile national-security cases regardless of their merits: the conviction of a famous defendant is the entry ticket to a partnership at a large firm, a congressional candidacy, or a run for governor.

from-alien-and-sedition-to-espionage.title: The Laura Ingraham exchange
from-alien-and-sedition-to-espionage.summary: John Kiriakou's account of an on-air exchange with Fox News host Laura Ingraham about torture, in which she told him she hated his position and he replied that anyone who wants torture as an instrument of policy should have the courage to go to Capitol Hill and change the law rather than pretend the existing law does not apply.

frus-greece-turkey-cyprus-volume.title: Cofer Black's warning to the liaison class
frus-greece-turkey-cyprus-volume.summary: The briefing Cofer Black gave to a class of visiting foreign liaison officers weeks before 11 September 2001 — code words about a honey salesman, a great football match and an enormous wedding — and the private exchange afterwards in which he told John Kiriakou he had been deadly serious.

frus-greece-turkey-cyprus-volume.title: Cofer Black
frus-greece-turkey-cyprus-volume.summary: Former head of the CIA Counterterrorism Center during and immediately after the September 11 attacks; principal architect of the agency's paramilitary turn on September 12, 2001; later Vice President of Blackwater under Erik Prince.

frus-greece-turkey-cyprus-volume.title: The liaison class
frus-greece-turkey-cyprus-volume.summary: The course John Kiriakou ran at the CIA for visiting officers of allied intelligence services — the setting for Cofer Black's warning weeks before 9/11, and the reason Kiriakou was in the counterterrorism chief's office to ask whether he had meant it.

frus-greece-turkey-cyprus-volume.title: Alfreda Bikowsky
frus-greece-turkey-cyprus-volume.summary: Senior CIA officer who headed Alec Station and, before that, served as its chief of operations, overseeing the CIA's torture program; per John Kiriakou, "bad news from the get-go," and part of a failed attempt with Rich Blee to turn a San Diego al-Qaeda cell into double agents.

frus-greece-turkey-cyprus-volume.title: John Kiriakou
frus-greece-turkey-cyprus-volume.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

frus-greece-turkey-cyprus-volume.title: The referee in a Greek-Turkish war
frus-greece-turkey-cyprus-volume.summary: John Kiriakou's assessment, given in Athens in 2025, that Greece cannot count on the United States taking its side against Turkey — Washington would position itself as an honest broker between the two — but that NATO support, particularly from Italy, France, Germany and Britain, would make Greece able to cope even without American leadership.

fusha-and-the-gulf-dialect.title: Djibouti
fusha-and-the-gulf-dialect.summary: The small Horn of Africa state a few miles across the water from Yemen that hosts Camp Lemonnier — the American drone base for the Yemen and Somalia wars, inherited from the departing French, and shared with China's only overseas military base behind a fence down the middle, in what John Kiriakou calls the worst kept secret in the world.

fusha-and-the-gulf-dialect.title: John Kiriakou
fusha-and-the-gulf-dialect.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

fusha-and-the-gulf-dialect.title: The Bab el-Mandeb
fusha-and-the-gulf-dialect.summary: The strait between Yemen and the Horn of Africa through which everything leaving the Suez Canal must pass — narrower than the Strait of Hormuz, in John Kiriakou's account the one genuine American national interest in Yemen, and the reason Israel has offered diplomatic recognition to Somaliland in exchange for a military base.

fusha-and-the-gulf-dialect.title: Chinese overseas police stations
fusha-and-the-gulf-dialect.summary: John Kiriakou's account of a New York Times revelation about Chinese nationals with apparent ties to the Chinese police operating out of storefronts around Manhattan and travelling around the United States to threaten Chinese people with reprisals against relatives in Beijing — and his puzzlement that the FBI missed it.

fusha-and-the-gulf-dialect.title: Central Intelligence Agency
fusha-and-the-gulf-dialect.summary: U.S. foreign intelligence service; John Kiriakou's employer from 1990 to 2004 and the central institution of KiriPedia

fusha-and-the-gulf-dialect.title: The Yemen jazz radio plan
fusha-and-the-gulf-dialect.summary: A scheme John Kiriakou says the American defence attaché in Sanaa described to him on his last visit to Yemen in 2011: a propaganda programme modelled on NPR that would play jazz and run call-in shows for young Yemenis. It lasted about two weeks before it shuttered, because nobody was going to listen to it.

gail-slater.title: Pam Bondi
gail-slater.summary: Panelists alongside Kiriakou on why Trump picked Bondi for loyalty above all, and called her handling of the Epstein files a farce.

gail-slater.title: Bill Barr
gail-slater.summary: Per Sean Davis, speaking on the same Megyn Kelly panel as Kiriakou, the attorney general under the first Trump administration, seen as competent but not fully loyal, whose relationship with Trump ended in a "breakup."

gail-slater.title: Lee Zeldon
gail-slater.summary: Per Megyn Kelly's opening monologue, the EPA administrator reportedly considered by Trump as a possible replacement for Attorney General Pam Bondi.

gail-slater.title: Alexa
gail-slater.summary: Per John Kiriakou, Amazon''s Alexa smart speaker reports directly to the NSA — and he owns one anyway. The device recurs across his interviews as the standing example of the surveillance trade-off in modern smart-home technology, and of his own negotiated exception to it: one speaker, in one room, against the advice of every intelligence officer he has ever known.

gail-slater.title: Anwar al-Awlaki
gail-slater.summary: American-born al-Qaeda propagandist; in 1993 the imam of the Falls Church, Virginia mosque visited by John Kiriakou's CIA Arabic-language class on a field trip; in 2001 the cleric at whose mosque the 9/11 hijackers prayed the night before the attacks; killed by U.S. drone strike in Yemen in approximately 2011.

gail-slater.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
gail-slater.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

galls-com-sponsor-story.title: Abu Zubaydah
galls-com-sponsor-story.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

galls-com-sponsor-story.title: Alex Station
galls-com-sponsor-story.summary: CIA unit that tracked Osama bin Laden beginning in 1995; per John Kiriakou, who served as chief of its counterintelligence branch, the unit kept extremely tight security around its files, limited FBI investigators' access to information about future 9/11 hijackers Khaled al-Mihdhar and Nawaf al-Hazmi, and — under a deliberate policy of non-cooperation with the FBI — failed to watchlist participants in the Malaysia summit where al-Qaeda planned the attacks.

galls-com-sponsor-story.title: Bahrain Posting (1994–1996)
galls-com-sponsor-story.summary: John Kiriakou's 1994–1996 assignment to Bahrain under U.S. State Department cover as second secretary for economic affairs — arriving with his wife Joanne and infant son Chris on August 1, 1994, into a tiny Gulf monarchy whose sectarian tensions erupted, two months later, into the first Intifada.

galls-com-sponsor-story.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
galls-com-sponsor-story.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

galls-com-sponsor-story.title: Cofer Black
galls-com-sponsor-story.summary: Former head of the CIA Counterterrorism Center during and immediately after the September 11 attacks; principal architect of the agency's paramilitary turn on September 12, 2001; later Vice President of Blackwater under Erik Prince.

galls-com-sponsor-story.title: Counterterrorism Center
galls-com-sponsor-story.summary: The CIA's Counterterrorism Center (CTC) — the unit where John Kiriakou spent the defining years of his operational career. He joined in the late 1990s as the only officer in the entire CIA fluent in both Greek and Arabic, served as chief of counterintelligence in the bin Laden unit, watched the Center swell from a few hundred employees to nearly 2,000 by September 12, 2001, and it was to CTC that he walked back down in May 2002 to refuse the torture program — the moment, he says, the CIA began to turn on him.

gangstalking-claims.title: Cancelling the 2026 midterms
gangstalking-claims.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that the 2026 war cannot win the midterm elections for the Republicans, and his flagged-as-paranoid worry that it may instead furnish the pretext for a national emergency and a cancelled election.

gangstalking-claims.title: CIA liaison relationships
gangstalking-claims.summary: John Kiriakou's critique of CIA intelligence-liaison relationships with foreign governments — sharply expanded after 9/11 — arguing that officers do not consider the long-term risk that disclosing sensitive operations to foreign services hands those governments leverage, including potential blackmail material, over the United States, and that no one left in Congress has the will to provide real oversight of the practice.

gangstalking-claims.title: Civilian ships and piracy
gangstalking-claims.summary: Why merchant crews cannot defend themselves: by international treaty no civilian ship may carry a weapon. John Kiriakou handled international piracy as a Senate Foreign Relations Committee staffer and brought Captain Richard Phillips to testify.

gangstalking-claims.title: Counterterrorism Center
gangstalking-claims.summary: The CIA's Counterterrorism Center (CTC) — the unit where John Kiriakou spent the defining years of his operational career. He joined in the late 1990s as the only officer in the entire CIA fluent in both Greek and Arabic, served as chief of counterintelligence in the bin Laden unit, watched the Center swell from a few hundred employees to nearly 2,000 by September 12, 2001, and it was to CTC that he walked back down in May 2002 to refuse the torture program — the moment, he says, the CIA began to turn on him.

gangstalking-claims.title: David Ransom
gangstalking-claims.summary: U.S. Ambassador to Bahrain during the period of John Kiriakou's posting there; characterized by Kiriakou as one of the finest people he worked for in his CIA career

gangstalking-claims.title: Defense Intelligence Agency
gangstalking-claims.summary: The Pentagon's intelligence arm, of which John Kiriakou holds a low opinion he states plainly and expects to be criticised for. He attributes the targeting data behind the 2026 Iranian elementary school strike to the agency.

gary-johnson.title: The Libertarian Party
gary-johnson.summary: The third party a lifelong Democrat joined on release from prison, after its 2016 presidential nominee had written to him in his cell and to the Attorney General on his behalf — the party John Kiriakou says was the only one talking about whistleblowing and the security-versus-liberty trade-off, and the one whose structural problem, he was told, is that it has no benefactor.

gary-johnson.title: FISA court
gary-johnson.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the secret Foreign Intelligence Surveillance court — created under Carter, sitting atop the Justice Department, issuing warrants that are never public — which he says was abused against Carter Page as part of what he believes was John Brennan's plan to deny Trump the presidency.

gary-johnson.title: Oliver Stone
gary-johnson.summary: American film director with whom John Kiriakou struck up a friendship after his release from prison. Stone optioned the rights to one chapter of Kiriakou's first book, co-developed an unmade History Channel series with him, blurbed his book on Abu Zubaydah, and was among the public figures who campaigned against the Bureau of Prisons' attempt to shut down Kiriakou's prison blog. The two disagree sharply over whether the CIA killed John F. Kennedy.

gary-johnson.title: Donald Trump
gary-johnson.summary: 45th and 47th U.S. president. Per John Kiriakou, a man genuinely convinced he was doing right by bombing Iran, "duped" by the same Netanyahu nuclear bluff Obama once rejected — and, at the same time, the most blindly pro-Israel president in history, an admirer of autocrats who has never once criticized Vladimir Putin, and prone to gestures — from the Gulf of America to a since-abandoned "Department of War" rename — that test the edges of his actual authority.

gary-johnson.title: The Libertarian Christmas party
gary-johnson.summary: The party John Kiriakou attended in a townhouse in Old Town Alexandria, held at the end of January because — being Libertarians — the organisers could not get their act together in December, and at which the head of the Libertarian Party of Virginia asked him to run for governor and was refused on the spot.

gary-schroen.title: The post-9/11 name traces
gary-schroen.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of his own assignment in the weeks after the September 11 attacks: with people walking into American embassies all over the world offering information on al-Qaeda, the CIA was buried under tens of thousands of names — sometimes thousands arriving in a single day — and needed, as he put it, an army of clerks to search them against its databases.

gary-schroen.title: The live satellite feed myth
gary-schroen.summary: John Kiriakou''s flat rejection of one of the most common screen conventions about American intelligence: that officers can call up a live satellite picture and watch a target walk through the streets of a city. There was no such thing then, he says, and there is no such thing now.

gary-schroen.title: Kandahar
gary-schroen.summary: The southern Afghan city and province that recurs across John Kiriakou's Afghanistan material — site of one of the two al-Qaeda training camps Abu Zubaydah founded, whose commanders were captured in the same March 2002 raids; the town Bill Clinton said he would have had to destroy, killing 300 innocents, to kill bin Laden in the 1990s; and a stop on Kiriakou's Senate-era heroin-poppy investigation, when the military helicoptered him down before refusing to let him walk the poppy fields.

gary-schroen.title: Renting Afghan warlords
gary-schroen.summary: The CIA's opening strategy in Afghanistan after the September 11 attacks — paying the country's warlords in cash rather than trying to buy their loyalty outright, captured in an agency saying that you cannot buy an Afghan warlord but you can certainly rent one.

gary-schroen.title: Condoleezza Rice
gary-schroen.summary: U.S. National Security Advisor on 9/11; John Kiriakou had a meeting booked with her that morning, watched her tell George Tenet to "take one for the team" rather than correct the record on Abu Zubaydah, and offers her failure to act on the CIA's warnings as his alternative to any theory that the attacks were allowed to happen.

gary-schroen.title: Heather Kiriakou
gary-schroen.summary: John Kiriakou's wife, a senior CIA analyst who — in his account — was one of the best analysts in the entire intelligence community and who lost her job at the agency for no reason other than being married to him. She sat off camera at his December 2007 ABC News interview and told him afterwards that he had said nothing classified.

gary-webb-kill-the-messenger.title: Contra rebels
gary-webb-kill-the-messenger.summary: The right-wing Nicaraguan insurgency armed by the Reagan administration against the Sandinista government. In John Kiriakou's account they were conservatives, right-wingers, in some cases fascists, and disgruntled military officers; they were split into a northern group the United States armed and a southern group that financed itself by selling cocaine — a distinction that became the pivot of the Gary Webb affair, and that Kiriakou uses to answer the CIA's standing denial that it had anything to do with the drug trade.

gary-webb-kill-the-messenger.title: CIA Drug Facilitation
gary-webb-kill-the-messenger.summary: Per John Kiriakou, the CIA''s reported involvement in facilitating the arrival of cocaine into the United States during the era that became the crack epidemic, and his own firsthand discovery — as a Senate Foreign Relations Committee investigator — that under American military control Afghanistan produced 93% of the world''s heroin. A DEA contact told him the report would never be published because ''we want Iran and Russia to be addicted to heroin. It weakens their societies.'' Kiriakou draws a direct parallel to the current fentanyl crisis: China is doing to the US what the US did to Iran and Russia.

gary-webb-kill-the-messenger.title: Dark Alliance
gary-webb-kill-the-messenger.summary: Gary Webb's seven-part San Jose Mercury News investigation reporting that cocaine reaching Los Angeles and fuelling the crack epidemic had travelled through Nicaragua with the CIA's knowledge. John Kiriakou's account stresses what Webb did and did not claim — that the agency turned a blind eye rather than ran the operation — and that three separate federal investigations later found his reporting correct.

gary-webb-kill-the-messenger.title: Walter Pincus
gary-webb-kill-the-messenger.summary: The Washington Post reporter who, in John Kiriakou's account of the Gary Webb affair, took the CIA's side of the cocaine story and put it on the paper's front page — wrong, and Kiriakou believes knowingly so.

gary-webb-kill-the-messenger.title: Oscar Blandón
gary-webb-kill-the-messenger.summary: The senior Contra leader whom Gary Webb's reporting identified as running the cocaine operation that moved product from Nicaragua to Los Angeles, and one of two men named in the Dark Alliance series.

gary-webb-kill-the-messenger.title: Domino theory
gary-webb-kill-the-messenger.summary: The Cold War doctrine, described by John Kiriakou as Ronald Reagan's organising obsession in Central America, holding that if one country there fell to communism the rest would fall in sequence up to the American border — the stated rationale for backing the Contra rebels against the Sandinistas.

gavin-newsom.title: Kiriakou's case-officer rankings
gavin-newsom.summary: A recurring segment in which John Kiriakou grades serving and former American politicians on how good a CIA case officer each would make, using an S-to-F scale. The criterion is character and the ability to attract confidence rather than politics, and he repeatedly grades allies low and opponents high.

gavin-newsom.title: Thomas Massie
gavin-newsom.summary: Republican U.S. Representative from Kentucky known for a constitutionalist voting record and consistent opposition to foreign military intervention; per John Kiriakou, a principled America-First congressman who votes with the president on the vast majority of issues, and whose opposition to U.S. funding of Israel and foreign wars is the only plausible explanation for the roughly $30 million spent by the Israel lobby to unseat him in a primary.

gavin-newsom.title: Abu Omar rendition
gavin-newsom.summary: The CIA's kidnapping of a Milan cleric, Abu Omar, who was sent to Egypt to be tortured; John Kiriakou calls it a case that ought to be taught at the CIA as how not to run a rendition, and it is what ultimately sent him to prison, after he confirmed a former colleague's surname to a journalist claiming to be writing a book about it.

gavin-newsom.title: Democratic Party 2025 Political Snapshot
gavin-newsom.summary: John Kiriakou's 2025 assessment of Democratic Party weakness — a record-low 24% approval rating, seven Senate Democrats crossing over to hand Trump a spending-bill win with no concessions, and California governor Gavin Newsom's surprising denial of parole to a large group of long-incarcerated eligible inmates, which Kiriakou reads as Newsom "playing the long game."

gavin-newsom.title: Kiriakou's Omega Seamaster
gavin-newsom.summary: The wristwatch John Kiriakou bought himself in the Athens duty-free the day after Christmas 1999, on his way to recruit an asset in another European country, at the end of a Christmas that had gone badly in a failing first marriage.

gavin-newsom.title: The Jerusalem bluff
gavin-newsom.summary: An interrogation in Pakistan in 2002 in which John Kiriakou, faced with a senior al-Qaeda prisoner working through the organisation's own resistance training, threatened to send him to Jerusalem rather than Guantánamo. Kiriakou supplied the account to explain a clip of the exchange circulating without its context.

gay-diplomat-operation.title: Kompromat
gay-diplomat-operation.summary: Russian-derived term for compromising material — recordings, photographs, or documentation of an individual''s criminal, sexual, or embarrassing behavior — used to coerce cooperation or silence. Per John Kiriakou, the CIA''s formal policy conclusion is that kompromat doesn''t work as a recruitment tool: faced with the binary choice between confessing to a spouse and committing treason, most targets confess. The agency therefore prefers voluntary, ideologically or financially motivated recruitment.

gay-diplomat-operation.title: Asset acquisition cycle
gay-diplomat-operation.summary: The four-step process — spot, assess, develop, recruit — taught as the first lesson of CIA case officer training

gay-diplomat-operation.title: John Kiriakou
gay-diplomat-operation.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

gay-diplomat-operation.title: Sociopathic Tendencies
gay-diplomat-operation.summary: Per John Kiriakou, the CIA actively recruits for what its instructors call 'sociopathic tendencies' — not full clinical sociopathy, but the capacity to operate in legal, moral, and ethical gray areas without being paralyzed by regret. Kiriakou describes this as the trait that makes case officers effective at recruitment and adaptable in the field, and offers his own act of whistleblowing as evidence he does not possess the deeper sociopathy that, in his view, characterizes the most institutionally successful intelligence officers.

gay-diplomat-operation.title: David Boies
gay-diplomat-operation.summary: The American litigator John Kiriakou has appeared alongside on Piers Morgan's programme, and whose observation about Alan Dershowitz — that he was not merely Epstein's attorney but his publicist — Kiriakou treats as the key distinction in the case.

gay-diplomat-operation.title: Jeffrey Epstein
gay-diplomat-operation.summary: Convicted sex offender; per John Kiriakou, was "an Israeli access agent" rather than a CIA asset, because the CIA collects foreign intelligence and Epstein's targets — Bill Clinton, Bill Gates, Prince Andrew — were not foreign. Kiriakou further holds that Epstein did die by suicide in federal custody, because in the Bureau of Prisons the cameras never work and the guards are always asleep.

gaza-famine.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
gaza-famine.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

gaza-famine.title: Hamas
gaza-famine.summary: The Palestinian movement behind the October 7, 2023 attack; John Kiriakou argues that a case could be made for calling it a freedom-fighting organization dedicated to the liberation of its people rather than simply a terrorist group, notes it is labeled a terrorist organization by only a small minority of UN member states, and has ruled Gaza since Israel's 2005 withdrawal.

gaza-famine.title: Roger Waters
gaza-famine.summary: Founding member of the British rock band Pink Floyd; outspoken supporter of Palestinian human rights; anonymously paid off John Kiriakou's second mortgage during his federal prison sentence, sparing his wife and children the loss of the family home; only discovered to be the benefactor years later; subsequently a personal friend of Kiriakou and a recurring guest on his programme.

gaza-famine.title: No band-aids since the early nineties
gaza-famine.summary: What doctors told John Kiriakou when he visited an Afghan hospital in 2000, during the first Taliban government — that they had not seen a band-aid since the early 1990s — and his conclusion that the humanitarian carve-outs in the Clinton-era sanctions did not exist in practice.

gaza-famine.title: October 7 attack
gaza-famine.summary: John Kiriakou's analysis of the October 7, 2023 Hamas attack as a policy failure, not an intelligence one — Israel was warned repeatedly, but Itamar Ben-Gvir diverted response forces to the West Bank, and Kiriakou believes Israel welcomed a pretext for overwhelming retaliation.

gaza-famine.title: France recognises Palestine
gaza-famine.summary: Emmanuel Macron's decision in July 2025 to extend formal recognition to the Republic of Palestine and exchange ambassadors, which John Kiriakou called a turning point that could not be overstated — the first serious crack in Western support for Israel, and significant precisely because France is a historic colonial power in the Middle East with a Security Council veto.

general-dostum.title: Dasht-i-Leili massacre
general-dostum.summary: Late-November 2001 mass suffocation of approximately 2,000 surrendered Taliban prisoners in unventilated shipping containers in the Afghan desert; the prisoners' surrender was negotiated by the CIA via the Northern Alliance, the transport order was issued by the CIA, and the operation was overseen by Northern Alliance warlord Abdul Rashid Dostum; John Kiriakou in 2009 as Senate Foreign Relations Committee investigator attempted to reopen the case under a 2008 Obama campaign promise; the CIA's classified response was, per Kiriakou, "go fuck yourself."

general-dostum.title: Brian Ross
general-dostum.summary: American investigative journalist and seven-time Emmy Award winner who was a prominent reporter at ABC News when, in December 2007, he conducted the on-camera interview with John Kiriakou that produced the first public confirmation by a U.S. official that the CIA waterboarded prisoners. Per Kiriakou, Ross called him out of the blue with the assertion that a source said Kiriakou had personally tortured Abu Zubaydah; Kiriakou's decision to give the interview anyway — driven by the conclusion that 'Brian Ross's source is at the White House and they're going to pin this on me' — became the pivot point of his entire post-CIA life.

general-dostum.title: John Kiriakou
general-dostum.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

general-dostum.title: Abu Zubaydah
general-dostum.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

general-dostum.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
general-dostum.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

general-dostum.title: The AIPAC "Holy Land" trip offer
general-dostum.summary: An approach John Kiriakou says he received within days of becoming chief investigator of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee: two AIPAC representatives offered him an all-expenses-paid trip to what they called the Holy Land, never using the word Israel, and told him it was cleared by the Senate ethics committee. He declined; colleagues of his went. He pairs the story with his account of AIPAC staff stationed in congressional offices, while insisting the practice is not unique to them.

general-intelligence-directorate.title: The Brüno shoot in Jordan
general-intelligence-directorate.summary: The scene John Kiriakou set up for Sacha Baron Cohen in Amman — four retired Palestinian militants, found in the Damascus telephone book at the Library of Congress, shown hardcore pornography by a character they believed to be an Austrian documentary journalist — which produced no reaction at all and was cut from the film entirely.

general-intelligence-directorate.title: MOSSAD
general-intelligence-directorate.summary: Israel's primary external intelligence service; characterized by John Kiriakou as universally hostile in his and his CIA colleagues' professional dealings with it ("never had a positive encounter with Mossad"); operates almost exclusively in the operational rather than analytical domain; the CIA is, per Kiriakou, categorically forbidden from spying on it.

general-intelligence-directorate.title: Abraxas Corporation
general-intelligence-directorate.summary: The private intelligence company founded in the 1990s by retired CIA operations officers as a tax pass-through and a place to smoke cigars and tell stories — which, after 9/11, made its founders, in John Kiriakou's phrase, Mega Millions rich.

general-intelligence-directorate.title: The Directorate of Science and Technology
general-intelligence-directorate.summary: One of the CIA's four directorates, which in John Kiriakou's time was an afterthought responsible for disguises and briefcases with hidden compartments, and which he says now works with Palantir, Amazon, Nvidia and Elon Musk's companies on work closer to DARPA's than to anything the agency did in the past.

general-intelligence-directorate.title: Hamas
general-intelligence-directorate.summary: The Palestinian movement behind the October 7, 2023 attack; John Kiriakou argues that a case could be made for calling it a freedom-fighting organization dedicated to the liberation of its people rather than simply a terrorist group, notes it is labeled a terrorist organization by only a small minority of UN member states, and has ruled Gaza since Israel's 2005 withdrawal.

general-intelligence-directorate.title: Abraham Accords
general-intelligence-directorate.summary: The Trump-brokered normalization deals between Israel and Gulf Arab states — in John Kiriakou's judgment "a terrible idea in the first place," a great victory for Israel and the Gulf Arabs that was "a punch in the throat to the Palestinians." He argues the Accords are how Trump meant to "solve the Middle East in a day" — by screwing the Palestinians — that Hamas read the abandonment correctly, that October 7 shattered the project, and that reviving the Accords (Saudis in, victory declared, Nobel collected) remains the organizing goal of Trump's regional policy.

general-muhammad-equipment-gift.title: Security, medical and finance
general-muhammad-equipment-gift.summary: The warning John Kiriakou says his first station chief gave him and that he passed on in turn to a first-tour case officer in Pakistan: there are only three offices at the CIA that can wreck your career — security, medical and finance — and only finance can send you to prison.

general-muhammad-equipment-gift.title: Business class after 9/11
general-muhammad-equipment-gift.summary: John Kiriakou''s illustration of what the post-attack money did to the CIA''s habits: Cofer Black telling him to just do whatever operation he was proposing because there was so much money it could not possibly be spent, and everyone at the agency flying business class from then on, anywhere in the world.

general-muhammad-equipment-gift.title: ''Don''t try to save the government money''
general-muhammad-equipment-gift.summary: The instruction John Kiriakou says a CIA supervisor gave him for parking in the nine-dollar economy lot at Dulles instead of the twenty-five-dollar daily lot, and the two trips it produced: a Pittsburgh approach funded entirely by a five-dollar bill, and a $195 fattoush salad in a Dubai nightclub.

general-muhammad-equipment-gift.title: The Punjab Elite Force
general-muhammad-equipment-gift.summary: The Pakistani provincial counterterrorism unit that supplied part of the assault manpower for the Abu Zubaydah raids of March 2002 — black trousers, black t-shirts stencilled with a pistol, and, in John Kiriakou's telling, a refusal to wear body armour on the grounds that if God called them that night they would go.

general-muhammad-equipment-gift.title: Kiriakou on wine
general-muhammad-equipment-gift.summary: John Kiriakou's long-standing interest in wine — a subscription to Wine Spectator running a quarter of a century, a climate-controlled cellar built into his house, an eye that has twice caught a host passing off a cheap bottle as something better, and a professional life in which wine served in turn as cover story, surveillance-detection errand, recruitment currency and diplomatic catastrophe.

general-muhammad-equipment-gift.title: No-bid contracts
general-muhammad-equipment-gift.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of the mechanism he considers the real corruption of American national security: an officer retires on a Friday, returns Monday on a contractor badge at ten times the salary, and is fed no-bid contracts by the friends he left behind — including, in one unnamed case he describes, a tax shelter that became a multi-billion dollar company inside a decade.

generals-in-national-security-posts.title: The US overseas basing footprint
generals-in-national-security-posts.summary: John Kiriakou''s summary of the one thing he says Democrats and Republicans in Washington genuinely agree on: that the United States needs a military presence in about 110 countries and bases in about 86 of them, along with the newest nuclear weapons, the biggest ships, the best aircraft and the biggest bombs.

generals-in-national-security-posts.title: John Bolton
generals-in-national-security-posts.summary: Former U.S. National Security Advisor. Per John Kiriakou, one of the most dangerous men in America and the real driver — with Elliott Abrams — of the 2019 pressure campaign against Venezuela; the signature at the National Security Council through which a covert action finding passes on its way to the president. Kiriakou predicted his 2019 departure from the Trump administration on the basis of White House chatter and Trump's premium on loyalty.

generals-in-national-security-posts.title: Bill Binney
generals-in-national-security-posts.summary: Former NSA technical director whom John Kiriakou cites as having debunked the DNC hack. Asked by Veteran Intelligence Professionals for Sanity to examine the science, Binney analyzed the speed of the upload and concluded the emails could only have been copied in person to a thumb drive, not taken remotely by Russia — an argument he later made to Donald Trump in the Oval Office. Kiriakou calls him a friend, the most brilliant person he has met on electronics, and a member of the whistleblower circle he belongs to.

generals-in-national-security-posts.title: Consulting job entrapment offers
generals-in-national-security-posts.summary: John Kiriakou's claim that he receives a steady stream of emails and telephone calls offering him work — always consulting — that he reads as attempts to bait him into violating federal law, and which he says happens all the time.

generals-in-national-security-posts.title: The John Kiriakou Task Force
generals-in-national-security-posts.summary: The dedicated FBI unit that John Kiriakou says was created inside the Bureau to investigate him after he blew the whistle on the CIA''s torture program: twelve agents appointed under director Robert Mueller who tapped his phones, intercepted his email and followed him in pairs to work, to church and to the grocery store for three years, trying to catch him committing a crime.

generals-in-national-security-posts.title: The regime change approval process
generals-in-national-security-posts.summary: John Kiriakou's step-by-step account of how a proposal to overthrow a foreign government travels through the United States government — beginning as a memo written at an officer's own desk, cleared by lawyers at the Justice Department and the National Security Council, signed by the president as an executive order, and ending in a safe on the seventh floor at CIA headquarters while the order itself goes to the Pentagon.

geneva-conventions.title: Counterterrorism Center
geneva-conventions.summary: The CIA's Counterterrorism Center (CTC) — the unit where John Kiriakou spent the defining years of his operational career. He joined in the late 1990s as the only officer in the entire CIA fluent in both Greek and Arabic, served as chief of counterintelligence in the bin Laden unit, watched the Center swell from a few hundred employees to nearly 2,000 by September 12, 2001, and it was to CTC that he walked back down in May 2002 to refuse the torture program — the moment, he says, the CIA began to turn on him.

geneva-conventions.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
geneva-conventions.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

geneva-conventions.title: Abu Zubaydah
geneva-conventions.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

geneva-conventions.title: The 1994 women''s class action
geneva-conventions.summary: A class action brought by female CIA employees who had been passed over for promotion produced, in John Kiriakou''s account, a judicial finding that the Agency had documented its own crime and a remedy of an across-the-board two-level promotion for every woman at the CIA.

geneva-conventions.title: The Clinton-era asset cull
geneva-conventions.summary: In the 1990s the CIA reviewed the file of every recruited asset in the world and dismissed any with a history of human rights abuses — roughly a third of its agents, in John Kiriakou''s account, in a reform he says was reversed as though by a switch after 11 September.

geneva-conventions.title: The unexplained false statement charge
geneva-conventions.summary: One of the five counts against John Kiriakou was making a false statement, and neither he nor his eleven lawyers could establish what the statement was supposed to have been; the government withdrew the count after his defence had spent six figures on it.

geo-risk-solutions.title: The University of Salamanca professorship
geo-risk-solutions.summary: John Kiriakou's teaching post in the graduate intelligence studies programme at the University of Salamanca, where he lectures on introductory intelligence studies and the history of terrorism, at an institution he describes as older than Spain itself.

geo-risk-solutions.title: Fake CIA résumés
geo-risk-solutions.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of being used as a human authenticator in the private sector: at the consulting firm he joined after leaving the CIA, every job applicant claiming agency service was sent to dinner with him, and by his count fully half of them had never set foot inside the CIA.

geo-risk-solutions.title: Gulf secret prisons for hire
geo-risk-solutions.summary: Asked whether the CIA knew of Gulf royals operating underground torture facilities and secret prisons, John Kiriakou answered that it did — one hundred per cent — then refused to give details, saying he would risk returning to prison. He described the arrangement instead: the United States sought out these countries precisely because they had no parliament and no free press to answer to, and paid for the use of their cells.

geo-risk-solutions.title: CIA attention to West Africa
geo-risk-solutions.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer on whether the CIA is likely to be operating in Burkina Faso: for all the years he was at the agency it cared very little about Africa and especially West Africa, but the presence of al-Qaeda and Islamic State affiliates plus the drug trade makes CIA and special forces involvement probable — and, he adds, the American public will not hear about it.

geo-risk-solutions.title: CIA–FBI incompatible computer systems
geo-risk-solutions.summary: John Kiriakou's claim that from the CIA's founding in 1947 until 2009 the computer systems of the CIA and the FBI were not compatible with one another — no message could be sent from one to the other and no intelligence shared — which he offers both as the material substrate of the interagency hatred that helped make September 11 possible, and as the gap through which James Mitchell and Bruce Jessen were able to pass Ali Soufan's FBI debriefings of Abu Zubaydah off as the fruits of torture.

geo-risk-solutions.title: Forcing Iran toward a bomb
geo-risk-solutions.summary: John Kiriakou''s argument that Western pressure risks producing the very outcome it claims to prevent: repeated Israeli assassinations of Iranian scientists and generals and strikes on Iranian sites may eventually leave Ayatollah Khamenei with no choice but to permit a defensive weapon — despite the religious prohibition Kiriakou credits him with maintaining, and despite successive American estimates that Iran is not seeking one.

george-habash.title: Iraqi invasion of Kuwait
george-habash.summary: John Kiriakou''s most detailed account of the intelligence process around the 1990 Iraqi invasion of Kuwait and its 1991 liberation. As a first-year CIA analyst on a ''training account'' covering Iraq, Kiriakou produced the June 30, 1990 warning paper for the White House; suggested calling the US Defense Attaché in Baghdad to drive to the border and report what he saw (the answer: ''Literally the entire Iraqi military is heading south''); briefed the August 2 Oval Office meeting with Bush; and later took a single phone call from General Colin Powell that led, eight hours later, to 47 cruise missiles striking the Iraqi Intelligence Service headquarters in Baghdad.

george-habash.title: Ahmed Khatib
george-habash.summary: Iraqi-installed occupation governor of Kuwait announced on August 2, 1990, hours after the invasion; medical doctor trained at the American University of Beirut whose mother had been a Sudanese slave in the Kuwaiti royal household; college roommate of George Habash and co-founder of the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine.

george-habash.title: William Webster
george-habash.summary: Director of Central Intelligence during the 1990 invasion of Kuwait, and before that a federal judge and Director of the FBI; per John Kiriakou, "a lovely man … just a very kind, nice man" and "a giant in my mind" — the director Kiriakou first briefed at four in the morning, on fifteen minutes' notice, during the Kuwait task force, and who sat two seats away from him in the Oval Office on the morning of the invasion.

george-habash.title: The Oval Office briefing of 2 August 1990
george-habash.summary: The morning Iraq invaded Kuwait, a 25-year-old John Kiriakou was driven from CIA headquarters to the White House and found himself briefing President George H. W. Bush, Vice President Quayle, Brent Scowcroft and the CIA director — and answering the question *"well, now what do we do?"*

george-habash.title: Saddam Hussein's classified biographer
