george-habash.summary: John Kiriakou''s first job at the CIA: writing the classified biography and psychological profile of Saddam Hussein in the Office of Leadership Analysis — the desk from which he watched the agency conclude, on 30 June 1990, that Iraq would invade Kuwait, and get the scale of the invasion wrong.

george-habash.title: *Now is not the time to go wobbly*
george-habash.summary: The telephone call from Margaret Thatcher to George H. W. Bush on the afternoon of the Kuwait invasion which, in John Kiriakou's account of that day inside the CIA, was what finally decided the president to expel Iraqi troops from Kuwait.

george-hw-bush.title: Iraqi invasion of Kuwait
george-hw-bush.summary: John Kiriakou''s most detailed account of the intelligence process around the 1990 Iraqi invasion of Kuwait and its 1991 liberation. As a first-year CIA analyst on a ''training account'' covering Iraq, Kiriakou produced the June 30, 1990 warning paper for the White House; suggested calling the US Defense Attaché in Baghdad to drive to the border and report what he saw (the answer: ''Literally the entire Iraqi military is heading south''); briefed the August 2 Oval Office meeting with Bush; and later took a single phone call from General Colin Powell that led, eight hours later, to 47 cruise missiles striking the Iraqi Intelligence Service headquarters in Baghdad.

george-hw-bush.title: George W. Bush
george-hw-bush.summary: 43rd President of the United States. In John Kiriakou's telling, Bush signed the August 1, 2002 executive order that authorized the CIA torture program, spent years telling the public "we don't torture," and — days after Kiriakou's 2007 ABC interview — blamed torture on "a rogue CIA officer" while walking from the White House South Portico to Marine One, a moment Kiriakou instantly read as the White House preparing to pin the program on him. Bush also ordered the FBI removed from Abu Zubaydah's black site, flew the bin Laden family out of the country after 9/11, and loosened the assassination ban of Executive Order 12333.

george-hw-bush.title: Oliver Stone
george-hw-bush.summary: American film director with whom John Kiriakou struck up a friendship after his release from prison. Stone optioned the rights to one chapter of Kiriakou's first book, co-developed an unmade History Channel series with him, blurbed his book on Abu Zubaydah, and was among the public figures who campaigned against the Bureau of Prisons' attempt to shut down Kiriakou's prison blog. The two disagree sharply over whether the CIA killed John F. Kennedy.

george-hw-bush.title: Freedom of Information Act
george-hw-bush.summary: The U.S. transparency law that runs through John Kiriakou's story from every direction — his plea agreement banned him from ever filing a FOIA request on himself, so he filed one with the Bureau of Prisons anyway and got back pages stamped "FOIA EXEMPT — DO NOT RELEASE TO INMATE"; a FOIA request exposed the prison commissary skim; Jason Leopold's requests revealed that a detainee's eye was removed under sedation without his knowledge and that NBC's Ken Dilanian sent his stories to the CIA before his own editor; and a FOIA request is how Kiriakou learned Gary Johnson had quietly lobbied for his early release.

george-hw-bush.title: Kiriakou's transfer to the Directorate of Operations
george-hw-bush.summary: John Kiriakou's roughly two-month internal campaign to transfer from the CIA's analytic Directorate of Intelligence to the operational Directorate of Operations, overcoming what he calls a "natural bias in operations against the eggheads on the analytic side," followed by an Athens posting secured because he was the only person in the entire CIA fluent in both Greek and Arabic. Covers his full CIA career arc from 1988/1990 recruitment through analyst years on Iraq, the switch to operations, 9/11, the enhanced-interrogation refusal, executive assistant to the deputy director for operations, and his eventual resignation and post-CIA career.

george-hw-bush.title: The polygraph
george-hw-bush.summary: The lie-detector examination that gates entry to the CIA, described by John Kiriakou from the inside: the twenty-minute wiring-up, the psychiatrist''s advice to stare at a speck on the wall, the deliberately planted false accusation used to test a candidate''s reaction, and his contention that the machine screens out exactly the wrong people.

george-mcgovern.title: The draft argument
george-mcgovern.summary: The disagreement John Kiriakou had at eighteen with a fellow College Democrat over Vietnam — that he thought the war immoral and illegal and would have served anyway if drafted, because his country had asked him to — which he identifies as the clearest surviving statement of the belief he later lost.

george-mcgovern.title: Invasion of Grenada
george-mcgovern.summary: The 1983 American invasion of Grenada, which John Kiriakou supported as a nineteen-year-old College Democrat at George Washington University on the grounds that American medical students had to be rescued — an episode he now cites as the clearest example of how completely he once accepted the government's own account of what it was doing.

george-mcgovern.title: Superdelegates
george-mcgovern.summary: The Democratic Party's automatic-delegate system, which John Kiriakou describes as created after George McGovern's 1972 landslide loss to return nominating power to party insiders. He cites West Virginia and Wyoming in 2016, where Bernie Sanders won the vote and Hillary Clinton took every delegate, and notes the Republican Party has no equivalent — which is why an insurgent like Donald Trump could win its nomination.

george-mcgovern.title: John Kiriakou
george-mcgovern.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

george-mcgovern.title: Tulsi Gabbard
george-mcgovern.summary: U.S. Director of National Intelligence; a longtime family friend of John Kiriakou's, who has known her since she was 12; Kiriakou calls her appointment "an inspired choice" despite disagreeing with her decision to join the Republican Party, and says she appears to have given up her opposition to Section 702 surveillance to secure Senate confirmation.

george-mcgovern.title: The translator for the Italian occupation
george-mcgovern.summary: John Kiriakou's grandmother — the only one of three sisters sent to school, a teacher who then taught Italian soldiers to speak Greek during the occupation, a lifelong royalist on Greek politics and a Democrat in America — and the divided household from which his own account of the Greek civil war descends.

george-tenet.title: Groupthink at the CIA
george-tenet.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the institutional conformity he says has made the CIA wrong about nearly every major international development since its creation — a failure he attributes to analysts agreeing with one another around a conference table while invoking red-team and outside-the-box vocabulary that changes nothing. He and his attorney Bruce Fein discussed writing a book about it.

george-tenet.title: The rebuttal book
george-tenet.summary: The volume published by a group of retired senior CIA leaders — George Tenet, Jim Pavitt, Jose Rodriguez and Cofer Black among them — answering the Senate torture report with the claim that the programme worked, saved lives and involved no mistakes, while continuing to refuse the word torture.

george-tenet.title: "When did you become a fascist?"
george-tenet.summary: The exchange John Kiriakou recalls with a former intern of his, a Yale sophomore he had supervised in Bahrain in the mid-1990s who resurfaced ten years later as a Pentagon under-secretariat for intelligence hire, briefing the CIA on Iraq. Walking him to his car after the briefing, Kiriakou asked *"Michael, when did you become a fascist?"* and got the answer he uses to date the neoconservative capture of the Bush administration, *"We're in charge now. We're in charge and Saddam Hussein's going to die."*

george-tenet.title: Assange plea deal
george-tenet.summary: The 2024 agreement under which Julian Assange pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit espionage, was processed in Saipan, and returned to Australia; John Kiriakou details its odd terms — a Chelsea Manning purge affidavit and a 25-year green-card ban — and the debate over whether it sets a precedent.

george-tenet.title: Barry Pollock
george-tenet.summary: Washington defense attorney who represented Julian Assange; John Kiriakou credits Pollock with negotiating the deal that let Assange be processed in Saipan — the U.S. district closest to Australia — rather than be brought to Virginia.

george-tenet.title: Omar al-Bayoumi
george-tenet.summary: The Saudi national who housed and funded two of the 9/11 hijackers in California; John Kiriakou describes him as a Saudi intelligence officer working under a ghost job, places him at President Bush's Crawford ranch before the attacks, and says the CIA blocked the 9/11 Commission from investigating him.

george-w-bush.title: Central American Task Force
george-w-bush.summary: CIA unit that led the agency's early-to-mid-1980s effort to overthrow the Sandinista government and support the Contras in Nicaragua. John Kiriakou describes serving as assistant to the unit's head as one of his first, and most controversial, CIA jobs; he denies the accusation that the CIA trained Contra and Salvadoran insurgents to garrote nuns, saying the agency instead worked to stop such atrocities, while acknowledging it was associated with people who did terrible things.

george-w-bush.title: The Taft joke
george-w-bush.summary: The moment at a White House briefing that John Kiriakou offers as the whole difference between the two men at the top of the Bush administration — a self-deprecating crack about William Howard Taft that left the president helpless with laughter and the vice president standing like a statue.

george-w-bush.title: The whiskers rule
george-w-bush.summary: John Kiriakou's description of the cultural practice he says American personnel encountered with some regularity in Afghanistan — that a boy who has not yet reached puberty is treated as available for sexual abuse — and his account of what he understood to have happened, and not happened, at Abu Ghraib.

george-w-bush.title: Learned Helplessness
george-w-bush.summary: Psychological concept adapted by the CIA as the theoretical basis for its post-9/11 enhanced interrogation program; per John Kiriakou, the goal of techniques including waterboarding was not primarily to elicit specific information but to render the prisoner so terrified of his captors that he would volunteer confessions on demand. In practice, applied to Abu Zubaydah, it meant a dog cage he would climb into on command, a coffin filled with cockroaches, and a towel whose mere appearance made him crumple — a programme Kiriakou says had far less to do with gathering intelligence than with ruining a man's life.

george-w-bush.title: The applicant who invented a CIA career
george-w-bush.summary: The job interview John Kiriakou conducted in the private sector at which he took a candidate to lunch, asked two questions any real CIA officer could answer, and was told: "I''m really sorry. I really need this job."

george-washington-university.title: The polygraph
george-washington-university.summary: The lie-detector examination that gates entry to the CIA, described by John Kiriakou from the inside: the twenty-minute wiring-up, the psychiatrist''s advice to stare at a speck on the wall, the deliberately planted false accusation used to test a candidate''s reaction, and his contention that the machine screens out exactly the wrong people.

george-washington-university.title: United Food and Commercial Workers
george-washington-university.summary: The huge K Street labor union where a young John Kiriakou — from a family with a long labor history — was working when Dr. Jerrold Post''s class assignment changed his life: shadow your boss for a week and write his psychological profile. Kiriakou''s boss was a mean old-school organizer whose back had been broken by scabs; halfway through the week Kiriakou called him a racist ("which he was"), and the resulting paper diagnosed the man as a sociopath and potentially dangerous. The paper is what put Kiriakou on the CIA''s radar.

george-washington-university.title: Arabic and Greek
george-washington-university.summary: The qualification John Kiriakou says opened the door to his transfer from CIA analysis to operations: a post in Athens wanted Greek or Arabic, and he had both — by most of his tellings the only officer in the agency who did. The chief who hired him gave the reason in one sentence: it is easier and cheaper to take a linguist and teach him operations than the other way round. The pairing also became a detection tool, since the language nobody speaks in Pakistan is Arabic.

george-washington-university.title: Kiriakou's transfer to the Directorate of Operations
george-washington-university.summary: John Kiriakou's roughly two-month internal campaign to transfer from the CIA's analytic Directorate of Intelligence to the operational Directorate of Operations, overcoming what he calls a "natural bias in operations against the eggheads on the analytic side," followed by an Athens posting secured because he was the only person in the entire CIA fluent in both Greek and Arabic. Covers his full CIA career arc from 1988/1990 recruitment through analyst years on Iraq, the switch to operations, 9/11, the enhanced-interrogation refusal, executive assistant to the deputy director for operations, and his eventual resignation and post-CIA career.

george-washington-university.title: New Castle, Pennsylvania
george-washington-university.summary: John Kiriakou's home town, an hour north of Pittsburgh on the edge of Amish country — a rust-belt city of roughly 40,000 to 50,000 people when he was growing up and around 18,000 to 20,000 now, whose decline he measures by the arrival of DEA and ATF field offices. It is also where, aged eight or nine and hunting salamanders in Oak Park Cemetery, he found the grave of a Medal of Honor private and acquired the lifelong interest in cemeteries that became a book.

george-washington-university.title: The translator for the Italian occupation
george-washington-university.summary: John Kiriakou's grandmother — the only one of three sisters sent to school, a teacher who then taught Italian soldiers to speak Greek during the occupation, a lifelong royalist on Greek politics and a Democrat in America — and the divided household from which his own account of the Greek civil war descends.

gerald-bull.title: MOSSAD
gerald-bull.summary: Israel's primary external intelligence service; characterized by John Kiriakou as universally hostile in his and his CIA colleagues' professional dealings with it ("never had a positive encounter with Mossad"); operates almost exclusively in the operational rather than analytical domain; the CIA is, per Kiriakou, categorically forbidden from spying on it.

gerald-bull.title: Adnan Khashoggi
gerald-bull.summary: Saudi arms dealer and Iran-Contra middleman whom John Kiriakou says was mentioned 'all the time' at the CIA — in pointed contrast to Jeffrey Epstein, whose name he never once heard there.

gerald-bull.title: Beef jerky anomaly in the Epstein files
gerald-bull.summary: A pattern John Kiriakou has flagged in the released Epstein correspondence: on the order of 1,300 to 1,500 emails discuss beef jerky — making it, teaching others to make it, freezing and storing it — and none discuss eating it. Kiriakou treats it as an unexplained code and declines to speculate about what it stands for.

gerald-bull.title: Jeffrey Epstein
gerald-bull.summary: Convicted sex offender; per John Kiriakou, was "an Israeli access agent" rather than a CIA asset, because the CIA collects foreign intelligence and Epstein's targets — Bill Clinton, Bill Gates, Prince Andrew — were not foreign. Kiriakou further holds that Epstein did die by suicide in federal custody, because in the Bureau of Prisons the cameras never work and the guards are always asleep.

gerald-bull.title: Iran-Contra
gerald-bull.summary: The mid-1980s scandal in which the Reagan administration secretly sold weapons to Iran and diverted the proceeds — laundered through Cyprus — to fund the Contra rebels in Nicaragua. Per John Kiriakou, Iran-Contra marks the precise end of what he calls the ''golden age'' of congressional intelligence oversight: the roughly 1975–1982 window opened by the Church and Pike Committees, when ''serious people, heavyweights'' actually held the CIA accountable. After Iran-Contra, he says, the oversight committees reverted to being ''cheerleaders'' for the agency — a posture that has held ever since.

gerald-bull.title: David Rockefeller in Bahrain
gerald-bull.summary: Per John Kiriakou — economic officer at the American Embassy in Bahrain, 1994–1996, and control officer for a David Rockefeller visit — Rockefeller''s award from the US-Bahrain Banking Society was a cover stop. After three days of documented public appearances, Rockefeller flew on a military plane to Baghdad to deliver a secret message to Saddam Hussein: stop violating sanctions, or the United States would take military action. Kiriakou cites the trip as a textbook case of how public figures are used as deniable back-channel intermediaries.

german-pow-chess-analogy.title: Abu Zubaydah as a sounding board
german-pow-chess-analogy.summary: The second, longer phase of Abu Zubaydah''s usefulness to the CIA, described by John Kiriakou in his December 2007 ABC News interview: once the prisoner had given up what he knew about current operations, his value shifted from threat reporting to analysis, with case officers reading him the names of men arrested in European capitals and asking whether the operations attributed to them made sense.

german-pow-chess-analogy.title: The slap approval cable
german-pow-chess-analogy.summary: The cable-by-cable approval chain that governed each escalation of the CIA''s enhanced interrogation techniques, described by John Kiriakou in his December 2007 ABC News interview: permission for even a single open-handed slap of Abu Zubaydah came from Washington after a discussion, was granted by the deputy director for operations, and had to be reported back by cable afterwards.

german-pow-chess-analogy.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
german-pow-chess-analogy.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

german-pow-chess-analogy.title: Abu Zubaydah
german-pow-chess-analogy.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

german-pow-chess-analogy.title: Brian Ross
german-pow-chess-analogy.summary: American investigative journalist and seven-time Emmy Award winner who was a prominent reporter at ABC News when, in December 2007, he conducted the on-camera interview with John Kiriakou that produced the first public confirmation by a U.S. official that the CIA waterboarded prisoners. Per Kiriakou, Ross called him out of the blue with the assertion that a source said Kiriakou had personally tortured Abu Zubaydah; Kiriakou's decision to give the interview anyway — driven by the conclusion that 'Brian Ross's source is at the White House and they're going to pin this on me' — became the pivot point of his entire post-CIA life.

german-pow-chess-analogy.title: The CIA defense
german-pow-chess-analogy.summary: John Kiriakou's account of what happens when a CIA asset is arrested — either the station chief privately asks the host country's intelligence service for the man's release, which he says works ninety-nine times out of a hundred, or the agency declines, leaving the defendant to argue at trial that he was acting on the CIA's behalf while the agency says nothing at all.

germany-and-israel.title: Antisemitism and anti-Zionism
germany-and-israel.summary: The conflation of criticism of the Israeli state with hatred of Jews, which John Kiriakou describes as a worldwide confusion and, according to a young Israeli he spoke to, an explicit lesson of the Israeli school system; a subject Kiriakou says he personally struggles with.

germany-and-israel.title: Roger Waters
germany-and-israel.summary: Founding member of the British rock band Pink Floyd; outspoken supporter of Palestinian human rights; anonymously paid off John Kiriakou's second mortgage during his federal prison sentence, sparing his wife and children the loss of the family home; only discovered to be the benefactor years later; subsequently a personal friend of Kiriakou and a recurring guest on his programme.

germany-and-israel.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
germany-and-israel.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

germany-and-israel.title: Famine in Gaza
germany-and-israel.summary: The starvation of the civilian population of the Gaza Strip, which John Kiriakou describes as a United Nations-declared famine caused not by an absence of food but by an Israeli refusal to let food reach the people who need it; Kiriakou characterises it as a war crime, a crime against humanity and a form of genocide, attributing that characterisation to the United Nations and the International Court of Justice rather than to himself.

germany-and-israel.title: Christian Zionism
germany-and-israel.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that American evangelical Christianity functions as an arm of Zionism, and that its support for Israel is helping extinguish the oldest Christian communities on earth — a position he says he argued directly with the evangelical students he was invited to teach, and which he grounds in the projection that Nazareth, Christian for two thousand years, may soon have no Christians left.

germany-and-israel.title: Israeli property acquisition in Greece and Cyprus
germany-and-israel.summary: John Kiriakou's account of Israelis buying land in Greece and Cyprus at a scale he considers destabilising — entire villages rather than holiday homes, a Jewish-only village outside Paphos with a casino attached, a rejected bid for an island in the Ionian Sea, and a request to open the first Zionist high school in Cyprus.

get-better-enough-to-go-back.title: The CIA divorce rate
get-better-enough-to-go-back.summary: John Kiriakou's account of why marriages fail at the CIA at a rate he says exceeds that of any other part of the U.S. government — the impossibility of explaining a midnight departure to a spouse without a clearance, and the difficulty officers have switching off a professional habit of deception. He gives the figure variously as over 75 percent and upwards of 80 percent, says he was determined not to become a statistic and became one anyway, and dates the end of his first marriage to a sentence spoken in an armoured car on the way to Athens airport. Both his divorces have been costly; of the second he says the agency played an active role he is barred by court order from explaining.

get-better-enough-to-go-back.title: Hire a lawyer first
get-better-enough-to-go-back.summary: The single piece of practical advice John Kiriakou gives to anyone considering blowing the whistle: retain a lawyer before saying anything, and have that lawyer sitting beside you when you do.

get-better-enough-to-go-back.title: Never meet my grandchildren
get-better-enough-to-go-back.summary: The threat John Kiriakou says one of the prosecutors in his case made to him — that he was going to die in prison and would never meet his grandchildren — set against the forty-five years he faced under the original charges.

get-better-enough-to-go-back.title: The detractors who died
get-better-enough-to-go-back.summary: John Kiriakou's observation that the senior CIA officials who wanted him dead or wanted him to die in prison have themselves since died, while a new generation of officers reaches out to tell him he did the right thing.

get-better-enough-to-go-back.title: They deserve an apology
get-better-enough-to-go-back.summary: John Kiriakou's statement that he feels he owes the men his government tortured an apology, that they deserve compensation they will never receive, and that at the very least they are owed the apology.

get-better-enough-to-go-back.title: Too much work to be Mrs Kiriakou
get-better-enough-to-go-back.summary: The reason John Kiriakou says his wife gave for leaving in 2017 — that it was simply too much work to be Mrs John Kiriakou — and his statement that he does not blame her.

get-thrown-out-spicily.title: Decorum in the Reagan years
get-thrown-out-spicily.summary: John Kiriakou's contrast between the State of the Union addresses he watched as a college student under Ronald Reagan — divided, substantive, but conducted with decorum — and the 2026 address he called a clown show with no decorum on either side.

get-thrown-out-spicily.title: The six-hour queue for seats
get-thrown-out-spicily.summary: John Kiriakou on learning that members of Congress arrive six hours early with packed meals to hold a seat for the State of the Union, and that in 2026 the absence of 112 Democrats freed those seats for the cabinet, the sub-cabinet and visitors.

get-thrown-out-spicily.title: Impeach him again
get-thrown-out-spicily.summary: John Kiriakou's warning that if the Democrats win a House majority in 2026 and immediately move to impeach Donald Trump again, they should never win another race — and his prediction that this is exactly what they will do.

get-thrown-out-spicily.title: Nationalizing the midterms
get-thrown-out-spicily.summary: John Kiriakou's recurring comparison between contemporary party messaging and Newt Gingrich's 1994 Contract with America, including his advice that Speaker Mike Johnson should keep Gingrich on his couch and ask him nightly how the 1994 midterms were nationalised.

get-thrown-out-spicily.title: The Trump appointees to the Court
get-thrown-out-spicily.summary: John Kiriakou's assessment that Donald Trump's Supreme Court appointees have been surprisingly good, and that the justices he regards as disasters — Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas — were appointed by more moderate presidents.

get-thrown-out-spicily.title: Ted Rall
get-thrown-out-spicily.summary: American editorial cartoonist and two-time Pulitzer Prize finalist; co-host with John Kiriakou of the daily news-commentary podcast "Deprogram," launched in September 2025 and by late 2025 running every weekday morning.

ghislaine-maxwell.title: Jeffrey Epstein
ghislaine-maxwell.summary: Convicted sex offender; per John Kiriakou, was "an Israeli access agent" rather than a CIA asset, because the CIA collects foreign intelligence and Epstein's targets — Bill Clinton, Bill Gates, Prince Andrew — were not foreign. Kiriakou further holds that Epstein did die by suicide in federal custody, because in the Bureau of Prisons the cameras never work and the guards are always asleep.

ghislaine-maxwell.title: MOSSAD
ghislaine-maxwell.summary: Israel's primary external intelligence service; characterized by John Kiriakou as universally hostile in his and his CIA colleagues' professional dealings with it ("never had a positive encounter with Mossad"); operates almost exclusively in the operational rather than analytical domain; the CIA is, per Kiriakou, categorically forbidden from spying on it.

ghislaine-maxwell.title: Robert Maxwell
ghislaine-maxwell.summary: British media proprietor and father of Ghislaine Maxwell; described by John Kiriakou as "a prolific Mossad spy — that's a historic fact," and as the family channel through which the Epstein operation, in Kiriakou's phrase, was "kept all in the family."

ghislaine-maxwell.title: Kiriakou's prison designation
ghislaine-maxwell.summary: The discrepancy between the minimum-security work camp John Kiriakou was sentenced to and the low-security prison the Bureau of Prisons actually placed him in, which he cites whenever the subject of preferential designations arises.

ghislaine-maxwell.title: Les Wexner
ghislaine-maxwell.summary: Ohio billionaire retail magnate; John Kiriakou cites Vanity Fair allegations that Wexner funneled millions to Jeffrey Epstein as his 'tax advisor,' offering it as evidence for his own view that Epstein's money and access served the Israelis.

ghislaine-maxwell.title: Sacha Baron Cohen
ghislaine-maxwell.summary: British comedian and actor; per John Kiriakou, "a comedic genius" who hired Kiriakou as a Middle East script advisor for the film Bruno, and whose attempt to film in Jordan without notifying the Jordanian Intelligence Service resulted in King Abdullah II personally greeting him at the Royal Palace.

gina-haspel.title: Kiriakou on influencing Trump
gina-haspel.summary: John Kiriakou's 2019 account of how to move Donald Trump on a policy question — that the president is malleable but needs to hear the same thing from three different people he respects, illustrated with an episode in which Rand Paul mentioned Kiriakou to Trump two weeks after an aide had, and Trump remembered the earlier mention. Kiriakou used the theory to argue that a pardon for Julian Assange was reachable.

gina-haspel.title: Jean Gately
gina-haspel.summary: The CIA officer who commanded the 1961 Bay of Pigs operation and, decades later, served alongside John Kiriakou as an elderly contractor at the CIA's Pakistan station, where he still blamed Kennedy for the defeat — 'We could have won that thing.'

gina-haspel.title: The Melber walkout
gina-haspel.summary: An incident on MSNBC in which John Kiriakou removed his microphone and threatened to leave the set after host Ari Melber introduced him as a leaker and a convicted felon, on a segment about whistleblowing recorded alongside Daniel Ellsberg. Kiriakou recounts it as the sharpest instance of the naming fight he has waged with the networks for over a decade.

gina-haspel.title: Torture as a recruiting tool
gina-haspel.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that interrogations, drone strikes and targeted killings have generated more enemies than they removed — supported by the arithmetic he uses, from an al-Qaeda core of a few hundred in Afghanistan to an ISIS he numbered at some thirty-five thousand, by the fighters he personally captured who told him they had no quarrel with America until a drone killed their families, and by his answer to the charge that it was his disclosure rather than the programme that put Americans at risk.

gina-haspel.title: Truman's CIA op-ed
gina-haspel.summary: A 1963 Washington Post op-ed in which former President Harry Truman — who signed the CIA into being in 1947 — called it a 'damn fool mistake' that should be disbanded; John Kiriakou notes the piece ran in the morning edition and vanished from the evening one.

gina-haspel.title: Ken Dilanian
gina-haspel.summary: Chief national-security correspondent at NBC News and MSNBC; documented — through a Jason Leopold Freedom of Information Act lawsuit against the CIA — to have sent his own articles to the CIA Office of Public Affairs for clearance before sending them to his own editor.

girls-madrasa-raid-error.title: Bob Grenier
girls-madrasa-raid-error.summary: Career CIA officer who served as station chief in Islamabad before, during, and after 9/11; later associate deputy director of operations for policy support and Iraq Mission Manager; John Kiriakou's boss and, for one year, his supervisor as executive assistant.

girls-madrasa-raid-error.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
girls-madrasa-raid-error.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

girls-madrasa-raid-error.title: Guantánamo Bay detention camp
girls-madrasa-raid-error.summary: Per John Kiriakou — as chief of counterterrorism operations in Pakistan after September 11, 2001 — the Guantanamo detention facility began as a temporary holding measure intended to last two to three weeks while the CIA and Justice Department determined which federal district court should try each prisoner, not as a long-term detention infrastructure. The Rawalpindi jail had reached capacity, Pakistani intelligence demanded the prisoners be removed, and CIA headquarters directed Kiriakou to load them onto a C-12 cargo plane and fly them to Cuba.

girls-madrasa-raid-error.title: Jennifer Keenan
girls-madrasa-raid-error.summary: FBI agent who partnered with John Kiriakou in Islamabad on the handling of an unreliable walk-in informant who had confessed to firing a rocket at the American embassy in 1996. After the informant's leads to weapons caches in Peshawar and a safe in Multan both turned up empty, Kiriakou and Keenan decided to lure him back to the embassy and arrest him on the strength of his original confession, which carried no statute of limitations.

girls-madrasa-raid-error.title: Senate Torture Report
girls-madrasa-raid-error.summary: The December 2014 executive summary of the U.S. Senate Select Committee on Intelligence's study of the CIA's post-9/11 detention and interrogation program; the first public disclosure of techniques including rectal feeding with hummus, sexual assault with broomsticks, and prolonged sleep deprivation.

girls-madrasa-raid-error.title: Tommy McHale
girls-madrasa-raid-error.summary: Highly decorated Port Authority of New York and New Jersey detective who worked as a terrorist hunter alongside John Kiriakou in Islamabad, Pakistan after 9/11; a survivor of the 1993 World Trade Center bombing whose best friend died on 9/11.

giuliani-pardon-solicitation.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
giuliani-pardon-solicitation.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

giuliani-pardon-solicitation.title: Alex Padilla
giuliani-pardon-solicitation.summary: U.S. Senator from California who was forced to the ground and handcuffed at a June 2025 press event after identifying himself as a sitting senator; per John Kiriakou, DHS Secretary Kristi Noem's claim that he failed to identify himself was false, and the White House's stated interest in prosecuting him was legally baseless because sitting senators have congressional immunity while acting in the course of their duties.

giuliani-pardon-solicitation.title: The hundred-and-fifty-foot limousine
giuliani-pardon-solicitation.summary: A detail John Kiriakou recalls from his years as a congressional staffer — that Mitch McConnell lived in a townhouse four doors from the Hart Senate Office Building, roughly a hundred and fifty feet away, and took a limousine to work every morning anyway, to be booed by staff as he passed.

giuliani-pardon-solicitation.title: Rick Praau
giuliani-pardon-solicitation.summary: Career CIA officer, chief of operations at the Counterterrorism Center and previously of the Special Activities Division, whose retirement memoir John Kiriakou reviewed critically in Covert Action Magazine. Kiriakou's objection is not to what the book contains but to what it omits — published reports that before joining the agency its author was investigated by Miami-Dade police over seven contract killings for the Medellín cartel. The surname is given here as the source transcript's auto-captions render it and may be mis-transcribed.

giuliani-pardon-solicitation.title: The contrition requirement
giuliani-pardon-solicitation.summary: The rule John Kiriakou says defeats his own pardon applications before they begin — that an applicant must show proof of contrition — and his refusal to meet it. Asked whether he is sorry for the crime he committed, his answer is no, and that he would do it again.

giuliani-pardon-solicitation.title: Military Ethics
giuliani-pardon-solicitation.summary: The hypothetical Kiriakou puts to college audiences — and the line no CIA training class ever teaches an officer where to draw.

glenn-symington-act.title: MOSSAD
glenn-symington-act.summary: Israel's primary external intelligence service; characterized by John Kiriakou as universally hostile in his and his CIA colleagues' professional dealings with it ("never had a positive encounter with Mossad"); operates almost exclusively in the operational rather than analytical domain; the CIA is, per Kiriakou, categorically forbidden from spying on it.

glenn-symington-act.title: Israeli Nuclear Program
glenn-symington-act.summary: Israel's widely assumed but officially unacknowledged nuclear arsenal; per John Kiriakou, the conventional wisdom within the CIA is that Israel possesses between 120 and 220 nuclear weapons, and the U.S. government's refusal to formally acknowledge this is driven by a specific legal obligation under the Glenn-Symington Act, which would require cutting off all foreign aid to any nuclear-armed country not party to the Non-Proliferation Treaty.

glenn-symington-act.title: AIPAC
glenn-symington-act.summary: The American Israel Public Affairs Committee — the U.S. political organization that, in John Kiriakou's framing, ought to be registered as a foreign-lobbying entity but is not, and that wields decisive electoral power against U.S. elected officials who express support for Palestinian human rights.

glenn-symington-act.title: Thomas Massie
glenn-symington-act.summary: Republican U.S. Representative from Kentucky known for a constitutionalist voting record and consistent opposition to foreign military intervention; per John Kiriakou, a principled America-First congressman who votes with the president on the vast majority of issues, and whose opposition to U.S. funding of Israel and foreign wars is the only plausible explanation for the roughly $30 million spent by the Israel lobby to unseat him in a primary.

glenn-symington-act.title: Iran Nuclear Assessment
glenn-symington-act.summary: Per John Kiriakou's assessment, the US–Israeli military campaign against Iran was a war of choice driven by Israeli political pressure rather than genuine intelligence indicating an Iranian nuclear weapons threat. The CIA produced two National Intelligence Estimates concluding Iran had no nuclear weapons program; Supreme Leader Ayatollah Khamenei issued a fatwa in the 1980s forbidding such a program. The U.S. went to war anyway, in Kiriakou's view, after President Trump replaced the Joint Chiefs of Staff with officers willing to accept Israeli intelligence and proceed.

glenn-symington-act.title: Church Committee
glenn-symington-act.summary: U.S. Senate investigative committee operating in 1975–1976 that examined domestic intelligence abuses by the CIA, FBI, and NSA; per John Kiriakou, the Church Committee — alongside the concurrent Pike Committee in the House — was the last genuine moment of legislative oversight over the intelligence community, born of a national consensus that government had gone dangerously off course. Its work led to the creation of the permanent Senate Select Committee on Intelligence, which Kiriakou says ceased to function as real oversight roughly seven years after its founding.

global-services.title: Special Activities Division
global-services.summary: The CIA's paramilitary arm; described by John Kiriakou as having two organizationally distinct components — the pre-9/11 SAD, a covert-action division within the Directorate of Operations, and a post-9/11 special activities group within the Counterterrorism Center, staffed largely by personnel on secondment from Delta Force, SEAL Team 6, and other special-operations units.

global-services.title: Tuesday morning kill list
global-services.summary: Weekly CIA targeting meeting instituted by John Brennan in 2009 during his service as Deputy National Security Advisor for Counterterrorism in the Obama administration; produced a written list of individuals to be killed in the following week; per John Kiriakou, the program was a source of pride within the Obama administration and was made operationally possible by the targeting-software sophistication of the period.

global-services.title: Vault 7
global-services.summary: The 2017 WikiLeaks disclosure of thousands of pages of CIA Directorate of Science and Technology documents — leaked by agency engineer Joshua Schulte — revealing CIA technical capabilities including remote takeover of internet-connected cars, conversion of smart-TV speakers into covert microphones, and the planting of Russian or Persian language fragments in foreign systems to mislead attribution.

global-services.title: Executive Order 12333
global-services.summary: The U.S. presidential directive — in its post-9/11 amended form — that grants the CIA the legal authority to kill any individual anywhere in the world deemed by the agency to pose a "clear and present danger" to the United States; the legal foundation underlying both CIA paramilitary operations and the agency's contractor relationships including with Blackwater.

global-services.title: How the CIA kills
global-services.summary: John Kiriakou''s description of the methods used when the CIA is ordered to kill someone outside a war zone: a team parachuting in miles away, stealing a car, a locks-and-picks specialist opening the door and suppressed weapons inside; a snatch into a van bound for an airport or a boat; or a brush past in a market with something poisoned — a technique he says the Russians used often and taught the Bulgarians into the early 1980s.

global-services.title: SEALs on loan to the CIA
global-services.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer to why the CIA did not use its own paramilitary team against Osama bin Laden: it did. The raid was a CIA operation directed by the Counterterrorism Center, and every Navy SEAL involved was temporarily a CIA contractor, on loan to the agency for the duration.

glyburide-incident.title: Frank's heart attack
glyburide-incident.summary: The 65-year-old insulin-dependent diabetic who shared a cell with John Kiriakou at FCI Loretto, reported chest tightness for months, was given Tylenol and a request for an EKG that the regional office never approved, and collapsed in the insulin line.

glyburide-incident.title: Kiriakou's type 2 diabetes
glyburide-incident.summary: The disease John Kiriakou was diagnosed with after leaving the CIA for a desk job, which he first fought down with a nutritionist's diet and a 70-pound weight loss, then lost ground to when insulin slowed his metabolism to a halt — reaching an A1C of 12.1 before he had his stomach removed to end it.

glyburide-incident.title: Larry
glyburide-incident.summary: The prisoner at FCI Loretto who complained of back pain for more than a year, was given Tylenol, and progressed from a cane to a walker to a wheelchair before a chaplain forced an outside hospital referral — which found stage four cancer of the spine. He died in his bunk two weeks later.

glyburide-incident.title: Kiriakou's gastrectomy
glyburide-incident.summary: The experimental operation John Kiriakou paid for with a bank loan in September 2022, in which his stomach was removed to reverse an uncontrolled type 2 diabetes — a procedure he had found in a Lancet paper by a Scottish surgeon, and which cost him 55 kilos and, he says, the disease itself.

glyburide-incident.title: Five per cent of the population, twenty-five per cent of the prisoners
glyburide-incident.summary: The statistic John Kiriakou returns to from inside prison — that the United States holds five per cent of the world''s people and a quarter of its prisoners, more per head than Russia, China or Iran — and the causes he assigns: the war on drugs, election-year lawmaking, and a Congress creating some fifty new crimes a year.

glyburide-incident.title: Kiriakou's post-gastrectomy complications
glyburide-incident.summary: The aftermath of John Kiriakou''s stomach removal: eighteen months of daily vomiting that turned out to be scar tissue, a diagnosis of malnutrition, and a night on his kitchen floor with a blood pressure of 80 over 52, caused by a blood clot sitting on an ulcer at the surgical site — one hour, his surgeon told him, from being too late.

gore-vidal.title: Remains of the Day (book)
gore-vidal.summary: John Kiriakou's book, announced for publication by Simon and Schuster in March 2026, billed as a definitive guide to the historic cemeteries of Washington DC and the first in a planned series; the second installment will cover the Mafia graves of New York City.

gore-vidal.title: Arkady Shevchenko
gore-vidal.summary: Soviet diplomat and Undersecretary General of the United Nations who secretly spied for the CIA before defecting to the United States in 1978 — described by John Kiriakou as the single most important spy the CIA ever had inside the Soviet power structure.

gore-vidal.title: Joseph B. Chambers
gore-vidal.summary: Civil War Medal of Honor recipient buried at Oak Park Cemetery in New Castle, Pennsylvania, whose grave John Kiriakou discovered as a child while looking for salamanders — sparking a lifelong interest in history.

gore-vidal.title: New Castle, Pennsylvania
gore-vidal.summary: John Kiriakou's home town, an hour north of Pittsburgh on the edge of Amish country — a rust-belt city of roughly 40,000 to 50,000 people when he was growing up and around 18,000 to 20,000 now, whose decline he measures by the arrival of DEA and ATF field offices. It is also where, aged eight or nine and hunting salamanders in Oak Park Cemetery, he found the grave of a Medal of Honor private and acquired the lifelong interest in cemeteries that became a book.

gore-vidal.title: Greek death rituals
gore-vidal.summary: The five-year grave rental, exhumation and ossuary practice of rural Greece as John Kiriakou describes it — bones washed in red wine, blessed, boxed, and eventually laid beneath the foundations of a new church, with cremation strictly forbidden. He visits the ossuary in his ancestral Rhodes village, where the records stop in the nineteenth century because the Ottomans burned everything earlier.

gore-vidal.title: Israel Boyd and the Wonder Bread story
gore-vidal.summary: John Kiriakou's account of finding the grave of Israel Boyd, one of two brothers forced by their parents into the family bakery business, who went on to invent the first industrial dough mixer and dough-cutting machine, pioneer adding milk to bread dough, and build the largest bakery in America before World War I — before selling the business, whose flagship "Mrs. McGill's Delicious Bread" was renamed Wonder Bread by its buyer.

government-accountability-project.title: John Walker Lindh
government-accountability-project.summary: American citizen captured while fighting alongside the Taliban in late 2001, present at the Qala-i-Jangi fortress at the start of the prisoner uprising that killed CIA officer Mike Spann. In John Kiriakou's account his case matters less for what Lindh did than for what was done around him — the false claim that he had been read his rights, the destruction of the career of the Justice Department lawyer who said so, and his place on the docket of the one judge who reserves national-security cases for herself.

government-accountability-project.title: The MintPress prediction
government-accountability-project.summary: The forecast John Kiriakou volunteers against himself — that asked in a post-election interview alongside Thomas Drake and Jesselyn Radack whether whistleblowers would fare better or worse under Donald Trump, he alone answered that nothing could be worse than Barack Obama, and was wrong.

government-accountability-project.title: The Americans Who Tell the Truth portrait
government-accountability-project.summary: The portrait of John Kiriakou painted by Robert Shetterly for his long-running series Americans Who Tell the Truth, unveiled at Busboys and Poets in Washington on February 7, 2013 — weeks before Kiriakou reported to prison — and inscribed with the words 'Even if torture works it cannot be tolerated.'

government-accountability-project.title: Ola Bini
government-accountability-project.summary: The Swedish programmer and friend of Julian Assange arrested in Ecuador in 2019 on the order of President Lenín Moreno, whose open-ended detention John Kiriakou treats as the collateral consequence of the same government's decision to hand Assange to the British.

government-accountability-project.title: The Senate WikiLeaks ban
government-accountability-project.summary: The instruction John Kiriakou watched the Senate security officer deliver in person to all one hundred senators and every committee after the WikiLeaks cables were published — that opening the material on a Senate computer would be the crime of unauthorized access to classified information, and that anyone who did so would be prosecuted.

government-accountability-project.title: The Uyghur resettlement trade
government-accountability-project.summary: The exchange John Kiriakou says the WikiLeaks cables revealed behind the prosecution of UBS whistleblower Brad Birkenfeld — Switzerland agreeing to accept two Uyghur prisoners out of Guantanamo on the condition that the United States arrest the man whose disclosure had exposed Swiss banking secrecy.

government-metadata-purchase.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
government-metadata-purchase.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

government-metadata-purchase.title: National security letters
government-metadata-purchase.summary: The demand letters the FBI began sending internet service providers after 2001, which John Kiriakou describes as one of three mechanisms that between them retired the warrant requirement for obtaining Americans' personal information. The other two are the FISA process and the outright purchase of metadata from social-media companies.

government-metadata-purchase.title: San Bernardino iPhone Case
government-metadata-purchase.summary: The 2015–16 legal standoff in which Apple refused to unlock the San Bernardino shooter's iPhone for the FBI, which instead paid an Israeli firm $6 million to crack it — though, per John Kiriakou, the intelligence that could have disrupted the attack never came from the phone at all.

government-metadata-purchase.title: AIPAC
government-metadata-purchase.summary: The American Israel Public Affairs Committee — the U.S. political organization that, in John Kiriakou's framing, ought to be registered as a foreign-lobbying entity but is not, and that wields decisive electoral power against U.S. elected officials who express support for Palestinian human rights.

government-metadata-purchase.title: Allen Dulles
government-metadata-purchase.summary: Long-serving CIA director whom John Kiriakou calls a 'monster' and a 'very dark figure in American history' — a United Fruit board member who ran the agency that overthrew Guatemala's Árbenz, who went to Truman's house to talk him out of criticising the CIA, and who stayed in touch with the men Kiriakou believes killed John F. Kennedy.

government-metadata-purchase.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
government-metadata-purchase.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

graham-netanyahu-icc-tapes.title: Espionage Act
graham-netanyahu-icc-tapes.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

graham-netanyahu-icc-tapes.title: International Criminal Court
graham-netanyahu-icc-tapes.summary: The Hague tribunal created by the Rome Statute, which has charged Benjamin Netanyahu with war crimes and crimes against humanity. John Kiriakou supports it as the necessary successor to Nuremberg, notes that neither the United States nor Israel is a signatory, and observes that a forced landing in a signatory state would oblige that country to arrest Netanyahu.

graham-netanyahu-icc-tapes.title: Lindsey Graham
graham-netanyahu-icc-tapes.summary: Republican senator from South Carolina who died in July 2026, and John Kiriakou's standing shorthand for the permanent war caucus — a "show horse" rather than a workhorse, a "chameleon" who "never saw a war that he didn't want to jump into with both feet," and, on posthumously released documentary footage, a man offering the US Air Force to bomb a country America was not at war with.

graham-netanyahu-icc-tapes.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
graham-netanyahu-icc-tapes.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

graham-netanyahu-icc-tapes.title: Hague Invasion Act
graham-netanyahu-icc-tapes.summary: The American statute, described by John Kiriakou as having been passed during the Obama administration, that authorises the president to use the United States military to invade the Netherlands and free an American or allied national held by the International Criminal Court — the standing legal answer to the possibility that Benjamin Netanyahu might be arrested abroad.

graham-netanyahu-icc-tapes.title: Netanyahu arrest poll
graham-netanyahu-icc-tapes.summary: The 2026 survey finding that a majority of Americans — not a plurality — support the arrest of Benjamin Netanyahu, a figure John Kiriakou notes is higher than the share who supported arresting Nicolás Maduro and which, per CNN, represents a fifty-point move in American opinion over five years.

greater-and-lesser-tunb-islands.title: 2026 Iran war economic shock
greater-and-lesser-tunb-islands.summary: John Kiriakou''s running assessment of the economic damage from the 2026 Iran war — an oil shock he says already exceeds both 1970s shocks combined, a natural-gas shock worse than the Nord Stream destruction, and a chokepoint problem that runs through fertilizer as much as fuel, since 65% of the world''s supply must transit the Strait of Hormuz. His summary: "This is an economic slowdown of choice."

greater-and-lesser-tunb-islands.title: Al-Julani
greater-and-lesser-tunb-islands.summary: The former al-Qaeda commander and, per John Kiriakou, co-founder of ISIS who was installed as president of Syria and received at the White House. Kiriakou''s initial reading was that no one moves from a ten-million-dollar American bounty to a state visit in months without being a long-term CIA asset — until a senior Turkish official told him over dinner that al-Julani was Turkey''s: ''We created him from nothing and we installed him in Syria.'' Kiriakou judged that version more plausible than his own.

greater-and-lesser-tunb-islands.title: Dead drop
greater-and-lesser-tunb-islands.summary: The classic tradecraft technique of passing material through a hidden location rather than a meeting. Per John Kiriakou, the hard part is not the drop but everything around it — in a sophisticated counterintelligence environment, merely identifying a viable site is very difficult, and the drop itself is bracketed by surveillance detection routes and a signal mark that can turn a single document into a sixteen-hour workday. It was the only element of clandestine training he struggled with, and the only exercise he was ever criticized for.

greater-and-lesser-tunb-islands.title: Dead Drop (podcast)
greater-and-lesser-tunb-islands.summary: John Kiriakou''s narrative podcast, launched in late 2025 — a season-long, memoir-style retelling of his life in intelligence, from recruitment ("The New Recruit") through Athens ("Golden Boy") to the post-9/11 hunt ("The Hunt Begins"), with mini-episodes like "A Spy''s Guide to Sofia." Written by Kiriakou with Alan Katz, produced by Costard & Touchstone Productions, with Kiriakou, Katz, and Nick Mechanic as executive producers. Its stated goal: "the deepest possible perspective on the world of spying and what makes any spy tick."

greater-and-lesser-tunb-islands.title: Death threats against Kiriakou
greater-and-lesser-tunb-islands.summary: The threats John Kiriakou has received across two decades — first after going public about the CIA torture program, when FBI advice that at least two were credible sent his family out of the country, and later in waves tied to his opposition to Gina Haspel, his remarks about Pakistan, and his advocacy on Palestine and the Epstein case.

greater-and-lesser-tunb-islands.title: ISIS
greater-and-lesser-tunb-islands.summary: The Islamic State, in John Kiriakou''s account, is an American policy failure made flesh — created because a faction decided al-Qaeda was not radical or violent enough, founded by Baghdadi while he sat in a U.S. military prison in Iraq, armed with hardware captured from the U.S.-supplied Iraqi army, and — per an email he cites from Hillary Clinton to John Podesta — funded by the governments of Saudi Arabia and Qatar. Kiriakou repeatedly punctured the anti-ISIS coalition''s logic: ISIS operated in seven countries while the U.S. bombed two, and Turkey had no real quarrel with ISIS at all — their common enemy was the Kurds.

greater-israel.title: Naftali Bennett
greater-israel.summary: The former Israeli prime minister, cited by John Kiriakou through 2026 for the position that Turkey would be the next target after Iran — a claim Kiriakou uses to identify the second obstacle, alongside Iran, to the Greater Israel project, and which by May 2026 he was stating in his own voice as an active Israeli intention rather than a Bennett prediction.

greater-israel.title: The seven countries argument
greater-israel.summary: John Kiriakou's dissent from the claim that America's post-2001 wars were fought on Israel's behalf. Taking the list of seven countries country by country, he argues Libya, Somalia and Afghanistan were American decisions made for American reasons — and concludes that the United States cannot blame all of its problems on Israel.

greater-israel.title: Lebanon-Israeli Conflict
greater-israel.summary: Per John Kiriakou, no Israeli government will allow Lebanon to flourish as a nation; he expects continued Israeli attacks and forced displacement of civilians, citing a statistic of up to 700,000 Lebanese internally displaced, and links the war to the "Greater Israel" rhetoric of US ambassador Mike Huckabee.

greater-israel.title: Mike Huckabee
greater-israel.summary: The United States ambassador to Israel under Donald Trump, and the subject of a public call for resignation from John Kiriakou after Huckabee received Jonathan Pollard at the American embassy. Kiriakou''s assessment separates two charges: Huckabee is not a traitor but an idiot who did not think the meeting was a big deal, and a former governor of a small state who still behaves as though he can set policy without the State Department or the National Security Council.

greater-israel.title: South Lebanon displacement, 2026
greater-israel.summary: John Kiriakou''s assessment of the Israeli campaign in southern Lebanon running alongside the 2026 Iran war: mass evacuation orders, hundreds of thousands internally displaced, and his conclusion that Israel has guaranteed Lebanon will be a failed state. He notes the world is not watching because it is watching Iran.

greater-israel.title: The Cyprus naval buildup, 2026
greater-israel.summary: The concentration of European warships and defence ministers on Cyprus during the 2026 Iran war, and John Kiriakou''s explanation of it: NATO and EU militaries feel compelled to appear supportive of Israel and the United States, whatever they say behind closed doors.

greek-ambassador-dinner-encounter.title: Ron Wyden
greek-ambassador-dinner-encounter.summary: U.S. senator and the lone real challenger of the CIA on the intelligence committees; John Kiriakou faults Wyden for challenging the agency only 'by the agency's rules' — refusing to read the Senate torture report into the record, and admitting at a dinner that fighting harder would cost him his security clearance.

greek-ambassador-dinner-encounter.title: Congressional intelligence oversight
greek-ambassador-dinner-encounter.summary: John Kiriakou''s standing criticism of the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence and the House Permanent Select Committee — that unlike the armed services and foreign relations committees, they do not perform oversight at all: "They''re just cheerleaders." His illustration is a sitting committee chairman who summoned him privately, then asked whether Kiriakou would write the criticism publicly on his behalf.

greek-ambassador-dinner-encounter.title: The CIA's internal social culture
greek-ambassador-dinner-encounter.summary: John Kiriakou's one-word characterisation of the agency's internal culture — "incestuous" — describing a club for every conceivable interest, actively encouraged officer-to-officer romances, and a design intent that officers should have no need of friends or activities outside the building.

greek-ambassador-dinner-encounter.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
greek-ambassador-dinner-encounter.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

greek-ambassador-dinner-encounter.title: John Brennan
greek-ambassador-dinner-encounter.summary: Former Director of the CIA; characterized in KiriPedia's source corpus as the principal architect of the agency's enhanced interrogation program and as having plotted against an elected President

greek-ambassador-dinner-encounter.title: MK-Ultra
greek-ambassador-dinner-encounter.summary: The CIA's mid-twentieth-century umbrella program of mind-control, behavioral-modification, and biological-warfare experimentation, encompassing subprojects such as MK-Chickwit and MK-Seesaw; active 1952–1975; documented practices included LSD dosing of unwitting American citizens in CIA-rented brothels and the aerosolized release of pathogens into the San Francisco fog; 80% of the program's documentation was destroyed by the CIA in defiance of a 1975 preservation order from Senator Frank Church.

greek-community-of-warren-ohio.title: The Tiffany stationery letter
greek-community-of-warren-ohio.summary: The deliberately expensive note John Kiriakou wrote to his first wife on Tiffany & Co. stationery, telling her he was halving her child support on the advice of counsel — a tactic suggested by his divorce lawyer to force her to file, and which worked the next day.

greek-community-of-warren-ohio.title: The CIA divorce rate
greek-community-of-warren-ohio.summary: John Kiriakou's account of why marriages fail at the CIA at a rate he says exceeds that of any other part of the U.S. government — the impossibility of explaining a midnight departure to a spouse without a clearance, and the difficulty officers have switching off a professional habit of deception. He gives the figure variously as over 75 percent and upwards of 80 percent, says he was determined not to become a statistic and became one anyway, and dates the end of his first marriage to a sentence spoken in an armoured car on the way to Athens airport. Both his divorces have been costly; of the second he says the agency played an active role he is barred by court order from explaining.

greek-community-of-warren-ohio.title: Consulting for royal families
greek-community-of-warren-ohio.summary: The work John Kiriakou says he was hired to do by members of two different royal families following the 2026 virality of his interviews — advising on ethics in their own intelligence operations — which he offers as evidence of how far the reversal in his standing had gone.

greek-community-of-warren-ohio.title: Double-Agent Capture
greek-community-of-warren-ohio.summary: Clandestine operation in which an intelligence service, having identified a recruited agent as working simultaneously for a hostile service, arranges a controlled final meeting to apprehend the agent before the agent can carry out orders — which may include killing the handler. Per John Kiriakou, he ran one such operation in the Middle East in the early 2000s after an NSA analyst warned him that his agent had just been ordered to shoot him in the next meeting.

greek-community-of-warren-ohio.title: John Kiriakou
greek-community-of-warren-ohio.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

greek-community-of-warren-ohio.title: Mary Jane Stevens
greek-community-of-warren-ohio.summary: The lawyer who represented John Kiriakou through his custody dispute — who told him to wait for Monday and go to court, was ignored, and then got the assurance from a hostile police chief that let him walk into the hearing without being arrested.

greek-death-rituals.title: Rhodes Jewish deportation and family rescue story
greek-death-rituals.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the 1944 Nazi roundup and deportation of roughly 2,000 Jewish residents of the island of Rhodes to Auschwitz, of whom only 14 survived — and of his own great-grandfather, a chauffeur, hiding his Jewish employer from the Nazis until the war's end.

greek-death-rituals.title: Remains of the Day (book)
greek-death-rituals.summary: John Kiriakou's book, announced for publication by Simon and Schuster in March 2026, billed as a definitive guide to the historic cemeteries of Washington DC and the first in a planned series; the second installment will cover the Mafia graves of New York City.

greek-death-rituals.title: Whispers in the Dirt
greek-death-rituals.summary: John Kiriakou's second cemetery book — a guide to the mafia graves of New York City, and the sequel Simon & Schuster commissioned after Remains of the Day. Reporting it produced the moment he realised an inmate who had told him a body was found in a barrel in his storage unit had been telling the truth.

greek-death-rituals.title: Israel Boyd and the Wonder Bread story
greek-death-rituals.summary: John Kiriakou's account of finding the grave of Israel Boyd, one of two brothers forced by their parents into the family bakery business, who went on to invent the first industrial dough mixer and dough-cutting machine, pioneer adding milk to bread dough, and build the largest bakery in America before World War I — before selling the business, whose flagship "Mrs. McGill's Delicious Bread" was renamed Wonder Bread by its buyer.

greek-death-rituals.title: Kiriakou's writing process
greek-death-rituals.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of how he actually writes — books in waves over roughly nine months, op-eds in forty-five minutes to an hour once an idea has sat for a few days, and a habit of getting up at two in the morning to write one because he cannot sleep. He wrote *Remains of the Day* in six weeks during COVID, losing whole evenings to it: "I look at the clock again, it''s 2:00 in the morning. I''m like, oh my god, what happened?"

greek-death-rituals.title: Abraham Accords
greek-death-rituals.summary: The Trump-brokered normalization deals between Israel and Gulf Arab states — in John Kiriakou's judgment "a terrible idea in the first place," a great victory for Israel and the Gulf Arabs that was "a punch in the throat to the Palestinians." He argues the Accords are how Trump meant to "solve the Middle East in a day" — by screwing the Palestinians — that Hamas read the abandonment correctly, that October 7 shattered the project, and that reviving the Accords (Saudis in, victory declared, Nobel collected) remains the organizing goal of Trump's regional policy.

greek-health-care-system.title: Americans and the word socialism
greek-health-care-system.summary: Two exchanges John Kiriakou uses to argue that the political vocabulary of the United States has stopped carrying meaning — a Thanksgiving conversation with a woman who denounced socialism and lived on Social Security, and a newspaper comment thread in which a restaurant owner taking his staff's tips was described as socialism.

greek-health-care-system.title: Kiriakou's Greek citizenship
greek-health-care-system.summary: The Greek nationality John Kiriakou acquired in 2010, after his CIA career and before his prosecution — offered, he says, by the Greek ambassador who asked what could be done to help when his troubles began, and granted when he answered "you could give me Greek citizenship." Held by his children too, it made him a Greek national at the moment he became, in Greece, a national hero; it brought him the commission to write the country's whistleblower protection law, and the Athens job that turned out to be a money laundering operation.

greek-health-care-system.title: Candace Owens
greek-health-care-system.summary: The commentator whose claims about the killing of Charlie Kirk John Kiriakou has publicly declined to accept. He credits her reach and her intelligence and rejects her method, citing an earlier occasion — a conference call he says he was on — at which she claimed irrefutable proof that the Italian government had stolen the 2020 election and that its release would return Donald Trump to office.

greek-health-care-system.title: Charlie Kirk shooting
greek-health-care-system.summary: Kiriakou questions the official account: a court filing says the ATF could not match the autopsy bullet to the rifle tied to the suspect.

greek-health-care-system.title: CIA Arabic hiring practices
greek-health-care-system.summary: John Kiriakou's account of how few CIA officers historically spoke Arabic — he was one of only two people in the entire agency fluent in both Greek and Arabic — and of how the agency's more recent pool of Arabic speakers, dominated by Arab Christian hires who clear background checks easily, often carries an innate anti-Muslim bias that limits their operational usefulness.

greek-health-care-system.title: Death threats against Kiriakou
greek-health-care-system.summary: The threats John Kiriakou has received across two decades — first after going public about the CIA torture program, when FBI advice that at least two were credible sent his family out of the country, and later in waves tied to his opposition to Gina Haspel, his remarks about Pakistan, and his advocacy on Palestine and the Epstein case.

greek-intelligence-service.title: John Kiriakou
greek-intelligence-service.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

greek-intelligence-service.title: Saint Nectarios of Aegina
greek-intelligence-service.summary: Early-20th-century Greek Orthodox saint whom John Kiriakou identifies with more than any other and carries a photograph of in his wallet; falsely accused and driven from his post, Nectarios forgave his accusers, and posthumous miracles led to his canonization.

greek-intelligence-service.title: Steven Lalas
greek-intelligence-service.summary: American with top-secret clearance recruited as a spy for Greece's National Intelligence Service (EYP) in a provocative mid-1990s operation run by the country's conservative government. Per John Kiriakou, who did not know Lawless personally, the case was so sensitive that his handler reported directly to the EYP director out of fear the CIA had planted a mole inside the service. Lawless was caught, served about seven years, and was given Greek citizenship on release.

greek-intelligence-service.title: Jerry Falwell Jr.
greek-intelligence-service.summary: Evangelical leader and former president of Liberty University; John Kiriakou recounts that Falwell personally recruited him to lecture at Liberty's Jesse Helms School of Government after his whistleblowing, with the reasoning that "torture is not Christian."

greek-intelligence-service.title: Six different passports
greek-intelligence-service.summary: John Kiriakou's answer to what has changed for intelligence officers since his own service — that he carried six different passports, and that he does not know how officers cross borders now that AI and facial recognition mean everything is scanned and stored — coupled with his advice not to let the technology take over the job.

greek-intelligence-service.title: Taybeh
greek-intelligence-service.summary: The only fully Christian village in the West Bank, home to the Holy Land's oldest brewery; John Kiriakou recounts it being set on fire and its Marian festival attacked by the IDF with drones, helicopters and stun grenades.

greek-orthodox-church.title: PFLP
greek-orthodox-church.summary: Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine; Palestinian armed group co-founded by George Habash and Ahmed Khatib, college roommates at the American University of Beirut. It is one of the Arab organizations John Kiriakou worked against during his Athens tour, where a semi-secret 1980s deal let the Arab groups transit Greece unmolested so long as they did not kill Greeks. Kiriakou's chance paper on Khatib made him the White House expert on the occupation governor of Kuwait in August 1990, and two of the Front's retired cadres later sat across a table from him in Jordan for a Sacha Baron Cohen shoot.

greek-orthodox-church.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
greek-orthodox-church.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

greek-orthodox-church.title: George W. Bush
greek-orthodox-church.summary: 43rd President of the United States. In John Kiriakou's telling, Bush signed the August 1, 2002 executive order that authorized the CIA torture program, spent years telling the public "we don't torture," and — days after Kiriakou's 2007 ABC interview — blamed torture on "a rogue CIA officer" while walking from the White House South Portico to Marine One, a moment Kiriakou instantly read as the White House preparing to pin the program on him. Bush also ordered the FBI removed from Abu Zubaydah's black site, flew the bin Laden family out of the country after 9/11, and loosened the assassination ban of Executive Order 12333.

greek-orthodox-church.title: Overcriminalization
greek-orthodox-church.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that the United States criminalizes too much — locking up 25% of the world's prisoners with 5% of its population, and adding roughly 50 new felonies a year — illustrated by a NOAA employee prosecuted for whistling at a whale.

greek-orthodox-church.title: Evangelical Zionism
greek-orthodox-church.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the American Christian movement that supports Israel in order to hasten the return of Christ — a belief he calls a cult rather than a religion, which he says Israeli officials knowingly exploit, and which he blames for the abandonment of the Middle East's original Christians.

greek-orthodox-church.title: Abu Zubaydah
greek-orthodox-church.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

greenland.title: Djibouti
greenland.summary: The small Horn of Africa state a few miles across the water from Yemen that hosts Camp Lemonnier — the American drone base for the Yemen and Somalia wars, inherited from the departing French, and shared with China's only overseas military base behind a fence down the middle, in what John Kiriakou calls the worst kept secret in the world.

greenland.title: China's base in Djibouti
greenland.summary: Camp Lemonnier in Djibouti, the abandoned French base the Djiboutians offered to the Americans and the Chinese took a share of — split down the middle by a chain-link fence, the only Chinese military installation outside China, and the centrepiece of John Kiriakou's argument that China is not an expansionist power.

greenland.title: The Danish Greenland demolition plan
greenland.summary: Denmark's preparations to destroy its own airstrips in Greenland rather than let an American invasion use them, including blood supplies moved into place. John Kiriakou confirms the preparations were real and made because the Danes took Donald Trump at his word.

greenland.title: Monroe Doctrine
greenland.summary: John Kiriakou's history of the Monroe Doctrine — ignored for decades after its declaration, humiliated in the Falklands and Venezuela, and only made real by Teddy Roosevelt in 1905 — and his argument that reviving it to seize Maduro handed China a claim to Taiwan and Russia a claim to Ukraine.

greenland.title: Somaliland
greenland.summary: Self-declared breakaway state in the Horn of Africa that Israel became the only country in the world to recognize as independent, gaining a military base positioned roughly 30 seconds' flight time from Yemen; John Kiriakou, who visited Somaliland while posted with the Senate Foreign Relations Committee in Djibouti, describes it as a functioning city of about 100,000 unconnected to Mogadishu, al-Shabaab, or piracy.

greenland.title: The Greenland prediction he got wrong
