hezbollah.summary: Per John Kiriakou's assessment, the US–Israeli military campaign against Iran was a war of choice driven by Israeli political pressure rather than genuine intelligence indicating an Iranian nuclear weapons threat. The CIA produced two National Intelligence Estimates concluding Iran had no nuclear weapons program; Supreme Leader Ayatollah Khamenei issued a fatwa in the 1980s forbidding such a program. The U.S. went to war anyway, in Kiriakou's view, after President Trump replaced the Joint Chiefs of Staff with officers willing to accept Israeli intelligence and proceed.

hezbollah.title: MOSSAD
hezbollah.summary: Israel's primary external intelligence service; characterized by John Kiriakou as universally hostile in his and his CIA colleagues' professional dealings with it ("never had a positive encounter with Mossad"); operates almost exclusively in the operational rather than analytical domain; the CIA is, per Kiriakou, categorically forbidden from spying on it.

hezbollah.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
hezbollah.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

hezbollah.title: Hassan Nasrallah
hezbollah.summary: Long-serving Secretary-General of Hezbollah, killed in an Israeli strike on a complex in southern Lebanon; the strike, which killed approximately 300 people in addition to Nasrallah, decapitated Hezbollah's leadership and is characterized by John Kiriakou as a war crime under international law.

hezbollah.title: Khobar Towers bombing
hezbollah.summary: June 25, 1996 truck bombing of a U.S. military housing complex in Khobar, Saudi Arabia, that killed 19 U.S. Air Force personnel. John Kiriakou, then a CIA officer living across the water in Bahrain, felt the blast shatter his own windows and drove to the scene the next morning. He says the U.S. government worked hard to blame Iran and a small Saudi Hezbollah cell with no evidence, when the attack was in fact carried out by a radical Saudi group — a predecessor of al-Qaeda, which took credit for it.

hezbollah.title: "The American war against Iran"
hezbollah.summary: A correction Benjamin Netanyahu issued to an Israeli reporter during the 2026 war — that it was the American war against Iran, and that Israel was merely America's ally. John Kiriakou treats it as the moment Israel walked away from a war it had spent years demanding, leaving the United States to fight it alone.

hillary-clinton.title: Reza Pahlavi
hillary-clinton.summary: The exiled Iranian crown prince whom John Kiriakou dismisses as an Israeli-backed fantasy candidate to rule Iran — a man who has not lived there since his teens, supported mainly by Beverly Hills exiles, whom Kiriakou says 'wouldn't survive the walk from the plane to the terminal.'

hillary-clinton.title: Angela Merkel
hillary-clinton.summary: German chancellor whose mobile phone the NSA was intercepting, in what John Kiriakou treats as the cleanest illustration of the two-tier American attitude to surveillance: the interception of one of Washington''s closest allies was big news, Hillary Clinton flew to Germany to apologise, and — per Kiriakou — the United States then did it again. Asked about it in Berlin, his answer was that intercepting her phone is exactly what he wants the CIA to be doing.

hillary-clinton.title: Mujahedin-e Khalq (MEK)
hillary-clinton.summary: Iranian opposition group that John Kiriakou describes as 'a quasi-communist cult' and a former U.S.-designated terrorist organization. Founded by a husband-and-wife team in the 1960s and based in northeastern Iraq, the MEK launched cross-border terrorist attacks into Iran and, per Kiriakou, attempted to murder the American ambassador and the senior U.S. general in Iran — carrying out anti-American attacks for decades. After Saddam Hussein expelled them they relocated to Paris; current leader Maryam Rajavi is widely believed to have killed or had killed her vanished husband to take over. In 2009 the MEK hired high-powered Washington lobbyists (from Howard Dean to Rudy Giuliani) to get off the terrorism list, and Kiriakou says it is now funded by Israel and used as assassins-for-hire in Tehran.

hillary-clinton.title: Somaliland
hillary-clinton.summary: Self-declared breakaway state in the Horn of Africa that Israel became the only country in the world to recognize as independent, gaining a military base positioned roughly 30 seconds' flight time from Yemen; John Kiriakou, who visited Somaliland while posted with the Senate Foreign Relations Committee in Djibouti, describes it as a functioning city of about 100,000 unconnected to Mogadishu, al-Shabaab, or piracy.

hillary-clinton.title: SPLC 2025 indictment
hillary-clinton.summary: Federal criminal case unveiled by FBI director Kash Patel and Deputy Attorney General Todd Blanche against the Southern Poverty Law Center on multiple felony counts, described by John Kiriakou as concerning alleged payments to the Ku Klux Klan and Nazi groups and alleged money laundering; Kiriakou judges the charges are of the documentary kind that either happened or did not and that they could bring an end to an organisation whose 2024 balance sheet showed assets of roughly $786 to $822 million.

hillary-clinton.title: Crypto AG
hillary-clinton.summary: The Swiss encryption-machine company revealed in February 2020 to have been secretly owned by the CIA and West German intelligence, which sold riggable ciphers to governments around the world for decades. John Kiriakou, who held senior positions at the agency, says he knew nothing about it — it was held that closely — and refuses to describe it as a scandal: nobody will be prosecuted, several people will probably win medals, and an intelligence operation is not supposed to be honest or fair.

hillary-in-a-kamala-suit.title: One hundred and twenty-three investigations
hillary-in-a-kamala-suit.summary: The figure John Kiriakou attributes to Attorney General Jeff Sessions and what he calls his big mouth: 123 active national security leak investigations under way, which Kiriakou uses to argue the Trump administration was worse for whistleblowers than Obama''s.

hillary-in-a-kamala-suit.title: The Chilean newspaper prediction
hillary-in-a-kamala-suit.summary: The forecast John Kiriakou says he got wrong: asked by a Chilean newspaper the week Donald Trump was elected whether things would improve for national security whistleblowers, he said he was cautiously optimistic, on the ground that they could not get worse than under Obama.

hillary-in-a-kamala-suit.title: Barack Obama
hillary-in-a-kamala-suit.summary: 44th U.S. president; in John Kiriakou's account, Obama publicly recounted refusing Benjamin Netanyahu's demand to bomb Iran and calling Israel's threat to use nuclear weapons a bluff — a bluff Kiriakou says Donald Trump later believed.

hillary-in-a-kamala-suit.title: The 2023 classified documents scandal
hillary-in-a-kamala-suit.summary: The run of discoveries of classified material in the private possession of Donald Trump, Joe Biden and Mike Pence, which John Kiriakou treats not as a scandal about any of them but as proof that the Espionage Act as currently applied makes almost everyone technically guilty. He rates Pence's briefing books as more highly classified than anything Julian Assange published, and says Biden's Senate-era documents are the ones that cannot be explained away.

hillary-in-a-kamala-suit.title: Anwar al-Awlaki
hillary-in-a-kamala-suit.summary: American-born al-Qaeda propagandist; in 1993 the imam of the Falls Church, Virginia mosque visited by John Kiriakou's CIA Arabic-language class on a field trip; in 2001 the cleric at whose mosque the 9/11 hijackers prayed the night before the attacks; killed by U.S. drone strike in Yemen in approximately 2011.

hire-a-lawyer-first.title: The detractors who died
hire-a-lawyer-first.summary: John Kiriakou's observation that the senior CIA officials who wanted him dead or wanted him to die in prison have themselves since died, while a new generation of officers reaches out to tell him he did the right thing.

hire-a-lawyer-first.title: The CIA divorce rate
hire-a-lawyer-first.summary: John Kiriakou's account of why marriages fail at the CIA at a rate he says exceeds that of any other part of the U.S. government — the impossibility of explaining a midnight departure to a spouse without a clearance, and the difficulty officers have switching off a professional habit of deception. He gives the figure variously as over 75 percent and upwards of 80 percent, says he was determined not to become a statistic and became one anyway, and dates the end of his first marriage to a sentence spoken in an armoured car on the way to Athens airport. Both his divorces have been costly; of the second he says the agency played an active role he is barred by court order from explaining.

hire-a-lawyer-first.title: Espionage Act
hire-a-lawyer-first.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

hire-a-lawyer-first.title: Get better enough to go back
hire-a-lawyer-first.summary: John Kiriakou's warning that the CIA does not care whether an officer has a mental breakdown, and cares about recovery only far enough to send them overseas again — advice he says means the officer has to look after themselves.

hire-a-lawyer-first.title: Never meet my grandchildren
hire-a-lawyer-first.summary: The threat John Kiriakou says one of the prosecutors in his case made to him — that he was going to die in prison and would never meet his grandchildren — set against the forty-five years he faced under the original charges.

hire-a-lawyer-first.title: Sixteen people knew
hire-a-lawyer-first.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer to why deeply held secrets do not leak: at the outset only sixteen people in the entire federal government knew about the CIA torture programme, which is why it stayed hidden for years.

home-confinement.title: Mark McDougall
home-confinement.summary: U.S. criminal defense attorney; chairman of the white-collar defense practice at Akin Gump Strauss and a law professor at Georgetown, who joined John Kiriakou's defense team pro bono in the 2012–2013 prosecution. Two separate Washington lawyers independently warned Kiriakou on the same day that McDougall was "the meanest man in Washington"; Kiriakou says he was never anything but kind to him, liked him best of the eleven attorneys on the case, and credits the line that persuaded him to take the final plea — "you think this is about justice, and it's not about justice; it's about mitigating damage."

home-confinement.title: The halfway house
home-confinement.summary: The re-entry stage of a federal sentence — up to twelve months of it by law, in practice a fortnight before conversion to house arrest — which John Kiriakou was denied entirely for writing about prison conditions from inside, and which he describes as a system designed to make released prisoners fail.

home-confinement.title: The Italians at Loretto
home-confinement.summary: The mafia contingent at FCI Loretto — men with last names like Gambino, Bonanno, Lucchese, Genovese, DeCavalcante — who adopted John Kiriakou in his second year, largely because he hated the FBI as much as they did. The cast included the boss of the Gambino family (in on a dozen-plus murder counts, the man who replaced John Gotti), Pete the Bonanno captain across the hall who asked why he sat "with those Nazi retards," and a crooked guard on the payroll delivering pork loin and fresh mozzarella. When the FBI later came to Kiriakou's door asking him to inform on Pete, his answer was "get off my property."

home-confinement.title: Bureau of Prisons
home-confinement.summary: The federal agency that ran John Kiriakou's incarceration — and one of his most persistent post-prison targets. The BOP overrode his judge's camp recommendation by deeming him "a threat to the public safety," threatened him with "diesel therapy" until 1,600 logged phone calls and letters from a dozen House members and two senators backed it off, and, per Kiriakou, functions as "an employment agency for unemployable semi-literate rural white men" and "a dumping ground for failed medical professionals" — an agency for which a prisoner's death is cheaper than his treatment.

home-confinement.title: Daniel Hale
home-confinement.summary: Per John Kiriakou, drone whistleblower Daniel Hale — an NSA contractor and drone targeting analyst who exposed an 80% civilian death rate in the U.S. drone program, was ordered to fire on two young girls his superior called "goats," and was sentenced to 45 months (of which Kiriakou says he actually served about 18) despite prosecutors seeking nine to eleven years.

home-confinement.title: Kiriakou's transfer to the Directorate of Operations
home-confinement.summary: John Kiriakou's roughly two-month internal campaign to transfer from the CIA's analytic Directorate of Intelligence to the operational Directorate of Operations, overcoming what he calls a "natural bias in operations against the eggheads on the analytic side," followed by an Athens posting secured because he was the only person in the entire CIA fluent in both Greek and Arabic. Covers his full CIA career arc from 1988/1990 recruitment through analyst years on Iraq, the switch to operations, 9/11, the enhanced-interrogation refusal, executive assistant to the deputy director for operations, and his eventual resignation and post-CIA career.

hope-is-not-a-strategy.title: A virtual state of war with Venezuela
hope-is-not-a-strategy.summary: John Kiriakou said in February 2025 that he was mystified by the choice of Marco Rubio as Secretary of State, describing him as a neoconservative in the mould of George W. Bush, and predicted that on Venezuela the second Trump administration would simply continue the Biden policy — which had itself continued the first Trump policy — leaving the two countries in what he called a virtual state of war.

hope-is-not-a-strategy.title: Donald Trump
hope-is-not-a-strategy.summary: 45th and 47th U.S. president. Per John Kiriakou, a man genuinely convinced he was doing right by bombing Iran, "duped" by the same Netanyahu nuclear bluff Obama once rejected — and, at the same time, the most blindly pro-Israel president in history, an admirer of autocrats who has never once criticized Vladimir Putin, and prone to gestures — from the Gulf of America to a since-abandoned "Department of War" rename — that test the edges of his actual authority.

hope-is-not-a-strategy.title: Marco Rubio
hope-is-not-a-strategy.summary: U.S. official whom John Kiriakou identifies as the real motivator behind pressure on Venezuela; Kiriakou argues Venezuela is not a meaningful drug threat to the U.S. and that Rubio simply wants Maduro gone.

hope-is-not-a-strategy.title: The Putin call and the China exception
hope-is-not-a-strategy.summary: In February 2025 John Kiriakou said he was optimistic that relations with Russia would improve, on the strength of a telephone call being arranged between Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin — but drew a sharp exception for China, arguing that nobody in the American government was sincere about improving those relations and that Washington, not Beijing, was instigating talk of war.

hope-is-not-a-strategy.title: 2028 presidential field
hope-is-not-a-strategy.summary: John Kiriakou's assessment of the wide-open 2028 presidential race — the first in his life, he says, where he has no idea who either party will nominate. Predictive markets were listing 44 Democrats and 26 Republicans as possible candidates. His own preferred candidate is Tucker Carlson, whom he says he has repeatedly begged to run; his working assumption about anyone who does want the job is that they are "a narcissist and probably a sociopath on top of it."

hope-is-not-a-strategy.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
hope-is-not-a-strategy.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

hostages-and-prisoners.title: The burden of peace
hostages-and-prisoners.summary: John Kiriakou's rule for asymmetric wars — that in any lopsided military conflict most of the burden of making peace falls on the superior military force, which will have to make most of the concessions — together with his rejection of unconditional surrender as a war aim.

hostages-and-prisoners.title: Famine in Gaza
hostages-and-prisoners.summary: The starvation of the civilian population of the Gaza Strip, which John Kiriakou describes as a United Nations-declared famine caused not by an absence of food but by an Israeli refusal to let food reach the people who need it; Kiriakou characterises it as a war crime, a crime against humanity and a form of genocide, attributing that characterisation to the United Nations and the International Court of Justice rather than to himself.

hostages-and-prisoners.title: France recognises Palestine
hostages-and-prisoners.summary: Emmanuel Macron's decision in July 2025 to extend formal recognition to the Republic of Palestine and exchange ambassadors, which John Kiriakou called a turning point that could not be overstated — the first serious crack in Western support for Israel, and significant precisely because France is a historic colonial power in the Middle East with a Security Council veto.

hostages-and-prisoners.title: The Egyptian berm
hostages-and-prisoners.summary: The earthwork Egypt built along its Gaza frontier more than a year before July 2025, which John Kiriakou describes as a defence not against Palestinians but against Israel — built because Cairo feared the border being thrown open from the other side, and because Egyptian troops would not fire on two million people.

hostages-and-prisoners.title: No band-aids since the early nineties
hostages-and-prisoners.summary: What doctors told John Kiriakou when he visited an Afghan hospital in 2000, during the first Taliban government — that they had not seen a band-aid since the early 1990s — and his conclusion that the humanitarian carve-outs in the Clinton-era sanctions did not exist in practice.

hostages-and-prisoners.title: Proposals to relocate the Palestinians
hostages-and-prisoners.summary: John Kiriakou's account of recurring schemes to solve the Palestinian question by moving the population somewhere else — including a 1980s proposal to rename a barren diamond of land on the Saudi–Iraqi border "Palestine" and resettle everyone there — and his verdict that picking up an entire people and moving them is unprecedented and untenable.

hostile-border-crossing.title: The shooting house
hostile-border-crossing.summary: The live-fire decision course at the Farm where a trainee has about three quarters of a second to decide whether the figure at the window is a gunman or a woman holding a baby — and where John Kiriakou says he never missed, which he connects to his own account of the temperament the CIA selects for.

hostile-border-crossing.title: Planning a surveillance detection route
hostile-border-crossing.summary: The hours of paperwork behind every CIA meeting before satellite mapping existed — photocopied road-atlas pages taped into sheets six feet across, legs and stops marked in coloured highlighter, submitted to instructors for approval and then driven in advance to check for no-left-turns and closed roads. John Kiriakou ran routes to and from work every day in Athens against 17 November, taught surveillance detection as an agency instructor, spent four or five hours of a night on the route around a single emergency meeting, and wrote the CIA Insider's Guide to the subject — from which the agency redacted six pages.

hostile-border-crossing.title: The Farm
hostile-border-crossing.summary: The CIA's clandestine training facility in Virginia; site of approximately 80% of all CIA operational training

hostile-border-crossing.title: Counterterrorist driving
hostile-border-crossing.summary: The vehicle training at the Farm — the PIT manoeuvre and how to avoid one, when to ram a roadblock and where to hit it, reversing at sixty miles an hour — conducted in a fleet of junkyard beaters the CIA bought expressly to be wrecked.

hostile-border-crossing.title: Kiriakou's skeet shooting
hostile-border-crossing.summary: The competitive shooting hobby that began when an octogenarian instructor at the Farm watched John Kiriakou — who had never fired a shotgun — hit steel plates at seven, twelve and twenty-five metres with a Remington pump action, and took him aside afterwards.

hostile-border-crossing.title: The operations course graduation
hostile-border-crossing.summary: The end of CIA field training: a graduation ceremony at which the whole class wore full disguises for the photograph, and a certificate that is itself classified and therefore cannot be displayed — it stays in the officer''s personnel file.

hot-bunking.title: The USS Gerald Ford plumbing failure
hot-bunking.summary: Days before the 2026 war, John Kiriakou raised the possibility that a sewage failure severe enough to send the carrier USS Gerald R. Ford back to Norfolk was sabotage by a crew that did not want to go to war with Iran.

hot-bunking.title: Frank Snepp
hot-bunking.summary: The CIA analyst who wrote Decent Interval, and whom John Kiriakou calls a giant — one of the great analysts of his generation, practically the first to say publicly that the United States was losing in Vietnam and committing atrocities there, who paid for it with his career and spent most of the rest of his life fighting the agency's publications review board.

hot-bunking.title: Kyriakos Mitsotakis
hot-bunking.summary: The Greek prime minister John Kiriakou names when asked which world leader he would put in Donald Trump's place — a choice he qualifies by admitting he did not vote for the man the first time and has since been pleasantly surprised.

hot-bunking.title: Sports and the Steelers bar
hot-bunking.summary: Asked whether he enjoys any sport, John Kiriakou named baseball and football, and described walking to a Steelers bar in Clarendon, Arlington, to watch a game he could have watched at home — for the five hundred screaming Pittsburgh fans.

hot-bunking.title: Trump's Supreme Court appointees
hot-bunking.summary: An assessment John Kiriakou volunteered in February 2026 and that runs against his politics elsewhere: that Donald Trump''s appointees to the Supreme Court have been surprisingly good, and that the justices he regards as disasters — Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas — were put there by moderate presidents.

hot-bunking.title: The Vietnam speech
hot-bunking.summary: A paid speaking engagement John Kiriakou described in February 2026 — booked by a New York speakers bureau for the morning of 10 August, addressing three hundred Australian investment bankers at their annual convention in a country he had never visited and had always wanted to.

houthis.title: Bab al-Mandab
houthis.summary: The strait where the Horn of Africa nearly meets the south-western tip of the Arabian Peninsula, which John Kiriakou identifies as one of the few American national interests in Yemen and as a chokepoint whose closure would push the global economy into recession.

houthis.title: Ali Abdullah Saleh
houthis.summary: President of Yemen for decades, close to both Saudi Arabia and the United States until Yemen's 1990 Security Council vote on Kuwait, after which his country collapsed into civil war; he fled to Saudi Arabia and was killed by a bomb planted in the palace where he had taken refuge.

houthis.title: Iran regional war (2026)
houthis.summary: The widening of the 2026 Iran conflict from a war between Iran on one side and the United States and Israel on the other into a regional war — Iranian missiles striking a US base in Jordan, Iranian strikes across the Gulf states, Houthi attacks on Saudi shipping and oil, and Saudi forces striking pro-Iranian militias in Iraq. John Kiriakou notes he had forecast the expansion a week earlier.

houthis.title: Mecca Agreement
houthis.summary: A trilateral mutual-defence pact between Pakistan, Turkey and Saudi Arabia signed in Mecca in August 2026. John Kiriakou treats it as the most consequential development in the region and one the American media largely ignored, because it makes three separate bilateral enmities collectively enforceable and leaves the United States out of the arrangement entirely.

houthis.title: Yemen
houthis.summary: Country on the southern Arabian Peninsula; setting of five John Kiriakou trips between 1990 and approximately 2010, spanning the country's brief unification, its civil war, and its present condition as a high-threat operating environment for U.S. and allied diplomatic personnel.

houthis.title: Somaliland and Israeli recognition
houthis.summary: Israel''s diplomatic recognition of Somaliland, which John Kiriakou describes as a trade: recognition no other state offers, in exchange for an air base within reach of Yemen. He calls it the one smart move in Israel''s response to the Mecca Agreement.

how-can-i-keep-from-singing.title: Pete Seeger
how-can-i-keep-from-singing.summary: American folk singer; John Kiriakou's personal hero alongside his father and grandfather; pleaded the First Amendment (rather than the Fifth) before the House Un-American Activities Committee in 1958 and was sent to prison for it (later overturned on appeal); befriended by Kiriakou over decades of concert-going and correspondence; rallied to Kiriakou's defense after Kiriakou's 2012 arrest; the subject of Kiriakou's favorite book, How Can I Keep From Singing?

how-can-i-keep-from-singing.title: Aldrich Ames
how-can-i-keep-from-singing.summary: Senior CIA officer — a GS-15 who rose to chief of counterintelligence for the Soviet branch — who spied for the KGB for nine years. Per John Kiriakou, Ames walked into the Soviet embassy in Washington in April 1985 and sold the identities of two CIA-recruited double agents for $50,000 to clear a debt run up by his second marriage; both were executed. He went on to identify more than thirty agents, compromise over a hundred clandestine operations, cause at least twelve deaths and take more than $2 million, while being known throughout the agency as a daily drunk and promoted at every turn. The KGB protected him with a decoy mole hunt; analyst Sandy Grimes caught him by matching his handler meetings to his bank deposits.

how-can-i-keep-from-singing.title: Beirut
how-can-i-keep-from-singing.summary: The Lebanese capital John Kiriakou confirms was a genuine espionage playground — though he dates the peak to the 1950s through the mid-1970s, when Beirut was the Paris and the banking centre of the Middle East, and when, beneath the CIA, KGB and Israeli presence, "more secretly the French ran the place." He also explains why the enormous new American embassy there is about fortification rather than a regional CIA headquarters.

how-can-i-keep-from-singing.title: Central Intelligence Agency
how-can-i-keep-from-singing.summary: U.S. foreign intelligence service; John Kiriakou's employer from 1990 to 2004 and the central institution of KiriPedia

how-can-i-keep-from-singing.title: John Kiriakou
how-can-i-keep-from-singing.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

how-can-i-keep-from-singing.title: Psychiatric evacuation
how-can-i-keep-from-singing.summary: The CIA's practice of pulling an officer out of a posting and flying him home when he breaks down — known inside the agency as being psychovac'd — and the desk-bound evaluation period that follows before he is allowed to travel again.

how-chinese-intelligence-recruits.title: The Chinese professor on LinkedIn
how-chinese-intelligence-recruits.summary: The year-long approach John Kiriakou says he received through LinkedIn from a professor at a Chinese university he had never heard of — an invitation to speak that became five arranged stops across eastern China without his agreement, and which ended when he wrote back that he does not work for the Chinese intelligence service and was immediately blocked.

how-chinese-intelligence-recruits.title: Craig Murray
how-chinese-intelligence-recruits.summary: Former British Ambassador to Uzbekistan whom John Kiriakou cites as a whistleblower of extreme torture: during a meeting at the Uzbek intelligence service, Murray heard screaming, walked in, and saw a man being boiled in oil — reporting it cost him his career.

how-chinese-intelligence-recruits.title: Dumping cash in a Moscow bathroom
how-chinese-intelligence-recruits.summary: John Kiriakou's examples of what covert action has actually meant in practice — American commandos blowing up the Trans-Siberian oil pipeline, Afghan guerrillas hired to cross the Amu Darya and attack a refinery inside the southern USSR, and cash dumped in a Moscow bathroom to undermine the rouble.

how-chinese-intelligence-recruits.title: MK-ULTRA in Canada
how-chinese-intelligence-recruits.summary: John Kiriakou''s confirmation that many MK-ULTRA experiments took place on Canadian soil, and his explanation of why: the CIA asked the Canadian intelligence service for help with its anti-Soviet, anti-Chinese remote-viewing and LSD work, and the Canadians gladly gave it.

how-chinese-intelligence-recruits.title: The voice vote on the Epstein files
how-chinese-intelligence-recruits.summary: John Kiriakou's account of how the Senate passed the Epstein files release without a roll call — a voice vote he says Chuck Schumer requested to save the majority leader, leaving no written record of how anyone voted and allowing every senator but one House holdout to claim they had stood up to the pedophiles.

how-chinese-intelligence-recruits.title: The Solomon Islands trip
how-chinese-intelligence-recruits.summary: The reporting trip John Kiriakou announced for July 2026 — ten days on Guadalcanal with Jeremy Kuzmarov of CovertAction Magazine, travelling via Fiji, to cover the dispute between the United States and China over access to Japan's Second World War military bases.

how-the-cia-kills.title: SEALs on loan to the CIA
how-the-cia-kills.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer to why the CIA did not use its own paramilitary team against Osama bin Laden: it did. The raid was a CIA operation directed by the Counterterrorism Center, and every Navy SEAL involved was temporarily a CIA contractor, on loan to the agency for the duration.

how-the-cia-kills.title: Nine recruitments in twenty-five years
how-the-cia-kills.summary: The conversation in which John Kiriakou''s Athens station chief, a twenty-five-year operations officer who had reached senior intelligence service level four with nine recruitments to his name, pointed out that Kiriakou had recruited five in two years — and Kiriakou''s explanation of the knack: that he could hide his disdain for a man completely while talking about whatever interested him.

how-the-cia-kills.title: The strongly worded protest
how-the-cia-kills.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of what actually happens when one state violates another''s airspace: not an act of war but a démarche. He notes that the Russians do it to the United States over Alaska all the time, that the Americans do it back with some frequency, that the Norwegians, Swedes and Turks do it too — and that the response is to send an ambassador in to lodge a formal protest.

how-the-cia-kills.title: The twenty-two-month clearance
how-the-cia-kills.summary: John Kiriakou''s figures for getting his first book through CIA prepublication review: nine months to write it, twenty-two months to clear it, and 120 pages rejected. He says everything he writes still goes to the agency for clearance, but that the process has become much easier as his detractors there have died or retired.

how-the-cia-kills.title: The divorce at the airport
how-the-cia-kills.summary: The end of John Kiriakou''s first marriage, as he tells it: after 17 November assassinated his next-door neighbour and left a manifesto saying they had set out that morning to kill him instead, the embassy put him in an armoured car, collected his children and his wife, and packed out the house. His wife reached the airport, walked up to him and said she wanted a divorce. They flew home on the same plane.

how-the-cia-kills.title: The Nordstream patsy
how-the-cia-kills.summary: John Kiriakou''s assessment of the man arrested in Italy over the Nordstream pipeline sabotage: a patsy. He says he cannot imagine otherwise, feels for whoever the man is, and thinks the authorities found somebody they could take a dump on — while maintaining that the operation itself required not just real expertise but state expertise and capability.

hr-mcmaster.title: Declassifying for a foreign government
hr-mcmaster.summary: The CIA procedure John Kiriakou describes for passing classified intelligence to a foreign service — the originating office extracts the substance onto a fresh sheet marked releasable to that country, so that no source or method travels with it — set out in 2017 as the thing Donald Trump did not do when he spoke to the Russian foreign minister and ambassador in the Oval Office.

hr-mcmaster.title: Donald Trump
hr-mcmaster.summary: 45th and 47th U.S. president. Per John Kiriakou, a man genuinely convinced he was doing right by bombing Iran, "duped" by the same Netanyahu nuclear bluff Obama once rejected — and, at the same time, the most blindly pro-Israel president in history, an admirer of autocrats who has never once criticized Vladimir Putin, and prone to gestures — from the Gulf of America to a since-abandoned "Department of War" rename — that test the edges of his actual authority.

hr-mcmaster.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
hr-mcmaster.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

hr-mcmaster.title: David Petraeus
hr-mcmaster.summary: Retired U.S. Army general and director of the CIA who, per John Kiriakou, confirmed the names of ten covert CIA operatives to his biographer and girlfriend and was never criminally charged — a contrast Kiriakou cites repeatedly as proof that his own prosecution under the Intelligence Identities Protection Act was selective. Kiriakou''s explanation for the disparity: Petraeus had not blown the whistle on the torture program and embarrassed the agency.

hr-mcmaster.title: Intelligence Identities Protection Act
hr-mcmaster.summary: U.S. law enacted in 1982 that makes it a crime to knowingly disclose the identity of a covert intelligence officer; per John Kiriakou, his 2012 prosecution under the act arose from confirming a single surname of a former CIA colleague to a journalist — a confirmation that was never published. The name passed through a chain from journalist to Human Rights Watch to Guantanamo defense attorneys before reaching a judge and ultimately the FBI, which traced it back to Kiriakou.

hr-mcmaster.title: James Risen
hr-mcmaster.summary: The New York Times reporter whose refusal to testify in the Jeffrey Sterling prosecution — through the Fourth Circuit, the Supreme Court and a Justice Department climbdown — John Kiriakou treats as the precedent that a later administration would want to overturn by making an example of a journalist.

hugh-francis-redmond.title: Fake CIA résumés
hugh-francis-redmond.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of being used as a human authenticator in the private sector: at the consulting firm he joined after leaving the CIA, every job applicant claiming agency service was sent to dinner with him, and by his count fully half of them had never set foot inside the CIA.

hugh-francis-redmond.title: The Fox News military analyst
hugh-francis-redmond.summary: The cable-news commentator John Kiriakou says he identified as a fraud within a single green-room conversation, because the man used movie vocabulary — black ops, wet work — where a real officer would have named a directorate. The man had obtained a Defense Department clearance on the strength of his claimed CIA service, advised generals in Afghanistan, and was later arrested and imprisoned for fraud.

hugh-francis-redmond.title: CIA attention to West Africa
hugh-francis-redmond.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer on whether the CIA is likely to be operating in Burkina Faso: for all the years he was at the agency it cared very little about Africa and especially West Africa, but the presence of al-Qaeda and Islamic State affiliates plus the drug trade makes CIA and special forces involvement probable — and, he adds, the American public will not hear about it.

hugh-francis-redmond.title: CIA–FBI incompatible computer systems
hugh-francis-redmond.summary: John Kiriakou's claim that from the CIA's founding in 1947 until 2009 the computer systems of the CIA and the FBI were not compatible with one another — no message could be sent from one to the other and no intelligence shared — which he offers both as the material substrate of the interagency hatred that helped make September 11 possible, and as the gap through which James Mitchell and Bruce Jessen were able to pass Ali Soufan's FBI debriefings of Abu Zubaydah off as the fruits of torture.

hugh-francis-redmond.title: Forcing Iran toward a bomb
hugh-francis-redmond.summary: John Kiriakou''s argument that Western pressure risks producing the very outcome it claims to prevent: repeated Israeli assassinations of Iranian scientists and generals and strikes on Iranian sites may eventually leave Ayatollah Khamenei with no choice but to permit a defensive weapon — despite the religious prohibition Kiriakou credits him with maintaining, and despite successive American estimates that Iran is not seeking one.

hugh-francis-redmond.title: Freemasons and Opus Dei at the CIA
hugh-francis-redmond.summary: John Kiriakou's characterisation of the affinity networks at the top of the CIA — a great many senior officers who are Freemasons, and periods in which most of the leadership belonged to Opus Dei and attended the same church in Great Falls, Virginia. He rejects the idea that these are plots, describing them instead as accidental clusters of men who look out for one another.

human-rights-watch.title: Amnesty International
human-rights-watch.summary: The human rights organization whose torture report forms part of John Kiriakou's core defense — the CIA's crimes were already public knowledge before he confirmed them on ABC, and the Justice Department's own declination letter said so — and the organization whose silence during his prosecution he cannot forgive. He begged Amnesty for a one-sentence statement and got a New Yorker subscription instead; it took Ai Weiwei to change their minds, and by then he was walking out of prison.

human-rights-watch.title: Reality Winner
human-rights-watch.summary: National Security Agency linguist imprisoned for sending a single classified page on Russian interference in the 2016 election to The Intercept. John Kiriakou attributes her arrest to the two reporters who received it, and to a printer-tracking countermeasure they appear not to have known about; he also treats her prosecution as an operation that served the intelligence community on three fronts at once.

human-rights-watch.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
human-rights-watch.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

human-rights-watch.title: Senate Intelligence Committee
human-rights-watch.summary: The Senate Select Committee on Intelligence — the CIA's designated overseer, which John Kiriakou credits with the torture report's unimpeachable method (6 million contemporaneous CIA field cables) and simultaneously dismisses, along with its House counterpart, as "little more than cheerleaders for the CIA" since the mid-1980s. It sits in the official whistleblower channel he calls a proven dead end, and its own investigation was famously spied on by the very agency it oversees.

human-rights-watch.title: Deuce Martinez
human-rights-watch.summary: The former CIA analyst whose business card was the basis of two of the three Espionage Act charges brought against John Kiriakou. Kiriakou scanned and emailed the card — which showed Martinez had gone to work for Mitchell and Jessen, the firm of the torture programme's architects — to a New York Times reporter and later to an ABC News reporter. The judge threw the espionage counts out.

hummus.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
hummus.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

hummus.title: Senate Torture Report
hummus.summary: The December 2014 executive summary of the U.S. Senate Select Committee on Intelligence's study of the CIA's post-9/11 detention and interrogation program; the first public disclosure of techniques including rectal feeding with hummus, sexual assault with broomsticks, and prolonged sleep deprivation.

hummus.title: Guantanamo Bay
hummus.summary: U.S. naval base in Cuba; site of CIA detention operations during the post-9/11 enhanced interrogation program; briefly served by John Kiriakou as interim Chief during the summer of 2002.

hummus.title: Strawberry Fields
hummus.summary: The CIA's nickname for a secret black-site annex at the Guantanamo Bay Naval Base used for the post-9/11 detention and interrogation program.

hummus.title: Jeff Fahey
hummus.summary: American actor; star of the Tyrell Vanto film in which John Kiriakou made his acting debut in late 2025; characterized by Kiriakou as generous with his time and on-set advice.

hummus.title: Tyrell Vanto
hummus.summary: Hollywood screenwriter and director; son of Jesse Vanto; friend of John Kiriakou; wrote and directed the late-2025 film in which Kiriakou made his acting debut.

hunter-biden-laptop.title: National Security vs Civil Liberties
hunter-biden-laptop.summary: Kiriakou's recurring argument that invoking "national security" is used to excuse the erosion of civil liberties and that the secrecy regime cannot coexist with constitutional democracy.

hunter-biden-laptop.title: Kamala Harris
hunter-biden-laptop.summary: Vice President under Joe Biden and 2024 Democratic presidential nominee; per John Kiriakou, installed as the party's nominee without a competitive primary despite having failed to reach the 2020 Iowa caucus, and closed out her 2024 campaign courting the Cheney family as a symbol of American values. Kiriakou, a lifelong progressive, says her pursuit of Dick Cheney's endorsement is what decided him against voting for her.

hunter-biden-laptop.title: Abolish the CIA
hunter-biden-laptop.summary: John Kiriakou's position that the CIA should be abolished because its functions are already duplicated by the other 17 U.S. intelligence agencies — analysis by the State Department, human spying by the Pentagon, technology by DARPA, NSA and the private sector.

hunter-biden-laptop.title: Abu Omar rendition
hunter-biden-laptop.summary: The CIA's kidnapping of a Milan cleric, Abu Omar, who was sent to Egypt to be tortured; John Kiriakou calls it a case that ought to be taught at the CIA as how not to run a rendition, and it is what ultimately sent him to prison, after he confirmed a former colleague's surname to a journalist claiming to be writing a book about it.

hunter-biden-laptop.title: Afghanistan 2011 Kerry Trip
hunter-biden-laptop.summary: John Kiriakou's 2011 trip to Afghanistan as senior investigator for the Senate Foreign Relations Committee under Chairman John Kerry, where the pair sat through a briefing with 11 one-to-four-star generals presenting an optimistic account of the war — after which Kerry mused the U.S. might win, only for Kiriakou to tell him the U.S. controlled only Kabul, and that the same rosy briefing had been given every year since 2002.

hunter-biden-laptop.title: CIA/FBI Budget Fearmongering
hunter-biden-laptop.summary: John Kiriakou's account of how the FBI, under J. Edgar Hoover, pioneered the tactic of citing a shifting parade of enemies before Congress to justify annual budget increases — communists, anarchists, gangsters, beatniks, anti-war protesters — a tactic the CIA later adopted wholesale, citing "communism" until 2001 and "terrorism" since, without needing further explanation to win budget increases.

hussein-kamel.title: Saddam Hussein
hussein-kamel.summary: President of Iraq from 1979 until the 2003 U.S. invasion; subject of John Kiriakou's CIA portfolio from January 1990 onward, in which capacity Kiriakou became, at age 25, "Saddam Hussein's intelligence community biographer" and the analyst who briefed President George H. W. Bush in the Oval Office on the morning of the 1990 invasion of Kuwait.

hussein-kamel.title: Uday Hussein
hussein-kamel.summary: Eldest son of Saddam Hussein; described by John Kiriakou as so dangerous a successor-in-waiting that Saddam's two sons-in-law — Hussein Kamel and Saddam Kamel — defected to Jordan in January 1993 specifically out of fear of him.

hussein-kamel.title: Ali Hassan al-Majid
hussein-kamel.summary: Saddam Hussein cousin known as "Chemical Ali" and "the Butcher of Kurdistan"; per John Kiriakou, also briefly served as the Iraqi-installed governor of occupied Kuwait — "the Butcher of Kuwait" — and was engaged in the wholesale slaughter of Kurds in the north, Shia in the south, and Kuwaitis under occupation.

hussein-kamel.title: April Glaspie
hussein-kamel.summary: U.S. Ambassador to Iraq in the run-up to the 1990 invasion of Kuwait; per John Kiriakou, delivered to Saddam Hussein — on a NODIS cable from Secretary of State James Baker — the line that the United States took no position on Arab-Arab border disputes, which Saddam is widely held to have read as a green light to invade. Kiriakou, who was in the CIA operations center the night her reporting cable came back, holds that she got a bum rap.

hussein-kamel.title: Iraq WMD intelligence
hussein-kamel.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of how the case for Iraqi weapons of mass destruction was fabricated: the intelligence community''s consensus was that Iraq had no WMD, but the White House had already decided to invade and sought analysis to fit the policy.

hussein-kamel.title: Norman Schwarzkopf
hussein-kamel.summary: U.S. Army general and commander of CENTCOM during the 1991 Gulf War; per John Kiriakou, the architect of the "visionary" flanking maneuver that bypassed Iraq's fortified Kuwait–Saudi border, struck from the north, and produced the Highway of Death.

hypersonic-missiles.title: The Bridgeton and the tanker escorts
hypersonic-missiles.summary: John Kiriakou's recollection of the 1980s American naval escort of oil tankers through the Strait of Hormuz, and of seeing the SS Bridgeton — then the largest oil tanker in the world, set ablaze by the Iranians — from a boat in the Persian Gulf.

hypersonic-missiles.title: "Iran posed no threat"
hypersonic-missiles.summary: John Kiriakou''s core objection to the 2026 war, stated as a chain of negatives: Iran had no nuclear weapon, no nuclear weapons programme, no wish for one, a religious ruling against one, and no delivery system if it had had one — findings he says were confirmed twice by the CIA and by the IAEA.

hypersonic-missiles.title: Killing Khamenei
hypersonic-missiles.summary: John Kiriakou's assessment that the killing of Ayatollah Khamenei during the 2026 war would change nothing, because the West had seriously overestimated his authority — an argument he extends to the American habit of expecting a war to end when a leader is removed.

hypersonic-missiles.title: THAAD stocks in the Gulf
hypersonic-missiles.summary: John Kiriakou's report, during the 2026 war, that the United Arab Emirates were seven days from exhausting their THAAD interceptors and Qatar four days — with American resupply unable to keep pace.

hypersonic-missiles.title: Chaos as the Israeli objective
hypersonic-missiles.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer to whether Netanyahu''s government actually wanted an American invasion of Iran: what the Israelis want in Iran is what they got in Libya — chaos, civil war, and as many dead Iranians as possible.

hypersonic-missiles.title: Marco Rubio and Iran policy
hypersonic-missiles.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer to who was actually driving American policy toward Iran in 2026: with the Vice President, the Director of National Intelligence and the Chairman of the Joint Chiefs all reported as opposed, and with Marco Rubio holding both the State Department and the National Security Adviser''s job, the policy was Rubio''s.

i-had-no-intent.title: The legal bills
i-had-no-intent.summary: The cost of John Kiriakou's defence, which he has given variously as more than half a million dollars, approaching a million, and more than a million — a figure he treats not as a hardship but as the mechanism of the prosecution itself, since bankruptcy is what makes a defendant accept a plea.

i-had-no-intent.title: The weight of the government
i-had-no-intent.summary: John Kiriakou's comparison, made on the eve of his imprisonment, between the danger of his overseas career — including two attempts on his life by different terrorist groups — and being prosecuted at home, which he says none of it prepared him for.

i-had-no-intent.title: Espionage Act
i-had-no-intent.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

i-had-no-intent.title: "The government is the biggest leaker"
i-had-no-intent.summary: John Kiriakou's answer, given on the eve of his imprisonment, to the argument that leaks make clandestine work impossible — that the United States government is itself the largest leaker of classified information in the country, sanctioning disclosure whenever it suits, as with the makers of Zero Dark Thirty and with drone-strike details given to the New York Times during an election campaign.

i-had-no-intent.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
i-had-no-intent.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

i-had-no-intent.title: The supporters who could not be public
i-had-no-intent.summary: The thanks John Kiriakou offered on the day of his sentencing — to dozens of former and serving CIA officers, FBI agents and assistant United States attorneys who rallied to him, almost all of them privately, with cards, emails and donations to his defence fund.

i-only-wanted-to-kill-jews.title: Fusha and the Gulf dialect
i-only-wanted-to-kill-jews.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of his own Arabic training — a first year in fusha, high standard Arabic, followed by a second year in khaleeji, the Gulf dialect — and what he reports of both: that Yemen is the only place pure fusha is spoken, that Saudis asked him why he spoke Arabic like Shakespeare, that the Gulf dialect is marked by a hard J other Arabs dislike, and that the Maghreb defeats him entirely.

i-only-wanted-to-kill-jews.title: The let-them-in strategy
i-only-wanted-to-kill-jews.summary: John Kiriakou has claimed one of the ideas he contributed as CIA counterterrorism chief in Pakistan was to stop trying to intercept al-Qaeda fighters one at a time on the Afghan border, and instead let them cross into Pakistan and take them ten at a time in their safe houses.

i-only-wanted-to-kill-jews.title: The two ISIs
i-only-wanted-to-kill-jews.summary: Asked how much cooperation he got from Pakistan''s intelligence service after 9/11, John Kiriakou answered that the honest answer was two answers: the counterterrorism officers he worked with had all been trained in America and Britain, while the men who gave him the stink eye in the corridors of ISI headquarters were the ones who had created the Taliban.

i-only-wanted-to-kill-jews.title: Whether anyone is still looking for Zawahiri
i-only-wanted-to-kill-jews.summary: Asked in December 2019 why Ayman al-Zawahiri had never been found, John Kiriakou offered a speculation he was careful to label as an outsider''s: that the United States might simply have stopped looking for him, because al-Qaeda had become largely irrelevant and attention had moved to ISIS.

i-only-wanted-to-kill-jews.title: Abu Zubaydah
i-only-wanted-to-kill-jews.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

i-only-wanted-to-kill-jews.title: Faisalabad Hospital
i-only-wanted-to-kill-jews.summary: The hospital where a dying Abu Zubaydah was taken after the raid of March 2002 — open windows, animals in the corridors, mosquitoes on open wounds, and a bar of Irish Spring soap used as a pincushion for reusable syringes — which came under fire from the street while he was on the operating table.

i-should-have-gone-to-film-school.title: The Kiriakou children
i-should-have-gone-to-film-school.summary: The five children of John Kiriakou, and what they do — a bond trader, an elementary school music teacher, a college junior studying supply chain economics, a sophomore who has not yet decided, and a fourteen-year-old. None of them, to their father's declared relief, has any interest in the CIA.

i-should-have-gone-to-film-school.title: Kiriakou's writing process
i-should-have-gone-to-film-school.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of how he actually writes — books in waves over roughly nine months, op-eds in forty-five minutes to an hour once an idea has sat for a few days, and a habit of getting up at two in the morning to write one because he cannot sleep. He wrote *Remains of the Day* in six weeks during COVID, losing whole evenings to it: "I look at the clock again, it''s 2:00 in the morning. I''m like, oh my god, what happened?"

i-should-have-gone-to-film-school.title: Remains of the Day (book)
i-should-have-gone-to-film-school.summary: John Kiriakou's book, announced for publication by Simon and Schuster in March 2026, billed as a definitive guide to the historic cemeteries of Washington DC and the first in a planned series; the second installment will cover the Mafia graves of New York City.

i-should-have-gone-to-film-school.title: The beer and the couch
i-should-have-gone-to-film-school.summary: What John Kiriakou says he did with the CIA''s spot-assessment training after leaving the agency. He still sizes up strangers within moments of meeting them, but the question is no longer what they can do for him: it is whether he would want to have a beer with them, and whether, if he were down on his luck, they would let him sleep on their couch.

i-should-have-gone-to-film-school.title: The Pentagon press contract
i-should-have-gone-to-film-school.summary: A contract John Kiriakou says every news outlet covering the Pentagon was required to sign in mid-2026, undertaking to publish no information that had not been officially provided by the department. Almost nobody signed: by his count Newsmax, One America News, a Turkish paper, a Hungarian paper and a couple of bloggers.

i-should-have-gone-to-film-school.title: Coffee with a cabinet member
i-should-have-gone-to-film-school.summary: John Kiriakou's disclosure that he had coffee with a member of the cabinet who told him to be patient about his pardon — and told him to watch what he said. He reports the meeting while stating plainly that there is nothing further he can do to make his case, and that he is not confident the outcome will be decided on justice.

i-want-my-fifty-bucks-back.title: Salt Typhoon
i-want-my-fifty-bucks-back.summary: The Chinese intelligence operation John Kiriakou describes as having hit the jackpot — collecting data on effectively every American through the telephone companies — and his blunt assessment that the Chinese cyber unit is good and American defences are not.

i-want-my-fifty-bucks-back.title: The Ai Weiwei Lego portrait
i-want-my-fifty-bucks-back.summary: The Alcatraz installation for which Ai Weiwei built 178 portraits of political prisoners out of Lego, and John Kiriakou's account of how his own inclusion was nearly blocked — Amnesty International told the artist it did not regard Kiriakou as a political prisoner, and only relented the week he left prison.

i-want-my-fifty-bucks-back.title: The Bolton raid
i-want-my-fifty-bucks-back.summary: John Kiriakou's reading of the August 2025 FBI search of John Bolton's home and office — that emailing national defense information to family members is the Espionage Act's definition of espionage, on a precedent set in Kiriakou's own case — together with the FBI evidence sticker he says is still on the back of his own computer.

i-want-my-fifty-bucks-back.title: The disappearance of Daniel Hale
i-want-my-fifty-bucks-back.summary: John Kiriakou's account of losing touch with the drone whistleblower Daniel Hale after his release from prison — a brief reappearance on social media, a shut-down account a week later, and a circle of friends none of whom has heard from him since.

i-want-my-fifty-bucks-back.title: The Iranian interest section
i-want-my-fifty-bucks-back.summary: How John Kiriakou obtained a visa to travel to Iran in the absence of diplomatic relations — through an Iranian interest section housed in the Pakistani embassy in Washington — and the argument he draws from it, that withholding recognition only makes diplomats' work harder.

i-want-my-fifty-bucks-back.title: The Pezeshkian invitation
i-want-my-fifty-bucks-back.summary: The invitation John Kiriakou disclosed in September 2025 to meet the Iranian president in New York during the UN General Assembly, as one of six people asked — an invitation he says he accepted without asking what it was about.

ian-henderson.title: The Belgian intelligence director
ian-henderson.summary: The brother of John Kiriakou's oldest friend, a Belgian exchange student at his high school, who rose to run Belgium's intelligence service and become deputy prime minister — and the exchange in which Kiriakou answered the standard defence of an intelligence chief's prejudices with his own experience.

ian-henderson.title: The embassy swap
ian-henderson.summary: The 1970s agreement under which the United States and the Soviet Union each built a new embassy in the other's capital — the Russians choosing the highest ground in Washington, the Americans being sold a dry riverbed in Moscow, and the American building having to be demolished because listening devices had been built into every beam.

ian-henderson.title: Salt Typhoon
ian-henderson.summary: The Chinese intelligence operation John Kiriakou describes as having hit the jackpot — collecting data on effectively every American through the telephone companies — and his blunt assessment that the Chinese cyber unit is good and American defences are not.

ian-henderson.title: The Ai Weiwei Lego portrait
ian-henderson.summary: The Alcatraz installation for which Ai Weiwei built 178 portraits of political prisoners out of Lego, and John Kiriakou's account of how his own inclusion was nearly blocked — Amnesty International told the artist it did not regard Kiriakou as a political prisoner, and only relented the week he left prison.

ian-henderson.title: The Iranian interest section
ian-henderson.summary: How John Kiriakou obtained a visa to travel to Iran in the absence of diplomatic relations — through an Iranian interest section housed in the Pakistani embassy in Washington — and the argument he draws from it, that withholding recognition only makes diplomats' work harder.

ian-henderson.title: The Pezeshkian invitation
ian-henderson.summary: The invitation John Kiriakou disclosed in September 2025 to meet the Iranian president in New York during the UN General Assembly, as one of six people asked — an invitation he says he accepted without asking what it was about.

ibrahim-traore.title: Amnesty International
ibrahim-traore.summary: The human rights organization whose torture report forms part of John Kiriakou's core defense — the CIA's crimes were already public knowledge before he confirmed them on ABC, and the Justice Department's own declination letter said so — and the organization whose silence during his prosecution he cannot forgive. He begged Amnesty for a one-sentence statement and got a New Yorker subscription instead; it took Ai Weiwei to change their minds, and by then he was walking out of prison.

ibrahim-traore.title: Djibouti
ibrahim-traore.summary: The small Horn of Africa state a few miles across the water from Yemen that hosts Camp Lemonnier — the American drone base for the Yemen and Somalia wars, inherited from the departing French, and shared with China's only overseas military base behind a fence down the middle, in what John Kiriakou calls the worst kept secret in the world.

ibrahim-traore.title: I want my fifty bucks back
ibrahim-traore.summary: What John Kiriakou says he shouted at John Fetterman from ten rows back at an Ohio State football game — and his explanation, as a Pennsylvanian furious about the senator, of why Fetterman keeps his seat anyway.

ibrahim-traore.title: Ian Henderson
ibrahim-traore.summary: The British colonial police officer who ran Bahrain's intelligence service during John Kiriakou's posting there — a man Kiriakou says even the heir presumptive to the throne was afraid to name aloud, and whom Kiriakou, seated at the crown prince's table at a dinner for George H. W. Bush, mistook for a corpse.

ibrahim-traore.title: Kimberly Guilfoyle in Athens
ibrahim-traore.summary: John Kiriakou's assessment of Kimberly Guilfoyle's appointment as American ambassador to Greece — that she got it because Donald Trump Jr. wanted her out of the way, a manoeuvre he compares to Saddam Hussein's habit of exiling successful generals as ambassadors — and his reluctant conclusion that Greece could have done worse.

ibrahim-traore.title: The magazines that bought her freedom
ibrahim-traore.summary: John Kiriakou's account of his grandmother's imprisonment by the collaborationist government in wartime Athens, and of his grandfather buying her release from a prison guard with American magazines — after which the couple escaped to the United States.

ilhan-omar.title: Espionage Act
ilhan-omar.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

ilhan-omar.title: Albert Stubblebine
ilhan-omar.summary: Per John Kiriakou, General Albert "Bert" Stubblebine was among the Army Intelligence figures behind the original Project Stargate remote-viewing program; Kiriakou interviewed the program's top people and says Stubblebine, like remote viewer Lyn Buchanan, had to sign non-disclosure agreements with the NSA and CIA.

ilhan-omar.title: Amnesty International
ilhan-omar.summary: The human rights organization whose torture report forms part of John Kiriakou's core defense — the CIA's crimes were already public knowledge before he confirmed them on ABC, and the Justice Department's own declination letter said so — and the organization whose silence during his prosecution he cannot forgive. He begged Amnesty for a one-sentence statement and got a New Yorker subscription instead; it took Ai Weiwei to change their minds, and by then he was walking out of prison.

ilhan-omar.title: Bahrain Posting (1994–1996)
ilhan-omar.summary: John Kiriakou's 1994–1996 assignment to Bahrain under U.S. State Department cover as second secretary for economic affairs — arriving with his wife Joanne and infant son Chris on August 1, 1994, into a tiny Gulf monarchy whose sectarian tensions erupted, two months later, into the first Intifada.

ilhan-omar.title: Bay Path University
ilhan-omar.summary: Per John Kiriakou, he teaches in the graduate intelligence-studies program at Bay Path University in Massachusetts, covering introduction to intelligence, the history of terrorism, and intelligence and cybersecurity.

ilhan-omar.title: The killing of Alex Pretty
ilhan-omar.summary: John Kiriakou''s verdict on the shooting of a man by immigration agents in Minneapolis in January 2026: a Kent State moment for the administration, a cover-up in progress, and — because there is no statute of limitations on murder — a case that will outlive the presidency and put people in prison.

imia-crisis.title: The Eastern Mediterranean gas field
imia-crisis.summary: The natural gas discovered off the south-eastern coast of Cyprus and running toward Lebanon, Israel and Palestine, which John Kiriakou identifies as the real source of Greek–Turkish tension. Turkey feels excluded although none of the gas lies in its waters; and although the founding agreement acknowledged a Palestinian share, Israel decides its size — an amount Kiriakou predicts will be zero.

imia-crisis.title: Article 5, invoked once
imia-crisis.summary: John Kiriakou's argument against NATO's continued necessity, resting on the observation that in the alliance's whole history it has been called on to defend a member from attack exactly once — on 11 September 2001 — and on the repeated American promises to Russia not to expand toward its borders, which he says four presidents in a row have broken.

imia-crisis.title: Afghan heroin policy
imia-crisis.summary: The post-2001 U.S. policy in Afghanistan of protecting, and per John Kiriakou actively encouraging, the cultivation of heroin poppy. Under the Taliban in 2000 Afghanistan produced 0% of the world's heroin; by 2009 under American occupation it produced 93%. Per a DEA officer Kiriakou consulted with on the policy paper he was preparing for Senator Kerry, the strategic rationale was that nearly all of the heroin flowed to Iran and Russia, addiction in those countries was considered desirable as a long-run societal weakener, and the same logic now operates in reverse with Chinese fentanyl flowing into the United States.

imia-crisis.title: The Arab states and the Gaza war
imia-crisis.summary: John Kiriakou's country-by-country reading of how the Arab governments positioned themselves after October 2023 — the Gulf states ranked by their fear of Iran, Jordan caught between its border and its population, Egypt sealing Rafah to prevent a repeat of earlier refugee flows — and his conclusion that every one of them is calculating damage to itself first and the Palestinians second.

imia-crisis.title: China as mediator
imia-crisis.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that China is the plausible mediator of Middle Eastern and Ukrainian conflicts, grounded in his claim that — Tibet and its border wars aside — China has no history of invading other countries, and his observation of how quickly Beijing accepted an offhand suggestion that it might mediate between Israel and Iran.

imia-crisis.title: China as economic threat
imia-crisis.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that China is the real threat to the West not militarily — it has one aircraft carrier to America's two dozen and rarely invades — but economically, buying friends worldwide while the U.S. spends a trillion dollars a year on weapons.

impeach-him-again.title: Nationalizing the midterms
impeach-him-again.summary: John Kiriakou's recurring comparison between contemporary party messaging and Newt Gingrich's 1994 Contract with America, including his advice that Speaker Mike Johnson should keep Gingrich on his couch and ask him nightly how the 1994 midterms were nationalised.

impeach-him-again.title: Decorum in the Reagan years
impeach-him-again.summary: John Kiriakou's contrast between the State of the Union addresses he watched as a college student under Ronald Reagan — divided, substantive, but conducted with decorum — and the 2026 address he called a clown show with no decorum on either side.

impeach-him-again.title: Get thrown out spicily
impeach-him-again.summary: John Kiriakou''s criticism of Representative Al Green''s protest at the 2026 State of the Union address: that holding up a banned sign and then walking out quietly accomplished nothing, and that if you are going to be removed you should struggle and fight back.

impeach-him-again.title: The six-hour queue for seats
impeach-him-again.summary: John Kiriakou on learning that members of Congress arrive six hours early with packed meals to hold a seat for the State of the Union, and that in 2026 the absence of 112 Democrats freed those seats for the cabinet, the sub-cabinet and visitors.

impeach-him-again.title: The Trump appointees to the Court
impeach-him-again.summary: John Kiriakou's assessment that Donald Trump's Supreme Court appointees have been surprisingly good, and that the justices he regards as disasters — Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas — were appointed by more moderate presidents.

impeach-him-again.title: Donald Trump
impeach-him-again.summary: 45th and 47th U.S. president. Per John Kiriakou, a man genuinely convinced he was doing right by bombing Iran, "duped" by the same Netanyahu nuclear bluff Obama once rejected — and, at the same time, the most blindly pro-Israel president in history, an admirer of autocrats who has never once criticized Vladimir Putin, and prone to gestures — from the Gulf of America to a since-abandoned "Department of War" rename — that test the edges of his actual authority.

imran-khan.title: The Imran Khan apology demand
imran-khan.summary: The demand issued by Imran Khan's party in late October 2025 that John Kiriakou apologise in writing to Khan, to the party and to the Pakistani people over a single sentence he had given an Indian outlet — that India would win a conventional war because it has five times the population — together with his refusal, the death threats, his lawyer's advice, and the blanket policy on South Asian media he adopted afterwards.

imran-khan.title: Abolish the CIA
imran-khan.summary: John Kiriakou's position that the CIA should be abolished because its functions are already duplicated by the other 17 U.S. intelligence agencies — analysis by the State Department, human spying by the Pentagon, technology by DARPA, NSA and the private sector.

imran-khan.title: Alex Karp
imran-khan.summary: Co-founder and CEO of Palantir Technologies; subject of a biographical assessment commissioned from John Kiriakou by an unnamed interest group; characterized as militarily-industrially conservative despite a Democratic Party registration, religious, extremely patriotic, and "driven by profit."

imran-khan.title: Another Bentley
imran-khan.summary: The scene John Kiriakou describes from a meeting with Benazir Bhutto during her exile in Dubai — a five-million-dollar palace on the Gulf, a car pulling up outside, and Bhutto saying that so help her God, if her husband had come home with another Bentley she would kill him — which Kiriakou uses as his measure of Pakistani political corruption.

imran-khan.title: Arrais Corporation
imran-khan.summary: Private intelligence firm; companion entity to The Analysis Corporation; originally an LLC pass-through for retired Senior Intelligence Service personnel from the CIA's operations side; subsequently acquired by IBM for over $1 billion.

imran-khan.title: Asset acquisition cycle
imran-khan.summary: The four-step process — spot, assess, develop, recruit — taught as the first lesson of CIA case officer training

in-q-tel.title: Palantir Technologies
in-q-tel.summary: U.S. data-analytics and intelligence-software company; received its first $1.5 million in seed funding from the CIA's In-Q-Tel venture-capital arm around 2002; characterized by John Kiriakou as functionally inseparable from the CIA in 2025, drawing the majority of its revenue from agency contracts and operating across DARPA, NSA, and the broader U.S. national-security apparatus.

in-q-tel.title: Will Hurd
in-q-tel.summary: Former CIA case officer, congressman and OpenAI board member whom John Kiriakou says he mentored at the agency; Kiriakou cites him as an example of the intelligence and tech worlds merging.

in-q-tel.title: Alex Karp
in-q-tel.summary: Co-founder and CEO of Palantir Technologies; subject of a biographical assessment commissioned from John Kiriakou by an unnamed interest group; characterized as militarily-industrially conservative despite a Democratic Party registration, religious, extremely patriotic, and "driven by profit."

in-q-tel.title: Peter Thiel
in-q-tel.summary: U.S. venture capitalist; co-founder of Palantir Technologies; subject of a biographical assessment commissioned from John Kiriakou by an unnamed interest group alongside Palantir CEO Alex Karp.

in-q-tel.title: US Military Venture Capital
in-q-tel.summary: Per John Kiriakou, the U.S. military now purchases technology using a venture-capital investment model, a shift he cites as a warning sign about how national-security institutions acquire emerging tech.

in-q-tel.title: The spy shop
in-q-tel.summary: A London shop, with branches in New York and briefly Washington, where John Kiriakou says the CIA bought a good deal of the equipment it needed — on the reasoning that a thousand-dollar purchase beat a million-dollar development programme. Any member of the public could walk in and buy the same things; much of the rest, he says, came from Radio Shack. In six months in Pakistan he used more gadgets than in the whole of the rest of his career, and all but one of them were bought online.

india.title: The Intercept
india.summary: The investigative news outlet that published Daniel Hale's drone leak; John Kiriakou notes that the same Intercept reporter, Matthew Cole, was involved in cases that led to the exposure of both Kiriakou himself and NSA leaker Reality Winner — though he insists Hale outed himself rather than being burned by the outlet.

india.title: Kashmir
india.summary: The disputed territory John Kiriakou says is front and centre for every Pakistani and largely absent from Indian minds, and on which his own sympathies lie with Pakistan — a promised 1940s referendum that never happened. He also describes the appearance that ended his participation in South Asian media: an Indian programme cut his pro-Pakistani answer, aired only his prediction that India would win a conventional war, and the death threats resumed.

india.title: Sanctions Effectiveness
india.summary: John Kiriakou's assessment that U.S. sanctions have been so overused against disfavored countries that nations like China now route around them entirely, and that sanctions work only when reserved for the worst actors and imposed in concert with other countries — citing apartheid South Africa as a success and Cuba/Venezuela as failures that instead entrench nationalist narratives.

india.title: The 2025 India–Pakistan clash assessment
india.summary: John Kiriakou''s verdict on the most recent India–Pakistan confrontation, delivered after an unusually explicit declaration of his own bias: he loved living in Pakistan, favours Pakistan on Kashmir, and judges that India accomplished nothing while Pakistan lost nothing, leaving the Pakistanis slightly ahead.

india.title: The CNN India refusal
india.summary: The interview request John Kiriakou turned down on the morning of 19 November 2025 — the latest of many from Indian broadcasters — because, he says, every answer he gives about India or Pakistan is turned into a banner headline with three exclamation points, stripped of context, and followed by a dozen death threats.

influencing-trump-rule-of-three.title: Gina Haspel
influencing-trump-rule-of-three.summary: Director of the Central Intelligence Agency under President Trump's first term; known to John Kiriakou and others at the CIA as "Bloody Gina"; per Kiriakou, flew out to the secret black site to sit in on one of the enhanced-interrogation torture sessions "just because she could," personally supervised the torture of USS Cole bombing suspect Rahim al-Nashiri, and later fed the CIA's torture tapes into an industrial document grinder after being explicitly told by White House Counsel not to destroy them.

influencing-trump-rule-of-three.title: Julian Assange
influencing-trump-rule-of-three.summary: Kiriakou — a 15-year friend and former WikiLeaks board member — on why Assange is a publisher owed a journalist's immunity, and a political prisoner.

influencing-trump-rule-of-three.title: Consortium News
influencing-trump-rule-of-three.summary: Independent investigative news outlet John Kiriakou has written for since at least 2017, founded by Polk Award-winning journalist Robert Parry, who broke major stories on Iran-Contra.
