Kiriakou's columns there have covered John Bolton's exit, the entrapment of Maria Butina, his own first tour in Saudi Arabia and the 2019 Ukraine-call whistleblower. He says PayPal permanently shuttered the outlet's account and briefly seized its funds before backing down under public pressure, while still refusing to reinstate it.

influencing-trump-rule-of-three.title: Donald Trump
influencing-trump-rule-of-three.summary: 45th and 47th U.S. president. Per John Kiriakou, a man genuinely convinced he was doing right by bombing Iran, "duped" by the same Netanyahu nuclear bluff Obama once rejected — and, at the same time, the most blindly pro-Israel president in history, an admirer of autocrats who has never once criticized Vladimir Putin, and prone to gestures — from the Gulf of America to a since-abandoned "Department of War" rename — that test the edges of his actual authority.

influencing-trump-rule-of-three.title: "Admit nothing, deny everything, make counter-accusations"
influencing-trump-rule-of-three.summary: One of the twenty life lessons John Kiriakou says the CIA taught him in training, and a slogan sold on coffee mugs and t-shirts in the headquarters gift shop — by far the most popular mug in the building. It was treated at Langley as a joke that was not quite a joke; in federal prison Kiriakou used it as an operating rule, and credits it with getting him out of an investigation into a prison-yard fight with nothing given up.

intelligence-agencies.title: FBI
intelligence-agencies.summary: Kiriakou says FBI agents were sticklers for the law in a way the CIA never was — and that the bureau 'leaks like a sieve.'

intelligence-agencies.title: NSA
intelligence-agencies.summary: Kiriakou on the agency whose Utah facility boasts room to store every American's calls, texts and emails for the next 500 years.

intelligence-agencies.title: President's Daily Brief
intelligence-agencies.summary: Per John Kiriakou, the President's Daily Brief (PDB) is a roughly 16-page, top-secret intelligence document produced daily for the president, written in a uniform CIA house style, briefed each morning, and — in his account — used partly to gauge and flatter incoming presidents.

intelligence-agencies.title: CIA Democrats (2016)
intelligence-agencies.summary: John Kiriakou's term for a wave of 2016-era congressional candidates with intelligence or military backgrounds who ran for office opposing Trump from the right on Russia — including former CIA officer Abigail Spanberger, who won a one-term-limited Virginia governorship, and former DIA official Elissa Slotkin, who moved from intelligence into Congress and the Senate — both of whom Kiriakou suggests are positioning for future presidential runs.

intelligence-agencies.title: Thomas Drake
intelligence-agencies.summary: NSA whistleblower; per John Kiriakou, the source for the statement that on the morning of September 11, 2001, NSA Director Mike Hayden told agency personnel NSA had been 'waiting for a 9/11' to implement the mass-electronic-surveillance program that NSA's founding charter forbids.

intelligence-agencies.title: 1953 Iran coup
intelligence-agencies.summary: The U.S.- and UK-backed overthrow of Iran's democratically elected prime minister, Mohammad Mossadegh; per John Kiriakou, the coup served British national interests rather than American ones, and the subsequent outlawing of secular political opposition under the Shah forced dissent into the mosques — producing a religious rather than secular revolution in 1979.

intelligence-fabrication.title: The hotel bar operation
intelligence-fabrication.summary: The night a visiting foreign delegation's security detail was expected in a boutique hotel bar and every seat in it turned out to be occupied by a CIA officer — an episode John Kiriakou offers as an example of bad leadership, and which left his colleagues personally out of pocket for their espresso martinis.

intelligence-fabrication.title: Denied areas
intelligence-fabrication.summary: The CIA term for countries so hostile and so heavily surveilled that ordinary operational movement is impossible — the Soviet Union, Cuba, Syria, and later Russia, China, North Korea and Iran — and the reason, in John Kiriakou's account, that officers heading to one get specialist briefings, eight-hour surveillance detection routes, and that the Agency has to fall back on liaison services instead of its own sources.

intelligence-fabrication.title: The Directorate of Operations
intelligence-fabrication.summary: The CIA's clandestine service, which John Kiriakou joined from analysis because he spoke both Greek and Arabic — a culture he describes as wildly different from the analytic side, short on institutional memory and organised around the race to become a station chief.

intelligence-fabrication.title: Abraxas Corporation
intelligence-fabrication.summary: The private intelligence company founded in the 1990s by retired CIA operations officers as a tax pass-through and a place to smoke cigars and tell stories — which, after 9/11, made its founders, in John Kiriakou's phrase, Mega Millions rich.

intelligence-fabrication.title: The Brüno shoot in Jordan
intelligence-fabrication.summary: The scene John Kiriakou set up for Sacha Baron Cohen in Amman — four retired Palestinian militants, found in the Damascus telephone book at the Library of Congress, shown hardcore pornography by a character they believed to be an Austrian documentary journalist — which produced no reaction at all and was cut from the film entirely.

intelligence-fabrication.title: Chief of station
intelligence-fabrication.summary: The CIA's senior officer in a foreign country — appointed by the CIA director alone, outranking the ambassador's intelligence equities in practice, and in John Kiriakou's account the figure who sets the moral temperature of a station, from the officer who handed him his first counterterrorism assignment to the one who walks into a minister's office fifteen minutes after the human rights officer has left.

intelligence-identities-protection-act.title: Haroon Yenor trial
intelligence-identities-protection-act.summary: Federal terrorism prosecution in which John Kiriakou testified as a defense expert witness; Yenor, arrested in November 2024 on charges tied to an alleged plot to bomb the New York Stock Exchange and a synagogue, was acquitted on all six charges on June 30; Kiriakou's expert testimony argued the FBI supplied the idea, the bomb, the explosives, the timer, the detonation cord, and the getaway car.

intelligence-identities-protection-act.title: Public safety factor
intelligence-identities-protection-act.summary: The Bureau of Prisons classification that barred Kiriakou from a minimum-security camp by rating him as dangerous as a murderer, applied over the objections of both his sentencing judge and the prosecutor who convicted him.

intelligence-identities-protection-act.title: The CIA–State Department cover agreement
intelligence-identities-protection-act.summary: The standing arrangement under which CIA officers serve abroad under State Department cover. As a senior investigator for the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, John Kiriakou was told the agency was misusing the agreement to place officers from the torture program under diplomatic cover so that publishing their names would expose journalists to the Intelligence Identities Protection Act. His written query, sent over Senator John Kerry''s signature, came back classified above his own clearance.

intelligence-identities-protection-act.title: Jim Moran
intelligence-identities-protection-act.summary: Twelve-term Democratic congressman from Northern Virginia and John Kiriakou's own representative, who took the floor of the House to call for his release and a presidential pardon, and wrote twice to the director of the Bureau of Prisons asking that his constituent receive halfway-house time. In Kiriakou's account he was one of only a handful of elected officials willing to help at all.

intelligence-identities-protection-act.title: The business-card espionage charges
intelligence-identities-protection-act.summary: Two of the three Espionage Act counts brought against John Kiriakou rested on his having passed a former CIA colleague's business card to two reporters — a man who had left the agency and had never been undercover — and were dropped after an exchange in open court in which the prosecutor's only answer to the judge was that Kiriakou should have been more careful.

intelligence-identities-protection-act.title: The Los Angeles Times Iran op-ed
intelligence-identities-protection-act.summary: An op-ed on Iranian foreign policy in Latin America that John Kiriakou was commissioned to write about six months after blowing the whistle on the torture programme. He had barely begun when the CIA general counsel's office telephoned to warn him off the subject — a call he could not explain for fourteen years, and which he now attributes to his own wife rather than to a source inside the newspaper.

intelligence-peddlers.title: Counterterrorism Center
intelligence-peddlers.summary: The CIA's Counterterrorism Center (CTC) — the unit where John Kiriakou spent the defining years of his operational career. He joined in the late 1990s as the only officer in the entire CIA fluent in both Greek and Arabic, served as chief of counterintelligence in the bin Laden unit, watched the Center swell from a few hundred employees to nearly 2,000 by September 12, 2001, and it was to CTC that he walked back down in May 2002 to refuse the torture program — the moment, he says, the CIA began to turn on him.

intelligence-peddlers.title: Walk-in
intelligence-peddlers.summary: In John Kiriakou's telling, someone who walks into an embassy offering information; 95% are lunatics or liars, some are 'intelligence peddlers' or hostile 'probes,' and about 1% are 'the real McCoy' — a framework he used to see through a supposed 'walk-in' tip during the Abu Zubaydah hunt. A genuine walk-in — a witness to a terrorist assassination — was later hypnotized by CIA psychologists in a London hotel room and read back a stolen van's license plate, verifying his account.

intelligence-peddlers.title: John Kiriakou
intelligence-peddlers.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

intelligence-peddlers.title: The walk-in who was a probe
intelligence-peddlers.summary: The man who presented himself at the American embassy in Athens claiming to be an Arab with information, and whom John Kiriakou interrogated the next day in a rolling meeting through the city — catching him reversing his own alias, while a hostile embassy's surveillance car followed and Kiriakou's boss ended it by putting a pistol to the man's cheek.

intelligence-peddlers.title: Cover stop
intelligence-peddlers.summary: A routine, innocuous errand run in the middle of a surveillance detection route so that an intelligence officer has a plausible reason to be where he is — the 7-Eleven, the dry cleaner, the wine shop — and, in John Kiriakou's account, also a petty-expense line item that has ended CIA careers.

intelligence-peddlers.title: The Snickers bar
intelligence-peddlers.summary: The ritual in John Kiriakou''s Athens station: when an officer made a recruitment, the boss announced it in the staff meeting, everyone applauded, and he threw the officer a Snickers bar.

international-criminal-court.title: Hague Invasion Act
international-criminal-court.summary: The American statute, described by John Kiriakou as having been passed during the Obama administration, that authorises the president to use the United States military to invade the Netherlands and free an American or allied national held by the International Criminal Court — the standing legal answer to the possibility that Benjamin Netanyahu might be arrested abroad.

international-criminal-court.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
international-criminal-court.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

international-criminal-court.title: Graham–Netanyahu ICC tapes
international-criminal-court.summary: Recordings of Lindsey Graham coordinating with Benjamin Netanyahu on how to discredit the International Criminal Court over its arrest warrant. On the tapes Graham lines up Senate signatories for a protest letter, jokes that he should be paid "tons of shekels," and asks Netanyahu to telephone two Democratic senators to thank them. John Kiriakou argues the conduct meets the definition of espionage his own judge applied to him.

international-criminal-court.title: Espionage Act
international-criminal-court.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

international-criminal-court.title: Lindsey Graham
international-criminal-court.summary: Republican senator from South Carolina who died in July 2026, and John Kiriakou's standing shorthand for the permanent war caucus — a "show horse" rather than a workhorse, a "chameleon" who "never saw a war that he didn't want to jump into with both feet," and, on posthumously released documentary footage, a man offering the US Air Force to bomb a country America was not at war with.

international-criminal-court.title: Netanyahu arrest poll
international-criminal-court.summary: The 2026 survey finding that a majority of Americans — not a plurality — support the arrest of Benjamin Netanyahu, a figure John Kiriakou notes is higher than the share who supported arresting Nicolás Maduro and which, per CNN, represents a fifty-point move in American opinion over five years.

international-spy-museum.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
international-spy-museum.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

international-spy-museum.title: John Kiriakou
international-spy-museum.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

international-spy-museum.title: 2028 presidential field
international-spy-museum.summary: John Kiriakou's assessment of the wide-open 2028 presidential race — the first in his life, he says, where he has no idea who either party will nominate. Predictive markets were listing 44 Democrats and 26 Republicans as possible candidates. His own preferred candidate is Tucker Carlson, whom he says he has repeatedly begged to run; his working assumption about anyone who does want the job is that they are "a narcissist and probably a sociopath on top of it."

international-spy-museum.title: Amaryllis Fox Kennedy
international-spy-museum.summary: Former CIA non-official-cover officer who worked under commercial cover as an international art consultant, later a Trump campaign manager and nominee for deputy CIA director. Per John Kiriakou, Senator Tom Cotton threatened to filibuster her appointment; the president responded by naming her deputy national security adviser instead — a job Kiriakou considers more powerful, since the CIA director reports to the national security adviser.

international-spy-museum.title: Andrew Bustamante
international-spy-museum.summary: Former CIA officer who sells CIA-style training online; John Kiriakou identifies him as the lone critic of his work hosting a show on a Russian network, and argues Bustamante's training business — open to anyone who pays — is the more problematic of the two.

international-spy-museum.title: Angry Birds
international-spy-museum.summary: The mobile game John Kiriakou describes as his only vice besides buying art, played every morning for nine consecutive years and cited by his ex-wife as a grievance in their marriage.

iran-12-day-war.title: Hassan Nasrallah
iran-12-day-war.summary: Long-serving Secretary-General of Hezbollah, killed in an Israeli strike on a complex in southern Lebanon; the strike, which killed approximately 300 people in addition to Nasrallah, decapitated Hezbollah's leadership and is characterized by John Kiriakou as a war crime under international law.

iran-12-day-war.title: Mohsen Rafighdoost
iran-12-day-war.summary: Iranian journalist and political figure whom John Kiriakou identifies as a co-founder of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and the propaganda voice behind the audio tapes distributed in Iran before the 1979 revolution; interviewed on the PBD Podcast, he conceded that the Shah's regime held only 3,000–3,500 political prisoners rather than the 100,000 opposition figures claimed at the time and that the Shah was, in his own judgment, a better man than Ayatollah Khomeini.

iran-12-day-war.title: The Russian nuclear umbrella
iran-12-day-war.summary: John Kiriakou's report, two days after the Israeli strikes on Iran began in June 2025, that Russia had declared Iran to be under the protection of its nuclear umbrella — and his conclusion that this rules out any Israeli nuclear use against Iran, because it would risk Russian nuclear retaliation against Israel.

iran-12-day-war.title: Mexican 9 Month Work Visas
iran-12-day-war.summary: A George W. Bush-administration proposal, negotiated with Mexico in the six to eight months before 9/11, to give undocumented Mexican workers renewable nine-month U.S. work visas requiring federal income tax payment — killed by the September 11 attacks before it could be ratified.

iran-12-day-war.title: The unarmed ship
iran-12-day-war.summary: John Kiriakou's enumeration of war crimes committed in the 2026 Iran war — striking civilian targets, rocketing a school and killing 160 children, and sinking a naval vessel and then refusing to aid the survivors — and his insistence that the objection is not confined to Israeli conduct.

iran-12-day-war.title: The three legal ways to enter another country
iran-12-day-war.summary: The test John Kiriakou applies to American military action abroad: that there are only three lawful ways for one country to move into another — with the approval of the UN Security Council, at that country''s invitation, or after being attacked by it — and that the United States, in his account, never meets any of the three.

iran-2024-drone-retaliation.title: The Iron Dome
iran-2024-drone-retaliation.summary: Israel's air-defence system as John Kiriakou reads it — impressive against a wave of slow Iranian drones, but shown by the handful that got through, and later by Iranian ballistic missiles, to be not all it is cracked up to be; each exchange, in his account, buying Iran intelligence about the gaps.

iran-2024-drone-retaliation.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
iran-2024-drone-retaliation.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

iran-2024-drone-retaliation.title: Israel's cell-phone assassinations in Iran
iran-2024-drone-retaliation.summary: John Kiriakou's account of how Israel wiped out Iran's military leadership by tracking cell phones — recruiting destitute Afghan refugees as $100-a-month spotters, and, when the generals stopped carrying phones, targeting their bodyguards' phones instead.

iran-2024-drone-retaliation.title: Itamar Ben-Gvir
iran-2024-drone-retaliation.summary: Israel's far-right Minister of National Security; John Kiriakou cites him as a convicted hate-crime felon placed in charge of security in Gaza and the West Bank over his victims, blames his insistence that any attack would come from the West Bank for diverting forces before October 7, and cites the death-penalty law passed under his portfolio for Palestinian detainees as the first reinstatement of capital punishment in Israel since it was abolished in 1956, excepting only the execution of Adolf Eichmann.

iran-2024-drone-retaliation.title: Israeli intelligence presence in the United States
iran-2024-drone-retaliation.summary: John Kiriakou's account of Israeli intelligence activity inside the United States — dozens of undeclared Mossad and Shin Bet officers identified by the FBI, a critical-threat counterintelligence classification alongside Russia, North Korea and Cuba, and a pattern of harassment and intimidation directed at declared CIA officers posted to Israel.

iran-2024-drone-retaliation.title: October 7 attack
iran-2024-drone-retaliation.summary: John Kiriakou's analysis of the October 7, 2023 Hamas attack as a policy failure, not an intelligence one — Israel was warned repeatedly, but Itamar Ben-Gvir diverted response forces to the West Bank, and Kiriakou believes Israel welcomed a pretext for overwhelming retaliation.

iran-contra.title: Adnan Khashoggi
iran-contra.summary: Saudi arms dealer and Iran-Contra middleman whom John Kiriakou says was mentioned 'all the time' at the CIA — in pointed contrast to Jeffrey Epstein, whose name he never once heard there.

iran-contra.title: Contra rebels
iran-contra.summary: The right-wing Nicaraguan insurgency armed by the Reagan administration against the Sandinista government. In John Kiriakou's account they were conservatives, right-wingers, in some cases fascists, and disgruntled military officers; they were split into a northern group the United States armed and a southern group that financed itself by selling cocaine — a distinction that became the pivot of the Gary Webb affair, and that Kiriakou uses to answer the CIA's standing denial that it had anything to do with the drug trade.

iran-contra.title: CIA Drug Facilitation
iran-contra.summary: Per John Kiriakou, the CIA''s reported involvement in facilitating the arrival of cocaine into the United States during the era that became the crack epidemic, and his own firsthand discovery — as a Senate Foreign Relations Committee investigator — that under American military control Afghanistan produced 93% of the world''s heroin. A DEA contact told him the report would never be published because ''we want Iran and Russia to be addicted to heroin. It weakens their societies.'' Kiriakou draws a direct parallel to the current fentanyl crisis: China is doing to the US what the US did to Iran and Russia.

iran-contra.title: MOSSAD
iran-contra.summary: Israel's primary external intelligence service; characterized by John Kiriakou as universally hostile in his and his CIA colleagues' professional dealings with it ("never had a positive encounter with Mossad"); operates almost exclusively in the operational rather than analytical domain; the CIA is, per Kiriakou, categorically forbidden from spying on it.

iran-contra.title: John Kiriakou
iran-contra.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

iran-contra.title: Central American Task Force
iran-contra.summary: CIA unit that led the agency's early-to-mid-1980s effort to overthrow the Sandinista government and support the Contras in Nicaragua. John Kiriakou describes serving as assistant to the unit's head as one of his first, and most controversial, CIA jobs; he denies the accusation that the CIA trained Contra and Salvadoran insurgents to garrote nuns, saying the agency instead worked to stop such atrocities, while acknowledging it was associated with people who did terrible things.

iran-elementary-school-strike.title: Defense Intelligence Agency
iran-elementary-school-strike.summary: The Pentagon's intelligence arm, of which John Kiriakou holds a low opinion he states plainly and expects to be criticised for. He attributes the targeting data behind the 2026 Iranian elementary school strike to the agency.

iran-elementary-school-strike.title: Targeting analyst
iran-elementary-school-strike.summary: A specialized CIA analyst — distinct from an intelligence analyst — who sifts millions of pieces of data, much of it metadata, to physically locate a person for capture or killing; John Kiriakou credits one with finding Abu Zubaydah down to 14 sites.

iran-elementary-school-strike.title: Iranian sleeper cells
iran-elementary-school-strike.summary: John Kiriakou's assessment of Iran's clandestine reach abroad — that the IRGC and the Ministry of Intelligence and Security do run sleeper cells worldwide, but probably not in the United States, Canada or the UK, and that the greater danger is the unaffiliated lone attacker. He also argues Iranian operatives are consistently poor, and identifies the Gulf's real vulnerability as its tourist landmarks rather than its military bases.

iran-elementary-school-strike.title: 2026 Iran war
iran-elementary-school-strike.summary: The open-ended American and Israeli war against Iran that John Kiriakou tracked week by week on his own show — a conflict he says was sold as three weeks, ran into its fifth month, achieved every decapitation objective it set, and continued anyway. His grade for it is a D, and his forecast is a Truth Social post declaring victory while nothing changes.

iran-elementary-school-strike.title: Al Jazeera blocked in the United States
iran-elementary-school-strike.summary: Within hours of the first strikes on Iran, John Kiriakou reported that American cable carriers had pulled Al Jazeera — a friend in Florida texted him that Dish Network had blocked it, and viewers reported the same of Comcast Xfinity in Boston. His reading was blunt: they do not want Americans to see what is happening in the Middle East.

iran-elementary-school-strike.title: The strike on Ahmadinejad's house
iran-elementary-school-strike.summary: On the first day of the 2026 war, reports placed one of the targets in Tehran at Narmak, believed to be the residence of former Iranian president Mahmoud Ahmadinejad. John Kiriakou broke into the broadcast to call it gratuitous and an act of murder: Ahmadinejad is retired, holds no authority, and — in Kiriakou''s description — was a moderate.

iran-iraq-war-intelligence-switching.title: Saddam Hussein
iran-iraq-war-intelligence-switching.summary: President of Iraq from 1979 until the 2003 U.S. invasion; subject of John Kiriakou's CIA portfolio from January 1990 onward, in which capacity Kiriakou became, at age 25, "Saddam Hussein's intelligence community biographer" and the analyst who briefed President George H. W. Bush in the Oval Office on the morning of the 1990 invasion of Kuwait.

iran-iraq-war-intelligence-switching.title: Bahrain Posting (1994–1996)
iran-iraq-war-intelligence-switching.summary: John Kiriakou's 1994–1996 assignment to Bahrain under U.S. State Department cover as second secretary for economic affairs — arriving with his wife Joanne and infant son Chris on August 1, 1994, into a tiny Gulf monarchy whose sectarian tensions erupted, two months later, into the first Intifada.

iran-iraq-war-intelligence-switching.title: Deep state
iran-iraq-war-intelligence-switching.summary: John Kiriakou''s position on the deep state — that it is not a right-wing trope but an accurate description of something he served inside for fifteen years at the CIA and two more on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee staff. He is indifferent to the label ("call it the state, call it the federal bureaucracy") and insists on the substance: "It''s there to stay. It''s not going anywhere."

iran-iraq-war-intelligence-switching.title: Dick Cheney
iran-iraq-war-intelligence-switching.summary: U.S. Vice President under George W. Bush. Per John Kiriakou — recounting CIA Director George Tenet's memoir — Cheney intercepted the presidential finding authorizing the CIA's enhanced interrogation program in the Oval Office anteroom and took it from Tenet before Bush could sign it. Tenet later concluded the president probably never actually signed the finding and probably told the truth when he said he had no idea the program was taking place. Kiriakou characterizes Cheney as the one who actually ran foreign policy, intelligence policy, and defense policy during the Bush years.

iran-iraq-war-intelligence-switching.title: Iraq WMD intelligence
iran-iraq-war-intelligence-switching.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of how the case for Iraqi weapons of mass destruction was fabricated: the intelligence community''s consensus was that Iraq had no WMD, but the White House had already decided to invade and sought analysis to fit the policy.

iran-iraq-war-intelligence-switching.title: MOSSAD
iran-iraq-war-intelligence-switching.summary: Israel's primary external intelligence service; characterized by John Kiriakou as universally hostile in his and his CIA colleagues' professional dealings with it ("never had a positive encounter with Mossad"); operates almost exclusively in the operational rather than analytical domain; the CIA is, per Kiriakou, categorically forbidden from spying on it.

iran-nuclear-assessment.title: Mujahedin-e Khalq (MEK)
iran-nuclear-assessment.summary: Iranian opposition group that John Kiriakou describes as 'a quasi-communist cult' and a former U.S.-designated terrorist organization. Founded by a husband-and-wife team in the 1960s and based in northeastern Iraq, the MEK launched cross-border terrorist attacks into Iran and, per Kiriakou, attempted to murder the American ambassador and the senior U.S. general in Iran — carrying out anti-American attacks for decades. After Saddam Hussein expelled them they relocated to Paris; current leader Maryam Rajavi is widely believed to have killed or had killed her vanished husband to take over. In 2009 the MEK hired high-powered Washington lobbyists (from Howard Dean to Rudy Giuliani) to get off the terrorism list, and Kiriakou says it is now funded by Israel and used as assassins-for-hire in Tehran.

iran-nuclear-assessment.title: Serving at the pleasure of the president
iran-nuclear-assessment.summary: The employment rule John Kiriakou says he was taught in his first week at the CIA: agency employees have none of the protections of the Civil Service Act and can be dismissed at will, over a bad tie or an unwelcome line in the President''s Daily Brief. He treats the rule as long-standing and harmless in itself, because every previous president wanted unbiased analysis — and as newly dangerous when a president fires the analysts whose assessments he dislikes.

iran-nuclear-assessment.title: The Russian nuclear umbrella
iran-nuclear-assessment.summary: John Kiriakou's report, two days after the Israeli strikes on Iran began in June 2025, that Russia had declared Iran to be under the protection of its nuclear umbrella — and his conclusion that this rules out any Israeli nuclear use against Iran, because it would risk Russian nuclear retaliation against Israel.

iran-nuclear-assessment.title: Trita Parsi
iran-nuclear-assessment.summary: Iran scholar; in a Foreign Affairs piece published August 10, 2025, predicted a renewed Israeli–Iranian war by the end of August 2025; described by John Kiriakou as "one of the greatest Iran scholars on the planet."

iran-nuclear-assessment.title: Mexican 9 Month Work Visas
iran-nuclear-assessment.summary: A George W. Bush-administration proposal, negotiated with Mexico in the six to eight months before 9/11, to give undocumented Mexican workers renewable nine-month U.S. work visas requiring federal income tax payment — killed by the September 11 attacks before it could be ratified.

iran-nuclear-assessment.title: Mossad networks in Iran
iran-nuclear-assessment.summary: The Israeli human-intelligence penetration of Iran that John Kiriakou calls larger than anyone suspected — thousands of clandestine reporters, many of them undocumented Afghan refugees paid the equivalent of fifty or a hundred dollars a month, run in person by spymasters inside the country and compartmentalized so that rolling up one network yields nothing about the others.

iran-posed-no-threat.title: Killing Khamenei
iran-posed-no-threat.summary: John Kiriakou's assessment that the killing of Ayatollah Khamenei during the 2026 war would change nothing, because the West had seriously overestimated his authority — an argument he extends to the American habit of expecting a war to end when a leader is removed.

iran-posed-no-threat.title: Chaos as the Israeli objective
iran-posed-no-threat.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer to whether Netanyahu''s government actually wanted an American invasion of Iran: what the Israelis want in Iran is what they got in Libya — chaos, civil war, and as many dead Iranians as possible.

iran-posed-no-threat.title: Marco Rubio and Iran policy
iran-posed-no-threat.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer to who was actually driving American policy toward Iran in 2026: with the Vice President, the Director of National Intelligence and the Chairman of the Joint Chiefs all reported as opposed, and with Marco Rubio holding both the State Department and the National Security Adviser''s job, the policy was Rubio''s.

iran-posed-no-threat.title: Hypersonic missiles
iran-posed-no-threat.summary: John Kiriakou confirms that hypersonic missiles are real and that Russia, China and Iran all have them; that a weapon travelling 2,500 miles an hour cannot be defended against; and that Iran holds too few of them to do anything but make each one count.

iran-posed-no-threat.title: The Truth Social announcement
iran-posed-no-threat.summary: John Kiriakou''s objection to how the 2026 war was announced: at two o''clock in the morning on Truth Social, with no address from the East Room, and with a president shuttling between Washington and Mar-a-Lago rather than explaining to the country why Americans were being sent to fight.

iran-posed-no-threat.title: MBS and Netanyahu asked Trump to attack Iran
iran-posed-no-threat.summary: John Kiriakou's account that Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu jointly went to Donald Trump and asked him to attack Iran — a move Kiriakou finds hard to reconcile with MBS's own years of work to improve Saudi relations with Tehran.

iran-regional-war-2026.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
iran-regional-war-2026.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

iran-regional-war-2026.title: Houthis
iran-regional-war-2026.summary: The Iran-aligned movement that controls the most important parts of Yemen, described by John Kiriakou as fierce fighters who beat the Saudi military over a decade of war and who in July 2026 declared a naval blockade of Saudi shipping.

iran-regional-war-2026.title: Reza Pahlavi
iran-regional-war-2026.summary: The exiled Iranian crown prince whom John Kiriakou dismisses as an Israeli-backed fantasy candidate to rule Iran — a man who has not lived there since his teens, supported mainly by Beverly Hills exiles, whom Kiriakou says 'wouldn't survive the walk from the plane to the terminal.'

iran-regional-war-2026.title: South Caucasus realignment
iran-regional-war-2026.summary: John Kiriakou''s reading of the post-election South Caucasus: Russia has lost Armenia, Georgia has split from Armenia and moved closer to Moscow, and Iran — contrary to the assumption that two Muslim neighbours would be natural partners — keeps far closer relations with Christian Armenia than with Azerbaijan.

iran-regional-war-2026.title: Pickaxe Mountain
iran-regional-war-2026.summary: The Iranian site whose ongoing excavation Benjamin Netanyahu publicised in July 2026 and which Donald Trump, in response, said he already knew about — using the exchange to tell an ally publicly not to brief the press ahead of him. John Kiriakou reads the episode as Netanyahu attempting to move American public opinion and Trump refusing to be moved.

iran-regional-war-2026.title: Ahmed Chalabi
iran-regional-war-2026.summary: Iraqi exile and founder of the Iraqi National Congress; per John Kiriakou, a Shia-Kurdish con man who looted Petra Bank in Jordan of $36 million in the 1980s, was sentenced to death in absentia, was pardoned at CIA request, then pocketed $6 million in CIA seed funding for the INC and bought a Mayfair house in cash; later resurrected by Dick Cheney to feed the Pentagon fabricated WMD intelligence used to justify the 2003 invasion of Iraq.

iran-strike-factions-2026.title: Reza Pahlavi
iran-strike-factions-2026.summary: The exiled Iranian crown prince whom John Kiriakou dismisses as an Israeli-backed fantasy candidate to rule Iran — a man who has not lived there since his teens, supported mainly by Beverly Hills exiles, whom Kiriakou says 'wouldn't survive the walk from the plane to the terminal.'

iran-strike-factions-2026.title: Iran 12-Day War
iran-strike-factions-2026.summary: 2025 Israeli air campaign against Iran during which Israel killed at least fourteen Iranian nuclear scientists by destroying the apartment buildings they lived in; preceded for each scientist by Farsi-language telephone calls from Iranian-Jewish Mossad and Shin Bet officers offering defection in lieu of certain death; characterized by John Kiriakou as a categorical departure from CIA targeting doctrine in its acceptable-civilian-casualty calculus.

iran-strike-factions-2026.title: Marco Rubio
iran-strike-factions-2026.summary: U.S. official whom John Kiriakou identifies as the real motivator behind pressure on Venezuela; Kiriakou argues Venezuela is not a meaningful drug threat to the U.S. and that Rubio simply wants Maduro gone.

iran-strike-factions-2026.title: Mark Levin Iran Policy
iran-strike-factions-2026.summary: Per Sean Davis, speaking on the same Megyn Kelly panel as Kiriakou, radio host Mark Levin was among the "outside voices" — alongside Senator Lindsey Graham — who effectively made the real policy call to invade Iran. Separately, per John Kiriakou, Levin is one of the very few prominent commentators who consistently defends Israel publicly online.

iran-strike-factions-2026.title: The three legal ways to enter another country
iran-strike-factions-2026.summary: The test John Kiriakou applies to American military action abroad: that there are only three lawful ways for one country to move into another — with the approval of the UN Security Council, at that country''s invitation, or after being attacked by it — and that the United States, in his account, never meets any of the three.

iran-strike-factions-2026.title: U.S. diplomatic vacancies
iran-strike-factions-2026.summary: John Kiriakou's account of how the mass dismissal of career U.S. ambassadors — never replaced — left the Gulf without American envoys as war with Iran loomed, so allied royals had to ask him personally whether the U.S. would attack.

iran-under-sanctions-daily-life.title: China as economic threat
iran-under-sanctions-daily-life.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that China is the real threat to the West not militarily — it has one aircraft carrier to America's two dozen and rarely invades — but economically, buying friends worldwide while the U.S. spends a trillion dollars a year on weapons.

iran-under-sanctions-daily-life.title: Richard D. Wolff
iran-under-sanctions-daily-life.summary: American Marxian economist, professor emeritus at the University of Massachusetts Amherst and a recurring guest of John Kiriakou, who calls him one of his favourite people and says he feels smarter after every conversation; Wolff's appearances supply Kiriakou's audience with a class analysis of tariffs, federal debt and the periodic crashes of capitalism.

iran-under-sanctions-daily-life.title: 2026 Iran war
iran-under-sanctions-daily-life.summary: The open-ended American and Israeli war against Iran that John Kiriakou tracked week by week on his own show — a conflict he says was sold as three weeks, ran into its fifth month, achieved every decapitation objective it set, and continued anyway. His grade for it is a D, and his forecast is a Truth Social post declaring victory while nothing changes.

iran-under-sanctions-daily-life.title: Trump tariffs
iran-under-sanctions-daily-life.summary: The across-the-board tariffs imposed by Donald Trump on United States trading partners, which John Kiriakou describes as having shaken up the economy faster than any president in generations — causing chaos in global stock markets, laying the groundwork for inflation and economic contraction, and producing political upheaval at home.

iran-under-sanctions-daily-life.title: 2026 Iran war economic shock
iran-under-sanctions-daily-life.summary: John Kiriakou''s running assessment of the economic damage from the 2026 Iran war — an oil shock he says already exceeds both 1970s shocks combined, a natural-gas shock worse than the Nord Stream destruction, and a chokepoint problem that runs through fertilizer as much as fuel, since 65% of the world''s supply must transit the Strait of Hormuz. His summary: "This is an economic slowdown of choice."

iran-under-sanctions-daily-life.title: The 2026 strike wave
iran-under-sanctions-daily-life.summary: The proliferation of American strikes in early 2026, from Minneapolis to the Southern California ports, which John Kiriakou raised alongside a February reversal in the job market and the question of whether union membership was rising after years of decline. The economist Richard D. Wolff's answer placed it in the ordinary rhythm of capitalist downturns and ended on employers squeezing workers who were, he said, beginning to really fight back.

iranian-intelligence-capability.title: Iranian strikes on Gulf hotels
iranian-intelligence-capability.summary: John Kiriakou''s reading of the Iranian drone and missile attacks on hotels in Abu Dhabi, Dubai and Muscat during the 2026 war: not targeted killings, but deliberate strikes at the tourist economies of the Gulf states, aimed at hotels famous enough to empty the country of visitors.

iranian-intelligence-capability.title: Embassy fortification after 9/11
iranian-intelligence-capability.summary: The post-2001 rebuilding of American embassies as hardened compounds, which John Kiriakou explains as a direct answer to Iranian Revolutionary Guard reconnaissance of diplomatic premises. His illustration is Doha: an embassy sitting above a grocery store in 1990, and an embassy occupying an entire city block and fortified "nine ways from Sunday" today.

iranian-intelligence-capability.title: Bombing the Omanis
iranian-intelligence-capability.summary: John Kiriakou's judgement that Iran's strikes on the Gulf states — and above all on Oman, which had been trying to broker peace — made enemies Iran did not need to make, of governments that would otherwise have sat the war out.

iranian-intelligence-capability.title: Dubai as Iran's window
iranian-intelligence-capability.summary: John Kiriakou''s explanation of why Iran did not hit Dubai hard during the 2026 war: the city is full of Iranian businessmen and is Iran''s outlet to the Western world and its principal means of evading sanctions.

iranian-intelligence-capability.title: Italian intelligence services
iranian-intelligence-capability.summary: John Kiriakou's assessment of the Italian services as very good and very close partners of the CIA — except in the Abu Omar case, when they refused to help, were ignored, and responded by investigating the CIA and identifying twenty-one of its officers.

iranian-intelligence-capability.title: "Most other countries are more moral than the CIA"
iranian-intelligence-capability.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer to a viewer who asked whether the United States has the most moral intelligence agency: it does not, and a hundred countries could be named whose services behave better — the disqualifying practice being the killing of people who pose no threat to the United States.

iranian-oil-sanctions-relief-2026.title: Asian fuel reserves, 2026
iranian-oil-sanctions-relief-2026.summary: The effect of the Strait of Hormuz closure on oil-importing Asian economies as John Kiriakou described it — countries counting their remaining fuel in days rather than months, with no substitute supply available, and economies he expects simply to stop.

iranian-oil-sanctions-relief-2026.title: 2026 Iran war economic shock
iranian-oil-sanctions-relief-2026.summary: John Kiriakou''s running assessment of the economic damage from the 2026 Iran war — an oil shock he says already exceeds both 1970s shocks combined, a natural-gas shock worse than the Nord Stream destruction, and a chokepoint problem that runs through fertilizer as much as fuel, since 65% of the world''s supply must transit the Strait of Hormuz. His summary: "This is an economic slowdown of choice."

iranian-oil-sanctions-relief-2026.title: Donald Trump
iranian-oil-sanctions-relief-2026.summary: 45th and 47th U.S. president. Per John Kiriakou, a man genuinely convinced he was doing right by bombing Iran, "duped" by the same Netanyahu nuclear bluff Obama once rejected — and, at the same time, the most blindly pro-Israel president in history, an admirer of autocrats who has never once criticized Vladimir Putin, and prone to gestures — from the Gulf of America to a since-abandoned "Department of War" rename — that test the edges of his actual authority.

iranian-oil-sanctions-relief-2026.title: Strait of Hormuz
iranian-oil-sanctions-relief-2026.summary: The shipping chokepoint at the mouth of the Persian Gulf, and the centre of gravity of the 2026 Iran war in John Kiriakou''s account — a strait whose only navigable deep water lies on the Iranian side of the maritime border, closed not by Iran''s aggression but, as he insists, by the American and Israeli attack that provoked it: "The Strait of Hormuz was open. We''re the ones that forced the closure."

iranian-oil-sanctions-relief-2026.title: Air wars are overrated
iranian-oil-sanctions-relief-2026.summary: John Kiriakou''s summary judgement on the 2026 Iran and Lebanon campaigns, delivered as the meta-headline of the whole war: air power flattened Gaza without destroying Hamas, is bogging down against Hezbollah, and cannot produce the outcome the war requires.

iranian-sleeper-cells.title: 2026 Iran war
iranian-sleeper-cells.summary: The open-ended American and Israeli war against Iran that John Kiriakou tracked week by week on his own show — a conflict he says was sold as three weeks, ran into its fifth month, achieved every decapitation objective it set, and continued anyway. His grade for it is a D, and his forecast is a Truth Social post declaring victory while nothing changes.

iranian-sleeper-cells.title: Sarah Adams
iranian-sleeper-cells.summary: A former CIA open-source analyst and frequent television commentator on terrorist threats, whom John Kiriakou dismisses in unusually direct terms: that she never held access to classified information, that she analysed press rather than intelligence, and that she has built a living out of predicting imminent disaster.

iranian-sleeper-cells.title: CIA liaison relationships
iranian-sleeper-cells.summary: John Kiriakou's critique of CIA intelligence-liaison relationships with foreign governments — sharply expanded after 9/11 — arguing that officers do not consider the long-term risk that disclosing sensitive operations to foreign services hands those governments leverage, including potential blackmail material, over the United States, and that no one left in Congress has the will to provide real oversight of the practice.

iranian-sleeper-cells.title: The Iranian elementary school strike
iranian-sleeper-cells.summary: A Tomahawk cruise missile strike at the start of the 2026 war that killed more than 175 people at an Iranian elementary school. The United States denied responsibility until its own investigation confirmed it; John Kiriakou traces the failure to targeting data a decade out of date and expects no one to be punished for it.

iranian-sleeper-cells.title: John Kiriakou
iranian-sleeper-cells.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

iranian-strikes-on-gulf-hotels.title: Bombing the Omanis
iranian-strikes-on-gulf-hotels.summary: John Kiriakou's judgement that Iran's strikes on the Gulf states — and above all on Oman, which had been trying to broker peace — made enemies Iran did not need to make, of governments that would otherwise have sat the war out.

iranian-strikes-on-gulf-hotels.title: Why the UAE was targeted
iranian-strikes-on-gulf-hotels.summary: John Kiriakou''s explanation for the disproportionate weight of Iranian fire falling on the United Arab Emirates in 2026: not the American presence but the Emirati role at the forefront of the war against the Houthis — and a wish to bloody Emirati noses despite the thousands of Iranians living in Dubai.

iranian-strikes-on-gulf-hotels.title: Iranian intelligence capability
iranian-strikes-on-gulf-hotels.summary: John Kiriakou's assessment of Iranian intelligence as poor and always having been poor, on the ground that Iranian officers do not receive good training and are essentially on their own, with only marginal help from the Russians and the Chinese.

iranian-strikes-on-gulf-hotels.title: THAAD stocks in the Gulf
iranian-strikes-on-gulf-hotels.summary: John Kiriakou's report, during the 2026 war, that the United Arab Emirates were seven days from exhausting their THAAD interceptors and Qatar four days — with American resupply unable to keep pace.

iranian-strikes-on-gulf-hotels.title: Embassy fortification after 9/11
iranian-strikes-on-gulf-hotels.summary: The post-2001 rebuilding of American embassies as hardened compounds, which John Kiriakou explains as a direct answer to Iranian Revolutionary Guard reconnaissance of diplomatic premises. His illustration is Doha: an embassy sitting above a grocery store in 1990, and an embassy occupying an entire city block and fortified "nine ways from Sunday" today.

iranian-strikes-on-gulf-hotels.title: A dangerous neighborhood
iranian-strikes-on-gulf-hotels.summary: The contrast John Kiriakou drew between his Gulf contacts on the second day of the 2026 Iran war — friends in Dubai who were panicked as drones struck the city's landmark towers, and the son of a senior Qatari official who simply chuckled and said 'this is life in the Middle East. We live in a dangerous neighborhood.'

iranian-suicide-drones.title: The Iron Dome
iranian-suicide-drones.summary: Israel's air-defence system as John Kiriakou reads it — impressive against a wave of slow Iranian drones, but shown by the handful that got through, and later by Iranian ballistic missiles, to be not all it is cracked up to be; each exchange, in his account, buying Iran intelligence about the gaps.

iranian-suicide-drones.title: 2026 Iran war
iranian-suicide-drones.summary: The open-ended American and Israeli war against Iran that John Kiriakou tracked week by week on his own show — a conflict he says was sold as three weeks, ran into its fifth month, achieved every decapitation objective it set, and continued anyway. His grade for it is a D, and his forecast is a Truth Social post declaring victory while nothing changes.

iranian-suicide-drones.title: The indicator he'd be watching
iranian-suicide-drones.summary: Asked what single sign would most alarm him if he were still inside the CIA on the first day of the 2026 Iran war, John Kiriakou named the movement of ground forces: about fifty thousand American troops are in the region, which cannot invade a country of ninety-two million, and it is the arrival of hundreds of thousands more — plus the last uncommitted carrier battle group — that would frighten him.

iranian-suicide-drones.title: Akrotiri Village Evacuation
iranian-suicide-drones.summary: Kiriakou says the drone that hit Britain's Akrotiri base in Cyprus was likely an Israeli operation, staged and then falsely blamed on Iran.

iranian-suicide-drones.title: John Kiriakou
iranian-suicide-drones.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

iranian-suicide-drones.title: The Fifth Fleet in Bahrain
iranian-suicide-drones.summary: The United States naval presence based in Bahrain since 1976 — the naval component of Central Command, headquartered at Manama. For John Kiriakou as a young diplomat it was mainly a social resource: the officers'' club for its salad bar, the enlisted club for football and cheap beer. It was also, he came to understand, the reason his reporting on Bahraini extrajudicial killings went nowhere. The ambassador''s summary of the alliance was four words long. In 2026 the headquarters was itself hit by Iranian missiles — an outcome that, in Kiriakou''s reading, inverts the entire purpose of the Gulf basing architecture.

iranian-underground-missile-silos.title: The obliteration claim
iranian-underground-missile-silos.summary: Donald Trump's statement that the Iranian nuclear programme had been "obliterated", and John Kiriakou's reading of it. Kiriakou offers three possibilities — the president lied, was tricked, or did not understand what had been achieved — and notes the claim's incompatibility with the later justification that Iran was days away from a weapon.

iranian-underground-missile-silos.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
iranian-underground-missile-silos.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

iranian-underground-missile-silos.title: 2026 Iran war
iranian-underground-missile-silos.summary: The open-ended American and Israeli war against Iran that John Kiriakou tracked week by week on his own show — a conflict he says was sold as three weeks, ran into its fifth month, achieved every decapitation objective it set, and continued anyway. His grade for it is a D, and his forecast is a Truth Social post declaring victory while nothing changes.

iranian-underground-missile-silos.title: Cost of the 2026 Iran war
iranian-underground-missile-silos.summary: The daily cost of the 2026 Iran war as John Kiriakou reported it — between two and three billion dollars a day, per Axios — and the comparison he draws with the Gulf War, when a president was rendered speechless by a figure of one hundred million dollars a day.

iranian-underground-missile-silos.title: Donald Trump
iranian-underground-missile-silos.summary: 45th and 47th U.S. president. Per John Kiriakou, a man genuinely convinced he was doing right by bombing Iran, "duped" by the same Netanyahu nuclear bluff Obama once rejected — and, at the same time, the most blindly pro-Israel president in history, an admirer of autocrats who has never once criticized Vladimir Putin, and prone to gestures — from the Gulf of America to a since-abandoned "Department of War" rename — that test the edges of his actual authority.

iranian-underground-missile-silos.title: The hundred-million-a-day briefing
iranian-underground-missile-silos.summary: A story John Kiriakou tells from his time as a CIA analyst during the Gulf War: the president''s morning briefer returned to the office and reported that the president had been shocked speechless on being told the United States was spending one hundred million dollars a day in the Gulf.

iraq-the-training-account.title: The Powell telephone call
iraq-the-training-account.summary: The morning call John Kiriakou says he took from General Colin Powell, then chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, asking who would have run an Iraqi operation to kill former President George H. W. Bush; Kiriakou named the Iraqi Intelligence Service station in Basra and its headquarters in Baghdad, and eight hours later the United States fired forty-eight cruise missiles at that building.

iraq-the-training-account.title: Arabic and Greek
iraq-the-training-account.summary: The qualification John Kiriakou says opened the door to his transfer from CIA analysis to operations: a post in Athens wanted Greek or Arabic, and he had both — by most of his tellings the only officer in the agency who did. The chief who hired him gave the reason in one sentence: it is easier and cheaper to take a linguist and teach him operations than the other way round. The pairing also became a detection tool, since the language nobody speaks in Pakistan is Arabic.

iraq-the-training-account.title: Training to kill
iraq-the-training-account.summary: John Kiriakou's account of arriving at the CIA's clandestine training facility expecting to learn how to recruit sources at diplomatic cocktail parties, and finding instead parachute training, resistance-to-interrogation instruction, and — as his old supervisor had warned him — training to kill people.

iraq-the-training-account.title: Bankruptcy and the dropped charges
iraq-the-training-account.summary: The sequence John Kiriakou places at the centre of his case: that the espionage counts against him were dropped only after his legal fees had bankrupted him, which he presents as evidence that the government''s aim was attrition rather than conviction.

iraq-the-training-account.title: Curtailment cables
iraq-the-training-account.summary: The career-ending requests John Kiriakou says he read coming back from the CIA's black sites — officers, doctors, psychologists and nurses asking to end their tours early rather than continue to take part in the interrogation programme — and his conclusion that if that many people were objecting in classified channels, someone would surely go public.

iraq-the-training-account.title: "It''s about mitigating damage"
iraq-the-training-account.summary: The sentence John Kiriakou credits with changing his mind about going to trial — one of his own attorneys telling him that his problem was that he thought the case was about justice, when it was about mitigating damage — and the two lawyers who drove to his house after he emailed at six in the morning to refuse the plea.

iraq-war-israeli-tower-sabotage.title: Guantánamo Bay detention camp
iraq-war-israeli-tower-sabotage.summary: Per John Kiriakou — as chief of counterterrorism operations in Pakistan after September 11, 2001 — the Guantanamo detention facility began as a temporary holding measure intended to last two to three weeks while the CIA and Justice Department determined which federal district court should try each prisoner, not as a long-term detention infrastructure. The Rawalpindi jail had reached capacity, Pakistani intelligence demanded the prisoners be removed, and CIA headquarters directed Kiriakou to load them onto a C-12 cargo plane and fly them to Cuba.

iraq-war-israeli-tower-sabotage.title: Pakistan Station (2002)
iraq-war-israeli-tower-sabotage.summary: John Kiriakou's January 2002 arrival in Islamabad to become CIA chief of counterterrorism operations — a journey via London and Kuwait with lost luggage, a warning that steered him away from the soon-to-be-bombed Marriott, a skeleton counterterrorism branch of seven CIA retirees, and the raids that followed.

iraq-war-israeli-tower-sabotage.title: 9/11 Commission
iraq-war-israeli-tower-sabotage.summary: The federal commission of inquiry into the September 11 attacks, which John Kiriakou describes as structurally incapable of reaching the truth because it was barred from interviewing serving CIA officers or any Guantanamo detainee, and was blocked by the CIA from pursuing the Saudi thread.

iraq-war-israeli-tower-sabotage.title: 9/11 plea agreements
iraq-war-israeli-tower-sabotage.summary: The Biden-era plea deals under which Khalid Sheikh Mohammed and co-defendants agreed to plead guilty to murdering 2,976 people in exchange for life without parole and a guarantee against transfer to the Colorado supermax — vacated by the Secretary of Defense after public backlash. Per John Kiriakou, the deals existed because torture had rendered every confession inadmissible, leaving no usable evidence.

iraq-war-israeli-tower-sabotage.title: Abu Zubaydah
iraq-war-israeli-tower-sabotage.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

iraq-war-israeli-tower-sabotage.title: Agnes von Kurowsky grave story
iraq-war-israeli-tower-sabotage.summary: John Kiriakou's account of discovering the Washington, D.C. grave of Agnes von Kurowsky, the World War I Red Cross nurse whose four-month wartime romance with a young ambulance driver, Ernest Hemingway, made her the model for the lead female character in six of his books, including A Farewell to Arms.

iraq-wmd-intelligence.title: Dick Cheney
iraq-wmd-intelligence.summary: U.S. Vice President under George W. Bush. Per John Kiriakou — recounting CIA Director George Tenet's memoir — Cheney intercepted the presidential finding authorizing the CIA's enhanced interrogation program in the Oval Office anteroom and took it from Tenet before Bush could sign it. Tenet later concluded the president probably never actually signed the finding and probably told the truth when he said he had no idea the program was taking place. Kiriakou characterizes Cheney as the one who actually ran foreign policy, intelligence policy, and defense policy during the Bush years.

iraq-wmd-intelligence.title: Principals Committee Meeting (February 2003)
iraq-wmd-intelligence.summary: Senior-most interagency forum of the U.S. national security apparatus, normally chaired by the president. Per John Kiriakou — who served as notetaker for CIA Director George Tenet at the eve-of-Iraq-invasion meeting on February 19–20, 2003 — Vice President Dick Cheney chaired in place of Bush, General Tommy Franks ended his order-of-battle briefing with 'If all goes as planned, we can be in Tehran by August,' and an NSC senior director said 'When we cross that border tomorrow morning, they're going to throw flowers at us.'

iraq-wmd-intelligence.title: Wesley Clark
iraq-wmd-intelligence.summary: Retired U.S. Army four-star general and former Clinton administration adviser; per John Kiriakou, "a very good guy", "one of the very, very few people at that level", and the public source of the account that in the weeks after 9/11 the Pentagon was working to a memo listing seven governments to be overthrown. Kiriakou treats Clark's story as corroborated by his own — on 6 May 2002 a CIA security officer told him, in the course of signing him onto the agency's most sensitive programmes, that the United States would invade Iraq the following year.

iraq-wmd-intelligence.title: The Taft joke
iraq-wmd-intelligence.summary: The moment at a White House briefing that John Kiriakou offers as the whole difference between the two men at the top of the Bush administration — a self-deprecating crack about William Howard Taft that left the president helpless with laughter and the vice president standing like a statue.

iraq-wmd-intelligence.title: The counterfeit dollar trade
iraq-wmd-intelligence.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of high-quality counterfeit US currency — the Swiss paper that makes it possible, an estimate that five to ten percent of the notes in circulation may be forged, and a quiet policy of buying up caches at thirty cents on the dollar and incinerating them.

iraq-wmd-intelligence.title: Lawrence Wilkerson
iraq-wmd-intelligence.summary: Retired Army colonel, chief of staff and closest friend to Secretary of State Colin Powell; John Kiriakou counts him among the most consequential military whistleblowers, cites his count of 108 deaths in military custody, and says Wilkerson confirmed on air that Powell's UN case for the Iraq war was knowingly "sold."

ireland-recognizes-palestine.title: France recognises Palestine
ireland-recognizes-palestine.summary: Emmanuel Macron's decision in July 2025 to extend formal recognition to the Republic of Palestine and exchange ambassadors, which John Kiriakou called a turning point that could not be overstated — the first serious crack in Western support for Israel, and significant precisely because France is a historic colonial power in the Middle East with a Security Council veto.

ireland-recognizes-palestine.title: The General Assembly workaround
ireland-recognizes-palestine.summary: A proposal John Kiriakou says a Russian diplomat described to him: letting the United Nations General Assembly take implementable decisions without Security Council permission, so that a supermajority of states could override an American veto. Kiriakou, whose last CIA tour was at the United Nations and who found the institution paralysed, says he thinks it is a good idea.

ireland-recognizes-palestine.title: The Greek turn toward Israel
ireland-recognizes-palestine.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of why Athens abandoned its traditional pro-Arab alignment and embraced Israel — a 180-degree flip he attributes to the collapse of Turkey''s relationship with Israel and, above all, to money: Israeli property buying that he says has tripled Greek house prices, and Cypriot gas fields Greece hopes to develop with Israeli partners.

ireland-recognizes-palestine.title: Proposals to relocate the Palestinians
ireland-recognizes-palestine.summary: John Kiriakou's account of recurring schemes to solve the Palestinian question by moving the population somewhere else — including a 1980s proposal to rename a barren diamond of land on the Saudi–Iraqi border "Palestine" and resettle everyone there — and his verdict that picking up an entire people and moving them is unprecedented and untenable.

ireland-recognizes-palestine.title: Ali from Newark
ireland-recognizes-palestine.summary: The Black shot caller at FCI Loretto, near the end of a twenty-five-year drug sentence, who came to embrace John Kiriakou at the close of his term and tell him how much he respected him — a friendship possible only because Kiriakou had decided on arrival to ignore the prison's racial divisions.

ireland-recognizes-palestine.title: Bezalel Smotrich
ireland-recognizes-palestine.summary: Israeli far-right minister whom John Kiriakou, alongside Itamar Ben-Gvir, blames for leaving Israel unprepared on October 7 by insisting any attack would come from the West Bank rather than Gaza.

irish-intelligence-services.title: Al-Qaeda training manual interrogation-resistance tactics
irish-intelligence-services.summary: A captured al-Qaeda training manual instructing operatives on how to resist interrogation, including feigning illness — a technique John Kiriakou says he saw a detainee use, and recognized, during a capture and interrogation in Pakistan.

irish-intelligence-services.title: China's base in Djibouti
irish-intelligence-services.summary: Camp Lemonnier in Djibouti, the abandoned French base the Djiboutians offered to the Americans and the Chinese took a share of — split down the middle by a chain-link fence, the only Chinese military installation outside China, and the centrepiece of John Kiriakou's argument that China is not an expansionist power.

irish-intelligence-services.title: Kent State shooting
irish-intelligence-services.summary: The 1970 shooting of unarmed student protesters by the Ohio National Guard; John Kiriakou says a family friend's daughter was among those killed — the closing event of a 1968–69 upheaval he treats both as the formation of his own politics and as the historical measure against which he judges the present.

irish-intelligence-services.title: Small-country intelligence services
irish-intelligence-services.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of dealing with the intelligence services of very small states — Djibouti, whose entire service he says occupied less space than his rented townhouse, and whose director''s office was half the size of his living room. His operating rule is that respect is the whole of the tradecraft: address the director as Your Excellency, and doors open that money cannot.

irish-intelligence-services.title: John Kiriakou
irish-intelligence-services.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

irish-intelligence-services.title: 2026 Iran war
irish-intelligence-services.summary: The open-ended American and Israeli war against Iran that John Kiriakou tracked week by week on his own show — a conflict he says was sold as three weeks, ran into its fifth month, achieved every decapitation objective it set, and continued anyway. His grade for it is a D, and his forecast is a Truth Social post declaring victory while nothing changes.

iron-dome.title: Iran's 2024 drone retaliation
iron-dome.summary: John Kiriakou's account of Iran's telegraphed 2024 drone strike on Israel — hundreds of slow drones, launched with advance warning to the U.S. and Jordan, nearly all shot down, which he reads as a controlled show of force and an intelligence victory that exposed the Iron Dome.

iron-dome.title: Evangelical Zionism
iron-dome.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the American Christian movement that supports Israel in order to hasten the return of Christ — a belief he calls a cult rather than a religion, which he says Israeli officials knowingly exploit, and which he blames for the abandonment of the Middle East's original Christians.

iron-dome.title: The Cyprus fruit relabel
iron-dome.summary: The 1970s workaround John Kiriakou has described for the Arab boycott of Israeli produce, Israeli fruit shipped to Cyprus, repacked in *"Produce of Cyprus"* boxes, then sold on into the Gulf. Kiriakou uses it as the specific answer to why the Abraham Accords look, in his account, less like a diplomatic breakthrough than the final removal of a fig leaf on a trade that had already been happening for half a century.

iron-dome.title: Josh Shapiro
iron-dome.summary: Governor of Pennsylvania; veteran of the Israel Defense Forces, in which he served during his late-teen kibbutz year before returning to U.S. citizenship; cited by John Kiriakou as the principal example of the loyalty question raised by American elected officials who have served the Israeli state — a disqualification Kiriakou states in absolute terms, and one he judges to have ended Shapiro's national prospects.

iron-dome.title: Strategic patience
iron-dome.summary: The doctrine John Kiriakou uses to describe a state that absorbs an attack and answers with a response calibrated to be smaller than the provocation — Iran's telegraphed drone waves against Israel, and India's refusal to escalate against Pakistan, which he says kept a war from becoming a nuclear one.

iron-dome.title: The Iran–Israel exchange assessment
iron-dome.summary: John Kiriakou''s judgement — which he expects to be unpopular — that Iran came out ahead of Israel in their direct missile exchange: the Iron Dome proved fallible, Iranian targeting was selective where Israel''s was not, and the ceasefire came, in his reading, because Israel had run out of missiles.

irs-audits-of-kiriakou.title: CIA crimes reports against Kiriakou
irs-audits-of-kiriakou.summary: The referral mechanism by which the Central Intelligence Agency asked the Justice Department to investigate John Kiriakou, used not once but repeatedly — by his account after every op-ed, television interview and university speech he gave following his 2007 disclosure of the torture program. The Justice Department declined every time, and Kiriakou treats the pattern as retaliation conducted through a lawful channel.

irs-audits-of-kiriakou.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
irs-audits-of-kiriakou.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

irs-audits-of-kiriakou.title: Publications Review Board
irs-audits-of-kiriakou.summary: The CIA office that must clear anything a former officer publishes. John Kiriakou says everything he writes goes to it — books, articles, "even a letter to the editor of Home and Garden magazine" — and describes how the turnaround tracked his standing at the agency: his first book took 22 months to clear while the leadership hated him; his most recent six cleared in days.

irs-audits-of-kiriakou.title: Intelligence Identities Protection Act
irs-audits-of-kiriakou.summary: U.S. law enacted in 1982 that makes it a crime to knowingly disclose the identity of a covert intelligence officer; per John Kiriakou, his 2012 prosecution under the act arose from confirming a single surname of a former CIA colleague to a journalist — a confirmation that was never published. The name passed through a chain from journalist to Human Rights Watch to Guantanamo defense attorneys before reaching a judge and ultimately the FBI, which traced it back to Kiriakou.

irs-audits-of-kiriakou.title: The CIPA hearing in Kiriakou's case
irs-audits-of-kiriakou.summary: The closed pre-trial proceeding under the Classified Information Procedures Act at which John Kiriakou's defence filed seventy motions to declassify the material it needed to mount a defence, and the judge denied all seventy at once. Kiriakou describes the ruling as the moment the case ended — his lead attorney told him on the way out of the courtroom that they had just lost — and as the point at which plea negotiations began.

irs-audits-of-kiriakou.title: Leonie Brinkema
irs-audits-of-kiriakou.summary: U.S. federal judge in the Eastern District of Virginia — informally the 'Espionage Court' — a Reagan appointee John Kiriakou calls "a hanging judge." Per Kiriakou, Brinkema systematically reserved all major national security cases for herself rather than allowing them to be distributed randomly among judges, and ruled in Kiriakou's case that his reason for blowing the whistle was legally irrelevant and that classified documents could not be used in his defense — effectively making it impossible to mount one.

isa-bin-salman-al-khalifa.title: Bahrain Posting (1994–1996)
isa-bin-salman-al-khalifa.summary: John Kiriakou's 1994–1996 assignment to Bahrain under U.S. State Department cover as second secretary for economic affairs — arriving with his wife Joanne and infant son Chris on August 1, 1994, into a tiny Gulf monarchy whose sectarian tensions erupted, two months later, into the first Intifada.

isa-bin-salman-al-khalifa.title: Bahrain Intifada (1994)
isa-bin-salman-al-khalifa.summary: The first Bahraini Intifada, a Shia uprising against the Sunni Al Khalifa monarchy that began roughly two months into John Kiriakou's 1994 Bahrain posting with a bombing at the Ministry of Labor, led by Abdul Amir Al-Jamri, and met by the government first with police, then armored personnel carriers and tanks, and executions.

isa-bin-salman-al-khalifa.title: Bahrain Prime Minister "Mr. 10 Percent"
isa-bin-salman-al-khalifa.summary: John Kiriakou's account of Bahrain's long-serving prime minister, the Amir's uncle, universally nicknamed "Mr. 10 Percent" for allegedly requiring a 10 percent cash cut on business deals — a cold, calculating figure Kiriakou calls "the definition of corruption," pointedly excluded from the national motto, yet credited with turning Bahrain into the Gulf's banking hub.

isa-bin-salman-al-khalifa.title: ''An unusually violent society''
isa-bin-salman-al-khalifa.summary: The judgment the Amir of Bahrain delivered to John Kiriakou in the mid-1990s, shortly after the Oklahoma City bombing — that Americans are accepting of violence 'that would be unacceptable in any other civilized country,' even by Arab standards. Kiriakou says he had no answer, because it was true, and he has since used it as the frame for political shootings in the United States.

isa-bin-salman-al-khalifa.title: Abdul Amir al-Jamri
isa-bin-salman-al-khalifa.summary: The Bahraini cleric who led the Shia opposition during the 1990s uprising, and whom John Kiriakou interviewed for a human rights report in 1991 — an interview that had the Bahraini prime minister demanding, within the hour, that both American officers be expelled from the country.

isa-bin-salman-al-khalifa.title: Salman bin Hamad
isa-bin-salman-al-khalifa.summary: The Bahraini heir presumptive who became John Kiriakou's friend during his 1994–96 posting — president of the Bahrain Center for Studies and Research and patron of the environmental association, both of which fell in Kiriakou's economic brief, and a companion on nights out at a nightclub by the naval base.

isi.title: Abu Zubaydah
isi.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

isi.title: A.Q. Khan
isi.summary: Pakistani nuclear scientist and the architect of Pakistan's bomb, who ran a black-market proliferation network that, per John Kiriakou, smuggled nuclear material and technology to North Korea and Libya. Kiriakou says the U.S. could easily have killed him — 'we knew where he lived, we knew how he spent his day' — but the Saudi government insisted the U.S. leave him alone, which Kiriakou calls a grave mistake and speculates was because the Saudis were pursuing their own nuclear capability. Khan was eventually pardoned by Pervez Musharraf, ending all investigations.

isi.title: Pervez Musharraf
isi.summary: Pakistani general and military dictator who ruled during John Kiriakou's 2002 posting as CIA chief of counterterrorism operations in Pakistan. Per Kiriakou, the United States 'essentially just purchased Musharraf,' paying tens of millions in cash to the ISI and meeting him several times a week — and in return 'he would let us do whatever we wanted.' Kiriakou says Musharraf, fearing the nuclear arsenal could fall into terrorist hands, unofficially turned control of Pakistan's nuclear weapons over to the Pentagon. Musharraf later pardoned proliferator A.Q. Khan.

isi.title: Tora Bora
isi.summary: Mountainous cave complex in eastern Afghanistan that served as an al-Qaeda redoubt after the September 11 attacks. Per John Kiriakou — chief of counterterrorism operations in Pakistan at the time — the CIA killed al-Qaeda military-affairs chief Mohammed Atef there in October 2001, and Tora Bora was the backdrop to the hunt for the senior al-Qaeda leadership that culminated in the capture of Abu Zubaydah.
