james-morris.summary: Israel's air-defence system as John Kiriakou reads it — impressive against a wave of slow Iranian drones, but shown by the handful that got through, and later by Iranian ballistic missiles, to be not all it is cracked up to be; each exchange, in his account, buying Iran intelligence about the gaps.

james-morris.title: Presidents asleep in meetings
james-morris.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer to who is the highest-profile person he ever saw fall asleep in a meeting — George H. W. Bush — together with his explanation that presidents do it all the time because the demands on their time leave too few hours in the day, and his father''s account of Ronald Reagan doing it constantly.

james-risen.title: Donald Trump
james-risen.summary: 45th and 47th U.S. president. Per John Kiriakou, a man genuinely convinced he was doing right by bombing Iran, "duped" by the same Netanyahu nuclear bluff Obama once rejected — and, at the same time, the most blindly pro-Israel president in history, an admirer of autocrats who has never once criticized Vladimir Putin, and prone to gestures — from the Gulf of America to a since-abandoned "Department of War" rename — that test the edges of his actual authority.

james-risen.title: Leaking versus whistleblowing
james-risen.summary: The distinction John Kiriakou insists is legal rather than rhetorical — whistleblowing being the disclosure of waste, fraud, abuse, illegality or threats to public health and safety, and leaking being everything else. He applies the same statutory test to Edward Snowden, to Chelsea Manning and to his own case, holds that motive is irrelevant to whether the test is met, and had to have the definition explained to him by his own attorney, because no whistleblower thinks he is one.

james-risen.title: Espionage Act
james-risen.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

james-risen.title: Official leaks
james-risen.summary: The category of disclosure John Kiriakou says is both the largest and the only one that is never prosecuted — trial balloons and opinion-shaping put out by the White House, the National Security Council and the Pentagon, with the president himself as the most prolific leaker in Washington.

james-risen.title: Declassifying for a foreign government
james-risen.summary: The CIA procedure John Kiriakou describes for passing classified intelligence to a foreign service — the originating office extracts the substance onto a fresh sheet marked releasable to that country, so that no source or method travels with it — set out in 2017 as the thing Donald Trump did not do when he spoke to the Russian foreign minister and ambassador in the Oval Office.

james-risen.title: H. R. McMaster
james-risen.summary: National Security Adviser during the May 2017 controversy over Donald Trump's disclosure of intelligence to Russian officials, whose public defence — that the president had not been briefed on the source of the information — John Kiriakou treated as a fork in which either answer reflects badly on McMaster himself.

james-woolsey.title: President's Daily Brief
james-woolsey.summary: Per John Kiriakou, the President's Daily Brief (PDB) is a roughly 16-page, top-secret intelligence document produced daily for the president, written in a uniform CIA house style, briefed each morning, and — in his account — used partly to gauge and flatter incoming presidents.

james-woolsey.title: Aldrich Ames
james-woolsey.summary: Senior CIA officer — a GS-15 who rose to chief of counterintelligence for the Soviet branch — who spied for the KGB for nine years. Per John Kiriakou, Ames walked into the Soviet embassy in Washington in April 1985 and sold the identities of two CIA-recruited double agents for $50,000 to clear a debt run up by his second marriage; both were executed. He went on to identify more than thirty agents, compromise over a hundred clandestine operations, cause at least twelve deaths and take more than $2 million, while being known throughout the agency as a daily drunk and promoted at every turn. The KGB protected him with a decoy mole hunt; analyst Sandy Grimes caught him by matching his handler meetings to his bank deposits.

james-woolsey.title: Bill Clinton
james-woolsey.summary: 42nd U.S. president whom John Kiriakou describes as wholly disinterested in intelligence — briefed by the CIA only twice in eight years, with Vice President Al Gore taking the daily briefing instead and relaying anything important.

james-woolsey.title: Havana Syndrome
james-woolsey.summary: Cluster of neurological symptoms — including nausea, ringing in the ears, vertigo, and traumatic brain injury — reported by American diplomatic and intelligence personnel beginning in Havana, Cuba, and subsequently at posts around the world. Per John Kiriakou, his initial skepticism gave way when a friend developed Havana Syndrome with an MRI-confirmed traumatic brain injury after a meeting outside the Russian Foreign Ministry; Kiriakou attributes the syndrome to Russian or Chinese directed-energy weapons and acknowledges the United States used a similar weapon during the operation to capture Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro.

james-woolsey.title: Bill Binney
james-woolsey.summary: Former NSA technical director whom John Kiriakou cites as having debunked the DNC hack. Asked by Veteran Intelligence Professionals for Sanity to examine the science, Binney analyzed the speed of the upload and concluded the emails could only have been copied in person to a thumb drive, not taken remotely by Russia — an argument he later made to Donald Trump in the Oval Office. Kiriakou calls him a friend, the most brilliant person he has met on electronics, and a member of the whistleblower circle he belongs to.

james-woolsey.title: Democratic redistricting collapse
james-woolsey.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of why Republicans remain competitive despite historically low approval ratings: a 1992 decision he attributes to Hillary Clinton to spend only in presidential battlegrounds, which he says ceded state legislatures and the congressional map for decades.

jane-harman.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
jane-harman.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

jane-harman.title: Senate Torture Report
jane-harman.summary: The December 2014 executive summary of the U.S. Senate Select Committee on Intelligence's study of the CIA's post-9/11 detention and interrogation program; the first public disclosure of techniques including rectal feeding with hummus, sexual assault with broomsticks, and prolonged sleep deprivation.

jane-harman.title: Abu Zubaydah
jane-harman.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

jane-harman.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
jane-harman.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

jane-harman.title: Cold cell
jane-harman.summary: A CIA interrogation technique in which a stripped detainee is chained to a ceiling eyebolt in a cell chilled to 50°F, then doused with a bucket of ice water at hourly intervals; never authorized; documented to have killed at least two prisoners.

jane-harman.title: Federal Torture Act
jane-harman.summary: United States statute criminalizing torture; per John Kiriakou, on the books since at least 1946, with concrete enforcement history — after World War II the United States executed Japanese soldiers convicted of waterboarding American prisoners of war, meaning waterboarding was at that time a capital offense under U.S. law. The act was effectively set aside for the CIA's enhanced interrogation program after 2002.

japanese-diplomat-fbi-sting.title: Edward Snowden
japanese-diplomat-fbi-sting.summary: Former NSA contractor who in 2013 disclosed the scope of U.S. [mass surveillance](/wiki/mass-surveillance), including the Section 702 collection program. Per John Kiriakou — who counts Snowden among the small group of national-security whistleblowers prosecuted under the Espionage Act — Snowden was ''stuck between two awful slippery slopes'': breaking his oath and chain of command on one side, and on the other catching something ''cut and dry against the Constitution'' that no one would act on. Kiriakou notes Snowden could not use his chain of command (as Kiriakou could not, his own chain being Jose Rodriguez), and that Judge Leonie Brinkema had reserved the Snowden case for herself before he fled the country.

japanese-diplomat-fbi-sting.title: Federal plea coercion
japanese-diplomat-fbi-sting.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that the federal justice system coerces guilty pleas by stacking charges and winning 98.2% of its cases — so that even innocent defendants take deals, as he did, told by his own attorney that the system is 'not about justice; it's about mitigating damage.'

japanese-diplomat-fbi-sting.title: Recruitment attempts on Kiriakou
japanese-diplomat-fbi-sting.summary: A series of episodes in which foreign intelligence officers tried to recruit John Kiriakou himself — an over-eager Hungarian during his CIA application, a French counterterrorism officer who staged a car pickup in Islamabad, and a Shin Bet officer at his first liaison briefing.

japanese-diplomat-fbi-sting.title: The 2016 research pitch
japanese-diplomat-fbi-sting.summary: An approach made to John Kiriakou in October 2016, roughly eighteen months after his release from prison, by a caller claiming to be a former CIA colleague who offered him five thousand dollars a month to conduct classified research. Kiriakou reads it as a second entrapment attempt, mounted after his sentence was already served, and says he identified it by the caller's mistakes with agency vocabulary.

japanese-diplomat-fbi-sting.title: Abu Zubaydah
japanese-diplomat-fbi-sting.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

japanese-diplomat-fbi-sting.title: The Warren, Ohio tail
japanese-diplomat-fbi-sting.summary: John Kiriakou's account of being followed around Warren, Ohio in January 2012 — to his grandparents' old house, to their graves, and to the Packard Museum car park — while he assumed the car behind him belonged to a private investigator hired by his ex-wife, and of realising four days later, in an FBI conference room, that the Bureau had followed him from Virginia.

jared-kushner.title: Bruce Fein
jared-kushner.summary: John Kiriakou's longtime attorney and one of his closest friends; a Harvard Law-trained constitutional scholar, former Deputy Attorney General under President Reagan and former General Counsel of the Federal Communications Commission. Fein took the call from Jared Kushner's attorney that opened Kiriakou's first pardon track, sat beside him at the 2018 Trump International Hotel meeting at which Rudy Giuliani's aide solicited $2 million for a presidential pardon, and is his co-author on a long-planned book about the CIA's record of failure.

jared-kushner.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
jared-kushner.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

jared-kushner.title: Donald Trump
jared-kushner.summary: 45th and 47th U.S. president. Per John Kiriakou, a man genuinely convinced he was doing right by bombing Iran, "duped" by the same Netanyahu nuclear bluff Obama once rejected — and, at the same time, the most blindly pro-Israel president in history, an admirer of autocrats who has never once criticized Vladimir Putin, and prone to gestures — from the Gulf of America to a since-abandoned "Department of War" rename — that test the edges of his actual authority.

jared-kushner.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
jared-kushner.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

jared-kushner.title: Itamar Ben-Gvir
jared-kushner.summary: Israel's far-right Minister of National Security; John Kiriakou cites him as a convicted hate-crime felon placed in charge of security in Gaza and the West Bank over his victims, blames his insistence that any attack would come from the West Bank for diverting forces before October 7, and cites the death-penalty law passed under his portfolio for Palestinian detainees as the first reinstatement of capital punishment in Israel since it was abolished in 1956, excepting only the execution of Adolf Eichmann.

jared-kushner.title: Mitchell and Jessen
jared-kushner.summary: The two American psychologists who pitched the CIA's enhanced interrogation program to Director George Tenet at a cocktail party in late October 2001; designers of the program and its theoretical underpinning, "learned helplessness."

jason-leopold.title: Ken Dilanian
jason-leopold.summary: Chief national-security correspondent at NBC News and MSNBC; documented — through a Jason Leopold Freedom of Information Act lawsuit against the CIA — to have sent his own articles to the CIA Office of Public Affairs for clearance before sending them to his own editor.

jason-leopold.title: John Kiriakou
jason-leopold.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

jason-leopold.title: Operation Mockingbird
jason-leopold.summary: The CIA's mid-twentieth-century program of recruiting and managing American journalists as influence assets; in John Kiriakou's account, no longer operationally necessary in the contemporary period because the U.S. media voluntarily reprints CIA-supplied material, and in at least one documented case sends articles to the agency for clearance before sending them to its own editor.

jason-leopold.title: Central Intelligence Agency
jason-leopold.summary: U.S. foreign intelligence service; John Kiriakou's employer from 1990 to 2004 and the central institution of KiriPedia

jason-leopold.title: Balochistan drone base
jason-leopold.summary: Secret CIA drone surveillance base in southwestern Pakistan's Balochistan region; its location was inadvertently disclosed when investigative journalist Jason Leopold filed a Freedom of Information Act request for Pentagon aviation-fuel-delivery records and identified an outsized fuel flow to the otherwise-undocumented base.

jason-leopold.title: Will Hurd
jason-leopold.summary: Former CIA case officer, congressman and OpenAI board member whom John Kiriakou says he mentored at the agency; Kiriakou cites him as an example of the intelligence and tech worlds merging.

jason-miyares.title: The Jay Jones texts
jason-miyares.summary: The leaked 2022 text messages in which Virginia''s Democratic candidate for attorney general joked about shooting Republicans — which John Kiriakou called shameful on reflex, before landing on the position he now holds: that everyone talks that way privately, that Republicans do it constantly, and that he no longer cares.

jason-miyares.title: Winsome Earle-Sears and the machine gun
jason-miyares.summary: John Kiriakou's verdict on the lieutenant governor of Virginia who ran for the top job in 2025 — that she is a nut, that her earlier campaign photographs showed her smiling and holding a machine gun, and that at the gubernatorial debate she had to be repeatedly slapped down for talking over her opponent.

jason-miyares.title: The pardoned January 6th defendants
jason-miyares.summary: John Kiriakou's observation that a striking number of the January 6th defendants pardoned by Donald Trump have got into trouble since their release — one arrested for threatening to kill the House minority leader, another shot dead in a gunfight with a police officer in Indiana — and his agreement that the base rate may explain all of it.

jason-miyares.title: The George Mason confrontation
jason-miyares.summary: The videotaped encounter at George Mason University in which former CIA director John Brennan poked a questioner in the chest — an incident John Kiriakou says at least a dozen friends sent him, and which showed him, for the first time in thirty-five years of knowing the man, a frightened John Brennan.

jason-miyares.title: The mobile passport lane
jason-miyares.summary: John Kiriakou's report of flying home from Spain during the longest government shutdown in American history — ridiculous security lines, and an immigration officer who said four words, "Look at the camera. Welcome home," which Kiriakou attributes to the man not being paid.

jason-miyares.title: The Perplexity subscription
jason-miyares.summary: The free lifetime account John Kiriakou says the chief executive of Perplexity emailed him at ten o'clock at night, days after he told Joe Rogan's audience that ChatGPT had invented a University of Maryland degree and a Belgian graduate school for him — and that when he corrected it, the machine argued back.

jcpoa.title: The permanent multipolar world
jcpoa.summary: John Kiriakou's assessment that the unipolar period following the collapse of the Soviet Union has ended permanently, and that the arrangement was not inevitable — he attributes it to American strategic choices, principally leaving the Iran nuclear agreement and choosing confrontation with China and Russia over the cooperation that was available.

jcpoa.title: The Iron Dome
jcpoa.summary: Israel's air-defence system as John Kiriakou reads it — impressive against a wave of slow Iranian drones, but shown by the handful that got through, and later by Iranian ballistic missiles, to be not all it is cracked up to be; each exchange, in his account, buying Iran intelligence about the gaps.

jcpoa.title: The Al Mayadeen debate
jcpoa.summary: Two days before the 2026 attack on Iran, John Kiriakou went on the Lebanese network Al Mayadeen expecting the usual point-counterpoint with an academic and found himself opposite Iran's lead nuclear negotiator. His argument to the negotiator — that what the two sides were then negotiating was the JCPOA under another name — was rejected outright before being accepted.

jcpoa.title: Iran Nuclear Assessment
jcpoa.summary: Per John Kiriakou's assessment, the US–Israeli military campaign against Iran was a war of choice driven by Israeli political pressure rather than genuine intelligence indicating an Iranian nuclear weapons threat. The CIA produced two National Intelligence Estimates concluding Iran had no nuclear weapons program; Supreme Leader Ayatollah Khamenei issued a fatwa in the 1980s forbidding such a program. The U.S. went to war anyway, in Kiriakou's view, after President Trump replaced the Joint Chiefs of Staff with officers willing to accept Israeli intelligence and proceed.

jcpoa.title: 2026 Iran war
jcpoa.summary: The open-ended American and Israeli war against Iran that John Kiriakou tracked week by week on his own show — a conflict he says was sold as three weeks, ran into its fifth month, achieved every decapitation objective it set, and continued anyway. His grade for it is a D, and his forecast is a Truth Social post declaring victory while nothing changes.

jcpoa.title: "A policy support organization"
jcpoa.summary: Asked how the CIA workforce would be reacting to the war on Iran, John Kiriakou answered from the Iraq war: people put their heads down and did as they were told, after a boss told an assembled group — all of whom opposed the invasion — that the agency is not a policy organization but a policy support organization, and would do what the White House told it to do.

jd-vance.title: Marco Rubio
jd-vance.summary: U.S. official whom John Kiriakou identifies as the real motivator behind pressure on Venezuela; Kiriakou argues Venezuela is not a meaningful drug threat to the U.S. and that Rubio simply wants Maduro gone.

jd-vance.title: Donald Trump
jd-vance.summary: 45th and 47th U.S. president. Per John Kiriakou, a man genuinely convinced he was doing right by bombing Iran, "duped" by the same Netanyahu nuclear bluff Obama once rejected — and, at the same time, the most blindly pro-Israel president in history, an admirer of autocrats who has never once criticized Vladimir Putin, and prone to gestures — from the Gulf of America to a since-abandoned "Department of War" rename — that test the edges of his actual authority.

jd-vance.title: The Republican split over the Iran war
jd-vance.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the division inside the Republican Party over the 2026 war with Iran — between the voters who backed Donald Trump as the no-foreign-wars candidate and an administration Kiriakou says has reverted to the neoconservative posture of John McCain's party, with Tulsi Gabbard and J.D. Vance on one side and Marco Rubio on the other.

jd-vance.title: Tulsi Gabbard
jd-vance.summary: U.S. Director of National Intelligence; a longtime family friend of John Kiriakou's, who has known her since she was 12; Kiriakou calls her appointment "an inspired choice" despite disagreeing with her decision to join the Republican Party, and says she appears to have given up her opposition to Section 702 surveillance to secure Senate confirmation.

jd-vance.title: John McCain
jd-vance.summary: Late U.S. Senator from Arizona who gave the most consequential Senate-floor defense of John Kiriakou — declaring that 'if it weren't for John Kiriakou, the American people would never have had any idea what the CIA was doing in their name' — and sponsored the McCain–Feinstein amendment banning torture.

jd-vance.title: John Kiriakou
jd-vance.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

jean-gately.title: JFK assassination
jean-gately.summary: November 22, 1963 killing of President John F. Kennedy in Dallas, Texas. John Kiriakou's position, drawn from a Pakistan-station encounter with Bay of Pigs commander Jean Gately, an RFK Jr. account of CIA Director John McCone's same-day exchange with Bobby Kennedy Sr., and a White House contact's confirmation that the remaining classified Kennedy documents all contain the word "Israel," is that elements of the CIA were probably involved and that Israeli intelligence was involved as well.

jean-gately.title: John McCone
jean-gately.summary: Director of the Central Intelligence Agency on November 22, 1963; per John Kiriakou's retelling of an account from Robert F. Kennedy Jr., responded to Bobby Kennedy Sr.'s same-day question "Tell me your people didn't do this" not with denial but with "I don't know who did it."

jean-gately.title: Gina Haspel
jean-gately.summary: Director of the Central Intelligence Agency under President Trump's first term; known to John Kiriakou and others at the CIA as "Bloody Gina"; per Kiriakou, flew out to the secret black site to sit in on one of the enhanced-interrogation torture sessions "just because she could," personally supervised the torture of USS Cole bombing suspect Rahim al-Nashiri, and later fed the CIA's torture tapes into an industrial document grinder after being explicitly told by White House Counsel not to destroy them.

jean-gately.title: Jeffrey Epstein
jean-gately.summary: Convicted sex offender; per John Kiriakou, was "an Israeli access agent" rather than a CIA asset, because the CIA collects foreign intelligence and Epstein's targets — Bill Clinton, Bill Gates, Prince Andrew — were not foreign. Kiriakou further holds that Epstein did die by suicide in federal custody, because in the Bureau of Prisons the cameras never work and the guards are always asleep.

jean-gately.title: Charlie Kirk shooting
jean-gately.summary: Kiriakou questions the official account: a court filing says the ATF could not match the autopsy bullet to the rifle tied to the suspect.

jean-gately.title: National Security Act of 1947
jean-gately.summary: The law that created the CIA and the National Security Council — passed, in John Kiriakou's telling, only because Harry Truman lied to J. Edgar Hoover. Hoover lobbied Capitol Hill to kill the bill until Truman promised the CIA would be a division of the FBI; the bill passed, Hoover realized he'd been duped, and ordered the FBI not to cooperate with the new agency — a freeze that lasted, incredibly, until after 9/11. Kiriakou's account of how the agency was designed at all runs through a room in New York where MI6 officers sat down with Bill Donovan, Prescott Bush and some pads of paper.

jeff-fahey.title: Tyrell Vanto
jeff-fahey.summary: Hollywood screenwriter and director; son of Jesse Vanto; friend of John Kiriakou; wrote and directed the late-2025 film in which Kiriakou made his acting debut.

jeff-fahey.title: Erik Prince
jeff-fahey.summary: Founder of Blackwater; CIA non-official-cover officer with a 201 file; identified publicly by Leon Panetta in front of the House Intelligence Committee; lives in Dubai outside U.S. jurisdiction; in popular culture invoked, alongside Elon Musk, as the composite figure for the billionaire in the Tyrell Vanto film featuring John Kiriakou.

jeff-fahey.title: Hummus
jeff-fahey.summary: The CIA's coercive 'rectal feeding' of detainees using pureed hummus — an unauthorized interrogation technique used at post-9/11 black sites, exposed in the 2014 Senate Torture Report, and the abuse for which John Kiriakou became most associated in popular culture.

jeff-fahey.title: John Kiriakou
jeff-fahey.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

jeff-fahey.title: Lincoln's last turd
jeff-fahey.summary: A purported piece of human waste attributed by a Pennsylvania circus-freak-show museum to Abraham Lincoln on the night of his assassination; auctioned for $5,000; subsequent DNA analysis disproved the attribution. John Kiriakou's failed bid for the artifact is the anecdote that, recirculated in early 2026, made him an internet meme figure.

jeff-fahey.title: The washed-out road to the airport
jeff-fahey.summary: The drive to catch a flight to the Joe Rogan taping, after a hurricane took out the only road from the Baja resort — thirty-five miles in almost two hours, driven by his co-star Jeff Fahey and by Tyrel Ventura, over a dune, across cactus, with the animals jumping out of the way.

jeffrey-epstein.title: Kathryn Ruemmler
jeffrey-epstein.summary: Obama White House counsel whose Epstein-file emails show her repeatedly trying to introduce Jeffrey Epstein to CIA director John Brennan; John Kiriakou notes she personally received a rare CIA award from Brennan and, as the White House's top lawyer, would have been the final legal authority approving the Tuesday-morning kill list.

jeffrey-epstein.title: Nick Bryant
jeffrey-epstein.summary: Investigative journalist, activist and co-founder of Epstein Justice, author of The Franklin Scandal, and a repeat guest on John Kiriakou's programme, where Kiriakou describes him as knowing the Epstein case better than anybody else in America.

jeffrey-epstein.title: CIA record deniability
jeffrey-epstein.summary: John Kiriakou's account of how senior CIA officers occasionally decide to keep an event out of the written record — illustrated by a recruited asset who committed a public murder, after which the Deputy Director for Operations told Kiriakou, on second thought, 'let's not put that in writing.'

jeffrey-epstein.title: Epstein and more than one service
jeffrey-epstein.summary: John Kiriakou's revision of his own position after the release of a further tranche of Epstein documents — that while he continues to believe Jeffrey Epstein was working for the Israelis, the papers indicate he was probably also working for the British, probably for the Americans, and possibly for the Germans.

jeffrey-epstein.title: Felix Rodriguez
jeffrey-epstein.summary: Cuban-American CIA officer and Bay of Pigs veteran; involved in the Vietnam War and reportedly present at the killing of Che Guevara; distinct from [Jose Rodriguez](/wiki/jose-rodriguez), the post-9/11 CIA official.

jeffrey-epstein.title: Kiriakou's prison designation
jeffrey-epstein.summary: The discrepancy between the minimum-security work camp John Kiriakou was sentenced to and the low-security prison the Bureau of Prisons actually placed him in, which he cites whenever the subject of preferential designations arises.

jeffrey-sterling.title: Espionage Act
jeffrey-sterling.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

jeffrey-sterling.title: Leonie Brinkema
jeffrey-sterling.summary: U.S. federal judge in the Eastern District of Virginia — informally the 'Espionage Court' — a Reagan appointee John Kiriakou calls "a hanging judge." Per Kiriakou, Brinkema systematically reserved all major national security cases for herself rather than allowing them to be distributed randomly among judges, and ruled in Kiriakou's case that his reason for blowing the whistle was legally irrelevant and that classified documents could not be used in his defense — effectively making it impossible to mount one.

jeffrey-sterling.title: The Intercept
jeffrey-sterling.summary: The investigative news outlet that published Daniel Hale's drone leak; John Kiriakou notes that the same Intercept reporter, Matthew Cole, was involved in cases that led to the exposure of both Kiriakou himself and NSA leaker Reality Winner — though he insists Hale outed himself rather than being burned by the outlet.

jeffrey-sterling.title: Chelsea Manning
jeffrey-sterling.summary: Former U.S. Army intelligence analyst who provided WikiLeaks its 2010 trove of military and diplomatic documents. Per John Kiriakou, Manning meets the legal definition of whistleblower for exposing war crimes, was a torture victim of prolonged solitary confinement with forced nudity, and was sentenced to 35 years in prison before Barack Obama commuted — not pardoned — her sentence. Kiriakou says Manning later refused a grand jury's offer of immunity and chose renewed jail time rather than testify against Julian Assange.

jeffrey-sterling.title: The 2016 research pitch
jeffrey-sterling.summary: An approach made to John Kiriakou in October 2016, roughly eighteen months after his release from prison, by a caller claiming to be a former CIA colleague who offered him five thousand dollars a month to conduct classified research. Kiriakou reads it as a second entrapment attempt, mounted after his sentence was already served, and says he identified it by the caller's mistakes with agency vocabulary.

jeffrey-sterling.title: The sources and methods red herring
jeffrey-sterling.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that the federal government invokes the exposure of sources and methods in every leak prosecution as a matter of routine, has never produced proof in any of them — not against Julian Assange, Edward Snowden or Chelsea Manning — and that American claims of damage to national security should therefore not be taken seriously.

jennifer-keenan-fbi.title: Guantánamo Bay detention camp
jennifer-keenan-fbi.summary: Per John Kiriakou — as chief of counterterrorism operations in Pakistan after September 11, 2001 — the Guantanamo detention facility began as a temporary holding measure intended to last two to three weeks while the CIA and Justice Department determined which federal district court should try each prisoner, not as a long-term detention infrastructure. The Rawalpindi jail had reached capacity, Pakistani intelligence demanded the prisoners be removed, and CIA headquarters directed Kiriakou to load them onto a C-12 cargo plane and fly them to Cuba.

jennifer-keenan-fbi.title: Tommy McHale
jennifer-keenan-fbi.summary: Highly decorated Port Authority of New York and New Jersey detective who worked as a terrorist hunter alongside John Kiriakou in Islamabad, Pakistan after 9/11; a survivor of the 1993 World Trade Center bombing whose best friend died on 9/11.

jennifer-keenan-fbi.title: Bob Grenier
jennifer-keenan-fbi.summary: Career CIA officer who served as station chief in Islamabad before, during, and after 9/11; later associate deputy director of operations for policy support and Iraq Mission Manager; John Kiriakou's boss and, for one year, his supervisor as executive assistant.

jennifer-keenan-fbi.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
jennifer-keenan-fbi.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

jennifer-keenan-fbi.title: Girls' madrasa raid error
jennifer-keenan-fbi.summary: A mistaken CIA raid, conducted the night of the Abu Zubaydah operation, on the home of an elderly Pakistani man running an unlicensed girls' madrasa — the only phone in the neighborhood, which al-Qaeda fighters had been using and the CIA had been intercepting. John Kiriakou personally apologized to the man on the president's behalf and arranged compensation.

jennifer-keenan-fbi.title: Senate Torture Report
jennifer-keenan-fbi.summary: The December 2014 executive summary of the U.S. Senate Select Committee on Intelligence's study of the CIA's post-9/11 detention and interrogation program; the first public disclosure of techniques including rectal feeding with hummus, sexual assault with broomsticks, and prolonged sleep deprivation.

jennifer-matthews.title: Senior Intelligence Service
jennifer-matthews.summary: The CIA's executive rank above the General Schedule, entry to which requires a tour outside an officer's own directorate and a tour in the policy community — a box-checking requirement John Kiriakou identifies as the reason an untrained analyst was sent to run a base in Afghanistan. Its officers are career staff rather than political appointees, some with thirty or forty years in place, which is why Kiriakou describes the service as capable of simply waiting a president out — or slow-rolling him. Its officers in the Counterterrorism Center were also the authors of the torture techniques.

jennifer-matthews.title: Alfreda Bikowsky
jennifer-matthews.summary: Senior CIA officer who headed Alec Station and, before that, served as its chief of operations, overseeing the CIA's torture program; per John Kiriakou, "bad news from the get-go," and part of a failed attempt with Rich Blee to turn a San Diego al-Qaeda cell into double agents.

jennifer-matthews.title: Forward Operating Base Chapman Attack
jennifer-matthews.summary: December 30, 2009 suicide bombing at Forward Operating Base Chapman in Khost, Afghanistan, killing seven CIA officers and wounding more than a dozen others — the deadliest single day in CIA history. Per John Kiriakou, the officer who led the base was a GS-14 with zero security training, assigned to the post as a career-promotion checkbox before her required elevation to the Senior Intelligence Service. The bomber — a Jordanian national who walked into the American consulate in Istanbul claiming to be Osama bin Laden's doctor — was never polygraphed because CIA personnel 'wanted so badly for this to be true.'

jennifer-matthews.title: Abbottabad
jennifer-matthews.summary: The Pakistani garrison city where Osama bin Laden was found and killed — named for a British major who was Pakistan's first military trainer, home to the Pakistani military's leadership, and in John Kiriakou's judgement the last place bin Laden could have lived unnoticed by the Pakistani state.

jennifer-matthews.title: Abu Zubaydah
jennifer-matthews.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

jennifer-matthews.title: Agent payment mechanics
jennifer-matthews.summary: How the CIA physically pays a recruited agent — cash every month, a receipt signed with any alias the agent chooses, and a polygraph regime built around the assumption that the officer handling the money is the person most likely to steal it.

jennings-randolph.title: Abu Omar rendition
jennings-randolph.summary: The CIA's kidnapping of a Milan cleric, Abu Omar, who was sent to Egypt to be tortured; John Kiriakou calls it a case that ought to be taught at the CIA as how not to run a rendition, and it is what ultimately sent him to prison, after he confirmed a former colleague's surname to a journalist claiming to be writing a book about it.

jennings-randolph.title: Abu Zubaydah
jennings-randolph.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

jennings-randolph.title: Aldrich Ames
jennings-randolph.summary: Senior CIA officer — a GS-15 who rose to chief of counterintelligence for the Soviet branch — who spied for the KGB for nine years. Per John Kiriakou, Ames walked into the Soviet embassy in Washington in April 1985 and sold the identities of two CIA-recruited double agents for $50,000 to clear a debt run up by his second marriage; both were executed. He went on to identify more than thirty agents, compromise over a hundred clandestine operations, cause at least twelve deaths and take more than $2 million, while being known throughout the agency as a daily drunk and promoted at every turn. The KGB protected him with a decoy mole hunt; analyst Sandy Grimes caught him by matching his handler meetings to his bank deposits.

jennings-randolph.title: CIA animal surveillance experiments
jennings-randolph.summary: Cold-War CIA efforts to turn animals into listening devices, which John Kiriakou describes as failures — including microphones and cameras mounted on pigeons trained to land on the Soviet embassy, which could reach the compound but never captured anything meaningful.

jennings-randolph.title: The CIA divorce rate
jennings-randolph.summary: John Kiriakou's account of why marriages fail at the CIA at a rate he says exceeds that of any other part of the U.S. government — the impossibility of explaining a midnight departure to a spouse without a clearance, and the difficulty officers have switching off a professional habit of deception. He gives the figure variously as over 75 percent and upwards of 80 percent, says he was determined not to become a statistic and became one anyway, and dates the end of his first marriage to a sentence spoken in an armoured car on the way to Athens airport. Both his divorces have been costly; of the second he says the agency played an active role he is barred by court order from explaining.

jennings-randolph.title: The CIA Insider's Guide to Surveillance and Surveillance Detection
jennings-randolph.summary: Book by John Kiriakou drawing on his experience as a surveillance detection instructor at the CIA and as a private surveillance training consultant. The book covers the techniques used by intelligence professionals to identify whether they are being followed — including the four-phase surveillance detection route, concealment device placement and retrieval, and counter-surveillance strategy — adapted for use by corporate executives, journalists, and others who want to confirm whether they are being followed.

jeremy-hammond.title: RDAP
jeremy-hammond.summary: The Bureau of Prisons' Residential Drug and Alcohol Program, which takes a year off a federal sentence on completion — the single most valuable piece of advice John Kiriakou says he gives to people facing prison time, alongside good-conduct credit and halfway-house conversion.

jeremy-hammond.title: Julian Assange
jeremy-hammond.summary: Kiriakou — a 15-year friend and former WikiLeaks board member — on why Assange is a publisher owed a journalist's immunity, and a political prisoner.

jeremy-hammond.title: Chelsea Manning
jeremy-hammond.summary: Former U.S. Army intelligence analyst who provided WikiLeaks its 2010 trove of military and diplomatic documents. Per John Kiriakou, Manning meets the legal definition of whistleblower for exposing war crimes, was a torture victim of prolonged solitary confinement with forced nudity, and was sentenced to 35 years in prison before Barack Obama commuted — not pardoned — her sentence. Kiriakou says Manning later refused a grand jury's offer of immunity and chose renewed jail time rather than testify against Julian Assange.

jeremy-hammond.title: Mike Pompeo
jeremy-hammond.summary: CIA director and later Secretary of State under Trump. John Kiriakou read Pompeo's 2017 speech branding WikiLeaks a "hostile non-state intelligence service" as the groundwork for an Espionage Act case against Julian Assange in the Eastern District of Virginia — the "Espionage Court" where Kiriakou himself was prosecuted. Friends who briefed Pompeo told Kiriakou he was extraordinarily bright but wrong on Iran; Kiriakou's own verdict soured permanently when Pompeo named Gina Haspel deputy director, flirted publicly with reinstating torture, and called Chelsea Manning a traitor — a crime she was never convicted of.

jeremy-hammond.title: The Latin American newspaper prediction
jeremy-hammond.summary: The prediction John Kiriakou gave to a Latin American newspaper a week or two after Donald Trump's first inauguration — that things would be better for whistleblowers under Trump because they could not possibly be worse than under Barack Obama — and his later verdict that he had been "very foolish" to say it, since the Trump administration opened three times as many leak investigations and won longer sentences.

jeremy-hammond.title: The play the CIA killed
jeremy-hammond.summary: A stage play about John Kiriakou's case, written in 2015 by the screenwriter Scott Burns for a New York theatre, which Kiriakou says was never performed because the CIA applied enough pressure on the theatre owner to stop it — an account he offered as a counterpoint to the Reality Winner play that was running unmolested at the same moment.

jerome-post.title: United Food and Commercial Workers
jerome-post.summary: The huge K Street labor union where a young John Kiriakou — from a family with a long labor history — was working when Dr. Jerrold Post''s class assignment changed his life: shadow your boss for a week and write his psychological profile. Kiriakou''s boss was a mean old-school organizer whose back had been broken by scabs; halfway through the week Kiriakou called him a racist ("which he was"), and the resulting paper diagnosed the man as a sociopath and potentially dangerous. The paper is what put Kiriakou on the CIA''s radar.

jerome-post.title: John Kiriakou
jerome-post.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

jerome-post.title: The polygraph
jerome-post.summary: The lie-detector examination that gates entry to the CIA, described by John Kiriakou from the inside: the twenty-minute wiring-up, the psychiatrist''s advice to stare at a speck on the wall, the deliberately planted false accusation used to test a candidate''s reaction, and his contention that the machine screens out exactly the wrong people.

jerome-post.title: Bob (CIA HR)
jerome-post.summary: Pseudonym for the CIA officer who served as director of human resources for the agency in the late 1980s and personally oversaw John Kiriakou's hiring

jerome-post.title: The CIA entrance examinations
jerome-post.summary: The two rounds of testing John Kiriakou sat before joining the CIA in 1990: a current-affairs multiple choice he found trivially easy, a blank fold-out map of the world, and a psychological inventory of several thousand agree-or-disagree statements that repeated the same proposition hundreds of questions apart to catch inconsistency — followed by an interview panel of a psychologist, a psychiatrist and an anthropologist.

jerome-post.title: Stansfield Turner
jerome-post.summary: Admiral and Director of Central Intelligence under Jimmy Carter from 1977 to 1981; named by John Kiriakou as one of only two CIA directors he considers good, because he tried to rein the organization in, and remembered inside the agency for the October 1977 mass firing of Directorate of Operations officers that CIA officers call the Friday Night Massacre.

jerry-falwell-jr.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
jerry-falwell-jr.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

jerry-falwell-jr.title: MOSSAD
jerry-falwell-jr.summary: Israel's primary external intelligence service; characterized by John Kiriakou as universally hostile in his and his CIA colleagues' professional dealings with it ("never had a positive encounter with Mossad"); operates almost exclusively in the operational rather than analytical domain; the CIA is, per Kiriakou, categorically forbidden from spying on it.

jerry-falwell-jr.title: Church of Saint Porphyrios
jerry-falwell-jr.summary: The Greek Orthodox church in Gaza that John Kiriakou describes as the oldest continuously operating church in the world; per Kiriakou, Israel bombed it while 24 women and children were sheltering inside.

jerry-falwell-jr.title: AIPAC
jerry-falwell-jr.summary: The American Israel Public Affairs Committee — the U.S. political organization that, in John Kiriakou's framing, ought to be registered as a foreign-lobbying entity but is not, and that wields decisive electoral power against U.S. elected officials who express support for Palestinian human rights.

jerry-falwell-jr.title: Donald Trump
jerry-falwell-jr.summary: 45th and 47th U.S. president. Per John Kiriakou, a man genuinely convinced he was doing right by bombing Iran, "duped" by the same Netanyahu nuclear bluff Obama once rejected — and, at the same time, the most blindly pro-Israel president in history, an admirer of autocrats who has never once criticized Vladimir Putin, and prone to gestures — from the Gulf of America to a since-abandoned "Department of War" rename — that test the edges of his actual authority.

jerry-falwell-jr.title: Greek Intelligence Service
jerry-falwell-jr.summary: Greece's intelligence service, with which John Kiriakou worked closely during his Athens posting; its head of surveillance called off surveillance on him after watching him make a large offering at Saint Nectarios's tomb on the island of Aegina.

jesse-jackson.title: Kiriakou's acting career
jesse-jackson.summary: The film role John Kiriakou took in 2025 after Tyrel Ventura wrote a part for him — a former CIA officer running a billionaire's security detail — which he shot in Mexico for a month and which made him, at sixty-odd, a member of the Screen Actors Guild.

jesse-jackson.title: The conscientious objectors book
jesse-jackson.summary: A long out-of-print volume of interviews with American conscientious objectors, published around 1972 and given to John Kiriakou from the personal collection of an objector he was friendly with in prison — a book whose harrowing accounts of objectors sent to real federal prisons rather than to camps convinced him that refusing to serve was often more physically dangerous than serving.

jesse-jackson.title: The Egyptian intelligence chief''s son
jesse-jackson.summary: A coincidence John Kiriakou reported from Oxford, Ohio in November 2025: his own son''s marketing professor turned out to be the son of Muhammad Farag, head of the Egyptian intelligence service some thirty-five years earlier, whom Kiriakou had met in Cairo when the professor was a boy of seven or eight — and the two families went out to dinner together.

jesse-jackson.title: The Giuliani–Epstein emails
jesse-jackson.summary: A cache of correspondence that a former chief of business development for Giuliani Partners told John Kiriakou she holds — thousands of pages of emails between Rudy Giuliani and Jeffrey Epstein, which she says she has offered to news organisations and to congressional committees and which nobody wanted, together with her claim that a second British prince and other former heads of state are implicated.

jesse-jackson.title: The mob vote for Trump
jesse-jackson.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer to a viewer asking whether he discussed politics with organised crime figures in prison: that he did, a great deal, that they love Donald Trump without qualification, and that the reason is a New York real estate developer''s unavoidable daily contact with the unions the mob controls.

jesse-jackson.title: The visa reciprocity rule
jesse-jackson.summary: The bilateral arrangement John Kiriakou describes by which each country sets the price of its own visas and the other matches it — and his conclusion that a United States policy of refusing visas to applicants who are overweight or who have cancer or diabetes must, under the same rule, license every other country to weigh American travellers at the door.

jesselyn-radack.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
jesselyn-radack.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

jesselyn-radack.title: John Kiriakou
jesselyn-radack.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

jesselyn-radack.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
jesselyn-radack.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

jesselyn-radack.title: John Walker Lindh
jesselyn-radack.summary: American citizen captured while fighting alongside the Taliban in late 2001, present at the Qala-i-Jangi fortress at the start of the prisoner uprising that killed CIA officer Mike Spann. In John Kiriakou's account his case matters less for what Lindh did than for what was done around him — the false claim that he had been read his rights, the destruction of the career of the Justice Department lawyer who said so, and his place on the docket of the one judge who reserves national-security cases for herself.

jesselyn-radack.title: Edward Snowden
jesselyn-radack.summary: Former NSA contractor who in 2013 disclosed the scope of U.S. [mass surveillance](/wiki/mass-surveillance), including the Section 702 collection program. Per John Kiriakou — who counts Snowden among the small group of national-security whistleblowers prosecuted under the Espionage Act — Snowden was ''stuck between two awful slippery slopes'': breaking his oath and chain of command on one side, and on the other catching something ''cut and dry against the Constitution'' that no one would act on. Kiriakou notes Snowden could not use his chain of command (as Kiriakou could not, his own chain being Jose Rodriguez), and that Judge Leonie Brinkema had reserved the Snowden case for herself before he fled the country.

jesselyn-radack.title: The night the Snowden story broke
jesselyn-radack.summary: How John Kiriakou learned about Edward Snowden. Three months into his sentence at FCI Loretto, a cellmate who could not sleep was listening to Coast to Coast AM in the middle of the night and woke him. Kiriakou turned on his own radio and followed the story through the distant stations that reach central Pennsylvania after dark.

jfk-assassination.title: Kiriakou's transfer to the Directorate of Operations
jfk-assassination.summary: John Kiriakou's roughly two-month internal campaign to transfer from the CIA's analytic Directorate of Intelligence to the operational Directorate of Operations, overcoming what he calls a "natural bias in operations against the eggheads on the analytic side," followed by an Athens posting secured because he was the only person in the entire CIA fluent in both Greek and Arabic. Covers his full CIA career arc from 1988/1990 recruitment through analyst years on Iraq, the switch to operations, 9/11, the enhanced-interrogation refusal, executive assistant to the deputy director for operations, and his eventual resignation and post-CIA career.

jfk-assassination.title: Jean Gately
jfk-assassination.summary: The CIA officer who commanded the 1961 Bay of Pigs operation and, decades later, served alongside John Kiriakou as an elderly contractor at the CIA's Pakistan station, where he still blamed Kennedy for the defeat — 'We could have won that thing.'

jfk-assassination.title: Felix Rodriguez
jfk-assassination.summary: Cuban-American CIA officer and Bay of Pigs veteran; involved in the Vietnam War and reportedly present at the killing of Che Guevara; distinct from [Jose Rodriguez](/wiki/jose-rodriguez), the post-9/11 CIA official.

jfk-assassination.title: MLK assassination
jfk-assassination.summary: The April 1968 killing of Martin Luther King Jr. John Kiriakou, having set out to read everything he could find on it, concluded that if James Earl Ray fired the shot he was a patsy — citing the implausibility of a lifelong alcoholic making a perfect shot from a flophouse bathroom a block away, and the FBI's documented attempt two years earlier to push King into suicide.

jfk-assassination.title: Robert F. Kennedy Jr.
jfk-assassination.summary: Son of Robert F. Kennedy; the source of an anecdote John Kiriakou repeats in which, on the day of the JFK assassination, RFK Sr. asked CIA director John McCone "Tell me your people didn't do this," and McCone answered only "I don't know who did it."

jfk-assassination.title: Thirty-year mandatory declassification
jfk-assassination.summary: The statutory requirement, described by John Kiriakou, that classified American documents be released after thirty years — a law he says virtually nobody knows about, and which he raises against the continued withholding of Kennedy assassination records more than sixty years on. He also describes the redaction practice that operates alongside it.

jihad-means-to-struggle.title: Islam in America
jihad-means-to-struggle.summary: John Kiriakou's response to a widely circulated clip of thousands of American Muslims at prayer, captioned as evidence that Islam is the fastest-growing religion in the United States. He notes that nothing in the clip establishes where or what the event was, and that most new American Muslims are African Americans converting — often, in his experience, in the prison system.

jihad-means-to-struggle.title: The Texas Muslim development
jihad-means-to-struggle.summary: A housing development planned by a group of wealthy Muslim professionals in Texas — twenty-five or thirty large houses on an empty tract with a mosque at the centre, marketed to other Muslim doctors, lawyers and engineers. John Kiriakou cites the alarm it caused, up to and including Governor Greg Abbott, as a case study in unnecessary panic.

jihad-means-to-struggle.title: CIA sexpionage
jihad-means-to-struggle.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of the CIA''s use of sex in espionage — routine from its founding through the early 1980s, including MK-Ultra and honey-pot operations — and why the agency largely abandoned it: coercion cannot build the trust a long-term source requires. Other services never stopped.

jihad-means-to-struggle.title: Olof Palme assassination
jihad-means-to-struggle.summary: The 1986 street murder of the Swedish prime minister, which John Kiriakou revisited step by step in Stockholm with researchers who had spent years on it. His conclusion — drawn from dozens of witness reports of two-man cars with walkie-talkies, some identified as police vehicles — is that much of the surveillance that night was carried out by people who believed they were running a practice exercise, until someone walked up and shot Palme dead.

jihad-means-to-struggle.title: Ro Khanna
jihad-means-to-struggle.summary: Democratic congressman from California, whom John Kiriakou describes as one of the very few selfless people in Congress and grades highly in his case-officer rankings.

jihad-means-to-struggle.title: Syrian minorities and the Israeli strikes
jihad-means-to-struggle.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of a conflict inside American policy toward post-Assad Syria: Washington wants the country''s Christian, Jewish and Druze communities protected and has recognised the new government and moved to reopen its embassy, while Israel continues to strike Syrian territory despite repeated instructions from Donald Trump to stop.

jim-bamford.title: Peter Strzok
jim-bamford.summary: Senior FBI counterintelligence officer who, per John Kiriakou, oversaw the FBI operation that included a fake Japanese-diplomat sting designed to induce Kiriakou to commit espionage, and who personally placed Kiriakou in handcuffs when he was arrested on January 12, 2012. Kiriakou did not learn Strzok's identity until 2017, when a Washington Post reporter called to ask for comment on Strzok's firing.

jim-bamford.title: The FBI raids on Kiriakou's home
jim-bamford.summary: Twenty-two agents, eight hours, a sledgehammer hole in the kitchen wall that is still there, potted plants emptied onto the floor and every piece of electronics removed — twice, and with no charge arising from either. John Kiriakou uses the raids as the ground for his flat description of the bureau as an outlaw organization.

jim-bamford.title: Church Committee
jim-bamford.summary: U.S. Senate investigative committee operating in 1975–1976 that examined domestic intelligence abuses by the CIA, FBI, and NSA; per John Kiriakou, the Church Committee — alongside the concurrent Pike Committee in the House — was the last genuine moment of legislative oversight over the intelligence community, born of a national consensus that government had gone dangerously off course. Its work led to the creation of the permanent Senate Select Committee on Intelligence, which Kiriakou says ceased to function as real oversight roughly seven years after its founding.

jim-bamford.title: COINTELPRO
jim-bamford.summary: The FBI programme of warrantless surveillance and disruption directed at Americans, and one of the four abuses John Kiriakou names when explaining what the Church Committee actually investigated. He treats it as the historical benchmark for what a real congressional inquiry into the security agencies looks like — and, through the campaign against Martin Luther King, as proof that the state will destroy a citizen it considers a threat.

jim-bamford.title: David Petraeus
jim-bamford.summary: Retired U.S. Army general and director of the CIA who, per John Kiriakou, confirmed the names of ten covert CIA operatives to his biographer and girlfriend and was never criminally charged — a contrast Kiriakou cites repeatedly as proof that his own prosecution under the Intelligence Identities Protection Act was selective. Kiriakou''s explanation for the disparity: Petraeus had not blown the whistle on the torture program and embarrassed the agency.

jim-bamford.title: Jim Jordan
jim-bamford.summary: Republican congressman from Ohio and chairman of the House Judiciary Committee. John Kiriakou describes a genuinely divided view of him: one of only four members of Congress he names as a friend of whistleblowers, and simultaneously the chairman whose Weaponization subcommittee he says is a partisan counterfeit of the Church Committee — with the whole question settled against Jordan by the Ohio State wrestlers who told him their team doctor was abusing them.

jim-jordan.title: Chuck Grassley
jim-jordan.summary: The senior senator from Iowa, and in John Kiriakou's assessment the one member of Congress who has taken whistleblower protection seriously as a legislative project — a count he has variously put at one finger, at two names, and at four out of 535. Grassley wrote the whistleblower protection statutes, speaks every year at the National Whistleblower Day luncheon, and is the name Kiriakou gives prospective whistleblowers as the single friendly ear on Capitol Hill. Kiriakou's personal verdict is colder — Grassley, he has said, never did anything for him.

jim-jordan.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
jim-jordan.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

jim-jordan.title: Kiriakou's case-officer rankings
jim-jordan.summary: A recurring segment in which John Kiriakou grades serving and former American politicians on how good a CIA case officer each would make, using an S-to-F scale. The criterion is character and the ability to attract confidence rather than politics, and he repeatedly grades allies low and opponents high.

jim-jordan.title: Church Committee
jim-jordan.summary: U.S. Senate investigative committee operating in 1975–1976 that examined domestic intelligence abuses by the CIA, FBI, and NSA; per John Kiriakou, the Church Committee — alongside the concurrent Pike Committee in the House — was the last genuine moment of legislative oversight over the intelligence community, born of a national consensus that government had gone dangerously off course. Its work led to the creation of the permanent Senate Select Committee on Intelligence, which Kiriakou says ceased to function as real oversight roughly seven years after its founding.

jim-jordan.title: COINTELPRO
jim-jordan.summary: The FBI programme of warrantless surveillance and disruption directed at Americans, and one of the four abuses John Kiriakou names when explaining what the Church Committee actually investigated. He treats it as the historical benchmark for what a real congressional inquiry into the security agencies looks like — and, through the campaign against Martin Luther King, as proof that the state will destroy a citizen it considers a threat.

jim-jordan.title: The Weaponization Subcommittee
jim-jordan.summary: The Select Subcommittee on the Weaponization of the Federal Government, created in January 2023 and promoted as a second Church Committee. John Kiriakou says he is a thousand per cent in favour of a second Church Committee and that this is not one: it was created on a straight party-line vote, the Democrats refused to take their seats, and its remit is the FBI''s treatment of conservatives rather than the crimes the original committee exposed.

jim-moran.title: John Kiriakou
jim-moran.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

jim-moran.title: Intelligence Identities Protection Act
jim-moran.summary: U.S. law enacted in 1982 that makes it a crime to knowingly disclose the identity of a covert intelligence officer; per John Kiriakou, his 2012 prosecution under the act arose from confirming a single surname of a former CIA colleague to a journalist — a confirmation that was never published. The name passed through a chain from journalist to Human Rights Watch to Guantanamo defense attorneys before reaching a judge and ultimately the FBI, which traced it back to Kiriakou.

jim-moran.title: Bureau of Prisons
jim-moran.summary: The federal agency that ran John Kiriakou's incarceration — and one of his most persistent post-prison targets. The BOP overrode his judge's camp recommendation by deeming him "a threat to the public safety," threatened him with "diesel therapy" until 1,600 logged phone calls and letters from a dozen House members and two senators backed it off, and, per Kiriakou, functions as "an employment agency for unemployable semi-literate rural white men" and "a dumping ground for failed medical professionals" — an agency for which a prisoner's death is cheaper than his treatment.

jim-moran.title: FCI Loretto
jim-moran.summary: U.S. Federal Correctional Institution in Loretto, Pennsylvania; the low-medium-security prison at which John Kiriakou served 23 months of a 30-month sentence following his 2013 Espionage Act–era plea deal; the originally ordered "minimum security work camp" placement was countermanded — per Kiriakou, on Brennan's direct intervention — to place him in the actual prison alongside the general population.

jim-moran.title: Letter from Loretto
jim-moran.summary: Prison newsletter written by John Kiriakou from FCI Loretto, modeled on Martin Luther King's "Letter from Birmingham Jail," which exposed two crimes committed against him by guards and went viral after being relayed to the Huffington Post, drawing national press to the prison.

jim-moran.title: Chuck Grassley
jim-moran.summary: The senior senator from Iowa, and in John Kiriakou's assessment the one member of Congress who has taken whistleblower protection seriously as a legislative project — a count he has variously put at one finger, at two names, and at four out of 535. Grassley wrote the whistleblower protection statutes, speaks every year at the National Whistleblower Day luncheon, and is the name Kiriakou gives prospective whistleblowers as the single friendly ear on Capitol Hill. Kiriakou's personal verdict is colder — Grassley, he has said, never did anything for him.

jim-pavitt.title: George Tenet
jim-pavitt.summary: Director of Central Intelligence from 1997 to 2004, spanning the September 11 attacks and the early enhanced-interrogation program; identified by John Kiriakou as John Brennan's institutional patron at the agency; the figure who ordered the Five Eyes intelligence services to "open the files" to each other in the early 2000s.

jim-pavitt.title: John Brennan
jim-pavitt.summary: Former Director of the CIA; characterized in KiriPedia's source corpus as the principal architect of the agency's enhanced interrogation program and as having plotted against an elected President

jim-pavitt.title: Bojinka plot
jim-pavitt.summary: 1996 Khalid Sheikh Mohammed–planned operation, prepared in a Manila, Philippines apartment, to hijack as many as fourteen Boeing 747s and crash them into buildings along the U.S. West Coast; disrupted only by accident, when a cleaning lady let herself into the apartment while the planner was out, recognized the materials laid out as a terrorist plot, and called the police — who alerted Filipino intelligence and, in turn, the CIA. The plot's architect was known to U.S. intelligence for the next six years only by the alias "Mukhtar," his true identity as Khalid Sheikh Mohammed surfacing only when Abu Zubaydah named him to FBI agent Ali Soufan in 2002.

jim-pavitt.title: Expanding your realm
jim-pavitt.summary: The lesson in CIA office politics John Kiriakou says he was taught in his first week — that to make yourself as important as possible you must constantly expand your realm and be king of as many people as you can — and his argument that at the senior-most level the same instinct starts reaching across agencies.

jim-pavitt.title: The twenty-five in Pakistan
jim-pavitt.summary: The answer John Kiriakou heard given to Senator Jeanne Shaheen in the spring of 2009, when she asked how many members of al-Qaeda were in Pakistan — twenty-five — and which he uses as the measure of how long the war outlived its stated object.

jim-pavitt.title: Martha Kesler
jim-pavitt.summary: Long-serving CIA Syria analyst; author of the standard-issue analytical primer "Syria: Fragile Mosaic of Power"; John Brennan''s first supervisor and the figure who first fired him from the agency, before being herself fired by Brennan when their roles inverted under George Tenet''s patronage.

jimmy-dimora.title: Frank Russo
jimmy-dimora.summary: The former auditor of Cuyahoga County, Ohio, who shared a bunk with John Kiriakou at FCI Loretto — a corruption defendant who cooperated against Jimmy Dimora, was marked in prison as a rat, and whom Kiriakou describes as a sweetheart with a hilarious sense of humour who won everybody over anyway.

jimmy-dimora.title: The rat and pedophile table
jimmy-dimora.summary: The cafeteria table at FCI Loretto reserved for cooperating witnesses and sex offenders — a placement that also carried a ban from the television room, and which John Kiriakou describes as an outcome cooperators knew to expect before they agreed to testify.

jimmy-dimora.title: Pete Calabrese
jimmy-dimora.summary: The senior Bonanno family member at FCI Loretto, known as Peter the Rabbit, who challenged John Kiriakou over his friendship with the cooperating witness Frank Russo and told him Russo brought dishonour to the Italians.

jimmy-dimora.title: FCI Loretto
jimmy-dimora.summary: U.S. Federal Correctional Institution in Loretto, Pennsylvania; the low-medium-security prison at which John Kiriakou served 23 months of a 30-month sentence following his 2013 Espionage Act–era plea deal; the originally ordered "minimum security work camp" placement was countermanded — per Kiriakou, on Brennan's direct intervention — to place him in the actual prison alongside the general population.

jimmy-dimora.title: Cell transfers at Loretto
jimmy-dimora.summary: How a prisoner at FCI Loretto moved from one cell to another — a process requiring six months in place, the written agreement of the receiving cell and the signature of the counselor, which John Kiriakou describes as a guard assigned to be a designated pain in the ass.

jimmy-dimora.title: Blue
jimmy-dimora.summary: The FCI Loretto correctional officer, widely considered the most unpopular in the prison, who covered his own nameplate with masking tape so released prisoners could not find him — and who told a colleague of John Kiriakou's that he would never touch the CIA man because of the press attention.

joby-warrick-washington-post-resignation.title: Lincoln's last turd
joby-warrick-washington-post-resignation.summary: A purported piece of human waste attributed by a Pennsylvania circus-freak-show museum to Abraham Lincoln on the night of his assassination; auctioned for $5,000; subsequent DNA analysis disproved the attribution. John Kiriakou's failed bid for the artifact is the anecdote that, recirculated in early 2026, made him an internet meme figure.

joby-warrick-washington-post-resignation.title: RFK Assassination
joby-warrick-washington-post-resignation.summary: Assassination of Robert F. Kennedy on June 5, 1968 in Los Angeles; per John Kiriakou, physically impossible to attribute to Sirhan Sirhan alone — Los Angeles County coroner Thomas Noguchi determined the fatal shot was fired from behind and below Kennedy's right ear at close range while Sirhan stood in front, the crime scene yielded more bullets than Sirhan's revolver could hold, and a hotel security guard named 'Caesar' was captured on video standing behind Kennedy at the moment of the shooting.

joby-warrick-washington-post-resignation.title: Bashar al-Assad
joby-warrick-washington-post-resignation.summary: President of Syria; John Kiriakou recounts warning Senator John Kerry to stop publicly calling Assad 'my dear friend' after a speech enraged Washington's Lebanese community, with Kerry citing motorcycle rides they had taken together to the Golan Heights.

joby-warrick-washington-post-resignation.title: Kiriakou's Abraham Lincoln collection
joby-warrick-washington-post-resignation.summary: John Kiriakou''s private collection of Abraham Lincoln relics, assembled at auction over many years and governed by a strict standard of provenance: a blood-soaked fragment of the pillowcase Lincoln died on, wallpaper from the Petersen House death room, a swatch of Mary Todd Lincoln''s funeral dress, and wood from the gallows on which the conspirators were hanged.

joby-warrick-washington-post-resignation.title: John Kiriakou
joby-warrick-washington-post-resignation.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

joby-warrick-washington-post-resignation.title: Al-Qaeda training manual interrogation-resistance tactics
joby-warrick-washington-post-resignation.summary: A captured al-Qaeda training manual instructing operatives on how to resist interrogation, including feigning illness — a technique John Kiriakou says he saw a detainee use, and recognized, during a capture and interrogation in Pakistan.

joe-biden.title: Barack Obama
joe-biden.summary: 44th U.S. president; in John Kiriakou's account, Obama publicly recounted refusing Benjamin Netanyahu's demand to bomb Iran and calling Israel's threat to use nuclear weapons a bluff — a bluff Kiriakou says Donald Trump later believed.

joe-biden.title: "It''s either him or it''s Manning"
joe-biden.summary: John Kiriakou's account of why Barack Obama commuted Chelsea Manning's sentence — that Joe Biden, lobbied by a wealthy Greek-American businessman, argued Kiriakou's clemency case to the president directly, and that Obama cut the discussion off ten minutes in by saying he would do one or the other but not both. Kiriakou's conclusion is that the commutation was an arithmetic judgement about a 35-year sentence rather than an act of conscience.

joe-biden.title: John Kerry
joe-biden.summary: U.S. Senator from Massachusetts; chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee during John Kiriakou's 2009 service as the committee's senior investigator; subsequently U.S. Secretary of State; characterized by Kiriakou as a coward who buckled under CIA pressure on the Dasht-i-Leili reopening and as personally fixated on his perceived theft of the Secretary of State position by Hillary Clinton; the famously thrown medals were duplicates purchased at the post exchange.

joe-biden.title: Kiriakou pardon request
joe-biden.summary: John Kiriakou's public campaign for a presidential pardon from Donald Trump to restore the pension and firearm rights he lost after his 2013 felony conviction for disclosing the identity of a covert CIA officer; includes a five-second Mar-a-Lago encounter in which Trump referred him to Attorney General Pam Bondi, a Kalshi prediction-market contract that opened at roughly 19 to 20 percent odds on his being pardoned, and letters of support from Tucker Carlson, Judge Andrew Napolitano and Dr. Phil.

joe-biden.title: Chelsea Manning
joe-biden.summary: Former U.S. Army intelligence analyst who provided WikiLeaks its 2010 trove of military and diplomatic documents. Per John Kiriakou, Manning meets the legal definition of whistleblower for exposing war crimes, was a torture victim of prolonged solitary confinement with forced nudity, and was sentenced to 35 years in prison before Barack Obama commuted — not pardoned — her sentence. Kiriakou says Manning later refused a grand jury's offer of immunity and chose renewed jail time rather than testify against Julian Assange.

joe-biden.title: Ranking Bush, Obama, Trump and Biden
joe-biden.summary: John Kiriakou's answer to a viewer asking which of four presidents he would choose to live under. He begins by picking Barack Obama as the least bad face to the world, reverses himself over the whistleblower prosecutions, and ends by naming Joe Biden — on the grounds that the country was effectively running itself.

joe-bidenopoulos.title: The Virginia pardon and voting rights
joe-bidenopoulos.summary: John Kiriakou's account of applying to have his voting rights restored in Virginia after leaving prison and receiving, unasked, a full state pardon delivered by courier from the office of Governor Terry McAuliffe — followed by a courthouse clerk and a state employee who between them got him registered in time to vote.

joe-bidenopoulos.title: Consulting job entrapment offers
joe-bidenopoulos.summary: John Kiriakou's claim that he receives a steady stream of emails and telephone calls offering him work — always consulting — that he reads as attempts to bait him into violating federal law, and which he says happens all the time.

joe-bidenopoulos.title: Heather Kiriakou
joe-bidenopoulos.summary: John Kiriakou's wife, a senior CIA analyst who — in his account — was one of the best analysts in the entire intelligence community and who lost her job at the agency for no reason other than being married to him. She sat off camera at his December 2007 ABC News interview and told him afterwards that he had said nothing classified.

joe-bidenopoulos.title: Kiriakou pardon request
