joe-bidenopoulos.summary: John Kiriakou's public campaign for a presidential pardon from Donald Trump to restore the pension and firearm rights he lost after his 2013 felony conviction for disclosing the identity of a covert CIA officer; includes a five-second Mar-a-Lago encounter in which Trump referred him to Attorney General Pam Bondi, a Kalshi prediction-market contract that opened at roughly 19 to 20 percent odds on his being pardoned, and letters of support from Tucker Carlson, Judge Andrew Napolitano and Dr. Phil.

joe-bidenopoulos.title: The Mohamed Atta Prague claim
joe-bidenopoulos.summary: Dick Cheney's televised assertion tying the September 11 hijacker Mohamed Atta to Saddam Hussein by way of a meeting with the Iraqi intelligence station chief in Prague, which John Kiriakou calls an out-and-out lie made up without a shred of supporting evidence.

joe-bidenopoulos.title: The asset recruitment cycle
joe-bidenopoulos.summary: The four-step professional standard John Kiriakou says governed CIA operations before September 11 — spot, assess, develop, recruit — and without which an officer did not get promoted. He calls it the asset acquisition cycle as often as the recruitment cycle. Spotting looks for access, not rank; assessment looks for a vulnerability, a word he insists is less ugly than it sounds; development is months or years of friendship bought on an unlimited expense account; and the recruitment itself rests not on money, revenge or ideology but on the target believing the officer is his best friend. Threats are forbidden — partly on ethics, partly because the target may come to the next meeting with a gun.

joe-kent.title: Veteran Intelligence Professionals for Sanity
joe-kent.summary: A group of former U.S. intelligence officials, of which John Kiriakou is a member, that issues the Sam Adams Award for Integrity in Intelligence — which Kiriakou arranged to give to whistleblower-adjacent figure Joe Kent.

joe-kent.title: Charlie Kirk shooting
joe-kent.summary: Kiriakou questions the official account: a court filing says the ATF could not match the autopsy bullet to the rifle tied to the suspect.

joe-kent.title: Bill Clinton
joe-kent.summary: 42nd U.S. president whom John Kiriakou describes as wholly disinterested in intelligence — briefed by the CIA only twice in eight years, with Vice President Al Gore taking the daily briefing instead and relaying anything important.

joe-kent.title: JFK assassination
joe-kent.summary: November 22, 1963 killing of President John F. Kennedy in Dallas, Texas. John Kiriakou's position, drawn from a Pakistan-station encounter with Bay of Pigs commander Jean Gately, an RFK Jr. account of CIA Director John McCone's same-day exchange with Bobby Kennedy Sr., and a White House contact's confirmation that the remaining classified Kennedy documents all contain the word "Israel," is that elements of the CIA were probably involved and that Israeli intelligence was involved as well.

joe-kent.title: Donald Trump
joe-kent.summary: 45th and 47th U.S. president. Per John Kiriakou, a man genuinely convinced he was doing right by bombing Iran, "duped" by the same Netanyahu nuclear bluff Obama once rejected — and, at the same time, the most blindly pro-Israel president in history, an admirer of autocrats who has never once criticized Vladimir Putin, and prone to gestures — from the Gulf of America to a since-abandoned "Department of War" rename — that test the edges of his actual authority.

joe-kent.title: Felix Rodriguez
joe-kent.summary: Cuban-American CIA officer and Bay of Pigs veteran; involved in the Vietnam War and reportedly present at the killing of Che Guevara; distinct from [Jose Rodriguez](/wiki/jose-rodriguez), the post-9/11 CIA official.

joe-rogan.title: Mike Baker
joe-rogan.summary: Former CIA case officer and John Kiriakou's direct predecessor in Athens on the 17 November problem; "the real deal," in Kiriakou's phrase, until a botched surveillance operation got him expelled from Greece and forced out of the agency the same day he expected a commendation.

joe-rogan.title: Martha Kesler
joe-rogan.summary: Long-serving CIA Syria analyst; author of the standard-issue analytical primer "Syria: Fragile Mosaic of Power"; John Brennan''s first supervisor and the figure who first fired him from the agency, before being herself fired by Brennan when their roles inverted under George Tenet''s patronage.

joe-rogan.title: Patrick Bet-David
joe-rogan.summary: The podcast host whom John Kiriakou described on another programme as a hardcore Zionist and a total backer of Reza Pahlavi, and who then played the clip back to him on air. Kiriakou withdrew the characterisation on the record, one of the few occasions where he has retracted a public statement about a named individual.

joe-rogan.title: The bunker busters as preemption
joe-rogan.summary: What John Kiriakou says friends in the CIA, the Defense Department and the White House told him about why Donald Trump broke with every previous president and struck Iran — that Benjamin Netanyahu said Israel was so certain of an Iranian nuclear attack that it was prepared to use nuclear weapons itself, and that Trump used bunker-buster bombs so that Israel would not.

joe-rogan.title: The manager's ranking
joe-rogan.summary: John Kiriakou's answer to a viewer who asked whether he would ever appear on Joe Rogan's show alongside Mike Baker — that his new manager, who represents some very senior people, told him he is more highly sought after than Baker is, so there is no reason to legitimise him.

joe-rogan.title: The mobile passport lane
joe-rogan.summary: John Kiriakou's report of flying home from Spain during the longest government shutdown in American history — ridiculous security lines, and an immigration officer who said four words, "Look at the camera. Welcome home," which Kiriakou attributes to the man not being paid.

joe-weisberg.title: Revolutionary Organization 17 November
joe-weisberg.summary: Greek far-left urban guerrilla group active 1975–2002; the deadliest terrorist organization in Greek history

joe-weisberg.title: John Kiriakou
joe-weisberg.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

joe-weisberg.title: French village LSD bread experiment
joe-weisberg.summary: John Kiriakou's account of a compartmented MK-Ultra experiment in which the CIA dosed the only bakery of a small French village he does not name with LSD — in some tellings by breaking in at night and spiking the yeast, in others by contaminating the flour supplied to it — so that the hapless baker sold the whole village an unwitting trip. Kiriakou places it as the sequel to the San Francisco bacterium release and calls it, in the agency's own terms, a successful operation.

joe-weisberg.title: Sleeper Agent
joe-weisberg.summary: Per John Kiriakou, a person taken in early childhood, raised in a simulated version of a target country, given a false identity built from the birth record of a deceased infant, inserted into the target country, and then left dormant — sometimes for decades — until activated. Kiriakou says only Russia is known to use sleeper agents; no other country's intelligence service employs the technique. A former East German sleeper agent he interviewed on his podcast defected to the FBI after his daughter was born and a kill threat was delivered to him on the New York subway.

joe-weisberg.title: John le Carré
joe-weisberg.summary: British novelist and former MI6 officer, the subject of a full episode of John Kiriakou's Dead Drop podcast. Kiriakou's argument is that le Carré is the only spy novelist to have changed the business of spying itself — supplying its working vocabulary, from 'Joes' and 'lamplighters' to 'honey trap', and shaping how officers understood their own world.

joe-weisberg.title: Larry Devlin
joe-weisberg.summary: CIA officer and former chief of station in the Congo, whose memoir Chief of Station, Congo was published on his instruction the day after he died — never submitted to the agency's Publications Review Board. John Kiriakou cites it as an act of nerve he admits he does not have.

joe-wilson.title: Valerie Plame
joe-wilson.summary: Covert CIA case officer whose identity was publicly outed by the Bush administration in retaliation for her husband, former U.S. ambassador to Niger Joseph Wilson, publishing a New York Times op-ed debunking the administration's claim that Iraq had attempted to purchase yellowcake uranium from Niger. Per John Kiriakou, Plame's CIA career ended on the day her cover was blown — she could never travel overseas under cover again; no one was prosecuted for the leak.

joe-wilson.title: Curveball
joe-wilson.summary: Cryptonym for the German-handled Iraqi defector whose fabricated WMD intelligence the German BND laundered to the CIA in the run-up to the 2003 Iraq War; per John Kiriakou, in fact a dishwasher at a Shish Kebab restaurant who scraped fake reports from newspaper articles and told the Germans he was an Iraqi scientist with access to weapons of mass destruction; the Germans refused to let the CIA meet or polygraph him, and his fabricated intelligence — biological, chemical, nuclear, and long-range delivery — became one of the central pillars of the Bush administration's WMD case.

joe-wilson.title: Abu Zubaydah
joe-wilson.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

joe-wilson.title: Cofer Black
joe-wilson.summary: Former head of the CIA Counterterrorism Center during and immediately after the September 11 attacks; principal architect of the agency's paramilitary turn on September 12, 2001; later Vice President of Blackwater under Erik Prince.

joe-wilson.title: Counterterrorism Center
joe-wilson.summary: The CIA's Counterterrorism Center (CTC) — the unit where John Kiriakou spent the defining years of his operational career. He joined in the late 1990s as the only officer in the entire CIA fluent in both Greek and Arabic, served as chief of counterintelligence in the bin Laden unit, watched the Center swell from a few hundred employees to nearly 2,000 by September 12, 2001, and it was to CTC that he walked back down in May 2002 to refuse the torture program — the moment, he says, the CIA began to turn on him.

joe-wilson.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
joe-wilson.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

john-bolton.title: National Security Council
john-bolton.summary: The White House body that, in John Kiriakou's telling, sat on the pro-war side of every fight that defined his era — gung-ho for the Iraq invasion alongside Cheney's and Rumsfeld's offices while the CIA, State Department, and Joint Chiefs opposed it; the place where an official predicted Iraqis would "throw flowers at us"; a signature stop in the approval chain for both the torture program and covert action findings; and the perch from which John Brennan, as its number two, urged the Justice Department to secretly reopen the case against Kiriakou.

john-bolton.title: Elliott Abrams
john-bolton.summary: The Reagan-era assistant secretary of state whose 2023 appointment to a Biden administration advisory board John Kiriakou treated as proof that neoliberal and neoconservative foreign policy are the same policy with interchangeable players — a man who pleaded guilty over Iran-Contra, was pardoned, helped sell the Iraqi weapons of mass destruction case, and then served Donald Trump on Iran and Venezuela.

john-bolton.title: Consortium News
john-bolton.summary: Independent investigative news outlet John Kiriakou has written for since at least 2017, founded by Polk Award-winning journalist Robert Parry, who broke major stories on Iran-Contra. Kiriakou's columns there have covered John Bolton's exit, the entrapment of Maria Butina, his own first tour in Saudi Arabia and the 2019 Ukraine-call whistleblower. He says PayPal permanently shuttered the outlet's account and briefly seized its funds before backing down under public pressure, while still refusing to reinstate it.

john-bolton.title: Henry Kissinger
john-bolton.summary: The former secretary of state John Kiriakou calls the biggest living war criminal — "the butcher of Cyprus, the butcher of Chile" — and blames, via the declassified record, for keeping the Greek junta in power. Kiriakou met him once as a new CIA officer, jokes that your natural impulse on meeting him "should be to become involuntarily violent," and marvels that both parties treat him as a foreign policy god. Yet he concedes the dark craftsman his due: Kissinger had goals, realpolitik was real, and it was Kissinger who got Nixon to China.

john-bolton.title: Donald Trump
john-bolton.summary: 45th and 47th U.S. president. Per John Kiriakou, a man genuinely convinced he was doing right by bombing Iran, "duped" by the same Netanyahu nuclear bluff Obama once rejected — and, at the same time, the most blindly pro-Israel president in history, an admirer of autocrats who has never once criticized Vladimir Putin, and prone to gestures — from the Gulf of America to a since-abandoned "Department of War" rename — that test the edges of his actual authority.

john-bolton.title: Generals in national security posts
john-bolton.summary: John Kiriakou''s blanket objection to putting retired generals in charge of the CIA, the Office of the Director of National Intelligence, the Defense Department or the National Security Council, resting on a single argument about how officers reach flag rank: generals became generals by saying ''yes sir'', and what a president needs is somebody who can tell him why an idea is terrible.

john-brennan.title: Kathryn Ruemmler
john-brennan.summary: Obama White House counsel whose Epstein-file emails show her repeatedly trying to introduce Jeffrey Epstein to CIA director John Brennan; John Kiriakou notes she personally received a rare CIA award from Brennan and, as the White House's top lawyer, would have been the final legal authority approving the Tuesday-morning kill list.

john-brennan.title: Obama's drone escalation
john-brennan.summary: The pair of figures John Kiriakou uses to measure what changed between the Bush and Obama administrations — twenty-four people killed by drones in George W. Bush's last month in office against four hundred and forty in Barack Obama's — offered as the answer to anyone who treats the drone programme as an inherited policy rather than an expanded one.

john-brennan.title: Pick the man, then find the crime
john-brennan.summary: Robert H. Jackson's 1940 doctrine — recurringly invoked by John Kiriakou — that a prosecutor's worst abuse is to select a target and then comb the law books for an offense to charge him with

john-brennan.title: The Analysis Corporation
john-brennan.summary: Arlington, Virginia–based [private intelligence firm](/wiki/private-intelligence); one of two companion entities (alongside Arrais Corporation) created as LLC pass-throughs for retired Senior Intelligence Service personnel; John Brennan was appointed its CEO in 2005.

john-brennan.title: Balochistan drone base
john-brennan.summary: Secret CIA drone surveillance base in southwestern Pakistan's Balochistan region; its location was inadvertently disclosed when investigative journalist Jason Leopold filed a Freedom of Information Act request for Pentagon aviation-fuel-delivery records and identified an outsized fuel flow to the otherwise-undocumented base.

john-brennan.title: "Only Fox came to my defence"
john-brennan.summary: John Kiriakou's account of how the American networks labelled him — MSNBC never using the word whistleblower and calling him a CIA leaker, CNN taking a year to change, and Fox, he says, being the only outlet that defended him at the time — offered as evidence that the label a case receives is drawn along political lines rather than factual ones.

john-durham.title: FISA court
john-durham.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the secret Foreign Intelligence Surveillance court — created under Carter, sitting atop the Justice Department, issuing warrants that are never public — which he says was abused against Carter Page as part of what he believes was John Brennan's plan to deny Trump the presidency.

john-durham.title: James Comey
john-durham.summary: Former FBI director indicted under the second Trump administration, whose prosecution John Kiriakou reads as a search for charges to fit a man rather than evidence of a crime — and which he expects to collapse, unlike the parallel case against John Brennan.

john-durham.title: John Brennan
john-durham.summary: Former Director of the CIA; characterized in KiriPedia's source corpus as the principal architect of the agency's enhanced interrogation program and as having plotted against an elected President

john-durham.title: Carter Page
john-durham.summary: Trump campaign adviser against whom, per John Kiriakou, the FBI lied to the FISA court multiple times in order to obtain surveillance warrants. Kiriakou offers the episode as evidence less of a conspiracy than of an assumption — that at that level, with everything classified, officials believe the truth will simply never come out.

john-durham.title: Tucker Carlson
john-durham.summary: American broadcaster and former Fox News host; a personal friend of John Kiriakou's for years, appearing on Kiriakou's radio and podcast work and hosting him roughly a dozen times on his own Fox show. Kiriakou calls him possibly the most brilliant and best-informed person he has ever encountered, and relays Glenn Greenwald's belief that Carlson could win the presidency — an idea Carlson privately dismisses.

john-durham.title: John Kiriakou
john-durham.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

john-fetterman.title: AIPAC
john-fetterman.summary: The American Israel Public Affairs Committee — the U.S. political organization that, in John Kiriakou's framing, ought to be registered as a foreign-lobbying entity but is not, and that wields decisive electoral power against U.S. elected officials who express support for Palestinian human rights.

john-fetterman.title: Abdul El-Sayed
john-fetterman.summary: Physician and Democratic Socialists of America-backed candidate in Michigan's 2026 Democratic Senate primary. John Kiriakou, who discloses a $100 donation to the campaign, presents him as the test case for whether the electability argument still works for establishment Democrats.

john-fetterman.title: AIPAC and foreign-agent registration
john-fetterman.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that AIPAC is the only organization of its kind exempt from registering under the Foreign Agents Registration Act — set against his own experience around 2008, when a contract worth five or six thousand dollars to write four op-eds praising the Abu Dhabi Chamber of Commerce obliged him to register as a foreign agent.

john-fetterman.title: BDS movement
john-fetterman.summary: The Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions movement against Israel; John Kiriakou notes that some 40 U.S. states now have anti-BDS laws that can require a speaker at a publicly funded university to sign a pledge of support for Israel — which he refuses to do.

john-fetterman.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
john-fetterman.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

john-fetterman.title: Bilderberg and weapon sales
john-fetterman.summary: John Kiriakou's claim, sourced to someone he knew who attended, that elite gatherings like Bilderberg and the Shangri-La Dialogue are — beneath the talk of global issues — fundamentally 'all about weapon sales' and defense-contractor deals.

john-kerry.title: Afghan heroin policy
john-kerry.summary: The post-2001 U.S. policy in Afghanistan of protecting, and per John Kiriakou actively encouraging, the cultivation of heroin poppy. Under the Taliban in 2000 Afghanistan produced 0% of the world's heroin; by 2009 under American occupation it produced 93%. Per a DEA officer Kiriakou consulted with on the policy paper he was preparing for Senator Kerry, the strategic rationale was that nearly all of the heroin flowed to Iran and Russia, addiction in those countries was considered desirable as a long-run societal weakener, and the same logic now operates in reverse with Chinese fentanyl flowing into the United States.

john-kerry.title: John Kiriakou
john-kerry.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

john-kerry.title: John Brennan
john-kerry.summary: Former Director of the CIA; characterized in KiriPedia's source corpus as the principal architect of the agency's enhanced interrogation program and as having plotted against an elected President

john-kerry.title: Bill Richardson
john-kerry.summary: U.S. Congressman, Ambassador to the United Nations, Secretary of Energy, and Governor of New Mexico; became friends with John Kiriakou at McClarty Associates; promised Secretary of State in exchange for endorsing Barack Obama in the 2008 Democratic primary; ultimately offered Commerce instead, then CIA director informally, before withdrawing his Commerce nomination.

john-kerry.title: SPLC 2025 indictment
john-kerry.summary: Federal criminal case unveiled by FBI director Kash Patel and Deputy Attorney General Todd Blanche against the Southern Poverty Law Center on multiple felony counts, described by John Kiriakou as concerning alleged payments to the Ku Klux Klan and Nazi groups and alleged money laundering; Kiriakou judges the charges are of the documentary kind that either happened or did not and that they could bring an end to an organisation whose 2024 balance sheet showed assets of roughly $786 to $822 million.

john-kerry.title: The Capitol switchboard
john-kerry.summary: John Kiriakou's advice, drawn from years as a congressional staffer, on how ordinary constituents actually move members of Congress — that the House will act on a single letter, that the Senate needs ten or twenty calls to put an issue on a senator's agenda, and that the Capitol operator will identify a caller's own representative for them.

john-kiriakou-task-force.title: John Brennan
john-kiriakou-task-force.summary: Former Director of the CIA; characterized in KiriPedia's source corpus as the principal architect of the agency's enhanced interrogation program and as having plotted against an elected President

john-kiriakou-task-force.title: Robert Mueller
john-kiriakou-task-force.summary: Director of the FBI in the years after September 11, 2001; per John Kiriakou, the official who, upon learning on July 31, 2002 that the CIA had won presidential approval to take primacy over Abu Zubaydah's interrogation away from the FBI's Ali Soufan, withdrew not just FBI personnel from the black site but every FBI employee from the country itself within 48 hours — "we know what these CIA guys are going to do; they're going to go completely nuts; we don't want any part of it."

john-kiriakou-task-force.title: Espionage Act
john-kiriakou-task-force.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

john-kiriakou-task-force.title: Prosecution as promotion
john-kiriakou-task-force.summary: John Kiriakou''s structural explanation of national-security prosecutions: that the FBI agents and Justice Department attorneys who bring them advance their careers by collecting convictions, which is why cases survive investigations that found no crime and why charges like false statement, perjury and wire fraud get filed when nothing else will stick.

john-kiriakou-task-force.title: The Warren, Ohio tail
john-kiriakou-task-force.summary: John Kiriakou's account of being followed around Warren, Ohio in January 2012 — to his grandparents' old house, to their graves, and to the Packard Museum car park — while he assumed the car behind him belonged to a private investigator hired by his ex-wife, and of realising four days later, in an FBI conference room, that the Bureau had followed him from Virginia.

john-kiriakou-task-force.title: Japanese diplomat FBI sting
john-kiriakou-task-force.summary: John Kiriakou's account of an FBI entrapment operation in which an agent posing as a Japanese diplomat cold-pitched him for classified information over five lunches, hoping he would commit actual espionage they could charge — a scheme he discovered only in his own case discovery.

john-kiriakou.title: Bob (CIA HR)
john-kiriakou.summary: Pseudonym for the CIA officer who served as director of human resources for the agency in the late 1980s and personally oversaw John Kiriakou's hiring

john-kiriakou.title: Breaking the nuclear taboo
john-kiriakou.summary: John Kiriakou's reporting that Donald Trump considered using a tactical nuclear weapon in Iran not for military necessity but to break what he regards as warfare's final taboo, freeing future presidents to use larger weapons — and the related account that the chairman of the Joint Chiefs refused him the nuclear codes.

john-kiriakou.title: International Spy Museum
john-kiriakou.summary: The Washington museum of espionage. John Kiriakou, who gives private tours of it, describes its room on the CIA torture program as a video loop in which only the torturers are given a voice — and in which he, the officer who exposed the program, is never mentioned.

john-kiriakou.title: Louis Farrakhan
john-kiriakou.summary: Leader of the Nation of Islam; per John Kiriakou, issued a perfectly timed statement during Kiriakou's imprisonment at FCI Loretto identifying him as a hero of the Muslim people for standing up for human rights — protecting Kiriakou from the prison's Muslim population at a moment when the Aryans were simultaneously protecting him under the cover story that he was a "Muslim hunter."

john-kiriakou.title: Mahmud (alias)
john-kiriakou.summary: Pseudonym for an Egyptian al-Qaeda fighter recruited by John Kiriakou in an unnamed country during the early 2000s

john-kiriakou.title: Prison as temporary duty
john-kiriakou.summary: The frame John Kiriakou and his wife adopted in the weeks between his sentencing and his surrender: that a thirty-month sentence was to be treated as a long overseas posting. He had spent much of his CIA career deployed for months at a time, once for two years, and says the family handled the separation the way it had handled those. The analogy borrowed a specific piece of agency vocabulary — TDY, the assignment nobody asks you about.

john-larson.title: The Graham Senate succession
john-larson.summary: John Kiriakou's comment on the appointment of Lindsey Graham's sister to serve out the remainder of his Senate term, and her announcement that she would run for a full term of her own — a candidacy whose only qualification, in Kiriakou's assessment, is her relation to the late senator.

john-larson.title: The Qatari 747
john-larson.summary: The Boeing 747 given to the United States by the government of Qatar to serve as Air Force One. John Kiriakou reported in July 2026 that it had been delivered to the president while he was overseas and that he declined to fly home in it, because it had not been fitted with the protective equipment — countermeasures, radar jamming — that the role requires.

john-larson.title: Bill Clinton
john-larson.summary: 42nd U.S. president whom John Kiriakou describes as wholly disinterested in intelligence — briefed by the CIA only twice in eight years, with Vice President Al Gore taking the daily briefing instead and relaying anything important.

john-larson.title: The CIA Insider's Guide to Surveillance and Surveillance Detection
john-larson.summary: Book by John Kiriakou drawing on his experience as a surveillance detection instructor at the CIA and as a private surveillance training consultant. The book covers the techniques used by intelligence professionals to identify whether they are being followed — including the four-phase surveillance detection route, concealment device placement and retrieval, and counter-surveillance strategy — adapted for use by corporate executives, journalists, and others who want to confirm whether they are being followed.

john-larson.title: Dimitris Koufodinas
john-larson.summary: The primary assassin of Revolutionary Organization 17 November, known as the Black Hand because everything he touched died — the one member who briefly escaped the collapse of the group, and who was found on a nudist beach on a Greek island.

john-larson.title: Fidel Castro
john-larson.summary: The Cuban leader John Kiriakou uses as his standing example of a relationship the United States could have had and chose not to — a rebel who liked America and had pitched in its minor leagues, written off because Washington had already committed itself to Batista. Castro also recurs across Kiriakou's account of the CIA as the agency's most-attempted assassination target, as the man who never cashed the rent cheques for Guantánamo, and as the figure American policy is still fighting years after his death.

john-le-carre.title: The scholar-in-residence pipeline
john-le-carre.summary: John Kiriakou's description of retired CIA operations officers taking scholar-in-residence posts at universities and teaching literature courses that function, by their own account, as a recruitment funnel — students enrol knowing the instructor is a former officer and hoping for help getting in.

john-le-carre.title: John Kiriakou
john-le-carre.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

john-le-carre.title: Asset acquisition cycle
john-le-carre.summary: The four-step process — spot, assess, develop, recruit — taught as the first lesson of CIA case officer training

john-le-carre.title: Joe Weisberg
john-le-carre.summary: Former CIA Counterterrorism Center officer and colleague of John Kiriakou who resigned abruptly, saying he did not have it in him to convince people to commit treason, then moved to Hollywood, wrote a well-regarded novel that sold poorly, and created the television series The Americans — which Kiriakou calls the best intelligence show ever made and one hundred per cent true to life, and every script of which the CIA redacted.

john-le-carre.title: Kiriakou's shortwave listening
john-le-carre.summary: The childhood hobby John Kiriakou identifies as the reason he went to work for the CIA — a fifty-cent auction radio, a walk-in closet turned radio shack with a pinned world map, membership of the American Shortwave Listeners Club, and a verified logging of Radio Ulan Bator that put him on the cover of the club's magazine at fourteen.

john-le-carre.title: Larry Devlin
john-le-carre.summary: CIA officer and former chief of station in the Congo, whose memoir Chief of Station, Congo was published on his instruction the day after he died — never submitted to the agency's Publications Review Board. John Kiriakou cites it as an act of nerve he admits he does not have.

john-mccain.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
john-mccain.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

john-mccain.title: John Kiriakou
john-mccain.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

john-mccain.title: Senate Torture Report
john-mccain.summary: The December 2014 executive summary of the U.S. Senate Select Committee on Intelligence's study of the CIA's post-9/11 detention and interrogation program; the first public disclosure of techniques including rectal feeding with hummus, sexual assault with broomsticks, and prolonged sleep deprivation.

john-mccain.title: Intelligence Identities Protection Act
john-mccain.summary: U.S. law enacted in 1982 that makes it a crime to knowingly disclose the identity of a covert intelligence officer; per John Kiriakou, his 2012 prosecution under the act arose from confirming a single surname of a former CIA colleague to a journalist — a confirmation that was never published. The name passed through a chain from journalist to Human Rights Watch to Guantanamo defense attorneys before reaching a judge and ultimately the FBI, which traced it back to Kiriakou.

john-mccain.title: Abu Zubaydah
john-mccain.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

john-mccain.title: The Republican split over the Iran war
john-mccain.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the division inside the Republican Party over the 2026 war with Iran — between the voters who backed Donald Trump as the no-foreign-wars candidate and an administration Kiriakou says has reverted to the neoconservative posture of John McCain's party, with Tulsi Gabbard and J.D. Vance on one side and Marco Rubio on the other.

john-mccone.title: JFK assassination
john-mccone.summary: November 22, 1963 killing of President John F. Kennedy in Dallas, Texas. John Kiriakou's position, drawn from a Pakistan-station encounter with Bay of Pigs commander Jean Gately, an RFK Jr. account of CIA Director John McCone's same-day exchange with Bobby Kennedy Sr., and a White House contact's confirmation that the remaining classified Kennedy documents all contain the word "Israel," is that elements of the CIA were probably involved and that Israeli intelligence was involved as well.

john-mccone.title: Robert F. Kennedy Jr.
john-mccone.summary: Son of Robert F. Kennedy; the source of an anecdote John Kiriakou repeats in which, on the day of the JFK assassination, RFK Sr. asked CIA director John McCone "Tell me your people didn't do this," and McCone answered only "I don't know who did it."

john-mccone.title: Tuesday morning kill list
john-mccone.summary: Weekly CIA targeting meeting instituted by John Brennan in 2009 during his service as Deputy National Security Advisor for Counterterrorism in the Obama administration; produced a written list of individuals to be killed in the following week; per John Kiriakou, the program was a source of pride within the Obama administration and was made operationally possible by the targeting-software sophistication of the period.

john-mccone.title: Executive Order 12333
john-mccone.summary: The U.S. presidential directive — in its post-9/11 amended form — that grants the CIA the legal authority to kill any individual anywhere in the world deemed by the agency to pose a "clear and present danger" to the United States; the legal foundation underlying both CIA paramilitary operations and the agency's contractor relationships including with Blackwater.

john-mccone.title: Jean Gately
john-mccone.summary: The CIA officer who commanded the 1961 Bay of Pigs operation and, decades later, served alongside John Kiriakou as an elderly contractor at the CIA's Pakistan station, where he still blamed Kennedy for the defeat — 'We could have won that thing.'

john-mccone.title: Stansfield Turner
john-mccone.summary: Admiral and Director of Central Intelligence under Jimmy Carter from 1977 to 1981; named by John Kiriakou as one of only two CIA directors he considers good, because he tried to rein the organization in, and remembered inside the agency for the October 1977 mass firing of Directorate of Operations officers that CIA officers call the Friday Night Massacre.

john-oneill.title: Mike Scheuer
john-oneill.summary: Founder and chief of "Alec Station", the CIA unit dedicated to tracking Osama bin Laden in the years before September 11, 2001; per John Kiriakou — alongside his New York FBI counterpart John O'Neill — "100 percent correct" about bin Laden, and uniformly hated for it inside the agency.

john-oneill.title: Abu Zubaydah
john-oneill.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

john-oneill.title: Alex Station
john-oneill.summary: CIA unit that tracked Osama bin Laden beginning in 1995; per John Kiriakou, who served as chief of its counterintelligence branch, the unit kept extremely tight security around its files, limited FBI investigators' access to information about future 9/11 hijackers Khaled al-Mihdhar and Nawaf al-Hazmi, and — under a deliberate policy of non-cooperation with the FBI — failed to watchlist participants in the Malaysia summit where al-Qaeda planned the attacks.

john-oneill.title: Ali Soufan
john-oneill.summary: FBI special agent who handled Abu Zubaydah immediately after his March 2002 capture; through patient, respectful interrogation produced the only actionable intelligence ever obtained from the detainee, including the first identification of "Mukhtar" as Khalid Sheikh Mohammed.

john-oneill.title: CIA–FBI interagency rivalry and 9/11
john-oneill.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the historical CIA–FBI rivalry, dating to J. Edgar Hoover's opposition to the 1947 National Security Act, and how it manifested before September 11 when Cofer Black's Counterterrorism Center withheld from the FBI that hijackers Nawaf al-Hazmi and Khalid al-Mihdhar had been granted U.S. visas.

john-oneill.title: Hezbollah
john-oneill.summary: Lebanese Shia militant organization and political party. Per John Kiriakou, Israel''s strategic goal regarding Hezbollah is not to defeat it outright but to keep Lebanon in a state of chaos that serves Israeli interests. He cites two Israeli operations: the simultaneous pager-detonation attack that decapitated Hezbollah''s leadership, which he called ''the most incredible operation I''ve ever seen,'' and the strike that killed former leader Hassan Nasrallah by leveling an entire complex and killing roughly 300 people — which he characterized as a war crime.

john-paul-ii-cia.title: Operation Gladio
john-paul-ii-cia.summary: A CIA, MI6, Vatican and NATO operation to leave 'stay-behind' sleeper networks across Western Europe after World War II in case of a Soviet invasion; John Kiriakou, who learned of it only after leaving the CIA, notes it was made public by Italian PM Andreotti in 1990.

john-paul-ii-cia.title: Doctor Zhivago operation
john-paul-ii-cia.summary: John Kiriakou's account of a joint CIA-Vatican operation to smuggle Russian-language copies of Boris Pasternak's banned Doctor Zhivago into the Soviet Union via an international book fair — an example of 'declaring victory in small increments.'

john-paul-ii-cia.title: Active measures
john-paul-ii-cia.summary: The in-house name John Kiriakou gives to the CIA branch responsible for propaganda and for countering hostile propaganda — a division he describes as running twenty-four hours a day, paired with an opposing anti-active-measures branch, and as the ancestor of the political action group that remains the agency's clandestine propaganda arm.

john-paul-ii-cia.title: Bilderberg and weapon sales
john-paul-ii-cia.summary: John Kiriakou's claim, sourced to someone he knew who attended, that elite gatherings like Bilderberg and the Shangri-La Dialogue are — beneath the talk of global issues — fundamentally 'all about weapon sales' and defense-contractor deals.

john-paul-ii-cia.title: Carlos the Jackal
john-paul-ii-cia.summary: Venezuelan-born militant (Ilich Ramírez Sánchez) active in the 1970s and 1980s; per John Kiriakou, 'the Osama bin Laden of the 70s and 80s.' Kiriakou spent his Athens posting trying to identify the middleman linking Carlos to the Greek terrorist group 17 November, then six months working the lead with MI5 in London; Carlos was finally run down by CIA contractor Billy Waugh in a Khartoum vegetable market and captured in 1994.

john-paul-ii-cia.title: Mormons in intelligence
john-paul-ii-cia.summary: John Kiriakou's observation that Mormons are heavily overrepresented in the CIA and FBI — because their clean-living record lets them pass the polygraph easily, and their missionary years leave them fluent in rare languages the agencies need.

john-ratcliffe.title: Tulsi Gabbard
john-ratcliffe.summary: U.S. Director of National Intelligence; a longtime family friend of John Kiriakou's, who has known her since she was 12; Kiriakou calls her appointment "an inspired choice" despite disagreeing with her decision to join the Republican Party, and says she appears to have given up her opposition to Section 702 surveillance to secure Senate confirmation.

john-ratcliffe.title: Donald Trump
john-ratcliffe.summary: 45th and 47th U.S. president. Per John Kiriakou, a man genuinely convinced he was doing right by bombing Iran, "duped" by the same Netanyahu nuclear bluff Obama once rejected — and, at the same time, the most blindly pro-Israel president in history, an admirer of autocrats who has never once criticized Vladimir Putin, and prone to gestures — from the Gulf of America to a since-abandoned "Department of War" rename — that test the edges of his actual authority.

john-ratcliffe.title: John Brennan
john-ratcliffe.summary: Former Director of the CIA; characterized in KiriPedia's source corpus as the principal architect of the agency's enhanced interrogation program and as having plotted against an elected President

john-ratcliffe.title: John Kiriakou
john-ratcliffe.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

john-ratcliffe.title: Martha Kesler
john-ratcliffe.summary: Long-serving CIA Syria analyst; author of the standard-issue analytical primer "Syria: Fragile Mosaic of Power"; John Brennan''s first supervisor and the figure who first fired him from the agency, before being herself fired by Brennan when their roles inverted under George Tenet''s patronage.

john-ratcliffe.title: Mar-a-Lago pardon pitch
john-ratcliffe.summary: The lunch at which John Kiriakou put his pardon request directly to Donald Trump. Flown to Palm Beach by a wealthy friend who also wanted a pardon, Kiriakou delivered a prepared line as the president worked the dining room, was told to take it to Pam Bondi, and was afterwards vouched for on a speakerphone call to Trump by a political fixer who then asked him for $25,000 a month until the pardon came through.

john-rendon.title: Kuwait Liberation Day
john-rendon.summary: February 1991 expulsion of Iraqi forces from Kuwait by the U.S.-led coalition; John Kiriakou entered the country with U.S. Marines on the day of liberation; the small American flags waved by the crowds — and the post-liberation arrival of Democratic and Republican National Committee personnel ostensibly to assist the country's transition to democracy — were, per Kiriakou, the work of professional propagandist John Rendon.

john-rendon.title: National Endowment for Democracy
john-rendon.summary: U.S. federally chartered organization characterized by John Kiriakou as a proxy for CIA propaganda — the funding vehicle by which the agency promotes pro-U.S. political leaders in foreign countries; explicitly not an operational entity in the boots-on-the-ground sense.

john-rendon.title: Karl Rove
john-rendon.summary: U.S. political strategist; manager of George W. Bush's 2000 and 2004 presidential campaigns; in 2008 he and John Kiriakou were hired by John Rendon to rehabilitate the reputation of an Indonesian general banned from the United States on human-rights grounds — a job Kiriakou says produced four unpublishable op-eds and nothing else.

john-rendon.title: Joko Widodo
john-rendon.summary: Indonesian general; former Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff of Indonesia; banned from the United States on human-rights grounds for personally killing six pro-democracy college student protesters by stabbing each in the heart in front of the others; subsequently elected Vice President of Indonesia; subject of an unsuccessful 2008 reputation-rehabilitation campaign conducted by John Rendon's firm with Karl Rove and John Kiriakou.

john-rendon.title: Operation Mockingbird
john-rendon.summary: The CIA's mid-twentieth-century program of recruiting and managing American journalists as influence assets; in John Kiriakou's account, no longer operationally necessary in the contemporary period because the U.S. media voluntarily reprints CIA-supplied material, and in at least one documented case sends articles to the agency for clearance before sending them to its own editor.

john-rendon.title: John Kiriakou
john-rendon.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

john-walker-lindh.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
john-walker-lindh.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

john-walker-lindh.title: Government Accountability Project
john-walker-lindh.summary: The Washington whistleblower-advocacy law firm and NGO, known as GAP, whose attorney Jesselyn Radack took John Kiriakou's case after his 2012 arrest and told him he was a whistleblower whether he thought so or not.

john-walker-lindh.title: Jesselyn Radack
john-walker-lindh.summary: American national-security attorney and former Justice Department ethics official who directs the whistleblower-defense practice at the Government Accountability Project. Per John Kiriakou, Radack was herself driven out of the Justice Department, had her law license threatened, and was placed on the no-fly list after blowing the whistle in the John Walker Lindh case; she went on to represent Kiriakou after his 2012 arrest and, separately, helped connect him to a path to reach Edward Snowden in 2013.

john-walker-lindh.title: Mike Spann
john-walker-lindh.summary: CIA officer; first American killed in combat in Afghanistan after the September 11 attacks and, in John Kiriakou's telling, the first of his own colleagues to die in the line of duty in the war that followed; killed during the November 2001 Qala-i-Jangi prison uprising; worked ten feet from Kiriakou in the Counterterrorism Center bullpen. Kiriakou, who lives within walking distance of Arlington National Cemetery, still visits his grave.

john-walker-lindh.title: Arabic and Greek
john-walker-lindh.summary: The qualification John Kiriakou says opened the door to his transfer from CIA analysis to operations: a post in Athens wanted Greek or Arabic, and he had both — by most of his tellings the only officer in the agency who did. The chief who hired him gave the reason in one sentence: it is easier and cheaper to take a linguist and teach him operations than the other way round. The pairing also became a detection tool, since the language nobody speaks in Pakistan is Arabic.

john-walker-lindh.title: Extraordinary Rendition
john-walker-lindh.summary: Per John Kiriakou, the CIA practice of seizing terrorism suspects in one country and transporting them to a third country — often a country with no due-process protections — to be held, interrogated, or tortured outside U.S. legal jurisdiction. The program operated alongside the enhanced-interrogation program and was the operational mechanism by which prisoners reached secret CIA facilities and allied torture sites in countries like Bahrain. Kiriakou himself was not in the rendition line of work but became a federal felon under the Intelligence Identities Protection Act for a single confirmation of a colleague's surname to a journalist who claimed to be writing a book on the Abu Omar rendition from Milan.

johns-briefing-room.title: Lindsey Graham
johns-briefing-room.summary: Republican senator from South Carolina who died in July 2026, and John Kiriakou's standing shorthand for the permanent war caucus — a "show horse" rather than a workhorse, a "chameleon" who "never saw a war that he didn't want to jump into with both feet," and, on posthumously released documentary footage, a man offering the US Air Force to bomb a country America was not at war with.

johns-briefing-room.title: Dead Drop (podcast)
johns-briefing-room.summary: John Kiriakou''s narrative podcast, launched in late 2025 — a season-long, memoir-style retelling of his life in intelligence, from recruitment ("The New Recruit") through Athens ("Golden Boy") to the post-9/11 hunt ("The Hunt Begins"), with mini-episodes like "A Spy''s Guide to Sofia." Written by Kiriakou with Alan Katz, produced by Costard & Touchstone Productions, with Kiriakou, Katz, and Nick Mechanic as executive producers. Its stated goal: "the deepest possible perspective on the world of spying and what makes any spy tick."

johns-briefing-room.title: Reza Pahlavi
johns-briefing-room.summary: The exiled Iranian crown prince whom John Kiriakou dismisses as an Israeli-backed fantasy candidate to rule Iran — a man who has not lived there since his teens, supported mainly by Beverly Hills exiles, whom Kiriakou says 'wouldn't survive the walk from the plane to the terminal.'

johns-briefing-room.title: Death threats against Kiriakou
johns-briefing-room.summary: The threats John Kiriakou has received across two decades — first after going public about the CIA torture program, when FBI advice that at least two were credible sent his family out of the country, and later in waves tied to his opposition to Gina Haspel, his remarks about Pakistan, and his advocacy on Palestine and the Epstein case.

johns-briefing-room.title: Leadership profiling
johns-briefing-room.summary: The CIA practice of producing classified psychological profiles of foreign leaders for the president, vice president, national security advisor and the secretaries of state and defense before any meeting. It was John Kiriakou's first job at the agency, where he served as Saddam Hussein's classified psychological biographer working alongside psychiatrists, psychologists and anthropologists.

johns-briefing-room.title: The TikTok fan edits
johns-briefing-room.summary: The short-form videos made by a University of Texas sophomore, giving John Kiriakou a chipmunk voice and laser eyes, which reached Gen Z at scale and led within weeks to representation by a major talent agency and meetings about film and television.

johns-rules-for-prison-survival.title: Ten-minute moves and the count
johns-rules-for-prison-survival.summary: The clock that governs a federal prison: a fixed daily timetable, movement permitted only during ten-minute windows on the hour, and five counts a day — two standing, three conducted with a flashlight in the face of a sleeping man, which John Kiriakou argues serve no purpose except sleep disruption.

johns-rules-for-prison-survival.title: FCI Loretto
johns-rules-for-prison-survival.summary: U.S. Federal Correctional Institution in Loretto, Pennsylvania; the low-medium-security prison at which John Kiriakou served 23 months of a 30-month sentence following his 2013 Espionage Act–era plea deal; the originally ordered "minimum security work camp" placement was countermanded — per Kiriakou, on Brennan's direct intervention — to place him in the actual prison alongside the general population.

johns-rules-for-prison-survival.title: The prison service economy
johns-rules-for-prison-survival.summary: The trade in goods and services at FCI Loretto as John Kiriakou describes it — used shoes resold on commission, convenience stores run out of lockers at a thirty per cent markup, a dozen bookmakers, unlicensed chiropractic, and sexual services priced in books of postage stamps.

johns-rules-for-prison-survival.title: Raymond Davis Lahore shooting
johns-rules-for-prison-survival.summary: A 2011 incident in Lahore, Pakistan in which CIA contractor Raymond Davis shot and killed two Pakistani men who approached his car with drawn guns; per John Kiriakou, Davis stayed at the scene per CIA "getting off the X" tradecraft, and the consulate SUV sent to rescue him struck and killed an uninvolved bystander en route.

johns-rules-for-prison-survival.title: Robert the arsonist
johns-rules-for-prison-survival.summary: The Australian prisoner who became John Kiriakou's roommate at FCI Loretto — convicted of burning down a Buffalo motor vehicles office over a sales tax dispute, a pathological liar who Kiriakou concluded was a clinical sociopath, and whom he says was easy to manipulate because he was an excitement junkie.

johns-rules-for-prison-survival.title: The chapel job
johns-rules-for-prison-survival.summary: The work assignment John Kiriakou was given at FCI Loretto after he volunteered to teach a class — *"if I want you to teach a class I'll ask you to teach a class"* — and was made a janitor in the chapel instead, at $1.08 a month.

joko-widodo.title: Karl Rove
joko-widodo.summary: U.S. political strategist; manager of George W. Bush's 2000 and 2004 presidential campaigns; in 2008 he and John Kiriakou were hired by John Rendon to rehabilitate the reputation of an Indonesian general banned from the United States on human-rights grounds — a job Kiriakou says produced four unpublishable op-eds and nothing else.

joko-widodo.title: John Kiriakou
joko-widodo.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

joko-widodo.title: John Rendon
joko-widodo.summary: Self-described "professional propagandist"; organizer of the pre-distributed American flags waved by Kuwaiti crowds on the 1991 Kuwait Liberation Day; in 2008 hired John Kiriakou (alongside Karl Rove) to produce op-eds attempting to rehabilitate the U.S. travel ban imposed on Indonesian general Joko Widodo.

joko-widodo.title: Kuwait Liberation Day
joko-widodo.summary: February 1991 expulsion of Iraqi forces from Kuwait by the U.S.-led coalition; John Kiriakou entered the country with U.S. Marines on the day of liberation; the small American flags waved by the crowds — and the post-liberation arrival of Democratic and Republican National Committee personnel ostensibly to assist the country's transition to democracy — were, per Kiriakou, the work of professional propagandist John Rendon.

joko-widodo.title: National Endowment for Democracy
joko-widodo.summary: U.S. federally chartered organization characterized by John Kiriakou as a proxy for CIA propaganda — the funding vehicle by which the agency promotes pro-U.S. political leaders in foreign countries; explicitly not an operational entity in the boots-on-the-ground sense.

jon-ossoff.title: Kiriakou's case-officer rankings
jon-ossoff.summary: A recurring segment in which John Kiriakou grades serving and former American politicians on how good a CIA case officer each would make, using an S-to-F scale. The criterion is character and the ability to attract confidence rather than politics, and he repeatedly grades allies low and opponents high.

jon-ossoff.title: Mark Warner
jon-ossoff.summary: Vice chairman of the Senate Intelligence Committee and former governor of Virginia. John Kiriakou reports being told, by a congressman who had campaigned for his release, that Warner had said in a room he should be hanging from a tree; he counts Warner among the Democrats who switched at the last minute to confirm Gina Haspel, and cites him as evidence that congressional oversight of the CIA is a joke — and then, asked to grade him, puts him at the top of the scale anyway.

jon-ossoff.title: Ro Khanna
jon-ossoff.summary: Democratic congressman from California, whom John Kiriakou describes as one of the very few selfless people in Congress and grades highly in his case-officer rankings.

jon-ossoff.title: Thomas Massie
jon-ossoff.summary: Republican U.S. Representative from Kentucky known for a constitutionalist voting record and consistent opposition to foreign military intervention; per John Kiriakou, a principled America-First congressman who votes with the president on the vast majority of issues, and whose opposition to U.S. funding of Israel and foreign wars is the only plausible explanation for the roughly $30 million spent by the Israel lobby to unseat him in a primary.

jon-ossoff.title: Jim Jordan
jon-ossoff.summary: Republican congressman from Ohio and chairman of the House Judiciary Committee. John Kiriakou describes a genuinely divided view of him: one of only four members of Congress he names as a friend of whistleblowers, and simultaneously the chairman whose Weaponization subcommittee he says is a partisan counterfeit of the Church Committee — with the whole question settled against Jordan by the Ohio State wrestlers who told him their team doctor was abusing them.

jon-ossoff.title: Kiriakou's gun rights appeal
jon-ossoff.summary: John Kiriakou's effort to have the firearms disability attached to his felony conviction lifted, by suing the Justice Department over a restoration process announced in 2025 and never built, and separately by applying for a presidential pardon he says he cannot count on.

jon-stewart.title: Jake Tapper
jon-stewart.summary: CNN anchor who drove to FCI Loretto to interview the imprisoned John Kiriakou — and who asked President Obama at a press conference why he had insisted on prosecuting a man who exposed a crime, a question Obama answered by walking away from the podium. Tapper's visit was the head of a media wave that began with a smuggled-out letter on the Huffington Post, and it became Kiriakou's protection inside; even a guard known as a psychopath left him alone rather than find CNN parked beside his car.

jon-stewart.title: Cancelling the 2026 midterms
jon-stewart.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that the 2026 war cannot win the midterm elections for the Republicans, and his flagged-as-paranoid worry that it may instead furnish the pretext for a national emergency and a cancelled election.

jon-stewart.title: CIA liaison relationships
jon-stewart.summary: John Kiriakou's critique of CIA intelligence-liaison relationships with foreign governments — sharply expanded after 9/11 — arguing that officers do not consider the long-term risk that disclosing sensitive operations to foreign services hands those governments leverage, including potential blackmail material, over the United States, and that no one left in Congress has the will to provide real oversight of the practice.

jon-stewart.title: Civilian ships and piracy
jon-stewart.summary: Why merchant crews cannot defend themselves: by international treaty no civilian ship may carry a weapon. John Kiriakou handled international piracy as a Senate Foreign Relations Committee staffer and brought Captain Richard Phillips to testify.

jon-stewart.title: Counterterrorism Center
jon-stewart.summary: The CIA's Counterterrorism Center (CTC) — the unit where John Kiriakou spent the defining years of his operational career. He joined in the late 1990s as the only officer in the entire CIA fluent in both Greek and Arabic, served as chief of counterintelligence in the bin Laden unit, watched the Center swell from a few hundred employees to nearly 2,000 by September 12, 2001, and it was to CTC that he walked back down in May 2002 to refuse the torture program — the moment, he says, the CIA began to turn on him.

jon-stewart.title: David Ransom
jon-stewart.summary: U.S. Ambassador to Bahrain during the period of John Kiriakou's posting there; characterized by Kiriakou as one of the finest people he worked for in his CIA career

jonathan-pollard.title: Caspar Weinberger
jonathan-pollard.summary: U.S. Secretary of Defense under Ronald Reagan; John Kiriakou cites Weinberger's assessment that Jonathan Pollard's espionage caused "grave damage" — the highest category of harm — to U.S. national security.

jonathan-pollard.title: The debate with the Mossad director
jonathan-pollard.summary: John Kiriakou's account of his first appearance on Piers Morgan's programme, where he debated a former director of the Mossad who he says could not stop chuckling, and the exchange about Israeli espionage that ended in "no comment".

jonathan-pollard.title: Cory Booker
jonathan-pollard.summary: Per John Kiriakou, he was "especially furious" with Democratic senator Cory Booker for running through the halls of Congress to get to a photo op standing behind Benjamin Netanyahu, which Kiriakou cites as an example of Democratic silence in the face of AIPAC pressure.

jonathan-pollard.title: Democratic silence on the Iran war
jonathan-pollard.summary: John Kiriakou's observation that the only front-facing critics of the 2026 Iran war came from the isolationist right, while Democrats said nothing. He attributes the silence to fear of an AIPAC-funded primary challenge, and singles out Senator Cory Booker as the illustration.

jonathan-pollard.title: Mark Levin Iran Policy
jonathan-pollard.summary: Per Sean Davis, speaking on the same Megyn Kelly panel as Kiriakou, radio host Mark Levin was among the "outside voices" — alongside Senator Lindsey Graham — who effectively made the real policy call to invade Iran. Separately, per John Kiriakou, Levin is one of the very few prominent commentators who consistently defends Israel publicly online.

jonathan-pollard.title: Scott Horton
jonathan-pollard.summary: American antiwar journalist and interviewer whom John Kiriakou calls one of the most brilliant people he has ever engaged with, and the man he found sitting opposite Alan Dershowitz and Danny Ayalon when both he and Horton were called in as last-minute fill-ins on a Piers Morgan panel about Jeffrey Epstein and Israeli espionage.

jordanian-al-qaeda-detainee.title: Abu Zubaydah
jordanian-al-qaeda-detainee.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

jordanian-al-qaeda-detainee.title: Tora Bora
jordanian-al-qaeda-detainee.summary: Mountainous cave complex in eastern Afghanistan that served as an al-Qaeda redoubt after the September 11 attacks. Per John Kiriakou — chief of counterterrorism operations in Pakistan at the time — the CIA killed al-Qaeda military-affairs chief Mohammed Atef there in October 2001, and Tora Bora was the backdrop to the hunt for the senior al-Qaeda leadership that culminated in the capture of Abu Zubaydah. Kiriakou also recounts an Egyptian al-Qaeda fighter he later recruited who survived a cruise-missile strike on a Tora Bora cave — one of only two who came out alive, his ears bleeding, describing the explosion as the most hideous sound he had ever heard.

jordanian-al-qaeda-detainee.title: The martyrdom bonus
jordanian-al-qaeda-detainee.summary: The recruitment offer John Kiriakou says captured al-Qaeda foot soldiers described to him in Pakistan: a monthly wage to go and fight the Americans in Afghanistan, and five hundred dollars paid to the fighter''s parents if he was killed. He uses it to argue that the men he captured had no religious or political motive at all — most had never read the Quran — and that the only way out of the cycle is education and economic development.

jordanian-al-qaeda-detainee.title: Active measures
jordanian-al-qaeda-detainee.summary: The in-house name John Kiriakou gives to the CIA branch responsible for propaganda and for countering hostile propaganda — a division he describes as running twenty-four hours a day, paired with an opposing anti-active-measures branch, and as the ancestor of the political action group that remains the agency's clandestine propaganda arm.

jordanian-al-qaeda-detainee.title: Athens bank fraud report
jordanian-al-qaeda-detainee.summary: John Kiriakou's account of taking a dream job as COO of an Athens investment firm in 2020, discovering it was an elaborate bank fraud, and being unable to get the FBI to act — an agent telling him that without 'terrorism, China, or January 6th,' they were not interested.

jordanian-al-qaeda-detainee.title: Bahrain Posting (1994–1996)
jordanian-al-qaeda-detainee.summary: John Kiriakou's 1994–1996 assignment to Bahrain under U.S. State Department cover as second secretary for economic affairs — arriving with his wife Joanne and infant son Chris on August 1, 1994, into a tiny Gulf monarchy whose sectarian tensions erupted, two months later, into the first Intifada.

jose-rodriguez.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
jose-rodriguez.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

jose-rodriguez.title: The 2026 KSM confession ruling
jose-rodriguez.summary: The Guantanamo military commission ruling, issued by Lieutenant Colonel Michael Shramma in late August 2026 and reported by John Kiriakou as breaking news on September 1, that threw out Khalid Sheikh Mohammed's confession as inadmissible because the CIA had waterboarded him 183 times, and further threw out his 2007 non-torture Guantanamo interrogations because FBI agents *"intentionally failed to explicitly tell KSM that he had a right to remain silent, that he had a right to consult an attorney, and that what he told them could be used against him at trial."* Kiriakou reads it as the moment the American torture programme made the trial of the man who murdered three thousand Americans impossible.

jose-rodriguez.title: Twenty-five al-Qaeda members
jose-rodriguez.summary: The Senate Foreign Relations Committee study John Kiriakou cites as finding that by the end of 2001 there were twenty-five active al-Qaeda members still in Afghanistan — the basis for his claim that the group was finished as a fighting force by Christmas.

jose-rodriguez.title: "Dig a hole and put him in the hole"
jose-rodriguez.summary: The classified CIA cable John Kiriakou has repeatedly cited as the one that convinced him the torture programme had crossed into murder, a field station reporting that interrogators had killed a detainee during a session and asking headquarters what to do, and a Base-office cable answering *"Dig a hole and put him in the hole."* Kiriakou frames it as the moment the answer to *"nobody ever gave the CIA permission to torture people to death"* stopped being a hypothetical.

jose-rodriguez.title: Public-interest defense
jose-rodriguez.summary: The affirmative defense the Espionage Act does not allow: John Kiriakou explains that a defendant cannot tell a jury he acted in the public interest, and that Edward Snowden''s willingness to come home hinged on getting that chance — which the Justice Department refused.

jose-rodriguez.title: The promotion panel
jose-rodriguez.summary: The CIA board that reviews an officer for advancement, and the one that reviewed John Kiriakou weeks after the Abu Zubaydah capture — where his refusal to be trained in the enhanced interrogation techniques was recorded as *"a shocking lack of commitment to counterterrorism"*, and he was passed over.

joseph-b-chambers.title: Arkady Shevchenko
joseph-b-chambers.summary: Soviet diplomat and Undersecretary General of the United Nations who secretly spied for the CIA before defecting to the United States in 1978 — described by John Kiriakou as the single most important spy the CIA ever had inside the Soviet power structure.

joseph-b-chambers.title: Gore Vidal
joseph-b-chambers.summary: American novelist and essayist; per John Kiriakou, a Sidwell Friends/St. Albans/Phillips Exeter alumnus who enlisted after Pearl Harbor rather than attend college, wrote the controversial 1948 novel The City and the Pillar, won a National Book Award in 1993, and was buried near his one lasting partner, Howard Austen, and his boyhood best friend, James Trimble, who was killed at Iwo Jima.

joseph-b-chambers.title: New Castle, Pennsylvania
joseph-b-chambers.summary: John Kiriakou's home town, an hour north of Pittsburgh on the edge of Amish country — a rust-belt city of roughly 40,000 to 50,000 people when he was growing up and around 18,000 to 20,000 now, whose decline he measures by the arrival of DEA and ATF field offices. It is also where, aged eight or nine and hunting salamanders in Oak Park Cemetery, he found the grave of a Medal of Honor private and acquired the lifelong interest in cemeteries that became a book.

joseph-b-chambers.title: Remains of the Day (book)
joseph-b-chambers.summary: John Kiriakou's book, announced for publication by Simon and Schuster in March 2026, billed as a definitive guide to the historic cemeteries of Washington DC and the first in a planned series; the second installment will cover the Mafia graves of New York City.

josh-shapiro.title: Kiriakou pardon request
josh-shapiro.summary: John Kiriakou's public campaign for a presidential pardon from Donald Trump to restore the pension and firearm rights he lost after his 2013 felony conviction for disclosing the identity of a covert CIA officer; includes a five-second Mar-a-Lago encounter in which Trump referred him to Attorney General Pam Bondi, a Kalshi prediction-market contract that opened at roughly 19 to 20 percent odds on his being pardoned, and letters of support from Tucker Carlson, Judge Andrew Napolitano and Dr. Phil.

josh-shapiro.title: AIPAC
josh-shapiro.summary: The American Israel Public Affairs Committee — the U.S. political organization that, in John Kiriakou's framing, ought to be registered as a foreign-lobbying entity but is not, and that wields decisive electoral power against U.S. elected officials who express support for Palestinian human rights.

josh-shapiro.title: The Iron Dome
josh-shapiro.summary: Israel's air-defence system as John Kiriakou reads it — impressive against a wave of slow Iranian drones, but shown by the handful that got through, and later by Iranian ballistic missiles, to be not all it is cracked up to be; each exchange, in his account, buying Iran intelligence about the gaps.

josh-shapiro.title: 1953 Iran coup
josh-shapiro.summary: The U.S.- and UK-backed overthrow of Iran's democratically elected prime minister, Mohammad Mossadegh; per John Kiriakou, the coup served British national interests rather than American ones, and the subsequent outlawing of secular political opposition under the Shah forced dissent into the mosques — producing a religious rather than secular revolution in 1979.

josh-shapiro.title: Alexa
josh-shapiro.summary: Per John Kiriakou, Amazon''s Alexa smart speaker reports directly to the NSA — and he owns one anyway. The device recurs across his interviews as the standing example of the surveillance trade-off in modern smart-home technology, and of his own negotiated exception to it: one speaker, in one room, against the advice of every intelligence officer he has ever known.

josh-shapiro.title: Cori Bush
josh-shapiro.summary: Former U.S. Representative from St. Louis (Missouri's 1st congressional district); cited by John Kiriakou as one of the two named cases of AIPAC successfully primarying an incumbent for delivering a House floor speech describing the Gaza war as a "wholesale massacre of Palestinian civilians."

joshua-schulte.title: Vault 7
joshua-schulte.summary: The 2017 WikiLeaks disclosure of thousands of pages of CIA Directorate of Science and Technology documents — leaked by agency engineer Joshua Schulte — revealing CIA technical capabilities including remote takeover of internet-connected cars, conversion of smart-TV speakers into covert microphones, and the planting of Russian or Persian language fragments in foreign systems to mislead attribution.

joshua-schulte.title: Julian Assange
joshua-schulte.summary: Kiriakou — a 15-year friend and former WikiLeaks board member — on why Assange is a publisher owed a journalist's immunity, and a political prisoner.

joshua-schulte.title: Marble Framework
joshua-schulte.summary: A CIA obfuscation tool revealed in the Vault 7 leaks; per John Kiriakou, the agency embedded snippets of Farsi and Cyrillic in the code of domestic hacking operations so that any discovery could be falsely attributed to Iran or Russia.

joshua-schulte.title: Sentencing enhancements
joshua-schulte.summary: John Kiriakou''s explanation of how a nine-year federal offence becomes a forty-year sentence: the sentencing table''s forty offence levels and seven criminal-history columns, and the enhancements stacked on top of a base level — for terrorism, for hacking, and, in the case he considers most perverse, for having pleaded not guilty and lost.

joshua-schulte.title: Michael Hastings
joshua-schulte.summary: American investigative journalist whose 2013 death in a single-vehicle Los Angeles car crash is invoked by John Kiriakou as the canonical real-world referent for the CIA car-remote-takeover capability disclosed in the 2017 Vault 7 documents.

joshua-schulte.title: UC Global and the state secrets privilege
joshua-schulte.summary: The Spanish private security company that John Kiriakou says copied the electronic devices of everyone visiting Julian Assange at the Ecuadorian embassy in London and passed the contents to the CIA. When two journalists and two attorneys sued and the case survived dismissal, the agency moved to invoke the state secrets privilege — which Kiriakou treats as proof that a plain constitutional violation can be left without any remedy at all.

juan-guaido.title: María Corina Machado
juan-guaido.summary: The Venezuelan opposition leader and Nobel Peace Prize laureate whom John Kiriakou rates no higher than Juan Guaidó: a figure in a permanently divided right-wing opposition who commands no armies and no troops. He reads the prize itself as part of the propaganda campaign against Maduro, and expects that if Maduro leaves the next leader of Venezuela will be a senior military officer rather than a civilian politician.

juan-guaido.title: Aafia Siddiqui
juan-guaido.summary: Pakistani-American neuroscientist arrested in Afghanistan and convicted in the United States of attempting to shoot FBI agents; per John Kiriakou, who covered the arrest as a terrorism consultant for ABC News and has followed the case since, she never had a gun and never fired, the bullet holes offered as proof predated her capture, and the CIA took her three children — two later recovered, the youngest never found.

juan-guaido.title: Afghan heroin policy
juan-guaido.summary: The post-2001 U.S. policy in Afghanistan of protecting, and per John Kiriakou actively encouraging, the cultivation of heroin poppy. Under the Taliban in 2000 Afghanistan produced 0% of the world's heroin; by 2009 under American occupation it produced 93%. Per a DEA officer Kiriakou consulted with on the policy paper he was preparing for Senator Kerry, the strategic rationale was that nearly all of the heroin flowed to Iran and Russia, addiction in those countries was considered desirable as a long-run societal weakener, and the same logic now operates in reverse with Chinese fentanyl flowing into the United States.

juan-guaido.title: The CIA divorce rate
juan-guaido.summary: John Kiriakou's account of why marriages fail at the CIA at a rate he says exceeds that of any other part of the U.S. government — the impossibility of explaining a midnight departure to a spouse without a clearance, and the difficulty officers have switching off a professional habit of deception. He gives the figure variously as over 75 percent and upwards of 80 percent, says he was determined not to become a statistic and became one anyway, and dates the end of his first marriage to a sentence spoken in an armoured car on the way to Athens airport. Both his divorces have been costly; of the second he says the agency played an active role he is barred by court order from explaining.

juan-guaido.title: Venezuelan embassy occupation (2019)
juan-guaido.summary: A 2019 sit-in at the Venezuelan embassy in Washington, D.C., which John Kiriakou says he joined at the Venezuelan government's request the night the United States broke relations with Venezuela; he says he still keeps Venezuelan government property from that night at his house.

juan-guaido.title: The Stratfor cables on Venezuela
juan-guaido.summary: Material John Kiriakou says WikiLeaks exposed on American operations against Venezuela — the training of opposition figures including Juan Guaidó and Leopoldo López, and plotting to sabotage dams inside the country to help bring down Hugo Chávez. He offers it as an example of detail so obscure that few journalists know it, and as the real reason for the pursuit of Julian Assange.

julian-assange.title: The Department of Education SWAT raid
julian-assange.summary: John Kiriakou's account of a pre-dawn armed raid on the home of a Washington Times journalist and her husband, an official at the Department of Education — carried out, he says, by the Department of Education's own armed SWAT team, which seized the reporter's notes and refused to return them. He uses the episode to point out that several civilian federal departments maintain armed tactical units, and that no other journalist covered it.

julian-assange.title: Kiriakou on influencing Trump
julian-assange.summary: John Kiriakou's 2019 account of how to move Donald Trump on a policy question — that the president is malleable but needs to hear the same thing from three different people he respects, illustrated with an episode in which Rand Paul mentioned Kiriakou to Trump two weeks after an aide had, and Trump remembered the earlier mention. Kiriakou used the theory to argue that a pardon for Julian Assange was reachable.

julian-assange.title: Kiriakou Introduction to WikiLeaks
julian-assange.summary: Kiriakou first heard of WikiLeaks as a warning inside the secret spaces it existed to expose: ''Don''t touch that. Don''t go near that.''

julian-assange.title: Leonard Peltier
julian-assange.summary: The American Indian Movement prisoner John Kiriakou names when asked which cases deserve attention alongside Assange's — an old and ailing man whom he calls factually innocent, and whose continued imprisonment he offers as evidence that the system's incentives run only one way.

julian-assange.title: Matt DeHart
julian-assange.summary: American Army veteran and whistleblower prosecuted on charges including child pornography that the Justice Department later admitted, in court, did not exist; per John Kiriakou, DeHart fled to Canada at the first sign of military trouble, was returned to the U.S., and was held without bond as a flight risk.

julian-assange.title: The 2020 extradition hearing
