julian-assange.summary: The London hearing on the United States' request to extradite Julian Assange, described by John Kiriakou two days into it — a proceeding scheduled to run to July with a month-long recess inserted at the American prosecutors' request, held in a courtroom whose microphones did not work, with Assange behind a plastic screen and unable to hear his own case. Kiriakou called it more of a circus sideshow than a legal hearing, and warned that even a defence victory would leave Assange expelled to Australia and open to a fresh American request.

justice-department-self-immolation-attem.title: Cameo
justice-department-self-immolation-attem.summary: The personalised-video app John Kiriakou joined in February 2026 and turned into an unexpected second career — around 2,600 videos, roughly 900 of them in his first month alone. Half are birthday messages and most of the rest are requests for CIA stories, but about two hundred have been appeals for advice or a pep talk, and three of those people later told him he had talked them out of suicide.

justice-department-self-immolation-attem.title: Cold cell
justice-department-self-immolation-attem.summary: A CIA interrogation technique in which a stripped detainee is chained to a ceiling eyebolt in a cell chilled to 50°F, then doused with a bucket of ice water at hourly intervals; never authorized; documented to have killed at least two prisoners.

justice-department-self-immolation-attem.title: Death threats against Kiriakou
justice-department-self-immolation-attem.summary: The threats John Kiriakou has received across two decades — first after going public about the CIA torture program, when FBI advice that at least two were credible sent his family out of the country, and later in waves tied to his opposition to Gina Haspel, his remarks about Pakistan, and his advocacy on Palestine and the Epstein case.

justice-department-self-immolation-attem.title: Israeli foreknowledge of 9/11
justice-department-self-immolation-attem.summary: John Kiriakou's stated belief that Israeli intelligence had penetrated al-Qaeda and knew an attack was coming but withheld the warning as a policy decision, offered as his explanation for the dozens of Israelis arrested in New York in the days after the attacks.

justice-department-self-immolation-attem.title: The Italians at Loretto
justice-department-self-immolation-attem.summary: The mafia contingent at FCI Loretto — men with last names like Gambino, Bonanno, Lucchese, Genovese, DeCavalcante — who adopted John Kiriakou in his second year, largely because he hated the FBI as much as they did. The cast included the boss of the Gambino family (in on a dozen-plus murder counts, the man who replaced John Gotti), Pete the Bonanno captain across the hall who asked why he sat "with those Nazi retards," and a crooked guard on the payroll delivering pork loin and fresh mozzarella. When the FBI later came to Kiriakou's door asking him to inform on Pete, his answer was "get off my property."

justice-department-self-immolation-attem.title: John Kiriakou
justice-department-self-immolation-attem.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

kamala-harris.title: Marco Rubio
kamala-harris.summary: U.S. official whom John Kiriakou identifies as the real motivator behind pressure on Venezuela; Kiriakou argues Venezuela is not a meaningful drug threat to the U.S. and that Rubio simply wants Maduro gone.

kamala-harris.title: Donald Trump
kamala-harris.summary: 45th and 47th U.S. president. Per John Kiriakou, a man genuinely convinced he was doing right by bombing Iran, "duped" by the same Netanyahu nuclear bluff Obama once rejected — and, at the same time, the most blindly pro-Israel president in history, an admirer of autocrats who has never once criticized Vladimir Putin, and prone to gestures — from the Gulf of America to a since-abandoned "Department of War" rename — that test the edges of his actual authority.

kamala-harris.title: Edward Snowden
kamala-harris.summary: Former NSA contractor who in 2013 disclosed the scope of U.S. [mass surveillance](/wiki/mass-surveillance), including the Section 702 collection program. Per John Kiriakou — who counts Snowden among the small group of national-security whistleblowers prosecuted under the Espionage Act — Snowden was ''stuck between two awful slippery slopes'': breaking his oath and chain of command on one side, and on the other catching something ''cut and dry against the Constitution'' that no one would act on. Kiriakou notes Snowden could not use his chain of command (as Kiriakou could not, his own chain being Jose Rodriguez), and that Judge Leonie Brinkema had reserved the Snowden case for herself before he fled the country.

kamala-harris.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
kamala-harris.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

kamala-harris.title: Richard Perle
kamala-harris.summary: Prominent neoconservative adviser to the George W. Bush White House whom John Kiriakou credits with planting the idea of invading Iraq in Dick Cheney's mind the day after 9/11.

kamala-harris.title: Democratic Party 2025 Political Snapshot
kamala-harris.summary: John Kiriakou's 2025 assessment of Democratic Party weakness — a record-low 24% approval rating, seven Senate Democrats crossing over to hand Trump a spending-bill win with no concessions, and California governor Gavin Newsom's surprising denial of parole to a large group of long-incarcerated eligible inmates, which Kiriakou reads as Newsom "playing the long game."

kandahar.title: Kiriakou's transfer to the Directorate of Operations
kandahar.summary: John Kiriakou's roughly two-month internal campaign to transfer from the CIA's analytic Directorate of Intelligence to the operational Directorate of Operations, overcoming what he calls a "natural bias in operations against the eggheads on the analytic side," followed by an Athens posting secured because he was the only person in the entire CIA fluent in both Greek and Arabic. Covers his full CIA career arc from 1988/1990 recruitment through analyst years on Iraq, the switch to operations, 9/11, the enhanced-interrogation refusal, executive assistant to the deputy director for operations, and his eventual resignation and post-CIA career.

kandahar.title: Afghan heroin policy
kandahar.summary: The post-2001 U.S. policy in Afghanistan of protecting, and per John Kiriakou actively encouraging, the cultivation of heroin poppy. Under the Taliban in 2000 Afghanistan produced 0% of the world's heroin; by 2009 under American occupation it produced 93%. Per a DEA officer Kiriakou consulted with on the policy paper he was preparing for Senator Kerry, the strategic rationale was that nearly all of the heroin flowed to Iran and Russia, addiction in those countries was considered desirable as a long-run societal weakener, and the same logic now operates in reverse with Chinese fentanyl flowing into the United States.

kandahar.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
kandahar.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

kandahar.title: David Hicks
kandahar.summary: Australian national captured in Afghanistan in late 2001 and held at Guantanamo, whose case John Kiriakou uses as the measure of what the Australian government can achieve for one of its citizens when it decides to act — and therefore as the indictment of its slowness over Julian Assange.

kandahar.title: The post-9/11 name traces
kandahar.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of his own assignment in the weeks after the September 11 attacks: with people walking into American embassies all over the world offering information on al-Qaeda, the CIA was buried under tens of thousands of names — sometimes thousands arriving in a single day — and needed, as he put it, an army of clerks to search them against its databases.

kandahar.title: The live satellite feed myth
kandahar.summary: John Kiriakou''s flat rejection of one of the most common screen conventions about American intelligence: that officers can call up a live satellite picture and watch a target walk through the streets of a city. There was no such thing then, he says, and there is no such thing now.

karl-rove.title: Joko Widodo
karl-rove.summary: Indonesian general; former Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff of Indonesia; banned from the United States on human-rights grounds for personally killing six pro-democracy college student protesters by stabbing each in the heart in front of the others; subsequently elected Vice President of Indonesia; subject of an unsuccessful 2008 reputation-rehabilitation campaign conducted by John Rendon's firm with Karl Rove and John Kiriakou.

karl-rove.title: John Rendon
karl-rove.summary: Self-described "professional propagandist"; organizer of the pre-distributed American flags waved by Kuwaiti crowds on the 1991 Kuwait Liberation Day; in 2008 hired John Kiriakou (alongside Karl Rove) to produce op-eds attempting to rehabilitate the U.S. travel ban imposed on Indonesian general Joko Widodo.

karl-rove.title: Administrative remedy process
karl-rove.summary: The Bureau of Prisons' internal grievance system, which Kiriakou describes as a fig leaf designed to run out the clock on prisoners' complaints rather than resolve them.

karl-rove.title: Bureau of Prisons
karl-rove.summary: The federal agency that ran John Kiriakou's incarceration — and one of his most persistent post-prison targets. The BOP overrode his judge's camp recommendation by deeming him "a threat to the public safety," threatened him with "diesel therapy" until 1,600 logged phone calls and letters from a dozen House members and two senators backed it off, and, per Kiriakou, functions as "an employment agency for unemployable semi-literate rural white men" and "a dumping ground for failed medical professionals" — an agency for which a prisoner's death is cheaper than his treatment.

karl-rove.title: Cold War
karl-rove.summary: The U.S.–Soviet confrontation that built the CIA John Kiriakou joined. Kiriakou argues the Cold War was real "but also at a certain level desired" — America has always needed an ism to oppose — and that its habits never died: "The Russians thought the Cold War was over, but no one told the US." From its memoirs he draws a standing tradecraft lesson (the CIA''s best recruits were always walk-ins), and in the new Russia and China confrontations he sees a Cold War 2.0 rebuilt on the old exaggerations.

karl-rove.title: David Petraeus
karl-rove.summary: Retired U.S. Army general and director of the CIA who, per John Kiriakou, confirmed the names of ten covert CIA operatives to his biographer and girlfriend and was never criminally charged — a contrast Kiriakou cites repeatedly as proof that his own prosecution under the Intelligence Identities Protection Act was selective. Kiriakou''s explanation for the disparity: Petraeus had not blown the whistle on the torture program and embarrassed the agency.

kashmir.title: The Imran Khan apology demand
kashmir.summary: The demand issued by Imran Khan's party in late October 2025 that John Kiriakou apologise in writing to Khan, to the party and to the Pakistani people over a single sentence he had given an Indian outlet — that India would win a conventional war because it has five times the population — together with his refusal, the death threats, his lawyer's advice, and the blanket policy on South Asian media he adopted afterwards.

kashmir.title: Al-Julani
kashmir.summary: The former al-Qaeda commander and, per John Kiriakou, co-founder of ISIS who was installed as president of Syria and received at the White House. Kiriakou''s initial reading was that no one moves from a ten-million-dollar American bounty to a state visit in months without being a long-term CIA asset — until a senior Turkish official told him over dinner that al-Julani was Turkey''s: ''We created him from nothing and we installed him in Syria.'' Kiriakou judged that version more plausible than his own.

kashmir.title: Death threats against Kiriakou
kashmir.summary: The threats John Kiriakou has received across two decades — first after going public about the CIA torture program, when FBI advice that at least two were credible sent his family out of the country, and later in waves tied to his opposition to Gina Haspel, his remarks about Pakistan, and his advocacy on Palestine and the Epstein case.

kashmir.title: Greater and Lesser Tunb Islands
kashmir.summary: Two small, largely uninhabited islands in the Persian Gulf, belonging to the emirate of Sharjah in the UAE, occupied by Iran in a 1990s incident John Kiriakou recounts as CIA analyst; Kiriakou correctly predicted the UAE would not go to war over them given Sharjah's heavy trade dependence on Iran, and has since used the case against 2026 speculation that the United States would seize them back.

kashmir.title: The 2025 India–Pakistan clash assessment
kashmir.summary: John Kiriakou''s verdict on the most recent India–Pakistan confrontation, delivered after an unusually explicit declaration of his own bias: he loved living in Pakistan, favours Pakistan on Kashmir, and judges that India accomplished nothing while Pakistan lost nothing, leaving the Pakistanis slightly ahead.

kashmir.title: India
kashmir.summary: The country John Kiriakou names as his least favourite of all the places he has worked — not, he stresses, for poverty or danger, both of which he has seen worse of, but for the caste system and "the way Indians treat one another." His illustration is an afternoon in Hyderabad when two separate restaurants refused to admit the driver he had invited to lunch.

kathryn-ruemmler.title: John Brennan
kathryn-ruemmler.summary: Former Director of the CIA; characterized in KiriPedia's source corpus as the principal architect of the agency's enhanced interrogation program and as having plotted against an elected President

kathryn-ruemmler.title: Jeffrey Epstein
kathryn-ruemmler.summary: Convicted sex offender; per John Kiriakou, was "an Israeli access agent" rather than a CIA asset, because the CIA collects foreign intelligence and Epstein's targets — Bill Clinton, Bill Gates, Prince Andrew — were not foreign. Kiriakou further holds that Epstein did die by suicide in federal custody, because in the Bureau of Prisons the cameras never work and the guards are always asleep.

kathryn-ruemmler.title: Tuesday morning kill list
kathryn-ruemmler.summary: Weekly CIA targeting meeting instituted by John Brennan in 2009 during his service as Deputy National Security Advisor for Counterterrorism in the Obama administration; produced a written list of individuals to be killed in the following week; per John Kiriakou, the program was a source of pride within the Obama administration and was made operationally possible by the targeting-software sophistication of the period.

kathryn-ruemmler.title: Extraordinary Rendition
kathryn-ruemmler.summary: Per John Kiriakou, the CIA practice of seizing terrorism suspects in one country and transporting them to a third country — often a country with no due-process protections — to be held, interrogated, or tortured outside U.S. legal jurisdiction. The program operated alongside the enhanced-interrogation program and was the operational mechanism by which prisoners reached secret CIA facilities and allied torture sites in countries like Bahrain. Kiriakou himself was not in the rendition line of work but became a federal felon under the Intelligence Identities Protection Act for a single confirmation of a colleague's surname to a journalist who claimed to be writing a book on the Abu Omar rendition from Milan.

kathryn-ruemmler.title: James Clapper
kathryn-ruemmler.summary: Director of National Intelligence under Obama, and in John Kiriakou's account the standing example of two arguments at once — that lying to Congress carries no consequence at the top of the intelligence community, and that career military officers make poor intelligence chiefs because they cannot tell a president no.

kathryn-ruemmler.title: 2026 Iran war
kathryn-ruemmler.summary: The open-ended American and Israeli war against Iran that John Kiriakou tracked week by week on his own show — a conflict he says was sold as three weeks, ran into its fifth month, achieved every decapitation objective it set, and continued anyway. His grade for it is a D, and his forecast is a Truth Social post declaring victory while nothing changes.

ken-dilanian.title: Jason Leopold
ken-dilanian.summary: Bloomberg investigative journalist; characterized by John Kiriakou as the leading practitioner of Freedom of Information Act litigation against U.S. [intelligence agencies](/wiki/intelligence-agencies); broke the Hillary Clinton private-email-server story; whose FOIA suit against the CIA Office of Public Affairs produced documentary evidence that NBC's chief national-security correspondent had been sending articles to the CIA for clearance before sending them to his own editor.

ken-dilanian.title: Central Intelligence Agency
ken-dilanian.summary: U.S. foreign intelligence service; John Kiriakou's employer from 1990 to 2004 and the central institution of KiriPedia

ken-dilanian.title: John Kiriakou
ken-dilanian.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

ken-dilanian.title: John Brennan
ken-dilanian.summary: Former Director of the CIA; characterized in KiriPedia's source corpus as the principal architect of the agency's enhanced interrogation program and as having plotted against an elected President

ken-dilanian.title: Julian Assange
ken-dilanian.summary: Kiriakou — a 15-year friend and former WikiLeaks board member — on why Assange is a publisher owed a journalist's immunity, and a political prisoner.

ken-dilanian.title: Operation Mockingbird
ken-dilanian.summary: The CIA's mid-twentieth-century program of recruiting and managing American journalists as influence assets; in John Kiriakou's account, no longer operationally necessary in the contemporary period because the U.S. media voluntarily reprints CIA-supplied material, and in at least one documented case sends articles to the agency for clearance before sending them to its own editor.

ken-schaefer.title: The astrophotographer lawyer
ken-schaefer.summary: The Philadelphia attorney who represented Ken Schaefer's victim and who, in John Kiriakou's account, was flown to Israel as the guest of a school he had shown his telescope to — and there asked by a government minister to make the case go away.

ken-schaefer.title: The shank planting incident
ken-schaefer.summary: The episode at FCI Loretto in which Dave Phillips made two homemade weapons, planted them on a pedophile the group was feuding with and informed on him anonymously — a plan John Kiriakou refused to join, and which cost Phillips a transfer while leaving Kiriakou untouched.

ken-schaefer.title: Dave Phillips
ken-schaefer.summary: The FCI Loretto prisoner who claimed to have been a CIA operations officer and whom John Kiriakou exposed as a fake by testing him on agency vocabulary — a possessive, risk-taking companion who planted shanks on a pedophile, was caught, and was shipped to another prison.

ken-schaefer.title: FCI Loretto
ken-schaefer.summary: U.S. Federal Correctional Institution in Loretto, Pennsylvania; the low-medium-security prison at which John Kiriakou served 23 months of a 30-month sentence following his 2013 Espionage Act–era plea deal; the originally ordered "minimum security work camp" placement was countermanded — per Kiriakou, on Brennan's direct intervention — to place him in the actual prison alongside the general population.

ken-schaefer.title: The merry-go-round prank
ken-schaefer.summary: The dirty trick John Kiriakou played on an FCI Loretto prisoner he calls Wallace — planting a release form and a laundry bag on his bunk on a Friday evening, when no official was available to contradict them, and letting him give away his possessions and hold a farewell dinner before he was arrested for attempted escape.

ken-schaefer.title: Rule six: the body endures more than the brain says
ken-schaefer.summary: The CIA maxim John Kiriakou carried into prison — that the human body can take much more punishment than the brain believes — which he applied first to being punched in the face and then, more importantly, to depression.

kent-state.title: John Kiriakou
kent-state.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

kent-state.title: RFK Assassination
kent-state.summary: Assassination of Robert F. Kennedy on June 5, 1968 in Los Angeles; per John Kiriakou, physically impossible to attribute to Sirhan Sirhan alone — Los Angeles County coroner Thomas Noguchi determined the fatal shot was fired from behind and below Kennedy's right ear at close range while Sirhan stood in front, the crime scene yielded more bullets than Sirhan's revolver could hold, and a hotel security guard named 'Caesar' was captured on video standing behind Kennedy at the moment of the shooting.

kent-state.title: Phil Ochs
kent-state.summary: 1960s–70s protest folk singer; John Kiriakou retells a story from Pete Seeger about the night Ochs — who had fallen into depression after being unable to sing following a mugging in Africa — called Seeger just before taking his own life.

kent-state.title: MK-Ultra
kent-state.summary: The CIA's mid-twentieth-century umbrella program of mind-control, behavioral-modification, and biological-warfare experimentation, encompassing subprojects such as MK-Chickwit and MK-Seesaw; active 1952–1975; documented practices included LSD dosing of unwitting American citizens in CIA-rented brothels and the aerosolized release of pathogens into the San Francisco fog; 80% of the program's documentation was destroyed by the CIA in defiance of a 1975 preservation order from Senator Frank Church.

kent-state.title: Al-Qaeda training manual interrogation-resistance tactics
kent-state.summary: A captured al-Qaeda training manual instructing operatives on how to resist interrogation, including feigning illness — a technique John Kiriakou says he saw a detainee use, and recognized, during a capture and interrogation in Pakistan.

kent-state.title: Alexa
kent-state.summary: Per John Kiriakou, Amazon''s Alexa smart speaker reports directly to the NSA — and he owns one anyway. The device recurs across his interviews as the standing example of the surveillance trade-off in modern smart-home technology, and of his own negotiated exception to it: one speaker, in one room, against the advice of every intelligence officer he has ever known.

kermit-roosevelt-and-mosaddegh.title: The nineteen intelligence agencies
kermit-roosevelt-and-mosaddegh.summary: Asked how many American intelligence agencies there are, John Kiriakou put the number at about nineteen, said there are no genuinely secret ones left, and argued that the sprawl is empire-building by the Pentagon — before asking why the Department of Agriculture and the Department of Commerce need intelligence agencies at all.

kermit-roosevelt-and-mosaddegh.title: Economic roots of terrorism
kermit-roosevelt-and-mosaddegh.summary: John Kiriakou's argument, drawn from interrogating young al-Qaeda fighters in Pakistan, that jihadi recruitment is driven by poverty and hopelessness rather than religion — illiterate villagers paid $300 a month who could not find the U.S. on a map and had never read the Quran.

kermit-roosevelt-and-mosaddegh.title: From the Alien and Sedition Acts to the Espionage Act
kermit-roosevelt-and-mosaddegh.summary: A lineage John Kiriakou endorsed on the In Limine podcast: that language was lifted from the Alien and Sedition Acts into the Espionage Act of 1917 during the anti-radical hysteria of that period, making a straight line from the earliest American political prosecutions to the statute used against modern whistleblowers.

kermit-roosevelt-and-mosaddegh.title: The Colonial Pipeline hack
kermit-roosevelt-and-mosaddegh.summary: Days after the May 2021 ransomware attack that shut the East Coast's main fuel pipeline, John Kiriakou said an FBI contact told him the bureau was fairly confident the Russian government was not behind it — and turned the episode into an indictment of the National Security Agency for watching Americans instead of defending them.

kermit-roosevelt-and-mosaddegh.title: Al Qaeda Software
kermit-roosevelt-and-mosaddegh.summary: A claim raised on a Kiriakou-appearance podcast that "Al-Qaeda" is also the name of a terrorist-tracking software, alongside its use as the name of the terrorist organization.

kermit-roosevelt-and-mosaddegh.title: The Laura Ingraham exchange
kermit-roosevelt-and-mosaddegh.summary: John Kiriakou's account of an on-air exchange with Fox News host Laura Ingraham about torture, in which she told him she hated his position and he replied that anyone who wants torture as an instrument of policy should have the courage to go to Capitol Hill and change the law rather than pretend the existing law does not apply.

kevin-shipp.title: The whistleblower support network
kevin-shipp.summary: The informal circle of American national security whistleblowers that John Kiriakou describes as 'something of a club' — Daniel Ellsberg, Bill Binney, Kirk Wiebe, Ed Loomis, Thomas Drake, Jesselyn Radack and others — whose members in the Washington area meet socially and without which, Kiriakou says, none of them could have got through it.

kevin-shipp.title: Bill Binney
kevin-shipp.summary: Former NSA technical director whom John Kiriakou cites as having debunked the DNC hack. Asked by Veteran Intelligence Professionals for Sanity to examine the science, Binney analyzed the speed of the upload and concluded the emails could only have been copied in person to a thumb drive, not taken remotely by Russia — an argument he later made to Donald Trump in the Oval Office. Kiriakou calls him a friend, the most brilliant person he has met on electronics, and a member of the whistleblower circle he belongs to.

kevin-shipp.title: Generals in national security posts
kevin-shipp.summary: John Kiriakou''s blanket objection to putting retired generals in charge of the CIA, the Office of the Director of National Intelligence, the Defense Department or the National Security Council, resting on a single argument about how officers reach flag rank: generals became generals by saying ''yes sir'', and what a president needs is somebody who can tell him why an idea is terrible.

kevin-shipp.title: John Bolton
kevin-shipp.summary: Former U.S. National Security Advisor. Per John Kiriakou, one of the most dangerous men in America and the real driver — with Elliott Abrams — of the 2019 pressure campaign against Venezuela; the signature at the National Security Council through which a covert action finding passes on its way to the president. Kiriakou predicted his 2019 departure from the Trump administration on the basis of White House chatter and Trump's premium on loyalty.

kevin-shipp.title: The John Kiriakou Task Force
kevin-shipp.summary: The dedicated FBI unit that John Kiriakou says was created inside the Bureau to investigate him after he blew the whistle on the CIA''s torture program: twelve agents appointed under director Robert Mueller who tapped his phones, intercepted his email and followed him in pairs to work, to church and to the grocery store for three years, trying to catch him committing a crime.

kevin-shipp.title: The oath to the Constitution
kevin-shipp.summary: The oath sworn with a raised right hand on the first day at the CIA, in an auditorium full of new hires, to protect the Constitution against all enemies foreign and domestic — and the secrecy agreement signed alongside it, which John Kiriakou and Ray McGovern both treat as merely a contract. Kiriakou uses the oath to answer the charge that he broke a promise, to explain why torture had to be disclosed, and to state a rule of precedence: when a law, a policy or a signed agreement conflicts with the Constitution, the Constitution wins every time. He suspects he was the only person in the room who meant it.

khaled-mashal.title: MOSSAD
khaled-mashal.summary: Israel's primary external intelligence service; characterized by John Kiriakou as universally hostile in his and his CIA colleagues' professional dealings with it ("never had a positive encounter with Mossad"); operates almost exclusively in the operational rather than analytical domain; the CIA is, per Kiriakou, categorically forbidden from spying on it.

khaled-mashal.title: Mahmoud al-Mabhouh
khaled-mashal.summary: Senior Hamas figure assassinated by Mossad in a Dubai hotel room in January 2010; the operation has been studied by intelligence services worldwide for its tradecraft, in particular the unsolved question of how the assassination team locked the hotel-room door from the inside after killing him.

khaled-mashal.title: The Siemens control room
khaled-mashal.summary: The underground surveillance facility in Dubai that John Kiriakou says he was given a tour of — built by Siemens, five storeys of monitors covering every inch of the city — and the taxi crash he watched unfold on the wall in real time.

khalid-el-masri.title: Maher Arar
khalid-el-masri.summary: Canadian-Syrian political-science professor at the University of Toronto; in 2002, returning from a family visit in Tunis, was seized by the FBI at JFK at CIA request, secretly rendered to Damascus, and tortured by Syrian intelligence for eight to nine months until they concluded he was the wrong man. The U.S. denied any involvement to the Canadian government until Arar's wife produced a credit-card receipt from his return flight. He sued the U.S. and lost on national-security grounds, then sued the Canadian government and won six million dollars. Per John Kiriakou, his case is the canonical illustration of the CIA rendition program rendering the wrong person.

khalid-el-masri.title: Mohamedou Ould Slahi
khalid-el-masri.summary: Mauritanian citizen, medical student in Germany at the time of his 2001 detention; held at Guantánamo Bay for fourteen years on the basis of one phone call from his cousin asking him to relay news of a family death to a second cousin who was in al-Qaeda; identified by John Kiriakou as one of the most morally significant figures of the post-9/11 period; subject of the film The Mauritanian; became a personal friend of Kiriakou's after both men were released.

khalid-el-masri.title: Edward Snowden
khalid-el-masri.summary: Former NSA contractor who in 2013 disclosed the scope of U.S. [mass surveillance](/wiki/mass-surveillance), including the Section 702 collection program. Per John Kiriakou — who counts Snowden among the small group of national-security whistleblowers prosecuted under the Espionage Act — Snowden was ''stuck between two awful slippery slopes'': breaking his oath and chain of command on one side, and on the other catching something ''cut and dry against the Constitution'' that no one would act on. Kiriakou notes Snowden could not use his chain of command (as Kiriakou could not, his own chain being Jose Rodriguez), and that Judge Leonie Brinkema had reserved the Snowden case for herself before he fled the country.

khalid-el-masri.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
khalid-el-masri.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

khalid-el-masri.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
khalid-el-masri.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

khalid-el-masri.title: Extraordinary Rendition
khalid-el-masri.summary: Per John Kiriakou, the CIA practice of seizing terrorism suspects in one country and transporting them to a third country — often a country with no due-process protections — to be held, interrogated, or tortured outside U.S. legal jurisdiction. The program operated alongside the enhanced-interrogation program and was the operational mechanism by which prisoners reached secret CIA facilities and allied torture sites in countries like Bahrain. Kiriakou himself was not in the rendition line of work but became a federal felon under the Intelligence Identities Protection Act for a single confirmation of a colleague's surname to a journalist who claimed to be writing a book on the Abu Omar rendition from Milan.

khalid-sheikh-mohammed.title: Abu Zubaydah
khalid-sheikh-mohammed.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

khalid-sheikh-mohammed.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
khalid-sheikh-mohammed.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

khalid-sheikh-mohammed.title: Waterboarding
khalid-sheikh-mohammed.summary: Torture technique in which a prisoner is restrained on an inclined board with the head lower than the feet, a cloth placed over the face, and water poured continuously over it to simulate drowning. Per John Kiriakou, waterboarding was treated as a criminal act under U.S. and international law for decades before 2002 — including a post–World War II execution of Japanese soldiers who waterboarded American POWs, and a 1968 court-martial of a U.S. soldier photographed waterboarding a North Vietnamese prisoner — before the CIA reauthorized it after September 11. Abu Zubaydah was waterboarded 83 times; Khalid Sheikh Mohammed 187 times.

khalid-sheikh-mohammed.title: Mitchell and Jessen
khalid-sheikh-mohammed.summary: The two American psychologists who pitched the CIA's enhanced interrogation program to Director George Tenet at a cocktail party in late October 2001; designers of the program and its theoretical underpinning, "learned helplessness."

khalid-sheikh-mohammed.title: Bojinka plot
khalid-sheikh-mohammed.summary: 1996 Khalid Sheikh Mohammed–planned operation, prepared in a Manila, Philippines apartment, to hijack as many as fourteen Boeing 747s and crash them into buildings along the U.S. West Coast; disrupted only by accident, when a cleaning lady let herself into the apartment while the planner was out, recognized the materials laid out as a terrorist plot, and called the police — who alerted Filipino intelligence and, in turn, the CIA. The plot's architect was known to U.S. intelligence for the next six years only by the alias "Mukhtar," his true identity as Khalid Sheikh Mohammed surfacing only when Abu Zubaydah named him to FBI agent Ali Soufan in 2002.

kharg-island.title: Mohammad Reza Pahlavi
kharg-island.summary: The last Shah of Iran, whom John Kiriakou describes as an absolute monarch and dictator who ran a bloodthirsty intelligence service against his own citizens, held formal diplomatic relations with Israel, and sent Iran's oil to the United States and the United Kingdom. Restored to the throne after the 1953 overthrow of Mohammad Mosaddegh, he left the country on a ski vacation in February 1979 and never returned.

kharg-island.title: Watching naval movements
kharg-island.summary: One of the first lessons John Kiriakou says he learned at the CIA: to read American military intentions, watch naval movements — one carrier strike group means business, two means war. He used it to correctly predict the 2026 strike on Iran days in advance.

kharg-island.title: 1953 Iran coup
kharg-island.summary: The U.S.- and UK-backed overthrow of Iran's democratically elected prime minister, Mohammad Mossadegh; per John Kiriakou, the coup served British national interests rather than American ones, and the subsequent outlawing of secular political opposition under the Shah forced dissent into the mosques — producing a religious rather than secular revolution in 1979.

kharg-island.title: SAVAK
kharg-island.summary: The intelligence service of the Shah of Iran, which John Kiriakou describes as bloodthirsty and as having spent far more effort investigating and murdering Iranian citizens than operating abroad. He credits its record — torture, executions of tens of thousands, and bodies dismembered and left in the street — with the durability of Iranian hostility to the Pahlavi family half a century later.

kharg-island.title: Alexa
kharg-island.summary: Per John Kiriakou, Amazon''s Alexa smart speaker reports directly to the NSA — and he owns one anyway. The device recurs across his interviews as the standing example of the surveillance trade-off in modern smart-home technology, and of his own negotiated exception to it: one speaker, in one room, against the advice of every intelligence officer he has ever known.

kharg-island.title: Consortium News
kharg-island.summary: Independent investigative news outlet John Kiriakou has written for since at least 2017, founded by Polk Award-winning journalist Robert Parry, who broke major stories on Iran-Contra. Kiriakou's columns there have covered John Bolton's exit, the entrapment of Maria Butina, his own first tour in Saudi Arabia and the 2019 Ukraine-call whistleblower. He says PayPal permanently shuttered the outlet's account and briefly seized its funds before backing down under public pressure, while still refusing to reinstate it.

khobar-towers-bombing.title: Hezbollah
khobar-towers-bombing.summary: Lebanese Shia militant organization and political party. Per John Kiriakou, Israel''s strategic goal regarding Hezbollah is not to defeat it outright but to keep Lebanon in a state of chaos that serves Israeli interests. He cites two Israeli operations: the simultaneous pager-detonation attack that decapitated Hezbollah''s leadership, which he called ''the most incredible operation I''ve ever seen,'' and the strike that killed former leader Hassan Nasrallah by leveling an entire complex and killing roughly 300 people — which he characterized as a war crime.

khobar-towers-bombing.title: Alex Station
khobar-towers-bombing.summary: CIA unit that tracked Osama bin Laden beginning in 1995; per John Kiriakou, who served as chief of its counterintelligence branch, the unit kept extremely tight security around its files, limited FBI investigators' access to information about future 9/11 hijackers Khaled al-Mihdhar and Nawaf al-Hazmi, and — under a deliberate policy of non-cooperation with the FBI — failed to watchlist participants in the Malaysia summit where al-Qaeda planned the attacks.

khobar-towers-bombing.title: Ali Soufan
khobar-towers-bombing.summary: FBI special agent who handled Abu Zubaydah immediately after his March 2002 capture; through patient, respectful interrogation produced the only actionable intelligence ever obtained from the detainee, including the first identification of "Mukhtar" as Khalid Sheikh Mohammed.

khobar-towers-bombing.title: CIA–FBI interagency rivalry and 9/11
khobar-towers-bombing.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the historical CIA–FBI rivalry, dating to J. Edgar Hoover's opposition to the 1947 National Security Act, and how it manifested before September 11 when Cofer Black's Counterterrorism Center withheld from the FBI that hijackers Nawaf al-Hazmi and Khalid al-Mihdhar had been granted U.S. visas.

khobar-towers-bombing.title: Counterterrorism Center
khobar-towers-bombing.summary: The CIA's Counterterrorism Center (CTC) — the unit where John Kiriakou spent the defining years of his operational career. He joined in the late 1990s as the only officer in the entire CIA fluent in both Greek and Arabic, served as chief of counterintelligence in the bin Laden unit, watched the Center swell from a few hundred employees to nearly 2,000 by September 12, 2001, and it was to CTC that he walked back down in May 2002 to refuse the torture program — the moment, he says, the CIA began to turn on him.

khobar-towers-bombing.title: John O'Neill
khobar-towers-bombing.summary: Special Agent in Charge of the FBI's New York field office for counterterrorism; "brash, flawed" but, per John Kiriakou, "spot-on about Osama bin Laden — 100 percent correct." Mentored FBI Arabic translator Ali Soufan. The principal subject of Lawrence Wright's book The Looming Tower.

kiki-camarena-case.title: Overcriminalization
kiki-camarena-case.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that the United States criminalizes too much — locking up 25% of the world's prisoners with 5% of its population, and adding roughly 50 new felonies a year — illustrated by a NOAA employee prosecuted for whistling at a whale.

kiki-camarena-case.title: 9/11 Commission
kiki-camarena-case.summary: The federal commission of inquiry into the September 11 attacks, which John Kiriakou describes as structurally incapable of reaching the truth because it was barred from interviewing serving CIA officers or any Guantanamo detainee, and was blocked by the CIA from pursuing the Saudi thread.

kiki-camarena-case.title: Abu Zubaydah
kiki-camarena-case.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

kiki-camarena-case.title: Afghan heroin policy
kiki-camarena-case.summary: The post-2001 U.S. policy in Afghanistan of protecting, and per John Kiriakou actively encouraging, the cultivation of heroin poppy. Under the Taliban in 2000 Afghanistan produced 0% of the world's heroin; by 2009 under American occupation it produced 93%. Per a DEA officer Kiriakou consulted with on the policy paper he was preparing for Senator Kerry, the strategic rationale was that nearly all of the heroin flowed to Iran and Russia, addiction in those countries was considered desirable as a long-run societal weakener, and the same logic now operates in reverse with Chinese fentanyl flowing into the United States.

kiki-camarena-case.title: Ahmed Khatib
kiki-camarena-case.summary: Iraqi-installed occupation governor of Kuwait announced on August 2, 1990, hours after the invasion; medical doctor trained at the American University of Beirut whose mother had been a Sudanese slave in the Kuwaiti royal household; college roommate of George Habash and co-founder of the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine.

kiki-camarena-case.title: Allen Dulles
kiki-camarena-case.summary: Long-serving CIA director whom John Kiriakou calls a 'monster' and a 'very dark figure in American history' — a United Fruit board member who ran the agency that overthrew Guatemala's Árbenz, who went to Truman's house to talk him out of criticising the CIA, and who stayed in touch with the men Kiriakou believes killed John F. Kennedy.

kill-them-all.title: *The human rights guy*
kill-them-all.summary: The nickname John Kiriakou says colleagues at the CIA used for him behind his back after he refused to be trained in the enhanced interrogation program and reported another officer for hooding prisoners at the Abu Zubaydah takedown safe house. He learned it from a friend, an Army Reserve brigadier general and psychiatrist named Steve, who framed it as a warning, and Kiriakou answered *"I'm not afraid of them. I'm right and they're wrong."*

kill-them-all.title: Cofer Black
kill-them-all.summary: Former head of the CIA Counterterrorism Center during and immediately after the September 11 attacks; principal architect of the agency's paramilitary turn on September 12, 2001; later Vice President of Blackwater under Erik Prince.

kill-them-all.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
kill-them-all.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

kill-them-all.title: Alex Station
kill-them-all.summary: CIA unit that tracked Osama bin Laden beginning in 1995; per John Kiriakou, who served as chief of its counterintelligence branch, the unit kept extremely tight security around its files, limited FBI investigators' access to information about future 9/11 hijackers Khaled al-Mihdhar and Nawaf al-Hazmi, and — under a deliberate policy of non-cooperation with the FBI — failed to watchlist participants in the Malaysia summit where al-Qaeda planned the attacks.

kill-them-all.title: Amnesty International
kill-them-all.summary: The human rights organization whose torture report forms part of John Kiriakou's core defense — the CIA's crimes were already public knowledge before he confirmed them on ABC, and the Justice Department's own declination letter said so — and the organization whose silence during his prosecution he cannot forgive. He begged Amnesty for a one-sentence statement and got a New Yorker subscription instead; it took Ai Weiwei to change their minds, and by then he was walking out of prison.

kill-them-all.title: Billy Waugh
kill-them-all.summary: Long-serving CIA paramilitary contractor; U.S. Army Special Forces ("Green Beret") veteran of World War II, Korea, and Vietnam; holder of approximately seventeen Purple Hearts (license plate "17 HITS"); resident of Niceville, Florida; died in his nineties.

killing-khamenei.title: "Iran posed no threat"
killing-khamenei.summary: John Kiriakou''s core objection to the 2026 war, stated as a chain of negatives: Iran had no nuclear weapon, no nuclear weapons programme, no wish for one, a religious ruling against one, and no delivery system if it had had one — findings he says were confirmed twice by the CIA and by the IAEA.

killing-khamenei.title: Chaos as the Israeli objective
killing-khamenei.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer to whether Netanyahu''s government actually wanted an American invasion of Iran: what the Israelis want in Iran is what they got in Libya — chaos, civil war, and as many dead Iranians as possible.

killing-khamenei.title: Marco Rubio and Iran policy
killing-khamenei.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer to who was actually driving American policy toward Iran in 2026: with the Vice President, the Director of National Intelligence and the Chairman of the Joint Chiefs all reported as opposed, and with Marco Rubio holding both the State Department and the National Security Adviser''s job, the policy was Rubio''s.

killing-khamenei.title: MBS and Netanyahu asked Trump to attack Iran
killing-khamenei.summary: John Kiriakou's account that Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu jointly went to Donald Trump and asked him to attack Iran — a move Kiriakou finds hard to reconcile with MBS's own years of work to improve Saudi relations with Tehran.

killing-khamenei.title: Hypersonic missiles
killing-khamenei.summary: John Kiriakou confirms that hypersonic missiles are real and that Russia, China and Iran all have them; that a weapon travelling 2,500 miles an hour cannot be defended against; and that Iran holds too few of them to do anything but make each one count.

killing-khamenei.title: The unarmed ship
killing-khamenei.summary: John Kiriakou's enumeration of war crimes committed in the 2026 Iran war — striking civilian targets, rocketing a school and killing 160 children, and sinking a naval vessel and then refusing to aid the survivors — and his insistence that the objection is not confined to Israeli conduct.

killing-of-iranian-police.title: Iran's conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz
killing-of-iranian-police.summary: The six demands issued by Iran's Supreme National Security Council in August 2026 as the price of reopening the Strait of Hormuz. John Kiriakou's observation is that they are the old nuclear-deal conditions transposed onto a new lever, and that the transposition is both smart and very difficult for Washington.

killing-of-iranian-police.title: 2026 Iran war
killing-of-iranian-police.summary: The open-ended American and Israeli war against Iran that John Kiriakou tracked week by week on his own show — a conflict he says was sold as three weeks, ran into its fifth month, achieved every decapitation objective it set, and continued anyway. His grade for it is a D, and his forecast is a Truth Social post declaring victory while nothing changes.

killing-of-iranian-police.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
killing-of-iranian-police.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

killing-of-iranian-police.title: Strait of Hormuz
killing-of-iranian-police.summary: The shipping chokepoint at the mouth of the Persian Gulf, and the centre of gravity of the 2026 Iran war in John Kiriakou''s account — a strait whose only navigable deep water lies on the Iranian side of the maritime border, closed not by Iran''s aggression but, as he insists, by the American and Israeli attack that provoked it: "The Strait of Hormuz was open. We''re the ones that forced the closure."

killing-of-iranian-police.title: The McDonald's theory of regime change
killing-of-iranian-police.summary: John Kiriakou''s argument, drawn from Vietnam and Cuba, that commerce accomplishes what force cannot: to turn a country pro-Western, open a McDonald''s rather than bomb it.

killing-of-iranian-police.title: Abraham Accords
killing-of-iranian-police.summary: The Trump-brokered normalization deals between Israel and Gulf Arab states — in John Kiriakou's judgment "a terrible idea in the first place," a great victory for Israel and the Gulf Arabs that was "a punch in the throat to the Palestinians." He argues the Accords are how Trump meant to "solve the Middle East in a day" — by screwing the Palestinians — that Hamas read the abandonment correctly, that October 7 shattered the project, and that reviving the Accords (Saudis in, victory declared, Nobel collected) remains the organizing goal of Trump's regional policy.

kim-philby.title: Aldrich Ames
kim-philby.summary: Senior CIA officer — a GS-15 who rose to chief of counterintelligence for the Soviet branch — who spied for the KGB for nine years. Per John Kiriakou, Ames walked into the Soviet embassy in Washington in April 1985 and sold the identities of two CIA-recruited double agents for $50,000 to clear a debt run up by his second marriage; both were executed. He went on to identify more than thirty agents, compromise over a hundred clandestine operations, cause at least twelve deaths and take more than $2 million, while being known throughout the agency as a daily drunk and promoted at every turn. The KGB protected him with a decoy mole hunt; analyst Sandy Grimes caught him by matching his handler meetings to his bank deposits.

kim-philby.title: James Jesus Angleton
kim-philby.summary: The CIA counterintelligence chief old-timers were 'genuinely afraid' of — and the wall of illegal files on American citizens kept in his office.

kim-philby.title: James Angleton
kim-philby.summary: Long-serving chief of CIA counterintelligence; in John Kiriakou's account the man whose wall of files at headquarters were all dossiers on American citizens, who was best man at Kim Philby's wedding and never recovered from learning Philby was the mole, and who — per the declassified JFK files — ordered CIA officers to recruit Lee Harvey Oswald.

kim-philby.title: Operation Paperclip
kim-philby.summary: The program by which the CIA's predecessor brought Nazi scientists to the United States after World War II; John Kiriakou notes the FBI opposed it, that the Nazis surrendered to the U.S. fearing the Soviets, and that V-2 rocket father Wernher von Braun is buried near his home in Virginia.

kim-philby.title: Warrenton Training Center
kim-philby.summary: A secret CIA communications facility in Warrenton, Virginia, which — per John Kiriakou — the KGB used as a decoy to protect Aldrich Ames. When Ames warned Moscow in 1986 that he feared becoming a suspect, a Soviet case officer told a CIA contact that the mole was posted to Warrenton; agency mole hunters then spent almost a year investigating ninety employees there and produced ten suspects, none of them Ames.

kim-philby.title: Allen Dulles
kim-philby.summary: Long-serving CIA director whom John Kiriakou calls a 'monster' and a 'very dark figure in American history' — a United Fruit board member who ran the agency that overthrew Guatemala's Árbenz, who went to Truman's house to talk him out of criticising the CIA, and who stayed in touch with the men Kiriakou believes killed John F. Kennedy.

kimberly-guilfoyle-in-athens.title: The Pondiki cartoon
kimberly-guilfoyle-in-athens.summary: The satirical Greek newspaper that ran a doctored photograph of the American ambassador Nicholas Burns naked in a dog collar, being whipped by the education minister — and John Kiriakou's account of the ambassador's official protest, and of the staff who taped the page above their desks where he could not see it.

kimberly-guilfoyle-in-athens.title: Abraham Accords
kimberly-guilfoyle-in-athens.summary: The Trump-brokered normalization deals between Israel and Gulf Arab states — in John Kiriakou's judgment "a terrible idea in the first place," a great victory for Israel and the Gulf Arabs that was "a punch in the throat to the Palestinians." He argues the Accords are how Trump meant to "solve the Middle East in a day" — by screwing the Palestinians — that Hamas read the abandonment correctly, that October 7 shattered the project, and that reviving the Accords (Saudis in, victory declared, Nobel collected) remains the organizing goal of Trump's regional policy.

kimberly-guilfoyle-in-athens.title: Nicholas Burns
kimberly-guilfoyle-in-athens.summary: The United States ambassador to Greece during John Kiriakou''s Athens tour — an envoy Kiriakou says he has always disliked and disrespected, whose unpopularity extended to his own staff, and whom he credits with exactly one good decision: drawing the assignments for a presidential visit out of a hat.

kimberly-guilfoyle-in-athens.title: The magazines that bought her freedom
kimberly-guilfoyle-in-athens.summary: John Kiriakou's account of his grandmother's imprisonment by the collaborationist government in wartime Athens, and of his grandfather buying her release from a prison guard with American magazines — after which the couple escaped to the United States.

kimberly-guilfoyle-in-athens.title: Amnesty International
kimberly-guilfoyle-in-athens.summary: The human rights organization whose torture report forms part of John Kiriakou's core defense — the CIA's crimes were already public knowledge before he confirmed them on ABC, and the Justice Department's own declination letter said so — and the organization whose silence during his prosecution he cannot forgive. He begged Amnesty for a one-sentence statement and got a New Yorker subscription instead; it took Ai Weiwei to change their minds, and by then he was walking out of prison.

kimberly-guilfoyle-in-athens.title: The CIA's internal social culture
kimberly-guilfoyle-in-athens.summary: John Kiriakou's one-word characterisation of the agency's internal culture — "incestuous" — describing a club for every conceivable interest, actively encouraged officer-to-officer romances, and a design intent that officers should have no need of friends or activities outside the building.

king-abdullah-ii.title: Abraham Accords
king-abdullah-ii.summary: The Trump-brokered normalization deals between Israel and Gulf Arab states — in John Kiriakou's judgment "a terrible idea in the first place," a great victory for Israel and the Gulf Arabs that was "a punch in the throat to the Palestinians." He argues the Accords are how Trump meant to "solve the Middle East in a day" — by screwing the Palestinians — that Hamas read the abandonment correctly, that October 7 shattered the project, and that reviving the Accords (Saudis in, victory declared, Nobel collected) remains the organizing goal of Trump's regional policy.

king-abdullah-ii.title: Church of Saint Porphyrios
king-abdullah-ii.summary: The Greek Orthodox church in Gaza that John Kiriakou describes as the oldest continuously operating church in the world; per Kiriakou, Israel bombed it while 24 women and children were sheltering inside.

king-abdullah-ii.title: The 1991 Saudi plan for Gaza
king-abdullah-ii.summary: A proposal John Kiriakou says he watched Ambassador Chas Freeman float to the Saudis during his first overseas tour in 1991 — that Saudi Arabia fund a port, an airport, a desalination plant and an electrical grid in Gaza. The Saudis agreed; Israel refused outright. Kiriakou raises it because the identical arrangement resurfaced in the Israeli press more than three decades later.

king-abdullah-ii.title: Alan Dershowitz
king-abdullah-ii.summary: American attorney and Harvard Law professor; John Kiriakou describes debating him on Piers Morgan's show over Jeffrey Epstein, telling Dershowitz he would have wanted to see him "hanging from a tree" had he sought leniency for Epstein as an Israeli spy — and cites attorney David Boies's on-air statement that Dershowitz was far more than Epstein's lawyer, also serving as his publicist, friend, and a guest on Epstein's island.

king-abdullah-ii.title: Arrais Corporation
king-abdullah-ii.summary: Private intelligence firm; companion entity to The Analysis Corporation; originally an LLC pass-through for retired Senior Intelligence Service personnel from the CIA's operations side; subsequently acquired by IBM for over $1 billion.

king-abdullah-ii.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
king-abdullah-ii.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

kiriakou-2026-viral-wave.title: ''Once CIA, always CIA''
kiriakou-2026-viral-wave.summary: The comment-section accusation John Kiriakou says angers him more than any other — that no one who has served in the CIA ever really leaves it, and that whistleblowers are therefore still working for the agency. He calls it "the most intellectually lazy, stupid, thoughtless position that anybody could take", says the agency actively benefits from it because it splits the anti-CIA public, and answers the version aimed at himself by pointing at his prison sentence.

kiriakou-2026-viral-wave.title: 2026 Iran war
kiriakou-2026-viral-wave.summary: The open-ended American and Israeli war against Iran that John Kiriakou tracked week by week on his own show — a conflict he says was sold as three weeks, ran into its fifth month, achieved every decapitation objective it set, and continued anyway. His grade for it is a D, and his forecast is a Truth Social post declaring victory while nothing changes.

kiriakou-2026-viral-wave.title: Advice to the next generation
kiriakou-2026-viral-wave.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer to a Gen Z viewer who said he felt helpless — that helplessness is not new, that 1968 and 1969 were worse, and that the remedy is four concrete things: run for any office at all, starting with the local water board; demonstrate; ride your elected officials and vote them out if they will not do what they are told; and write.

kiriakou-2026-viral-wave.title: Al-Qaeda training manual interrogation-resistance tactics
kiriakou-2026-viral-wave.summary: A captured al-Qaeda training manual instructing operatives on how to resist interrogation, including feigning illness — a technique John Kiriakou says he saw a detainee use, and recognized, during a capture and interrogation in Pakistan.

kiriakou-2026-viral-wave.title: China's base in Djibouti
kiriakou-2026-viral-wave.summary: Camp Lemonnier in Djibouti, the abandoned French base the Djiboutians offered to the Americans and the Chinese took a share of — split down the middle by a chain-link fence, the only Chinese military installation outside China, and the centrepiece of John Kiriakou's argument that China is not an expansionist power.

kiriakou-2026-viral-wave.title: The death of investigative journalism
kiriakou-2026-viral-wave.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the collapse of investigative reporting inside the American mainstream press — Joby Warrick's resignation from the *Washington Post*, the paper that brought down a president, and the 80 per cent of its staff Kiriakou says have gone since Jeff Bezos bought it — together with the outlets he says are doing the work instead, and his advice to a student who wants to do it anyway.

kiriakou-acting-career.title: The Brüno shoot in Jordan
kiriakou-acting-career.summary: The scene John Kiriakou set up for Sacha Baron Cohen in Amman — four retired Palestinian militants, found in the Damascus telephone book at the Library of Congress, shown hardcore pornography by a character they believed to be an Austrian documentary journalist — which produced no reaction at all and was cut from the film entirely.

kiriakou-acting-career.title: Alexander Acosta and the sweetheart deal
kiriakou-acting-career.summary: The US attorney who gave Jeffrey Epstein his 2006 non-prosecution agreement and later said he had been ordered to — a chain of command John Kiriakou traces upward to an attorney general famous for his powerlessness, and therefore to somebody above him whom nobody has ever named.

kiriakou-acting-career.title: American missile stockpiles
kiriakou-acting-career.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that the United States has run its interceptor stocks down to the point of strategic vulnerability — that the conventional wisdom in Washington was that a round of the Iran war ended because the Patriots ran out, and that a country which cannot fight a two-front war certainly cannot do it below maximum production.

kiriakou-acting-career.title: Anwar al-Awlaki
kiriakou-acting-career.summary: American-born al-Qaeda propagandist; in 1993 the imam of the Falls Church, Virginia mosque visited by John Kiriakou's CIA Arabic-language class on a field trip; in 2001 the cleric at whose mosque the 9/11 hijackers prayed the night before the attacks; killed by U.S. drone strike in Yemen in approximately 2011.

kiriakou-acting-career.title: Central Intelligence Agency
kiriakou-acting-career.summary: U.S. foreign intelligence service; John Kiriakou's employer from 1990 to 2004 and the central institution of KiriPedia

kiriakou-acting-career.title: The visa reciprocity rule
kiriakou-acting-career.summary: The bilateral arrangement John Kiriakou describes by which each country sets the price of its own visas and the other matches it — and his conclusion that a United States policy of refusing visas to applicants who are overweight or who have cancer or diabetes must, under the same rule, license every other country to weigh American travellers at the door.

kiriakou-and-cenk-uygur.title: AIPAC
kiriakou-and-cenk-uygur.summary: The American Israel Public Affairs Committee — the U.S. political organization that, in John Kiriakou's framing, ought to be registered as a foreign-lobbying entity but is not, and that wields decisive electoral power against U.S. elected officials who express support for Palestinian human rights.

kiriakou-and-cenk-uygur.title: Anwar al-Awlaki
kiriakou-and-cenk-uygur.summary: American-born al-Qaeda propagandist; in 1993 the imam of the Falls Church, Virginia mosque visited by John Kiriakou's CIA Arabic-language class on a field trip; in 2001 the cleric at whose mosque the 9/11 hijackers prayed the night before the attacks; killed by U.S. drone strike in Yemen in approximately 2011.

kiriakou-and-cenk-uygur.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
kiriakou-and-cenk-uygur.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

kiriakou-and-cenk-uygur.title: Cofer Black
kiriakou-and-cenk-uygur.summary: Former head of the CIA Counterterrorism Center during and immediately after the September 11 attacks; principal architect of the agency's paramilitary turn on September 12, 2001; later Vice President of Blackwater under Erik Prince.

kiriakou-and-cenk-uygur.title: F-35 avionics dispute with Israel
kiriakou-and-cenk-uygur.summary: John Kiriakou's account of how Israel demanded F-35 fighters without the deliberately degraded avionics the U.S. installs on export models — and, refused, allegedly worked through American defense contractors to steal the technology instead.

kiriakou-and-cenk-uygur.title: Israeli integration into U.S. agencies
kiriakou-and-cenk-uygur.summary: John Kiriakou''s objection to the formal embedding of Israeli personnel inside American defense and intelligence institutions — a National Defense Authorization Act provision collocating them with the Pentagon and opening Five Eyes-style liaison with the CIA, arriving in the same weeks as a DIA all-hands warning that Israeli services were unusually aggressive in recruiting inside DIA. His argument is that the two cannot both be true: either Israel is a critical counterintelligence threat or it is a partner.

kiriakou-and-third-parties.title: Overcriminalization
kiriakou-and-third-parties.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that the United States criminalizes too much — locking up 25% of the world's prisoners with 5% of its population, and adding roughly 50 new felonies a year — illustrated by a NOAA employee prosecuted for whistling at a whale.

kiriakou-and-third-parties.title: Charlie Kirk shooting
kiriakou-and-third-parties.summary: Kiriakou questions the official account: a court filing says the ATF could not match the autopsy bullet to the rifle tied to the suspect.

kiriakou-and-third-parties.title: Iran's 2024 drone retaliation
kiriakou-and-third-parties.summary: John Kiriakou's account of Iran's telegraphed 2024 drone strike on Israel — hundreds of slow drones, launched with advance warning to the U.S. and Jordan, nearly all shot down, which he reads as a controlled show of force and an intelligence victory that exposed the Iron Dome.

kiriakou-and-third-parties.title: Israel's cell-phone assassinations in Iran
kiriakou-and-third-parties.summary: John Kiriakou's account of how Israel wiped out Iran's military leadership by tracking cell phones — recruiting destitute Afghan refugees as $100-a-month spotters, and, when the generals stopped carrying phones, targeting their bodyguards' phones instead.

kiriakou-and-third-parties.title: JFK assassination
kiriakou-and-third-parties.summary: November 22, 1963 killing of President John F. Kennedy in Dallas, Texas. John Kiriakou's position, drawn from a Pakistan-station encounter with Bay of Pigs commander Jean Gately, an RFK Jr. account of CIA Director John McCone's same-day exchange with Bobby Kennedy Sr., and a White House contact's confirmation that the remaining classified Kennedy documents all contain the word "Israel," is that elements of the CIA were probably involved and that Israeli intelligence was involved as well.

kiriakou-and-third-parties.title: Americans and the word socialism
kiriakou-and-third-parties.summary: Two exchanges John Kiriakou uses to argue that the political vocabulary of the United States has stopped carrying meaning — a Thanksgiving conversation with a woman who denounced socialism and lived on Social Security, and a newspaper comment thread in which a restaurant owner taking his staff's tips was described as socialism.

kiriakou-athens-house.title: The Nordeen house
kiriakou-athens-house.summary: The embassy housing on Deliyani Street in Athens that John Kiriakou refused on arrival in 1998 — the house outside which the American defence attaché had been blown to pieces by 17 November, his head landing on the neighbouring roof.

kiriakou-athens-house.title: The Athens carjacking
kiriakou-athens-house.summary: The motorcyclist who followed John Kiriakou''s car through Athens two months into his posting — leading to a gun drawn on a ten-lane intersection, a shot fired, a disabled motorcycle, and a question asked back in Washington: *is John a hothead?*

kiriakou-athens-house.title: There is no such thing as bad food in Athens
kiriakou-athens-house.summary: The lesson John Kiriakou says he learned at a lorry drivers' stop outside Corinth, where the food was as good as his grandmother's — reached on the three-and-a-half-hour drives he made to meet a source too sensitive to be met in Athens, with a vineyard tour as his cover story.

kiriakou-athens-house.title: How Kiriakou went armed in Athens
kiriakou-athens-house.summary: The load John Kiriakou carried every day during his Athens tour — a 9mm in a tear-away waist pack with three magazines, a snub-nosed .38 on his ankle, about 47 rounds in total, and a buck knife his boss handed him on his first day *"just in case things go to shit"*.

kiriakou-athens-house.title: American shoes
kiriakou-athens-house.summary: The detail by which the chief of the Greek intelligence service identified John Kiriakou as an American within minutes of meeting him — not his Greek, which was fluent, but his footwear — and which sent Kiriakou straight to a shoe shop before working the anarchist quarters of Athens.

kiriakou-athens-house.title: Kiriakou's first recruitment
kiriakou-athens-house.summary: How John Kiriakou made his first CIA recruitment in Athens: by combing 25-year-old Greek police files not for people who had talked but for people who had answered back, finding one such man in a communist neighbourhood coffee shop, and buying his telephone number from a waiter for the price of a fifty.

kiriakou-cameo-practice.title: John Kiriakou
kiriakou-cameo-practice.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

kiriakou-cameo-practice.title: Consulting for royal families
kiriakou-cameo-practice.summary: The work John Kiriakou says he was hired to do by members of two different royal families following the 2026 virality of his interviews — advising on ethics in their own intelligence operations — which he offers as evidence of how far the reversal in his standing had gone.

kiriakou-cameo-practice.title: Diary of a CEO — January 2026 Kiriakou interview
kiriakou-cameo-practice.summary: The January 2026 long-form appearance by John Kiriakou on Steven Bartlett's Diary of a CEO podcast that a University of Texas at Austin sophomore then cut into TikTok shorts — sped and slowed, with lasers added — kicking off the Gen Z discovery of Kiriakou that pushed his cameo requests past 1,900 and drew a 2:30 a.m. representation call in Dubai from the Creative Artists Agency; Kiriakou treats it as the pivot after which stories he had been telling for nineteen years finally landed.

kiriakou-cameo-practice.title: 2026 Iran war
kiriakou-cameo-practice.summary: The open-ended American and Israeli war against Iran that John Kiriakou tracked week by week on his own show — a conflict he says was sold as three weeks, ran into its fifth month, achieved every decapitation objective it set, and continued anyway. His grade for it is a D, and his forecast is a Truth Social post declaring victory while nothing changes.

kiriakou-cameo-practice.title: Abraham Accords
kiriakou-cameo-practice.summary: The Trump-brokered normalization deals between Israel and Gulf Arab states — in John Kiriakou's judgment "a terrible idea in the first place," a great victory for Israel and the Gulf Arabs that was "a punch in the throat to the Palestinians." He argues the Accords are how Trump meant to "solve the Middle East in a day" — by screwing the Palestinians — that Hamas read the abandonment correctly, that October 7 shattered the project, and that reviving the Accords (Saudis in, victory declared, Nobel collected) remains the organizing goal of Trump's regional policy.

kiriakou-cameo-practice.title: Alexa
kiriakou-cameo-practice.summary: Per John Kiriakou, Amazon''s Alexa smart speaker reports directly to the NSA — and he owns one anyway. The device recurs across his interviews as the standing example of the surveillance trade-off in modern smart-home technology, and of his own negotiated exception to it: one speaker, in one room, against the advice of every intelligence officer he has ever known.

kiriakou-case-officer-rankings.title: Jim Jordan
kiriakou-case-officer-rankings.summary: Republican congressman from Ohio and chairman of the House Judiciary Committee. John Kiriakou describes a genuinely divided view of him: one of only four members of Congress he names as a friend of whistleblowers, and simultaneously the chairman whose Weaponization subcommittee he says is a partisan counterfeit of the Church Committee — with the whole question settled against Jordan by the Ohio State wrestlers who told him their team doctor was abusing them.

kiriakou-case-officer-rankings.title: Jon Ossoff
kiriakou-case-officer-rankings.summary: United States senator from Georgia, whom John Kiriakou places among the rare honest figures on Capitol Hill and grades at the top of his case-officer rankings. Kiriakou also notes a family connection to the wartime liberation of Greece.

kiriakou-case-officer-rankings.title: Mark Warner
kiriakou-case-officer-rankings.summary: Vice chairman of the Senate Intelligence Committee and former governor of Virginia. John Kiriakou reports being told, by a congressman who had campaigned for his release, that Warner had said in a room he should be hanging from a tree; he counts Warner among the Democrats who switched at the last minute to confirm Gina Haspel, and cites him as evidence that congressional oversight of the CIA is a joke — and then, asked to grade him, puts him at the top of the scale anyway.

kiriakou-case-officer-rankings.title: Ro Khanna
kiriakou-case-officer-rankings.summary: Democratic congressman from California, whom John Kiriakou describes as one of the very few selfless people in Congress and grades highly in his case-officer rankings.

kiriakou-case-officer-rankings.title: Tucker Carlson
kiriakou-case-officer-rankings.summary: American broadcaster and former Fox News host; a personal friend of John Kiriakou's for years, appearing on Kiriakou's radio and podcast work and hosting him roughly a dozen times on his own Fox show. Kiriakou calls him possibly the most brilliant and best-informed person he has ever encountered, and relays Glenn Greenwald's belief that Carlson could win the presidency — an idea Carlson privately dismisses.

kiriakou-case-officer-rankings.title: Kiriakou's gun rights appeal
kiriakou-case-officer-rankings.summary: John Kiriakou's effort to have the firearms disability attached to his felony conviction lifted, by suing the Justice Department over a restoration process announced in 2025 and never built, and separately by applying for a presidential pardon he says he cannot count on.

kiriakou-cipa-hearing.title: Julian Assange
kiriakou-cipa-hearing.summary: Kiriakou — a 15-year friend and former WikiLeaks board member — on why Assange is a publisher owed a journalist's immunity, and a political prisoner.

kiriakou-cipa-hearing.title: Leonie Brinkema
kiriakou-cipa-hearing.summary: U.S. federal judge in the Eastern District of Virginia — informally the 'Espionage Court' — a Reagan appointee John Kiriakou calls "a hanging judge." Per Kiriakou, Brinkema systematically reserved all major national security cases for herself rather than allowing them to be distributed randomly among judges, and ruled in Kiriakou's case that his reason for blowing the whistle was legally irrelevant and that classified documents could not be used in his defense — effectively making it impossible to mount one.

kiriakou-cipa-hearing.title: Eastern District of Virginia
kiriakou-cipa-hearing.summary: The U.S. federal district covering northern Virginia — home to Langley, the Pentagon, DHS and much of the intelligence-contractor industry — which John Kiriakou calls 'the espionage court' because the Justice Department files the great majority of its national security prosecutions there and because, in his telling, no national-security defendant has ever won a case in it; Kiriakou, Julian Assange, Edward Snowden and Jeffrey Sterling were all charged there.

kiriakou-cipa-hearing.title: Espionage Act
kiriakou-cipa-hearing.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

kiriakou-cipa-hearing.title: Intelligence Identities Protection Act
kiriakou-cipa-hearing.summary: U.S. law enacted in 1982 that makes it a crime to knowingly disclose the identity of a covert intelligence officer; per John Kiriakou, his 2012 prosecution under the act arose from confirming a single surname of a former CIA colleague to a journalist — a confirmation that was never published. The name passed through a chain from journalist to Human Rights Watch to Guantanamo defense attorneys before reaching a judge and ultimately the FBI, which traced it back to Kiriakou.

kiriakou-cipa-hearing.title: Lenín Moreno
kiriakou-cipa-hearing.summary: President of Ecuador during the final year of Julian Assange's asylum in the country's London embassy. John Kiriakou, speaking four days before Assange's removal, called Moreno a two-faced traitor who was trading Assange for American money, tariffs and debt relief, and dismissed the INA Papers accusations against Assange as factually untrue.

kiriakou-cuba-trip.title: Gina Haspel
