langley.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

langley.title: Defense HUMINT Service
langley.summary: The Pentagon's human collection outfit, which John Kiriakou names as one of the three agencies that already do everything the CIA does — alongside the State Department's Bureau of Intelligence and Research for analysis and the NSA for interception — and which is therefore the core of his argument that Langley is redundant rather than merely badly run.

langley.title: The New Jersey drones
langley.summary: John Kiriakou''s shifting account of the New Jersey drone flap: his state trooper friend''s report of a missing Defense or Energy Department convoy load, and the 60 Minutes segment in which Air Force generals concluded the drones were hostile and probably Chinese.

larry-devlin.title: Publications Review Board
larry-devlin.summary: The CIA office that must clear anything a former officer publishes. John Kiriakou says everything he writes goes to it — books, articles, "even a letter to the editor of Home and Garden magazine" — and describes how the turnaround tracked his standing at the agency: his first book took 22 months to clear while the leadership hated him; his most recent six cleared in days.

larry-devlin.title: Joe Weisberg
larry-devlin.summary: Former CIA Counterterrorism Center officer and colleague of John Kiriakou who resigned abruptly, saying he did not have it in him to convince people to commit treason, then moved to Hollywood, wrote a well-regarded novel that sold poorly, and created the television series The Americans — which Kiriakou calls the best intelligence show ever made and one hundred per cent true to life, and every script of which the CIA redacted.

larry-devlin.title: John Kiriakou
larry-devlin.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

larry-devlin.title: The scholar-in-residence pipeline
larry-devlin.summary: John Kiriakou's description of retired CIA operations officers taking scholar-in-residence posts at universities and teaching literature courses that function, by their own account, as a recruitment funnel — students enrol knowing the instructor is a former officer and hoping for help getting in.

larry-devlin.title: John le Carré
larry-devlin.summary: British novelist and former MI6 officer, the subject of a full episode of John Kiriakou's Dead Drop podcast. Kiriakou's argument is that le Carré is the only spy novelist to have changed the business of spying itself — supplying its working vocabulary, from 'Joes' and 'lamplighters' to 'honey trap', and shaping how officers understood their own world.

larry-devlin.title: Kiriakou's shortwave listening
larry-devlin.summary: The childhood hobby John Kiriakou identifies as the reason he went to work for the CIA — a fifty-cent auction radio, a walk-in closet turned radio shack with a pinned world map, membership of the American Shortwave Listeners Club, and a verified logging of Radio Ulan Bator that put him on the cover of the club's magazine at fourteen.

larry-raviv.title: FCI Loretto
larry-raviv.summary: U.S. Federal Correctional Institution in Loretto, Pennsylvania; the low-medium-security prison at which John Kiriakou served 23 months of a 30-month sentence following his 2013 Espionage Act–era plea deal; the originally ordered "minimum security work camp" placement was countermanded — per Kiriakou, on Brennan's direct intervention — to place him in the actual prison alongside the general population.

larry-raviv.title: Truck
larry-raviv.summary: The convicted serial killer at FCI Loretto who sought John Kiriakou's approval, claimed to have run guns to Angolan rebels in a shrimp boat, and beat a prisoner unconscious after Kiriakou told him the man had called him a pedophile.

larry-raviv.title: Chomo
larry-raviv.summary: The prison term for a child molester, which John Kiriakou first heard on his first day at FCI Loretto when two skinheads at the Aryan table put it to him as the last of three vetting questions before deciding whether he could eat with them.

larry-raviv.title: Clint Goswick
larry-raviv.summary: Fellow federal prisoner of John Kiriakou at FCI Loretto; a devout Christian and Wichita Falls, Texas heating-and-air-conditioning business owner convicted of drug conspiracy and a gun charge despite never having used, possessed, manufactured, or distributed drugs.

larry-raviv.title: Doing Time Like a Spy
larry-raviv.summary: Prison memoir by John Kiriakou, full title Doing Time Like a Spy: How the CIA Taught Me to Survive and Thrive in Prison; winner of two literary awards and reissued in a second edition by Simon and Schuster.

larry-raviv.title: Federal prison security levels
larry-raviv.summary: The ladder of federal custody as John Kiriakou describes it — penitentiary, medium, low and minimum-security camp — the transfer rules that let long-sentence prisoners descend it, and why that placed dangerous men inside the low-security prison where he served his sentence.

larry-spinal-cancer.title: Frank's heart attack
larry-spinal-cancer.summary: The 65-year-old insulin-dependent diabetic who shared a cell with John Kiriakou at FCI Loretto, reported chest tightness for months, was given Tylenol and a request for an EKG that the regional office never approved, and collapsed in the insulin line.

larry-spinal-cancer.title: The glyburide incident
larry-spinal-cancer.summary: The episode John Kiriakou described in a Letter from Loretto of 12 September 2014: handed a bottle of glyburide by the prison pharmacy without explanation, he crashed twice and passed out on the floor — and his physician father-in-law told him the drug could have put him into heart failure.

larry-spinal-cancer.title: Administrative remedy process
larry-spinal-cancer.summary: The Bureau of Prisons' internal grievance system, which Kiriakou describes as a fig leaf designed to run out the clock on prisoners' complaints rather than resolve them.

larry-spinal-cancer.title: The chapel job
larry-spinal-cancer.summary: The work assignment John Kiriakou was given at FCI Loretto after he volunteered to teach a class — *"if I want you to teach a class I'll ask you to teach a class"* — and was made a janitor in the chapel instead, at $1.08 a month.

larry-spinal-cancer.title: Medical care in federal prison
larry-spinal-cancer.summary: Kiriakou's account of health care at FCI Loretto, where a bunkmate's months of reported chest pain ended in a heart attack, a prisoner with untreated back pain was diagnosed with terminal cancer weeks before he died, and Kiriakou himself collapsed after being handed a drug nobody had explained to him.

larry-spinal-cancer.title: Four deaths at Loretto
larry-spinal-cancer.summary: John Kiriakou's tally of the prisoners who died during his twenty-three months at FCI Loretto — four, all of preventable illness, two of heart attacks and two of cancer — and his account of one of them, a man he ate with daily who was given Tylenol for months before an outside x-ray found stage four spinal cancer.

laura-loomer.title: Louise Mensch
laura-loomer.summary: The former British parliamentarian who attacked John Kiriakou on social media, prompting the only defamation action he describes having threatened. On his lawyer's advice he demanded a retraction; Mensch retracted in full and kept a pinned apology on her account for six months.

laura-loomer.title: Podcasters on foreign payrolls
laura-loomer.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of being told by an investigative journalist he respects that four household-name podcasters were taking CIA money — an allegation she could not corroborate and would not publish. He treats it as credible and extends the logic: if the agency is paying podcasters, foreign governments will be paying them too.

laura-loomer.title: Donald Trump
laura-loomer.summary: 45th and 47th U.S. president. Per John Kiriakou, a man genuinely convinced he was doing right by bombing Iran, "duped" by the same Netanyahu nuclear bluff Obama once rejected — and, at the same time, the most blindly pro-Israel president in history, an admirer of autocrats who has never once criticized Vladimir Putin, and prone to gestures — from the Gulf of America to a since-abandoned "Department of War" rename — that test the edges of his actual authority.

laura-loomer.title: 2026 Iran war
laura-loomer.summary: The open-ended American and Israeli war against Iran that John Kiriakou tracked week by week on his own show — a conflict he says was sold as three weeks, ran into its fifth month, achieved every decapitation objective it set, and continued anyway. His grade for it is a D, and his forecast is a Truth Social post declaring victory while nothing changes.

laura-loomer.title: Ahmed Chalabi
laura-loomer.summary: Iraqi exile and founder of the Iraqi National Congress; per John Kiriakou, a Shia-Kurdish con man who looted Petra Bank in Jordan of $36 million in the 1980s, was sentenced to death in absentia, was pardoned at CIA request, then pocketed $6 million in CIA seed funding for the INC and bought a Mayfair house in cash; later resurrected by Dick Cheney to feed the Pentagon fabricated WMD intelligence used to justify the 2003 invasion of Iraq.

lavrov-on-sanctions.title: Dumping the treasury bonds
lavrov-on-sanctions.summary: The second economic weapon John Kiriakou says China holds against the United States — its position as the second or third largest holder of long-term government treasury bonds, which it could simply dump, and which he says would crash the entire American economy.

lavrov-on-sanctions.title: "Beyond Your Dreams"
lavrov-on-sanctions.summary: The gloss a host gave John Kiriakou on his first trip to China when he asked what the beautiful car with the BYD badge was — and the answer he got when he asked why he had never heard of it, which was that the United States is the only country where they are not sold.

lavrov-on-sanctions.title: Carving up Iran
lavrov-on-sanctions.summary: The Israeli end goal John Kiriakou says has been discussed with increasingly less discretion — dividing Iran into five small rump countries including Balochistan, Arabistan and Kurdistan, on the reasoning that small states are more easily controlled — and which he expects Israel will eventually try to get Donald Trump to carry out.

lavrov-on-sanctions.title: Sanctions and the Russian adjustment
lavrov-on-sanctions.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of why sanctions stopped hurting Russia: Sergey Lavrov''s admission that Moscow was caught off balance by the speed of the American response, the three or four weeks that shock lasted, and the discovery that Russia did not need the United States or its banking system once India and China agreed to buy whatever oil it had.

lavrov-on-sanctions.title: Sitting on my father's lap
lavrov-on-sanctions.summary: John Kiriakou's earliest political memory — being four or five years old, watching buildings burn on television, and asking his father why, to be told that some bad men had killed Martin Luther King and Robert Kennedy and people were very upset — which he uses as his benchmark for how divided the United States has become.

lawrence-wilkerson.title: Colin Powell
lawrence-wilkerson.summary: U.S. Secretary of State whose 2003 UN testimony made the case for the Iraq war; John Kiriakou says the white powder in Powell's prop tube was nothing, and that Powell's own chief of staff later told him the presentation was knowingly 'sold.'

lawrence-wilkerson.title: Iraq WMD intelligence
lawrence-wilkerson.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of how the case for Iraqi weapons of mass destruction was fabricated: the intelligence community''s consensus was that Iraq had no WMD, but the White House had already decided to invade and sought analysis to fit the policy.

lawrence-wilkerson.title: Salt Pit
lawrence-wilkerson.summary: A CIA black site north of Kabul — a former Soviet, then Taliban, dungeon the CIA took over for its post-9/11 detention programme. Gul Rahman froze to death there in a cold cell, a technique John Kiriakou considers worse than waterboarding and says killed several prisoners; he suspects others were killed off the books and never reported.

lawrence-wilkerson.title: John Kiriakou
lawrence-wilkerson.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

lawrence-wilkerson.title: Chelsea Manning
lawrence-wilkerson.summary: Former U.S. Army intelligence analyst who provided WikiLeaks its 2010 trove of military and diplomatic documents. Per John Kiriakou, Manning meets the legal definition of whistleblower for exposing war crimes, was a torture victim of prolonged solitary confinement with forced nudity, and was sentenced to 35 years in prison before Barack Obama commuted — not pardoned — her sentence. Kiriakou says Manning later refused a grand jury's offer of immunity and chose renewed jail time rather than testify against Julian Assange.

lawrence-wilkerson.title: Daniel Ellsberg
lawrence-wilkerson.summary: The Pentagon Papers whistleblower Kiriakou calls 'the Godfather of all national security whistleblowers' — and one of the great mentors of his life.

leadership-profiling.title: Reza Pahlavi
leadership-profiling.summary: The exiled Iranian crown prince whom John Kiriakou dismisses as an Israeli-backed fantasy candidate to rule Iran — a man who has not lived there since his teens, supported mainly by Beverly Hills exiles, whom Kiriakou says 'wouldn't survive the walk from the plane to the terminal.'

leadership-profiling.title: John Kiriakou's Briefing Room
leadership-profiling.summary: A twice-weekly news and commentary programme launched by John Kiriakou in July 2026, presented as analysis rather than partisan opinion, and distinct from his storytelling podcast Dead Drop.

leadership-profiling.title: Ahmed Chalabi
leadership-profiling.summary: Iraqi exile and founder of the Iraqi National Congress; per John Kiriakou, a Shia-Kurdish con man who looted Petra Bank in Jordan of $36 million in the 1980s, was sentenced to death in absentia, was pardoned at CIA request, then pocketed $6 million in CIA seed funding for the INC and bought a Mayfair house in cash; later resurrected by Dick Cheney to feed the Pentagon fabricated WMD intelligence used to justify the 2003 invasion of Iraq.

leadership-profiling.title: Saddam Hussein
leadership-profiling.summary: President of Iraq from 1979 until the 2003 U.S. invasion; subject of John Kiriakou's CIA portfolio from January 1990 onward, in which capacity Kiriakou became, at age 25, "Saddam Hussein's intelligence community biographer" and the analyst who briefed President George H. W. Bush in the Oval Office on the morning of the 1990 invasion of Kuwait.

leadership-profiling.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
leadership-profiling.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

leadership-profiling.title: Lindsey Graham
leadership-profiling.summary: Republican senator from South Carolina who died in July 2026, and John Kiriakou's standing shorthand for the permanent war caucus — a "show horse" rather than a workhorse, a "chameleon" who "never saw a war that he didn't want to jump into with both feet," and, on posthumously released documentary footage, a man offering the US Air Force to bomb a country America was not at war with.

leaker-versus-whistleblower.title: The Melber walkout
leaker-versus-whistleblower.summary: An incident on MSNBC in which John Kiriakou removed his microphone and threatened to leave the set after host Ari Melber introduced him as a leaker and a convicted felon, on a segment about whistleblowing recorded alongside Daniel Ellsberg. Kiriakou recounts it as the sharpest instance of the naming fight he has waged with the networks for over a decade.

leaker-versus-whistleblower.title: The Ukraine call whistleblower
leaker-versus-whistleblower.summary: The intelligence officer whose complaint triggered Donald Trump's first impeachment, and whom John Kiriakou declines to accept as a whistleblower at all — not on partisan grounds but on procedural ones. The complaint went to the Justice Department rather than the oversight committees, and its prose, he says, is lawyers' prose rather than the uniform CIA analytic style every analyst is trained into. He is nonetheless emphatic that naming the man was indefensible.

leaker-versus-whistleblower.title: Jesselyn Radack
leaker-versus-whistleblower.summary: American national-security attorney and former Justice Department ethics official who directs the whistleblower-defense practice at the Government Accountability Project. Per John Kiriakou, Radack was herself driven out of the Justice Department, had her law license threatened, and was placed on the no-fly list after blowing the whistle in the John Walker Lindh case; she went on to represent Kiriakou after his 2012 arrest and, separately, helped connect him to a path to reach Edward Snowden in 2013.

leaker-versus-whistleblower.title: Gina Haspel
leaker-versus-whistleblower.summary: Director of the Central Intelligence Agency under President Trump's first term; known to John Kiriakou and others at the CIA as "Bloody Gina"; per Kiriakou, flew out to the secret black site to sit in on one of the enhanced-interrogation torture sessions "just because she could," personally supervised the torture of USS Cole bombing suspect Rahim al-Nashiri, and later fed the CIA's torture tapes into an industrial document grinder after being explicitly told by White House Counsel not to destroy them.

leaker-versus-whistleblower.title: Chuck Grassley
leaker-versus-whistleblower.summary: The senior senator from Iowa, and in John Kiriakou's assessment the one member of Congress who has taken whistleblower protection seriously as a legislative project — a count he has variously put at one finger, at two names, and at four out of 535. Grassley wrote the whistleblower protection statutes, speaks every year at the National Whistleblower Day luncheon, and is the name Kiriakou gives prospective whistleblowers as the single friendly ear on Capitol Hill. Kiriakou's personal verdict is colder — Grassley, he has said, never did anything for him.

leaker-versus-whistleblower.title: Over-classification
leaker-versus-whistleblower.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of why the American government classifies far more than it can ever review: not conspiracy but incentive. At lesser agencies a classification stamp is a status marker — it puts you in the in-crowd and above the colleague who lacks access — and at the CIA everything carries a stamp by default. His complaint about press coverage of classified-document scandals is that it never reaches the underlying question of why the documents were secret at all.

leaking-vs-whistleblowing.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
leaking-vs-whistleblowing.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

leaking-vs-whistleblowing.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
leaking-vs-whistleblowing.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

leaking-vs-whistleblowing.title: Federal Torture Act
leaking-vs-whistleblowing.summary: United States statute criminalizing torture; per John Kiriakou, on the books since at least 1946, with concrete enforcement history — after World War II the United States executed Japanese soldiers convicted of waterboarding American prisoners of war, meaning waterboarding was at that time a capital offense under U.S. law. The act was effectively set aside for the CIA's enhanced interrogation program after 2002.

leaking-vs-whistleblowing.title: Official leaks
leaking-vs-whistleblowing.summary: The category of disclosure John Kiriakou says is both the largest and the only one that is never prosecuted — trial balloons and opinion-shaping put out by the White House, the National Security Council and the Pentagon, with the president himself as the most prolific leaker in Washington.

leaking-vs-whistleblowing.title: Barack Obama
leaking-vs-whistleblowing.summary: 44th U.S. president; in John Kiriakou's account, Obama publicly recounted refusing Benjamin Netanyahu's demand to bomb Iran and calling Israel's threat to use nuclear weapons a bluff — a bluff Kiriakou says Donald Trump later believed.

leaking-vs-whistleblowing.title: Espionage Act
leaking-vs-whistleblowing.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

leaks-come-from-the-pentagon.title: Area 58
leaks-come-from-the-pentagon.summary: The claim John Kiriakou says was put to him by a man who presents as entirely serious and is writing a book about it: that beyond Area 51 there is an Area 58 — seven more, and that much more secret — containing an underground bunker where alien craft land, known to those involved as the embassy because it is where the United States liaises with the aliens.

leaks-come-from-the-pentagon.title: Luis Elizondo
leaks-come-from-the-pentagon.summary: Why John Kiriakou never booked the best-known public advocate for unidentified aerial phenomena on his RT programme: viewers kept insisting Elizondo was an expert, so Kiriakou researched him and found chiefly Elizondo saying he was an expert. He says he does not know what the man is an expert on, and that it was not a fit for the show.

leaks-come-from-the-pentagon.title: SEALs on loan to the CIA
leaks-come-from-the-pentagon.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer to why the CIA did not use its own paramilitary team against Osama bin Laden: it did. The raid was a CIA operation directed by the Counterterrorism Center, and every Navy SEAL involved was temporarily a CIA contractor, on loan to the agency for the duration.

leaks-come-from-the-pentagon.title: The alternative obituaries
leaks-come-from-the-pentagon.summary: The obituaries John Kiriakou writes for CovertAction Magazine whenever someone associated with the CIA's torture program dies — deliberately mean-spirited pieces arguing the world is better off without them — and the phone call he took from one subject's daughter, who called him a monster, and what he said back to her.

leaks-come-from-the-pentagon.title: The Australian pilot
leaks-come-from-the-pentagon.summary: The disappearance John Kiriakou recounts as an argument for declassification rather than as proof of anything: a pilot in his early twenties flying on 10 September 1978 who radioed that a silver cylinder was above his aircraft matching his speed exactly, said it was not an aircraft, was cut off by a loud sound of electronic interference, and was never seen again — along with the plane.

leaks-come-from-the-pentagon.title: The 9/11 truth honorarium
leaks-come-from-the-pentagon.summary: How John Kiriakou came to headline a 9/11 truth event he had not realised was one: a $500 speaking fee from a PR man he had known through better days, a poster that revealed the sponsor, a sister telling him to withdraw, and his decision to honour the commitment anyway — while telling the audience to their faces that he would never believe Building 7 was a controlled demolition or that explosive thermite paint exists.

learned-helplessness.title: Abu Zubaydah
learned-helplessness.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

learned-helplessness.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
learned-helplessness.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

learned-helplessness.title: George W. Bush
learned-helplessness.summary: 43rd President of the United States. In John Kiriakou's telling, Bush signed the August 1, 2002 executive order that authorized the CIA torture program, spent years telling the public "we don't torture," and — days after Kiriakou's 2007 ABC interview — blamed torture on "a rogue CIA officer" while walking from the White House South Portico to Marine One, a moment Kiriakou instantly read as the White House preparing to pin the program on him. Bush also ordered the FBI removed from Abu Zubaydah's black site, flew the bin Laden family out of the country after 9/11, and loosened the assassination ban of Executive Order 12333.

learned-helplessness.title: Khalid Sheikh Mohammed
learned-helplessness.summary: Mastermind of the September 11, 2001 attacks; identified to the CIA by Abu Zubaydah, in the course of FBI interrogator Ali Soufan's rapport-based debriefing at the black site, as the man behind the kunya "Mukhtar" the agency had been hunting since at least 1996 for the Bojinka plot; per Kiriakou's relay of his self-account, radicalized by news video of an Israeli soldier with his boot on the neck of a Palestinian woman.

learned-helplessness.title: Waterboarding
learned-helplessness.summary: Torture technique in which a prisoner is restrained on an inclined board with the head lower than the feet, a cloth placed over the face, and water poured continuously over it to simulate drowning. Per John Kiriakou, waterboarding was treated as a criminal act under U.S. and international law for decades before 2002 — including a post–World War II execution of Japanese soldiers who waterboarded American POWs, and a 1968 court-martial of a U.S. soldier photographed waterboarding a North Vietnamese prisoner — before the CIA reauthorized it after September 11. Abu Zubaydah was waterboarded 83 times; Khalid Sheikh Mohammed 187 times.

learned-helplessness.title: Salt Pit
learned-helplessness.summary: A CIA black site north of Kabul — a former Soviet, then Taliban, dungeon the CIA took over for its post-9/11 detention programme. Gul Rahman froze to death there in a cold cell, a technique John Kiriakou considers worse than waterboarding and says killed several prisoners; he suspects others were killed off the books and never reported.

learning-to-dive-in-the-embassy-pool.title: The Nordstream patsy
learning-to-dive-in-the-embassy-pool.summary: John Kiriakou''s assessment of the man arrested in Italy over the Nordstream pipeline sabotage: a patsy. He says he cannot imagine otherwise, feels for whoever the man is, and thinks the authorities found somebody they could take a dump on — while maintaining that the operation itself required not just real expertise but state expertise and capability.

learning-to-dive-in-the-embassy-pool.title: The divorce at the airport
learning-to-dive-in-the-embassy-pool.summary: The end of John Kiriakou''s first marriage, as he tells it: after 17 November assassinated his next-door neighbour and left a manifesto saying they had set out that morning to kill him instead, the embassy put him in an armoured car, collected his children and his wife, and packed out the house. His wife reached the airport, walked up to him and said she wanted a divorce. They flew home on the same plane.

learning-to-dive-in-the-embassy-pool.title: How the CIA kills
learning-to-dive-in-the-embassy-pool.summary: John Kiriakou''s description of the methods used when the CIA is ordered to kill someone outside a war zone: a team parachuting in miles away, stealing a car, a locks-and-picks specialist opening the door and suppressed weapons inside; a snatch into a van bound for an airport or a boat; or a brush past in a market with something poisoned — a technique he says the Russians used often and taught the Bulgarians into the early 1980s.

learning-to-dive-in-the-embassy-pool.title: Mark Polymeropoulos
learning-to-dive-in-the-embassy-pool.summary: The CIA officer John Kiriakou describes as a friend who was in his first tour when Aldrich Ames blew his identity, was brought in from the cold, and later became station chief in Moscow — an appointment Kiriakou characterises as a deliberate thumb in the Russians'' eye: the officer their spy had burned, put in charge of operations against them.

learning-to-dive-in-the-embassy-pool.title: Nine recruitments in twenty-five years
learning-to-dive-in-the-embassy-pool.summary: The conversation in which John Kiriakou''s Athens station chief, a twenty-five-year operations officer who had reached senior intelligence service level four with nine recruitments to his name, pointed out that Kiriakou had recruited five in two years — and Kiriakou''s explanation of the knack: that he could hide his disdain for a man completely while talking about whatever interested him.

learning-to-dive-in-the-embassy-pool.title: Qatari money in Egypt
learning-to-dive-in-the-embassy-pool.summary: John Kiriakou''s explanation for Qatar injecting seven and a half billion dollars into the Egyptian economy: to annoy Saudi Arabia. He describes a long, close Saudi–Egyptian relationship dating back to the mid-1960s, a terrible Qatari–Saudi one, and an Egypt happy to take the money — including the year the Egyptians thanked the Saudis for their generosity with an uninhabited island in the Red Sea.

lebanon-israeli-conflict.title: MOSSAD
lebanon-israeli-conflict.summary: Israel's primary external intelligence service; characterized by John Kiriakou as universally hostile in his and his CIA colleagues' professional dealings with it ("never had a positive encounter with Mossad"); operates almost exclusively in the operational rather than analytical domain; the CIA is, per Kiriakou, categorically forbidden from spying on it.

lebanon-israeli-conflict.title: Hezbollah
lebanon-israeli-conflict.summary: Lebanese Shia militant organization and political party. Per John Kiriakou, Israel''s strategic goal regarding Hezbollah is not to defeat it outright but to keep Lebanon in a state of chaos that serves Israeli interests. He cites two Israeli operations: the simultaneous pager-detonation attack that decapitated Hezbollah''s leadership, which he called ''the most incredible operation I''ve ever seen,'' and the strike that killed former leader Hassan Nasrallah by leveling an entire complex and killing roughly 300 people — which he characterized as a war crime.

lebanon-israeli-conflict.title: Iran 12-Day War
lebanon-israeli-conflict.summary: 2025 Israeli air campaign against Iran during which Israel killed at least fourteen Iranian nuclear scientists by destroying the apartment buildings they lived in; preceded for each scientist by Farsi-language telephone calls from Iranian-Jewish Mossad and Shin Bet officers offering defection in lieu of certain death; characterized by John Kiriakou as a categorical departure from CIA targeting doctrine in its acceptable-civilian-casualty calculus.

lebanon-israeli-conflict.title: Donald Trump
lebanon-israeli-conflict.summary: 45th and 47th U.S. president. Per John Kiriakou, a man genuinely convinced he was doing right by bombing Iran, "duped" by the same Netanyahu nuclear bluff Obama once rejected — and, at the same time, the most blindly pro-Israel president in history, an admirer of autocrats who has never once criticized Vladimir Putin, and prone to gestures — from the Gulf of America to a since-abandoned "Department of War" rename — that test the edges of his actual authority.

lebanon-israeli-conflict.title: The Cyprus naval buildup, 2026
lebanon-israeli-conflict.summary: The concentration of European warships and defence ministers on Cyprus during the 2026 Iran war, and John Kiriakou''s explanation of it: NATO and EU militaries feel compelled to appear supportive of Israel and the United States, whatever they say behind closed doors.

lebanon-israeli-conflict.title: The seven countries argument
lebanon-israeli-conflict.summary: John Kiriakou's dissent from the claim that America's post-2001 wars were fought on Israel's behalf. Taking the list of seven countries country by country, he argues Libya, Somalia and Afghanistan were American decisions made for American reasons — and concludes that the United States cannot blame all of its problems on Israel.

lee-zeldon.title: Todd Blanch
lee-zeldon.summary: Per Megyn Kelly, reading Trump's own statement live during her interview with Kiriakou, Todd Blanch was named the incoming acting Attorney General, replacing Pam Bondi.

lee-zeldon.title: Pam Bondi
lee-zeldon.summary: Panelists alongside Kiriakou on why Trump picked Bondi for loyalty above all, and called her handling of the Epstein files a farce.

lee-zeldon.title: Bill Barr
lee-zeldon.summary: Per Sean Davis, speaking on the same Megyn Kelly panel as Kiriakou, the attorney general under the first Trump administration, seen as competent but not fully loyal, whose relationship with Trump ended in a "breakup."

lee-zeldon.title: Gail Slater
lee-zeldon.summary: Per Sean Davis, speaking on the same Megyn Kelly panel as Kiriakou, the head of the DOJ antitrust unit under Pam Bondi who was stripped of authority and then fired.

lee-zeldon.title: Alexa
lee-zeldon.summary: Per John Kiriakou, Amazon''s Alexa smart speaker reports directly to the NSA — and he owns one anyway. The device recurs across his interviews as the standing example of the surveillance trade-off in modern smart-home technology, and of his own negotiated exception to it: one speaker, in one room, against the advice of every intelligence officer he has ever known.

lee-zeldon.title: Anwar al-Awlaki
lee-zeldon.summary: American-born al-Qaeda propagandist; in 1993 the imam of the Falls Church, Virginia mosque visited by John Kiriakou's CIA Arabic-language class on a field trip; in 2001 the cleric at whose mosque the 9/11 hijackers prayed the night before the attacks; killed by U.S. drone strike in Yemen in approximately 2011.

legal-mail.title: Seven thousand letters
legal-mail.summary: The correspondence John Kiriakou conducted from FCI Loretto — 7,000 letters to 675 different people over 23 months, begun because of an unsolicited postcard of a rose that reached him four hours into his sentence.

legal-mail.title: Arianna Huffington
legal-mail.summary: Founder of the Huffington Post and the accidental amplifier who turned John Kiriakou's prison writing into a phenomenon. His first Letter from Loretto went to his attorney, then to a friend running Firedoglake who — unknown to Kiriakou — was close to Huffington; she plastered it as a banner headline and it drew over a million hits, bringing CNN and 60 Minutes to the prison gates. She published his open letter to Snowden, ran the diesel-therapy exposé that triggered the "hands off John Kiriakou" campaign, and came to Loretto herself with two young journalists.

legal-mail.title: FCI Loretto
legal-mail.summary: U.S. Federal Correctional Institution in Loretto, Pennsylvania; the low-medium-security prison at which John Kiriakou served 23 months of a 30-month sentence following his 2013 Espionage Act–era plea deal; the originally ordered "minimum security work camp" placement was countermanded — per Kiriakou, on Brennan's direct intervention — to place him in the actual prison alongside the general population.

legal-mail.title: Sarge
legal-mail.summary: The FCI Loretto correctional officer John Kiriakou named in a Letter from Loretto for swearing at him and trashing his cell — conduct he later learned was not merely a Bureau of Prisons infraction but a misdemeanour crime, and one of two offences he says the letter inadvertently exposed.

legal-mail.title: Letter from Loretto
legal-mail.summary: Prison newsletter written by John Kiriakou from FCI Loretto, modeled on Martin Luther King's "Letter from Birmingham Jail," which exposed two crimes committed against him by guards and went viral after being relayed to the Huffington Post, drawing national press to the prison.

legal-mail.title: The black box
legal-mail.summary: The restraint apparatus in which John Kiriakou was moved from FCI Loretto to an outside medical appointment — handcuffs, leg irons, a waist chain and a steel box locked over the cuffs so the lock could not be picked — and the form he refused to sign because it required him to call everybody sir.

lenin-moreno.title: Julian Assange
lenin-moreno.summary: Kiriakou — a 15-year friend and former WikiLeaks board member — on why Assange is a publisher owed a journalist's immunity, and a political prisoner.

lenin-moreno.title: Ola Bini
lenin-moreno.summary: The Swedish programmer and friend of Julian Assange arrested in Ecuador in 2019 on the order of President Lenín Moreno, whose open-ended detention John Kiriakou treats as the collateral consequence of the same government's decision to hand Assange to the British.

lenin-moreno.title: The CIPA hearing in Kiriakou's case
lenin-moreno.summary: The closed pre-trial proceeding under the Classified Information Procedures Act at which John Kiriakou's defence filed seventy motions to declassify the material it needed to mount a defence, and the judge denied all seventy at once. Kiriakou describes the ruling as the moment the case ended — his lead attorney told him on the way out of the courtroom that they had just lost — and as the point at which plea negotiations began.

lenin-moreno.title: Espionage Act
lenin-moreno.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

lenin-moreno.title: "Admit nothing, deny everything, make counter-accusations"
lenin-moreno.summary: One of the twenty life lessons John Kiriakou says the CIA taught him in training, and a slogan sold on coffee mugs and t-shirts in the headquarters gift shop — by far the most popular mug in the building. It was treated at Langley as a joke that was not quite a joke; in federal prison Kiriakou used it as an operating rule, and credits it with getting him out of an investigation into a prison-yard fight with nothing given up.

lenin-moreno.title: Anwar al-Awlaki
lenin-moreno.summary: American-born al-Qaeda propagandist; in 1993 the imam of the Falls Church, Virginia mosque visited by John Kiriakou's CIA Arabic-language class on a field trip; in 2001 the cleric at whose mosque the 9/11 hijackers prayed the night before the attacks; killed by U.S. drone strike in Yemen in approximately 2011.

leon-panetta.title: David Petraeus
leon-panetta.summary: Retired U.S. Army general and director of the CIA who, per John Kiriakou, confirmed the names of ten covert CIA operatives to his biographer and girlfriend and was never criminally charged — a contrast Kiriakou cites repeatedly as proof that his own prosecution under the Intelligence Identities Protection Act was selective. Kiriakou''s explanation for the disparity: Petraeus had not blown the whistle on the torture program and embarrassed the agency.

leon-panetta.title: Espionage Act
leon-panetta.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

leon-panetta.title: Abu Zubaydah
leon-panetta.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

leon-panetta.title: Thomas Drake
leon-panetta.summary: NSA whistleblower; per John Kiriakou, the source for the statement that on the morning of September 11, 2001, NSA Director Mike Hayden told agency personnel NSA had been 'waiting for a 9/11' to implement the mass-electronic-surveillance program that NSA's founding charter forbids.

leon-panetta.title: The Panetta bin Laden disclosure
leon-panetta.summary: Leon Panetta's accidental naming of the special forces ground commander of the bin Laden raid in front of a Hollywood screenwriter, which Kiriakou uses as the control case for his argument that Espionage Act enforcement is selective.

leon-panetta.title: Cofer Black
leon-panetta.summary: Former head of the CIA Counterterrorism Center during and immediately after the September 11 attacks; principal architect of the agency's paramilitary turn on September 12, 2001; later Vice President of Blackwater under Erik Prince.

leonard-peltier.title: Julian Assange
leonard-peltier.summary: Kiriakou — a 15-year friend and former WikiLeaks board member — on why Assange is a publisher owed a journalist's immunity, and a political prisoner.

leonard-peltier.title: Daniel Hale
leonard-peltier.summary: Per John Kiriakou, drone whistleblower Daniel Hale — an NSA contractor and drone targeting analyst who exposed an 80% civilian death rate in the U.S. drone program, was ordered to fire on two young girls his superior called "goats," and was sentenced to 45 months (of which Kiriakou says he actually served about 18) despite prosecutors seeking nine to eleven years.

leonard-peltier.title: Anwar al-Awlaki
leonard-peltier.summary: American-born al-Qaeda propagandist; in 1993 the imam of the Falls Church, Virginia mosque visited by John Kiriakou's CIA Arabic-language class on a field trip; in 2001 the cleric at whose mosque the 9/11 hijackers prayed the night before the attacks; killed by U.S. drone strike in Yemen in approximately 2011.

leonard-peltier.title: Brad Birkenfeld
leonard-peltier.summary: The UBS banking whistleblower, who was prosecuted and imprisoned before winning a $104 million settlement from the Treasury Department and spending it on the legal defence of other whistleblowers. John Kiriakou uses him as the measure of the gap between financial and national-security whistleblowing, and names him among the visitors whose devices he believes were copied at the Ecuadorian embassy in London.

leonard-peltier.title: Government Accountability Project
leonard-peltier.summary: The Washington whistleblower-advocacy law firm and NGO, known as GAP, whose attorney Jesselyn Radack took John Kiriakou's case after his 2012 arrest and told him he was a whistleblower whether he thought so or not.

leonard-peltier.title: Intelligence Identities Protection Act
leonard-peltier.summary: U.S. law enacted in 1982 that makes it a crime to knowingly disclose the identity of a covert intelligence officer; per John Kiriakou, his 2012 prosecution under the act arose from confirming a single surname of a former CIA colleague to a journalist — a confirmation that was never published. The name passed through a chain from journalist to Human Rights Watch to Guantanamo defense attorneys before reaching a judge and ultimately the FBI, which traced it back to Kiriakou.

leonie-brinkema.title: Espionage Act
leonie-brinkema.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

leonie-brinkema.title: Julian Assange
leonie-brinkema.summary: Kiriakou — a 15-year friend and former WikiLeaks board member — on why Assange is a publisher owed a journalist's immunity, and a political prisoner.

leonie-brinkema.title: National Archives declassification
leonie-brinkema.summary: John Kiriakou''s exposé of why U.S. records go undeclassified: the National Archives runs a 20-year-old computer with no connectivity, its head has asked for a smaller budget, and Freedom of Information Act requests face what he calls a 500-year backlog.

leonie-brinkema.title: The Panetta bin Laden disclosure
leonie-brinkema.summary: Leon Panetta's accidental naming of the special forces ground commander of the bin Laden raid in front of a Hollywood screenwriter, which Kiriakou uses as the control case for his argument that Espionage Act enforcement is selective.

leonie-brinkema.title: Public-interest defense
leonie-brinkema.summary: The affirmative defense the Espionage Act does not allow: John Kiriakou explains that a defendant cannot tell a jury he acted in the public interest, and that Edward Snowden''s willingness to come home hinged on getting that chance — which the Justice Department refused.

leonie-brinkema.title: The New York Times problem
leonie-brinkema.summary: Barack Obama''s reason, as John Kiriakou reports it, for never charging Julian Assange: the Washington Post, the New York Times, the Wall Street Journal and the Associated Press publish classified information every single day, so a publisher charged with espionage cannot be the only one. Kiriakou treats it as the central First Amendment question of the case, and notes that Joe Biden — who was in the room for the original argument — doubled down instead of dropping the charges.

les-wexner.title: Jeffrey Epstein
les-wexner.summary: Convicted sex offender; per John Kiriakou, was "an Israeli access agent" rather than a CIA asset, because the CIA collects foreign intelligence and Epstein's targets — Bill Clinton, Bill Gates, Prince Andrew — were not foreign. Kiriakou further holds that Epstein did die by suicide in federal custody, because in the Bureau of Prisons the cameras never work and the guards are always asleep.

les-wexner.title: Prince Andrew
les-wexner.summary: British royal, now Andrew Mountbatten Windsor, named repeatedly by John Kiriakou as one of the un-recruitable principals whose access made Jeffrey Epstein valuable to a foreign intelligence service. Kiriakou has asked why Andrew was never charged over conduct with minors, reads his alleged provision of classified Ministry of Defence documents to Epstein as evidence of espionage rather than vanity — and expects him to face no criminal consequence at all, because the statute of limitations has run.

les-wexner.title: Ghislaine Maxwell
les-wexner.summary: British socialite and convicted sex offender; per John Kiriakou, her father Robert Maxwell was a prolific Mossad spy, and she is the likely conduit through whom Jeffrey Epstein was introduced to and recruited by Mossad.

les-wexner.title: MOSSAD
les-wexner.summary: Israel's primary external intelligence service; characterized by John Kiriakou as universally hostile in his and his CIA colleagues' professional dealings with it ("never had a positive encounter with Mossad"); operates almost exclusively in the operational rather than analytical domain; the CIA is, per Kiriakou, categorically forbidden from spying on it.

les-wexner.title: Peter Mandelson
les-wexner.summary: British politician; described by John Kiriakou as the former British ambassador to Washington and as someone likely to be charged with serious crimes in connection with Jeffrey Epstein.

les-wexner.title: Beef jerky anomaly in the Epstein files
les-wexner.summary: A pattern John Kiriakou has flagged in the released Epstein correspondence: on the order of 1,300 to 1,500 emails discuss beef jerky — making it, teaching others to make it, freezing and storing it — and none discuss eating it. Kiriakou treats it as an unexplained code and declines to speculate about what it stands for.

letter-from-loretto.title: FCI Loretto
letter-from-loretto.summary: U.S. Federal Correctional Institution in Loretto, Pennsylvania; the low-medium-security prison at which John Kiriakou served 23 months of a 30-month sentence following his 2013 Espionage Act–era plea deal; the originally ordered "minimum security work camp" placement was countermanded — per Kiriakou, on Brennan's direct intervention — to place him in the actual prison alongside the general population.

letter-from-loretto.title: Arianna Huffington
letter-from-loretto.summary: Founder of the Huffington Post and the accidental amplifier who turned John Kiriakou's prison writing into a phenomenon. His first Letter from Loretto went to his attorney, then to a friend running Firedoglake who — unknown to Kiriakou — was close to Huffington; she plastered it as a banner headline and it drew over a million hits, bringing CNN and 60 Minutes to the prison gates. She published his open letter to Snowden, ran the diesel-therapy exposé that triggered the "hands off John Kiriakou" campaign, and came to Loretto herself with two young journalists.

letter-from-loretto.title: This desk kills fascism
letter-from-loretto.summary: The sign Kiriakou taped to the cell desk on which he wrote the letters from Loretto, borrowed from Woody Guthrie's guitar, torn down by a guard within hours and kept by Kiriakou ever since.

letter-from-loretto.title: Education at FCI Loretto
letter-from-loretto.summary: The classes, drug programme and good-conduct rules at FCI Loretto, which Kiriakou described in a letter from Loretto as correcting nothing — and which taught him, he wrote, how to cook methamphetamine and defraud a mortgage company.

letter-from-loretto.title: Sarge
letter-from-loretto.summary: The FCI Loretto correctional officer John Kiriakou named in a Letter from Loretto for swearing at him and trashing his cell — conduct he later learned was not merely a Bureau of Prisons infraction but a misdemeanour crime, and one of two offences he says the letter inadvertently exposed.

letter-from-loretto.title: The mailroom standoff
letter-from-loretto.summary: Told at FCI Loretto that he had no right to write to journalists, John Kiriakou printed the Bureau of Prisons regulations in the law library and laid them out in the mailroom until the staff gave up and sent the letter.

letters-the-cabinet-ignored.title: The FLETC badge
letters-the-cabinet-ignored.summary: The shiny gold badge John Kiriakou carried before joining the CIA, issued after he trained at the Federal Law Enforcement Training Center — and which he insists never made him a law enforcement officer, a distinction he uses to deny the same status to ICE agents and federal prison guards.

letters-the-cabinet-ignored.title: The Bureau of Prisons polos
letters-the-cabinet-ignored.summary: What John Kiriakou says he saw on the morning of 6 January 2021 while parking on Capitol Hill for a meeting with his attorney Bruce Fein — a group of men stripping off Bureau of Prisons logo polo shirts and pulling on black ones — and the sentence he says he shouted at them.

letters-the-cabinet-ignored.title: Ali from Newark
letters-the-cabinet-ignored.summary: The Black shot caller at FCI Loretto, near the end of a twenty-five-year drug sentence, who came to embrace John Kiriakou at the close of his term and tell him how much he respected him — a friendship possible only because Kiriakou had decided on arrival to ignore the prison's racial divisions.

letters-the-cabinet-ignored.title: Bezalel Smotrich
letters-the-cabinet-ignored.summary: Israeli far-right minister whom John Kiriakou, alongside Itamar Ben-Gvir, blames for leaving Israel unprepared on October 7 by insisting any attack would come from the West Bank rather than Gaza.

letters-the-cabinet-ignored.title: Candace Owens
letters-the-cabinet-ignored.summary: The commentator whose claims about the killing of Charlie Kirk John Kiriakou has publicly declined to accept. He credits her reach and her intelligence and rejects her method, citing an earlier occasion — a conference call he says he was on — at which she claimed irrefutable proof that the Italian government had stolen the 2020 election and that its release would return Donald Trump to office.

letters-the-cabinet-ignored.title: Clyde Hall
letters-the-cabinet-ignored.summary: The imprisoned Ohio congressman John Kiriakou says served at his prison a few years before him, whose remark on release — that he had made some of the best friends of his life inside — Kiriakou thought insane at the time and came to understand after his own sentence.

liam-o-grady.title: Communications management unit
liam-o-grady.summary: The two restricted-contact units inside the American federal prison system, at Terre Haute and Marion; built for "the worst of the worst" but, in John Kiriakou's account, used to silence prisoners whose messages are inconvenient — and a practice he groups with solitary confinement as torture. He served part of his own sentence in a modified one.

liam-o-grady.title: Daniel Hale
liam-o-grady.summary: Per John Kiriakou, drone whistleblower Daniel Hale — an NSA contractor and drone targeting analyst who exposed an 80% civilian death rate in the U.S. drone program, was ordered to fire on two young girls his superior called "goats," and was sentenced to 45 months (of which Kiriakou says he actually served about 18) despite prosecutors seeking nine to eleven years.

liam-o-grady.title: Espionage Act
liam-o-grady.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

liam-o-grady.title: Matthew Cole
liam-o-grady.summary: American national-security journalist whose reporting tradecraft, per John Kiriakou, has led to the federal incarceration of five whistleblowers — including Kiriakou himself. In Kiriakou's account, Cole emailed him in 2010 ostensibly researching a book on the rendition of Abu Omar, asked Kiriakou to confirm the surname of a CIA officer who appeared in Kiriakou's own first book under the alias 'John', and Kiriakou's confirmation was the act of confirming a covert officer's identity for which he was eventually prosecuted under the Intelligence Identities Protection Act.

liam-o-grady.title: The roadblock strike
liam-o-grady.summary: The drone strike Daniel Hale described at his own sentencing and that John Kiriakou retells as the reason Hale became a whistleblower: a car approaching a U.S. roadblock in Afghanistan, two girls aged six and nine visible inside, an order to fire given twice over Hale''s objection, and a father who afterwards hid his daughters'' bodies in a village dumpster for fear that special forces would take them.

libertarian-party.title: Gary Johnson
libertarian-party.summary: The former Republican governor of New Mexico and Libertarian nominee for president who wrote to John Kiriakou in prison, wrote separately to Attorney General Eric Holder asking that he be released — a letter Kiriakou learned of only later through a Freedom of Information Act request — and telephoned him within days of his coming home.

libertarian-party.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
libertarian-party.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

libertarian-party.title: FCI Loretto
libertarian-party.summary: U.S. Federal Correctional Institution in Loretto, Pennsylvania; the low-medium-security prison at which John Kiriakou served 23 months of a 30-month sentence following his 2013 Espionage Act–era plea deal; the originally ordered "minimum security work camp" placement was countermanded — per Kiriakou, on Brennan's direct intervention — to place him in the actual prison alongside the general population.

libertarian-party.title: Encryption before the key
libertarian-party.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of where encryption actually fails, offered against John McAfee''s claim that no communication can be private. Kiriakou defers to the technologists he knows — Edward Snowden, Bill Binney, Thomas Drake and Kirk Wiebe — who tell him sufficiently sophisticated encryption does work. The exposure is upstream of the cipher: if an agency can reach your machine as you type, before you hit the encryption key, the encryption never gets a chance. He nonetheless encrypts everything he sends, and rejects the argument that encryption is what lets attacks through.

libertarian-party.title: The three legal ways to enter another country
libertarian-party.summary: The test John Kiriakou applies to American military action abroad: that there are only three lawful ways for one country to move into another — with the approval of the UN Security Council, at that country''s invitation, or after being attacked by it — and that the United States, in his account, never meets any of the three.

libertarian-party.title: The Libertarian Christmas party
libertarian-party.summary: The party John Kiriakou attended in a townhouse in Old Town Alexandria, held at the end of January because — being Libertarians — the organisers could not get their act together in December, and at which the head of the Libertarian Party of Virginia asked him to run for governor and was refused on the spot.

liberty-university.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
liberty-university.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

liberty-university.title: The four-question torture exam
liberty-university.summary: A final examination set by a former CIA officer teaching alongside John Kiriakou at Liberty University, consisting of four escalating questions about whether the student would torture — the terrorist, then his wife in front of him, then their children — with the last question asking the student to justify the previous three answers to God. Kiriakou describes it as the most powerful exam he has ever seen.

liberty-university.title: Christian Zionism
liberty-university.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that American evangelical Christianity functions as an arm of Zionism, and that its support for Israel is helping extinguish the oldest Christian communities on earth — a position he says he argued directly with the evangelical students he was invited to teach, and which he grounds in the projection that Nazareth, Christian for two thousand years, may soon have no Christians left.

liberty-university.title: Agent payment mechanics
liberty-university.summary: How the CIA physically pays a recruited agent — cash every month, a receipt signed with any alias the agent chooses, and a polygraph regime built around the assumption that the officer handling the money is the person most likely to steal it.

liberty-university.title: AIPAC
liberty-university.summary: The American Israel Public Affairs Committee — the U.S. political organization that, in John Kiriakou's framing, ought to be registered as a foreign-lobbying entity but is not, and that wields decisive electoral power against U.S. elected officials who express support for Palestinian human rights.

liberty-university.title: Allen Dulles
liberty-university.summary: Long-serving CIA director whom John Kiriakou calls a 'monster' and a 'very dark figure in American history' — a United Fruit board member who ran the agency that overthrew Guatemala's Árbenz, who went to Truman's house to talk him out of criticising the CIA, and who stayed in touch with the men Kiriakou believes killed John F. Kennedy.

lie-detection.title: Critical Analytic Thinking
lie-detection.summary: Per John Kiriakou, the foundational discipline of CIA analyst training and the most practically valuable skill he carried into civilian life: questioning all incoming information — including, especially, sources whose ideological positions align with one''s own — and arriving at conclusions from evidence rather than prior belief. Kiriakou cites his own COVID lab-leak conclusion, reached against his initial instinct, as an example of the method in practice.

lie-detection.title: John Kiriakou
lie-detection.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

lie-detection.title: Safe Housekeeper
lie-detection.summary: Per John Kiriakou, a person recruited by a CIA officer to rent and maintain an apartment or other premises as a safe house, using their own name and identity to conceal any CIA connection. The role itself is minimal — rent the apartment, keep it clean, keep it stocked with water — but the recruitment is itself a covert operation requiring the same persuasion and pressure techniques used to acquire any sensitive asset. Kiriakou recruited a safe housekeeper overseas and believes the pressure he applied may have caused her a nervous breakdown.

lie-detection.title: FCI Loretto
lie-detection.summary: U.S. Federal Correctional Institution in Loretto, Pennsylvania; the low-medium-security prison at which John Kiriakou served 23 months of a 30-month sentence following his 2013 Espionage Act–era plea deal; the originally ordered "minimum security work camp" placement was countermanded — per Kiriakou, on Brennan's direct intervention — to place him in the actual prison alongside the general population.

lie-detection.title: Moral Injury
lie-detection.summary: Psychological diagnosis John Kiriakou received from a friend — a CIA veteran, brigadier general, and psychiatrist — who identified it as the source of Kiriakou's post-divorce PTSD. The concept describes the psychological damage caused when a person you fully trust does something that violates the moral framework you were raised to believe in; the brain cannot process that such a violation has occurred, and the result is a form of PTSD. Kiriakou had no PTSD from Pakistan or his CIA career but was, in his own description, destroyed by his divorce.

lie-detection.title: Rebetiko music
lie-detection.summary: The Greek genre born in the prisons and opium dens of Constantinople that John Kiriakou reaches for when he is feeling particularly down — one half of a listening diet he describes as classic rock and Greek folk, the music his parents and grandparents played, and which he names as what would bring back his memories if he ever lost them.

lincolns-candlelight-pardons.title: Pardons nobody asked for
lincolns-candlelight-pardons.summary: Two cases John Kiriakou cites of people pardoned without applying: the Binance founder, who said publicly that he had never met the president, never asked for a pardon and never applied for one; and Darryl Strawberry, a New York Mets great with tax and drug problems behind him. Kiriakou raises both while waiting, unsuccessfully, for a pardon he has actively sought for years.

lincolns-candlelight-pardons.title: Coffee with a cabinet member
lincolns-candlelight-pardons.summary: John Kiriakou's disclosure that he had coffee with a member of the cabinet who told him to be patient about his pardon — and told him to watch what he said. He reports the meeting while stating plainly that there is nothing further he can do to make his case, and that he is not confident the outcome will be decided on justice.

lincolns-candlelight-pardons.title: Ed Martin and the pardon file
lincolns-candlelight-pardons.summary: The US pardon attorney whose office John Kiriakou directed supporters to write to, and the message a mutual friend brought back from him: that he was the third person that day to call about Kiriakou, that Kiriakou should relax, and that his file was literally on Martin''s desk. Kiriakou''s advice to letter-writers was to send physical mail rather than email.

lincolns-candlelight-pardons.title: The Crenshaw text messages
lincolns-candlelight-pardons.summary: John Kiriakou's account of taking his girlfriend's phone at midnight, finding a message from Dan Crenshaw asking what she was wearing, and texting back that he was her boyfriend and Crenshaw should ask his own wife — who had a ten-month-old baby at the time. Kiriakou says the woman showed him other messages that were filthy, and that she had saved them in case she needed to use them.

lincolns-candlelight-pardons.title: The January 6 pipe bomber report
lincolns-candlelight-pardons.summary: The story John Kiriakou says he posted to Facebook and nobody else picked up: a report that the FBI had identified the person who placed pipe bombs outside the RNC and DNC as a former Capitol Police officer who had been on rotation to the CIA doing physical security, recognised from a limp caused by a college sports injury, at a stated confidence of 94 per cent. She had not been charged, and Kiriakou lists the questions it would raise if true.

lincolns-candlelight-pardons.title: The Red Fort bombing
lincolns-candlelight-pardons.summary: John Kiriakou''s on-air attribution of a car bombing outside the Red Fort in New Delhi to Kashmiri separatist groups — offered with the acknowledgement that saying so brings him death threats from Pakistanis, and with a flat definition: groups that murder civilians for political purposes are terrorist groups, whatever their political point may be.

lincolns-last-turd.title: John Kiriakou
lincolns-last-turd.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

lincolns-last-turd.title: Kiriakou's Abraham Lincoln collection
lincolns-last-turd.summary: John Kiriakou''s private collection of Abraham Lincoln relics, assembled at auction over many years and governed by a strict standard of provenance: a blood-soaked fragment of the pillowcase Lincoln died on, wallpaper from the Petersen House death room, a swatch of Mary Todd Lincoln''s funeral dress, and wood from the gallows on which the conspirators were hanged.

lincolns-last-turd.title: Joby Warrick's Washington Post resignation
lincolns-last-turd.summary: John Kiriakou's account of his friend Joby Warrick, a multiple Pulitzer Prize-winning investigative journalist, resigning from the Washington Post because investigative journalism at the paper was dead — amid an 80% staff reduction since Jeff Bezos bought the paper.

lincolns-last-turd.title: Hummus
lincolns-last-turd.summary: The CIA's coercive 'rectal feeding' of detainees using pureed hummus — an unauthorized interrogation technique used at post-9/11 black sites, exposed in the 2014 Senate Torture Report, and the abuse for which John Kiriakou became most associated in popular culture.

lincolns-last-turd.title: Abu Zubaydah
lincolns-last-turd.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

lincolns-last-turd.title: Kiriakou's money-laundering tip
lincolns-last-turd.summary: John Kiriakou's account of taking a chief operating officer job at a boutique investment firm early in the COVID pandemic that he came to believe was an international money-laundering operation possibly backed by Iran — downloading 15,000 pages of supporting documents before an FBI agent told him the bureau would only take interest if the case involved Russia, China, terrorism, or January 6th.

lindsey-graham.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
lindsey-graham.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

lindsey-graham.title: The Caspian drone strike
lindsey-graham.summary: The July 2026 incident in which Ukrainian drones, unleashed by Volodymyr Zelensky as part of a declared 40-day drone war on June 25 to make the Russian people feel pain, strayed onto an Iranian ship in the Caspian Sea and killed an Iranian sailor. John Kiriakou treats Zelensky's subsequent attempt to spin the mistake into a request that the United States expand its Iran war into the Caspian as a probable Netanyahu suggestion, and Iran's decision to accept an apology and reparations as evidence that Iran no longer needs the mistake to be a war.

lindsey-graham.title: The GUR-SBU gun battle
lindsey-graham.summary: The daylight shootout on Shumsky Street in Kyiv, in which Ukraine's two most senior intelligence services, the GUR (military intelligence) and the SBU (domestic security), fired on each other after the SBU detained a GUR officer. John Kiriakou, asked to react on the Sanchez Effect, said he had tried to think of a precedent and could not; he treats the fight as *"the breakdown of the Ukrainian side."*

lindsey-graham.title: Gulf intelligence services
lindsey-graham.summary: John Kiriakou's assessment of the intelligence services of the Gulf Cooperation Council states, which he worked with closely during his CIA career and rates uniformly excellent — highly trained, multilingual and experienced worldwide — with the Emiratis and Qataris the strongest of them and the Emiratis, in his ranking, the best of all.

lindsey-graham.title: The White House pastry chef
lindsey-graham.summary: John Kiriakou''s former next-door neighbour, a White House pastry chef who was in the building when Donald Trump came to meet Barack Obama four days after the 2016 election, and who told Kiriakou that the president-elect looked sick and looked scared.

lindsey-graham.title: The Italian schoolchildren
lindsey-graham.summary: An encounter John Kiriakou described in July 2026 as a measure of how far his late-career fame had spread: walking down Fifth Avenue in New York, a bus pulled up, a boy of about thirteen shouted his name in Italian, and sixty-five Italian middle schoolers ran off the bus. The selfies took half an hour.

litani-river.title: Evangelical Zionism
litani-river.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the American Christian movement that supports Israel in order to hasten the return of Christ — a belief he calls a cult rather than a religion, which he says Israeli officials knowingly exploit, and which he blames for the abandonment of the Middle East's original Christians.

litani-river.title: American missile stockpiles
litani-river.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that the United States has run its interceptor stocks down to the point of strategic vulnerability — that the conventional wisdom in Washington was that a round of the Iran war ended because the Patriots ran out, and that a country which cannot fight a two-front war certainly cannot do it below maximum production.

litani-river.title: The Bab el-Mandeb
litani-river.summary: The strait between Yemen and the Horn of Africa through which everything leaving the Suez Canal must pass — narrower than the Strait of Hormuz, in John Kiriakou's account the one genuine American national interest in Yemen, and the reason Israel has offered diplomatic recognition to Somaliland in exchange for a military base.

litani-river.title: Djibouti
litani-river.summary: The small Horn of Africa state a few miles across the water from Yemen that hosts Camp Lemonnier — the American drone base for the Yemen and Somalia wars, inherited from the departing French, and shared with China's only overseas military base behind a fence down the middle, in what John Kiriakou calls the worst kept secret in the world.

litani-river.title: Gary Johnson
litani-river.summary: The former Republican governor of New Mexico and Libertarian nominee for president who wrote to John Kiriakou in prison, wrote separately to Attorney General Eric Holder asking that he be released — a letter Kiriakou learned of only later through a Freedom of Information Act request — and telephoned him within days of his coming home.

litani-river.title: The Greek Orthodox Church
litani-river.summary: The church John Kiriakou was raised in and still belongs to — the institution behind his Greek fluency and his family''s immigrant history, a recurring thread in his accounts of Athens, Damascus, Bethlehem and Washington, and, in two cases, an actor in his own story: the church the FBI followed him into, and the priest who tried to get him a pardon.

lobbyists-writing-legislation.title: The Speaker's office as gatekeeper
lobbyists-writing-legislation.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of how legislative power moved in the mid-1990s from committee chairmen and the Rules Committee into the office of the Speaker of the House, where it has stayed because no subsequent Speaker has wanted to give it back — and the member of Congress who explained the death of his own whistleblower bill in four words: ''Nancy said I couldn''t.''

lobbyists-writing-legislation.title: Think tank financing
lobbyists-writing-legislation.summary: John Kiriakou's warning that Washington's think tanks — more than 1,200 of them by a Washington Post count — must be read through their funding, illustrated with the case of someone close to him who controlled about $200,000 a year in donations for a Fortune 100 defence contractor and moved the money when a household-name institute proved insufficiently pro-contractor.

lobbyists-writing-legislation.title: The Trumpcare confusion
lobbyists-writing-legislation.summary: A television interview John Kiriakou says he watched, in which a woman from Arkansas wept with gratitude to President Trump because a website had insured her son's cancer treatment — and, told by the reporter that this was in fact the Affordable Care Act, insisted that Obamacare had been repealed and replaced and that what she had was Trumpcare.

lobbyists-writing-legislation.title: Progressive taxation
lobbyists-writing-legislation.summary: John Kiriakou''s argument that the United States abandoned a system it was once proud of: taxation based, in Theodore Roosevelt''s formulation, on a person''s ability to pay. It fell apart under Ronald Reagan, he says, and the regressive substitutes now proposed — a higher gas tax among them — hit the people least able to absorb them.

lobbyists-writing-legislation.title: The Iron Dome
lobbyists-writing-legislation.summary: Israel's air-defence system as John Kiriakou reads it — impressive against a wave of slow Iranian drones, but shown by the handful that got through, and later by Iranian ballistic missiles, to be not all it is cracked up to be; each exchange, in his account, buying Iran intelligence about the gaps.

lobbyists-writing-legislation.title: John Kerry
lobbyists-writing-legislation.summary: U.S. Senator from Massachusetts; chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee during John Kiriakou's 2009 service as the committee's senior investigator; subsequently U.S. Secretary of State; characterized by Kiriakou as a coward who buckled under CIA pressure on the Dasht-i-Leili reopening and as personally fixated on his perceived theft of the Secretary of State position by Hillary Clinton; the famously thrown medals were duplicates purchased at the post exchange.

loretto-correctional-officers.title: Prison phone monitoring
loretto-correctional-officers.summary: Kiriakou treated the recording of his prison telephone calls as an intelligence channel rather than a constraint, planting messages for staff he knew were listening — a practice that produced a confrontation with a lieutenant over the word 'Nimrod'.

loretto-correctional-officers.title: Solitary confinement
loretto-correctional-officers.summary: The prison isolation practice the United Nations calls a form of torture; John Kiriakou, drawing on his own ten days in a six-by-sixteen-foot cell, argues that jailing depressed prisoners like Daniel Hale in solitary 'for their own safety' is precisely what drives them to suicide.

loretto-correctional-officers.title: Bureau of Prisons
loretto-correctional-officers.summary: The federal agency that ran John Kiriakou's incarceration — and one of his most persistent post-prison targets. The BOP overrode his judge's camp recommendation by deeming him "a threat to the public safety," threatened him with "diesel therapy" until 1,600 logged phone calls and letters from a dozen House members and two senators backed it off, and, per Kiriakou, functions as "an employment agency for unemployable semi-literate rural white men" and "a dumping ground for failed medical professionals" — an agency for which a prisoner's death is cheaper than his treatment.

loretto-correctional-officers.title: Central Intelligence Agency
loretto-correctional-officers.summary: U.S. foreign intelligence service; John Kiriakou's employer from 1990 to 2004 and the central institution of KiriPedia

loretto-correctional-officers.title: FCI Loretto
