mark-polymeropoulos.summary: John Kiriakou''s figures for getting his first book through CIA prepublication review: nine months to write it, twenty-two months to clear it, and 120 pages rejected. He says everything he writes still goes to the agency for clearance, but that the process has become much easier as his detractors there have died or retired.

mark-polymeropoulos.title: The divorce at the airport
mark-polymeropoulos.summary: The end of John Kiriakou''s first marriage, as he tells it: after 17 November assassinated his next-door neighbour and left a manifesto saying they had set out that morning to kill him instead, the embassy put him in an armoured car, collected his children and his wife, and packed out the house. His wife reached the airport, walked up to him and said she wanted a divorce. They flew home on the same plane.

mark-warner.title: John Kiriakou
mark-warner.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

mark-warner.title: Pete Seeger
mark-warner.summary: American folk singer; John Kiriakou's personal hero alongside his father and grandfather; pleaded the First Amendment (rather than the Fifth) before the House Un-American Activities Committee in 1958 and was sent to prison for it (later overturned on appeal); befriended by Kiriakou over decades of concert-going and correspondence; rallied to Kiriakou's defense after Kiriakou's 2012 arrest; the subject of Kiriakou's favorite book, How Can I Keep From Singing?

mark-warner.title: Jon Ossoff
mark-warner.summary: United States senator from Georgia, whom John Kiriakou places among the rare honest figures on Capitol Hill and grades at the top of his case-officer rankings. Kiriakou also notes a family connection to the wartime liberation of Greece.

mark-warner.title: Kiriakou's case-officer rankings
mark-warner.summary: A recurring segment in which John Kiriakou grades serving and former American politicians on how good a CIA case officer each would make, using an S-to-F scale. The criterion is character and the ability to attract confidence rather than politics, and he repeatedly grades allies low and opponents high.

mark-warner.title: Kiriakou's gun rights appeal
mark-warner.summary: John Kiriakou's effort to have the firearms disability attached to his felony conviction lifted, by suing the Justice Department over a restoration process announced in 2025 and never built, and separately by applying for a presidential pardon he says he cannot count on.

mark-warner.title: Alexa
mark-warner.summary: Per John Kiriakou, Amazon''s Alexa smart speaker reports directly to the NSA — and he owns one anyway. The device recurs across his interviews as the standing example of the surveillance trade-off in modern smart-home technology, and of his own negotiated exception to it: one speaker, in one room, against the advice of every intelligence officer he has ever known.

mark-zuckerberg-angela-merkel-meeting.title: John Kiriakou
mark-zuckerberg-angela-merkel-meeting.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

mark-zuckerberg-angela-merkel-meeting.title: Operation Mockingbird
mark-zuckerberg-angela-merkel-meeting.summary: The CIA's mid-twentieth-century program of recruiting and managing American journalists as influence assets; in John Kiriakou's account, no longer operationally necessary in the contemporary period because the U.S. media voluntarily reprints CIA-supplied material, and in at least one documented case sends articles to the agency for clearance before sending them to its own editor.

mark-zuckerberg-angela-merkel-meeting.title: Project Stargate
mark-zuckerberg-angela-merkel-meeting.summary: The CIA's remote-viewing program, which Kiriakou says burned millions for decades and failed — and which he understands is being revisited.

mark-zuckerberg-angela-merkel-meeting.title: DARPA LifeLog
mark-zuckerberg-angela-merkel-meeting.summary: A Pentagon research program meant to track every email, photo, location and purchase of a person; John Kiriakou notes it was killed on February 4, 2004 — one day before Mark Zuckerberg filed the Facebook LLC.

mark-zuckerberg-angela-merkel-meeting.title: In-Q-Tel
mark-zuckerberg-angela-merkel-meeting.summary: The CIA's openly acknowledged venture capital arm; provided Palantir Technologies its first $1.5 million in seed funding; in John Kiriakou's account the principal vehicle by which the agency finances private-sector development of technologies it intends to use.

mark-zuckerberg-angela-merkel-meeting.title: Joe Rogan
mark-zuckerberg-angela-merkel-meeting.summary: The podcast host whose show John Kiriakou finally sat for in October 2025 — an experience that began with signing a non-disclosure agreement and ended with his verdict that Rogan is "a nice guy, very down to earth, very normal." The first thing Rogan asked, walking into the studio ten minutes late: "Hey, do you know my friend Mike Baker?" Kiriakou defends Rogan as unfairly characterized as a right-winger, and had long cited the show as the venue where Zuckerberg admitted Facebook suppressed the Hunter Biden laptop story at the FBI''s behest.

marlon-beard.title: FCI Loretto
marlon-beard.summary: U.S. Federal Correctional Institution in Loretto, Pennsylvania; the low-medium-security prison at which John Kiriakou served 23 months of a 30-month sentence following his 2013 Espionage Act–era plea deal; the originally ordered "minimum security work camp" placement was countermanded — per Kiriakou, on Brennan's direct intervention — to place him in the actual prison alongside the general population.

marlon-beard.title: Cell transfers at Loretto
marlon-beard.summary: How a prisoner at FCI Loretto moved from one cell to another — a process requiring six months in place, the written agreement of the receiving cell and the signature of the counselor, which John Kiriakou describes as a guard assigned to be a designated pain in the ass.

marlon-beard.title: Blue
marlon-beard.summary: The FCI Loretto correctional officer, widely considered the most unpopular in the prison, who covered his own nameplate with masking tape so released prisoners could not find him — and who told a colleague of John Kiriakou's that he would never touch the CIA man because of the press attention.

marlon-beard.title: The dog food memo
marlon-beard.summary: The internal announcement circulated by the warden of FCI Loretto apologising for having served prisoners dog food on a taco night, which John Kiriakou cites as evidence not of the error but of how bad the ordinary food was — because nobody noticed.

marlon-beard.title: Correctional officers at FCI Loretto
marlon-beard.summary: Kiriakou's portraits of the staff at FCI Loretto — including two officers who tried to trick him into a fight, a lieutenant forced out of several prisons for harassment, and an officer whose abuse of prisoners he successfully reported.

marlon-beard.title: Kiriakou's FOIA request from prison
marlon-beard.summary: The Freedom of Information Act request John Kiriakou filed on himself six weeks into his sentence at FCI Loretto — despite a plea agreement promising he never would — which returned 250 pages including a warden's memorandum warning staff that the incoming prisoner had access to the media.

martha-kesler.title: John Brennan
martha-kesler.summary: Former Director of the CIA; characterized in KiriPedia's source corpus as the principal architect of the agency's enhanced interrogation program and as having plotted against an elected President

martha-kesler.title: John Ratcliffe
martha-kesler.summary: CIA director under Trump's second term; per John Kiriakou, a "bombthrower" he mostly disagrees with politically but supported as a needed disruptor for the agency — "a good guy, expert in what he does," though "not a visionary thinker" and, on Kiriakou's later assessment, a neocon who has outmanoeuvred Tulsi Gabbard for primacy over U.S. intelligence. Ratcliffe told the White House the CIA had no objection to pardoning Kiriakou.

martha-kesler.title: Jim Pavitt
martha-kesler.summary: Long-serving CIA Deputy Director for Operations during the early post-9/11 period; characterized by John Kiriakou as "a legendary officer and a really great guy"; mocked John Brennan openly within the agency for Brennan's recurring stated ambition to head his own intelligence agency.

martha-kesler.title: Joe Rogan
martha-kesler.summary: The podcast host whose show John Kiriakou finally sat for in October 2025 — an experience that began with signing a non-disclosure agreement and ended with his verdict that Rogan is "a nice guy, very down to earth, very normal." The first thing Rogan asked, walking into the studio ten minutes late: "Hey, do you know my friend Mike Baker?" Kiriakou defends Rogan as unfairly characterized as a right-winger, and had long cited the show as the venue where Zuckerberg admitted Facebook suppressed the Hunter Biden laptop story at the FBI''s behest.

martha-kesler.title: Abu Zubaydah
martha-kesler.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

martha-kesler.title: Ali Soufan
martha-kesler.summary: FBI special agent who handled Abu Zubaydah immediately after his March 2002 capture; through patient, respectful interrogation produced the only actionable intelligence ever obtained from the detainee, including the first identification of "Mukhtar" as Khalid Sheikh Mohammed.

martin-luther-king.title: FCI Loretto
martin-luther-king.summary: U.S. Federal Correctional Institution in Loretto, Pennsylvania; the low-medium-security prison at which John Kiriakou served 23 months of a 30-month sentence following his 2013 Espionage Act–era plea deal; the originally ordered "minimum security work camp" placement was countermanded — per Kiriakou, on Brennan's direct intervention — to place him in the actual prison alongside the general population.

martin-luther-king.title: MLK assassination
martin-luther-king.summary: The April 1968 killing of Martin Luther King Jr. John Kiriakou, having set out to read everything he could find on it, concluded that if James Earl Ray fired the shot he was a patsy — citing the implausibility of a lifelong alcoholic making a perfect shot from a flophouse bathroom a block away, and the FBI's documented attempt two years earlier to push King into suicide.

martin-luther-king.title: Vault 7
martin-luther-king.summary: The 2017 WikiLeaks disclosure of thousands of pages of CIA Directorate of Science and Technology documents — leaked by agency engineer Joshua Schulte — revealing CIA technical capabilities including remote takeover of internet-connected cars, conversion of smart-TV speakers into covert microphones, and the planting of Russian or Persian language fragments in foreign systems to mislead attribution.

martin-luther-king.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
martin-luther-king.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

martin-luther-king.title: Arianna Huffington
martin-luther-king.summary: Founder of the Huffington Post and the accidental amplifier who turned John Kiriakou's prison writing into a phenomenon. His first Letter from Loretto went to his attorney, then to a friend running Firedoglake who — unknown to Kiriakou — was close to Huffington; she plastered it as a banner headline and it drew over a million hits, bringing CNN and 60 Minutes to the prison gates. She published his open letter to Snowden, ran the diesel-therapy exposé that triggered the "hands off John Kiriakou" campaign, and came to Loretto herself with two young journalists.

martin-luther-king.title: Aryan Brotherhood
martin-luther-king.summary: The white prison gang that adopted John Kiriakou on his first day at FCI Loretto. Two hours in, two Aryans with swastika neck tattoos walked into his cell to check his paperwork — not a rat, not a "chomo" — and invited him to the Aryan table, which ran from hardcore Nazis at one end to merely white guys at the other. A rumor that he had been a CIA assassin earned him the nickname "the Muslim killer," which he never corrected; asked directly, he answered "we all did stuff we weren't proud of — it was wartime," and the Aryans loved it. He sat with them a year before the Italians took him in.

marty-gottesfeld.title: Donnie Reynolds Jr.
marty-gottesfeld.summary: Tennessee businessman and antique-firearms collector serving a life-plus-75-year federal sentence at the Communications Management Unit in Terre Haute, Indiana; per John Kiriakou and Marty Gottesfeld, a scapegoat for the fallout of the ATF's Operation Fast and Furious after refusing to become an undercover cartel weapons source.

marty-gottesfeld.title: Operation Fast and Furious
marty-gottesfeld.summary: The ATF gun-walking operation John Kiriakou describes as the background to the Donnie Reynolds Jr case — in which agents let 2,000 weapons reach Mexican cartel buyers in the hope of tracing them upward, arrested nobody at the top, and then turned back on the small players when Congress demanded answers.

marty-gottesfeld.title: Abu Nidal Organization
marty-gottesfeld.summary: Per John Kiriakou, the CIA destroyed the Abu Nidal Organization from within by exploiting Abu Nidal''s pathological paranoia: rather than recruiting members (impossible given the group''s extreme anti-American orientation), the agency planted false signals that various members were already cooperating with US intelligence. Members began killing each other one by one. Kiriakou: ''Next thing you know, they''ve all killed each other and the only one left is Abu Nidal.'' He also disbelieves the official heart-attack cause of Abu Nidal''s death, attributing it to a Saddam Hussein ''control'' decision.

marty-gottesfeld.title: Abu Zubaydah
marty-gottesfeld.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

marty-gottesfeld.title: British Bases in Cyprus
marty-gottesfeld.summary: British sovereign bases in Cyprus host a large American contingent. Kiriakou, a quarter Cypriot, on the bases as evacuation hub, missile target, and suspected nuclear site — and on the 46-year US weapons embargo almost no American knows about.

marty-gottesfeld.title: Church Committee
marty-gottesfeld.summary: U.S. Senate investigative committee operating in 1975–1976 that examined domestic intelligence abuses by the CIA, FBI, and NSA; per John Kiriakou, the Church Committee — alongside the concurrent Pike Committee in the House — was the last genuine moment of legislative oversight over the intelligence community, born of a national consensus that government had gone dangerously off course. Its work led to the creation of the permanent Senate Select Committee on Intelligence, which Kiriakou says ceased to function as real oversight roughly seven years after its founding.

mary-jane-stevens.title: The custody standoff
mary-jane-stevens.summary: The week John Kiriakou used his CIA surveillance training to find his own sons after his ex-wife hid them in breach of a custody order — ending with him carrying his eight-year-old out of a Greek Orthodox church during the consecration, a felony charge that was dropped, and a hostage-style handover at a diner on the state line.

mary-jane-stevens.title: Cofer Black
mary-jane-stevens.summary: Former head of the CIA Counterterrorism Center during and immediately after the September 11 attacks; principal architect of the agency's paramilitary turn on September 12, 2001; later Vice President of Blackwater under Erik Prince.

mary-jane-stevens.title: Cofer Black's warning to the liaison class
mary-jane-stevens.summary: The briefing Cofer Black gave to a class of visiting foreign liaison officers weeks before 11 September 2001 — code words about a honey salesman, a great football match and an enormous wedding — and the private exchange afterwards in which he told John Kiriakou he had been deadly serious.

mary-jane-stevens.title: The Foreign Relations volume and the sources still alive
mary-jane-stevens.summary: The errand that put John Kiriakou and Cofer Black in a car to the White House on the morning of 11 September 2001: three declassified cables due to be printed in a State Department history volume named CIA sources who were still living — and an obscure law requiring the United States to resettle any source it outs.

mary-jane-stevens.title: The Greek community of Warren, Ohio
mary-jane-stevens.summary: The Greek-American community John Kiriakou's mother and first wife both came from — overwhelmingly from the island of Chios, closely enough knit that his divorce started a fistfight in a coffee house between men who had never met him.

mary-jane-stevens.title: John Kiriakou
mary-jane-stevens.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

mary-margaret-graham.title: Wesley Clark
mary-margaret-graham.summary: Retired U.S. Army four-star general and former Clinton administration adviser; per John Kiriakou, "a very good guy", "one of the very, very few people at that level", and the public source of the account that in the weeks after 9/11 the Pentagon was working to a memo listing seven governments to be overthrown. Kiriakou treats Clark's story as corroborated by his own — on 6 May 2002 a CIA security officer told him, in the course of signing him onto the agency's most sensitive programmes, that the United States would invade Iraq the following year.

mary-margaret-graham.title: Concealment of the CIA budget
mary-margaret-graham.summary: John Kiriakou''s description of how the CIA hides its spending: there is no publicly available written CIA budget, and individual line items are distributed across unrelated federal departments under invented cover programmes — a practice he says persists unchanged, and which once repeatedly exposed the agency to Senator William Proxmire''s Golden Fleece Award.

mary-margaret-graham.title: AIPAC
mary-margaret-graham.summary: The American Israel Public Affairs Committee — the U.S. political organization that, in John Kiriakou's framing, ought to be registered as a foreign-lobbying entity but is not, and that wields decisive electoral power against U.S. elected officials who express support for Palestinian human rights.

mary-margaret-graham.title: Bahrain Posting (1994–1996)
mary-margaret-graham.summary: John Kiriakou's 1994–1996 assignment to Bahrain under U.S. State Department cover as second secretary for economic affairs — arriving with his wife Joanne and infant son Chris on August 1, 1994, into a tiny Gulf monarchy whose sectarian tensions erupted, two months later, into the first Intifada.

mary-margaret-graham.title: China as economic threat
mary-margaret-graham.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that China is the real threat to the West not militarily — it has one aircraft carrier to America's two dozen and rarely invades — but economically, buying friends worldwide while the U.S. spends a trillion dollars a year on weapons.

mary-margaret-graham.title: Andrew Warren
mary-margaret-graham.summary: Former CIA officer and station chief who, per John Kiriakou, was protected and lavishly funded by his supervisor "Mary Margaret," then convicted of raping 23 women — videotaping every attack — before a post-prison religious conversion and further sexual assault convictions.

mass-incarceration-critique.title: Bureau of Prisons
mass-incarceration-critique.summary: The federal agency that ran John Kiriakou's incarceration — and one of his most persistent post-prison targets. The BOP overrode his judge's camp recommendation by deeming him "a threat to the public safety," threatened him with "diesel therapy" until 1,600 logged phone calls and letters from a dozen House members and two senators backed it off, and, per Kiriakou, functions as "an employment agency for unemployable semi-literate rural white men" and "a dumping ground for failed medical professionals" — an agency for which a prisoner's death is cheaper than his treatment.

mass-incarceration-critique.title: Education at FCI Loretto
mass-incarceration-critique.summary: The classes, drug programme and good-conduct rules at FCI Loretto, which Kiriakou described in a letter from Loretto as correcting nothing — and which taught him, he wrote, how to cook methamphetamine and defraud a mortgage company.

mass-incarceration-critique.title: Administrative remedy process
mass-incarceration-critique.summary: The Bureau of Prisons' internal grievance system, which Kiriakou describes as a fig leaf designed to run out the clock on prisoners' complaints rather than resolve them.

mass-incarceration-critique.title: Medical care in federal prison
mass-incarceration-critique.summary: Kiriakou's account of health care at FCI Loretto, where a bunkmate's months of reported chest pain ended in a heart attack, a prisoner with untreated back pain was diagnosed with terminal cancer weeks before he died, and Kiriakou himself collapsed after being handed a drug nobody had explained to him.

mass-incarceration-critique.title: FCI Loretto
mass-incarceration-critique.summary: U.S. Federal Correctional Institution in Loretto, Pennsylvania; the low-medium-security prison at which John Kiriakou served 23 months of a 30-month sentence following his 2013 Espionage Act–era plea deal; the originally ordered "minimum security work camp" placement was countermanded — per Kiriakou, on Brennan's direct intervention — to place him in the actual prison alongside the general population.

mass-incarceration-critique.title: Letter from Loretto
mass-incarceration-critique.summary: Prison newsletter written by John Kiriakou from FCI Loretto, modeled on Martin Luther King's "Letter from Birmingham Jail," which exposed two crimes committed against him by guards and went viral after being relayed to the Huffington Post, drawing national press to the prison.

mass-surveillance.title: NSA Surveillance
mass-surveillance.summary: ''It is part of NSA''s founding charter that it is not allowed to spy on Americans'' — Kiriakou on warrantless collection and the Bluffdale warehouse.

mass-surveillance.title: Purchased data as a warrant workaround
mass-surveillance.summary: John Kiriakou's account of U.S. federal agencies buying Americans' personal data from social-media platforms and data brokers rather than seeking a warrant — a practice he describes as an ethical and legal problem likely to reach the Supreme Court, and one in which no judge is aware a case is being built.

mass-surveillance.title: Flock cameras
mass-surveillance.summary: Automated licence-plate reading cameras mounted on police vehicles and on poles disguised as utility poles. John Kiriakou describes them as blanket, constant surveillance and a direct assault on civil liberties, more dangerous than the public realises, and says they are the point at which Edward Snowden's predictions have already come true.

mass-surveillance.title: Kiriakou on artificial intelligence
mass-surveillance.summary: John Kiriakou's stated experience with and objections to large language models — a ChatGPT exchange in which the system stated his degrees incorrectly, refused his correction and then cut him off, and a test in which every scholarly citation it produced for his university syllabus turned out to be fabricated. He also describes AI as the flagging layer of contemporary surveillance.

mass-surveillance.title: WLDragnet
mass-surveillance.summary: Free search tool documenting U.S. defense contractors' monitoring of social-media users by political affiliation. John Kiriakou says a search of his own name in the tool's beta showed Northrop Grumman had queried him hundreds of times, and that his attorneys used the data in separate litigation against the company.

mass-surveillance.title: The MI5 model for America
mass-surveillance.summary: The discussions John Kiriakou says he took part in on his first trip to London as a CIA officer in 1992 or 1993, about creating an American equivalent of Britain’s MI5 — a domestic intelligence service, without arrest powers, that would spy on citizens and hand what it found to the FBI — and his observation thirty years later that it looked to be coming to pass.

matt-dehart.title: Julian Assange
matt-dehart.summary: Kiriakou — a 15-year friend and former WikiLeaks board member — on why Assange is a publisher owed a journalist's immunity, and a political prisoner.

matt-dehart.title: Bob Grenier
matt-dehart.summary: Career CIA officer who served as station chief in Islamabad before, during, and after 9/11; later associate deputy director of operations for policy support and Iraq Mission Manager; John Kiriakou's boss and, for one year, his supervisor as executive assistant.

matt-dehart.title: CIA Remote Vehicle Control
matt-dehart.summary: John Kiriakou's account, corroborated by Forbes' Andy Greenberg's real-world demonstration, that the CIA can remotely take over a car's systems and cause a fatal crash disguised as an accident.

matt-dehart.title: Classification compartments
matt-dehart.summary: John Kiriakou's explanation of the U.S. secrecy tiers above 'top secret' — the TS/SCI/TK/gamma clearances everyone at the CIA gets, and the additional compartments that mean even senior officials can be barred from a single cable.

matt-dehart.title: Cofer Black
matt-dehart.summary: Former head of the CIA Counterterrorism Center during and immediately after the September 11 attacks; principal architect of the agency's paramilitary turn on September 12, 2001; later Vice President of Blackwater under Erik Prince.

matt-dehart.title: Espionage Act
matt-dehart.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

matthew-cole.title: Reality Winner
matthew-cole.summary: National Security Agency linguist imprisoned for sending a single classified page on Russian interference in the 2016 election to The Intercept. John Kiriakou attributes her arrest to the two reporters who received it, and to a printer-tracking countermeasure they appear not to have known about; he also treats her prosecution as an operation that served the intelligence community on three fronts at once.

matthew-cole.title: The Intercept
matthew-cole.summary: The investigative news outlet that published Daniel Hale's drone leak; John Kiriakou notes that the same Intercept reporter, Matthew Cole, was involved in cases that led to the exposure of both Kiriakou himself and NSA leaker Reality Winner — though he insists Hale outed himself rather than being burned by the outlet.

matthew-cole.title: Human Rights Watch
matthew-cole.summary: The organization whose 2005 report that the CIA was torturing its prisoners — two years before John Kiriakou''s ABC interview — anchors his defense that he confirmed rather than revealed the program. It is also the middle link in the chain that ended in his arrest: working with the John Adams Project, Human Rights Watch employed the investigator who carried a classified name from journalist Matthew Cole to the Guantánamo defense attorneys, and when the FBI walked that chain backwards it arrived at Kiriakou''s door.

matthew-cole.title: The Intercept's exposed sources
matthew-cole.summary: John Kiriakou's charge that national security whistleblowers who take material to The Intercept end up in prison. He names Reality Winner and Terry Albury as sources whose identities the outlet exposed, says the same thing happened to Daniel Hale, and identifies the outlet's two national security reporters, Richard Esposito and Matthew Cole, as the journalists responsible for sending him to prison. His question is whether the pattern is incompetence or something worse.

matthew-cole.title: Valerie Plame
matthew-cole.summary: Covert CIA case officer whose identity was publicly outed by the Bush administration in retaliation for her husband, former U.S. ambassador to Niger Joseph Wilson, publishing a New York Times op-ed debunking the administration's claim that Iraq had attempted to purchase yellowcake uranium from Niger. Per John Kiriakou, Plame's CIA career ended on the day her cover was blown — she could never travel overseas under cover again; no one was prosecuted for the leak.

max-blumenthal.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
max-blumenthal.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

max-blumenthal.title: China's base in Djibouti
max-blumenthal.summary: Camp Lemonnier in Djibouti, the abandoned French base the Djiboutians offered to the Americans and the Chinese took a share of — split down the middle by a chain-link fence, the only Chinese military installation outside China, and the centrepiece of John Kiriakou's argument that China is not an expansionist power.

max-blumenthal.title: Iran Nuclear Assessment
max-blumenthal.summary: Per John Kiriakou's assessment, the US–Israeli military campaign against Iran was a war of choice driven by Israeli political pressure rather than genuine intelligence indicating an Iranian nuclear weapons threat. The CIA produced two National Intelligence Estimates concluding Iran had no nuclear weapons program; Supreme Leader Ayatollah Khamenei issued a fatwa in the 1980s forbidding such a program. The U.S. went to war anyway, in Kiriakou's view, after President Trump replaced the Joint Chiefs of Staff with officers willing to accept Israeli intelligence and proceed.

max-blumenthal.title: John Kiriakou
max-blumenthal.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

max-blumenthal.title: NewsGuard
max-blumenthal.summary: A media-rating organization, founded by the former head of Court TV and a former Wall Street Journal publisher, that scores news outlets 0-100 for reliability. Per John Kiriakou, NewsGuard docks any outlet that takes a position on Ukraine or Syria contrary to its preferred line, is subscribed to mostly by government entities (chiefly the Pentagon), and singled out Consortium News, the Grayzone, Antiwar.com, and ScheerPost over their criticism of U.S. policy — prompting a First Amendment lawsuit.

max-blumenthal.title: Trita Parsi
max-blumenthal.summary: Iran scholar; in a Foreign Affairs piece published August 10, 2025, predicted a renewed Israeli–Iranian war by the end of August 2025; described by John Kiriakou as "one of the greatest Iran scholars on the planet."

max-miller.title: Bernie Moreno
max-miller.summary: Republican senator from Ohio and father-in-law of Congressman Max Miller. John Kiriakou raises, without asserting, the possibility that Moreno's two-year public silence about the abuse of his daughter was the product of blackmail.

max-miller.title: Blackmail of closeted politicians
max-miller.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that a significant number of senior American politicians are concealing their sexuality and are vulnerable to blackmail because of it, illustrated with a roll-call of congressional outings from the 1980s onward.

max-miller.title: Kiriakou's case-officer rankings
max-miller.summary: A recurring segment in which John Kiriakou grades serving and former American politicians on how good a CIA case officer each would make, using an S-to-F scale. The criterion is character and the ability to attract confidence rather than politics, and he repeatedly grades allies low and opponents high.

max-miller.title: Thomas Massie
max-miller.summary: Republican U.S. Representative from Kentucky known for a constitutionalist voting record and consistent opposition to foreign military intervention; per John Kiriakou, a principled America-First congressman who votes with the president on the vast majority of issues, and whose opposition to U.S. funding of Israel and foreign wars is the only plausible explanation for the roughly $30 million spent by the Israel lobby to unseat him in a primary.

max-miller.title: Jim Jordan
max-miller.summary: Republican congressman from Ohio and chairman of the House Judiciary Committee. John Kiriakou describes a genuinely divided view of him: one of only four members of Congress he names as a friend of whistleblowers, and simultaneously the chairman whose Weaponization subcommittee he says is a partisan counterfeit of the Church Committee — with the whole question settled against Jordan by the Ohio State wrestlers who told him their team doctor was abusing them.

max-miller.title: John Kiriakou
max-miller.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

maxwell-at-a-work-camp.title: The Maxwell Justice Department interview
maxwell-at-a-work-camp.summary: Ghislaine Maxwell's July 2025 interview with the Justice Department, in which her counsel said she took the fifth on nothing and answered every question — a risk John Kiriakou reads as evidence she was probably telling the truth, and as an approach for a commutation or a pardon.

maxwell-at-a-work-camp.title: The question about the showers
maxwell-at-a-work-camp.summary: The single thing John Kiriakou says he most wanted to know before going to prison, and the lunch his attorneys arranged with a former George Washington University professor — himself recently released — to answer it.

maxwell-at-a-work-camp.title: The forty-seven suffix
maxwell-at-a-work-camp.summary: The last two digits of a federal prisoner number that, according to John Kiriakou, mark the holder as a member of an organised gang — and which the Italians at FCI Loretto carried along with MS-13, the Bloods, the Crips and the Mexican Mafia.

maxwell-at-a-work-camp.title: The hierarchy of charges
maxwell-at-a-work-camp.summary: How federal prisoners ranked one another by offence, in John Kiriakou's account — RICO at the top, usually with a murder conspiracy attached; wealthy white-collar convicts despised as soft; and arson, insurance fraud and mortgage fraud attracting no interest at all.

maxwell-at-a-work-camp.title: The Mayflower Madam analogy
maxwell-at-a-work-camp.summary: John Kiriakou's argument, borrowed from the 1980s Mayflower Madam case, that the Epstein 'list' will disappoint anyone expecting a schedule of clients — because address books contain the dry cleaner and the Chinese takeaway alongside everyone else, and nobody keeps a spreadsheet of their crimes.

maxwell-at-a-work-camp.title: Ali from Newark
maxwell-at-a-work-camp.summary: The Black shot caller at FCI Loretto, near the end of a twenty-five-year drug sentence, who came to embrace John Kiriakou at the close of his term and tell him how much he respected him — a friendship possible only because Kiriakou had decided on arrival to ignore the prison's racial divisions.

mbs-and-netanyahu-asked-trump-to-attack-.title: Chaos as the Israeli objective
mbs-and-netanyahu-asked-trump-to-attack-.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer to whether Netanyahu''s government actually wanted an American invasion of Iran: what the Israelis want in Iran is what they got in Libya — chaos, civil war, and as many dead Iranians as possible.

mbs-and-netanyahu-asked-trump-to-attack-.title: Marco Rubio and Iran policy
mbs-and-netanyahu-asked-trump-to-attack-.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer to who was actually driving American policy toward Iran in 2026: with the Vice President, the Director of National Intelligence and the Chairman of the Joint Chiefs all reported as opposed, and with Marco Rubio holding both the State Department and the National Security Adviser''s job, the policy was Rubio''s.

mbs-and-netanyahu-asked-trump-to-attack-.title: Killing Khamenei
mbs-and-netanyahu-asked-trump-to-attack-.summary: John Kiriakou's assessment that the killing of Ayatollah Khamenei during the 2026 war would change nothing, because the West had seriously overestimated his authority — an argument he extends to the American habit of expecting a war to end when a leader is removed.

mbs-and-netanyahu-asked-trump-to-attack-.title: The difficulty of getting out
mbs-and-netanyahu-asked-trump-to-attack-.summary: John Kiriakou''s standing formulation about regime change: it is easy to invade a country and easy to overthrow a government, and very difficult to leave. He measures it in the twenty years the United States spent in Afghanistan and the nineteen in Iraq.

mbs-and-netanyahu-asked-trump-to-attack-.title: The clear and present danger finding
mbs-and-netanyahu-asked-trump-to-attack-.summary: The presidential determination John Kiriakou says must precede any CIA paramilitary targeted killing — an assertion that the person concerned is a clear and present danger to the United States, to an American installation, or to an American person — and his judgement that in early 2026 that threshold had not been reached in Iran.

mbs-and-netanyahu-asked-trump-to-attack-.title: Bombing the Omanis
mbs-and-netanyahu-asked-trump-to-attack-.summary: John Kiriakou's judgement that Iran's strikes on the Gulf states — and above all on Oman, which had been trying to broker peace — made enemies Iran did not need to make, of governments that would otherwise have sat the war out.

mccain-feinstein-amendment.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
mccain-feinstein-amendment.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

mccain-feinstein-amendment.title: Espionage Act
mccain-feinstein-amendment.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

mccain-feinstein-amendment.title: Overcriminalization
mccain-feinstein-amendment.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that the United States criminalizes too much — locking up 25% of the world's prisoners with 5% of its population, and adding roughly 50 new felonies a year — illustrated by a NOAA employee prosecuted for whistling at a whale.

mccain-feinstein-amendment.title: Senate Torture Report
mccain-feinstein-amendment.summary: The December 2014 executive summary of the U.S. Senate Select Committee on Intelligence's study of the CIA's post-9/11 detention and interrogation program; the first public disclosure of techniques including rectal feeding with hummus, sexual assault with broomsticks, and prolonged sleep deprivation.

mccain-feinstein-amendment.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
mccain-feinstein-amendment.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

mccain-feinstein-amendment.title: Abolish the CIA
mccain-feinstein-amendment.summary: John Kiriakou's position that the CIA should be abolished because its functions are already duplicated by the other 17 U.S. intelligence agencies — analysis by the State Department, human spying by the Pentagon, technology by DARPA, NSA and the private sector.

mecca-agreement.title: A Turkey–Israel confrontation
mecca-agreement.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of what two senior Turkish foreign ministry officials told him over dinner in March 2026 about the prospect of war with Israel: that it will not happen, that Turkey would win if it did, and that Turkey would not ask NATO for help.

mecca-agreement.title: Somaliland and Israeli recognition
mecca-agreement.summary: Israel''s diplomatic recognition of Somaliland, which John Kiriakou describes as a trade: recognition no other state offers, in exchange for an air base within reach of Yemen. He calls it the one smart move in Israel''s response to the Mecca Agreement.

mecca-agreement.title: Abraham Accords
mecca-agreement.summary: The Trump-brokered normalization deals between Israel and Gulf Arab states — in John Kiriakou's judgment "a terrible idea in the first place," a great victory for Israel and the Gulf Arabs that was "a punch in the throat to the Palestinians." He argues the Accords are how Trump meant to "solve the Middle East in a day" — by screwing the Palestinians — that Hamas read the abandonment correctly, that October 7 shattered the project, and that reviving the Accords (Saudis in, victory declared, Nobel collected) remains the organizing goal of Trump's regional policy.

mecca-agreement.title: Dewey Clarridge
mecca-agreement.summary: The CIA operations officer John Kiriakou calls a legendary figure and a giant of the 1980s — prosecuted over Iran-Contra, and the man who said publicly that Saudi Arabia already had nuclear weapons. Kiriakou believes him, holds that the Saudis financed the Pakistani bomb and were repaid in access to it, and believes Clarridge was also involved in the movement of cocaine into the United States.

mecca-agreement.title: Houthis
mecca-agreement.summary: The Iran-aligned movement that controls the most important parts of Yemen, described by John Kiriakou as fierce fighters who beat the Saudi military over a decade of war and who in July 2026 declared a naval blockade of Saudi shipping.

mecca-agreement.title: Romania and US military positioning
mecca-agreement.summary: John Kiriakou's assessment that Romania has become the United States' next staging option toward the Middle East, because Greece is full and Turkey is pursuing its own course.

medea-benjamins-broken-arm.title: The Palestinian middle class in the Gulf
medea-benjamins-broken-arm.summary: John Kiriakou's stated puzzlement, after a career spent on and in the Middle East, at what he calls a region-wide dislike of Palestinians among Arab governments — given that Palestinians constitute the entire professional middle class of the Gulf states, and are themselves Arabs and mostly Muslims.

medea-benjamins-broken-arm.title: Expulsion of Palestinians from the Gulf
medea-benjamins-broken-arm.summary: The mass expulsion of the Palestinian professional class from the Gulf Arab states in the aftermath of Iraq's 1990 invasion of Kuwait, which John Kiriakou witnessed from the region and identifies as the reason Gulf governments are willing to normalise relations with Israel. He dates the Kuwaiti decision to a wedding he attended weeks after the liberation, says Western and Egyptian pressure stopped it being total, and has repeatedly said he has never understood the grudge himself.

medea-benjamins-broken-arm.title: The call about rebuilding Gaza
medea-benjamins-broken-arm.summary: A telephone call John Kiriakou says he received on 7 November 2025 from a contact in the Israeli government, reporting that Israel had approached private American companies to redevelop Gaza — not Gazan Palestinians — and that the widely reported Saudi-administration plan was newspaper talk rather than anything the Israeli military was discussing. His conclusion: ''the fix is already in.''

medea-benjamins-broken-arm.title: The synagogue in Damascus
medea-benjamins-broken-arm.summary: John Kiriakou's account of visiting an operating, practising Jewish synagogue in Damascus, and the forecast he attaches to it — that he would not bet money on the safety of Christians, Jews, Alawites or any other religious minority in Syria under the present government or any other, whatever else is said of Bashar al-Assad.

medea-benjamins-broken-arm.title: Code Pink
medea-benjamins-broken-arm.summary: The women-led peace group co-founded by Medea Benjamin. John Kiriakou first met them as a Senate staffer — he was the man who threw them out of a hearing he had produced, and got a lecture from Senator Shaheen for it. When he was arrested they were "right there next to me"; they threw his going-away party on the roof of the Hay-Adams, commissioned a folk group to sing a song rewritten about him, and quietly arranged for Roger Waters to pay off the second mortgage so his family could keep the house. He calls them his angels, and the one institution in American life he still trusts.

medea-benjamins-broken-arm.title: Julian Assange
medea-benjamins-broken-arm.summary: Kiriakou — a 15-year friend and former WikiLeaks board member — on why Assange is a publisher owed a journalist's immunity, and a political prisoner.

mek.title: Hillary Clinton
mek.summary: Former U.S. Secretary of State and 2016 presidential candidate; John Kiriakou describes her as arguably the most neoconservative candidate Democrats could have nominated, more militarist even than her husband, and credits her — separately — with correctly describing Iran as a military dictatorship run by the IRGC rather than a genuine theocracy.

mek.title: Iran Nuclear Assessment
mek.summary: Per John Kiriakou's assessment, the US–Israeli military campaign against Iran was a war of choice driven by Israeli political pressure rather than genuine intelligence indicating an Iranian nuclear weapons threat. The CIA produced two National Intelligence Estimates concluding Iran had no nuclear weapons program; Supreme Leader Ayatollah Khamenei issued a fatwa in the 1980s forbidding such a program. The U.S. went to war anyway, in Kiriakou's view, after President Trump replaced the Joint Chiefs of Staff with officers willing to accept Israeli intelligence and proceed.

mek.title: Congressional intelligence oversight
mek.summary: John Kiriakou''s standing criticism of the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence and the House Permanent Select Committee — that unlike the armed services and foreign relations committees, they do not perform oversight at all: "They''re just cheerleaders." His illustration is a sitting committee chairman who summoned him privately, then asked whether Kiriakou would write the criticism publicly on his behalf.

mek.title: Federal Torture Act
mek.summary: United States statute criminalizing torture; per John Kiriakou, on the books since at least 1946, with concrete enforcement history — after World War II the United States executed Japanese soldiers convicted of waterboarding American prisoners of war, meaning waterboarding was at that time a capital offense under U.S. law. The act was effectively set aside for the CIA's enhanced interrogation program after 2002.

mek.title: Jeffrey Epstein
mek.summary: Convicted sex offender; per John Kiriakou, was "an Israeli access agent" rather than a CIA asset, because the CIA collects foreign intelligence and Epstein's targets — Bill Clinton, Bill Gates, Prince Andrew — were not foreign. Kiriakou further holds that Epstein did die by suicide in federal custody, because in the Bureau of Prisons the cameras never work and the guards are always asleep.

mek.title: Maduro Capture
mek.summary: CIA-driven nighttime operation in which a team of Delta Force commandos entered Venezuela and removed Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro and his wife from their beds. Per John Kiriakou, the key enabling intelligence — per a New York Times account he cited — came from a CIA asset inside Maduro''s presidential palace who called when Maduro went to sleep: ''He''s sound asleep. If you''re going to do it, do it now.'' At least eighty people were killed in the operation, including approximately thirty-five Cubans. Kiriakou compares it to the 1989 capture of Manuel Noriega, in which US forces blasted death metal at the Vatican Embassy until Noriega was asked to leave.

mental-health-as-a-disciplinary-problem.title: Three square meals and a warm bed
mental-health-as-a-disciplinary-problem.summary: John Kiriakou has said he will never forget a remark he overheard from three men playing cards in an empty television room at FCI Loretto, who counted up the meals, the bed, the clothes, the television and the medical care they were given and concluded that the place was very nearly paradise.

mental-health-as-a-disciplinary-problem.title: The case against work camps
mental-health-as-a-disciplinary-problem.summary: John Kiriakou, who asked to serve his own sentence at a minimum-security work camp and was sent to the prison across the street instead, came out of prison arguing that the camps should not exist at all — and, in the same breath, that some prisoners are dangerous enough that prisons certainly should.

mental-health-as-a-disciplinary-problem.title: Domingo's television
mental-health-as-a-disciplinary-problem.summary: John Kiriakou has used the television rooms at FCI Loretto as his sharpest illustration of prison segregation: sets owned by racial blocs since a riot in the 1990s, a seat in front of one costing fourteen dollars, and one set left tuned to Law & Order every morning because a man named Domingo had paid four hundred dollars for it and had been gone for years.

mental-health-as-a-disciplinary-problem.title: The chapel rule
mental-health-as-a-disciplinary-problem.summary: The chapel and the library at FCI Loretto were the two places child molesters could be certain of safety, because a correctional officer was always present; John Kiriakou, who worked in the chapel, has described the house rule against discussing your case there and the indignation with which it was met.

mental-health-as-a-disciplinary-problem.title: The CIA that never existed
mental-health-as-a-disciplinary-problem.summary: A former senior CIA officer once told John Kiriakou that the agency he spoke about so fondly had never really existed — that it had only existed in his mind, that it had always been troubled and antithetical to American life, and that he had simply been too junior to see what was happening at the top. Kiriakou has come to think the man was right.

mental-health-as-a-disciplinary-problem.title: The Official Secrets Act comparison
mental-health-as-a-disciplinary-problem.summary: John Kiriakou has argued that for whistleblowers the United Kingdom is far worse than the United States, because the Official Secrets Act bars anyone from saying anything touching national security and is used, in his phrase, as an iron fist against whistleblowers and potential whistleblowers alike.

meredith-whittaker.title: Andrew Feinstein
meredith-whittaker.summary: Referenced on the same WikiLeaks-conference panel as John Kiriakou; the description of Feinstein's talk on the multiple factors that ended apartheid was given by another panelist putting a question to Kiriakou, not by Kiriakou himself.

meredith-whittaker.title: Securedrop
meredith-whittaker.summary: The encrypted submission tool pioneered by WikiLeaks to let sources hand over documents without exposing themselves.

meredith-whittaker.title: Ai Whistleblower Initiative
meredith-whittaker.summary: The AI Whistleblower Initiative, working on legal protections for the wave of whistleblowers now coming out of the artificial-intelligence industry.

meredith-whittaker.title: Belmarsh Prison
meredith-whittaker.summary: The maximum-security London prison where Julian Assange was held for years on a bail-jumping sentence John Kiriakou calls a fabrication — kept in solitary confinement alongside the worst offenders in the United Kingdom, and held past the expiry of his sentence at the request of the United States. Kiriakou corresponded with Assange there and watched the letters change.

meredith-whittaker.title: Chaos Computer Club Wikileaks
meredith-whittaker.summary: The Berlin hacker collective that shaped WikiLeaks' early years — and where a journalist first met Daniel Domscheit-Berg under a pseudonym.

meredith-whittaker.title: Chelsea Manning
meredith-whittaker.summary: Former U.S. Army intelligence analyst who provided WikiLeaks its 2010 trove of military and diplomatic documents. Per John Kiriakou, Manning meets the legal definition of whistleblower for exposing war crimes, was a torture victim of prolonged solitary confinement with forced nudity, and was sentenced to 35 years in prison before Barack Obama commuted — not pardoned — her sentence. Kiriakou says Manning later refused a grand jury's offer of immunity and chose renewed jail time rather than testify against Julian Assange.

merry-go-round-prank.title: The self-destructing terrorist cell
merry-go-round-prank.summary: The CIA operation John Kiriakou describes in which a terrorist group was destroyed without a single agency killing — by approaching each member abroad in turn and implying that a colleague had informed, until they had murdered one another and the last man was killed by his own head of state.

merry-go-round-prank.title: FCI Loretto
merry-go-round-prank.summary: U.S. Federal Correctional Institution in Loretto, Pennsylvania; the low-medium-security prison at which John Kiriakou served 23 months of a 30-month sentence following his 2013 Espionage Act–era plea deal; the originally ordered "minimum security work camp" placement was countermanded — per Kiriakou, on Brennan's direct intervention — to place him in the actual prison alongside the general population.

merry-go-round-prank.title: Ken Schaefer
merry-go-round-prank.summary: The FCI Loretto prisoner who told others he was inside for securities irregularities, was in fact convicted of transporting a child for sex, fled to Israel on bail, and — after John Kiriakou exposed and confronted him — offered money to prisoners to have Kiriakou attacked.

merry-go-round-prank.title: The shank planting incident
merry-go-round-prank.summary: The episode at FCI Loretto in which Dave Phillips made two homemade weapons, planted them on a pedophile the group was feuding with and informed on him anonymously — a plan John Kiriakou refused to join, and which cost Phillips a transfer while leaving Kiriakou untouched.

merry-go-round-prank.title: The astrophotographer lawyer
merry-go-round-prank.summary: The Philadelphia attorney who represented Ken Schaefer's victim and who, in John Kiriakou's account, was flown to Israel as the guest of a school he had shown his telescope to — and there asked by a government minister to make the case go away.

merry-go-round-prank.title: Dave Phillips
merry-go-round-prank.summary: The FCI Loretto prisoner who claimed to have been a CIA operations officer and whom John Kiriakou exposed as a fake by testing him on agency vocabulary — a possessive, risk-taking companion who planted shanks on a pedophile, was caught, and was shipped to another prison.

mexican-9-month-work-visas.title: AIPAC
mexican-9-month-work-visas.summary: The American Israel Public Affairs Committee — the U.S. political organization that, in John Kiriakou's framing, ought to be registered as a foreign-lobbying entity but is not, and that wields decisive electoral power against U.S. elected officials who express support for Palestinian human rights.

mexican-9-month-work-visas.title: Donald Trump
mexican-9-month-work-visas.summary: 45th and 47th U.S. president. Per John Kiriakou, a man genuinely convinced he was doing right by bombing Iran, "duped" by the same Netanyahu nuclear bluff Obama once rejected — and, at the same time, the most blindly pro-Israel president in history, an admirer of autocrats who has never once criticized Vladimir Putin, and prone to gestures — from the Gulf of America to a since-abandoned "Department of War" rename — that test the edges of his actual authority.

mexican-9-month-work-visas.title: Iran 12-Day War
mexican-9-month-work-visas.summary: 2025 Israeli air campaign against Iran during which Israel killed at least fourteen Iranian nuclear scientists by destroying the apartment buildings they lived in; preceded for each scientist by Farsi-language telephone calls from Iranian-Jewish Mossad and Shin Bet officers offering defection in lieu of certain death; characterized by John Kiriakou as a categorical departure from CIA targeting doctrine in its acceptable-civilian-casualty calculus.

mexican-9-month-work-visas.title: Iran Nuclear Assessment
mexican-9-month-work-visas.summary: Per John Kiriakou's assessment, the US–Israeli military campaign against Iran was a war of choice driven by Israeli political pressure rather than genuine intelligence indicating an Iranian nuclear weapons threat. The CIA produced two National Intelligence Estimates concluding Iran had no nuclear weapons program; Supreme Leader Ayatollah Khamenei issued a fatwa in the 1980s forbidding such a program. The U.S. went to war anyway, in Kiriakou's view, after President Trump replaced the Joint Chiefs of Staff with officers willing to accept Israeli intelligence and proceed.

mexican-9-month-work-visas.title: Israel-United States relations
mexican-9-month-work-visas.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the U.S.-Israel relationship, including his own first visit to Israel as a tourist in 2022 and his characterization of Israel's willingness to destroy an entire city block to kill a single target, confident that the United States will not object.

mexican-9-month-work-visas.title: Eric Swallwell
mexican-9-month-work-visas.summary: Kiriakou names Swalwell once — a passing aside contrasting today's partisan Congress with the Church and Pike Committees of 1975.

mexico-city-as-an-espionage-hub.title: The embassy local hire
mexico-city-as-an-espionage-hub.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of how a foreign service recruits inside an American embassy without ever approaching an American: by paying long-serving local staff a supplement they cannot refuse, and letting them assemble the identity of the station from fragments — most conclusively the office a new arrival names when he answers his telephone.

mexico-city-as-an-espionage-hub.title: Lindsey Graham
mexico-city-as-an-espionage-hub.summary: Republican senator from South Carolina who died in July 2026, and John Kiriakou's standing shorthand for the permanent war caucus — a "show horse" rather than a workhorse, a "chameleon" who "never saw a war that he didn't want to jump into with both feet," and, on posthumously released documentary footage, a man offering the US Air Force to bomb a country America was not at war with.

mexico-city-as-an-espionage-hub.title: Pakistani prisons
mexico-city-as-an-espionage-hub.summary: John Kiriakou''s flat refusal, in a discussion of Imran Khan''s detention, of the idea that a Pakistani prison offers VIP treatment to a former prime minister — grounded in his having visited many of them himself during the period when the CIA was locking people up there.

mexico-city-as-an-espionage-hub.title: Savas Kalenderidis
mexico-city-as-an-espionage-hub.summary: Greek intelligence officer, national hero and personal friend of John Kiriakou''s, who was involved in the operation to protect the PKK founder Abdullah Öcalan at the Greek embassy in Nairobi in 1999 — an operation that ended when Turkish and Kenyan intelligence diverted part of Öcalan''s motorcade and seized him. Kiriakou flatly denies the claim that the CIA and Turkish intelligence tried to kill Kalenderidis there.

mexico-city-as-an-espionage-hub.title: The Afghan Zero Units
mexico-city-as-an-espionage-hub.summary: The CIA-trained Afghan paramilitary units whose surviving members were resettled in the United States, and John Kiriakou''s account of why so many of them have broken down: recruited without training or therapy, taken out at night to kill their own tribesmen and extended family, promised the land of milk and honey, and then met on arrival with no work permit, no treatment and no help at all.

mexico-city-as-an-espionage-hub.title: The White House pastry chef
mexico-city-as-an-espionage-hub.summary: John Kiriakou''s former next-door neighbour, a White House pastry chef who was in the building when Donald Trump came to meet Barack Obama four days after the 2016 election, and who told Kiriakou that the president-elect looked sick and looked scared.

mi6.title: China's base in Djibouti
mi6.summary: Camp Lemonnier in Djibouti, the abandoned French base the Djiboutians offered to the Americans and the Chinese took a share of — split down the middle by a chain-link fence, the only Chinese military installation outside China, and the centrepiece of John Kiriakou's argument that China is not an expansionist power.

mi6.title: China as economic threat
mi6.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that China is the real threat to the West not militarily — it has one aircraft carrier to America's two dozen and rarely invades — but economically, buying friends worldwide while the U.S. spends a trillion dollars a year on weapons.

mi6.title: Five Eyes
mi6.summary: The intelligence-sharing partnership of the United States, United Kingdom, Canada, Australia, and New Zealand

mi6.title: Revolutionary Organization 17 November
mi6.summary: Greek far-left urban guerrilla group active 1975–2002; the deadliest terrorist organization in Greek history

mi6.title: John Kiriakou
mi6.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

mi6.title: The Chinese embassy in London
mi6.summary: John Kiriakou's assessment of the Chinese mission planned for London — an embassy occupying an entire city block that would be the largest in the world, approved over street protests, and which he calls 'the mother of all spy dens.' He contrasts it with Washington's refusal of the same proposal, and predicts China will now build such embassies everywhere.

michael-hastings.title: Vault 7
michael-hastings.summary: The 2017 WikiLeaks disclosure of thousands of pages of CIA Directorate of Science and Technology documents — leaked by agency engineer Joshua Schulte — revealing CIA technical capabilities including remote takeover of internet-connected cars, conversion of smart-TV speakers into covert microphones, and the planting of Russian or Persian language fragments in foreign systems to mislead attribution.

michael-hastings.title: Joshua Schulte
michael-hastings.summary: Former CIA Directorate of Science and Technology engineer; source of the 2017 Vault 7 WikiLeaks disclosure of the agency's offensive technical capabilities; currently serving a 40-year federal sentence for espionage; maintains his innocence.

michael-hastings.title: Bluffdale NSA Data Center
michael-hastings.summary: The NSA's purpose-built facility in the Utah desert, characterized by John Kiriakou as having storage capacity for every phone call, text message, and email of every American for the next 500 years.

michael-hastings.title: CIA Remote Vehicle Control
michael-hastings.summary: John Kiriakou's account, corroborated by Forbes' Andy Greenberg's real-world demonstration, that the CIA can remotely take over a car's systems and cause a fatal crash disguised as an accident.

michael-hastings.title: Espionage Act
michael-hastings.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

michael-hastings.title: In-Q-Tel
michael-hastings.summary: The CIA's openly acknowledged venture capital arm; provided Palantir Technologies its first $1.5 million in seed funding; in John Kiriakou's account the principal vehicle by which the agency finances private-sector development of technologies it intends to use.

michigan-2026-democratic-senate-primary.title: Abdul El-Sayed
michigan-2026-democratic-senate-primary.summary: Physician and Democratic Socialists of America-backed candidate in Michigan's 2026 Democratic Senate primary. John Kiriakou, who discloses a $100 donation to the campaign, presents him as the test case for whether the electability argument still works for establishment Democrats.

michigan-2026-democratic-senate-primary.title: Mike Rogers
michigan-2026-democratic-senate-primary.summary: Former Republican congressman from Michigan and repeat Senate candidate, who lost narrowly in 2024 and ran again in 2026. John Kiriakou singles out his campaign advertisement calling Abdul El-Sayed a communist Trojan horse as an insult to the intelligence of Michigan voters.

michigan-2026-democratic-senate-primary.title: AIPAC
michigan-2026-democratic-senate-primary.summary: The American Israel Public Affairs Committee — the U.S. political organization that, in John Kiriakou's framing, ought to be registered as a foreign-lobbying entity but is not, and that wields decisive electoral power against U.S. elected officials who express support for Palestinian human rights.

michigan-2026-democratic-senate-primary.title: Americans and the word socialism
michigan-2026-democratic-senate-primary.summary: Two exchanges John Kiriakou uses to argue that the political vocabulary of the United States has stopped carrying meaning — a Thanksgiving conversation with a woman who denounced socialism and lived on Social Security, and a newspaper comment thread in which a restaurant owner taking his staff's tips was described as socialism.

michigan-2026-democratic-senate-primary.title: Thomas Massie
michigan-2026-democratic-senate-primary.summary: Republican U.S. Representative from Kentucky known for a constitutionalist voting record and consistent opposition to foreign military intervention; per John Kiriakou, a principled America-First congressman who votes with the president on the vast majority of issues, and whose opposition to U.S. funding of Israel and foreign wars is the only plausible explanation for the roughly $30 million spent by the Israel lobby to unseat him in a primary.

michigan-2026-democratic-senate-primary.title: Bernie Moreno
michigan-2026-democratic-senate-primary.summary: Republican senator from Ohio and father-in-law of Congressman Max Miller. John Kiriakou raises, without asserting, the possibility that Moreno's two-year public silence about the abuse of his daughter was the product of blackmail.

middle-east-forum.title: MOSSAD
middle-east-forum.summary: Israel's primary external intelligence service; characterized by John Kiriakou as universally hostile in his and his CIA colleagues' professional dealings with it ("never had a positive encounter with Mossad"); operates almost exclusively in the operational rather than analytical domain; the CIA is, per Kiriakou, categorically forbidden from spying on it.

middle-east-forum.title: Senate Foreign Relations Committee
middle-east-forum.summary: Kiriakou was senior investigator under John Kerry — and still held the post when his own federal prosecution came to a head in January 2012.

middle-east-forum.title: Antisemitism and anti-Zionism
middle-east-forum.summary: The conflation of criticism of the Israeli state with hatred of Jews, which John Kiriakou describes as a worldwide confusion and, according to a young Israeli he spoke to, an explicit lesson of the Israeli school system; a subject Kiriakou says he personally struggles with.

middle-east-forum.title: AIPAC
middle-east-forum.summary: The American Israel Public Affairs Committee — the U.S. political organization that, in John Kiriakou's framing, ought to be registered as a foreign-lobbying entity but is not, and that wields decisive electoral power against U.S. elected officials who express support for Palestinian human rights.

middle-east-forum.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
middle-east-forum.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

middle-east-forum.title: Charlie Kirk
middle-east-forum.summary: American conservative activist, founder of the movement John Kiriakou calls the centre of MAGA's youth vote, and — in the only meeting between them — a seventeen-year-old lobbyist Kiriakou watched run a Senate press conference and concluded was going places. Kiriakou disagreed with him on roughly eighty per cent of the issues, ranked his generational political impact alongside Martin Luther King and Robert F. Kennedy Sr., and notes that Kirk had turned against Israeli conduct in Gaza shortly before he was killed.

mike-baker.title: Joe Rogan
mike-baker.summary: The podcast host whose show John Kiriakou finally sat for in October 2025 — an experience that began with signing a non-disclosure agreement and ended with his verdict that Rogan is "a nice guy, very down to earth, very normal." The first thing Rogan asked, walking into the studio ten minutes late: "Hey, do you know my friend Mike Baker?" Kiriakou defends Rogan as unfairly characterized as a right-winger, and had long cited the show as the venue where Zuckerberg admitted Facebook suppressed the Hunter Biden laptop story at the FBI''s behest.

mike-baker.title: Revolutionary Organization 17 November
mike-baker.summary: Greek far-left urban guerrilla group active 1975–2002; the deadliest terrorist organization in Greek history

mike-baker.title: John Kiriakou
mike-baker.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

mike-baker.title: Abraham Accords
mike-baker.summary: The Trump-brokered normalization deals between Israel and Gulf Arab states — in John Kiriakou's judgment "a terrible idea in the first place," a great victory for Israel and the Gulf Arabs that was "a punch in the throat to the Palestinians." He argues the Accords are how Trump meant to "solve the Middle East in a day" — by screwing the Palestinians — that Hamas read the abandonment correctly, that October 7 shattered the project, and that reviving the Accords (Saudis in, victory declared, Nobel collected) remains the organizing goal of Trump's regional policy.

mike-baker.title: Abu Zubaydah
mike-baker.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

mike-baker.title: Ali Soufan
mike-baker.summary: FBI special agent who handled Abu Zubaydah immediately after his March 2002 capture; through patient, respectful interrogation produced the only actionable intelligence ever obtained from the detainee, including the first identification of "Mukhtar" as Khalid Sheikh Mohammed.

mike-hayden.title: Thomas Drake
mike-hayden.summary: NSA whistleblower; per John Kiriakou, the source for the statement that on the morning of September 11, 2001, NSA Director Mike Hayden told agency personnel NSA had been 'waiting for a 9/11' to implement the mass-electronic-surveillance program that NSA's founding charter forbids.

mike-hayden.title: Section 702
mike-hayden.summary: Section of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act under which the U.S. government conducts warrantless electronic surveillance; per John Kiriakou the principal post-9/11 mechanism by which the CIA, NSA, and FBI surveil American citizens; renewed by Congress every two years over the objection of a small bipartisan minority; the subject of an estimated 200,000+ illegal FBI database queries — per the Brennan Center for Justice, including ~78,000 misused queries over a two-year window; the disclosure that Edward Snowden made public in summer 2013.

mike-hayden.title: CIA adultery culture
mike-hayden.summary: John Kiriakou's recurring characterization of the CIA officer corps as riddled with adultery and casual sex — which he frames not as gossip but as a systemic counterintelligence vulnerability that makes officers easy to recruit.

mike-hayden.title: Donald Trump
mike-hayden.summary: 45th and 47th U.S. president. Per John Kiriakou, a man genuinely convinced he was doing right by bombing Iran, "duped" by the same Netanyahu nuclear bluff Obama once rejected — and, at the same time, the most blindly pro-Israel president in history, an admirer of autocrats who has never once criticized Vladimir Putin, and prone to gestures — from the Gulf of America to a since-abandoned "Department of War" rename — that test the edges of his actual authority.

mike-hayden.title: Guantánamo Bay detention camp
mike-hayden.summary: Per John Kiriakou — as chief of counterterrorism operations in Pakistan after September 11, 2001 — the Guantanamo detention facility began as a temporary holding measure intended to last two to three weeks while the CIA and Justice Department determined which federal district court should try each prisoner, not as a long-term detention infrastructure. The Rawalpindi jail had reached capacity, Pakistani intelligence demanded the prisoners be removed, and CIA headquarters directed Kiriakou to load them onto a C-12 cargo plane and fly them to Cuba.

mike-hayden.title: Jeffrey Epstein
mike-hayden.summary: Convicted sex offender; per John Kiriakou, was "an Israeli access agent" rather than a CIA asset, because the CIA collects foreign intelligence and Epstein's targets — Bill Clinton, Bill Gates, Prince Andrew — were not foreign. Kiriakou further holds that Epstein did die by suicide in federal custody, because in the Bureau of Prisons the cameras never work and the guards are always asleep.

mike-huckabee.title: Jonathan Pollard
mike-huckabee.summary: U.S. Navy civilian intelligence analyst convicted in 1985 of spying for Israel; the canonical proven case of Israeli espionage against the United States; cited by John Kiriakou in his 2024 Piers Morgan debate with a former Mossad director who denied any Israeli spying on the U.S.

mike-huckabee.title: Greater Israel
mike-huckabee.summary: The territorial project John Kiriakou believes the Israeli government genuinely holds: the expulsion of every Palestinian, beginning in Gaza and continuing into the West Bank, pursued on a hundred- or two-hundred-year horizon in the confidence that the United States will never push back.

mike-huckabee.title: Lebanon-Israeli Conflict
mike-huckabee.summary: Per John Kiriakou, no Israeli government will allow Lebanon to flourish as a nation; he expects continued Israeli attacks and forced displacement of civilians, citing a statistic of up to 700,000 Lebanese internally displaced, and links the war to the "Greater Israel" rhetoric of US ambassador Mike Huckabee.

mike-huckabee.title: Naftali Bennett
mike-huckabee.summary: The former Israeli prime minister, cited by John Kiriakou through 2026 for the position that Turkey would be the next target after Iran — a claim Kiriakou uses to identify the second obstacle, alongside Iran, to the Greater Israel project, and which by May 2026 he was stating in his own voice as an active Israeli intention rather than a Bennett prediction.

mike-huckabee.title: South Lebanon displacement, 2026
mike-huckabee.summary: John Kiriakou''s assessment of the Israeli campaign in southern Lebanon running alongside the 2026 Iran war: mass evacuation orders, hundreds of thousands internally displaced, and his conclusion that Israel has guaranteed Lebanon will be a failed state. He notes the world is not watching because it is watching Iran.

mike-huckabee.title: The seven countries argument
mike-huckabee.summary: John Kiriakou's dissent from the claim that America's post-2001 wars were fought on Israel's behalf. Taking the list of seven countries country by country, he argues Libya, Somalia and Afghanistan were American decisions made for American reasons — and concludes that the United States cannot blame all of its problems on Israel.

mike-johnson.title: Epstein Files Transparency Act
mike-johnson.summary: The law compelling the Justice Department to release the Epstein files by a fixed deadline, passed 419 to 1 in the House and 99 to nothing in the Senate and then, in John Kiriakou's account, simply not complied with.

mike-johnson.title: Jeffrey Epstein
mike-johnson.summary: Convicted sex offender; per John Kiriakou, was "an Israeli access agent" rather than a CIA asset, because the CIA collects foreign intelligence and Epstein's targets — Bill Clinton, Bill Gates, Prince Andrew — were not foreign. Kiriakou further holds that Epstein did die by suicide in federal custody, because in the Bureau of Prisons the cameras never work and the guards are always asleep.

mike-johnson.title: Marjorie Taylor Greene
mike-johnson.summary: American congresswoman whom John Kiriakou, despite deep political disagreement, has repeatedly credited for breaking with her party on the Epstein files, on military aid to Israel, and on Gaza. He describes her as courageous for pressing Donald Trump to release the files unredacted, and says the pressure ultimately forced her out of Washington.

mike-johnson.title: John Kiriakou
mike-johnson.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

mike-johnson.title: The Fifth Fleet in Bahrain
mike-johnson.summary: The United States naval presence based in Bahrain since 1976 — the naval component of Central Command, headquartered at Manama. For John Kiriakou as a young diplomat it was mainly a social resource: the officers'' club for its salad bar, the enlisted club for football and cheap beer. It was also, he came to understand, the reason his reporting on Bahraini extrajudicial killings went nowhere. The ambassador''s summary of the alliance was four words long. In 2026 the headquarters was itself hit by Iranian missiles — an outcome that, in Kiriakou''s reading, inverts the entire purpose of the Gulf basing architecture.

mike-johnson.title: Democratic redistricting collapse
mike-johnson.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of why Republicans remain competitive despite historically low approval ratings: a 1992 decision he attributes to Hillary Clinton to spend only in presidential battlegrounds, which he says ceded state legislatures and the congressional map for decades.

mike-mastrovito.title: Sara Jane Moore
