mossad.title: Glenn-Symington Act
mossad.summary: U.S. federal statute, co-authored by Senators John Glenn and Stuart Symington, that prohibits the U.S. government from providing foreign aid of any kind to any country possessing a nuclear weapons program that has not signed the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty; per John Kiriakou, Israel is the only country in the world meeting both criteria, making the law the principal reason the U.S. government officially declines to acknowledge the Israeli nuclear program.

mossad.title: Hassan Nasrallah
mossad.summary: Long-serving Secretary-General of Hezbollah, killed in an Israeli strike on a complex in southern Lebanon; the strike, which killed approximately 300 people in addition to Nasrallah, decapitated Hezbollah's leadership and is characterized by John Kiriakou as a war crime under international law.

mossad.title: Israeli False Flags
mossad.summary: Per John Kiriakou, the Mossad has been carrying out false flag operations since the founding of the state of Israel and is "usually very good at it"; he says his first suspicion on hearing of attacks on Saudi oil fields, Azerbaijan, and Cyprus was that they were Israeli false flags, and he fears a false flag against the Al-Aqsa Mosque blamed on Iran or the Arabs.

mossad.title: James Fishback
mossad.summary: Florida gubernatorial candidate whom Kiriakou says he never personally endorsed, despite viral claims and a since-deleted tweet posted by his assistant; Kiriakou calls Fishback's stance on Israel well-considered but distances himself from Fishback's other stated positions, including a proposed sin tax on OnlyFans creators, an immigration moratorium, and comments Kiriakou calls racist.

mossad.title: Maria Butina
mossad.summary: Russian gun-rights activist convicted in the United States of failing to register as a foreign agent; John Kiriakou cites her case as an example of the "process crime" of FARA violations, contrasting the severity of her 18-month solitary-confinement sentence with federal guidelines calling for 0-6 months.

mount-weather.title: Five Eyes
mount-weather.summary: The intelligence-sharing partnership of the United States, United Kingdom, Canada, Australia, and New Zealand

mount-weather.title: Abraham Accords
mount-weather.summary: The Trump-brokered normalization deals between Israel and Gulf Arab states — in John Kiriakou's judgment "a terrible idea in the first place," a great victory for Israel and the Gulf Arabs that was "a punch in the throat to the Palestinians." He argues the Accords are how Trump meant to "solve the Middle East in a day" — by screwing the Palestinians — that Hamas read the abandonment correctly, that October 7 shattered the project, and that reviving the Accords (Saudis in, victory declared, Nobel collected) remains the organizing goal of Trump's regional policy.

mount-weather.title: Abu Zubaydah
mount-weather.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

mount-weather.title: Access Agent
mount-weather.summary: CIA (and foreign intelligence service) term for a recruited asset whose value lies not in the secrets they hold directly but in their regular social access to high-value targets — politicians, executives, heads of state — who cannot themselves be recruited. Per John Kiriakou, the access agent is funded generously to maintain an environment in which the targets feel comfortable and return repeatedly; kompromat — compromising photographs or recordings — may be collected as a secondary tool. Kiriakou identifies Jeffrey Epstein as a textbook access agent, in his assessment working for Israeli intelligence.

mount-weather.title: AIPAC
mount-weather.summary: The American Israel Public Affairs Committee — the U.S. political organization that, in John Kiriakou's framing, ought to be registered as a foreign-lobbying entity but is not, and that wields decisive electoral power against U.S. elected officials who express support for Palestinian human rights.

mount-weather.title: Asset acquisition cycle
mount-weather.summary: The four-step process — spot, assess, develop, recruit — taught as the first lesson of CIA case officer training

moving-a-satellite-to-kuwait.title: The operational cable
moving-a-satellite-to-kuwait.summary: The written product of every CIA field meeting — drafted the same day, printed and handed to the instructors at the Farm, who critiqued the prose, the conduct of the meeting and what the officer had been wearing.

moving-a-satellite-to-kuwait.title: Bill Buckley
moving-a-satellite-to-kuwait.summary: CIA station chief in Beirut kidnapped by Palestinian Islamic Jihad in March 1984; tortured at length over fifteen months; killed in captivity; the case from which the agency derived a generation of operational-security lessons including the abandonment of single-point tracking devices in CIA officers' personal kit.

moving-a-satellite-to-kuwait.title: Iraqi invasion of Kuwait
moving-a-satellite-to-kuwait.summary: John Kiriakou''s most detailed account of the intelligence process around the 1990 Iraqi invasion of Kuwait and its 1991 liberation. As a first-year CIA analyst on a ''training account'' covering Iraq, Kiriakou produced the June 30, 1990 warning paper for the White House; suggested calling the US Defense Attaché in Baghdad to drive to the border and report what he saw (the answer: ''Literally the entire Iraqi military is heading south''); briefed the August 2 Oval Office meeting with Bush; and later took a single phone call from General Colin Powell that led, eight hours later, to 47 cruise missiles striking the Iraqi Intelligence Service headquarters in Baghdad.

moving-a-satellite-to-kuwait.title: Mr. Fish
moving-a-satellite-to-kuwait.summary: The cover name the CIA used for Abu Zubaydah in Pakistan in 2002 — invented because the Americans would not tell their Pakistani partners who the target was, and derived from the only thing they would say about him: that he was a big fish.

moving-a-satellite-to-kuwait.title: Navigating Pakistan without maps
moving-a-satellite-to-kuwait.summary: The logistical problem John Kiriakou says nearly undid the Abu Zubaydah operation: in 2002 Pakistan had no maps to buy, no street signs and no addresses, so the CIA team navigated a city of twelve million by shoe advertisement, traffic policeman, British school and McDonald''s — rehearsing the route twice in the small hours before the raids.

moving-a-satellite-to-kuwait.title: Planning a surveillance detection route
moving-a-satellite-to-kuwait.summary: The hours of paperwork behind every CIA meeting before satellite mapping existed — photocopied road-atlas pages taped into sheets six feet across, legs and stops marked in coloured highlighter, submitted to instructors for approval and then driven in advance to check for no-left-turns and closed roads. John Kiriakou ran routes to and from work every day in Athens against 17 November, taught surveillance detection as an agency instructor, spent four or five hours of a night on the route around a single emergency meeting, and wrote the CIA Insider's Guide to the subject — from which the agency redacted six pages.

mr-fish.title: The Directorate of Science and Technology
mr-fish.summary: One of the CIA's four directorates, which in John Kiriakou's time was an afterthought responsible for disguises and briefcases with hidden compartments, and which he says now works with Palantir, Amazon, Nvidia and Elon Musk's companies on work closer to DARPA's than to anything the agency did in the past.

mr-fish.title: The Punjab Elite Force
mr-fish.summary: The Pakistani provincial counterterrorism unit that supplied part of the assault manpower for the Abu Zubaydah raids of March 2002 — black trousers, black t-shirts stencilled with a pistol, and, in John Kiriakou's telling, a refusal to wear body armour on the grounds that if God called them that night they would go.

mr-fish.title: Abu Zubaydah
mr-fish.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

mr-fish.title: The mosquito cloud
mr-fish.summary: The night John Kiriakou waited beside Abu Zubaydah's hospital bed in Faisalabad in a room full of mosquitoes, having stopped taking his anti-malarial because of the nightmares — and turned the ceiling fan to full blast in a cold March room until an FBI agent asked what he was doing.

mr-fish.title: The royal family at Taif
mr-fish.summary: John Kiriakou''s first overseas assignment sent him at twenty-five to the Kuwaiti government in exile at Taif in Saudi Arabia, where he found a king weeping over a dug-up rose garden and repeated a mantra to a despondent royal family: we are going to get you your country back.

mr-fish.title: The lapsed film rights
mr-fish.summary: John Kiriakou has sold the rights to his life story three separate times — to Universal, 20th Century Fox and Paramount — and all three studios let the option lapse, telling him there was too much detail and too many stories to fit into two hours.

muammar-gaddafi.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
muammar-gaddafi.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

muammar-gaddafi.title: Osama bin Laden
muammar-gaddafi.summary: Founder and leader of al-Qaeda and the central target of the manhunt that shaped John Kiriakou's counterterrorism career. Per Kiriakou, bin Laden came from a billionaire Saudi construction family, was never one of the CIA-funded Afghan mujahideen, overruled subordinates who wanted to attack Israel and insisted the 9/11 attacks hit the United States to crash its economy, escaped Tora Bora dressed as a woman, and spent his final years next to Pakistan's equivalent of West Point — where, Kiriakou says, you would have to be a "mental defective" not to know he was there. Kiriakou believes the United States never intended to capture him alive.

muammar-gaddafi.title: ISIS
muammar-gaddafi.summary: The Islamic State, in John Kiriakou''s account, is an American policy failure made flesh — created because a faction decided al-Qaeda was not radical or violent enough, founded by Baghdadi while he sat in a U.S. military prison in Iraq, armed with hardware captured from the U.S.-supplied Iraqi army, and — per an email he cites from Hillary Clinton to John Podesta — funded by the governments of Saudi Arabia and Qatar. Kiriakou repeatedly punctured the anti-ISIS coalition''s logic: ISIS operated in seven countries while the U.S. bombed two, and Turkey had no real quarrel with ISIS at all — their common enemy was the Kurds.

muammar-gaddafi.title: Maduro Capture
muammar-gaddafi.summary: CIA-driven nighttime operation in which a team of Delta Force commandos entered Venezuela and removed Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro and his wife from their beds. Per John Kiriakou, the key enabling intelligence — per a New York Times account he cited — came from a CIA asset inside Maduro''s presidential palace who called when Maduro went to sleep: ''He''s sound asleep. If you''re going to do it, do it now.'' At least eighty people were killed in the operation, including approximately thirty-five Cubans. Kiriakou compares it to the 1989 capture of Manuel Noriega, in which US forces blasted death metal at the Vatican Embassy until Noriega was asked to leave.

muammar-gaddafi.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
muammar-gaddafi.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

muammar-gaddafi.title: Saddam Hussein
muammar-gaddafi.summary: President of Iraq from 1979 until the 2003 U.S. invasion; subject of John Kiriakou's CIA portfolio from January 1990 onward, in which capacity Kiriakou became, at age 25, "Saddam Hussein's intelligence community biographer" and the analyst who briefed President George H. W. Bush in the Oval Office on the morning of the 1990 invasion of Kuwait.

muddling-through.title: The NATO expansion promises
muddling-through.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the assurances American presidents gave Russia that NATO would not expand to its borders or admit Ukraine — promises he says were made repeatedly, broken repeatedly, and, in his blunt formulation, never meant. He couples the account with an equally explicit statement that he opposes the Russian invasion of Ukraine.

muddling-through.title: The Paris rifle serial number
muddling-through.summary: The case John Kiriakou uses to argue that American weapons sent to Ukraine are leaking onto the black market: a rifle used to shoot and severely wound a policeman in Paris whose serial number, he says, matched a shipment of assault rifles the United States had sent to Ukraine some six months earlier.

muddling-through.title: CIA attention to West Africa
muddling-through.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer on whether the CIA is likely to be operating in Burkina Faso: for all the years he was at the agency it cared very little about Africa and especially West Africa, but the presence of al-Qaeda and Islamic State affiliates plus the drug trade makes CIA and special forces involvement probable — and, he adds, the American public will not hear about it.

muddling-through.title: The African diplomat's remark
muddling-through.summary: The line John Kiriakou says an African diplomat gave him at a White House summit, and which he uses to explain Chinese success on the continent: you Americans always offer us democracy and military aid, and the Chinese offer us food and new roads. Kiriakou traces the consequence to Chinese bases across Africa and a State Department that did not see it coming.

muddling-through.title: The Hersh publishing collapse
muddling-through.summary: John Kiriakou's account of Seymour Hersh's disappearance from mainstream print — from the London Review of Books in 2017, which Hersh told him was already the only outlet that would take his work, to Substack five years later. Kiriakou, who helped give Hersh an award for integrity in intelligence, presents the trajectory as a measure of how bad conditions for American journalism have become.

muddling-through.title: The secret Sahel appropriations
muddling-through.summary: John Kiriakou's complaint that the United States is quietly pumping billions of dollars into Niger, Mali, Burkina Faso, Guinea-Conakry and Guinea-Bissau — spending he says is supposed to be a big secret, addresses a French problem rather than an American one, and which American taxpayers have a right to know about and to judge.

muhammad-atar.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
muhammad-atar.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

muhammad-atar.title: Walling
muhammad-atar.summary: A CIA interrogation technique in which a detainee is slammed against a wall; designed on paper to use a padded fiberboard surface and a rolled towel around the neck, but applied in practice against bare concrete-block walls without protective measures, producing in at least one case permanent brain damage.

muhammad-atar.title: Ramzi bin al-Shibh
muhammad-atar.summary: Alleged September 11 co-conspirator, captured in Pakistan in the summer of 2002 and taken to a secret prison rather than to trial. John Kiriakou, who is often wrongly credited with his capture, cites him as the clearest demonstration of what torture cost the United States — declared clinically insane by the Pentagon's own psychiatrist as a result of CIA sleep deprivation, and therefore untriable.

muhammad-atar.title: Mitchell and Jessen
muhammad-atar.summary: The two American psychologists who pitched the CIA's enhanced interrogation program to Director George Tenet at a cocktail party in late October 2001; designers of the program and its theoretical underpinning, "learned helplessness."

muhammad-atar.title: Hummus
muhammad-atar.summary: The CIA's coercive 'rectal feeding' of detainees using pureed hummus — an unauthorized interrogation technique used at post-9/11 black sites, exposed in the 2014 Senate Torture Report, and the abuse for which John Kiriakou became most associated in popular culture.

muhammad-atar.title: Sleep deprivation
muhammad-atar.summary: A CIA interrogation technique used against high-value detainees post-9/11; the agency was authorized to deny prisoners sleep for up to 12 days continuously; people died; at least one detainee was rendered permanently clinically insane.

music-as-torture.title: Cold cell
music-as-torture.summary: A CIA interrogation technique in which a stripped detainee is chained to a ceiling eyebolt in a cell chilled to 50°F, then doused with a bucket of ice water at hourly intervals; never authorized; documented to have killed at least two prisoners.

music-as-torture.title: Waterboarding
music-as-torture.summary: Torture technique in which a prisoner is restrained on an inclined board with the head lower than the feet, a cloth placed over the face, and water poured continuously over it to simulate drowning. Per John Kiriakou, waterboarding was treated as a criminal act under U.S. and international law for decades before 2002 — including a post–World War II execution of Japanese soldiers who waterboarded American POWs, and a 1968 court-martial of a U.S. soldier photographed waterboarding a North Vietnamese prisoner — before the CIA reauthorized it after September 11. Abu Zubaydah was waterboarded 83 times; Khalid Sheikh Mohammed 187 times.

music-as-torture.title: Sleep deprivation
music-as-torture.summary: A CIA interrogation technique used against high-value detainees post-9/11; the agency was authorized to deny prisoners sleep for up to 12 days continuously; people died; at least one detainee was rendered permanently clinically insane.

music-as-torture.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
music-as-torture.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

music-as-torture.title: Cameo
music-as-torture.summary: The personalised-video app John Kiriakou joined in February 2026 and turned into an unexpected second career — around 2,600 videos, roughly 900 of them in his first month alone. Half are birthday messages and most of the rest are requests for CIA stories, but about two hundred have been appeals for advice or a pep talk, and three of those people later told him he had talked them out of suicide.

music-as-torture.title: Death threats against Kiriakou
music-as-torture.summary: The threats John Kiriakou has received across two decades — first after going public about the CIA torture program, when FBI advice that at least two were credible sent his family out of the country, and later in waves tied to his opposition to Gina Haspel, his remarks about Pakistan, and his advocacy on Palestine and the Epstein case.

muslim-brotherhood-designation.title: Islamofascism
muslim-brotherhood-designation.summary: A term John Kiriakou says was introduced into American media around 2004 and 2005, was created by a public relations firm working for the Republican National Committee, was pushed hard into everyday usage, failed to catch on, and was quietly abandoned. He offers it as his clearest example of manufactured vocabulary intended as domestic propaganda.

muslim-brotherhood-designation.title: Abu Zubaydah
muslim-brotherhood-designation.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

muslim-brotherhood-designation.title: Counterterrorism Center
muslim-brotherhood-designation.summary: The CIA's Counterterrorism Center (CTC) — the unit where John Kiriakou spent the defining years of his operational career. He joined in the late 1990s as the only officer in the entire CIA fluent in both Greek and Arabic, served as chief of counterintelligence in the bin Laden unit, watched the Center swell from a few hundred employees to nearly 2,000 by September 12, 2001, and it was to CTC that he walked back down in May 2002 to refuse the torture program — the moment, he says, the CIA began to turn on him.

muslim-brotherhood-designation.title: Dick Cheney
muslim-brotherhood-designation.summary: U.S. Vice President under George W. Bush. Per John Kiriakou — recounting CIA Director George Tenet's memoir — Cheney intercepted the presidential finding authorizing the CIA's enhanced interrogation program in the Oval Office anteroom and took it from Tenet before Bush could sign it. Tenet later concluded the president probably never actually signed the finding and probably told the truth when he said he had no idea the program was taking place. Kiriakou characterizes Cheney as the one who actually ran foreign policy, intelligence policy, and defense policy during the Bush years.

muslim-brotherhood-designation.title: George Tenet
muslim-brotherhood-designation.summary: Director of Central Intelligence from 1997 to 2004, spanning the September 11 attacks and the early enhanced-interrogation program; identified by John Kiriakou as John Brennan's institutional patron at the agency; the figure who ordered the Five Eyes intelligence services to "open the files" to each other in the early 2000s.

muslim-brotherhood-designation.title: Air India Flight 182
muslim-brotherhood-designation.summary: The 1985 bombing of a Boeing 747 over the Atlantic, which John Kiriakou has attributed to the government of India in the course of arguing that state sponsorship of terrorism is not confined to the countries formally designated for it.

myanmar-civil-war-kiriakou-view.title: 1953 Iran coup
myanmar-civil-war-kiriakou-view.summary: The U.S.- and UK-backed overthrow of Iran's democratically elected prime minister, Mohammad Mossadegh; per John Kiriakou, the coup served British national interests rather than American ones, and the subsequent outlawing of secular political opposition under the Shah forced dissent into the mosques — producing a religious rather than secular revolution in 1979.

myanmar-civil-war-kiriakou-view.title: AIPAC
myanmar-civil-war-kiriakou-view.summary: The American Israel Public Affairs Committee — the U.S. political organization that, in John Kiriakou's framing, ought to be registered as a foreign-lobbying entity but is not, and that wields decisive electoral power against U.S. elected officials who express support for Palestinian human rights.

myanmar-civil-war-kiriakou-view.title: Bahrain fishing officer demarche
myanmar-civil-war-kiriakou-view.summary: Kiriakou's account of serving, while stationed in Bahrain, as the embassy's econ officer and by extension its fishing, banking, aviation, and environment officer — including delivering a formal U.S. demarche to Bahrain's deputy foreign minister over a U.S.-Canada dispute about whether clams legally count as fish.

myanmar-civil-war-kiriakou-view.title: Barack Obama
myanmar-civil-war-kiriakou-view.summary: 44th U.S. president; in John Kiriakou's account, Obama publicly recounted refusing Benjamin Netanyahu's demand to bomb Iran and calling Israel's threat to use nuclear weapons a bluff — a bluff Kiriakou says Donald Trump later believed.

myanmar-civil-war-kiriakou-view.title: Below World's End
myanmar-civil-war-kiriakou-view.summary: Film in which John Kiriakou made his acting debut, filmed entirely in Mexico during October 2025; Kiriakou's performance earned him a Screen Actors Guild membership card, and Sean Penn told him after a private screening that he had unknowingly been acting throughout his entire CIA career.

myanmar-civil-war-kiriakou-view.title: Big Assawoman Bay NASA launch
myanmar-civil-war-kiriakou-view.summary: John Kiriakou's account of being taken, as a junior CIA analyst, to watch a NASA rocket launch near the village of Big Assawoman on Virginia's Eastern Shore, where he was startled to find foreign space-agency officials present unsupervised.

naftali-bennett.title: Greater Israel
naftali-bennett.summary: The territorial project John Kiriakou believes the Israeli government genuinely holds: the expulsion of every Palestinian, beginning in Gaza and continuing into the West Bank, pursued on a hundred- or two-hundred-year horizon in the confidence that the United States will never push back.

naftali-bennett.title: Lebanon-Israeli Conflict
naftali-bennett.summary: Per John Kiriakou, no Israeli government will allow Lebanon to flourish as a nation; he expects continued Israeli attacks and forced displacement of civilians, citing a statistic of up to 700,000 Lebanese internally displaced, and links the war to the "Greater Israel" rhetoric of US ambassador Mike Huckabee.

naftali-bennett.title: Israeli Nuclear Program
naftali-bennett.summary: Israel's widely assumed but officially unacknowledged nuclear arsenal; per John Kiriakou, the conventional wisdom within the CIA is that Israel possesses between 120 and 220 nuclear weapons, and the U.S. government's refusal to formally acknowledge this is driven by a specific legal obligation under the Glenn-Symington Act, which would require cutting off all foreign aid to any nuclear-armed country not party to the Non-Proliferation Treaty.

naftali-bennett.title: Mike Huckabee
naftali-bennett.summary: The United States ambassador to Israel under Donald Trump, and the subject of a public call for resignation from John Kiriakou after Huckabee received Jonathan Pollard at the American embassy. Kiriakou''s assessment separates two charges: Huckabee is not a traitor but an idiot who did not think the meeting was a big deal, and a former governor of a small state who still behaves as though he can set policy without the State Department or the National Security Council.

naftali-bennett.title: South Lebanon displacement, 2026
naftali-bennett.summary: John Kiriakou''s assessment of the Israeli campaign in southern Lebanon running alongside the 2026 Iran war: mass evacuation orders, hundreds of thousands internally displaced, and his conclusion that Israel has guaranteed Lebanon will be a failed state. He notes the world is not watching because it is watching Iran.

naftali-bennett.title: The Samson Option
naftali-bennett.summary: John Kiriakou's assessment, given during the 2026 Iran war, that Israel would use nuclear weapons if it believed the state itself was about to collapse. He notes that a year earlier he would have called the idea ridiculous, and that analysts put the Israeli arsenal at between eighty and two hundred warheads.

narcotics-under-cover.title: Qat in Yemen
narcotics-under-cover.summary: The afternoon shrub-chewing habit of Yemen, and the special dispensation the CIA had to issue so that its officers could take part in it. John Kiriakou explains that no source could be developed in a qat-chewing country by an officer who would not chew.

narcotics-under-cover.title: "Most other countries are more moral than the CIA"
narcotics-under-cover.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer to a viewer who asked whether the United States has the most moral intelligence agency: it does not, and a hundred countries could be named whose services behave better — the disqualifying practice being the killing of people who pose no threat to the United States.

narcotics-under-cover.title: Spies traded home
narcotics-under-cover.summary: What happens to intelligence officers and agents after they are exchanged and sent back, in John Kiriakou''s account: not usually execution, but a career that is irreparably damaged, because every service you would want to hide from now knows exactly who you are.

narcotics-under-cover.title: The clear and present danger finding
narcotics-under-cover.summary: The presidential determination John Kiriakou says must precede any CIA paramilitary targeted killing — an assertion that the person concerned is a clear and present danger to the United States, to an American installation, or to an American person — and his judgement that in early 2026 that threshold had not been reached in Iran.

narcotics-under-cover.title: The Islamabad guest house
narcotics-under-cover.summary: The sixteen-room guest house in Islamabad that CIA officers took over entirely during the post-9/11 deployments — a place John Kiriakou says the agency still will not let him name, which came with breakfast, dinner and laundry for about thirty-five dollars a day against a per diem of five hundred.

narcotics-under-cover.title: A Middle East reading list
narcotics-under-cover.summary: The books and the starting point John Kiriakou recommends to anyone trying to understand the modern Middle East: begin at the end of the Second World War, not five thousand years earlier, and start with The House of Saud, the Sykes-Picot Agreement and From Beirut to Jerusalem.

nation-of-islam-at-loretto.title: Aryan Brotherhood
nation-of-islam-at-loretto.summary: The white prison gang that adopted John Kiriakou on his first day at FCI Loretto. Two hours in, two Aryans with swastika neck tattoos walked into his cell to check his paperwork — not a rat, not a "chomo" — and invited him to the Aryan table, which ran from hardcore Nazis at one end to merely white guys at the other. A rumor that he had been a CIA assassin earned him the nickname "the Muslim killer," which he never corrected; asked directly, he answered "we all did stuff we weren't proud of — it was wartime," and the Aryans loved it. He sat with them a year before the Italians took him in.

nation-of-islam-at-loretto.title: FCI Loretto
nation-of-islam-at-loretto.summary: U.S. Federal Correctional Institution in Loretto, Pennsylvania; the low-medium-security prison at which John Kiriakou served 23 months of a 30-month sentence following his 2013 Espionage Act–era plea deal; the originally ordered "minimum security work camp" placement was countermanded — per Kiriakou, on Brennan's direct intervention — to place him in the actual prison alongside the general population.

nation-of-islam-at-loretto.title: Prison racial segregation
nation-of-islam-at-loretto.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the rigid racial and ethnic division of American prisons — a cafeteria split like the 1950s South — and his argument that segregating and hardening inmates for years, then releasing them with no skills, makes society less safe.

nation-of-islam-at-loretto.title: Doing Time Like a Spy
nation-of-islam-at-loretto.summary: Prison memoir by John Kiriakou, full title Doing Time Like a Spy: How the CIA Taught Me to Survive and Thrive in Prison; winner of two literary awards and reissued in a second edition by Simon and Schuster.

nation-of-islam-at-loretto.title: Louis Farrakhan
nation-of-islam-at-loretto.summary: Leader of the Nation of Islam; per John Kiriakou, issued a perfectly timed statement during Kiriakou's imprisonment at FCI Loretto identifying him as a hero of the Muslim people for standing up for human rights — protecting Kiriakou from the prison's Muslim population at a moment when the Aryans were simultaneously protecting him under the cover story that he was a "Muslim hunter."

nation-of-islam-at-loretto.title: The Pisces prison gang
nation-of-islam-at-loretto.summary: The umbrella gang every Hispanic prisoner at FCI Loretto was required to join on pain of a beating — which subordinated street rivalries like MS-13, the Norteños and the Zetas to a single inside identity and required every member to work out daily against the possibility of a race riot.

national-archives-declassification.title: Espionage Act
national-archives-declassification.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

national-archives-declassification.title: Leonie Brinkema
national-archives-declassification.summary: U.S. federal judge in the Eastern District of Virginia — informally the 'Espionage Court' — a Reagan appointee John Kiriakou calls "a hanging judge." Per Kiriakou, Brinkema systematically reserved all major national security cases for herself rather than allowing them to be distributed randomly among judges, and ruled in Kiriakou's case that his reason for blowing the whistle was legally irrelevant and that classified documents could not be used in his defense — effectively making it impossible to mount one.

national-archives-declassification.title: Julian Assange
national-archives-declassification.summary: Kiriakou — a 15-year friend and former WikiLeaks board member — on why Assange is a publisher owed a journalist's immunity, and a political prisoner.

national-archives-declassification.title: Thomas Drake
national-archives-declassification.summary: NSA whistleblower; per John Kiriakou, the source for the statement that on the morning of September 11, 2001, NSA Director Mike Hayden told agency personnel NSA had been 'waiting for a 9/11' to implement the mass-electronic-surveillance program that NSA's founding charter forbids.

national-archives-declassification.title: Classified email
national-archives-declassification.summary: John Kiriakou was serving overseas the day classified email was introduced at the CIA, and remembers his station chief saying there was no way to control it. His own illustration of what followed is a lunch invitation to his wife — a fellow senior CIA officer — marked Secret HUM 4-82, and her reply naming a deli and a time, marked the same way.

national-archives-declassification.title: Edward Snowden
national-archives-declassification.summary: Former NSA contractor who in 2013 disclosed the scope of U.S. [mass surveillance](/wiki/mass-surveillance), including the Section 702 collection program. Per John Kiriakou — who counts Snowden among the small group of national-security whistleblowers prosecuted under the Espionage Act — Snowden was ''stuck between two awful slippery slopes'': breaking his oath and chain of command on one side, and on the other catching something ''cut and dry against the Constitution'' that no one would act on. Kiriakou notes Snowden could not use his chain of command (as Kiriakou could not, his own chain being Jose Rodriguez), and that Judge Leonie Brinkema had reserved the Snowden case for herself before he fled the country.

national-bird.title: Daniel Hale
national-bird.summary: Per John Kiriakou, drone whistleblower Daniel Hale — an NSA contractor and drone targeting analyst who exposed an 80% civilian death rate in the U.S. drone program, was ordered to fire on two young girls his superior called "goats," and was sentenced to 45 months (of which Kiriakou says he actually served about 18) despite prosecutors seeking nine to eleven years.

national-bird.title: The Drone Papers
national-bird.summary: The trove of classified documents leaked by Daniel Hale and published by The Intercept — later collected in book form as 'The Assassination Complex' — exposing how the U.S. drone program selected and killed targets; John Kiriakou relied on it in his own writing on the war in Afghanistan.

national-bird.title: Signature strikes
national-bird.summary: The drone-targeting doctrine, exposed by Daniel Hale's leak, under which the U.S. kills people not for who they are but for patterns of behavior or association; John Kiriakou says operators treat any male over 12 as a legitimate target on the theory that he 'could pick up a gun.'

national-bird.title: PTSD
national-bird.summary: Post-traumatic stress disorder runs through John Kiriakou''s life and worldview — he had it coming out of Greece after an assassination attempt, brought it home from Pakistan alongside his shock at colleagues'' willingness to kill, and was blindsided by a delayed post-prison version that helped end his marriage. For six months after release he dreamed the same dream nightly: that he was out by mistake and had to get back inside before midnight count. He still takes a repurposed blood-pressure drug that stops the dreams, and he extends the diagnosis outward — to secret-site interrogators who came back crying, to drone pilots, and to prisoners released angry and untreated.

national-bird.title: Code Pink
national-bird.summary: The women-led peace group co-founded by Medea Benjamin. John Kiriakou first met them as a Senate staffer — he was the man who threw them out of a hearing he had produced, and got a lecture from Senator Shaheen for it. When he was arrested they were "right there next to me"; they threw his going-away party on the roof of the Hay-Adams, commissioned a folk group to sing a song rewritten about him, and quietly arranged for Roger Waters to pay off the second mortgage so his family could keep the house. He calls them his angels, and the one institution in American life he still trusts.

national-bird.title: Espionage Act
national-bird.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

national-endowment-for-democracy.title: John Rendon
national-endowment-for-democracy.summary: Self-described "professional propagandist"; organizer of the pre-distributed American flags waved by Kuwaiti crowds on the 1991 Kuwait Liberation Day; in 2008 hired John Kiriakou (alongside Karl Rove) to produce op-eds attempting to rehabilitate the U.S. travel ban imposed on Indonesian general Joko Widodo.

national-endowment-for-democracy.title: Kuwait Liberation Day
national-endowment-for-democracy.summary: February 1991 expulsion of Iraqi forces from Kuwait by the U.S.-led coalition; John Kiriakou entered the country with U.S. Marines on the day of liberation; the small American flags waved by the crowds — and the post-liberation arrival of Democratic and Republican National Committee personnel ostensibly to assist the country's transition to democracy — were, per Kiriakou, the work of professional propagandist John Rendon.

national-endowment-for-democracy.title: Operation Mockingbird
national-endowment-for-democracy.summary: The CIA's mid-twentieth-century program of recruiting and managing American journalists as influence assets; in John Kiriakou's account, no longer operationally necessary in the contemporary period because the U.S. media voluntarily reprints CIA-supplied material, and in at least one documented case sends articles to the agency for clearance before sending them to its own editor.

national-endowment-for-democracy.title: CIA political action group
national-endowment-for-democracy.summary: The CIA's most secretive clandestine propaganda arm — successor to the Cold War 'active measures group' — which John Kiriakou says places and funds propagandists worldwide; no officer of it has been publicly identified since 1982, and he encountered its work funding the DNC's and RNC's international arms in post-war Kuwait.

national-endowment-for-democracy.title: Andres Serrano
national-endowment-for-democracy.summary: American artist; in the 1980s the creator of Piss Christ — a beaker of urine containing an inverted crucifix — which so enraged President Ronald Reagan that he cut off funding to the National Endowment for the Arts. Per John Kiriakou, also the photographer of a torture-chamber series at Tate Modern, London, in which one panel is a photograph of Kiriakou next to a panel of a U.S. military torturer.

national-endowment-for-democracy.title: Code Pink
national-endowment-for-democracy.summary: The women-led peace group co-founded by Medea Benjamin. John Kiriakou first met them as a Senate staffer — he was the man who threw them out of a hearing he had produced, and got a lecture from Senator Shaheen for it. When he was arrested they were "right there next to me"; they threw his going-away party on the roof of the Hay-Adams, commissioned a folk group to sing a song rewritten about him, and quietly arranged for Roger Waters to pay off the second mortgage so his family could keep the house. He calls them his angels, and the one institution in American life he still trusts.

national-intelligence-council.title: Counterterrorism Center
national-intelligence-council.summary: The CIA's Counterterrorism Center (CTC) — the unit where John Kiriakou spent the defining years of his operational career. He joined in the late 1990s as the only officer in the entire CIA fluent in both Greek and Arabic, served as chief of counterintelligence in the bin Laden unit, watched the Center swell from a few hundred employees to nearly 2,000 by September 12, 2001, and it was to CTC that he walked back down in May 2002 to refuse the torture program — the moment, he says, the CIA began to turn on him.

national-intelligence-council.title: Dick Cheney
national-intelligence-council.summary: U.S. Vice President under George W. Bush. Per John Kiriakou — recounting CIA Director George Tenet's memoir — Cheney intercepted the presidential finding authorizing the CIA's enhanced interrogation program in the Oval Office anteroom and took it from Tenet before Bush could sign it. Tenet later concluded the president probably never actually signed the finding and probably told the truth when he said he had no idea the program was taking place. Kiriakou characterizes Cheney as the one who actually ran foreign policy, intelligence policy, and defense policy during the Bush years.

national-intelligence-council.title: Iraq WMD intelligence
national-intelligence-council.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of how the case for Iraqi weapons of mass destruction was fabricated: the intelligence community''s consensus was that Iraq had no WMD, but the White House had already decided to invade and sought analysis to fit the policy.

national-intelligence-council.title: Jonathan Pollard
national-intelligence-council.summary: U.S. Navy civilian intelligence analyst convicted in 1985 of spying for Israel; the canonical proven case of Israeli espionage against the United States; cited by John Kiriakou in his 2024 Piers Morgan debate with a former Mossad director who denied any Israeli spying on the U.S.

national-intelligence-council.title: Principals Committee Meeting (February 2003)
national-intelligence-council.summary: Senior-most interagency forum of the U.S. national security apparatus, normally chaired by the president. Per John Kiriakou — who served as notetaker for CIA Director George Tenet at the eve-of-Iraq-invasion meeting on February 19–20, 2003 — Vice President Dick Cheney chaired in place of Bush, General Tommy Franks ended his order-of-battle briefing with 'If all goes as planned, we can be in Tehran by August,' and an NSC senior director said 'When we cross that border tomorrow morning, they're going to throw flowers at us.'

national-intelligence-council.title: Saddam Hussein
national-intelligence-council.summary: President of Iraq from 1979 until the 2003 U.S. invasion; subject of John Kiriakou's CIA portfolio from January 1990 onward, in which capacity Kiriakou became, at age 25, "Saddam Hussein's intelligence community biographer" and the analyst who briefed President George H. W. Bush in the Oval Office on the morning of the 1990 invasion of Kuwait.

national-security-act.title: J. Edgar Hoover
national-security-act.summary: The FBI's founding director — 48 years in the chair — whose opposition nearly strangled the CIA at birth. Per John Kiriakou, Truman lifted Hoover's objection to the National Security Act of 1947 by disingenuously assuring him the CIA would be a division of the FBI; the lie seeded the two agencies' permanent mutual hatred. Kiriakou also credits Hoover with perfecting the annual ritual the CIA later copied — scaring Congress witless and demanding budget increases — and with controlling Hollywood's FBI image so tightly that no film could be made without his approval.

national-security-act.title: CIA–FBI interagency rivalry and 9/11
national-security-act.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the historical CIA–FBI rivalry, dating to J. Edgar Hoover's opposition to the 1947 National Security Act, and how it manifested before September 11 when Cofer Black's Counterterrorism Center withheld from the FBI that hijackers Nawaf al-Hazmi and Khalid al-Mihdhar had been granted U.S. visas.

national-security-act.title: William Donovan
national-security-act.summary: General William "Wild Bill" Donovan — Medal of Honor recipient, decorated World War I veteran, Wall Street figure, and founder of the wartime Office of Strategic Services (OSS). Per John Kiriakou, Donovan had President Truman's ear and insisted the new agency be independent rather than a division of the FBI; he was among the men who sat down with visiting MI6 officers in New York in 1946–47 and sketched out a centralized intelligence service on pads of paper, and he became — in Kiriakou's telling — the first director of the CIA, over the sustained opposition of J. Edgar Hoover.

national-security-act.title: Founding of the CIA (1947)
national-security-act.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the CIA's creation under the National Security Act of 1947 — built with British MI6 help after a chaotic 1945-47 interregnum, and opposed by J. Edgar Hoover until Truman falsely promised him the new agency would be part of the FBI.

national-security-act.title: Revolutionary Organization 17 November
national-security-act.summary: Greek far-left urban guerrilla group active 1975–2002; the deadliest terrorist organization in Greek history

national-security-act.title: Truman's CIA op-ed
national-security-act.summary: A 1963 Washington Post op-ed in which former President Harry Truman — who signed the CIA into being in 1947 — called it a 'damn fool mistake' that should be disbanded; John Kiriakou notes the piece ran in the morning edition and vanished from the evening one.

national-security-agency.title: Thomas Drake
national-security-agency.summary: NSA whistleblower; per John Kiriakou, the source for the statement that on the morning of September 11, 2001, NSA Director Mike Hayden told agency personnel NSA had been 'waiting for a 9/11' to implement the mass-electronic-surveillance program that NSA's founding charter forbids.

national-security-agency.title: Abu Zubaydah
national-security-agency.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

national-security-agency.title: NSA
national-security-agency.summary: Kiriakou on the agency whose Utah facility boasts room to store every American's calls, texts and emails for the next 500 years.

national-security-agency.title: NSA Surveillance
national-security-agency.summary: ''It is part of NSA''s founding charter that it is not allowed to spy on Americans'' — Kiriakou on warrantless collection and the Bluffdale warehouse.

national-security-agency.title: PTSD
national-security-agency.summary: Post-traumatic stress disorder runs through John Kiriakou''s life and worldview — he had it coming out of Greece after an assassination attempt, brought it home from Pakistan alongside his shock at colleagues'' willingness to kill, and was blindsided by a delayed post-prison version that helped end his marriage. For six months after release he dreamed the same dream nightly: that he was out by mistake and had to get back inside before midnight count. He still takes a repurposed blood-pressure drug that stops the dreams, and he extends the diagnosis outward — to secret-site interrogators who came back crying, to drone pilots, and to prisoners released angry and untreated.

national-security-agency.title: Pegasus spyware
national-security-agency.summary: Israeli-developed phone-interception software that requires no action by the target — no link clicked, no message answered — and gives its operator the contents of the device along with live use of its camera and microphone. John Kiriakou describes it as having escaped state control: sold on commercially, routed through an American contractor and then directly by the Israelis, used against Americans, and implicated in a Greek interception scandal that he says brought down a government.

national-security-council.title: Osama bin Laden
national-security-council.summary: Founder and leader of al-Qaeda and the central target of the manhunt that shaped John Kiriakou's counterterrorism career. Per Kiriakou, bin Laden came from a billionaire Saudi construction family, was never one of the CIA-funded Afghan mujahideen, overruled subordinates who wanted to attack Israel and insisted the 9/11 attacks hit the United States to crash its economy, escaped Tora Bora dressed as a woman, and spent his final years next to Pakistan's equivalent of West Point — where, Kiriakou says, you would have to be a "mental defective" not to know he was there. Kiriakou believes the United States never intended to capture him alive.

national-security-council.title: John Bolton
national-security-council.summary: Former U.S. National Security Advisor. Per John Kiriakou, one of the most dangerous men in America and the real driver — with Elliott Abrams — of the 2019 pressure campaign against Venezuela; the signature at the National Security Council through which a covert action finding passes on its way to the president. Kiriakou predicted his 2019 departure from the Trump administration on the basis of White House chatter and Trump's premium on loyalty.

national-security-council.title: Counterterrorism Center
national-security-council.summary: The CIA's Counterterrorism Center (CTC) — the unit where John Kiriakou spent the defining years of his operational career. He joined in the late 1990s as the only officer in the entire CIA fluent in both Greek and Arabic, served as chief of counterintelligence in the bin Laden unit, watched the Center swell from a few hundred employees to nearly 2,000 by September 12, 2001, and it was to CTC that he walked back down in May 2002 to refuse the torture program — the moment, he says, the CIA began to turn on him.

national-security-council.title: American Psychological Association
national-security-council.summary: The world's largest body of psychologists, which John Kiriakou cites constantly for one devastating datum — its research shows people begin to lose their minds at around day seven without sleep, and begin to die at day nine as their organs shut down. Mitchell and Jessen were nonetheless authorized to keep chained, naked prisoners awake for up to twelve days, which is why Kiriakou insists sleep deprivation was always worse than waterboarding. The organization's own role in the interrogation program later became the subject of an internal revolt and a 500-page independent report.

national-security-council.title: Donald Rumsfeld
national-security-council.summary: U.S. Secretary of Defense during the post-9/11 torture program and, per John Kiriakou, joined at the hip with Dick Cheney in pushing the Iraq war from inside the Office of the Secretary of Defense. Kiriakou recounts Rumsfeld dismissing sleep deprivation as a real technique by pointing to his own standup desk, and names him among the war criminals who would be prosecuted in any other country.

national-security-council.title: Presidential call memcons
national-security-council.summary: How a call between the president and a foreign leader is staffed and recorded, as John Kiriakou describes it. Four people are usually on the line and rarely five — not the twenty reported during the Ukraine affair — and the write-up, a memorandum of conversation or memcon, is held so tightly inside the National Security Council that a CIA analyst, he says, would never see one.

national-security-letters.title: Panquake
national-security-letters.summary: Open-source, blockchain-based social platform developed by the Iceland-registered company Talk Liberation, for which John Kiriakou has served as brand ambassador since 2020. Kiriakou describes it as advertising-free, subscription-funded, free of back doors, and run on servers powered by Icelandic geothermal steam — a project he frames as a David-and-Goliath fight against banks, big technology and governments.

national-security-letters.title: Government Purchase of Social Media Metadata
national-security-letters.summary: Per John Kiriakou, the practice by which U.S. intelligence and law enforcement agencies — including the NSA and FBI — buy bulk user metadata from social media companies such as Facebook, Instagram, and X (formerly Twitter), bypassing the warrant requirements that would otherwise apply to direct surveillance. The practice exploits a provision in platform terms of service under which users surrender ownership of their metadata to the company, which may then sell it freely.

national-security-letters.title: CIA–Big Tech revolving door
national-security-letters.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of the traffic between the CIA and the major technology companies — "they work hand in glove" — illustrated by a supervisor who resigned five years short of his thirty-year pension for a Microsoft job paying eight times his government salary. The exchange, he argues, benefits both sides and is for that reason dangerous: the agency gains access to the most advanced companies in the world, and the companies gain a direct channel into the intelligence community.

national-security-letters.title: Bill Binney
national-security-letters.summary: Former NSA technical director whom John Kiriakou cites as having debunked the DNC hack. Asked by Veteran Intelligence Professionals for Sanity to examine the science, Binney analyzed the speed of the upload and concluded the emails could only have been copied in person to a thumb drive, not taken remotely by Russia — an argument he later made to Donald Trump in the Oval Office. Kiriakou calls him a friend, the most brilliant person he has met on electronics, and a member of the whistleblower circle he belongs to.

national-security-letters.title: Edward Snowden
national-security-letters.summary: Former NSA contractor who in 2013 disclosed the scope of U.S. [mass surveillance](/wiki/mass-surveillance), including the Section 702 collection program. Per John Kiriakou — who counts Snowden among the small group of national-security whistleblowers prosecuted under the Espionage Act — Snowden was ''stuck between two awful slippery slopes'': breaking his oath and chain of command on one side, and on the other catching something ''cut and dry against the Constitution'' that no one would act on. Kiriakou notes Snowden could not use his chain of command (as Kiriakou could not, his own chain being Jose Rodriguez), and that Judge Leonie Brinkema had reserved the Snowden case for herself before he fled the country.

national-security-letters.title: Pegasus spyware
national-security-letters.summary: Israeli-developed phone-interception software that requires no action by the target — no link clicked, no message answered — and gives its operator the contents of the device along with live use of its camera and microphone. John Kiriakou describes it as having escaped state control: sold on commercially, routed through an American contractor and then directly by the Israelis, used against Americans, and implicated in a Greek interception scandal that he says brought down a government.

national-security-vs-civil-liberties.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
national-security-vs-civil-liberties.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

national-security-vs-civil-liberties.title: John Kiriakou
national-security-vs-civil-liberties.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

national-security-vs-civil-liberties.title: AIPAC
national-security-vs-civil-liberties.summary: The American Israel Public Affairs Committee — the U.S. political organization that, in John Kiriakou's framing, ought to be registered as a foreign-lobbying entity but is not, and that wields decisive electoral power against U.S. elected officials who express support for Palestinian human rights.

national-security-vs-civil-liberties.title: Bahrain Posting (1994–1996)
national-security-vs-civil-liberties.summary: John Kiriakou's 1994–1996 assignment to Bahrain under U.S. State Department cover as second secretary for economic affairs — arriving with his wife Joanne and infant son Chris on August 1, 1994, into a tiny Gulf monarchy whose sectarian tensions erupted, two months later, into the first Intifada.

national-security-vs-civil-liberties.title: The CIA Insider's Guide to Surveillance and Surveillance Detection
national-security-vs-civil-liberties.summary: Book by John Kiriakou drawing on his experience as a surveillance detection instructor at the CIA and as a private surveillance training consultant. The book covers the techniques used by intelligence professionals to identify whether they are being followed — including the four-phase surveillance detection route, concealment device placement and retrieval, and counter-surveillance strategy — adapted for use by corporate executives, journalists, and others who want to confirm whether they are being followed.

national-security-vs-civil-liberties.title: Hunter Biden Laptop
national-security-vs-civil-liberties.summary: John Kiriakou's assessment of the Hunter Biden laptop controversy — he saw nothing related to child sex abuse in the material but says the Biden family, particularly Hunter, has serious documented substance-abuse problems; and that the 2020 open letter in which 51 former intelligence officials called the story a Russian/KGB-style operation used deliberately hedged, CIA-trained language and was later shown (per Michael Morell's testimony) to have been solicited by the Biden campaign.

national-whistleblower-day.title: The Berlin conference list
national-whistleblower-day.summary: Checking into a Berlin hotel for a conference, John Kiriakou was handed the guest list when the clerk could not find his booking — and discovered that every one of the dozen names on it was a friend of his, and every one of them an outspoken whistleblower.

national-whistleblower-day.title: "The least I could do"
national-whistleblower-day.summary: Told that he had kept another whistleblower from slipping, John Kiriakou declined the credit and described the work in the plainest possible terms: getting somebody out of the house for three or four hours, or taking them to dinner, because so many people had done exactly that for him when he was at his lowest.

national-whistleblower-day.title: Do what is right or what is easy
national-whistleblower-day.summary: Asked what he would tell the boy who once told his father he wanted to be a spy, John Kiriakou said he would tell him to always tell the truth and do the right thing — arguing that everyone already knows in their gut the difference between right and wrong, and that the only real question is whether they then do what is right or what is easy.

national-whistleblower-day.title: The cousin who stopped speaking
national-whistleblower-day.summary: An older first cousin told John Kiriakou after his conviction that he could no longer speak to him because Kiriakou had brought shame on the family; Kiriakou's reply was to point out that the cousin had imported drugs from Colombia, had appeared in the Washington Post as a mayor's cocaine dealer, and had fled to Greece until the statute of limitations expired.

national-whistleblower-day.title: The orange jumpsuits
national-whistleblower-day.summary: John Kiriakou has argued that the clothing ISIS put on the Western hostages it beheaded was not a coincidence but a citation: the group dressed its prisoners in orange jumpsuits because the United States dressed its own prisoners in orange jumpsuits, and once a government tortures, it has licensed every other government to do the same to its people.

national-whistleblower-day.title: The postcards for Daniel Hale
national-whistleblower-day.summary: The letter-writing appeal John Kiriakou ran for Daniel Hale in May and June 2021 — naming Hale as the whistleblower most in need of help, posting his jail address publicly, and relaying from the prisoner himself the exact rules a letter had to satisfy to reach him: ten stamps a week, plain unlined white paper, black ink, and no photographs.

nationalizing-the-midterms.title: Impeach him again
nationalizing-the-midterms.summary: John Kiriakou's warning that if the Democrats win a House majority in 2026 and immediately move to impeach Donald Trump again, they should never win another race — and his prediction that this is exactly what they will do.

nationalizing-the-midterms.title: Albright in Pyongyang
nationalizing-the-midterms.summary: John Kiriakou's account of Bill Clinton's stated regret over the final week of his presidency — that he wished he had pursued diplomatic relations with North Korea instead of Israeli-Palestinian peace — and of Madeleine Albright being in Pyongyang rather than at the talks.

nationalizing-the-midterms.title: Decorum in the Reagan years
nationalizing-the-midterms.summary: John Kiriakou's contrast between the State of the Union addresses he watched as a college student under Ronald Reagan — divided, substantive, but conducted with decorum — and the 2026 address he called a clown show with no decorum on either side.

nationalizing-the-midterms.title: Failure to accept responsibility
nationalizing-the-midterms.summary: The federal sentencing enhancement that John Kiriakou says explains why 98 per cent of federal criminal cases end in a plea bargain: a defendant who refuses a deal, goes to trial and loses has time added to the sentence for failing to accept responsibility.

nationalizing-the-midterms.title: Get thrown out spicily
nationalizing-the-midterms.summary: John Kiriakou''s criticism of Representative Al Green''s protest at the 2026 State of the Union address: that holding up a banned sign and then walking out quietly accomplished nothing, and that if you are going to be removed you should struggle and fight back.

nationalizing-the-midterms.title: The French in the streets
nationalizing-the-midterms.summary: John Kiriakou's stated admiration for how quickly the French take to the streets, offered while questioning Ted Rall about the chances of violence during the 2025 French political crisis, alongside his observation that he could not recall a French president ever resigning.

nato-article-5-invoked-once.title: Major non-NATO ally status for Ukraine
nato-article-5-invoked-once.summary: John Kiriakou''s forecast of how the Russian demand that Ukraine never join NATO can be met without leaving Ukraine unprotected: the designation of major non-NATO ally, already held by Australia, Japan, South Korea, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates, which he says confers essentially the same rights without the membership.

nato-article-5-invoked-once.title: Ukraine as a proxy war
nato-article-5-invoked-once.summary: John Kiriakou's assessment, given two months into the 2022 Russian invasion, that the United States was funding a proxy war it knew Ukraine could not win in order to bog Russia down — and that the outcome was already fixed, so peace talks should happen at once.

nato-article-5-invoked-once.title: China as mediator
nato-article-5-invoked-once.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that China is the plausible mediator of Middle Eastern and Ukrainian conflicts, grounded in his claim that — Tibet and its border wars aside — China has no history of invading other countries, and his observation of how quickly Beijing accepted an offhand suggestion that it might mediate between Israel and Iran.

nato-article-5-invoked-once.title: China as economic threat
nato-article-5-invoked-once.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that China is the real threat to the West not militarily — it has one aircraft carrier to America's two dozen and rarely invades — but economically, buying friends worldwide while the U.S. spends a trillion dollars a year on weapons.

nato-article-5-invoked-once.title: F-35 sale to Turkey
nato-article-5-invoked-once.summary: The proposed sale of F-35 fighters to Turkey, opposed for decades by Greece and Greek-Americans who fear the aircraft would be used against Greece, and opposed by Benjamin Netanyahu for the same reason with respect to Israel. When Netanyahu raised the objection publicly in July 2026, Donald Trump answered that he does not take orders from a foreign leader about arms sales — a rebuke John Kiriakou describes as unprecedented.

nato-article-5-invoked-once.title: The Imia crisis
nato-article-5-invoked-once.summary: The 1996 confrontation between Greece and Turkey over an uninhabited Aegean islet, which John Kiriakou cites as the last time the two came close to exchanging fire — a flag raised, a flag taken down, warships dispatched, and Bill Clinton telephoning both capitals to tell them to stop.

ndaa-2027-israel-fusion.title: MOSSAD
ndaa-2027-israel-fusion.summary: Israel's primary external intelligence service; characterized by John Kiriakou as universally hostile in his and his CIA colleagues' professional dealings with it ("never had a positive encounter with Mossad"); operates almost exclusively in the operational rather than analytical domain; the CIA is, per Kiriakou, categorically forbidden from spying on it.

ndaa-2027-israel-fusion.title: F-35 avionics dispute with Israel
ndaa-2027-israel-fusion.summary: John Kiriakou's account of how Israel demanded F-35 fighters without the deliberately degraded avionics the U.S. installs on export models — and, refused, allegedly worked through American defense contractors to steal the technology instead.

ndaa-2027-israel-fusion.title: Israel's counterintelligence threat ranking
ndaa-2027-israel-fusion.summary: John Kiriakou's repeated point that the American intelligence community formally ranks Israel a critical counterintelligence threat — the same tier as North Korea, China, Russia, Iran and Cuba — specifically for spying on and infiltrating the US government, and that policy has responded by giving Israel more access rather than less.

ndaa-2027-israel-fusion.title: Jonathan Pollard
ndaa-2027-israel-fusion.summary: U.S. Navy civilian intelligence analyst convicted in 1985 of spying for Israel; the canonical proven case of Israeli espionage against the United States; cited by John Kiriakou in his 2024 Piers Morgan debate with a former Mossad director who denied any Israeli spying on the U.S.

ndaa-2027-israel-fusion.title: Veterans' benefits for IDF service
ndaa-2027-israel-fusion.summary: A bill sponsored by a Republican congressman from Pennsylvania and one from Ohio that would extend US veterans' benefits to any American who joins the Israel Defense Forces. John Kiriakou calls it an outrage and, as an American, treason.

ndaa-2027-israel-fusion.title: Iran Nuclear Assessment
ndaa-2027-israel-fusion.summary: Per John Kiriakou's assessment, the US–Israeli military campaign against Iran was a war of choice driven by Israeli political pressure rather than genuine intelligence indicating an Iranian nuclear weapons threat. The CIA produced two National Intelligence Estimates concluding Iran had no nuclear weapons program; Supreme Leader Ayatollah Khamenei issued a fatwa in the 1980s forbidding such a program. The U.S. went to war anyway, in Kiriakou's view, after President Trump replaced the Joint Chiefs of Staff with officers willing to accept Israeli intelligence and proceed.

ndaa-section-219.title: Israeli espionage in the United States
ndaa-section-219.summary: The long-running Israeli intelligence effort against American targets, which John Kiriakou describes from inside the CIA: Israelis barred from the headquarters building, 187 spies identified by the FBI in 1990, a critical-threat counterintelligence ranking alongside Russia and China, and a 2026 warning that activity had intensified.

ndaa-section-219.title: F-35 avionics dispute with Israel
ndaa-section-219.summary: John Kiriakou's account of how Israel demanded F-35 fighters without the deliberately degraded avionics the U.S. installs on export models — and, refused, allegedly worked through American defense contractors to steal the technology instead.

ndaa-section-219.title: AIPAC
ndaa-section-219.summary: The American Israel Public Affairs Committee — the U.S. political organization that, in John Kiriakou's framing, ought to be registered as a foreign-lobbying entity but is not, and that wields decisive electoral power against U.S. elected officials who express support for Palestinian human rights.

ndaa-section-219.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
ndaa-section-219.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

ndaa-section-219.title: Israeli training of American police
ndaa-section-219.summary: The practice, which John Kiriakou opposes, of Israeli police and IDF personnel training American local police departments, including at the Atlanta facility known as Cop City.

ndaa-section-219.title: Israeli interception of US secure calls
ndaa-section-219.summary: John Kiriakou's account of overhearing evidence, within six months of joining the CIA, that Israeli intelligence was listening to encrypted American government calls — a colleague's secure line dropped mid-conversation and two Israeli voices could be heard on the open channel discussing whether the call had ended. He treats the episode as the concrete basis for assuming that American principals are intercepted as a matter of routine.

netanyahu-and-the-tel-aviv-police-chief.title: The Jenin incursion
netanyahu-and-the-tel-aviv-police-chief.summary: The Israeli military operation in Jenin of early July 2023, which John Kiriakou cited by its casualty figures — nine Palestinians dead and about a hundred wounded before the withdrawal — and which he called only the very beginning of what the most right-wing government in Israeli history would do.

netanyahu-and-the-tel-aviv-police-chief.title: The Israeli electorate shift
netanyahu-and-the-tel-aviv-police-chief.summary: John Kiriakou's structural explanation for why he does not expect Israeli politics to swing back — that the influx of Russian and Ukrainian Jewish immigrants over the preceding ten or fifteen years has moved the electorate so far right that a viable socialist movement or Labour party is, in his view, gone for good.

netanyahu-and-the-tel-aviv-police-chief.title: The Greek neo-Nazi seats
netanyahu-and-the-tel-aviv-police-chief.summary: John Kiriakou''s tally of the June 2023 Greek parliamentary election, which he treats as the most disturbing case of a Europe-wide trend: eight parties won seats, six of them right-wing, four of them right-wing extremist, and two of them neo-Nazi parties taking thirteen seats between them.

netanyahu-and-the-tel-aviv-police-chief.title: The Rwanda deportations
netanyahu-and-the-tel-aviv-police-chief.summary: The British policy of removing asylum seekers to Rwanda for resettlement, which John Kiriakou cited in 2023 as evidence that the United Kingdom belongs on the list of countries with entrenched right-wing governments — a policy he called right-wing extremist and probably illegal.

netanyahu-and-the-tel-aviv-police-chief.title: Elliott Abrams
netanyahu-and-the-tel-aviv-police-chief.summary: The Reagan-era assistant secretary of state whose 2023 appointment to a Biden administration advisory board John Kiriakou treated as proof that neoliberal and neoconservative foreign policy are the same policy with interchangeable players — a man who pleaded guilty over Iran-Contra, was pardoned, helped sell the Iraqi weapons of mass destruction case, and then served Donald Trump on Iran and Venezuela.

netanyahu-and-the-tel-aviv-police-chief.title: Frances Haugen
netanyahu-and-the-tel-aviv-police-chief.summary: The Facebook employee John Kiriakou refuses to call a whistleblower — arguing that against the legal definition, bringing to light waste, fraud, abuse, illegality or threats to public health or safety, she qualifies as a corporate spokesperson whose motive was to improve the company's bottom line, not to expose wrongdoing.

netanyahu-arrest-poll.title: Maduro Capture
netanyahu-arrest-poll.summary: CIA-driven nighttime operation in which a team of Delta Force commandos entered Venezuela and removed Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro and his wife from their beds. Per John Kiriakou, the key enabling intelligence — per a New York Times account he cited — came from a CIA asset inside Maduro''s presidential palace who called when Maduro went to sleep: ''He''s sound asleep. If you''re going to do it, do it now.'' At least eighty people were killed in the operation, including approximately thirty-five Cubans. Kiriakou compares it to the 1989 capture of Manuel Noriega, in which US forces blasted death metal at the Vatican Embassy until Noriega was asked to leave.

netanyahu-arrest-poll.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
netanyahu-arrest-poll.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

netanyahu-arrest-poll.title: International Criminal Court
netanyahu-arrest-poll.summary: The Hague tribunal created by the Rome Statute, which has charged Benjamin Netanyahu with war crimes and crimes against humanity. John Kiriakou supports it as the necessary successor to Nuremberg, notes that neither the United States nor Israel is a signatory, and observes that a forced landing in a signatory state would oblige that country to arrest Netanyahu.

netanyahu-arrest-poll.title: Graham–Netanyahu ICC tapes
netanyahu-arrest-poll.summary: Recordings of Lindsey Graham coordinating with Benjamin Netanyahu on how to discredit the International Criminal Court over its arrest warrant. On the tapes Graham lines up Senate signatories for a protest letter, jokes that he should be paid "tons of shekels," and asks Netanyahu to telephone two Democratic senators to thank them. John Kiriakou argues the conduct meets the definition of espionage his own judge applied to him.

netanyahu-arrest-poll.title: Hague Invasion Act
netanyahu-arrest-poll.summary: The American statute, described by John Kiriakou as having been passed during the Obama administration, that authorises the president to use the United States military to invade the Netherlands and free an American or allied national held by the International Criminal Court — the standing legal answer to the possibility that Benjamin Netanyahu might be arrested abroad.

netanyahu-arrest-poll.title: Ahmed Chalabi
netanyahu-arrest-poll.summary: Iraqi exile and founder of the Iraqi National Congress; per John Kiriakou, a Shia-Kurdish con man who looted Petra Bank in Jordan of $36 million in the 1980s, was sentenced to death in absentia, was pardoned at CIA request, then pocketed $6 million in CIA seed funding for the INC and bought a Mayfair house in cash; later resurrected by Dick Cheney to feed the Pentagon fabricated WMD intelligence used to justify the 2003 invasion of Iraq.

netanyahu-in-hiding.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
netanyahu-in-hiding.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

netanyahu-in-hiding.title: Itamar Ben-Gvir
netanyahu-in-hiding.summary: Israel's far-right Minister of National Security; John Kiriakou cites him as a convicted hate-crime felon placed in charge of security in Gaza and the West Bank over his victims, blames his insistence that any attack would come from the West Bank for diverting forces before October 7, and cites the death-penalty law passed under his portfolio for Palestinian detainees as the first reinstatement of capital punishment in Israel since it was abolished in 1956, excepting only the execution of Adolf Eichmann.

netanyahu-in-hiding.title: Targeting information between allies
netanyahu-in-hiding.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that Russian targeting support to Iran during the 2026 war was unremarkable rather than scandalous — the same thing the United States was doing for Ukraine, the Soviet Union did for North Vietnam, and Washington did for the Afghan mujahideen. His conclusion is that the way to stop it is to ask Moscow directly.

netanyahu-in-hiding.title: Trump Iran Ceasefire Efforts
netanyahu-in-hiding.summary: Per John Kiriakou, Donald Trump reached out behind the scenes twice in ten days seeking a ceasefire with Iran and was rebuffed; Kiriakou also says Benjamin Netanyahu called the White House to check reports of the outreach, and that on foreign policy Netanyahu "has just as much authority as whoever happens to be president of the United States."

netanyahu-in-hiding.title: Cost of the 2026 Iran war
netanyahu-in-hiding.summary: The daily cost of the 2026 Iran war as John Kiriakou reported it — between two and three billion dollars a day, per Axios — and the comparison he draws with the Gulf War, when a president was rendered speechless by a figure of one hundred million dollars a day.

netanyahu-in-hiding.title: Donald Trump
