The complaint went to the Justice Department rather than the oversight committees, and its prose, he says, is lawyers' prose rather than the uniform CIA analytic style every analyst is trained into. He is nonetheless emphatic that naming the man was indefensible.

presidential-call-memcons.title: National Security Council
presidential-call-memcons.summary: The White House body that, in John Kiriakou's telling, sat on the pro-war side of every fight that defined his era — gung-ho for the Iraq invasion alongside Cheney's and Rumsfeld's offices while the CIA, State Department, and Joint Chiefs opposed it; the place where an official predicted Iraqis would "throw flowers at us"; a signature stop in the approval chain for both the torture program and covert action findings; and the perch from which John Brennan, as its number two, urged the Justice Department to secretly reopen the case against Kiriakou.

presidential-call-memcons.title: Chuck Grassley
presidential-call-memcons.summary: The senior senator from Iowa, and in John Kiriakou's assessment the one member of Congress who has taken whistleblower protection seriously as a legislative project — a count he has variously put at one finger, at two names, and at four out of 535. Grassley wrote the whistleblower protection statutes, speaks every year at the National Whistleblower Day luncheon, and is the name Kiriakou gives prospective whistleblowers as the single friendly ear on Capitol Hill. Kiriakou's personal verdict is colder — Grassley, he has said, never did anything for him.

presidential-call-memcons.title: Gina Haspel
presidential-call-memcons.summary: Director of the Central Intelligence Agency under President Trump's first term; known to John Kiriakou and others at the CIA as "Bloody Gina"; per Kiriakou, flew out to the secret black site to sit in on one of the enhanced-interrogation torture sessions "just because she could," personally supervised the torture of USS Cole bombing suspect Rahim al-Nashiri, and later fed the CIA's torture tapes into an industrial document grinder after being explicitly told by White House Counsel not to destroy them.

presidential-call-memcons.title: Leaker versus whistleblower
presidential-call-memcons.summary: The fight over what the American networks would call John Kiriakou. It took his lawyers, above all Jesselyn Radack, a year of work between January 2012 and January 2013 to get CNN and MSNBC to stop introducing him as 'CIA leaker John Kiriakou'. CNN changed and Fox, he notes, never needed to; MSNBC in his account never did, and Rachel Maddow settled on a formula he quotes with some precision — a man 'who styles himself a whistleblower'.

presidential-call-memcons.title: Over-classification
presidential-call-memcons.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of why the American government classifies far more than it can ever review: not conspiracy but incentive. At lesser agencies a classification stamp is a status marker — it puts you in the in-crowd and above the colleague who lacks access — and at the CIA everything carries a stamp by default. His complaint about press coverage of classified-document scandals is that it never reaches the underlying question of why the documents were secret at all.

presidents-and-the-cia.title: Allen Dulles
presidents-and-the-cia.summary: Long-serving CIA director whom John Kiriakou calls a 'monster' and a 'very dark figure in American history' — a United Fruit board member who ran the agency that overthrew Guatemala's Árbenz, who went to Truman's house to talk him out of criticising the CIA, and who stayed in touch with the men Kiriakou believes killed John F. Kennedy.

presidents-and-the-cia.title: Andrew Bustamante
presidents-and-the-cia.summary: Former CIA officer who sells CIA-style training online; John Kiriakou identifies him as the lone critic of his work hosting a show on a Russian network, and argues Bustamante's training business — open to anyone who pays — is the more problematic of the two.

presidents-and-the-cia.title: Barack Obama
presidents-and-the-cia.summary: 44th U.S. president; in John Kiriakou's account, Obama publicly recounted refusing Benjamin Netanyahu's demand to bomb Iran and calling Israel's threat to use nuclear weapons a bluff — a bluff Kiriakou says Donald Trump later believed.

presidents-and-the-cia.title: Bill Burns
presidents-and-the-cia.summary: Career U.S. diplomat named CIA director in 2021, and the one senior appointment John Kiriakou has endorsed without qualification — a man he has known for thirty years, "apolitical to a fault," untouched by torture, Guantánamo or the secret prisons, and the only figure he thought had the standing to reform the agency. Kiriakou wrote an op-ed calling him "finally, an adult in the room," and says Burns ended up serving as the Biden administration's de facto Secretary of State before being drawn into the CIA's culture of drone warfare, rendition and domestic spying.

presidents-and-the-cia.title: Church Committee
presidents-and-the-cia.summary: U.S. Senate investigative committee operating in 1975–1976 that examined domestic intelligence abuses by the CIA, FBI, and NSA; per John Kiriakou, the Church Committee — alongside the concurrent Pike Committee in the House — was the last genuine moment of legislative oversight over the intelligence community, born of a national consensus that government had gone dangerously off course. Its work led to the creation of the permanent Senate Select Committee on Intelligence, which Kiriakou says ceased to function as real oversight roughly seven years after its founding.

presidents-and-the-cia.title: Central Intelligence Agency
presidents-and-the-cia.summary: U.S. foreign intelligence service; John Kiriakou's employer from 1990 to 2004 and the central institution of KiriPedia

presidents-asleep-in-meetings.title: The Ann Coulter dinner
presidents-asleep-in-meetings.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of an unplanned dinner in Los Angeles around 2016 at which a college friend arrived with Ann Coulter, and of finding her interesting, well-informed and lovely — from which he concludes that the public hatred she trades in is an act, and one he says she has seriously cashed in on.

presidents-asleep-in-meetings.title: Barrett Brown
presidents-asleep-in-meetings.summary: American journalist and former Anonymous associate whom John Kiriakou describes as one of the most intelligent writers and analysts he has ever encountered, with long-standing mental health problems and a two-decade heroin addiction he has now been clear of for at least a year, expelled from the United Kingdom and relocated to Mexico.

presidents-asleep-in-meetings.title: Censorship on the left
presidents-asleep-in-meetings.summary: John Kiriakou''s observation that he was censored far less by Forbes and Fortune than by The Nation and Mother Jones, which he offers as an instance of a general rule that a writer''s own side censors them hardest — the counterpart to Ted Rall''s account of being made to fit a particular kind of leftism rather than any kind.

presidents-asleep-in-meetings.title: Dr Oz and the Armenian hospices
presidents-asleep-in-meetings.summary: John Kiriakou''s reaction to a television segment by Mehmet Oz alleging fraud by Armenian-run hospices in Los Angeles — that a man he identifies as a veteran of the Turkish special forces zeroing in on Armenians in California is not a coincidence, and that each of the administration''s appointees appears to arrive with a racial scandal of their own.

presidents-asleep-in-meetings.title: The Iron Dome
presidents-asleep-in-meetings.summary: Israel's air-defence system as John Kiriakou reads it — impressive against a wave of slow Iranian drones, but shown by the handful that got through, and later by Iranian ballistic missiles, to be not all it is cracked up to be; each exchange, in his account, buying Iran intelligence about the gaps.

presidents-asleep-in-meetings.title: James Morris
presidents-asleep-in-meetings.summary: A close friend of John Kiriakou''s who served seventeen years of a twenty-year sentence for a crime committed at sixteen, found on release that a violent felony conviction closed off employment, made his own way to Turkey and across the border into Syria, spent two years fighting alongside the Kurds against ISIS, and later took his own life.

presidents-daily-brief.title: Central Intelligence Agency
presidents-daily-brief.summary: U.S. foreign intelligence service; John Kiriakou's employer from 1990 to 2004 and the central institution of KiriPedia

presidents-daily-brief.title: John Kiriakou
presidents-daily-brief.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

presidents-daily-brief.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
presidents-daily-brief.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

presidents-daily-brief.title: Democratic redistricting collapse
presidents-daily-brief.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of why Republicans remain competitive despite historically low approval ratings: a 1992 decision he attributes to Hillary Clinton to spend only in presidential battlegrounds, which he says ceded state legislatures and the congressional map for decades.

presidents-daily-brief.title: Cheney's airstrip question
presidents-daily-brief.summary: A one-line request from Vice President Dick Cheney — what is the longest airstrip in northern Iraq made of? — that nobody in the CIA's operations directorate could answer, and that John Kiriakou eventually resolved by asking the agency librarian. The answer came back within a day, with the exact mix. The purpose was to work out whether the runway would take a transport aircraft carrying two tanks.

presidents-daily-brief.title: James Woolsey
presidents-daily-brief.summary: Director of Central Intelligence for twenty-three months at the start of the Clinton administration, forced out over his refusal to discipline anyone after the exposure of Aldrich Ames, and later chairman of Booz Allen Hamilton; John Kiriakou notes that his family attributed four years of illness before his death to Havana syndrome.

press-tv-website-seizure.title: The 2022 deplatforming
press-tv-website-seizure.summary: The removal of John Kiriakou's radio programme from every major podcast platform after Russia's invasion of Ukraine, on the basis of his work for Sputnik News — preceded, he says, by a Washington Post article and a CSIS paper arguing that his weekly segment on American prison conditions was Russian propaganda weakening American democracy.

press-tv-website-seizure.title: Julian Assange
press-tv-website-seizure.summary: Kiriakou — a 15-year friend and former WikiLeaks board member — on why Assange is a publisher owed a journalist's immunity, and a political prisoner.

press-tv-website-seizure.title: Ed Schultz
press-tv-website-seizure.summary: American broadcaster, a friend of John Kiriakou''s and later his colleague at RT, whom Kiriakou cites twice over: as a man forbidden by MSNBC to discuss Bernie Sanders during a primary, and as a dead man still being labelled a Russian government mouthpiece four years after his death.

press-tv-website-seizure.title: Kiriakou's Russian media work
press-tv-website-seizure.summary: John Kiriakou's account of hosting a daily Sputnik radio show for seven and a half years with full contractual freedom to criticize anyone, including Putin — which he did on the morning of the Ukraine invasion — offered as a rebuttal to claims that Russian outlets are mere propaganda.

press-tv-website-seizure.title: Panquake
press-tv-website-seizure.summary: Open-source, blockchain-based social platform developed by the Iceland-registered company Talk Liberation, for which John Kiriakou has served as brand ambassador since 2020. Kiriakou describes it as advertising-free, subscription-funded, free of back doors, and run on servers powered by Icelandic geothermal steam — a project he frames as a David-and-Goliath fight against banks, big technology and governments.

press-tv-website-seizure.title: The state-affiliated media labels
press-tv-website-seizure.summary: The warning tags applied by social media platforms from 2020 identifying accounts as mouthpieces of foreign governments, which John Kiriakou describes checking his own account for daily. His standing example of how indiscriminate the practice became is the labelling of Ed Schultz, who had been dead for years.

pricewaterhousecoopers.title: China as economic threat
pricewaterhousecoopers.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that China is the real threat to the West not militarily — it has one aircraft carrier to America's two dozen and rarely invades — but economically, buying friends worldwide while the U.S. spends a trillion dollars a year on weapons.

pricewaterhousecoopers.title: Kiriakou's transfer to the Directorate of Operations
pricewaterhousecoopers.summary: John Kiriakou's roughly two-month internal campaign to transfer from the CIA's analytic Directorate of Intelligence to the operational Directorate of Operations, overcoming what he calls a "natural bias in operations against the eggheads on the analytic side," followed by an Athens posting secured because he was the only person in the entire CIA fluent in both Greek and Arabic. Covers his full CIA career arc from 1988/1990 recruitment through analyst years on Iraq, the switch to operations, 9/11, the enhanced-interrogation refusal, executive assistant to the deputy director for operations, and his eventual resignation and post-CIA career.

pricewaterhousecoopers.title: Central Intelligence Agency
pricewaterhousecoopers.summary: U.S. foreign intelligence service; John Kiriakou's employer from 1990 to 2004 and the central institution of KiriPedia

pricewaterhousecoopers.title: Dead drop
pricewaterhousecoopers.summary: The classic tradecraft technique of passing material through a hidden location rather than a meeting. Per John Kiriakou, the hard part is not the drop but everything around it — in a sophisticated counterintelligence environment, merely identifying a viable site is very difficult, and the drop itself is bracketed by surveillance detection routes and a signal mark that can turn a single document into a sixteen-hour workday. It was the only element of clandestine training he struggled with, and the only exercise he was ever criticized for.

pricewaterhousecoopers.title: Iran 12-Day War
pricewaterhousecoopers.summary: 2025 Israeli air campaign against Iran during which Israel killed at least fourteen Iranian nuclear scientists by destroying the apartment buildings they lived in; preceded for each scientist by Farsi-language telephone calls from Iranian-Jewish Mossad and Shin Bet officers offering defection in lieu of certain death; characterized by John Kiriakou as a categorical departure from CIA targeting doctrine in its acceptable-civilian-casualty calculus.

pricewaterhousecoopers.title: JFK assassination
pricewaterhousecoopers.summary: November 22, 1963 killing of President John F. Kennedy in Dallas, Texas. John Kiriakou's position, drawn from a Pakistan-station encounter with Bay of Pigs commander Jean Gately, an RFK Jr. account of CIA Director John McCone's same-day exchange with Bobby Kennedy Sr., and a White House contact's confirmation that the remaining classified Kennedy documents all contain the word "Israel," is that elements of the CIA were probably involved and that Israeli intelligence was involved as well.

prince-andrew.title: Peter Mandelson
prince-andrew.summary: British politician; described by John Kiriakou as the former British ambassador to Washington and as someone likely to be charged with serious crimes in connection with Jeffrey Epstein.

prince-andrew.title: "All it takes is a signature"
prince-andrew.summary: John Kiriakou's answer, drawn from his years as a Senate investigator, to the claim that Congress had run out of time to obtain the Epstein flight logs — that a committee's investigative power is exercised by one senator signing a piece of paper, which can be done at any hour, and that the excuse is therefore not a sensible one.

prince-andrew.title: Les Wexner
prince-andrew.summary: Ohio billionaire retail magnate; John Kiriakou cites Vanity Fair allegations that Wexner funneled millions to Jeffrey Epstein as his 'tax advisor,' offering it as evidence for his own view that Epstein's money and access served the Israelis.

prince-andrew.title: Signal and the parking lot
prince-andrew.summary: John Kiriakou's account of how a clandestine source is actually contacted — an innocuous telephone question with a pre-agreed answer standing for a time and a place fixed in advance, and a physical signal such as the flowerpot on Bob Woodward's balcony — offered as the reason investigators looking for an email trail between a service and its agent will not find one.

prince-andrew.title: The Epstein files and the Starmer government
prince-andrew.summary: John Kiriakou's prediction that the Epstein disclosures could bring down Keir Starmer's government, on the strength of evidence that Prince Andrew and Peter Mandelson gave Epstein classified British Ministry of Defence documents — an Official Secrets Act matter that in America would fall under the Espionage Act.

prince-andrew.title: Eli Cohen
prince-andrew.summary: Israeli Mossad spy who infiltrated Damascus in the early 1960s under cover as a wealthy Syrian-Argentine businessman; per John Kiriakou, he was on the verge of being named deputy defense minister of Syria before being detected through a burst-transmission intercept and publicly hanged.

prince-muhammad-bin-naif.title: Anwar al-Awlaki
prince-muhammad-bin-naif.summary: American-born al-Qaeda propagandist; in 1993 the imam of the Falls Church, Virginia mosque visited by John Kiriakou's CIA Arabic-language class on a field trip; in 2001 the cleric at whose mosque the 9/11 hijackers prayed the night before the attacks; killed by U.S. drone strike in Yemen in approximately 2011.

prince-muhammad-bin-naif.title: Yemen
prince-muhammad-bin-naif.summary: Country on the southern Arabian Peninsula; setting of five John Kiriakou trips between 1990 and approximately 2010, spanning the country's brief unification, its civil war, and its present condition as a high-threat operating environment for U.S. and allied diplomatic personnel.

prince-muhammad-bin-naif.title: China's base in Djibouti
prince-muhammad-bin-naif.summary: Camp Lemonnier in Djibouti, the abandoned French base the Djiboutians offered to the Americans and the Chinese took a share of — split down the middle by a chain-link fence, the only Chinese military installation outside China, and the centrepiece of John Kiriakou's argument that China is not an expansionist power.

prince-muhammad-bin-naif.title: Djibouti
prince-muhammad-bin-naif.summary: The small Horn of Africa state a few miles across the water from Yemen that hosts Camp Lemonnier — the American drone base for the Yemen and Somalia wars, inherited from the departing French, and shared with China's only overseas military base behind a fence down the middle, in what John Kiriakou calls the worst kept secret in the world.

prince-muhammad-bin-naif.title: Admiral William Crowe
prince-muhammad-bin-naif.summary: Former Chairman of the U.S. Joint Chiefs of Staff and former CENTCOM commander who had lived in Bahrain, author of the "pound for pound" formula every Bahraini and every American ambassador quotes, and the visiting dignitary John Kiriakou was assigned to escort — a week that ended with the Bahraini Prime Minister refusing to let go of Kiriakou's hand.

prince-muhammad-bin-naif.title: The Grasshopper
prince-muhammad-bin-naif.summary: A recruited terrorist source John Kiriakou ran under a cryptonym, who called him after midnight on a dedicated burner, met him behind a church with a paper bag of his wife's gold jewellery, and was given five thousand dollars from station funds as what the chief of station called an early Christmas bonus.

principals-committee-meeting.title: MOSSAD
principals-committee-meeting.summary: Israel's primary external intelligence service; characterized by John Kiriakou as universally hostile in his and his CIA colleagues' professional dealings with it ("never had a positive encounter with Mossad"); operates almost exclusively in the operational rather than analytical domain; the CIA is, per Kiriakou, categorically forbidden from spying on it.

principals-committee-meeting.title: Iraq WMD intelligence
principals-committee-meeting.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of how the case for Iraqi weapons of mass destruction was fabricated: the intelligence community''s consensus was that Iraq had no WMD, but the White House had already decided to invade and sought analysis to fit the policy.

principals-committee-meeting.title: Dick Cheney
principals-committee-meeting.summary: U.S. Vice President under George W. Bush. Per John Kiriakou — recounting CIA Director George Tenet's memoir — Cheney intercepted the presidential finding authorizing the CIA's enhanced interrogation program in the Oval Office anteroom and took it from Tenet before Bush could sign it. Tenet later concluded the president probably never actually signed the finding and probably told the truth when he said he had no idea the program was taking place. Kiriakou characterizes Cheney as the one who actually ran foreign policy, intelligence policy, and defense policy during the Bush years.

principals-committee-meeting.title: Saddam Hussein
principals-committee-meeting.summary: President of Iraq from 1979 until the 2003 U.S. invasion; subject of John Kiriakou's CIA portfolio from January 1990 onward, in which capacity Kiriakou became, at age 25, "Saddam Hussein's intelligence community biographer" and the analyst who briefed President George H. W. Bush in the Oval Office on the morning of the 1990 invasion of Kuwait.

principals-committee-meeting.title: Condoleezza Rice
principals-committee-meeting.summary: U.S. National Security Advisor on 9/11; John Kiriakou had a meeting booked with her that morning, watched her tell George Tenet to "take one for the team" rather than correct the record on Abu Zubaydah, and offers her failure to act on the CIA's warnings as his alternative to any theory that the attacks were allowed to happen.

principals-committee-meeting.title: Bahrain Posting (1994–1996)
principals-committee-meeting.summary: John Kiriakou's 1994–1996 assignment to Bahrain under U.S. State Department cover as second secretary for economic affairs — arriving with his wife Joanne and infant son Chris on August 1, 1994, into a tiny Gulf monarchy whose sectarian tensions erupted, two months later, into the first Intifada.

prison-as-temporary-duty.title: John Kiriakou
prison-as-temporary-duty.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

prison-as-temporary-duty.title: Heather Kiriakou
prison-as-temporary-duty.summary: John Kiriakou's wife, a senior CIA analyst who — in his account — was one of the best analysts in the entire intelligence community and who lost her job at the agency for no reason other than being married to him. She sat off camera at his December 2007 ABC News interview and told him afterwards that he had said nothing classified.

prison-as-temporary-duty.title: CIA crimes reports against Kiriakou
prison-as-temporary-duty.summary: The referral mechanism by which the Central Intelligence Agency asked the Justice Department to investigate John Kiriakou, used not once but repeatedly — by his account after every op-ed, television interview and university speech he gave following his 2007 disclosure of the torture program. The Justice Department declined every time, and Kiriakou treats the pattern as retaliation conducted through a lawful channel.

prison-as-temporary-duty.title: Abu Zubaydah
prison-as-temporary-duty.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

prison-as-temporary-duty.title: Amir
prison-as-temporary-duty.summary: The pseudonym John Kiriakou gives the Muslim, ethnically Arab domestic officer sent on temporary duty to Pakistan to help with the Abu Zubaydah hunt — the colleague who drove them into India by GPS, drank the roadside tea and had diarrhoea for six weeks, and invented the textile-baron cover story on the spot.

prison-as-temporary-duty.title: Barack Obama
prison-as-temporary-duty.summary: 44th U.S. president; in John Kiriakou's account, Obama publicly recounted refusing Benjamin Netanyahu's demand to bomb Iran and calling Israel's threat to use nuclear weapons a bluff — a bluff Kiriakou says Donald Trump later believed.

prison-cell-transfers.title: Cleanliness in prison
prison-cell-transfers.summary: John Kiriakou's account of hygiene and order at FCI Loretto — where everybody showered daily on pain of a beating, everybody was constantly cleaning, and the rules on possessions and bedmaking left almost no room for clutter.

prison-cell-transfers.title: Dave Phillips
prison-cell-transfers.summary: The FCI Loretto prisoner who claimed to have been a CIA operations officer and whom John Kiriakou exposed as a fake by testing him on agency vocabulary — a possessive, risk-taking companion who planted shanks on a pedophile, was caught, and was shipped to another prison.

prison-cell-transfers.title: Frank Russo
prison-cell-transfers.summary: The former auditor of Cuyahoga County, Ohio, who shared a bunk with John Kiriakou at FCI Loretto — a corruption defendant who cooperated against Jimmy Dimora, was marked in prison as a rat, and whom Kiriakou describes as a sweetheart with a hilarious sense of humour who won everybody over anyway.

prison-cell-transfers.title: Marlon Beard
prison-cell-transfers.summary: The career drug dealer who shared a cell with John Kiriakou at FCI Loretto and told him to keep writing when shakedowns over the Letters from Loretto were being used to provoke the other prisoners against him — advice Kiriakou credits with making him double down.

prison-cell-transfers.title: Prison nicknames
prison-cell-transfers.summary: The naming convention John Kiriakou describes at FCI Loretto — where nearly every Black and Hispanic prisoner went by a nickname, most white prisoners did not, and the nickname rather than the legal name was what a man gave when signing up for the basketball tournament.

prison-cell-transfers.title: Sewer trout
prison-cell-transfers.summary: The name prisoners at FCI Loretto gave the fish served on Fridays — which John Kiriakou says arrived in boxes stacked illegally behind the serving line, marked Alaskan cod, product of China, and not for human consumption, feed use only.

prison-chapel-job.title: Bureau of Prisons
prison-chapel-job.summary: The federal agency that ran John Kiriakou's incarceration — and one of his most persistent post-prison targets. The BOP overrode his judge's camp recommendation by deeming him "a threat to the public safety," threatened him with "diesel therapy" until 1,600 logged phone calls and letters from a dozen House members and two senators backed it off, and, per Kiriakou, functions as "an employment agency for unemployable semi-literate rural white men" and "a dumping ground for failed medical professionals" — an agency for which a prisoner's death is cheaper than his treatment.

prison-chapel-job.title: Intelligence Identities Protection Act
prison-chapel-job.summary: U.S. law enacted in 1982 that makes it a crime to knowingly disclose the identity of a covert intelligence officer; per John Kiriakou, his 2012 prosecution under the act arose from confirming a single surname of a former CIA colleague to a journalist — a confirmation that was never published. The name passed through a chain from journalist to Human Rights Watch to Guantanamo defense attorneys before reaching a judge and ultimately the FBI, which traced it back to Kiriakou.

prison-chapel-job.title: Private prison system
prison-chapel-job.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the U.S. private prison industry as an incentive to keep beds filled and cut costs on food and medicine — illustrated by the 'sewer trout,' dog-food, and dead-rat-in-the-Kool-Aid stories from his own incarceration.

prison-chapel-job.title: Solitary confinement
prison-chapel-job.summary: The prison isolation practice the United Nations calls a form of torture; John Kiriakou, drawing on his own ten days in a six-by-sixteen-foot cell, argues that jailing depressed prisoners like Daniel Hale in solitary 'for their own safety' is precisely what drives them to suicide.

prison-chapel-job.title: FCI Loretto
prison-chapel-job.summary: U.S. Federal Correctional Institution in Loretto, Pennsylvania; the low-medium-security prison at which John Kiriakou served 23 months of a 30-month sentence following his 2013 Espionage Act–era plea deal; the originally ordered "minimum security work camp" placement was countermanded — per Kiriakou, on Brennan's direct intervention — to place him in the actual prison alongside the general population.

prison-chapel-job.title: Raymond Davis Lahore shooting
prison-chapel-job.summary: A 2011 incident in Lahore, Pakistan in which CIA contractor Raymond Davis shot and killed two Pakistani men who approached his car with drawn guns; per John Kiriakou, Davis stayed at the scene per CIA "getting off the X" tradecraft, and the consulate SUV sent to rescue him struck and killed an uninvolved bystander en route.

prison-cleanliness.title: Cell transfers at Loretto
prison-cleanliness.summary: How a prisoner at FCI Loretto moved from one cell to another — a process requiring six months in place, the written agreement of the receiving cell and the signature of the counselor, which John Kiriakou describes as a guard assigned to be a designated pain in the ass.

prison-cleanliness.title: FCI Loretto
prison-cleanliness.summary: U.S. Federal Correctional Institution in Loretto, Pennsylvania; the low-medium-security prison at which John Kiriakou served 23 months of a 30-month sentence following his 2013 Espionage Act–era plea deal; the originally ordered "minimum security work camp" placement was countermanded — per Kiriakou, on Brennan's direct intervention — to place him in the actual prison alongside the general population.

prison-cleanliness.title: The dog food memo
prison-cleanliness.summary: The internal announcement circulated by the warden of FCI Loretto apologising for having served prisoners dog food on a taco night, which John Kiriakou cites as evidence not of the error but of how bad the ordinary food was — because nobody noticed.

prison-cleanliness.title: Prison nicknames
prison-cleanliness.summary: The naming convention John Kiriakou describes at FCI Loretto — where nearly every Black and Hispanic prisoner went by a nickname, most white prisoners did not, and the nickname rather than the legal name was what a man gave when signing up for the basketball tournament.

prison-cleanliness.title: Sewer trout
prison-cleanliness.summary: The name prisoners at FCI Loretto gave the fish served on Fridays — which John Kiriakou says arrived in boxes stacked illegally behind the serving line, marked Alaskan cod, product of China, and not for human consumption, feed use only.

prison-cleanliness.title: Blue
prison-cleanliness.summary: The FCI Loretto correctional officer, widely considered the most unpopular in the prison, who covered his own nameplate with masking tape so released prisoners could not find him — and who told a colleague of John Kiriakou's that he would never touch the CIA man because of the press attention.

prison-commissary.title: Bureau of Prisons
prison-commissary.summary: The federal agency that ran John Kiriakou's incarceration — and one of his most persistent post-prison targets. The BOP overrode his judge's camp recommendation by deeming him "a threat to the public safety," threatened him with "diesel therapy" until 1,600 logged phone calls and letters from a dozen House members and two senators backed it off, and, per Kiriakou, functions as "an employment agency for unemployable semi-literate rural white men" and "a dumping ground for failed medical professionals" — an agency for which a prisoner's death is cheaper than his treatment.

prison-commissary.title: Arianna Huffington
prison-commissary.summary: Founder of the Huffington Post and the accidental amplifier who turned John Kiriakou's prison writing into a phenomenon. His first Letter from Loretto went to his attorney, then to a friend running Firedoglake who — unknown to Kiriakou — was close to Huffington; she plastered it as a banner headline and it drew over a million hits, bringing CNN and 60 Minutes to the prison gates. She published his open letter to Snowden, ran the diesel-therapy exposé that triggered the "hands off John Kiriakou" campaign, and came to Loretto herself with two young journalists.

prison-commissary.title: Freedom of Information Act
prison-commissary.summary: The U.S. transparency law that runs through John Kiriakou's story from every direction — his plea agreement banned him from ever filing a FOIA request on himself, so he filed one with the Bureau of Prisons anyway and got back pages stamped "FOIA EXEMPT — DO NOT RELEASE TO INMATE"; a FOIA request exposed the prison commissary skim; Jason Leopold's requests revealed that a detainee's eye was removed under sedation without his knowledge and that NBC's Ken Dilanian sent his stories to the CIA before his own editor; and a FOIA request is how Kiriakou learned Gary Johnson had quietly lobbied for his early release.

prison-commissary.title: Paul Wright
prison-commissary.summary: The former prisoner who founded the Human Rights Defense Center and co-created Prison Legal News — the longest-running publication produced by and for current and former prisoners in American history — and whose reporting John Kiriakou draws on for the finding that the Bureau of Prisons' own grievance system increases prison violence.

prison-commissary.title: Prison tattoos
prison-commissary.summary: Tattoos as John Kiriakou encountered them at FCI Loretto — the swastika-necked welcoming committee on his first day, the Lady Justice piece that made him laugh and then think, the constant pressure on him to get one, and his flat refusal to take a souvenir of the place.

prison-commissary.title: Jake Tapper
prison-commissary.summary: CNN anchor who drove to FCI Loretto to interview the imprisoned John Kiriakou — and who asked President Obama at a press conference why he had insisted on prosecuting a man who exposed a crime, a question Obama answered by walking away from the podium. Tapper's visit was the head of a media wave that began with a smuggled-out letter on the Huffington Post, and it became Kiriakou's protection inside; even a guard known as a psychopath left him alone rather than find CNN parked beside his car.

prison-depression.title: Passing time at Loretto
prison-depression.summary: How prisoners at FCI Loretto filled days John Kiriakou describes as Groundhog Day — working out and watching television on a set of screens divided between factions, while Kiriakou himself read, answered mail and wrote a book.

prison-depression.title: Seven thousand letters
prison-depression.summary: The correspondence John Kiriakou conducted from FCI Loretto — 7,000 letters to 675 different people over 23 months, begun because of an unsolicited postcard of a rose that reached him four hours into his sentence.

prison-depression.title: FCI Loretto
prison-depression.summary: U.S. Federal Correctional Institution in Loretto, Pennsylvania; the low-medium-security prison at which John Kiriakou served 23 months of a 30-month sentence following his 2013 Espionage Act–era plea deal; the originally ordered "minimum security work camp" placement was countermanded — per Kiriakou, on Brennan's direct intervention — to place him in the actual prison alongside the general population.

prison-depression.title: Rule six: the body endures more than the brain says
prison-depression.summary: The CIA maxim John Kiriakou carried into prison — that the human body can take much more punishment than the brain believes — which he applied first to being punched in the face and then, more importantly, to depression.

prison-depression.title: Dave Phillips
prison-depression.summary: The FCI Loretto prisoner who claimed to have been a CIA operations officer and whom John Kiriakou exposed as a fake by testing him on agency vocabulary — a possessive, risk-taking companion who planted shanks on a pedophile, was caught, and was shipped to another prison.

prison-depression.title: The shank planting incident
prison-depression.summary: The episode at FCI Loretto in which Dave Phillips made two homemade weapons, planted them on a pedophile the group was feuding with and informed on him anonymously — a plan John Kiriakou refused to join, and which cost Phillips a transfer while leaving Kiriakou untouched.

prison-foia-request.title: Blue
prison-foia-request.summary: The FCI Loretto correctional officer, widely considered the most unpopular in the prison, who covered his own nameplate with masking tape so released prisoners could not find him — and who told a colleague of John Kiriakou's that he would never touch the CIA man because of the press attention.

prison-foia-request.title: FCI Loretto

prison-foia-request.title: Marlon Beard
prison-foia-request.summary: The career drug dealer who shared a cell with John Kiriakou at FCI Loretto and told him to keep writing when shakedowns over the Letters from Loretto were being used to provoke the other prisoners against him — advice Kiriakou credits with making him double down.

prison-foia-request.title: The stinger
prison-foia-request.summary: The improvised prison cooking rig John Kiriakou describes at FCI Loretto — a wall-plug faceplate wired to live current and dropped into a bucket of water — which produced restaurant-quality Italian food daily and, on one occasion, killed a correctional officer.

prison-foia-request.title: Dave Phillips
prison-foia-request.summary: The FCI Loretto prisoner who claimed to have been a CIA operations officer and whom John Kiriakou exposed as a fake by testing him on agency vocabulary — a possessive, risk-taking companion who planted shanks on a pedophile, was caught, and was shipped to another prison.

prison-foia-request.title: The dog food memo
prison-foia-request.summary: The internal announcement circulated by the warden of FCI Loretto apologising for having served prisoners dog food on a taco night, which John Kiriakou cites as evidence not of the error but of how bad the ordinary food was — because nobody noticed.

prison-food-economy.title: The Italians at Loretto
prison-food-economy.summary: The mafia contingent at FCI Loretto — men with last names like Gambino, Bonanno, Lucchese, Genovese, DeCavalcante — who adopted John Kiriakou in his second year, largely because he hated the FBI as much as they did. The cast included the boss of the Gambino family (in on a dozen-plus murder counts, the man who replaced John Gotti), Pete the Bonanno captain across the hall who asked why he sat "with those Nazi retards," and a crooked guard on the payroll delivering pork loin and fresh mozzarella. prison-food-economy.title: Medical care in federal prison
prison-food-economy.summary: Kiriakou's account of health care at FCI Loretto, where a bunkmate's months of reported chest pain ended in a heart attack, a prisoner with untreated back pain was diagnosed with terminal cancer weeks before he died, and Kiriakou himself collapsed after being handed a drug nobody had explained to him.

prison-food-economy.title: John Kiriakou
prison-food-economy.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

prison-food-economy.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
prison-food-economy.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

prison-guard-hiring-standards.title: The suicide watch protocol
prison-guard-hiring-standards.summary: The federal suicide watch procedure as John Kiriakou describes it from inside — a room with windows on four sides, volunteer prisoners watching in four-hour shifts around the clock, and paper sheets that cannot be knotted — which he uses to enumerate, step by step, everything that failed in the case of Jeffrey Epstein.

prison-guard-hiring-standards.title: Kiriakou on wine
prison-guard-hiring-standards.summary: John Kiriakou's long-standing interest in wine — a subscription to Wine Spectator running a quarter of a century, a climate-controlled cellar built into his house, an eye that has twice caught a host passing off a cheap bottle as something better, and a professional life in which wine served in turn as cover story, surveillance-detection errand, recruitment currency and diplomatic catastrophe.

prison-guard-hiring-standards.title: Correctional officers at FCI Loretto
prison-guard-hiring-standards.summary: Kiriakou's portraits of the staff at FCI Loretto — including two officers who tried to trick him into a fight, a lieutenant forced out of several prisons for harassment, and an officer whose abuse of prisoners he successfully reported.

prison-guard-hiring-standards.title: Business class after 9/11
prison-guard-hiring-standards.summary: John Kiriakou''s illustration of what the post-attack money did to the CIA''s habits: Cofer Black telling him to just do whatever operation he was proposing because there was so much money it could not possibly be spent, and everyone at the agency flying business class from then on, anywhere in the world.

prison-guard-hiring-standards.title: ''Don''t try to save the government money''
prison-guard-hiring-standards.summary: The instruction John Kiriakou says a CIA supervisor gave him for parking in the nine-dollar economy lot at Dulles instead of the twenty-five-dollar daily lot, and the two trips it produced: a Pittsburgh approach funded entirely by a five-dollar bill, and a $195 fattoush salad in a Dubai nightclub.

prison-guard-hiring-standards.title: The General Muhammad equipment gift
prison-guard-hiring-standards.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the end of the Abu Zubaydah operation in Pakistan, when headquarters told him to throw away or hand over the truckloads of equipment his station had bought — and of learning weeks later from his day-to-day Pakistani contact that the brigadier general who accepted the gift had simply taken it all himself.

prison-legal-news.title: Administrative remedy process
prison-legal-news.summary: The Bureau of Prisons' internal grievance system, which Kiriakou describes as a fig leaf designed to run out the clock on prisoners' complaints rather than resolve them.

prison-legal-news.title: Medical care in federal prison
prison-legal-news.summary: Kiriakou's account of health care at FCI Loretto, where a bunkmate's months of reported chest pain ended in a heart attack, a prisoner with untreated back pain was diagnosed with terminal cancer weeks before he died, and Kiriakou himself collapsed after being handed a drug nobody had explained to him.

prison-legal-news.title: Paul Wright
prison-legal-news.summary: The former prisoner who founded the Human Rights Defense Center and co-created Prison Legal News — the longest-running publication produced by and for current and former prisoners in American history — and whose reporting John Kiriakou draws on for the finding that the Bureau of Prisons' own grievance system increases prison violence.

prison-legal-news.title: Bureau of Prisons
prison-legal-news.summary: The federal agency that ran John Kiriakou's incarceration — and one of his most persistent post-prison targets. The BOP overrode his judge's camp recommendation by deeming him "a threat to the public safety," threatened him with "diesel therapy" until 1,600 logged phone calls and letters from a dozen House members and two senators backed it off, and, per Kiriakou, functions as "an employment agency for unemployable semi-literate rural white men" and "a dumping ground for failed medical professionals" — an agency for which a prisoner's death is cheaper than his treatment.

prison-legal-news.title: Larry
prison-legal-news.summary: The prisoner at FCI Loretto who complained of back pain for more than a year, was given Tylenol, and progressed from a cane to a walker to a wheelchair before a chaplain forced an outside hospital referral — which found stage four cancer of the spine. He died in his bunk two weeks later.

prison-legal-news.title: Kiriakou on mass incarceration
prison-legal-news.summary: The argument Kiriakou developed in the letters from Loretto and has repeated since: that the United States holds a quarter of the world''s prisoners with five per cent of its people, that the cause is the drug war and election-year legislating, and that reform died in the Senate without a vote.

prison-medical-care.title: Prison Legal News
prison-medical-care.summary: The longest-running publication produced by and for current and former prisoners in American history, co-founded by former prisoner Paul Wright, and a recurring source in Kiriakou's account of Bureau of Prisons practice.

prison-medical-care.title: Kiriakou on mass incarceration
prison-medical-care.summary: The argument Kiriakou developed in the letters from Loretto and has repeated since: that the United States holds a quarter of the world''s prisoners with five per cent of its people, that the cause is the drug war and election-year legislating, and that reform died in the Senate without a vote.

prison-medical-care.title: Paul Wright
prison-medical-care.summary: The former prisoner who founded the Human Rights Defense Center and co-created Prison Legal News — the longest-running publication produced by and for current and former prisoners in American history — and whose reporting John Kiriakou draws on for the finding that the Bureau of Prisons' own grievance system increases prison violence.

prison-medical-care.title: The Public Health Service in the prisons
prison-medical-care.summary: John Kiriakou's contrast between the United States Public Health Service officers he worked with during fifteen years at the CIA, whom he found excellent, and the Public Health Service physician assistants he encountered as a prisoner at FCI Loretto, whom he describes as the dregs of the service — people dumped into the Bureau of Prisons because they could not work anywhere else in government.

prison-medical-care.title: The suicide watch protocol
prison-medical-care.summary: The federal suicide watch procedure as John Kiriakou describes it from inside — a room with windows on four sides, volunteer prisoners watching in four-hour shifts around the clock, and paper sheets that cannot be knotted — which he uses to enumerate, step by step, everything that failed in the case of Jeffrey Epstein.

prison-medical-care.title: Frank's heart attack
prison-medical-care.summary: The 65-year-old insulin-dependent diabetic who shared a cell with John Kiriakou at FCI Loretto, reported chest tightness for months, was given Tylenol and a request for an EKG that the regional office never approved, and collapsed in the insulin line.

prison-nicknames.title: Cell transfers at Loretto
prison-nicknames.summary: How a prisoner at FCI Loretto moved from one cell to another — a process requiring six months in place, the written agreement of the receiving cell and the signature of the counselor, which John Kiriakou describes as a guard assigned to be a designated pain in the ass.

prison-nicknames.title: FCI Loretto
prison-nicknames.summary: U.S. Federal Correctional Institution in Loretto, Pennsylvania; the low-medium-security prison at which John Kiriakou served 23 months of a 30-month sentence following his 2013 Espionage Act–era plea deal; the originally ordered "minimum security work camp" placement was countermanded — per Kiriakou, on Brennan's direct intervention — to place him in the actual prison alongside the general population.

prison-nicknames.title: Cleanliness in prison
prison-nicknames.summary: John Kiriakou's account of hygiene and order at FCI Loretto — where everybody showered daily on pain of a beating, everybody was constantly cleaning, and the rules on possessions and bedmaking left almost no room for clutter.

prison-nicknames.title: The dog food memo
prison-nicknames.summary: The internal announcement circulated by the warden of FCI Loretto apologising for having served prisoners dog food on a taco night, which John Kiriakou cites as evidence not of the error but of how bad the ordinary food was — because nobody noticed.

prison-nicknames.title: Passing time at Loretto
prison-nicknames.summary: How prisoners at FCI Loretto filled days John Kiriakou describes as Groundhog Day — working out and watching television on a set of screens divided between factions, while Kiriakou himself read, answered mail and wrote a book.

prison-nicknames.title: Depression in prison
prison-nicknames.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the condition he says everybody inside has, and the three-part regime he set against it — eating right, exercising daily and finding a distraction — which in his own case meant more than a hundred books, 7,000 letters and a book written in longhand.

prison-pedophile-accounts.title: 2026 Iran war
prison-pedophile-accounts.summary: The open-ended American and Israeli war against Iran that John Kiriakou tracked week by week on his own show — a conflict he says was sold as three weeks, ran into its fifth month, achieved every decapitation objective it set, and continued anyway. His grade for it is a D, and his forecast is a Truth Social post declaring victory while nothing changes.

prison-pedophile-accounts.title: Abolish the CIA
prison-pedophile-accounts.summary: John Kiriakou's position that the CIA should be abolished because its functions are already duplicated by the other 17 U.S. intelligence agencies — analysis by the State Department, human spying by the Pentagon, technology by DARPA, NSA and the private sector.

prison-pedophile-accounts.title: Adnan Khashoggi
prison-pedophile-accounts.summary: Saudi arms dealer and Iran-Contra middleman whom John Kiriakou says was mentioned 'all the time' at the CIA — in pointed contrast to Jeffrey Epstein, whose name he never once heard there.

prison-pedophile-accounts.title: AIPAC
prison-pedophile-accounts.summary: The American Israel Public Affairs Committee — the U.S. political organization that, in John Kiriakou's framing, ought to be registered as a foreign-lobbying entity but is not, and that wields decisive electoral power against U.S. elected officials who express support for Palestinian human rights.

prison-pedophile-accounts.title: CIA culture of lying
prison-pedophile-accounts.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of deception as an occupational condition at the CIA — the tradecraft of detecting it, the training that instils it, and the institutional rot he says follows when officers cannot switch it off: a deputy director who married five successive secretaries, promotion panels that traded advancement for sex, and staff psychiatrists overheard planning how to push a colleague toward resignation or suicide.

prison-pedophile-accounts.title: The CIA Insider's Guide to Surveillance and Surveillance Detection
prison-pedophile-accounts.summary: Book by John Kiriakou drawing on his experience as a surveillance detection instructor at the CIA and as a private surveillance training consultant. The book covers the techniques used by intelligence professionals to identify whether they are being followed — including the four-phase surveillance detection route, concealment device placement and retrieval, and counter-surveillance strategy — adapted for use by corporate executives, journalists, and others who want to confirm whether they are being followed.

prison-phone-monitoring.title: Correctional officers at FCI Loretto
prison-phone-monitoring.summary: Kiriakou's portraits of the staff at FCI Loretto — including two officers who tried to trick him into a fight, a lieutenant forced out of several prisons for harassment, and an officer whose abuse of prisoners he successfully reported.

prison-phone-monitoring.title: Doing Time Like a Spy
prison-phone-monitoring.summary: Prison memoir by John Kiriakou, full title Doing Time Like a Spy: How the CIA Taught Me to Survive and Thrive in Prison; winner of two literary awards and reissued in a second edition by Simon and Schuster.

prison-phone-monitoring.title: The prison visiting room
prison-phone-monitoring.summary: The room where a federal prisoner sees his family, reached through a strip-search cell — where John Kiriakou's children came to accept where their father was, where a former CIA boss turned up unannounced, and which is closed entirely to prisoners held under special administrative measures.

prison-phone-monitoring.title: Solitary confinement
prison-phone-monitoring.summary: The prison isolation practice the United Nations calls a form of torture; John Kiriakou, drawing on his own ten days in a six-by-sixteen-foot cell, argues that jailing depressed prisoners like Daniel Hale in solitary 'for their own safety' is precisely what drives them to suicide.

prison-phone-monitoring.title: Central Intelligence Agency
prison-phone-monitoring.summary: U.S. foreign intelligence service; John Kiriakou's employer from 1990 to 2004 and the central institution of KiriPedia

prison-phone-monitoring.title: Espionage Act
prison-phone-monitoring.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

prison-racial-segregation.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
prison-racial-segregation.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

prison-racial-segregation.title: Kiriakou's transfer to the Directorate of Operations
prison-racial-segregation.summary: John Kiriakou's roughly two-month internal campaign to transfer from the CIA's analytic Directorate of Intelligence to the operational Directorate of Operations, overcoming what he calls a "natural bias in operations against the eggheads on the analytic side," followed by an Athens posting secured because he was the only person in the entire CIA fluent in both Greek and Arabic. Covers his full CIA career arc from 1988/1990 recruitment through analyst years on Iraq, the switch to operations, 9/11, the enhanced-interrogation refusal, executive assistant to the deputy director for operations, and his eventual resignation and post-CIA career.

prison-racial-segregation.title: Kiriakou prison manipulation tactics
prison-racial-segregation.summary: John Kiriakou's account of applying CIA tradecraft — including deliberate deception, forged paperwork, and manipulating other inmates into violence — to protect himself and control his environment during his federal prison sentence.

prison-racial-segregation.title: Mark Lanzotti
prison-racial-segregation.summary: John Kiriakou's best friend in prison — an Italian sentenced to triple life without parole for a first-time nonviolent meth conspiracy he was the only man to voluntarily leave; Kiriakou wrote the appeal that won his release, and he is now the top-selling realtor on the Jersey Shore.

prison-service-economy.title: John's rules for prison survival
prison-service-economy.summary: The code John Kiriakou says he wrote for himself at FCI Loretto out of his CIA training — rule one, recruit prisoners as sources using the same motivations the agency teaches; rule two, seek cover and blend in — illustrated with a plan to obtain contraband binder clips.

prison-service-economy.title: The chapel job
prison-service-economy.summary: The work assignment John Kiriakou was given at FCI Loretto after he volunteered to teach a class — *"if I want you to teach a class I'll ask you to teach a class"* — and was made a janitor in the chapel instead, at $1.08 a month.

prison-service-economy.title: Ten-minute moves and the count
prison-service-economy.summary: The clock that governs a federal prison: a fixed daily timetable, movement permitted only during ten-minute windows on the hour, and five counts a day — two standing, three conducted with a flashlight in the face of a sleeping man, which John Kiriakou argues serve no purpose except sleep disruption.

prison-service-economy.title: The prison commissary
prison-service-economy.summary: The federal prison store as John Kiriakou describes it: a captive market with a flat thirty per cent mark-up whose proceeds were supposed to buy library books and athletic equipment for prisoners and instead bought a large-screen television for the guards'' lounge — a diversion he established through a Freedom of Information Act request.

prison-service-economy.title: Raymond Davis Lahore shooting
prison-service-economy.summary: A 2011 incident in Lahore, Pakistan in which CIA contractor Raymond Davis shot and killed two Pakistani men who approached his car with drawn guns; per John Kiriakou, Davis stayed at the scene per CIA "getting off the X" tradecraft, and the consulate SUV sent to rescue him struck and killed an uninvolved bystander en route.

prison-tattoos.summary: The white prison gang that adopted John Kiriakou on his first day at FCI Loretto. Two hours in, two Aryans with swastika neck tattoos walked into his cell to check his paperwork — not a rat, not a "chomo" — and invited him to the Aryan table, which ran from hardcore Nazis at one end to merely white guys at the other. A rumor that he had been a CIA assassin earned him the nickname "the Muslim killer," which he never corrected; asked directly, he answered "we all did stuff we weren't proud of — it was wartime," and the Aryans loved it. He sat with them a year before the Italians took him in.

prison-visiting-room.title: Thomas Drake
prison-visiting-room.summary: NSA whistleblower; per John Kiriakou, the source for the statement that on the morning of September 11, 2001, NSA Director Mike Hayden told agency personnel NSA had been 'waiting for a 9/11' to implement the mass-electronic-surveillance program that NSA's founding charter forbids.

prison-visiting-room.title: Julian Assange
prison-visiting-room.summary: Kiriakou — a 15-year friend and former WikiLeaks board member — on why Assange is a publisher owed a journalist's immunity, and a political prisoner.

prison-visiting-room.title: Prison phone monitoring
prison-visiting-room.summary: Kiriakou treated the recording of his prison telephone calls as an intelligence channel rather than a constraint, planting messages for staff he knew were listening — a practice that produced a confrontation with a lieutenant over the word 'Nimrod'.

prison-visiting-room.title: Correctional officers at FCI Loretto
prison-visiting-room.summary: Kiriakou's portraits of the staff at FCI Loretto — including two officers who tried to trick him into a fight, a lieutenant forced out of several prisons for harassment, and an officer whose abuse of prisoners he successfully reported.

prisoner-disposition-from-pakistan.title: The first prisoner who cooperated
prisoner-disposition-from-pakistan.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of the first al-Qaeda prisoner in Pakistan who agreed to talk to him, the reason the man gave — that he was a prisoner and got nothing out of refusing — and the intelligence that followed: a foot-by-foot description of his crossing from Afghanistan and the locations of safe houses that were then raided.

prisoner-disposition-from-pakistan.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
prisoner-disposition-from-pakistan.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

prisoner-disposition-from-pakistan.title: The families of the captured
prisoner-disposition-from-pakistan.summary: John Kiriakou's statement that the wives and children of men captured in the post-9/11 raids in Pakistan were separated from them and sent back to their home countries — and that the prisoners were not told, and were left believing their wives were still in American custody.

prisoner-disposition-from-pakistan.title: Afghan heroin policy
prisoner-disposition-from-pakistan.summary: The post-2001 U.S. policy in Afghanistan of protecting, and per John Kiriakou actively encouraging, the cultivation of heroin poppy. Under the Taliban in 2000 Afghanistan produced 0% of the world's heroin; by 2009 under American occupation it produced 93%. Per a DEA officer Kiriakou consulted with on the policy paper he was preparing for Senator Kerry, the strategic rationale was that nearly all of the heroin flowed to Iran and Russia, addiction in those countries was considered desirable as a long-run societal weakener, and the same logic now operates in reverse with Chinese fentanyl flowing into the United States.

prisoner-disposition-from-pakistan.title: Tora Bora
prisoner-disposition-from-pakistan.summary: Mountainous cave complex in eastern Afghanistan that served as an al-Qaeda redoubt after the September 11 attacks. Per John Kiriakou — chief of counterterrorism operations in Pakistan at the time — the CIA killed al-Qaeda military-affairs chief Mohammed Atef there in October 2001, and Tora Bora was the backdrop to the hunt for the senior al-Qaeda leadership that culminated in the capture of Abu Zubaydah. Kiriakou also recounts an Egyptian al-Qaeda fighter he later recruited who survived a cruise-missile strike on a Tora Bora cave — one of only two who came out alive, his ears bleeding, describing the explosion as the most hideous sound he had ever heard.

prisoner-disposition-from-pakistan.title: Abu Zubaydah
prisoner-disposition-from-pakistan.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

private-intelligence.title: Arrais Corporation
private-intelligence.summary: Private intelligence firm; companion entity to The Analysis Corporation; originally an LLC pass-through for retired Senior Intelligence Service personnel from the CIA's operations side; subsequently acquired by IBM for over $1 billion.

private-intelligence.title: Abraxas Corporation
private-intelligence.summary: The private intelligence company founded in the 1990s by retired CIA operations officers as a tax pass-through and a place to smoke cigars and tell stories — which, after 9/11, made its founders, in John Kiriakou's phrase, Mega Millions rich.

private-intelligence.title: The Analysis Corporation
private-intelligence.summary: Arlington, Virginia–based [private intelligence firm](/wiki/private-intelligence); one of two companion entities (alongside Arrais Corporation) created as LLC pass-throughs for retired Senior Intelligence Service personnel; John Brennan was appointed its CEO in 2005.

private-intelligence.title: No-bid contracts
private-intelligence.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of the mechanism he considers the real corruption of American national security: an officer retires on a Friday, returns Monday on a contractor badge at ten times the salary, and is fed no-bid contracts by the friends he left behind — including, in one unnamed case he describes, a tax shelter that became a multi-billion dollar company inside a decade.

private-intelligence.title: The Cypriot billionaire's investigation
private-intelligence.summary: The six-week private-intelligence job John Kiriakou describes as operational rather than analytic: a Cypriot billionaire wanted to know about the man engaged to his only daughter, and Kiriakou bribed a police captain in Cyprus, ran surveillance in London, and reported back that the fiancé was a thief with drug convictions.

private-intelligence.title: The Oman oil lease
private-intelligence.summary: A private-intelligence assignment in which an oil company that had leased a field on Oman's border with Yemen for ninety-nine years discovered al-Qaeda controlled the ground, and sent John Kiriakou to Muscat to ask whether the Omani government would clear them out.

private-prison-system.title: Overcriminalization
private-prison-system.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that the United States criminalizes too much — locking up 25% of the world's prisoners with 5% of its population, and adding roughly 50 new felonies a year — illustrated by a NOAA employee prosecuted for whistling at a whale.

private-prison-system.title: Doing Time Like a Spy
private-prison-system.summary: Prison memoir by John Kiriakou, full title Doing Time Like a Spy: How the CIA Taught Me to Survive and Thrive in Prison; winner of two literary awards and reissued in a second edition by Simon and Schuster.

private-prison-system.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
private-prison-system.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

private-prison-system.title: FCI Loretto
private-prison-system.summary: U.S. Federal Correctional Institution in Loretto, Pennsylvania; the low-medium-security prison at which John Kiriakou served 23 months of a 30-month sentence following his 2013 Espionage Act–era plea deal; the originally ordered "minimum security work camp" placement was countermanded — per Kiriakou, on Brennan's direct intervention — to place him in the actual prison alongside the general population.

private-prison-system.title: Donnie Reynolds Jr.
private-prison-system.summary: Tennessee businessman and antique-firearms collector serving a life-plus-75-year federal sentence at the Communications Management Unit in Terre Haute, Indiana; per John Kiriakou and Marty Gottesfeld, a scapegoat for the fallout of the ATF's Operation Fast and Furious after refusing to become an undercover cartel weapons source.

private-prison-system.title: The sentencing reform bills that died
private-prison-system.summary: The bipartisan legislation John Kiriakou watched from prison and campaigned for afterwards — the Recidivism Reduction and Public Safety Act and the Smarter Sentencing Act, alongside a Sentencing Commission move to lower drug guidelines — which would have freed thousands and abolished most mandatory minimums, and which died in the Senate without a vote. Kiriakou blames two majority leaders and two attorneys general, and sets out both the arithmetic behind the bills and the limiting principle he attaches to them.

progressive-taxation.title: The Trumpcare confusion
progressive-taxation.summary: A television interview John Kiriakou says he watched, in which a woman from Arkansas wept with gratitude to President Trump because a website had insured her son's cancer treatment — and, told by the reporter that this was in fact the Affordable Care Act, insisted that Obamacare had been repealed and replaced and that what she had was Trumpcare.

progressive-taxation.title: The Speaker's office as gatekeeper
progressive-taxation.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of how legislative power moved in the mid-1990s from committee chairmen and the Rules Committee into the office of the Speaker of the House, where it has stayed because no subsequent Speaker has wanted to give it back — and the member of Congress who explained the death of his own whistleblower bill in four words: ''Nancy said I couldn''t.''

progressive-taxation.title: Think tank financing
progressive-taxation.summary: John Kiriakou's warning that Washington's think tanks — more than 1,200 of them by a Washington Post count — must be read through their funding, illustrated with the case of someone close to him who controlled about $200,000 a year in donations for a Fortune 100 defence contractor and moved the money when a household-name institute proved insufficiently pro-contractor.

progressive-taxation.title: Lobbyists writing legislation
progressive-taxation.summary: John Kiriakou''s first-hand account from the Senate Foreign Relations Committee: told that the committee would take part in the carbon offsets debate and protesting that he knew nothing about carbon offsets, he was told not to worry — and the next day strangers came into the office, took over most of the desks, logged on and began writing the bill.

progressive-taxation.title: The Iron Dome
progressive-taxation.summary: Israel's air-defence system as John Kiriakou reads it — impressive against a wave of slow Iranian drones, but shown by the handful that got through, and later by Iranian ballistic missiles, to be not all it is cracked up to be; each exchange, in his account, buying Iran intelligence about the gaps.

progressive-taxation.title: The tax rates from Eisenhower to Nixon
progressive-taxation.summary: John Kiriakou's explanation for the American wealth gap and the size of the deficit — that from Eisenhower through Nixon the top rate of tax ran upwards of seventy-five per cent and the wealthy whittled it down from there, whereas now they begin at almost nothing and whittle down from that.

project-gateway.title: MK-Ultra
project-gateway.summary: The CIA's mid-twentieth-century umbrella program of mind-control, behavioral-modification, and biological-warfare experimentation, encompassing subprojects such as MK-Chickwit and MK-Seesaw; active 1952–1975; documented practices included LSD dosing of unwitting American citizens in CIA-rented brothels and the aerosolized release of pathogens into the San Francisco fog; 80% of the program's documentation was destroyed by the CIA in defiance of a 1975 preservation order from Senator Frank Church.

project-gateway.title: Executive Order 12333
project-gateway.summary: The U.S. presidential directive — in its post-9/11 amended form — that grants the CIA the legal authority to kill any individual anywhere in the world deemed by the agency to pose a "clear and present danger" to the United States; the legal foundation underlying both CIA paramilitary operations and the agency's contractor relationships including with Blackwater.

project-gateway.title: Family Jewels
project-gateway.summary: The CIA's internal catalogue of its own abuses, demanded in full by the Church and Pike Committees in 1975; per John Kiriakou, MK-Ultra and its assassination programs surfaced first, 85 percent of the MK-Ultra files were shredded in defiance of a direct order, and new officers were taught that everything in the file belonged to the era before 1975.

project-gateway.title: French village LSD bread experiment
project-gateway.summary: John Kiriakou's account of a compartmented MK-Ultra experiment in which the CIA dosed the only bakery of a small French village he does not name with LSD — in some tellings by breaking in at night and spiking the yeast, in others by contaminating the flour supplied to it — so that the hapless baker sold the whole village an unwitting trip. Kiriakou places it as the sequel to the San Francisco bacterium release and calls it, in the agency's own terms, a successful operation.

project-gateway.title: Alexa
project-gateway.summary: Per John Kiriakou, Amazon''s Alexa smart speaker reports directly to the NSA — and he owns one anyway. The device recurs across his interviews as the standing example of the surveillance trade-off in modern smart-home technology, and of his own negotiated exception to it: one speaker, in one room, against the advice of every intelligence officer he has ever known.

project-gateway.title: CIA adultery culture
project-gateway.summary: John Kiriakou's recurring characterization of the CIA officer corps as riddled with adultery and casual sex — which he frames not as gossip but as a systemic counterintelligence vulnerability that makes officers easy to recruit.

project-stargate.title: Russell Targ
project-stargate.summary: Named in a post-produced narration segment appended to an interview featuring John Kiriakou, describing Targ as an original Stanford Research Institute scientist behind government remote-viewing protocols — not a claim made by Kiriakou himself, who elsewhere expresses skepticism that remote viewing ever worked.

project-stargate.title: Espionage Act
project-stargate.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

project-stargate.title: Gina Haspel
project-stargate.summary: Director of the Central Intelligence Agency under President Trump's first term; known to John Kiriakou and others at the CIA as "Bloody Gina"; per Kiriakou, flew out to the secret black site to sit in on one of the enhanced-interrogation torture sessions "just because she could," personally supervised the torture of USS Cole bombing suspect Rahim al-Nashiri, and later fed the CIA's torture tapes into an industrial document grinder after being explicitly told by White House Counsel not to destroy them.

project-stargate.title: Overcriminalization
project-stargate.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that the United States criminalizes too much — locking up 25% of the world's prisoners with 5% of its population, and adding roughly 50 new felonies a year — illustrated by a NOAA employee prosecuted for whistling at a whale.

project-stargate.title: Private prison system
project-stargate.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the U.S. private prison industry as an incentive to keep beds filled and cut costs on food and medicine — illustrated by the 'sewer trout,' dog-food, and dead-rat-in-the-Kool-Aid stories from his own incarceration.

promotion-panel.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
promotion-panel.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

promotion-panel.title: Jose Rodriguez
promotion-panel.summary: Senior CIA officer of the post-9/11 era; identified by John Kiriakou as among those responsible for crimes committed in the name of national security; described as believing himself to be a good guy.

promotion-panel.title: New Castle, Pennsylvania
promotion-panel.summary: John Kiriakou's home town, an hour north of Pittsburgh on the edge of Amish country — a rust-belt city of roughly 40,000 to 50,000 people when he was growing up and around 18,000 to 20,000 now, whose decline he measures by the arrival of DEA and ATF field offices. It is also where, aged eight or nine and hunting salamanders in Oak Park Cemetery, he found the grave of a Medal of Honor private and acquired the lifelong interest in cemeteries that became a book.

promotion-panel.title: Counterterrorism Center
promotion-panel.summary: The CIA's Counterterrorism Center (CTC) — the unit where John Kiriakou spent the defining years of his operational career. He joined in the late 1990s as the only officer in the entire CIA fluent in both Greek and Arabic, served as chief of counterintelligence in the bin Laden unit, watched the Center swell from a few hundred employees to nearly 2,000 by September 12, 2001, and it was to CTC that he walked back down in May 2002 to refuse the torture program — the moment, he says, the CIA began to turn on him.

promotion-panel.title: Dick Cheney
promotion-panel.summary: U.S. Vice President under George W. Bush. Per John Kiriakou — recounting CIA Director George Tenet's memoir — Cheney intercepted the presidential finding authorizing the CIA's enhanced interrogation program in the Oval Office anteroom and took it from Tenet before Bush could sign it. Tenet later concluded the president probably never actually signed the finding and probably told the truth when he said he had no idea the program was taking place. Kiriakou characterizes Cheney as the one who actually ran foreign policy, intelligence policy, and defense policy during the Bush years.

promotion-panel.title: The Directorate of Operations
promotion-panel.summary: The CIA's clandestine service, which John Kiriakou joined from analysis because he spoke both Greek and Arabic — a culture he describes as wildly different from the analytic side, short on institutional memory and organised around the race to become a station chief.

propane-truck-ruse.title: The weapons cache map
propane-truck-ruse.summary: The single sheet of paper found inside an otherwise empty gun safe in the Middle East — a childlike map marked with an X and written directions past a palm tree and a large rock, which led John Kiriakou's team to a desert bunker packed to the ceiling with Hezbollah's arsenal.

propane-truck-ruse.title: Training foreign intelligence services
propane-truck-ruse.summary: The CIA job John Kiriakou took after returning from Athens — travelling the world to teach foreign services how to carry out counterterrorist raids, break down doors, seize people, conduct interrogations and disrupt cells — and why, he says, those countries asked the Americans rather than the Israelis or the British.

propane-truck-ruse.title: Double-Agent Capture
propane-truck-ruse.summary: Clandestine operation in which an intelligence service, having identified a recruited agent as working simultaneously for a hostile service, arranges a controlled final meeting to apprehend the agent before the agent can carry out orders — which may include killing the handler. Per John Kiriakou, he ran one such operation in the Middle East in the early 2000s after an NSA analyst warned him that his agent had just been ordered to shoot him in the next meeting.
