sandy-grimes.title: Rosario Ames
sandy-grimes.summary: Colombian cultural attaché recruited to work for the CIA, and the second wife of Aldrich Ames. Per John Kiriakou, Ames began an affair with her in Mexico in 1981 in violation of agency regulations; when he brought her and her mother to America his first marriage collapsed, and their taste for high living put him deep enough in debt that he walked into the Soviet embassy to sell it away. She was arrested alongside him at their Arlington home in 1994 and served four years of a 63-month sentence before returning to Colombia.

sandy-grimes.title: Warrenton Training Center
sandy-grimes.summary: A secret CIA communications facility in Warrenton, Virginia, which — per John Kiriakou — the KGB used as a decoy to protect Aldrich Ames. When Ames warned Moscow in 1986 that he feared becoming a suspect, a Soviet case officer told a CIA contact that the mole was posted to Warrenton; agency mole hunters then spent almost a year investigating ninety employees there and produced ten suspects, none of them Ames.

sara-jane-moore.title: Mike Mastrovito
sara-jane-moore.summary: Twenty-five-year Secret Service veteran; founder and first director of the Secret Service Intelligence Division; later, after a forced retirement, a CIA contractor specializing in Greek terrorism; close colleague of John Kiriakou in Athens. Started his career at the end of the Eisenhower administration, was in Dallas with President Kennedy, and was effectively removed from the Secret Service after Sara Jane Moore's 1975 attempt on President Ford — having interviewed Moore two weeks earlier on a threatening letter she had sent.

sara-jane-moore.title: Secret Service
sara-jane-moore.summary: The U.S. agency protecting the president. John Kiriakou, who worked alongside it for 35 years, describes a culture of complacency and poor follow-up — great with guns, weak on training and follow-through — and calls the 2024 Butler rally shooting a colossal historic screw-up in which coverage of the surrounding buildings was outsourced to a county sheriff's department. He has also encountered the Service as an adversary, outside the Venezuelan embassy in Washington in 2019.

sara-jane-moore.title: Permanent wartime economy
sara-jane-moore.summary: John Kiriakou's thesis that since 9/11 the United States has run a permanent wartime economy so large that cutting the defense budget would trigger a depression — likening the dependency to crack addiction and warning it makes war almost inevitable.

sara-jane-moore.title: Arnon Milchan
sara-jane-moore.summary: Israeli-American Hollywood producer and, per John Kiriakou, an Israeli super-spy and arms dealer for LAKAM; central to a Netanyahu corruption charge, and named in FBI documents alongside Netanyahu in the smuggling of U.S. nuclear secrets.

sara-jane-moore.title: BDS movement
sara-jane-moore.summary: The Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions movement against Israel; John Kiriakou notes that some 40 U.S. states now have anti-BDS laws that can require a speaker at a publicly funded university to sign a pledge of support for Israel — which he refuses to do.

sara-jane-moore.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
sara-jane-moore.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

sarah-adams.title: Iranian sleeper cells
sarah-adams.summary: John Kiriakou's assessment of Iran's clandestine reach abroad — that the IRGC and the Ministry of Intelligence and Security do run sleeper cells worldwide, but probably not in the United States, Canada or the UK, and that the greater danger is the unaffiliated lone attacker. He also argues Iranian operatives are consistently poor, and identifies the Gulf's real vulnerability as its tourist landmarks rather than its military bases.

sarah-adams.title: 2026 Iran war
sarah-adams.summary: The open-ended American and Israeli war against Iran that John Kiriakou tracked week by week on his own show — a conflict he says was sold as three weeks, ran into its fifth month, achieved every decapitation objective it set, and continued anyway. His grade for it is a D, and his forecast is a Truth Social post declaring victory while nothing changes.

sarah-adams.title: Andrew Bustamante
sarah-adams.summary: Former CIA officer who sells CIA-style training online; John Kiriakou identifies him as the lone critic of his work hosting a show on a Russian network, and argues Bustamante's training business — open to anyone who pays — is the more problematic of the two.

sarah-adams.title: John Kiriakou
sarah-adams.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

sarah-adams.title: The White House tip
sarah-adams.summary: A week and a half before the 2026 attack on Iran, John Kiriakou said publicly that a friend at the White House had told him the decision to attack had been made and that it would come the following Monday or Tuesday. A podcaster mocked him for it — how could a man twenty years out of the CIA know that? On the morning the strikes began, Kiriakou answered: people with access do call, because they are opposed to the war.

sarah-adams.title: "A policy support organization"
sarah-adams.summary: Asked how the CIA workforce would be reacting to the war on Iran, John Kiriakou answered from the Iraq war: people put their heads down and did as they were told, after a boss told an assembled group — all of whom opposed the invasion — that the agency is not a policy organization but a policy support organization, and would do what the White House told it to do.

sarge-the-guard.title: Legal mail
sarge-the-guard.summary: The privileged correspondence category John Kiriakou used to smuggle the Letters from Loretto and the manuscript of his book out of prison — addressed to his attorney Jesselyn Radack and marked legal mail, which staff were forbidden to open.

sarge-the-guard.title: Dave Phillips
sarge-the-guard.summary: The FCI Loretto prisoner who claimed to have been a CIA operations officer and whom John Kiriakou exposed as a fake by testing him on agency vocabulary — a possessive, risk-taking companion who planted shanks on a pedophile, was caught, and was shipped to another prison.

sarge-the-guard.title: Letter from Loretto
sarge-the-guard.summary: Prison newsletter written by John Kiriakou from FCI Loretto, modeled on Martin Luther King's "Letter from Birmingham Jail," which exposed two crimes committed against him by guards and went viral after being relayed to the Huffington Post, drawing national press to the prison.

sarge-the-guard.title: Seven thousand letters
sarge-the-guard.summary: The correspondence John Kiriakou conducted from FCI Loretto — 7,000 letters to 675 different people over 23 months, begun because of an unsolicited postcard of a rose that reached him four hours into his sentence.

sarge-the-guard.title: Arianna Huffington
sarge-the-guard.summary: Founder of the Huffington Post and the accidental amplifier who turned John Kiriakou's prison writing into a phenomenon. His first Letter from Loretto went to his attorney, then to a friend running Firedoglake who — unknown to Kiriakou — was close to Huffington; she plastered it as a banner headline and it drew over a million hits, bringing CNN and 60 Minutes to the prison gates. She published his open letter to Snowden, ran the diesel-therapy exposé that triggered the "hands off John Kiriakou" campaign, and came to Loretto herself with two young journalists.

sarge-the-guard.title: The Bob Jones frame-up
sarge-the-guard.summary: The operation John Kiriakou ran inside FCI Loretto against a man at his own cafeteria table — forging court papers in the prison law library from a genuine 1970s Ohio case involving a man of the same name, and using them to have him banished by the shot callers.

saud-nasir-al-sabah.title: Iraqi invasion of Kuwait
saud-nasir-al-sabah.summary: John Kiriakou''s most detailed account of the intelligence process around the 1990 Iraqi invasion of Kuwait and its 1991 liberation. As a first-year CIA analyst on a ''training account'' covering Iraq, Kiriakou produced the June 30, 1990 warning paper for the White House; suggested calling the US Defense Attaché in Baghdad to drive to the border and report what he saw (the answer: ''Literally the entire Iraqi military is heading south''); briefed the August 2 Oval Office meeting with Bush; and later took a single phone call from General Colin Powell that led, eight hours later, to 47 cruise missiles striking the Iraqi Intelligence Service headquarters in Baghdad.

saud-nasir-al-sabah.title: Sheikh Jaber al-Ahmad
saud-nasir-al-sabah.summary: Amir of Kuwait during the 1990 Iraqi invasion and the 1991 liberation; per John Kiriakou, "a very kind and decent man and a leader who genuinely loved and cared for his people"; the subject of a CIA cable Kiriakou wrote from Taif which led President George H. W. Bush to invite the Amir to Washington for "the red carpet treatment" — after which the Amir returned with renewed focus on driving the Iraqis out.

saud-nasir-al-sabah.title: Sheikh Saad al-Abdullah
saud-nasir-al-sabah.summary: Crown Prince and Prime Minister of Kuwait during the 1990–91 Iraqi occupation; per John Kiriakou, the day-to-day leader of the Kuwaiti government-in-exile in Taif — "very military," "hands-on," "the best leader Kuwait had for that situation," meeting twenty hours a day with everyone who needed to be met and simultaneously managing the Kuwaiti resistance on the ground.

saud-nasir-al-sabah.title: Skip Gnehm
saud-nasir-al-sabah.summary: U.S. Ambassador to Kuwait at the 1991 liberation; per John Kiriakou, "one of the finest men I've ever worked for anywhere in the world"; led the reopening of the U.S. embassy in Kuwait City on Liberation Day with the cable "American Embassy Kuwait City is now open for business"; famously complained that he could not stop Kuwaitis from writing pro-American graffiti on the side of the embassy.

saud-nasir-al-sabah.title: 1993 Bush Kuwait assassination plot
saud-nasir-al-sabah.summary: Iraqi intelligence plot, foiled by Kuwaiti authorities, to assassinate former President George H. W. Bush during his post-liberation "victory lap" visit to Kuwait; the U.S. response, per John Kiriakou's first-person account of his telephone call with Chairman of the Joint Chiefs Colin Powell, was 47 cruise missiles fired into the Iraqi Intelligence Service headquarters in Baghdad eight hours later.

saud-nasir-al-sabah.title: Afghan heroin policy
saud-nasir-al-sabah.summary: The post-2001 U.S. policy in Afghanistan of protecting, and per John Kiriakou actively encouraging, the cultivation of heroin poppy. Under the Taliban in 2000 Afghanistan produced 0% of the world's heroin; by 2009 under American occupation it produced 93%. Per a DEA officer Kiriakou consulted with on the policy paper he was preparing for Senator Kerry, the strategic rationale was that nearly all of the heroin flowed to Iran and Russia, addiction in those countries was considered desirable as a long-run societal weakener, and the same logic now operates in reverse with Chinese fentanyl flowing into the United States.

saudi-aid-priorities.title: The Saudi fear of an election
saudi-aid-priorities.summary: The explanation a Saudi diplomat gave John Kiriakou in the late 1990s for the royal family''s opposition to democracy in the kingdom: if there were an election in Saudi Arabia, Osama bin Laden would win it — a remark Kiriakou uses to argue that the regime''s problem was not that its princes loved al-Qaeda but that it feared its own population did.

saudi-aid-priorities.title: Saudi influence in Egypt

saudi-aid-priorities.title: The Yemen jazz radio plan

saudi-arabia-as-an-open-air-prison.title: The kafala sponsorship system
saudi-arabia-as-an-open-air-prison.summary: The Saudi sponsorship regime as John Kiriakou describes it — a Saudi national must own the majority of any company a foreigner works for, that sponsor holds the worker's passport, and a falling-out leaves the worker under effective house arrest, which he says is how South Asian women brought in as domestics are kept as sex slaves.

saudi-arabia-as-an-open-air-prison.title: The 1991 Saudi plan for Gaza
saudi-arabia-as-an-open-air-prison.summary: A proposal John Kiriakou says he watched Ambassador Chas Freeman float to the Saudis during his first overseas tour in 1991 — that Saudi Arabia fund a port, an airport, a desalination plant and an electrical grid in Gaza. The Saudis agreed; Israel refused outright. Kiriakou raises it because the identical arrangement resurfaced in the Israeli press more than three decades later.

saudi-arabia-as-an-open-air-prison.title: The Saudi demand for a political appointee
saudi-arabia-as-an-open-air-prison.summary: John Kiriakou's account of a standing Saudi condition on the American embassy in Riyadh — that the ambassador must never be a career diplomat, the opposite of what most countries want, because Riyadh wants someone whose telephone call the president of the United States will take.

saudi-arabia-as-an-open-air-prison.title: The Eric Adams ambassadorship
saudi-arabia-as-an-open-air-prison.summary: The September 2025 proposal, floated by Steve Witkoff, to remove Eric Adams from the New York mayoral race by offering him the embassy in Riyadh — which John Kiriakou thought likely to be attempted, on the reasoning that Donald Trump is not stupid, knows Adams cannot win, and would gain by forcing Zohran Mamdani to spend money.

saudi-arabia-as-an-open-air-prison.title: Aafia Siddiqui
saudi-arabia-as-an-open-air-prison.summary: Pakistani-American neuroscientist arrested in Afghanistan and convicted in the United States of attempting to shoot FBI agents; per John Kiriakou, who covered the arrest as a terrorism consultant for ABC News and has followed the case since, she never had a gun and never fired, the bullet holes offered as proof predated her capture, and the CIA took her three children — two later recovered, the youngest never found.

saudi-arabia-as-an-open-air-prison.title: Clive Stafford Smith
saudi-arabia-as-an-open-air-prison.summary: The British human rights lawyer who represents Aafia Siddiqui, described by John Kiriakou as a man who has never charged a client a dollar in his life, lives on donations, holds an OBE for his human rights work, and represented sixty-six Guantanamo detainees — securing the release of every one of them.

saudi-iran-diplomatic-rivalry.title: Djibouti
saudi-iran-diplomatic-rivalry.summary: The small Horn of Africa state a few miles across the water from Yemen that hosts Camp Lemonnier — the American drone base for the Yemen and Somalia wars, inherited from the departing French, and shared with China's only overseas military base behind a fence down the middle, in what John Kiriakou calls the worst kept secret in the world.

saudi-iran-diplomatic-rivalry.title: Donald Trump
saudi-iran-diplomatic-rivalry.summary: 45th and 47th U.S. president. Per John Kiriakou, a man genuinely convinced he was doing right by bombing Iran, "duped" by the same Netanyahu nuclear bluff Obama once rejected — and, at the same time, the most blindly pro-Israel president in history, an admirer of autocrats who has never once criticized Vladimir Putin, and prone to gestures — from the Gulf of America to a since-abandoned "Department of War" rename — that test the edges of his actual authority.

saudi-iran-diplomatic-rivalry.title: Kiriakou's daily news diet
saudi-iran-diplomatic-rivalry.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the wide range of mainstream and alternative outlets he reads each morning to compare competing angles, the two outlets — the Associated Press and ProPublica — he singles out as exceptional, and his broader habits of media consumption, from an admitted addiction to political polling to his distrust of AI chatbots after they repeatedly fabricated his own biography.

saudi-iran-diplomatic-rivalry.title: Russia-Ukraine war origins
saudi-iran-diplomatic-rivalry.summary: John Kiriakou's account that the war began in 2014, not 2022 — rooted in broken U.S. promises that NATO would not expand to Russia's borders, the 2014 removal of a pro-Russian Ukrainian leader, and the seizure of Crimea; he says Russia is now winning and has no reason to negotiate.

saudi-iran-diplomatic-rivalry.title: China as economic threat
saudi-iran-diplomatic-rivalry.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that China is the real threat to the West not militarily — it has one aircraft carrier to America's two dozen and rarely invades — but economically, buying friends worldwide while the U.S. spends a trillion dollars a year on weapons.

saudi-iran-diplomatic-rivalry.title: Code Pink
saudi-iran-diplomatic-rivalry.summary: The women-led peace group co-founded by Medea Benjamin. John Kiriakou first met them as a Senate staffer — he was the man who threw them out of a hearing he had produced, and got a lecture from Senator Shaheen for it. When he was arrested they were "right there next to me"; they threw his going-away party on the roof of the Hay-Adams, commissioned a folk group to sing a song rewritten about him, and quietly arranged for Roger Waters to pay off the second mortgage so his family could keep the house. He calls them his angels, and the one institution in American life he still trusts.

saudi-military-composition.title: The Hajj ban as leverage
saudi-military-composition.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer to what a Saudi retaliation against Iran would look like: not a military strike but a ban on Iranians making the pilgrimage to Mecca. He notes it was done at the turn of the 1980s, that it produced a crisis, and that Iranian terrorist attacks against Saudis followed.

saudi-military-composition.title: John Brennan
saudi-military-composition.summary: Former Director of the CIA; characterized in KiriPedia's source corpus as the principal architect of the agency's enhanced interrogation program and as having plotted against an elected President

saudi-military-composition.title: 2026 Iran war
saudi-military-composition.summary: The open-ended American and Israeli war against Iran that John Kiriakou tracked week by week on his own show — a conflict he says was sold as three weeks, ran into its fifth month, achieved every decapitation objective it set, and continued anyway. His grade for it is a D, and his forecast is a Truth Social post declaring victory while nothing changes.

saudi-military-composition.title: A.Q. Khan
saudi-military-composition.summary: Pakistani nuclear scientist and the architect of Pakistan's bomb, who ran a black-market proliferation network that, per John Kiriakou, smuggled nuclear material and technology to North Korea and Libya. Kiriakou says the U.S. could easily have killed him — 'we knew where he lived, we knew how he spent his day' — but the Saudi government insisted the U.S. leave him alone, which Kiriakou calls a grave mistake and speculates was because the Saudis were pursuing their own nuclear capability. Khan was eventually pardoned by Pervez Musharraf, ending all investigations.

saudi-military-composition.title: Iran Nuclear Assessment
saudi-military-composition.summary: Per John Kiriakou's assessment, the US–Israeli military campaign against Iran was a war of choice driven by Israeli political pressure rather than genuine intelligence indicating an Iranian nuclear weapons threat. The CIA produced two National Intelligence Estimates concluding Iran had no nuclear weapons program; Supreme Leader Ayatollah Khamenei issued a fatwa in the 1980s forbidding such a program. The U.S. went to war anyway, in Kiriakou's view, after President Trump replaced the Joint Chiefs of Staff with officers willing to accept Israeli intelligence and proceed.

saudi-nuclear-program.title: Dewey Clarridge
saudi-nuclear-program.summary: The CIA operations officer John Kiriakou calls a legendary figure and a giant of the 1980s — prosecuted over Iran-Contra, and the man who said publicly that Saudi Arabia already had nuclear weapons. Kiriakou believes him, holds that the Saudis financed the Pakistani bomb and were repaid in access to it, and believes Clarridge was also involved in the movement of cocaine into the United States.

saudi-nuclear-program.title: Jeffrey Epstein
saudi-nuclear-program.summary: Convicted sex offender; per John Kiriakou, was "an Israeli access agent" rather than a CIA asset, because the CIA collects foreign intelligence and Epstein's targets — Bill Clinton, Bill Gates, Prince Andrew — were not foreign. Kiriakou further holds that Epstein did die by suicide in federal custody, because in the Bureau of Prisons the cameras never work and the guards are always asleep.

saudi-nuclear-program.title: CIA Drug Facilitation
saudi-nuclear-program.summary: Per John Kiriakou, the CIA''s reported involvement in facilitating the arrival of cocaine into the United States during the era that became the crack epidemic, and his own firsthand discovery — as a Senate Foreign Relations Committee investigator — that under American military control Afghanistan produced 93% of the world''s heroin. A DEA contact told him the report would never be published because ''we want Iran and Russia to be addicted to heroin. It weakens their societies.'' Kiriakou draws a direct parallel to the current fentanyl crisis: China is doing to the US what the US did to Iran and Russia.

saudi-nuclear-program.title: Jack Devine
saudi-nuclear-program.summary: A former CIA officer John Kiriakou worked for briefly in 2001 or 2002, and describes with real warmth as a great officer and a true believer — while flatly rejecting his insistence that the agency was never involved with cocaine. Asked to choose between Devine and a thirty-year DEA veteran who agrees with him, Kiriakou picks the DEA man.

saudi-nuclear-program.summary: Senior CIA officer — a GS-15 who rose to chief of counterintelligence for the Soviet branch — who spied for the KGB for nine years. He went on to identify more than thirty agents, compromise over a hundred clandestine operations, cause at least twelve deaths and take more than $2 million, while being known throughout the agency as a daily drunk and promoted at every turn. The KGB protected him with a decoy mole hunt; analyst Sandy Grimes caught him by matching his handler meetings to his bank deposits.

saudi-nuclear-program.title: Ali Abdullah Saleh
saudi-nuclear-program.summary: President of Yemen for decades, close to both Saudi Arabia and the United States until Yemen's 1990 Security Council vote on Kuwait, after which his country collapsed into civil war; he fled to Saudi Arabia and was killed by a bomb planted in the palace where he had taken refuge.

saudi-pakistan-turkey-defense-pact.summary: John Kiriakou's account of what happened to the roughly one million Palestinians who had made up the middle class of Kuwait, Bahrain, the United Arab Emirates and Saudi Arabia, expelled en masse after the 1991 liberation of Kuwait as retaliation for the Palestine Liberation Organization's support for Saddam Hussein's invasion, and replaced with Filipino, Indian and Pakistani labour. Kiriakou treats it as the structural reason the Palestinians *"have never recovered"* and as the precedent for the Arab silence he sees today.

saudi-pakistan-turkey-defense-pact.summary: The recurring split John Kiriakou describes across successive U.S. wars, the CIA, the State Department, and the Joint Chiefs of Staff on one side counselling caution, and the office of the vice president, the office of the secretary of defense, and the National Security Council on the other pushing for military action, a division Kiriakou first heard laid out in May 2002 on his first day as executive assistant to the CIA's deputy director for operations, and which he says held again on Iran twenty-four years later.

saudi-pakistan-turkey-defense-pact.title: Laura Loomer
saudi-pakistan-turkey-defense-pact.summary: The American activist who publicly called John Kiriakou a Russian spy, a Russian asset and a common criminal. saudi-pakistan-turkey-defense-pact.title: Russia and NATO membership
saudi-pakistan-turkey-defense-pact.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the opening that was available with Moscow in the early 2000s and was refused — deep cooperation on terrorism, narcotics and proliferation offered only on terms of junior partnership, and approaches from both Yeltsin and Putin about joining NATO that met, in his words, the cold shoulder.

saudi-pakistan-turkey-defense-pact.title: The Hellenic Axis
saudi-pakistan-turkey-defense-pact.summary: The Greece-Cyprus-Israel bloc that Israeli officials framed in August 2026 as their strategic counterpoint to the Saudi-Pakistan-Turkey defense pact, an alignment John Kiriakou reads as Greek elites accepting an Israeli presence they can no longer control, while the Greek street pushes the other way. Kiriakou treats the Greek state's fear of Turkey as real, and the Israeli offer as a bargain Greeks will refuse in the 2027 elections.

saudi-princes-and-9-11.title: Abu Zubaydah
saudi-princes-and-9-11.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

saudi-princes-and-9-11.title: George Tenet
saudi-princes-and-9-11.summary: Director of Central Intelligence from 1997 to 2004, spanning the September 11 attacks and the early enhanced-interrogation program; identified by John Kiriakou as John Brennan's institutional patron at the agency; the figure who ordered the Five Eyes intelligence services to "open the files" to each other in the early 2000s.

saudi-princes-and-9-11.title: Carlos the Jackal
saudi-princes-and-9-11.summary: Venezuelan-born militant (Ilich Ramírez Sánchez) active in the 1970s and 1980s; per John Kiriakou, 'the Osama bin Laden of the 70s and 80s.' Kiriakou spent his Athens posting trying to identify the middleman linking Carlos to the Greek terrorist group 17 November, then six months working the lead with MI5 in London; Carlos was finally run down by CIA contractor Billy Waugh in a Khartoum vegetable market and captured in 1994.

saudi-princes-and-9-11.summary: Convicted sex offender; per John Kiriakou, was "an Israeli access agent" rather than a CIA asset, because the CIA collects foreign intelligence and Epstein's targets — Bill Clinton, Bill Gates, Prince Andrew — were not foreign. saudi-princes-and-9-11.summary: The CIA's mid-twentieth-century umbrella program of mind-control, behavioral-modification, and biological-warfare experimentation, encompassing subprojects such as MK-Chickwit and MK-Seesaw; active 1952–1975; documented practices included LSD dosing of unwitting American citizens in CIA-rented brothels and the aerosolized release of pathogens into the San Francisco fog; 80% of the program's documentation was destroyed by the CIA in defiance of a 1975 preservation order from Senator Frank Church.

savak.title: Mohammad Reza Pahlavi
savak.summary: The last Shah of Iran, whom John Kiriakou describes as an absolute monarch and dictator who ran a bloodthirsty intelligence service against his own citizens, held formal diplomatic relations with Israel, and sent Iran's oil to the United States and the United Kingdom. Restored to the throne after the 1953 overthrow of Mohammad Mosaddegh, he left the country on a ski vacation in February 1979 and never returned.

savak.title: 1953 Iran coup
savak.summary: The U.S.- and UK-backed overthrow of Iran's democratically elected prime minister, Mohammad Mossadegh; per John Kiriakou, the coup served British national interests rather than American ones, and the subsequent outlawing of secular political opposition under the Shah forced dissent into the mosques — producing a religious rather than secular revolution in 1979.

savak.title: Reza Pahlavi
savak.summary: The exiled Iranian crown prince whom John Kiriakou dismisses as an Israeli-backed fantasy candidate to rule Iran — a man who has not lived there since his teens, supported mainly by Beverly Hills exiles, whom Kiriakou says 'wouldn't survive the walk from the plane to the terminal.'

savak.title: Hillary Clinton
savak.summary: Former U.S. Secretary of State and 2016 presidential candidate; John Kiriakou describes her as arguably the most neoconservative candidate Democrats could have nominated, more militarist even than her husband, and credits her — separately — with correctly describing Iran as a military dictatorship run by the IRGC rather than a genuine theocracy.

savak.title: Kharg Island
savak.summary: The island where most of Iran's oil is refined, and in John Kiriakou's assessment a standing target whose destruction would be a crisis for world oil prices. It was bombed in the 1980s, causing a global price shock; Kiriakou considers a repeat by the United States or Israel possible, and expects the Iranians to answer it rather than absorb it.

savas-kalenderidis.title: The C-130 resettlements
savas-kalenderidis.summary: John Kiriakou''s confirmation that the Hmong communities of Minnesota were former CIA assets brought to the United States as refugees, and his extension of a rule Ted Rall proposed — that refugee populations end up wherever the aircraft carrying them happened to land — to the Kurds of Bismarck, North Dakota and St Louis.

savas-kalenderidis.title: Lindsey Graham
savas-kalenderidis.summary: Republican senator from South Carolina who died in July 2026, and John Kiriakou's standing shorthand for the permanent war caucus — a "show horse" rather than a workhorse, a "chameleon" who "never saw a war that he didn't want to jump into with both feet," and, on posthumously released documentary footage, a man offering the US Air Force to bomb a country America was not at war with.

savas-kalenderidis.title: Mexico City as an espionage hub
savas-kalenderidis.summary: John Kiriakou''s assessment of Mexico City as one of the world''s principal centres of international espionage, alongside Vienna, London, Paris and Washington — driven by a gargantuan American embassy that Russian services target from next door — and his reading of why Mexico simply ignored a dossier of suspected Russian officers handed over by the Biden administration.

savas-kalenderidis.title: Pakistani prisons
savas-kalenderidis.summary: John Kiriakou''s flat refusal, in a discussion of Imran Khan''s detention, of the idea that a Pakistani prison offers VIP treatment to a former prime minister — grounded in his having visited many of them himself during the period when the CIA was locking people up there.

savas-kalenderidis.title: The Afghan Zero Units
savas-kalenderidis.summary: The CIA-trained Afghan paramilitary units whose surviving members were resettled in the United States, and John Kiriakou''s account of why so many of them have broken down: recruited without training or therapy, taken out at night to kill their own tribesmen and extended family, promised the land of milk and honey, and then met on arrival with no work permit, no treatment and no help at all.

savas-kalenderidis.title: The embassy local hire
savas-kalenderidis.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of how a foreign service recruits inside an American embassy without ever approaching an American: by paying long-serving local staff a supplement they cannot refuse, and letting them assemble the identity of the station from fragments — most conclusively the office a new arrival names when he answers his telephone.

say-five-years.title: Ali from Newark
say-five-years.summary: The Black shot caller at FCI Loretto, near the end of a twenty-five-year drug sentence, who came to embrace John Kiriakou at the close of his term and tell him how much he respected him — a friendship possible only because Kiriakou had decided on arrival to ignore the prison's racial divisions.

say-five-years.title: The forty-seven suffix
say-five-years.summary: The last two digits of a federal prisoner number that, according to John Kiriakou, mark the holder as a member of an organised gang — and which the Italians at FCI Loretto carried along with MS-13, the Bloods, the Crips and the Mexican Mafia.

say-five-years.title: The quarterback with a personal chef
say-five-years.summary: The former New York Giants quarterback John Kiriakou says lived in the next row of cells at FCI Loretto — serving a long sentence for a Ponzi scheme, paying every prison gang $500 a month for his safety, and employing another prisoner to cook him three meals a day from food stolen out of the cafeteria.

say-five-years.title: Clyde Hall
say-five-years.summary: The imprisoned Ohio congressman John Kiriakou says served at his prison a few years before him, whose remark on release — that he had made some of the best friends of his life inside — Kiriakou thought insane at the time and came to understand after his own sentence.

say-five-years.title: The body in the barrel
say-five-years.summary: The exchange John Kiriakou reports having with a fellow prisoner who explained his conviction by saying the police had found a body in a barrel in his storage unit — and that a hundred people had access to the unit — to which Kiriakou's only reply was that he was not judging him.

say-five-years.title: The hierarchy of charges
say-five-years.summary: How federal prisoners ranked one another by offence, in John Kiriakou's account — RICO at the top, usually with a murder conspiracy attached; wealthy white-collar convicts despised as soft; and arson, insurance fraud and mortgage fraud attracting no interest at all.

scholar-in-residence-program.title: Counterterrorism Center
scholar-in-residence-program.summary: The CIA's Counterterrorism Center (CTC) — the unit where John Kiriakou spent the defining years of his operational career. He joined in the late 1990s as the only officer in the entire CIA fluent in both Greek and Arabic, served as chief of counterintelligence in the bin Laden unit, watched the Center swell from a few hundred employees to nearly 2,000 by September 12, 2001, and it was to CTC that he walked back down in May 2002 to refuse the torture program — the moment, he says, the CIA began to turn on him.

scholar-in-residence-program.title: The Ukraine call whistleblower
scholar-in-residence-program.summary: The intelligence officer whose complaint triggered Donald Trump's first impeachment, and whom John Kiriakou declines to accept as a whistleblower at all — not on partisan grounds but on procedural ones. The complaint went to the Justice Department rather than the oversight committees, and its prose, he says, is lawyers' prose rather than the uniform CIA analytic style every analyst is trained into. He is nonetheless emphatic that naming the man was indefensible.

scholar-in-residence-program.title: Cuban double agents
scholar-in-residence-program.summary: John Kiriakou's assessment of Cuban intelligence as one of the best services on the planet, defensive in nature and trained by the KGB, and his flat claim — repeated across several tellings — that the CIA has never recruited a Cuban who did not turn out to be working for Havana all along.

scholar-in-residence-program.title: Office of Leadership Analysis
scholar-in-residence-program.summary: CIA analytic office — internally called LDA, for Leadership Development Analysis — founded by CIA psychiatrist Jerome Post, where John Kiriakou was hired at the start of his CIA career and spent his first seven and a half years as Saddam Hussein's classified psychological profiler. His first assignment, given on his first day, was covering Iraq and Kuwait, a portfolio his boss described as so quiet the office sometimes went days without a single incoming cable.

scholar-in-residence-program.title: Thomas Drake
scholar-in-residence-program.summary: NSA whistleblower; per John Kiriakou, the source for the statement that on the morning of September 11, 2001, NSA Director Mike Hayden told agency personnel NSA had been 'waiting for a 9/11' to implement the mass-electronic-surveillance program that NSA's founding charter forbids.

scholar-in-residence-program.title: Abolish the CIA
scholar-in-residence-program.summary: John Kiriakou's position that the CIA should be abolished because its functions are already duplicated by the other 17 U.S. intelligence agencies — analysis by the State Department, human spying by the Pentagon, technology by DARPA, NSA and the private sector.

scott-horton.title: Piers Morgan
scott-horton.summary: British broadcaster whose panel show became John Kiriakou's 2025 sparring ring — "the equivalent of a WWE Smackdown with Alan Dershowitz<Cite s="2026-06-27-deep-focus-report-john-kiriakou-on-iran-endless-wars-and-u-s-fo" t="9:18" />." Paired with Scott Horton against Dershowitz and former Mossad chief Moshe Yaalon, Kiriakou said on air that Israel spies on the United States and that Jeffrey Epstein was an Israeli access agent, drawing a chuckle from the general and the claim that spying stopped when Pollard was caught — "General, with all due respect, that's just simply not true." Morgan's producer had to instruct the polite ex-spy not to be afraid to interrupt.

scott-horton.title: Jeffrey Epstein
scott-horton.summary: Convicted sex offender; per John Kiriakou, was "an Israeli access agent" rather than a CIA asset, because the CIA collects foreign intelligence and Epstein's targets — Bill Clinton, Bill Gates, Prince Andrew — were not foreign. Kiriakou further holds that Epstein did die by suicide in federal custody, because in the Bureau of Prisons the cameras never work and the guards are always asleep.

scott-horton.title: MOSSAD
scott-horton.summary: Israel's primary external intelligence service; characterized by John Kiriakou as universally hostile in his and his CIA colleagues' professional dealings with it ("never had a positive encounter with Mossad"); operates almost exclusively in the operational rather than analytical domain; the CIA is, per Kiriakou, categorically forbidden from spying on it.

scott-horton.title: Jonathan Pollard
scott-horton.summary: U.S. Navy civilian intelligence analyst convicted in 1985 of spying for Israel; the canonical proven case of Israeli espionage against the United States; cited by John Kiriakou in his 2024 Piers Morgan debate with a former Mossad director who denied any Israeli spying on the U.S.

scott-horton.title: Prince Andrew
scott-horton.summary: British royal, now Andrew Mountbatten Windsor, named repeatedly by John Kiriakou as one of the un-recruitable principals whose access made Jeffrey Epstein valuable to a foreign intelligence service. Kiriakou has asked why Andrew was never charged over conduct with minors, reads his alleged provision of classified Ministry of Defence documents to Epstein as evidence of espionage rather than vanity — and expects him to face no criminal consequence at all, because the statute of limitations has run.

scott-horton.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
scott-horton.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

seal-team-six-attrition.title: Bin Laden health rumors
seal-team-six-attrition.summary: John Kiriakou's dismissal of the claim that Osama bin Laden died years before the 2011 raid. He says the CIA received a steady stream of medical rumours about him — kidney failure, dialysis in a cave, a spinal disorder — none of which turned out to be true, and that bin Laden was in fine health apart from arthritis and a hip problem until the day he died.

seal-team-six-attrition.title: False flags are too hard
seal-team-six-attrition.summary: John Kiriakou''s practical objection to the idea that governments routinely stage false flag operations: they exist, and at the operational level the CIA used them constantly, but the bigger the operation the harder it is to run — too many moving parts, too many people who must buy into the conspiracy, and too much incompetence in government to keep any of it straight. He couples the objection with the observation that a government which is not transparent has no standing to complain about public suspicion.

seal-team-six-attrition.title: The cave myth
seal-team-six-attrition.summary: John Kiriakou's rejection of the popular image of al-Qaeda's leadership living in caves. He says the CIA knew its targets were in major cities, deliberately let them believe the search was concentrated on the tribal areas, and caught them because men who think they are unobserved get sloppy with their phones and email.

seal-team-six-attrition.title: The Obama recruitment thesis
seal-team-six-attrition.summary: John Kiriakou''s public explanation of what happened to Barack Obama: not that the CIA created him, but that a first-term senator with no national security experience is exactly the kind of president the agency wants, and that the first briefing several levels above top secret is enough to hook him. Kiriakou supports the reading with two quotations Obama gave to reporters, including that he never had any idea he would be so good at killing people.

seal-team-six-attrition.title: The Taliban lobbyist in Washington
seal-team-six-attrition.summary: A story put to John Kiriakou about a Taliban delegation''s American press conference and the Washington lobbyist who represented them. Kiriakou remembered the episode and the lobbyist''s New Jersey base but not the claim about her parentage, and explained why it caused so little controversy at the time: the United States had no historical quarrel with the Taliban, and had armed and fêted some of its future members during the war against the Soviets.

seal-team-six-attrition.title: The torture memo signature
seal-team-six-attrition.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of how the CIA''s torture programme was authorised: a list of about ten techniques sent from headquarters through the Justice Department, the National Security Council lawyers and Condoleezza Rice to the president — who, to the surprise of the agency''s own leadership, signed it. Kiriakou recalls the deputy director saying three times in one meeting that he could not believe the president had signed the memo.

sealing-the-courtroom.title: The jury consultant's advice
sealing-the-courtroom.summary: What John Kiriakou''s jury consultant told him about a national security trial in the Eastern District of Virginia: that in any other district in America he would say fight and win, but in that one, "buddy, you don''t have a prayer. Take the deal."

sealing-the-courtroom.title: The swimming pool substitution
sealing-the-courtroom.summary: John Kiriakou''s illustration of how classified words are handled at trial: prosecutors and judge agree in advance to replace them with harmless unclassified substitutes, so that "Vault 7" becomes "swimming pool" — and the jury, told the real words are too secret for their ears, concludes the defendant must be guilty.

sealing-the-courtroom.title: Assange and the European Court of Human Rights
sealing-the-courtroom.summary: The last legal avenue John Kiriakou identified for Julian Assange in 2022 — three precedents in which the Strasbourg court refused to let Britain extradite mentally ill defendants to American solitary confinement — and the procedural trap that made it useless: Britain said the appeal need not halt the extradition.

sealing-the-courtroom.title: Julian Assange
sealing-the-courtroom.summary: Kiriakou — a 15-year friend and former WikiLeaks board member — on why Assange is a publisher owed a journalist's immunity, and a political prisoner.

sealing-the-courtroom.title: Eastern District of Virginia
sealing-the-courtroom.summary: The U.S. federal district covering northern Virginia — home to Langley, the Pentagon, DHS and much of the intelligence-contractor industry — which John Kiriakou calls 'the espionage court' because the Justice Department files the great majority of its national security prosecutions there and because, in his telling, no national-security defendant has ever won a case in it; Kiriakou, Julian Assange, Edward Snowden and Jeffrey Sterling were all charged there.

sealing-the-courtroom.title: The CIPA hearing in Kiriakou's case
sealing-the-courtroom.summary: The closed pre-trial proceeding under the Classified Information Procedures Act at which John Kiriakou's defence filed seventy motions to declassify the material it needed to mount a defence, and the judge denied all seventy at once. Kiriakou describes the ruling as the moment the case ended — his lead attorney told him on the way out of the courtroom that they had just lost — and as the point at which plea negotiations began.

seals-on-loan-to-the-cia.title: How the CIA kills
seals-on-loan-to-the-cia.summary: John Kiriakou''s description of the methods used when the CIA is ordered to kill someone outside a war zone: a team parachuting in miles away, stealing a car, a locks-and-picks specialist opening the door and suppressed weapons inside; a snatch into a van bound for an airport or a boat; or a brush past in a market with something poisoned — a technique he says the Russians used often and taught the Bulgarians into the early 1980s.

seals-on-loan-to-the-cia.title: Nine recruitments in twenty-five years
seals-on-loan-to-the-cia.summary: The conversation in which John Kiriakou''s Athens station chief, a twenty-five-year operations officer who had reached senior intelligence service level four with nine recruitments to his name, pointed out that Kiriakou had recruited five in two years — and Kiriakou''s explanation of the knack: that he could hide his disdain for a man completely while talking about whatever interested him.

seals-on-loan-to-the-cia.title: The ayatollah and the photographs
seals-on-loan-to-the-cia.summary: The training story John Kiriakou says ended the CIA''s use of compromat: a prostitute lured a junior Iranian ayatollah into a hotel room wired for audio and video, the agency took dozens of pictures, and when confronted with them abroad he asked for two in 8×10, three in 5×7, and one on a slide for his wall.

seals-on-loan-to-the-cia.title: Mark Polymeropoulos
seals-on-loan-to-the-cia.summary: The CIA officer John Kiriakou describes as a friend who was in his first tour when Aldrich Ames blew his identity, was brought in from the cold, and later became station chief in Moscow — an appointment Kiriakou characterises as a deliberate thumb in the Russians'' eye: the officer their spy had burned, put in charge of operations against them.

seals-on-loan-to-the-cia.title: Suing the CIA
seals-on-loan-to-the-cia.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer to whether anyone has ever successfully sued the CIA in civil court: not that he knows of. He allows only what he calls small, picky victories — chiefly suing for the right to sue — and applies the same pessimism to the burned officer whose case prompted the question.

seals-on-loan-to-the-cia.title: The strongly worded protest
seals-on-loan-to-the-cia.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of what actually happens when one state violates another''s airspace: not an act of war but a démarche. He notes that the Russians do it to the United States over Alaska all the time, that the Americans do it back with some frequency, that the Norwegians, Swedes and Turks do it too — and that the response is to send an ambassador in to lodge a formal protest.

sebastian-gorka.title: Rudy Giuliani
sebastian-gorka.summary: Former U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of New York and Mayor of New York City; in 2018 attempted to extort $2 million from John Kiriakou in exchange for arranging a presidential pardon from President Trump; the attempt was reported to the New York Times by Kiriakou himself and corroborated by Giuliani's then-aide Noelle Dunphy after Giuliani sexually harassed her.

sebastian-gorka.title: Bruce Fein
sebastian-gorka.summary: John Kiriakou's longtime attorney and one of his closest friends; a Harvard Law-trained constitutional scholar, former Deputy Attorney General under President Reagan and former General Counsel of the Federal Communications Commission. Fein took the call from Jared Kushner's attorney that opened Kiriakou's first pardon track, sat beside him at the 2018 Trump International Hotel meeting at which Rudy Giuliani's aide solicited $2 million for a presidential pardon, and is his co-author on a long-planned book about the CIA's record of failure.

sebastian-gorka.title: James Bond
sebastian-gorka.summary: The fictional spy who got John Kiriakou — and, he says, half the Directorate of Operations — into the business. He asked for walkie-talkies at nine and told his father at sixteen that he wanted to be a spy in the Middle East; he concedes "literally none of it is true to life", but vouches for one scene: Bond always runs into the CIA officer at the party. The figure follows him to the end, too — a personality paper titled "Who is James Bond?" describes the officer type in terms he finds harsh, and federal prosecutors, he says, argued for his detention by talking about him "like I was 007."

sebastian-gorka.title: Amaryllis Fox Kennedy
sebastian-gorka.summary: Former CIA non-official-cover officer who worked under commercial cover as an international art consultant, later a Trump campaign manager and nominee for deputy CIA director. Per John Kiriakou, Senator Tom Cotton threatened to filibuster her appointment; the president responded by naming her deputy national security adviser instead — a job Kiriakou considers more powerful, since the CIA director reports to the national security adviser.

sebastian-gorka.title: Robert MacLean
sebastian-gorka.summary: TSA whistleblower; the person to whom John Kiriakou first described Rudy Giuliani's 2018 $2 million pardon-extortion attempt the same evening it occurred, and who in turn tipped the FBI (which declined interest) and then the New York Times.

sebastian-gorka.title: Bernie Kerik
sebastian-gorka.summary: Former New York Police Department Commissioner; the person who, in 2018, introduced John Kiriakou to Rudy Giuliani for what became Giuliani's $2 million pardon-extortion attempt.

second-chance-act.title: FCI Loretto
second-chance-act.summary: U.S. Federal Correctional Institution in Loretto, Pennsylvania; the low-medium-security prison at which John Kiriakou served 23 months of a 30-month sentence following his 2013 Espionage Act–era plea deal; the originally ordered "minimum security work camp" placement was countermanded — per Kiriakou, on Brennan's direct intervention — to place him in the actual prison alongside the general population.

second-chance-act.title: Mark Lanzalotti
second-chance-act.summary: The prisoner John Kiriakou describes as his closest friend at FCI Loretto and one of the finest human beings he has known — a first-time non-violent drug defendant sentenced to triple life without parole for refusing to inform, the prison's foremost cook and bookie, and the man whose release Kiriakou secured by writing his Second Chance Act petition.

second-chance-act.title: Clint Goswick
second-chance-act.summary: Fellow federal prisoner of John Kiriakou at FCI Loretto; a devout Christian and Wichita Falls, Texas heating-and-air-conditioning business owner convicted of drug conspiracy and a gun charge despite never having used, possessed, manufactured, or distributed drugs.

second-chance-act.title: Dave Phillips
second-chance-act.summary: The FCI Loretto prisoner who claimed to have been a CIA operations officer and whom John Kiriakou exposed as a fake by testing him on agency vocabulary — a possessive, risk-taking companion who planted shanks on a pedophile, was caught, and was shipped to another prison.

second-chance-act.title: Pete Calabrese
second-chance-act.summary: The senior Bonanno family member at FCI Loretto, known as Peter the Rabbit, who challenged John Kiriakou over his friendship with the cooperating witness Frank Russo and told him Russo brought dishonour to the Italians.

second-chance-act.title: The stinger
second-chance-act.summary: The improvised prison cooking rig John Kiriakou describes at FCI Loretto — a wall-plug faceplate wired to live current and dropped into a bucket of water — which produced restaurant-quality Italian food daily and, on one occasion, killed a correctional officer.

secret-service.title: Butler rally shooting
secret-service.summary: The July 2024 attempt on Donald Trump's life at a rally in Butler, Pennsylvania, on which John Kiriakou takes no position as to who was responsible but argues the published facts cannot be reconciled with a competent Secret Service — and that the questions it leaves open are owed an answer for the historical record whether or not anyone alive gets one.

secret-service.title: Permanent wartime economy
secret-service.summary: John Kiriakou's thesis that since 9/11 the United States has run a permanent wartime economy so large that cutting the defense budget would trigger a depression — likening the dependency to crack addiction and warning it makes war almost inevitable.

secret-service.title: Sara Jane Moore
secret-service.summary: American who attempted to assassinate President Gerald Ford in San Francisco in September 1975, two weeks after Mike Mastrovito of the Secret Service had interviewed her at her apartment regarding a threatening letter she had sent to the president. Per John Kiriakou, the case Mastrovito identified as having ended his Secret Service career.

secret-service.title: Hamilton 68
secret-service.summary: A company founded by former CIA, FBI, NSA and Director of National Intelligence officials that rates news sites as reliable or unreliable, contracting mainly with the Pentagon to flag articles on government computers with green or red check marks; John Kiriakou says it threatened Consortium News with a "Kremlin apologist" red-check designation, after which PayPal permanently suspended the outlet's account and confiscated its funds.

secret-service.title: John Kiriakou
secret-service.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

secret-service.title: Taking the ball and going home
secret-service.summary: John Kiriakou''s rule of thumb, offered after the July 2024 Butler shooting, that a failed state-run assassination is not retried: an operation with that many moving parts would not be attempted in front of thousands of people, would not be entrusted to a twenty-year-old, and once blown would be abandoned rather than repeated.

section-702.title: Thomas Drake
section-702.summary: NSA whistleblower; per John Kiriakou, the source for the statement that on the morning of September 11, 2001, NSA Director Mike Hayden told agency personnel NSA had been 'waiting for a 9/11' to implement the mass-electronic-surveillance program that NSA's founding charter forbids.

section-702.title: Mike Hayden
section-702.summary: Director of the National Security Agency on September 11, 2001; subsequently Director of the Central Intelligence Agency under President George W. Bush. Per John Kiriakou's relay of NSA whistleblower Tom Drake, on the morning of 9/11 Hayden told NSA personnel the agency had been 'waiting for a 9/11 so that they could implement the bigger program and grab everybody's electronics' — despite the agency's founding charter forbidding it from intercepting the communications of U.S. persons.

section-702.title: NSA Surveillance
section-702.summary: ''It is part of NSA''s founding charter that it is not allowed to spy on Americans'' — Kiriakou on warrantless collection and the Bluffdale warehouse.

section-702.title: San Bernardino iPhone Case
section-702.summary: The 2015–16 legal standoff in which Apple refused to unlock the San Bernardino shooter's iPhone for the FBI, which instead paid an Israeli firm $6 million to crack it — though, per John Kiriakou, the intelligence that could have disrupted the attack never came from the phone at all.

section-702.title: The Gabbard confirmation fight
section-702.summary: John Kiriakou's February 2025 assessment that Tulsi Gabbard was in real danger of not being confirmed as Director of National Intelligence — not because the Democrats opposed her, which they did, but because she was losing Republicans over Section 702, and had been telling them privately that she supported a renewal he knows she opposes.

section-702.title: Abu Zubaydah
section-702.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

securedrop.title: Julian Assange
securedrop.summary: Kiriakou — a 15-year friend and former WikiLeaks board member — on why Assange is a publisher owed a journalist's immunity, and a political prisoner.

securedrop.title: Encryption before the key
securedrop.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of where encryption actually fails, offered against John McAfee''s claim that no communication can be private. Kiriakou defers to the technologists he knows — Edward Snowden, Bill Binney, Thomas Drake and Kirk Wiebe — who tell him sufficiently sophisticated encryption does work. The exposure is upstream of the cipher: if an agency can reach your machine as you type, before you hit the encryption key, the encryption never gets a chance. He nonetheless encrypts everything he sends, and rejects the argument that encryption is what lets attacks through.

securedrop.title: Meredith Whittaker
securedrop.summary: Per John Kiriakou, Meredith Whittaker is developing a new, and by his account successful, business model for the encrypted-messaging app Signal, an alternative he cites alongside ProtonMail's compromised attempt at the same thing.

securedrop.title: Daniel Hale
securedrop.summary: Per John Kiriakou, drone whistleblower Daniel Hale — an NSA contractor and drone targeting analyst who exposed an 80% civilian death rate in the U.S. drone program, was ordered to fire on two young girls his superior called "goats," and was sentenced to 45 months (of which Kiriakou says he actually served about 18) despite prosecutors seeking nine to eleven years.

securedrop.title: Edward Snowden
securedrop.summary: Former NSA contractor who in 2013 disclosed the scope of U.S. [mass surveillance](/wiki/mass-surveillance), including the Section 702 collection program. Per John Kiriakou — who counts Snowden among the small group of national-security whistleblowers prosecuted under the Espionage Act — Snowden was ''stuck between two awful slippery slopes'': breaking his oath and chain of command on one side, and on the other catching something ''cut and dry against the Constitution'' that no one would act on. Kiriakou notes Snowden could not use his chain of command (as Kiriakou could not, his own chain being Jose Rodriguez), and that Judge Leonie Brinkema had reserved the Snowden case for herself before he fled the country.

securedrop.title: Espionage Act
securedrop.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

security-finance-and-medical.title: The Faisalabad cash run
security-finance-and-medical.summary: The drive John Kiriakou made to Faisalabad, Pakistan roughly two weeks before the capture of Abu Zubaydah, with two million dollars in cash in two duffel bags in the van, and the exchange with his colleague about why anyone would cheat the CIA out of twenty dollars.

security-finance-and-medical.title: Arabic and Greek
security-finance-and-medical.summary: The qualification John Kiriakou says opened the door to his transfer from CIA analysis to operations: a post in Athens wanted Greek or Arabic, and he had both — by most of his tellings the only officer in the agency who did. The chief who hired him gave the reason in one sentence: it is easier and cheaper to take a linguist and teach him operations than the other way round. The pairing also became a detection tool, since the language nobody speaks in Pakistan is Arabic.

security-finance-and-medical.title: Bankruptcy and the dropped charges
security-finance-and-medical.summary: The sequence John Kiriakou places at the centre of his case: that the espionage counts against him were dropped only after his legal fees had bankrupted him, which he presents as evidence that the government''s aim was attrition rather than conviction.

security-finance-and-medical.title: Curtailment cables
security-finance-and-medical.summary: The career-ending requests John Kiriakou says he read coming back from the CIA's black sites — officers, doctors, psychologists and nurses asking to end their tours early rather than continue to take part in the interrogation programme — and his conclusion that if that many people were objecting in classified channels, someone would surely go public.

security-finance-and-medical.title: The Indonesian recruitment question
security-finance-and-medical.summary: A hypothetical put to John Kiriakou and other CIA applicants during the interview process — what to do when a foreign official you have cultivated for a year turns out not to be recruitable — and the answer that Kiriakou later understood had been the point of the exercise: break into the embassy and steal the information.

security-finance-and-medical.title: The prostitute hypothetical
security-finance-and-medical.summary: The classroom exercise John Kiriakou uses in university lectures to demonstrate that the CIA gave its operations officers no ethical guidelines at all — a recruited terrorist source who demands a prostitute, and then the same demand for a child.

security-medical-and-finance.title: The General Muhammad equipment gift
security-medical-and-finance.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the end of the Abu Zubaydah operation in Pakistan, when headquarters told him to throw away or hand over the truckloads of equipment his station had bought — and of learning weeks later from his day-to-day Pakistani contact that the brigadier general who accepted the gift had simply taken it all himself.

security-medical-and-finance.title: Business class after 9/11
security-medical-and-finance.summary: John Kiriakou''s illustration of what the post-attack money did to the CIA''s habits: Cofer Black telling him to just do whatever operation he was proposing because there was so much money it could not possibly be spent, and everyone at the agency flying business class from then on, anywhere in the world.

security-medical-and-finance.title: ''Don''t try to save the government money''
security-medical-and-finance.summary: The instruction John Kiriakou says a CIA supervisor gave him for parking in the nine-dollar economy lot at Dulles instead of the twenty-five-dollar daily lot, and the two trips it produced: a Pittsburgh approach funded entirely by a five-dollar bill, and a $195 fattoush salad in a Dubai nightclub.

security-medical-and-finance.title: Agent payment mechanics
security-medical-and-finance.summary: How the CIA physically pays a recruited agent — cash every month, a receipt signed with any alias the agent chooses, and a polygraph regime built around the assumption that the officer handling the money is the person most likely to steal it.

security-medical-and-finance.title: Abu Zubaydah
security-medical-and-finance.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

security-medical-and-finance.title: CIA cash room
security-medical-and-finance.summary: John Kiriakou's description of the rooms at large CIA stations stacked floor-to-ceiling with cash — tens or hundreds of millions of dollars — from which an officer can sign out whatever an operation needs, as when he took $2 million to buy safe houses for the Abu Zubaydah capture.

self-destructing-terrorist-cell.title: The merry-go-round prank
self-destructing-terrorist-cell.summary: The dirty trick John Kiriakou played on an FCI Loretto prisoner he calls Wallace — planting a release form and a laundry bag on his bunk on a Friday evening, when no official was available to contradict them, and letting him give away his possessions and hold a farewell dinner before he was arrested for attempted escape.

self-destructing-terrorist-cell.title: FCI Loretto
self-destructing-terrorist-cell.summary: U.S. Federal Correctional Institution in Loretto, Pennsylvania; the low-medium-security prison at which John Kiriakou served 23 months of a 30-month sentence following his 2013 Espionage Act–era plea deal; the originally ordered "minimum security work camp" placement was countermanded — per Kiriakou, on Brennan's direct intervention — to place him in the actual prison alongside the general population.

self-destructing-terrorist-cell.title: The astrophotographer lawyer
self-destructing-terrorist-cell.summary: The Philadelphia attorney who represented Ken Schaefer's victim and who, in John Kiriakou's account, was flown to Israel as the guest of a school he had shown his telescope to — and there asked by a government minister to make the case go away.

self-destructing-terrorist-cell.title: Dave Phillips
self-destructing-terrorist-cell.summary: The FCI Loretto prisoner who claimed to have been a CIA operations officer and whom John Kiriakou exposed as a fake by testing him on agency vocabulary — a possessive, risk-taking companion who planted shanks on a pedophile, was caught, and was shipped to another prison.

self-destructing-terrorist-cell.title: Doing Time Like a Spy
self-destructing-terrorist-cell.summary: Prison memoir by John Kiriakou, full title Doing Time Like a Spy: How the CIA Taught Me to Survive and Thrive in Prison; winner of two literary awards and reissued in a second edition by Simon and Schuster.

self-destructing-terrorist-cell.title: Ken Schaefer
self-destructing-terrorist-cell.summary: The FCI Loretto prisoner who told others he was inside for securities irregularities, was in fact convicted of transporting a child for sex, fled to Israel on bail, and — after John Kiriakou exposed and confronted him — offered money to prisoners to have Kiriakou attacked.

senate-foreign-relations-committee.title: The Capitol switchboard
senate-foreign-relations-committee.summary: John Kiriakou's advice, drawn from years as a congressional staffer, on how ordinary constituents actually move members of Congress — that the House will act on a single letter, that the Senate needs ten or twenty calls to put an issue on a senator's agenda, and that the Capitol operator will identify a caller's own representative for them.

senate-foreign-relations-committee.title: Hawala system
senate-foreign-relations-committee.summary: Informal, ledger-based money-transfer network used across the Middle East, South Asia, and their diasporas to move funds without involving banks; per John Kiriakou's first-person account of testing one in the UAE — handing $50 to a grocer for a 16-digit number to redeem at an Arabic bakery in Bethesda, Maryland — completely untraceable; identified by Kiriakou (later, as Chief Investigator on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee) as one of the principal channels through which al-Qaeda moved operational money in the post-9/11 period, along with DHL.

senate-foreign-relations-committee.title: Middle East Forum
senate-foreign-relations-committee.summary: The publication — 'clearly an Israeli publication,' in John Kiriakou's words, and one he had never heard of before a Google alert surfaced it — that ran a piece by the political adviser to the Israeli foreign minister calling Kiriakou antisemitic and describing his writing as evidence of 'the rot' in the American intellectual left. Kiriakou took the phrase as a compliment and says the episode shows how closely Israel monitors even small independent outlets.

senate-foreign-relations-committee.title: The Kenya mission
senate-foreign-relations-committee.summary: Asked in March 2026 whether he had ever run a mission in Africa, John Kiriakou answered that he had — one, in Kenya — and then declined to say anything further about it, adding that he was not certain he was permitted to confirm even that he had been in the country. It is one of the clearest instances in the corpus of him marking the edge of what he will disclose.

senate-foreign-relations-committee.title: The State Department cover investigation
senate-foreign-relations-committee.summary: One of the inquiries John Kiriakou opened as senior investigator on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, on a reporter's tip that the CIA was placing some of its torturers under State Department cover in violation of the cover agreement between the two departments. He wrote to the State Department asking for clarification. Five or six weeks later a colleague told him a reply had come and had been classified above his clearance; asked what it said, the colleague summarised it as an obscenity. That was the end of the investigation.

senate-foreign-relations-committee.title: United States–DRC relations
senate-foreign-relations-committee.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of why American policy toward the Democratic Republic of the Congo is quietly comfortable while the east of the country is in chaos: the United States buys as much Congolese rare earth metal as can be dug out of the ground, and the central government''s weakness against Rwanda is a problem Donald Trump claimed to have solved for the purposes of a Nobel Peace Prize case, with a peace Kiriakou says lasted a couple of weeks.

senate-intelligence-committee.title: Dianne Feinstein
senate-intelligence-committee.summary: Longtime Democratic U.S. senator from California and chair of the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence. Per John Kiriakou, one of the greatest disappointments on Capitol Hill — an unusually friendly chairwoman who exercised no real oversight, good on torture and a cheerleader for the CIA on everything else. She co-authored the 2015 McCain-Feinstein Amendment that reiterated the federal ban on torture, and she blocked Gina Haspel's promotion in 2013 before publicly warming to her in 2018.

senate-intelligence-committee.title: Senate Torture Report
senate-intelligence-committee.summary: The December 2014 executive summary of the U.S. Senate Select Committee on Intelligence's study of the CIA's post-9/11 detention and interrogation program; the first public disclosure of techniques including rectal feeding with hummus, sexual assault with broomsticks, and prolonged sleep deprivation.

senate-intelligence-committee.title: Bureau of Prisons
senate-intelligence-committee.summary: The federal agency that ran John Kiriakou's incarceration — and one of his most persistent post-prison targets. The BOP overrode his judge's camp recommendation by deeming him "a threat to the public safety," threatened him with "diesel therapy" until 1,600 logged phone calls and letters from a dozen House members and two senators backed it off, and, per Kiriakou, functions as "an employment agency for unemployable semi-literate rural white men" and "a dumping ground for failed medical professionals" — an agency for which a prisoner's death is cheaper than his treatment.

senate-intelligence-committee.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
senate-intelligence-committee.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

senate-intelligence-committee.title: Human Rights Watch
senate-intelligence-committee.summary: The organization whose 2005 report that the CIA was torturing its prisoners — two years before John Kiriakou''s ABC interview — anchors his defense that he confirmed rather than revealed the program. It is also the middle link in the chain that ended in his arrest: working with the John Adams Project, Human Rights Watch employed the investigator who carried a classified name from journalist Matthew Cole to the Guantánamo defense attorneys, and when the FBI walked that chain backwards it arrived at Kiriakou''s door.

senate-intelligence-committee.title: John Kiriakou
senate-intelligence-committee.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

senate-torture-report.title: The cremation footnote
senate-torture-report.summary: A footnote John Kiriakou cites from the declassified executive summary of the Senate torture report, stating that Abu Zubaydah will never be permitted to leave Guantanamo — despite never having joined al-Qaeda, never having pledged fealty to Osama bin Laden and never having been charged — and that on his death the CIA will cremate his body and scatter the ashes at sea.

senate-torture-report.title: Jane Harman
senate-torture-report.summary: Former U.S. Representative from California who served as ranking member and later chair of the House Intelligence Committee. Per John Kiriakou, Harman was present in the room when congressional leadership was briefed on the CIA's enhanced interrogation program; when reporters later asked her about the program, she denied knowing about it. Kiriakou told the New York Times she had been in the room, after which Harman revised her account to say she had left early and that an aide remained as a notetaker.

senate-torture-report.title: Ruining the whistleblower
senate-torture-report.summary: John Kiriakou's account of what a prosecution of a whistleblower is actually for — not conviction but ruin, personally, professionally and financially — offered as the thing he did not think through before he spoke, and the thing he says then happened to him exactly as described.

senate-torture-report.title: Strawberry Fields
senate-torture-report.summary: The CIA's nickname for a secret black-site annex at the Guantanamo Bay Naval Base used for the post-9/11 detention and interrogation program.

senate-torture-report.title: The rebuttal book
senate-torture-report.summary: The volume published by a group of retired senior CIA leaders — George Tenet, Jim Pavitt, Jose Rodriguez and Cofer Black among them — answering the Senate torture report with the claim that the programme worked, saved lives and involved no mistakes, while continuing to refuse the word torture.

senate-torture-report.title: Ticking time bomb scenario
senate-torture-report.summary: The hypothetical case — an imminent attack only the captured terrorist's confession can prevent — used to justify the CIA's post-9/11 enhanced interrogation program; characterized by John Kiriakou as fictional and not corresponding to any real-world case.

senior-executive-service.title: Central Intelligence Agency
senior-executive-service.summary: U.S. foreign intelligence service; John Kiriakou's employer from 1990 to 2004 and the central institution of KiriPedia

senior-executive-service.title: Church Committee
senior-executive-service.summary: U.S. Senate investigative committee operating in 1975–1976 that examined domestic intelligence abuses by the CIA, FBI, and NSA; per John Kiriakou, the Church Committee — alongside the concurrent Pike Committee in the House — was the last genuine moment of legislative oversight over the intelligence community, born of a national consensus that government had gone dangerously off course. Its work led to the creation of the permanent Senate Select Committee on Intelligence, which Kiriakou says ceased to function as real oversight roughly seven years after its founding.

senior-executive-service.title: Pike Committee
senior-executive-service.summary: U.S. House investigative committee operating in 1975–1976 in parallel with the Senate's Church Committee; per John Kiriakou, the two committees together were the apex — and the last genuine exercise — of congressional oversight of the CIA, staffed by heavyweights and followed by a golden age that lasted only until Iran-Contra. Their work created the permanent House and Senate intelligence committees, which Kiriakou says degraded within a decade into cheerleaders for the agency.

senior-executive-service.title: National Intelligence Council
senior-executive-service.summary: Body housed at the CIA comprising the most senior analysts drawn from across the entire intelligence community. Its officers — National Intelligence Officers (NIOs) — hold positions at the Senior Intelligence Service level and are responsible for long-range strategic analysis on specific portfolio areas, as well as the production of National Intelligence Estimates. Per John Kiriakou, learning that the NIO for Warning had held the same job for forty-two years and just received a waiver to stay until seventy was the moment he first believed in the existence of the deep state.

senior-executive-service.title: Abu Zubaydah
senior-executive-service.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

senior-executive-service.title: AIPAC
senior-executive-service.summary: The American Israel Public Affairs Committee — the U.S. political organization that, in John Kiriakou's framing, ought to be registered as a foreign-lobbying entity but is not, and that wields decisive electoral power against U.S. elected officials who express support for Palestinian human rights.

senior-intelligence-service.title: Jennifer Matthews
senior-intelligence-service.summary: CIA analyst who was made chief of base at Khost, Afghanistan without operational or security training in order to complete the tour requirement for promotion, and who was killed there with six other officers by a Jordanian double agent she had gone outside the fortified perimeter to greet with a birthday cake.

senior-intelligence-service.title: John Brennan
senior-intelligence-service.summary: Former Director of the CIA; characterized in KiriPedia's source corpus as the principal architect of the agency's enhanced interrogation program and as having plotted against an elected President

senior-intelligence-service.title: Jose Rodriguez
senior-intelligence-service.summary: Senior CIA officer of the post-9/11 era; identified by John Kiriakou as among those responsible for crimes committed in the name of national security; described as believing himself to be a good guy.

senior-intelligence-service.title: Chief of station
