senior-intelligence-service.summary: The CIA's senior officer in a foreign country — appointed by the CIA director alone, outranking the ambassador's intelligence equities in practice, and in John Kiriakou's account the figure who sets the moral temperature of a station, from the officer who handed him his first counterterrorism assignment to the one who walks into a minister's office fifteen minutes after the human rights officer has left.

senior-intelligence-service.title: Mike Pompeo
senior-intelligence-service.summary: CIA director and later Secretary of State under Trump. John Kiriakou read Pompeo's 2017 speech branding WikiLeaks a "hostile non-state intelligence service" as the groundwork for an Espionage Act case against Julian Assange in the Eastern District of Virginia — the "Espionage Court" where Kiriakou himself was prosecuted. Friends who briefed Pompeo told Kiriakou he was extraordinarily bright but wrong on Iran; Kiriakou's own verdict soured permanently when Pompeo named Gina Haspel deputy director, flirted publicly with reinstating torture, and called Chelsea Manning a traitor — a crime she was never convicted of.

senior-intelligence-service.title: Forward Operating Base Chapman Attack
senior-intelligence-service.summary: December 30, 2009 suicide bombing at Forward Operating Base Chapman in Khost, Afghanistan, killing seven CIA officers and wounding more than a dozen others — the deadliest single day in CIA history. Per John Kiriakou, the officer who led the base was a GS-14 with zero security training, assigned to the post as a career-promotion checkbox before her required elevation to the Senior Intelligence Service. The bomber — a Jordanian national who walked into the American consulate in Istanbul claiming to be Osama bin Laden's doctor — was never polygraphed because CIA personnel 'wanted so badly for this to be true.'

sensitive-but-unclassified.title: Over-classification
sensitive-but-unclassified.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of why the American government classifies far more than it can ever review: not conspiracy but incentive. At lesser agencies a classification stamp is a status marker — it puts you in the in-crowd and above the colleague who lacks access — and at the CIA everything carries a stamp by default. His complaint about press coverage of classified-document scandals is that it never reaches the underlying question of why the documents were secret at all.

sensitive-but-unclassified.title: Espionage Act
sensitive-but-unclassified.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

sensitive-but-unclassified.title: Classified email
sensitive-but-unclassified.summary: John Kiriakou was serving overseas the day classified email was introduced at the CIA, and remembers his station chief saying there was no way to control it. His own illustration of what followed is a lunch invitation to his wife — a fellow senior CIA officer — marked Secret HUM 4-82, and her reply naming a deli and a time, marked the same way.

sensitive-but-unclassified.title: The mosaic concept
sensitive-but-unclassified.summary: The intelligence method John Kiriakou names for assembling a complete operational picture out of individually trivial fragments — one tile at a time, worthless alone, decisive together. He attributes the idea to Soviet thinking of the 1960s, cites Mossad's Iranian networks as the clearest modern demonstration, and warns that the same logic is what would let an American prosecutor charge a scholar with espionage for reading declassified documents.

sensitive-but-unclassified.title: The 2023 classified documents scandal
sensitive-but-unclassified.summary: The run of discoveries of classified material in the private possession of Donald Trump, Joe Biden and Mike Pence, which John Kiriakou treats not as a scandal about any of them but as proof that the Espionage Act as currently applied makes almost everyone technically guilty. He rates Pence's briefing books as more highly classified than anything Julian Assange published, and says Biden's Senate-era documents are the ones that cannot be explained away.

sensitive-but-unclassified.title: Carrying classified material out of a SCIF
sensitive-but-unclassified.summary: The two lawful procedures John Kiriakou describes for removing classified documents from a secure facility — a double-enveloped, double-marked package addressed to your home agency, or a leather bag with a double lock — and his flat statement that nothing about either allows a document to be forgotten in a garage for twelve years.

sentencing-enhancements.title: Joshua Schulte
sentencing-enhancements.summary: Former CIA Directorate of Science and Technology engineer; source of the 2017 Vault 7 WikiLeaks disclosure of the agency's offensive technical capabilities; currently serving a 40-year federal sentence for espionage; maintains his innocence.

sentencing-enhancements.title: Espionage Act
sentencing-enhancements.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

sentencing-enhancements.title: Brad Birkenfeld
sentencing-enhancements.summary: The UBS banking whistleblower, who was prosecuted and imprisoned before winning a $104 million settlement from the Treasury Department and spending it on the legal defence of other whistleblowers. John Kiriakou uses him as the measure of the gap between financial and national-security whistleblowing, and names him among the visitors whose devices he believes were copied at the Ecuadorian embassy in London.

sentencing-enhancements.title: The Charles Littlejohn prosecution
sentencing-enhancements.summary: The five-year sentence handed to an IRS contractor who disclosed Donald Trump's tax returns to the New York Times, which John Kiriakou calls stunning and unjustified — the material was protected but not classified, the Biden campaign made use of it, and the sentencing judge compared the disclosure to the January 6 attack on the Capitol.

sentencing-enhancements.title: Chelsea Manning
sentencing-enhancements.summary: Former U.S. Army intelligence analyst who provided WikiLeaks its 2010 trove of military and diplomatic documents. Per John Kiriakou, Manning meets the legal definition of whistleblower for exposing war crimes, was a torture victim of prolonged solitary confinement with forced nudity, and was sentenced to 35 years in prison before Barack Obama commuted — not pardoned — her sentence. Kiriakou says Manning later refused a grand jury's offer of immunity and chose renewed jail time rather than testify against Julian Assange.

sentencing-enhancements.title: CIA adultery culture
sentencing-enhancements.summary: John Kiriakou's recurring characterization of the CIA officer corps as riddled with adultery and casual sex — which he frames not as gossip but as a systemic counterintelligence vulnerability that makes officers easy to recruit.

sentencing-reform-bills.title: Five per cent of the population, twenty-five per cent of the prisoners
sentencing-reform-bills.summary: The statistic John Kiriakou returns to from inside prison — that the United States holds five per cent of the world''s people and a quarter of its prisoners, more per head than Russia, China or Iran — and the causes he assigns: the war on drugs, election-year lawmaking, and a Congress creating some fifty new crimes a year.

sentencing-reform-bills.title: Private prison system
sentencing-reform-bills.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the U.S. private prison industry as an incentive to keep beds filled and cut costs on food and medicine — illustrated by the 'sewer trout,' dog-food, and dead-rat-in-the-Kool-Aid stories from his own incarceration.

sentencing-reform-bills.title: The halfway house
sentencing-reform-bills.summary: The re-entry stage of a federal sentence — up to twelve months of it by law, in practice a fortnight before conversion to house arrest — which John Kiriakou was denied entirely for writing about prison conditions from inside, and which he describes as a system designed to make released prisoners fail.

sentencing-reform-bills.title: Administrative remedy process
sentencing-reform-bills.summary: The Bureau of Prisons' internal grievance system, which Kiriakou describes as a fig leaf designed to run out the clock on prisoners' complaints rather than resolve them.

sentencing-reform-bills.title: Bureau of Prisons
sentencing-reform-bills.summary: The federal agency that ran John Kiriakou's incarceration — and one of his most persistent post-prison targets. The BOP overrode his judge's camp recommendation by deeming him "a threat to the public safety," threatened him with "diesel therapy" until 1,600 logged phone calls and letters from a dozen House members and two senators backed it off, and, per Kiriakou, functions as "an employment agency for unemployable semi-literate rural white men" and "a dumping ground for failed medical professionals" — an agency for which a prisoner's death is cheaper than his treatment.

sentencing-reform-bills.title: The glyburide incident
sentencing-reform-bills.summary: The episode John Kiriakou described in a Letter from Loretto of 12 September 2014: handed a bottle of glyburide by the prison pharmacy without explanation, he crashed twice and passed out on the floor — and his physician father-in-law told him the drug could have put him into heart failure.

sergey-lavrov.title: Tony Blinken
sergey-lavrov.summary: American secretary of state under Joe Biden, and a former colleague of John Kiriakou's on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, whose desk Kiriakou inherited. Kiriakou calls him a lovely and very smart man who was completely over his head in the job — a great intellect who belonged at a think tank rather than in the cabinet, and who owed every position of his adult life to thirty years of proximity to Biden. In Kiriakou's account the proof is that the sensitive diplomacy of the Biden years was handed instead to CIA director Bill Burns, the de facto secretary of state.

sergey-lavrov.title: China as economic threat
sergey-lavrov.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that China is the real threat to the West not militarily — it has one aircraft carrier to America's two dozen and rarely invades — but economically, buying friends worldwide while the U.S. spends a trillion dollars a year on weapons.

sergey-lavrov.title: Afghan heroin policy
sergey-lavrov.summary: The post-2001 U.S. policy in Afghanistan of protecting, and per John Kiriakou actively encouraging, the cultivation of heroin poppy. Under the Taliban in 2000 Afghanistan produced 0% of the world's heroin; by 2009 under American occupation it produced 93%. Per a DEA officer Kiriakou consulted with on the policy paper he was preparing for Senator Kerry, the strategic rationale was that nearly all of the heroin flowed to Iran and Russia, addiction in those countries was considered desirable as a long-run societal weakener, and the same logic now operates in reverse with Chinese fentanyl flowing into the United States.

sergey-lavrov.title: Sanctions and the Russian adjustment
sergey-lavrov.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of why sanctions stopped hurting Russia: Sergey Lavrov''s admission that Moscow was caught off balance by the speed of the American response, the three or four weeks that shock lasted, and the discovery that Russia did not need the United States or its banking system once India and China agreed to buy whatever oil it had.

sergey-lavrov.title: Lindsey Graham
sergey-lavrov.summary: Republican senator from South Carolina who died in July 2026, and John Kiriakou's standing shorthand for the permanent war caucus — a "show horse" rather than a workhorse, a "chameleon" who "never saw a war that he didn't want to jump into with both feet," and, on posthumously released documentary footage, a man offering the US Air Force to bomb a country America was not at war with.

sergey-lavrov.title: CIA Drug Facilitation
sergey-lavrov.summary: Per John Kiriakou, the CIA''s reported involvement in facilitating the arrival of cocaine into the United States during the era that became the crack epidemic, and his own firsthand discovery — as a Senate Foreign Relations Committee investigator — that under American military control Afghanistan produced 93% of the world''s heroin. A DEA contact told him the report would never be published because ''we want Iran and Russia to be addicted to heroin. It weakens their societies.'' Kiriakou draws a direct parallel to the current fentanyl crisis: China is doing to the US what the US did to Iran and Russia.

serving-at-the-pleasure-of-the-president.title: Tulsi Gabbard
serving-at-the-pleasure-of-the-president.summary: U.S. Director of National Intelligence; a longtime family friend of John Kiriakou's, who has known her since she was 12; Kiriakou calls her appointment "an inspired choice" despite disagreeing with her decision to join the Republican Party, and says she appears to have given up her opposition to Section 702 surveillance to secure Senate confirmation.

serving-at-the-pleasure-of-the-president.title: Bill Clinton
serving-at-the-pleasure-of-the-president.summary: 42nd U.S. president whom John Kiriakou describes as wholly disinterested in intelligence — briefed by the CIA only twice in eight years, with Vice President Al Gore taking the daily briefing instead and relaying anything important.

serving-at-the-pleasure-of-the-president.title: Iran Nuclear Assessment
serving-at-the-pleasure-of-the-president.summary: Per John Kiriakou's assessment, the US–Israeli military campaign against Iran was a war of choice driven by Israeli political pressure rather than genuine intelligence indicating an Iranian nuclear weapons threat. The CIA produced two National Intelligence Estimates concluding Iran had no nuclear weapons program; Supreme Leader Ayatollah Khamenei issued a fatwa in the 1980s forbidding such a program. The U.S. went to war anyway, in Kiriakou's view, after President Trump replaced the Joint Chiefs of Staff with officers willing to accept Israeli intelligence and proceed.

serving-at-the-pleasure-of-the-president.title: 2026 Iran war
serving-at-the-pleasure-of-the-president.summary: The open-ended American and Israeli war against Iran that John Kiriakou tracked week by week on his own show — a conflict he says was sold as three weeks, ran into its fifth month, achieved every decapitation objective it set, and continued anyway. His grade for it is a D, and his forecast is a Truth Social post declaring victory while nothing changes.

serving-at-the-pleasure-of-the-president.title: Executive Order 12333
serving-at-the-pleasure-of-the-president.summary: The U.S. presidential directive — in its post-9/11 amended form — that grants the CIA the legal authority to kill any individual anywhere in the world deemed by the agency to pose a "clear and present danger" to the United States; the legal foundation underlying both CIA paramilitary operations and the agency's contractor relationships including with Blackwater.

serving-at-the-pleasure-of-the-president.title: Gulf consultations before the Iran war
serving-at-the-pleasure-of-the-president.summary: John Kiriakou's account of travelling in Kuwait, Abu Dhabi, Dubai and Doha in the weeks before the 2026 strikes on Iran, and finding that the United States had made no diplomatic case to its Gulf partners at all — in sharp contrast to the worldwide campaign that preceded the Iraq war. He told a senior Emirati royal that two carrier strike groups meant an attack was coming.

seven-cell-phones.title: The job in the medical practice
seven-cell-phones.summary: The made-up job that carried John Kiriakou through his first months out of prison — invented for him by the parents of a friend, both physicians, so that he would have something — and the patched-together living that followed it, including a think-tank post that ended in a mass layoff after a year.

seven-cell-phones.title: The hundred-city tour
seven-cell-phones.summary: The year-long, hundred-city speaking tour John Kiriakou described beginning in early 2026 — opening in Belfast, Dublin and Manchester, returning to Scotland and northern England, then the United States and Canada, Australia and New Zealand, continental Europe, the Persian Gulf and East Asia.

seven-cell-phones.title: The Nation of Islam at Loretto
seven-cell-phones.summary: The largest Muslim faction at FCI Loretto — African American converts to the Nation of Islam — two of whom walked into John Kiriakou's cell in his first days holding their own newspaper, in which Louis Farrakhan had called him a hero of the Muslim people for opposing torture. They told him he would have no trouble with them; one declined the handshake he offered, on the ground that he does not shake hands with the white devil. The Aryans, meanwhile, had decided he was a CIA assassin who killed Muslims. Kiriakou kept his mouth shut and let both beliefs stand.

seven-cell-phones.title: Seventy-two denied motions
seven-cell-phones.summary: The count John Kiriakou gives of the pretrial motions filed in his case and denied by Judge Leonie Brinkema — seventy-two denied and none granted — which he offers as the mechanism by which a national security defendant in the Eastern District of Virginia is prevented from mounting a defence at all.

seven-cell-phones.title: The professor and the Ellsberg profile
seven-cell-phones.summary: The story John Kiriakou says his CIA recruiter told him — that in 1971, as founder of the unit producing long-distance psychological profiles of foreign leaders, he was handed a file on Daniel Ellsberg, refused to profile an American citizen, and later discovered his boss had done it anyway under his name, which he testified to before the Watergate Committee.

seven-cell-phones.title: CIA adultery culture
seven-cell-phones.summary: John Kiriakou's recurring characterization of the CIA officer corps as riddled with adultery and casual sex — which he frames not as gossip but as a systemic counterintelligence vulnerability that makes officers easy to recruit.

seven-thousand-letters.title: Depression in prison
seven-thousand-letters.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the condition he says everybody inside has, and the three-part regime he set against it — eating right, exercising daily and finding a distraction — which in his own case meant more than a hundred books, 7,000 letters and a book written in longhand.

seven-thousand-letters.title: Passing time at Loretto
seven-thousand-letters.summary: How prisoners at FCI Loretto filled days John Kiriakou describes as Groundhog Day — working out and watching television on a set of screens divided between factions, while Kiriakou himself read, answered mail and wrote a book.

seven-thousand-letters.title: Dave Phillips
seven-thousand-letters.summary: The FCI Loretto prisoner who claimed to have been a CIA operations officer and whom John Kiriakou exposed as a fake by testing him on agency vocabulary — a possessive, risk-taking companion who planted shanks on a pedophile, was caught, and was shipped to another prison.

seven-thousand-letters.title: FCI Loretto
seven-thousand-letters.summary: U.S. Federal Correctional Institution in Loretto, Pennsylvania; the low-medium-security prison at which John Kiriakou served 23 months of a 30-month sentence following his 2013 Espionage Act–era plea deal; the originally ordered "minimum security work camp" placement was countermanded — per Kiriakou, on Brennan's direct intervention — to place him in the actual prison alongside the general population.

seven-thousand-letters.title: Legal mail
seven-thousand-letters.summary: The privileged correspondence category John Kiriakou used to smuggle the Letters from Loretto and the manuscript of his book out of prison — addressed to his attorney Jesselyn Radack and marked legal mail, which staff were forbidden to open.

seven-thousand-letters.title: The rat and pedophile table
seven-thousand-letters.summary: The cafeteria table at FCI Loretto reserved for cooperating witnesses and sex offenders — a placement that also carried a ban from the television room, and which John Kiriakou describes as an outcome cooperators knew to expect before they agreed to testify.

seventy-two-denied-motions.title: Jeffrey Sterling
seventy-two-denied-motions.summary: Former CIA officer convicted of nine felonies, including seven counts of espionage, after giving a New York Times interview about a racial discrimination lawsuit he had filed against the CIA. Per John Kiriakou, Sterling was not accused of spying for a foreign country; his underlying case was that the CIA had passed him over for promotion and told him explicitly it was because of his race. Daniel Ellsberg asked Sterling to go to trial specifically so the constitutionality of the Espionage Act could be challenged; Sterling did, was convicted, and was sentenced by Judge Leonie Brinkema to what she described as 'Kiriakou plus 12 months.'

seventy-two-denied-motions.title: Espionage Act
seventy-two-denied-motions.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

seventy-two-denied-motions.title: The Nation of Islam at Loretto
seventy-two-denied-motions.summary: The largest Muslim faction at FCI Loretto — African American converts to the Nation of Islam — two of whom walked into John Kiriakou's cell in his first days holding their own newspaper, in which Louis Farrakhan had called him a hero of the Muslim people for opposing torture. They told him he would have no trouble with them; one declined the handshake he offered, on the ground that he does not shake hands with the white devil. The Aryans, meanwhile, had decided he was a CIA assassin who killed Muslims. Kiriakou kept his mouth shut and let both beliefs stand.

seventy-two-denied-motions.title: Aryan Brotherhood
seventy-two-denied-motions.summary: The white prison gang that adopted John Kiriakou on his first day at FCI Loretto. Two hours in, two Aryans with swastika neck tattoos walked into his cell to check his paperwork — not a rat, not a "chomo" — and invited him to the Aryan table, which ran from hardcore Nazis at one end to merely white guys at the other. A rumor that he had been a CIA assassin earned him the nickname "the Muslim killer," which he never corrected; asked directly, he answered "we all did stuff we weren't proud of — it was wartime," and the Aryans loved it. He sat with them a year before the Italians took him in.

seventy-two-denied-motions.title: Bahrain Posting (1994–1996)
seventy-two-denied-motions.summary: John Kiriakou's 1994–1996 assignment to Bahrain under U.S. State Department cover as second secretary for economic affairs — arriving with his wife Joanne and infant son Chris on August 1, 1994, into a tiny Gulf monarchy whose sectarian tensions erupted, two months later, into the first Intifada.

seventy-two-denied-motions.title: "Ecuador is open for business"
seventy-two-denied-motions.summary: The Wall Street Journal headline John Kiriakou says appeared the day after he hand-delivered a letter to Ecuador's ambassador in Washington asking that Julian Assange's internet access be restored, and which made him fear Assange was about to be used as a bargaining chip.

sewer-trout.title: The dog food memo
sewer-trout.summary: The internal announcement circulated by the warden of FCI Loretto apologising for having served prisoners dog food on a taco night, which John Kiriakou cites as evidence not of the error but of how bad the ordinary food was — because nobody noticed.

sewer-trout.title: FCI Loretto
sewer-trout.summary: U.S. Federal Correctional Institution in Loretto, Pennsylvania; the low-medium-security prison at which John Kiriakou served 23 months of a 30-month sentence following his 2013 Espionage Act–era plea deal; the originally ordered "minimum security work camp" placement was countermanded — per Kiriakou, on Brennan's direct intervention — to place him in the actual prison alongside the general population.

sewer-trout.title: Cell transfers at Loretto
sewer-trout.summary: How a prisoner at FCI Loretto moved from one cell to another — a process requiring six months in place, the written agreement of the receiving cell and the signature of the counselor, which John Kiriakou describes as a guard assigned to be a designated pain in the ass.

sewer-trout.title: Cleanliness in prison
sewer-trout.summary: John Kiriakou's account of hygiene and order at FCI Loretto — where everybody showered daily on pain of a beating, everybody was constantly cleaning, and the rules on possessions and bedmaking left almost no room for clutter.

sewer-trout.title: The rat and pedophile table
sewer-trout.summary: The cafeteria table at FCI Loretto reserved for cooperating witnesses and sex offenders — a placement that also carried a ban from the television room, and which John Kiriakou describes as an outcome cooperators knew to expect before they agreed to testify.

sewer-trout.title: The stinger
sewer-trout.summary: The improvised prison cooking rig John Kiriakou describes at FCI Loretto — a wall-plug faceplate wired to live current and dropped into a bucket of water — which produced restaurant-quality Italian food daily and, on one occasion, killed a correctional officer.

seyyed-hossein-nasr.title: Saint Nectarios of Aegina
seyyed-hossein-nasr.summary: Early-20th-century Greek Orthodox saint whom John Kiriakou identifies with more than any other and carries a photograph of in his wallet; falsely accused and driven from his post, Nectarios forgave his accusers, and posthumous miracles led to his canonization.

seyyed-hossein-nasr.title: Sharia law
seyyed-hossein-nasr.summary: Islamic jurisprudence. Challenged by a viewer who equated it with executions of gay people, forced child marriage and the criminalisation of apostasy, John Kiriakou answers that those acts are largely the work of ISIS rather than of any government, and that Sharia is in substance a body of civil law covering inheritance, insurance, education, property ownership and commercial disputes.

seyyed-hossein-nasr.title: 2028 presidential field
seyyed-hossein-nasr.summary: John Kiriakou's assessment of the wide-open 2028 presidential race — the first in his life, he says, where he has no idea who either party will nominate. Predictive markets were listing 44 Democrats and 26 Republicans as possible candidates. His own preferred candidate is Tucker Carlson, whom he says he has repeatedly begged to run; his working assumption about anyone who does want the job is that they are "a narcissist and probably a sociopath on top of it."

seyyed-hossein-nasr.title: Amaryllis Fox Kennedy
seyyed-hossein-nasr.summary: Former CIA non-official-cover officer who worked under commercial cover as an international art consultant, later a Trump campaign manager and nominee for deputy CIA director. Per John Kiriakou, Senator Tom Cotton threatened to filibuster her appointment; the president responded by naming her deputy national security adviser instead — a job Kiriakou considers more powerful, since the CIA director reports to the national security adviser.

seyyed-hossein-nasr.title: Andrew Bustamante
seyyed-hossein-nasr.summary: Former CIA officer who sells CIA-style training online; John Kiriakou identifies him as the lone critic of his work hosting a show on a Russian network, and argues Bustamante's training business — open to anyone who pays — is the more problematic of the two.

seyyed-hossein-nasr.title: Angry Birds
seyyed-hossein-nasr.summary: The mobile game John Kiriakou describes as his only vice besides buying art, played every morning for nine consecutive years and cited by his ex-wife as a grievance in their marriage.

shank-planting-incident.title: Dave Phillips
shank-planting-incident.summary: The FCI Loretto prisoner who claimed to have been a CIA operations officer and whom John Kiriakou exposed as a fake by testing him on agency vocabulary — a possessive, risk-taking companion who planted shanks on a pedophile, was caught, and was shipped to another prison.

shank-planting-incident.title: FCI Loretto
shank-planting-incident.summary: U.S. Federal Correctional Institution in Loretto, Pennsylvania; the low-medium-security prison at which John Kiriakou served 23 months of a 30-month sentence following his 2013 Espionage Act–era plea deal; the originally ordered "minimum security work camp" placement was countermanded — per Kiriakou, on Brennan's direct intervention — to place him in the actual prison alongside the general population.

shank-planting-incident.title: Ken Schaefer
shank-planting-incident.summary: The FCI Loretto prisoner who told others he was inside for securities irregularities, was in fact convicted of transporting a child for sex, fled to Israel on bail, and — after John Kiriakou exposed and confronted him — offered money to prisoners to have Kiriakou attacked.

shank-planting-incident.title: Passing time at Loretto
shank-planting-incident.summary: How prisoners at FCI Loretto filled days John Kiriakou describes as Groundhog Day — working out and watching television on a set of screens divided between factions, while Kiriakou himself read, answered mail and wrote a book.

shank-planting-incident.title: Depression in prison
shank-planting-incident.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the condition he says everybody inside has, and the three-part regime he set against it — eating right, exercising daily and finding a distraction — which in his own case meant more than a hundred books, 7,000 letters and a book written in longhand.

shank-planting-incident.title: Seven thousand letters
shank-planting-incident.summary: The correspondence John Kiriakou conducted from FCI Loretto — 7,000 letters to 675 different people over 23 months, begun because of an unsolicited postcard of a rose that reached him four hours into his sentence.

sharia-law.title: Seyyed Hossein Nasr
sharia-law.summary: The scholar of Islamic philosophy under whom John Kiriakou studied Shiism as an undergraduate. Kiriakou calls him probably the most important Shia Muslim scholar in the world, notes that he is the father of Vali Nasr, and remarks that at ninety-eight he is still teaching.

sharia-law.title: 2028 presidential field
sharia-law.summary: John Kiriakou's assessment of the wide-open 2028 presidential race — the first in his life, he says, where he has no idea who either party will nominate. Predictive markets were listing 44 Democrats and 26 Republicans as possible candidates. His own preferred candidate is Tucker Carlson, whom he says he has repeatedly begged to run; his working assumption about anyone who does want the job is that they are "a narcissist and probably a sociopath on top of it."

sharia-law.title: Amaryllis Fox Kennedy
sharia-law.summary: Former CIA non-official-cover officer who worked under commercial cover as an international art consultant, later a Trump campaign manager and nominee for deputy CIA director. Per John Kiriakou, Senator Tom Cotton threatened to filibuster her appointment; the president responded by naming her deputy national security adviser instead — a job Kiriakou considers more powerful, since the CIA director reports to the national security adviser.

sharia-law.title: Andrew Bustamante
sharia-law.summary: Former CIA officer who sells CIA-style training online; John Kiriakou identifies him as the lone critic of his work hosting a show on a Russian network, and argues Bustamante's training business — open to anyone who pays — is the more problematic of the two.

sharia-law.title: Angry Birds
sharia-law.summary: The mobile game John Kiriakou describes as his only vice besides buying art, played every morning for nine consecutive years and cited by his ex-wife as a grievance in their marriage.

sharia-law.title: CIA intelligence failures
sharia-law.summary: John Kiriakou's standing position that the CIA has missed every major world event since its founding in 1947 — the building and the fall of the Berlin Wall, the collapse of the Soviet Union, the Iran hostage crisis, 9/11 — and that the remedy is therefore not more money but fewer overseas bases and actual accountability, of which he says there has been none.

sharon-scranage.title: Plato Cacheris
sharon-scranage.summary: Legendary Washington, D.C. defense attorney who served as John Kiriakou''s lead counsel in his 2012–2013 Espionage Act prosecution. Per Kiriakou, when discovery revealed the FBI had run a fake-diplomat sting against him, Cacheris explained the government''s posture bluntly: ''Because they have a shit case and they know it''s shit, and that''s why we''re going to trial.'' He spent most of the case urging trial, then drove to Kiriakou''s house on decision day and said ''You stupid son of a bitch — take the deal.'' Cacheris also represented FBI spy Robert Hanssen.

sharon-scranage.title: Bob Trout
sharon-scranage.summary: Washington defense attorney, Plato Cacheris''s partner at Trout Cacheris, and one of the eleven lawyers who represented John Kiriakou: the "elegant southern gentleman" who told him, "If you were my own brother, I would beg you to take this deal."

sharon-scranage.title: FCI Loretto
sharon-scranage.summary: U.S. Federal Correctional Institution in Loretto, Pennsylvania; the low-medium-security prison at which John Kiriakou served 23 months of a 30-month sentence following his 2013 Espionage Act–era plea deal; the originally ordered "minimum security work camp" placement was countermanded — per Kiriakou, on Brennan's direct intervention — to place him in the actual prison alongside the general population.

sharon-scranage.title: John Kiriakou
sharon-scranage.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

sharon-scranage.title: Mark McDougall
sharon-scranage.summary: U.S. criminal defense attorney; chairman of the white-collar defense practice at Akin Gump Strauss and a law professor at Georgetown, who joined John Kiriakou's defense team pro bono in the 2012–2013 prosecution. Two separate Washington lawyers independently warned Kiriakou on the same day that McDougall was "the meanest man in Washington"; Kiriakou says he was never anything but kind to him, liked him best of the eleven attorneys on the case, and credits the line that persuaded him to take the final plea — "you think this is about justice, and it's not about justice; it's about mitigating damage."

sharon-scranage.title: Abu Zubaydah
sharon-scranage.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

sheikh-jaber-al-ahmad.title: Sheikh Saad al-Abdullah
sheikh-jaber-al-ahmad.summary: Crown Prince and Prime Minister of Kuwait during the 1990–91 Iraqi occupation; per John Kiriakou, the day-to-day leader of the Kuwaiti government-in-exile in Taif — "very military," "hands-on," "the best leader Kuwait had for that situation," meeting twenty hours a day with everyone who needed to be met and simultaneously managing the Kuwaiti resistance on the ground.

sheikh-jaber-al-ahmad.title: Skip Gnehm
sheikh-jaber-al-ahmad.summary: U.S. Ambassador to Kuwait at the 1991 liberation; per John Kiriakou, "one of the finest men I've ever worked for anywhere in the world"; led the reopening of the U.S. embassy in Kuwait City on Liberation Day with the cable "American Embassy Kuwait City is now open for business"; famously complained that he could not stop Kuwaitis from writing pro-American graffiti on the side of the embassy.

sheikh-jaber-al-ahmad.title: 1993 Bush Kuwait assassination plot
sheikh-jaber-al-ahmad.summary: Iraqi intelligence plot, foiled by Kuwaiti authorities, to assassinate former President George H. W. Bush during his post-liberation "victory lap" visit to Kuwait; the U.S. response, per John Kiriakou's first-person account of his telephone call with Chairman of the Joint Chiefs Colin Powell, was 47 cruise missiles fired into the Iraqi Intelligence Service headquarters in Baghdad eight hours later.

sheikh-jaber-al-ahmad.title: George Habash
sheikh-jaber-al-ahmad.summary: Co-founder of the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine; as a young Lebanese medical student he was the college roommate at the American University of Beirut of Ahmed Khatib, the doctor whom Iraq installed as occupation governor of Kuwait on August 2, 1990 — a connection John Kiriakou carried into the Oval Office that day.

sheikh-jaber-al-ahmad.title: Iraqi invasion of Kuwait
sheikh-jaber-al-ahmad.summary: John Kiriakou''s most detailed account of the intelligence process around the 1990 Iraqi invasion of Kuwait and its 1991 liberation. As a first-year CIA analyst on a ''training account'' covering Iraq, Kiriakou produced the June 30, 1990 warning paper for the White House; suggested calling the US Defense Attaché in Baghdad to drive to the border and report what he saw (the answer: ''Literally the entire Iraqi military is heading south''); briefed the August 2 Oval Office meeting with Bush; and later took a single phone call from General Colin Powell that led, eight hours later, to 47 cruise missiles striking the Iraqi Intelligence Service headquarters in Baghdad.

sheikh-jaber-al-ahmad.title: William Webster
sheikh-jaber-al-ahmad.summary: Director of Central Intelligence during the 1990 invasion of Kuwait, and before that a federal judge and Director of the FBI; per John Kiriakou, "a lovely man … just a very kind, nice man" and "a giant in my mind" — the director Kiriakou first briefed at four in the morning, on fifteen minutes' notice, during the Kuwait task force, and who sat two seats away from him in the Oval Office on the morning of the invasion.

sheikh-saad-al-abdullah.title: Sheikh Jaber al-Ahmad
sheikh-saad-al-abdullah.summary: Amir of Kuwait during the 1990 Iraqi invasion and the 1991 liberation; per John Kiriakou, "a very kind and decent man and a leader who genuinely loved and cared for his people"; the subject of a CIA cable Kiriakou wrote from Taif which led President George H. W. Bush to invite the Amir to Washington for "the red carpet treatment" — after which the Amir returned with renewed focus on driving the Iraqis out.

sheikh-saad-al-abdullah.title: Saud Nasir Al-Sabah
sheikh-saad-al-abdullah.summary: Kuwaiti Ambassador to the United States in the run-up to the 1990 Iraqi invasion; per John Kiriakou, "just a lovely, lovely man, very generous with his time"; the diplomatic channel through which the CIA, working from the Kuwaiti embassy in Washington, communicated its escalating June–July 1990 warnings that Iraq was preparing to invade.

sheikh-saad-al-abdullah.title: Skip Gnehm
sheikh-saad-al-abdullah.summary: U.S. Ambassador to Kuwait at the 1991 liberation; per John Kiriakou, "one of the finest men I've ever worked for anywhere in the world"; led the reopening of the U.S. embassy in Kuwait City on Liberation Day with the cable "American Embassy Kuwait City is now open for business"; famously complained that he could not stop Kuwaitis from writing pro-American graffiti on the side of the embassy.

sheikh-saad-al-abdullah.title: 1993 Bush Kuwait assassination plot
sheikh-saad-al-abdullah.summary: Iraqi intelligence plot, foiled by Kuwaiti authorities, to assassinate former President George H. W. Bush during his post-liberation "victory lap" visit to Kuwait; the U.S. response, per John Kiriakou's first-person account of his telephone call with Chairman of the Joint Chiefs Colin Powell, was 47 cruise missiles fired into the Iraqi Intelligence Service headquarters in Baghdad eight hours later.

sheikh-saad-al-abdullah.title: Ahmed Chalabi
sheikh-saad-al-abdullah.summary: Iraqi exile and founder of the Iraqi National Congress; per John Kiriakou, a Shia-Kurdish con man who looted Petra Bank in Jordan of $36 million in the 1980s, was sentenced to death in absentia, was pardoned at CIA request, then pocketed $6 million in CIA seed funding for the INC and bought a Mayfair house in cash; later resurrected by Dick Cheney to feed the Pentagon fabricated WMD intelligence used to justify the 2003 invasion of Iraq.

sheikh-saad-al-abdullah.title: Ali Hassan al-Majid
sheikh-saad-al-abdullah.summary: Saddam Hussein cousin known as "Chemical Ali" and "the Butcher of Kurdistan"; per John Kiriakou, also briefly served as the Iraqi-installed governor of occupied Kuwait — "the Butcher of Kuwait" — and was engaged in the wholesale slaughter of Kurds in the north, Shia in the south, and Kuwaitis under occupation.

sheldon-adelson.title: Jonathan Pollard
sheldon-adelson.summary: U.S. Navy civilian intelligence analyst convicted in 1985 of spying for Israel; the canonical proven case of Israeli espionage against the United States; cited by John Kiriakou in his 2024 Piers Morgan debate with a former Mossad director who denied any Israeli spying on the U.S.

sheldon-adelson.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
sheldon-adelson.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

sheldon-adelson.title: Caspar Weinberger
sheldon-adelson.summary: U.S. Secretary of Defense under Ronald Reagan; John Kiriakou cites Weinberger's assessment that Jonathan Pollard's espionage caused "grave damage" — the highest category of harm — to U.S. national security.

sheldon-adelson.title: The CIA recruiting video
sheldon-adelson.summary: The Agency recruiting video John Kiriakou says he watched with dismay, in which a woman described herself as an autistic, depressed, anxious lesbian who had found a home at the CIA — and his reaction that this was not the CIA he joined.

sheldon-adelson.title: The Kuwaiti cargo in yuan
sheldon-adelson.summary: The shipment of Kuwaiti oil that John Kiriakou says the Chinese paid for in yuan rather than dollars for the first time, which he treats as the first step toward the end of the American empire.

sheldon-adelson.title: The Saudi question
sheldon-adelson.summary: John Kiriakou''s challenge to the premise of the Abraham Accords: that after a lifetime working in the Middle East he is unable to identify anything Saudi Arabia would actually gain from recognising Israel.

shia-populations-and-the-oil-fields.title: Kuwait as a sectarian model
shia-populations-and-the-oil-fields.summary: John Kiriakou's nomination of Kuwait as the one country in the Middle East to have managed a transition toward a workable form of democracy and sectarian coexistence — an argument he makes without concealing that it began with the royal family bulldozing an entire Shia neighbourhood in the early 1980s.

shia-populations-and-the-oil-fields.title: Bahrain's naturalisation policy
shia-populations-and-the-oil-fields.summary: John Kiriakou's account of how the Bahraini royal family changed the sectarian arithmetic of the country over thirty years — importing Syrians and naturalising Indian and Pakistani Sunni Muslims until a population that had been two-thirds to three-quarters Shia was closer to half and half.

shia-populations-and-the-oil-fields.title: Saudi Arabia and radicalism
shia-populations-and-the-oil-fields.summary: John Kiriakou's long-held position that Saudi Arabia is the primary generator of radical movements worldwide — a claim he locates not in the government alone but in the whole structure of Saudi government and society, in which a clerical establishment tells the rulers what to think while the rulers privately do as they please.

shia-populations-and-the-oil-fields.title: The U.S.–Saudi relationship
shia-populations-and-the-oil-fields.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the American alliance with Saudi Arabia as a straightforward trade — basing rights and oil in exchange for weapons sales and protection — and of the price the United States pays for it, which he describes as a demonstrated willingness to walk away from its own commitments to international law and human rights in order to protect the regime.

shia-populations-and-the-oil-fields.title: Democratic change in the Middle East
shia-populations-and-the-oil-fields.summary: John Kiriakou's answer to what it would take for Middle Eastern populations to free themselves of both Western influence and Saudi ambition — decades, a democratic rather than violent revolution on the early Tunisian model, and, in a conclusion he reaches reluctantly, blood in the streets, because he does not believe a bloodless model exists.

shia-populations-and-the-oil-fields.title: Saudi influence in Egypt
shia-populations-and-the-oil-fields.summary: John Kiriakou's account of Saudi Arabia's role in Egypt — not merely supporting the government that displaced the Muslim Brotherhood but bankrolling it and ensuring its survival — which he places within a history of Saudi interference in Egyptian internal affairs reaching back to the nationalist revolution of 1958.

shin-bet.title: Israeli intelligence presence in the United States
shin-bet.summary: John Kiriakou's account of Israeli intelligence activity inside the United States — dozens of undeclared Mossad and Shin Bet officers identified by the FBI, a critical-threat counterintelligence classification alongside Russia, North Korea and Cuba, and a pattern of harassment and intimidation directed at declared CIA officers posted to Israel.

shin-bet.title: F-35 avionics dispute with Israel
shin-bet.summary: John Kiriakou's account of how Israel demanded F-35 fighters without the deliberately degraded avionics the U.S. installs on export models — and, refused, allegedly worked through American defense contractors to steal the technology instead.

shin-bet.title: Recruitment attempts on Kiriakou
shin-bet.summary: A series of episodes in which foreign intelligence officers tried to recruit John Kiriakou himself — an over-eager Hungarian during his CIA application, a French counterterrorism officer who staged a car pickup in Islamabad, and a Shin Bet officer at his first liaison briefing.

shin-bet.title: MOSSAD
shin-bet.summary: Israel's primary external intelligence service; characterized by John Kiriakou as universally hostile in his and his CIA colleagues' professional dealings with it ("never had a positive encounter with Mossad"); operates almost exclusively in the operational rather than analytical domain; the CIA is, per Kiriakou, categorically forbidden from spying on it.

shin-bet.title: Sheldon Adelson
shin-bet.summary: American casino magnate and Republican megadonor. In John Kiriakou's account Adelson sent his private jet to fly Jonathan Pollard from prison to Israel, paid out of his own pocket to move the American embassy to Jerusalem, and functions as Kiriakou's standing unit of measurement for what political money can buy — including in the negative, as the patron the Libertarian Party never had.

shin-bet.title: The briefing held off campus
shin-bet.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of his first classified liaison briefing, given to the Israelis: the Israelis are never allowed into CIA headquarters because they spy on it, so the exchange was held miles away in rented space, with nothing above the secret level.

shireen-abu-akleh.title: Church of Saint Porphyrios
shireen-abu-akleh.summary: The Greek Orthodox church in Gaza that John Kiriakou describes as the oldest continuously operating church in the world; per Kiriakou, Israel bombed it while 24 women and children were sheltering inside.

shireen-abu-akleh.title: Taybeh
shireen-abu-akleh.summary: The only fully Christian village in the West Bank, home to the Holy Land's oldest brewery; John Kiriakou recounts it being set on fire and its Marian festival attacked by the IDF with drones, helicopters and stun grenades.

shireen-abu-akleh.title: Roger Waters
shireen-abu-akleh.summary: Founding member of the British rock band Pink Floyd; outspoken supporter of Palestinian human rights; anonymously paid off John Kiriakou's second mortgage during his federal prison sentence, sparing his wife and children the loss of the family home; only discovered to be the benefactor years later; subsequently a personal friend of Kiriakou and a recurring guest on his programme.

shireen-abu-akleh.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
shireen-abu-akleh.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

shireen-abu-akleh.title: Tuesday morning kill list
shireen-abu-akleh.summary: Weekly CIA targeting meeting instituted by John Brennan in 2009 during his service as Deputy National Security Advisor for Counterterrorism in the Obama administration; produced a written list of individuals to be killed in the following week; per John Kiriakou, the program was a source of pride within the Obama administration and was made operationally possible by the targeting-software sophistication of the period.

shireen-abu-akleh.title: No prosecution for a dead journalist
shireen-abu-akleh.summary: A fact John Kiriakou says he read the day he raised it — that the Israeli government has never prosecuted anyone over the death of any journalist, ever — and the conclusion he draws from it: that killing journalists is state policy, and that Israel should stop pretending otherwise and simply say reporters enter at their own risk.

shooting-house.title: Counterterrorist driving
shooting-house.summary: The vehicle training at the Farm — the PIT manoeuvre and how to avoid one, when to ram a roadblock and where to hit it, reversing at sixty miles an hour — conducted in a fleet of junkyard beaters the CIA bought expressly to be wrecked.

shooting-house.title: Kiriakou's skeet shooting
shooting-house.summary: The competitive shooting hobby that began when an octogenarian instructor at the Farm watched John Kiriakou — who had never fired a shotgun — hit steel plates at seven, twelve and twenty-five metres with a Remington pump action, and took him aside afterwards.

shooting-house.title: The bomb course
shooting-house.summary: The week-long CIA explosives course at a facility in another state, where John Kiriakou learned to build a Molotov cocktail, then a detonator rig, then an ammonium nitrate bomb — his final exam, which put a van's transmission three hundred yards into the woods.

shooting-house.title: The hostile border crossing exercise
shooting-house.summary: The training exercise run before dawn at a closed Dulles Airport in which CIA trainees crossed into the fictional Republic of Victoria — where John Kiriakou talked his way past a US-government-branded pen in his pocket, and the class clown ended up stripped to his underwear.

shooting-house.title: The operations course graduation
shooting-house.summary: The end of CIA field training: a graduation ceremony at which the whole class wore full disguises for the photograph, and a certificate that is itself classified and therefore cannot be displayed — it stays in the officer''s personnel file.

shooting-house.title: The El Salvador hotel drill
shooting-house.summary: A night exercise at the Farm in which trainees sat alone in a mock flea-bag hotel room in El Salvador, were visited by two men announcing housekeeping, and were shot with paint pellets. All eight failed, and the lesson John Kiriakou drew from it he says he never forgot.

shot-callers.title: The rat and pedophile table
shot-callers.summary: The cafeteria table at FCI Loretto reserved for cooperating witnesses and sex offenders — a placement that also carried a ban from the television room, and which John Kiriakou describes as an outcome cooperators knew to expect before they agreed to testify.

shot-callers.title: The Pisces prison gang
shot-callers.summary: The umbrella gang every Hispanic prisoner at FCI Loretto was required to join on pain of a beating — which subordinated street rivalries like MS-13, the Norteños and the Zetas to a single inside identity and required every member to work out daily against the possibility of a race riot.

shot-callers.title: The Bob Jones frame-up
shot-callers.summary: The operation John Kiriakou ran inside FCI Loretto against a man at his own cafeteria table — forging court papers in the prison law library from a genuine 1970s Ohio case involving a man of the same name, and using them to have him banished by the shot callers.

shot-callers.title: Pete Calabrese
shot-callers.summary: The senior Bonanno family member at FCI Loretto, known as Peter the Rabbit, who challenged John Kiriakou over his friendship with the cooperating witness Frank Russo and told him Russo brought dishonour to the Italians.

shot-callers.title: FCI Loretto
shot-callers.summary: U.S. Federal Correctional Institution in Loretto, Pennsylvania; the low-medium-security prison at which John Kiriakou served 23 months of a 30-month sentence following his 2013 Espionage Act–era plea deal; the originally ordered "minimum security work camp" placement was countermanded — per Kiriakou, on Brennan's direct intervention — to place him in the actual prison alongside the general population.

shot-callers.title: Chomo
shot-callers.summary: The prison term for a child molester, which John Kiriakou first heard on his first day at FCI Loretto when two skinheads at the Aryan table put it to him as the last of three vetting questions before deciding whether he could eat with them.

sigint-versus-humint-balance.title: Iraqi invasion of Kuwait
sigint-versus-humint-balance.summary: John Kiriakou''s most detailed account of the intelligence process around the 1990 Iraqi invasion of Kuwait and its 1991 liberation. As a first-year CIA analyst on a ''training account'' covering Iraq, Kiriakou produced the June 30, 1990 warning paper for the White House; suggested calling the US Defense Attaché in Baghdad to drive to the border and report what he saw (the answer: ''Literally the entire Iraqi military is heading south''); briefed the August 2 Oval Office meeting with Bush; and later took a single phone call from General Colin Powell that led, eight hours later, to 47 cruise missiles striking the Iraqi Intelligence Service headquarters in Baghdad.

sigint-versus-humint-balance.title: Agent payment mechanics
sigint-versus-humint-balance.summary: How the CIA physically pays a recruited agent — cash every month, a receipt signed with any alias the agent chooses, and a polygraph regime built around the assumption that the officer handling the money is the person most likely to steal it.

sigint-versus-humint-balance.title: Cuban double agents
sigint-versus-humint-balance.summary: John Kiriakou's assessment of Cuban intelligence as one of the best services on the planet, defensive in nature and trained by the KGB, and his flat claim — repeated across several tellings — that the CIA has never recruited a Cuban who did not turn out to be working for Havana all along.

sigint-versus-humint-balance.title: "He''s been ours since the ''70s"
sigint-versus-humint-balance.summary: An episode John Kiriakou uses to convey the scale of CIA penetration of foreign political classes: spotting a former prime minister at a diplomatic cocktail party, rushing back to the embassy to file for a name trace and vulnerability assessment before anyone else could approach him, and receiving a same-day instruction to cease and desist because the man had already been an agency asset for decades.

sigint-versus-humint-balance.title: Kompromat
sigint-versus-humint-balance.summary: Russian-derived term for compromising material — recordings, photographs, or documentation of an individual''s criminal, sexual, or embarrassing behavior — used to coerce cooperation or silence. Per John Kiriakou, the CIA''s formal policy conclusion is that kompromat doesn''t work as a recruitment tool: faced with the binary choice between confessing to a spouse and committing treason, most targets confess. The agency therefore prefers voluntary, ideologically or financially motivated recruitment.

sigint-versus-humint-balance.title: NSA Surveillance
sigint-versus-humint-balance.summary: ''It is part of NSA''s founding charter that it is not allowed to spy on Americans'' — Kiriakou on warrantless collection and the Bluffdale warehouse.

signal-and-the-parking-lot.title: Access Agent
signal-and-the-parking-lot.summary: CIA (and foreign intelligence service) term for a recruited asset whose value lies not in the secrets they hold directly but in their regular social access to high-value targets — politicians, executives, heads of state — who cannot themselves be recruited. Per John Kiriakou, the access agent is funded generously to maintain an environment in which the targets feel comfortable and return repeatedly; kompromat — compromising photographs or recordings — may be collected as a secondary tool. Kiriakou identifies Jeffrey Epstein as a textbook access agent, in his assessment working for Israeli intelligence.

signal-and-the-parking-lot.title: Jeffrey Epstein
signal-and-the-parking-lot.summary: Convicted sex offender; per John Kiriakou, was "an Israeli access agent" rather than a CIA asset, because the CIA collects foreign intelligence and Epstein's targets — Bill Clinton, Bill Gates, Prince Andrew — were not foreign. Kiriakou further holds that Epstein did die by suicide in federal custody, because in the Bureau of Prisons the cameras never work and the guards are always asleep.

signal-and-the-parking-lot.title: The Israelis are free agents
signal-and-the-parking-lot.summary: John Kiriakou's formulation of Israel as an intelligence partner whose cooperation is conditional rather than allied — friendly when it suits, and equally willing to deal with Russia, China or Germany — offered as the reason an Israeli-run source could end up passing American information to a service hostile to the United States, and given each time with an acknowledgement that saying it brings him threats.

signal-and-the-parking-lot.title: Prince Andrew
signal-and-the-parking-lot.summary: British royal, now Andrew Mountbatten Windsor, named repeatedly by John Kiriakou as one of the un-recruitable principals whose access made Jeffrey Epstein valuable to a foreign intelligence service. Kiriakou has asked why Andrew was never charged over conduct with minors, reads his alleged provision of classified Ministry of Defence documents to Epstein as evidence of espionage rather than vanity — and expects him to face no criminal consequence at all, because the statute of limitations has run.

signal-and-the-parking-lot.title: Alan Dershowitz
signal-and-the-parking-lot.summary: American attorney and Harvard Law professor; John Kiriakou describes debating him on Piers Morgan's show over Jeffrey Epstein, telling Dershowitz he would have wanted to see him "hanging from a tree" had he sought leniency for Epstein as an Israeli spy — and cites attorney David Boies's on-air statement that Dershowitz was far more than Epstein's lawyer, also serving as his publicist, friend, and a guest on Epstein's island.

signal-and-the-parking-lot.title: Alexander Acosta and the sweetheart deal
signal-and-the-parking-lot.summary: The US attorney who gave Jeffrey Epstein his 2006 non-prosecution agreement and later said he had been ordered to — a chain of command John Kiriakou traces upward to an attorney general famous for his powerlessness, and therefore to somebody above him whom nobody has ever named.

signature-strikes.title: Code Pink
signature-strikes.summary: The women-led peace group co-founded by Medea Benjamin. John Kiriakou first met them as a Senate staffer — he was the man who threw them out of a hearing he had produced, and got a lecture from Senator Shaheen for it. When he was arrested they were "right there next to me"; they threw his going-away party on the roof of the Hay-Adams, commissioned a folk group to sing a song rewritten about him, and quietly arranged for Roger Waters to pay off the second mortgage so his family could keep the house. He calls them his angels, and the one institution in American life he still trusts.

signature-strikes.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
signature-strikes.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

signature-strikes.title: The Drone Papers
signature-strikes.summary: The trove of classified documents leaked by Daniel Hale and published by The Intercept — later collected in book form as 'The Assassination Complex' — exposing how the U.S. drone program selected and killed targets; John Kiriakou relied on it in his own writing on the war in Afghanistan.

signature-strikes.title: Anwar al-Awlaki
signature-strikes.summary: American-born al-Qaeda propagandist; in 1993 the imam of the Falls Church, Virginia mosque visited by John Kiriakou's CIA Arabic-language class on a field trip; in 2001 the cleric at whose mosque the 9/11 hijackers prayed the night before the attacks; killed by U.S. drone strike in Yemen in approximately 2011.

signature-strikes.title: Espionage Act
signature-strikes.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

signature-strikes.title: National Bird
signature-strikes.summary: Award-winning documentary on the U.S. drone program featuring whistleblower Daniel Hale; John Kiriakou calls it essential viewing, noting its footage of drone operators debating on audio whether the figures in their crosshairs are children before firing.

signing-with-caa.title: Consulting for royal families
signing-with-caa.summary: The work John Kiriakou says he was hired to do by members of two different royal families following the 2026 virality of his interviews — advising on ethics in their own intelligence operations — which he offers as evidence of how far the reversal in his standing had gone.

signing-with-caa.title: "Embrace it and keep telling it"
signing-with-caa.summary: The advice John Kiriakou says he was given days after his arrest — that he could not hide from the prosecution but had to embrace it, and had to keep telling his side of the story until it became the side of record, because the government would eventually move on to its next target.

signing-with-caa.title: Kiriakou cameo practice
signing-with-caa.summary: John Kiriakou's post-2026 use of the Cameo personalised-video service — running at roughly 25 to 30 hours a week, some 900 messages in the month of March 2026 alone, nearly 2,000 messages in total by July 2026 — that he says has produced three cases in which the person receiving the video message afterwards told him he had talked them out of committing suicide, including a 15-year-old bulimic girl to whom Kiriakou gave his personal phone number.

signing-with-caa.title: Suggested responses
signing-with-caa.summary: The second email John Kiriakou says arrived before his first appearance on Fox News — a list of suggested responses to accompany the questions the producers had already sent him — which he ignored, and which he says was never sent again.

signing-with-caa.title: The convicted felon introduction
signing-with-caa.summary: The MSNBC appearance John Kiriakou says was his last: booked opposite Daniel Ellsberg, having agreed his on-air identification in advance with the producers, he was introduced instead as "convicted felon John Kiriakou", swore on tape, and began removing his microphone.

signing-with-caa.title: The underlying sadness
signing-with-caa.summary: The change several people have independently reported to John Kiriakou about himself since his prosecution — an underlying sadness that was not there before — which he says he does not see in himself, considering himself a happy and well-adjusted person.

sigurdur-thordarson.title: Julian Assange
sigurdur-thordarson.summary: Kiriakou — a 15-year friend and former WikiLeaks board member — on why Assange is a publisher owed a journalist's immunity, and a political prisoner.

sigurdur-thordarson.title: Prosecutorial careerism
sigurdur-thordarson.summary: John Kiriakou''s explanation for why senior federal prosecutors pursue high-profile national-security cases regardless of their merits: the conviction of a famous defendant is the entry ticket to a partnership at a large firm, a congressional candidacy, or a run for governor.

sigurdur-thordarson.title: CIA media relations
sigurdur-thordarson.summary: John Kiriakou's account of how the CIA shapes press coverage in the 2020s without needing an Operation Mockingbird-style infiltration program — because corporate media now recites CIA messaging willingly, most journalists simply rewrite emailed statements from the agency's Office of Public Affairs, and the CIA allegedly manipulates algorithms and backs podcasts to spread its point of view.

sigurdur-thordarson.title: Communications management unit
sigurdur-thordarson.summary: The two restricted-contact units inside the American federal prison system, at Terre Haute and Marion; built for "the worst of the worst" but, in John Kiriakou's account, used to silence prisoners whose messages are inconvenient — and a practice he groups with solitary confinement as torture. He served part of his own sentence in a modified one.

sigurdur-thordarson.title: Daniel Ellsberg
sigurdur-thordarson.summary: The Pentagon Papers whistleblower Kiriakou calls 'the Godfather of all national security whistleblowers' — and one of the great mentors of his life.

sigurdur-thordarson.title: Death threats against Kiriakou
sigurdur-thordarson.summary: The threats John Kiriakou has received across two decades — first after going public about the CIA torture program, when FBI advice that at least two were credible sent his family out of the country, and later in waves tied to his opposition to Gina Haspel, his remarks about Pakistan, and his advocacy on Palestine and the Epstein case.

site-13.title: The Punjab Elite Force
site-13.summary: The Pakistani provincial counterterrorism unit that supplied part of the assault manpower for the Abu Zubaydah raids of March 2002 — black trousers, black t-shirts stencilled with a pistol, and, in John Kiriakou's telling, a refusal to wear body armour on the grounds that if God called them that night they would go.

site-13.title: The toll booth plan
site-13.summary: John Kiriakou's first idea for catching Abu Zubaydah in 2002 — to put CIA officers dressed as Pakistanis in the toll booths of the Lahore–Faisalabad motorway and grab him as he came through — drawn from his own summer job as a toll collector on the Pennsylvania Turnpike, and abandoned as, in his own words, a terrible idea.

site-13.title: Faisalabad
site-13.summary: The Pakistani textile city of some seven or eight million people where Abu Zubaydah was captured in March 2002 — concrete, mud and corrugated tin in John Kiriakou's description, with a brand-new glass-and-steel McDonald's standing in the middle of it.

site-13.title: Abu Zubaydah
site-13.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

site-13.title: Faisalabad Hospital
site-13.summary: The hospital where a dying Abu Zubaydah was taken after the raid of March 2002 — open windows, animals in the corridors, mosquitoes on open wounds, and a bar of Irish Spring soap used as a pincushion for reusable syringes — which came under fire from the street while he was on the operating table.

site-13.title: CIA versus FBI at a raid
site-13.summary: John Kiriakou''s two-sentence account of the institutional difference between the two agencies, drawn from joint raids in Pakistan in 2002: the FBI numbers the four walls with sticky notes, photographs the inside of every drawer and collects every piece of paper, because it is building a case. The CIA breaks down the door, grabs all the men and sends them to Guantánamo.

sitting-on-my-fathers-lap.title: The ideological circle
sitting-on-my-fathers-lap.summary: John Kiriakou's long-held claim that the political spectrum is not a straight line from left to right but a circle, on which the two ends meet — and that in the case of MAGA and the progressive left, the point where they meet is war and peace.

sitting-on-my-fathers-lap.title: The Pentagon budget reversal
sitting-on-my-fathers-lap.summary: The pair of announcements John Kiriakou uses as his cleanest evidence of incoherence in the second Trump administration — a stated intention to cut the Pentagon budget by fifty per cent, celebrated at the time, followed a couple of months later by a stated intention to increase it by fifty per cent.

sitting-on-my-fathers-lap.title: "Beyond Your Dreams"
sitting-on-my-fathers-lap.summary: The gloss a host gave John Kiriakou on his first trip to China when he asked what the beautiful car with the BYD badge was — and the answer he got when he asked why he had never heard of it, which was that the United States is the only country where they are not sold.

sitting-on-my-fathers-lap.title: Carving up Iran
sitting-on-my-fathers-lap.summary: The Israeli end goal John Kiriakou says has been discussed with increasingly less discretion — dividing Iran into five small rump countries including Balochistan, Arabistan and Kurdistan, on the reasoning that small states are more easily controlled — and which he expects Israel will eventually try to get Donald Trump to carry out.

sitting-on-my-fathers-lap.title: Dumping the treasury bonds
sitting-on-my-fathers-lap.summary: The second economic weapon John Kiriakou says China holds against the United States — its position as the second or third largest holder of long-term government treasury bonds, which it could simply dump, and which he says would crash the entire American economy.

sitting-on-my-fathers-lap.title: Lavrov on sanctions
sitting-on-my-fathers-lap.summary: The two remarks by Russian foreign minister Sergey Lavrov that John Kiriakou pairs to summarise the failure of the sanctions weapon — that Russia was surprised by how swiftly the Americans imposed sanctions, and, a year or two later, surprised by how quickly Russia got around them.

six-different-passports.title: The referee in a Greek-Turkish war
six-different-passports.summary: John Kiriakou's assessment, given in Athens in 2025, that Greece cannot count on the United States taking its side against Turkey — Washington would position itself as an honest broker between the two — but that NATO support, particularly from Italy, France, Germany and Britain, would make Greece able to cope even without American leadership.

six-different-passports.title: Denied areas
six-different-passports.summary: The CIA term for countries so hostile and so heavily surveilled that ordinary operational movement is impossible — the Soviet Union, Cuba, Syria, and later Russia, China, North Korea and Iran — and the reason, in John Kiriakou's account, that officers heading to one get specialist briefings, eight-hour surveillance detection routes, and that the Agency has to fall back on liaison services instead of its own sources.

six-different-passports.title: Greek Intelligence Service
six-different-passports.summary: Greece's intelligence service, with which John Kiriakou worked closely during his Athens posting; its head of surveillance called off surveillance on him after watching him make a large offering at Saint Nectarios's tomb on the island of Aegina.

six-different-passports.title: Kiriakou on artificial intelligence
six-different-passports.summary: John Kiriakou's stated experience with and objections to large language models — a ChatGPT exchange in which the system stated his degrees incorrectly, refused his correction and then cut him off, and a test in which every scholarly citation it produced for his university syllabus turned out to be fabricated. He also describes AI as the flagging layer of contemporary surveillance.

six-different-passports.title: MOSSAD
six-different-passports.summary: Israel's primary external intelligence service; characterized by John Kiriakou as universally hostile in his and his CIA colleagues' professional dealings with it ("never had a positive encounter with Mossad"); operates almost exclusively in the operational rather than analytical domain; the CIA is, per Kiriakou, categorically forbidden from spying on it.

six-different-passports.title: Abu Zubaydah as a sounding board
six-different-passports.summary: The second, longer phase of Abu Zubaydah''s usefulness to the CIA, described by John Kiriakou in his December 2007 ABC News interview: once the prisoner had given up what he knew about current operations, his value shifted from threat reporting to analysis, with case officers reading him the names of men arrested in European capitals and asking whether the operations attributed to them made sense.

six-ways-from-sunday.title: John Brennan
six-ways-from-sunday.summary: Former Director of the CIA; characterized in KiriPedia's source corpus as the principal architect of the agency's enhanced interrogation program and as having plotted against an elected President

six-ways-from-sunday.title: Russiagate
six-ways-from-sunday.summary: John Kiriakou''s rebuttal of the claim that Russia swung the 2016 U.S. election: the Mueller report found no interference, the DNC emails were leaked in person rather than remotely hacked, and Russia''s roughly $50,000 in Facebook ads — half spent after the election — was trivial against billions in campaign spending.

six-ways-from-sunday.title: Misleading headlines
six-ways-from-sunday.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that the headline rather than the article is where American news does its work, that major papers routinely run headlines unsupported by the evidence beneath them, and that the problem was frequent enough for his radio show to devote a weekly segment to it.

six-ways-from-sunday.title: Treason
six-ways-from-sunday.summary: John Kiriakou's insistence on the constitutional definition of treason — a capital offence consisting of taking up arms against the United States or giving aid and comfort to the enemy in time of war — and his argument that a president who publicly disagrees with an intelligence assessment has not committed it, because the CIA does not set foreign policy.

six-ways-from-sunday.title: Ahmed Chalabi
six-ways-from-sunday.summary: Iraqi exile and founder of the Iraqi National Congress; per John Kiriakou, a Shia-Kurdish con man who looted Petra Bank in Jordan of $36 million in the 1980s, was sentenced to death in absentia, was pardoned at CIA request, then pocketed $6 million in CIA seed funding for the INC and bought a Mayfair house in cash; later resurrected by Dick Cheney to feed the Pentagon fabricated WMD intelligence used to justify the 2003 invasion of Iraq.

six-ways-from-sunday.title: Dick Cheney
six-ways-from-sunday.summary: U.S. Vice President under George W. Bush. Per John Kiriakou — recounting CIA Director George Tenet's memoir — Cheney intercepted the presidential finding authorizing the CIA's enhanced interrogation program in the Oval Office anteroom and took it from Tenet before Bush could sign it. Tenet later concluded the president probably never actually signed the finding and probably told the truth when he said he had no idea the program was taking place. Kiriakou characterizes Cheney as the one who actually ran foreign policy, intelligence policy, and defense policy during the Bush years.

sixteen-employees-to-twenty-thousand.title: Abbas and the three-state problem
sixteen-employees-to-twenty-thousand.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that no two-state solution is available — because there is already one state, because Mahmoud Abbas is nineteen years into a four-year term and has become a billionaire, and because East Bank, West Bank and Gaza Palestinians are so disconnected that the real arithmetic is three states, which nobody will discuss.

sixteen-employees-to-twenty-thousand.title: Bulldozing the olive orchards
sixteen-employees-to-twenty-thousand.summary: The sequence John Kiriakou describes preceding Israeli seizures of Palestinian land in the West Bank — olive orchards bulldozed and crops burned to make leaving easier, then the house demolished and a prefabricated one built for a settler family — and the different practice he says applies in East Jerusalem.

sixteen-employees-to-twenty-thousand.title: Elbridge Gerry and the salamander
sixteen-employees-to-twenty-thousand.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the origin of the word gerrymander — Elbridge Gerry, vice president and former governor of Massachusetts, drawing district boundaries to elect his friends, and Benjamin Franklin saying the shapes looked like salamanders — together with a piece of trivia from his unpublished book on cemeteries.

sixteen-employees-to-twenty-thousand.title: New Castle, Pennsylvania
sixteen-employees-to-twenty-thousand.summary: John Kiriakou's home town, an hour north of Pittsburgh on the edge of Amish country — a rust-belt city of roughly 40,000 to 50,000 people when he was growing up and around 18,000 to 20,000 now, whose decline he measures by the arrival of DEA and ATF field offices.
