Under the Taliban in 2000 Afghanistan produced 0% of the world's heroin; by 2009 under American occupation it produced 93%. Per a DEA officer Kiriakou consulted with on the policy paper he was preparing for Senator Kerry, the strategic rationale was that nearly all of the heroin flowed to Iran and Russia, addiction in those countries was considered desirable as a long-run societal weakener, and the same logic now operates in reverse with Chinese fentanyl flowing into the United States.

taliban.title: Bob Grenier
taliban.summary: Career CIA officer who served as station chief in Islamabad before, during, and after 9/11; later associate deputy director of operations for policy support and Iraq Mission Manager; John Kiriakou's boss and, for one year, his supervisor as executive assistant.

taliban.title: The twenty-five in Pakistan
taliban.summary: The answer John Kiriakou heard given to Senator Jeanne Shaheen in the spring of 2009, when she asked how many members of al-Qaeda were in Pakistan — twenty-five — and which he uses as the measure of how long the war outlived its stated object.

taliban.title: The Peace and Friendship Bridge
taliban.summary: A bridge across the narrow Pakistan–China frontier that John Kiriakou saw advertised on billboards across Pakistan while serving there, and the exchange it produced with a Pakistani general: asked why so much was being made of it, the general said the Chinese were the only friends Pakistan had who had never turned on them — and then looked at Kiriakou.

taliban.title: The Taliban truck escort origin
taliban.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of how the Taliban began: as a Pakistani government scheme under Benazir Bhutto to take madrasa students — talib, plural taliban — out of the religious schools and put them with Kalashnikovs aboard Pakistani trucks crossing Afghanistan to Iran, to stop mujahideen fighters from pirating the cargo.

taliban.title: Abu Zubaydah
taliban.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

talk-liberation-bank-freeze.title: Panquake
talk-liberation-bank-freeze.summary: Open-source, blockchain-based social platform developed by the Iceland-registered company Talk Liberation, for which John Kiriakou has served as brand ambassador since 2020. Kiriakou describes it as advertising-free, subscription-funded, free of back doors, and run on servers powered by Icelandic geothermal steam — a project he frames as a David-and-Goliath fight against banks, big technology and governments.

talk-liberation-bank-freeze.title: Suzie Dawson
talk-liberation-bank-freeze.summary: New Zealand activist and journalist, chief executive of Talk Liberation and the driving force behind the Panquake platform. John Kiriakou, who has known her for years and serves as the platform's brand ambassador, describes her as the most dogged person he has ever known — a characterisation he traces to her defence of Julian Assange before Assange was dragged out of the Ecuadorian embassy.

talk-liberation-bank-freeze.title: Julian Assange
talk-liberation-bank-freeze.summary: Kiriakou — a 15-year friend and former WikiLeaks board member — on why Assange is a publisher owed a journalist's immunity, and a political prisoner.

talk-liberation-bank-freeze.title: Elon Musk
talk-liberation-bank-freeze.summary: Kiriakou met Musk by chance at a Washington hotel bar in 2009, when he was worth $1 billion and talking about Tesla, SpaceX and colonizing Mars.

talk-liberation-bank-freeze.title: Government encryption back-door demands
talk-liberation-bank-freeze.summary: John Kiriakou's account of state pressure on technology companies for access to encrypted systems — the British government's demand for a back door into Apple's operating system, which he says Apple met with a threat to leave the United Kingdom, and his prediction that the second Trump administration would make the same demand of any new platform under a counterterrorism pretext.

talk-liberation-bank-freeze.title: The colleague who went to Microsoft
talk-liberation-bank-freeze.summary: In 2000, John Kiriakou''s supervisor left the CIA for Microsoft to do what he called "some really cool social media stuff" — a phrase that meant nothing to Kiriakou at the time, and which he later read as an early sign of the deliberate placement of intelligence officers inside technology companies.

targeting-analyst.title: Kiriakou's transfer to the Directorate of Operations
targeting-analyst.summary: John Kiriakou's roughly two-month internal campaign to transfer from the CIA's analytic Directorate of Intelligence to the operational Directorate of Operations, overcoming what he calls a "natural bias in operations against the eggheads on the analytic side," followed by an Athens posting secured because he was the only person in the entire CIA fluent in both Greek and Arabic. Covers his full CIA career arc from 1988/1990 recruitment through analyst years on Iraq, the switch to operations, 9/11, the enhanced-interrogation refusal, executive assistant to the deputy director for operations, and his eventual resignation and post-CIA career.

targeting-analyst.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
targeting-analyst.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

targeting-analyst.title: Abu Zubaydah
targeting-analyst.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

targeting-analyst.title: The Iranian elementary school strike
targeting-analyst.summary: A Tomahawk cruise missile strike at the start of the 2026 war that killed more than 175 people at an Iranian elementary school. The United States denied responsibility until its own investigation confirmed it; John Kiriakou traces the failure to targeting data a decade out of date and expects no one to be punished for it.

targeting-analyst.title: Magic box
targeting-analyst.summary: An improvised cell-phone locator that two CIA tech officers built from parts bought in a Pakistani bazaar during the hunt for Abu Zubaydah. It could point toward a phone while a call was live, and did so exactly once — long enough for John Kiriakou to conclude the device was wasted time and to fly in a targeting analyst instead.

targeting-analyst.title: The Directorate of Science and Technology
targeting-analyst.summary: One of the CIA's four directorates, which in John Kiriakou's time was an afterthought responsible for disguises and briefcases with hidden compartments, and which he says now works with Palantir, Amazon, Nvidia and Elon Musk's companies on work closer to DARPA's than to anything the agency did in the past.

targeting-information-between-allies.title: Russian refusal of US mediation
targeting-information-between-allies.summary: The Russian announcement during the 2026 Iran war that it would no longer take part in Ukraine settlement talks led by the United States, on the grounds that Washington had negotiated with Iran and attacked it mid-negotiation. John Kiriakou's assessment was that the reasoning was correct.

targeting-information-between-allies.title: Trump Iran Ceasefire Efforts
targeting-information-between-allies.summary: Per John Kiriakou, Donald Trump reached out behind the scenes twice in ten days seeking a ceasefire with Iran and was rebuffed; Kiriakou also says Benjamin Netanyahu called the White House to check reports of the outreach, and that on foreign policy Netanyahu "has just as much authority as whoever happens to be president of the United States."

targeting-information-between-allies.title: Donald Trump
targeting-information-between-allies.summary: 45th and 47th U.S. president. Per John Kiriakou, a man genuinely convinced he was doing right by bombing Iran, "duped" by the same Netanyahu nuclear bluff Obama once rejected — and, at the same time, the most blindly pro-Israel president in history, an admirer of autocrats who has never once criticized Vladimir Putin, and prone to gestures — from the Gulf of America to a since-abandoned "Department of War" rename — that test the edges of his actual authority.

targeting-information-between-allies.title: Netanyahu in hiding
targeting-information-between-allies.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the Israeli prime minister's disappearance from public view during the 2026 Iran war, when reports placed him in Germany and then Cyprus, and of Iran's adoption of Israel's own decapitation tactics — strikes on Netanyahu's house, which killed his brother, and on Itamar Ben-Gvir's.

targeting-information-between-allies.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
targeting-information-between-allies.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

targeting-information-between-allies.title: Cost of the 2026 Iran war
targeting-information-between-allies.summary: The daily cost of the 2026 Iran war as John Kiriakou reported it — between two and three billion dollars a day, per Axios — and the comparison he draws with the Gulf War, when a president was rendered speechless by a figure of one hundred million dollars a day.

tarpon-springs.title: The family that spans the spectrum
tarpon-springs.summary: John Kiriakou''s Greek relations, offered as a political cross-section: his grandmother''s first cousin sat on the politburo of the Communist Party of Greece, a close cousin was elected governor of the Dodecanese for the Conservatives, he has everybody in between — and all of them, to his bafflement, love the American ambassador.

tarpon-springs.title: Craig Murray
tarpon-springs.summary: Former British Ambassador to Uzbekistan whom John Kiriakou cites as a whistleblower of extreme torture: during a meeting at the Uzbek intelligence service, Murray heard screaming, walked in, and saw a man being boiled in oil — reporting it cost him his career.

tarpon-springs.title: Dumping cash in a Moscow bathroom
tarpon-springs.summary: John Kiriakou's examples of what covert action has actually meant in practice — American commandos blowing up the Trans-Siberian oil pipeline, Afghan guerrillas hired to cross the Amu Darya and attack a refinery inside the southern USSR, and cash dumped in a Moscow bathroom to undermine the rouble.

tarpon-springs.title: How Chinese intelligence recruits
tarpon-springs.summary: John Kiriakou''s assessment of the Ministry of State Security''s tradecraft: very effective with anyone who simply wants money, because the money is limitless, and very bad at cultivating a source who does not yet know who is cultivating him — with the target usually being access to sophisticated technology.

tarpon-springs.title: MK-ULTRA in Canada
tarpon-springs.summary: John Kiriakou''s confirmation that many MK-ULTRA experiments took place on Canadian soil, and his explanation of why: the CIA asked the Canadian intelligence service for help with its anti-Soviet, anti-Chinese remote-viewing and LSD work, and the Canadians gladly gave it.

tarpon-springs.title: Pakistani corruption and democracy
tarpon-springs.summary: John Kiriakou's assessment that corruption in Pakistan is so deep and so broad that a genuinely functioning democracy is almost impossible there — set against a long history of military coups, a habit of imprisoning former prime ministers, and his insistence that Imran Khan should not be in a cell.

taybeh.title: Shireen Abu Akleh
taybeh.summary: Al Jazeera journalist, U.S. citizen and Greek Orthodox Christian; John Kiriakou recounts that she was shot in the face by an Israeli sniper while wearing clearly marked press gear, and that the IDF then beat pallbearers at her funeral.

taybeh.title: Church of Saint Porphyrios
taybeh.summary: The Greek Orthodox church in Gaza that John Kiriakou describes as the oldest continuously operating church in the world; per Kiriakou, Israel bombed it while 24 women and children were sheltering inside.

taybeh.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
taybeh.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

taybeh.title: Greek Intelligence Service
taybeh.summary: Greece's intelligence service, with which John Kiriakou worked closely during his Athens posting; its head of surveillance called off surveillance on him after watching him make a large offering at Saint Nectarios's tomb on the island of Aegina.

taybeh.title: Jerry Falwell Jr.
taybeh.summary: Evangelical leader and former president of Liberty University; John Kiriakou recounts that Falwell personally recruited him to lecture at Liberty's Jesse Helms School of Government after his whistleblowing, with the reasoning that "torture is not Christian."

taybeh.title: Iraqi invasion of Kuwait
taybeh.summary: John Kiriakou''s most detailed account of the intelligence process around the 1990 Iraqi invasion of Kuwait and its 1991 liberation. As a first-year CIA analyst on a ''training account'' covering Iraq, Kiriakou produced the June 30, 1990 warning paper for the White House; suggested calling the US Defense Attaché in Baghdad to drive to the border and report what he saw (the answer: ''Literally the entire Iraqi military is heading south''); briefed the August 2 Oval Office meeting with Bush; and later took a single phone call from General Colin Powell that led, eight hours later, to 47 cruise missiles striking the Iraqi Intelligence Service headquarters in Baghdad.

ted-rall.title: Donald Trump
ted-rall.summary: 45th and 47th U.S. president. Per John Kiriakou, a man genuinely convinced he was doing right by bombing Iran, "duped" by the same Netanyahu nuclear bluff Obama once rejected — and, at the same time, the most blindly pro-Israel president in history, an admirer of autocrats who has never once criticized Vladimir Putin, and prone to gestures — from the Gulf of America to a since-abandoned "Department of War" rename — that test the edges of his actual authority.

ted-rall.title: Kurds
ted-rall.summary: The stateless people John Kiriakou calls generationally pro-American — he escorted visiting Kurdish delegations around Washington as a young analyst and bristled at officials who talked down to them. In his telling the Kurds were the only genuine opposition inside Saddam's Iraq, the only faction of the exile circus that ever amounted to anything (Jalal Talabani ended up president of Iraq), the victims of Saddam's chemical weapons and of a no-fly zone that forgot to ban helicopters — and the common enemy that actually united Turkey and ISIS.

ted-rall.title: Abraxas Corporation
ted-rall.summary: The private intelligence company founded in the 1990s by retired CIA operations officers as a tax pass-through and a place to smoke cigars and tell stories — which, after 9/11, made its founders, in John Kiriakou's phrase, Mega Millions rich.

ted-rall.title: AIPAC
ted-rall.summary: The American Israel Public Affairs Committee — the U.S. political organization that, in John Kiriakou's framing, ought to be registered as a foreign-lobbying entity but is not, and that wields decisive electoral power against U.S. elected officials who express support for Palestinian human rights.

ted-rall.title: The BBC and the sanctions coverage
ted-rall.summary: John Kiriakou's assessment of the BBC — that it has a long history of offering both sides, which American broadcasters do not — set against his memory of watching it from inside the CIA in the run-up to the liberation of Kuwait, when its reporting on starving Iraqi children under sanctions drove him mad, because food was not sanctioned and Saddam Hussein was refusing to distribute it.

ted-rall.title: Ranking Bush, Obama, Trump and Biden
ted-rall.summary: John Kiriakou's answer to a viewer asking which of four presidents he would choose to live under. He begins by picking Barack Obama as the least bad face to the world, reverses himself over the whistleblower prosecutions, and ends by naming Joe Biden — on the grounds that the country was effectively running itself.

temporary-protected-status.title: Haiti
temporary-protected-status.summary: A country John Kiriakou studied for the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, where he found that the seven largest merchant families — the families that run the entire Haitian economy — are white. He treats Haiti's poverty as manufactured rather than accidental, and its unrest as a story the American press declines to cover.

temporary-protected-status.title: Ceuta migrant crossings (2026)
temporary-protected-status.summary: The mass crossing of roughly 60,000 people from Morocco into the Spanish enclave of Ceuta in early August 2026. John Kiriakou reads the episode not as a spontaneous migration but as a deliberate act of Moroccan statecraft aimed at Spain, triggered by the Spanish prime minister's visit to Algeria, and rejects the widely circulated theory that Israel organised it.

temporary-protected-status.title: Morocco–Algeria rivalry
temporary-protected-status.summary: The long enmity between Morocco and Algeria over primacy in North Africa, which John Kiriakou identifies as the actual cause of the 2026 mass crossing into Ceuta after Spain's prime minister paid an official visit to Algiers.

temporary-protected-status.title: Spanish enclaves in North Africa
temporary-protected-status.summary: Ceuta and the smaller Spanish territories on the Moroccan coast, held under treaties more than four centuries old. In John Kiriakou's account they are colonial remnants that Morocco resents, that Israel has used to needle Spain over its criticism of Israeli occupation, and that United States policy now formally describes as an occupation.

temporary-protected-status.title: Thomas Massie
temporary-protected-status.summary: Republican U.S. Representative from Kentucky known for a constitutionalist voting record and consistent opposition to foreign military intervention; per John Kiriakou, a principled America-First congressman who votes with the president on the vast majority of issues, and whose opposition to U.S. funding of Israel and foreign wars is the only plausible explanation for the roughly $30 million spent by the Israel lobby to unseat him in a primary.

temporary-protected-status.title: Abdul El-Sayed
temporary-protected-status.summary: Physician and Democratic Socialists of America-backed candidate in Michigan's 2026 Democratic Senate primary. John Kiriakou, who discloses a $100 donation to the campaign, presents him as the test case for whether the electability argument still works for establishment Democrats.

ten-minute-moves.title: John's rules for prison survival
ten-minute-moves.summary: The code John Kiriakou says he wrote for himself at FCI Loretto out of his CIA training — rule one, recruit prisoners as sources using the same motivations the agency teaches; rule two, seek cover and blend in — illustrated with a plan to obtain contraband binder clips.

ten-minute-moves.title: FCI Loretto
ten-minute-moves.summary: U.S. Federal Correctional Institution in Loretto, Pennsylvania; the low-medium-security prison at which John Kiriakou served 23 months of a 30-month sentence following his 2013 Espionage Act–era plea deal; the originally ordered "minimum security work camp" placement was countermanded — per Kiriakou, on Brennan's direct intervention — to place him in the actual prison alongside the general population.

ten-minute-moves.title: The prison service economy
ten-minute-moves.summary: The trade in goods and services at FCI Loretto as John Kiriakou describes it — used shoes resold on commission, convenience stores run out of lockers at a thirty per cent markup, a dozen bookmakers, unlicensed chiropractic, and sexual services priced in books of postage stamps.

ten-minute-moves.title: The chapel job
ten-minute-moves.summary: The work assignment John Kiriakou was given at FCI Loretto after he volunteered to teach a class — *"if I want you to teach a class I'll ask you to teach a class"* — and was made a janitor in the chapel instead, at $1.08 a month.

ten-minute-moves.title: Robert the arsonist
ten-minute-moves.summary: The Australian prisoner who became John Kiriakou's roommate at FCI Loretto — convicted of burning down a Buffalo motor vehicles office over a sales tax dispute, a pathological liar who Kiriakou concluded was a clinical sociopath, and whom he says was easy to manipulate because he was an excitement junkie.

ten-minute-moves.title: Private prison system
ten-minute-moves.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the U.S. private prison industry as an incentive to keep beds filled and cut costs on food and medicine — illustrated by the 'sewer trout,' dog-food, and dead-rat-in-the-Kool-Aid stories from his own incarceration.

terry-albury.title: The Latin American newspaper prediction
terry-albury.summary: The prediction John Kiriakou gave to a Latin American newspaper a week or two after Donald Trump's first inauguration — that things would be better for whistleblowers under Trump because they could not possibly be worse than under Barack Obama — and his later verdict that he had been "very foolish" to say it, since the Trump administration opened three times as many leak investigations and won longer sentences.

terry-albury.title: The play the CIA killed
terry-albury.summary: A stage play about John Kiriakou's case, written in 2015 by the screenwriter Scott Burns for a New York theatre, which Kiriakou says was never performed because the CIA applied enough pressure on the theatre owner to stop it — an account he offered as a counterpoint to the Reality Winner play that was running unmolested at the same moment.

terry-albury.title: Hillary in a Kamala suit
terry-albury.summary: John Kiriakou''s assessment of the incoming Biden administration three weeks after the 2020 election: Biden as Obama 2.0, Kamala Harris as "Hillary in a Kamala suit", and a career prosecutor whose drug sentencings he says ruined thousands of lives.

terry-albury.title: Liam O'Grady
terry-albury.summary: The Eastern District of Virginia judge who sentenced Daniel Hale, and who in John Kiriakou''s account surprised the courtroom twice: with a sentence of 45 months rather than the far longer term expected, and with a recommendation that Hale serve it in a low-security prison where he could be treated for depression and addiction. The Bureau of Prisons ignored the recommendation and sent him to the communications management unit at Marion instead.

terry-albury.title: One hundred and twenty-three investigations
terry-albury.summary: The figure John Kiriakou attributes to Attorney General Jeff Sessions and what he calls his big mouth: 123 active national security leak investigations under way, which Kiriakou uses to argue the Trump administration was worse for whistleblowers than Obama''s.

terry-albury.title: The Chilean newspaper prediction
terry-albury.summary: The forecast John Kiriakou says he got wrong: asked by a Chilean newspaper the week Donald Trump was elected whether things would improve for national security whistleblowers, he said he was cautiously optimistic, on the ground that they could not get worse than under Obama.

terry-aubry.title: Watermark
terry-aubry.summary: Reality Winner, on Kiriakou's show, describes the printer watermark that let the NSA trace her leaked document to a specific office.

terry-aubry.title: Afghan Languages
terry-aubry.summary: The three major languages of Afghanistan — Pashto, Dari (a form of Persian), and Arabic — as discussed on John Kiriakou's show with NSA whistleblower and former military linguist Reality Winner.

terry-aubry.title: Angela Merkel
terry-aubry.summary: German chancellor whose mobile phone the NSA was intercepting, in what John Kiriakou treats as the cleanest illustration of the two-tier American attitude to surveillance: the interception of one of Washington''s closest allies was big news, Hillary Clinton flew to Germany to apologise, and — per Kiriakou — the United States then did it again. Asked about it in Berlin, his answer was that intercepting her phone is exactly what he wants the CIA to be doing.

terry-aubry.title: Chelsea Manning
terry-aubry.summary: Former U.S. Army intelligence analyst who provided WikiLeaks its 2010 trove of military and diplomatic documents. Per John Kiriakou, Manning meets the legal definition of whistleblower for exposing war crimes, was a torture victim of prolonged solitary confinement with forced nudity, and was sentenced to 35 years in prison before Barack Obama commuted — not pardoned — her sentence. Kiriakou says Manning later refused a grand jury's offer of immunity and chose renewed jail time rather than testify against Julian Assange.

terry-aubry.title: CIA disguise program
terry-aubry.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the CIA's disguise and forgery specialists — including a master disguise maker recruited from a beauty academy who built him a custom bald-head mask over six weeks, and a master forger recruited off his college newspaper cartoons.

terry-aubry.title: Donald Trump
terry-aubry.summary: 45th and 47th U.S. president. Per John Kiriakou, a man genuinely convinced he was doing right by bombing Iran, "duped" by the same Netanyahu nuclear bluff Obama once rejected — and, at the same time, the most blindly pro-Israel president in history, an admirer of autocrats who has never once criticized Vladimir Putin, and prone to gestures — from the Gulf of America to a since-abandoned "Department of War" rename — that test the edges of his actual authority.

thaad-stocks-in-the-gulf.title: Why the UAE was targeted
thaad-stocks-in-the-gulf.summary: John Kiriakou''s explanation for the disproportionate weight of Iranian fire falling on the United Arab Emirates in 2026: not the American presence but the Emirati role at the forefront of the war against the Houthis — and a wish to bloody Emirati noses despite the thousands of Iranians living in Dubai.

thaad-stocks-in-the-gulf.title: Bombing the Omanis
thaad-stocks-in-the-gulf.summary: John Kiriakou's judgement that Iran's strikes on the Gulf states — and above all on Oman, which had been trying to broker peace — made enemies Iran did not need to make, of governments that would otherwise have sat the war out.

thaad-stocks-in-the-gulf.title: Iranian strikes on Gulf hotels
thaad-stocks-in-the-gulf.summary: John Kiriakou''s reading of the Iranian drone and missile attacks on hotels in Abu Dhabi, Dubai and Muscat during the 2026 war: not targeted killings, but deliberate strikes at the tourist economies of the Gulf states, aimed at hotels famous enough to empty the country of visitors.

thaad-stocks-in-the-gulf.title: Bahrain's naturalisation policy
thaad-stocks-in-the-gulf.summary: John Kiriakou's account of how the Bahraini royal family changed the sectarian arithmetic of the country over thirty years — importing Syrians and naturalising Indian and Pakistani Sunni Muslims until a population that had been two-thirds to three-quarters Shia was closer to half and half.

thaad-stocks-in-the-gulf.title: Chaos as the Israeli objective
thaad-stocks-in-the-gulf.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer to whether Netanyahu''s government actually wanted an American invasion of Iran: what the Israelis want in Iran is what they got in Libya — chaos, civil war, and as many dead Iranians as possible.

thaad-stocks-in-the-gulf.title: Closing the Gulf embassies
thaad-stocks-in-the-gulf.summary: John Kiriakou''s reading of the American decision, announced live on air on 3 March 2026, to close its embassies in Saudi Arabia and Kuwait: that in the whole of the first Gulf War no American embassy was closed except Kuwait''s own, whose diplomats were taken to Iraq as human shields, and that shutting two at once meant Washington had concluded the war was about to get very much worse.

thatcher-wobbly-call.title: Saddam Hussein's classified biographer
thatcher-wobbly-call.summary: John Kiriakou''s first job at the CIA: writing the classified biography and psychological profile of Saddam Hussein in the Office of Leadership Analysis — the desk from which he watched the agency conclude, on 30 June 1990, that Iraq would invade Kuwait, and get the scale of the invasion wrong.

thatcher-wobbly-call.title: The Oval Office briefing of 2 August 1990
thatcher-wobbly-call.summary: The morning Iraq invaded Kuwait, a 25-year-old John Kiriakou was driven from CIA headquarters to the White House and found himself briefing President George H. W. Bush, Vice President Quayle, Brent Scowcroft and the CIA director — and answering the question *"well, now what do we do?"*

thatcher-wobbly-call.title: Bahrain Posting (1994–1996)
thatcher-wobbly-call.summary: John Kiriakou's 1994–1996 assignment to Bahrain under U.S. State Department cover as second secretary for economic affairs — arriving with his wife Joanne and infant son Chris on August 1, 1994, into a tiny Gulf monarchy whose sectarian tensions erupted, two months later, into the first Intifada.

thatcher-wobbly-call.title: George Habash
thatcher-wobbly-call.summary: Co-founder of the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine; as a young Lebanese medical student he was the college roommate at the American University of Beirut of Ahmed Khatib, the doctor whom Iraq installed as occupation governor of Kuwait on August 2, 1990 — a connection John Kiriakou carried into the Oval Office that day.

thatcher-wobbly-call.title: John Kiriakou
thatcher-wobbly-call.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

thatcher-wobbly-call.title: Abdul Amir al-Jamri
thatcher-wobbly-call.summary: The Bahraini cleric who led the Shia opposition during the 1990s uprising, and whom John Kiriakou interviewed for a human rights report in 1991 — an interview that had the Bahraini prime minister demanding, within the hour, that both American officers be expelled from the country.

the-189-undeclared-officers.title: Jonathan Pollard
the-189-undeclared-officers.summary: U.S. Navy civilian intelligence analyst convicted in 1985 of spying for Israel; the canonical proven case of Israeli espionage against the United States; cited by John Kiriakou in his 2024 Piers Morgan debate with a former Mossad director who denied any Israeli spying on the U.S.

the-189-undeclared-officers.title: Arabists
the-189-undeclared-officers.summary: The label applied inside the U.S. government to diplomats and analysts who knew Arabic and Middle Eastern history, and which John Kiriakou confirms functioned as a dismissal — the assumption being that anyone who understood the region was blindly prejudiced against Israel, or antisemitic.

the-189-undeclared-officers.title: AIPAC
the-189-undeclared-officers.summary: The American Israel Public Affairs Committee — the U.S. political organization that, in John Kiriakou's framing, ought to be registered as a foreign-lobbying entity but is not, and that wields decisive electoral power against U.S. elected officials who express support for Palestinian human rights.

the-189-undeclared-officers.title: The "spell your name" briefing
the-189-undeclared-officers.summary: The first time John Kiriakou dealt with the Israeli services: eight weeks into his CIA career, giving the junior slot in a liaison briefing on Saddam Hussein''s state of mind, he was interrupted by a Mossad representative who asked him to spell his name and then told him he was Jewish. Kiriakou''s reply — that he was not recruitable — became one of his recurring illustrations of the liaison relationship.

the-189-undeclared-officers.title: Abraham Accords
the-189-undeclared-officers.summary: The Trump-brokered normalization deals between Israel and Gulf Arab states — in John Kiriakou's judgment "a terrible idea in the first place," a great victory for Israel and the Gulf Arabs that was "a punch in the throat to the Palestinians." He argues the Accords are how Trump meant to "solve the Middle East in a day" — by screwing the Palestinians — that Hamas read the abandonment correctly, that October 7 shattered the project, and that reviving the Accords (Saudis in, victory declared, Nobel collected) remains the organizing goal of Trump's regional policy.

the-189-undeclared-officers.title: Amnesty International
the-189-undeclared-officers.summary: The human rights organization whose torture report forms part of John Kiriakou's core defense — the CIA's crimes were already public knowledge before he confirmed them on ABC, and the Justice Department's own declination letter said so — and the organization whose silence during his prosecution he cannot forgive. He begged Amnesty for a one-sentence statement and got a New Yorker subscription instead; it took Ai Weiwei to change their minds, and by then he was walking out of prison.

the-1968-waterboarding-conviction.title: The torture memo signature
the-1968-waterboarding-conviction.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of how the CIA''s torture programme was authorised: a list of about ten techniques sent from headquarters through the Justice Department, the National Security Council lawyers and Condoleezza Rice to the president — who, to the surprise of the agency''s own leadership, signed it. Kiriakou recalls the deputy director saying three times in one meeting that he could not believe the president had signed the memo.

the-1968-waterboarding-conviction.title: Abu Zubaydah
the-1968-waterboarding-conviction.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

the-1968-waterboarding-conviction.title: Bin Laden health rumors
the-1968-waterboarding-conviction.summary: John Kiriakou's dismissal of the claim that Osama bin Laden died years before the 2011 raid. He says the CIA received a steady stream of medical rumours about him — kidney failure, dialysis in a cave, a spinal disorder — none of which turned out to be true, and that bin Laden was in fine health apart from arthritis and a hip problem until the day he died.

the-1968-waterboarding-conviction.title: Fake CIA résumés
the-1968-waterboarding-conviction.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of being used as a human authenticator in the private sector: at the consulting firm he joined after leaving the CIA, every job applicant claiming agency service was sent to dinner with him, and by his count fully half of them had never set foot inside the CIA.

the-1968-waterboarding-conviction.title: False flags are too hard
the-1968-waterboarding-conviction.summary: John Kiriakou''s practical objection to the idea that governments routinely stage false flag operations: they exist, and at the operational level the CIA used them constantly, but the bigger the operation the harder it is to run — too many moving parts, too many people who must buy into the conspiracy, and too much incompetence in government to keep any of it straight. He couples the objection with the observation that a government which is not transparent has no standing to complain about public suspicion.

the-1968-waterboarding-conviction.title: SEAL Team Six attrition
the-1968-waterboarding-conviction.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer to the claim that the Navy SEALs who killed Osama bin Laden have since been killed off: the dead came from the broader unit rather than the raid party, SEAL Team Six numbers several hundred men rather than the dozen or so people imagine, and losing a high number of them to accidents and combat is, in his phrase, very sadly common.

the-1994-womens-class-action.title: Geneva Conventions
the-1994-womens-class-action.summary: The laws of war at the center of John Kiriakou''s most-told confrontation story: finding hooded prisoners in Pakistan, he demanded of the officer in charge — "Are you seriously telling me that you have never read the Geneva Convention? It is a war crime to put hoods on them. Take the hoods off." The two reported each other to headquarters; Kiriakou got in trouble — "they didn''t give two shits about the Geneva Convention." He indicts the Bush administration''s twin dodges: that al-Qaeda fighters, as non-state actors, fell outside the Conventions'' protections, and that the techniques weren''t torture at all.

the-1994-womens-class-action.title: The Clinton-era asset cull
the-1994-womens-class-action.summary: In the 1990s the CIA reviewed the file of every recruited asset in the world and dismissed any with a history of human rights abuses — roughly a third of its agents, in John Kiriakou''s account, in a reform he says was reversed as though by a switch after 11 September.

the-1994-womens-class-action.title: The new Iraqi flag
the-1994-womens-class-action.summary: Before the invasion of Iraq, John Kiriakou walked into the CIA''s Iraq Operations Group and found its director at his desk with Crayola markers, colouring in a design for a new Iraqi flag.

the-1994-womens-class-action.title: The unexplained false statement charge
the-1994-womens-class-action.summary: One of the five counts against John Kiriakou was making a false statement, and neither he nor his eleven lawyers could establish what the statement was supposed to have been; the government withdrew the count after his defence had spent six figures on it.

the-1994-womens-class-action.title: The scholar-in-residence pipeline
the-1994-womens-class-action.summary: John Kiriakou's description of retired CIA operations officers taking scholar-in-residence posts at universities and teaching literature courses that function, by their own account, as a recruitment funnel — students enrol knowing the instructor is a former officer and hoping for help getting in.

the-1994-womens-class-action.title: Eastern District of Virginia
the-1994-womens-class-action.summary: The U.S. federal district covering northern Virginia — home to Langley, the Pentagon, DHS and much of the intelligence-contractor industry — which John Kiriakou calls 'the espionage court' because the Justice Department files the great majority of its national security prosecutions there and because, in his telling, no national-security defendant has ever won a case in it; Kiriakou, Julian Assange, Edward Snowden and Jeffrey Sterling were all charged there.

the-1996-campaign-contribution-disclosur.title: The Ukraine call whistleblower
the-1996-campaign-contribution-disclosur.summary: The intelligence officer whose complaint triggered Donald Trump's first impeachment, and whom John Kiriakou declines to accept as a whistleblower at all — not on partisan grounds but on procedural ones. The complaint went to the Justice Department rather than the oversight committees, and its prose, he says, is lawyers' prose rather than the uniform CIA analytic style every analyst is trained into. He is nonetheless emphatic that naming the man was indefensible.

the-1996-campaign-contribution-disclosur.title: Whistleblower Protection Act
the-1996-campaign-contribution-disclosur.summary: United States statute protecting federal employees who disclose government wrongdoing from retaliation; per John Kiriakou, national security employees — including those at the CIA, Pentagon, FBI, NSA, DEA, White House, and Homeland Security — are explicitly exempt from its protections, leaving them with no legally safe avenue to report illegal activity within their agencies.

the-1996-campaign-contribution-disclosur.title: David Ransom
the-1996-campaign-contribution-disclosur.summary: U.S. Ambassador to Bahrain during the period of John Kiriakou's posting there; characterized by Kiriakou as one of the finest people he worked for in his CIA career

the-1996-campaign-contribution-disclosur.title: John Kiriakou
the-1996-campaign-contribution-disclosur.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

the-1996-campaign-contribution-disclosur.title: Chuck Grassley
the-1996-campaign-contribution-disclosur.summary: The senior senator from Iowa, and in John Kiriakou's assessment the one member of Congress who has taken whistleblower protection seriously as a legislative project — a count he has variously put at one finger, at two names, and at four out of 535. Grassley wrote the whistleblower protection statutes, speaks every year at the National Whistleblower Day luncheon, and is the name Kiriakou gives prospective whistleblowers as the single friendly ear on Capitol Hill. Kiriakou's personal verdict is colder — Grassley, he has said, never did anything for him.

the-1996-campaign-contribution-disclosur.title: The 2007 death threats
the-1996-campaign-contribution-disclosur.summary: The immediate personal consequence of John Kiriakou''s December 2007 television appearance confirming CIA waterboarding: hundreds of pieces of hate mail, and three threats against his life that the FBI classified as credible, one of which named his children and gave his home address. On the Bureau''s advice he took his family out of the country for a week; the FBI then interviewed the senders, judged them local cranks, and told him to come home.

the-2007-death-threats.title: The Ukraine call whistleblower
the-2007-death-threats.summary: The intelligence officer whose complaint triggered Donald Trump's first impeachment, and whom John Kiriakou declines to accept as a whistleblower at all — not on partisan grounds but on procedural ones. The complaint went to the Justice Department rather than the oversight committees, and its prose, he says, is lawyers' prose rather than the uniform CIA analytic style every analyst is trained into. He is nonetheless emphatic that naming the man was indefensible.

the-2007-death-threats.title: The chilling effect of whistleblower prosecutions
the-2007-death-threats.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that national-security prosecutions are not primarily about convictions but about deterrence — that the CIA cares about sending a message where the FBI cares about promotions, that his own case was meant to frighten anyone else considering disclosure, and that a New York Times reporter told him every national-security source the paper had went silent on the day of his arrest.

the-2007-death-threats.title: The 1996 campaign contribution disclosure
the-2007-death-threats.summary: The whistleblower disclosure John Kiriakou made inside the CIA in 1996, sixteen years before the one that ruined him. Serving overseas, he learned of a very large illegal contribution to the Dole presidential campaign, reported it to the CIA Inspector General, and watched the system work exactly as written: the IG investigated, found the information credible, and referred it to the Federal Election Commission. He offers it as the control case against which he judges every later complaint.

the-2007-death-threats.title: Thomas Drake
the-2007-death-threats.summary: NSA whistleblower; per John Kiriakou, the source for the statement that on the morning of September 11, 2001, NSA Director Mike Hayden told agency personnel NSA had been 'waiting for a 9/11' to implement the mass-electronic-surveillance program that NSA's founding charter forbids.

the-2007-death-threats.title: Chuck Grassley
the-2007-death-threats.summary: The senior senator from Iowa, and in John Kiriakou's assessment the one member of Congress who has taken whistleblower protection seriously as a legislative project — a count he has variously put at one finger, at two names, and at four out of 535. Grassley wrote the whistleblower protection statutes, speaks every year at the National Whistleblower Day luncheon, and is the name Kiriakou gives prospective whistleblowers as the single friendly ear on Capitol Hill. Kiriakou's personal verdict is colder — Grassley, he has said, never did anything for him.

the-2007-death-threats.title: Gina Haspel
the-2007-death-threats.summary: Director of the Central Intelligence Agency under President Trump's first term; known to John Kiriakou and others at the CIA as "Bloody Gina"; per Kiriakou, flew out to the secret black site to sit in on one of the enhanced-interrogation torture sessions "just because she could," personally supervised the torture of USS Cole bombing suspect Rahim al-Nashiri, and later fed the CIA's torture tapes into an industrial document grinder after being explicitly told by White House Counsel not to destroy them.

the-2016-research-pitch.title: Japanese diplomat FBI sting
the-2016-research-pitch.summary: John Kiriakou's account of an FBI entrapment operation in which an agent posing as a Japanese diplomat cold-pitched him for classified information over five lunches, hoping he would commit actual espionage they could charge — a scheme he discovered only in his own case discovery.

the-2016-research-pitch.title: Espionage Act
the-2016-research-pitch.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

the-2016-research-pitch.title: Jeffrey Sterling
the-2016-research-pitch.summary: Former CIA officer convicted of nine felonies, including seven counts of espionage, after giving a New York Times interview about a racial discrimination lawsuit he had filed against the CIA. Per John Kiriakou, Sterling was not accused of spying for a foreign country; his underlying case was that the CIA had passed him over for promotion and told him explicitly it was because of his race. Daniel Ellsberg asked Sterling to go to trial specifically so the constitutionality of the Espionage Act could be challenged; Sterling did, was convicted, and was sentenced by Judge Leonie Brinkema to what she described as 'Kiriakou plus 12 months.'

the-2016-research-pitch.title: Chelsea Manning
the-2016-research-pitch.summary: Former U.S. Army intelligence analyst who provided WikiLeaks its 2010 trove of military and diplomatic documents. Per John Kiriakou, Manning meets the legal definition of whistleblower for exposing war crimes, was a torture victim of prolonged solitary confinement with forced nudity, and was sentenced to 35 years in prison before Barack Obama commuted — not pardoned — her sentence. Kiriakou says Manning later refused a grand jury's offer of immunity and chose renewed jail time rather than testify against Julian Assange.

the-2016-research-pitch.title: John Kerry
the-2016-research-pitch.summary: U.S. Senator from Massachusetts; chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee during John Kiriakou's 2009 service as the committee's senior investigator; subsequently U.S. Secretary of State; characterized by Kiriakou as a coward who buckled under CIA pressure on the Dasht-i-Leili reopening and as personally fixated on his perceived theft of the Secretary of State position by Hillary Clinton; the famously thrown medals were duplicates purchased at the post exchange.

the-2017-european-tour.title: The Official Secrets Act comparison
the-2017-european-tour.summary: John Kiriakou has argued that for whistleblowers the United Kingdom is far worse than the United States, because the Official Secrets Act bars anyone from saying anything touching national security and is used, in his phrase, as an iron fist against whistleblowers and potential whistleblowers alike.

the-2017-european-tour.title: The CIA that never existed
the-2017-european-tour.summary: A former senior CIA officer once told John Kiriakou that the agency he spoke about so fondly had never really existed — that it had only existed in his mind, that it had always been troubled and antithetical to American life, and that he had simply been too junior to see what was happening at the top. Kiriakou has come to think the man was right.

the-2017-european-tour.title: Domingo's television
the-2017-european-tour.summary: John Kiriakou has used the television rooms at FCI Loretto as his sharpest illustration of prison segregation: sets owned by racial blocs since a riot in the 1990s, a seat in front of one costing fourteen dollars, and one set left tuned to Law & Order every morning because a man named Domingo had paid four hundred dollars for it and had been gone for years.

the-2017-european-tour.title: Mental health as a disciplinary problem
the-2017-european-tour.summary: John Kiriakou has said that before his own prosecution he never gave five seconds of thought to the American prison system, and that living inside it showed him a broken one — in particular a system in which mental health is treated as a disciplinary problem rather than a medical one.

the-2017-european-tour.title: The Ai Weiwei encounter in Berlin
the-2017-european-tour.summary: John Kiriakou met the artist Ai Weiwei by pure chance on a Berlin street while dragging a suitcase to the airport after a board meeting — an encounter that led to a tour of Ai Weiwei's studio and a signed iPhone case bearing the Lego portrait the artist had made of him for an exhibition at Alcatraz.

the-2017-european-tour.title: The Alcatraz walkthrough
the-2017-european-tour.summary: On his very first day of house arrest, the day Ai Weiwei's political-prisoner exhibition closed at Alcatraz, the San Francisco gallery that had helped stage the show telephoned John Kiriakou and walked him around the entire exhibition on an iPad so that he could see his own portrait and the ceramic flowers filling the sinks of the solitary confinement cells.

the-2020-extradition-hearing.title: Solitary confinement
the-2020-extradition-hearing.summary: The prison isolation practice the United Nations calls a form of torture; John Kiriakou, drawing on his own ten days in a six-by-sixteen-foot cell, argues that jailing depressed prisoners like Daniel Hale in solitary 'for their own safety' is precisely what drives them to suicide.

the-2020-extradition-hearing.title: Julian Assange
the-2020-extradition-hearing.summary: Kiriakou — a 15-year friend and former WikiLeaks board member — on why Assange is a publisher owed a journalist's immunity, and a political prisoner.

the-2020-extradition-hearing.title: Eastern District of Virginia
the-2020-extradition-hearing.summary: The U.S. federal district covering northern Virginia — home to Langley, the Pentagon, DHS and much of the intelligence-contractor industry — which John Kiriakou calls 'the espionage court' because the Justice Department files the great majority of its national security prosecutions there and because, in his telling, no national-security defendant has ever won a case in it; Kiriakou, Julian Assange, Edward Snowden and Jeffrey Sterling were all charged there.

the-2020-extradition-hearing.title: The solitary confinement precedents
the-2020-extradition-hearing.summary: The legal argument John Kiriakou made repeatedly between 2020 and 2022 in defence of Julian Assange, and revived in 2025 for the Australian pilot Daniel Duggan — that no extradition to the United States can succeed once a court is asked to find that American solitary confinement is not torture, a proposition already contradicted by the United Nations, by the United States' own federal torture statute, and by a line of British and European rulings blocking extraditions on exactly that ground.

the-2020-extradition-hearing.title: Assange and solitary confinement
the-2020-extradition-hearing.summary: John Kiriakou's 2018 argument that Julian Assange's isolation inside the Ecuadorian embassy amounted to solitary confinement — a practice the United Nations classes as torture — and that everybody breaks under it eventually, however strong they are.

the-2020-extradition-hearing.title: Bernie Sanders
the-2020-extradition-hearing.summary: United States senator from Vermont. John Kiriakou, who watched him daily from the Senate Foreign Relations Committee staff, describes Sanders holding open breakfast in the Senate cafeteria for anyone who walked in — insisting only that they call him "Bernie" — and names him the one 2016 candidate willing to talk about shrinking the military.

the-2025-india-pakistan-clash-assessment.title: The ISI as two organizations
the-2025-india-pakistan-clash-assessment.summary: John Kiriakou''s working model of Pakistan''s Inter-Services Intelligence during his time as CIA chief of counterterrorism operations there: one half made up of British-trained officers he calls great counterterrorism partners, and another half that created, trained, financed and armed the Taliban — a split that left him deciding case by case whom he could trust.

the-2025-india-pakistan-clash-assessment.title: CIA attention to West Africa
the-2025-india-pakistan-clash-assessment.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer on whether the CIA is likely to be operating in Burkina Faso: for all the years he was at the agency it cared very little about Africa and especially West Africa, but the presence of al-Qaeda and Islamic State affiliates plus the drug trade makes CIA and special forces involvement probable — and, he adds, the American public will not hear about it.

the-2025-india-pakistan-clash-assessment.title: CIA–FBI incompatible computer systems
the-2025-india-pakistan-clash-assessment.summary: John Kiriakou's claim that from the CIA's founding in 1947 until 2009 the computer systems of the CIA and the FBI were not compatible with one another — no message could be sent from one to the other and no intelligence shared — which he offers both as the material substrate of the interagency hatred that helped make September 11 possible, and as the gap through which James Mitchell and Bruce Jessen were able to pass Ali Soufan's FBI debriefings of Abu Zubaydah off as the fruits of torture.

the-2025-india-pakistan-clash-assessment.title: Fake CIA résumés
the-2025-india-pakistan-clash-assessment.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of being used as a human authenticator in the private sector: at the consulting firm he joined after leaving the CIA, every job applicant claiming agency service was sent to dinner with him, and by his count fully half of them had never set foot inside the CIA.

the-2025-india-pakistan-clash-assessment.title: Forcing Iran toward a bomb
the-2025-india-pakistan-clash-assessment.summary: John Kiriakou''s argument that Western pressure risks producing the very outcome it claims to prevent: repeated Israeli assassinations of Iranian scientists and generals and strikes on Iranian sites may eventually leave Ayatollah Khamenei with no choice but to permit a defensive weapon — despite the religious prohibition Kiriakou credits him with maintaining, and despite successive American estimates that Iran is not seeking one.

the-2025-india-pakistan-clash-assessment.title: Freemasons and Opus Dei at the CIA
the-2025-india-pakistan-clash-assessment.summary: John Kiriakou's characterisation of the affinity networks at the top of the CIA — a great many senior officers who are Freemasons, and periods in which most of the leadership belonged to Opus Dei and attended the same church in Great Falls, Virginia. He rejects the idea that these are plots, describing them instead as accidental clusters of men who look out for one another.

the-2026-world-cup-final.title: Kiriakou on soccer
the-2026-world-cup-final.summary: John Kiriakou's public reversal on football, a sport he had dismissed since his teens on the strength of a Saturday Night Live joke about a match between Yemen and Saudi Arabia being decided early by an insurmountable one-nil lead. Watching the 2026 World Cup, he concluded he had been wrong.

the-2026-world-cup-final.title: Acts of Service
the-2026-world-cup-final.summary: The Doja Cat song that John Kiriakou discovered, through a Cameo request, had become the soundtrack to a genre of montage about him. The clips set to it use footage from before his weight loss — he lost 77 pounds by 2007 and 115 pounds from 2022 — and he says he cannot watch them.

the-2026-world-cup-final.title: 2026 Iran war
the-2026-world-cup-final.summary: The open-ended American and Israeli war against Iran that John Kiriakou tracked week by week on his own show — a conflict he says was sold as three weeks, ran into its fifth month, achieved every decapitation objective it set, and continued anyway. His grade for it is a D, and his forecast is a Truth Social post declaring victory while nothing changes.

the-2026-world-cup-final.title: Strait of Hormuz
the-2026-world-cup-final.summary: The shipping chokepoint at the mouth of the Persian Gulf, and the centre of gravity of the 2026 Iran war in John Kiriakou''s account — a strait whose only navigable deep water lies on the Iranian side of the maritime border, closed not by Iran''s aggression but, as he insists, by the American and Israeli attack that provoked it: "The Strait of Hormuz was open. We''re the ones that forced the closure."

the-2026-world-cup-final.title: The General Assembly circus
the-2026-world-cup-final.summary: John Kiriakou's view of the annual United Nations General Assembly, which he calls the Super Bowl for global politics and which he disliked more than almost anything else in his CIA career. His last tour was at the United Nations in New York, where the September session brings the city to a halt and makes the American mission almost unreachable.

the-2026-world-cup-final.title: The Pentagon injury figures
the-2026-world-cup-final.summary: John Kiriakou''s explanation of why the Pentagon was able to withhold news of dozens of American casualties in the Iran war: not secrecy law, but the absence of any statute requiring disclosure. In his framing Congress is asleep at the switch, having never passed such a law, so the department reports nothing it is not obliged to report.

the-abraham-lincoln-off-oman.title: Canada as a bargaining chip
the-abraham-lincoln-off-oman.summary: John Kiriakou's reading of Mark Carney's Davos speech as the moment Canada stopped pretending the United States could be trusted as a long-term partner — and his account of what wore the relationship out, including Washington's insistence that Ottawa arrest Huawei's chief financial officer on a computer-hacking charge and hold her for three years to trade.

the-abraham-lincoln-off-oman.title: China's generals without combat experience
the-abraham-lincoln-off-oman.summary: Presented with the observation that China's purged and reshuffled top brass are now too young to have fought in any war, John Kiriakou agreed it mattered little in the near term and a great deal in the long term — because American military planning will have to account for an adversary whose senior commanders have never been in combat.

the-abraham-lincoln-off-oman.title: Ilhan Omar
the-abraham-lincoln-off-oman.summary: U.S. Representative whom John Kiriakou credits with sponsoring a rewrite of the Espionage Act in two consecutive Congresses — legislation he says is dead on arrival with a Republican House because of who she is. Kiriakou has also sat at her table — in January 2026 he was one of about twenty guests at a dinner where Omar described the federal operation in Minneapolis and the budget manoeuvre that funded every part of the government except Homeland Security.

the-abraham-lincoln-off-oman.title: Macron and the airplane steps
the-abraham-lincoln-off-oman.summary: Asked what he thought was behind the French president's bruised appearance at Davos, John Kiriakou gave the blunt answer — "honestly, I think she hits him" — and dated his own change of mind to the footage at the top of the airplane steps.

the-abraham-lincoln-off-oman.title: The Arlington house
the-abraham-lincoln-off-oman.summary: The 1,200-square-foot house John Kiriakou bought with his Pakistan overtime and danger pay for $347,000, sold two years later for $721,000, and now values at a million — the anchor of his repeated argument that his own children can never live in the Arlington, Virginia neighbourhood they grew up in.

the-abraham-lincoln-off-oman.title: The CIA performance metric
the-abraham-lincoln-off-oman.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer to a viewer who asked whether the CIA used key performance indicators: for case officers there was only one measure — how many genuine spies you had recruited to steal secrets — and recruiting the old lady who keeps the safe house clean might earn a pat on the back and nothing more.

the-addis-ababa-zoo.title: Quoted on NPR
the-addis-ababa-zoo.summary: John Kiriakou's discovery, via a standing Google alert on his own name, that National Public Radio had cited a DeProgram discussion between him and Ted Rall in an article on Palestinians killed while waiting for food — an outlet he had walked out on years earlier.

the-addis-ababa-zoo.title: The boring cover story
the-addis-ababa-zoo.summary: The CIA training principle John Kiriakou says governed how officers described their jobs to strangers: pick something so dull that nobody asks a second question. His own standard answer was the foreign service, training work, and some import-export negotiation.

the-addis-ababa-zoo.title: The rejected deposits
the-addis-ababa-zoo.summary: John Kiriakou''s explanation of why banks returned large deposits to Donald Trump — not political discrimination, in his account, but anti-money-laundering law: a bank that cannot get a credible account of where the money came from faces felony exposure, and no bank turns away deposits for any lesser reason.

the-addis-ababa-zoo.title: The Milan–Sofia flight
the-addis-ababa-zoo.summary: A flight John Kiriakou took from Milan to Sofia, routed away from Athens under a different passport for a sensitive operation, on which a persistent seatmate refused to accept a dull cover story — until Kiriakou told him he smuggled women and cigarettes out of Eastern Europe.

the-addis-ababa-zoo.title: The Saudi request on Gaddafi
the-addis-ababa-zoo.summary: John Kiriakou's account of an approach by Saudi Arabia to the CIA asking that Muammar Gaddafi be overthrown by any means necessary, with Riyadh offering to pay for everything — a request he says was declined, and which lapsed only when Gaddafi announced he would turn his attention from the Middle East to African unity.

the-addis-ababa-zoo.title: Home rule in Washington, DC
the-addis-ababa-zoo.summary: The governing arrangement under which the District of Columbia has run its own affairs since 1971, explained by John Kiriakou as a grant made by Richard Nixon that replaced direct rule by a congressional committee — and which he describes Donald Trump as wanting to take back, on the strength of a single assault on a well-known administration staffer.

the-afghan-womans-lesson.title: Rival factions in Libya
the-afghan-womans-lesson.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the CIA and the State Department backing opposing factions inside Libya — proxies funded by two arms of the same government that end up fighting each other, an arrangement he calls insane and treats as characteristic of American intervention in places nobody is reporting on.

the-afghan-womans-lesson.title: The Wagner coverage asymmetry
the-afghan-womans-lesson.summary: John Kiriakou''s explanation for why the Wagner Group saturates American media while American private military contractors do not: there is no desire or necessity in the American press to keep secret a private army that does not belong to the United States, and the coverage doubles as a device for keeping Americans engaged with Ukraine.

the-afghan-womans-lesson.title: Elliott Abrams
the-afghan-womans-lesson.summary: The Reagan-era assistant secretary of state whose 2023 appointment to a Biden administration advisory board John Kiriakou treated as proof that neoliberal and neoconservative foreign policy are the same policy with interchangeable players — a man who pleaded guilty over Iran-Contra, was pardoned, helped sell the Iraqi weapons of mass destruction case, and then served Donald Trump on Iran and Venezuela.

the-afghan-womans-lesson.title: Frances Haugen
the-afghan-womans-lesson.summary: The Facebook employee John Kiriakou refuses to call a whistleblower — arguing that against the legal definition, bringing to light waste, fraud, abuse, illegality or threats to public health or safety, she qualifies as a corporate spokesperson whose motive was to improve the company's bottom line, not to expose wrongdoing.

the-afghan-womans-lesson.title: Gavin Newsom
the-afghan-womans-lesson.summary: The California governor John Kiriakou described in 2023 as the consummate Democratic Party insider waiting his turn — a Pelosi relative who married into the Brown family, doing everything the Biden operation asked of him, including a pointless surrogate trip to Idaho, on the calculation that Joe Biden would not reach the nominating convention.

the-afghan-womans-lesson.title: Hamid Karzai
the-afghan-womans-lesson.summary: The president installed in Afghanistan after the American invasion, whom John Kiriakou uses as the standing illustration of what occupation actually buys: after twenty years and more than a trillion dollars, Karzai was ''little more than the mayor of Kabul'' — and did not control all of Kabul either. The line began as a joke among Senate Foreign Relations Committee staff, and Kiriakou used it to Senator John Kerry''s face ten years into the war.

the-afghan-zero-units.title: The C-130 resettlements
the-afghan-zero-units.summary: John Kiriakou''s confirmation that the Hmong communities of Minnesota were former CIA assets brought to the United States as refugees, and his extension of a rule Ted Rall proposed — that refugee populations end up wherever the aircraft carrying them happened to land — to the Kurds of Bismarck, North Dakota and St Louis.

the-afghan-zero-units.title: Lindsey Graham
the-afghan-zero-units.summary: Republican senator from South Carolina who died in July 2026, and John Kiriakou's standing shorthand for the permanent war caucus — a "show horse" rather than a workhorse, a "chameleon" who "never saw a war that he didn't want to jump into with both feet," and, on posthumously released documentary footage, a man offering the US Air Force to bomb a country America was not at war with.

the-afghan-zero-units.title: Mexico City as an espionage hub
the-afghan-zero-units.summary: John Kiriakou''s assessment of Mexico City as one of the world''s principal centres of international espionage, alongside Vienna, London, Paris and Washington — driven by a gargantuan American embassy that Russian services target from next door — and his reading of why Mexico simply ignored a dossier of suspected Russian officers handed over by the Biden administration.

the-afghan-zero-units.title: Pakistani prisons
the-afghan-zero-units.summary: John Kiriakou''s flat refusal, in a discussion of Imran Khan''s detention, of the idea that a Pakistani prison offers VIP treatment to a former prime minister — grounded in his having visited many of them himself during the period when the CIA was locking people up there.

the-afghan-zero-units.title: Savas Kalenderidis
the-afghan-zero-units.summary: Greek intelligence officer, national hero and personal friend of John Kiriakou''s, who was involved in the operation to protect the PKK founder Abdullah Öcalan at the Greek embassy in Nairobi in 1999 — an operation that ended when Turkish and Kenyan intelligence diverted part of Öcalan''s motorcade and seized him. Kiriakou flatly denies the claim that the CIA and Turkish intelligence tried to kill Kalenderidis there.

the-afghan-zero-units.title: The Afghans in diplomatic limbo
the-afghan-zero-units.summary: John Kiriakou''s two-sided answer on the Afghan evacuees still held at a base in Qatar years after the fall of Kabul: that anyone who works for an occupation government which then loses will probably end badly, and that the United States nevertheless owes a debt to people who worked for it and should not leave them hanging.

the-afghans-in-diplomatic-limbo.title: Barrett Brown
the-afghans-in-diplomatic-limbo.summary: American journalist and former Anonymous associate whom John Kiriakou describes as one of the most intelligent writers and analysts he has ever encountered, with long-standing mental health problems and a two-decade heroin addiction he has now been clear of for at least a year, expelled from the United Kingdom and relocated to Mexico.

the-afghans-in-diplomatic-limbo.title: Censorship on the left
the-afghans-in-diplomatic-limbo.summary: John Kiriakou''s observation that he was censored far less by Forbes and Fortune than by The Nation and Mother Jones, which he offers as an instance of a general rule that a writer''s own side censors them hardest — the counterpart to Ted Rall''s account of being made to fit a particular kind of leftism rather than any kind.

the-afghans-in-diplomatic-limbo.title: Dr Oz and the Armenian hospices
the-afghans-in-diplomatic-limbo.summary: John Kiriakou''s reaction to a television segment by Mehmet Oz alleging fraud by Armenian-run hospices in Los Angeles — that a man he identifies as a veteran of the Turkish special forces zeroing in on Armenians in California is not a coincidence, and that each of the administration''s appointees appears to arrive with a racial scandal of their own.

the-afghans-in-diplomatic-limbo.title: The Iron Dome
the-afghans-in-diplomatic-limbo.summary: Israel's air-defence system as John Kiriakou reads it — impressive against a wave of slow Iranian drones, but shown by the handful that got through, and later by Iranian ballistic missiles, to be not all it is cracked up to be; each exchange, in his account, buying Iran intelligence about the gaps.

the-afghans-in-diplomatic-limbo.title: James Morris
the-afghans-in-diplomatic-limbo.summary: A close friend of John Kiriakou''s who served seventeen years of a twenty-year sentence for a crime committed at sixteen, found on release that a violent felony conviction closed off employment, made his own way to Turkey and across the border into Syria, spent two years fighting alongside the Kurds against ISIS, and later took his own life.

the-afghans-in-diplomatic-limbo.title: Presidents asleep in meetings
the-afghans-in-diplomatic-limbo.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer to who is the highest-profile person he ever saw fall asleep in a meeting — George H. W. Bush — together with his explanation that presidents do it all the time because the demands on their time leave too few hours in the day, and his father''s account of Ronald Reagan doing it constantly.

the-african-diplomats-remark.title: The secret Sahel appropriations
the-african-diplomats-remark.summary: John Kiriakou's complaint that the United States is quietly pumping billions of dollars into Niger, Mali, Burkina Faso, Guinea-Conakry and Guinea-Bissau — spending he says is supposed to be a big secret, addresses a French problem rather than an American one, and which American taxpayers have a right to know about and to judge.

the-african-diplomats-remark.title: The Paris rifle serial number
the-african-diplomats-remark.summary: The case John Kiriakou uses to argue that American weapons sent to Ukraine are leaking onto the black market: a rifle used to shoot and severely wound a policeman in Paris whose serial number, he says, matched a shipment of assault rifles the United States had sent to Ukraine some six months earlier.

the-african-diplomats-remark.title: CIA attention to West Africa
the-african-diplomats-remark.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer on whether the CIA is likely to be operating in Burkina Faso: for all the years he was at the agency it cared very little about Africa and especially West Africa, but the presence of al-Qaeda and Islamic State affiliates plus the drug trade makes CIA and special forces involvement probable — and, he adds, the American public will not hear about it.

the-african-diplomats-remark.title: China as economic threat
the-african-diplomats-remark.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that China is the real threat to the West not militarily — it has one aircraft carrier to America's two dozen and rarely invades — but economically, buying friends worldwide while the U.S. spends a trillion dollars a year on weapons.

the-african-diplomats-remark.title: Muddling through
the-african-diplomats-remark.summary: An analytic term John Kiriakou says CIA analysts used all the time, and his defence of it: forecasters instinctively reach for either/or outcomes, when what actually happens most often is that the parties to a conflict muddle through and little changes over the medium term. He applies it to Ukraine, and to why he expects Russia not to use nuclear weapons.

the-african-diplomats-remark.title: Permanent wartime economy
the-african-diplomats-remark.summary: John Kiriakou's thesis that since 9/11 the United States has run a permanent wartime economy so large that cutting the defense budget would trigger a depression — likening the dependency to crack addiction and warning it makes war almost inevitable.

the-ai-he-uses.title: Al Jazeera blocked in the United States
the-ai-he-uses.summary: Within hours of the first strikes on Iran, John Kiriakou reported that American cable carriers had pulled Al Jazeera — a friend in Florida texted him that Dish Network had blocked it, and viewers reported the same of Comcast Xfinity in Boston. His reading was blunt: they do not want Americans to see what is happening in the Middle East.

the-ai-he-uses.title: 2026 Iran war
the-ai-he-uses.summary: The open-ended American and Israeli war against Iran that John Kiriakou tracked week by week on his own show — a conflict he says was sold as three weeks, ran into its fifth month, achieved every decapitation objective it set, and continued anyway. His grade for it is a D, and his forecast is a Truth Social post declaring victory while nothing changes.

the-ai-he-uses.title: "A policy support organization"
the-ai-he-uses.summary: Asked how the CIA workforce would be reacting to the war on Iran, John Kiriakou answered from the Iraq war: people put their heads down and did as they were told, after a boss told an assembled group — all of whom opposed the invasion — that the agency is not a policy organization but a policy support organization, and would do what the White House told it to do.

the-ai-he-uses.title: Akrotiri Village Evacuation
the-ai-he-uses.summary: Kiriakou says the drone that hit Britain's Akrotiri base in Cyprus was likely an Israeli operation, staged and then falsely blamed on Iran.

the-ai-he-uses.title: American missile stockpiles
the-ai-he-uses.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that the United States has run its interceptor stocks down to the point of strategic vulnerability — that the conventional wisdom in Washington was that a round of the Iran war ended because the Patriots ran out, and that a country which cannot fight a two-front war certainly cannot do it below maximum production.

the-ai-he-uses.title: Andrew Bustamante
the-ai-he-uses.summary: Former CIA officer who sells CIA-style training online; John Kiriakou identifies him as the lone critic of his work hosting a show on a Russian network, and argues Bustamante's training business — open to anyone who pays — is the more problematic of the two.

the-ai-weiwei-encounter-in-berlin.title: The Alcatraz walkthrough
the-ai-weiwei-encounter-in-berlin.summary: On his very first day of house arrest, the day Ai Weiwei's political-prisoner exhibition closed at Alcatraz, the San Francisco gallery that had helped stage the show telephoned John Kiriakou and walked him around the entire exhibition on an iPad so that he could see his own portrait and the ceramic flowers filling the sinks of the solitary confinement cells.

the-ai-weiwei-encounter-in-berlin.title: Domingo's television
the-ai-weiwei-encounter-in-berlin.summary: John Kiriakou has used the television rooms at FCI Loretto as his sharpest illustration of prison segregation: sets owned by racial blocs since a riot in the 1990s, a seat in front of one costing fourteen dollars, and one set left tuned to Law & Order every morning because a man named Domingo had paid four hundred dollars for it and had been gone for years.

the-ai-weiwei-encounter-in-berlin.title: Mental health as a disciplinary problem
the-ai-weiwei-encounter-in-berlin.summary: John Kiriakou has said that before his own prosecution he never gave five seconds of thought to the American prison system, and that living inside it showed him a broken one — in particular a system in which mental health is treated as a disciplinary problem rather than a medical one.

the-ai-weiwei-encounter-in-berlin.title: The 2017 European tour
the-ai-weiwei-encounter-in-berlin.summary: In May 2017 John Kiriakou spent a week speaking about national security whistleblowing in Iceland, Germany, Luxembourg, Belgium and Ireland, addressing the German Parliament and sharing panels with serving European ministers — an audience he contrasted sharply with his reception in the United States, and one he found newly willing to break with Washington because it was, in his word, panic-stricken about Donald Trump.

the-ai-weiwei-encounter-in-berlin.title: The attribution problem in the DNC hack
the-ai-weiwei-encounter-in-berlin.summary: Asked in 2017 whether he had any confidence in the intelligence community's assessments of Russian interference, John Kiriakou said he had none — objecting that no one had ever defined what was meant by hacking, that the published evidence told the public nothing, and that an agency asking to be taken at its word should not be.

the-ai-weiwei-encounter-in-berlin.title: The case against work camps
the-ai-weiwei-encounter-in-berlin.summary: John Kiriakou, who asked to serve his own sentence at a minimum-security work camp and was sent to the prison across the street instead, came out of prison arguing that the camps should not exist at all — and, in the same breath, that some prisoners are dangerous enough that prisons certainly should.

the-ai-weiwei-lego-portrait.title: Amnesty International
the-ai-weiwei-lego-portrait.summary: The human rights organization whose torture report forms part of John Kiriakou's core defense — the CIA's crimes were already public knowledge before he confirmed them on ABC, and the Justice Department's own declination letter said so — and the organization whose silence during his prosecution he cannot forgive. He begged Amnesty for a one-sentence statement and got a New Yorker subscription instead; it took Ai Weiwei to change their minds, and by then he was walking out of prison.

the-ai-weiwei-lego-portrait.title: I want my fifty bucks back
