the-baltimore-tunnel.summary: The California governor John Kiriakou described in 2023 as the consummate Democratic Party insider waiting his turn — a Pelosi relative who married into the Brown family, doing everything the Biden operation asked of him, including a pointless surrogate trip to Idaho, on the calculation that Joe Biden would not reach the nominating convention.

the-baltimore-tunnel.title: Netanyahu and the Tel Aviv police chief
the-baltimore-tunnel.summary: The July 2023 dismissal of Tel Aviv's police chief, which John Kiriakou identified as the moment Benjamin Netanyahu may have overstepped — arguing that the real threat to the Israeli prime minister came not from the Palestinians but from his own attempt to take over the court system, and from the strikes and demonstrations that had not subsided.

the-bamiyan-precedent.title: Destroying the Dome of the Rock
the-bamiyan-precedent.summary: John Kiriakou's agreement with Tucker Carlson that a Zionist extremist plan to demolish the Dome of the Rock and build a third temple would be the event that starts the Third World War — and his additional prediction that it would also be the beginning of the end for the Israeli government and all of its support.

the-bamiyan-precedent.title: Where he slept in Afghanistan
the-bamiyan-precedent.summary: John Kiriakou's inventory of his own Afghan accommodation across a decade of trips — a shared tent on the first visits, a tent of his own once ("living high on the hog"), the officers' quarters at Bagram once the American foothold was serious, and a three-star Afghan hotel when he returned as a private citizen to get the Kite Runner children out.

the-bamiyan-precedent.title: Abigail Spanberger
the-bamiyan-precedent.summary: Governor of Virginia from 2025 and, before Congress, a CIA officer alongside John Kiriakou in the Counterterrorism Center — whom he calls a perfectly nice person who would have been a middle-of-the-road Republican in the 1970s and 1980s, and whose victory speech, to his surprise, said all the right things.

the-bamiyan-precedent.title: Afghan heroin policy
the-bamiyan-precedent.summary: The post-2001 U.S. policy in Afghanistan of protecting, and per John Kiriakou actively encouraging, the cultivation of heroin poppy. Under the Taliban in 2000 Afghanistan produced 0% of the world's heroin; by 2009 under American occupation it produced 93%. Per a DEA officer Kiriakou consulted with on the policy paper he was preparing for Senator Kerry, the strategic rationale was that nearly all of the heroin flowed to Iran and Russia, addiction in those countries was considered desirable as a long-run societal weakener, and the same logic now operates in reverse with Chinese fentanyl flowing into the United States.

the-bamiyan-precedent.title: Jason Miyares
the-bamiyan-precedent.summary: The Cuban-born Republican attorney general of Virginia whom John Kiriakou expected to be a right-wing disaster and found instead to be excellent — a judgement he says is hard for him to make about a conservative Republican, and which he repeated on the night Miyares was unceremoniously thrown out of office.

the-bamiyan-precedent.title: The $230 million claim
the-bamiyan-precedent.summary: John Kiriakou's reaction to a sitting president demanding a quarter of a billion dollars in compensation from his own Justice Department — he telephoned his friend and former attorney Bruce Fein, expecting to be told it was impossible, and was told instead that an obscure nineteenth-century law makes it perfectly legal.

the-bay-of-piglets.title: No declaration of war since 1941
the-bay-of-piglets.summary: John Kiriakou's answer to whether Congress will assert its authority over military action against Venezuela — an unqualified no, resting on the fact that the last declaration of war was on 8 December 1941 and that even the Gulf War was fought on an authorisation to use force rather than a declaration.

the-bay-of-piglets.title: The thirty-year-old nominee
the-bay-of-piglets.summary: The nominee to head the Office of Special Counsel who withdrew in October 2025 after text messages surfaced in which he acknowledged a Nazi streak — and John Kiriakou's separate objection, which was that a man six years out of school has no business running an office at the Justice Department in the first place.

the-bay-of-piglets.title: Venezuela regime change (2026)
the-bay-of-piglets.summary: John Kiriakou''s assessment of the American operation that removed Venezuela''s president — a clear violation of international law, since none of the three recognised grounds for one state attacking another applied, but not a violation of US law, which since 1985 has expressly permitted special forces to cross borders and seize people for trial. His reluctant conclusion at the time: "as much as I hate admitting it, this regime change seems to be working right now."

the-bay-of-piglets.title: What we owed Mexico
the-bay-of-piglets.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer to why American and Mexican cooperation against the cartels achieves so little: the federales are incorruptible and outgunned, the government does not control parts of its own territory, and the United States spent a century punishing Mexico instead of helping it develop — allowing four families to own the entire economy.

the-bay-of-piglets.title: Abigail Spanberger
the-bay-of-piglets.summary: Governor of Virginia from 2025 and, before Congress, a CIA officer alongside John Kiriakou in the Counterterrorism Center — whom he calls a perfectly nice person who would have been a middle-of-the-road Republican in the 1970s and 1980s, and whose victory speech, to his surprise, said all the right things.

the-bay-of-piglets.title: Destroying the Dome of the Rock
the-bay-of-piglets.summary: John Kiriakou's agreement with Tucker Carlson that a Zionist extremist plan to demolish the Dome of the Rock and build a third temple would be the event that starts the Third World War — and his additional prediction that it would also be the beginning of the end for the Israeli government and all of its support.

the-bbc-and-the-sanctions-coverage.title: Ted Rall
the-bbc-and-the-sanctions-coverage.summary: American editorial cartoonist and two-time Pulitzer Prize finalist; co-host with John Kiriakou of the daily news-commentary podcast "Deprogram," launched in September 2025 and by late 2025 running every weekday morning.

the-bbc-and-the-sanctions-coverage.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
the-bbc-and-the-sanctions-coverage.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

the-bbc-and-the-sanctions-coverage.title: Kurds
the-bbc-and-the-sanctions-coverage.summary: The stateless people John Kiriakou calls generationally pro-American — he escorted visiting Kurdish delegations around Washington as a young analyst and bristled at officials who talked down to them. In his telling the Kurds were the only genuine opposition inside Saddam's Iraq, the only faction of the exile circus that ever amounted to anything (Jalal Talabani ended up president of Iraq), the victims of Saddam's chemical weapons and of a no-fly zone that forgot to ban helicopters — and the common enemy that actually united Turkey and ISIS.

the-bbc-and-the-sanctions-coverage.title: 2026 Iran war
the-bbc-and-the-sanctions-coverage.summary: The open-ended American and Israeli war against Iran that John Kiriakou tracked week by week on his own show — a conflict he says was sold as three weeks, ran into its fifth month, achieved every decapitation objective it set, and continued anyway. His grade for it is a D, and his forecast is a Truth Social post declaring victory while nothing changes.

the-bbc-and-the-sanctions-coverage.title: Arming the crazies
the-bbc-and-the-sanctions-coverage.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the American habit of arming the most radical faction available — the Mujahideen over any other Afghan force, the White Russians over the Red — and his expectation, stated days into the 2026 war, that the United States and Israel would begin arming factions inside Iran and that the factions chosen would be the radical ones.

the-bbc-and-the-sanctions-coverage.title: Chaos as the Israeli objective
the-bbc-and-the-sanctions-coverage.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer to whether Netanyahu''s government actually wanted an American invasion of Iran: what the Israelis want in Iran is what they got in Libya — chaos, civil war, and as many dead Iranians as possible.

the-beer-and-the-couch.title: I should have gone to film school
the-beer-and-the-couch.summary: One of the two answers John Kiriakou gives when asked whether, knowing what he knows now, he would join the CIA again. He is candid that he has answered the question differently over the years — sometimes yes, because the agency can only be changed from inside, and sometimes that he should have gone to film school, which he insists is not a joke.

the-beer-and-the-couch.title: Kiriakou's writing process
the-beer-and-the-couch.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of how he actually writes — books in waves over roughly nine months, op-eds in forty-five minutes to an hour once an idea has sat for a few days, and a habit of getting up at two in the morning to write one because he cannot sleep. He wrote *Remains of the Day* in six weeks during COVID, losing whole evenings to it: "I look at the clock again, it''s 2:00 in the morning. I''m like, oh my god, what happened?"

the-beer-and-the-couch.title: Remains of the Day (book)
the-beer-and-the-couch.summary: John Kiriakou's book, announced for publication by Simon and Schuster in March 2026, billed as a definitive guide to the historic cemeteries of Washington DC and the first in a planned series; the second installment will cover the Mafia graves of New York City.

the-beer-and-the-couch.title: The Kiriakou children
the-beer-and-the-couch.summary: The five children of John Kiriakou, and what they do — a bond trader, an elementary school music teacher, a college junior studying supply chain economics, a sophomore who has not yet decided, and a fourteen-year-old. None of them, to their father's declared relief, has any interest in the CIA.

the-beer-and-the-couch.title: The Pentagon press contract
the-beer-and-the-couch.summary: A contract John Kiriakou says every news outlet covering the Pentagon was required to sign in mid-2026, undertaking to publish no information that had not been officially provided by the department. Almost nobody signed: by his count Newsmax, One America News, a Turkish paper, a Hungarian paper and a couple of bloggers.

the-beer-and-the-couch.title: Asset acquisition cycle
the-beer-and-the-couch.summary: The four-step process — spot, assess, develop, recruit — taught as the first lesson of CIA case officer training

the-belgian-intelligence-director.title: Ian Henderson
the-belgian-intelligence-director.summary: The British colonial police officer who ran Bahrain's intelligence service during John Kiriakou's posting there — a man Kiriakou says even the heir presumptive to the throne was afraid to name aloud, and whom Kiriakou, seated at the crown prince's table at a dinner for George H. W. Bush, mistook for a corpse.

the-belgian-intelligence-director.title: The bug in the bedroom
the-belgian-intelligence-director.summary: The listening device John Kiriakou says fell out of an air conditioning vent onto his bare chest while he read in bed in Bahrain — planted, his chief told him, because he was writing the embassy's human rights report.

the-belgian-intelligence-director.title: The Russian soldier in Manama
the-belgian-intelligence-director.summary: The Russian soldier John Kiriakou says he met in Manama, Bahrain, who told him the Chechens were the only people on earth he was afraid of — a remark Kiriakou produced in a conversation about Chechnya's standing as a fighting nation.

the-belgian-intelligence-director.title: Amnesty International
the-belgian-intelligence-director.summary: The human rights organization whose torture report forms part of John Kiriakou's core defense — the CIA's crimes were already public knowledge before he confirmed them on ABC, and the Justice Department's own declination letter said so — and the organization whose silence during his prosecution he cannot forgive. He begged Amnesty for a one-sentence statement and got a New Yorker subscription instead; it took Ai Weiwei to change their minds, and by then he was walking out of prison.

the-belgian-intelligence-director.title: I want my fifty bucks back
the-belgian-intelligence-director.summary: What John Kiriakou says he shouted at John Fetterman from ten rows back at an Ohio State football game — and his explanation, as a Pennsylvanian furious about the senator, of why Fetterman keeps his seat anyway.

the-belgian-intelligence-director.title: Ibrahim Traoré
the-belgian-intelligence-director.summary: John Kiriakou's assessment of the military ruler of Burkina Faso — a young officer who took power promising a return to democracy, and who in Kiriakou's account has grown increasingly irrational, criminalising homosexuality, abolishing the electoral commission and moving to expel foreigners.

the-benghazi-hearings-critique.title: The Libya policy reversal
the-benghazi-hearings-critique.summary: John Kiriakou''s verdict on the overthrow of Muammar Gaddafi: the United States had a healthy working relationship with a man who hated al-Qaeda as much as it did, and flipping sides at the last minute was a terrible policy error that left the country in anarchy. Told that destabilisation may have been the objective all along, he called that an incredibly shortsighted policy, because power vacuums drag America in and it cannot get back out.

the-benghazi-hearings-critique.title: The September 10th country
the-benghazi-hearings-critique.summary: John Kiriakou''s formulation of what he wants back, and his ledger on the two wars: he never supported the invasion of Iraq, which he calls a war of choice and of family revenge, and he did support the war in Afghanistan until al-Qaeda was defeated in 2003, after which everything became nation building. He assigns the destruction of the pre-attack country to George W. Bush and Barack Obama equally.

the-benghazi-hearings-critique.title: Bin Laden health rumors
the-benghazi-hearings-critique.summary: John Kiriakou's dismissal of the claim that Osama bin Laden died years before the 2011 raid. He says the CIA received a steady stream of medical rumours about him — kidney failure, dialysis in a cave, a spinal disorder — none of which turned out to be true, and that bin Laden was in fine health apart from arthritis and a hip problem until the day he died.

the-benghazi-hearings-critique.title: Fake CIA résumés
the-benghazi-hearings-critique.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of being used as a human authenticator in the private sector: at the consulting firm he joined after leaving the CIA, every job applicant claiming agency service was sent to dinner with him, and by his count fully half of them had never set foot inside the CIA.

the-benghazi-hearings-critique.title: False flags are too hard
the-benghazi-hearings-critique.summary: John Kiriakou''s practical objection to the idea that governments routinely stage false flag operations: they exist, and at the operational level the CIA used them constantly, but the bigger the operation the harder it is to run — too many moving parts, too many people who must buy into the conspiracy, and too much incompetence in government to keep any of it straight. He couples the objection with the observation that a government which is not transparent has no standing to complain about public suspicion.

the-benghazi-hearings-critique.title: SEAL Team Six attrition
the-benghazi-hearings-critique.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer to the claim that the Navy SEALs who killed Osama bin Laden have since been killed off: the dead came from the broader unit rather than the raid party, SEAL Team Six numbers several hundred men rather than the dozen or so people imagine, and losing a high number of them to accidents and combat is, in his phrase, very sadly common.

the-berlin-conference-list.title: "The least I could do"
the-berlin-conference-list.summary: Told that he had kept another whistleblower from slipping, John Kiriakou declined the credit and described the work in the plainest possible terms: getting somebody out of the house for three or four hours, or taking them to dinner, because so many people had done exactly that for him when he was at his lowest.

the-berlin-conference-list.title: National Whistleblower Day
the-berlin-conference-list.summary: John Kiriakou has called National Whistleblower Day an event no whistleblower or supporter should miss — held every year in the Kennedy Caucus Room, which he describes as not merely the biggest room on Capitol Hill but the most historic single room anywhere on it, having hosted every major Senate hearing from the sinking of the Titanic to Watergate and Iran-Contra.

the-berlin-conference-list.title: Do what is right or what is easy
the-berlin-conference-list.summary: Asked what he would tell the boy who once told his father he wanted to be a spy, John Kiriakou said he would tell him to always tell the truth and do the right thing — arguing that everyone already knows in their gut the difference between right and wrong, and that the only real question is whether they then do what is right or what is easy.

the-berlin-conference-list.title: "We don''t hire felons"
the-berlin-conference-list.summary: After his release from prison John Kiriakou could not find work anywhere — turned down, he says, by Target, Safeway, McDonald's and Uber — and the one job he was eventually offered, at a Washington think tank, paid minimum wage on condition that he run a permanent crowdfunding campaign to raise his own salary.

the-berlin-conference-list.title: Edward Snowden
the-berlin-conference-list.summary: Former NSA contractor who in 2013 disclosed the scope of U.S. [mass surveillance](/wiki/mass-surveillance), including the Section 702 collection program. Per John Kiriakou — who counts Snowden among the small group of national-security whistleblowers prosecuted under the Espionage Act — Snowden was ''stuck between two awful slippery slopes'': breaking his oath and chain of command on one side, and on the other catching something ''cut and dry against the Constitution'' that no one would act on. Kiriakou notes Snowden could not use his chain of command (as Kiriakou could not, his own chain being Jose Rodriguez), and that Judge Leonie Brinkema had reserved the Snowden case for herself before he fled the country.

the-berlin-conference-list.title: Jesselyn Radack
the-berlin-conference-list.summary: American national-security attorney and former Justice Department ethics official who directs the whistleblower-defense practice at the Government Accountability Project. Per John Kiriakou, Radack was herself driven out of the Justice Department, had her law license threatened, and was placed on the no-fly list after blowing the whistle in the John Walker Lindh case; she went on to represent Kiriakou after his 2012 arrest and, separately, helped connect him to a path to reach Edward Snowden in 2013.

the-best-meal-overseas.title: The dandelion salad
the-best-meal-overseas.summary: The meal John Kiriakou assembled in the yard at FCI Loretto from foraged dandelions, commissary olive oil and sea salt, instant rice, a bouillon cube, peanuts, borrowed Sazón and a bag of chicken — which he calls the single most satisfying meal of his twenty-three months in prison.

the-best-meal-overseas.title: The Islamabad guest house
the-best-meal-overseas.summary: The sixteen-room guest house in Islamabad that CIA officers took over entirely during the post-9/11 deployments — a place John Kiriakou says the agency still will not let him name, which came with breakfast, dinner and laundry for about thirty-five dollars a day against a per diem of five hundred.

the-best-meal-overseas.title: A Middle East reading list
the-best-meal-overseas.summary: The books and the starting point John Kiriakou recommends to anyone trying to understand the modern Middle East: begin at the end of the Second World War, not five thousand years earlier, and start with The House of Saud, the Sykes-Picot Agreement and From Beirut to Jerusalem.

the-best-meal-overseas.title: Bombing the Omanis
the-best-meal-overseas.summary: John Kiriakou's judgement that Iran's strikes on the Gulf states — and above all on Oman, which had been trying to broker peace — made enemies Iran did not need to make, of governments that would otherwise have sat the war out.

the-best-meal-overseas.title: Bowe Bergdahl
the-best-meal-overseas.summary: The American soldier who walked off his base in Afghanistan, was captured by the Haqqani network and handed to the Taliban, and was repatriated in a prisoner trade — a man John Kiriakou says was treated as a traitor although he was not one.

the-best-meal-overseas.title: Chaos as the Israeli objective
the-best-meal-overseas.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer to whether Netanyahu''s government actually wanted an American invasion of Iran: what the Israelis want in Iran is what they got in Libya — chaos, civil war, and as many dead Iranians as possible.

the-blacked-out-grand-jury-minutes.title: The unredacted copy-paste
the-blacked-out-grand-jury-minutes.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of the flaw in the first tranche of released Epstein documents: highlighting a redaction, cutting it and pasting it into a new document revealed the blacked-out text, which turned out to be the names of victims.

the-blacked-out-grand-jury-minutes.title: The snapshots in the release
the-blacked-out-grand-jury-minutes.summary: John Kiriakou's summary of what the first Epstein tranches actually contained — investigative documents, grand jury testimony and snapshots taken by Epstein and his friends — and the two photographs that dominated the early coverage.

the-blacked-out-grand-jury-minutes.title: The letter to Larry Nassar
the-blacked-out-grand-jury-minutes.summary: The letter from Jeffrey Epstein to the convicted USA Gymnastics doctor Larry Nassar that John Kiriakou singled out from the released documents, in which Epstein wrote that he would have gone home by the time it arrived and blamed everything on Donald Trump.

the-blacked-out-grand-jury-minutes.title: Clickers and touchers
the-blacked-out-grand-jury-minutes.summary: The distinction John Kiriakou says prisoners at FCI Loretto drew between convicted sex offenders who had only viewed images of children and those who had travelled across state lines to molest them, and his account of why they are all held at low security.

the-blacked-out-grand-jury-minutes.title: Prince Andrew
the-blacked-out-grand-jury-minutes.summary: British royal, now Andrew Mountbatten Windsor, named repeatedly by John Kiriakou as one of the un-recruitable principals whose access made Jeffrey Epstein valuable to a foreign intelligence service. Kiriakou has asked why Andrew was never charged over conduct with minors, reads his alleged provision of classified Ministry of Defence documents to Epstein as evidence of espionage rather than vanity — and expects him to face no criminal consequence at all, because the statute of limitations has run.

the-blacked-out-grand-jury-minutes.title: The dorm as a reward
the-blacked-out-grand-jury-minutes.summary: John Kiriakou's explanation that moving a federal prisoner from a cell to a dormitory is a privilege earned over time, and why Ghislaine Maxwell's rapid promotion to dormitory living made no sense to him.

the-bloomingdale-precedent.title: The Epstein birthday book
the-bloomingdale-precedent.summary: The page attributed to Donald Trump in Jeffrey Epstein's 2003 fiftieth-birthday book, released by House Democrats in September 2025, which John Kiriakou read out in full and assessed as a banker who had studied handwriting and as an artist — concluding that whoever signed it probably drew it, and refusing to call it a hoax.

the-bloomingdale-precedent.title: E. Jean Carroll
the-bloomingdale-precedent.summary: The plaintiff whose persistence John Kiriakou singled out for deep respect — she kept suing after the political tide turned against her, and won an award he put at eighty-three or eighty-five million dollars on a day when Donald Trump won almost everything else in the federal courts.

the-bloomingdale-precedent.title: Astrology at the CIA
the-bloomingdale-precedent.summary: John Kiriakou''s confirmation that astrology played a role in CIA work in the 1950s and early 1960s as part of MK-ULTRA, alongside time travel and teleportation — and his explanation for why: officials with unlimited budgets and no obligation to report to the public reasoned that there was probably nothing to it, but that if there were, it would make them a star.

the-bloomingdale-precedent.title: Carrying passports in Washington
the-bloomingdale-precedent.summary: John Kiriakou's report in September 2025 that people in Washington had begun carrying their passports for fear of being scooped up by immigration enforcement — alongside the case of an American symphony violinist held for three weeks, and his own belief that ethnic profiling violates the Fourth Amendment.

the-bloomingdale-precedent.title: "Christians are suckers"
the-bloomingdale-precedent.summary: John Kiriakou's explanation for how a president who does not go to church, has no spiritual adviser and could not name a line of scripture can push school prayer without cost — that he thinks most Christians are suckers, an assessment Kiriakou says he hates to make and believes anyway.

the-bloomingdale-precedent.title: Find a Grave
the-bloomingdale-precedent.summary: The cemetery database John Kiriakou calls literally his favourite website on the internet, which he opens during the ten-minute countdown before broadcasts and uses to decide who goes into his cemetery books — and which supplied him the story of Greta Zimmer Friedman.

the-body-in-the-barrel.title: Clyde Hall
the-body-in-the-barrel.summary: The imprisoned Ohio congressman John Kiriakou says served at his prison a few years before him, whose remark on release — that he had made some of the best friends of his life inside — Kiriakou thought insane at the time and came to understand after his own sentence.

the-body-in-the-barrel.title: Ali from Newark
the-body-in-the-barrel.summary: The Black shot caller at FCI Loretto, near the end of a twenty-five-year drug sentence, who came to embrace John Kiriakou at the close of his term and tell him how much he respected him — a friendship possible only because Kiriakou had decided on arrival to ignore the prison's racial divisions.

the-body-in-the-barrel.title: Say five years
the-body-in-the-barrel.summary: The first piece of prison advice John Kiriakou says he was given — from a Bonanno family captain, walking laps of the snowed-in basketball court at FCI Loretto — to tell anyone who asked that he was serving five years rather than the thirty months he actually had.

the-body-in-the-barrel.title: The forty-seven suffix
the-body-in-the-barrel.summary: The last two digits of a federal prisoner number that, according to John Kiriakou, mark the holder as a member of an organised gang — and which the Italians at FCI Loretto carried along with MS-13, the Bloods, the Crips and the Mexican Mafia.

the-body-in-the-barrel.title: The hierarchy of charges
the-body-in-the-barrel.summary: How federal prisoners ranked one another by offence, in John Kiriakou's account — RICO at the top, usually with a murder conspiracy attached; wealthy white-collar convicts despised as soft; and arson, insurance fraud and mortgage fraud attracting no interest at all.

the-body-in-the-barrel.title: The quarterback with a personal chef
the-body-in-the-barrel.summary: The former New York Giants quarterback John Kiriakou says lived in the next row of cells at FCI Loretto — serving a long sentence for a Ponzi scheme, paying every prison gang $500 a month for his safety, and employing another prisoner to cook him three meals a day from food stolen out of the cafeteria.

the-bolivian-visa-line.title: Heather Kiriakou
the-bolivian-visa-line.summary: John Kiriakou's wife, a senior CIA analyst who — in his account — was one of the best analysts in the entire intelligence community and who lost her job at the agency for no reason other than being married to him. She sat off camera at his December 2007 ABC News interview and told him afterwards that he had said nothing classified.

the-bolivian-visa-line.title: Publications Review Board
the-bolivian-visa-line.summary: The CIA office that must clear anything a former officer publishes. John Kiriakou says everything he writes goes to it — books, articles, "even a letter to the editor of Home and Garden magazine" — and describes how the turnaround tracked his standing at the agency: his first book took 22 months to clear while the leadership hated him; his most recent six cleared in days.

the-bolivian-visa-line.title: Abu Zubaydah
the-bolivian-visa-line.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

the-bolivian-visa-line.title: Brian Ross
the-bolivian-visa-line.summary: American investigative journalist and seven-time Emmy Award winner who was a prominent reporter at ABC News when, in December 2007, he conducted the on-camera interview with John Kiriakou that produced the first public confirmation by a U.S. official that the CIA waterboarded prisoners. Per Kiriakou, Ross called him out of the blue with the assertion that a source said Kiriakou had personally tortured Abu Zubaydah; Kiriakou's decision to give the interview anyway — driven by the conclusion that 'Brian Ross's source is at the White House and they're going to pin this on me' — became the pivot point of his entire post-CIA life.

the-bolivian-visa-line.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
the-bolivian-visa-line.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

the-bolivian-visa-line.title: Corporate competitive intelligence
the-bolivian-visa-line.summary: The private-sector discipline John Kiriakou entered on leaving the CIA in 2004: collecting human-source intelligence on rival firms for a big-four accountancy. He was the fourth CIA officer Deloitte had hired into a group that paired former intelligence collectors with corporate research analysts, and his requirements were a rival''s pricing models, its discount structure, and which of its top-producing partners were unhappy enough to be poached. All the major firms, he says, run the same operation against each other.

the-bolton-raid.title: Amnesty International
the-bolton-raid.summary: The human rights organization whose torture report forms part of John Kiriakou's core defense — the CIA's crimes were already public knowledge before he confirmed them on ABC, and the Justice Department's own declination letter said so — and the organization whose silence during his prosecution he cannot forgive. He begged Amnesty for a one-sentence statement and got a New Yorker subscription instead; it took Ai Weiwei to change their minds, and by then he was walking out of prison.

the-bolton-raid.title: Espionage Act
the-bolton-raid.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

the-bolton-raid.title: I want my fifty bucks back
the-bolton-raid.summary: What John Kiriakou says he shouted at John Fetterman from ten rows back at an Ohio State football game — and his explanation, as a Pennsylvanian furious about the senator, of why Fetterman keeps his seat anyway.

the-bolton-raid.title: Ian Henderson
the-bolton-raid.summary: The British colonial police officer who ran Bahrain's intelligence service during John Kiriakou's posting there — a man Kiriakou says even the heir presumptive to the throne was afraid to name aloud, and whom Kiriakou, seated at the crown prince's table at a dinner for George H. W. Bush, mistook for a corpse.

the-bolton-raid.title: Ibrahim Traoré
the-bolton-raid.summary: John Kiriakou's assessment of the military ruler of Burkina Faso — a young officer who took power promising a return to democracy, and who in Kiriakou's account has grown increasingly irrational, criminalising homosexuality, abolishing the electoral commission and moving to expel foreigners.

the-bolton-raid.title: Kimberly Guilfoyle in Athens
the-bolton-raid.summary: John Kiriakou's assessment of Kimberly Guilfoyle's appointment as American ambassador to Greece — that she got it because Donald Trump Jr. wanted her out of the way, a manoeuvre he compares to Saddam Hussein's habit of exiling successful generals as ambassadors — and his reluctant conclusion that Greece could have done worse.

the-bomb-course.title: Counterterrorist driving
the-bomb-course.summary: The vehicle training at the Farm — the PIT manoeuvre and how to avoid one, when to ram a roadblock and where to hit it, reversing at sixty miles an hour — conducted in a fleet of junkyard beaters the CIA bought expressly to be wrecked.

the-bomb-course.title: The Advanced Counterterrorism Operations course
the-bomb-course.summary: The six-week CIA course for which John Kiriakou says he was one of only about a dozen officers in the entire agency selected — and which he finished, as he puts it, just in time for 9/11.

the-bomb-course.title: The operations course graduation
the-bomb-course.summary: The end of CIA field training: a graduation ceremony at which the whole class wore full disguises for the photograph, and a certificate that is itself classified and therefore cannot be displayed — it stays in the officer''s personnel file.

the-bomb-course.title: The shooting house
the-bomb-course.summary: The live-fire decision course at the Farm where a trainee has about three quarters of a second to decide whether the figure at the window is a gunman or a woman holding a baby — and where John Kiriakou says he never missed, which he connects to his own account of the temperament the CIA selects for.

the-bomb-course.title: The Farm
the-bomb-course.summary: The CIA's clandestine training facility in Virginia; site of approximately 80% of all CIA operational training

the-bomb-course.title: The hostile border crossing exercise
the-bomb-course.summary: The training exercise run before dawn at a closed Dulles Airport in which CIA trainees crossed into the fictional Republic of Victoria — where John Kiriakou talked his way past a US-government-branded pen in his pocket, and the class clown ended up stripped to his underwear.

the-booby-trapped-christmas-cards.title: The interrupted break-in
the-booby-trapped-christmas-cards.summary: A break-in in a friendly country nearly failed when the neighbour who was supposed to be at work turned out to have given birth the day before; John Kiriakou talked his way out of it at the door by claiming to be looking for his aunt''s flat in the wrong building.

the-booby-trapped-christmas-cards.title: The Satan dream
the-booby-trapped-christmas-cards.summary: Seventeen years after leaving Pakistan, John Kiriakou said he still dreamt about it every night — a recurring dream of Satan hunting him house to house — and described a failed blood pressure drug now used to erase the dreams of PTSD patients.

the-booby-trapped-christmas-cards.title: Corkscrew landings in Afghanistan
the-booby-trapped-christmas-cards.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the tight spiralling helicopter approaches used to evade rocket and Stinger fire on landings in Afghanistan after 9/11, with the side doors open, and of the passengers around him being sick while he found it exhilarating.

the-booby-trapped-christmas-cards.title: George Washington University
the-booby-trapped-christmas-cards.summary: The Washington university where John Kiriakou took a bachelor's degree in Middle Eastern studies and began a master's in legislative affairs, and where a professor who was in fact a CIA spotter recruited him into the agency — an institution that recurs throughout his account as the place his intelligence career began, as the venue of his first CIA tests, and later as a classroom he taught in himself.

the-booby-trapped-christmas-cards.title: No ethics training at the CIA
the-booby-trapped-christmas-cards.summary: John Kiriakou''s claim that the CIA provides no ethics training of any kind, so that an officer either arrives with a personal moral code or never acquires one — and the classroom hypothetical he uses to show where the line goes undrawn.

the-booby-trapped-christmas-cards.title: PTSD
the-booby-trapped-christmas-cards.summary: Post-traumatic stress disorder runs through John Kiriakou''s life and worldview — he had it coming out of Greece after an assassination attempt, brought it home from Pakistan alongside his shock at colleagues'' willingness to kill, and was blindsided by a delayed post-prison version that helped end his marriage. For six months after release he dreamed the same dream nightly: that he was out by mistake and had to get back inside before midnight count. He still takes a repurposed blood-pressure drug that stops the dreams, and he extends the diagnosis outward — to secret-site interrogators who came back crying, to drone pilots, and to prisoners released angry and untreated.

the-book-the-publisher-sat-on.title: The Sputnik shutdown
the-book-the-publisher-sat-on.summary: The 2020 cancellation of the radio programme John Kiriakou co-hosted at Sputnik, and what he says followed — a five-thousand-dollar crowdfunder for a camera and a microphone that became one of the more successful independent political podcasts.

the-book-the-publisher-sat-on.title: Ali from Newark
the-book-the-publisher-sat-on.summary: The Black shot caller at FCI Loretto, near the end of a twenty-five-year drug sentence, who came to embrace John Kiriakou at the close of his term and tell him how much he respected him — a friendship possible only because Kiriakou had decided on arrival to ignore the prison's racial divisions.

the-book-the-publisher-sat-on.title: Bezalel Smotrich
the-book-the-publisher-sat-on.summary: Israeli far-right minister whom John Kiriakou, alongside Itamar Ben-Gvir, blames for leaving Israel unprepared on October 7 by insisting any attack would come from the West Bank rather than Gaza.

the-book-the-publisher-sat-on.title: Candace Owens
the-book-the-publisher-sat-on.summary: The commentator whose claims about the killing of Charlie Kirk John Kiriakou has publicly declined to accept. He credits her reach and her intelligence and rejects her method, citing an earlier occasion — a conference call he says he was on — at which she claimed irrefutable proof that the Italian government had stolen the 2020 election and that its release would return Donald Trump to office.

the-book-the-publisher-sat-on.title: Cleaning up after Tora Bora
the-book-the-publisher-sat-on.summary: John Kiriakou was not at Tora Bora. He arrived in Pakistan in January 2002, two months after the bombing, and says he went specifically to clean up what the battle had left behind — scavenging material, detaining the fighters too slow to get away, and mapping the smugglers'' valleys the survivors had used to cross. In his account the clean-up was necessary because the encirclement failed: bin Laden, warned by an al-Qaeda operative working as translator to the commander of Central Command, left in the dark dressed as a woman in the back of a pickup truck, and at dawn there was nobody in Tora Bora to surrender.

the-book-the-publisher-sat-on.title: Clyde Hall
the-book-the-publisher-sat-on.summary: The imprisoned Ohio congressman John Kiriakou says served at his prison a few years before him, whose remark on release — that he had made some of the best friends of his life inside — Kiriakou thought insane at the time and came to understand after his own sentence.

the-boring-cover-story.title: The Milan–Sofia flight
the-boring-cover-story.summary: A flight John Kiriakou took from Milan to Sofia, routed away from Athens under a different passport for a sensitive operation, on which a persistent seatmate refused to accept a dull cover story — until Kiriakou told him he smuggled women and cigarettes out of Eastern Europe.

the-boring-cover-story.title: Quoted on NPR
the-boring-cover-story.summary: John Kiriakou's discovery, via a standing Google alert on his own name, that National Public Radio had cited a DeProgram discussion between him and Ted Rall in an article on Palestinians killed while waiting for food — an outlet he had walked out on years earlier.

the-boring-cover-story.title: The Addis Ababa zoo
the-boring-cover-story.summary: A visit John Kiriakou made to the zoo in Addis Ababa on a free half-day, where he watched keepers force a screaming donkey into the lion enclosure — and noted the two-tier admission price charged to foreigners.

the-boring-cover-story.title: The asset recruitment cycle
the-boring-cover-story.summary: The four-step professional standard John Kiriakou says governed CIA operations before September 11 — spot, assess, develop, recruit — and without which an officer did not get promoted. He calls it the asset acquisition cycle as often as the recruitment cycle. Spotting looks for access, not rank; assessment looks for a vulnerability, a word he insists is less ugly than it sounds; development is months or years of friendship bought on an unlimited expense account; and the recruitment itself rests not on money, revenge or ideology but on the target believing the officer is his best friend. Threats are forbidden — partly on ethics, partly because the target may come to the next meeting with a gun.

the-boring-cover-story.title: The election day 1992 poll
the-boring-cover-story.summary: An informal show of hands taken in a CIA branch office on election day 1992, which John Kiriakou describes as the moment he discovered he had no idea of the politics of the colleagues he sat three feet away from — and that he was not, as he had assumed, the only progressive in the room.

the-boring-cover-story.title: The rejected deposits
the-boring-cover-story.summary: John Kiriakou''s explanation of why banks returned large deposits to Donald Trump — not political discrimination, in his account, but anti-money-laundering law: a bank that cannot get a credible account of where the money came from faces felony exposure, and no bank turns away deposits for any lesser reason.

the-botched-pitch.title: Cover position
the-botched-pitch.summary: The occupational identity under which an intelligence officer operates abroad. John Kiriakou''s account collapses the popular idea that certain embassy jobs are tell-tale: because a diplomatic mission has to do its real work every day, every position in and out of an embassy is simultaneously a genuine job and a possible cover, which is precisely what makes cover work.

the-botched-pitch.title: Amaryllis Fox Kennedy
the-botched-pitch.summary: Former CIA non-official-cover officer who worked under commercial cover as an international art consultant, later a Trump campaign manager and nominee for deputy CIA director. Per John Kiriakou, Senator Tom Cotton threatened to filibuster her appointment; the president responded by naming her deputy national security adviser instead — a job Kiriakou considers more powerful, since the CIA director reports to the national security adviser.

the-botched-pitch.title: Andrew Bustamante
the-botched-pitch.summary: Former CIA officer who sells CIA-style training online; John Kiriakou identifies him as the lone critic of his work hosting a show on a Russian network, and argues Bustamante's training business — open to anyone who pays — is the more problematic of the two.

the-botched-pitch.title: Operational vehicles
the-botched-pitch.summary: The cars John Kiriakou used in the field. In the Middle East they were whatever the rental company supplied — usually a Toyota — on the reasoning that anonymity was the point; in Athens, where the threat justified it, he was issued a factory-built, level-four armoured BMW 540 that broke down constantly.

the-botched-pitch.title: 2028 presidential field
the-botched-pitch.summary: John Kiriakou's assessment of the wide-open 2028 presidential race — the first in his life, he says, where he has no idea who either party will nominate. Predictive markets were listing 44 Democrats and 26 Republicans as possible candidates. His own preferred candidate is Tucker Carlson, whom he says he has repeatedly begged to run; his working assumption about anyone who does want the job is that they are "a narcissist and probably a sociopath on top of it."

the-botched-pitch.title: Angry Birds
the-botched-pitch.summary: The mobile game John Kiriakou describes as his only vice besides buying art, played every morning for nine consecutive years and cited by his ex-wife as a grievance in their marriage.

the-bowl-of-dates.title: Curtailment cables
the-bowl-of-dates.summary: The career-ending requests John Kiriakou says he read coming back from the CIA's black sites — officers, doctors, psychologists and nurses asking to end their tours early rather than continue to take part in the interrogation programme — and his conclusion that if that many people were objecting in classified channels, someone would surely go public.

the-bowl-of-dates.title: "You were the first person that ever asked me about my children"
the-bowl-of-dates.summary: The answer John Kiriakou says he received when he asked a mid-level al-Qaeda member he had recruited in Pakistan why he had allowed the recruitment to happen: that in five years of detention Kiriakou had been the first person to ask about his children.

the-bowl-of-dates.title: Arabic and Greek
the-bowl-of-dates.summary: The qualification John Kiriakou says opened the door to his transfer from CIA analysis to operations: a post in Athens wanted Greek or Arabic, and he had both — by most of his tellings the only officer in the agency who did. The chief who hired him gave the reason in one sentence: it is easier and cheaper to take a linguist and teach him operations than the other way round. The pairing also became a detection tool, since the language nobody speaks in Pakistan is Arabic.

the-bowl-of-dates.title: Bankruptcy and the dropped charges
the-bowl-of-dates.summary: The sequence John Kiriakou places at the centre of his case: that the espionage counts against him were dropped only after his legal fees had bankrupted him, which he presents as evidence that the government''s aim was attrition rather than conviction.

the-bowl-of-dates.title: Security, finance and medical
the-bowl-of-dates.summary: The rule John Kiriakou says CIA recruits were taught in their first week on the job — that there are exactly three offices an officer may never lie to, because those three can end a career — and the reasoning he attaches to each.

the-bowl-of-dates.title: The declination letter
the-bowl-of-dates.summary: The letter the Justice Department sent John Kiriakou's attorneys in December 2008 declining to prosecute him, on the grounds that the torture allegations were already public through human rights organizations and that it is illegal to classify a crime — and the celebration dinner that was followed three weeks later by Barack Obama's inauguration.

the-brennan-felony-referral.title: Donald Trump
the-brennan-felony-referral.summary: 45th and 47th U.S. president. Per John Kiriakou, a man genuinely convinced he was doing right by bombing Iran, "duped" by the same Netanyahu nuclear bluff Obama once rejected — and, at the same time, the most blindly pro-Israel president in history, an admirer of autocrats who has never once criticized Vladimir Putin, and prone to gestures — from the Gulf of America to a since-abandoned "Department of War" rename — that test the edges of his actual authority.

the-brennan-felony-referral.title: Ali from Newark
the-brennan-felony-referral.summary: The Black shot caller at FCI Loretto, near the end of a twenty-five-year drug sentence, who came to embrace John Kiriakou at the close of his term and tell him how much he respected him — a friendship possible only because Kiriakou had decided on arrival to ignore the prison's racial divisions.

the-brennan-felony-referral.title: Bezalel Smotrich
the-brennan-felony-referral.summary: Israeli far-right minister whom John Kiriakou, alongside Itamar Ben-Gvir, blames for leaving Israel unprepared on October 7 by insisting any attack would come from the West Bank rather than Gaza.

the-brennan-felony-referral.title: Candace Owens
the-brennan-felony-referral.summary: The commentator whose claims about the killing of Charlie Kirk John Kiriakou has publicly declined to accept. He credits her reach and her intelligence and rejects her method, citing an earlier occasion — a conference call he says he was on — at which she claimed irrefutable proof that the Italian government had stolen the 2020 election and that its release would return Donald Trump to office.

the-brennan-felony-referral.title: Clyde Hall
the-brennan-felony-referral.summary: The imprisoned Ohio congressman John Kiriakou says served at his prison a few years before him, whose remark on release — that he had made some of the best friends of his life inside — Kiriakou thought insane at the time and came to understand after his own sentence.

the-brennan-felony-referral.title: Drunken border guards
the-brennan-felony-referral.summary: John Kiriakou's explanation for how quiet frontiers become shooting wars — bored, drinking troops with nothing to do and no supervision — which he applies to the Thailand-Cambodia clashes, to the India-China line, and to why Vladimir Putin objects to a NATO country on his border.

the-brett-stephens-column.title: Bezalel Smotrich
the-brett-stephens-column.summary: Israeli far-right minister whom John Kiriakou, alongside Itamar Ben-Gvir, blames for leaving Israel unprepared on October 7 by insisting any attack would come from the West Bank rather than Gaza.

the-brett-stephens-column.title: Famine in Gaza
the-brett-stephens-column.summary: The starvation of the civilian population of the Gaza Strip, which John Kiriakou describes as a United Nations-declared famine caused not by an absence of food but by an Israeli refusal to let food reach the people who need it; Kiriakou characterises it as a war crime, a crime against humanity and a form of genocide, attributing that characterisation to the United Nations and the International Court of Justice rather than to himself.

the-brett-stephens-column.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
the-brett-stephens-column.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

the-brett-stephens-column.title: France recognises Palestine
the-brett-stephens-column.summary: Emmanuel Macron's decision in July 2025 to extend formal recognition to the Republic of Palestine and exchange ambassadors, which John Kiriakou called a turning point that could not be overstated — the first serious crack in Western support for Israel, and significant precisely because France is a historic colonial power in the Middle East with a Security Council veto.

the-brett-stephens-column.title: Hostages and prisoners
the-brett-stephens-column.summary: John Kiriakou's objection to the vocabulary of the Gaza war — that Israelis held by Hamas are called hostages while Palestinians held by Israel without charge are called prisoners — which he treats as one instance of a wider pattern in which allies have governments and adversaries have regimes.

the-brett-stephens-column.title: Itamar Ben-Gvir
the-brett-stephens-column.summary: Israel's far-right Minister of National Security; John Kiriakou cites him as a convicted hate-crime felon placed in charge of security in Gaza and the West Bank over his victims, blames his insistence that any attack would come from the West Bank for diverting forces before October 7, and cites the death-penalty law passed under his portfolio for Palestinian detainees as the first reinstatement of capital punishment in Israel since it was abolished in 1956, excepting only the execution of Adolf Eichmann.

the-bridgeton-and-the-tanker-escorts.title: Hypersonic missiles
the-bridgeton-and-the-tanker-escorts.summary: John Kiriakou confirms that hypersonic missiles are real and that Russia, China and Iran all have them; that a weapon travelling 2,500 miles an hour cannot be defended against; and that Iran holds too few of them to do anything but make each one count.

the-bridgeton-and-the-tanker-escorts.title: Dubai as Iran's window
the-bridgeton-and-the-tanker-escorts.summary: John Kiriakou''s explanation of why Iran did not hit Dubai hard during the 2026 war: the city is full of Iranian businessmen and is Iran''s outlet to the Western world and its principal means of evading sanctions.

the-bridgeton-and-the-tanker-escorts.title: Bombing the Omanis
the-bridgeton-and-the-tanker-escorts.summary: John Kiriakou's judgement that Iran's strikes on the Gulf states — and above all on Oman, which had been trying to broker peace — made enemies Iran did not need to make, of governments that would otherwise have sat the war out.

the-bridgeton-and-the-tanker-escorts.title: THAAD stocks in the Gulf
the-bridgeton-and-the-tanker-escorts.summary: John Kiriakou's report, during the 2026 war, that the United Arab Emirates were seven days from exhausting their THAAD interceptors and Qatar four days — with American resupply unable to keep pace.

the-bridgeton-and-the-tanker-escorts.title: Why the UAE was targeted
the-bridgeton-and-the-tanker-escorts.summary: John Kiriakou''s explanation for the disproportionate weight of Iranian fire falling on the United Arab Emirates in 2026: not the American presence but the Emirati role at the forefront of the war against the Houthis — and a wish to bloody Emirati noses despite the thousands of Iranians living in Dubai.

the-briefing-held-off-campus.title: Shin Bet
the-briefing-held-off-campus.summary: Israel's internal security service; per John Kiriakou, one of the two declared Israeli intelligence officers at the Washington embassy, and the service whose officer, alongside a Mossad officer, he says tried to recruit him at his first CIA liaison briefing in the spring of 1990 — an approach his colleagues told him had been made to every one of them.

the-briefing-held-off-campus.title: Recruitment attempts on Kiriakou
the-briefing-held-off-campus.summary: A series of episodes in which foreign intelligence officers tried to recruit John Kiriakou himself — an over-eager Hungarian during his CIA application, a French counterterrorism officer who staged a car pickup in Islamabad, and a Shin Bet officer at his first liaison briefing.

the-briefing-held-off-campus.title: Israeli intelligence presence in the United States
the-briefing-held-off-campus.summary: John Kiriakou's account of Israeli intelligence activity inside the United States — dozens of undeclared Mossad and Shin Bet officers identified by the FBI, a critical-threat counterintelligence classification alongside Russia, North Korea and Cuba, and a pattern of harassment and intimidation directed at declared CIA officers posted to Israel.

the-briefing-held-off-campus.title: MOSSAD
the-briefing-held-off-campus.summary: Israel's primary external intelligence service; characterized by John Kiriakou as universally hostile in his and his CIA colleagues' professional dealings with it ("never had a positive encounter with Mossad"); operates almost exclusively in the operational rather than analytical domain; the CIA is, per Kiriakou, categorically forbidden from spying on it.

the-briefing-held-off-campus.title: Blackmail in agent recruitment
the-briefing-held-off-campus.summary: What John Kiriakou says CIA career trainees were taught about blackmail: that the agency does not use it, not on moral grounds but because a long-term agent relationship requires mutual trust and coercion cannot produce it. He allows two exceptions — the pre-Church Committee past, and cases where the objective is simply to stop a target doing something, which can also be handed to a friendlier service.

the-briefing-held-off-campus.title: Consulting job entrapment offers
the-briefing-held-off-campus.summary: John Kiriakou's claim that he receives a steady stream of emails and telephone calls offering him work — always consulting — that he reads as attempts to bait him into violating federal law, and which he says happens all the time.

the-broken-side-view-mirror.title: The code room and the buried weapons
the-broken-side-view-mirror.summary: What John Kiriakou demanded when the officer he had cold-pitched in Athens agreed to meet him — access to his embassy's code room and all of its weapons — and the meeting in a hotel coffee shop, surrounded by armed CIA officers at every table, at which the terms were set.

the-broken-side-view-mirror.title: The restaurants in witness protection
the-broken-side-view-mirror.summary: What became of the foreign intelligence officer John Kiriakou recruited in Athens — resettled in the United States under a made-up name, given citizenship for his family and seed money to start again, and last heard of owning seven restaurants — and the resettlement package Kiriakou says the CIA offers a burned agent.

the-broken-side-view-mirror.title: The Mallios argument
the-broken-side-view-mirror.summary: The confrontation John Kiriakou describes with his mentor Gust Avrakotos while the two worked the 17 November task force — Kiriakou remarked in passing that the group's second victim, the Greek police chief Mallios, had been a torturer under the junta; Avrakotos slammed him against a wall; and the exchange that followed became the basis of their friendship.

the-broken-side-view-mirror.title: Kiriakou's first recruitment
the-broken-side-view-mirror.summary: How John Kiriakou made his first CIA recruitment in Athens: by combing 25-year-old Greek police files not for people who had talked but for people who had answered back, finding one such man in a communist neighbourhood coffee shop, and buying his telephone number from a waiter for the price of a fifty.

the-broken-side-view-mirror.title: Asset acquisition cycle
the-broken-side-view-mirror.summary: The four-step process — spot, assess, develop, recruit — taught as the first lesson of CIA case officer training

the-broken-side-view-mirror.title: Gust Avrakotos
the-broken-side-view-mirror.summary: CIA case officer, John Kiriakou's operations mentor, and a central figure in Charlie Wilson's War — the prolific, divisive covert-war veteran Kiriakou credits as the greatest teacher of his adult life.

the-bug-in-the-bedroom.title: Ian Henderson
the-bug-in-the-bedroom.summary: The British colonial police officer who ran Bahrain's intelligence service during John Kiriakou's posting there — a man Kiriakou says even the heir presumptive to the throne was afraid to name aloud, and whom Kiriakou, seated at the crown prince's table at a dinner for George H. W. Bush, mistook for a corpse.

the-bug-in-the-bedroom.title: The embassy swap
the-bug-in-the-bedroom.summary: The 1970s agreement under which the United States and the Soviet Union each built a new embassy in the other's capital — the Russians choosing the highest ground in Washington, the Americans being sold a dry riverbed in Moscow, and the American building having to be demolished because listening devices had been built into every beam.

the-bug-in-the-bedroom.title: The Russian soldier in Manama
the-bug-in-the-bedroom.summary: The Russian soldier John Kiriakou says he met in Manama, Bahrain, who told him the Chechens were the only people on earth he was afraid of — a remark Kiriakou produced in a conversation about Chechnya's standing as a fighting nation.

the-bug-in-the-bedroom.title: The Belgian intelligence director
the-bug-in-the-bedroom.summary: The brother of John Kiriakou's oldest friend, a Belgian exchange student at his high school, who rose to run Belgium's intelligence service and become deputy prime minister — and the exchange in which Kiriakou answered the standard defence of an intelligence chief's prejudices with his own experience.

the-bug-in-the-bedroom.title: Amnesty International
the-bug-in-the-bedroom.summary: The human rights organization whose torture report forms part of John Kiriakou's core defense — the CIA's crimes were already public knowledge before he confirmed them on ABC, and the Justice Department's own declination letter said so — and the organization whose silence during his prosecution he cannot forgive. He begged Amnesty for a one-sentence statement and got a New Yorker subscription instead; it took Ai Weiwei to change their minds, and by then he was walking out of prison.

the-bug-in-the-bedroom.title: I want my fifty bucks back
the-bug-in-the-bedroom.summary: What John Kiriakou says he shouted at John Fetterman from ten rows back at an Ohio State football game — and his explanation, as a Pennsylvanian furious about the senator, of why Fetterman keeps his seat anyway.

the-bunker-busters-as-preemption.title: The dispersal of the Iranian program
the-bunker-busters-as-preemption.summary: John Kiriakou's assessment that neither the Israeli nor the American strikes had any lasting effect on Iran's nuclear programme, because the facilities are spread across the country and mostly deep underground — and his reading of Iran's shrugging response as the best evidence that the bombing did not work.

the-bunker-busters-as-preemption.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
the-bunker-busters-as-preemption.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

the-bunker-busters-as-preemption.title: Joe Rogan
the-bunker-busters-as-preemption.summary: The podcast host whose show John Kiriakou finally sat for in October 2025 — an experience that began with signing a non-disclosure agreement and ended with his verdict that Rogan is "a nice guy, very down to earth, very normal." The first thing Rogan asked, walking into the studio ten minutes late: "Hey, do you know my friend Mike Baker?" Kiriakou defends Rogan as unfairly characterized as a right-winger, and had long cited the show as the venue where Zuckerberg admitted Facebook suppressed the Hunter Biden laptop story at the FBI''s behest.

the-bunker-busters-as-preemption.title: 2026 Iran war
the-bunker-busters-as-preemption.summary: The open-ended American and Israeli war against Iran that John Kiriakou tracked week by week on his own show — a conflict he says was sold as three weeks, ran into its fifth month, achieved every decapitation objective it set, and continued anyway. His grade for it is a D, and his forecast is a Truth Social post declaring victory while nothing changes.

the-bunker-busters-as-preemption.title: Donald Trump
the-bunker-busters-as-preemption.summary: 45th and 47th U.S. president. Per John Kiriakou, a man genuinely convinced he was doing right by bombing Iran, "duped" by the same Netanyahu nuclear bluff Obama once rejected — and, at the same time, the most blindly pro-Israel president in history, an admirer of autocrats who has never once criticized Vladimir Putin, and prone to gestures — from the Gulf of America to a since-abandoned "Department of War" rename — that test the edges of his actual authority.

the-bunker-busters-as-preemption.title: Netanyahu's nuclear threat to Trump
the-bunker-busters-as-preemption.summary: John Kiriakou's account, sourced to friends in the White House and the administration, that Donald Trump agreed to bomb Iran because Benjamin Netanyahu threatened to use nuclear weapons against Iran if the United States did not act. Kiriakou presents it as the reason a request every previous president refused was finally granted.

the-burden-of-peace.title: Hostages and prisoners
the-burden-of-peace.summary: John Kiriakou's objection to the vocabulary of the Gaza war — that Israelis held by Hamas are called hostages while Palestinians held by Israel without charge are called prisoners — which he treats as one instance of a wider pattern in which allies have governments and adversaries have regimes.

the-burden-of-peace.title: Famine in Gaza
the-burden-of-peace.summary: The starvation of the civilian population of the Gaza Strip, which John Kiriakou describes as a United Nations-declared famine caused not by an absence of food but by an Israeli refusal to let food reach the people who need it; Kiriakou characterises it as a war crime, a crime against humanity and a form of genocide, attributing that characterisation to the United Nations and the International Court of Justice rather than to himself.

the-burden-of-peace.title: France recognises Palestine
the-burden-of-peace.summary: Emmanuel Macron's decision in July 2025 to extend formal recognition to the Republic of Palestine and exchange ambassadors, which John Kiriakou called a turning point that could not be overstated — the first serious crack in Western support for Israel, and significant precisely because France is a historic colonial power in the Middle East with a Security Council veto.

the-burden-of-peace.title: The Egyptian berm
the-burden-of-peace.summary: The earthwork Egypt built along its Gaza frontier more than a year before July 2025, which John Kiriakou describes as a defence not against Palestinians but against Israel — built because Cairo feared the border being thrown open from the other side, and because Egyptian troops would not fire on two million people.

the-burden-of-peace.title: No band-aids since the early nineties
the-burden-of-peace.summary: What doctors told John Kiriakou when he visited an Afghan hospital in 2000, during the first Taliban government — that they had not seen a band-aid since the early 1990s — and his conclusion that the humanitarian carve-outs in the Clinton-era sanctions did not exist in practice.

the-burden-of-peace.title: Proposals to relocate the Palestinians
the-burden-of-peace.summary: John Kiriakou's account of recurring schemes to solve the Palestinian question by moving the population somewhere else — including a 1980s proposal to rename a barren diamond of land on the Saudi–Iraqi border "Palestine" and resettle everyone there — and his verdict that picking up an entire people and moving them is unprecedented and untenable.

the-bureau-answers-to-no-one.title: The glass-eating prisoner
the-bureau-answers-to-no-one.summary: A case John Kiriakou cites from a 2015 New York Times Magazine investigation of federal solitary confinement: a prisoner held in the Special Housing Unit at the federal supermax in Florence, Colorado for roughly eighteen years who smashed his narrow cell window and ate the broken glass so that he would be taken to a hospital and could speak to another human being.

the-bureau-answers-to-no-one.title: The SHU loophole
the-bureau-answers-to-no-one.summary: John Kiriakou''s warning about the American assurances given to British courts in the Julian Assange extradition case: prosecutors promised not to place him in a communications management unit but said nothing about the Special Housing Unit, and in Kiriakou''s account a prison need only cite an overheard threat to hold a man in solitary indefinitely.

the-bureau-answers-to-no-one.title: The fifteen-minute call
the-bureau-answers-to-no-one.summary: How Marty Gottesfeld, held in the communications management unit at Terre Haute, allocated the single fifteen-minute telephone call he was permitted each week: an email to his wife, his two attorneys and John Kiriakou, with the call going to whoever answered first.

the-bureau-answers-to-no-one.title: The modified CMU
the-bureau-answers-to-no-one.summary: The communications restrictions imposed on John Kiriakou at FCI Loretto after his Letter from Loretto was published by the Huffington Post. Staff called it a modified communications management unit: a five-day delay on incoming and outgoing email, live monitoring of his telephone calls rather than recording, and a prohibition on speaking Greek to his family.

the-bureau-answers-to-no-one.title: The sixty-five-cent arrangement
the-bureau-answers-to-no-one.summary: The deal John Kiriakou struck with the chaplain at FCI Loretto: rather than keep his 65-cents-an-hour janitor''s wage, he asked to be kept on the books while the money went to the next man on the list, and to stop coming to work — which is how he found the time to write Doing Time Like a Spy.

the-bureau-answers-to-no-one.title: Evidence of previous heroism
the-bureau-answers-to-no-one.summary: A phrase John Kiriakou attributes to Judge Leonie Brinkema at his 2013 sentencing. When his service in Pakistan and his role in the capture of Abu Zubaydah were raised in mitigation, the judge ruled — in what Kiriakou gives as her exact words — that any evidence of previous heroism is irrelevant.

the-bureau-of-prisons-polos.title: The FLETC badge
the-bureau-of-prisons-polos.summary: The shiny gold badge John Kiriakou carried before joining the CIA, issued after he trained at the Federal Law Enforcement Training Center — and which he insists never made him a law enforcement officer, a distinction he uses to deny the same status to ICE agents and federal prison guards.

the-bureau-of-prisons-polos.title: Letters the cabinet ignored
the-bureau-of-prisons-polos.summary: John Kiriakou's account, from his years on the staff of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, of what happened to congressional oversight letters sent to cabinet secretaries and agency directors — mostly nothing — and why he expects the same of demands made from the minority side of the aisle.

the-bureau-of-prisons-polos.title: Ali from Newark
the-bureau-of-prisons-polos.summary: The Black shot caller at FCI Loretto, near the end of a twenty-five-year drug sentence, who came to embrace John Kiriakou at the close of his term and tell him how much he respected him — a friendship possible only because Kiriakou had decided on arrival to ignore the prison's racial divisions.

the-bureau-of-prisons-polos.title: Bezalel Smotrich
the-bureau-of-prisons-polos.summary: Israeli far-right minister whom John Kiriakou, alongside Itamar Ben-Gvir, blames for leaving Israel unprepared on October 7 by insisting any attack would come from the West Bank rather than Gaza.

the-bureau-of-prisons-polos.title: Candace Owens
the-bureau-of-prisons-polos.summary: The commentator whose claims about the killing of Charlie Kirk John Kiriakou has publicly declined to accept. He credits her reach and her intelligence and rejects her method, citing an earlier occasion — a conference call he says he was on — at which she claimed irrefutable proof that the Italian government had stolen the 2020 election and that its release would return Donald Trump to office.

the-bureau-of-prisons-polos.title: Clyde Hall
the-bureau-of-prisons-polos.summary: The imprisoned Ohio congressman John Kiriakou says served at his prison a few years before him, whose remark on release — that he had made some of the best friends of his life inside — Kiriakou thought insane at the time and came to understand after his own sentence.

the-buried-senate-documents.title: Freedom of Information Act
the-buried-senate-documents.summary: The U.S. transparency law that runs through John Kiriakou's story from every direction — his plea agreement banned him from ever filing a FOIA request on himself, so he filed one with the Bureau of Prisons anyway and got back pages stamped "FOIA EXEMPT — DO NOT RELEASE TO INMATE"; a FOIA request exposed the prison commissary skim; Jason Leopold's requests revealed that a detainee's eye was removed under sedation without his knowledge and that NBC's Ken Dilanian sent his stories to the CIA before his own editor; and a FOIA request is how Kiriakou learned Gary Johnson had quietly lobbied for his early release.

the-buried-senate-documents.title: Thirty-year mandatory declassification
the-buried-senate-documents.summary: The statutory requirement, described by John Kiriakou, that classified American documents be released after thirty years — a law he says virtually nobody knows about, and which he raises against the continued withholding of Kennedy assassination records more than sixty years on. He also describes the redaction practice that operates alongside it.

the-buried-senate-documents.title: Congressional intelligence oversight
the-buried-senate-documents.summary: John Kiriakou''s standing criticism of the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence and the House Permanent Select Committee — that unlike the armed services and foreign relations committees, they do not perform oversight at all: "They''re just cheerleaders." His illustration is a sitting committee chairman who summoned him privately, then asked whether Kiriakou would write the criticism publicly on his behalf.

the-buried-senate-documents.title: Podcasters on foreign payrolls
the-buried-senate-documents.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of being told by an investigative journalist he respects that four household-name podcasters were taking CIA money — an allegation she could not corroborate and would not publish. He treats it as credible and extends the logic: if the agency is paying podcasters, foreign governments will be paying them too.

the-buried-senate-documents.title: Pike Committee
the-buried-senate-documents.summary: U.S. House investigative committee operating in 1975–1976 in parallel with the Senate's Church Committee; per John Kiriakou, the two committees together were the apex — and the last genuine exercise — of congressional oversight of the CIA, staffed by heavyweights and followed by a golden age that lasted only until Iran-Contra. Their work created the permanent House and Senate intelligence committees, which Kiriakou says degraded within a decade into cheerleaders for the agency.

the-buried-senate-documents.title: "All it takes is a signature"
the-buried-senate-documents.summary: John Kiriakou's answer, drawn from his years as a Senate investigator, to the claim that Congress had run out of time to obtain the Epstein flight logs — that a committee's investigative power is exercised by one senator signing a piece of paper, which can be done at any hour, and that the excuse is therefore not a sensible one.

the-business-card-espionage-charges.title: Espionage Act
the-business-card-espionage-charges.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

the-business-card-espionage-charges.title: Intelligence Identities Protection Act
the-business-card-espionage-charges.summary: U.S. law enacted in 1982 that makes it a crime to knowingly disclose the identity of a covert intelligence officer; per John Kiriakou, his 2012 prosecution under the act arose from confirming a single surname of a former CIA colleague to a journalist — a confirmation that was never published. The name passed through a chain from journalist to Human Rights Watch to Guantanamo defense attorneys before reaching a judge and ultimately the FBI, which traced it back to Kiriakou.

the-business-card-espionage-charges.title: Eastern District of Virginia
the-business-card-espionage-charges.summary: The U.S. federal district covering northern Virginia — home to Langley, the Pentagon, DHS and much of the intelligence-contractor industry — which John Kiriakou calls 'the espionage court' because the Justice Department files the great majority of its national security prosecutions there and because, in his telling, no national-security defendant has ever won a case in it; Kiriakou, Julian Assange, Edward Snowden and Jeffrey Sterling were all charged there.

the-business-card-espionage-charges.title: Federal plea coercion
the-business-card-espionage-charges.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that the federal justice system coerces guilty pleas by stacking charges and winning 98.2% of its cases — so that even innocent defendants take deals, as he did, told by his own attorney that the system is 'not about justice; it's about mitigating damage.'

the-business-card-espionage-charges.title: Japanese diplomat FBI sting
the-business-card-espionage-charges.summary: John Kiriakou's account of an FBI entrapment operation in which an agent posing as a Japanese diplomat cold-pitched him for classified information over five lunches, hoping he would commit actual espionage they could charge — a scheme he discovered only in his own case discovery.

the-business-card-espionage-charges.title: Edward Snowden
the-business-card-espionage-charges.summary: Former NSA contractor who in 2013 disclosed the scope of U.S. [mass surveillance](/wiki/mass-surveillance), including the Section 702 collection program. Per John Kiriakou — who counts Snowden among the small group of national-security whistleblowers prosecuted under the Espionage Act — Snowden was ''stuck between two awful slippery slopes'': breaking his oath and chain of command on one side, and on the other catching something ''cut and dry against the Constitution'' that no one would act on. Kiriakou notes Snowden could not use his chain of command (as Kiriakou could not, his own chain being Jose Rodriguez), and that Judge Leonie Brinkema had reserved the Snowden case for herself before he fled the country.

the-c-130-resettlements.title: The Afghan Zero Units
