the-cia-recruiting-video.summary: John Kiriakou''s challenge to the premise of the Abraham Accords: that after a lifetime working in the Middle East he is unable to identify anything Saudi Arabia would actually gain from recognising Israel.

the-cia-recruiting-video.title: Bigger than the Russian embassy
the-cia-recruiting-video.summary: Why American embassies in small, strategically unimportant countries are enormous: the answer John Kiriakou says he was given by a station chief on one of his first CIA trips — that the building had to be bigger than the Soviet one across town. He describes American embassies in Africa as "absolutely gigantic" for that reason alone, and calls the US embassy in Cairo an enormous facility matched by an equally enormous Russian one.

the-cia-recruiting-video.title: How the CIA kills
the-cia-recruiting-video.summary: John Kiriakou''s description of the methods used when the CIA is ordered to kill someone outside a war zone: a team parachuting in miles away, stealing a car, a locks-and-picks specialist opening the door and suppressed weapons inside; a snatch into a van bound for an airport or a boat; or a brush past in a market with something poisoned — a technique he says the Russians used often and taught the Bulgarians into the early 1980s.

the-cia-spotter-professor.title: Bin Laden health rumors
the-cia-spotter-professor.summary: John Kiriakou's dismissal of the claim that Osama bin Laden died years before the 2011 raid. He says the CIA received a steady stream of medical rumours about him — kidney failure, dialysis in a cave, a spinal disorder — none of which turned out to be true, and that bin Laden was in fine health apart from arthritis and a hip problem until the day he died.

the-cia-spotter-professor.title: The scholar-in-residence pipeline
the-cia-spotter-professor.summary: John Kiriakou's description of retired CIA operations officers taking scholar-in-residence posts at universities and teaching literature courses that function, by their own account, as a recruitment funnel — students enrol knowing the instructor is a former officer and hoping for help getting in.

the-cia-spotter-professor.title: Fake CIA résumés
the-cia-spotter-professor.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of being used as a human authenticator in the private sector: at the consulting firm he joined after leaving the CIA, every job applicant claiming agency service was sent to dinner with him, and by his count fully half of them had never set foot inside the CIA.

the-cia-spotter-professor.title: False flags are too hard
the-cia-spotter-professor.summary: John Kiriakou''s practical objection to the idea that governments routinely stage false flag operations: they exist, and at the operational level the CIA used them constantly, but the bigger the operation the harder it is to run — too many moving parts, too many people who must buy into the conspiracy, and too much incompetence in government to keep any of it straight. He couples the objection with the observation that a government which is not transparent has no standing to complain about public suspicion.

the-cia-spotter-professor.title: Recruiting foreign students
the-cia-spotter-professor.summary: The long-horizon intelligence argument for admitting foreign students to American universities — that a doctoral student in the hard sciences recruited on campus goes home to a weapons programme as an asset already in place — and John Kiriakou's view that collapsing enrolment is an operational loss nobody at the top is thinking about.

the-cia-spotter-professor.title: SEAL Team Six attrition
the-cia-spotter-professor.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer to the claim that the Navy SEALs who killed Osama bin Laden have since been killed off: the dead came from the broader unit rather than the raid party, SEAL Team Six numbers several hundred men rather than the dozen or so people imagine, and losing a high number of them to accidents and combat is, in his phrase, very sadly common.

the-cia-that-never-existed.title: The 2017 European tour
the-cia-that-never-existed.summary: In May 2017 John Kiriakou spent a week speaking about national security whistleblowing in Iceland, Germany, Luxembourg, Belgium and Ireland, addressing the German Parliament and sharing panels with serving European ministers — an audience he contrasted sharply with his reception in the United States, and one he found newly willing to break with Washington because it was, in his word, panic-stricken about Donald Trump.

the-cia-that-never-existed.title: Domingo's television
the-cia-that-never-existed.summary: John Kiriakou has used the television rooms at FCI Loretto as his sharpest illustration of prison segregation: sets owned by racial blocs since a riot in the 1990s, a seat in front of one costing fourteen dollars, and one set left tuned to Law & Order every morning because a man named Domingo had paid four hundred dollars for it and had been gone for years.

the-cia-that-never-existed.title: Mental health as a disciplinary problem
the-cia-that-never-existed.summary: John Kiriakou has said that before his own prosecution he never gave five seconds of thought to the American prison system, and that living inside it showed him a broken one — in particular a system in which mental health is treated as a disciplinary problem rather than a medical one.

the-cia-that-never-existed.title: The Ai Weiwei encounter in Berlin
the-cia-that-never-existed.summary: John Kiriakou met the artist Ai Weiwei by pure chance on a Berlin street while dragging a suitcase to the airport after a board meeting — an encounter that led to a tour of Ai Weiwei's studio and a signed iPhone case bearing the Lego portrait the artist had made of him for an exhibition at Alcatraz.

the-cia-that-never-existed.title: The Alcatraz walkthrough
the-cia-that-never-existed.summary: On his very first day of house arrest, the day Ai Weiwei's political-prisoner exhibition closed at Alcatraz, the San Francisco gallery that had helped stage the show telephoned John Kiriakou and walked him around the entire exhibition on an iPad so that he could see his own portrait and the ceramic flowers filling the sinks of the solitary confinement cells.

the-cia-that-never-existed.title: The attribution problem in the DNC hack
the-cia-that-never-existed.summary: Asked in 2017 whether he had any confidence in the intelligence community's assessments of Russian interference, John Kiriakou said he had none — objecting that no one had ever defined what was meant by hacking, that the published evidence told the public nothing, and that an agency asking to be taken at its word should not be.

the-cia-under-a-left-wing-president.title: The NYPD intelligence post
the-cia-under-a-left-wing-president.summary: The New York Police Department position — deputy commissioner for intelligence — that John Kiriakou says traditionally goes to someone coming out of the CIA, and which he uses to explain why the agency is indifferent to who wins a New York mayoral election so long as the post and its liaison with the joint terrorism task force survive.

the-cia-under-a-left-wing-president.title: CIA operational psychologists
the-cia-under-a-left-wing-president.summary: The branch of the CIA's psychological staff that John Kiriakou says he worked with directly as a case officer — not the analysts who profile foreign leaders, but the clinicians who vet a prospective recruit for insanity or invention, and advise an officer on exactly how hard a source can be pushed before he breaks.

the-cia-under-a-left-wing-president.title: CIA psychological evaluations
the-cia-under-a-left-wing-president.summary: The two kinds of psychological work John Kiriakou describes inside the CIA — the recurring psychiatric screening every officer undergoes, before employment, again three years after hiring and every five years thereafter for life; and the long-distance evaluation of foreign leaders carried out by the analytic side. The agency's clinical psychologists are split between the two, with a third group in operations advising case officers on the sources they recruit.

the-cia-under-a-left-wing-president.title: The two officers who changed
the-cia-under-a-left-wing-president.summary: John Kiriakou's account of two colleagues he liked as junior officers and watched become something else — one who rose to deputy director for counterterrorism at both the CIA and the FBI and whom he calls a war criminal, and one who took over the bin Laden unit and became, in his phrase, a stone cold killer.

the-cia-under-a-left-wing-president.title: Torture and morale inside the CIA
the-cia-under-a-left-wing-president.summary: John Kiriakou's account of what the torture programme did to morale at the CIA — a compartment so tight that nobody knew for six or eight months, a workforce that split between objectors and true believers who enjoyed the work, and a pullback by George Tenet around 2005 that ended active torture at the secret sites while leaving the prisons open and Guantanamo untouched.

the-cia-under-a-left-wing-president.title: CIA political neutrality tradition
the-cia-under-a-left-wing-president.summary: The informal midcentury norm at the Central Intelligence Agency, described by John Kiriakou from his own 1990-era experience, under which employees did not share their partisan affiliations at work, small displays such as a Bob Dole campaign bumper sticker in a cubicle triggered severe internal discipline, and career officers steered clear of political endorsement — a tradition Kiriakou argues collapsed by 2020, when 51 former intelligence officials signed the letter dismissing the Hunter Biden laptop story.

the-clear-and-present-danger-finding.title: Marco Rubio and Iran policy
the-clear-and-present-danger-finding.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer to who was actually driving American policy toward Iran in 2026: with the Vice President, the Director of National Intelligence and the Chairman of the Joint Chiefs all reported as opposed, and with Marco Rubio holding both the State Department and the National Security Adviser''s job, the policy was Rubio''s.

the-clear-and-present-danger-finding.title: "Most other countries are more moral than the CIA"
the-clear-and-present-danger-finding.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer to a viewer who asked whether the United States has the most moral intelligence agency: it does not, and a hundred countries could be named whose services behave better — the disqualifying practice being the killing of people who pose no threat to the United States.

the-clear-and-present-danger-finding.title: MBS and Netanyahu asked Trump to attack Iran
the-clear-and-present-danger-finding.summary: John Kiriakou's account that Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu jointly went to Donald Trump and asked him to attack Iran — a move Kiriakou finds hard to reconcile with MBS's own years of work to improve Saudi relations with Tehran.

the-clear-and-present-danger-finding.title: Bombing the Omanis
the-clear-and-present-danger-finding.summary: John Kiriakou's judgement that Iran's strikes on the Gulf states — and above all on Oman, which had been trying to broker peace — made enemies Iran did not need to make, of governments that would otherwise have sat the war out.

the-clear-and-present-danger-finding.title: Chaos as the Israeli objective
the-clear-and-present-danger-finding.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer to whether Netanyahu''s government actually wanted an American invasion of Iran: what the Israelis want in Iran is what they got in Libya — chaos, civil war, and as many dead Iranians as possible.

the-clear-and-present-danger-finding.title: Dubai as Iran's window
the-clear-and-present-danger-finding.summary: John Kiriakou''s explanation of why Iran did not hit Dubai hard during the 2026 war: the city is full of Iranian businessmen and is Iran''s outlet to the Western world and its principal means of evading sanctions.

the-clemency-campaign-of-january-2013.title: Ralph Nader
the-clemency-campaign-of-january-2013.summary: American consumer advocate and perennial third-party presidential candidate. In January 2013 Nader co-signed a letter to the president asking for John Kiriakou to be pardoned; weeks later Kiriakou thanked him by name at his portrait unveiling as a steadfast supporter whose backing he described as humbling. Nader's 2000 independent run also anchors Kiriakou's account of how third-party candidates were shut out of the presidential debates.

the-clemency-campaign-of-january-2013.title: The legal bills
the-clemency-campaign-of-january-2013.summary: The cost of John Kiriakou's defence, which he has given variously as more than half a million dollars, approaching a million, and more than a million — a figure he treats not as a hardship but as the mechanism of the prosecution itself, since bankruptcy is what makes a defendant accept a plea.

the-clemency-campaign-of-january-2013.title: The second officer in the same case
the-clemency-campaign-of-january-2013.summary: A document John Kiriakou says his attorneys discovered shortly before his January 2013 sentencing, showing that a second CIA officer had given the same reporter the names of ten undercover officers along with information on counterterrorist operations and the flight plans of the aircraft serving a secret prison — and was never investigated or prosecuted, which Kiriakou takes as proof that his own case was about whistleblowing rather than disclosure.

the-clemency-campaign-of-january-2013.title: The seventh Espionage Act defendant
the-clemency-campaign-of-january-2013.summary: The case John Kiriakou cited two days before his own sentencing to correct the count of Espionage Act prosecutions brought under Barack Obama — a translator at the American naval base in Bahrain who had just been charged, making seven, against three in the whole history of the United States before 2009.

the-clemency-campaign-of-january-2013.title: Abu Zubaydah
the-clemency-campaign-of-january-2013.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

the-clemency-campaign-of-january-2013.title: Daniel Ellsberg
the-clemency-campaign-of-january-2013.summary: The Pentagon Papers whistleblower Kiriakou calls 'the Godfather of all national security whistleblowers' — and one of the great mentors of his life.

the-clinton-asset-purge.title: Bill Clinton
the-clinton-asset-purge.summary: 42nd U.S. president whom John Kiriakou describes as wholly disinterested in intelligence — briefed by the CIA only twice in eight years, with Vice President Al Gore taking the daily briefing instead and relaying anything important.

the-clinton-asset-purge.title: Church Committee
the-clinton-asset-purge.summary: U.S. Senate investigative committee operating in 1975–1976 that examined domestic intelligence abuses by the CIA, FBI, and NSA; per John Kiriakou, the Church Committee — alongside the concurrent Pike Committee in the House — was the last genuine moment of legislative oversight over the intelligence community, born of a national consensus that government had gone dangerously off course. Its work led to the creation of the permanent Senate Select Committee on Intelligence, which Kiriakou says ceased to function as real oversight roughly seven years after its founding.

the-clinton-asset-purge.title: Presidential appetite for intelligence
the-clinton-asset-purge.summary: John Kiriakou''s ranking of the presidents he served under by how much intelligence they actually wanted — from George H. W. Bush, who asked for special analytic products constantly, to Bill Clinton, who he says was briefed twice in eight years.

the-clinton-asset-purge.title: Fifty new crimes a year
the-clinton-asset-purge.summary: John Kiriakou''s argument that the United States has become a carceral country by legislative accretion — fifty newly created federal crimes every year for two decades, on top of five per cent of the world''s population holding twenty-five per cent of its prisoners.

the-clinton-asset-purge.title: How Kiriakou went armed in Athens
the-clinton-asset-purge.summary: The load John Kiriakou carried every day during his Athens tour — a 9mm in a tear-away waist pack with three magazines, a snub-nosed .38 on his ankle, about 47 rounds in total, and a buck knife his boss handed him on his first day *"just in case things go to shit"*.

the-clinton-asset-purge.title: The Al Udeid strike
the-clinton-asset-purge.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of Iran''s face-saving retaliation for the American bombing of its nuclear sites in June 2025 — a single missile fired at Al Udeid air base in Qatar, announced two hours in advance, which he says hit a geodesic dome housing top secret communications.

the-clinton-era-asset-cull.title: Geneva Conventions
the-clinton-era-asset-cull.summary: The laws of war at the center of John Kiriakou''s most-told confrontation story: finding hooded prisoners in Pakistan, he demanded of the officer in charge — "Are you seriously telling me that you have never read the Geneva Convention? It is a war crime to put hoods on them. Take the hoods off." The two reported each other to headquarters; Kiriakou got in trouble — "they didn''t give two shits about the Geneva Convention." He indicts the Bush administration''s twin dodges: that al-Qaeda fighters, as non-state actors, fell outside the Conventions'' protections, and that the techniques weren''t torture at all.

the-clinton-era-asset-cull.title: The 1994 women''s class action
the-clinton-era-asset-cull.summary: A class action brought by female CIA employees who had been passed over for promotion produced, in John Kiriakou''s account, a judicial finding that the Agency had documented its own crime and a remedy of an across-the-board two-level promotion for every woman at the CIA.

the-clinton-era-asset-cull.title: The new Iraqi flag
the-clinton-era-asset-cull.summary: Before the invasion of Iraq, John Kiriakou walked into the CIA''s Iraq Operations Group and found its director at his desk with Crayola markers, colouring in a design for a new Iraqi flag.

the-clinton-era-asset-cull.title: The unexplained false statement charge
the-clinton-era-asset-cull.summary: One of the five counts against John Kiriakou was making a false statement, and neither he nor his eleven lawyers could establish what the statement was supposed to have been; the government withdrew the count after his defence had spent six figures on it.

the-clinton-era-asset-cull.title: Church Committee
the-clinton-era-asset-cull.summary: U.S. Senate investigative committee operating in 1975–1976 that examined domestic intelligence abuses by the CIA, FBI, and NSA; per John Kiriakou, the Church Committee — alongside the concurrent Pike Committee in the House — was the last genuine moment of legislative oversight over the intelligence community, born of a national consensus that government had gone dangerously off course. Its work led to the creation of the permanent Senate Select Committee on Intelligence, which Kiriakou says ceased to function as real oversight roughly seven years after its founding.

the-clinton-era-asset-cull.title: Extraordinary Rendition
the-clinton-era-asset-cull.summary: Per John Kiriakou, the CIA practice of seizing terrorism suspects in one country and transporting them to a third country — often a country with no due-process protections — to be held, interrogated, or tortured outside U.S. legal jurisdiction. The program operated alongside the enhanced-interrogation program and was the operational mechanism by which prisoners reached secret CIA facilities and allied torture sites in countries like Bahrain. Kiriakou himself was not in the rendition line of work but became a federal felon under the Intelligence Identities Protection Act for a single confirmation of a colleague's surname to a journalist who claimed to be writing a book on the Abu Omar rendition from Milan.

the-clinton-pakistan-plane-switch.title: The catering truck transfer
the-clinton-pakistan-plane-switch.summary: The covert removal of Donald Trump from Air Force One at the end of a NATO summit in Turkey — boarded in front of the television cameras, driven across the tarmac inside an airport catering truck, and flown on to Britain aboard a smaller jet while the White House press corps travelled on the aircraft everyone believed he was on.

the-clinton-pakistan-plane-switch.title: The Baltimore plot
the-clinton-pakistan-plane-switch.summary: The 1861 conspiracy to assassinate president-elect Abraham Lincoln as his train passed through Baltimore, uncovered by Pinkerton detectives — and the overnight passage in a soft felt hat and shawl that got him to his inauguration and made the press call him a coward.

the-clinton-pakistan-plane-switch.title: Bill Clinton
the-clinton-pakistan-plane-switch.summary: 42nd U.S. president whom John Kiriakou describes as wholly disinterested in intelligence — briefed by the CIA only twice in eight years, with Vice President Al Gore taking the daily briefing instead and relaying anything important.

the-clinton-pakistan-plane-switch.title: The Air Force One bomb threat
the-clinton-pakistan-plane-switch.summary: The bomb threat telephoned to the classified telephone aboard Air Force One as Bill Clinton's aircraft lifted out of Athens in November 1999, disclosed by the ambassador at the embassy's after-action review — a detail John Kiriakou withheld from years of tellings of that visit until 2026.

the-clinton-pakistan-plane-switch.title: Fidel Castro
the-clinton-pakistan-plane-switch.summary: The Cuban leader John Kiriakou uses as his standing example of a relationship the United States could have had and chose not to — a rebel who liked America and had pitched in its minor leagues, written off because Washington had already committed itself to Batista. Castro also recurs across Kiriakou's account of the CIA as the agency's most-attempted assassination target, as the man who never cashed the rent cheques for Guantánamo, and as the figure American policy is still fighting years after his death.

the-clinton-pakistan-plane-switch.title: Nicholas Burns
the-clinton-pakistan-plane-switch.summary: The United States ambassador to Greece during John Kiriakou''s Athens tour — an envoy Kiriakou says he has always disliked and disrespected, whose unpopularity extended to his own staff, and whom he credits with exactly one good decision: drawing the assignments for a presidential visit out of a hat.

the-cnn-india-refusal.title: Pakistani corruption and democracy
the-cnn-india-refusal.summary: John Kiriakou's assessment that corruption in Pakistan is so deep and so broad that a genuinely functioning democracy is almost impossible there — set against a long history of military coups, a habit of imprisoning former prime ministers, and his insistence that Imran Khan should not be in a cell.

the-cnn-india-refusal.title: The Imran Khan apology demand
the-cnn-india-refusal.summary: The demand issued by Imran Khan's party in late October 2025 that John Kiriakou apologise in writing to Khan, to the party and to the Pakistani people over a single sentence he had given an Indian outlet — that India would win a conventional war because it has five times the population — together with his refusal, the death threats, his lawyer's advice, and the blanket policy on South Asian media he adopted afterwards.

the-cnn-india-refusal.title: Craig Murray
the-cnn-india-refusal.summary: Former British Ambassador to Uzbekistan whom John Kiriakou cites as a whistleblower of extreme torture: during a meeting at the Uzbek intelligence service, Murray heard screaming, walked in, and saw a man being boiled in oil — reporting it cost him his career.

the-cnn-india-refusal.title: Dumping cash in a Moscow bathroom
the-cnn-india-refusal.summary: John Kiriakou's examples of what covert action has actually meant in practice — American commandos blowing up the Trans-Siberian oil pipeline, Afghan guerrillas hired to cross the Amu Darya and attack a refinery inside the southern USSR, and cash dumped in a Moscow bathroom to undermine the rouble.

the-cnn-india-refusal.title: How Chinese intelligence recruits
the-cnn-india-refusal.summary: John Kiriakou''s assessment of the Ministry of State Security''s tradecraft: very effective with anyone who simply wants money, because the money is limitless, and very bad at cultivating a source who does not yet know who is cultivating him — with the target usually being access to sophisticated technology.

the-cnn-india-refusal.title: MK-ULTRA in Canada
the-cnn-india-refusal.summary: John Kiriakou''s confirmation that many MK-ULTRA experiments took place on Canadian soil, and his explanation of why: the CIA asked the Canadian intelligence service for help with its anti-Soviet, anti-Chinese remote-viewing and LSD work, and the Canadians gladly gave it.

the-co-who-wanted-the-cia.title: Domingo's television
the-co-who-wanted-the-cia.summary: John Kiriakou has used the television rooms at FCI Loretto as his sharpest illustration of prison segregation: sets owned by racial blocs since a riot in the 1990s, a seat in front of one costing fourteen dollars, and one set left tuned to Law & Order every morning because a man named Domingo had paid four hundred dollars for it and had been gone for years.

the-co-who-wanted-the-cia.title: The case against work camps
the-co-who-wanted-the-cia.summary: John Kiriakou, who asked to serve his own sentence at a minimum-security work camp and was sent to the prison across the street instead, came out of prison arguing that the camps should not exist at all — and, in the same breath, that some prisoners are dangerous enough that prisons certainly should.

the-co-who-wanted-the-cia.title: The persona in the first week
the-co-who-wanted-the-cia.summary: Five days into a sentence he had expected to serve at a minimum-security camp, John Kiriakou decided to fall back on his CIA training and adopt a deliberately aggressive exterior — reasoning that in a prison where the weak end up checking themselves into solitary for protection, he would rather be the man other people needed protection from.

the-co-who-wanted-the-cia.title: The professor in the visiting room
the-co-who-wanted-the-cia.summary: John Kiriakou has credited the idea for his prison memoir to a university professor who visited him at FCI Loretto, listened to him tell stories across a visiting-room table, and told him that although the whole thing was by its nature depressing, the stories were good and there were lessons in them, and that he should write a book.

the-co-who-wanted-the-cia.title: Mental health as a disciplinary problem
the-co-who-wanted-the-cia.summary: John Kiriakou has said that before his own prosecution he never gave five seconds of thought to the American prison system, and that living inside it showed him a broken one — in particular a system in which mental health is treated as a disciplinary problem rather than a medical one.

the-co-who-wanted-the-cia.title: The chapel rule
the-co-who-wanted-the-cia.summary: The chapel and the library at FCI Loretto were the two places child molesters could be certain of safety, because a correctional officer was always present; John Kiriakou, who worked in the chapel, has described the house rule against discussing your case there and the indignation with which it was met.

the-cocaine-in-the-west-wing.title: The Capitol Hill cocaine ring
the-cocaine-in-the-west-wing.summary: The 1983 congressional drug scandal John Kiriakou stumbled into at eighteen, when an FBI agent called at his father's house and then asked him whether he had ever seen his congressman trade stamps for cocaine — a question he answered no to, and which turned out to be exactly what the congressman was doing.

the-cocaine-in-the-west-wing.title: Elliott Abrams
the-cocaine-in-the-west-wing.summary: The Reagan-era assistant secretary of state whose 2023 appointment to a Biden administration advisory board John Kiriakou treated as proof that neoliberal and neoconservative foreign policy are the same policy with interchangeable players — a man who pleaded guilty over Iran-Contra, was pardoned, helped sell the Iraqi weapons of mass destruction case, and then served Donald Trump on Iran and Venezuela.

the-cocaine-in-the-west-wing.title: Frances Haugen
the-cocaine-in-the-west-wing.summary: The Facebook employee John Kiriakou refuses to call a whistleblower — arguing that against the legal definition, bringing to light waste, fraud, abuse, illegality or threats to public health or safety, she qualifies as a corporate spokesperson whose motive was to improve the company's bottom line, not to expose wrongdoing.

the-cocaine-in-the-west-wing.title: Gavin Newsom
the-cocaine-in-the-west-wing.summary: The California governor John Kiriakou described in 2023 as the consummate Democratic Party insider waiting his turn — a Pelosi relative who married into the Brown family, doing everything the Biden operation asked of him, including a pointless surrogate trip to Idaho, on the calculation that Joe Biden would not reach the nominating convention.

the-cocaine-in-the-west-wing.title: Netanyahu and the Tel Aviv police chief
the-cocaine-in-the-west-wing.summary: The July 2023 dismissal of Tel Aviv's police chief, which John Kiriakou identified as the moment Benjamin Netanyahu may have overstepped — arguing that the real threat to the Israeli prime minister came not from the Palestinians but from his own attempt to take over the court system, and from the strikes and demonstrations that had not subsided.

the-code-room-and-the-buried-weapons.title: The broken side-view mirror
the-code-room-and-the-buried-weapons.summary: The cold pitch John Kiriakou made in Athens against the incoming intelligence representative of a hostile Middle Eastern state — a manoeuvre suggested by his mentor Gust Avrakotos, in which Kiriakou snapped the mirror off the man's diplomatic car with a bag of books, established cover with the neighbour, apologised at the door, asked for a glass of water, and used the minute alone to kneel down and speak Arabic to the target's four-year-old daughter.

the-code-room-and-the-buried-weapons.title: The restaurants in witness protection
the-code-room-and-the-buried-weapons.summary: What became of the foreign intelligence officer John Kiriakou recruited in Athens — resettled in the United States under a made-up name, given citizenship for his family and seed money to start again, and last heard of owning seven restaurants — and the resettlement package Kiriakou says the CIA offers a burned agent.

the-code-room-and-the-buried-weapons.title: The Mallios argument
the-code-room-and-the-buried-weapons.summary: The confrontation John Kiriakou describes with his mentor Gust Avrakotos while the two worked the 17 November task force — Kiriakou remarked in passing that the group's second victim, the Greek police chief Mallios, had been a torturer under the junta; Avrakotos slammed him against a wall; and the exchange that followed became the basis of their friendship.

the-code-room-and-the-buried-weapons.title: Agent payment mechanics
the-code-room-and-the-buried-weapons.summary: How the CIA physically pays a recruited agent — cash every month, a receipt signed with any alias the agent chooses, and a polygraph regime built around the assumption that the officer handling the money is the person most likely to steal it.

the-code-room-and-the-buried-weapons.title: Gust Avrakotos
the-code-room-and-the-buried-weapons.summary: CIA case officer, John Kiriakou's operations mentor, and a central figure in Charlie Wilson's War — the prolific, divisive covert-war veteran Kiriakou credits as the greatest teacher of his adult life.

the-code-room-and-the-buried-weapons.title: Recruiting from the bottom
the-code-room-and-the-buried-weapons.summary: The targeting method John Kiriakou believes produced the killings of Iran''s leadership: not agents at the top of the state but destitute refugees at street level, paid a hundred dollars a month to write down when a general leaves his building and by which route. He contrasts it with the CIA''s own record in Iran, where it spent his career trying and failing to recruit inside the Ayatollah''s office, the foreign ministry and the IRGC.

the-coffee-with-the-jordanian-intern.title: Bulldozing the olive orchards
the-coffee-with-the-jordanian-intern.summary: The sequence John Kiriakou describes preceding Israeli seizures of Palestinian land in the West Bank — olive orchards bulldozed and crops burned to make leaving easier, then the house demolished and a prefabricated one built for a settler family — and the different practice he says applies in East Jerusalem.

the-coffee-with-the-jordanian-intern.title: Abbas and the three-state problem
the-coffee-with-the-jordanian-intern.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that no two-state solution is available — because there is already one state, because Mahmoud Abbas is nineteen years into a four-year term and has become a billionaire, and because East Bank, West Bank and Gaza Palestinians are so disconnected that the real arithmetic is three states, which nobody will discuss.

the-coffee-with-the-jordanian-intern.title: The three pro-Israel countries
the-coffee-with-the-jordanian-intern.summary: A global opinion poll John Kiriakou reported in August 2025 which, on his account, found only three countries with majority pro-Israel populations — Israel, the United States, and, to his own bafflement, Nigeria — with Turkey the most anti-Israel country outside the Middle East and Greece at 74 per cent against.

the-coffee-with-the-jordanian-intern.title: Elbridge Gerry and the salamander
the-coffee-with-the-jordanian-intern.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the origin of the word gerrymander — Elbridge Gerry, vice president and former governor of Massachusetts, drawing district boundaries to elect his friends, and Benjamin Franklin saying the shapes looked like salamanders — together with a piece of trivia from his unpublished book on cemeteries.

the-coffee-with-the-jordanian-intern.title: New Castle, Pennsylvania
the-coffee-with-the-jordanian-intern.summary: John Kiriakou's home town, an hour north of Pittsburgh on the edge of Amish country — a rust-belt city of roughly 40,000 to 50,000 people when he was growing up and around 18,000 to 20,000 now, whose decline he measures by the arrival of DEA and ATF field offices. It is also where, aged eight or nine and hunting salamanders in Oak Park Cemetery, he found the grave of a Medal of Honor private and acquired the lifelong interest in cemeteries that became a book.

the-coffee-with-the-jordanian-intern.title: From sixteen employees to twenty thousand
the-coffee-with-the-jordanian-intern.summary: John Kiriakou's support for cutting the staff of the Office of the Director of National Intelligence, on the ground that a body created after 9/11 with sixteen employees to coordinate the agencies had grown to twenty thousand.

the-colleague-who-went-to-microsoft.title: James Bond
the-colleague-who-went-to-microsoft.summary: The fictional spy who got John Kiriakou — and, he says, half the Directorate of Operations — into the business. He asked for walkie-talkies at nine and told his father at sixteen that he wanted to be a spy in the Middle East; he concedes "literally none of it is true to life", but vouches for one scene: Bond always runs into the CIA officer at the party. The figure follows him to the end, too — a personality paper titled "Who is James Bond?" describes the officer type in terms he finds harsh, and federal prosecutors, he says, argued for his detention by talking about him "like I was 007."

the-colleague-who-went-to-microsoft.title: The Talk Liberation bank freeze
the-colleague-who-went-to-microsoft.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the September 2022 freezing of Talk Liberation's Icelandic bank accounts — the seed funding behind the Panquake platform — on stated suspicion of money laundering and possible terrorist financing. Kiriakou, who deliberately declines to name the bank, calls the allegations nonsense, says in his personal opinion the freeze came at a government's behest, and notes the accounts were later unfrozen.

the-colleague-who-went-to-microsoft.title: The counterfeit dollar trade
the-colleague-who-went-to-microsoft.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of high-quality counterfeit US currency — the Swiss paper that makes it possible, an estimate that five to ten percent of the notes in circulation may be forged, and a quiet policy of buying up caches at thirty cents on the dollar and incinerating them.

the-colleague-who-went-to-microsoft.title: CIA and FBI embedded at social media firms
the-colleague-who-went-to-microsoft.summary: John Kiriakou's claim, citing the Twitter Files, that active-duty CIA and FBI officers were placed undercover inside Twitter, Facebook and other platforms — which he argues can only mean they were spying on Americans.

the-colleague-who-went-to-microsoft.title: Government Purchase of Social Media Metadata
the-colleague-who-went-to-microsoft.summary: Per John Kiriakou, the practice by which U.S. intelligence and law enforcement agencies — including the NSA and FBI — buy bulk user metadata from social media companies such as Facebook, Instagram, and X (formerly Twitter), bypassing the warrant requirements that would otherwise apply to direct surveillance. The practice exploits a provision in platform terms of service under which users surrender ownership of their metadata to the company, which may then sell it freely.

the-colleague-who-went-to-microsoft.title: Chinese overseas police stations
the-colleague-who-went-to-microsoft.summary: John Kiriakou's account of a New York Times revelation about Chinese nationals with apparent ties to the Chinese police operating out of storefronts around Manhattan and travelling around the United States to threaten Chinese people with reprisals against relatives in Beijing — and his puzzlement that the FBI missed it.

the-colombian-air-bridge-through-venezue.title: The plot to divert Maduro's plane
the-colombian-air-bridge-through-venezue.summary: The reported CIA attempt to recruit Nicolás Maduro's pilot so that a flight carrying him into exile in Havana would instead land at Key West, where the DEA would seize him — a Noriega repeat that prompted John Kiriakou to ask why a government pursuing regime change should care where the deposed ruler goes.

the-colombian-air-bridge-through-venezue.title: The fentanyl-from-cocaine claim
the-colombian-air-bridge-through-venezue.summary: The assertion that seventy per cent of American overdoses trace to fentanyl processed from Venezuelan cocaine, which John Kiriakou refuted on air by reading the DEA's own fact sheet — fentanyl is not made from cocaine, it is mixed into it, along with almost everything else on the market.

the-colombian-air-bridge-through-venezue.title: Venezuela Boat Strikes
the-colombian-air-bridge-through-venezue.summary: September 2025 U.S. military strike on a boat in the Caribbean that killed 11 people the White House called drug traffickers; John Kiriakou calls it piracy on the high seas followed by mass murder, arguing the victims were never charged with a crime and that the boat's unusual passenger count undercuts the drug-trafficking story.

the-colombian-air-bridge-through-venezue.title: Hamid Karzai
the-colombian-air-bridge-through-venezue.summary: The president installed in Afghanistan after the American invasion, whom John Kiriakou uses as the standing illustration of what occupation actually buys: after twenty years and more than a trillion dollars, Karzai was ''little more than the mayor of Kabul'' — and did not control all of Kabul either. The line began as a joke among Senate Foreign Relations Committee staff, and Kiriakou used it to Senator John Kerry''s face ten years into the war.

the-colombian-air-bridge-through-venezue.title: The Sahel church burnings
the-colombian-air-bridge-through-venezue.summary: John Kiriakou's account of al-Qaeda affiliates and Boko Haram in Chad, Mali and Nigeria attacking schools and churches — opening fire on teachers and administrators, kidnapping children, and burning congregations alive — and his observation that none of it is covered in the American media.

the-colombian-air-bridge-through-venezue.title: There are denials and then there are denials
the-colombian-air-bridge-through-venezue.summary: John Kiriakou's rule for reading official statements — that 'we have no such plans' is not a denial, because nothing counts as a plan until a head of government signs off on it, leaving a government free to discuss and even prepare something it can still credibly say it has no plans for.

the-colonial-pipeline-hack.title: The nineteen intelligence agencies
the-colonial-pipeline-hack.summary: Asked how many American intelligence agencies there are, John Kiriakou put the number at about nineteen, said there are no genuinely secret ones left, and argued that the sprawl is empire-building by the Pentagon — before asking why the Department of Agriculture and the Department of Commerce need intelligence agencies at all.

the-colonial-pipeline-hack.title: Kermit Roosevelt and Mosaddegh
the-colonial-pipeline-hack.summary: The CIA officer John Kiriakou names as the man who ran the 1953 overthrow of Iran's Prime Minister Mosaddegh on behalf of British Petroleum — who called it the gravest mistake of his life in the only interview he ever gave, and who, according to the documents Kiriakou has since read in the archives, did not actually run it at all.

the-colonial-pipeline-hack.title: Make it the blip
the-colonial-pipeline-hack.summary: Having stayed up all night reading law review journals and concluded that he had broken no law, John Kiriakou telephoned his attorneys at six in the morning to say he wanted to go to trial. They drove to his house, told him he was facing twelve to eighteen years, and the lawyer he respected most gave him the sentence that changed his mind.

the-colonial-pipeline-hack.title: Plato Kacheris
the-colonial-pipeline-hack.summary: A spelling variant of the name of John Kiriakou's lead defence attorney, who appears in the auto-generated transcripts as both "Kacheris" and "Cacheris". The article on him is at Plato Cacheris.

the-colonial-pipeline-hack.title: The four-day-old New York Times
the-colonial-pipeline-hack.summary: In December 2014, reading a four-day-old copy of the New York Times that prison staff had already cut articles out of, John Kiriakou found an interview in which Edward Snowden said that watching Kiriakou's case and Thomas Drake's — and seeing that neither man backed down — had inspired him to go public.

the-colonial-pipeline-hack.title: The postcards for Daniel Hale
the-colonial-pipeline-hack.summary: The letter-writing appeal John Kiriakou ran for Daniel Hale in May and June 2021 — naming Hale as the whistleblower most in need of help, posting his jail address publicly, and relaying from the prisoner himself the exact rules a letter had to satisfy to reach him: ten stamps a week, plain unlined white paper, black ink, and no photographs.

the-colour-coded-badges.title: The can of ravioli
the-colour-coded-badges.summary: John Kiriakou's confession that he eats tinned ravioli cold, straight from the can, and refuses on principle to pay more than ninety-nine cents for it — used, when the price reached $2.49, as his own answer to the polling finding that Americans care about prices more than anything else.

the-colour-coded-badges.title: Craig Murray
the-colour-coded-badges.summary: Former British Ambassador to Uzbekistan whom John Kiriakou cites as a whistleblower of extreme torture: during a meeting at the Uzbek intelligence service, Murray heard screaming, walked in, and saw a man being boiled in oil — reporting it cost him his career.

the-colour-coded-badges.title: Dumping cash in a Moscow bathroom
the-colour-coded-badges.summary: John Kiriakou's examples of what covert action has actually meant in practice — American commandos blowing up the Trans-Siberian oil pipeline, Afghan guerrillas hired to cross the Amu Darya and attack a refinery inside the southern USSR, and cash dumped in a Moscow bathroom to undermine the rouble.

the-colour-coded-badges.title: How Chinese intelligence recruits
the-colour-coded-badges.summary: John Kiriakou''s assessment of the Ministry of State Security''s tradecraft: very effective with anyone who simply wants money, because the money is limitless, and very bad at cultivating a source who does not yet know who is cultivating him — with the target usually being access to sophisticated technology.

the-colour-coded-badges.title: MK-ULTRA in Canada
the-colour-coded-badges.summary: John Kiriakou''s confirmation that many MK-ULTRA experiments took place on Canadian soil, and his explanation of why: the CIA asked the Canadian intelligence service for help with its anti-Soviet, anti-Chinese remote-viewing and LSD work, and the Canadians gladly gave it.

the-colour-coded-badges.title: Pakistani corruption and democracy
the-colour-coded-badges.summary: John Kiriakou's assessment that corruption in Pakistan is so deep and so broad that a genuinely functioning democracy is almost impossible there — set against a long history of military coups, a habit of imprisoning former prime ministers, and his insistence that Imran Khan should not be in a cell.

the-communist-party-of-greece.title: Arabic and Greek
the-communist-party-of-greece.summary: The qualification John Kiriakou says opened the door to his transfer from CIA analysis to operations: a post in Athens wanted Greek or Arabic, and he had both — by most of his tellings the only officer in the agency who did. The chief who hired him gave the reason in one sentence: it is easier and cheaper to take a linguist and teach him operations than the other way round. The pairing also became a detection tool, since the language nobody speaks in Pakistan is Arabic.

the-communist-party-of-greece.title: Barrett Brown
the-communist-party-of-greece.summary: American journalist and former Anonymous associate whom John Kiriakou describes as one of the most intelligent writers and analysts he has ever encountered, with long-standing mental health problems and a two-decade heroin addiction he has now been clear of for at least a year, expelled from the United Kingdom and relocated to Mexico.

the-communist-party-of-greece.title: Censorship on the left
the-communist-party-of-greece.summary: John Kiriakou''s observation that he was censored far less by Forbes and Fortune than by The Nation and Mother Jones, which he offers as an instance of a general rule that a writer''s own side censors them hardest — the counterpart to Ted Rall''s account of being made to fit a particular kind of leftism rather than any kind.

the-communist-party-of-greece.title: Dr Oz and the Armenian hospices
the-communist-party-of-greece.summary: John Kiriakou''s reaction to a television segment by Mehmet Oz alleging fraud by Armenian-run hospices in Los Angeles — that a man he identifies as a veteran of the Turkish special forces zeroing in on Armenians in California is not a coincidence, and that each of the administration''s appointees appears to arrive with a racial scandal of their own.

the-communist-party-of-greece.title: The Iron Dome
the-communist-party-of-greece.summary: Israel's air-defence system as John Kiriakou reads it — impressive against a wave of slow Iranian drones, but shown by the handful that got through, and later by Iranian ballistic missiles, to be not all it is cracked up to be; each exchange, in his account, buying Iran intelligence about the gaps.

the-communist-party-of-greece.title: James Morris
the-communist-party-of-greece.summary: A close friend of John Kiriakou''s who served seventeen years of a twenty-year sentence for a crime committed at sixteen, found on release that a violent felony conviction closed off employment, made his own way to Turkey and across the border into Syria, spent two years fighting alongside the Kurds against ISIS, and later took his own life.

the-concealed-carry-advertisements.title: The Office of Security arrangement
the-concealed-carry-advertisements.summary: The disclosure John Kiriakou says emerged from a 2020 custody hearing: that his wife, herself a senior CIA officer, had accompanied him to the 2007 ABC News whistleblowing interview on the instruction of the CIA''s Office of Security, and had continued to report on his activities.

the-concealed-carry-advertisements.title: Arabic and Greek
the-concealed-carry-advertisements.summary: The qualification John Kiriakou says opened the door to his transfer from CIA analysis to operations: a post in Athens wanted Greek or Arabic, and he had both — by most of his tellings the only officer in the agency who did. The chief who hired him gave the reason in one sentence: it is easier and cheaper to take a linguist and teach him operations than the other way round. The pairing also became a detection tool, since the language nobody speaks in Pakistan is Arabic.

the-concealed-carry-advertisements.title: Bankruptcy and the dropped charges
the-concealed-carry-advertisements.summary: The sequence John Kiriakou places at the centre of his case: that the espionage counts against him were dropped only after his legal fees had bankrupted him, which he presents as evidence that the government''s aim was attrition rather than conviction.

the-concealed-carry-advertisements.title: Curtailment cables
the-concealed-carry-advertisements.summary: The career-ending requests John Kiriakou says he read coming back from the CIA's black sites — officers, doctors, psychologists and nurses asking to end their tours early rather than continue to take part in the interrogation programme — and his conclusion that if that many people were objecting in classified channels, someone would surely go public.

the-concealed-carry-advertisements.title: Iraq, the training account
the-concealed-carry-advertisements.summary: The reason John Kiriakou says he was given the Iraq portfolio as a new CIA analyst in 1990 — that nothing ever happened there — and the promise that once he had learned tradecraft and the house writing style he would be moved to somewhere exciting, such as Romania.

the-concealed-carry-advertisements.title: "It''s about mitigating damage"
the-concealed-carry-advertisements.summary: The sentence John Kiriakou credits with changing his mind about going to trial — one of his own attorneys telling him that his problem was that he thought the case was about justice, when it was about mitigating damage — and the two lawyers who drove to his house after he emailed at six in the morning to refuse the plea.

the-condoleezza-rice-meeting.title: The second plane
the-condoleezza-rice-meeting.summary: John Kiriakou's account of where he was standing when United Airlines Flight 175 struck the South Tower — in Cofer Black's outer office, mid-sentence, explaining to a secretary why a pilot could not possibly fly into the World Trade Center on so clear a day.

the-condoleezza-rice-meeting.title: Dick Clarke
the-condoleezza-rice-meeting.summary: The White House counterterrorism chief John Kiriakou describes as the most highly respected non-ideological counterterrorism professional in government — demoted by the incoming Bush administration, ignored when he warned Condoleezza Rice that a terrible attack was coming, and, on Kiriakou's account, lied to by CIA director George Tenet about al-Qaeda operatives already inside the United States.

the-condoleezza-rice-meeting.title: Reading in on the Iraq invasion
the-condoleezza-rice-meeting.summary: John Kiriakou's account of his first day as executive assistant to the CIA's deputy director for operations, when he signed six secrecy agreements and was told that the United States would invade Iraq the following March, and that the agencies opposing the war had already lost the argument.

the-condoleezza-rice-meeting.title: The liaison class
the-condoleezza-rice-meeting.summary: The course John Kiriakou ran at the CIA for visiting officers of allied intelligence services — the setting for Cofer Black's warning weeks before 9/11, and the reason Kiriakou was in the counterterrorism chief's office to ask whether he had meant it.

the-condoleezza-rice-meeting.title: The Powell telephone call
the-condoleezza-rice-meeting.summary: The morning call John Kiriakou says he took from General Colin Powell, then chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, asking who would have run an Iraqi operation to kill former President George H. W. Bush; Kiriakou named the Iraqi Intelligence Service station in Basra and its headquarters in Baghdad, and eight hours later the United States fired forty-eight cruise missiles at that building.

the-condoleezza-rice-meeting.title: The seventy-two-year-old contractor
the-condoleezza-rice-meeting.summary: The hallway conversation John Kiriakou says explained why the CIA had not sent him, an Arabic speaker, to interrogate captured al-Qaeda fighters — a returning contractor's answer that he had been in Afghanistan killing people — and the demand Kiriakou made afterwards that got him sent to Pakistan the next day.

the-conscientious-objectors-book.title: The mob vote for Trump
the-conscientious-objectors-book.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer to a viewer asking whether he discussed politics with organised crime figures in prison: that he did, a great deal, that they love Donald Trump without qualification, and that the reason is a New York real estate developer''s unavoidable daily contact with the unions the mob controls.

the-conscientious-objectors-book.title: 1953 Iran coup
the-conscientious-objectors-book.summary: The U.S.- and UK-backed overthrow of Iran's democratically elected prime minister, Mohammad Mossadegh; per John Kiriakou, the coup served British national interests rather than American ones, and the subsequent outlawing of secular political opposition under the Shah forced dissent into the mosques — producing a religious rather than secular revolution in 1979.

the-conscientious-objectors-book.title: Active measures
the-conscientious-objectors-book.summary: The in-house name John Kiriakou gives to the CIA branch responsible for propaganda and for countering hostile propaganda — a division he describes as running twenty-four hours a day, paired with an opposing anti-active-measures branch, and as the ancestor of the political action group that remains the agency's clandestine propaganda arm.

the-conscientious-objectors-book.title: Admiral William Crowe
the-conscientious-objectors-book.summary: Former Chairman of the U.S. Joint Chiefs of Staff and former CENTCOM commander who had lived in Bahrain, author of the "pound for pound" formula every Bahraini and every American ambassador quotes, and the visiting dignitary John Kiriakou was assigned to escort — a week that ended with the Bahraini Prime Minister refusing to let go of Kiriakou's hand.

the-conscientious-objectors-book.title: AIPAC
the-conscientious-objectors-book.summary: The American Israel Public Affairs Committee — the U.S. political organization that, in John Kiriakou's framing, ought to be registered as a foreign-lobbying entity but is not, and that wields decisive electoral power against U.S. elected officials who express support for Palestinian human rights.

the-conscientious-objectors-book.title: Anwar al-Awlaki
the-conscientious-objectors-book.summary: American-born al-Qaeda propagandist; in 1993 the imam of the Falls Church, Virginia mosque visited by John Kiriakou's CIA Arabic-language class on a field trip; in 2001 the cleric at whose mosque the 9/11 hijackers prayed the night before the attacks; killed by U.S. drone strike in Yemen in approximately 2011.

the-contrition-requirement.title: The supporters who could not be public
the-contrition-requirement.summary: The thanks John Kiriakou offered on the day of his sentencing — to dozens of former and serving CIA officers, FBI agents and assistant United States attorneys who rallied to him, almost all of them privately, with cards, emails and donations to his defence fund.

the-contrition-requirement.title: Espionage Act
the-contrition-requirement.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

the-contrition-requirement.title: Federal plea coercion
the-contrition-requirement.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that the federal justice system coerces guilty pleas by stacking charges and winning 98.2% of its cases — so that even innocent defendants take deals, as he did, told by his own attorney that the system is 'not about justice; it's about mitigating damage.'

the-contrition-requirement.title: Giuliani Pardon Solicitation
the-contrition-requirement.summary: Per John Kiriakou, a meeting at the Trump International Hotel in Washington in which Rudy Giuliani's associate solicited $2 million in exchange for a presidential pardon — a story that subsequently appeared as a front-page New York Times article. Giuliani publicly denied ever meeting Kiriakou; Kiriakou sent the Times the photograph taken at the meeting that morning, and the paper published the story with the note that it had seen documentary proof.

the-contrition-requirement.title: Kiriakou pardon request
the-contrition-requirement.summary: John Kiriakou's public campaign for a presidential pardon from Donald Trump to restore the pension and firearm rights he lost after his 2013 felony conviction for disclosing the identity of a covert CIA officer; includes a five-second Mar-a-Lago encounter in which Trump referred him to Attorney General Pam Bondi, a Kalshi prediction-market contract that opened at roughly 19 to 20 percent odds on his being pardoned, and letters of support from Tucker Carlson, Judge Andrew Napolitano and Dr. Phil.

the-contrition-requirement.title: The 11(c)(1)(C) plea
the-contrition-requirement.summary: The unusual plea structure John Kiriakou's lawyers negotiated in 2012, in which the sentence is written into the agreement and the judge may accept or reject it but cannot change it. Judge Leonie Brinkema told the court she had never seen one in her career, said she did not like it, and told Kiriakou that if she could she would have given him ten years.

the-convenient-terrorist.title: Abu Zubaydah
the-convenient-terrorist.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

the-convenient-terrorist.title: Espionage Act
the-convenient-terrorist.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

the-convenient-terrorist.title: Whistleblower Protection Act
the-convenient-terrorist.summary: United States statute protecting federal employees who disclose government wrongdoing from retaliation; per John Kiriakou, national security employees — including those at the CIA, Pentagon, FBI, NSA, DEA, White House, and Homeland Security — are explicitly exempt from its protections, leaving them with no legally safe avenue to report illegal activity within their agencies.

the-convenient-terrorist.title: Doing Time Like a Spy
the-convenient-terrorist.summary: Prison memoir by John Kiriakou, full title Doing Time Like a Spy: How the CIA Taught Me to Survive and Thrive in Prison; winner of two literary awards and reissued in a second edition by Simon and Schuster.

the-convenient-terrorist.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
the-convenient-terrorist.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

the-convenient-terrorist.title: The Grand Mosque cover story
the-convenient-terrorist.summary: A single fabricated account of innocent travel that John Kiriakou says he heard roughly twenty-five times from Arab men detained in Pakistan after the September 11 attacks — a trip to Karachi to study Arabic, a lost passport, and a ride to the Grand Mosque. Its details were wrong in ways that gave it away, and Kiriakou treats its uniformity as evidence of poor operational security rather than of innocence.

the-convicted-felon-introduction.title: Suggested responses
the-convicted-felon-introduction.summary: The second email John Kiriakou says arrived before his first appearance on Fox News — a list of suggested responses to accompany the questions the producers had already sent him — which he ignored, and which he says was never sent again.

the-convicted-felon-introduction.title: The NPR walkout
the-convicted-felon-introduction.summary: The Saturday morning interview John Kiriakou says he ended after five minutes of a scheduled half hour, having been attacked on air over an op-ed about Gina Haspel, and which he closed by asking the host where NPR had been while he was blowing the whistle on the torture programme.

the-convicted-felon-introduction.title: The pre-interview
the-convicted-felon-introduction.summary: The booking practice John Kiriakou says all the American television networks use and which he finds maddening: an invitation to appear, a quick pre-interview to establish what he thinks, and then a call a minute later saying they have decided to go a different way on the story.

the-convicted-felon-introduction.title: Consulting for royal families
the-convicted-felon-introduction.summary: The work John Kiriakou says he was hired to do by members of two different royal families following the 2026 virality of his interviews — advising on ethics in their own intelligence operations — which he offers as evidence of how far the reversal in his standing had gone.

the-convicted-felon-introduction.title: "Embrace it and keep telling it"
the-convicted-felon-introduction.summary: The advice John Kiriakou says he was given days after his arrest — that he could not hide from the prosecution but had to embrace it, and had to keep telling his side of the story until it became the side of record, because the government would eventually move on to its next target.

the-convicted-felon-introduction.title: Signing with CAA
the-convicted-felon-introduction.summary: The representation John Kiriakou says followed the 2026 virality of his podcast clips: a contract with the Creative Artists Agency covering books, film, consulting and licensing, and a run of advertising approaches including one from the maker of the spectacle frames he already wore.

the-costa-rica-model.title: Sanctions and the Russian adjustment
the-costa-rica-model.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of why sanctions stopped hurting Russia: Sergey Lavrov''s admission that Moscow was caught off balance by the speed of the American response, the three or four weeks that shock lasted, and the discovery that Russia did not need the United States or its banking system once India and China agreed to buy whatever oil it had.

the-costa-rica-model.title: Bigger than the Russian embassy
the-costa-rica-model.summary: Why American embassies in small, strategically unimportant countries are enormous: the answer John Kiriakou says he was given by a station chief on one of his first CIA trips — that the building had to be bigger than the Soviet one across town. He describes American embassies in Africa as "absolutely gigantic" for that reason alone, and calls the US embassy in Cairo an enormous facility matched by an equally enormous Russian one.

the-costa-rica-model.title: Declare victory and go home
the-costa-rica-model.summary: The exit John Kiriakou prescribed for Israel in Gaza: turn the territory back to the United Nations, declare Hamas destroyed, declare victory, then engage the Saudis on the Abraham Accords and negotiate a deal later. His reasoning was that nothing remained to destroy, that killing as many people as possible is not a viable policy, and that Israel had no other way out.

the-costa-rica-model.title: "Do not ever attempt to contact me again"
the-costa-rica-model.summary: The reply John Kiriakou says he received from John Kerry, then Secretary of State, after emailing him privately in the days before reporting to prison to beg that his sentence be commuted. Kiriakou had worked closely with Kerry for two and a half years; the one-line answer, sent after two or three days, was the last he ever heard from him.

the-costa-rica-model.title: "Every Israeli I ever knew"
the-costa-rica-model.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the attitudes he encountered among Israelis he knew professionally and socially — that almost every one of them wanted the Palestinians killed or exiled — together with his description of a sensibility he says is palpable walking around Tel Aviv and Jerusalem, and his immediate self-correction when he overstated the claim.

the-costa-rica-model.title: Palestine House
the-costa-rica-model.summary: The Washington, DC meeting space and gallery for pro-Palestinian human rights groups, artists and musicians that John Kiriakou describes as newly opened on Capitol Hill — housed in a building donated by a Lebanese-American property developer, running programming several nights a week, and headed by Miko Peled.

the-counterfeit-dollar-trade.title: Iraq WMD intelligence
the-counterfeit-dollar-trade.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of how the case for Iraqi weapons of mass destruction was fabricated: the intelligence community''s consensus was that Iraq had no WMD, but the White House had already decided to invade and sought analysis to fit the policy.

the-counterfeit-dollar-trade.title: James Bond
the-counterfeit-dollar-trade.summary: The fictional spy who got John Kiriakou — and, he says, half the Directorate of Operations — into the business. He asked for walkie-talkies at nine and told his father at sixteen that he wanted to be a spy in the Middle East; he concedes "literally none of it is true to life", but vouches for one scene: Bond always runs into the CIA officer at the party. The figure follows him to the end, too — a personality paper titled "Who is James Bond?" describes the officer type in terms he finds harsh, and federal prosecutors, he says, argued for his detention by talking about him "like I was 007."

the-counterfeit-dollar-trade.title: The Talk Liberation bank freeze
the-counterfeit-dollar-trade.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the September 2022 freezing of Talk Liberation's Icelandic bank accounts — the seed funding behind the Panquake platform — on stated suspicion of money laundering and possible terrorist financing. Kiriakou, who deliberately declines to name the bank, calls the allegations nonsense, says in his personal opinion the freeze came at a government's behest, and notes the accounts were later unfrozen.

the-counterfeit-dollar-trade.title: The colleague who went to Microsoft
the-counterfeit-dollar-trade.summary: In 2000, John Kiriakou''s supervisor left the CIA for Microsoft to do what he called "some really cool social media stuff" — a phrase that meant nothing to Kiriakou at the time, and which he later read as an early sign of the deliberate placement of intelligence officers inside technology companies.

the-counterfeit-dollar-trade.title: Saddam Hussein
the-counterfeit-dollar-trade.summary: President of Iraq from 1979 until the 2003 U.S. invasion; subject of John Kiriakou's CIA portfolio from January 1990 onward, in which capacity Kiriakou became, at age 25, "Saddam Hussein's intelligence community biographer" and the analyst who briefed President George H. W. Bush in the Oval Office on the morning of the 1990 invasion of Kuwait.

the-counterfeit-dollar-trade.title: Ahmed Chalabi
the-counterfeit-dollar-trade.summary: Iraqi exile and founder of the Iraqi National Congress; per John Kiriakou, a Shia-Kurdish con man who looted Petra Bank in Jordan of $36 million in the 1980s, was sentenced to death in absentia, was pardoned at CIA request, then pocketed $6 million in CIA seed funding for the INC and bought a Mayfair house in cash; later resurrected by Dick Cheney to feed the Pentagon fabricated WMD intelligence used to justify the 2003 invasion of Iraq.

the-counterintelligence-exemption.title: Mike Pompeo
the-counterintelligence-exemption.summary: CIA director and later Secretary of State under Trump. John Kiriakou read Pompeo's 2017 speech branding WikiLeaks a "hostile non-state intelligence service" as the groundwork for an Espionage Act case against Julian Assange in the Eastern District of Virginia — the "Espionage Court" where Kiriakou himself was prosecuted. Friends who briefed Pompeo told Kiriakou he was extraordinarily bright but wrong on Iran; Kiriakou's own verdict soured permanently when Pompeo named Gina Haspel deputy director, flirted publicly with reinstating torture, and called Chelsea Manning a traitor — a crime she was never convicted of.

the-counterintelligence-exemption.title: Julian Assange
the-counterintelligence-exemption.summary: Kiriakou — a 15-year friend and former WikiLeaks board member — on why Assange is a publisher owed a journalist's immunity, and a political prisoner.

the-counterintelligence-exemption.title: The chilling effect of whistleblower prosecutions
the-counterintelligence-exemption.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that national-security prosecutions are not primarily about convictions but about deterrence — that the CIA cares about sending a message where the FBI cares about promotions, that his own case was meant to frighten anyone else considering disclosure, and that a New York Times reporter told him every national-security source the paper had went silent on the day of his arrest.

the-counterintelligence-exemption.title: Authorized leaks
the-counterintelligence-exemption.summary: The distinction John Kiriakou draws between the classified information Washington releases on purpose and the classified information it prosecutes people for releasing. The mechanism is the same and the legal status is identical; what differs is whether the leak flatters the leaker. His worked example is an agency leak claiming the CIA predicted the October 2023 attack on Israel three days out — a story the CIA can then piously report to the FBI, knowing the source will never be found.

the-counterintelligence-exemption.title: Central Intelligence Agency
the-counterintelligence-exemption.summary: U.S. foreign intelligence service; John Kiriakou's employer from 1990 to 2004 and the central institution of KiriPedia

the-counterintelligence-exemption.title: Eastern District of Virginia
the-counterintelligence-exemption.summary: The U.S. federal district covering northern Virginia — home to Langley, the Pentagon, DHS and much of the intelligence-contractor industry — which John Kiriakou calls 'the espionage court' because the Justice Department files the great majority of its national security prosecutions there and because, in his telling, no national-security defendant has ever won a case in it; Kiriakou, Julian Assange, Edward Snowden and Jeffrey Sterling were all charged there.

the-counterintelligence-report-that-stop.title: The Israelis were off limits
the-counterintelligence-report-that-stop.summary: John Kiriakou's flat denial, given on a televised panel, that the CIA collected against Israel in return — 'the Israelis were off limits to us at the CIA. We were not permitted' — and Alan Dershowitz's refusal to believe it.

the-counterintelligence-report-that-stop.title: The hundred and eighty-seven Israeli officers
the-counterintelligence-report-that-stop.summary: The figure John Kiriakou gives for undeclared Israeli intelligence officers working clandestinely in the United States when he joined the CIA around 1990 — 187 identified by the FBI, over and above the one declared Mossad officer and one declared Shin Bet officer at the Israeli embassy.

the-counterintelligence-report-that-stop.title: Dianne Feinstein
the-counterintelligence-report-that-stop.summary: Longtime Democratic U.S. senator from California and chair of the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence. Per John Kiriakou, one of the greatest disappointments on Capitol Hill — an unusually friendly chairwoman who exercised no real oversight, good on torture and a cheerleader for the CIA on everything else. She co-authored the 2015 McCain-Feinstein Amendment that reiterated the federal ban on torture, and she blocked Gina Haspel's promotion in 2013 before publicly warming to her in 2018.

the-counterintelligence-report-that-stop.title: Israel-United States relations
the-counterintelligence-report-that-stop.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the U.S.-Israel relationship, including his own first visit to Israel as a tourist in 2022 and his characterization of Israel's willingness to destroy an entire city block to kill a single target, confident that the United States will not object.

the-counterintelligence-report-that-stop.title: MOSSAD
the-counterintelligence-report-that-stop.summary: Israel's primary external intelligence service; characterized by John Kiriakou as universally hostile in his and his CIA colleagues' professional dealings with it ("never had a positive encounter with Mossad"); operates almost exclusively in the operational rather than analytical domain; the CIA is, per Kiriakou, categorically forbidden from spying on it.

the-counterintelligence-report-that-stop.title: Senate Torture Report
the-counterintelligence-report-that-stop.summary: The December 2014 executive summary of the U.S. Senate Select Committee on Intelligence's study of the CIA's post-9/11 detention and interrogation program; the first public disclosure of techniques including rectal feeding with hummus, sexual assault with broomsticks, and prolonged sleep deprivation.

the-cousin-who-stopped-speaking.title: Do what is right or what is easy
the-cousin-who-stopped-speaking.summary: Asked what he would tell the boy who once told his father he wanted to be a spy, John Kiriakou said he would tell him to always tell the truth and do the right thing — arguing that everyone already knows in their gut the difference between right and wrong, and that the only real question is whether they then do what is right or what is easy.

the-cousin-who-stopped-speaking.title: National Whistleblower Day
the-cousin-who-stopped-speaking.summary: John Kiriakou has called National Whistleblower Day an event no whistleblower or supporter should miss — held every year in the Kennedy Caucus Room, which he describes as not merely the biggest room on Capitol Hill but the most historic single room anywhere on it, having hosted every major Senate hearing from the sinking of the Titanic to Watergate and Iran-Contra.

the-cousin-who-stopped-speaking.title: The Berlin conference list
the-cousin-who-stopped-speaking.summary: Checking into a Berlin hotel for a conference, John Kiriakou was handed the guest list when the clerk could not find his booking — and discovered that every one of the dozen names on it was a friend of his, and every one of them an outspoken whistleblower.

the-cousin-who-stopped-speaking.title: "The least I could do"
the-cousin-who-stopped-speaking.summary: Told that he had kept another whistleblower from slipping, John Kiriakou declined the credit and described the work in the plainest possible terms: getting somebody out of the house for three or four hours, or taking them to dinner, because so many people had done exactly that for him when he was at his lowest.

the-cousin-who-stopped-speaking.title: The orange jumpsuits
the-cousin-who-stopped-speaking.summary: John Kiriakou has argued that the clothing ISIS put on the Western hostages it beheaded was not a coincidence but a citation: the group dressed its prisoners in orange jumpsuits because the United States dressed its own prisoners in orange jumpsuits, and once a government tortures, it has licensed every other government to do the same to its people.

the-cousin-who-stopped-speaking.title: The postcards for Daniel Hale
the-cousin-who-stopped-speaking.summary: The letter-writing appeal John Kiriakou ran for Daniel Hale in May and June 2021 — naming Hale as the whistleblower most in need of help, posting his jail address publicly, and relaying from the prisoner himself the exact rules a letter had to satisfy to reach him: ten stamps a week, plain unlined white paper, black ink, and no photographs.

the-crenshaw-text-messages.title: Coffee with a cabinet member
the-crenshaw-text-messages.summary: John Kiriakou's disclosure that he had coffee with a member of the cabinet who told him to be patient about his pardon — and told him to watch what he said. He reports the meeting while stating plainly that there is nothing further he can do to make his case, and that he is not confident the outcome will be decided on justice.

the-crenshaw-text-messages.title: Ed Martin and the pardon file
the-crenshaw-text-messages.summary: The US pardon attorney whose office John Kiriakou directed supporters to write to, and the message a mutual friend brought back from him: that he was the third person that day to call about Kiriakou, that Kiriakou should relax, and that his file was literally on Martin''s desk. Kiriakou''s advice to letter-writers was to send physical mail rather than email.

the-crenshaw-text-messages.title: Lincoln's candlelight pardons
the-crenshaw-text-messages.summary: The historical contrast John Kiriakou drew while discussing a mass grant of clemency: stories of Abraham Lincoln staying up late into the night pardoning Civil War deserters by candlelight, on the principle that nobody should be executed for cowardice — set against a modern president who Kiriakou says has pardoned more people than anyone in American history, whenever the mood strikes him.

the-crenshaw-text-messages.title: Pardons nobody asked for
the-crenshaw-text-messages.summary: Two cases John Kiriakou cites of people pardoned without applying: the Binance founder, who said publicly that he had never met the president, never asked for a pardon and never applied for one; and Darryl Strawberry, a New York Mets great with tax and drug problems behind him. Kiriakou raises both while waiting, unsuccessfully, for a pardon he has actively sought for years.

the-crenshaw-text-messages.title: Sergey Lavrov
the-crenshaw-text-messages.summary: Russian foreign minister, and previously Russian ambassador to the United Nations during John Kiriakou's assignment there, where the two worked the same Security Council.
