the-hardtalk-interview.summary: The introductory philosophy lecture at Miami University of Ohio in which John Kiriakou's own whistleblowing was set as the ethical dilemma, unknown to the professor with Kiriakou's son sitting in the room — the episode Kiriakou offers when asked how he survived losing his career, his pension and his marriage.

the-hardtalk-interview.title: Zero Dark Thirty
the-hardtalk-interview.summary: 2012 film dramatizing the CIA hunt for Osama bin Laden, criticized on release for suggesting torture produced the intelligence that led to his capture. John Kiriakou surveys the mixed critical reception — praise from Time and the New Yorker for its craft, condemnation from journalist Michael Wolff and director Kathryn Bigelow's critics for what they called pro-torture propaganda — and notes his friend Senator John McCain said the film left him "sick... because it is wrong."

the-hellenic-axis.title: The Saudi-Pakistan-Turkey defense pact
the-hellenic-axis.summary: The 2026 realignment John Kiriakou describes as a tectonic shift in Middle Eastern geopolitics, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan signing a mutual-defense treaty joined by Turkey and offered to Iran and Egypt, born of the perception that the United States can no longer defend its Gulf allies and that Israel's threat to strike NATO member Turkey has broken Article 5.

the-hersh-publishing-collapse.title: Wolf Blitzer at CIA headquarters
the-hersh-publishing-collapse.summary: What John Kiriakou says he saw a couple of weeks into his CIA career in 1990: the CNN correspondent Wolf Blitzer walking the halls of headquarters with a camera crew and no security escort, filming a stand-up in front of an agency sign. Kiriakou offers it, alongside the Bob Woodward episode, as evidence that the supposed wall between the CIA and the American press does not exist.

the-hersh-publishing-collapse.title: Bob Woodward's CIA headquarters access
the-hersh-publishing-collapse.summary: John Kiriakou's account of watching Washington Post journalist Bob Woodward walk the halls of CIA headquarters unescorted while researching a book, after the CIA director ordered staff to cooperate with him — an episode Kiriakou cites as evidence of how close the relationship between senior CIA officials and favored journalists really is.

the-hersh-publishing-collapse.title: CIA attention to West Africa
the-hersh-publishing-collapse.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer on whether the CIA is likely to be operating in Burkina Faso: for all the years he was at the agency it cared very little about Africa and especially West Africa, but the presence of al-Qaeda and Islamic State affiliates plus the drug trade makes CIA and special forces involvement probable — and, he adds, the American public will not hear about it.

the-hersh-publishing-collapse.title: Muddling through
the-hersh-publishing-collapse.summary: An analytic term John Kiriakou says CIA analysts used all the time, and his defence of it: forecasters instinctively reach for either/or outcomes, when what actually happens most often is that the parties to a conflict muddle through and little changes over the medium term. He applies it to Ukraine, and to why he expects Russia not to use nuclear weapons.

the-hersh-publishing-collapse.title: Nord Stream pipeline sabotage
the-hersh-publishing-collapse.summary: The 2022 destruction of the Nord Stream gas pipelines, whose responsibility John Kiriakou treats as genuinely unresolved — citing Seymour Hersh's reporting that the CIA did it, a later Ukrainian special-forces claim of a sailboat-based operation carried out without Zelensky's knowledge, and a retired CIA colleague's private theory that Putin blew up his own pipeline to blame the Americans.

the-hersh-publishing-collapse.title: The African diplomat's remark
the-hersh-publishing-collapse.summary: The line John Kiriakou says an African diplomat gave him at a White House summit, and which he uses to explain Chinese success on the continent: you Americans always offer us democracy and military aid, and the Chinese offer us food and new roads. Kiriakou traces the consequence to Chinese bases across Africa and a State Department that did not see it coming.

the-hierarchy-of-charges.title: The forty-seven suffix
the-hierarchy-of-charges.summary: The last two digits of a federal prisoner number that, according to John Kiriakou, mark the holder as a member of an organised gang — and which the Italians at FCI Loretto carried along with MS-13, the Bloods, the Crips and the Mexican Mafia.

the-hierarchy-of-charges.title: The golf course deed forgery
the-hierarchy-of-charges.summary: The property fraud John Kiriakou encountered at FCI Loretto — a prisoner who forged papers transferring ownership of a golf course to himself and then began charging people rent — and the place such crimes occupy in the prison's own hierarchy of offences.

the-hierarchy-of-charges.title: Ali from Newark
the-hierarchy-of-charges.summary: The Black shot caller at FCI Loretto, near the end of a twenty-five-year drug sentence, who came to embrace John Kiriakou at the close of his term and tell him how much he respected him — a friendship possible only because Kiriakou had decided on arrival to ignore the prison's racial divisions.

the-hierarchy-of-charges.title: Clyde Hall
the-hierarchy-of-charges.summary: The imprisoned Ohio congressman John Kiriakou says served at his prison a few years before him, whose remark on release — that he had made some of the best friends of his life inside — Kiriakou thought insane at the time and came to understand after his own sentence.

the-hierarchy-of-charges.title: Say five years
the-hierarchy-of-charges.summary: The first piece of prison advice John Kiriakou says he was given — from a Bonanno family captain, walking laps of the snowed-in basketball court at FCI Loretto — to tell anyone who asked that he was serving five years rather than the thirty months he actually had.

the-hierarchy-of-charges.title: The question about the showers
the-hierarchy-of-charges.summary: The single thing John Kiriakou says he most wanted to know before going to prison, and the lunch his attorneys arranged with a former George Washington University professor — himself recently released — to answer it.

the-homelessness-executive-order.title: The mental health parity gap
the-homelessness-executive-order.summary: John Kiriakou's account of American mental health provision — parity written into the Affordable Care Act and entirely unenforced, more mentally ill people in most county jails than in the mental hospitals, and his condition that nobody should be forced into treatment until the treatment is worth being forced into.

the-homelessness-executive-order.title: Ali from Newark
the-homelessness-executive-order.summary: The Black shot caller at FCI Loretto, near the end of a twenty-five-year drug sentence, who came to embrace John Kiriakou at the close of his term and tell him how much he respected him — a friendship possible only because Kiriakou had decided on arrival to ignore the prison's racial divisions.

the-homelessness-executive-order.title: Bezalel Smotrich
the-homelessness-executive-order.summary: Israeli far-right minister whom John Kiriakou, alongside Itamar Ben-Gvir, blames for leaving Israel unprepared on October 7 by insisting any attack would come from the West Bank rather than Gaza.

the-homelessness-executive-order.title: Candace Owens
the-homelessness-executive-order.summary: The commentator whose claims about the killing of Charlie Kirk John Kiriakou has publicly declined to accept. He credits her reach and her intelligence and rejects her method, citing an earlier occasion — a conference call he says he was on — at which she claimed irrefutable proof that the Italian government had stolen the 2020 election and that its release would return Donald Trump to office.

the-homelessness-executive-order.title: Clyde Hall
the-homelessness-executive-order.summary: The imprisoned Ohio congressman John Kiriakou says served at his prison a few years before him, whose remark on release — that he had made some of the best friends of his life inside — Kiriakou thought insane at the time and came to understand after his own sentence.

the-homelessness-executive-order.title: Donald Trump
the-homelessness-executive-order.summary: 45th and 47th U.S. president. Per John Kiriakou, a man genuinely convinced he was doing right by bombing Iran, "duped" by the same Netanyahu nuclear bluff Obama once rejected — and, at the same time, the most blindly pro-Israel president in history, an admirer of autocrats who has never once criticized Vladimir Putin, and prone to gestures — from the Gulf of America to a since-abandoned "Department of War" rename — that test the edges of his actual authority.

the-honey-salesman-warning.title: Arabic and Greek
the-honey-salesman-warning.summary: The qualification John Kiriakou says opened the door to his transfer from CIA analysis to operations: a post in Athens wanted Greek or Arabic, and he had both — by most of his tellings the only officer in the agency who did. The chief who hired him gave the reason in one sentence: it is easier and cheaper to take a linguist and teach him operations than the other way round. The pairing also became a detection tool, since the language nobody speaks in Pakistan is Arabic.

the-honey-salesman-warning.title: Bankruptcy and the dropped charges
the-honey-salesman-warning.summary: The sequence John Kiriakou places at the centre of his case: that the espionage counts against him were dropped only after his legal fees had bankrupted him, which he presents as evidence that the government''s aim was attrition rather than conviction.

the-honey-salesman-warning.title: Curtailment cables
the-honey-salesman-warning.summary: The career-ending requests John Kiriakou says he read coming back from the CIA's black sites — officers, doctors, psychologists and nurses asking to end their tours early rather than continue to take part in the interrogation programme — and his conclusion that if that many people were objecting in classified channels, someone would surely go public.

the-honey-salesman-warning.title: Security, finance and medical
the-honey-salesman-warning.summary: The rule John Kiriakou says CIA recruits were taught in their first week on the job — that there are exactly three offices an officer may never lie to, because those three can end a career — and the reasoning he attaches to each.

the-honey-salesman-warning.title: The bowl of dates
the-honey-salesman-warning.summary: The detail John Kiriakou uses to compress his argument about interrogation: that the intelligence the CIA''s contractors reported as the fruit of waterboarding had in fact been obtained by an FBI agent who offered Abu Zubaydah a bowl of dates.

the-honey-salesman-warning.title: The declination letter
the-honey-salesman-warning.summary: The letter the Justice Department sent John Kiriakou's attorneys in December 2008 declining to prosecute him, on the grounds that the torture allegations were already public through human rights organizations and that it is illegal to classify a crime — and the celebration dinner that was followed three weeks later by Barack Obama's inauguration.

the-hooding-dispute.title: "You were the first person that ever asked me about my children"
the-hooding-dispute.summary: The answer John Kiriakou says he received when he asked a mid-level al-Qaeda member he had recruited in Pakistan why he had allowed the recruitment to happen: that in five years of detention Kiriakou had been the first person to ask about his children.

the-hooding-dispute.title: The Faisalabad cash run
the-hooding-dispute.summary: The drive John Kiriakou made to Faisalabad, Pakistan roughly two weeks before the capture of Abu Zubaydah, with two million dollars in cash in two duffel bags in the van, and the exchange with his colleague about why anyone would cheat the CIA out of twenty dollars.

the-hooding-dispute.title: The martyrdom bonus
the-hooding-dispute.summary: The recruitment offer John Kiriakou says captured al-Qaeda foot soldiers described to him in Pakistan: a monthly wage to go and fight the Americans in Afghanistan, and five hundred dollars paid to the fighter''s parents if he was killed. He uses it to argue that the men he captured had no religious or political motive at all — most had never read the Quran — and that the only way out of the cycle is education and economic development.

the-hooding-dispute.title: The two Tunisians
the-hooding-dispute.summary: The first counterterrorist raid John Kiriakou led after arriving in Pakistan in January 2002, which produced two eighteen-year-olds from Tunisia who burst into tears when the door came down, one of them asking whether he could telephone his mother.

the-hooding-dispute.title: Arabic and Greek
the-hooding-dispute.summary: The qualification John Kiriakou says opened the door to his transfer from CIA analysis to operations: a post in Athens wanted Greek or Arabic, and he had both — by most of his tellings the only officer in the agency who did. The chief who hired him gave the reason in one sentence: it is easier and cheaper to take a linguist and teach him operations than the other way round. The pairing also became a detection tool, since the language nobody speaks in Pakistan is Arabic.

the-hooding-dispute.title: Bankruptcy and the dropped charges
the-hooding-dispute.summary: The sequence John Kiriakou places at the centre of his case: that the espionage counts against him were dropped only after his legal fees had bankrupted him, which he presents as evidence that the government''s aim was attrition rather than conviction.

the-hot-dog-lady-cable.title: The Directorate of Operations
the-hot-dog-lady-cable.summary: The CIA's clandestine service, which John Kiriakou joined from analysis because he spoke both Greek and Arabic — a culture he describes as wildly different from the analytic side, short on institutional memory and organised around the race to become a station chief.

the-hot-dog-lady-cable.title: The Directorate of Intelligence
the-hot-dog-lady-cable.summary: The CIA's analytic cadre, where John Kiriakou spent the first seven years of his career working on Iraq before switching to operations — a culture he describes as convinced it holds the smartest people in the room, and whose function he says is duplicated across a dozen other agencies.

the-hot-dog-lady-cable.title: Operating Directive
the-hot-dog-lady-cable.summary: The CIA's six-tier (0 through 5) intelligence priority system used to indicate the urgency with which case officers should pursue specific topics

the-hot-dog-lady-cable.title: President's Daily Brief
the-hot-dog-lady-cable.summary: Per John Kiriakou, the President's Daily Brief (PDB) is a roughly 16-page, top-secret intelligence document produced daily for the president, written in a uniform CIA house style, briefed each morning, and — in his account — used partly to gauge and flatter incoming presidents.

the-hot-dog-lady-cable.title: Office of the Director of National Intelligence
the-hot-dog-lady-cable.summary: The intelligence-community layer created in 2004, which John Kiriakou argues should never have existed. He traces its origin to George Tenet's failures over 9/11 and Iraq, notes it grew from sixteen employees to roughly twenty-four thousand, and points out that most agencies nominally under it are Defense Department bodies over which it controls nothing but the budget.

the-hot-dog-lady-cable.title: John Ratcliffe
the-hot-dog-lady-cable.summary: CIA director under Trump's second term; per John Kiriakou, a "bombthrower" he mostly disagrees with politically but supported as a needed disruptor for the agency — "a good guy, expert in what he does," though "not a visionary thinker" and, on Kiriakou's later assessment, a neocon who has outmanoeuvred Tulsi Gabbard for primacy over U.S. intelligence. Ratcliffe told the White House the CIA had no objection to pardoning Kiriakou.

the-hotel-bar-operation.title: Fabricated intelligence reporting
the-hotel-bar-operation.summary: The three things John Kiriakou says CIA case officers are caught doing — inventing intelligence outright, holding real reports back to smooth out a monthly quota, and padding cover-stop expenses — and his argument that the fabrication is driven by production targets set by bad managers.

the-hotel-bar-operation.title: Denied areas
the-hotel-bar-operation.summary: The CIA term for countries so hostile and so heavily surveilled that ordinary operational movement is impossible — the Soviet Union, Cuba, Syria, and later Russia, China, North Korea and Iran — and the reason, in John Kiriakou's account, that officers heading to one get specialist briefings, eight-hour surveillance detection routes, and that the Agency has to fall back on liaison services instead of its own sources.

the-hotel-bar-operation.title: Abraxas Corporation
the-hotel-bar-operation.summary: The private intelligence company founded in the 1990s by retired CIA operations officers as a tax pass-through and a place to smoke cigars and tell stories — which, after 9/11, made its founders, in John Kiriakou's phrase, Mega Millions rich.

the-hotel-bar-operation.title: The Brüno shoot in Jordan
the-hotel-bar-operation.summary: The scene John Kiriakou set up for Sacha Baron Cohen in Amman — four retired Palestinian militants, found in the Damascus telephone book at the Library of Congress, shown hardcore pornography by a character they believed to be an Austrian documentary journalist — which produced no reaction at all and was cut from the film entirely.

the-hotel-bar-operation.title: Chief of station
the-hotel-bar-operation.summary: The CIA's senior officer in a foreign country — appointed by the CIA director alone, outranking the ambassador's intelligence equities in practice, and in John Kiriakou's account the figure who sets the moral temperature of a station, from the officer who handed him his first counterterrorism assignment to the one who walks into a minister's office fifteen minutes after the human rights officer has left.

the-hotel-bar-operation.title: The hotel room cover
the-hotel-bar-operation.summary: John Kiriakou has described the improvised cover story taught for a clandestine meeting raided in progress: with a hostile service banging on the hotel door, both officer and source were to strip and get into the bed, on the reasoning that a surveillance team hunting a CIA meeting would lose interest the moment it found something else entirely.

the-hotel-room-cover.title: Surveillance detection route
the-hotel-room-cover.summary: Tradecraft technique used by intelligence officers and assets to determine whether they are being followed before, during, or after an operational meeting

the-hotel-room-cover.title: The hotel bar operation
the-hotel-room-cover.summary: The night a visiting foreign delegation's security detail was expected in a boutique hotel bar and every seat in it turned out to be occupied by a CIA officer — an episode John Kiriakou offers as an example of bad leadership, and which left his colleagues personally out of pocket for their espresso martinis.

the-hotel-room-cover.title: More money on security in Athens than Beirut
the-hotel-room-cover.summary: John Kiriakou''s measure of how dangerous Athens was for American officials at the turn of the century — that the United States spent more on security there than in Beirut — and the consequence he says followed: no diplomatic plates, because they would make Americans easier to identify and kill.

the-hotel-room-cover.title: The interrupted break-in
the-hotel-room-cover.summary: A break-in in a friendly country nearly failed when the neighbour who was supposed to be at work turned out to have given birth the day before; John Kiriakou talked his way out of it at the door by claiming to be looking for his aunt''s flat in the wrong building.

the-hotel-room-cover.title: The operational test
the-hotel-room-cover.summary: The vetting procedure John Kiriakou describes for moving a trusted source onto normal handling: put a full surveillance team on him without telling him, watch how he gets to the meeting, and then ask him to describe what he did.

the-hotel-room-cover.title: Abu Zubaydah as a sounding board
the-hotel-room-cover.summary: The second, longer phase of Abu Zubaydah''s usefulness to the CIA, described by John Kiriakou in his December 2007 ABC News interview: once the prisoner had given up what he knew about current operations, his value shifted from threat reporting to analysis, with case officers reading him the names of men arrested in European capitals and asking whether the operations attributed to them made sense.

the-house-of-cards-theory.title: Donald Trump
the-house-of-cards-theory.summary: 45th and 47th U.S. president. Per John Kiriakou, a man genuinely convinced he was doing right by bombing Iran, "duped" by the same Netanyahu nuclear bluff Obama once rejected — and, at the same time, the most blindly pro-Israel president in history, an admirer of autocrats who has never once criticized Vladimir Putin, and prone to gestures — from the Gulf of America to a since-abandoned "Department of War" rename — that test the edges of his actual authority.

the-house-of-cards-theory.title: Air wars are overrated
the-house-of-cards-theory.summary: John Kiriakou''s summary judgement on the 2026 Iran and Lebanon campaigns, delivered as the meta-headline of the whole war: air power flattened Gaza without destroying Hamas, is bogging down against Hezbollah, and cannot produce the outcome the war requires.

the-house-of-cards-theory.title: The Netanyahu death rumour
the-house-of-cards-theory.summary: A theory advanced by well-regarded podcasters during the 2026 Iran war that Benjamin Netanyahu had been killed and the fact concealed — his son's seven-day silence read as sitting shiva. John Kiriakou recounts it collapsing when Netanyahu gave a press conference, and sets it against the real decapitation campaign against the IRGC.

the-house-of-cards-theory.title: Strait of Hormuz
the-house-of-cards-theory.summary: The shipping chokepoint at the mouth of the Persian Gulf, and the centre of gravity of the 2026 Iran war in John Kiriakou''s account — a strait whose only navigable deep water lies on the Iranian side of the maritime border, closed not by Iran''s aggression but, as he insists, by the American and Israeli attack that provoked it: "The Strait of Hormuz was open. We''re the ones that forced the closure."

the-house-of-cards-theory.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
the-house-of-cards-theory.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

the-house-of-cards-theory.title: Hamas
the-house-of-cards-theory.summary: The Palestinian movement behind the October 7, 2023 attack; John Kiriakou argues that a case could be made for calling it a freedom-fighting organization dedicated to the liberation of its people rather than simply a terrorist group, notes it is labeled a terrorist organization by only a small minority of UN member states, and has ruled Gaza since Israel's 2005 withdrawal.

the-human-rights-guy.title: "Kill them all"
the-human-rights-guy.summary: The one-line departure hug John Kiriakou says he got from his own CIA boss, an elegant, thousand-dollar-suit man he calls John, whom he had joked belonged in the State Department, on the day Kiriakou left Washington to become chief of counterterrorism operations in Pakistan after 9/11. Kiriakou uses it as the compressed summary of the mood inside the building he was leaving behind.

the-human-rights-guy.title: Abu Zubaydah
the-human-rights-guy.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

the-human-rights-guy.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
the-human-rights-guy.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

the-hundred-and-fifty-foot-limousine.title: Julian Assange
the-hundred-and-fifty-foot-limousine.summary: Kiriakou — a 15-year friend and former WikiLeaks board member — on why Assange is a publisher owed a journalist's immunity, and a political prisoner.

the-hundred-and-fifty-foot-limousine.title: Prosecutorial careerism
the-hundred-and-fifty-foot-limousine.summary: John Kiriakou''s explanation for why senior federal prosecutors pursue high-profile national-security cases regardless of their merits: the conviction of a famous defendant is the entry ticket to a partnership at a large firm, a congressional candidacy, or a run for governor.

the-hundred-and-fifty-foot-limousine.title: Giuliani Pardon Solicitation
the-hundred-and-fifty-foot-limousine.summary: Per John Kiriakou, a meeting at the Trump International Hotel in Washington in which Rudy Giuliani's associate solicited $2 million in exchange for a presidential pardon — a story that subsequently appeared as a front-page New York Times article. Giuliani publicly denied ever meeting Kiriakou; Kiriakou sent the Times the photograph taken at the meeting that morning, and the paper published the story with the note that it had seen documentary proof.

the-hundred-and-fifty-foot-limousine.title: Kiriakou pardon request
the-hundred-and-fifty-foot-limousine.summary: John Kiriakou's public campaign for a presidential pardon from Donald Trump to restore the pension and firearm rights he lost after his 2013 felony conviction for disclosing the identity of a covert CIA officer; includes a five-second Mar-a-Lago encounter in which Trump referred him to Attorney General Pam Bondi, a Kalshi prediction-market contract that opened at roughly 19 to 20 percent odds on his being pardoned, and letters of support from Tucker Carlson, Judge Andrew Napolitano and Dr. Phil.

the-hundred-and-fifty-foot-limousine.title: The density of spies in Washington
the-hundred-and-fifty-foot-limousine.summary: John Kiriakou's claim that there are more spies in Washington DC than anywhere else in the world, that the FBI's counterintelligence division does nothing but try to root them out, and that the job cannot be finished short of becoming North Korea.

the-hundred-and-fifty-foot-limousine.title: Jared Kushner
the-hundred-and-fifty-foot-limousine.summary: Donald Trump's son-in-law and senior adviser during the first Trump administration, and the first person inside the White House to open a channel on John Kiriakou's pardon. After Trump saw Kiriakou on Tucker Carlson's show, Kushner's attorney called Kiriakou's attorney Bruce Fein; the meeting that followed produced a request for a one-page paper — three-quarters of it Kiriakou's story, the last quarter an argument for how pardoning him would help Trump get re-elected — after which Kiriakou never heard back.

the-hundred-city-tour.title: The job in the medical practice
the-hundred-city-tour.summary: The made-up job that carried John Kiriakou through his first months out of prison — invented for him by the parents of a friend, both physicians, so that he would have something — and the patched-together living that followed it, including a think-tank post that ended in a mass layoff after a year.

the-hundred-city-tour.title: Seven cell phones
the-hundred-city-tour.summary: John Kiriakou's account of why his first marriage ended — that his wife, a ballet teacher, knew only that he worked for the CIA, and that a career in which one of seven cell phones rang at midnight and he left speaking Arabic for a day at a time could not survive the questions it produced.

the-hundred-city-tour.title: The Nation of Islam at Loretto
the-hundred-city-tour.summary: The largest Muslim faction at FCI Loretto — African American converts to the Nation of Islam — two of whom walked into John Kiriakou's cell in his first days holding their own newspaper, in which Louis Farrakhan had called him a hero of the Muslim people for opposing torture. They told him he would have no trouble with them; one declined the handshake he offered, on the ground that he does not shake hands with the white devil. The Aryans, meanwhile, had decided he was a CIA assassin who killed Muslims. Kiriakou kept his mouth shut and let both beliefs stand.

the-hundred-city-tour.title: Seventy-two denied motions
the-hundred-city-tour.summary: The count John Kiriakou gives of the pretrial motions filed in his case and denied by Judge Leonie Brinkema — seventy-two denied and none granted — which he offers as the mechanism by which a national security defendant in the Eastern District of Virginia is prevented from mounting a defence at all.

the-hundred-city-tour.title: The professor and the Ellsberg profile
the-hundred-city-tour.summary: The story John Kiriakou says his CIA recruiter told him — that in 1971, as founder of the unit producing long-distance psychological profiles of foreign leaders, he was handed a file on Daniel Ellsberg, refused to profile an American citizen, and later discovered his boss had done it anyway under his name, which he testified to before the Watergate Committee.

the-hundred-city-tour.title: 1953 Iran coup
the-hundred-city-tour.summary: The U.S.- and UK-backed overthrow of Iran's democratically elected prime minister, Mohammad Mossadegh; per John Kiriakou, the coup served British national interests rather than American ones, and the subsequent outlawing of secular political opposition under the Shah forced dissent into the mosques — producing a religious rather than secular revolution in 1979.

the-hundred-dollar-informants.title: The diplomatic stool collection
the-hundred-dollar-informants.summary: John Kiriakou''s confirmation that visiting heads of state routinely carry their own faeces home rather than leave them in an American hotel — because, in his account, entities within the United States government will gladly collect the material for its DNA and health information, and the hotel employee who retrieves it is a CIA officer under cover.

the-hundred-dollar-informants.title: Phil Donahue
the-hundred-dollar-informants.summary: American talk-show host who, John Kiriakou discovered seven years after the fact, had been secretly paying his weekly newspaper column fee — $400 a week for nine years, routed through Reader Supported News — because Donahue had learned that Kiriakou came out of prison broke and did not want him sleeping in his car.

the-hundred-dollar-informants.title: Soviet Union
the-hundred-dollar-informants.summary: The superpower whose collapse framed the start of John Kiriakou's CIA career — it was "literally in the process of collapsing" when he joined in January 1990, ushering in a brief "peace dividend" era when the agency's new threats were environmental degradation and AIDS. Kiriakou cites Brzezinski's "Afghan trap" that lured the Soviets into Afghanistan, argues the U.S. abandoned the radicalized mujahideen the moment the Soviets were beaten, notes America then took "a vacation from history," and recalls that Jonathan Pollard's stolen documents were traded by Israel to the Soviets in exchange for Russian Jews.

the-hundred-dollar-informants.title: The Alaska glacier
the-hundred-dollar-informants.summary: The visitor centre John Kiriakou saw on a 2016 trip to Alaska with Gary Johnson, built at the foot of a glacier close enough to touch from the observation deck and by then a quarter of a mile away from it — an image he uses as the plainest available demonstration of climate change, and one he refuses to let pass as a joke.

the-hundred-dollar-informants.title: The armour at Union Station
the-hundred-dollar-informants.summary: John Kiriakou''s eyewitness account of stepping off an Amtrak train at Washington''s Union Station in August 2025 to find two armoured personnel carriers and a .50 calibre machine gun trained on the entrance — and of tourists posing for photographs with the National Guardsmen deployed in the parts of the city where, he says, there is no crime.

the-hundred-dollar-informants.title: The CIA and Iridium
the-hundred-dollar-informants.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of the Central Intelligence Agency buying the satellite telephone company Iridium when it was unprofitable and about to go out of business, because the agency needed the network — a purchase he places alongside its acquisition of Intelsat, and which he encountered personally when he had to rent the phones for Afghanistan.

the-hundred-drachma-coins.title: The Yugo factory argument
the-hundred-drachma-coins.summary: The dinner-table confrontation in which one of John Kiriakou's uncles in Greece demanded to know why the United States had bombed the Yugo factory — an accusation Kiriakou could answer only technically, because he thought the 1999 bombing of Yugoslavia was wrong in the first place.

the-hundred-drachma-coins.title: The Kosovo objection
the-hundred-drachma-coins.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the 1999 NATO bombing of Yugoslavia as seen from the American embassy in Athens — an Orthodox Christian American diplomat serving in an Orthodox country while the United States bombed one, and his view that Kosovo is a rump state invented on land holy to the Serbian Orthodox Church.

the-hundred-drachma-coins.title: Ali from Newark
the-hundred-drachma-coins.summary: The Black shot caller at FCI Loretto, near the end of a twenty-five-year drug sentence, who came to embrace John Kiriakou at the close of his term and tell him how much he respected him — a friendship possible only because Kiriakou had decided on arrival to ignore the prison's racial divisions.

the-hundred-drachma-coins.title: Bezalel Smotrich
the-hundred-drachma-coins.summary: Israeli far-right minister whom John Kiriakou, alongside Itamar Ben-Gvir, blames for leaving Israel unprepared on October 7 by insisting any attack would come from the West Bank rather than Gaza.

the-hundred-drachma-coins.title: Candace Owens
the-hundred-drachma-coins.summary: The commentator whose claims about the killing of Charlie Kirk John Kiriakou has publicly declined to accept. He credits her reach and her intelligence and rejects her method, citing an earlier occasion — a conference call he says he was on — at which she claimed irrefutable proof that the Italian government had stolen the 2020 election and that its release would return Donald Trump to office.

the-hundred-drachma-coins.title: Clyde Hall
the-hundred-drachma-coins.summary: The imprisoned Ohio congressman John Kiriakou says served at his prison a few years before him, whose remark on release — that he had made some of the best friends of his life inside — Kiriakou thought insane at the time and came to understand after his own sentence.

the-hundred-eighty-seven-israeli-officer.title: The Israelis were off limits
the-hundred-eighty-seven-israeli-officer.summary: John Kiriakou's flat denial, given on a televised panel, that the CIA collected against Israel in return — 'the Israelis were off limits to us at the CIA. We were not permitted' — and Alan Dershowitz's refusal to believe it.

the-hundred-eighty-seven-israeli-officer.title: The counterintelligence report that stopped
the-hundred-eighty-seven-israeli-officer.summary: John Kiriakou's account of an annual FBI assessment of the worst counterintelligence threats to the United States that named Russia, China and Israel every year, reported each time by Newsweek's Jeff Stein — until, he says, Dianne Feinstein changed the rules so that the report no longer had to be issued.

the-hundred-eighty-seven-israeli-officer.title: The anti-semite smear
the-hundred-eighty-seven-israeli-officer.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of the professional cost of saying publicly that Israel spies on the United States: Alan Dershowitz calls him names, and the political director of the Israeli foreign minister called him a noted anti-semite.

the-hundred-eighty-seven-israeli-officer.title: The Piers Morgan panel
the-hundred-eighty-seven-israeli-officer.summary: The televised debate John Kiriakou returns to most often — two against two, with Scott Horton and himself on one side and Alan Dershowitz and a senior former Israeli official on the other. Kiriakou set out his position on Hamas, October 7th and Gaza, and Piers Morgan told him at the end that he had come around and agreed. On a second appearance from the same panel he argued that Jeffrey Epstein was an Israeli access agent, provoked Dershowitz — Epstein's own attorney — into an interruption Kiriakou considers self-defeating, and got an unbothered "who knows?" from the Israeli.

the-hundred-eighty-seven-israeli-officer.title: Alan Dershowitz
the-hundred-eighty-seven-israeli-officer.summary: American attorney and Harvard Law professor; John Kiriakou describes debating him on Piers Morgan's show over Jeffrey Epstein, telling Dershowitz he would have wanted to see him "hanging from a tree" had he sought leniency for Epstein as an Israeli spy — and cites attorney David Boies's on-air statement that Dershowitz was far more than Epstein's lawyer, also serving as his publicist, friend, and a guest on Epstein's island.

the-hundred-eighty-seven-israeli-officer.title: Israel-United States relations
the-hundred-eighty-seven-israeli-officer.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the U.S.-Israel relationship, including his own first visit to Israel as a tourist in 2022 and his characterization of Israel's willingness to destroy an entire city block to kill a single target, confident that the United States will not object.

the-hundred-million-a-day-briefing.title: Cost of the 2026 Iran war
the-hundred-million-a-day-briefing.summary: The daily cost of the 2026 Iran war as John Kiriakou reported it — between two and three billion dollars a day, per Axios — and the comparison he draws with the Gulf War, when a president was rendered speechless by a figure of one hundred million dollars a day.

the-hundred-million-a-day-briefing.title: Strikes on US bases in the 2026 Iran war
the-hundred-million-a-day-briefing.summary: John Kiriakou's assessment of the damage Iranian retaliation did to the American basing network across the Middle East during the 2026 war — including the loss of Incirlik air base in Turkey — and of the resupply problem that followed, with matériel routed through European and Indian ports. His verdict is that none of it was unforeseeable; Iran had announced it in advance.

the-hundred-million-a-day-briefing.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
the-hundred-million-a-day-briefing.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

the-hundred-million-a-day-briefing.title: Donald Trump
the-hundred-million-a-day-briefing.summary: 45th and 47th U.S. president. Per John Kiriakou, a man genuinely convinced he was doing right by bombing Iran, "duped" by the same Netanyahu nuclear bluff Obama once rejected — and, at the same time, the most blindly pro-Israel president in history, an admirer of autocrats who has never once criticized Vladimir Putin, and prone to gestures — from the Gulf of America to a since-abandoned "Department of War" rename — that test the edges of his actual authority.

the-hundred-million-a-day-briefing.title: Iranian underground missile silos
the-hundred-million-a-day-briefing.summary: John Kiriakou''s assessment of why the American and Israeli air campaign against Iran could not disarm it: the missile silos are buried under featureless desert with nothing on the surface to mark them, and an air force cannot destroy what it cannot locate. He measures the problem against twenty years of failure against Taliban fighters who had only rifles and caves.

the-hundred-million-a-day-briefing.title: Itamar Ben-Gvir
the-hundred-million-a-day-briefing.summary: Israel's far-right Minister of National Security; John Kiriakou cites him as a convicted hate-crime felon placed in charge of security in Gaza and the West Bank over his victims, blames his insistence that any attack would come from the West Bank for diverting forces before October 7, and cites the death-penalty law passed under his portfolio for Palestinian detainees as the first reinstatement of capital punishment in Israel since it was abolished in 1956, excepting only the execution of Adolf Eichmann.

the-hyundai-robots.title: "Beyond Your Dreams"
the-hyundai-robots.summary: The gloss a host gave John Kiriakou on his first trip to China when he asked what the beautiful car with the BYD badge was — and the answer he got when he asked why he had never heard of it, which was that the United States is the only country where they are not sold.

the-hyundai-robots.title: "Whatever DARPA''s working on"
the-hyundai-robots.summary: John Kiriakou's standing rejoinder to the defence of American research spending — that the secrecy of DARPA's projects is the indictment rather than the excuse, because whatever it is working on should have been developed twenty years ago and be in the field today, and should be, in his phrase, Star Trek kind of stuff.

the-hyundai-robots.title: The Pentagon budget reversal
the-hyundai-robots.summary: The pair of announcements John Kiriakou uses as his cleanest evidence of incoherence in the second Trump administration — a stated intention to cut the Pentagon budget by fifty per cent, celebrated at the time, followed a couple of months later by a stated intention to increase it by fifty per cent.

the-hyundai-robots.title: The rare earth calculation
the-hyundai-robots.summary: John Kiriakou's explanation of how China came to control the world market in rare earth metals — not by holding the only deposits, which exist everywhere including under California's Salton Sea, but by being willing to absorb the economic loss of mining ore that is mostly waste, at a fraction of American defence spending.

the-hyundai-robots.title: Carving up Iran
the-hyundai-robots.summary: The Israeli end goal John Kiriakou says has been discussed with increasingly less discretion — dividing Iran into five small rump countries including Balochistan, Arabistan and Kurdistan, on the reasoning that small states are more easily controlled — and which he expects Israel will eventually try to get Donald Trump to carry out.

the-hyundai-robots.title: Dumping the treasury bonds
the-hyundai-robots.summary: The second economic weapon John Kiriakou says China holds against the United States — its position as the second or third largest holder of long-term government treasury bonds, which it could simply dump, and which he says would crash the entire American economy.

the-ideological-circle.title: Sitting on my father's lap
the-ideological-circle.summary: John Kiriakou's earliest political memory — being four or five years old, watching buildings burn on television, and asking his father why, to be told that some bad men had killed Martin Luther King and Robert Kennedy and people were very upset — which he uses as his benchmark for how divided the United States has become.

the-ideological-circle.title: The Pentagon budget reversal
the-ideological-circle.summary: The pair of announcements John Kiriakou uses as his cleanest evidence of incoherence in the second Trump administration — a stated intention to cut the Pentagon budget by fifty per cent, celebrated at the time, followed a couple of months later by a stated intention to increase it by fifty per cent.

the-ideological-circle.title: "Whatever DARPA''s working on"
the-ideological-circle.summary: John Kiriakou's standing rejoinder to the defence of American research spending — that the secrecy of DARPA's projects is the indictment rather than the excuse, because whatever it is working on should have been developed twenty years ago and be in the field today, and should be, in his phrase, Star Trek kind of stuff.

the-ideological-circle.title: "Beyond Your Dreams"
the-ideological-circle.summary: The gloss a host gave John Kiriakou on his first trip to China when he asked what the beautiful car with the BYD badge was — and the answer he got when he asked why he had never heard of it, which was that the United States is the only country where they are not sold.

the-ideological-circle.title: Carving up Iran
the-ideological-circle.summary: The Israeli end goal John Kiriakou says has been discussed with increasingly less discretion — dividing Iran into five small rump countries including Balochistan, Arabistan and Kurdistan, on the reasoning that small states are more easily controlled — and which he expects Israel will eventually try to get Donald Trump to carry out.

the-ideological-circle.title: Dumping the treasury bonds
the-ideological-circle.summary: The second economic weapon John Kiriakou says China holds against the United States — its position as the second or third largest holder of long-term government treasury bonds, which it could simply dump, and which he says would crash the entire American economy.

the-imran-khan-apology-demand.title: Death threats against Kiriakou
the-imran-khan-apology-demand.summary: The threats John Kiriakou has received across two decades — first after going public about the CIA torture program, when FBI advice that at least two were credible sent his family out of the country, and later in waves tied to his opposition to Gina Haspel, his remarks about Pakistan, and his advocacy on Palestine and the Epstein case.

the-imran-khan-apology-demand.title: Abraham Accords
the-imran-khan-apology-demand.summary: The Trump-brokered normalization deals between Israel and Gulf Arab states — in John Kiriakou's judgment "a terrible idea in the first place," a great victory for Israel and the Gulf Arabs that was "a punch in the throat to the Palestinians." He argues the Accords are how Trump meant to "solve the Middle East in a day" — by screwing the Palestinians — that Hamas read the abandonment correctly, that October 7 shattered the project, and that reviving the Accords (Saudis in, victory declared, Nobel collected) remains the organizing goal of Trump's regional policy.

the-imran-khan-apology-demand.title: Arrais Corporation
the-imran-khan-apology-demand.summary: Private intelligence firm; companion entity to The Analysis Corporation; originally an LLC pass-through for retired Senior Intelligence Service personnel from the CIA's operations side; subsequently acquired by IBM for over $1 billion.

the-imran-khan-apology-demand.title: Denied areas
the-imran-khan-apology-demand.summary: The CIA term for countries so hostile and so heavily surveilled that ordinary operational movement is impossible — the Soviet Union, Cuba, Syria, and later Russia, China, North Korea and Iran — and the reason, in John Kiriakou's account, that officers heading to one get specialist briefings, eight-hour surveillance detection routes, and that the Agency has to fall back on liaison services instead of its own sources.

the-imran-khan-apology-demand.title: Kashmir
the-imran-khan-apology-demand.summary: The disputed territory John Kiriakou says is front and centre for every Pakistani and largely absent from Indian minds, and on which his own sympathies lie with Pakistan — a promised 1940s referendum that never happened. He also describes the appearance that ended his participation in South Asian media: an Indian programme cut his pro-Pakistani answer, aired only his prediction that India would win a conventional war, and the death threats resumed.

the-imran-khan-apology-demand.title: The ISI-Mossad relationship
the-imran-khan-apology-demand.summary: John Kiriakou's characterisation of the relationship between Pakistani and Israeli intelligence — a formal relationship as recently as 1979 and none since, but no hostility either, because Pakistan is preoccupied with India and Afghanistan and Israel has never regarded Pakistan as a threat.

the-imran-khan-request.title: The Pentagon and the Pakistani arsenal
the-imran-khan-request.summary: What John Kiriakou says he was told unofficially while stationed in Pakistan in 2002 — that Pervez Musharraf had turned control of the Pakistani nuclear arsenal over to the United States, and that the Pentagon controlled it — and Pakistan's insistence in the years since that this was never true, which Kiriakou says would be the more worrying answer.

the-imran-khan-request.title: Another Bentley
the-imran-khan-request.summary: The scene John Kiriakou describes from a meeting with Benazir Bhutto during her exile in Dubai — a five-million-dollar palace on the Gulf, a car pulling up outside, and Bhutto saying that so help her God, if her husband had come home with another Bentley she would kill him — which Kiriakou uses as his measure of Pakistani political corruption.

the-imran-khan-request.title: Pakistani corruption and democracy
the-imran-khan-request.summary: John Kiriakou's assessment that corruption in Pakistan is so deep and so broad that a genuinely functioning democracy is almost impossible there — set against a long history of military coups, a habit of imprisoning former prime ministers, and his insistence that Imran Khan should not be in a cell.

the-imran-khan-request.title: Imran Khan
the-imran-khan-request.summary: Former Prime Minister of Pakistan; subsequently deposed and imprisoned; his political party, the PTI (Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf), sent John Kiriakou a formal demand for apology after a November 2025 Indian-media interview in which Kiriakou observed that India would prevail over Pakistan in a conventional conflict; Kiriakou's reply has not been transcribed in polite company.

the-imran-khan-request.title: ISI
the-imran-khan-request.summary: Pakistan''s Inter-Services Intelligence agency, the CIA''s principal counterterrorism partner during John Kiriakou''s 2002 posting. Per Kiriakou, there were effectively ''two parallel ISIs'': one made up of Sandhurst-trained, FBI-schooled professionals he calls heroes who risked their lives on counterterrorism, and another — ''people with long beards who gave you a dirty look'' — who had created Kashmiri terrorist groups like Jaish-e-Mohammed and were attacking Shia mosques and Americans. Because of this, the CIA never told the ISI the identity of high-value targets, referring to Abu Zubaydah only as ''Mr. Fish.''

the-imran-khan-request.title: The CNN India refusal
the-imran-khan-request.summary: The interview request John Kiriakou turned down on the morning of 19 November 2025 — the latest of many from Indian broadcasters — because, he says, every answer he gives about India or Pakistan is turned into a banner headline with three exclamation points, stripped of context, and followed by a dozen death threats.

the-indicator-hed-be-watching.title: "A policy support organization"
the-indicator-hed-be-watching.summary: Asked how the CIA workforce would be reacting to the war on Iran, John Kiriakou answered from the Iraq war: people put their heads down and did as they were told, after a boss told an assembled group — all of whom opposed the invasion — that the agency is not a policy organization but a policy support organization, and would do what the White House told it to do.

the-indicator-hed-be-watching.title: Iranian suicide drones
the-indicator-hed-be-watching.summary: John Kiriakou''s description of the weapon he expected to define Iran''s side of the 2026 war: one-way drones built inside Iran from Iranian parts, in large numbers, costing five to ten thousand dollars each, with explosives strapped on and flown remotely into a target. He treats them as the reason an aircraft carrier can no longer defend itself, the reason air defence fails on arithmetic rather than on technology, and the reason the Gulf states are reassessing the value of American bases.

the-indicator-hed-be-watching.title: 2026 Iran war
the-indicator-hed-be-watching.summary: The open-ended American and Israeli war against Iran that John Kiriakou tracked week by week on his own show — a conflict he says was sold as three weeks, ran into its fifth month, achieved every decapitation objective it set, and continued anyway. His grade for it is a D, and his forecast is a Truth Social post declaring victory while nothing changes.

the-indicator-hed-be-watching.title: The White House tip
the-indicator-hed-be-watching.summary: A week and a half before the 2026 attack on Iran, John Kiriakou said publicly that a friend at the White House had told him the decision to attack had been made and that it would come the following Monday or Tuesday. A podcaster mocked him for it — how could a man twenty years out of the CIA know that? On the morning the strikes began, Kiriakou answered: people with access do call, because they are opposed to the war.

the-indicator-hed-be-watching.title: American missile stockpiles
the-indicator-hed-be-watching.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that the United States has run its interceptor stocks down to the point of strategic vulnerability — that the conventional wisdom in Washington was that a round of the Iran war ended because the Patriots ran out, and that a country which cannot fight a two-front war certainly cannot do it below maximum production.

the-indicator-hed-be-watching.title: Andrew Bustamante
the-indicator-hed-be-watching.summary: Former CIA officer who sells CIA-style training online; John Kiriakou identifies him as the lone critic of his work hosting a show on a Russian network, and argues Bustamante's training business — open to anyone who pays — is the more problematic of the two.

the-indonesian-recruitment-question.title: Arabic and Greek
the-indonesian-recruitment-question.summary: The qualification John Kiriakou says opened the door to his transfer from CIA analysis to operations: a post in Athens wanted Greek or Arabic, and he had both — by most of his tellings the only officer in the agency who did. The chief who hired him gave the reason in one sentence: it is easier and cheaper to take a linguist and teach him operations than the other way round. The pairing also became a detection tool, since the language nobody speaks in Pakistan is Arabic.

the-indonesian-recruitment-question.title: Security, finance and medical
the-indonesian-recruitment-question.summary: The rule John Kiriakou says CIA recruits were taught in their first week on the job — that there are exactly three offices an officer may never lie to, because those three can end a career — and the reasoning he attaches to each.

the-indonesian-recruitment-question.title: The autographed basketball
the-indonesian-recruitment-question.summary: A recruitment John Kiriakou has cited as proof that an agent''s price is not always money: a source who loved the Chicago Bulls, an ordinary basketball bought from the NBA online store with a forged provenance involving Michael Jordan, and an acrylic display box.

the-indonesian-recruitment-question.title: The Faisalabad cash run
the-indonesian-recruitment-question.summary: The drive John Kiriakou made to Faisalabad, Pakistan roughly two weeks before the capture of Abu Zubaydah, with two million dollars in cash in two duffel bags in the van, and the exchange with his colleague about why anyone would cheat the CIA out of twenty dollars.

the-indonesian-recruitment-question.title: The prostitute hypothetical
the-indonesian-recruitment-question.summary: The classroom exercise John Kiriakou uses in university lectures to demonstrate that the CIA gave its operations officers no ethical guidelines at all — a recruited terrorist source who demands a prostitute, and then the same demand for a child.

the-indonesian-recruitment-question.title: "You were the first person that ever asked me about my children"
the-indonesian-recruitment-question.summary: The answer John Kiriakou says he received when he asked a mid-level al-Qaeda member he had recruited in Pakistan why he had allowed the recruitment to happen: that in five years of detention Kiriakou had been the first person to ask about his children.

the-inside-job-refusal.title: Bill Clinton
the-inside-job-refusal.summary: 42nd U.S. president whom John Kiriakou describes as wholly disinterested in intelligence — briefed by the CIA only twice in eight years, with Vice President Al Gore taking the daily briefing instead and relaying anything important.

the-inside-job-refusal.title: Church Committee
the-inside-job-refusal.summary: U.S. Senate investigative committee operating in 1975–1976 that examined domestic intelligence abuses by the CIA, FBI, and NSA; per John Kiriakou, the Church Committee — alongside the concurrent Pike Committee in the House — was the last genuine moment of legislative oversight over the intelligence community, born of a national consensus that government had gone dangerously off course. Its work led to the creation of the permanent Senate Select Committee on Intelligence, which Kiriakou says ceased to function as real oversight roughly seven years after its founding.

the-inside-job-refusal.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
the-inside-job-refusal.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

the-inside-job-refusal.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
the-inside-job-refusal.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

the-inside-job-refusal.title: Fifty new crimes a year
the-inside-job-refusal.summary: John Kiriakou''s argument that the United States has become a carceral country by legislative accretion — fifty newly created federal crimes every year for two decades, on top of five per cent of the world''s population holding twenty-five per cent of its prisoners.

the-inside-job-refusal.title: How Kiriakou went armed in Athens
the-inside-job-refusal.summary: The load John Kiriakou carried every day during his Athens tour — a 9mm in a tear-away waist pack with three magazines, a snub-nosed .38 on his ankle, about 47 rounds in total, and a buck knife his boss handed him on his first day *"just in case things go to shit"*.

the-intercept-source-exposures.title: The Intercept
the-intercept-source-exposures.summary: The investigative news outlet that published Daniel Hale's drone leak; John Kiriakou notes that the same Intercept reporter, Matthew Cole, was involved in cases that led to the exposure of both Kiriakou himself and NSA leaker Reality Winner — though he insists Hale outed himself rather than being burned by the outlet.

the-intercept-source-exposures.title: Matthew Cole
the-intercept-source-exposures.summary: American national-security journalist whose reporting tradecraft, per John Kiriakou, has led to the federal incarceration of five whistleblowers — including Kiriakou himself. In Kiriakou's account, Cole emailed him in 2010 ostensibly researching a book on the rendition of Abu Omar, asked Kiriakou to confirm the surname of a CIA officer who appeared in Kiriakou's own first book under the alias 'John', and Kiriakou's confirmation was the act of confirming a covert officer's identity for which he was eventually prosecuted under the Intelligence Identities Protection Act.

the-intercept-source-exposures.title: Daniel Hale
the-intercept-source-exposures.summary: Per John Kiriakou, drone whistleblower Daniel Hale — an NSA contractor and drone targeting analyst who exposed an 80% civilian death rate in the U.S. drone program, was ordered to fire on two young girls his superior called "goats," and was sentenced to 45 months (of which Kiriakou says he actually served about 18) despite prosecutors seeking nine to eleven years.

the-intercept-source-exposures.title: The Drone Papers
the-intercept-source-exposures.summary: The trove of classified documents leaked by Daniel Hale and published by The Intercept — later collected in book form as 'The Assassination Complex' — exposing how the U.S. drone program selected and killed targets; John Kiriakou relied on it in his own writing on the war in Afghanistan.

the-intercept-source-exposures.title: Communications management unit
the-intercept-source-exposures.summary: The two restricted-contact units inside the American federal prison system, at Terre Haute and Marion; built for "the worst of the worst" but, in John Kiriakou's account, used to silence prisoners whose messages are inconvenient — and a practice he groups with solitary confinement as torture. He served part of his own sentence in a modified one.

the-intercept.title: Matthew Cole
the-intercept.summary: American national-security journalist whose reporting tradecraft, per John Kiriakou, has led to the federal incarceration of five whistleblowers — including Kiriakou himself. In Kiriakou's account, Cole emailed him in 2010 ostensibly researching a book on the rendition of Abu Omar, asked Kiriakou to confirm the surname of a CIA officer who appeared in Kiriakou's own first book under the alias 'John', and Kiriakou's confirmation was the act of confirming a covert officer's identity for which he was eventually prosecuted under the Intelligence Identities Protection Act.

the-intercept.title: Jeffrey Sterling
the-intercept.summary: Former CIA officer convicted of nine felonies, including seven counts of espionage, after giving a New York Times interview about a racial discrimination lawsuit he had filed against the CIA. Per John Kiriakou, Sterling was not accused of spying for a foreign country; his underlying case was that the CIA had passed him over for promotion and told him explicitly it was because of his race. Daniel Ellsberg asked Sterling to go to trial specifically so the constitutionality of the Espionage Act could be challenged; Sterling did, was convicted, and was sentenced by Judge Leonie Brinkema to what she described as 'Kiriakou plus 12 months.'

the-intercept.title: Daniel Hale
the-intercept.summary: Per John Kiriakou, drone whistleblower Daniel Hale — an NSA contractor and drone targeting analyst who exposed an 80% civilian death rate in the U.S. drone program, was ordered to fire on two young girls his superior called "goats," and was sentenced to 45 months (of which Kiriakou says he actually served about 18) despite prosecutors seeking nine to eleven years.

the-intercept.title: India
the-intercept.summary: The country John Kiriakou names as his least favourite of all the places he has worked — not, he stresses, for poverty or danger, both of which he has seen worse of, but for the caste system and "the way Indians treat one another." His illustration is an afternoon in Hyderabad when two separate restaurants refused to admit the driver he had invited to lunch.

the-intercept.title: The Intercept's exposed sources
the-intercept.summary: John Kiriakou's charge that national security whistleblowers who take material to The Intercept end up in prison. He names Reality Winner and Terry Albury as sources whose identities the outlet exposed, says the same thing happened to Daniel Hale, and identifies the outlet's two national security reporters, Richard Esposito and Matthew Cole, as the journalists responsible for sending him to prison. His question is whether the pattern is incompetence or something worse.

the-intercept.title: Wikileaks as a System
the-intercept.summary: Per John Kiriakou, WikiLeaks functions less as a single leader than as a durable system — one that protected whistleblowers, helped popularize the term "whistleblower" itself, was credited with contributing to the Arab Spring, weathered pressure to become a defanged NGO, and outlasted the political fallout of its 2010 cable releases (including, in Kiriakou's account, an unintended assist to Donald Trump's election).

the-interrupted-break-in.title: The booby-trapped Christmas cards
the-interrupted-break-in.summary: Among the devices al-Qaeda left behind in positions it was forced to evacuate in Afghanistan, John Kiriakou describes a detonator laid flat inside a Christmas card, so that opening the card would take the reader''s hands off.

the-interrupted-break-in.title: The tomato patch surveillance
the-interrupted-break-in.summary: John Kiriakou''s earliest surveillance operation, run at the age of nine with walkie-talkies against the neighbourhood children he suspected of stealing his father''s tomatoes.

the-interrupted-break-in.title: George Washington University
the-interrupted-break-in.summary: The Washington university where John Kiriakou took a bachelor's degree in Middle Eastern studies and began a master's in legislative affairs, and where a professor who was in fact a CIA spotter recruited him into the agency — an institution that recurs throughout his account as the place his intelligence career began, as the venue of his first CIA tests, and later as a classroom he taught in himself.

the-interrupted-break-in.title: No ethics training at the CIA
the-interrupted-break-in.summary: John Kiriakou''s claim that the CIA provides no ethics training of any kind, so that an officer either arrives with a personal moral code or never acquires one — and the classroom hypothetical he uses to show where the line goes undrawn.

the-interrupted-break-in.title: PTSD
the-interrupted-break-in.summary: Post-traumatic stress disorder runs through John Kiriakou''s life and worldview — he had it coming out of Greece after an assassination attempt, brought it home from Pakistan alongside his shock at colleagues'' willingness to kill, and was blindsided by a delayed post-prison version that helped end his marriage. For six months after release he dreamed the same dream nightly: that he was out by mistake and had to get back inside before midnight count. He still takes a repurposed blood-pressure drug that stops the dreams, and he extends the diagnosis outward — to secret-site interrogators who came back crying, to drone pilots, and to prisoners released angry and untreated.

the-interrupted-break-in.title: The Satan dream
the-interrupted-break-in.summary: Seventeen years after leaving Pakistan, John Kiriakou said he still dreamt about it every night — a recurring dream of Satan hunting him house to house — and described a failed blood pressure drug now used to erase the dreams of PTSD patients.

the-iowa-republican-exchange.title: The balloon test
the-iowa-republican-exchange.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that Israel had warning of the 7 October 2023 attack — that settlers along the Gaza line had reported training for months, that balloons were sent over as a probe in the days beforehand, and that nothing was done.

the-iowa-republican-exchange.title: The Piers Morgan panel
the-iowa-republican-exchange.summary: The televised debate John Kiriakou returns to most often — two against two, with Scott Horton and himself on one side and Alan Dershowitz and a senior former Israeli official on the other. Kiriakou set out his position on Hamas, October 7th and Gaza, and Piers Morgan told him at the end that he had come around and agreed. On a second appearance from the same panel he argued that Jeffrey Epstein was an Israeli access agent, provoked Dershowitz — Epstein's own attorney — into an interruption Kiriakou considers self-defeating, and got an unbothered "who knows?" from the Israeli.

the-iowa-republican-exchange.title: Cleaning up after Tora Bora
the-iowa-republican-exchange.summary: John Kiriakou was not at Tora Bora. He arrived in Pakistan in January 2002, two months after the bombing, and says he went specifically to clean up what the battle had left behind — scavenging material, detaining the fighters too slow to get away, and mapping the smugglers'' valleys the survivors had used to cross. In his account the clean-up was necessary because the encirclement failed: bin Laden, warned by an al-Qaeda operative working as translator to the commander of Central Command, left in the dark dressed as a woman in the back of a pickup truck, and at dawn there was nobody in Tora Bora to surrender.

the-iowa-republican-exchange.title: Famine in Gaza
the-iowa-republican-exchange.summary: The starvation of the civilian population of the Gaza Strip, which John Kiriakou describes as a United Nations-declared famine caused not by an absence of food but by an Israeli refusal to let food reach the people who need it; Kiriakou characterises it as a war crime, a crime against humanity and a form of genocide, attributing that characterisation to the United Nations and the International Court of Justice rather than to himself.

the-iowa-republican-exchange.title: Hayden at the National Press Club
the-iowa-republican-exchange.summary: John Kiriakou's account of seeing Michael Hayden, after a series of strokes, at a National Press Club event sponsored by the intelligence centre that bears his name — and the two reactions it produced in him, neither of them satisfaction alone.

the-iowa-republican-exchange.title: Saddam and the journalists
the-iowa-republican-exchange.summary: John Kiriakou's comparison, drawn from fifteen years working the Iraq target at the CIA, between a dictator who hated the press and did not kill it and a government that he says kills journalists deliberately and in numbers.

the-iran-israel-exchange-assessment.title: Forcing Iran toward a bomb
the-iran-israel-exchange-assessment.summary: John Kiriakou''s argument that Western pressure risks producing the very outcome it claims to prevent: repeated Israeli assassinations of Iranian scientists and generals and strikes on Iranian sites may eventually leave Ayatollah Khamenei with no choice but to permit a defensive weapon — despite the religious prohibition Kiriakou credits him with maintaining, and despite successive American estimates that Iran is not seeking one.

the-iran-israel-exchange-assessment.title: The Iron Dome
the-iran-israel-exchange-assessment.summary: Israel's air-defence system as John Kiriakou reads it — impressive against a wave of slow Iranian drones, but shown by the handful that got through, and later by Iranian ballistic missiles, to be not all it is cracked up to be; each exchange, in his account, buying Iran intelligence about the gaps.

the-iran-israel-exchange-assessment.title: The Syria chemical attack correction
the-iran-israel-exchange-assessment.summary: John Kiriakou's public retraction of what he wrote about the August 2013 chemical attack near Damascus. Asked about the passage in his book on Iran, he said he had written it before United Nations whistleblowers came forward to say they did not believe it was a Syrian government attack, and thanked the questioner for the chance to correct it.

the-iran-israel-exchange-assessment.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
the-iran-israel-exchange-assessment.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

the-iran-israel-exchange-assessment.title: CIA attention to West Africa
the-iran-israel-exchange-assessment.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer on whether the CIA is likely to be operating in Burkina Faso: for all the years he was at the agency it cared very little about Africa and especially West Africa, but the presence of al-Qaeda and Islamic State affiliates plus the drug trade makes CIA and special forces involvement probable — and, he adds, the American public will not hear about it.

the-iran-israel-exchange-assessment.title: CIA–FBI incompatible computer systems
the-iran-israel-exchange-assessment.summary: John Kiriakou's claim that from the CIA's founding in 1947 until 2009 the computer systems of the CIA and the FBI were not compatible with one another — no message could be sent from one to the other and no intelligence shared — which he offers both as the material substrate of the interagency hatred that helped make September 11 possible, and as the gap through which James Mitchell and Bruce Jessen were able to pass Ali Soufan's FBI debriefings of Abu Zubaydah off as the fruits of torture.

the-iranian-interest-section.title: The Pezeshkian invitation
the-iranian-interest-section.summary: The invitation John Kiriakou disclosed in September 2025 to meet the Iranian president in New York during the UN General Assembly, as one of six people asked — an invitation he says he accepted without asking what it was about.

the-iranian-interest-section.title: Amnesty International
the-iranian-interest-section.summary: The human rights organization whose torture report forms part of John Kiriakou's core defense — the CIA's crimes were already public knowledge before he confirmed them on ABC, and the Justice Department's own declination letter said so — and the organization whose silence during his prosecution he cannot forgive. He begged Amnesty for a one-sentence statement and got a New Yorker subscription instead; it took Ai Weiwei to change their minds, and by then he was walking out of prison.

the-iranian-interest-section.title: I want my fifty bucks back
the-iranian-interest-section.summary: What John Kiriakou says he shouted at John Fetterman from ten rows back at an Ohio State football game — and his explanation, as a Pennsylvanian furious about the senator, of why Fetterman keeps his seat anyway.

the-iranian-interest-section.title: Ian Henderson
the-iranian-interest-section.summary: The British colonial police officer who ran Bahrain's intelligence service during John Kiriakou's posting there — a man Kiriakou says even the heir presumptive to the throne was afraid to name aloud, and whom Kiriakou, seated at the crown prince's table at a dinner for George H. W. Bush, mistook for a corpse.

the-iranian-interest-section.title: Ibrahim Traoré
the-iranian-interest-section.summary: John Kiriakou's assessment of the military ruler of Burkina Faso — a young officer who took power promising a return to democracy, and who in Kiriakou's account has grown increasingly irrational, criminalising homosexuality, abolishing the electoral commission and moving to expel foreigners.

the-iranian-interest-section.title: Kimberly Guilfoyle in Athens
the-iranian-interest-section.summary: John Kiriakou's assessment of Kimberly Guilfoyle's appointment as American ambassador to Greece — that she got it because Donald Trump Jr. wanted her out of the way, a manoeuvre he compares to Saddam Hussein's habit of exiling successful generals as ambassadors — and his reluctant conclusion that Greece could have done worse.

the-iranians-only-have-to-survive.title: Mojtaba Khamenei
the-iranians-only-have-to-survive.summary: The successor named as Iran's leader after the assassination of Ali Khamenei, and John Kiriakou's reading of the choice — that the only real objection is the shared surname, which exposes Iran to charges of hereditary succession, but that the appointment was an act of defiance aimed squarely at Donald Trump's declaration that he would choose Iran's next leader.

the-iranians-only-have-to-survive.title: The unarmed ship
the-iranians-only-have-to-survive.summary: John Kiriakou's enumeration of war crimes committed in the 2026 Iran war — striking civilian targets, rocketing a school and killing 160 children, and sinking a naval vessel and then refusing to aid the survivors — and his insistence that the objection is not confined to Israeli conduct.

the-iranians-only-have-to-survive.title: 2026 Iran war
the-iranians-only-have-to-survive.summary: The open-ended American and Israeli war against Iran that John Kiriakou tracked week by week on his own show — a conflict he says was sold as three weeks, ran into its fifth month, achieved every decapitation objective it set, and continued anyway. His grade for it is a D, and his forecast is a Truth Social post declaring victory while nothing changes.

the-iranians-only-have-to-survive.title: Bahrain's force majeure
the-iranians-only-have-to-survive.summary: John Kiriakou's explanation of Bahrain declaring force majeure on its energy commitments during the 2026 Iran war — why it is catastrophic for Bahrain and irrelevant to the global oil market, since the kingdom produces and consumes about a hundred thousand barrels a day and sells only the output of a small offshore field gifted to it by Saudi Arabia.

the-iranians-only-have-to-survive.title: Killing Khamenei
the-iranians-only-have-to-survive.summary: John Kiriakou's assessment that the killing of Ayatollah Khamenei during the 2026 war would change nothing, because the West had seriously overestimated his authority — an argument he extends to the American habit of expecting a war to end when a leader is removed.

the-iranians-only-have-to-survive.title: The empty Church of the Holy Sepulchre
the-iranians-only-have-to-survive.summary: A video John Kiriakou describes watching during the 2026 Iran war — the Church of the Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem completely deserted, filmed beside the Edicule that covers the tomb of Christ, with nothing audible but air raid sirens. He offers it alongside Israeli footage he reads as evidence that the country knows it is in trouble.

the-isi-as-two-organizations.title: The Taliban lobbyist in Washington
the-isi-as-two-organizations.summary: A story put to John Kiriakou about a Taliban delegation''s American press conference and the Washington lobbyist who represented them. Kiriakou remembered the episode and the lobbyist''s New Jersey base but not the claim about her parentage, and explained why it caused so little controversy at the time: the United States had no historical quarrel with the Taliban, and had armed and fêted some of its future members during the war against the Soviets.

the-isi-as-two-organizations.title: The 2025 India–Pakistan clash assessment
the-isi-as-two-organizations.summary: John Kiriakou''s verdict on the most recent India–Pakistan confrontation, delivered after an unusually explicit declaration of his own bias: he loved living in Pakistan, favours Pakistan on Kashmir, and judges that India accomplished nothing while Pakistan lost nothing, leaving the Pakistanis slightly ahead.

the-isi-as-two-organizations.title: The cave myth
the-isi-as-two-organizations.summary: John Kiriakou's rejection of the popular image of al-Qaeda's leadership living in caves. He says the CIA knew its targets were in major cities, deliberately let them believe the search was concentrated on the tribal areas, and caught them because men who think they are unobserved get sloppy with their phones and email.

the-isi-as-two-organizations.title: Benazir Bhutto
