the-lapis-lazuli-paperweight.title: The porn on bin Laden's computers
the-lapis-lazuli-paperweight.summary: The question a Pittsburgh newspaper editor put to John Kiriakou on live television hoping to embarrass him — about the pornography found on Osama bin Laden's computers — and the answer that left the programme's host saying he had been rendered speechless for the first time in twenty-five years.

the-lapis-lazuli-paperweight.title: The Russian soldier in Manama
the-lapis-lazuli-paperweight.summary: The Russian soldier John Kiriakou says he met in Manama, Bahrain, who told him the Chechens were the only people on earth he was afraid of — a remark Kiriakou produced in a conversation about Chechnya's standing as a fighting nation.

the-lapis-lazuli-paperweight.title: Amnesty International
the-lapis-lazuli-paperweight.summary: The human rights organization whose torture report forms part of John Kiriakou's core defense — the CIA's crimes were already public knowledge before he confirmed them on ABC, and the Justice Department's own declination letter said so — and the organization whose silence during his prosecution he cannot forgive. He begged Amnesty for a one-sentence statement and got a New Yorker subscription instead; it took Ai Weiwei to change their minds, and by then he was walking out of prison.

the-lapis-lazuli-paperweight.title: Hayden at the National Press Club
the-lapis-lazuli-paperweight.summary: John Kiriakou's account of seeing Michael Hayden, after a series of strokes, at a National Press Club event sponsored by the intelligence centre that bears his name — and the two reactions it produced in him, neither of them satisfaction alone.

the-lapis-lazuli-paperweight.title: I want my fifty bucks back
the-lapis-lazuli-paperweight.summary: What John Kiriakou says he shouted at John Fetterman from ten rows back at an Ohio State football game — and his explanation, as a Pennsylvanian furious about the senator, of why Fetterman keeps his seat anyway.

the-lapsed-film-rights.title: Mr. Fish
the-lapsed-film-rights.summary: The cover name the CIA used for Abu Zubaydah in Pakistan in 2002 — invented because the Americans would not tell their Pakistani partners who the target was, and derived from the only thing they would say about him: that he was a big fish.

the-lapsed-film-rights.title: The royal family at Taif
the-lapsed-film-rights.summary: John Kiriakou''s first overseas assignment sent him at twenty-five to the Kuwaiti government in exile at Taif in Saudi Arabia, where he found a king weeping over a dug-up rose garden and repeated a mantra to a despondent royal family: we are going to get you your country back.

the-lapsed-film-rights.title: Stephen Saunders
the-lapsed-film-rights.summary: British defense attaché in Athens assassinated by Revolutionary Organization 17 November in March 2000

the-lapsed-film-rights.title: The Reluctant Spy
the-lapsed-film-rights.summary: John Kiriakou''s 2009 memoir, The Reluctant Spy: My Secret Life in the CIA''s War on Terror, begun in secret months before he blew the whistle and reaching number five on the New York Times bestseller list.

the-lapsed-film-rights.title: Kiriakou''s recommended reading
the-lapsed-film-rights.summary: Asked in March 2026 what to read about the CIA, John Kiriakou named his own first two books and, beyond them, a 1980s history called The Rise and Fall of the CIA, which he says was his own first real introduction to covert action and its failures.

the-lapsed-film-rights.title: A Middle East reading list
the-lapsed-film-rights.summary: The books and the starting point John Kiriakou recommends to anyone trying to understand the modern Middle East: begin at the end of the Second World War, not five thousand years earlier, and start with The House of Saud, the Sykes-Picot Agreement and From Beirut to Jerusalem.

the-las-vegas-case.title: Abbas and the three-state problem
the-las-vegas-case.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that no two-state solution is available — because there is already one state, because Mahmoud Abbas is nineteen years into a four-year term and has become a billionaire, and because East Bank, West Bank and Gaza Palestinians are so disconnected that the real arithmetic is three states, which nobody will discuss.

the-las-vegas-case.title: Bulldozing the olive orchards
the-las-vegas-case.summary: The sequence John Kiriakou describes preceding Israeli seizures of Palestinian land in the West Bank — olive orchards bulldozed and crops burned to make leaving easier, then the house demolished and a prefabricated one built for a settler family — and the different practice he says applies in East Jerusalem.

the-las-vegas-case.title: Elbridge Gerry and the salamander
the-las-vegas-case.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the origin of the word gerrymander — Elbridge Gerry, vice president and former governor of Massachusetts, drawing district boundaries to elect his friends, and Benjamin Franklin saying the shapes looked like salamanders — together with a piece of trivia from his unpublished book on cemeteries.

the-las-vegas-case.title: New Castle, Pennsylvania
the-las-vegas-case.summary: John Kiriakou's home town, an hour north of Pittsburgh on the edge of Amish country — a rust-belt city of roughly 40,000 to 50,000 people when he was growing up and around 18,000 to 20,000 now, whose decline he measures by the arrival of DEA and ATF field offices. It is also where, aged eight or nine and hunting salamanders in Oak Park Cemetery, he found the grave of a Medal of Honor private and acquired the lifelong interest in cemeteries that became a book.

the-las-vegas-case.title: From sixteen employees to twenty thousand
the-las-vegas-case.summary: John Kiriakou's support for cutting the staff of the Office of the Director of National Intelligence, on the ground that a body created after 9/11 with sixteen employees to coordinate the agencies had grown to twenty thousand.

the-las-vegas-case.title: The coffee with the Jordanian intern
the-las-vegas-case.summary: A morning meeting John Kiriakou took with a young intern from the Jordanian embassy who had found him on LinkedIn — and which he credits with reminding him that Palestinians are not a monolith, a point he says pro-Palestinian Westerners in particular tend to get wrong.

the-latin-american-newspaper-prediction.title: The play the CIA killed
the-latin-american-newspaper-prediction.summary: A stage play about John Kiriakou's case, written in 2015 by the screenwriter Scott Burns for a New York theatre, which Kiriakou says was never performed because the CIA applied enough pressure on the theatre owner to stop it — an account he offered as a counterpoint to the Reality Winner play that was running unmolested at the same moment.

the-latin-american-newspaper-prediction.title: Espionage Act
the-latin-american-newspaper-prediction.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

the-latin-american-newspaper-prediction.title: Jeremy Hammond
the-latin-american-newspaper-prediction.summary: The hacker held in contempt for refusing to testify against Julian Assange before a grand jury. John Kiriakou''s point about his case is administrative rather than constitutional: Hammond was pulled out of the Bureau of Prisons drug and alcohol programme two months short of completing it, forfeiting the eighteen months it would have taken off his sentence — a penalty that applied whether or not he ever agreed to testify.

the-latin-american-newspaper-prediction.title: Reality Winner
the-latin-american-newspaper-prediction.summary: National Security Agency linguist imprisoned for sending a single classified page on Russian interference in the 2016 election to The Intercept. John Kiriakou attributes her arrest to the two reporters who received it, and to a printer-tracking countermeasure they appear not to have known about; he also treats her prosecution as an operation that served the intelligence community on three fronts at once.

the-latin-american-newspaper-prediction.title: Barack Obama
the-latin-american-newspaper-prediction.summary: 44th U.S. president; in John Kiriakou's account, Obama publicly recounted refusing Benjamin Netanyahu's demand to bomb Iran and calling Israel's threat to use nuclear weapons a bluff — a bluff Kiriakou says Donald Trump later believed.

the-laura-ingraham-exchange.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
the-laura-ingraham-exchange.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

the-laura-ingraham-exchange.title: Evidence of previous heroism
the-laura-ingraham-exchange.summary: A phrase John Kiriakou attributes to Judge Leonie Brinkema at his 2013 sentencing. When his service in Pakistan and his role in the capture of Abu Zubaydah were raised in mitigation, the judge ruled — in what Kiriakou gives as her exact words — that any evidence of previous heroism is irrelevant.

the-laura-ingraham-exchange.title: From the Alien and Sedition Acts to the Espionage Act
the-laura-ingraham-exchange.summary: A lineage John Kiriakou endorsed on the In Limine podcast: that language was lifted from the Alien and Sedition Acts into the Espionage Act of 1917 during the anti-radical hysteria of that period, making a straight line from the earliest American political prosecutions to the statute used against modern whistleblowers.

the-laura-ingraham-exchange.title: Kermit Roosevelt and Mosaddegh
the-laura-ingraham-exchange.summary: The CIA officer John Kiriakou names as the man who ran the 1953 overthrow of Iran's Prime Minister Mosaddegh on behalf of British Petroleum — who called it the gravest mistake of his life in the only interview he ever gave, and who, according to the documents Kiriakou has since read in the archives, did not actually run it at all.

the-laura-ingraham-exchange.title: Plato Cacheris
the-laura-ingraham-exchange.summary: Legendary Washington, D.C. defense attorney who served as John Kiriakou''s lead counsel in his 2012–2013 Espionage Act prosecution. Per Kiriakou, when discovery revealed the FBI had run a fake-diplomat sting against him, Cacheris explained the government''s posture bluntly: ''Because they have a shit case and they know it''s shit, and that''s why we''re going to trial.'' He spent most of the case urging trial, then drove to Kiriakou''s house on decision day and said ''You stupid son of a bitch — take the deal.'' Cacheris also represented FBI spy Robert Hanssen.

the-laura-ingraham-exchange.title: Prosecutorial careerism
the-laura-ingraham-exchange.summary: John Kiriakou''s explanation for why senior federal prosecutors pursue high-profile national-security cases regardless of their merits: the conviction of a famous defendant is the entry ticket to a partnership at a large firm, a congressional candidacy, or a run for governor.

the-lawfare-template.title: CIA attention to West Africa
the-lawfare-template.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer on whether the CIA is likely to be operating in Burkina Faso: for all the years he was at the agency it cared very little about Africa and especially West Africa, but the presence of al-Qaeda and Islamic State affiliates plus the drug trade makes CIA and special forces involvement probable — and, he adds, the American public will not hear about it.

the-lawfare-template.title: CIA–FBI incompatible computer systems
the-lawfare-template.summary: John Kiriakou's claim that from the CIA's founding in 1947 until 2009 the computer systems of the CIA and the FBI were not compatible with one another — no message could be sent from one to the other and no intelligence shared — which he offers both as the material substrate of the interagency hatred that helped make September 11 possible, and as the gap through which James Mitchell and Bruce Jessen were able to pass Ali Soufan's FBI debriefings of Abu Zubaydah off as the fruits of torture.

the-lawfare-template.title: Fake CIA résumés
the-lawfare-template.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of being used as a human authenticator in the private sector: at the consulting firm he joined after leaving the CIA, every job applicant claiming agency service was sent to dinner with him, and by his count fully half of them had never set foot inside the CIA.

the-lawfare-template.title: Forcing Iran toward a bomb
the-lawfare-template.summary: John Kiriakou''s argument that Western pressure risks producing the very outcome it claims to prevent: repeated Israeli assassinations of Iranian scientists and generals and strikes on Iranian sites may eventually leave Ayatollah Khamenei with no choice but to permit a defensive weapon — despite the religious prohibition Kiriakou credits him with maintaining, and despite successive American estimates that Iran is not seeking one.

the-lawfare-template.title: Freemasons and Opus Dei at the CIA
the-lawfare-template.summary: John Kiriakou's characterisation of the affinity networks at the top of the CIA — a great many senior officers who are Freemasons, and periods in which most of the leadership belonged to Opus Dei and attended the same church in Great Falls, Virginia. He rejects the idea that these are plots, describing them instead as accidental clusters of men who look out for one another.

the-lawfare-template.title: GeoRisk Solutions
the-lawfare-template.summary: The political risk consultancy John Kiriakou founded with the dean of the University of Salamanca's intelligence studies programme, staffed with academics and a former assistant secretary of state, with offices in Salamanca and Washington and a stated business of selling cost-effective country and regional risk analysis to banks, funds and companies.

the-least-i-could-do.title: The Berlin conference list
the-least-i-could-do.summary: Checking into a Berlin hotel for a conference, John Kiriakou was handed the guest list when the clerk could not find his booking — and discovered that every one of the dozen names on it was a friend of his, and every one of them an outspoken whistleblower.

the-least-i-could-do.title: Do what is right or what is easy
the-least-i-could-do.summary: Asked what he would tell the boy who once told his father he wanted to be a spy, John Kiriakou said he would tell him to always tell the truth and do the right thing — arguing that everyone already knows in their gut the difference between right and wrong, and that the only real question is whether they then do what is right or what is easy.

the-least-i-could-do.title: National Whistleblower Day
the-least-i-could-do.summary: John Kiriakou has called National Whistleblower Day an event no whistleblower or supporter should miss — held every year in the Kennedy Caucus Room, which he describes as not merely the biggest room on Capitol Hill but the most historic single room anywhere on it, having hosted every major Senate hearing from the sinking of the Titanic to Watergate and Iran-Contra.

the-least-i-could-do.title: "We don''t hire felons"
the-least-i-could-do.summary: After his release from prison John Kiriakou could not find work anywhere — turned down, he says, by Target, Safeway, McDonald's and Uber — and the one job he was eventually offered, at a Washington think tank, paid minimum wage on condition that he run a permanent crowdfunding campaign to raise his own salary.

the-least-i-could-do.title: Government Accountability Project
the-least-i-could-do.summary: The Washington whistleblower-advocacy law firm and NGO, known as GAP, whose attorney Jesselyn Radack took John Kiriakou's case after his 2012 arrest and told him he was a whistleblower whether he thought so or not.

the-least-i-could-do.title: The cousin who stopped speaking
the-least-i-could-do.summary: An older first cousin told John Kiriakou after his conviction that he could no longer speak to him because Kiriakou had brought shame on the family; Kiriakou's reply was to point out that the cousin had imported drugs from Colombia, had appeared in the Washington Post as a mayor's cocaine dealer, and had fled to Greece until the statute of limitations expired.

the-legal-bills.title: "I had no intent"
the-legal-bills.summary: The formula John Kiriakou used in the days around his January 2013 sentencing to describe his own guilty plea — that he had committed the act charged but had neither the intent to commit a crime nor the intent to harm the officer he named, having believed the man was retired and available to be interviewed.

the-legal-bills.title: The seventh Espionage Act defendant
the-legal-bills.summary: The case John Kiriakou cited two days before his own sentencing to correct the count of Espionage Act prosecutions brought under Barack Obama — a translator at the American naval base in Bahrain who had just been charged, making seven, against three in the whole history of the United States before 2009.

the-legal-bills.title: The nine months on food stamps
the-legal-bills.summary: The nine months John Kiriakou's family spent on public assistance after his arrest in January 2012 — his wife working out at the dining room table that they could not afford to buy food the following week, because everything they had had gone to the lawyers, and the Arlington County welfare office for which they qualified for everything.

the-legal-bills.title: The second officer in the same case
the-legal-bills.summary: A document John Kiriakou says his attorneys discovered shortly before his January 2013 sentencing, showing that a second CIA officer had given the same reporter the names of ten undercover officers along with information on counterterrorist operations and the flight plans of the aircraft serving a secret prison — and was never investigated or prosecuted, which Kiriakou takes as proof that his own case was about whistleblowing rather than disclosure.

the-legal-bills.title: Arianna Huffington
the-legal-bills.summary: Founder of the Huffington Post and the accidental amplifier who turned John Kiriakou's prison writing into a phenomenon. His first Letter from Loretto went to his attorney, then to a friend running Firedoglake who — unknown to Kiriakou — was close to Huffington; she plastered it as a banner headline and it drew over a million hits, bringing CNN and 60 Minutes to the prison gates. She published his open letter to Snowden, ran the diesel-therapy exposé that triggered the "hands off John Kiriakou" campaign, and came to Loretto herself with two young journalists.

the-legal-bills.title: The clemency campaign of January 2013
the-legal-bills.summary: The three parallel appeals for a pardon or commutation made on John Kiriakou's behalf in the days before his 25 January 2013 sentencing — a letter to the president from Ralph Nader, Bruce Fein and Joan Claybrook, a change.org petition with nearly two thousand signatures, a Greek-American community petition, and a letter signed by more than eighteen CIA officers and FBI agents alongside Pete Seeger, Oliver Stone and Daniel Ellsberg.

the-legal-definition-of-whistleblowing.title: Frank Serpico
the-legal-definition-of-whistleblowing.summary: The New York police officer John Kiriakou calls one of the giants of the twentieth century and ranks with Daniel Ellsberg among its greatest whistleblowers — a man shot in the face whose police colleagues did not call an ambulance, and whom Kiriakou counts as a friend.

the-legal-definition-of-whistleblowing.title: "There is almost no upside"
the-legal-definition-of-whistleblowing.summary: John Kiriakou''s accounting of what blowing the whistle cost him — pension, friends, freedom and finally family — set against the single thing he says is left: knowing he did the right thing. And his timeline, from the whistle in 2007 to a vindication he says took eleven years.

the-legal-definition-of-whistleblowing.title: Frances Haugen
the-legal-definition-of-whistleblowing.summary: The Facebook employee John Kiriakou refuses to call a whistleblower — arguing that against the legal definition, bringing to light waste, fraud, abuse, illegality or threats to public health or safety, she qualifies as a corporate spokesperson whose motive was to improve the company's bottom line, not to expose wrongdoing.

the-legal-definition-of-whistleblowing.title: Leaker versus whistleblower
the-legal-definition-of-whistleblowing.summary: The fight over what the American networks would call John Kiriakou. It took his lawyers, above all Jesselyn Radack, a year of work between January 2012 and January 2013 to get CNN and MSNBC to stop introducing him as 'CIA leaker John Kiriakou'. CNN changed and Fox, he notes, never needed to; MSNBC in his account never did, and Rachel Maddow settled on a formula he quotes with some precision — a man 'who styles himself a whistleblower'.

the-legal-definition-of-whistleblowing.title: The Bay of Piglets
the-legal-definition-of-whistleblowing.summary: The phrase John Kiriakou wished he had coined for the twice-attempted amphibious landings in Venezuela — and his account of one of the men rounded up coming ashore, who emailed him years later asking to appear on his show as a whistleblower on communism, and was told no.

the-legal-definition-of-whistleblowing.title: The culture of secrecy and the truth
the-legal-definition-of-whistleblowing.summary: Asked how he decided what counted as true inside an institution built on secrecy, and whether that changed after he left, John Kiriakou answered no twice — because in his account everyone knows the difference in their gut, and the job is to stop the culture of secrecy from bastardising what you already know.

the-let-them-in-strategy.title: The two ISIs
the-let-them-in-strategy.summary: Asked how much cooperation he got from Pakistan''s intelligence service after 9/11, John Kiriakou answered that the honest answer was two answers: the counterterrorism officers he worked with had all been trained in America and Britain, while the men who gave him the stink eye in the corridors of ISI headquarters were the ones who had created the Taliban.

the-let-them-in-strategy.title: Fusha and the Gulf dialect
the-let-them-in-strategy.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of his own Arabic training — a first year in fusha, high standard Arabic, followed by a second year in khaleeji, the Gulf dialect — and what he reports of both: that Yemen is the only place pure fusha is spoken, that Saudis asked him why he spoke Arabic like Shakespeare, that the Gulf dialect is marked by a hard J other Arabs dislike, and that the Maghreb defeats him entirely.

the-let-them-in-strategy.title: Whether anyone is still looking for Zawahiri
the-let-them-in-strategy.summary: Asked in December 2019 why Ayman al-Zawahiri had never been found, John Kiriakou offered a speculation he was careful to label as an outsider''s: that the United States might simply have stopped looking for him, because al-Qaeda had become largely irrelevant and attention had moved to ISIS.

the-let-them-in-strategy.title: "I only wanted to kill Jews"
the-let-them-in-strategy.summary: In the hospital room at a Pakistani military base, after telling the wounded Abu Zubaydah that fifty thousand people had been in the towers and that he was not the victim, John Kiriakou says the prisoner answered that he had only wanted to kill Jews and had been overruled.

the-let-them-in-strategy.title: Abu Zubaydah
the-let-them-in-strategy.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

the-let-them-in-strategy.title: The Punjab Elite Force
the-let-them-in-strategy.summary: The Pakistani provincial counterterrorism unit that supplied part of the assault manpower for the Abu Zubaydah raids of March 2002 — black trousers, black t-shirts stencilled with a pistol, and, in John Kiriakou's telling, a refusal to wear body armour on the grounds that if God called them that night they would go.

the-letter-to-larry-nassar.title: The blacked-out grand jury minutes
the-letter-to-larry-nassar.summary: John Kiriakou on the 119 pages of grand jury minutes released in the Epstein document tranches with every single word blacked out, despite two federal judges having ordered their release.

the-letter-to-larry-nassar.title: The snapshots in the release
the-letter-to-larry-nassar.summary: John Kiriakou's summary of what the first Epstein tranches actually contained — investigative documents, grand jury testimony and snapshots taken by Epstein and his friends — and the two photographs that dominated the early coverage.

the-letter-to-larry-nassar.title: The unredacted copy-paste
the-letter-to-larry-nassar.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of the flaw in the first tranche of released Epstein documents: highlighting a redaction, cutting it and pasting it into a new document revealed the blacked-out text, which turned out to be the names of victims.

the-letter-to-larry-nassar.title: Clickers and touchers
the-letter-to-larry-nassar.summary: The distinction John Kiriakou says prisoners at FCI Loretto drew between convicted sex offenders who had only viewed images of children and those who had travelled across state lines to molest them, and his account of why they are all held at low security.

the-letter-to-larry-nassar.title: Prince Andrew
the-letter-to-larry-nassar.summary: British royal, now Andrew Mountbatten Windsor, named repeatedly by John Kiriakou as one of the un-recruitable principals whose access made Jeffrey Epstein valuable to a foreign intelligence service. Kiriakou has asked why Andrew was never charged over conduct with minors, reads his alleged provision of classified Ministry of Defence documents to Epstein as evidence of espionage rather than vanity — and expects him to face no criminal consequence at all, because the statute of limitations has run.

the-letter-to-larry-nassar.title: The dorm as a reward
the-letter-to-larry-nassar.summary: John Kiriakou's explanation that moving a federal prisoner from a cell to a dormitory is a privilege earned over time, and why Ghislaine Maxwell's rapid promotion to dormitory living made no sense to him.

the-letter-to-the-shah.title: Reza Pahlavi
the-letter-to-the-shah.summary: The exiled Iranian crown prince whom John Kiriakou dismisses as an Israeli-backed fantasy candidate to rule Iran — a man who has not lived there since his teens, supported mainly by Beverly Hills exiles, whom Kiriakou says 'wouldn't survive the walk from the plane to the terminal.'

the-letter-to-the-shah.title: George Washington University
the-letter-to-the-shah.summary: The Washington university where John Kiriakou took a bachelor's degree in Middle Eastern studies and began a master's in legislative affairs, and where a professor who was in fact a CIA spotter recruited him into the agency — an institution that recurs throughout his account as the place his intelligence career began, as the venue of his first CIA tests, and later as a classroom he taught in himself.

the-letter-to-the-shah.title: Invasion of Grenada
the-letter-to-the-shah.summary: The 1983 American invasion of Grenada, which John Kiriakou supported as a nineteen-year-old College Democrat at George Washington University on the grounds that American medical students had to be rescued — an episode he now cites as the clearest example of how completely he once accepted the government's own account of what it was doing.

the-letter-to-the-shah.title: George McGovern
the-letter-to-the-shah.summary: The 1972 Democratic presidential nominee, whose landslide defeat John Kiriakou identifies as the pretext for creating superdelegates. As a George Washington University sophomore in 1983, Kiriakou wrote to McGovern offering the campus theater for a campaign launch; McGovern telephoned him personally, announced his 1984 candidacy there, and afterwards took him home for tuna sandwiches made by his wife.

the-letter-to-the-shah.title: John Kiriakou
the-letter-to-the-shah.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

the-letter-to-the-shah.title: The draft argument
the-letter-to-the-shah.summary: The disagreement John Kiriakou had at eighteen with a fellow College Democrat over Vietnam — that he thought the war immoral and illegal and would have served anyway if drafted, because his country had asked him to — which he identifies as the clearest surviving statement of the belief he later lost.

the-liaison-class.title: Cofer Black's warning to the liaison class
the-liaison-class.summary: The briefing Cofer Black gave to a class of visiting foreign liaison officers weeks before 11 September 2001 — code words about a honey salesman, a great football match and an enormous wedding — and the private exchange afterwards in which he told John Kiriakou he had been deadly serious.

the-liaison-class.title: Cofer Black
the-liaison-class.summary: Former head of the CIA Counterterrorism Center during and immediately after the September 11 attacks; principal architect of the agency's paramilitary turn on September 12, 2001; later Vice President of Blackwater under Erik Prince.

the-liaison-class.title: The Foreign Relations volume and the sources still alive
the-liaison-class.summary: The errand that put John Kiriakou and Cofer Black in a car to the White House on the morning of 11 September 2001: three declassified cables due to be printed in a State Department history volume named CIA sources who were still living — and an obscure law requiring the United States to resettle any source it outs.

the-liaison-class.title: John Kiriakou
the-liaison-class.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

the-liaison-class.title: The Condoleezza Rice meeting
the-liaison-class.summary: The nine o'clock White House appointment John Kiriakou and Cofer Black never kept on the morning of 11 September 2001. The Government Printing Office was about to issue a volume of declassified Greece-Turkey-Cyprus cables in an edition of five or ten copies; three of them named CIA sources who were still alive, and an obscure statute obliges the government to offer citizenship and resettlement to any recruited source it outs. The two men were going to ask the National Security Advisor to quietly pull three cables nobody would miss. The car was at the East entrance at 8.15.

the-liaison-class.title: Counterterrorism Center
the-liaison-class.summary: The CIA's Counterterrorism Center (CTC) — the unit where John Kiriakou spent the defining years of his operational career. He joined in the late 1990s as the only officer in the entire CIA fluent in both Greek and Arabic, served as chief of counterintelligence in the bin Laden unit, watched the Center swell from a few hundred employees to nearly 2,000 by September 12, 2001, and it was to CTC that he walked back down in May 2002 to refuse the torture program — the moment, he says, the CIA began to turn on him.

the-libertarian-christmas-party.title: The White House pastry chef
the-libertarian-christmas-party.summary: John Kiriakou''s former next-door neighbour, a White House pastry chef who was in the building when Donald Trump came to meet Barack Obama four days after the 2016 election, and who told Kiriakou that the president-elect looked sick and looked scared.

the-libertarian-christmas-party.title: Gary Johnson
the-libertarian-christmas-party.summary: The former Republican governor of New Mexico and Libertarian nominee for president who wrote to John Kiriakou in prison, wrote separately to Attorney General Eric Holder asking that he be released — a letter Kiriakou learned of only later through a Freedom of Information Act request — and telephoned him within days of his coming home.

the-libertarian-christmas-party.title: The Libertarian Party
the-libertarian-christmas-party.summary: The third party a lifelong Democrat joined on release from prison, after its 2016 presidential nominee had written to him in his cell and to the Attorney General on his behalf — the party John Kiriakou says was the only one talking about whistleblowing and the security-versus-liberty trade-off, and the one whose structural problem, he was told, is that it has no benefactor.

the-libertarian-christmas-party.title: Lindsey Graham
the-libertarian-christmas-party.summary: Republican senator from South Carolina who died in July 2026, and John Kiriakou's standing shorthand for the permanent war caucus — a "show horse" rather than a workhorse, a "chameleon" who "never saw a war that he didn't want to jump into with both feet," and, on posthumously released documentary footage, a man offering the US Air Force to bomb a country America was not at war with.

the-libertarian-christmas-party.title: Mexico City as an espionage hub
the-libertarian-christmas-party.summary: John Kiriakou''s assessment of Mexico City as one of the world''s principal centres of international espionage, alongside Vienna, London, Paris and Washington — driven by a gargantuan American embassy that Russian services target from next door — and his reading of why Mexico simply ignored a dossier of suspected Russian officers handed over by the Biden administration.

the-libertarian-christmas-party.title: Pakistani prisons
the-libertarian-christmas-party.summary: John Kiriakou''s flat refusal, in a discussion of Imran Khan''s detention, of the idea that a Pakistani prison offers VIP treatment to a former prime minister — grounded in his having visited many of them himself during the period when the CIA was locking people up there.

the-libya-policy-reversal.title: The Benghazi hearings critique
the-libya-policy-reversal.summary: John Kiriakou''s complaint about the congressional inquiry into Benghazi, which he watched all the way through: he believes there is some evidence of gun running, doubts anyone will ever establish who was behind it, and objects that the hearings were not trying to find out — having devolved into a political contest that served the American people not at all.

the-libya-policy-reversal.title: The September 10th country
the-libya-policy-reversal.summary: John Kiriakou''s formulation of what he wants back, and his ledger on the two wars: he never supported the invasion of Iraq, which he calls a war of choice and of family revenge, and he did support the war in Afghanistan until al-Qaeda was defeated in 2003, after which everything became nation building. He assigns the destruction of the pre-attack country to George W. Bush and Barack Obama equally.

the-libya-policy-reversal.title: Bin Laden health rumors
the-libya-policy-reversal.summary: John Kiriakou's dismissal of the claim that Osama bin Laden died years before the 2011 raid. He says the CIA received a steady stream of medical rumours about him — kidney failure, dialysis in a cave, a spinal disorder — none of which turned out to be true, and that bin Laden was in fine health apart from arthritis and a hip problem until the day he died.

the-libya-policy-reversal.title: Fake CIA résumés
the-libya-policy-reversal.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of being used as a human authenticator in the private sector: at the consulting firm he joined after leaving the CIA, every job applicant claiming agency service was sent to dinner with him, and by his count fully half of them had never set foot inside the CIA.

the-libya-policy-reversal.title: False flags are too hard
the-libya-policy-reversal.summary: John Kiriakou''s practical objection to the idea that governments routinely stage false flag operations: they exist, and at the operational level the CIA used them constantly, but the bigger the operation the harder it is to run — too many moving parts, too many people who must buy into the conspiracy, and too much incompetence in government to keep any of it straight. He couples the objection with the observation that a government which is not transparent has no standing to complain about public suspicion.

the-libya-policy-reversal.title: SEAL Team Six attrition
the-libya-policy-reversal.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer to the claim that the Navy SEALs who killed Osama bin Laden have since been killed off: the dead came from the broader unit rather than the raid party, SEAL Team Six numbers several hundred men rather than the dozen or so people imagine, and losing a high number of them to accidents and combat is, in his phrase, very sadly common.

the-libyan-constitution-unveiling.title: No plan for day two
the-libyan-constitution-unveiling.summary: The lesson John Kiriakou says he learned early at the CIA: the United States is very good at overthrowing governments and has no idea what to do afterwards. The planning is all about day one. He lists Iraq, Afghanistan, Libya, Syria, Sudan and Somalia as the record, and gives three reasons the same officials keep repeating the mistake.

the-libyan-constitution-unveiling.title: Venezuela regime change (2026)
the-libyan-constitution-unveiling.summary: John Kiriakou''s assessment of the American operation that removed Venezuela''s president — a clear violation of international law, since none of the three recognised grounds for one state attacking another applied, but not a violation of US law, which since 1985 has expressly permitted special forces to cross borders and seize people for trial. His reluctant conclusion at the time: "as much as I hate admitting it, this regime change seems to be working right now."

the-libyan-constitution-unveiling.title: Covert action programs
the-libyan-constitution-unveiling.summary: The most tightly held category of American intelligence activity — so tightly held, John Kiriakou says, that a serving CIA officer may not utter the phrase in public. Which is why he found it extraordinary that a president announced one on television, and doubts the announcement was straightforwardly true.

the-libyan-constitution-unveiling.title: María Corina Machado
the-libyan-constitution-unveiling.summary: The Venezuelan opposition leader and Nobel Peace Prize laureate whom John Kiriakou rates no higher than Juan Guaidó: a figure in a permanently divided right-wing opposition who commands no armies and no troops. He reads the prize itself as part of the propaganda campaign against Maduro, and expects that if Maduro leaves the next leader of Venezuela will be a senior military officer rather than a civilian politician.

the-libyan-constitution-unveiling.title: The West Africa cocaine route
the-libyan-constitution-unveiling.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of where cocaine transiting Venezuela actually goes: not north to the United States but east to West Africa, onto camels along an old Tuareg track to Morocco, and by boat to Spain. The drugs, he says, are meant for Western Europe — and are not Venezuelan to begin with, but Colombian and Ecuadorian.

the-libyan-constitution-unveiling.title: Venezuelan heavy crude and the refining bottleneck
the-libyan-constitution-unveiling.summary: John Kiriakou''s economic explanation for American pressure on Venezuela: the country''s oil is unusually high in sulfur and requires specialty refining, which for years could only be done in Houston. He says sanctions pushed India and China to build refineries capable of processing it, and that a Chinese announcement of a Caribbean refinery for Venezuelan crude left Washington with a policy it could not admit had failed.

the-live-satellite-feed-myth.title: The post-9/11 name traces
the-live-satellite-feed-myth.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of his own assignment in the weeks after the September 11 attacks: with people walking into American embassies all over the world offering information on al-Qaeda, the CIA was buried under tens of thousands of names — sometimes thousands arriving in a single day — and needed, as he put it, an army of clerks to search them against its databases.

the-live-satellite-feed-myth.title: Gary Schroen
the-live-satellite-feed-myth.summary: The senior CIA officer whom John Kiriakou describes as legendary and who, with a small team of agency special operations officers, was the first CIA group into Afghanistan after the September 11 attacks — going in, Kiriakou says, on something like September 12, and later writing a book about it called First In.

the-live-satellite-feed-myth.title: Kandahar
the-live-satellite-feed-myth.summary: The southern Afghan city and province that recurs across John Kiriakou's Afghanistan material — site of one of the two al-Qaeda training camps Abu Zubaydah founded, whose commanders were captured in the same March 2002 raids; the town Bill Clinton said he would have had to destroy, killing 300 innocents, to kill bin Laden in the 1990s; and a stop on Kiriakou's Senate-era heroin-poppy investigation, when the military helicoptered him down before refusing to let him walk the poppy fields.

the-live-satellite-feed-myth.title: Condoleezza Rice
the-live-satellite-feed-myth.summary: U.S. National Security Advisor on 9/11; John Kiriakou had a meeting booked with her that morning, watched her tell George Tenet to "take one for the team" rather than correct the record on Abu Zubaydah, and offers her failure to act on the CIA's warnings as his alternative to any theory that the attacks were allowed to happen.

the-live-satellite-feed-myth.title: Heather Kiriakou
the-live-satellite-feed-myth.summary: John Kiriakou's wife, a senior CIA analyst who — in his account — was one of the best analysts in the entire intelligence community and who lost her job at the agency for no reason other than being married to him. She sat off camera at his December 2007 ABC News interview and told him afterwards that he had said nothing classified.

the-live-satellite-feed-myth.title: The Mohamed Atta Prague claim
the-live-satellite-feed-myth.summary: Dick Cheney's televised assertion tying the September 11 hijacker Mohamed Atta to Saddam Hussein by way of a meeting with the Iraqi intelligence station chief in Prague, which John Kiriakou calls an out-and-out lie made up without a shred of supporting evidence.

the-logic-of-radicalization.title: The Knesset death penalty law
the-logic-of-radicalization.summary: The Israeli law imposing a mandatory death sentence by hanging on Palestinians convicted of killing during a terrorist act, and John Kiriakou's response to it. He notes that the government defining what counts as terrorism is the same government whose settlers the law exempts, and calls the result a codification of racial discrimination.

the-logic-of-radicalization.title: Antisemitism and anti-Zionism
the-logic-of-radicalization.summary: The conflation of criticism of the Israeli state with hatred of Jews, which John Kiriakou describes as a worldwide confusion and, according to a young Israeli he spoke to, an explicit lesson of the Israeli school system; a subject Kiriakou says he personally struggles with.

the-logic-of-radicalization.title: Israel's rightward shift
the-logic-of-radicalization.summary: John Kiriakou's explanation for why Israeli politics moved sharply right over roughly two decades — that immigration from Russia, Ukraine and the United States brought in a conservatism the Israeli electorate had not seen before, displacing the socialist politics of the earlier European arrivals.

the-logic-of-radicalization.title: Itamar Ben-Gvir
the-logic-of-radicalization.summary: Israel's far-right Minister of National Security; John Kiriakou cites him as a convicted hate-crime felon placed in charge of security in Gaza and the West Bank over his victims, blames his insistence that any attack would come from the West Bank for diverting forces before October 7, and cites the death-penalty law passed under his portfolio for Palestinian detainees as the first reinstatement of capital punishment in Israel since it was abolished in 1956, excepting only the execution of Adolf Eichmann.

the-logic-of-radicalization.title: The empire on the ropes
the-logic-of-radicalization.summary: John Kiriakou's answer to whether the American empire is finished — that it is on the ropes but certainly not over — and, in the same exchange, his first unqualified statement that Israeli tactics were inspired by Nazi Germany, a comparison he says he hesitated for years to make.

the-logic-of-radicalization.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
the-logic-of-radicalization.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

the-loretto-camp-mixup.title: The sentencing remark
the-loretto-camp-mixup.summary: The comment John Kiriakou says the judge made at his sentencing — that she wished she could give him the maximum, because that is what she would give him — and his reading of it as a performance for the national security reporters filling the gallery.

the-loretto-camp-mixup.title: "It''s about mitigating damage"
the-loretto-camp-mixup.summary: The sentence John Kiriakou credits with changing his mind about going to trial — one of his own attorneys telling him that his problem was that he thought the case was about justice, when it was about mitigating damage — and the two lawyers who drove to his house after he emailed at six in the morning to refuse the plea.

the-loretto-camp-mixup.title: Passing time at Loretto
the-loretto-camp-mixup.summary: How prisoners at FCI Loretto filled days John Kiriakou describes as Groundhog Day — working out and watching television on a set of screens divided between factions, while Kiriakou himself read, answered mail and wrote a book.

the-loretto-camp-mixup.title: Arabic and Greek
the-loretto-camp-mixup.summary: The qualification John Kiriakou says opened the door to his transfer from CIA analysis to operations: a post in Athens wanted Greek or Arabic, and he had both — by most of his tellings the only officer in the agency who did. The chief who hired him gave the reason in one sentence: it is easier and cheaper to take a linguist and teach him operations than the other way round. The pairing also became a detection tool, since the language nobody speaks in Pakistan is Arabic.

the-loretto-camp-mixup.title: Bankruptcy and the dropped charges
the-loretto-camp-mixup.summary: The sequence John Kiriakou places at the centre of his case: that the espionage counts against him were dropped only after his legal fees had bankrupted him, which he presents as evidence that the government''s aim was attrition rather than conviction.

the-loretto-camp-mixup.title: Curtailment cables
the-loretto-camp-mixup.summary: The career-ending requests John Kiriakou says he read coming back from the CIA's black sites — officers, doctors, psychologists and nurses asking to end their tours early rather than continue to take part in the interrogation programme — and his conclusion that if that many people were objecting in classified channels, someone would surely go public.

the-macron-defamation-suit.title: Candace Owens
the-macron-defamation-suit.summary: The commentator whose claims about the killing of Charlie Kirk John Kiriakou has publicly declined to accept. He credits her reach and her intelligence and rejects her method, citing an earlier occasion — a conference call he says he was on — at which she claimed irrefutable proof that the Italian government had stolen the 2020 election and that its release would return Donald Trump to office.

the-macron-defamation-suit.title: Ali from Newark
the-macron-defamation-suit.summary: The Black shot caller at FCI Loretto, near the end of a twenty-five-year drug sentence, who came to embrace John Kiriakou at the close of his term and tell him how much he respected him — a friendship possible only because Kiriakou had decided on arrival to ignore the prison's racial divisions.

the-macron-defamation-suit.title: Bezalel Smotrich
the-macron-defamation-suit.summary: Israeli far-right minister whom John Kiriakou, alongside Itamar Ben-Gvir, blames for leaving Israel unprepared on October 7 by insisting any attack would come from the West Bank rather than Gaza.

the-macron-defamation-suit.title: Clyde Hall
the-macron-defamation-suit.summary: The imprisoned Ohio congressman John Kiriakou says served at his prison a few years before him, whose remark on release — that he had made some of the best friends of his life inside — Kiriakou thought insane at the time and came to understand after his own sentence.

the-macron-defamation-suit.title: Drunken border guards
the-macron-defamation-suit.summary: John Kiriakou's explanation for how quiet frontiers become shooting wars — bored, drinking troops with nothing to do and no supervision — which he applies to the Thailand-Cambodia clashes, to the India-China line, and to why Vladimir Putin objects to a NATO country on his border.

the-macron-defamation-suit.title: France recognises Palestine
the-macron-defamation-suit.summary: Emmanuel Macron's decision in July 2025 to extend formal recognition to the Republic of Palestine and exchange ambassadors, which John Kiriakou called a turning point that could not be overstated — the first serious crack in Western support for Israel, and significant precisely because France is a historic colonial power in the Middle East with a Security Council veto.

the-magazines-that-bought-her-freedom.title: Kimberly Guilfoyle in Athens
the-magazines-that-bought-her-freedom.summary: John Kiriakou's assessment of Kimberly Guilfoyle's appointment as American ambassador to Greece — that she got it because Donald Trump Jr. wanted her out of the way, a manoeuvre he compares to Saddam Hussein's habit of exiling successful generals as ambassadors — and his reluctant conclusion that Greece could have done worse.

the-magazines-that-bought-her-freedom.title: The Pondiki cartoon
the-magazines-that-bought-her-freedom.summary: The satirical Greek newspaper that ran a doctored photograph of the American ambassador Nicholas Burns naked in a dog collar, being whipped by the education minister — and John Kiriakou's account of the ambassador's official protest, and of the staff who taped the page above their desks where he could not see it.

the-magazines-that-bought-her-freedom.title: Amnesty International
the-magazines-that-bought-her-freedom.summary: The human rights organization whose torture report forms part of John Kiriakou's core defense — the CIA's crimes were already public knowledge before he confirmed them on ABC, and the Justice Department's own declination letter said so — and the organization whose silence during his prosecution he cannot forgive. He begged Amnesty for a one-sentence statement and got a New Yorker subscription instead; it took Ai Weiwei to change their minds, and by then he was walking out of prison.

the-magazines-that-bought-her-freedom.title: I want my fifty bucks back
the-magazines-that-bought-her-freedom.summary: What John Kiriakou says he shouted at John Fetterman from ten rows back at an Ohio State football game — and his explanation, as a Pennsylvanian furious about the senator, of why Fetterman keeps his seat anyway.

the-magazines-that-bought-her-freedom.title: Ian Henderson
the-magazines-that-bought-her-freedom.summary: The British colonial police officer who ran Bahrain's intelligence service during John Kiriakou's posting there — a man Kiriakou says even the heir presumptive to the throne was afraid to name aloud, and whom Kiriakou, seated at the crown prince's table at a dinner for George H. W. Bush, mistook for a corpse.

the-magazines-that-bought-her-freedom.title: Ibrahim Traoré
the-magazines-that-bought-her-freedom.summary: John Kiriakou's assessment of the military ruler of Burkina Faso — a young officer who took power promising a return to democracy, and who in Kiriakou's account has grown increasingly irrational, criminalising homosexuality, abolishing the electoral commission and moving to expel foreigners.

the-mailroom-standoff.title: The Kurd from Terre Haute
the-mailroom-standoff.summary: An Iraqi Kurd who reached the modified communications management unit at FCI Loretto after four years inside the CMU at Terre Haute, and who told John Kiriakou that the only way out was to keep your mouth shut for years.

the-mailroom-standoff.title: Communications management unit
the-mailroom-standoff.summary: The two restricted-contact units inside the American federal prison system, at Terre Haute and Marion; built for "the worst of the worst" but, in John Kiriakou's account, used to silence prisoners whose messages are inconvenient — and a practice he groups with solitary confinement as torture. He served part of his own sentence in a modified one.

the-mailroom-standoff.title: FCI Loretto
the-mailroom-standoff.summary: U.S. Federal Correctional Institution in Loretto, Pennsylvania; the low-medium-security prison at which John Kiriakou served 23 months of a 30-month sentence following his 2013 Espionage Act–era plea deal; the originally ordered "minimum security work camp" placement was countermanded — per Kiriakou, on Brennan's direct intervention — to place him in the actual prison alongside the general population.

the-mailroom-standoff.title: The Walmart phone call
the-mailroom-standoff.summary: John Kiriakou''s account, from a White House friend, that Jared Kushner personally telephoned the chief executive of Walmart to find a job for a woman whose life sentence Donald Trump had commuted, and rang back every six months to check on her.

the-mailroom-standoff.title: Letter from Loretto
the-mailroom-standoff.summary: Prison newsletter written by John Kiriakou from FCI Loretto, modeled on Martin Luther King's "Letter from Birmingham Jail," which exposed two crimes committed against him by guards and went viral after being relayed to the Huffington Post, drawing national press to the prison.

the-mailroom-standoff.title: Kiriakou's FOIA request from prison
the-mailroom-standoff.summary: The Freedom of Information Act request John Kiriakou filed on himself six weeks into his sentence at FCI Loretto — despite a plea agreement promising he never would — which returned 250 pages including a warden's memorandum warning staff that the incoming prisoner had access to the media.

the-mallios-argument.title: The broken side-view mirror
the-mallios-argument.summary: The cold pitch John Kiriakou made in Athens against the incoming intelligence representative of a hostile Middle Eastern state — a manoeuvre suggested by his mentor Gust Avrakotos, in which Kiriakou snapped the mirror off the man's diplomatic car with a bag of books, established cover with the neighbour, apologised at the door, asked for a glass of water, and used the minute alone to kneel down and speak Arabic to the target's four-year-old daughter.

the-mallios-argument.title: The code room and the buried weapons
the-mallios-argument.summary: What John Kiriakou demanded when the officer he had cold-pitched in Athens agreed to meet him — access to his embassy's code room and all of its weapons — and the meeting in a hotel coffee shop, surrounded by armed CIA officers at every table, at which the terms were set.

the-mallios-argument.title: Gust Avrakotos
the-mallios-argument.summary: CIA case officer, John Kiriakou's operations mentor, and a central figure in Charlie Wilson's War — the prolific, divisive covert-war veteran Kiriakou credits as the greatest teacher of his adult life.

the-mallios-argument.title: Greek Intelligence Service
the-mallios-argument.summary: Greece's intelligence service, with which John Kiriakou worked closely during his Athens posting; its head of surveillance called off surveillance on him after watching him make a large offering at Saint Nectarios's tomb on the island of Aegina.

the-mallios-argument.title: Revolutionary Organization 17 November
the-mallios-argument.summary: Greek far-left urban guerrilla group active 1975–2002; the deadliest terrorist organization in Greek history

the-mallios-argument.title: John Kiriakou
the-mallios-argument.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

the-managers-ranking.title: Joe Rogan
the-managers-ranking.summary: The podcast host whose show John Kiriakou finally sat for in October 2025 — an experience that began with signing a non-disclosure agreement and ended with his verdict that Rogan is "a nice guy, very down to earth, very normal." The first thing Rogan asked, walking into the studio ten minutes late: "Hey, do you know my friend Mike Baker?" Kiriakou defends Rogan as unfairly characterized as a right-winger, and had long cited the show as the venue where Zuckerberg admitted Facebook suppressed the Hunter Biden laptop story at the FBI''s behest.

the-managers-ranking.title: The Perplexity subscription
the-managers-ranking.summary: The free lifetime account John Kiriakou says the chief executive of Perplexity emailed him at ten o'clock at night, days after he told Joe Rogan's audience that ChatGPT had invented a University of Maryland degree and a Belgian graduate school for him — and that when he corrected it, the machine argued back.

the-managers-ranking.title: Abigail Spanberger
the-managers-ranking.summary: Governor of Virginia from 2025 and, before Congress, a CIA officer alongside John Kiriakou in the Counterterrorism Center — whom he calls a perfectly nice person who would have been a middle-of-the-road Republican in the 1970s and 1980s, and whose victory speech, to his surprise, said all the right things.

the-managers-ranking.title: Jason Miyares
the-managers-ranking.summary: The Cuban-born Republican attorney general of Virginia whom John Kiriakou expected to be a right-wing disaster and found instead to be excellent — a judgement he says is hard for him to make about a conservative Republican, and which he repeated on the night Miyares was unceremoniously thrown out of office.

the-managers-ranking.title: Mike Baker
the-managers-ranking.summary: Former CIA case officer and John Kiriakou's direct predecessor in Athens on the 17 November problem; "the real deal," in Kiriakou's phrase, until a botched surveillance operation got him expelled from Greece and forced out of the agency the same day he expected a commendation.

the-managers-ranking.title: The Arlington house
the-managers-ranking.summary: The 1,200-square-foot house John Kiriakou bought with his Pakistan overtime and danger pay for $347,000, sold two years later for $721,000, and now values at a million — the anchor of his repeated argument that his own children can never live in the Arlington, Virginia neighbourhood they grew up in.

the-martyrdom-bonus.title: The two Tunisians
the-martyrdom-bonus.summary: The first counterterrorist raid John Kiriakou led after arriving in Pakistan in January 2002, which produced two eighteen-year-olds from Tunisia who burst into tears when the door came down, one of them asking whether he could telephone his mother.

the-martyrdom-bonus.title: Economic roots of terrorism
the-martyrdom-bonus.summary: John Kiriakou's argument, drawn from interrogating young al-Qaeda fighters in Pakistan, that jihadi recruitment is driven by poverty and hopelessness rather than religion — illiterate villagers paid $300 a month who could not find the U.S. on a map and had never read the Quran.

the-martyrdom-bonus.title: "You were the first person that ever asked me about my children"
the-martyrdom-bonus.summary: The answer John Kiriakou says he received when he asked a mid-level al-Qaeda member he had recruited in Pakistan why he had allowed the recruitment to happen: that in five years of detention Kiriakou had been the first person to ask about his children.

the-martyrdom-bonus.title: Chief of station
the-martyrdom-bonus.summary: The CIA's senior officer in a foreign country — appointed by the CIA director alone, outranking the ambassador's intelligence equities in practice, and in John Kiriakou's account the figure who sets the moral temperature of a station, from the officer who handed him his first counterterrorism assignment to the one who walks into a minister's office fifteen minutes after the human rights officer has left.

the-martyrdom-bonus.title: Jordanian al-Qaeda detainee
the-martyrdom-bonus.summary: The subject of John Kiriakou's first-ever interrogation in Pakistan — a Jordanian who had gone to Afghanistan to run an orphanage, joined al-Qaeda for its funding, and told the truth about his escape route because 'I'm your prisoner; what good would it do to lie?'

the-martyrdom-bonus.title: The hooding dispute
the-martyrdom-bonus.summary: The argument John Kiriakou says he had with a subordinate at a CIA safe house in Pakistan on the night of the Abu Zubaydah raid, over hoods placed on captured prisoners; both men reported each other to headquarters, and Kiriakou was the one reprimanded.

the-maxwell-justice-department-interview.title: The Mayflower Madam analogy
the-maxwell-justice-department-interview.summary: John Kiriakou's argument, borrowed from the 1980s Mayflower Madam case, that the Epstein 'list' will disappoint anyone expecting a schedule of clients — because address books contain the dry cleaner and the Chinese takeaway alongside everyone else, and nobody keeps a spreadsheet of their crimes.

the-maxwell-justice-department-interview.title: Maxwell at a work camp
the-maxwell-justice-department-interview.summary: John Kiriakou's objection to Ghislaine Maxwell's placement in a minimum security work camp — that convicted sex offenders are, in his experience, never eligible for minimums — and his refusal, when pressed, to offer any explanation for the exception.

the-maxwell-justice-department-interview.title: Ali from Newark
the-maxwell-justice-department-interview.summary: The Black shot caller at FCI Loretto, near the end of a twenty-five-year drug sentence, who came to embrace John Kiriakou at the close of his term and tell him how much he respected him — a friendship possible only because Kiriakou had decided on arrival to ignore the prison's racial divisions.

the-maxwell-justice-department-interview.title: Bezalel Smotrich
the-maxwell-justice-department-interview.summary: Israeli far-right minister whom John Kiriakou, alongside Itamar Ben-Gvir, blames for leaving Israel unprepared on October 7 by insisting any attack would come from the West Bank rather than Gaza.

the-maxwell-justice-department-interview.title: Candace Owens
the-maxwell-justice-department-interview.summary: The commentator whose claims about the killing of Charlie Kirk John Kiriakou has publicly declined to accept. He credits her reach and her intelligence and rejects her method, citing an earlier occasion — a conference call he says he was on — at which she claimed irrefutable proof that the Italian government had stolen the 2020 election and that its release would return Donald Trump to office.

the-maxwell-justice-department-interview.title: Clyde Hall
the-maxwell-justice-department-interview.summary: The imprisoned Ohio congressman John Kiriakou says served at his prison a few years before him, whose remark on release — that he had made some of the best friends of his life inside — Kiriakou thought insane at the time and came to understand after his own sentence.

the-mayflower-madam-analogy.title: The Maxwell Justice Department interview
the-mayflower-madam-analogy.summary: Ghislaine Maxwell's July 2025 interview with the Justice Department, in which her counsel said she took the fifth on nothing and answered every question — a risk John Kiriakou reads as evidence she was probably telling the truth, and as an approach for a commutation or a pardon.

the-mayflower-madam-analogy.title: Maxwell at a work camp
the-mayflower-madam-analogy.summary: John Kiriakou's objection to Ghislaine Maxwell's placement in a minimum security work camp — that convicted sex offenders are, in his experience, never eligible for minimums — and his refusal, when pressed, to offer any explanation for the exception.

the-mayflower-madam-analogy.title: Ali from Newark
the-mayflower-madam-analogy.summary: The Black shot caller at FCI Loretto, near the end of a twenty-five-year drug sentence, who came to embrace John Kiriakou at the close of his term and tell him how much he respected him — a friendship possible only because Kiriakou had decided on arrival to ignore the prison's racial divisions.

the-mayflower-madam-analogy.title: Bezalel Smotrich
the-mayflower-madam-analogy.summary: Israeli far-right minister whom John Kiriakou, alongside Itamar Ben-Gvir, blames for leaving Israel unprepared on October 7 by insisting any attack would come from the West Bank rather than Gaza.

the-mayflower-madam-analogy.title: Candace Owens
the-mayflower-madam-analogy.summary: The commentator whose claims about the killing of Charlie Kirk John Kiriakou has publicly declined to accept. He credits her reach and her intelligence and rejects her method, citing an earlier occasion — a conference call he says he was on — at which she claimed irrefutable proof that the Italian government had stolen the 2020 election and that its release would return Donald Trump to office.

the-mayflower-madam-analogy.title: Clyde Hall
the-mayflower-madam-analogy.summary: The imprisoned Ohio congressman John Kiriakou says served at his prison a few years before him, whose remark on release — that he had made some of the best friends of his life inside — Kiriakou thought insane at the time and came to understand after his own sentence.

the-mcconnell-obituary.title: The Graham Senate succession
the-mcconnell-obituary.summary: John Kiriakou's comment on the appointment of Lindsey Graham's sister to serve out the remainder of his Senate term, and her announcement that she would run for a full term of her own — a candidacy whose only qualification, in Kiriakou's assessment, is her relation to the late senator.

the-mcconnell-obituary.title: Lindsey Graham
the-mcconnell-obituary.summary: Republican senator from South Carolina who died in July 2026, and John Kiriakou's standing shorthand for the permanent war caucus — a "show horse" rather than a workhorse, a "chameleon" who "never saw a war that he didn't want to jump into with both feet," and, on posthumously released documentary footage, a man offering the US Air Force to bomb a country America was not at war with.

the-mcconnell-obituary.title: 2026 Iran war
the-mcconnell-obituary.summary: The open-ended American and Israeli war against Iran that John Kiriakou tracked week by week on his own show — a conflict he says was sold as three weeks, ran into its fifth month, achieved every decapitation objective it set, and continued anyway. His grade for it is a D, and his forecast is a Truth Social post declaring victory while nothing changes.

the-mcconnell-obituary.title: Embassy movie night
the-mcconnell-obituary.summary: The weekly diversion John Kiriakou remembers from his posting to Pakistan after September 11th, when the station worked seven days a week and fourteen hours a day: on Wednesday nights the ambassador hosted a film in the embassy''s small theatre, and the audience shouted at the screen and threw popcorn at whatever they had managed to get hold of.

the-mcconnell-obituary.title: The Espionage Act and the Rosenbergs
the-mcconnell-obituary.summary: John Kiriakou''s short legislative history of the Espionage Act: written in 1917 to counter German saboteurs, slightly amended in 1950 after the execution of Julius and Ethel Rosenberg, and never meaningfully updated since. It does not use the words classified information, because the classification system did not exist when it was drafted.

the-mcconnell-obituary.title: The Qatari 747
the-mcconnell-obituary.summary: The Boeing 747 given to the United States by the government of Qatar to serve as Air Force One. John Kiriakou reported in July 2026 that it had been delivered to the president while he was overseas and that he declined to fly home in it, because it had not been fitted with the protective equipment — countermeasures, radar jamming — that the role requires.

the-mcdonalds-theory.title: Kiriakou's visit to Vietnam (2026)
the-mcdonalds-theory.summary: A week in Vietnam in August 2026, taken around a paid speech to Australian investment bankers and shaped by four cousins who fought there. John Kiriakou broadcast an episode from Ho Chi Minh City and used the trip to argue that commerce, not force, is what turns a country pro-American.

the-mcdonalds-theory.title: Iran's conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz
the-mcdonalds-theory.summary: The six demands issued by Iran's Supreme National Security Council in August 2026 as the price of reopening the Strait of Hormuz. John Kiriakou's observation is that they are the old nuclear-deal conditions transposed onto a new lever, and that the transposition is both smart and very difficult for Washington.

the-mcdonalds-theory.title: 2026 Iran war
the-mcdonalds-theory.summary: The open-ended American and Israeli war against Iran that John Kiriakou tracked week by week on his own show — a conflict he says was sold as three weeks, ran into its fifth month, achieved every decapitation objective it set, and continued anyway. His grade for it is a D, and his forecast is a Truth Social post declaring victory while nothing changes.

the-mcdonalds-theory.title: Củ Chi tunnels
the-mcdonalds-theory.summary: The 250-kilometre tunnel network dug by the Viet Cong outside Saigon, which John Kiriakou visited in 2026 and could not physically enter. He attributes the tunnels' viability to the malnutrition of the people who dug them.

the-mcdonalds-theory.title: The killing of Iranian police
the-mcdonalds-theory.summary: A campaign of assassinations against individual Iranian police officers and domestic security personnel during the 2026 war, intended to provoke popular revolt by removing the state's capacity to suppress it. John Kiriakou attributes the killings to Israeli operatives and reports that they produced the opposite of the intended effect.

the-mcdonalds-theory.title: The Saigon CIA station photograph
the-mcdonalds-theory.summary: The Pulitzer-winning image of evacuees climbing a ladder to a helicopter during the fall of Saigon in 1975. John Kiriakou, who talked his way onto the roof in 2026, points out that the building most Americans take for the embassy was in fact an apartment block that secretly housed the CIA's Saigon station.

the-melber-walkout.title: Leaker versus whistleblower
the-melber-walkout.summary: The fight over what the American networks would call John Kiriakou. It took his lawyers, above all Jesselyn Radack, a year of work between January 2012 and January 2013 to get CNN and MSNBC to stop introducing him as 'CIA leaker John Kiriakou'. CNN changed and Fox, he notes, never needed to; MSNBC in his account never did, and Rachel Maddow settled on a formula he quotes with some precision — a man 'who styles himself a whistleblower'.

the-melber-walkout.title: Gina Haspel
the-melber-walkout.summary: Director of the Central Intelligence Agency under President Trump's first term; known to John Kiriakou and others at the CIA as "Bloody Gina"; per Kiriakou, flew out to the secret black site to sit in on one of the enhanced-interrogation torture sessions "just because she could," personally supervised the torture of USS Cole bombing suspect Rahim al-Nashiri, and later fed the CIA's torture tapes into an industrial document grinder after being explicitly told by White House Counsel not to destroy them.

the-melber-walkout.title: The Ukraine call whistleblower
the-melber-walkout.summary: The intelligence officer whose complaint triggered Donald Trump's first impeachment, and whom John Kiriakou declines to accept as a whistleblower at all — not on partisan grounds but on procedural ones. The complaint went to the Justice Department rather than the oversight committees, and its prose, he says, is lawyers' prose rather than the uniform CIA analytic style every analyst is trained into. He is nonetheless emphatic that naming the man was indefensible.

the-melber-walkout.title: Daniel Ellsberg
the-melber-walkout.summary: The Pentagon Papers whistleblower Kiriakou calls 'the Godfather of all national security whistleblowers' — and one of the great mentors of his life.

the-melber-walkout.title: The Fox News military analyst
the-melber-walkout.summary: The cable-news commentator John Kiriakou says he identified as a fraud within a single green-room conversation, because the man used movie vocabulary — black ops, wet work — where a real officer would have named a directorate. The man had obtained a Defense Department clearance on the strength of his claimed CIA service, advised generals in Afghanistan, and was later arrested and imprisoned for fraud.

the-melber-walkout.title: Bill Binney
the-melber-walkout.summary: Former NSA technical director whom John Kiriakou cites as having debunked the DNC hack. Asked by Veteran Intelligence Professionals for Sanity to examine the science, Binney analyzed the speed of the upload and concluded the emails could only have been copied in person to a thumb drive, not taken remotely by Russia — an argument he later made to Donald Trump in the Oval Office. Kiriakou calls him a friend, the most brilliant person he has met on electronics, and a member of the whistleblower circle he belongs to.

the-mental-health-parity-gap.title: The homelessness executive order
the-mental-health-parity-gap.summary: Donald Trump's July 2025 executive order on homelessness, which John Kiriakou criticised on the ground that it understates the population by two thirds and proposes forcible commitment to facilities that do not exist — while conceding that Trump diagnoses the problem better than his predecessors did.

the-mental-health-parity-gap.title: Ali from Newark
the-mental-health-parity-gap.summary: The Black shot caller at FCI Loretto, near the end of a twenty-five-year drug sentence, who came to embrace John Kiriakou at the close of his term and tell him how much he respected him — a friendship possible only because Kiriakou had decided on arrival to ignore the prison's racial divisions.

the-mental-health-parity-gap.title: Bezalel Smotrich
the-mental-health-parity-gap.summary: Israeli far-right minister whom John Kiriakou, alongside Itamar Ben-Gvir, blames for leaving Israel unprepared on October 7 by insisting any attack would come from the West Bank rather than Gaza.

the-mental-health-parity-gap.title: Candace Owens
the-mental-health-parity-gap.summary: The commentator whose claims about the killing of Charlie Kirk John Kiriakou has publicly declined to accept. He credits her reach and her intelligence and rejects her method, citing an earlier occasion — a conference call he says he was on — at which she claimed irrefutable proof that the Italian government had stolen the 2020 election and that its release would return Donald Trump to office.

the-mental-health-parity-gap.title: Clyde Hall
the-mental-health-parity-gap.summary: The imprisoned Ohio congressman John Kiriakou says served at his prison a few years before him, whose remark on release — that he had made some of the best friends of his life inside — Kiriakou thought insane at the time and came to understand after his own sentence.

the-mental-health-parity-gap.title: Drunken border guards
the-mental-health-parity-gap.summary: John Kiriakou's explanation for how quiet frontiers become shooting wars — bored, drinking troops with nothing to do and no supervision — which he applies to the Thailand-Cambodia clashes, to the India-China line, and to why Vladimir Putin objects to a NATO country on his border.

the-mi5-model-for-america.title: Expanding your realm
the-mi5-model-for-america.summary: The lesson in CIA office politics John Kiriakou says he was taught in his first week — that to make yourself as important as possible you must constantly expand your realm and be king of as many people as you can — and his argument that at the senior-most level the same instinct starts reaching across agencies.

the-mi5-model-for-america.title: Mass Surveillance
the-mi5-model-for-america.summary: Kiriakou says the NSA has dropped any pretext of protecting civil liberties, warehousing every call, text and email in the Utah desert.

the-mi5-model-for-america.title: Russia is not the gravest threat
the-mi5-model-for-america.summary: John Kiriakou's rejection of the first policy speech by MI6's first woman chief, Blaise Metreweli, which named Russia and the Russo-Ukrainian war as the greatest danger to Britain and Europe. His counter-case is demographic and fiscal — Russia is practically bankrupt with a birth rate that would empty it in a century — and his own candidate for the real threat is not a state at all.

the-mi5-model-for-america.title: MI6
the-mi5-model-for-america.summary: The United Kingdom''s Secret Intelligence Service, the foreign-intelligence service of the British government and the closest CIA liaison partner under the Five Eyes framework. Per John Kiriakou, MI6 was the parent organization that asked Truman after WWII to set up a ''central intelligence agency'' on the model of its own service — making the CIA in effect MI6''s little brother. Kiriakou''s stated view of the historical relationship: MI6 saw the CIA as its little brother, then after the empire fell apart as its big brother, and then after 9/11 as ''strangers'' because U.S. policy became ''simply to kill everybody.''

the-mi5-model-for-america.title: National Security vs Civil Liberties
the-mi5-model-for-america.summary: Kiriakou's recurring argument that invoking "national security" is used to excuse the erosion of civil liberties and that the secrecy regime cannot coexist with constitutional democracy.

the-mi5-model-for-america.title: The MI5 model
the-mi5-model-for-america.summary: The proposal John Kiriakou says was already being discussed with the British in 1992 or 1993 — an American domestic intelligence service on the MI5 pattern, without arrest powers, feeding what it collected on citizens to the FBI — and which he believes the post-January 6 legislation would finally deliver.

the-mi5-model.title: The Grenier counterinsurgency op-ed
the-mi5-model.summary: The New York Times piece by former CIA officer Robert Grenier arguing that the storming of the Capitol should be treated as an insurgency, and John Kiriakou's published answer to it — that a colleague of thirty years using that word is asking for people to be killed, and that counterinsurgency describes a set of practices the Constitution forbids at home.

the-mi5-model.title: Deep state
the-mi5-model.summary: John Kiriakou''s position on the deep state — that it is not a right-wing trope but an accurate description of something he served inside for fifteen years at the CIA and two more on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee staff. He is indifferent to the label ("call it the state, call it the federal bureaucracy") and insists on the substance: "It''s there to stay. It''s not going anywhere."

the-mi5-model.title: Bahrain Posting (1994–1996)
