the-mi5-model.summary: John Kiriakou's 1994–1996 assignment to Bahrain under U.S. State Department cover as second secretary for economic affairs — arriving with his wife Joanne and infant son Chris on August 1, 1994, into a tiny Gulf monarchy whose sectarian tensions erupted, two months later, into the first Intifada.

the-mi5-model.title: Bashar al-Assad
the-mi5-model.summary: President of Syria; John Kiriakou recounts warning Senator John Kerry to stop publicly calling Assad 'my dear friend' after a speech enraged Washington's Lebanese community, with Kerry citing motorcycle rides they had taken together to the Golan Heights.

the-mi5-model.title: Bob Grenier
the-mi5-model.summary: Career CIA officer who served as station chief in Islamabad before, during, and after 9/11; later associate deputy director of operations for policy support and Iraq Mission Manager; John Kiriakou's boss and, for one year, his supervisor as executive assistant.

the-mi5-model.title: Jim Pavitt
the-mi5-model.summary: Long-serving CIA Deputy Director for Operations during the early post-9/11 period; characterized by John Kiriakou as "a legendary officer and a really great guy"; mocked John Brennan openly within the agency for Brennan's recurring stated ambition to head his own intelligence agency.

the-milan-sofia-flight.title: The boring cover story
the-milan-sofia-flight.summary: The CIA training principle John Kiriakou says governed how officers described their jobs to strangers: pick something so dull that nobody asks a second question. His own standard answer was the foreign service, training work, and some import-export negotiation.

the-milan-sofia-flight.title: Quoted on NPR
the-milan-sofia-flight.summary: John Kiriakou's discovery, via a standing Google alert on his own name, that National Public Radio had cited a DeProgram discussion between him and Ted Rall in an article on Palestinians killed while waiting for food — an outlet he had walked out on years earlier.

the-milan-sofia-flight.title: The Addis Ababa zoo
the-milan-sofia-flight.summary: A visit John Kiriakou made to the zoo in Addis Ababa on a free half-day, where he watched keepers force a screaming donkey into the lion enclosure — and noted the two-tier admission price charged to foreigners.

the-milan-sofia-flight.title: The election day 1992 poll
the-milan-sofia-flight.summary: An informal show of hands taken in a CIA branch office on election day 1992, which John Kiriakou describes as the moment he discovered he had no idea of the politics of the colleagues he sat three feet away from — and that he was not, as he had assumed, the only progressive in the room.

the-milan-sofia-flight.title: The ex-prisoner at the Bureau of Prisons
the-milan-sofia-flight.summary: John Kiriakou's approving account of the appointment of a former federal prisoner — recently released after five years on a drug conspiracy charge — as deputy director of the Bureau of Prisons, which he calls an inspired choice and one of the few things he has praised Donald Trump for.

the-milan-sofia-flight.title: The fifteen-dollar maintenance fee
the-milan-sofia-flight.summary: An appointment John Kiriakou made at his bank on the morning of a broadcast to ask for the return of a $15 monthly maintenance fee that had taken his account to minus fifteen dollars — a story he told on air as a plain statement of what his finances looked like after prison.

the-minister-of-awqaf-compliment.title: The Jerusalem harassment campaign
the-minister-of-awqaf-compliment.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of what happened to a CIA colleague and his wife during a declared two-year State Department rotation in Jerusalem: furniture rearranged after one embassy party, all three toilets in the house defecated in after another, and, before they left, the family dog''s tail cut off and bandaged. Kiriakou presents the three break-ins as routine rather than exceptional.

the-minister-of-awqaf-compliment.title: CIA attention to West Africa
the-minister-of-awqaf-compliment.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer on whether the CIA is likely to be operating in Burkina Faso: for all the years he was at the agency it cared very little about Africa and especially West Africa, but the presence of al-Qaeda and Islamic State affiliates plus the drug trade makes CIA and special forces involvement probable — and, he adds, the American public will not hear about it.

the-minister-of-awqaf-compliment.title: CIA–FBI incompatible computer systems
the-minister-of-awqaf-compliment.summary: John Kiriakou's claim that from the CIA's founding in 1947 until 2009 the computer systems of the CIA and the FBI were not compatible with one another — no message could be sent from one to the other and no intelligence shared — which he offers both as the material substrate of the interagency hatred that helped make September 11 possible, and as the gap through which James Mitchell and Bruce Jessen were able to pass Ali Soufan's FBI debriefings of Abu Zubaydah off as the fruits of torture.

the-minister-of-awqaf-compliment.title: CIA language training
the-minister-of-awqaf-compliment.summary: The agency''s language pipeline as John Kiriakou experienced and describes it: a full year of Arabic at nine hours a day, an optional second year at the State Department''s school, and the calculation that made his own career — that it is cheaper to teach a linguist operations than to teach an operations officer Greek and Arabic.

the-minister-of-awqaf-compliment.title: Fake CIA résumés
the-minister-of-awqaf-compliment.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of being used as a human authenticator in the private sector: at the consulting firm he joined after leaving the CIA, every job applicant claiming agency service was sent to dinner with him, and by his count fully half of them had never set foot inside the CIA.

the-minister-of-awqaf-compliment.title: Forcing Iran toward a bomb
the-minister-of-awqaf-compliment.summary: John Kiriakou''s argument that Western pressure risks producing the very outcome it claims to prevent: repeated Israeli assassinations of Iranian scientists and generals and strikes on Iranian sites may eventually leave Ayatollah Khamenei with no choice but to permit a defensive weapon — despite the religious prohibition Kiriakou credits him with maintaining, and despite successive American estimates that Iran is not seeking one.

the-mintpress-prediction.title: Anwar al-Awlaki
the-mintpress-prediction.summary: American-born al-Qaeda propagandist; in 1993 the imam of the Falls Church, Virginia mosque visited by John Kiriakou's CIA Arabic-language class on a field trip; in 2001 the cleric at whose mosque the 9/11 hijackers prayed the night before the attacks; killed by U.S. drone strike in Yemen in approximately 2011.

the-mintpress-prediction.title: Daniel Hale
the-mintpress-prediction.summary: Per John Kiriakou, drone whistleblower Daniel Hale — an NSA contractor and drone targeting analyst who exposed an 80% civilian death rate in the U.S. drone program, was ordered to fire on two young girls his superior called "goats," and was sentenced to 45 months (of which Kiriakou says he actually served about 18) despite prosecutors seeking nine to eleven years.

the-mintpress-prediction.title: Government Accountability Project
the-mintpress-prediction.summary: The Washington whistleblower-advocacy law firm and NGO, known as GAP, whose attorney Jesselyn Radack took John Kiriakou's case after his 2012 arrest and told him he was a whistleblower whether he thought so or not.

the-mintpress-prediction.title: John Brennan
the-mintpress-prediction.summary: Former Director of the CIA; characterized in KiriPedia's source corpus as the principal architect of the agency's enhanced interrogation program and as having plotted against an elected President

the-mintpress-prediction.title: Julian Assange
the-mintpress-prediction.summary: Kiriakou — a 15-year friend and former WikiLeaks board member — on why Assange is a publisher owed a journalist's immunity, and a political prisoner.

the-mintpress-prediction.title: Brad Birkenfeld
the-mintpress-prediction.summary: The UBS banking whistleblower, who was prosecuted and imprisoned before winning a $104 million settlement from the Treasury Department and spending it on the legal defence of other whistleblowers. John Kiriakou uses him as the measure of the gap between financial and national-security whistleblowing, and names him among the visitors whose devices he believes were copied at the Ecuadorian embassy in London.

the-mob-vote-for-trump.title: The conscientious objectors book
the-mob-vote-for-trump.summary: A long out-of-print volume of interviews with American conscientious objectors, published around 1972 and given to John Kiriakou from the personal collection of an objector he was friendly with in prison — a book whose harrowing accounts of objectors sent to real federal prisons rather than to camps convinced him that refusing to serve was often more physically dangerous than serving.

the-mob-vote-for-trump.title: Jesse Jackson
the-mob-vote-for-trump.summary: American civil rights leader and two-time presidential candidate whose hospitalisation in November 2025 John Kiriakou discussed at length — explaining progressive supranuclear palsy, the condition Jackson was diagnosed with two years after Parkinson''s, from his own family''s experience of the same disease, and giving a poor prognosis.

the-mob-vote-for-trump.title: Kiriakou's acting career
the-mob-vote-for-trump.summary: The film role John Kiriakou took in 2025 after Tyrel Ventura wrote a part for him — a former CIA officer running a billionaire's security detail — which he shot in Mexico for a month and which made him, at sixty-odd, a member of the Screen Actors Guild.

the-mob-vote-for-trump.title: The Egyptian intelligence chief''s son
the-mob-vote-for-trump.summary: A coincidence John Kiriakou reported from Oxford, Ohio in November 2025: his own son''s marketing professor turned out to be the son of Muhammad Farag, head of the Egyptian intelligence service some thirty-five years earlier, whom Kiriakou had met in Cairo when the professor was a boy of seven or eight — and the two families went out to dinner together.

the-mob-vote-for-trump.title: The Giuliani–Epstein emails
the-mob-vote-for-trump.summary: A cache of correspondence that a former chief of business development for Giuliani Partners told John Kiriakou she holds — thousands of pages of emails between Rudy Giuliani and Jeffrey Epstein, which she says she has offered to news organisations and to congressional committees and which nobody wanted, together with her claim that a second British prince and other former heads of state are implicated.

the-mob-vote-for-trump.title: The Outer Banks seasonal workers
the-mob-vote-for-trump.summary: John Kiriakou''s observation, from years of family summers on the Outer Banks of North Carolina, that he never encountered an American lifeguard and almost no American shop clerks or waiters — the staff being Bulgarian, Romanian, Moldovan and otherwise Eastern European, working on the cheap, housed eight to twelve to a house and sent home at the end of the season.

the-mobile-passport-lane.title: The Farragut West encounter
the-mobile-passport-lane.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of walking up to two National Guardsmen in the Farragut West Metro station — the safest station on the network, in his estimate — telling himself the whole way not to say anything, and then saying one sentence: "You guys should be ashamed of yourselves."

the-mobile-passport-lane.title: Abigail Spanberger
the-mobile-passport-lane.summary: Governor of Virginia from 2025 and, before Congress, a CIA officer alongside John Kiriakou in the Counterterrorism Center — whom he calls a perfectly nice person who would have been a middle-of-the-road Republican in the 1970s and 1980s, and whose victory speech, to his surprise, said all the right things.

the-mobile-passport-lane.title: Jason Miyares
the-mobile-passport-lane.summary: The Cuban-born Republican attorney general of Virginia whom John Kiriakou expected to be a right-wing disaster and found instead to be excellent — a judgement he says is hard for him to make about a conservative Republican, and which he repeated on the night Miyares was unceremoniously thrown out of office.

the-mobile-passport-lane.title: Joe Rogan
the-mobile-passport-lane.summary: The podcast host whose show John Kiriakou finally sat for in October 2025 — an experience that began with signing a non-disclosure agreement and ended with his verdict that Rogan is "a nice guy, very down to earth, very normal." The first thing Rogan asked, walking into the studio ten minutes late: "Hey, do you know my friend Mike Baker?" Kiriakou defends Rogan as unfairly characterized as a right-winger, and had long cited the show as the venue where Zuckerberg admitted Facebook suppressed the Hunter Biden laptop story at the FBI''s behest.

the-mobile-passport-lane.title: The Arlington house
the-mobile-passport-lane.summary: The 1,200-square-foot house John Kiriakou bought with his Pakistan overtime and danger pay for $347,000, sold two years later for $721,000, and now values at a million — the anchor of his repeated argument that his own children can never live in the Arlington, Virginia neighbourhood they grew up in.

the-mobile-passport-lane.title: The Crete blood feud
the-mobile-passport-lane.summary: John Kiriakou's explanation of the mass shooting on Crete as neither terrorism nor politics but a family feud that boiled over — an answer he gives smiling, because in his account every Greek already knows that on Crete everybody is armed and everybody is angry with somebody.

the-modified-cmu.title: The fifteen-minute call
the-modified-cmu.summary: How Marty Gottesfeld, held in the communications management unit at Terre Haute, allocated the single fifteen-minute telephone call he was permitted each week: an email to his wife, his two attorneys and John Kiriakou, with the call going to whoever answered first.

the-modified-cmu.title: The SHU loophole
the-modified-cmu.summary: John Kiriakou''s warning about the American assurances given to British courts in the Julian Assange extradition case: prosecutors promised not to place him in a communications management unit but said nothing about the Special Housing Unit, and in Kiriakou''s account a prison need only cite an overheard threat to hold a man in solitary indefinitely.

the-modified-cmu.title: The Bureau of Prisons answers to no one
the-modified-cmu.summary: John Kiriakou''s summary of what he calls the hardest lesson of his incarceration: that the Bureau of Prisons sits under the Justice Department but is accountable to nobody in practice, disregarding what sentencing judges order and what its own prosecutors have agreed, and placing prisoners wherever it chooses.

the-modified-cmu.title: The glass-eating prisoner
the-modified-cmu.summary: A case John Kiriakou cites from a 2015 New York Times Magazine investigation of federal solitary confinement: a prisoner held in the Special Housing Unit at the federal supermax in Florence, Colorado for roughly eighteen years who smashed his narrow cell window and ate the broken glass so that he would be taken to a hospital and could speak to another human being.

the-modified-cmu.title: The Kurd from Terre Haute
the-modified-cmu.summary: An Iraqi Kurd who reached the modified communications management unit at FCI Loretto after four years inside the CMU at Terre Haute, and who told John Kiriakou that the only way out was to keep your mouth shut for years.

the-modified-cmu.title: The sixty-five-cent arrangement
the-modified-cmu.summary: The deal John Kiriakou struck with the chaplain at FCI Loretto: rather than keep his 65-cents-an-hour janitor''s wage, he asked to be kept on the books while the money went to the next man on the list, and to stop coming to work — which is how he found the time to write Doing Time Like a Spy.

the-mosquito-cloud.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
the-mosquito-cloud.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

the-mosquito-cloud.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
the-mosquito-cloud.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

the-mosquito-cloud.title: Mr. Fish
the-mosquito-cloud.summary: The cover name the CIA used for Abu Zubaydah in Pakistan in 2002 — invented because the Americans would not tell their Pakistani partners who the target was, and derived from the only thing they would say about him: that he was a big fish.

the-mosquito-cloud.title: The standard operating procedure assignment
the-mosquito-cloud.summary: The task John Kiriakou says he was given on arriving in Pakistan in January 2002 — to write a standard operating procedure for taking down an al-Qaeda safe house — the legal pad he wrote it on, the high value target list it was built around, and the first raid it produced.

the-mosquito-cloud.title: Amnesty International
the-mosquito-cloud.summary: The human rights organization whose torture report forms part of John Kiriakou's core defense — the CIA's crimes were already public knowledge before he confirmed them on ABC, and the Justice Department's own declination letter said so — and the organization whose silence during his prosecution he cannot forgive. He begged Amnesty for a one-sentence statement and got a New Yorker subscription instead; it took Ai Weiwei to change their minds, and by then he was walking out of prison.

the-mosquito-cloud.title: Astrology at the CIA
the-mosquito-cloud.summary: John Kiriakou''s confirmation that astrology played a role in CIA work in the 1950s and early 1960s as part of MK-ULTRA, alongside time travel and teleportation — and his explanation for why: officials with unlimited budgets and no obligation to report to the public reasoned that there was probably nothing to it, but that if there were, it would make them a star.

the-move-to-fort-myer.title: Abraham Accords
the-move-to-fort-myer.summary: The Trump-brokered normalization deals between Israel and Gulf Arab states — in John Kiriakou's judgment "a terrible idea in the first place," a great victory for Israel and the Gulf Arabs that was "a punch in the throat to the Palestinians." He argues the Accords are how Trump meant to "solve the Middle East in a day" — by screwing the Palestinians — that Hamas read the abandonment correctly, that October 7 shattered the project, and that reviving the Accords (Saudis in, victory declared, Nobel collected) remains the organizing goal of Trump's regional policy.

the-move-to-fort-myer.title: The CIA's internal social culture
the-move-to-fort-myer.summary: John Kiriakou's one-word characterisation of the agency's internal culture — "incestuous" — describing a club for every conceivable interest, actively encouraged officer-to-officer romances, and a design intent that officers should have no need of friends or activities outside the building.

the-move-to-fort-myer.title: Death threats against Kiriakou
the-move-to-fort-myer.summary: The threats John Kiriakou has received across two decades — first after going public about the CIA torture program, when FBI advice that at least two were credible sent his family out of the country, and later in waves tied to his opposition to Gina Haspel, his remarks about Pakistan, and his advocacy on Palestine and the Epstein case.

the-move-to-fort-myer.title: Fridays at the agency
the-move-to-fort-myer.summary: John Kiriakou's observation that Fridays were always very slow at the CIA, because the Middle East weekend falls on Thursday-Friday or Friday-Saturday depending on the country and the quiet propagates back to Washington — a rhythm he says bled into the United States generally.

the-move-to-fort-myer.title: Hamid Karzai
the-move-to-fort-myer.summary: The president installed in Afghanistan after the American invasion, whom John Kiriakou uses as the standing illustration of what occupation actually buys: after twenty years and more than a trillion dollars, Karzai was ''little more than the mayor of Kabul'' — and did not control all of Kabul either. The line began as a joke among Senate Foreign Relations Committee staff, and Kiriakou used it to Senator John Kerry''s face ten years into the war.

the-move-to-fort-myer.title: Kimberly Guilfoyle in Athens
the-move-to-fort-myer.summary: John Kiriakou's assessment of Kimberly Guilfoyle's appointment as American ambassador to Greece — that she got it because Donald Trump Jr. wanted her out of the way, a manoeuvre he compares to Saddam Hussein's habit of exiling successful generals as ambassadors — and his reluctant conclusion that Greece could have done worse.

the-multi-state-permit.title: "Stefanik will not be governor"
the-multi-state-permit.summary: John Kiriakou's flat, on-the-record prediction about the New York governor's race, made against a friend he describes as irrationally conservative who insisted the contest would turn on a single issue — the right to carry a gun. Kiriakou called it the most ridiculous thing he had heard the man say, and argued that Elise Stefanik's political career is finished.

the-multi-state-permit.title: Coffee with a cabinet member
the-multi-state-permit.summary: John Kiriakou's disclosure that he had coffee with a member of the cabinet who told him to be patient about his pardon — and told him to watch what he said. He reports the meeting while stating plainly that there is nothing further he can do to make his case, and that he is not confident the outcome will be decided on justice.

the-multi-state-permit.title: The nineteen-hundred-dollar premium
the-multi-state-permit.summary: John Kiriakou''s own stake in the collapse of the Affordable Care Act subsidies: a monthly health insurance premium going from roughly $900 to $1,900. He says plainly that he cannot do it — that he does not have $1,900 a month for health insurance — and notes that the figure exceeds what the broadcast pays him.

the-multi-state-permit.title: Ed Martin and the pardon file
the-multi-state-permit.summary: The US pardon attorney whose office John Kiriakou directed supporters to write to, and the message a mutual friend brought back from him: that he was the third person that day to call about Kiriakou, that Kiriakou should relax, and that his file was literally on Martin''s desk. Kiriakou''s advice to letter-writers was to send physical mail rather than email.

the-multi-state-permit.title: Lincoln's candlelight pardons
the-multi-state-permit.summary: The historical contrast John Kiriakou drew while discussing a mass grant of clemency: stories of Abraham Lincoln staying up late into the night pardoning Civil War deserters by candlelight, on the principle that nobody should be executed for cowardice — set against a modern president who Kiriakou says has pardoned more people than anyone in American history, whenever the mood strikes him.

the-multi-state-permit.title: Pardons nobody asked for
the-multi-state-permit.summary: Two cases John Kiriakou cites of people pardoned without applying: the Binance founder, who said publicly that he had never met the president, never asked for a pardon and never applied for one; and Darryl Strawberry, a New York Mets great with tax and drug problems behind him. Kiriakou raises both while waiting, unsuccessfully, for a pardon he has actively sought for years.

the-national-guard-in-washington.title: The Lafayette Square tents
the-national-guard-in-washington.summary: The long-running protest encampment across from the White House that a New Jersey congressman wanted removed by force in 2025, and John Kiriakou's observation that tents have stood on that spot for as long as he has lived in Washington — since 1982.

the-national-guard-in-washington.title: The third-term workaround
the-national-guard-in-washington.summary: John Kiriakou's constitutional argument that Donald Trump cannot reach a third term by running as vice president and having J.D. Vance resign — because a vice president barred from the presidency cannot assume it, so the speakership takes precedence.

the-national-guard-in-washington.title: Cleaning up after Tora Bora
the-national-guard-in-washington.summary: John Kiriakou was not at Tora Bora. He arrived in Pakistan in January 2002, two months after the bombing, and says he went specifically to clean up what the battle had left behind — scavenging material, detaining the fighters too slow to get away, and mapping the smugglers'' valleys the survivors had used to cross. In his account the clean-up was necessary because the encirclement failed: bin Laden, warned by an al-Qaeda operative working as translator to the commander of Central Command, left in the dark dressed as a woman in the back of a pickup truck, and at dawn there was nobody in Tora Bora to surrender.

the-national-guard-in-washington.title: Hayden at the National Press Club
the-national-guard-in-washington.summary: John Kiriakou's account of seeing Michael Hayden, after a series of strokes, at a National Press Club event sponsored by the intelligence centre that bears his name — and the two reactions it produced in him, neither of them satisfaction alone.

the-national-guard-in-washington.title: Saddam and the journalists
the-national-guard-in-washington.summary: John Kiriakou's comparison, drawn from fifteen years working the Iraq target at the CIA, between a dictator who hated the press and did not kill it and a government that he says kills journalists deliberately and in numbers.

the-national-guard-in-washington.title: The balloon test
the-national-guard-in-washington.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that Israel had warning of the 7 October 2023 attack — that settlers along the Gaza line had reported training for months, that balloons were sent over as a probe in the days beforehand, and that nothing was done.

the-nato-expansion-promises.title: CIA attention to West Africa
the-nato-expansion-promises.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer on whether the CIA is likely to be operating in Burkina Faso: for all the years he was at the agency it cared very little about Africa and especially West Africa, but the presence of al-Qaeda and Islamic State affiliates plus the drug trade makes CIA and special forces involvement probable — and, he adds, the American public will not hear about it.

the-nato-expansion-promises.title: Muddling through
the-nato-expansion-promises.summary: An analytic term John Kiriakou says CIA analysts used all the time, and his defence of it: forecasters instinctively reach for either/or outcomes, when what actually happens most often is that the parties to a conflict muddle through and little changes over the medium term. He applies it to Ukraine, and to why he expects Russia not to use nuclear weapons.

the-nato-expansion-promises.title: The Paris rifle serial number
the-nato-expansion-promises.summary: The case John Kiriakou uses to argue that American weapons sent to Ukraine are leaking onto the black market: a rifle used to shoot and severely wound a policeman in Paris whose serial number, he says, matched a shipment of assault rifles the United States had sent to Ukraine some six months earlier.

the-nato-expansion-promises.title: CIA–FBI incompatible computer systems
the-nato-expansion-promises.summary: John Kiriakou's claim that from the CIA's founding in 1947 until 2009 the computer systems of the CIA and the FBI were not compatible with one another — no message could be sent from one to the other and no intelligence shared — which he offers both as the material substrate of the interagency hatred that helped make September 11 possible, and as the gap through which James Mitchell and Bruce Jessen were able to pass Ali Soufan's FBI debriefings of Abu Zubaydah off as the fruits of torture.

the-nato-expansion-promises.title: Drunken border guards
the-nato-expansion-promises.summary: John Kiriakou's explanation for how quiet frontiers become shooting wars — bored, drinking troops with nothing to do and no supervision — which he applies to the Thailand-Cambodia clashes, to the India-China line, and to why Vladimir Putin objects to a NATO country on his border.

the-nato-expansion-promises.title: Fake CIA résumés
the-nato-expansion-promises.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of being used as a human authenticator in the private sector: at the consulting firm he joined after leaving the CIA, every job applicant claiming agency service was sent to dinner with him, and by his count fully half of them had never set foot inside the CIA.

the-netanyahu-death-rumour.title: The house of cards theory
the-netanyahu-death-rumour.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the strategic premise behind the 2026 Iran war — that decapitating the Iranian government would bring the whole state down — and of why it fails. To win, he argues, the United States would have to destroy the entire Iranian government and military and install a puppet; Iran wins simply by surviving.

the-netanyahu-death-rumour.title: Air wars are overrated
the-netanyahu-death-rumour.summary: John Kiriakou''s summary judgement on the 2026 Iran and Lebanon campaigns, delivered as the meta-headline of the whole war: air power flattened Gaza without destroying Hamas, is bogging down against Hezbollah, and cannot produce the outcome the war requires.

the-netanyahu-death-rumour.title: Donald Trump
the-netanyahu-death-rumour.summary: 45th and 47th U.S. president. Per John Kiriakou, a man genuinely convinced he was doing right by bombing Iran, "duped" by the same Netanyahu nuclear bluff Obama once rejected — and, at the same time, the most blindly pro-Israel president in history, an admirer of autocrats who has never once criticized Vladimir Putin, and prone to gestures — from the Gulf of America to a since-abandoned "Department of War" rename — that test the edges of his actual authority.

the-netanyahu-death-rumour.title: 2026 Iran war economic shock
the-netanyahu-death-rumour.summary: John Kiriakou''s running assessment of the economic damage from the 2026 Iran war — an oil shock he says already exceeds both 1970s shocks combined, a natural-gas shock worse than the Nord Stream destruction, and a chokepoint problem that runs through fertilizer as much as fuel, since 65% of the world''s supply must transit the Strait of Hormuz. His summary: "This is an economic slowdown of choice."

the-netanyahu-death-rumour.title: Advice to an aspiring intelligence analyst
the-netanyahu-death-rumour.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer to a 21-year-old student asking what to study and what to read: pick a geographic area, become the go-to person on it, and consume everything published in the field — including the journals written by people who have never made policy.

the-netanyahu-death-rumour.title: Asian fuel reserves, 2026
the-netanyahu-death-rumour.summary: The effect of the Strait of Hormuz closure on oil-importing Asian economies as John Kiriakou described it — countries counting their remaining fuel in days rather than months, with no substitute supply available, and economies he expects simply to stop.

the-new-iraqi-flag.title: Saddam Hussein
the-new-iraqi-flag.summary: President of Iraq from 1979 until the 2003 U.S. invasion; subject of John Kiriakou's CIA portfolio from January 1990 onward, in which capacity Kiriakou became, at age 25, "Saddam Hussein's intelligence community biographer" and the analyst who briefed President George H. W. Bush in the Oval Office on the morning of the 1990 invasion of Kuwait.

the-new-iraqi-flag.title: American Psychological Association
the-new-iraqi-flag.summary: The world's largest body of psychologists, which John Kiriakou cites constantly for one devastating datum — its research shows people begin to lose their minds at around day seven without sleep, and begin to die at day nine as their organs shut down. Mitchell and Jessen were nonetheless authorized to keep chained, naked prisoners awake for up to twelve days, which is why Kiriakou insists sleep deprivation was always worse than waterboarding. The organization's own role in the interrogation program later became the subject of an internal revolt and a 500-page independent report.

the-new-iraqi-flag.title: Counterterrorism Center
the-new-iraqi-flag.summary: The CIA's Counterterrorism Center (CTC) — the unit where John Kiriakou spent the defining years of his operational career. He joined in the late 1990s as the only officer in the entire CIA fluent in both Greek and Arabic, served as chief of counterintelligence in the bin Laden unit, watched the Center swell from a few hundred employees to nearly 2,000 by September 12, 2001, and it was to CTC that he walked back down in May 2002 to refuse the torture program — the moment, he says, the CIA began to turn on him.

the-new-iraqi-flag.title: Ahmed Chalabi
the-new-iraqi-flag.summary: Iraqi exile and founder of the Iraqi National Congress; per John Kiriakou, a Shia-Kurdish con man who looted Petra Bank in Jordan of $36 million in the 1980s, was sentenced to death in absentia, was pardoned at CIA request, then pocketed $6 million in CIA seed funding for the INC and bought a Mayfair house in cash; later resurrected by Dick Cheney to feed the Pentagon fabricated WMD intelligence used to justify the 2003 invasion of Iraq.

the-new-iraqi-flag.title: Bahrain Posting (1994–1996)
the-new-iraqi-flag.summary: John Kiriakou's 1994–1996 assignment to Bahrain under U.S. State Department cover as second secretary for economic affairs — arriving with his wife Joanne and infant son Chris on August 1, 1994, into a tiny Gulf monarchy whose sectarian tensions erupted, two months later, into the first Intifada.

the-new-iraqi-flag.title: Bob Baer
the-new-iraqi-flag.summary: Former CIA case officer; per John Kiriakou, "pretty famous"; the subject of George Clooney's film Syriana; pulled out of northern Iraq by the Clinton White House in the 1990s after [NSA intercepted](/wiki/the-intercept) a communication revealing he was developing a network of sources to assassinate Saddam Hussein — National Security Adviser Sandy Berger called CIA and threatened him with a conspiracy charge.

the-new-jersey-drones.title: The Lake Michigan sightings
the-new-jersey-drones.summary: The Netflix-documented Lake Michigan case John Kiriakou raised with a UFO podcaster: National Weather Service employees who watched objects for hours on radar and by eye, the objects avoiding the frozen part of the lake, and the principal witness quitting his job.

the-new-jersey-drones.title: The pilot who saw it drink
the-new-jersey-drones.summary: The F-14 pilot John Kiriakou met at his godfather's Alexandria restaurant in the late 1970s, who described following a cigar-shaped object that submerged, stayed under and came back up — and being told by other pilots that they had all seen the same thing.

the-new-jersey-drones.title: Langley
the-new-jersey-drones.summary: The Virginia location of CIA headquarters and, in John Kiriakou''s usage, shorthand for the agency''s permanent power. It''s where he worked as the CIA''s lone Iraq-Kuwait analyst — told to start on Iraq "because nothing ever happened there" — where a cafeteria conversation invited him into the torture program, where he walked past the Kryptos sculpture every day for fifteen years without solving it, and the place agencies return to after apologizing to Congress, "where of course nothing ever changes." When a host suggested the real government of America is out in Langley and Washington''s white marble is for show, Kiriakou''s answer was: "that''s about the shape of it."

the-new-jersey-drones.title: CIA and the UFO question
the-new-jersey-drones.summary: John Kiriakou's consistent answer that UFOs and alien technology are a Pentagon matter, not a CIA one — though he says nearly every former fighter-pilot friend of his has seen something inexplicable, sometimes emerging from the ocean.

the-new-jersey-drones.title: Area 58
the-new-jersey-drones.summary: The claim John Kiriakou says was put to him by a man who presents as entirely serious and is writing a book about it: that beyond Area 51 there is an Area 58 — seven more, and that much more secret — containing an underground bunker where alien craft land, known to those involved as the embassy because it is where the United States liaises with the aliens.

the-new-jersey-drones.title: John Kiriakou
the-new-jersey-drones.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

the-new-york-times-problem.title: Julian Assange
the-new-york-times-problem.summary: Kiriakou — a 15-year friend and former WikiLeaks board member — on why Assange is a publisher owed a journalist's immunity, and a political prisoner.

the-new-york-times-problem.title: Authorized leaks
the-new-york-times-problem.summary: The distinction John Kiriakou draws between the classified information Washington releases on purpose and the classified information it prosecutes people for releasing. The mechanism is the same and the legal status is identical; what differs is whether the leak flatters the leaker. His worked example is an agency leak claiming the CIA predicted the October 2023 attack on Israel three days out — a story the CIA can then piously report to the FBI, knowing the source will never be found.

the-new-york-times-problem.title: Espionage Act
the-new-york-times-problem.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

the-new-york-times-problem.title: Eastern District of Virginia
the-new-york-times-problem.summary: The U.S. federal district covering northern Virginia — home to Langley, the Pentagon, DHS and much of the intelligence-contractor industry — which John Kiriakou calls 'the espionage court' because the Justice Department files the great majority of its national security prosecutions there and because, in his telling, no national-security defendant has ever won a case in it; Kiriakou, Julian Assange, Edward Snowden and Jeffrey Sterling were all charged there.

the-new-york-times-problem.title: Edward Snowden
the-new-york-times-problem.summary: Former NSA contractor who in 2013 disclosed the scope of U.S. [mass surveillance](/wiki/mass-surveillance), including the Section 702 collection program. Per John Kiriakou — who counts Snowden among the small group of national-security whistleblowers prosecuted under the Espionage Act — Snowden was ''stuck between two awful slippery slopes'': breaking his oath and chain of command on one side, and on the other catching something ''cut and dry against the Constitution'' that no one would act on. Kiriakou notes Snowden could not use his chain of command (as Kiriakou could not, his own chain being Jose Rodriguez), and that Judge Leonie Brinkema had reserved the Snowden case for herself before he fled the country.

the-new-york-times-problem.title: Leonie Brinkema
the-new-york-times-problem.summary: U.S. federal judge in the Eastern District of Virginia — informally the 'Espionage Court' — a Reagan appointee John Kiriakou calls "a hanging judge." Per Kiriakou, Brinkema systematically reserved all major national security cases for herself rather than allowing them to be distributed randomly among judges, and ruled in Kiriakou's case that his reason for blowing the whistle was legally irrelevant and that classified documents could not be used in his defense — effectively making it impossible to mount one.

the-newcastle-news.title: The three pro-Israel countries
the-newcastle-news.summary: A global opinion poll John Kiriakou reported in August 2025 which, on his account, found only three countries with majority pro-Israel populations — Israel, the United States, and, to his own bafflement, Nigeria — with Turkey the most anti-Israel country outside the Middle East and Greece at 74 per cent against.

the-newcastle-news.title: Abbas and the three-state problem
the-newcastle-news.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that no two-state solution is available — because there is already one state, because Mahmoud Abbas is nineteen years into a four-year term and has become a billionaire, and because East Bank, West Bank and Gaza Palestinians are so disconnected that the real arithmetic is three states, which nobody will discuss.

the-newcastle-news.title: Bulldozing the olive orchards
the-newcastle-news.summary: The sequence John Kiriakou describes preceding Israeli seizures of Palestinian land in the West Bank — olive orchards bulldozed and crops burned to make leaving easier, then the house demolished and a prefabricated one built for a settler family — and the different practice he says applies in East Jerusalem.

the-newcastle-news.title: Elbridge Gerry and the salamander
the-newcastle-news.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the origin of the word gerrymander — Elbridge Gerry, vice president and former governor of Massachusetts, drawing district boundaries to elect his friends, and Benjamin Franklin saying the shapes looked like salamanders — together with a piece of trivia from his unpublished book on cemeteries.

the-newcastle-news.title: New Castle, Pennsylvania
the-newcastle-news.summary: John Kiriakou's home town, an hour north of Pittsburgh on the edge of Amish country — a rust-belt city of roughly 40,000 to 50,000 people when he was growing up and around 18,000 to 20,000 now, whose decline he measures by the arrival of DEA and ATF field offices. It is also where, aged eight or nine and hunting salamanders in Oak Park Cemetery, he found the grave of a Medal of Honor private and acquired the lifelong interest in cemeteries that became a book.

the-newcastle-news.title: From sixteen employees to twenty thousand
the-newcastle-news.summary: John Kiriakou's support for cutting the staff of the Office of the Director of National Intelligence, on the ground that a body created after 9/11 with sixteen employees to coordinate the agencies had grown to twenty thousand.

the-night-the-snowden-story-broke.title: Edward Snowden
the-night-the-snowden-story-broke.summary: Former NSA contractor who in 2013 disclosed the scope of U.S. [mass surveillance](/wiki/mass-surveillance), including the Section 702 collection program. Per John Kiriakou — who counts Snowden among the small group of national-security whistleblowers prosecuted under the Espionage Act — Snowden was ''stuck between two awful slippery slopes'': breaking his oath and chain of command on one side, and on the other catching something ''cut and dry against the Constitution'' that no one would act on. Kiriakou notes Snowden could not use his chain of command (as Kiriakou could not, his own chain being Jose Rodriguez), and that Judge Leonie Brinkema had reserved the Snowden case for herself before he fled the country.

the-night-the-snowden-story-broke.title: Jesselyn Radack
the-night-the-snowden-story-broke.summary: American national-security attorney and former Justice Department ethics official who directs the whistleblower-defense practice at the Government Accountability Project. Per John Kiriakou, Radack was herself driven out of the Justice Department, had her law license threatened, and was placed on the no-fly list after blowing the whistle in the John Walker Lindh case; she went on to represent Kiriakou after his 2012 arrest and, separately, helped connect him to a path to reach Edward Snowden in 2013.

the-night-the-snowden-story-broke.title: Thomas Drake
the-night-the-snowden-story-broke.summary: NSA whistleblower; per John Kiriakou, the source for the statement that on the morning of September 11, 2001, NSA Director Mike Hayden told agency personnel NSA had been 'waiting for a 9/11' to implement the mass-electronic-surveillance program that NSA's founding charter forbids.

the-night-the-snowden-story-broke.title: FCI Loretto
the-night-the-snowden-story-broke.summary: U.S. Federal Correctional Institution in Loretto, Pennsylvania; the low-medium-security prison at which John Kiriakou served 23 months of a 30-month sentence following his 2013 Espionage Act–era plea deal; the originally ordered "minimum security work camp" placement was countermanded — per Kiriakou, on Brennan's direct intervention — to place him in the actual prison alongside the general population.

the-night-the-snowden-story-broke.title: The four-day-old New York Times
the-night-the-snowden-story-broke.summary: In December 2014, reading a four-day-old copy of the New York Times that prison staff had already cut articles out of, John Kiriakou found an interview in which Edward Snowden said that watching Kiriakou's case and Thomas Drake's — and seeing that neither man backed down — had inspired him to go public.

the-night-the-snowden-story-broke.title: The chilling effect of whistleblower prosecutions
the-night-the-snowden-story-broke.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that national-security prosecutions are not primarily about convictions but about deterrence — that the CIA cares about sending a message where the FBI cares about promotions, that his own case was meant to frighten anyone else considering disclosure, and that a New York Times reporter told him every national-security source the paper had went silent on the day of his arrest.

the-nine-eighty-three-premium.title: Albright in Pyongyang
the-nine-eighty-three-premium.summary: John Kiriakou's account of Bill Clinton's stated regret over the final week of his presidency — that he wished he had pursued diplomatic relations with North Korea instead of Israeli-Palestinian peace — and of Madeleine Albright being in Pyongyang rather than at the talks.

the-nine-eighty-three-premium.title: Failure to accept responsibility
the-nine-eighty-three-premium.summary: The federal sentencing enhancement that John Kiriakou says explains why 98 per cent of federal criminal cases end in a plea bargain: a defendant who refuses a deal, goes to trial and loses has time added to the sentence for failing to accept responsibility.

the-nine-eighty-three-premium.title: Nationalizing the midterms
the-nine-eighty-three-premium.summary: John Kiriakou's recurring comparison between contemporary party messaging and Newt Gingrich's 1994 Contract with America, including his advice that Speaker Mike Johnson should keep Gingrich on his couch and ask him nightly how the 1994 midterms were nationalised.

the-nine-eighty-three-premium.title: The French in the streets
the-nine-eighty-three-premium.summary: John Kiriakou's stated admiration for how quickly the French take to the streets, offered while questioning Ted Rall about the chances of violence during the 2025 French political crisis, alongside his observation that he could not recall a French president ever resigning.

the-nine-eighty-three-premium.title: Ted Rall
the-nine-eighty-three-premium.summary: American editorial cartoonist and two-time Pulitzer Prize finalist; co-host with John Kiriakou of the daily news-commentary podcast "Deprogram," launched in September 2025 and by late 2025 running every weekday morning.

the-nine-eighty-three-premium.title: The nineteen-hundred-dollar premium
the-nine-eighty-three-premium.summary: John Kiriakou''s own stake in the collapse of the Affordable Care Act subsidies: a monthly health insurance premium going from roughly $900 to $1,900. He says plainly that he cannot do it — that he does not have $1,900 a month for health insurance — and notes that the figure exceeds what the broadcast pays him.

the-nine-eleven-truth-honorarium.title: The alternative obituaries
the-nine-eleven-truth-honorarium.summary: The obituaries John Kiriakou writes for CovertAction Magazine whenever someone associated with the CIA's torture program dies — deliberately mean-spirited pieces arguing the world is better off without them — and the phone call he took from one subject's daughter, who called him a monster, and what he said back to her.

the-nine-eleven-truth-honorarium.title: The unswept roof
the-nine-eleven-truth-honorarium.summary: John Kiriakou''s two security observations after the killing of Charlie Kirk: that drone surveillance of outdoor events is cheap, easy and has no reason not to be used; and that the building the shooter is said to have fired from had been closed for renovation since April and supposedly locked up tight, yet nobody in the campus police department appears to have walked up to the roof to check.

the-nine-eleven-truth-honorarium.title: Area 58
the-nine-eleven-truth-honorarium.summary: The claim John Kiriakou says was put to him by a man who presents as entirely serious and is writing a book about it: that beyond Area 51 there is an Area 58 — seven more, and that much more secret — containing an underground bunker where alien craft land, known to those involved as the embassy because it is where the United States liaises with the aliens.

the-nine-eleven-truth-honorarium.title: Leaks come from the Pentagon
the-nine-eleven-truth-honorarium.summary: John Kiriakou''s rule of attribution for national security leaks, drawn from his own CIA experience: ninety-nine times out of a hundred the leak came from the Pentagon — which he says leaks constantly, is so gigantic that the source cannot be traced, and does not polygraph anybody. He adds the motive: somebody who opposed the operation and was overruled.

the-nine-eleven-truth-honorarium.title: Luis Elizondo
the-nine-eleven-truth-honorarium.summary: Why John Kiriakou never booked the best-known public advocate for unidentified aerial phenomena on his RT programme: viewers kept insisting Elizondo was an expert, so Kiriakou researched him and found chiefly Elizondo saying he was an expert. He says he does not know what the man is an expert on, and that it was not a fit for the show.

the-nine-eleven-truth-honorarium.title: The Australian pilot
the-nine-eleven-truth-honorarium.summary: The disappearance John Kiriakou recounts as an argument for declassification rather than as proof of anything: a pilot in his early twenties flying on 10 September 1978 who radioed that a silver cylinder was above his aircraft matching his speed exactly, said it was not an aircraft, was cut off by a loud sound of electronic interference, and was never seen again — along with the plane.

the-nine-months-on-food-stamps.title: The tax rates from Eisenhower to Nixon
the-nine-months-on-food-stamps.summary: John Kiriakou's explanation for the American wealth gap and the size of the deficit — that from Eisenhower through Nixon the top rate of tax ran upwards of seventy-five per cent and the wealthy whittled it down from there, whereas now they begin at almost nothing and whittle down from that.

the-nine-months-on-food-stamps.title: The legal bills
the-nine-months-on-food-stamps.summary: The cost of John Kiriakou's defence, which he has given variously as more than half a million dollars, approaching a million, and more than a million — a figure he treats not as a hardship but as the mechanism of the prosecution itself, since bankruptcy is what makes a defendant accept a plea.

the-nine-months-on-food-stamps.title: Abraham Accords
the-nine-months-on-food-stamps.summary: The Trump-brokered normalization deals between Israel and Gulf Arab states — in John Kiriakou's judgment "a terrible idea in the first place," a great victory for Israel and the Gulf Arabs that was "a punch in the throat to the Palestinians." He argues the Accords are how Trump meant to "solve the Middle East in a day" — by screwing the Palestinians — that Hamas read the abandonment correctly, that October 7 shattered the project, and that reviving the Accords (Saudis in, victory declared, Nobel collected) remains the organizing goal of Trump's regional policy.

the-nine-months-on-food-stamps.title: Bankruptcy and the dropped charges
the-nine-months-on-food-stamps.summary: The sequence John Kiriakou places at the centre of his case: that the espionage counts against him were dropped only after his legal fees had bankrupted him, which he presents as evidence that the government''s aim was attrition rather than conviction.

the-nine-months-on-food-stamps.title: The CIA's internal social culture
the-nine-months-on-food-stamps.summary: John Kiriakou's one-word characterisation of the agency's internal culture — "incestuous" — describing a club for every conceivable interest, actively encouraged officer-to-officer romances, and a design intent that officers should have no need of friends or activities outside the building.

the-nine-months-on-food-stamps.title: Death threats against Kiriakou
the-nine-months-on-food-stamps.summary: The threats John Kiriakou has received across two decades — first after going public about the CIA torture program, when FBI advice that at least two were credible sent his family out of the country, and later in waves tied to his opposition to Gina Haspel, his remarks about Pakistan, and his advocacy on Palestine and the Epstein case.

the-nineteen-hundred-dollar-premium.title: Three Republican congressmen
the-nineteen-hundred-dollar-premium.summary: John Kiriakou''s arithmetic for why the shutdown fight was not over when the Senate cut its deal: the Senate produced its own agreement rather than voting on the House bill, so the House has to be recalled to vote on the Senate version. Republicans needed seven Democratic senators; the House needs only three Republican congressmen to kill it — which is why he thought attention should shift to the House.

the-nineteen-hundred-dollar-premium.title: Whipping votes
the-nineteen-hundred-dollar-premium.summary: John Kiriakou''s explanation of what a party whip does and why Chuck Schumer''s failure to do it mattered: a leader who tells his caucus to vote their conscience has not whipped the vote at all. Kiriakou traces the office to a figurative whip used in the 1700s and 1800s, and calls the concession very dangerous — an admission that you have lost.

the-nineteen-hundred-dollar-premium.title: Coffee with a cabinet member
the-nineteen-hundred-dollar-premium.summary: John Kiriakou's disclosure that he had coffee with a member of the cabinet who told him to be patient about his pardon — and told him to watch what he said. He reports the meeting while stating plainly that there is nothing further he can do to make his case, and that he is not confident the outcome will be decided on justice.

the-nineteen-hundred-dollar-premium.title: The multi-state permit
the-nineteen-hundred-dollar-premium.summary: The warning John Kiriakou says he was given when he obtained his concealed carry permit: that the multi-state permit is not recognised in New York, New Jersey or Maryland, and that he should not carry a concealed weapon in any of them. He raised it while rejecting a friend''s theory that gun rights would decide a New York governor''s race.

the-nineteen-hundred-dollar-premium.title: Ed Martin and the pardon file
the-nineteen-hundred-dollar-premium.summary: The US pardon attorney whose office John Kiriakou directed supporters to write to, and the message a mutual friend brought back from him: that he was the third person that day to call about Kiriakou, that Kiriakou should relax, and that his file was literally on Martin''s desk. Kiriakou''s advice to letter-writers was to send physical mail rather than email.

the-nineteen-hundred-dollar-premium.title: Lincoln's candlelight pardons
the-nineteen-hundred-dollar-premium.summary: The historical contrast John Kiriakou drew while discussing a mass grant of clemency: stories of Abraham Lincoln staying up late into the night pardoning Civil War deserters by candlelight, on the principle that nobody should be executed for cowardice — set against a modern president who Kiriakou says has pardoned more people than anyone in American history, whenever the mood strikes him.

the-nineteen-intelligence-agencies.title: The Colonial Pipeline hack
the-nineteen-intelligence-agencies.summary: Days after the May 2021 ransomware attack that shut the East Coast's main fuel pipeline, John Kiriakou said an FBI contact told him the bureau was fairly confident the Russian government was not behind it — and turned the episode into an indictment of the National Security Agency for watching Americans instead of defending them.

the-nineteen-intelligence-agencies.title: Kermit Roosevelt and Mosaddegh
the-nineteen-intelligence-agencies.summary: The CIA officer John Kiriakou names as the man who ran the 1953 overthrow of Iran's Prime Minister Mosaddegh on behalf of British Petroleum — who called it the gravest mistake of his life in the only interview he ever gave, and who, according to the documents Kiriakou has since read in the archives, did not actually run it at all.

the-nineteen-intelligence-agencies.title: Abolish the CIA
the-nineteen-intelligence-agencies.summary: John Kiriakou's position that the CIA should be abolished because its functions are already duplicated by the other 17 U.S. intelligence agencies — analysis by the State Department, human spying by the Pentagon, technology by DARPA, NSA and the private sector.

the-nineteen-intelligence-agencies.title: Make it the blip
the-nineteen-intelligence-agencies.summary: Having stayed up all night reading law review journals and concluded that he had broken no law, John Kiriakou telephoned his attorneys at six in the morning to say he wanted to go to trial. They drove to his house, told him he was facing twelve to eighteen years, and the lawyer he respected most gave him the sentence that changed his mind.

the-nineteen-intelligence-agencies.title: Plato Kacheris
the-nineteen-intelligence-agencies.summary: A spelling variant of the name of John Kiriakou's lead defence attorney, who appears in the auto-generated transcripts as both "Kacheris" and "Cacheris". The article on him is at Plato Cacheris.

the-nineteen-intelligence-agencies.title: The four-day-old New York Times
the-nineteen-intelligence-agencies.summary: In December 2014, reading a four-day-old copy of the New York Times that prison staff had already cut articles out of, John Kiriakou found an interview in which Edward Snowden said that watching Kiriakou's case and Thomas Drake's — and seeing that neither man backed down — had inspired him to go public.

the-nordstream-patsy.title: Learning to dive in the embassy pool
the-nordstream-patsy.summary: John Kiriakou''s brief diving history, offered when the Nordstream sabotage discussion turned to the physics of deep water: lessons in the pool of the American embassy in 1991, one dive in the Red Sea at Sharm el-Sheikh in about 1992, and never again after that.

the-nordstream-patsy.title: Zaluzhny and the Nordstream prosecution
the-nordstream-patsy.summary: John Kiriakou''s reaction to German investigators drawing a bead on the former commander-in-chief of the Ukrainian armed forces over the Nordstream sabotage: that the CIA and the Pentagon now wish the case would go away, that the truth is not supposed to come out in such an operation, that Seymour Hersh probably had the kernel but not the details, and that it was very likely a joint operation. He expects somebody to go to prison.

the-nordstream-patsy.title: How the CIA kills
the-nordstream-patsy.summary: John Kiriakou''s description of the methods used when the CIA is ordered to kill someone outside a war zone: a team parachuting in miles away, stealing a car, a locks-and-picks specialist opening the door and suppressed weapons inside; a snatch into a van bound for an airport or a boat; or a brush past in a market with something poisoned — a technique he says the Russians used often and taught the Bulgarians into the early 1980s.

the-nordstream-patsy.title: Mark Polymeropoulos
the-nordstream-patsy.summary: The CIA officer John Kiriakou describes as a friend who was in his first tour when Aldrich Ames blew his identity, was brought in from the cold, and later became station chief in Moscow — an appointment Kiriakou characterises as a deliberate thumb in the Russians'' eye: the officer their spy had burned, put in charge of operations against them.

the-nordstream-patsy.title: Nine recruitments in twenty-five years
the-nordstream-patsy.summary: The conversation in which John Kiriakou''s Athens station chief, a twenty-five-year operations officer who had reached senior intelligence service level four with nine recruitments to his name, pointed out that Kiriakou had recruited five in two years — and Kiriakou''s explanation of the knack: that he could hide his disdain for a man completely while talking about whatever interested him.

the-nordstream-patsy.title: Qatari money in Egypt
the-nordstream-patsy.summary: John Kiriakou''s explanation for Qatar injecting seven and a half billion dollars into the Egyptian economy: to annoy Saudi Arabia. He describes a long, close Saudi–Egyptian relationship dating back to the mid-1960s, a terrible Qatari–Saudi one, and an Egypt happy to take the money — including the year the Egyptians thanked the Saudis for their generosity with an uninhabited island in the Red Sea.

the-north-korea-seal-team-six-operation.title: The Gang of Four and Gang of Eight
the-north-korea-seal-team-six-operation.summary: John Kiriakou''s description of how the CIA restricts notification of its most sensitive covert operations to four or eight congressional leaders, and his verdict on the practice: because a member of an intelligence committee can be an overseer without being cleared for what is being overseen, the arrangement is not oversight but, in his word, gangsterism.

the-north-korea-seal-team-six-operation.title: Aafia Siddiqui
the-north-korea-seal-team-six-operation.summary: Pakistani-American neuroscientist arrested in Afghanistan and convicted in the United States of attempting to shoot FBI agents; per John Kiriakou, who covered the arrest as a terrorism consultant for ABC News and has followed the case since, she never had a gun and never fired, the bullet holes offered as proof predated her capture, and the CIA took her three children — two later recovered, the youngest never found.

the-north-korea-seal-team-six-operation.title: The 1991 Saudi plan for Gaza
the-north-korea-seal-team-six-operation.summary: A proposal John Kiriakou says he watched Ambassador Chas Freeman float to the Saudis during his first overseas tour in 1991 — that Saudi Arabia fund a port, an airport, a desalination plant and an electrical grid in Gaza. The Saudis agreed; Israel refused outright. Kiriakou raises it because the identical arrangement resurfaced in the Israeli press more than three decades later.

the-north-korea-seal-team-six-operation.title: Clive Stafford Smith
the-north-korea-seal-team-six-operation.summary: The British human rights lawyer who represents Aafia Siddiqui, described by John Kiriakou as a man who has never charged a client a dollar in his life, lives on donations, holds an OBE for his human rights work, and represented sixty-six Guantanamo detainees — securing the release of every one of them.

the-north-korea-seal-team-six-operation.title: Hamid Karzai
the-north-korea-seal-team-six-operation.summary: The president installed in Afghanistan after the American invasion, whom John Kiriakou uses as the standing illustration of what occupation actually buys: after twenty years and more than a trillion dollars, Karzai was ''little more than the mayor of Kabul'' — and did not control all of Kabul either. The line began as a joke among Senate Foreign Relations Committee staff, and Kiriakou used it to Senator John Kerry''s face ten years into the war.

the-north-korea-seal-team-six-operation.title: Kiriakou on travel
the-north-korea-seal-team-six-operation.summary: John Kiriakou''s own ranking of the countries he has visited: Greece his favourite and, he insists, the best food anywhere; Oman the most beautiful landscape; Syria the most extraordinary civilisation; and Chile the cheapest, illustrated by a bottle of a vineyard''s locked-away reserve that cost $8.50 on his honeymoon.

the-npr-walkout.title: The pre-interview
the-npr-walkout.summary: The booking practice John Kiriakou says all the American television networks use and which he finds maddening: an invitation to appear, a quick pre-interview to establish what he thinks, and then a call a minute later saying they have decided to go a different way on the story.

the-npr-walkout.title: The convicted felon introduction
the-npr-walkout.summary: The MSNBC appearance John Kiriakou says was his last: booked opposite Daniel Ellsberg, having agreed his on-air identification in advance with the producers, he was introduced instead as "convicted felon John Kiriakou", swore on tape, and began removing his microphone.

the-npr-walkout.title: Suggested responses
the-npr-walkout.summary: The second email John Kiriakou says arrived before his first appearance on Fox News — a list of suggested responses to accompany the questions the producers had already sent him — which he ignored, and which he says was never sent again.

the-npr-walkout.title: Consulting for royal families
the-npr-walkout.summary: The work John Kiriakou says he was hired to do by members of two different royal families following the 2026 virality of his interviews — advising on ethics in their own intelligence operations — which he offers as evidence of how far the reversal in his standing had gone.

the-npr-walkout.title: "Embrace it and keep telling it"
the-npr-walkout.summary: The advice John Kiriakou says he was given days after his arrest — that he could not hide from the prosecution but had to embrace it, and had to keep telling his side of the story until it became the side of record, because the government would eventually move on to its next target.

the-npr-walkout.title: Signing with CAA
the-npr-walkout.summary: The representation John Kiriakou says followed the 2026 virality of his podcast clips: a contract with the Creative Artists Agency covering books, film, consulting and licensing, and a run of advertising approaches including one from the maker of the spectacle frames he already wore.

the-nuclear-testing-legacy.title: The Zaporizhzhia accusations
the-nuclear-testing-legacy.summary: John Kiriakou''s inverted reading of the 2023 standoff over Ukraine''s Zaporizhzhia nuclear plant: that Russia and Ukraine publicly accusing each other of planning a false-flag attack on the plant is precisely what prevented one, because ratting each other out forced the whole world to watch.

the-nuclear-testing-legacy.title: Elliott Abrams
the-nuclear-testing-legacy.summary: The Reagan-era assistant secretary of state whose 2023 appointment to a Biden administration advisory board John Kiriakou treated as proof that neoliberal and neoconservative foreign policy are the same policy with interchangeable players — a man who pleaded guilty over Iran-Contra, was pardoned, helped sell the Iraqi weapons of mass destruction case, and then served Donald Trump on Iran and Venezuela.

the-nuclear-testing-legacy.title: Frances Haugen
the-nuclear-testing-legacy.summary: The Facebook employee John Kiriakou refuses to call a whistleblower — arguing that against the legal definition, bringing to light waste, fraud, abuse, illegality or threats to public health or safety, she qualifies as a corporate spokesperson whose motive was to improve the company's bottom line, not to expose wrongdoing.

the-nuclear-testing-legacy.title: Gavin Newsom
the-nuclear-testing-legacy.summary: The California governor John Kiriakou described in 2023 as the consummate Democratic Party insider waiting his turn — a Pelosi relative who married into the Brown family, doing everything the Biden operation asked of him, including a pointless surrogate trip to Idaho, on the calculation that Joe Biden would not reach the nominating convention.

the-nuclear-testing-legacy.title: Netanyahu and the Tel Aviv police chief
the-nuclear-testing-legacy.summary: The July 2023 dismissal of Tel Aviv's police chief, which John Kiriakou identified as the moment Benjamin Netanyahu may have overstepped — arguing that the real threat to the Israeli prime minister came not from the Palestinians but from his own attempt to take over the court system, and from the strikes and demonstrations that had not subsided.

the-nypd-intelligence-post.title: The CIA under a left-wing president
the-nypd-intelligence-post.summary: John Kiriakou's two-part answer to a hypothetical about a socialist administration — that most of the CIA would carry on as though nothing had happened, because officers serve at the pleasure of the president, while elements of the directorate of operations would actively seek to remove such a president. His supporting example is John F. Kennedy.

the-nypd-intelligence-post.title: CIA operational psychologists
the-nypd-intelligence-post.summary: The branch of the CIA's psychological staff that John Kiriakou says he worked with directly as a case officer — not the analysts who profile foreign leaders, but the clinicians who vet a prospective recruit for insanity or invention, and advise an officer on exactly how hard a source can be pushed before he breaks.

the-nypd-intelligence-post.title: CIA psychological evaluations
the-nypd-intelligence-post.summary: The two kinds of psychological work John Kiriakou describes inside the CIA — the recurring psychiatric screening every officer undergoes, before employment, again three years after hiring and every five years thereafter for life; and the long-distance evaluation of foreign leaders carried out by the analytic side. The agency's clinical psychologists are split between the two, with a third group in operations advising case officers on the sources they recruit.

the-nypd-intelligence-post.title: The two officers who changed
the-nypd-intelligence-post.summary: John Kiriakou's account of two colleagues he liked as junior officers and watched become something else — one who rose to deputy director for counterterrorism at both the CIA and the FBI and whom he calls a war criminal, and one who took over the bin Laden unit and became, in his phrase, a stone cold killer.

the-nypd-intelligence-post.title: Torture and morale inside the CIA
the-nypd-intelligence-post.summary: John Kiriakou's account of what the torture programme did to morale at the CIA — a compartment so tight that nobody knew for six or eight months, a workforce that split between objectors and true believers who enjoyed the work, and a pullback by George Tenet around 2005 that ended active torture at the secret sites while leaving the prisons open and Guantanamo untouched.

the-nypd-intelligence-post.title: Bernie Kerik
the-nypd-intelligence-post.summary: Former New York Police Department Commissioner; the person who, in 2018, introduced John Kiriakou to Rudy Giuliani for what became Giuliani's $2 million pardon-extortion attempt.

the-oath-in-the-auditorium.title: Arabic and Greek
the-oath-in-the-auditorium.summary: The qualification John Kiriakou says opened the door to his transfer from CIA analysis to operations: a post in Athens wanted Greek or Arabic, and he had both — by most of his tellings the only officer in the agency who did. The chief who hired him gave the reason in one sentence: it is easier and cheaper to take a linguist and teach him operations than the other way round. The pairing also became a detection tool, since the language nobody speaks in Pakistan is Arabic.

the-oath-in-the-auditorium.title: Bankruptcy and the dropped charges
the-oath-in-the-auditorium.summary: The sequence John Kiriakou places at the centre of his case: that the espionage counts against him were dropped only after his legal fees had bankrupted him, which he presents as evidence that the government''s aim was attrition rather than conviction.

the-oath-in-the-auditorium.title: Curtailment cables
the-oath-in-the-auditorium.summary: The career-ending requests John Kiriakou says he read coming back from the CIA's black sites — officers, doctors, psychologists and nurses asking to end their tours early rather than continue to take part in the interrogation programme — and his conclusion that if that many people were objecting in classified channels, someone would surely go public.

the-oath-in-the-auditorium.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
the-oath-in-the-auditorium.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

the-oath-in-the-auditorium.title: Iraq, the training account
the-oath-in-the-auditorium.summary: The reason John Kiriakou says he was given the Iraq portfolio as a new CIA analyst in 1990 — that nothing ever happened there — and the promise that once he had learned tradecraft and the house writing style he would be moved to somewhere exciting, such as Romania.

the-oath-in-the-auditorium.title: "It''s about mitigating damage"
the-oath-in-the-auditorium.summary: The sentence John Kiriakou credits with changing his mind about going to trial — one of his own attorneys telling him that his problem was that he thought the case was about justice, when it was about mitigating damage — and the two lawyers who drove to his house after he emailed at six in the morning to refuse the plea.

the-oath-to-the-constitution.title: Amnesty International
the-oath-to-the-constitution.summary: The human rights organization whose torture report forms part of John Kiriakou's core defense — the CIA's crimes were already public knowledge before he confirmed them on ABC, and the Justice Department's own declination letter said so — and the organization whose silence during his prosecution he cannot forgive. He begged Amnesty for a one-sentence statement and got a New Yorker subscription instead; it took Ai Weiwei to change their minds, and by then he was walking out of prison.

the-oath-to-the-constitution.title: Human Rights Watch
the-oath-to-the-constitution.summary: The organization whose 2005 report that the CIA was torturing its prisoners — two years before John Kiriakou''s ABC interview — anchors his defense that he confirmed rather than revealed the program. It is also the middle link in the chain that ended in his arrest: working with the John Adams Project, Human Rights Watch employed the investigator who carried a classified name from journalist Matthew Cole to the Guantánamo defense attorneys, and when the FBI walked that chain backwards it arrived at Kiriakou''s door.

the-oath-to-the-constitution.title: Dead drop
the-oath-to-the-constitution.summary: The classic tradecraft technique of passing material through a hidden location rather than a meeting. Per John Kiriakou, the hard part is not the drop but everything around it — in a sophisticated counterintelligence environment, merely identifying a viable site is very difficult, and the drop itself is bracketed by surveillance detection routes and a signal mark that can turn a single document into a sixteen-hour workday. It was the only element of clandestine training he struggled with, and the only exercise he was ever criticized for.

the-oath-to-the-constitution.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
the-oath-to-the-constitution.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

the-oath-to-the-constitution.title: Ray McGovern
the-oath-to-the-constitution.summary: Former senior CIA analyst turned antiwar dissident, and one of John Kiriakou's closest friends — "like a brother to me." Kiriakou began working at the CIA on the Monday after the Friday McGovern retired in January 1990, so the two never overlapped inside; they became comrades in the whistleblower world instead. McGovern coined the "MICIMATT" framing Kiriakou often borrows, went into Putin's office with Oliver Stone for a 40-minute meeting, and — per Kiriakou — believes 9/11 was a conspiracy, a view Kiriakou affectionately notes is far from his own.

the-oath-to-the-constitution.title: Prepublication review
the-oath-to-the-constitution.summary: The CIA clearance process every former officer's writing must pass through, and John Kiriakou's account of what it did to his eighth book — five weeks instead of two, a missed publisher's deadline, six pages redacted as classified that he says the agency had itself declassified a decade earlier, and an appeal route requiring another ninety days.

the-obama-recruitment-thesis.title: The September 10th country
the-obama-recruitment-thesis.summary: John Kiriakou''s formulation of what he wants back, and his ledger on the two wars: he never supported the invasion of Iraq, which he calls a war of choice and of family revenge, and he did support the war in Afghanistan until al-Qaeda was defeated in 2003, after which everything became nation building. He assigns the destruction of the pre-attack country to George W. Bush and Barack Obama equally.

the-obama-recruitment-thesis.title: False flags are too hard
the-obama-recruitment-thesis.summary: John Kiriakou''s practical objection to the idea that governments routinely stage false flag operations: they exist, and at the operational level the CIA used them constantly, but the bigger the operation the harder it is to run — too many moving parts, too many people who must buy into the conspiracy, and too much incompetence in government to keep any of it straight. He couples the objection with the observation that a government which is not transparent has no standing to complain about public suspicion.

the-obama-recruitment-thesis.title: SEAL Team Six attrition
the-obama-recruitment-thesis.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer to the claim that the Navy SEALs who killed Osama bin Laden have since been killed off: the dead came from the broader unit rather than the raid party, SEAL Team Six numbers several hundred men rather than the dozen or so people imagine, and losing a high number of them to accidents and combat is, in his phrase, very sadly common.

the-obama-recruitment-thesis.title: Bin Laden health rumors
the-obama-recruitment-thesis.summary: John Kiriakou's dismissal of the claim that Osama bin Laden died years before the 2011 raid. He says the CIA received a steady stream of medical rumours about him — kidney failure, dialysis in a cave, a spinal disorder — none of which turned out to be true, and that bin Laden was in fine health apart from arthritis and a hip problem until the day he died.

the-obama-recruitment-thesis.title: Fake CIA résumés
