the-obama-recruitment-thesis.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of being used as a human authenticator in the private sector: at the consulting firm he joined after leaving the CIA, every job applicant claiming agency service was sent to dinner with him, and by his count fully half of them had never set foot inside the CIA.

the-obama-recruitment-thesis.title: The 1968 waterboarding conviction
the-obama-recruitment-thesis.summary: The precedent John Kiriakou uses to dispose of the argument that waterboarding was legally uncertain after 2002: a January 1968 Washington Post front page showing an American soldier waterboarding a North Vietnamese prisoner, an investigation ordered by Defense Secretary Robert McNamara, and the soldier''s arrest, conviction for torture and imprisonment. The law, Kiriakou points out, never changed in between.

the-obliteration-claim.title: Iranian underground missile silos
the-obliteration-claim.summary: John Kiriakou''s assessment of why the American and Israeli air campaign against Iran could not disarm it: the missile silos are buried under featureless desert with nothing on the surface to mark them, and an air force cannot destroy what it cannot locate. He measures the problem against twenty years of failure against Taliban fighters who had only rifles and caves.

the-obliteration-claim.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
the-obliteration-claim.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

the-obliteration-claim.title: Donald Trump
the-obliteration-claim.summary: 45th and 47th U.S. president. Per John Kiriakou, a man genuinely convinced he was doing right by bombing Iran, "duped" by the same Netanyahu nuclear bluff Obama once rejected — and, at the same time, the most blindly pro-Israel president in history, an admirer of autocrats who has never once criticized Vladimir Putin, and prone to gestures — from the Gulf of America to a since-abandoned "Department of War" rename — that test the edges of his actual authority.

the-obliteration-claim.title: Cost of the 2026 Iran war
the-obliteration-claim.summary: The daily cost of the 2026 Iran war as John Kiriakou reported it — between two and three billion dollars a day, per Axios — and the comparison he draws with the Gulf War, when a president was rendered speechless by a figure of one hundred million dollars a day.

the-obliteration-claim.title: Itamar Ben-Gvir
the-obliteration-claim.summary: Israel's far-right Minister of National Security; John Kiriakou cites him as a convicted hate-crime felon placed in charge of security in Gaza and the West Bank over his victims, blames his insistence that any attack would come from the West Bank for diverting forces before October 7, and cites the death-penalty law passed under his portfolio for Palestinian detainees as the first reinstatement of capital punishment in Israel since it was abolished in 1956, excepting only the execution of Adolf Eichmann.

the-obliteration-claim.title: Jared Kushner
the-obliteration-claim.summary: Donald Trump's son-in-law and senior adviser during the first Trump administration, and the first person inside the White House to open a channel on John Kiriakou's pardon. After Trump saw Kiriakou on Tucker Carlson's show, Kushner's attorney called Kiriakou's attorney Bruce Fein; the meeting that followed produced a request for a one-page paper — three-quarters of it Kiriakou's story, the last quarter an argument for how pardoning him would help Trump get re-elected — after which Kiriakou never heard back.

the-october-2025-poll-of-american-jews.title: Clock Tower X
the-october-2025-poll-of-american-jews.summary: The American firm John Kiriakou described as being paid $6 million by the Israeli government to make ChatGPT more pro-Israeli by generating content, gaming algorithms and managing AI frameworks.

the-october-2025-poll-of-american-jews.title: The Armenian podcasters
the-october-2025-poll-of-american-jews.summary: Three naturalised Armenian-American podcasters who, independently of one another, told John Kiriakou during a week in Los Angeles that the Turks were outspending and out-lobbying Armenia in Washington — and his reply as a dual Greek citizen.

the-october-2025-poll-of-american-jews.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
the-october-2025-poll-of-american-jews.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

the-october-2025-poll-of-american-jews.title: AIPAC
the-october-2025-poll-of-american-jews.summary: The American Israel Public Affairs Committee — the U.S. political organization that, in John Kiriakou's framing, ought to be registered as a foreign-lobbying entity but is not, and that wields decisive electoral power against U.S. elected officials who express support for Palestinian human rights.

the-october-2025-poll-of-american-jews.title: Abdul El-Sayed
the-october-2025-poll-of-american-jews.summary: Physician and Democratic Socialists of America-backed candidate in Michigan's 2026 Democratic Senate primary. John Kiriakou, who discloses a $100 donation to the campaign, presents him as the test case for whether the electability argument still works for establishment Democrats.

the-october-2025-poll-of-american-jews.title: AIPAC and foreign-agent registration
the-october-2025-poll-of-american-jews.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that AIPAC is the only organization of its kind exempt from registering under the Foreign Agents Registration Act — set against his own experience around 2008, when a contract worth five or six thousand dollars to write four op-eds praising the Abu Dhabi Chamber of Commerce obliged him to register as a foreign agent.

the-october-8-gaza-cars.title: October 7 attack
the-october-8-gaza-cars.summary: John Kiriakou's analysis of the October 7, 2023 Hamas attack as a policy failure, not an intelligence one — Israel was warned repeatedly, but Itamar Ben-Gvir diverted response forces to the West Bank, and Kiriakou believes Israel welcomed a pretext for overwhelming retaliation.

the-october-8-gaza-cars.title: Abraham Accords
the-october-8-gaza-cars.summary: The Trump-brokered normalization deals between Israel and Gulf Arab states — in John Kiriakou's judgment "a terrible idea in the first place," a great victory for Israel and the Gulf Arabs that was "a punch in the throat to the Palestinians." He argues the Accords are how Trump meant to "solve the Middle East in a day" — by screwing the Palestinians — that Hamas read the abandonment correctly, that October 7 shattered the project, and that reviving the Accords (Saudis in, victory declared, Nobel collected) remains the organizing goal of Trump's regional policy.

the-october-8-gaza-cars.title: The Arab states and the Gaza war
the-october-8-gaza-cars.summary: John Kiriakou's country-by-country reading of how the Arab governments positioned themselves after October 2023 — the Gulf states ranked by their fear of Iran, Jordan caught between its border and its population, Egypt sealing Rafah to prevent a repeat of earlier refugee flows — and his conclusion that every one of them is calculating damage to itself first and the Palestinians second.

the-october-8-gaza-cars.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
the-october-8-gaza-cars.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

the-october-8-gaza-cars.title: Bezalel Smotrich
the-october-8-gaza-cars.summary: Israeli far-right minister whom John Kiriakou, alongside Itamar Ben-Gvir, blames for leaving Israel unprepared on October 7 by insisting any attack would come from the West Bank rather than Gaza.

the-october-8-gaza-cars.title: The 1991 Saudi plan for Gaza
the-october-8-gaza-cars.summary: A proposal John Kiriakou says he watched Ambassador Chas Freeman float to the Saudis during his first overseas tour in 1991 — that Saudi Arabia fund a port, an airport, a desalination plant and an electrical grid in Gaza. The Saudis agreed; Israel refused outright. Kiriakou raises it because the identical arrangement resurfaced in the Israeli press more than three decades later.

the-office-of-security-arrangement.title: The Los Angeles Times Iran op-ed
the-office-of-security-arrangement.summary: An op-ed on Iranian foreign policy in Latin America that John Kiriakou was commissioned to write about six months after blowing the whistle on the torture programme. He had barely begun when the CIA general counsel's office telephoned to warn him off the subject — a call he could not explain for fourteen years, and which he now attributes to his own wife rather than to a source inside the newspaper.

the-office-of-security-arrangement.title: The concealed carry advertisements
the-office-of-security-arrangement.summary: The anecdote John Kiriakou offers about surveillance capitalism: a private telephone conversation in which a friend told him he needed a concealed carry permit, followed within the hour by a Facebook feed consisting entirely of advertisements for concealed carry classes.

the-office-of-security-arrangement.title: Abu Omar rendition
the-office-of-security-arrangement.summary: The CIA's kidnapping of a Milan cleric, Abu Omar, who was sent to Egypt to be tortured; John Kiriakou calls it a case that ought to be taught at the CIA as how not to run a rendition, and it is what ultimately sent him to prison, after he confirmed a former colleague's surname to a journalist claiming to be writing a book about it.

the-office-of-security-arrangement.title: The declination letter
the-office-of-security-arrangement.summary: The letter the Justice Department sent John Kiriakou's attorneys in December 2008 declining to prosecute him, on the grounds that the torture allegations were already public through human rights organizations and that it is illegal to classify a crime — and the celebration dinner that was followed three weeks later by Barack Obama's inauguration.

the-office-of-security-arrangement.title: The rogue officer remark
the-office-of-security-arrangement.summary: The answer President George W. Bush shouted to a reporter on his way to the helicopter — that if there was torture, it was the work of a rogue CIA officer — which John Kiriakou has said convinced him he was about to be made the scapegoat, and which led him to accept Brian Ross's interview offer.

the-office-of-security-arrangement.title: Arabic and Greek
the-office-of-security-arrangement.summary: The qualification John Kiriakou says opened the door to his transfer from CIA analysis to operations: a post in Athens wanted Greek or Arabic, and he had both — by most of his tellings the only officer in the agency who did. The chief who hired him gave the reason in one sentence: it is easier and cheaper to take a linguist and teach him operations than the other way round. The pairing also became a detection tool, since the language nobody speaks in Pakistan is Arabic.

the-official-secrets-act-comparison.title: The 2017 European tour
the-official-secrets-act-comparison.summary: In May 2017 John Kiriakou spent a week speaking about national security whistleblowing in Iceland, Germany, Luxembourg, Belgium and Ireland, addressing the German Parliament and sharing panels with serving European ministers — an audience he contrasted sharply with his reception in the United States, and one he found newly willing to break with Washington because it was, in his word, panic-stricken about Donald Trump.

the-official-secrets-act-comparison.title: Domingo's television
the-official-secrets-act-comparison.summary: John Kiriakou has used the television rooms at FCI Loretto as his sharpest illustration of prison segregation: sets owned by racial blocs since a riot in the 1990s, a seat in front of one costing fourteen dollars, and one set left tuned to Law & Order every morning because a man named Domingo had paid four hundred dollars for it and had been gone for years.

the-official-secrets-act-comparison.title: Mental health as a disciplinary problem
the-official-secrets-act-comparison.summary: John Kiriakou has said that before his own prosecution he never gave five seconds of thought to the American prison system, and that living inside it showed him a broken one — in particular a system in which mental health is treated as a disciplinary problem rather than a medical one.

the-official-secrets-act-comparison.title: The Ai Weiwei encounter in Berlin
the-official-secrets-act-comparison.summary: John Kiriakou met the artist Ai Weiwei by pure chance on a Berlin street while dragging a suitcase to the airport after a board meeting — an encounter that led to a tour of Ai Weiwei's studio and a signed iPhone case bearing the Lego portrait the artist had made of him for an exhibition at Alcatraz.

the-official-secrets-act-comparison.title: The Alcatraz walkthrough
the-official-secrets-act-comparison.summary: On his very first day of house arrest, the day Ai Weiwei's political-prisoner exhibition closed at Alcatraz, the San Francisco gallery that had helped stage the show telephoned John Kiriakou and walked him around the entire exhibition on an iPad so that he could see his own portrait and the ceramic flowers filling the sinks of the solitary confinement cells.

the-official-secrets-act-comparison.title: The attribution problem in the DNC hack
the-official-secrets-act-comparison.summary: Asked in 2017 whether he had any confidence in the intelligence community's assessments of Russian interference, John Kiriakou said he had none — objecting that no one had ever defined what was meant by hacking, that the published evidence told the public nothing, and that an agency asking to be taken at its word should not be.

the-open-letter-to-edward-snowden.title: Arianna Huffington
the-open-letter-to-edward-snowden.summary: Founder of the Huffington Post and the accidental amplifier who turned John Kiriakou's prison writing into a phenomenon. His first Letter from Loretto went to his attorney, then to a friend running Firedoglake who — unknown to Kiriakou — was close to Huffington; she plastered it as a banner headline and it drew over a million hits, bringing CNN and 60 Minutes to the prison gates. She published his open letter to Snowden, ran the diesel-therapy exposé that triggered the "hands off John Kiriakou" campaign, and came to Loretto herself with two young journalists.

the-open-letter-to-edward-snowden.title: Brad Birkenfeld
the-open-letter-to-edward-snowden.summary: The UBS banking whistleblower, who was prosecuted and imprisoned before winning a $104 million settlement from the Treasury Department and spending it on the legal defence of other whistleblowers. John Kiriakou uses him as the measure of the gap between financial and national-security whistleblowing, and names him among the visitors whose devices he believes were copied at the Ecuadorian embassy in London.

the-open-letter-to-edward-snowden.title: FCI Loretto
the-open-letter-to-edward-snowden.summary: U.S. Federal Correctional Institution in Loretto, Pennsylvania; the low-medium-security prison at which John Kiriakou served 23 months of a 30-month sentence following his 2013 Espionage Act–era plea deal; the originally ordered "minimum security work camp" placement was countermanded — per Kiriakou, on Brennan's direct intervention — to place him in the actual prison alongside the general population.

the-open-letter-to-edward-snowden.title: Snowden did not defect
the-open-letter-to-edward-snowden.summary: John Kiriakou's two corrections to the treatment of Edward Snowden at Tulsi Gabbard's 2025 confirmation hearing — that "traitor" has a constitutional definition Snowden does not meet, there having been no declaration of war since December 1941, and that Snowden did not defect to Russia but was stranded in a Moscow transit lounge en route to Ecuador when John Kerry revoked his passport.

the-open-letter-to-edward-snowden.title: The legal bills
the-open-letter-to-edward-snowden.summary: The cost of John Kiriakou's defence, which he has given variously as more than half a million dollars, approaching a million, and more than a million — a figure he treats not as a hardship but as the mechanism of the prosecution itself, since bankruptcy is what makes a defendant accept a plea.

the-open-letter-to-edward-snowden.title: The seventh Espionage Act defendant
the-open-letter-to-edward-snowden.summary: The case John Kiriakou cited two days before his own sentencing to correct the count of Espionage Act prosecutions brought under Barack Obama — a translator at the American naval base in Bahrain who had just been charged, making seven, against three in the whole history of the United States before 2009.

the-operational-test.title: Running into former sources
the-operational-test.summary: John Kiriakou has twice met people he once ran as agents by accident, years after leaving the CIA — once at an airport and once in the street — and both times they came to him with a bear hug. One of them was astonished to discover he spoke English.

the-operational-test.title: Sources are not traitors
the-operational-test.summary: Asked whether CIA officers privately regarded their recruited agents as traitors and held them in contempt, John Kiriakou answered that they did not — because the officers believed they were the good guys, and a recruited source had become one of them.

the-operational-test.title: The Greek colonel and China
the-operational-test.summary: The arrest of a Greek colonel assigned to NATO on charges of spying for China — a case John Kiriakou calls highly unusual not because espionage arrests are rare in Greece, but because they are almost always for Russia, and which he says shows the Chinese have begun caring about NATO communications.

the-operational-test.title: The density of spies in Washington
the-operational-test.summary: John Kiriakou's claim that there are more spies in Washington DC than anywhere else in the world, that the FBI's counterintelligence division does nothing but try to root them out, and that the job cannot be finished short of becoming North Korea.

the-operational-test.title: Prince Andrew
the-operational-test.summary: British royal, now Andrew Mountbatten Windsor, named repeatedly by John Kiriakou as one of the un-recruitable principals whose access made Jeffrey Epstein valuable to a foreign intelligence service. Kiriakou has asked why Andrew was never charged over conduct with minors, reads his alleged provision of classified Ministry of Defence documents to Epstein as evidence of espionage rather than vanity — and expects him to face no criminal consequence at all, because the statute of limitations has run.

the-operational-test.title: Qat in Yemen
the-operational-test.summary: The afternoon shrub-chewing habit of Yemen, and the special dispensation the CIA had to issue so that its officers could take part in it. John Kiriakou explains that no source could be developed in a qat-chewing country by an officer who would not chew.

the-orange-jumpsuits.title: The woman escorted from the White House
the-orange-jumpsuits.summary: Before John Kiriakou spoke to ABC News, someone else had already blown the whistle on the CIA's secret prisons — a woman at the White House whom he respected deeply, who was escorted out of the building, stripped of her badge and told never to come back, and who has always insisted it was not her.

the-orange-jumpsuits.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
the-orange-jumpsuits.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

the-orange-jumpsuits.title: Do what is right or what is easy
the-orange-jumpsuits.summary: Asked what he would tell the boy who once told his father he wanted to be a spy, John Kiriakou said he would tell him to always tell the truth and do the right thing — arguing that everyone already knows in their gut the difference between right and wrong, and that the only real question is whether they then do what is right or what is easy.

the-orange-jumpsuits.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
the-orange-jumpsuits.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

the-orange-jumpsuits.title: Guantanamo Bay
the-orange-jumpsuits.summary: U.S. naval base in Cuba; site of CIA detention operations during the post-9/11 enhanced interrogation program; briefly served by John Kiriakou as interim Chief during the summer of 2002.

the-orange-jumpsuits.title: National Whistleblower Day
the-orange-jumpsuits.summary: John Kiriakou has called National Whistleblower Day an event no whistleblower or supporter should miss — held every year in the Kennedy Caucus Room, which he describes as not merely the biggest room on Capitol Hill but the most historic single room anywhere on it, having hosted every major Senate hearing from the sinking of the Titanic to Watergate and Iran-Contra.

the-orb-off-yemen.title: The density of spies in Washington
the-orb-off-yemen.summary: John Kiriakou's claim that there are more spies in Washington DC than anywhere else in the world, that the FBI's counterintelligence division does nothing but try to root them out, and that the job cannot be finished short of becoming North Korea.

the-orb-off-yemen.title: The Greek colonel and China
the-orb-off-yemen.summary: The arrest of a Greek colonel assigned to NATO on charges of spying for China — a case John Kiriakou calls highly unusual not because espionage arrests are rare in Greece, but because they are almost always for Russia, and which he says shows the Chinese have begun caring about NATO communications.

the-orb-off-yemen.title: Kiriakou's UFO sighting
the-orb-off-yemen.summary: The object John Kiriakou and his father watched from the side of Route 60 in Amish country, western Pennsylvania, on a Friday night in 1981 — three flashes of white light, then a silent orange trapezoid hanging a couple of thousand feet up, which left at a speed he had never seen before or since.

the-orb-off-yemen.title: Prince Andrew
the-orb-off-yemen.summary: British royal, now Andrew Mountbatten Windsor, named repeatedly by John Kiriakou as one of the un-recruitable principals whose access made Jeffrey Epstein valuable to a foreign intelligence service. Kiriakou has asked why Andrew was never charged over conduct with minors, reads his alleged provision of classified Ministry of Defence documents to Epstein as evidence of espionage rather than vanity — and expects him to face no criminal consequence at all, because the statute of limitations has run.

the-orb-off-yemen.title: Running into former sources
the-orb-off-yemen.summary: John Kiriakou has twice met people he once ran as agents by accident, years after leaving the CIA — once at an airport and once in the street — and both times they came to him with a bear hug. One of them was astonished to discover he spoke English.

the-orb-off-yemen.title: Sources are not traitors
the-orb-off-yemen.summary: Asked whether CIA officers privately regarded their recruited agents as traitors and held them in contempt, John Kiriakou answered that they did not — because the officers believed they were the good guys, and a recruited source had become one of them.

the-order-of-the-whistleblower-process.title: "Only Fox came to my defence"
the-order-of-the-whistleblower-process.summary: John Kiriakou's account of how the American networks labelled him — MSNBC never using the word whistleblower and calling him a CIA leaker, CNN taking a year to change, and Fox, he says, being the only outlet that defended him at the time — offered as evidence that the label a case receives is drawn along political lines rather than factual ones.

the-order-of-the-whistleblower-process.title: Espionage Act
the-order-of-the-whistleblower-process.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

the-order-of-the-whistleblower-process.title: The Ukraine call whistleblower
the-order-of-the-whistleblower-process.summary: The intelligence officer whose complaint triggered Donald Trump's first impeachment, and whom John Kiriakou declines to accept as a whistleblower at all — not on partisan grounds but on procedural ones. The complaint went to the Justice Department rather than the oversight committees, and its prose, he says, is lawyers' prose rather than the uniform CIA analytic style every analyst is trained into. He is nonetheless emphatic that naming the man was indefensible.

the-order-of-the-whistleblower-process.title: Whistleblower Protection Act
the-order-of-the-whistleblower-process.summary: United States statute protecting federal employees who disclose government wrongdoing from retaliation; per John Kiriakou, national security employees — including those at the CIA, Pentagon, FBI, NSA, DEA, White House, and Homeland Security — are explicitly exempt from its protections, leaving them with no legally safe avenue to report illegal activity within their agencies.

the-order-of-the-whistleblower-process.title: Chuck Grassley
the-order-of-the-whistleblower-process.summary: The senior senator from Iowa, and in John Kiriakou's assessment the one member of Congress who has taken whistleblower protection seriously as a legislative project — a count he has variously put at one finger, at two names, and at four out of 535. Grassley wrote the whistleblower protection statutes, speaks every year at the National Whistleblower Day luncheon, and is the name Kiriakou gives prospective whistleblowers as the single friendly ear on Capitol Hill. Kiriakou's personal verdict is colder — Grassley, he has said, never did anything for him.

the-order-of-the-whistleblower-process.title: The 1996 campaign contribution disclosure
the-order-of-the-whistleblower-process.summary: The whistleblower disclosure John Kiriakou made inside the CIA in 1996, sixteen years before the one that ruined him. Serving overseas, he learned of a very large illegal contribution to the Dole presidential campaign, reported it to the CIA Inspector General, and watched the system work exactly as written: the IG investigated, found the information credible, and referred it to the Federal Election Commission. He offers it as the control case against which he judges every later complaint.

the-oreilly-exclusivity-rule.title: The Trump weave
the-oreilly-exclusivity-rule.summary: The name a speakers' bureau gave to John Kiriakou's platform manner — starting one story, turning off into another, and coming back to finish the first — a habit he attributes to never writing anything down before he walks to the podium.

the-oreilly-exclusivity-rule.title: The Piers Morgan panel
the-oreilly-exclusivity-rule.summary: The televised debate John Kiriakou returns to most often — two against two, with Scott Horton and himself on one side and Alan Dershowitz and a senior former Israeli official on the other. Kiriakou set out his position on Hamas, October 7th and Gaza, and Piers Morgan told him at the end that he had come around and agreed. On a second appearance from the same panel he argued that Jeffrey Epstein was an Israeli access agent, provoked Dershowitz — Epstein's own attorney — into an interruption Kiriakou considers self-defeating, and got an unbothered "who knows?" from the Israeli.

the-oreilly-exclusivity-rule.title: Cleaning up after Tora Bora
the-oreilly-exclusivity-rule.summary: John Kiriakou was not at Tora Bora. He arrived in Pakistan in January 2002, two months after the bombing, and says he went specifically to clean up what the battle had left behind — scavenging material, detaining the fighters too slow to get away, and mapping the smugglers'' valleys the survivors had used to cross. In his account the clean-up was necessary because the encirclement failed: bin Laden, warned by an al-Qaeda operative working as translator to the commander of Central Command, left in the dark dressed as a woman in the back of a pickup truck, and at dawn there was nobody in Tora Bora to surrender.

the-oreilly-exclusivity-rule.title: Hayden at the National Press Club
the-oreilly-exclusivity-rule.summary: John Kiriakou's account of seeing Michael Hayden, after a series of strokes, at a National Press Club event sponsored by the intelligence centre that bears his name — and the two reactions it produced in him, neither of them satisfaction alone.

the-oreilly-exclusivity-rule.title: Saddam and the journalists
the-oreilly-exclusivity-rule.summary: John Kiriakou's comparison, drawn from fifteen years working the Iraq target at the CIA, between a dictator who hated the press and did not kill it and a government that he says kills journalists deliberately and in numbers.

the-oreilly-exclusivity-rule.title: The balloon test
the-oreilly-exclusivity-rule.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that Israel had warning of the 7 October 2023 attack — that settlers along the Gaza line had reported training for months, that balloons were sent over as a probe in the days beforehand, and that nothing was done.

the-other-five-percent.title: "Every Israeli I ever knew"
the-other-five-percent.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the attitudes he encountered among Israelis he knew professionally and socially — that almost every one of them wanted the Palestinians killed or exiled — together with his description of a sensibility he says is palpable walking around Tel Aviv and Jerusalem, and his immediate self-correction when he overstated the claim.

the-other-five-percent.title: Palestine House
the-other-five-percent.summary: The Washington, DC meeting space and gallery for pro-Palestinian human rights groups, artists and musicians that John Kiriakou describes as newly opened on Capitol Hill — housed in a building donated by a Lebanese-American property developer, running programming several nights a week, and headed by Miko Peled.

the-other-five-percent.title: Bigger than the Russian embassy
the-other-five-percent.summary: Why American embassies in small, strategically unimportant countries are enormous: the answer John Kiriakou says he was given by a station chief on one of his first CIA trips — that the building had to be bigger than the Soviet one across town. He describes American embassies in Africa as "absolutely gigantic" for that reason alone, and calls the US embassy in Cairo an enormous facility matched by an equally enormous Russian one.

the-other-five-percent.title: Declare victory and go home
the-other-five-percent.summary: The exit John Kiriakou prescribed for Israel in Gaza: turn the territory back to the United Nations, declare Hamas destroyed, declare victory, then engage the Saudis on the Abraham Accords and negotiate a deal later. His reasoning was that nothing remained to destroy, that killing as many people as possible is not a viable policy, and that Israel had no other way out.

the-other-five-percent.title: "Do not ever attempt to contact me again"
the-other-five-percent.summary: The reply John Kiriakou says he received from John Kerry, then Secretary of State, after emailing him privately in the days before reporting to prison to beg that his sentence be commuted. Kiriakou had worked closely with Kerry for two and a half years; the one-line answer, sent after two or three days, was the last he ever heard from him.

the-other-five-percent.title: Sanctions and the Russian adjustment
the-other-five-percent.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of why sanctions stopped hurting Russia: Sergey Lavrov''s admission that Moscow was caught off balance by the speed of the American response, the three or four weeks that shock lasted, and the discovery that Russia did not need the United States or its banking system once India and China agreed to buy whatever oil it had.

the-outer-banks-seasonal-workers.title: The visa reciprocity rule
the-outer-banks-seasonal-workers.summary: The bilateral arrangement John Kiriakou describes by which each country sets the price of its own visas and the other matches it — and his conclusion that a United States policy of refusing visas to applicants who are overweight or who have cancer or diabetes must, under the same rule, license every other country to weigh American travellers at the door.

the-outer-banks-seasonal-workers.title: Jesse Jackson
the-outer-banks-seasonal-workers.summary: American civil rights leader and two-time presidential candidate whose hospitalisation in November 2025 John Kiriakou discussed at length — explaining progressive supranuclear palsy, the condition Jackson was diagnosed with two years after Parkinson''s, from his own family''s experience of the same disease, and giving a poor prognosis.

the-outer-banks-seasonal-workers.title: Kiriakou's acting career
the-outer-banks-seasonal-workers.summary: The film role John Kiriakou took in 2025 after Tyrel Ventura wrote a part for him — a former CIA officer running a billionaire's security detail — which he shot in Mexico for a month and which made him, at sixty-odd, a member of the Screen Actors Guild.

the-outer-banks-seasonal-workers.title: The conscientious objectors book
the-outer-banks-seasonal-workers.summary: A long out-of-print volume of interviews with American conscientious objectors, published around 1972 and given to John Kiriakou from the personal collection of an objector he was friendly with in prison — a book whose harrowing accounts of objectors sent to real federal prisons rather than to camps convinced him that refusing to serve was often more physically dangerous than serving.

the-outer-banks-seasonal-workers.title: The Egyptian intelligence chief''s son
the-outer-banks-seasonal-workers.summary: A coincidence John Kiriakou reported from Oxford, Ohio in November 2025: his own son''s marketing professor turned out to be the son of Muhammad Farag, head of the Egyptian intelligence service some thirty-five years earlier, whom Kiriakou had met in Cairo when the professor was a boy of seven or eight — and the two families went out to dinner together.

the-outer-banks-seasonal-workers.title: The Giuliani–Epstein emails
the-outer-banks-seasonal-workers.summary: A cache of correspondence that a former chief of business development for Giuliani Partners told John Kiriakou she holds — thousands of pages of emails between Rudy Giuliani and Jeffrey Epstein, which she says she has offered to news organisations and to congressional committees and which nobody wanted, together with her claim that a second British prince and other former heads of state are implicated.

the-oz-analogy.title: The Club Fed myth
the-oz-analogy.summary: John Kiriakou''s standing objection to the phrase ''Club Fed'' and the idea that federal prison is a soft landing for white-collar convicts: there is no such thing, he says, no golf and no gardening, only an institution designed to humiliate and emasculate and to make a man count the days.

the-oz-analogy.title: Truck and Cat in the Hat
the-oz-analogy.summary: An incident at FCI Loretto in which John Kiriakou, told by one prisoner that another had called him a rat, invented a slur he knew would enrage a convicted serial killer — who beat the accuser badly enough to require a helicopter medevac. Kiriakou presents it as a live application of two rules he says he learned at the CIA: let others do your dirty work, and admit nothing, deny everything, make counter-accusations.

the-oz-analogy.title: The Italians at Loretto
the-oz-analogy.summary: The mafia contingent at FCI Loretto — men with last names like Gambino, Bonanno, Lucchese, Genovese, DeCavalcante — who adopted John Kiriakou in his second year, largely because he hated the FBI as much as they did. The cast included the boss of the Gambino family (in on a dozen-plus murder counts, the man who replaced John Gotti), Pete the Bonanno captain across the hall who asked why he sat "with those Nazi retards," and a crooked guard on the payroll delivering pork loin and fresh mozzarella. When the FBI later came to Kiriakou's door asking him to inform on Pete, his answer was "get off my property."

the-oz-analogy.title: Prison racial segregation
the-oz-analogy.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the rigid racial and ethnic division of American prisons — a cafeteria split like the 1950s South — and his argument that segregating and hardening inmates for years, then releasing them with no skills, makes society less safe.

the-oz-analogy.title: Supervised release travel restrictions
the-oz-analogy.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the years of court supervision that followed his prison term, in which a judge refused him permission to travel abroad to give paid speeches while he was expected to earn a living, and in which he had to surrender his passport on returning from every trip he was allowed to take.

the-oz-analogy.title: The culling of friendships
the-oz-analogy.summary: John Kiriakou''s description of what happened to his private life after he confirmed the CIA''s torture program: friends and even family members began walking away from him before any charge was filed, a process he came to regard, oddly, as a culling exercise that dispatched phonies and left the people who genuinely loved him.

the-palestinian-middle-class-in-the-gulf.title: Medea Benjamin's broken arm
the-palestinian-middle-class-in-the-gulf.summary: John Kiriakou's account of Egyptian authorities breaking the arm of the CODEPINK co-founder Medea Benjamin while arresting her, as she attempted to reach the Rafah crossing to escort a food shipment into Gaza — an incident he offers as a measure of what Egyptian policing of the border looks like in practice.

the-palestinian-middle-class-in-the-gulf.title: Expulsion of Palestinians from the Gulf
the-palestinian-middle-class-in-the-gulf.summary: The mass expulsion of the Palestinian professional class from the Gulf Arab states in the aftermath of Iraq's 1990 invasion of Kuwait, which John Kiriakou witnessed from the region and identifies as the reason Gulf governments are willing to normalise relations with Israel. He dates the Kuwaiti decision to a wedding he attended weeks after the liberation, says Western and Egyptian pressure stopped it being total, and has repeatedly said he has never understood the grudge himself.

the-palestinian-middle-class-in-the-gulf.title: The call about rebuilding Gaza
the-palestinian-middle-class-in-the-gulf.summary: A telephone call John Kiriakou says he received on 7 November 2025 from a contact in the Israeli government, reporting that Israel had approached private American companies to redevelop Gaza — not Gazan Palestinians — and that the widely reported Saudi-administration plan was newspaper talk rather than anything the Israeli military was discussing. His conclusion: ''the fix is already in.''

the-palestinian-middle-class-in-the-gulf.title: The synagogue in Damascus
the-palestinian-middle-class-in-the-gulf.summary: John Kiriakou's account of visiting an operating, practising Jewish synagogue in Damascus, and the forecast he attaches to it — that he would not bet money on the safety of Christians, Jews, Alawites or any other religious minority in Syria under the present government or any other, whatever else is said of Bashar al-Assad.

the-palestinian-middle-class-in-the-gulf.title: Bahrain Posting (1994–1996)
the-palestinian-middle-class-in-the-gulf.summary: John Kiriakou's 1994–1996 assignment to Bahrain under U.S. State Department cover as second secretary for economic affairs — arriving with his wife Joanne and infant son Chris on August 1, 1994, into a tiny Gulf monarchy whose sectarian tensions erupted, two months later, into the first Intifada.

the-palestinian-middle-class-in-the-gulf.title: Qatari money in Egypt
the-palestinian-middle-class-in-the-gulf.summary: John Kiriakou''s explanation for Qatar injecting seven and a half billion dollars into the Egyptian economy: to annoy Saudi Arabia. He describes a long, close Saudi–Egyptian relationship dating back to the mid-1960s, a terrible Qatari–Saudi one, and an Egypt happy to take the money — including the year the Egyptians thanked the Saudis for their generosity with an uninhabited island in the Red Sea.

the-panda-card.title: Europe without Russian gas
the-panda-card.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that Europe needs Russia more than Russia needs Europe, made from what he has physically encountered rather than from figures. Speaking in Nottingham in 2025 he found the concert hall so cold that the audience complained, and was told by the manager that the venue could not afford to heat itself without Russian gas. He reports the same of homes in Britain, Germany and Greece, where American gas is simply too expensive to substitute.

the-panda-card.title: Nuclear war is winnable
the-panda-card.summary: The belief John Kiriakou says is held by a real faction in both Ukraine and the United States: that a nuclear exchange can be survived and won. He traces the American version to Pat Buchanan''s 1992 presidential campaign — we come out from our caves and continue the fight — and reconstructs the Ukrainian version as a bet that if Russia went nuclear, the American, British and French arsenals would answer. He calls the reasoning insanity and thinks it is nonetheless being done.

the-panda-card.title: The scholar-in-residence pipeline
the-panda-card.summary: John Kiriakou's description of retired CIA operations officers taking scholar-in-residence posts at universities and teaching literature courses that function, by their own account, as a recruitment funnel — students enrol knowing the instructor is a former officer and hoping for help getting in.

the-panda-card.title: Operation Spiderweb
the-panda-card.summary: The Ukrainian drone attack on Russia's strategic bomber fleet in June 2025, which John Kiriakou calls a brilliant operation and — against Volodymyr Zelensky's account — one Ukraine could not have run alone. Eighteen months of preparation, drones smuggled across eleven time zones by human couriers, and command from Kyiv all required outside help, he argues; and Donald Trump's uncharacteristic public silence afterwards is his evidence that Washington was in on it.

the-panda-card.title: Recruiting foreign students
the-panda-card.summary: The long-horizon intelligence argument for admitting foreign students to American universities — that a doctoral student in the hard sciences recruited on campus goes home to a weapons programme as an asset already in place — and John Kiriakou's view that collapsing enrolment is an operational loss nobody at the top is thinking about.

the-panda-card.title: Ted Rall
the-panda-card.summary: American editorial cartoonist and two-time Pulitzer Prize finalist; co-host with John Kiriakou of the daily news-commentary podcast "Deprogram," launched in September 2025 and by late 2025 running every weekday morning.

the-pardoned-january-6th-defendants.title: Abigail Spanberger
the-pardoned-january-6th-defendants.summary: Governor of Virginia from 2025 and, before Congress, a CIA officer alongside John Kiriakou in the Counterterrorism Center — whom he calls a perfectly nice person who would have been a middle-of-the-road Republican in the 1970s and 1980s, and whose victory speech, to his surprise, said all the right things.

the-pardoned-january-6th-defendants.title: Destroying the Dome of the Rock
the-pardoned-january-6th-defendants.summary: John Kiriakou's agreement with Tucker Carlson that a Zionist extremist plan to demolish the Dome of the Rock and build a third temple would be the event that starts the Third World War — and his additional prediction that it would also be the beginning of the end for the Israeli government and all of its support.

the-pardoned-january-6th-defendants.title: Donald Trump
the-pardoned-january-6th-defendants.summary: 45th and 47th U.S. president. Per John Kiriakou, a man genuinely convinced he was doing right by bombing Iran, "duped" by the same Netanyahu nuclear bluff Obama once rejected — and, at the same time, the most blindly pro-Israel president in history, an admirer of autocrats who has never once criticized Vladimir Putin, and prone to gestures — from the Gulf of America to a since-abandoned "Department of War" rename — that test the edges of his actual authority.

the-pardoned-january-6th-defendants.title: Jason Miyares
the-pardoned-january-6th-defendants.summary: The Cuban-born Republican attorney general of Virginia whom John Kiriakou expected to be a right-wing disaster and found instead to be excellent — a judgement he says is hard for him to make about a conservative Republican, and which he repeated on the night Miyares was unceremoniously thrown out of office.

the-pardoned-january-6th-defendants.title: Joe Rogan
the-pardoned-january-6th-defendants.summary: The podcast host whose show John Kiriakou finally sat for in October 2025 — an experience that began with signing a non-disclosure agreement and ended with his verdict that Rogan is "a nice guy, very down to earth, very normal." The first thing Rogan asked, walking into the studio ten minutes late: "Hey, do you know my friend Mike Baker?" Kiriakou defends Rogan as unfairly characterized as a right-winger, and had long cited the show as the venue where Zuckerberg admitted Facebook suppressed the Hunter Biden laptop story at the FBI''s behest.

the-pardoned-january-6th-defendants.title: No declaration of war since 1941
the-pardoned-january-6th-defendants.summary: John Kiriakou's answer to whether Congress will assert its authority over military action against Venezuela — an unqualified no, resting on the fact that the last declaration of war was on 8 December 1941 and that even the Gulf War was fought on an authorisation to use force rather than a declaration.

the-paris-rifle-serial-number.title: The secret Sahel appropriations
the-paris-rifle-serial-number.summary: John Kiriakou's complaint that the United States is quietly pumping billions of dollars into Niger, Mali, Burkina Faso, Guinea-Conakry and Guinea-Bissau — spending he says is supposed to be a big secret, addresses a French problem rather than an American one, and which American taxpayers have a right to know about and to judge.

the-paris-rifle-serial-number.title: The African diplomat's remark
the-paris-rifle-serial-number.summary: The line John Kiriakou says an African diplomat gave him at a White House summit, and which he uses to explain Chinese success on the continent: you Americans always offer us democracy and military aid, and the Chinese offer us food and new roads. Kiriakou traces the consequence to Chinese bases across Africa and a State Department that did not see it coming.

the-paris-rifle-serial-number.title: CIA attention to West Africa
the-paris-rifle-serial-number.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer on whether the CIA is likely to be operating in Burkina Faso: for all the years he was at the agency it cared very little about Africa and especially West Africa, but the presence of al-Qaeda and Islamic State affiliates plus the drug trade makes CIA and special forces involvement probable — and, he adds, the American public will not hear about it.

the-paris-rifle-serial-number.title: Muddling through
the-paris-rifle-serial-number.summary: An analytic term John Kiriakou says CIA analysts used all the time, and his defence of it: forecasters instinctively reach for either/or outcomes, when what actually happens most often is that the parties to a conflict muddle through and little changes over the medium term. He applies it to Ukraine, and to why he expects Russia not to use nuclear weapons.

the-paris-rifle-serial-number.title: The NATO expansion promises
the-paris-rifle-serial-number.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the assurances American presidents gave Russia that NATO would not expand to its borders or admit Ukraine — promises he says were made repeatedly, broken repeatedly, and, in his blunt formulation, never meant. He couples the account with an equally explicit statement that he opposes the Russian invasion of Ukraine.

the-paris-rifle-serial-number.title: The Hersh publishing collapse
the-paris-rifle-serial-number.summary: John Kiriakou's account of Seymour Hersh's disappearance from mainstream print — from the London Review of Books in 2017, which Hersh told him was already the only outlet that would take his work, to Substack five years later. Kiriakou, who helped give Hersh an award for integrity in intelligence, presents the trajectory as a measure of how bad conditions for American journalism have become.

the-parthenon-view-condo.title: The cats of Athens
the-parthenon-view-condo.summary: John Kiriakou's explanation for why there are no rats in Athens — the enormous population of street cats that tourists feed at restaurant tables — offered as a contrast to Washington, where he says the rats are the size of small dogs.

the-parthenon-view-condo.title: The Greek brain drain
the-parthenon-view-condo.summary: The editorial John Kiriakou read in a Greek newspaper tracking where educated Greeks emigrate — the United States, Britain, Germany, Australia — and the line he took from it: that when fifteen hundred Greeks with master''s degrees, law degrees, MDs and PhDs move to Turkey for better opportunity, you know you are finished.

the-parthenon-view-condo.title: Washington, rat central
the-parthenon-view-condo.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the rat population of Washington, D.C. — one he saw the size of a small dog, and the night he drove to Southeast Washington at quarter to two in the morning to collect two eighteen-year-olds whose van had been stolen, and found them panicking not about the theft but about the rats eating a sleeping homeless man's toes.

the-parthenon-view-condo.title: Astrology at the CIA
the-parthenon-view-condo.summary: John Kiriakou''s confirmation that astrology played a role in CIA work in the 1950s and early 1960s as part of MK-ULTRA, alongside time travel and teleportation — and his explanation for why: officials with unlimited budgets and no obligation to report to the public reasoned that there was probably nothing to it, but that if there were, it would make them a star.

the-parthenon-view-condo.title: Carrying passports in Washington
the-parthenon-view-condo.summary: John Kiriakou's report in September 2025 that people in Washington had begun carrying their passports for fear of being scooped up by immigration enforcement — alongside the case of an American symphony violinist held for three weeks, and his own belief that ethnic profiling violates the Fourth Amendment.

the-parthenon-view-condo.title: "Christians are suckers"
the-parthenon-view-condo.summary: John Kiriakou's explanation for how a president who does not go to church, has no spiritual adviser and could not name a line of scripture can push school prayer without cost — that he thinks most Christians are suckers, an assessment Kiriakou says he hates to make and believes anyway.

the-penn-state-textbooks.title: The Rashid family
the-penn-state-textbooks.summary: The dynasty that controlled the Arabian peninsula before the House of Saud, and John Kiriakou''s account of meeting one of its descendants while stationed in Saudi Arabia — a man who told him the kingdom had once been theirs.

the-penn-state-textbooks.title: The Emir of Bahrain''s verdict
the-penn-state-textbooks.summary: The judgement John Kiriakou says the Emir of Bahrain delivered to him at his beach house — that George H. W. Bush was the last American president to give the Arabs a fair shake — and Kiriakou''s reasons for agreeing with it.

the-penn-state-textbooks.title: Bill Clinton
the-penn-state-textbooks.summary: 42nd U.S. president whom John Kiriakou describes as wholly disinterested in intelligence — briefed by the CIA only twice in eight years, with Vice President Al Gore taking the daily briefing instead and relaying anything important.

the-penn-state-textbooks.title: Church Committee
the-penn-state-textbooks.summary: U.S. Senate investigative committee operating in 1975–1976 that examined domestic intelligence abuses by the CIA, FBI, and NSA; per John Kiriakou, the Church Committee — alongside the concurrent Pike Committee in the House — was the last genuine moment of legislative oversight over the intelligence community, born of a national consensus that government had gone dangerously off course. Its work led to the creation of the permanent Senate Select Committee on Intelligence, which Kiriakou says ceased to function as real oversight roughly seven years after its founding.

the-penn-state-textbooks.title: Fifty new crimes a year
the-penn-state-textbooks.summary: John Kiriakou''s argument that the United States has become a carceral country by legislative accretion — fifty newly created federal crimes every year for two decades, on top of five per cent of the world''s population holding twenty-five per cent of its prisoners.

the-penn-state-textbooks.title: How Kiriakou went armed in Athens
the-penn-state-textbooks.summary: The load John Kiriakou carried every day during his Athens tour — a 9mm in a tear-away waist pack with three magazines, a snub-nosed .38 on his ankle, about 47 rounds in total, and a buck knife his boss handed him on his first day *"just in case things go to shit"*.

the-pentagon-and-the-pakistani-arsenal.title: The Imran Khan request
the-pentagon-and-the-pakistani-arsenal.summary: John Kiriakou's account of Imran Khan's dealings with the United States — that while still prime minister Khan warned the Americans he would start blaming them for everything, drawing the reply that they were blamed for everything anyway; and that after his arrest he got word out asking for help, which produced an approach to his former wife Jemima Goldsmith and a refusal from Pakistan.

the-pentagon-and-the-pakistani-arsenal.title: A.Q. Khan
the-pentagon-and-the-pakistani-arsenal.summary: Pakistani nuclear scientist and the architect of Pakistan's bomb, who ran a black-market proliferation network that, per John Kiriakou, smuggled nuclear material and technology to North Korea and Libya. Kiriakou says the U.S. could easily have killed him — 'we knew where he lived, we knew how he spent his day' — but the Saudi government insisted the U.S. leave him alone, which Kiriakou calls a grave mistake and speculates was because the Saudis were pursuing their own nuclear capability. Khan was eventually pardoned by Pervez Musharraf, ending all investigations.

the-pentagon-and-the-pakistani-arsenal.title: ISI
the-pentagon-and-the-pakistani-arsenal.summary: Pakistan''s Inter-Services Intelligence agency, the CIA''s principal counterterrorism partner during John Kiriakou''s 2002 posting. Per Kiriakou, there were effectively ''two parallel ISIs'': one made up of Sandhurst-trained, FBI-schooled professionals he calls heroes who risked their lives on counterterrorism, and another — ''people with long beards who gave you a dirty look'' — who had created Kashmiri terrorist groups like Jaish-e-Mohammed and were attacking Shia mosques and Americans. Because of this, the CIA never told the ISI the identity of high-value targets, referring to Abu Zubaydah only as ''Mr. Fish.''

the-pentagon-and-the-pakistani-arsenal.title: Strategic patience
the-pentagon-and-the-pakistani-arsenal.summary: The doctrine John Kiriakou uses to describe a state that absorbs an attack and answers with a response calibrated to be smaller than the provocation — Iran's telegraphed drone waves against Israel, and India's refusal to escalate against Pakistan, which he says kept a war from becoming a nuclear one.

the-pentagon-and-the-pakistani-arsenal.title: Another Bentley
the-pentagon-and-the-pakistani-arsenal.summary: The scene John Kiriakou describes from a meeting with Benazir Bhutto during her exile in Dubai — a five-million-dollar palace on the Gulf, a car pulling up outside, and Bhutto saying that so help her God, if her husband had come home with another Bentley she would kill him — which Kiriakou uses as his measure of Pakistani political corruption.

the-pentagon-and-the-pakistani-arsenal.title: Pervez Musharraf
the-pentagon-and-the-pakistani-arsenal.summary: Pakistani general and military dictator who ruled during John Kiriakou's 2002 posting as CIA chief of counterterrorism operations in Pakistan. Per Kiriakou, the United States 'essentially just purchased Musharraf,' paying tens of millions in cash to the ISI and meeting him several times a week — and in return 'he would let us do whatever we wanted.' Kiriakou says Musharraf, fearing the nuclear arsenal could fall into terrorist hands, unofficially turned control of Pakistan's nuclear weapons over to the Pentagon. Musharraf later pardoned proliferator A.Q. Khan.

the-pentagon-budget-reversal.title: The ideological circle
the-pentagon-budget-reversal.summary: John Kiriakou's long-held claim that the political spectrum is not a straight line from left to right but a circle, on which the two ends meet — and that in the case of MAGA and the progressive left, the point where they meet is war and peace.

the-pentagon-budget-reversal.title: "Whatever DARPA''s working on"
the-pentagon-budget-reversal.summary: John Kiriakou's standing rejoinder to the defence of American research spending — that the secrecy of DARPA's projects is the indictment rather than the excuse, because whatever it is working on should have been developed twenty years ago and be in the field today, and should be, in his phrase, Star Trek kind of stuff.

the-pentagon-budget-reversal.title: Sitting on my father's lap
the-pentagon-budget-reversal.summary: John Kiriakou's earliest political memory — being four or five years old, watching buildings burn on television, and asking his father why, to be told that some bad men had killed Martin Luther King and Robert Kennedy and people were very upset — which he uses as his benchmark for how divided the United States has become.

the-pentagon-budget-reversal.title: The Hyundai robots
the-pentagon-budget-reversal.summary: The South Korean robots John Kiriakou cites as the answer to a promise the Pentagon has been making for decades — long-life batteries solved by a Hyundai subsidiary, robots ready to go to market that can get into a self-driving car and do the grocery shopping, and his question of why DARPA has not managed it.

the-pentagon-budget-reversal.title: "Beyond Your Dreams"
the-pentagon-budget-reversal.summary: The gloss a host gave John Kiriakou on his first trip to China when he asked what the beautiful car with the BYD badge was — and the answer he got when he asked why he had never heard of it, which was that the United States is the only country where they are not sold.

the-pentagon-budget-reversal.title: Carving up Iran
the-pentagon-budget-reversal.summary: The Israeli end goal John Kiriakou says has been discussed with increasingly less discretion — dividing Iran into five small rump countries including Balochistan, Arabistan and Kurdistan, on the reasoning that small states are more easily controlled — and which he expects Israel will eventually try to get Donald Trump to carry out.

the-pentagon-injury-figures.title: The Pentagon press contract
the-pentagon-injury-figures.summary: A contract John Kiriakou says every news outlet covering the Pentagon was required to sign in mid-2026, undertaking to publish no information that had not been officially provided by the department. Almost nobody signed: by his count Newsmax, One America News, a Turkish paper, a Hungarian paper and a couple of bloggers.

the-pentagon-injury-figures.title: 2026 Iran war
the-pentagon-injury-figures.summary: The open-ended American and Israeli war against Iran that John Kiriakou tracked week by week on his own show — a conflict he says was sold as three weeks, ran into its fifth month, achieved every decapitation objective it set, and continued anyway. His grade for it is a D, and his forecast is a Truth Social post declaring victory while nothing changes.

the-pentagon-injury-figures.title: Acts of Service
the-pentagon-injury-figures.summary: The Doja Cat song that John Kiriakou discovered, through a Cameo request, had become the soundtrack to a genre of montage about him. The clips set to it use footage from before his weight loss — he lost 77 pounds by 2007 and 115 pounds from 2022 — and he says he cannot watch them.

the-pentagon-injury-figures.title: Kiriakou on soccer
the-pentagon-injury-figures.summary: John Kiriakou's public reversal on football, a sport he had dismissed since his teens on the strength of a Saturday Night Live joke about a match between Yemen and Saudi Arabia being decided early by an insurmountable one-nil lead. Watching the 2026 World Cup, he concluded he had been wrong.

the-pentagon-injury-figures.title: Strait of Hormuz
the-pentagon-injury-figures.summary: The shipping chokepoint at the mouth of the Persian Gulf, and the centre of gravity of the 2026 Iran war in John Kiriakou''s account — a strait whose only navigable deep water lies on the Iranian side of the maritime border, closed not by Iran''s aggression but, as he insists, by the American and Israeli attack that provoked it: "The Strait of Hormuz was open. We''re the ones that forced the closure."

the-pentagon-injury-figures.title: The 2026 World Cup final
the-pentagon-injury-figures.summary: Spain''s victory over Argentina in a final John Kiriakou described as dirty on the losers'' part and notable for a red card, and the awkwardness that followed: Donald Trump, who had exerted considerable influence over FIFA and whose country was hosting, had to present the trophy to a nation whose leadership he had spent weeks publicly attacking. The Spanish press cropped him out of the celebration photographs.

the-pentagon-press-contract.title: The Pentagon injury figures
the-pentagon-press-contract.summary: John Kiriakou''s explanation of why the Pentagon was able to withhold news of dozens of American casualties in the Iran war: not secrecy law, but the absence of any statute requiring disclosure. In his framing Congress is asleep at the switch, having never passed such a law, so the department reports nothing it is not obliged to report.

the-pentagon-press-contract.title: Remains of the Day (book)
the-pentagon-press-contract.summary: John Kiriakou's book, announced for publication by Simon and Schuster in March 2026, billed as a definitive guide to the historic cemeteries of Washington DC and the first in a planned series; the second installment will cover the Mafia graves of New York City.

the-pentagon-press-contract.title: I should have gone to film school
the-pentagon-press-contract.summary: One of the two answers John Kiriakou gives when asked whether, knowing what he knows now, he would join the CIA again. He is candid that he has answered the question differently over the years — sometimes yes, because the agency can only be changed from inside, and sometimes that he should have gone to film school, which he insists is not a joke.

the-pentagon-press-contract.title: Kiriakou's writing process
the-pentagon-press-contract.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of how he actually writes — books in waves over roughly nine months, op-eds in forty-five minutes to an hour once an idea has sat for a few days, and a habit of getting up at two in the morning to write one because he cannot sleep. He wrote *Remains of the Day* in six weeks during COVID, losing whole evenings to it: "I look at the clock again, it''s 2:00 in the morning. I''m like, oh my god, what happened?"

the-pentagon-press-contract.title: The beer and the couch
the-pentagon-press-contract.summary: What John Kiriakou says he did with the CIA''s spot-assessment training after leaving the agency. He still sizes up strangers within moments of meeting them, but the question is no longer what they can do for him: it is whether he would want to have a beer with them, and whether, if he were down on his luck, they would let him sleep on their couch.

the-pentagon-press-contract.title: The Kiriakou children
the-pentagon-press-contract.summary: The five children of John Kiriakou, and what they do — a bond trader, an elementary school music teacher, a college junior studying supply chain economics, a sophomore who has not yet decided, and a fourteen-year-old. None of them, to their father's declared relief, has any interest in the CIA.

the-perplexity-subscription.title: Joe Rogan
the-perplexity-subscription.summary: The podcast host whose show John Kiriakou finally sat for in October 2025 — an experience that began with signing a non-disclosure agreement and ended with his verdict that Rogan is "a nice guy, very down to earth, very normal." The first thing Rogan asked, walking into the studio ten minutes late: "Hey, do you know my friend Mike Baker?" Kiriakou defends Rogan as unfairly characterized as a right-winger, and had long cited the show as the venue where Zuckerberg admitted Facebook suppressed the Hunter Biden laptop story at the FBI''s behest.

the-perplexity-subscription.title: The manager's ranking
the-perplexity-subscription.summary: John Kiriakou's answer to a viewer who asked whether he would ever appear on Joe Rogan's show alongside Mike Baker — that his new manager, who represents some very senior people, told him he is more highly sought after than Baker is, so there is no reason to legitimise him.

the-perplexity-subscription.title: Abigail Spanberger
the-perplexity-subscription.summary: Governor of Virginia from 2025 and, before Congress, a CIA officer alongside John Kiriakou in the Counterterrorism Center — whom he calls a perfectly nice person who would have been a middle-of-the-road Republican in the 1970s and 1980s, and whose victory speech, to his surprise, said all the right things.

the-perplexity-subscription.title: Jason Miyares
the-perplexity-subscription.summary: The Cuban-born Republican attorney general of Virginia whom John Kiriakou expected to be a right-wing disaster and found instead to be excellent — a judgement he says is hard for him to make about a conservative Republican, and which he repeated on the night Miyares was unceremoniously thrown out of office.

the-perplexity-subscription.title: The Arlington house
the-perplexity-subscription.summary: The 1,200-square-foot house John Kiriakou bought with his Pakistan overtime and danger pay for $347,000, sold two years later for $721,000, and now values at a million — the anchor of his repeated argument that his own children can never live in the Arlington, Virginia neighbourhood they grew up in.

the-perplexity-subscription.title: The Crete blood feud
the-perplexity-subscription.summary: John Kiriakou's explanation of the mass shooting on Crete as neither terrorism nor politics but a family feud that boiled over — an answer he gives smiling, because in his account every Greek already knows that on Crete everybody is armed and everybody is angry with somebody.

the-persona-in-the-first-week.title: The professor in the visiting room
the-persona-in-the-first-week.summary: John Kiriakou has credited the idea for his prison memoir to a university professor who visited him at FCI Loretto, listened to him tell stories across a visiting-room table, and told him that although the whole thing was by its nature depressing, the stories were good and there were lessons in them, and that he should write a book.

the-persona-in-the-first-week.title: Domingo's television
the-persona-in-the-first-week.summary: John Kiriakou has used the television rooms at FCI Loretto as his sharpest illustration of prison segregation: sets owned by racial blocs since a riot in the 1990s, a seat in front of one costing fourteen dollars, and one set left tuned to Law & Order every morning because a man named Domingo had paid four hundred dollars for it and had been gone for years.

the-persona-in-the-first-week.title: The CO who wanted the CIA
the-persona-in-the-first-week.summary: A young correctional officer at FCI Loretto once pulled John Kiriakou aside and asked in a whisper how to get into the CIA; when Kiriakou told him he was bright and did not belong there, the man explained that both his parents and his grandfather had been correctional officers and that his wife would never leave Loretto, a town of twelve hundred people.

the-persona-in-the-first-week.title: The psychology chairman's letter
the-persona-in-the-first-week.summary: Unsure how to deal with the child molesters who made up a large share of the population at FCI Loretto, John Kiriakou wrote to a professor friend for advice; the reply, from the chairman of a university psychology department, told him that pedophiles cannot be cured and that they talk about their crimes constantly because reliving them is itself gratifying.

the-persona-in-the-first-week.title: Mental health as a disciplinary problem
the-persona-in-the-first-week.summary: John Kiriakou has said that before his own prosecution he never gave five seconds of thought to the American prison system, and that living inside it showed him a broken one — in particular a system in which mental health is treated as a disciplinary problem rather than a medical one.

the-persona-in-the-first-week.title: The case against work camps
the-persona-in-the-first-week.summary: John Kiriakou, who asked to serve his own sentence at a minimum-security work camp and was sent to the prison across the street instead, came out of prison arguing that the camps should not exist at all — and, in the same breath, that some prisoners are dangerous enough that prisons certainly should.

the-pezeshkian-invitation.title: The Iranian interest section
the-pezeshkian-invitation.summary: How John Kiriakou obtained a visa to travel to Iran in the absence of diplomatic relations — through an Iranian interest section housed in the Pakistani embassy in Washington — and the argument he draws from it, that withholding recognition only makes diplomats' work harder.

the-pezeshkian-invitation.title: Amnesty International
the-pezeshkian-invitation.summary: The human rights organization whose torture report forms part of John Kiriakou's core defense — the CIA's crimes were already public knowledge before he confirmed them on ABC, and the Justice Department's own declination letter said so — and the organization whose silence during his prosecution he cannot forgive. He begged Amnesty for a one-sentence statement and got a New Yorker subscription instead; it took Ai Weiwei to change their minds, and by then he was walking out of prison.

the-pezeshkian-invitation.title: I want my fifty bucks back
the-pezeshkian-invitation.summary: What John Kiriakou says he shouted at John Fetterman from ten rows back at an Ohio State football game — and his explanation, as a Pennsylvanian furious about the senator, of why Fetterman keeps his seat anyway.

the-pezeshkian-invitation.title: Ian Henderson
the-pezeshkian-invitation.summary: The British colonial police officer who ran Bahrain's intelligence service during John Kiriakou's posting there — a man Kiriakou says even the heir presumptive to the throne was afraid to name aloud, and whom Kiriakou, seated at the crown prince's table at a dinner for George H. W. Bush, mistook for a corpse.

the-pezeshkian-invitation.title: Ibrahim Traoré
the-pezeshkian-invitation.summary: John Kiriakou's assessment of the military ruler of Burkina Faso — a young officer who took power promising a return to democracy, and who in Kiriakou's account has grown increasingly irrational, criminalising homosexuality, abolishing the electoral commission and moving to expel foreigners.

the-pezeshkian-invitation.title: Kimberly Guilfoyle in Athens
the-pezeshkian-invitation.summary: John Kiriakou's assessment of Kimberly Guilfoyle's appointment as American ambassador to Greece — that she got it because Donald Trump Jr. wanted her out of the way, a manoeuvre he compares to Saddam Hussein's habit of exiling successful generals as ambassadors — and his reluctant conclusion that Greece could have done worse.

the-philosophy-class.title: Whistleblower psychology
the-philosophy-class.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of what distinguishes people who come forward: psychological studies showing whistleblowers hold a much more sharply defined sense of right and wrong than the general population, weighed against his own claim that there is no whistleblower who has not contemplated suicide in the period after going public.

the-philosophy-class.title: David Petraeus
the-philosophy-class.summary: Retired U.S. Army general and director of the CIA who, per John Kiriakou, confirmed the names of ten covert CIA operatives to his biographer and girlfriend and was never criminally charged — a contrast Kiriakou cites repeatedly as proof that his own prosecution under the Intelligence Identities Protection Act was selective. Kiriakou''s explanation for the disparity: Petraeus had not blown the whistle on the torture program and embarrassed the agency.

the-philosophy-class.title: Senate Torture Report
the-philosophy-class.summary: The December 2014 executive summary of the U.S. Senate Select Committee on Intelligence's study of the CIA's post-9/11 detention and interrogation program; the first public disclosure of techniques including rectal feeding with hummus, sexual assault with broomsticks, and prolonged sleep deprivation.

the-philosophy-class.title: The HardTalk interview
the-philosophy-class.summary: The first interview John Kiriakou gave after leaving prison, on the BBC programme he describes as hard-hitting and mean-spirited, in which a host pressing him to show remorse drew the formulation he has used ever since: it is not a crime to reveal a crime.

the-philosophy-class.title: Abu Zubaydah
the-philosophy-class.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

the-philosophy-class.title: Ali Soufan
the-philosophy-class.summary: FBI special agent who handled Abu Zubaydah immediately after his March 2002 capture; through patient, respectful interrogation produced the only actionable intelligence ever obtained from the detainee, including the first identification of "Mukhtar" as Khalid Sheikh Mohammed.

the-piers-morgan-panel.title: Piers Morgan
the-piers-morgan-panel.summary: British broadcaster whose panel show became John Kiriakou's 2025 sparring ring — "the equivalent of a WWE Smackdown with Alan Dershowitz<Cite s="2026-06-27-deep-focus-report-john-kiriakou-on-iran-endless-wars-and-u-s-fo" t="9:18" />." Paired with Scott Horton against Dershowitz and former Mossad chief Moshe Yaalon, Kiriakou said on air that Israel spies on the United States and that Jeffrey Epstein was an Israeli access agent, drawing a chuckle from the general and the claim that spying stopped when Pollard was caught — "General, with all due respect, that's just simply not true." Morgan's producer had to instruct the polite ex-spy not to be afraid to interrupt.

the-piers-morgan-panel.title: Jeffrey Epstein
the-piers-morgan-panel.summary: Convicted sex offender; per John Kiriakou, was "an Israeli access agent" rather than a CIA asset, because the CIA collects foreign intelligence and Epstein's targets — Bill Clinton, Bill Gates, Prince Andrew — were not foreign. Kiriakou further holds that Epstein did die by suicide in federal custody, because in the Bureau of Prisons the cameras never work and the guards are always asleep.

the-piers-morgan-panel.title: MOSSAD
the-piers-morgan-panel.summary: Israel's primary external intelligence service; characterized by John Kiriakou as universally hostile in his and his CIA colleagues' professional dealings with it ("never had a positive encounter with Mossad"); operates almost exclusively in the operational rather than analytical domain; the CIA is, per Kiriakou, categorically forbidden from spying on it.

the-piers-morgan-panel.title: Scott Horton
the-piers-morgan-panel.summary: American antiwar journalist and interviewer whom John Kiriakou calls one of the most brilliant people he has ever engaged with, and the man he found sitting opposite Alan Dershowitz and Danny Ayalon when both he and Horton were called in as last-minute fill-ins on a Piers Morgan panel about Jeffrey Epstein and Israeli espionage.

the-piers-morgan-panel.title: The O'Reilly exclusivity rule
the-piers-morgan-panel.summary: The condition Bill O'Reilly's producer attached to booking John Kiriakou — that he appear on no other programme for three days either side — and Kiriakou's refusal to surrender a week of his diary, which meant he never appeared on the show at all.

the-piers-morgan-panel.title: The Trump weave
the-piers-morgan-panel.summary: The name a speakers' bureau gave to John Kiriakou's platform manner — starting one story, turning off into another, and coming back to finish the first — a habit he attributes to never writing anything down before he walks to the podium.

the-pillow-talk-leak-case.title: "Don''t charge Donald Trump with espionage"
the-pillow-talk-leak-case.summary: An opinion piece John Kiriakou wrote for Consortium News after the classified documents were found at Mar-a-Lago, arguing against an Espionage Act prosecution of Trump — and, in its subheading, against Espionage Act prosecutions of anyone else either. He uses it as the frame for his position that the statute should be scrapped and rewritten to reach only those who mean the country harm.

the-pillow-talk-leak-case.title: Espionage Act
the-pillow-talk-leak-case.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

the-pillow-talk-leak-case.title: CIA adultery culture
