the-pillow-talk-leak-case.summary: John Kiriakou's recurring characterization of the CIA officer corps as riddled with adultery and casual sex — which he frames not as gossip but as a systemic counterintelligence vulnerability that makes officers easy to recruit.

the-pillow-talk-leak-case.title: Classification compartments
the-pillow-talk-leak-case.summary: John Kiriakou's explanation of the U.S. secrecy tiers above 'top secret' — the TS/SCI/TK/gamma clearances everyone at the CIA gets, and the additional compartments that mean even senior officials can be barred from a single cable.

the-pillow-talk-leak-case.title: The Charles Littlejohn prosecution
the-pillow-talk-leak-case.summary: The five-year sentence handed to an IRS contractor who disclosed Donald Trump's tax returns to the New York Times, which John Kiriakou calls stunning and unjustified — the material was protected but not classified, the Biden campaign made use of it, and the sentencing judge compared the disclosure to the January 6 attack on the Capitol.

the-pillow-talk-leak-case.title: Chelsea Manning
the-pillow-talk-leak-case.summary: Former U.S. Army intelligence analyst who provided WikiLeaks its 2010 trove of military and diplomatic documents. Per John Kiriakou, Manning meets the legal definition of whistleblower for exposing war crimes, was a torture victim of prolonged solitary confinement with forced nudity, and was sentenced to 35 years in prison before Barack Obama commuted — not pardoned — her sentence. Kiriakou says Manning later refused a grand jury's offer of immunity and chose renewed jail time rather than testify against Julian Assange.

the-pilot-who-saw-it-drink.title: The Lake Michigan sightings
the-pilot-who-saw-it-drink.summary: The Netflix-documented Lake Michigan case John Kiriakou raised with a UFO podcaster: National Weather Service employees who watched objects for hours on radar and by eye, the objects avoiding the frozen part of the lake, and the principal witness quitting his job.

the-pilot-who-saw-it-drink.title: The New Jersey drones
the-pilot-who-saw-it-drink.summary: John Kiriakou''s shifting account of the New Jersey drone flap: his state trooper friend''s report of a missing Defense or Energy Department convoy load, and the 60 Minutes segment in which Air Force generals concluded the drones were hostile and probably Chinese.

the-pilot-who-saw-it-drink.title: Kiriakou's UFO sighting
the-pilot-who-saw-it-drink.summary: The object John Kiriakou and his father watched from the side of Route 60 in Amish country, western Pennsylvania, on a Friday night in 1981 — three flashes of white light, then a silent orange trapezoid hanging a couple of thousand feet up, which left at a speed he had never seen before or since.

the-pilot-who-saw-it-drink.title: Langley
the-pilot-who-saw-it-drink.summary: The Virginia location of CIA headquarters and, in John Kiriakou''s usage, shorthand for the agency''s permanent power. It''s where he worked as the CIA''s lone Iraq-Kuwait analyst — told to start on Iraq "because nothing ever happened there" — where a cafeteria conversation invited him into the torture program, where he walked past the Kryptos sculpture every day for fifteen years without solving it, and the place agencies return to after apologizing to Congress, "where of course nothing ever changes." When a host suggested the real government of America is out in Langley and Washington''s white marble is for show, Kiriakou''s answer was: "that''s about the shape of it."

the-pilot-who-saw-it-drink.title: Area 58
the-pilot-who-saw-it-drink.summary: The claim John Kiriakou says was put to him by a man who presents as entirely serious and is writing a book about it: that beyond Area 51 there is an Area 58 — seven more, and that much more secret — containing an underground bunker where alien craft land, known to those involved as the embassy because it is where the United States liaises with the aliens.

the-pilot-who-saw-it-drink.title: CIA and the UFO question
the-pilot-who-saw-it-drink.summary: John Kiriakou's consistent answer that UFOs and alien technology are a Pentagon matter, not a CIA one — though he says nearly every former fighter-pilot friend of his has seen something inexplicable, sometimes emerging from the ocean.

the-pineapple-militia-case.title: "Dig a hole and put him in the hole"
the-pineapple-militia-case.summary: The classified CIA cable John Kiriakou has repeatedly cited as the one that convinced him the torture programme had crossed into murder, a field station reporting that interrogators had killed a detainee during a session and asking headquarters what to do, and a Base-office cable answering *"Dig a hole and put him in the hole."* Kiriakou frames it as the moment the answer to *"nobody ever gave the CIA permission to torture people to death"* stopped being a hypothetical.

the-pineapple-militia-case.title: Consulting job entrapment offers
the-pineapple-militia-case.summary: John Kiriakou's claim that he receives a steady stream of emails and telephone calls offering him work — always consulting — that he reads as attempts to bait him into violating federal law, and which he says happens all the time.

the-pineapple-militia-case.title: FBI
the-pineapple-militia-case.summary: Kiriakou says FBI agents were sticklers for the law in a way the CIA never was — and that the bureau 'leaks like a sieve.'

the-pineapple-militia-case.title: Kiriakou's legal counteroffensive
the-pineapple-militia-case.summary: John Kiriakou's announcement in February 2021 that after thirteen years of being reactive and responsive to his detractors he intended to start going after people, having connected with Harvard and Georgetown law professors — a plan he described without giving detail, saying only that things were turning around.

the-pineapple-militia-case.title: Phone microphone ad targeting
the-pineapple-militia-case.summary: John Kiriakou's account of a spoken telephone conversation about concealed carry permits being followed, five minutes later, by a Facebook feed in which every single advertisement was for a concealed carry class — offered as evidence for his claim that the platforms go further than they admit and listen when the phone is turned off.

the-play-the-cia-killed.title: The Latin American newspaper prediction
the-play-the-cia-killed.summary: The prediction John Kiriakou gave to a Latin American newspaper a week or two after Donald Trump's first inauguration — that things would be better for whistleblowers under Trump because they could not possibly be worse than under Barack Obama — and his later verdict that he had been "very foolish" to say it, since the Trump administration opened three times as many leak investigations and won longer sentences.

the-play-the-cia-killed.title: Jeremy Hammond
the-play-the-cia-killed.summary: The hacker held in contempt for refusing to testify against Julian Assange before a grand jury. John Kiriakou''s point about his case is administrative rather than constitutional: Hammond was pulled out of the Bureau of Prisons drug and alcohol programme two months short of completing it, forfeiting the eighteen months it would have taken off his sentence — a penalty that applied whether or not he ever agreed to testify.

the-play-the-cia-killed.title: Reality Winner
the-play-the-cia-killed.summary: National Security Agency linguist imprisoned for sending a single classified page on Russian interference in the 2016 election to The Intercept. John Kiriakou attributes her arrest to the two reporters who received it, and to a printer-tracking countermeasure they appear not to have known about; he also treats her prosecution as an operation that served the intelligence community on three fronts at once.

the-play-the-cia-killed.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
the-play-the-cia-killed.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

the-play-the-cia-killed.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
the-play-the-cia-killed.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

the-plea-hearing-objection.title: Julian Assange
the-plea-hearing-objection.summary: Kiriakou — a 15-year friend and former WikiLeaks board member — on why Assange is a publisher owed a journalist's immunity, and a political prisoner.

the-plea-hearing-objection.title: Federal plea coercion
the-plea-hearing-objection.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that the federal justice system coerces guilty pleas by stacking charges and winning 98.2% of its cases — so that even innocent defendants take deals, as he did, told by his own attorney that the system is 'not about justice; it's about mitigating damage.'

the-plea-hearing-objection.title: Eastern District of Virginia
the-plea-hearing-objection.summary: The U.S. federal district covering northern Virginia — home to Langley, the Pentagon, DHS and much of the intelligence-contractor industry — which John Kiriakou calls 'the espionage court' because the Justice Department files the great majority of its national security prosecutions there and because, in his telling, no national-security defendant has ever won a case in it; Kiriakou, Julian Assange, Edward Snowden and Jeffrey Sterling were all charged there.

the-plea-hearing-objection.title: The CIPA hearing in Kiriakou's case
the-plea-hearing-objection.summary: The closed pre-trial proceeding under the Classified Information Procedures Act at which John Kiriakou's defence filed seventy motions to declassify the material it needed to mount a defence, and the judge denied all seventy at once. Kiriakou describes the ruling as the moment the case ended — his lead attorney told him on the way out of the courtroom that they had just lost — and as the point at which plea negotiations began.

the-plea-hearing-objection.title: Leonie Brinkema
the-plea-hearing-objection.summary: U.S. federal judge in the Eastern District of Virginia — informally the 'Espionage Court' — a Reagan appointee John Kiriakou calls "a hanging judge." Per Kiriakou, Brinkema systematically reserved all major national security cases for herself rather than allowing them to be distributed randomly among judges, and ruled in Kiriakou's case that his reason for blowing the whistle was legally irrelevant and that classified documents could not be used in his defense — effectively making it impossible to mount one.

the-plea-hearing-objection.title: Jeffrey Sterling
the-plea-hearing-objection.summary: Former CIA officer convicted of nine felonies, including seven counts of espionage, after giving a New York Times interview about a racial discrimination lawsuit he had filed against the CIA. Per John Kiriakou, Sterling was not accused of spying for a foreign country; his underlying case was that the CIA had passed him over for promotion and told him explicitly it was because of his race. Daniel Ellsberg asked Sterling to go to trial specifically so the constitutionality of the Espionage Act could be challenged; Sterling did, was convicted, and was sentenced by Judge Leonie Brinkema to what she described as 'Kiriakou plus 12 months.'

the-plot-to-divert-maduros-plane.title: The Colombian air bridge through Venezuela
the-plot-to-divert-maduros-plane.summary: What John Kiriakou says his own Senate Foreign Relations Committee investigation found about drug trafficking through Venezuela — that it exists, that it consists of Colombian aircraft landing there en route to Africa, and that there is no evidence Nicolás Maduro controls it or knows when and where it happens.

the-plot-to-divert-maduros-plane.title: Venezuela Boat Strikes
the-plot-to-divert-maduros-plane.summary: September 2025 U.S. military strike on a boat in the Caribbean that killed 11 people the White House called drug traffickers; John Kiriakou calls it piracy on the high seas followed by mass murder, arguing the victims were never charged with a crime and that the boat's unusual passenger count undercuts the drug-trafficking story.

the-plot-to-divert-maduros-plane.title: Hamid Karzai
the-plot-to-divert-maduros-plane.summary: The president installed in Afghanistan after the American invasion, whom John Kiriakou uses as the standing illustration of what occupation actually buys: after twenty years and more than a trillion dollars, Karzai was ''little more than the mayor of Kabul'' — and did not control all of Kabul either. The line began as a joke among Senate Foreign Relations Committee staff, and Kiriakou used it to Senator John Kerry''s face ten years into the war.

the-plot-to-divert-maduros-plane.title: The fentanyl-from-cocaine claim
the-plot-to-divert-maduros-plane.summary: The assertion that seventy per cent of American overdoses trace to fentanyl processed from Venezuelan cocaine, which John Kiriakou refuted on air by reading the DEA's own fact sheet — fentanyl is not made from cocaine, it is mixed into it, along with almost everything else on the market.

the-plot-to-divert-maduros-plane.title: There are denials and then there are denials
the-plot-to-divert-maduros-plane.summary: John Kiriakou's rule for reading official statements — that 'we have no such plans' is not a denial, because nothing counts as a plan until a head of government signs off on it, leaving a government free to discuss and even prepare something it can still credibly say it has no plans for.

the-plot-to-divert-maduros-plane.title: Venezuela regime change (2026)
the-plot-to-divert-maduros-plane.summary: John Kiriakou''s assessment of the American operation that removed Venezuela''s president — a clear violation of international law, since none of the three recognised grounds for one state attacking another applied, but not a violation of US law, which since 1985 has expressly permitted special forces to cross borders and seize people for trial. His reluctant conclusion at the time: "as much as I hate admitting it, this regime change seems to be working right now."

the-pondiki-cartoon.title: Kimberly Guilfoyle in Athens
the-pondiki-cartoon.summary: John Kiriakou's assessment of Kimberly Guilfoyle's appointment as American ambassador to Greece — that she got it because Donald Trump Jr. wanted her out of the way, a manoeuvre he compares to Saddam Hussein's habit of exiling successful generals as ambassadors — and his reluctant conclusion that Greece could have done worse.

the-pondiki-cartoon.title: Nicholas Burns
the-pondiki-cartoon.summary: The United States ambassador to Greece during John Kiriakou''s Athens tour — an envoy Kiriakou says he has always disliked and disrespected, whose unpopularity extended to his own staff, and whom he credits with exactly one good decision: drawing the assignments for a presidential visit out of a hat.

the-pondiki-cartoon.title: The magazines that bought her freedom
the-pondiki-cartoon.summary: John Kiriakou's account of his grandmother's imprisonment by the collaborationist government in wartime Athens, and of his grandfather buying her release from a prison guard with American magazines — after which the couple escaped to the United States.

the-pondiki-cartoon.title: Amnesty International
the-pondiki-cartoon.summary: The human rights organization whose torture report forms part of John Kiriakou's core defense — the CIA's crimes were already public knowledge before he confirmed them on ABC, and the Justice Department's own declination letter said so — and the organization whose silence during his prosecution he cannot forgive. He begged Amnesty for a one-sentence statement and got a New Yorker subscription instead; it took Ai Weiwei to change their minds, and by then he was walking out of prison.

the-pondiki-cartoon.title: I want my fifty bucks back
the-pondiki-cartoon.summary: What John Kiriakou says he shouted at John Fetterman from ten rows back at an Ohio State football game — and his explanation, as a Pennsylvanian furious about the senator, of why Fetterman keeps his seat anyway.

the-pondiki-cartoon.title: Ian Henderson
the-pondiki-cartoon.summary: The British colonial police officer who ran Bahrain's intelligence service during John Kiriakou's posting there — a man Kiriakou says even the heir presumptive to the throne was afraid to name aloud, and whom Kiriakou, seated at the crown prince's table at a dinner for George H. W. Bush, mistook for a corpse.

the-porn-on-bin-ladens-computers.title: The lapis lazuli paperweight
the-porn-on-bin-ladens-computers.summary: The chunk of raw lapis lazuli John Kiriakou says he took from Osama bin Laden's house in Afghanistan and still keeps — described on air as magnificent, and agreed on air to have probably served as bin Laden's paperweight.

the-porn-on-bin-ladens-computers.title: Cleaning up after Tora Bora
the-porn-on-bin-ladens-computers.summary: John Kiriakou was not at Tora Bora. He arrived in Pakistan in January 2002, two months after the bombing, and says he went specifically to clean up what the battle had left behind — scavenging material, detaining the fighters too slow to get away, and mapping the smugglers'' valleys the survivors had used to cross. In his account the clean-up was necessary because the encirclement failed: bin Laden, warned by an al-Qaeda operative working as translator to the commander of Central Command, left in the dark dressed as a woman in the back of a pickup truck, and at dawn there was nobody in Tora Bora to surrender.

the-porn-on-bin-ladens-computers.title: Hayden at the National Press Club
the-porn-on-bin-ladens-computers.summary: John Kiriakou's account of seeing Michael Hayden, after a series of strokes, at a National Press Club event sponsored by the intelligence centre that bears his name — and the two reactions it produced in him, neither of them satisfaction alone.

the-porn-on-bin-ladens-computers.title: Saddam and the journalists
the-porn-on-bin-ladens-computers.summary: John Kiriakou's comparison, drawn from fifteen years working the Iraq target at the CIA, between a dictator who hated the press and did not kill it and a government that he says kills journalists deliberately and in numbers.

the-porn-on-bin-ladens-computers.title: The balloon test
the-porn-on-bin-ladens-computers.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that Israel had warning of the 7 October 2023 attack — that settlers along the Gaza line had reported training for months, that balloons were sent over as a probe in the days beforehand, and that nothing was done.

the-porn-on-bin-ladens-computers.title: The book the publisher sat on
the-porn-on-bin-ladens-computers.summary: The manuscript John Kiriakou says he delivered to his publisher three years before August 2025 and had still not seen printed, and the email he finally sent telling them it was time to fish or cut bait.

the-postcards-for-daniel-hale.title: The solitary confinement precedents
the-postcards-for-daniel-hale.summary: The legal argument John Kiriakou made repeatedly between 2020 and 2022 in defence of Julian Assange, and revived in 2025 for the Australian pilot Daniel Duggan — that no extradition to the United States can succeed once a court is asked to find that American solitary confinement is not torture, a proposition already contradicted by the United Nations, by the United States' own federal torture statute, and by a line of British and European rulings blocking extraditions on exactly that ground.

the-postcards-for-daniel-hale.title: Julian Assange
the-postcards-for-daniel-hale.summary: Kiriakou — a 15-year friend and former WikiLeaks board member — on why Assange is a publisher owed a journalist's immunity, and a political prisoner.

the-postcards-for-daniel-hale.title: PTSD
the-postcards-for-daniel-hale.summary: Post-traumatic stress disorder runs through John Kiriakou''s life and worldview — he had it coming out of Greece after an assassination attempt, brought it home from Pakistan alongside his shock at colleagues'' willingness to kill, and was blindsided by a delayed post-prison version that helped end his marriage. For six months after release he dreamed the same dream nightly: that he was out by mistake and had to get back inside before midnight count. He still takes a repurposed blood-pressure drug that stops the dreams, and he extends the diagnosis outward — to secret-site interrogators who came back crying, to drone pilots, and to prisoners released angry and untreated.

the-postcards-for-daniel-hale.title: The Intercept
the-postcards-for-daniel-hale.summary: The investigative news outlet that published Daniel Hale's drone leak; John Kiriakou notes that the same Intercept reporter, Matthew Cole, was involved in cases that led to the exposure of both Kiriakou himself and NSA leaker Reality Winner — though he insists Hale outed himself rather than being burned by the outlet.

the-postcards-for-daniel-hale.title: Chelsea Manning
the-postcards-for-daniel-hale.summary: Former U.S. Army intelligence analyst who provided WikiLeaks its 2010 trove of military and diplomatic documents. Per John Kiriakou, Manning meets the legal definition of whistleblower for exposing war crimes, was a torture victim of prolonged solitary confinement with forced nudity, and was sentenced to 35 years in prison before Barack Obama commuted — not pardoned — her sentence. Kiriakou says Manning later refused a grand jury's offer of immunity and chose renewed jail time rather than testify against Julian Assange.

the-postcards-for-daniel-hale.title: Daniel Ellsberg
the-postcards-for-daniel-hale.summary: The Pentagon Papers whistleblower Kiriakou calls 'the Godfather of all national security whistleblowers' — and one of the great mentors of his life.

the-powell-telephone-call.title: Iraq, the training account
the-powell-telephone-call.summary: The reason John Kiriakou says he was given the Iraq portfolio as a new CIA analyst in 1990 — that nothing ever happened there — and the promise that once he had learned tradecraft and the house writing style he would be moved to somewhere exciting, such as Romania.

the-powell-telephone-call.title: Arabic and Greek
the-powell-telephone-call.summary: The qualification John Kiriakou says opened the door to his transfer from CIA analysis to operations: a post in Athens wanted Greek or Arabic, and he had both — by most of his tellings the only officer in the agency who did. The chief who hired him gave the reason in one sentence: it is easier and cheaper to take a linguist and teach him operations than the other way round. The pairing also became a detection tool, since the language nobody speaks in Pakistan is Arabic.

the-powell-telephone-call.title: The Condoleezza Rice meeting
the-powell-telephone-call.summary: The nine o'clock White House appointment John Kiriakou and Cofer Black never kept on the morning of 11 September 2001. The Government Printing Office was about to issue a volume of declassified Greece-Turkey-Cyprus cables in an edition of five or ten copies; three of them named CIA sources who were still alive, and an obscure statute obliges the government to offer citizenship and resettlement to any recruited source it outs. The two men were going to ask the National Security Advisor to quietly pull three cables nobody would miss. The car was at the East entrance at 8.15.

the-powell-telephone-call.title: The Tehran slip
the-powell-telephone-call.summary: The moment John Kiriakou says he witnessed as note-taker in a secure video teleconference a day or two before the 2003 invasion of Iraq, when a briefing general said that if all went as planned American forces could be in Tehran by August, and CIA Director George Tenet turned off his microphone and asked Kiriakou whether the man had said Tehran or Baghdad.

the-powell-telephone-call.title: Training to kill
the-powell-telephone-call.summary: John Kiriakou's account of arriving at the CIA's clandestine training facility expecting to learn how to recruit sources at diplomatic cocktail parties, and finding instead parachute training, resistance-to-interrogation instruction, and — as his old supervisor had warned him — training to kill people.

the-powell-telephone-call.title: Bankruptcy and the dropped charges
the-powell-telephone-call.summary: The sequence John Kiriakou places at the centre of his case: that the espionage counts against him were dropped only after his legal fees had bankrupted him, which he presents as evidence that the government''s aim was attrition rather than conviction.

the-pre-interview.title: Suggested responses
the-pre-interview.summary: The second email John Kiriakou says arrived before his first appearance on Fox News — a list of suggested responses to accompany the questions the producers had already sent him — which he ignored, and which he says was never sent again.

the-pre-interview.title: The NPR walkout
the-pre-interview.summary: The Saturday morning interview John Kiriakou says he ended after five minutes of a scheduled half hour, having been attacked on air over an op-ed about Gina Haspel, and which he closed by asking the host where NPR had been while he was blowing the whistle on the torture programme.

the-pre-interview.title: The convicted felon introduction
the-pre-interview.summary: The MSNBC appearance John Kiriakou says was his last: booked opposite Daniel Ellsberg, having agreed his on-air identification in advance with the producers, he was introduced instead as "convicted felon John Kiriakou", swore on tape, and began removing his microphone.

the-pre-interview.title: Consulting for royal families
the-pre-interview.summary: The work John Kiriakou says he was hired to do by members of two different royal families following the 2026 virality of his interviews — advising on ethics in their own intelligence operations — which he offers as evidence of how far the reversal in his standing had gone.

the-pre-interview.title: "Embrace it and keep telling it"
the-pre-interview.summary: The advice John Kiriakou says he was given days after his arrest — that he could not hide from the prosecution but had to embrace it, and had to keep telling his side of the story until it became the side of record, because the government would eventually move on to its next target.

the-pre-interview.title: Signing with CAA
the-pre-interview.summary: The representation John Kiriakou says followed the 2026 virality of his podcast clips: a contract with the Creative Artists Agency covering books, film, consulting and licensing, and a run of advertising approaches including one from the maker of the spectacle frames he already wore.

the-professor-and-the-ellsberg-profile.title: The Nation of Islam at Loretto
the-professor-and-the-ellsberg-profile.summary: The largest Muslim faction at FCI Loretto — African American converts to the Nation of Islam — two of whom walked into John Kiriakou's cell in his first days holding their own newspaper, in which Louis Farrakhan had called him a hero of the Muslim people for opposing torture. They told him he would have no trouble with them; one declined the handshake he offered, on the ground that he does not shake hands with the white devil. The Aryans, meanwhile, had decided he was a CIA assassin who killed Muslims. Kiriakou kept his mouth shut and let both beliefs stand.

the-professor-and-the-ellsberg-profile.title: Seven cell phones
the-professor-and-the-ellsberg-profile.summary: John Kiriakou's account of why his first marriage ended — that his wife, a ballet teacher, knew only that he worked for the CIA, and that a career in which one of seven cell phones rang at midnight and he left speaking Arabic for a day at a time could not survive the questions it produced.

the-professor-and-the-ellsberg-profile.title: Seventy-two denied motions
the-professor-and-the-ellsberg-profile.summary: The count John Kiriakou gives of the pretrial motions filed in his case and denied by Judge Leonie Brinkema — seventy-two denied and none granted — which he offers as the mechanism by which a national security defendant in the Eastern District of Virginia is prevented from mounting a defence at all.

the-professor-and-the-ellsberg-profile.title: The hundred-city tour
the-professor-and-the-ellsberg-profile.summary: The year-long, hundred-city speaking tour John Kiriakou described beginning in early 2026 — opening in Belfast, Dublin and Manchester, returning to Scotland and northern England, then the United States and Canada, Australia and New Zealand, continental Europe, the Persian Gulf and East Asia.

the-professor-and-the-ellsberg-profile.title: The job in the medical practice
the-professor-and-the-ellsberg-profile.summary: The made-up job that carried John Kiriakou through his first months out of prison — invented for him by the parents of a friend, both physicians, so that he would have something — and the patched-together living that followed it, including a think-tank post that ended in a mass layoff after a year.

the-professor-and-the-ellsberg-profile.title: Church Committee
the-professor-and-the-ellsberg-profile.summary: U.S. Senate investigative committee operating in 1975–1976 that examined domestic intelligence abuses by the CIA, FBI, and NSA; per John Kiriakou, the Church Committee — alongside the concurrent Pike Committee in the House — was the last genuine moment of legislative oversight over the intelligence community, born of a national consensus that government had gone dangerously off course. Its work led to the creation of the permanent Senate Select Committee on Intelligence, which Kiriakou says ceased to function as real oversight roughly seven years after its founding.

the-professor-in-the-visiting-room.title: The psychology chairman's letter
the-professor-in-the-visiting-room.summary: Unsure how to deal with the child molesters who made up a large share of the population at FCI Loretto, John Kiriakou wrote to a professor friend for advice; the reply, from the chairman of a university psychology department, told him that pedophiles cannot be cured and that they talk about their crimes constantly because reliving them is itself gratifying.

the-professor-in-the-visiting-room.title: The persona in the first week
the-professor-in-the-visiting-room.summary: Five days into a sentence he had expected to serve at a minimum-security camp, John Kiriakou decided to fall back on his CIA training and adopt a deliberately aggressive exterior — reasoning that in a prison where the weak end up checking themselves into solitary for protection, he would rather be the man other people needed protection from.

the-professor-in-the-visiting-room.title: Domingo's television
the-professor-in-the-visiting-room.summary: John Kiriakou has used the television rooms at FCI Loretto as his sharpest illustration of prison segregation: sets owned by racial blocs since a riot in the 1990s, a seat in front of one costing fourteen dollars, and one set left tuned to Law & Order every morning because a man named Domingo had paid four hundred dollars for it and had been gone for years.

the-professor-in-the-visiting-room.title: The chapel rule
the-professor-in-the-visiting-room.summary: The chapel and the library at FCI Loretto were the two places child molesters could be certain of safety, because a correctional officer was always present; John Kiriakou, who worked in the chapel, has described the house rule against discussing your case there and the indignation with which it was met.

the-professor-in-the-visiting-room.title: The CO who wanted the CIA
the-professor-in-the-visiting-room.summary: A young correctional officer at FCI Loretto once pulled John Kiriakou aside and asked in a whisper how to get into the CIA; when Kiriakou told him he was bright and did not belong there, the man explained that both his parents and his grandfather had been correctional officers and that his wife would never leave Loretto, a town of twelve hundred people.

the-professor-in-the-visiting-room.title: Mental health as a disciplinary problem
the-professor-in-the-visiting-room.summary: John Kiriakou has said that before his own prosecution he never gave five seconds of thought to the American prison system, and that living inside it showed him a broken one — in particular a system in which mental health is treated as a disciplinary problem rather than a medical one.

the-prostitute-hypothetical.title: College tuition as an inducement
the-prostitute-hypothetical.summary: The recruitment inducement John Kiriakou describes as among the CIA's most effective — enrolling a source's child at any American university and paying for it — and the arrangements with universities and corporations he says make it possible.

the-prostitute-hypothetical.title: Security, finance and medical
the-prostitute-hypothetical.summary: The rule John Kiriakou says CIA recruits were taught in their first week on the job — that there are exactly three offices an officer may never lie to, because those three can end a career — and the reasoning he attaches to each.

the-prostitute-hypothetical.title: The Faisalabad cash run
the-prostitute-hypothetical.summary: The drive John Kiriakou made to Faisalabad, Pakistan roughly two weeks before the capture of Abu Zubaydah, with two million dollars in cash in two duffel bags in the van, and the exchange with his colleague about why anyone would cheat the CIA out of twenty dollars.

the-prostitute-hypothetical.title: The Indonesian recruitment question
the-prostitute-hypothetical.summary: A hypothetical put to John Kiriakou and other CIA applicants during the interview process — what to do when a foreign official you have cultivated for a year turns out not to be recruitable — and the answer that Kiriakou later understood had been the point of the exercise: break into the embassy and steal the information.

the-prostitute-hypothetical.title: Arabic and Greek
the-prostitute-hypothetical.summary: The qualification John Kiriakou says opened the door to his transfer from CIA analysis to operations: a post in Athens wanted Greek or Arabic, and he had both — by most of his tellings the only officer in the agency who did. The chief who hired him gave the reason in one sentence: it is easier and cheaper to take a linguist and teach him operations than the other way round. The pairing also became a detection tool, since the language nobody speaks in Pakistan is Arabic.

the-prostitute-hypothetical.title: "You were the first person that ever asked me about my children"
the-prostitute-hypothetical.summary: The answer John Kiriakou says he received when he asked a mid-level al-Qaeda member he had recruited in Pakistan why he had allowed the recruitment to happen: that in five years of detention Kiriakou had been the first person to ask about his children.

the-psychology-chairmans-letter.title: The professor in the visiting room
the-psychology-chairmans-letter.summary: John Kiriakou has credited the idea for his prison memoir to a university professor who visited him at FCI Loretto, listened to him tell stories across a visiting-room table, and told him that although the whole thing was by its nature depressing, the stories were good and there were lessons in them, and that he should write a book.

the-psychology-chairmans-letter.title: The chapel rule
the-psychology-chairmans-letter.summary: The chapel and the library at FCI Loretto were the two places child molesters could be certain of safety, because a correctional officer was always present; John Kiriakou, who worked in the chapel, has described the house rule against discussing your case there and the indignation with which it was met.

the-psychology-chairmans-letter.title: The persona in the first week
the-psychology-chairmans-letter.summary: Five days into a sentence he had expected to serve at a minimum-security camp, John Kiriakou decided to fall back on his CIA training and adopt a deliberately aggressive exterior — reasoning that in a prison where the weak end up checking themselves into solitary for protection, he would rather be the man other people needed protection from.

the-psychology-chairmans-letter.title: Chomo
the-psychology-chairmans-letter.summary: The prison term for a child molester, which John Kiriakou first heard on his first day at FCI Loretto when two skinheads at the Aryan table put it to him as the last of three vetting questions before deciding whether he could eat with them.

the-psychology-chairmans-letter.title: Domingo's television
the-psychology-chairmans-letter.summary: John Kiriakou has used the television rooms at FCI Loretto as his sharpest illustration of prison segregation: sets owned by racial blocs since a riot in the 1990s, a seat in front of one costing fourteen dollars, and one set left tuned to Law & Order every morning because a man named Domingo had paid four hundred dollars for it and had been gone for years.

the-psychology-chairmans-letter.title: Mental health as a disciplinary problem
the-psychology-chairmans-letter.summary: John Kiriakou has said that before his own prosecution he never gave five seconds of thought to the American prison system, and that living inside it showed him a broken one — in particular a system in which mental health is treated as a disciplinary problem rather than a medical one.

the-puerto-rico-thirds.title: The gamma globulin shot
the-puerto-rico-thirds.summary: The yellow fever inoculation John Kiriakou says every CIA officer took from his hiring through about 2000 — a gamma globulin injection he compares to having maple syrup put into the buttock, which raised a knot the size of a tennis ball and earned an hour of paid administrative time to walk it out around the compound.

the-puerto-rico-thirds.title: Typhoid fever in Bangkok
the-puerto-rico-thirds.summary: The illness John Kiriakou calls the sickest he has ever been — typhoid fever caught in Bangkok in 2002, which he had assumed the inoculation would prevent, and which put him in hospital twice. The doctor''s correction: the shot does not stop you catching typhoid, only makes it slightly less virulent when you do.

the-puerto-rico-thirds.title: Abu Zubaydah
the-puerto-rico-thirds.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

the-puerto-rico-thirds.title: Ali from Newark
the-puerto-rico-thirds.summary: The Black shot caller at FCI Loretto, near the end of a twenty-five-year drug sentence, who came to embrace John Kiriakou at the close of his term and tell him how much he respected him — a friendship possible only because Kiriakou had decided on arrival to ignore the prison's racial divisions.

the-puerto-rico-thirds.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
the-puerto-rico-thirds.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

the-puerto-rico-thirds.title: Bezalel Smotrich
the-puerto-rico-thirds.summary: Israeli far-right minister whom John Kiriakou, alongside Itamar Ben-Gvir, blames for leaving Israel unprepared on October 7 by insisting any attack would come from the West Bank rather than Gaza.

the-putin-call-and-the-china-exception.title: China as mediator
the-putin-call-and-the-china-exception.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that China is the plausible mediator of Middle Eastern and Ukrainian conflicts, grounded in his claim that — Tibet and its border wars aside — China has no history of invading other countries, and his observation of how quickly Beijing accepted an offhand suggestion that it might mediate between Israel and Iran.

the-putin-call-and-the-china-exception.title: Donald Trump
the-putin-call-and-the-china-exception.summary: 45th and 47th U.S. president. Per John Kiriakou, a man genuinely convinced he was doing right by bombing Iran, "duped" by the same Netanyahu nuclear bluff Obama once rejected — and, at the same time, the most blindly pro-Israel president in history, an admirer of autocrats who has never once criticized Vladimir Putin, and prone to gestures — from the Gulf of America to a since-abandoned "Department of War" rename — that test the edges of his actual authority.

the-putin-call-and-the-china-exception.title: Hope is not a strategy
the-putin-call-and-the-china-exception.summary: Opening a February 2025 commentary with a maxim he attributes to business school — that hope is not a strategy — John Kiriakou nonetheless set out four things he was hoping the second Trump administration meant, on the grounds that if they did not come from Trump he did not expect them from anyone else in American politics.

the-putin-call-and-the-china-exception.title: Vladimir Putin
the-putin-call-and-the-china-exception.summary: President of Russia. Per John Kiriakou, Putin twice raised joining NATO — floating it to Bill Clinton and later telling Barack Obama Russia would like to explore membership — and was refused both times; Kiriakou has never believed Putin wants to conquer Ukraine or Eastern Europe, argues U.S. hostility toward Russia is driven by defense contractors and a permanent wartime economy, and notes the irony that Putin was the anti-communist the U.S. itself backed in the Yeltsin era.

the-putin-call-and-the-china-exception.title: Ukraine as a proxy war
the-putin-call-and-the-china-exception.summary: John Kiriakou's assessment, given two months into the 2022 Russian invasion, that the United States was funding a proxy war it knew Ukraine could not win in order to bog Russia down — and that the outcome was already fixed, so peace talks should happen at once.

the-putin-call-and-the-china-exception.title: Canada as a bargaining chip
the-putin-call-and-the-china-exception.summary: John Kiriakou's reading of Mark Carney's Davos speech as the moment Canada stopped pretending the United States could be trusted as a long-term partner — and his account of what wore the relationship out, including Washington's insistence that Ottawa arrest Huawei's chief financial officer on a computer-hacking charge and hold her for three years to trade.

the-qatari-seven-forty-seven.title: The Graham Senate succession
the-qatari-seven-forty-seven.summary: John Kiriakou's comment on the appointment of Lindsey Graham's sister to serve out the remainder of his Senate term, and her announcement that she would run for a full term of her own — a candidacy whose only qualification, in Kiriakou's assessment, is her relation to the late senator.

the-qatari-seven-forty-seven.title: The catering truck transfer
the-qatari-seven-forty-seven.summary: The covert removal of Donald Trump from Air Force One at the end of a NATO summit in Turkey — boarded in front of the television cameras, driven across the tarmac inside an airport catering truck, and flown on to Britain aboard a smaller jet while the White House press corps travelled on the aircraft everyone believed he was on.

the-qatari-seven-forty-seven.title: Lindsey Graham
the-qatari-seven-forty-seven.summary: Republican senator from South Carolina who died in July 2026, and John Kiriakou's standing shorthand for the permanent war caucus — a "show horse" rather than a workhorse, a "chameleon" who "never saw a war that he didn't want to jump into with both feet," and, on posthumously released documentary footage, a man offering the US Air Force to bomb a country America was not at war with.

the-qatari-seven-forty-seven.title: Fidel Castro
the-qatari-seven-forty-seven.summary: The Cuban leader John Kiriakou uses as his standing example of a relationship the United States could have had and chose not to — a rebel who liked America and had pitched in its minor leagues, written off because Washington had already committed itself to Batista. Castro also recurs across Kiriakou's account of the CIA as the agency's most-attempted assassination target, as the man who never cashed the rent cheques for Guantánamo, and as the figure American policy is still fighting years after his death.

the-qatari-seven-forty-seven.title: John Larson
the-qatari-seven-forty-seven.summary: The twenty-eight-year congressman from Connecticut's first district whose primary defeat John Kiriakou reads as a verdict on both the Democratic Party's campaign theory and the age of its incumbents.

the-qatari-seven-forty-seven.title: The Air Force One bomb threat
the-qatari-seven-forty-seven.summary: The bomb threat telephoned to the classified telephone aboard Air Force One as Bill Clinton's aircraft lifted out of Athens in November 1999, disclosed by the ambassador at the embassy's after-action review — a detail John Kiriakou withheld from years of tellings of that visit until 2026.

the-quarterback-with-a-personal-chef.title: The golf course deed forgery
the-quarterback-with-a-personal-chef.summary: The property fraud John Kiriakou encountered at FCI Loretto — a prisoner who forged papers transferring ownership of a golf course to himself and then began charging people rent — and the place such crimes occupy in the prison's own hierarchy of offences.

the-quarterback-with-a-personal-chef.title: Ali from Newark
the-quarterback-with-a-personal-chef.summary: The Black shot caller at FCI Loretto, near the end of a twenty-five-year drug sentence, who came to embrace John Kiriakou at the close of his term and tell him how much he respected him — a friendship possible only because Kiriakou had decided on arrival to ignore the prison's racial divisions.

the-quarterback-with-a-personal-chef.title: Say five years
the-quarterback-with-a-personal-chef.summary: The first piece of prison advice John Kiriakou says he was given — from a Bonanno family captain, walking laps of the snowed-in basketball court at FCI Loretto — to tell anyone who asked that he was serving five years rather than the thirty months he actually had.

the-quarterback-with-a-personal-chef.title: The forty-seven suffix
the-quarterback-with-a-personal-chef.summary: The last two digits of a federal prisoner number that, according to John Kiriakou, mark the holder as a member of an organised gang — and which the Italians at FCI Loretto carried along with MS-13, the Bloods, the Crips and the Mexican Mafia.

the-quarterback-with-a-personal-chef.title: Clyde Hall
the-quarterback-with-a-personal-chef.summary: The imprisoned Ohio congressman John Kiriakou says served at his prison a few years before him, whose remark on release — that he had made some of the best friends of his life inside — Kiriakou thought insane at the time and came to understand after his own sentence.

the-quarterback-with-a-personal-chef.title: The body in the barrel
the-quarterback-with-a-personal-chef.summary: The exchange John Kiriakou reports having with a fellow prisoner who explained his conviction by saying the police had found a body in a barrel in his storage unit — and that a hundred people had access to the unit — to which Kiriakou's only reply was that he was not judging him.

the-question-about-the-showers.title: Maxwell at a work camp
the-question-about-the-showers.summary: John Kiriakou's objection to Ghislaine Maxwell's placement in a minimum security work camp — that convicted sex offenders are, in his experience, never eligible for minimums — and his refusal, when pressed, to offer any explanation for the exception.

the-question-about-the-showers.title: The forty-seven suffix
the-question-about-the-showers.summary: The last two digits of a federal prisoner number that, according to John Kiriakou, mark the holder as a member of an organised gang — and which the Italians at FCI Loretto carried along with MS-13, the Bloods, the Crips and the Mexican Mafia.

the-question-about-the-showers.title: The hierarchy of charges
the-question-about-the-showers.summary: How federal prisoners ranked one another by offence, in John Kiriakou's account — RICO at the top, usually with a murder conspiracy attached; wealthy white-collar convicts despised as soft; and arson, insurance fraud and mortgage fraud attracting no interest at all.

the-question-about-the-showers.title: Ali from Newark
the-question-about-the-showers.summary: The Black shot caller at FCI Loretto, near the end of a twenty-five-year drug sentence, who came to embrace John Kiriakou at the close of his term and tell him how much he respected him — a friendship possible only because Kiriakou had decided on arrival to ignore the prison's racial divisions.

the-question-about-the-showers.title: Clyde Hall
the-question-about-the-showers.summary: The imprisoned Ohio congressman John Kiriakou says served at his prison a few years before him, whose remark on release — that he had made some of the best friends of his life inside — Kiriakou thought insane at the time and came to understand after his own sentence.

the-question-about-the-showers.title: Say five years
the-question-about-the-showers.summary: The first piece of prison advice John Kiriakou says he was given — from a Bonanno family captain, walking laps of the snowed-in basketball court at FCI Loretto — to tell anyone who asked that he was serving five years rather than the thirty months he actually had.

the-ramot-junction-shooting.title: Astrology at the CIA
the-ramot-junction-shooting.summary: John Kiriakou''s confirmation that astrology played a role in CIA work in the 1950s and early 1960s as part of MK-ULTRA, alongside time travel and teleportation — and his explanation for why: officials with unlimited budgets and no obligation to report to the public reasoned that there was probably nothing to it, but that if there were, it would make them a star.

the-ramot-junction-shooting.title: Carrying passports in Washington
the-ramot-junction-shooting.summary: John Kiriakou's report in September 2025 that people in Washington had begun carrying their passports for fear of being scooped up by immigration enforcement — alongside the case of an American symphony violinist held for three weeks, and his own belief that ethnic profiling violates the Fourth Amendment.

the-ramot-junction-shooting.title: "Christians are suckers"
the-ramot-junction-shooting.summary: John Kiriakou's explanation for how a president who does not go to church, has no spiritual adviser and could not name a line of scripture can push school prayer without cost — that he thinks most Christians are suckers, an assessment Kiriakou says he hates to make and believes anyway.

the-ramot-junction-shooting.title: E. Jean Carroll
the-ramot-junction-shooting.summary: The plaintiff whose persistence John Kiriakou singled out for deep respect — she kept suing after the political tide turned against her, and won an award he put at eighty-three or eighty-five million dollars on a day when Donald Trump won almost everything else in the federal courts.

the-ramot-junction-shooting.title: Find a Grave
the-ramot-junction-shooting.summary: The cemetery database John Kiriakou calls literally his favourite website on the internet, which he opens during the ten-minute countdown before broadcasts and uses to decide who goes into his cemetery books — and which supplied him the story of Greta Zimmer Friedman.

the-ramot-junction-shooting.title: Greta Zimmer Friedman
the-ramot-junction-shooting.summary: The Austrian-born dental assistant John Kiriakou found listed on Find a Grave as a "pop culture icon" — the woman a sailor grabbed and kissed in Times Square on V-J Day 1945, misidentified for years as a nurse, buried at Arlington, and whose story Kiriakou tells as the reason he writes cemetery books.

the-rare-earth-calculation.title: Dumping the treasury bonds
the-rare-earth-calculation.summary: The second economic weapon John Kiriakou says China holds against the United States — its position as the second or third largest holder of long-term government treasury bonds, which it could simply dump, and which he says would crash the entire American economy.

the-rare-earth-calculation.title: "Beyond Your Dreams"
the-rare-earth-calculation.summary: The gloss a host gave John Kiriakou on his first trip to China when he asked what the beautiful car with the BYD badge was — and the answer he got when he asked why he had never heard of it, which was that the United States is the only country where they are not sold.

the-rare-earth-calculation.title: The Hyundai robots
the-rare-earth-calculation.summary: The South Korean robots John Kiriakou cites as the answer to a promise the Pentagon has been making for decades — long-life batteries solved by a Hyundai subsidiary, robots ready to go to market that can get into a self-driving car and do the grocery shopping, and his question of why DARPA has not managed it.

the-rare-earth-calculation.title: Afghan rare earth minerals
the-rare-earth-calculation.summary: John Kiriakou's argument, made days after the fall of Kabul in August 2021, that the country with real leverage in Afghanistan was China — which holds an exclusive contract to mine rare earth metals valued in a Defense Department report at one trillion dollars, and therefore has a stake in a stable long-term Afghan government even a Taliban one.

the-rare-earth-calculation.title: Carving up Iran
the-rare-earth-calculation.summary: The Israeli end goal John Kiriakou says has been discussed with increasingly less discretion — dividing Iran into five small rump countries including Balochistan, Arabistan and Kurdistan, on the reasoning that small states are more easily controlled — and which he expects Israel will eventually try to get Donald Trump to carry out.

the-rare-earth-calculation.title: Lavrov on sanctions
the-rare-earth-calculation.summary: The two remarks by Russian foreign minister Sergey Lavrov that John Kiriakou pairs to summarise the failure of the sanctions weapon — that Russia was surprised by how swiftly the Americans imposed sanctions, and, a year or two later, surprised by how quickly Russia got around them.

the-ras-laffan-strike.title: South Pars and the North Dome
the-ras-laffan-strike.summary: The gas field beneath the Persian Gulf that Iran and Qatar share, and John Kiriakou''s explanation of why the Israeli strike on the Iranian third was not an accident: hit one and you hit the other automatically, and Israel had reason to want Qatar hit.

the-ras-laffan-strike.title: Why Iran targets the Gulf states
the-ras-laffan-strike.summary: John Kiriakou''s explanation of why Iranian missiles fell more heavily on Gulf Arab states than on Israel during the 2026 war: the Gulf has no Iron Dome, a finite missile stock has to be spent where it counts, and hosting American forces converted an uneasy coexistence into open enmity.

the-ras-laffan-strike.title: 2026 Iran war economic shock
the-ras-laffan-strike.summary: John Kiriakou''s running assessment of the economic damage from the 2026 Iran war — an oil shock he says already exceeds both 1970s shocks combined, a natural-gas shock worse than the Nord Stream destruction, and a chokepoint problem that runs through fertilizer as much as fuel, since 65% of the world''s supply must transit the Strait of Hormuz. His summary: "This is an economic slowdown of choice."

the-ras-laffan-strike.title: Asian fuel reserves, 2026
the-ras-laffan-strike.summary: The effect of the Strait of Hormuz closure on oil-importing Asian economies as John Kiriakou described it — countries counting their remaining fuel in days rather than months, with no substitute supply available, and economies he expects simply to stop.

the-ras-laffan-strike.title: Iranian oil sanctions relief, 2026
the-ras-laffan-strike.summary: The American decision, during the war it was fighting against Iran, to lift sanctions on Iranian oil at sea in order to hold prices down. John Kiriakou pairs it with the moment an Indian ship paid Iran for oil in yuan and was waved through — after which, he says, the sanctions came off.

the-ras-laffan-strike.title: Advice to an aspiring intelligence analyst
the-ras-laffan-strike.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer to a 21-year-old student asking what to study and what to read: pick a geographic area, become the go-to person on it, and consume everything published in the field — including the journals written by people who have never made policy.

the-rashid-family.title: The Emir of Bahrain''s verdict
the-rashid-family.summary: The judgement John Kiriakou says the Emir of Bahrain delivered to him at his beach house — that George H. W. Bush was the last American president to give the Arabs a fair shake — and Kiriakou''s reasons for agreeing with it.

the-rashid-family.title: The Penn State textbooks
the-rashid-family.summary: How a week-long high-school scholarship to Penn State sent the teenage John Kiriakou into the university bookstore to buy the textbooks for Middle East courses he was not enrolled in — the purchase he credits with turning a childhood fascination into a field of study.

the-rashid-family.title: The Saudi-administered Gaza proposal
the-rashid-family.summary: An arrangement reported in the Israeli left-wing press and repeated by John Kiriakou as a possible basis for future talks: a disarmed, semi-independent Gaza policed and rebuilt by Saudi Arabia, with a port, an airport, a power grid and a sewage system.

the-rashid-family.title: Bill Clinton
the-rashid-family.summary: 42nd U.S. president whom John Kiriakou describes as wholly disinterested in intelligence — briefed by the CIA only twice in eight years, with Vice President Al Gore taking the daily briefing instead and relaying anything important.

the-rashid-family.title: Church Committee
the-rashid-family.summary: U.S. Senate investigative committee operating in 1975–1976 that examined domestic intelligence abuses by the CIA, FBI, and NSA; per John Kiriakou, the Church Committee — alongside the concurrent Pike Committee in the House — was the last genuine moment of legislative oversight over the intelligence community, born of a national consensus that government had gone dangerously off course. Its work led to the creation of the permanent Senate Select Committee on Intelligence, which Kiriakou says ceased to function as real oversight roughly seven years after its founding.

the-rashid-family.title: Fifty new crimes a year
the-rashid-family.summary: John Kiriakou''s argument that the United States has become a carceral country by legislative accretion — fifty newly created federal crimes every year for two decades, on top of five per cent of the world''s population holding twenty-five per cent of its prisoners.

the-rebuttal-book.title: George Tenet
the-rebuttal-book.summary: Director of Central Intelligence from 1997 to 2004, spanning the September 11 attacks and the early enhanced-interrogation program; identified by John Kiriakou as John Brennan's institutional patron at the agency; the figure who ordered the Five Eyes intelligence services to "open the files" to each other in the early 2000s.

the-rebuttal-book.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
the-rebuttal-book.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

the-rebuttal-book.title: Mitchell and Jessen
the-rebuttal-book.summary: The two American psychologists who pitched the CIA's enhanced interrogation program to Director George Tenet at a cocktail party in late October 2001; designers of the program and its theoretical underpinning, "learned helplessness."

the-rebuttal-book.title: Senate Torture Report
the-rebuttal-book.summary: The December 2014 executive summary of the U.S. Senate Select Committee on Intelligence's study of the CIA's post-9/11 detention and interrogation program; the first public disclosure of techniques including rectal feeding with hummus, sexual assault with broomsticks, and prolonged sleep deprivation.

the-rebuttal-book.title: Abu Zubaydah
the-rebuttal-book.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

the-rebuttal-book.title: John Brennan
the-rebuttal-book.summary: Former Director of the CIA; characterized in KiriPedia's source corpus as the principal architect of the agency's enhanced interrogation program and as having plotted against an elected President

the-red-fort-bombing.title: Coffee with a cabinet member
the-red-fort-bombing.summary: John Kiriakou's disclosure that he had coffee with a member of the cabinet who told him to be patient about his pardon — and told him to watch what he said. He reports the meeting while stating plainly that there is nothing further he can do to make his case, and that he is not confident the outcome will be decided on justice.

the-red-fort-bombing.title: Ed Martin and the pardon file
the-red-fort-bombing.summary: The US pardon attorney whose office John Kiriakou directed supporters to write to, and the message a mutual friend brought back from him: that he was the third person that day to call about Kiriakou, that Kiriakou should relax, and that his file was literally on Martin''s desk. Kiriakou''s advice to letter-writers was to send physical mail rather than email.

the-red-fort-bombing.title: Lincoln's candlelight pardons
the-red-fort-bombing.summary: The historical contrast John Kiriakou drew while discussing a mass grant of clemency: stories of Abraham Lincoln staying up late into the night pardoning Civil War deserters by candlelight, on the principle that nobody should be executed for cowardice — set against a modern president who Kiriakou says has pardoned more people than anyone in American history, whenever the mood strikes him.

the-red-fort-bombing.title: Pardons nobody asked for
the-red-fort-bombing.summary: Two cases John Kiriakou cites of people pardoned without applying: the Binance founder, who said publicly that he had never met the president, never asked for a pardon and never applied for one; and Darryl Strawberry, a New York Mets great with tax and drug problems behind him. Kiriakou raises both while waiting, unsuccessfully, for a pardon he has actively sought for years.

the-red-fort-bombing.title: Sergey Lavrov
the-red-fort-bombing.summary: Russian foreign minister, and previously Russian ambassador to the United Nations during John Kiriakou's assignment there, where the two worked the same Security Council. Kiriakou describes him as the most admired diplomat in the building — the most powerful, important and strategic ambassador there despite operating with far smaller resources than his American, British, French and Chinese counterparts, and better than most of the American diplomats Kiriakou worked for. When Lavrov was abruptly sidelined in late 2025, Kiriakou's reading was retirement rather than disgrace.

the-red-fort-bombing.title: "Stefanik will not be governor"
the-red-fort-bombing.summary: John Kiriakou's flat, on-the-record prediction about the New York governor's race, made against a friend he describes as irrationally conservative who insisted the contest would turn on a single issue — the right to carry a gun. Kiriakou called it the most ridiculous thing he had heard the man say, and argued that Elise Stefanik's political career is finished.

the-referee-in-a-greek-turkish-war.title: Six different passports
the-referee-in-a-greek-turkish-war.summary: John Kiriakou's answer to what has changed for intelligence officers since his own service — that he carried six different passports, and that he does not know how officers cross borders now that AI and facial recognition mean everything is scanned and stored — coupled with his advice not to let the technology take over the job.

the-referee-in-a-greek-turkish-war.title: The east Mediterranean gas partnership
the-referee-in-a-greek-turkish-war.summary: John Kiriakou''s explanation for why the Greek government is solidly pro-Israel while the Greek public is solidly anti-Israel: Cyprus sits on an ocean of natural gas, and the Greeks, Cypriots, Israelis and — to a lesser extent — Egyptians lift it together and share the money. The arrangement drives Turkey to distraction, and in his reading puts Greek–Turkish relations on track to get worse.

the-referee-in-a-greek-turkish-war.title: The Foreign Relations volume and the sources still alive
the-referee-in-a-greek-turkish-war.summary: The errand that put John Kiriakou and Cofer Black in a car to the White House on the morning of 11 September 2001: three declassified cables due to be printed in a State Department history volume named CIA sources who were still living — and an obscure law requiring the United States to resettle any source it outs.

the-referee-in-a-greek-turkish-war.title: Greek Intelligence Service
the-referee-in-a-greek-turkish-war.summary: Greece's intelligence service, with which John Kiriakou worked closely during his Athens posting; its head of surveillance called off surveillance on him after watching him make a large offering at Saint Nectarios's tomb on the island of Aegina.

the-referee-in-a-greek-turkish-war.title: Israel, Turkey, and NATO Article 5
the-referee-in-a-greek-turkish-war.summary: John Kiriakou's scenario in which an Israeli attack on Turkey would oblige every NATO member, the United States included, to come to Turkey's defence — and in which the alliance would sooner dissolve than honour that obligation against Israel.

the-referee-in-a-greek-turkish-war.title: Cofer Black's warning to the liaison class
the-referee-in-a-greek-turkish-war.summary: The briefing Cofer Black gave to a class of visiting foreign liaison officers weeks before 11 September 2001 — code words about a honey salesman, a great football match and an enormous wedding — and the private exchange afterwards in which he told John Kiriakou he had been deadly serious.

the-regime-change-approval-process.title: CIA political action group
the-regime-change-approval-process.summary: The CIA's most secretive clandestine propaganda arm — successor to the Cold War 'active measures group' — which John Kiriakou says places and funds propagandists worldwide; no officer of it has been publicly identified since 1982, and he encountered its work funding the DNC's and RNC's international arms in post-war Kuwait.

the-regime-change-approval-process.title: Generals in national security posts
the-regime-change-approval-process.summary: John Kiriakou''s blanket objection to putting retired generals in charge of the CIA, the Office of the Director of National Intelligence, the Defense Department or the National Security Council, resting on a single argument about how officers reach flag rank: generals became generals by saying ''yes sir'', and what a president needs is somebody who can tell him why an idea is terrible.

the-regime-change-approval-process.title: The assassination approval process
the-regime-change-approval-process.summary: Why John Kiriakou thinks arranging the death of a foreign leader is far harder for the CIA than the public assumes. It is not the 1960s: there is congressional oversight, and before any proposal reaches the president''s signature it must clear layers of lawyers at the Justice Department''s Office of Legal Counsel, the National Security Council and the agency''s own General Counsel. Pressuring a leader into flight, he notes, is both easier and more legal.

the-regime-change-approval-process.title: National Security Council
the-regime-change-approval-process.summary: The White House body that, in John Kiriakou's telling, sat on the pro-war side of every fight that defined his era — gung-ho for the Iraq invasion alongside Cheney's and Rumsfeld's offices while the CIA, State Department, and Joint Chiefs opposed it; the place where an official predicted Iraqis would "throw flowers at us"; a signature stop in the approval chain for both the torture program and covert action findings; and the perch from which John Brennan, as its number two, urged the Justice Department to secretly reopen the case against Kiriakou.

the-regime-change-approval-process.title: The CIA-Pentagon war divide
the-regime-change-approval-process.summary: The recurring split John Kiriakou describes across successive U.S. wars, the CIA, the State Department, and the Joint Chiefs of Staff on one side counselling caution, and the office of the vice president, the office of the secretary of defense, and the National Security Council on the other pushing for military action, a division Kiriakou first heard laid out in May 2002 on his first day as executive assistant to the CIA's deputy director for operations, and which he says held again on Iran twenty-four years later.

the-regime-change-approval-process.title: Elliott Abrams
the-regime-change-approval-process.summary: The Reagan-era assistant secretary of state whose 2023 appointment to a Biden administration advisory board John Kiriakou treated as proof that neoliberal and neoconservative foreign policy are the same policy with interchangeable players — a man who pleaded guilty over Iran-Contra, was pardoned, helped sell the Iraqi weapons of mass destruction case, and then served Donald Trump on Iran and Venezuela.

the-rejected-deposits.title: Quoted on NPR
the-rejected-deposits.summary: John Kiriakou's discovery, via a standing Google alert on his own name, that National Public Radio had cited a DeProgram discussion between him and Ted Rall in an article on Palestinians killed while waiting for food — an outlet he had walked out on years earlier.

the-rejected-deposits.title: The Addis Ababa zoo
the-rejected-deposits.summary: A visit John Kiriakou made to the zoo in Addis Ababa on a free half-day, where he watched keepers force a screaming donkey into the lion enclosure — and noted the two-tier admission price charged to foreigners.

the-rejected-deposits.title: The boring cover story
the-rejected-deposits.summary: The CIA training principle John Kiriakou says governed how officers described their jobs to strangers: pick something so dull that nobody asks a second question. His own standard answer was the foreign service, training work, and some import-export negotiation.

the-rejected-deposits.title: The election day 1992 poll
the-rejected-deposits.summary: An informal show of hands taken in a CIA branch office on election day 1992, which John Kiriakou describes as the moment he discovered he had no idea of the politics of the colleagues he sat three feet away from — and that he was not, as he had assumed, the only progressive in the room.

the-rejected-deposits.title: The ex-prisoner at the Bureau of Prisons
the-rejected-deposits.summary: John Kiriakou's approving account of the appointment of a former federal prisoner — recently released after five years on a drug conspiracy charge — as deputy director of the Bureau of Prisons, which he calls an inspired choice and one of the few things he has praised Donald Trump for.

the-rejected-deposits.title: The fifteen-dollar maintenance fee
the-rejected-deposits.summary: An appointment John Kiriakou made at his bank on the morning of a broadcast to ask for the return of a $15 monthly maintenance fee that had taken his account to minus fifteen dollars — a story he told on air as a plain statement of what his finances looked like after prison.

the-reluctant-spy.title: Espionage Act
the-reluctant-spy.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

the-reluctant-spy.title: Recruitment attempts on Kiriakou
the-reluctant-spy.summary: A series of episodes in which foreign intelligence officers tried to recruit John Kiriakou himself — an over-eager Hungarian during his CIA application, a French counterterrorism officer who staged a car pickup in Islamabad, and a Shin Bet officer at his first liaison briefing.

the-reluctant-spy.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
the-reluctant-spy.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

the-reluctant-spy.title: Kiriakou's transfer to the Directorate of Operations
the-reluctant-spy.summary: John Kiriakou's roughly two-month internal campaign to transfer from the CIA's analytic Directorate of Intelligence to the operational Directorate of Operations, overcoming what he calls a "natural bias in operations against the eggheads on the analytic side," followed by an Athens posting secured because he was the only person in the entire CIA fluent in both Greek and Arabic. Covers his full CIA career arc from 1988/1990 recruitment through analyst years on Iraq, the switch to operations, 9/11, the enhanced-interrogation refusal, executive assistant to the deputy director for operations, and his eventual resignation and post-CIA career.

the-reluctant-spy.title: PTSD
the-reluctant-spy.summary: Post-traumatic stress disorder runs through John Kiriakou''s life and worldview — he had it coming out of Greece after an assassination attempt, brought it home from Pakistan alongside his shock at colleagues'' willingness to kill, and was blindsided by a delayed post-prison version that helped end his marriage. For six months after release he dreamed the same dream nightly: that he was out by mistake and had to get back inside before midnight count. He still takes a repurposed blood-pressure drug that stops the dreams, and he extends the diagnosis outward — to secret-site interrogators who came back crying, to drone pilots, and to prisoners released angry and untreated.

the-reluctant-spy.title: Sweat Lodge
the-reluctant-spy.summary: Per John Kiriakou, the federal prison where he was incarcerated had a Native American sweat lodge that was shut down after it was misused for sex rather than religious ceremony; he says he has never personally been in a sweat lodge.

the-resort-with-no-air-conditioning.title: The tarantula on the mini fridge
the-resort-with-no-air-conditioning.summary: The wildlife of the Baja resort as John Kiriakou catalogued it — rattlesnakes everywhere, an emailed instruction never to go barefoot, shoes shaken out before every midnight walk to the mini fridge kept outdoors, a flashlight in hand, and one night at three in the morning a tarantula sitting on the fridge itself.

the-resort-with-no-air-conditioning.title: The fox that ate the scraps
the-resort-with-no-air-conditioning.summary: The small grey desert fox that lived on the grounds of the Baja resort, which the cook told John Kiriakou would finish anything left on the plate — and which, every single night, defecated on exactly the spot he crossed to reach his outdoor mini fridge.

the-resort-with-no-air-conditioning.title: Where he slept in Afghanistan
the-resort-with-no-air-conditioning.summary: John Kiriakou's inventory of his own Afghan accommodation across a decade of trips — a shared tent on the first visits, a tent of his own once ("living high on the hog"), the officers' quarters at Bagram once the American foothold was serious, and a three-star Afghan hotel when he returned as a private citizen to get the Kite Runner children out.

the-resort-with-no-air-conditioning.title: The washed-out road to the airport
the-resort-with-no-air-conditioning.summary: The drive to catch a flight to the Joe Rogan taping, after a hurricane took out the only road from the Baja resort — thirty-five miles in almost two hours, driven by his co-star Jeff Fahey and by Tyrel Ventura, over a dune, across cactus, with the animals jumping out of the way.

the-resort-with-no-air-conditioning.title: Joe Rogan
the-resort-with-no-air-conditioning.summary: The podcast host whose show John Kiriakou finally sat for in October 2025 — an experience that began with signing a non-disclosure agreement and ended with his verdict that Rogan is "a nice guy, very down to earth, very normal." The first thing Rogan asked, walking into the studio ten minutes late: "Hey, do you know my friend Mike Baker?" Kiriakou defends Rogan as unfairly characterized as a right-winger, and had long cited the show as the venue where Zuckerberg admitted Facebook suppressed the Hunter Biden laptop story at the FBI''s behest.

the-resort-with-no-air-conditioning.title: Abigail Spanberger
the-resort-with-no-air-conditioning.summary: Governor of Virginia from 2025 and, before Congress, a CIA officer alongside John Kiriakou in the Counterterrorism Center — whom he calls a perfectly nice person who would have been a middle-of-the-road Republican in the 1970s and 1980s, and whose victory speech, to his surprise, said all the right things.

the-restaurants-in-witness-protection.title: The code room and the buried weapons
the-restaurants-in-witness-protection.summary: What John Kiriakou demanded when the officer he had cold-pitched in Athens agreed to meet him — access to his embassy's code room and all of its weapons — and the meeting in a hotel coffee shop, surrounded by armed CIA officers at every table, at which the terms were set.

the-restaurants-in-witness-protection.title: The broken side-view mirror
the-restaurants-in-witness-protection.summary: The cold pitch John Kiriakou made in Athens against the incoming intelligence representative of a hostile Middle Eastern state — a manoeuvre suggested by his mentor Gust Avrakotos, in which Kiriakou snapped the mirror off the man's diplomatic car with a bag of books, established cover with the neighbour, apologised at the door, asked for a glass of water, and used the minute alone to kneel down and speak Arabic to the target's four-year-old daughter.

the-restaurants-in-witness-protection.title: Agent inducements
the-restaurants-in-witness-protection.summary: The non-cash things the CIA can offer a recruited agent — a child's university place anywhere in America, treatment at a top hospital for a sick spouse, or a carefully staged personal gift — and the standing arrangements with universities and large corporations that make them possible.

the-restaurants-in-witness-protection.title: Asset acquisition cycle
the-restaurants-in-witness-protection.summary: The four-step process — spot, assess, develop, recruit — taught as the first lesson of CIA case officer training

the-restaurants-in-witness-protection.title: Agent payment mechanics
the-restaurants-in-witness-protection.summary: How the CIA physically pays a recruited agent — cash every month, a receipt signed with any alias the agent chooses, and a polygraph regime built around the assumption that the officer handling the money is the person most likely to steal it.
