the-restaurants-in-witness-protection.title: Access Agent
the-restaurants-in-witness-protection.summary: CIA (and foreign intelligence service) term for a recruited asset whose value lies not in the secrets they hold directly but in their regular social access to high-value targets — politicians, executives, heads of state — who cannot themselves be recruited. Per John Kiriakou, the access agent is funded generously to maintain an environment in which the targets feel comfortable and return repeatedly; kompromat — compromising photographs or recordings — may be collected as a secondary tool. Kiriakou identifies Jeffrey Epstein as a textbook access agent, in his assessment working for Israeli intelligence.

the-roadblock-drone-strike.title: Daniel Hale
the-roadblock-drone-strike.summary: Per John Kiriakou, drone whistleblower Daniel Hale — an NSA contractor and drone targeting analyst who exposed an 80% civilian death rate in the U.S. drone program, was ordered to fire on two young girls his superior called "goats," and was sentenced to 45 months (of which Kiriakou says he actually served about 18) despite prosecutors seeking nine to eleven years.

the-roadblock-drone-strike.title: Communications management unit
the-roadblock-drone-strike.summary: The two restricted-contact units inside the American federal prison system, at Terre Haute and Marion; built for "the worst of the worst" but, in John Kiriakou's account, used to silence prisoners whose messages are inconvenient — and a practice he groups with solitary confinement as torture. He served part of his own sentence in a modified one.

the-roadblock-drone-strike.title: Espionage Act
the-roadblock-drone-strike.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

the-roadblock-drone-strike.title: Liam O'Grady
the-roadblock-drone-strike.summary: The Eastern District of Virginia judge who sentenced Daniel Hale, and who in John Kiriakou''s account surprised the courtroom twice: with a sentence of 45 months rather than the far longer term expected, and with a recommendation that Hale serve it in a low-security prison where he could be treated for depression and addiction. The Bureau of Prisons ignored the recommendation and sent him to the communications management unit at Marion instead.

the-roadblock-drone-strike.title: Daniel Ellsberg
the-roadblock-drone-strike.summary: The Pentagon Papers whistleblower Kiriakou calls 'the Godfather of all national security whistleblowers' — and one of the great mentors of his life.

the-rogue-officer-remark.title: The declination letter
the-rogue-officer-remark.summary: The letter the Justice Department sent John Kiriakou's attorneys in December 2008 declining to prosecute him, on the grounds that the torture allegations were already public through human rights organizations and that it is illegal to classify a crime — and the celebration dinner that was followed three weeks later by Barack Obama's inauguration.

the-rogue-officer-remark.title: Curtailment cables
the-rogue-officer-remark.summary: The career-ending requests John Kiriakou says he read coming back from the CIA's black sites — officers, doctors, psychologists and nurses asking to end their tours early rather than continue to take part in the interrogation programme — and his conclusion that if that many people were objecting in classified channels, someone would surely go public.

the-rogue-officer-remark.title: Bankruptcy and the dropped charges
the-rogue-officer-remark.summary: The sequence John Kiriakou places at the centre of his case: that the espionage counts against him were dropped only after his legal fees had bankrupted him, which he presents as evidence that the government''s aim was attrition rather than conviction.

the-rogue-officer-remark.title: Arabic and Greek
the-rogue-officer-remark.summary: The qualification John Kiriakou says opened the door to his transfer from CIA analysis to operations: a post in Athens wanted Greek or Arabic, and he had both — by most of his tellings the only officer in the agency who did. The chief who hired him gave the reason in one sentence: it is easier and cheaper to take a linguist and teach him operations than the other way round. The pairing also became a detection tool, since the language nobody speaks in Pakistan is Arabic.

the-rogue-officer-remark.title: Security, finance and medical
the-rogue-officer-remark.summary: The rule John Kiriakou says CIA recruits were taught in their first week on the job — that there are exactly three offices an officer may never lie to, because those three can end a career — and the reasoning he attaches to each.

the-rogue-officer-remark.title: The bowl of dates
the-rogue-officer-remark.summary: The detail John Kiriakou uses to compress his argument about interrogation: that the intelligence the CIA''s contractors reported as the fruit of waterboarding had in fact been obtained by an FBI agent who offered Abu Zubaydah a bowl of dates.

the-rooftop-double-agent.title: 2026 Iran war

the-rooftop-double-agent.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
the-rooftop-double-agent.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

the-rooftop-double-agent.title: Củ Chi tunnels
the-rooftop-double-agent.summary: The 250-kilometre tunnel network dug by the Viet Cong outside Saigon, which John Kiriakou visited in 2026 and could not physically enter. He attributes the tunnels' viability to the malnutrition of the people who dug them.

the-rooftop-double-agent.title: Dewey Clarridge
the-rooftop-double-agent.summary: The CIA operations officer John Kiriakou calls a legendary figure and a giant of the 1980s — prosecuted over Iran-Contra, and the man who said publicly that Saudi Arabia already had nuclear weapons. Kiriakou believes him, holds that the Saudis financed the Pakistani bomb and were repaid in access to it, and believes Clarridge was also involved in the movement of cocaine into the United States.

the-royal-family-at-taif.title: Mr. Fish
the-royal-family-at-taif.summary: The cover name the CIA used for Abu Zubaydah in Pakistan in 2002 — invented because the Americans would not tell their Pakistani partners who the target was, and derived from the only thing they would say about him: that he was a big fish.

the-royal-family-at-taif.title: The lapsed film rights
the-royal-family-at-taif.summary: John Kiriakou has sold the rights to his life story three separate times — to Universal, 20th Century Fox and Paramount — and all three studios let the option lapse, telling him there was too much detail and too many stories to fit into two hours.

the-royal-family-at-taif.title: Gulf security bargain
the-royal-family-at-taif.summary: The decades-old arrangement — traced by John Kiriakou to FDR and the Saudi king, and originally British — under which Gulf Arab monarchies host U.S. bases and sell oil in dollars in exchange for American protection; a bargain Kiriakou says collapsed when those bases failed to shield them during the war on Iran.

the-royal-family-at-taif.title: Iraqi invasion of Kuwait
the-royal-family-at-taif.summary: John Kiriakou''s most detailed account of the intelligence process around the 1990 Iraqi invasion of Kuwait and its 1991 liberation. As a first-year CIA analyst on a ''training account'' covering Iraq, Kiriakou produced the June 30, 1990 warning paper for the White House; suggested calling the US Defense Attaché in Baghdad to drive to the border and report what he saw (the answer: ''Literally the entire Iraqi military is heading south''); briefed the August 2 Oval Office meeting with Bush; and later took a single phone call from General Colin Powell that led, eight hours later, to 47 cruise missiles striking the Iraqi Intelligence Service headquarters in Baghdad.

the-royal-family-at-taif.title: Sheikh Saad al-Abdullah
the-royal-family-at-taif.summary: Crown Prince and Prime Minister of Kuwait during the 1990–91 Iraqi occupation; per John Kiriakou, the day-to-day leader of the Kuwaiti government-in-exile in Taif — "very military," "hands-on," "the best leader Kuwait had for that situation," meeting twenty hours a day with everyone who needed to be met and simultaneously managing the Kuwaiti resistance on the ground.

the-royal-family-at-taif.title: April Glaspie
the-royal-family-at-taif.summary: U.S. Ambassador to Iraq in the run-up to the 1990 invasion of Kuwait; per John Kiriakou, delivered to Saddam Hussein — on a NODIS cable from Secretary of State James Baker — the line that the United States took no position on Arab-Arab border disputes, which Saddam is widely held to have read as a green light to invade. Kiriakou, who was in the CIA operations center the night her reporting cable came back, holds that she got a bum rap.

the-russian-nuclear-umbrella.title: 2026 Iran war
the-russian-nuclear-umbrella.summary: The open-ended American and Israeli war against Iran that John Kiriakou tracked week by week on his own show — a conflict he says was sold as three weeks, ran into its fifth month, achieved every decapitation objective it set, and continued anyway. His grade for it is a D, and his forecast is a Truth Social post declaring victory while nothing changes.

the-russian-nuclear-umbrella.title: Iran 12-Day War
the-russian-nuclear-umbrella.summary: 2025 Israeli air campaign against Iran during which Israel killed at least fourteen Iranian nuclear scientists by destroying the apartment buildings they lived in; preceded for each scientist by Farsi-language telephone calls from Iranian-Jewish Mossad and Shin Bet officers offering defection in lieu of certain death; characterized by John Kiriakou as a categorical departure from CIA targeting doctrine in its acceptable-civilian-casualty calculus.

the-russian-nuclear-umbrella.title: Iran Nuclear Assessment
the-russian-nuclear-umbrella.summary: Per John Kiriakou's assessment, the US–Israeli military campaign against Iran was a war of choice driven by Israeli political pressure rather than genuine intelligence indicating an Iranian nuclear weapons threat. The CIA produced two National Intelligence Estimates concluding Iran had no nuclear weapons program; Supreme Leader Ayatollah Khamenei issued a fatwa in the 1980s forbidding such a program. The U.S. went to war anyway, in Kiriakou's view, after President Trump replaced the Joint Chiefs of Staff with officers willing to accept Israeli intelligence and proceed.

the-russian-nuclear-umbrella.title: Israel's cell-phone assassinations in Iran
the-russian-nuclear-umbrella.summary: John Kiriakou's account of how Israel wiped out Iran's military leadership by tracking cell phones — recruiting destitute Afghan refugees as $100-a-month spotters, and, when the generals stopped carrying phones, targeting their bodyguards' phones instead.

the-russian-nuclear-umbrella.title: Reza Pahlavi
the-russian-nuclear-umbrella.summary: The exiled Iranian crown prince whom John Kiriakou dismisses as an Israeli-backed fantasy candidate to rule Iran — a man who has not lived there since his teens, supported mainly by Beverly Hills exiles, whom Kiriakou says 'wouldn't survive the walk from the plane to the terminal.'

the-russian-nuclear-umbrella.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
the-russian-nuclear-umbrella.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

the-russian-soldier-in-manama.title: Ian Henderson
the-russian-soldier-in-manama.summary: The British colonial police officer who ran Bahrain's intelligence service during John Kiriakou's posting there — a man Kiriakou says even the heir presumptive to the throne was afraid to name aloud, and whom Kiriakou, seated at the crown prince's table at a dinner for George H. W. Bush, mistook for a corpse.

the-russian-soldier-in-manama.title: The bug in the bedroom
the-russian-soldier-in-manama.summary: The listening device John Kiriakou says fell out of an air conditioning vent onto his bare chest while he read in bed in Bahrain — planted, his chief told him, because he was writing the embassy's human rights report.

the-russian-soldier-in-manama.title: The lapis lazuli paperweight
the-russian-soldier-in-manama.summary: The chunk of raw lapis lazuli John Kiriakou says he took from Osama bin Laden's house in Afghanistan and still keeps — described on air as magnificent, and agreed on air to have probably served as bin Laden's paperweight.

the-russian-soldier-in-manama.title: The Belgian intelligence director
the-russian-soldier-in-manama.summary: The brother of John Kiriakou's oldest friend, a Belgian exchange student at his high school, who rose to run Belgium's intelligence service and become deputy prime minister — and the exchange in which Kiriakou answered the standard defence of an intelligence chief's prejudices with his own experience.

the-russian-soldier-in-manama.title: The embassy swap
the-russian-soldier-in-manama.summary: The 1970s agreement under which the United States and the Soviet Union each built a new embassy in the other's capital — the Russians choosing the highest ground in Washington, the Americans being sold a dry riverbed in Moscow, and the American building having to be demolished because listening devices had been built into every beam.

the-russian-soldier-in-manama.title: Amnesty International
the-russian-soldier-in-manama.summary: The human rights organization whose torture report forms part of John Kiriakou's core defense — the CIA's crimes were already public knowledge before he confirmed them on ABC, and the Justice Department's own declination letter said so — and the organization whose silence during his prosecution he cannot forgive. He begged Amnesty for a one-sentence statement and got a New Yorker subscription instead; it took Ai Weiwei to change their minds, and by then he was walking out of prison.

the-rwanda-deportations.title: The Greek neo-Nazi seats
the-rwanda-deportations.summary: John Kiriakou''s tally of the June 2023 Greek parliamentary election, which he treats as the most disturbing case of a Europe-wide trend: eight parties won seats, six of them right-wing, four of them right-wing extremist, and two of them neo-Nazi parties taking thirteen seats between them.

the-rwanda-deportations.title: The Israeli electorate shift
the-rwanda-deportations.summary: John Kiriakou's structural explanation for why he does not expect Israeli politics to swing back — that the influx of Russian and Ukrainian Jewish immigrants over the preceding ten or fifteen years has moved the electorate so far right that a viable socialist movement or Labour party is, in his view, gone for good.

the-rwanda-deportations.title: Netanyahu and the Tel Aviv police chief
the-rwanda-deportations.summary: The July 2023 dismissal of Tel Aviv's police chief, which John Kiriakou identified as the moment Benjamin Netanyahu may have overstepped — arguing that the real threat to the Israeli prime minister came not from the Palestinians but from his own attempt to take over the court system, and from the strikes and demonstrations that had not subsided.

the-rwanda-deportations.title: The Jenin incursion
the-rwanda-deportations.summary: The Israeli military operation in Jenin of early July 2023, which John Kiriakou cited by its casualty figures — nine Palestinians dead and about a hundred wounded before the withdrawal — and which he called only the very beginning of what the most right-wing government in Israeli history would do.

the-rwanda-deportations.title: Elliott Abrams
the-rwanda-deportations.summary: The Reagan-era assistant secretary of state whose 2023 appointment to a Biden administration advisory board John Kiriakou treated as proof that neoliberal and neoconservative foreign policy are the same policy with interchangeable players — a man who pleaded guilty over Iran-Contra, was pardoned, helped sell the Iraqi weapons of mass destruction case, and then served Donald Trump on Iran and Venezuela.

the-rwanda-deportations.title: Frances Haugen
the-rwanda-deportations.summary: The Facebook employee John Kiriakou refuses to call a whistleblower — arguing that against the legal definition, bringing to light waste, fraud, abuse, illegality or threats to public health or safety, she qualifies as a corporate spokesperson whose motive was to improve the company's bottom line, not to expose wrongdoing.

the-sahel-church-burnings.title: The Sudan massacre
the-sahel-church-burnings.summary: The killing of at least 624 civilians by a government-affiliated militia in Sudan in late October 2025, which John Kiriakou called a crime against humanity — and which he reads as a proxy war financed by the United Arab Emirates on one side and Saudi Arabia on the other, with a Wahhabi component traceable to Hassan al-Turabi.

the-sahel-church-burnings.title: CIA attention to West Africa
the-sahel-church-burnings.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer on whether the CIA is likely to be operating in Burkina Faso: for all the years he was at the agency it cared very little about Africa and especially West Africa, but the presence of al-Qaeda and Islamic State affiliates plus the drug trade makes CIA and special forces involvement probable — and, he adds, the American public will not hear about it.

the-sahel-church-burnings.title: The Colombian air bridge through Venezuela
the-sahel-church-burnings.summary: What John Kiriakou says his own Senate Foreign Relations Committee investigation found about drug trafficking through Venezuela — that it exists, that it consists of Colombian aircraft landing there en route to Africa, and that there is no evidence Nicolás Maduro controls it or knows when and where it happens.

the-sahel-church-burnings.title: The secret Sahel appropriations
the-sahel-church-burnings.summary: John Kiriakou's complaint that the United States is quietly pumping billions of dollars into Niger, Mali, Burkina Faso, Guinea-Conakry and Guinea-Bissau — spending he says is supposed to be a big secret, addresses a French problem rather than an American one, and which American taxpayers have a right to know about and to judge.

the-sahel-church-burnings.title: The Tajik civil war
the-sahel-church-burnings.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the Tajik civil war of the 1990s as the pattern that later conflicts follow — a quarter to a third of the population dead by some accounts, ethnic massacres routine enough that captives were roped together and drowned when the bullets ran out, and a war that lasted exactly as long as its foreign sponsors stayed interested.

the-sahel-church-burnings.title: Abraham Accords
the-sahel-church-burnings.summary: The Trump-brokered normalization deals between Israel and Gulf Arab states — in John Kiriakou's judgment "a terrible idea in the first place," a great victory for Israel and the Gulf Arabs that was "a punch in the throat to the Palestinians." He argues the Accords are how Trump meant to "solve the Middle East in a day" — by screwing the Palestinians — that Hamas read the abandonment correctly, that October 7 shattered the project, and that reviving the Accords (Saudis in, victory declared, Nobel collected) remains the organizing goal of Trump's regional policy.

the-saigon-cia-station-photograph.title: Kiriakou's visit to Vietnam (2026)
the-saigon-cia-station-photograph.summary: A week in Vietnam in August 2026, taken around a paid speech to Australian investment bankers and shaped by four cousins who fought there. John Kiriakou broadcast an episode from Ho Chi Minh City and used the trip to argue that commerce, not force, is what turns a country pro-American.

the-saigon-cia-station-photograph.title: Củ Chi tunnels

the-saigon-cia-station-photograph.title: The McDonald's theory of regime change
the-saigon-cia-station-photograph.summary: John Kiriakou''s argument, drawn from Vietnam and Cuba, that commerce accomplishes what force cannot: to turn a country pro-Western, open a McDonald''s rather than bomb it.

the-saigon-cia-station-photograph.summary: The white prison gang that adopted John Kiriakou on his first day at FCI Loretto. the-samson-option.title: Israeli Nuclear Program
the-samson-option.summary: Israel's widely assumed but officially unacknowledged nuclear arsenal; per John Kiriakou, the conventional wisdom within the CIA is that Israel possesses between 120 and 220 nuclear weapons, and the U.S. government's refusal to formally acknowledge this is driven by a specific legal obligation under the Glenn-Symington Act, which would require cutting off all foreign aid to any nuclear-armed country not party to the Non-Proliferation Treaty.

the-samson-option.title: Greater Israel
the-samson-option.summary: The territorial project John Kiriakou believes the Israeli government genuinely holds: the expulsion of every Palestinian, beginning in Gaza and continuing into the West Bank, pursued on a hundred- or two-hundred-year horizon in the confidence that the United States will never push back.

the-samson-option.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
the-samson-option.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

the-samson-option.title: Lebanon-Israeli Conflict
the-samson-option.summary: Per John Kiriakou, no Israeli government will allow Lebanon to flourish as a nation; he expects continued Israeli attacks and forced displacement of civilians, citing a statistic of up to 700,000 Lebanese internally displaced, and links the war to the "Greater Israel" rhetoric of US ambassador Mike Huckabee.

the-samson-option.title: Mike Huckabee
the-samson-option.summary: The United States ambassador to Israel under Donald Trump, and the subject of a public call for resignation from John Kiriakou after Huckabee received Jonathan Pollard at the American embassy. Kiriakou''s assessment separates two charges: Huckabee is not a traitor but an idiot who did not think the meeting was a big deal, and a former governor of a small state who still behaves as though he can set policy without the State Department or the National Security Council.

the-samson-option.title: Decapitation strikes
the-samson-option.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that killing an adversary's leadership does not defeat the adversary — grounded in a standing joke from his own service that the CIA had killed twenty-seven separate "number three" figures in al-Qaeda, and applied to the 2026 Iran war, where the entire political, military and scientific leadership was killed in the opening days and the fighting continued regardless.

the-san-francisco-bacterium-release.title: French village LSD bread experiment
the-san-francisco-bacterium-release.summary: John Kiriakou's account of a compartmented MK-Ultra experiment in which the CIA dosed the only bakery of a small French village he does not name with LSD — in some tellings by breaking in at night and spiking the yeast, in others by contaminating the flour supplied to it — so that the hapless baker sold the whole village an unwitting trip. Kiriakou places it as the sequel to the San Francisco bacterium release and calls it, in the agency's own terms, a successful operation.

the-san-francisco-bacterium-release.title: MK-Ultra
the-san-francisco-bacterium-release.summary: The CIA's mid-twentieth-century umbrella program of mind-control, behavioral-modification, and biological-warfare experimentation, encompassing subprojects such as MK-Chickwit and MK-Seesaw; active 1952–1975; documented practices included LSD dosing of unwitting American citizens in CIA-rented brothels and the aerosolized release of pathogens into the San Francisco fog; 80% of the program's documentation was destroyed by the CIA in defiance of a 1975 preservation order from Senator Frank Church.

the-san-francisco-bacterium-release.title: Richard Helms
the-san-francisco-bacterium-release.summary: CIA director who, per John Kiriakou, ordered the destruction of all MK-Ultra documents on the same day the Church Committee explicitly told him not to destroy them — and who, in Kiriakou's telling, illegally destroyed most of the agency's JFK material as well. He was held in contempt of Congress and fined a nominal sum that colleagues covered by passing a hat down the corridor to his office. Because of the destruction, only about 15% of the MK-Ultra record survives — largely financial records, from which the program had to be pieced back together.

the-san-francisco-bacterium-release.title: MK-ULTRA in Canada
the-san-francisco-bacterium-release.summary: John Kiriakou''s confirmation that many MK-ULTRA experiments took place on Canadian soil, and his explanation of why: the CIA asked the Canadian intelligence service for help with its anti-Soviet, anti-Chinese remote-viewing and LSD work, and the Canadians gladly gave it.

the-san-francisco-bacterium-release.title: Operation Midnight Climax
the-san-francisco-bacterium-release.summary: Sub-project of the CIA's MK-Ultra program, conducted in San Francisco. Per John Kiriakou, the CIA rented a safe house and paid sex workers to bring men back to it, where agents dosed the men with LSD without their knowledge or consent, then observed their behavior through one-way mirrors. The operation followed an earlier phase in which the CIA had dosed its own employees; when that produced suicides, it moved to using unconsenting members of the public.

the-san-francisco-bacterium-release.title: "Our job is to break the law"
the-san-francisco-bacterium-release.summary: The line John Kiriakou says CIA instructors repeated in training, and the qualification he attached to it at the time: the job is to break the law over there, not here. He describes participating willingly in break-ins abroad while insisting a warrant is required at home.

the-satan-dream.title: PTSD
the-satan-dream.summary: Post-traumatic stress disorder runs through John Kiriakou''s life and worldview — he had it coming out of Greece after an assassination attempt, brought it home from Pakistan alongside his shock at colleagues'' willingness to kill, and was blindsided by a delayed post-prison version that helped end his marriage. For six months after release he dreamed the same dream nightly: that he was out by mistake and had to get back inside before midnight count. He still takes a repurposed blood-pressure drug that stops the dreams, and he extends the diagnosis outward — to secret-site interrogators who came back crying, to drone pilots, and to prisoners released angry and untreated.

the-satan-dream.title: The booby-trapped Christmas cards
the-satan-dream.summary: Among the devices al-Qaeda left behind in positions it was forced to evacuate in Afghanistan, John Kiriakou describes a detonator laid flat inside a Christmas card, so that opening the card would take the reader''s hands off.

the-satan-dream.title: The tomato patch surveillance
the-satan-dream.summary: John Kiriakou''s earliest surveillance operation, run at the age of nine with walkie-talkies against the neighbourhood children he suspected of stealing his father''s tomatoes.

the-satan-dream.title: George Washington University
the-satan-dream.summary: The Washington university where John Kiriakou took a bachelor's degree in Middle Eastern studies and began a master's in legislative affairs, and where a professor who was in fact a CIA spotter recruited him into the agency — an institution that recurs throughout his account as the place his intelligence career began, as the venue of his first CIA tests, and later as a classroom he taught in himself.

the-satan-dream.title: No ethics training at the CIA
the-satan-dream.summary: John Kiriakou''s claim that the CIA provides no ethics training of any kind, so that an officer either arrives with a personal moral code or never acquires one — and the classroom hypothetical he uses to show where the line goes undrawn.

the-satan-dream.title: The interrupted break-in
the-satan-dream.summary: A break-in in a friendly country nearly failed when the neighbour who was supposed to be at work turned out to have given birth the day before; John Kiriakou talked his way out of it at the door by claiming to be looking for his aunt''s flat in the wrong building.

the-saudi-administered-gaza-proposal.title: The Al Udeid strike
the-saudi-administered-gaza-proposal.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of Iran''s face-saving retaliation for the American bombing of its nuclear sites in June 2025 — a single missile fired at Al Udeid air base in Qatar, announced two hours in advance, which he says hit a geodesic dome housing top secret communications.

the-saudi-administered-gaza-proposal.title: The Emir of Bahrain''s verdict
the-saudi-administered-gaza-proposal.summary: The judgement John Kiriakou says the Emir of Bahrain delivered to him at his beach house — that George H. W. Bush was the last American president to give the Arabs a fair shake — and Kiriakou''s reasons for agreeing with it.

the-saudi-administered-gaza-proposal.title: The Rashid family
the-saudi-administered-gaza-proposal.summary: The dynasty that controlled the Arabian peninsula before the House of Saud, and John Kiriakou''s account of meeting one of its descendants while stationed in Saudi Arabia — a man who told him the kingdom had once been theirs.

the-saudi-administered-gaza-proposal.title: Bill Clinton
the-saudi-administered-gaza-proposal.summary: 42nd U.S. president whom John Kiriakou describes as wholly disinterested in intelligence — briefed by the CIA only twice in eight years, with Vice President Al Gore taking the daily briefing instead and relaying anything important.

the-saudi-administered-gaza-proposal.title: Church Committee
the-saudi-administered-gaza-proposal.summary: U.S. Senate investigative committee operating in 1975–1976 that examined domestic intelligence abuses by the CIA, FBI, and NSA; per John Kiriakou, the Church Committee — alongside the concurrent Pike Committee in the House — was the last genuine moment of legislative oversight over the intelligence community, born of a national consensus that government had gone dangerously off course. Its work led to the creation of the permanent Senate Select Committee on Intelligence, which Kiriakou says ceased to function as real oversight roughly seven years after its founding.

the-saudi-administered-gaza-proposal.title: Fifty new crimes a year
the-saudi-administered-gaza-proposal.summary: John Kiriakou''s argument that the United States has become a carceral country by legislative accretion — fifty newly created federal crimes every year for two decades, on top of five per cent of the world''s population holding twenty-five per cent of its prisoners.

the-saudi-demand-for-a-political-appoint.title: The Eric Adams ambassadorship
the-saudi-demand-for-a-political-appoint.summary: The September 2025 proposal, floated by Steve Witkoff, to remove Eric Adams from the New York mayoral race by offering him the embassy in Riyadh — which John Kiriakou thought likely to be attempted, on the reasoning that Donald Trump is not stupid, knows Adams cannot win, and would gain by forcing Zohran Mamdani to spend money.

the-saudi-demand-for-a-political-appoint.title: Saudi Arabia as an open-air prison
the-saudi-demand-for-a-political-appoint.summary: John Kiriakou's verdict on the country he served in — 'the biggest open air prison in the world' — together with his account of what the ambassador's life there is like inside the residence and outside it, the two ambassadors he served under, and the annual migration of the entire Saudi government to Jeddah to escape the heat.

the-saudi-demand-for-a-political-appoint.title: The kafala sponsorship system
the-saudi-demand-for-a-political-appoint.summary: The Saudi sponsorship regime as John Kiriakou describes it — a Saudi national must own the majority of any company a foreigner works for, that sponsor holds the worker's passport, and a falling-out leaves the worker under effective house arrest, which he says is how South Asian women brought in as domestics are kept as sex slaves.

the-saudi-demand-for-a-political-appoint.title: The 1991 Saudi plan for Gaza
the-saudi-demand-for-a-political-appoint.summary: A proposal John Kiriakou says he watched Ambassador Chas Freeman float to the Saudis during his first overseas tour in 1991 — that Saudi Arabia fund a port, an airport, a desalination plant and an electrical grid in Gaza. The Saudis agreed; Israel refused outright. Kiriakou raises it because the identical arrangement resurfaced in the Israeli press more than three decades later.

the-saudi-demand-for-a-political-appoint.title: Zohran Mamdani
the-saudi-demand-for-a-political-appoint.summary: John Kiriakou's assessment of the New York mayoral candidate in September 2025 — a smart young man running a very good campaign, surrounding himself with older seasoned New Yorkers rather than going in like a bull in a china shop, and gaining rather than losing ground the more the establishment attacked him.

the-saudi-demand-for-a-political-appoint.title: Aafia Siddiqui
the-saudi-demand-for-a-political-appoint.summary: Pakistani-American neuroscientist arrested in Afghanistan and convicted in the United States of attempting to shoot FBI agents; per John Kiriakou, who covered the arrest as a terrorism consultant for ABC News and has followed the case since, she never had a gun and never fired, the bullet holes offered as proof predated her capture, and the CIA took her three children — two later recovered, the youngest never found.

the-saudi-question.title: The Kuwaiti cargo in yuan
the-saudi-question.summary: The shipment of Kuwaiti oil that John Kiriakou says the Chinese paid for in yuan rather than dollars for the first time, which he treats as the first step toward the end of the American empire.

the-saudi-question.title: Sheldon Adelson
the-saudi-question.summary: American casino magnate and Republican megadonor. In John Kiriakou's account Adelson sent his private jet to fly Jonathan Pollard from prison to Israel, paid out of his own pocket to move the American embassy to Jerusalem, and functions as Kiriakou's standing unit of measurement for what political money can buy — including in the negative, as the patron the Libertarian Party never had.

the-saudi-question.title: Shin Bet
the-saudi-question.summary: Israel's internal security service; per John Kiriakou, one of the two declared Israeli intelligence officers at the Washington embassy, and the service whose officer, alongside a Mossad officer, he says tried to recruit him at his first CIA liaison briefing in the spring of 1990 — an approach his colleagues told him had been made to every one of them.

the-saudi-question.title: The CIA recruiting video
the-saudi-question.summary: The Agency recruiting video John Kiriakou says he watched with dismay, in which a woman described herself as an autistic, depressed, anxious lesbian who had found a home at the CIA — and his reaction that this was not the CIA he joined.

the-saudi-question.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
the-saudi-question.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

the-saudi-request-on-gaddafi.title: The Hannity Lockerbie exchange
the-saudi-request-on-gaddafi.summary: A televised argument in which John Kiriakou says he embarrassed Sean Hannity by pointing out that the 1986 American bombing that killed Muammar Gaddafi's daughter came three years before the Lockerbie bombing, and so could not have been revenge for it.

the-saudi-request-on-gaddafi.title: Quoted on NPR
the-saudi-request-on-gaddafi.summary: John Kiriakou's discovery, via a standing Google alert on his own name, that National Public Radio had cited a DeProgram discussion between him and Ted Rall in an article on Palestinians killed while waiting for food — an outlet he had walked out on years earlier.

the-saudi-request-on-gaddafi.title: The Addis Ababa zoo
the-saudi-request-on-gaddafi.summary: A visit John Kiriakou made to the zoo in Addis Ababa on a free half-day, where he watched keepers force a screaming donkey into the lion enclosure — and noted the two-tier admission price charged to foreigners.

the-saudi-request-on-gaddafi.title: The boring cover story
the-saudi-request-on-gaddafi.summary: The CIA training principle John Kiriakou says governed how officers described their jobs to strangers: pick something so dull that nobody asks a second question. His own standard answer was the foreign service, training work, and some import-export negotiation.

the-saudi-request-on-gaddafi.title: The election day 1992 poll
the-saudi-request-on-gaddafi.summary: An informal show of hands taken in a CIA branch office on election day 1992, which John Kiriakou describes as the moment he discovered he had no idea of the politics of the colleagues he sat three feet away from — and that he was not, as he had assumed, the only progressive in the room.

the-saudi-request-on-gaddafi.title: The ex-prisoner at the Bureau of Prisons
the-saudi-request-on-gaddafi.summary: John Kiriakou's approving account of the appointment of a former federal prisoner — recently released after five years on a drug conspiracy charge — as deputy director of the Bureau of Prisons, which he calls an inspired choice and one of the few things he has praised Donald Trump for.

the-science-fiction-writer-foia-request.title: CIA attention to West Africa
the-science-fiction-writer-foia-request.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer on whether the CIA is likely to be operating in Burkina Faso: for all the years he was at the agency it cared very little about Africa and especially West Africa, but the presence of al-Qaeda and Islamic State affiliates plus the drug trade makes CIA and special forces involvement probable — and, he adds, the American public will not hear about it.

the-science-fiction-writer-foia-request.title: CIA–FBI incompatible computer systems
the-science-fiction-writer-foia-request.summary: John Kiriakou's claim that from the CIA's founding in 1947 until 2009 the computer systems of the CIA and the FBI were not compatible with one another — no message could be sent from one to the other and no intelligence shared — which he offers both as the material substrate of the interagency hatred that helped make September 11 possible, and as the gap through which James Mitchell and Bruce Jessen were able to pass Ali Soufan's FBI debriefings of Abu Zubaydah off as the fruits of torture.

the-science-fiction-writer-foia-request.title: Fake CIA résumés
the-science-fiction-writer-foia-request.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of being used as a human authenticator in the private sector: at the consulting firm he joined after leaving the CIA, every job applicant claiming agency service was sent to dinner with him, and by his count fully half of them had never set foot inside the CIA.

the-science-fiction-writer-foia-request.title: Forcing Iran toward a bomb
the-science-fiction-writer-foia-request.summary: John Kiriakou''s argument that Western pressure risks producing the very outcome it claims to prevent: repeated Israeli assassinations of Iranian scientists and generals and strikes on Iranian sites may eventually leave Ayatollah Khamenei with no choice but to permit a defensive weapon — despite the religious prohibition Kiriakou credits him with maintaining, and despite successive American estimates that Iran is not seeking one.

the-science-fiction-writer-foia-request.title: Freemasons and Opus Dei at the CIA
the-science-fiction-writer-foia-request.summary: John Kiriakou's characterisation of the affinity networks at the top of the CIA — a great many senior officers who are Freemasons, and periods in which most of the leadership belonged to Opus Dei and attended the same church in Great Falls, Virginia. He rejects the idea that these are plots, describing them instead as accidental clusters of men who look out for one another.

the-science-fiction-writer-foia-request.title: GeoRisk Solutions
the-science-fiction-writer-foia-request.summary: The political risk consultancy John Kiriakou founded with the dean of the University of Salamanca's intelligence studies programme, staffed with academics and a former assistant secretary of state, with offices in Salamanca and Washington and a stated business of selling cost-effective country and regional risk analysis to banks, funds and companies.

the-scooter-libby-deposition.title: Dumping cash in a Moscow bathroom
the-scooter-libby-deposition.summary: John Kiriakou's examples of what covert action has actually meant in practice — American commandos blowing up the Trans-Siberian oil pipeline, Afghan guerrillas hired to cross the Amu Darya and attack a refinery inside the southern USSR, and cash dumped in a Moscow bathroom to undermine the rouble.

the-scooter-libby-deposition.title: Abigail Spanberger
the-scooter-libby-deposition.summary: Governor of Virginia from 2025 and, before Congress, a CIA officer alongside John Kiriakou in the Counterterrorism Center — whom he calls a perfectly nice person who would have been a middle-of-the-road Republican in the 1970s and 1980s, and whose victory speech, to his surprise, said all the right things.

the-scooter-libby-deposition.title: Craig Murray
the-scooter-libby-deposition.summary: Former British Ambassador to Uzbekistan whom John Kiriakou cites as a whistleblower of extreme torture: during a meeting at the Uzbek intelligence service, Murray heard screaming, walked in, and saw a man being boiled in oil — reporting it cost him his career.

the-scooter-libby-deposition.title: Destroying the Dome of the Rock
the-scooter-libby-deposition.summary: John Kiriakou's agreement with Tucker Carlson that a Zionist extremist plan to demolish the Dome of the Rock and build a third temple would be the event that starts the Third World War — and his additional prediction that it would also be the beginning of the end for the Israeli government and all of its support.

the-scooter-libby-deposition.title: How Chinese intelligence recruits
the-scooter-libby-deposition.summary: John Kiriakou''s assessment of the Ministry of State Security''s tradecraft: very effective with anyone who simply wants money, because the money is limitless, and very bad at cultivating a source who does not yet know who is cultivating him — with the target usually being access to sophisticated technology.

the-scooter-libby-deposition.title: Jason Miyares
the-scooter-libby-deposition.summary: The Cuban-born Republican attorney general of Virginia whom John Kiriakou expected to be a right-wing disaster and found instead to be excellent — a judgement he says is hard for him to make about a conservative Republican, and which he repeated on the night Miyares was unceremoniously thrown out of office.

the-search-for-a-country-to-take-gaza.title: Walking Robert Morgenthau to the hearing room
the-search-for-a-country-to-take-gaza.summary: John Kiriakou's recollection of taking the arm of a very elderly Robert Morgenthau in a Senate corridor and walking him to a Foreign Relations Committee hearing — and of telling him he had just read a book about Smyrna, and had not known his father coined the word genocide.

the-search-for-a-country-to-take-gaza.title: "An actual summit"
the-search-for-a-country-to-take-gaza.summary: John Kiriakou's reading of the August 2025 Anchorage meeting between Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin — that the Russian delegation's seniority proved Moscow was serious, that Putin is not the erratic figure American media portray, and that there is never any downside to diplomacy.

the-search-for-a-country-to-take-gaza.title: Sergey Lavrov
the-search-for-a-country-to-take-gaza.summary: Russian foreign minister, and previously Russian ambassador to the United Nations during John Kiriakou's assignment there, where the two worked the same Security Council. Kiriakou describes him as the most admired diplomat in the building — the most powerful, important and strategic ambassador there despite operating with far smaller resources than his American, British, French and Chinese counterparts, and better than most of the American diplomats Kiriakou worked for. When Lavrov was abruptly sidelined in late 2025, Kiriakou's reading was retirement rather than disgrace.

the-search-for-a-country-to-take-gaza.title: The seat-belt roadblocks
the-search-for-a-country-to-take-gaza.summary: What John Kiriakou reported the federalised National Guard, police, FBI, ATF and DEA were actually doing at roadblocks on Washington's main thoroughfares in August 2025 — writing tickets for unworn seat belts and broken brake lights, in neighbourhoods he says have no street crime to speak of.

the-search-for-a-country-to-take-gaza.title: The Sue Mi Terry case
the-search-for-a-country-to-take-gaza.summary: John Kiriakou's reading of the prosecution of analyst Sue Mi Terry — charged not under the Espionage Act but under the Foreign Agents Registration Act, an offence he reduces to failing to fill out a form on the internet, and one whose nominal sentencing range he says means nothing in practice.

the-search-for-a-country-to-take-gaza.title: The thrown sandwich
the-search-for-a-country-to-take-gaza.summary: The arrest of a man who threw a sandwich at a National Guardsman at 14th and U Street in Washington in August 2025, charged with felony assault on a police officer with a stated demand for ten years — an overcharge John Kiriakou said no Washington jury would ever convict on.

the-seat-belt-roadblocks.title: The thrown sandwich
the-seat-belt-roadblocks.summary: The arrest of a man who threw a sandwich at a National Guardsman at 14th and U Street in Washington in August 2025, charged with felony assault on a police officer with a stated demand for ten years — an overcharge John Kiriakou said no Washington jury would ever convict on.

the-seat-belt-roadblocks.title: Home rule in Washington, DC
the-seat-belt-roadblocks.summary: The governing arrangement under which the District of Columbia has run its own affairs since 1971, explained by John Kiriakou as a grant made by Richard Nixon that replaced direct rule by a congressional committee — and which he describes Donald Trump as wanting to take back, on the strength of a single assault on a well-known administration staffer.

the-seat-belt-roadblocks.title: "An actual summit"
the-seat-belt-roadblocks.summary: John Kiriakou's reading of the August 2025 Anchorage meeting between Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin — that the Russian delegation's seniority proved Moscow was serious, that Putin is not the erratic figure American media portray, and that there is never any downside to diplomacy.

the-seat-belt-roadblocks.title: Sergey Lavrov
the-seat-belt-roadblocks.summary: Russian foreign minister, and previously Russian ambassador to the United Nations during John Kiriakou's assignment there, where the two worked the same Security Council. Kiriakou describes him as the most admired diplomat in the building — the most powerful, important and strategic ambassador there despite operating with far smaller resources than his American, British, French and Chinese counterparts, and better than most of the American diplomats Kiriakou worked for. When Lavrov was abruptly sidelined in late 2025, Kiriakou's reading was retirement rather than disgrace.

the-seat-belt-roadblocks.title: The Lafayette Square tents
the-seat-belt-roadblocks.summary: The long-running protest encampment across from the White House that a New Jersey congressman wanted removed by force in 2025, and John Kiriakou's observation that tents have stood on that spot for as long as he has lived in Washington — since 1982.

the-seat-belt-roadblocks.title: The National Guard in Washington
the-seat-belt-roadblocks.summary: John Kiriakou's response to the August 2025 federalisation of the District of Columbia police — a decision he says was taken without informing the mayor or the police chief, in a city where crime was falling, and which he expected to expire after three days for want of congressional authorisation.

the-second-officer-in-the-same-case.title: David Petraeus
the-second-officer-in-the-same-case.summary: Retired U.S. Army general and director of the CIA who, per John Kiriakou, confirmed the names of ten covert CIA operatives to his biographer and girlfriend and was never criminally charged — a contrast Kiriakou cites repeatedly as proof that his own prosecution under the Intelligence Identities Protection Act was selective. Kiriakou''s explanation for the disparity: Petraeus had not blown the whistle on the torture program and embarrassed the agency.

the-second-officer-in-the-same-case.title: The legal bills
the-second-officer-in-the-same-case.summary: The cost of John Kiriakou's defence, which he has given variously as more than half a million dollars, approaching a million, and more than a million — a figure he treats not as a hardship but as the mechanism of the prosecution itself, since bankruptcy is what makes a defendant accept a plea.

the-second-officer-in-the-same-case.title: The seventh Espionage Act defendant
the-second-officer-in-the-same-case.summary: The case John Kiriakou cited two days before his own sentencing to correct the count of Espionage Act prosecutions brought under Barack Obama — a translator at the American naval base in Bahrain who had just been charged, making seven, against three in the whole history of the United States before 2009.

the-second-officer-in-the-same-case.title: Espionage Act
the-second-officer-in-the-same-case.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

the-second-officer-in-the-same-case.title: Ralph Nader
the-second-officer-in-the-same-case.summary: American consumer advocate and perennial third-party presidential candidate. In January 2013 Nader co-signed a letter to the president asking for John Kiriakou to be pardoned; weeks later Kiriakou thanked him by name at his portrait unveiling as a steadfast supporter whose backing he described as humbling. Nader's 2000 independent run also anchors Kiriakou's account of how third-party candidates were shut out of the presidential debates.

the-second-officer-in-the-same-case.title: The clemency campaign of January 2013
the-second-officer-in-the-same-case.summary: The three parallel appeals for a pardon or commutation made on John Kiriakou's behalf in the days before his 25 January 2013 sentencing — a letter to the president from Ralph Nader, Bruce Fein and Joan Claybrook, a change.org petition with nearly two thousand signatures, a Greek-American community petition, and a letter signed by more than eighteen CIA officers and FBI agents alongside Pete Seeger, Oliver Stone and Daniel Ellsberg.

the-second-plane.title: The Condoleezza Rice meeting
the-second-plane.summary: The nine o'clock White House appointment John Kiriakou and Cofer Black never kept on the morning of 11 September 2001. The Government Printing Office was about to issue a volume of declassified Greece-Turkey-Cyprus cables in an edition of five or ten copies; three of them named CIA sources who were still alive, and an obscure statute obliges the government to offer citizenship and resettlement to any recruited source it outs. The two men were going to ask the National Security Advisor to quietly pull three cables nobody would miss. The car was at the East entrance at 8.15.

the-second-plane.title: "We''re at war today"
the-second-plane.summary: The short speech John Kiriakou says Cofer Black delivered standing on his desk in the CIA's Counterterrorism Center on the morning of 11 September 2001, telling his officers that not all of them would make it home and that anyone for whom this was not enough could walk out without being thought less of. Nobody moved.

the-second-plane.title: Cofer Black's warning to the liaison class
the-second-plane.summary: The briefing Cofer Black gave to a class of visiting foreign liaison officers weeks before 11 September 2001 — code words about a honey salesman, a great football match and an enormous wedding — and the private exchange afterwards in which he told John Kiriakou he had been deadly serious.

the-second-plane.title: The honey salesman warning
the-second-plane.summary: The al-Qaeda briefing Cofer Black delivered unannounced to a visiting delegation of Middle Eastern intelligence officers at CIA headquarters on 6 July 2001, in which he described intercepted code words — a honey salesman arriving with vast quantities of honey, a great wedding, a great football match — as signals of an imminent attack on a massive scale, and begged the visitors for any source inside al-Qaeda.

the-second-plane.title: The seventy-two-year-old contractor
the-second-plane.summary: The hallway conversation John Kiriakou says explained why the CIA had not sent him, an Arabic speaker, to interrogate captured al-Qaeda fighters — a returning contractor's answer that he had been in Afghanistan killing people — and the demand Kiriakou made afterwards that got him sent to Pakistan the next day.

the-second-plane.title: The Tehran slip
the-second-plane.summary: The moment John Kiriakou says he witnessed as note-taker in a secure video teleconference a day or two before the 2003 invasion of Iraq, when a briefing general said that if all went as planned American forces could be in Tehran by August, and CIA Director George Tenet turned off his microphone and asked Kiriakou whether the man had said Tehran or Baghdad.

the-secret-prisons-the-heads-of-state-di.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
the-secret-prisons-the-heads-of-state-di.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

the-secret-prisons-the-heads-of-state-di.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
the-secret-prisons-the-heads-of-state-di.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

the-secret-prisons-the-heads-of-state-di.title: Extraordinary Rendition
the-secret-prisons-the-heads-of-state-di.summary: Per John Kiriakou, the CIA practice of seizing terrorism suspects in one country and transporting them to a third country — often a country with no due-process protections — to be held, interrogated, or tortured outside U.S. legal jurisdiction. The program operated alongside the enhanced-interrogation program and was the operational mechanism by which prisoners reached secret CIA facilities and allied torture sites in countries like Bahrain. Kiriakou himself was not in the rendition line of work but became a federal felon under the Intelligence Identities Protection Act for a single confirmation of a colleague's surname to a journalist who claimed to be writing a book on the Abu Omar rendition from Milan.

the-secret-prisons-the-heads-of-state-di.title: Guantánamo Bay detention camp
the-secret-prisons-the-heads-of-state-di.summary: Per John Kiriakou — as chief of counterterrorism operations in Pakistan after September 11, 2001 — the Guantanamo detention facility began as a temporary holding measure intended to last two to three weeks while the CIA and Justice Department determined which federal district court should try each prisoner, not as a long-term detention infrastructure. The Rawalpindi jail had reached capacity, Pakistani intelligence demanded the prisoners be removed, and CIA headquarters directed Kiriakou to load them onto a C-12 cargo plane and fly them to Cuba.

the-secret-prisons-the-heads-of-state-di.title: "Take our word for it"
the-secret-prisons-the-heads-of-state-di.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the standing justification given after American strikes kill civilians — that there was a terrorist present, and that the public would agree if it could see the intelligence — set against his statement that he saw that intelligence and it was fabricated, and applied to the 2021 Kabul strike that killed seven children.

the-secret-prisons-the-heads-of-state-di.title: Abu Omar rendition
the-secret-prisons-the-heads-of-state-di.summary: The CIA's kidnapping of a Milan cleric, Abu Omar, who was sent to Egypt to be tortured; John Kiriakou calls it a case that ought to be taught at the CIA as how not to run a rendition, and it is what ultimately sent him to prison, after he confirmed a former colleague's surname to a journalist claiming to be writing a book about it.

the-secret-sahel-appropriations.title: CIA attention to West Africa
the-secret-sahel-appropriations.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer on whether the CIA is likely to be operating in Burkina Faso: for all the years he was at the agency it cared very little about Africa and especially West Africa, but the presence of al-Qaeda and Islamic State affiliates plus the drug trade makes CIA and special forces involvement probable — and, he adds, the American public will not hear about it.

the-secret-sahel-appropriations.title: The Paris rifle serial number
the-secret-sahel-appropriations.summary: The case John Kiriakou uses to argue that American weapons sent to Ukraine are leaking onto the black market: a rifle used to shoot and severely wound a policeman in Paris whose serial number, he says, matched a shipment of assault rifles the United States had sent to Ukraine some six months earlier.

the-secret-sahel-appropriations.title: The African diplomat's remark
the-secret-sahel-appropriations.summary: The line John Kiriakou says an African diplomat gave him at a White House summit, and which he uses to explain Chinese success on the continent: you Americans always offer us democracy and military aid, and the Chinese offer us food and new roads. Kiriakou traces the consequence to Chinese bases across Africa and a State Department that did not see it coming.

the-secret-sahel-appropriations.title: The Sahel church burnings
the-secret-sahel-appropriations.summary: John Kiriakou's account of al-Qaeda affiliates and Boko Haram in Chad, Mali and Nigeria attacking schools and churches — opening fire on teachers and administrators, kidnapping children, and burning congregations alive — and his observation that none of it is covered in the American media.

the-secret-sahel-appropriations.title: Muddling through
the-secret-sahel-appropriations.summary: An analytic term John Kiriakou says CIA analysts used all the time, and his defence of it: forecasters instinctively reach for either/or outcomes, when what actually happens most often is that the parties to a conflict muddle through and little changes over the medium term. He applies it to Ukraine, and to why he expects Russia not to use nuclear weapons.

the-secret-sahel-appropriations.title: The Hersh publishing collapse
the-secret-sahel-appropriations.summary: John Kiriakou's account of Seymour Hersh's disappearance from mainstream print — from the London Review of Books in 2017, which Hersh told him was already the only outlet that would take his work, to Substack five years later. Kiriakou, who helped give Hersh an award for integrity in intelligence, presents the trajectory as a measure of how bad conditions for American journalism have become.

the-senate-wikileaks-ban.title: Julian Assange
the-senate-wikileaks-ban.summary: Kiriakou — a 15-year friend and former WikiLeaks board member — on why Assange is a publisher owed a journalist's immunity, and a political prisoner.

the-senate-wikileaks-ban.title: Anwar al-Awlaki
the-senate-wikileaks-ban.summary: American-born al-Qaeda propagandist; in 1993 the imam of the Falls Church, Virginia mosque visited by John Kiriakou's CIA Arabic-language class on a field trip; in 2001 the cleric at whose mosque the 9/11 hijackers prayed the night before the attacks; killed by U.S. drone strike in Yemen in approximately 2011.

the-senate-wikileaks-ban.title: Intelligence Identities Protection Act
the-senate-wikileaks-ban.summary: U.S. law enacted in 1982 that makes it a crime to knowingly disclose the identity of a covert intelligence officer; per John Kiriakou, his 2012 prosecution under the act arose from confirming a single surname of a former CIA colleague to a journalist — a confirmation that was never published. The name passed through a chain from journalist to Human Rights Watch to Guantanamo defense attorneys before reaching a judge and ultimately the FBI, which traced it back to Kiriakou.

the-senate-wikileaks-ban.title: The Uyghur resettlement trade
the-senate-wikileaks-ban.summary: The exchange John Kiriakou says the WikiLeaks cables revealed behind the prosecution of UBS whistleblower Brad Birkenfeld — Switzerland agreeing to accept two Uyghur prisoners out of Guantanamo on the condition that the United States arrest the man whose disclosure had exposed Swiss banking secrecy.

the-senate-wikileaks-ban.title: Brad Birkenfeld
the-senate-wikileaks-ban.summary: The UBS banking whistleblower, who was prosecuted and imprisoned before winning a $104 million settlement from the Treasury Department and spending it on the legal defence of other whistleblowers. John Kiriakou uses him as the measure of the gap between financial and national-security whistleblowing, and names him among the visitors whose devices he believes were copied at the Ecuadorian embassy in London.

the-senate-wikileaks-ban.title: Daniel Hale
the-senate-wikileaks-ban.summary: Per John Kiriakou, drone whistleblower Daniel Hale — an NSA contractor and drone targeting analyst who exposed an 80% civilian death rate in the U.S. drone program, was ordered to fire on two young girls his superior called "goats," and was sentenced to 45 months (of which Kiriakou says he actually served about 18) despite prosecutors seeking nine to eleven years.

the-sentencing-remark.title: "It''s about mitigating damage"
the-sentencing-remark.summary: The sentence John Kiriakou credits with changing his mind about going to trial — one of his own attorneys telling him that his problem was that he thought the case was about justice, when it was about mitigating damage — and the two lawyers who drove to his house after he emailed at six in the morning to refuse the plea.

the-sentencing-remark.title: The Loretto camp mix-up
the-sentencing-remark.summary: John Kiriakou's account of turning himself in at the federal work camp at Loretto, Pennsylvania as the court had ordered, being sent across the street to the prison to be processed, and then being handcuffed and walked into the prison itself — with nobody on the outside knowing where he was for five days.

the-sentencing-remark.title: Thursday arrests
the-sentencing-remark.summary: The scheduling practice John Kiriakou attributes to the FBI — arresting on a Thursday so that a defendant, unable to be arraigned on a Friday, spends four nights in jail before seeing a judge — and the single sentence that he says kept him out of it.

the-sentencing-remark.title: Arabic and Greek
the-sentencing-remark.summary: The qualification John Kiriakou says opened the door to his transfer from CIA analysis to operations: a post in Athens wanted Greek or Arabic, and he had both — by most of his tellings the only officer in the agency who did. The chief who hired him gave the reason in one sentence: it is easier and cheaper to take a linguist and teach him operations than the other way round. The pairing also became a detection tool, since the language nobody speaks in Pakistan is Arabic.

the-sentencing-remark.title: Bankruptcy and the dropped charges
the-sentencing-remark.summary: The sequence John Kiriakou places at the centre of his case: that the espionage counts against him were dropped only after his legal fees had bankrupted him, which he presents as evidence that the government''s aim was attrition rather than conviction.

the-sentencing-remark.title: Curtailment cables
the-sentencing-remark.summary: The career-ending requests John Kiriakou says he read coming back from the CIA's black sites — officers, doctors, psychologists and nurses asking to end their tours early rather than continue to take part in the interrogation programme — and his conclusion that if that many people were objecting in classified channels, someone would surely go public.

the-september-tenth-country.title: The Obama recruitment thesis
the-september-tenth-country.summary: John Kiriakou''s public explanation of what happened to Barack Obama: not that the CIA created him, but that a first-term senator with no national security experience is exactly the kind of president the agency wants, and that the first briefing several levels above top secret is enough to hook him. Kiriakou supports the reading with two quotations Obama gave to reporters, including that he never had any idea he would be so good at killing people.

the-september-tenth-country.title: The Libya policy reversal
the-september-tenth-country.summary: John Kiriakou''s verdict on the overthrow of Muammar Gaddafi: the United States had a healthy working relationship with a man who hated al-Qaeda as much as it did, and flipping sides at the last minute was a terrible policy error that left the country in anarchy. Told that destabilisation may have been the objective all along, he called that an incredibly shortsighted policy, because power vacuums drag America in and it cannot get back out.

the-september-tenth-country.title: The Benghazi hearings critique
the-september-tenth-country.summary: John Kiriakou''s complaint about the congressional inquiry into Benghazi, which he watched all the way through: he believes there is some evidence of gun running, doubts anyone will ever establish who was behind it, and objects that the hearings were not trying to find out — having devolved into a political contest that served the American people not at all.

the-september-tenth-country.title: Bin Laden health rumors
the-september-tenth-country.summary: John Kiriakou's dismissal of the claim that Osama bin Laden died years before the 2011 raid. He says the CIA received a steady stream of medical rumours about him — kidney failure, dialysis in a cave, a spinal disorder — none of which turned out to be true, and that bin Laden was in fine health apart from arthritis and a hip problem until the day he died.

the-september-tenth-country.title: Fake CIA résumés
the-september-tenth-country.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of being used as a human authenticator in the private sector: at the consulting firm he joined after leaving the CIA, every job applicant claiming agency service was sent to dinner with him, and by his count fully half of them had never set foot inside the CIA.

the-september-tenth-country.title: False flags are too hard
the-september-tenth-country.summary: John Kiriakou''s practical objection to the idea that governments routinely stage false flag operations: they exist, and at the operational level the CIA used them constantly, but the bigger the operation the harder it is to run — too many moving parts, too many people who must buy into the conspiracy, and too much incompetence in government to keep any of it straight. He couples the objection with the observation that a government which is not transparent has no standing to complain about public suspicion.

the-seven-countries-argument.title: Greater Israel
the-seven-countries-argument.summary: The territorial project John Kiriakou believes the Israeli government genuinely holds: the expulsion of every Palestinian, beginning in Gaza and continuing into the West Bank, pursued on a hundred- or two-hundred-year horizon in the confidence that the United States will never push back.

the-seven-countries-argument.title: Lebanon-Israeli Conflict
the-seven-countries-argument.summary: Per John Kiriakou, no Israeli government will allow Lebanon to flourish as a nation; he expects continued Israeli attacks and forced displacement of civilians, citing a statistic of up to 700,000 Lebanese internally displaced, and links the war to the "Greater Israel" rhetoric of US ambassador Mike Huckabee.

the-seven-countries-argument.title: Mike Huckabee
the-seven-countries-argument.summary: The United States ambassador to Israel under Donald Trump, and the subject of a public call for resignation from John Kiriakou after Huckabee received Jonathan Pollard at the American embassy. Kiriakou''s assessment separates two charges: Huckabee is not a traitor but an idiot who did not think the meeting was a big deal, and a former governor of a small state who still behaves as though he can set policy without the State Department or the National Security Council.

the-seven-countries-argument.title: Naftali Bennett
the-seven-countries-argument.summary: The former Israeli prime minister, cited by John Kiriakou through 2026 for the position that Turkey would be the next target after Iran — a claim Kiriakou uses to identify the second obstacle, alongside Iran, to the Greater Israel project, and which by May 2026 he was stating in his own voice as an active Israeli intention rather than a Bennett prediction.

the-seven-countries-argument.title: South Lebanon displacement, 2026
the-seven-countries-argument.summary: John Kiriakou''s assessment of the Israeli campaign in southern Lebanon running alongside the 2026 Iran war: mass evacuation orders, hundreds of thousands internally displaced, and his conclusion that Israel has guaranteed Lebanon will be a failed state. He notes the world is not watching because it is watching Iran.

the-seven-countries-argument.title: The Samson Option
the-seven-countries-argument.summary: John Kiriakou's assessment, given during the 2026 Iran war, that Israel would use nuclear weapons if it believed the state itself was about to collapse. He notes that a year earlier he would have called the idea ridiculous, and that analysts put the Israeli arsenal at between eighty and two hundred warheads.

the-seventh-espionage-defendant.title: The legal bills
the-seventh-espionage-defendant.summary: The cost of John Kiriakou's defence, which he has given variously as more than half a million dollars, approaching a million, and more than a million — a figure he treats not as a hardship but as the mechanism of the prosecution itself, since bankruptcy is what makes a defendant accept a plea.

the-seventh-espionage-defendant.title: The second officer in the same case
the-seventh-espionage-defendant.summary: A document John Kiriakou says his attorneys discovered shortly before his January 2013 sentencing, showing that a second CIA officer had given the same reporter the names of ten undercover officers along with information on counterterrorist operations and the flight plans of the aircraft serving a secret prison — and was never investigated or prosecuted, which Kiriakou takes as proof that his own case was about whistleblowing rather than disclosure.

the-seventh-espionage-defendant.title: Arianna Huffington
the-seventh-espionage-defendant.summary: Founder of the Huffington Post and the accidental amplifier who turned John Kiriakou's prison writing into a phenomenon. His first Letter from Loretto went to his attorney, then to a friend running Firedoglake who — unknown to Kiriakou — was close to Huffington; she plastered it as a banner headline and it drew over a million hits, bringing CNN and 60 Minutes to the prison gates. She published his open letter to Snowden, ran the diesel-therapy exposé that triggered the "hands off John Kiriakou" campaign, and came to Loretto herself with two young journalists.

the-seventh-espionage-defendant.title: Brad Birkenfeld
the-seventh-espionage-defendant.summary: The UBS banking whistleblower, who was prosecuted and imprisoned before winning a $104 million settlement from the Treasury Department and spending it on the legal defence of other whistleblowers. John Kiriakou uses him as the measure of the gap between financial and national-security whistleblowing, and names him among the visitors whose devices he believes were copied at the Ecuadorian embassy in London.

the-seventh-espionage-defendant.title: Espionage Act
the-seventh-espionage-defendant.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

the-seventh-espionage-defendant.title: The whiskers rule
the-seventh-espionage-defendant.summary: John Kiriakou's description of the cultural practice he says American personnel encountered with some regularity in Afghanistan — that a boy who has not yet reached puberty is treated as available for sexual abuse — and his account of what he understood to have happened, and not happened, at Abu Ghraib.

the-seventy-two-year-old-contractor.title: The Condoleezza Rice meeting
the-seventy-two-year-old-contractor.summary: The nine o'clock White House appointment John Kiriakou and Cofer Black never kept on the morning of 11 September 2001. The Government Printing Office was about to issue a volume of declassified Greece-Turkey-Cyprus cables in an edition of five or ten copies; three of them named CIA sources who were still alive, and an obscure statute obliges the government to offer citizenship and resettlement to any recruited source it outs. The two men were going to ask the National Security Advisor to quietly pull three cables nobody would miss. The car was at the East entrance at 8.15.

the-seventy-two-year-old-contractor.title: The Faisalabad cash run
the-seventy-two-year-old-contractor.summary: The drive John Kiriakou made to Faisalabad, Pakistan roughly two weeks before the capture of Abu Zubaydah, with two million dollars in cash in two duffel bags in the van, and the exchange with his colleague about why anyone would cheat the CIA out of twenty dollars.

the-seventy-two-year-old-contractor.title: The honey salesman warning
the-seventy-two-year-old-contractor.summary: The al-Qaeda briefing Cofer Black delivered unannounced to a visiting delegation of Middle Eastern intelligence officers at CIA headquarters on 6 July 2001, in which he described intercepted code words — a honey salesman arriving with vast quantities of honey, a great wedding, a great football match — as signals of an imminent attack on a massive scale, and begged the visitors for any source inside al-Qaeda.

the-seventy-two-year-old-contractor.title: The second plane
the-seventy-two-year-old-contractor.summary: John Kiriakou's account of where he was standing when United Airlines Flight 175 struck the South Tower — in Cofer Black's outer office, mid-sentence, explaining to a secretary why a pilot could not possibly fly into the World Trade Center on so clear a day.

the-seventy-two-year-old-contractor.title: "We''re at war today"
the-seventy-two-year-old-contractor.summary: The short speech John Kiriakou says Cofer Black delivered standing on his desk in the CIA's Counterterrorism Center on the morning of 11 September 2001, telling his officers that not all of them would make it home and that anyone for whom this was not enough could walk out without being thought less of. Nobody moved.

the-seventy-two-year-old-contractor.title: Arabic and Greek
the-seventy-two-year-old-contractor.summary: The qualification John Kiriakou says opened the door to his transfer from CIA analysis to operations: a post in Athens wanted Greek or Arabic, and he had both — by most of his tellings the only officer in the agency who did. The chief who hired him gave the reason in one sentence: it is easier and cheaper to take a linguist and teach him operations than the other way round. The pairing also became a detection tool, since the language nobody speaks in Pakistan is Arabic.

the-shu-loophole.title: The fifteen-minute call
the-shu-loophole.summary: How Marty Gottesfeld, held in the communications management unit at Terre Haute, allocated the single fifteen-minute telephone call he was permitted each week: an email to his wife, his two attorneys and John Kiriakou, with the call going to whoever answered first.

the-shu-loophole.title: The glass-eating prisoner
the-shu-loophole.summary: A case John Kiriakou cites from a 2015 New York Times Magazine investigation of federal solitary confinement: a prisoner held in the Special Housing Unit at the federal supermax in Florence, Colorado for roughly eighteen years who smashed his narrow cell window and ate the broken glass so that he would be taken to a hospital and could speak to another human being.

the-shu-loophole.title: The Bureau of Prisons answers to no one
the-shu-loophole.summary: John Kiriakou''s summary of what he calls the hardest lesson of his incarceration: that the Bureau of Prisons sits under the Justice Department but is accountable to nobody in practice, disregarding what sentencing judges order and what its own prosecutors have agreed, and placing prisoners wherever it chooses.

the-shu-loophole.title: The modified CMU
the-shu-loophole.summary: The communications restrictions imposed on John Kiriakou at FCI Loretto after his Letter from Loretto was published by the Huffington Post. Staff called it a modified communications management unit: a five-day delay on incoming and outgoing email, live monitoring of his telephone calls rather than recording, and a prohibition on speaking Greek to his family.

the-shu-loophole.title: Julian Assange
