the-shu-loophole.summary: Kiriakou — a 15-year friend and former WikiLeaks board member — on why Assange is a publisher owed a journalist's immunity, and a political prisoner.

the-shu-loophole.title: The sixty-five-cent arrangement
the-shu-loophole.summary: The deal John Kiriakou struck with the chaplain at FCI Loretto: rather than keep his 65-cents-an-hour janitor''s wage, he asked to be kept on the books while the money went to the next man on the list, and to stop coming to work — which is how he found the time to write Doing Time Like a Spy.

the-siemens-control-room.title: MOSSAD
the-siemens-control-room.summary: Israel's primary external intelligence service; characterized by John Kiriakou as universally hostile in his and his CIA colleagues' professional dealings with it ("never had a positive encounter with Mossad"); operates almost exclusively in the operational rather than analytical domain; the CIA is, per Kiriakou, categorically forbidden from spying on it.

the-siemens-control-room.title: The debate with the Mossad director
the-siemens-control-room.summary: John Kiriakou's account of his first appearance on Piers Morgan's programme, where he debated a former director of the Mossad who he says could not stop chuckling, and the exchange about Israeli espionage that ended in "no comment".

the-siemens-control-room.title: Mahmoud al-Mabhouh
the-siemens-control-room.summary: Senior Hamas figure assassinated by Mossad in a Dubai hotel room in January 2010; the operation has been studied by intelligence services worldwide for its tradecraft, in particular the unsolved question of how the assassination team locked the hotel-room door from the inside after killing him.

the-siemens-control-room.title: Khaled Mashal
the-siemens-control-room.summary: Senior Hamas political leader; survived a 1997 Mossad poisoning attempt in Amman, Jordan; the operation's failure and the political fallout in Jordan are the canonical example, in John Kiriakou's account, of Israeli operational hostility carried out in friendly third-country territory without regard for the diplomatic consequences.

the-six-hour-queue-for-seats.title: Get thrown out spicily
the-six-hour-queue-for-seats.summary: John Kiriakou''s criticism of Representative Al Green''s protest at the 2026 State of the Union address: that holding up a banned sign and then walking out quietly accomplished nothing, and that if you are going to be removed you should struggle and fight back.

the-six-hour-queue-for-seats.title: Decorum in the Reagan years
the-six-hour-queue-for-seats.summary: John Kiriakou's contrast between the State of the Union addresses he watched as a college student under Ronald Reagan — divided, substantive, but conducted with decorum — and the 2026 address he called a clown show with no decorum on either side.

the-six-hour-queue-for-seats.title: Impeach him again
the-six-hour-queue-for-seats.summary: John Kiriakou's warning that if the Democrats win a House majority in 2026 and immediately move to impeach Donald Trump again, they should never win another race — and his prediction that this is exactly what they will do.

the-six-hour-queue-for-seats.title: Nationalizing the midterms
the-six-hour-queue-for-seats.summary: John Kiriakou's recurring comparison between contemporary party messaging and Newt Gingrich's 1994 Contract with America, including his advice that Speaker Mike Johnson should keep Gingrich on his couch and ask him nightly how the 1994 midterms were nationalised.

the-six-hour-queue-for-seats.title: The Trump appointees to the Court
the-six-hour-queue-for-seats.summary: John Kiriakou's assessment that Donald Trump's Supreme Court appointees have been surprisingly good, and that the justices he regards as disasters — Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas — were appointed by more moderate presidents.

the-six-hour-queue-for-seats.title: Ted Rall
the-six-hour-queue-for-seats.summary: American editorial cartoonist and two-time Pulitzer Prize finalist; co-host with John Kiriakou of the daily news-commentary podcast "Deprogram," launched in September 2025 and by late 2025 running every weekday morning.

the-sixty-five-cent-arrangement.title: The Bureau of Prisons answers to no one
the-sixty-five-cent-arrangement.summary: John Kiriakou''s summary of what he calls the hardest lesson of his incarceration: that the Bureau of Prisons sits under the Justice Department but is accountable to nobody in practice, disregarding what sentencing judges order and what its own prosecutors have agreed, and placing prisoners wherever it chooses.

the-sixty-five-cent-arrangement.title: The fifteen-minute call
the-sixty-five-cent-arrangement.summary: How Marty Gottesfeld, held in the communications management unit at Terre Haute, allocated the single fifteen-minute telephone call he was permitted each week: an email to his wife, his two attorneys and John Kiriakou, with the call going to whoever answered first.

the-sixty-five-cent-arrangement.title: The glass-eating prisoner
the-sixty-five-cent-arrangement.summary: A case John Kiriakou cites from a 2015 New York Times Magazine investigation of federal solitary confinement: a prisoner held in the Special Housing Unit at the federal supermax in Florence, Colorado for roughly eighteen years who smashed his narrow cell window and ate the broken glass so that he would be taken to a hospital and could speak to another human being.

the-sixty-five-cent-arrangement.title: The modified CMU
the-sixty-five-cent-arrangement.summary: The communications restrictions imposed on John Kiriakou at FCI Loretto after his Letter from Loretto was published by the Huffington Post. Staff called it a modified communications management unit: a five-day delay on incoming and outgoing email, live monitoring of his telephone calls rather than recording, and a prohibition on speaking Greek to his family.

the-sixty-five-cent-arrangement.title: The SHU loophole
the-sixty-five-cent-arrangement.summary: John Kiriakou''s warning about the American assurances given to British courts in the Julian Assange extradition case: prosecutors promised not to place him in a communications management unit but said nothing about the Special Housing Unit, and in Kiriakou''s account a prison need only cite an overheard threat to hold a man in solitary indefinitely.

the-sixty-five-cent-arrangement.title: Evidence of previous heroism
the-sixty-five-cent-arrangement.summary: A phrase John Kiriakou attributes to Judge Leonie Brinkema at his 2013 sentencing. When his service in Pakistan and his role in the capture of Abu Zubaydah were raised in mitigation, the judge ruled — in what Kiriakou gives as her exact words — that any evidence of previous heroism is irrelevant.

the-slap-approval-cable.title: Abu Zubaydah as a sounding board
the-slap-approval-cable.summary: The second, longer phase of Abu Zubaydah''s usefulness to the CIA, described by John Kiriakou in his December 2007 ABC News interview: once the prisoner had given up what he knew about current operations, his value shifted from threat reporting to analysis, with case officers reading him the names of men arrested in European capitals and asking whether the operations attributed to them made sense.

the-slap-approval-cable.title: The German POW chess analogy
the-slap-approval-cable.summary: The reasoning John Kiriakou gave ABC News in December 2007 for why he had believed at the time that waterboarding was necessary: he had heard of Second World War German prisoners who, over months of playing chess with their interrogators, built enough rapport to talk, and he judged that al-Qaeda prisoners were a different order of adversary who would never be seduced into cooperating.

the-slap-approval-cable.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
the-slap-approval-cable.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

the-slap-approval-cable.title: Abu Zubaydah
the-slap-approval-cable.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

the-slap-approval-cable.title: Brian Ross
the-slap-approval-cable.summary: American investigative journalist and seven-time Emmy Award winner who was a prominent reporter at ABC News when, in December 2007, he conducted the on-camera interview with John Kiriakou that produced the first public confirmation by a U.S. official that the CIA waterboarded prisoners. Per Kiriakou, Ross called him out of the blue with the assertion that a source said Kiriakou had personally tortured Abu Zubaydah; Kiriakou's decision to give the interview anyway — driven by the conclusion that 'Brian Ross's source is at the White House and they're going to pin this on me' — became the pivot point of his entire post-CIA life.

the-slap-approval-cable.title: Waterboarding
the-slap-approval-cable.summary: Torture technique in which a prisoner is restrained on an inclined board with the head lower than the feet, a cloth placed over the face, and water poured continuously over it to simulate drowning. Per John Kiriakou, waterboarding was treated as a criminal act under U.S. and international law for decades before 2002 — including a post–World War II execution of Japanese soldiers who waterboarded American POWs, and a 1968 court-martial of a U.S. soldier photographed waterboarding a North Vietnamese prisoner — before the CIA reauthorized it after September 11. Abu Zubaydah was waterboarded 83 times; Khalid Sheikh Mohammed 187 times.

the-snapshots-in-the-release.title: The blacked-out grand jury minutes
the-snapshots-in-the-release.summary: John Kiriakou on the 119 pages of grand jury minutes released in the Epstein document tranches with every single word blacked out, despite two federal judges having ordered their release.

the-snapshots-in-the-release.title: The unredacted copy-paste
the-snapshots-in-the-release.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of the flaw in the first tranche of released Epstein documents: highlighting a redaction, cutting it and pasting it into a new document revealed the blacked-out text, which turned out to be the names of victims.

the-snapshots-in-the-release.title: Prince Andrew
the-snapshots-in-the-release.summary: British royal, now Andrew Mountbatten Windsor, named repeatedly by John Kiriakou as one of the un-recruitable principals whose access made Jeffrey Epstein valuable to a foreign intelligence service. Kiriakou has asked why Andrew was never charged over conduct with minors, reads his alleged provision of classified Ministry of Defence documents to Epstein as evidence of espionage rather than vanity — and expects him to face no criminal consequence at all, because the statute of limitations has run.

the-snapshots-in-the-release.title: The letter to Larry Nassar
the-snapshots-in-the-release.summary: The letter from Jeffrey Epstein to the convicted USA Gymnastics doctor Larry Nassar that John Kiriakou singled out from the released documents, in which Epstein wrote that he would have gone home by the time it arrived and blamed everything on Donald Trump.

the-snapshots-in-the-release.title: Bill Clinton
the-snapshots-in-the-release.summary: 42nd U.S. president whom John Kiriakou describes as wholly disinterested in intelligence — briefed by the CIA only twice in eight years, with Vice President Al Gore taking the daily briefing instead and relaying anything important.

the-snapshots-in-the-release.title: Clickers and touchers
the-snapshots-in-the-release.summary: The distinction John Kiriakou says prisoners at FCI Loretto drew between convicted sex offenders who had only viewed images of children and those who had travelled across state lines to molest them, and his account of why they are all held at low security.

the-snickers-bar.title: Kiriakou's first recruitment
the-snickers-bar.summary: How John Kiriakou made his first CIA recruitment in Athens: by combing 25-year-old Greek police files not for people who had talked but for people who had answered back, finding one such man in a communist neighbourhood coffee shop, and buying his telephone number from a waiter for the price of a fifty.

the-snickers-bar.title: John Kiriakou
the-snickers-bar.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

the-snickers-bar.title: American shoes
the-snickers-bar.summary: The detail by which the chief of the Greek intelligence service identified John Kiriakou as an American within minutes of meeting him — not his Greek, which was fluent, but his footwear — and which sent Kiriakou straight to a shoe shop before working the anarchist quarters of Athens.

the-snickers-bar.title: Intelligence peddlers
the-snickers-bar.summary: John Kiriakou''s breakdown of who actually walks into an American embassy offering information: the overwhelming majority are fabricators or probes, a few per cent are peddlers selling the same nugget to five embassies in a month, and about one per cent are the real thing.

the-snickers-bar.title: How Kiriakou went armed in Athens
the-snickers-bar.summary: The load John Kiriakou carried every day during his Athens tour — a 9mm in a tear-away waist pack with three magazines, a snub-nosed .38 on his ankle, about 47 rounds in total, and a buck knife his boss handed him on his first day *"just in case things go to shit"*.

the-snickers-bar.title: There is no such thing as bad food in Athens
the-snickers-bar.summary: The lesson John Kiriakou says he learned at a lorry drivers' stop outside Corinth, where the food was as good as his grandmother's — reached on the three-and-a-half-hour drives he made to meet a source too sensitive to be met in Athens, with a vineyard tour as his cover story.

the-sociopath-next-door.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
the-sociopath-next-door.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

the-sociopath-next-door.title: Vietnam War
the-sociopath-next-door.summary: The war John Kiriakou grew up in the shadow of — his parents marched against it — and the deep precedent for everything he fights: entered on the Gulf of Tonkin lie, prosecuted by generals who knew for a decade they were losing (per the Pentagon Papers), studded with torture whose victims recited the Green Bay Packers'' starting lineup as "intelligence," and ended in part by Daniel Ellsberg, "the godfather of all modern national security whistleblowers." Even Robert McNamara, he notes, understood waterboarding was a bridge too far.

the-sociopath-next-door.title: Chuck Grassley
the-sociopath-next-door.summary: The senior senator from Iowa, and in John Kiriakou's assessment the one member of Congress who has taken whistleblower protection seriously as a legislative project — a count he has variously put at one finger, at two names, and at four out of 535. Grassley wrote the whistleblower protection statutes, speaks every year at the National Whistleblower Day luncheon, and is the name Kiriakou gives prospective whistleblowers as the single friendly ear on Capitol Hill. Kiriakou's personal verdict is colder — Grassley, he has said, never did anything for him.

the-sociopath-next-door.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
the-sociopath-next-door.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

the-sociopath-next-door.title: Jim Jordan
the-sociopath-next-door.summary: Republican congressman from Ohio and chairman of the House Judiciary Committee. John Kiriakou describes a genuinely divided view of him: one of only four members of Congress he names as a friend of whistleblowers, and simultaneously the chairman whose Weaponization subcommittee he says is a partisan counterfeit of the Church Committee — with the whole question settled against Jordan by the Ohio State wrestlers who told him their team doctor was abusing them.

the-sociopath-next-door.title: Prison racial segregation
the-sociopath-next-door.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the rigid racial and ethnic division of American prisons — a cafeteria split like the 1950s South — and his argument that segregating and hardening inmates for years, then releasing them with no skills, makes society less safe.

the-solitary-confinement-precedents.title: Julian Assange
the-solitary-confinement-precedents.summary: Kiriakou — a 15-year friend and former WikiLeaks board member — on why Assange is a publisher owed a journalist's immunity, and a political prisoner.

the-solitary-confinement-precedents.title: Solitary confinement
the-solitary-confinement-precedents.summary: The prison isolation practice the United Nations calls a form of torture; John Kiriakou, drawing on his own ten days in a six-by-sixteen-foot cell, argues that jailing depressed prisoners like Daniel Hale in solitary 'for their own safety' is precisely what drives them to suicide.

the-solitary-confinement-precedents.title: The postcards for Daniel Hale
the-solitary-confinement-precedents.summary: The letter-writing appeal John Kiriakou ran for Daniel Hale in May and June 2021 — naming Hale as the whistleblower most in need of help, posting his jail address publicly, and relaying from the prisoner himself the exact rules a letter had to satisfy to reach him: ten stamps a week, plain unlined white paper, black ink, and no photographs.

the-solitary-confinement-precedents.title: Daniel Duggan
the-solitary-confinement-precedents.summary: The former US Marine pilot and naturalised Australian citizen held in Australian custody for three years, uncharged in Australia, while the United States sought his extradition over flight training given in China years earlier. John Kiriakou submitted an affidavit in the case on the effects of solitary confinement, has spoken to both his Australian and American legal teams, and argues the selective prosecution "just stinks of politics" — and that extradition would end the case: "if he is extradited to the US, he''s lost."

the-solitary-confinement-precedents.title: Eastern State Penitentiary
the-solitary-confinement-precedents.summary: The Philadelphia prison where, per John Kiriakou, solitary confinement was invented in 1829 — a neo-Gothic stone penitentiary of tiny cells arranged as spokes around a central guard post, each containing a bed, a chair, a table, a chamber pot and a Bible, on the theory that a man left alone with scripture would emerge a law-abiding Christian. What happened instead, Kiriakou says, is that everybody went insane — and the practice was kept anyway, because it worked as punishment.

the-solitary-confinement-precedents.title: The EU whistleblower directive
the-solitary-confinement-precedents.summary: The European Union whistleblower protection directive, which John Kiriakou describes as a watered-down descendant of the Greek law he helped write in 2015. His objection is to its exemption: the directive does not apply to Brussels itself. He treats that as an instance of a general legislative habit rather than a European failing — Congress, he notes, routinely exempts itself from the laws it passes, including the Occupational Safety and Health Act.

the-solomon-islands-trip.title: The Chinese professor on LinkedIn
the-solomon-islands-trip.summary: The year-long approach John Kiriakou says he received through LinkedIn from a professor at a Chinese university he had never heard of — an invitation to speak that became five arranged stops across eastern China without his agreement, and which ended when he wrote back that he does not work for the Chinese intelligence service and was immediately blocked.

the-solomon-islands-trip.title: Craig Murray
the-solomon-islands-trip.summary: Former British Ambassador to Uzbekistan whom John Kiriakou cites as a whistleblower of extreme torture: during a meeting at the Uzbek intelligence service, Murray heard screaming, walked in, and saw a man being boiled in oil — reporting it cost him his career.

the-solomon-islands-trip.title: Dumping cash in a Moscow bathroom
the-solomon-islands-trip.summary: John Kiriakou's examples of what covert action has actually meant in practice — American commandos blowing up the Trans-Siberian oil pipeline, Afghan guerrillas hired to cross the Amu Darya and attack a refinery inside the southern USSR, and cash dumped in a Moscow bathroom to undermine the rouble.

the-solomon-islands-trip.title: How Chinese intelligence recruits
the-solomon-islands-trip.summary: John Kiriakou''s assessment of the Ministry of State Security''s tradecraft: very effective with anyone who simply wants money, because the money is limitless, and very bad at cultivating a source who does not yet know who is cultivating him — with the target usually being access to sophisticated technology.

the-solomon-islands-trip.title: MK-ULTRA in Canada
the-solomon-islands-trip.summary: John Kiriakou''s confirmation that many MK-ULTRA experiments took place on Canadian soil, and his explanation of why: the CIA asked the Canadian intelligence service for help with its anti-Soviet, anti-Chinese remote-viewing and LSD work, and the Canadians gladly gave it.

the-solomon-islands-trip.title: Pakistani corruption and democracy
the-solomon-islands-trip.summary: John Kiriakou's assessment that corruption in Pakistan is so deep and so broad that a genuinely functioning democracy is almost impossible there — set against a long history of military coups, a habit of imprisoning former prime ministers, and his insistence that Imran Khan should not be in a cell.

the-sources-and-methods-red-herring.title: The Stratfor cables on Venezuela
the-sources-and-methods-red-herring.summary: Material John Kiriakou says WikiLeaks exposed on American operations against Venezuela — the training of opposition figures including Juan Guaidó and Leopoldo López, and plotting to sabotage dams inside the country to help bring down Hugo Chávez. He offers it as an example of detail so obscure that few journalists know it, and as the real reason for the pursuit of Julian Assange.

the-sources-and-methods-red-herring.title: Espionage Act
the-sources-and-methods-red-herring.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

the-sources-and-methods-red-herring.title: Julian Assange
the-sources-and-methods-red-herring.summary: Kiriakou — a 15-year friend and former WikiLeaks board member — on why Assange is a publisher owed a journalist's immunity, and a political prisoner.

the-sources-and-methods-red-herring.title: Chelsea Manning
the-sources-and-methods-red-herring.summary: Former U.S. Army intelligence analyst who provided WikiLeaks its 2010 trove of military and diplomatic documents. Per John Kiriakou, Manning meets the legal definition of whistleblower for exposing war crimes, was a torture victim of prolonged solitary confinement with forced nudity, and was sentenced to 35 years in prison before Barack Obama commuted — not pardoned — her sentence. Kiriakou says Manning later refused a grand jury's offer of immunity and chose renewed jail time rather than testify against Julian Assange.

the-sources-and-methods-red-herring.title: Edward Snowden
the-sources-and-methods-red-herring.summary: Former NSA contractor who in 2013 disclosed the scope of U.S. [mass surveillance](/wiki/mass-surveillance), including the Section 702 collection program. Per John Kiriakou — who counts Snowden among the small group of national-security whistleblowers prosecuted under the Espionage Act — Snowden was ''stuck between two awful slippery slopes'': breaking his oath and chain of command on one side, and on the other catching something ''cut and dry against the Constitution'' that no one would act on. Kiriakou notes Snowden could not use his chain of command (as Kiriakou could not, his own chain being Jose Rodriguez), and that Judge Leonie Brinkema had reserved the Snowden case for herself before he fled the country.

the-sources-and-methods-red-herring.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
the-sources-and-methods-red-herring.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

the-spell-your-name-briefing.title: The Israeli listening devices ban
the-spell-your-name-briefing.summary: Why Mossad and Shin Bet representatives were barred from CIA headquarters, per John Kiriakou: the gifts they brought to liaison meetings kept turning up with listening devices and batteries embedded inside, so the agency stopped admitting them and rented meeting space in Virginia instead.

the-spell-your-name-briefing.title: The Jerusalem harassment campaign
the-spell-your-name-briefing.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of what happened to a CIA colleague and his wife during a declared two-year State Department rotation in Jerusalem: furniture rearranged after one embassy party, all three toilets in the house defecated in after another, and, before they left, the family dog''s tail cut off and bandaged. Kiriakou presents the three break-ins as routine rather than exceptional.

the-spell-your-name-briefing.title: Gulf secret prisons for hire
the-spell-your-name-briefing.summary: Asked whether the CIA knew of Gulf royals operating underground torture facilities and secret prisons, John Kiriakou answered that it did — one hundred per cent — then refused to give details, saying he would risk returning to prison. He described the arrangement instead: the United States sought out these countries precisely because they had no parliament and no free press to answer to, and paid for the use of their cells.

the-spell-your-name-briefing.title: Jonathan Pollard
the-spell-your-name-briefing.summary: U.S. Navy civilian intelligence analyst convicted in 1985 of spying for Israel; the canonical proven case of Israeli espionage against the United States; cited by John Kiriakou in his 2024 Piers Morgan debate with a former Mossad director who denied any Israeli spying on the U.S.

the-spell-your-name-briefing.title: The 189 undeclared officers
the-spell-your-name-briefing.summary: A figure John Kiriakou attributes to the CIA''s director of security, given to his intake class on his first day at the agency in January 1990: against two declared Israeli intelligence officers at the embassy in Washington, the FBI counted at least 189 undeclared ones operating across the United States. He pairs it with the fact that Israeli liaison officers were barred from CIA headquarters.

the-spell-your-name-briefing.title: AIPAC
the-spell-your-name-briefing.summary: The American Israel Public Affairs Committee — the U.S. political organization that, in John Kiriakou's framing, ought to be registered as a foreign-lobbying entity but is not, and that wields decisive electoral power against U.S. elected officials who express support for Palestinian human rights.

the-sputnik-shutdown.title: The book the publisher sat on
the-sputnik-shutdown.summary: The manuscript John Kiriakou says he delivered to his publisher three years before August 2025 and had still not seen printed, and the email he finally sent telling them it was time to fish or cut bait.

the-sputnik-shutdown.title: Cleaning up after Tora Bora
the-sputnik-shutdown.summary: John Kiriakou was not at Tora Bora. He arrived in Pakistan in January 2002, two months after the bombing, and says he went specifically to clean up what the battle had left behind — scavenging material, detaining the fighters too slow to get away, and mapping the smugglers'' valleys the survivors had used to cross. In his account the clean-up was necessary because the encirclement failed: bin Laden, warned by an al-Qaeda operative working as translator to the commander of Central Command, left in the dark dressed as a woman in the back of a pickup truck, and at dawn there was nobody in Tora Bora to surrender.

the-sputnik-shutdown.title: Hayden at the National Press Club
the-sputnik-shutdown.summary: John Kiriakou's account of seeing Michael Hayden, after a series of strokes, at a National Press Club event sponsored by the intelligence centre that bears his name — and the two reactions it produced in him, neither of them satisfaction alone.

the-sputnik-shutdown.title: Saddam and the journalists
the-sputnik-shutdown.summary: John Kiriakou's comparison, drawn from fifteen years working the Iraq target at the CIA, between a dictator who hated the press and did not kill it and a government that he says kills journalists deliberately and in numbers.

the-sputnik-shutdown.title: The balloon test
the-sputnik-shutdown.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that Israel had warning of the 7 October 2023 attack — that settlers along the Gaza line had reported training for months, that balloons were sent over as a probe in the days beforehand, and that nothing was done.

the-sputnik-shutdown.title: The green room with Hayden
the-sputnik-shutdown.summary: The 2008 television booking at which John Kiriakou and Michael Hayden were to appear together — and which Hayden, according to Kiriakou, walked out of after Kiriakou greeted him as "Mike" and refused to call him General Hayden.

the-spy-shop.title: Abu Zubaydah
the-spy-shop.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

the-spy-shop.title: Palantir Technologies
the-spy-shop.summary: U.S. data-analytics and intelligence-software company; received its first $1.5 million in seed funding from the CIA's In-Q-Tel venture-capital arm around 2002; characterized by John Kiriakou as functionally inseparable from the CIA in 2025, drawing the majority of its revenue from agency contracts and operating across DARPA, NSA, and the broader U.S. national-security apparatus.

the-spy-shop.title: Surveillance detection route
the-spy-shop.summary: Tradecraft technique used by intelligence officers and assets to determine whether they are being followed before, during, or after an operational meeting

the-spy-shop.title: Spy films John Kiriakou considers accurate
the-spy-shop.summary: Kiriakou's assessment of which espionage films get it right — Argo, The Recruit and Bridge of Spies — and his flat rejection of the action genre's premises, including the hidden weapons stash.

the-spy-shop.title: Central Intelligence Agency
the-spy-shop.summary: U.S. foreign intelligence service; John Kiriakou's employer from 1990 to 2004 and the central institution of KiriPedia

the-spy-shop.title: In-Q-Tel
the-spy-shop.summary: The CIA's openly acknowledged venture capital arm; provided Palantir Technologies its first $1.5 million in seed funding; in John Kiriakou's account the principal vehicle by which the agency finances private-sector development of technologies it intends to use.

the-spy-who-talked-too-much.title: The CIA Insider's Guide omnibus
the-spy-who-talked-too-much.summary: Skyhorse Publishing's plan to reissue John Kiriakou's three CIA Insider's Guides as a single updated volume of some 550 pages, with an introduction Tucker Carlson wrote in a day — part of what Kiriakou described in 2026 as a big book year.

the-spy-who-talked-too-much.title: The CIA Insider's Guide to Surveillance and Surveillance Detection
the-spy-who-talked-too-much.summary: Book by John Kiriakou drawing on his experience as a surveillance detection instructor at the CIA and as a private surveillance training consultant. The book covers the techniques used by intelligence professionals to identify whether they are being followed — including the four-phase surveillance detection route, concealment device placement and retrieval, and counter-surveillance strategy — adapted for use by corporate executives, journalists, and others who want to confirm whether they are being followed.

the-spy-who-talked-too-much.title: Remains of the Day (book)
the-spy-who-talked-too-much.summary: John Kiriakou's book, announced for publication by Simon and Schuster in March 2026, billed as a definitive guide to the historic cemeteries of Washington DC and the first in a planned series; the second installment will cover the Mafia graves of New York City.

the-spy-who-talked-too-much.title: 2026 Iran war economic shock
the-spy-who-talked-too-much.summary: John Kiriakou''s running assessment of the economic damage from the 2026 Iran war — an oil shock he says already exceeds both 1970s shocks combined, a natural-gas shock worse than the Nord Stream destruction, and a chokepoint problem that runs through fertilizer as much as fuel, since 65% of the world''s supply must transit the Strait of Hormuz. His summary: "This is an economic slowdown of choice."

the-spy-who-talked-too-much.title: Advice to an aspiring intelligence analyst
the-spy-who-talked-too-much.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer to a 21-year-old student asking what to study and what to read: pick a geographic area, become the go-to person on it, and consume everything published in the field — including the journals written by people who have never made policy.

the-spy-who-talked-too-much.title: Air wars are overrated
the-spy-who-talked-too-much.summary: John Kiriakou''s summary judgement on the 2026 Iran and Lebanon campaigns, delivered as the meta-headline of the whole war: air power flattened Gaza without destroying Hamas, is bogging down against Hezbollah, and cannot produce the outcome the war requires.

the-spys-guide-to-a-city.title: Olof Palme assassination
the-spys-guide-to-a-city.summary: The 1986 street murder of the Swedish prime minister, which John Kiriakou revisited step by step in Stockholm with researchers who had spent years on it. His conclusion — drawn from dozens of witness reports of two-man cars with walkie-talkies, some identified as police vehicles — is that much of the surveillance that night was carried out by people who believed they were running a practice exercise, until someone walked up and shot Palme dead.

the-spys-guide-to-a-city.title: The au pair who became a Stockholm police officer
the-spys-guide-to-a-city.summary: A young Swedish woman who lived with John Kiriakou and his then wife in Arlington, Virginia for a year around 2016. The daughter of Syrian Christian refugees, she went home to join the Stockholm police and, because she spoke fluent Swedish, English and Arabic, was posted to community outreach in a minority neighbourhood — a placement Kiriakou took at the time as evidence of a progressive Sweden he later concluded he had misread.

the-spys-guide-to-a-city.title: CIA sexpionage
the-spys-guide-to-a-city.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of the CIA''s use of sex in espionage — routine from its founding through the early 1980s, including MK-Ultra and honey-pot operations — and why the agency largely abandoned it: coercion cannot build the trust a long-term source requires. Other services never stopped.

the-spys-guide-to-a-city.title: Islam in America
the-spys-guide-to-a-city.summary: John Kiriakou's response to a widely circulated clip of thousands of American Muslims at prayer, captioned as evidence that Islam is the fastest-growing religion in the United States. He notes that nothing in the clip establishes where or what the event was, and that most new American Muslims are African Americans converting — often, in his experience, in the prison system.

the-spys-guide-to-a-city.title: Jihad means to struggle
the-spys-guide-to-a-city.summary: John Kiriakou's insistence, as a graduate in Islamic theology and an Arabic speaker, that jihad does not mean and has never meant holy war. He traces the American usage to media coverage of the 1979 Iranian revolution and the embassy hostage crisis, and points out that one can declare a jihad against poverty or in favour of education.

the-spys-guide-to-a-city.title: Ro Khanna
the-spys-guide-to-a-city.summary: Democratic congressman from California, whom John Kiriakou describes as one of the very few selfless people in Congress and grades highly in his case-officer rankings.

the-standard-operating-procedure-assignm.title: Abu Zubaydah
the-standard-operating-procedure-assignm.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

the-standard-operating-procedure-assignm.title: Mr. Fish
the-standard-operating-procedure-assignm.summary: The cover name the CIA used for Abu Zubaydah in Pakistan in 2002 — invented because the Americans would not tell their Pakistani partners who the target was, and derived from the only thing they would say about him: that he was a big fish.

the-standard-operating-procedure-assignm.title: Counterterrorism Center
the-standard-operating-procedure-assignm.summary: The CIA's Counterterrorism Center (CTC) — the unit where John Kiriakou spent the defining years of his operational career. He joined in the late 1990s as the only officer in the entire CIA fluent in both Greek and Arabic, served as chief of counterintelligence in the bin Laden unit, watched the Center swell from a few hundred employees to nearly 2,000 by September 12, 2001, and it was to CTC that he walked back down in May 2002 to refuse the torture program — the moment, he says, the CIA began to turn on him.

the-standard-operating-procedure-assignm.title: John Kiriakou
the-standard-operating-procedure-assignm.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

the-standard-operating-procedure-assignm.title: Billy Waugh
the-standard-operating-procedure-assignm.summary: Long-serving CIA paramilitary contractor; U.S. Army Special Forces ("Green Beret") veteran of World War II, Korea, and Vietnam; holder of approximately seventeen Purple Hearts (license plate "17 HITS"); resident of Niceville, Florida; died in his nineties.

the-standard-operating-procedure-assignm.title: The mosquito cloud
the-standard-operating-procedure-assignm.summary: The night John Kiriakou waited beside Abu Zubaydah's hospital bed in Faisalabad in a room full of mosquitoes, having stopped taking his anti-malarial because of the nightmares — and turned the ceiling fan to full blast in a cold March room until an FBI agent asked what he was doing.

the-stapler-in-the-dirksen-building.title: The DNC in debt
the-stapler-in-the-dirksen-building.summary: John Kiriakou''s July 2026 summary of the Democratic National Committee''s finances, drawn from New York Times reporting: two million dollars in debt against Republican reserves of $130 million, vendors asked to hold their invoices until after the elections, the party headquarters pledged as loan collateral, and a chairman who threw his phone at a junior aide.

the-stapler-in-the-dirksen-building.title: Embassy movie night
the-stapler-in-the-dirksen-building.summary: The weekly diversion John Kiriakou remembers from his posting to Pakistan after September 11th, when the station worked seven days a week and fourteen hours a day: on Wednesday nights the ambassador hosted a film in the embassy''s small theatre, and the audience shouted at the screen and threw popcorn at whatever they had managed to get hold of.

the-stapler-in-the-dirksen-building.title: The Italian schoolchildren
the-stapler-in-the-dirksen-building.summary: An encounter John Kiriakou described in July 2026 as a measure of how far his late-career fame had spread: walking down Fifth Avenue in New York, a bus pulled up, a boy of about thirteen shouted his name in Italian, and sixty-five Italian middle schoolers ran off the bus. The selfies took half an hour.

the-stapler-in-the-dirksen-building.title: 2026 Iran war
the-stapler-in-the-dirksen-building.summary: The open-ended American and Israeli war against Iran that John Kiriakou tracked week by week on his own show — a conflict he says was sold as three weeks, ran into its fifth month, achieved every decapitation objective it set, and continued anyway. His grade for it is a D, and his forecast is a Truth Social post declaring victory while nothing changes.

the-stapler-in-the-dirksen-building.title: Lindsey Graham
the-stapler-in-the-dirksen-building.summary: Republican senator from South Carolina who died in July 2026, and John Kiriakou's standing shorthand for the permanent war caucus — a "show horse" rather than a workhorse, a "chameleon" who "never saw a war that he didn't want to jump into with both feet," and, on posthumously released documentary footage, a man offering the US Air Force to bomb a country America was not at war with.

the-stapler-in-the-dirksen-building.title: The Espionage Act and the Rosenbergs
the-stapler-in-the-dirksen-building.summary: John Kiriakou''s short legislative history of the Espionage Act: written in 1917 to counter German saboteurs, slightly amended in 1950 after the execution of Julius and Ethel Rosenberg, and never meaningfully updated since. It does not use the words classified information, because the classification system did not exist when it was drafted.

the-state-department-cover-investigation.title: Senate Foreign Relations Committee
the-state-department-cover-investigation.summary: Kiriakou was senior investigator under John Kerry — and still held the post when his own federal prosecution came to a head in January 2012.

the-state-department-cover-investigation.title: Dasht-i-Leili massacre
the-state-department-cover-investigation.summary: Late-November 2001 mass suffocation of approximately 2,000 surrendered Taliban prisoners in unventilated shipping containers in the Afghan desert; the prisoners' surrender was negotiated by the CIA via the Northern Alliance, the transport order was issued by the CIA, and the operation was overseen by Northern Alliance warlord Abdul Rashid Dostum; John Kiriakou in 2009 as Senate Foreign Relations Committee investigator attempted to reopen the case under a 2008 Obama campaign promise; the CIA's classified response was, per Kiriakou, "go fuck yourself."

the-state-department-cover-investigation.title: Abu Zubaydah
the-state-department-cover-investigation.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

the-state-department-cover-investigation.title: Brian Ross
the-state-department-cover-investigation.summary: American investigative journalist and seven-time Emmy Award winner who was a prominent reporter at ABC News when, in December 2007, he conducted the on-camera interview with John Kiriakou that produced the first public confirmation by a U.S. official that the CIA waterboarded prisoners. Per Kiriakou, Ross called him out of the blue with the assertion that a source said Kiriakou had personally tortured Abu Zubaydah; Kiriakou's decision to give the interview anyway — driven by the conclusion that 'Brian Ross's source is at the White House and they're going to pin this on me' — became the pivot point of his entire post-CIA life.

the-state-department-cover-investigation.title: General Abdul Rashid Dostum
the-state-department-cover-investigation.summary: Northern Alliance Afghan warlord; overseer of the November–December 2001 Dasht-i-Leili massacre; characterized by John Kiriakou as a serial defector between the Taliban and the Northern Alliance and as a psychopath.

the-state-department-cover-investigation.title: Qala-i-Jangi uprising
the-state-department-cover-investigation.summary: The late-November 2001 prisoner uprising at a fortress in northern Afghanistan during which CIA officer Mike Spann was killed; the event during which the American al-Qaeda figure John Walker Lindh was captured; among the first major firefights of the post-9/11 Afghan campaign.

the-stinger.title: Mark Lanzalotti
the-stinger.summary: The prisoner John Kiriakou describes as his closest friend at FCI Loretto and one of the finest human beings he has known — a first-time non-violent drug defendant sentenced to triple life without parole for refusing to inform, the prison's foremost cook and bookie, and the man whose release Kiriakou secured by writing his Second Chance Act petition.

the-stinger.title: FCI Loretto
the-stinger.summary: U.S. Federal Correctional Institution in Loretto, Pennsylvania; the low-medium-security prison at which John Kiriakou served 23 months of a 30-month sentence following his 2013 Espionage Act–era plea deal; the originally ordered "minimum security work camp" placement was countermanded — per Kiriakou, on Brennan's direct intervention — to place him in the actual prison alongside the general population.

the-stinger.title: Pete Calabrese
the-stinger.summary: The senior Bonanno family member at FCI Loretto, known as Peter the Rabbit, who challenged John Kiriakou over his friendship with the cooperating witness Frank Russo and told him Russo brought dishonour to the Italians.

the-stinger.title: The rat and pedophile table
the-stinger.summary: The cafeteria table at FCI Loretto reserved for cooperating witnesses and sex offenders — a placement that also carried a ban from the television room, and which John Kiriakou describes as an outcome cooperators knew to expect before they agreed to testify.

the-stinger.title: Frank Russo
the-stinger.summary: The former auditor of Cuyahoga County, Ohio, who shared a bunk with John Kiriakou at FCI Loretto — a corruption defendant who cooperated against Jimmy Dimora, was marked in prison as a rat, and whom Kiriakou describes as a sweetheart with a hilarious sense of humour who won everybody over anyway.

the-stinger.title: Passing time at Loretto
the-stinger.summary: How prisoners at FCI Loretto filled days John Kiriakou describes as Groundhog Day — working out and watching television on a set of screens divided between factions, while Kiriakou himself read, answered mail and wrote a book.

the-stratfor-cables-on-venezuela.title: The sources and methods red herring
the-stratfor-cables-on-venezuela.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that the federal government invokes the exposure of sources and methods in every leak prosecution as a matter of routine, has never produced proof in any of them — not against Julian Assange, Edward Snowden or Chelsea Manning — and that American claims of damage to national security should therefore not be taken seriously.

the-stratfor-cables-on-venezuela.title: The Caracas checklist
the-stratfor-cables-on-venezuela.summary: The sequence of steps John Kiriakou says an operation to overthrow the Venezuelan government would run through — pressure Maduro into flight, secure the presidential palace, co-opt or bombard the military, take the television and radio stations, hold the main intersections of the capital — and his insistence that none of it is the hard part.

the-stratfor-cables-on-venezuela.title: Juan Guaidó
the-stratfor-cables-on-venezuela.summary: Venezuelan opposition figure whom the United States recognized as interim president starting in 2019; John Kiriakou dismisses him as having been, in substance, nothing more than a George Washington University grad student, and says the U.S. attempt to install him — followed later by María Corina Machado — failed because Venezuelan support for Nicolás Maduro rests on loyalty to Chavista revolutionary ideology rather than to Maduro personally.

the-stratfor-cables-on-venezuela.title: Julian Assange
the-stratfor-cables-on-venezuela.summary: Kiriakou — a 15-year friend and former WikiLeaks board member — on why Assange is a publisher owed a journalist's immunity, and a political prisoner.

the-stratfor-cables-on-venezuela.title: Khalid El-Masri
the-stratfor-cables-on-venezuela.summary: German grocery-store owner; rendered by the CIA in 2003 because his name — Khaled the Egyptian — happened to match that of a different Khaled the Egyptian whom a sister agency had reported was traveling to Albania to bomb the U.S. embassy. Tortured in Cairo to within an inch of his life. Released when Egyptian interrogators concluded he was the wrong man. Per John Kiriakou, returned to Germany with a waist-length beard and a Quran, telling a reporter: ''All I want to do is kill Americans.''

the-stratfor-cables-on-venezuela.title: The Colombian air bridge through Venezuela
the-stratfor-cables-on-venezuela.summary: What John Kiriakou says his own Senate Foreign Relations Committee investigation found about drug trafficking through Venezuela — that it exists, that it consists of Colombian aircraft landing there en route to Africa, and that there is no evidence Nicolás Maduro controls it or knows when and where it happens.

the-strike-on-ahmadinejads-house.title: 2026 Iran war
the-strike-on-ahmadinejads-house.summary: The open-ended American and Israeli war against Iran that John Kiriakou tracked week by week on his own show — a conflict he says was sold as three weeks, ran into its fifth month, achieved every decapitation objective it set, and continued anyway. His grade for it is a D, and his forecast is a Truth Social post declaring victory while nothing changes.

the-strike-on-ahmadinejads-house.title: The Iranian elementary school strike
the-strike-on-ahmadinejads-house.summary: A Tomahawk cruise missile strike at the start of the 2026 war that killed more than 175 people at an Iranian elementary school. The United States denied responsibility until its own investigation confirmed it; John Kiriakou traces the failure to targeting data a decade out of date and expects no one to be punished for it.

the-strike-on-ahmadinejads-house.title: Al Jazeera blocked in the United States
the-strike-on-ahmadinejads-house.summary: Within hours of the first strikes on Iran, John Kiriakou reported that American cable carriers had pulled Al Jazeera — a friend in Florida texted him that Dish Network had blocked it, and viewers reported the same of Comcast Xfinity in Boston. His reading was blunt: they do not want Americans to see what is happening in the Middle East.

the-strike-on-ahmadinejads-house.title: "A policy support organization"
the-strike-on-ahmadinejads-house.summary: Asked how the CIA workforce would be reacting to the war on Iran, John Kiriakou answered from the Iraq war: people put their heads down and did as they were told, after a boss told an assembled group — all of whom opposed the invasion — that the agency is not a policy organization but a policy support organization, and would do what the White House told it to do.

the-strike-on-ahmadinejads-house.title: Akrotiri Village Evacuation
the-strike-on-ahmadinejads-house.summary: Kiriakou says the drone that hit Britain's Akrotiri base in Cyprus was likely an Israeli operation, staged and then falsely blamed on Iran.

the-strike-on-ahmadinejads-house.title: American missile stockpiles
the-strike-on-ahmadinejads-house.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that the United States has run its interceptor stocks down to the point of strategic vulnerability — that the conventional wisdom in Washington was that a round of the Iran war ended because the Patriots ran out, and that a country which cannot fight a two-front war certainly cannot do it below maximum production.

the-strongly-worded-protest.title: How the CIA kills
the-strongly-worded-protest.summary: John Kiriakou''s description of the methods used when the CIA is ordered to kill someone outside a war zone: a team parachuting in miles away, stealing a car, a locks-and-picks specialist opening the door and suppressed weapons inside; a snatch into a van bound for an airport or a boat; or a brush past in a market with something poisoned — a technique he says the Russians used often and taught the Bulgarians into the early 1980s.

the-strongly-worded-protest.title: Nine recruitments in twenty-five years
the-strongly-worded-protest.summary: The conversation in which John Kiriakou''s Athens station chief, a twenty-five-year operations officer who had reached senior intelligence service level four with nine recruitments to his name, pointed out that Kiriakou had recruited five in two years — and Kiriakou''s explanation of the knack: that he could hide his disdain for a man completely while talking about whatever interested him.

the-strongly-worded-protest.title: SEALs on loan to the CIA
the-strongly-worded-protest.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer to why the CIA did not use its own paramilitary team against Osama bin Laden: it did. The raid was a CIA operation directed by the Counterterrorism Center, and every Navy SEAL involved was temporarily a CIA contractor, on loan to the agency for the duration.

the-strongly-worded-protest.title: The ayatollah and the photographs
the-strongly-worded-protest.summary: The training story John Kiriakou says ended the CIA''s use of compromat: a prostitute lured a junior Iranian ayatollah into a hotel room wired for audio and video, the agency took dozens of pictures, and when confronted with them abroad he asked for two in 8×10, three in 5×7, and one on a slide for his wall.

the-strongly-worded-protest.title: Learning to dive in the embassy pool
the-strongly-worded-protest.summary: John Kiriakou''s brief diving history, offered when the Nordstream sabotage discussion turned to the physics of deep water: lessons in the pool of the American embassy in 1991, one dive in the Red Sea at Sharm el-Sheikh in about 1992, and never again after that.

the-strongly-worded-protest.title: Mark Polymeropoulos
the-strongly-worded-protest.summary: The CIA officer John Kiriakou describes as a friend who was in his first tour when Aldrich Ames blew his identity, was brought in from the cold, and later became station chief in Moscow — an appointment Kiriakou characterises as a deliberate thumb in the Russians'' eye: the officer their spy had burned, put in charge of operations against them.

the-sudan-massacre.title: The Sahel church burnings
the-sudan-massacre.summary: John Kiriakou's account of al-Qaeda affiliates and Boko Haram in Chad, Mali and Nigeria attacking schools and churches — opening fire on teachers and administrators, kidnapping children, and burning congregations alive — and his observation that none of it is covered in the American media.

the-sudan-massacre.title: The Tajik civil war
the-sudan-massacre.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the Tajik civil war of the 1990s as the pattern that later conflicts follow — a quarter to a third of the population dead by some accounts, ethnic massacres routine enough that captives were roped together and drowned when the bullets ran out, and a war that lasted exactly as long as its foreign sponsors stayed interested.

the-sudan-massacre.title: Abraham Accords
the-sudan-massacre.summary: The Trump-brokered normalization deals between Israel and Gulf Arab states — in John Kiriakou's judgment "a terrible idea in the first place," a great victory for Israel and the Gulf Arabs that was "a punch in the throat to the Palestinians." He argues the Accords are how Trump meant to "solve the Middle East in a day" — by screwing the Palestinians — that Hamas read the abandonment correctly, that October 7 shattered the project, and that reviving the Accords (Saudis in, victory declared, Nobel collected) remains the organizing goal of Trump's regional policy.

the-sudan-massacre.title: The CIA's internal social culture
the-sudan-massacre.summary: John Kiriakou's one-word characterisation of the agency's internal culture — "incestuous" — describing a club for every conceivable interest, actively encouraged officer-to-officer romances, and a design intent that officers should have no need of friends or activities outside the building.

the-sudan-massacre.title: Death threats against Kiriakou
the-sudan-massacre.summary: The threats John Kiriakou has received across two decades — first after going public about the CIA torture program, when FBI advice that at least two were credible sent his family out of the country, and later in waves tied to his opposition to Gina Haspel, his remarks about Pakistan, and his advocacy on Palestine and the Epstein case.

the-sudan-massacre.title: Fridays at the agency
the-sudan-massacre.summary: John Kiriakou's observation that Fridays were always very slow at the CIA, because the Middle East weekend falls on Thursday-Friday or Friday-Saturday depending on the country and the quiet propagates back to Washington — a rhythm he says bled into the United States generally.

the-sue-mi-terry-case.title: "An actual summit"
the-sue-mi-terry-case.summary: John Kiriakou's reading of the August 2025 Anchorage meeting between Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin — that the Russian delegation's seniority proved Moscow was serious, that Putin is not the erratic figure American media portray, and that there is never any downside to diplomacy.

the-sue-mi-terry-case.title: Sergey Lavrov
the-sue-mi-terry-case.summary: Russian foreign minister, and previously Russian ambassador to the United Nations during John Kiriakou's assignment there, where the two worked the same Security Council. Kiriakou describes him as the most admired diplomat in the building — the most powerful, important and strategic ambassador there despite operating with far smaller resources than his American, British, French and Chinese counterparts, and better than most of the American diplomats Kiriakou worked for. When Lavrov was abruptly sidelined in late 2025, Kiriakou's reading was retirement rather than disgrace.

the-sue-mi-terry-case.title: The search for a country to take Gaza
the-sue-mi-terry-case.summary: John Kiriakou's account of Israel approaching one country after another — Albania, Indonesia, Egypt, Saudi Arabia and finally South Sudan — to accept expelled Gazans, a project he calls the literal definition of ethnic cleansing and says cannot be done because it is illegal.

the-sue-mi-terry-case.title: The seat-belt roadblocks
the-sue-mi-terry-case.summary: What John Kiriakou reported the federalised National Guard, police, FBI, ATF and DEA were actually doing at roadblocks on Washington's main thoroughfares in August 2025 — writing tickets for unworn seat belts and broken brake lights, in neighbourhoods he says have no street crime to speak of.

the-sue-mi-terry-case.title: The thrown sandwich
the-sue-mi-terry-case.summary: The arrest of a man who threw a sandwich at a National Guardsman at 14th and U Street in Washington in August 2025, charged with felony assault on a police officer with a stated demand for ten years — an overcharge John Kiriakou said no Washington jury would ever convict on.

the-sue-mi-terry-case.title: Walking Robert Morgenthau to the hearing room
the-sue-mi-terry-case.summary: John Kiriakou's recollection of taking the arm of a very elderly Robert Morgenthau in a Senate corridor and walking him to a Foreign Relations Committee hearing — and of telling him he had just read a book about Smyrna, and had not known his father coined the word genocide.

the-supporters-who-could-not-be-public.title: Espionage Act
the-supporters-who-could-not-be-public.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

the-supporters-who-could-not-be-public.title: The contrition requirement
the-supporters-who-could-not-be-public.summary: The rule John Kiriakou says defeats his own pardon applications before they begin — that an applicant must show proof of contrition — and his refusal to meet it. Asked whether he is sorry for the crime he committed, his answer is no, and that he would do it again.

the-supporters-who-could-not-be-public.title: FCI Loretto
the-supporters-who-could-not-be-public.summary: U.S. Federal Correctional Institution in Loretto, Pennsylvania; the low-medium-security prison at which John Kiriakou served 23 months of a 30-month sentence following his 2013 Espionage Act–era plea deal; the originally ordered "minimum security work camp" placement was countermanded — per Kiriakou, on Brennan's direct intervention — to place him in the actual prison alongside the general population.

the-supporters-who-could-not-be-public.title: Intelligence Identities Protection Act
the-supporters-who-could-not-be-public.summary: U.S. law enacted in 1982 that makes it a crime to knowingly disclose the identity of a covert intelligence officer; per John Kiriakou, his 2012 prosecution under the act arose from confirming a single surname of a former CIA colleague to a journalist — a confirmation that was never published. The name passed through a chain from journalist to Human Rights Watch to Guantanamo defense attorneys before reaching a judge and ultimately the FBI, which traced it back to Kiriakou.

the-supporters-who-could-not-be-public.title: Prosecutorial careerism
the-supporters-who-could-not-be-public.summary: John Kiriakou''s explanation for why senior federal prosecutors pursue high-profile national-security cases regardless of their merits: the conviction of a famous defendant is the entry ticket to a partnership at a large firm, a congressional candidacy, or a run for governor.

the-supporters-who-could-not-be-public.title: "I had no intent"
the-supporters-who-could-not-be-public.summary: The formula John Kiriakou used in the days around his January 2013 sentencing to describe his own guilty plea — that he had committed the act charged but had neither the intent to commit a crime nor the intent to harm the officer he named, having believed the man was retired and available to be interviewed.

the-swimming-pool-substitution.title: Sealing the courtroom
the-swimming-pool-substitution.summary: The physical measures John Kiriakou describes as accompanying a classified-information trial: plastic sheeting and duct tape over the windows so lasers cannot read the vibrations, white noise in the vestibule, and the clearing of everyone but the judge, jury, bailiff, clerk, lawyers and defendant.

the-swimming-pool-substitution.title: The jury consultant's advice
the-swimming-pool-substitution.summary: What John Kiriakou''s jury consultant told him about a national security trial in the Eastern District of Virginia: that in any other district in America he would say fight and win, but in that one, "buddy, you don''t have a prayer. Take the deal."

the-swimming-pool-substitution.title: Assange and the European Court of Human Rights
the-swimming-pool-substitution.summary: The last legal avenue John Kiriakou identified for Julian Assange in 2022 — three precedents in which the Strasbourg court refused to let Britain extradite mentally ill defendants to American solitary confinement — and the procedural trap that made it useless: Britain said the appeal need not halt the extradition.

the-swimming-pool-substitution.title: Julian Assange
the-swimming-pool-substitution.summary: Kiriakou — a 15-year friend and former WikiLeaks board member — on why Assange is a publisher owed a journalist's immunity, and a political prisoner.

the-swimming-pool-substitution.title: Pan Quake
the-swimming-pool-substitution.summary: An open-source, nonprofit, advertising-free social media platform hosted in Iceland on geothermal power and built on a content blockchain, conceived by Suzie Dawson and promoted by John Kiriakou as a brand ambassador from 2021. Kiriakou described its offshore incorporation and subscription model as deliberate defences against the attacks he expected from the CIA and NSA, and later said its Icelandic bank account was frozen at the FBI's request over the platform's association with Julian Assange supporters.

the-swimming-pool-substitution.title: The Istanbul peace talks
the-swimming-pool-substitution.summary: The early Russia–Ukraine negotiations in Istanbul that John Kiriakou says lasted three days and were never revived — talks the United States neither attended nor encouraged the Ukrainians to attend, and after which, he notes, the words "peace talks" disappeared from American discourse.

the-synagogue-in-damascus.title: Al-Julani
the-synagogue-in-damascus.summary: The former al-Qaeda commander and, per John Kiriakou, co-founder of ISIS who was installed as president of Syria and received at the White House. Kiriakou''s initial reading was that no one moves from a ten-million-dollar American bounty to a state visit in months without being a long-term CIA asset — until a senior Turkish official told him over dinner that al-Julani was Turkey''s: ''We created him from nothing and we installed him in Syria.'' Kiriakou judged that version more plausible than his own.

the-synagogue-in-damascus.title: Medea Benjamin's broken arm
the-synagogue-in-damascus.summary: John Kiriakou's account of Egyptian authorities breaking the arm of the CODEPINK co-founder Medea Benjamin while arresting her, as she attempted to reach the Rafah crossing to escort a food shipment into Gaza — an incident he offers as a measure of what Egyptian policing of the border looks like in practice.

the-synagogue-in-damascus.title: Expulsion of Palestinians from the Gulf
the-synagogue-in-damascus.summary: The mass expulsion of the Palestinian professional class from the Gulf Arab states in the aftermath of Iraq's 1990 invasion of Kuwait, which John Kiriakou witnessed from the region and identifies as the reason Gulf governments are willing to normalise relations with Israel. He dates the Kuwaiti decision to a wedding he attended weeks after the liberation, says Western and Egyptian pressure stopped it being total, and has repeatedly said he has never understood the grudge himself.

the-synagogue-in-damascus.title: The call about rebuilding Gaza
the-synagogue-in-damascus.summary: A telephone call John Kiriakou says he received on 7 November 2025 from a contact in the Israeli government, reporting that Israel had approached private American companies to redevelop Gaza — not Gazan Palestinians — and that the widely reported Saudi-administration plan was newspaper talk rather than anything the Israeli military was discussing. His conclusion: ''the fix is already in.''

the-synagogue-in-damascus.title: The Palestinian middle class in the Gulf
the-synagogue-in-damascus.summary: John Kiriakou's stated puzzlement, after a career spent on and in the Middle East, at what he calls a region-wide dislike of Palestinians among Arab governments — given that Palestinians constitute the entire professional middle class of the Gulf states, and are themselves Arabs and mostly Muslims.

the-synagogue-in-damascus.title: Bashar al-Assad
the-synagogue-in-damascus.summary: President of Syria; John Kiriakou recounts warning Senator John Kerry to stop publicly calling Assad 'my dear friend' after a speech enraged Washington's Lebanese community, with Kerry citing motorcycle rides they had taken together to the Golan Heights.

the-syria-chemical-attack-correction.title: Forcing Iran toward a bomb
the-syria-chemical-attack-correction.summary: John Kiriakou''s argument that Western pressure risks producing the very outcome it claims to prevent: repeated Israeli assassinations of Iranian scientists and generals and strikes on Iranian sites may eventually leave Ayatollah Khamenei with no choice but to permit a defensive weapon — despite the religious prohibition Kiriakou credits him with maintaining, and despite successive American estimates that Iran is not seeking one.

the-syria-chemical-attack-correction.title: The Iran–Israel exchange assessment
the-syria-chemical-attack-correction.summary: John Kiriakou''s judgement — which he expects to be unpopular — that Iran came out ahead of Israel in their direct missile exchange: the Iron Dome proved fallible, Iranian targeting was selective where Israel''s was not, and the ceasefire came, in his reading, because Israel had run out of missiles.

the-syria-chemical-attack-correction.title: CIA attention to West Africa
the-syria-chemical-attack-correction.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer on whether the CIA is likely to be operating in Burkina Faso: for all the years he was at the agency it cared very little about Africa and especially West Africa, but the presence of al-Qaeda and Islamic State affiliates plus the drug trade makes CIA and special forces involvement probable — and, he adds, the American public will not hear about it.

the-syria-chemical-attack-correction.title: CIA–FBI incompatible computer systems
the-syria-chemical-attack-correction.summary: John Kiriakou's claim that from the CIA's founding in 1947 until 2009 the computer systems of the CIA and the FBI were not compatible with one another — no message could be sent from one to the other and no intelligence shared — which he offers both as the material substrate of the interagency hatred that helped make September 11 possible, and as the gap through which James Mitchell and Bruce Jessen were able to pass Ali Soufan's FBI debriefings of Abu Zubaydah off as the fruits of torture.

the-syria-chemical-attack-correction.title: The Damascus consulate strike
the-syria-chemical-attack-correction.summary: The April 2024 Israeli attack on Iran's consulate in Damascus, which John Kiriakou describes as an unambiguous violation of the Vienna Convention, and whose official Israeli explanation — that it had not occurred to anyone the world would read it as a provocation — he calls disingenuous and intended purely for domestic audiences.

the-syria-chemical-attack-correction.title: Fake CIA résumés
the-syria-chemical-attack-correction.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of being used as a human authenticator in the private sector: at the consulting firm he joined after leaving the CIA, every job applicant claiming agency service was sent to dinner with him, and by his count fully half of them had never set foot inside the CIA.

the-taft-joke.title: Dick Cheney
the-taft-joke.summary: U.S. Vice President under George W. Bush. Per John Kiriakou — recounting CIA Director George Tenet's memoir — Cheney intercepted the presidential finding authorizing the CIA's enhanced interrogation program in the Oval Office anteroom and took it from Tenet before Bush could sign it. Tenet later concluded the president probably never actually signed the finding and probably told the truth when he said he had no idea the program was taking place. Kiriakou characterizes Cheney as the one who actually ran foreign policy, intelligence policy, and defense policy during the Bush years.

the-taft-joke.title: George W. Bush
the-taft-joke.summary: 43rd President of the United States. In John Kiriakou's telling, Bush signed the August 1, 2002 executive order that authorized the CIA torture program, spent years telling the public "we don't torture," and — days after Kiriakou's 2007 ABC interview — blamed torture on "a rogue CIA officer" while walking from the White House South Portico to Marine One, a moment Kiriakou instantly read as the White House preparing to pin the program on him. Bush also ordered the FBI removed from Abu Zubaydah's black site, flew the bin Laden family out of the country after 9/11, and loosened the assassination ban of Executive Order 12333.

the-taft-joke.title: Iraq WMD intelligence
the-taft-joke.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of how the case for Iraqi weapons of mass destruction was fabricated: the intelligence community''s consensus was that Iraq had no WMD, but the White House had already decided to invade and sought analysis to fit the policy.

the-taft-joke.title: Billy Waugh
the-taft-joke.summary: Long-serving CIA paramilitary contractor; U.S. Army Special Forces ("Green Beret") veteran of World War II, Korea, and Vietnam; holder of approximately seventeen Purple Hearts (license plate "17 HITS"); resident of Niceville, Florida; died in his nineties.

the-taft-joke.title: Donald Rumsfeld
the-taft-joke.summary: U.S. Secretary of Defense during the post-9/11 torture program and, per John Kiriakou, joined at the hip with Dick Cheney in pushing the Iraq war from inside the Office of the Secretary of Defense. Kiriakou recounts Rumsfeld dismissing sleep deprivation as a real technique by pointing to his own standup desk, and names him among the war criminals who would be prosecuted in any other country.

the-taiwan-blank-check.title: The Richard Haass back channel
the-taiwan-blank-check.summary: The April 2023 Track 2 meeting between Richard Haass, two former National Security Council deputies and Russian foreign minister Sergey Lavrov, which John Kiriakou explained as unofficial diplomacy requiring White House approval to be legal — and which he judged a good thing, because it built a mechanism for talks before the politics allowed them.

the-taiwan-blank-check.title: The Baltimore tunnel
the-taiwan-blank-check.summary: The rail tunnel built in 1850 just north of Baltimore that John Kiriakou names as the physical reason the American northeast has no high-speed rail — it is too narrow to admit a high-speed train, so every train on the corridor must be built to fit through it.

the-taiwan-blank-check.title: The Wagner coverage asymmetry
the-taiwan-blank-check.summary: John Kiriakou''s explanation for why the Wagner Group saturates American media while American private military contractors do not: there is no desire or necessity in the American press to keep secret a private army that does not belong to the United States, and the coverage doubles as a device for keeping Americans engaged with Ukraine.

the-taiwan-blank-check.title: China as mediator
the-taiwan-blank-check.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that China is the plausible mediator of Middle Eastern and Ukrainian conflicts, grounded in his claim that — Tibet and its border wars aside — China has no history of invading other countries, and his observation of how quickly Beijing accepted an offhand suggestion that it might mediate between Israel and Iran.

the-taiwan-blank-check.title: China as economic threat
the-taiwan-blank-check.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that China is the real threat to the West not militarily — it has one aircraft carrier to America's two dozen and rarely invades — but economically, buying friends worldwide while the U.S. spends a trillion dollars a year on weapons.

the-taiwan-blank-check.title: Elliott Abrams
the-taiwan-blank-check.summary: The Reagan-era assistant secretary of state whose 2023 appointment to a Biden administration advisory board John Kiriakou treated as proof that neoliberal and neoconservative foreign policy are the same policy with interchangeable players — a man who pleaded guilty over Iran-Contra, was pardoned, helped sell the Iraqi weapons of mass destruction case, and then served Donald Trump on Iran and Venezuela.

the-tajik-civil-war.title: The Sudan massacre
the-tajik-civil-war.summary: The killing of at least 624 civilians by a government-affiliated militia in Sudan in late October 2025, which John Kiriakou called a crime against humanity — and which he reads as a proxy war financed by the United Arab Emirates on one side and Saudi Arabia on the other, with a Wahhabi component traceable to Hassan al-Turabi.

the-tajik-civil-war.title: Hamid Karzai
the-tajik-civil-war.summary: The president installed in Afghanistan after the American invasion, whom John Kiriakou uses as the standing illustration of what occupation actually buys: after twenty years and more than a trillion dollars, Karzai was ''little more than the mayor of Kabul'' — and did not control all of Kabul either. The line began as a joke among Senate Foreign Relations Committee staff, and Kiriakou used it to Senator John Kerry''s face ten years into the war.

the-tajik-civil-war.title: The Sahel church burnings
the-tajik-civil-war.summary: John Kiriakou's account of al-Qaeda affiliates and Boko Haram in Chad, Mali and Nigeria attacking schools and churches — opening fire on teachers and administrators, kidnapping children, and burning congregations alive — and his observation that none of it is covered in the American media.

the-tajik-civil-war.title: Abraham Accords
the-tajik-civil-war.summary: The Trump-brokered normalization deals between Israel and Gulf Arab states — in John Kiriakou's judgment "a terrible idea in the first place," a great victory for Israel and the Gulf Arabs that was "a punch in the throat to the Palestinians." He argues the Accords are how Trump meant to "solve the Middle East in a day" — by screwing the Palestinians — that Hamas read the abandonment correctly, that October 7 shattered the project, and that reviving the Accords (Saudis in, victory declared, Nobel collected) remains the organizing goal of Trump's regional policy.

the-tajik-civil-war.title: The CIA's internal social culture
the-tajik-civil-war.summary: John Kiriakou's one-word characterisation of the agency's internal culture — "incestuous" — describing a club for every conceivable interest, actively encouraged officer-to-officer romances, and a design intent that officers should have no need of friends or activities outside the building.

the-tajik-civil-war.title: Death threats against Kiriakou
the-tajik-civil-war.summary: The threats John Kiriakou has received across two decades — first after going public about the CIA torture program, when FBI advice that at least two were credible sent his family out of the country, and later in waves tied to his opposition to Gina Haspel, his remarks about Pakistan, and his advocacy on Palestine and the Epstein case.

the-taliban-lobbyist-in-washington.title: The ISI as two organizations
