the-taliban-lobbyist-in-washington.summary: John Kiriakou''s working model of Pakistan''s Inter-Services Intelligence during his time as CIA chief of counterterrorism operations there: one half made up of British-trained officers he calls great counterterrorism partners, and another half that created, trained, financed and armed the Taliban — a split that left him deciding case by case whom he could trust.

the-taliban-lobbyist-in-washington.title: The cave myth
the-taliban-lobbyist-in-washington.summary: John Kiriakou's rejection of the popular image of al-Qaeda's leadership living in caves. He says the CIA knew its targets were in major cities, deliberately let them believe the search was concentrated on the tribal areas, and caught them because men who think they are unobserved get sloppy with their phones and email.

the-taliban-lobbyist-in-washington.title: Bin Laden health rumors
the-taliban-lobbyist-in-washington.summary: John Kiriakou's dismissal of the claim that Osama bin Laden died years before the 2011 raid. He says the CIA received a steady stream of medical rumours about him — kidney failure, dialysis in a cave, a spinal disorder — none of which turned out to be true, and that bin Laden was in fine health apart from arthritis and a hip problem until the day he died.

the-taliban-lobbyist-in-washington.title: SEAL Team Six attrition
the-taliban-lobbyist-in-washington.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer to the claim that the Navy SEALs who killed Osama bin Laden have since been killed off: the dead came from the broader unit rather than the raid party, SEAL Team Six numbers several hundred men rather than the dozen or so people imagine, and losing a high number of them to accidents and combat is, in his phrase, very sadly common.

the-taliban-lobbyist-in-washington.title: The torture memo signature
the-taliban-lobbyist-in-washington.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of how the CIA''s torture programme was authorised: a list of about ten techniques sent from headquarters through the Justice Department, the National Security Council lawyers and Condoleezza Rice to the president — who, to the surprise of the agency''s own leadership, signed it. Kiriakou recalls the deputy director saying three times in one meeting that he could not believe the president had signed the memo.

the-taliban-lobbyist-in-washington.title: Fake CIA résumés
the-taliban-lobbyist-in-washington.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of being used as a human authenticator in the private sector: at the consulting firm he joined after leaving the CIA, every job applicant claiming agency service was sent to dinner with him, and by his count fully half of them had never set foot inside the CIA.

the-tarantula-on-the-mini-fridge.title: The resort with no air conditioning
the-tarantula-on-the-mini-fridge.summary: The Baja California resort where John Kiriakou spent a month filming in 2025 — built in the 1960s as a commune by long-haired left-wing Angelenos funded by Thomas Hart Benton's daughter, a dozen buildings on the southernmost tip of the peninsula, no air conditioning, and nothing whatsoever to do unless you dive.

the-tarantula-on-the-mini-fridge.title: The fox that ate the scraps
the-tarantula-on-the-mini-fridge.summary: The small grey desert fox that lived on the grounds of the Baja resort, which the cook told John Kiriakou would finish anything left on the plate — and which, every single night, defecated on exactly the spot he crossed to reach his outdoor mini fridge.

the-tarantula-on-the-mini-fridge.title: Where he slept in Afghanistan
the-tarantula-on-the-mini-fridge.summary: John Kiriakou's inventory of his own Afghan accommodation across a decade of trips — a shared tent on the first visits, a tent of his own once ("living high on the hog"), the officers' quarters at Bagram once the American foothold was serious, and a three-star Afghan hotel when he returned as a private citizen to get the Kite Runner children out.

the-tarantula-on-the-mini-fridge.title: The washed-out road to the airport
the-tarantula-on-the-mini-fridge.summary: The drive to catch a flight to the Joe Rogan taping, after a hurricane took out the only road from the Baja resort — thirty-five miles in almost two hours, driven by his co-star Jeff Fahey and by Tyrel Ventura, over a dune, across cactus, with the animals jumping out of the way.

the-tarantula-on-the-mini-fridge.title: Abigail Spanberger
the-tarantula-on-the-mini-fridge.summary: Governor of Virginia from 2025 and, before Congress, a CIA officer alongside John Kiriakou in the Counterterrorism Center — whom he calls a perfectly nice person who would have been a middle-of-the-road Republican in the 1970s and 1980s, and whose victory speech, to his surprise, said all the right things.

the-tarantula-on-the-mini-fridge.title: Destroying the Dome of the Rock
the-tarantula-on-the-mini-fridge.summary: John Kiriakou's agreement with Tucker Carlson that a Zionist extremist plan to demolish the Dome of the Rock and build a third temple would be the event that starts the Third World War — and his additional prediction that it would also be the beginning of the end for the Israeli government and all of its support.

the-tax-rates-from-eisenhower-to-nixon.title: The nine months on food stamps
the-tax-rates-from-eisenhower-to-nixon.summary: The nine months John Kiriakou's family spent on public assistance after his arrest in January 2012 — his wife working out at the dining room table that they could not afford to buy food the following week, because everything they had had gone to the lawyers, and the Arlington County welfare office for which they qualified for everything.

the-tax-rates-from-eisenhower-to-nixon.title: Abraham Accords
the-tax-rates-from-eisenhower-to-nixon.summary: The Trump-brokered normalization deals between Israel and Gulf Arab states — in John Kiriakou's judgment "a terrible idea in the first place," a great victory for Israel and the Gulf Arabs that was "a punch in the throat to the Palestinians." He argues the Accords are how Trump meant to "solve the Middle East in a day" — by screwing the Palestinians — that Hamas read the abandonment correctly, that October 7 shattered the project, and that reviving the Accords (Saudis in, victory declared, Nobel collected) remains the organizing goal of Trump's regional policy.

the-tax-rates-from-eisenhower-to-nixon.title: The CIA's internal social culture
the-tax-rates-from-eisenhower-to-nixon.summary: John Kiriakou's one-word characterisation of the agency's internal culture — "incestuous" — describing a club for every conceivable interest, actively encouraged officer-to-officer romances, and a design intent that officers should have no need of friends or activities outside the building.

the-tax-rates-from-eisenhower-to-nixon.title: Death threats against Kiriakou
the-tax-rates-from-eisenhower-to-nixon.summary: The threats John Kiriakou has received across two decades — first after going public about the CIA torture program, when FBI advice that at least two were credible sent his family out of the country, and later in waves tied to his opposition to Gina Haspel, his remarks about Pakistan, and his advocacy on Palestine and the Epstein case.

the-tax-rates-from-eisenhower-to-nixon.title: Fridays at the agency
the-tax-rates-from-eisenhower-to-nixon.summary: John Kiriakou's observation that Fridays were always very slow at the CIA, because the Middle East weekend falls on Thursday-Friday or Friday-Saturday depending on the country and the quiet propagates back to Washington — a rhythm he says bled into the United States generally.

the-tax-rates-from-eisenhower-to-nixon.title: Hamid Karzai
the-tax-rates-from-eisenhower-to-nixon.summary: The president installed in Afghanistan after the American invasion, whom John Kiriakou uses as the standing illustration of what occupation actually buys: after twenty years and more than a trillion dollars, Karzai was ''little more than the mayor of Kabul'' — and did not control all of Kabul either. The line began as a joke among Senate Foreign Relations Committee staff, and Kiriakou used it to Senator John Kerry''s face ten years into the war.

the-tehran-slip.title: Reading in on the Iraq invasion
the-tehran-slip.summary: John Kiriakou's account of his first day as executive assistant to the CIA's deputy director for operations, when he signed six secrecy agreements and was told that the United States would invade Iraq the following March, and that the agencies opposing the war had already lost the argument.

the-tehran-slip.title: George Tenet
the-tehran-slip.summary: Director of Central Intelligence from 1997 to 2004, spanning the September 11 attacks and the early enhanced-interrogation program; identified by John Kiriakou as John Brennan's institutional patron at the agency; the figure who ordered the Five Eyes intelligence services to "open the files" to each other in the early 2000s.

the-tehran-slip.title: Dick Cheney
the-tehran-slip.summary: U.S. Vice President under George W. Bush. Per John Kiriakou — recounting CIA Director George Tenet's memoir — Cheney intercepted the presidential finding authorizing the CIA's enhanced interrogation program in the Oval Office anteroom and took it from Tenet before Bush could sign it. Tenet later concluded the president probably never actually signed the finding and probably told the truth when he said he had no idea the program was taking place. Kiriakou characterizes Cheney as the one who actually ran foreign policy, intelligence policy, and defense policy during the Bush years.

the-tehran-slip.title: The Condoleezza Rice meeting
the-tehran-slip.summary: The nine o'clock White House appointment John Kiriakou and Cofer Black never kept on the morning of 11 September 2001. The Government Printing Office was about to issue a volume of declassified Greece-Turkey-Cyprus cables in an edition of five or ten copies; three of them named CIA sources who were still alive, and an obscure statute obliges the government to offer citizenship and resettlement to any recruited source it outs. The two men were going to ask the National Security Advisor to quietly pull three cables nobody would miss. The car was at the East entrance at 8.15.

the-tehran-slip.title: Iraq WMD intelligence
the-tehran-slip.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of how the case for Iraqi weapons of mass destruction was fabricated: the intelligence community''s consensus was that Iraq had no WMD, but the White House had already decided to invade and sought analysis to fit the policy.

the-tehran-slip.title: Ahmed Chalabi
the-tehran-slip.summary: Iraqi exile and founder of the Iraqi National Congress; per John Kiriakou, a Shia-Kurdish con man who looted Petra Bank in Jordan of $36 million in the 1980s, was sentenced to death in absentia, was pardoned at CIA request, then pocketed $6 million in CIA seed funding for the INC and bought a Mayfair house in cash; later resurrected by Dick Cheney to feed the Pentagon fabricated WMD intelligence used to justify the 2003 invasion of Iraq.

the-texas-muslim-development.title: Islam in America
the-texas-muslim-development.summary: John Kiriakou's response to a widely circulated clip of thousands of American Muslims at prayer, captioned as evidence that Islam is the fastest-growing religion in the United States. He notes that nothing in the clip establishes where or what the event was, and that most new American Muslims are African Americans converting — often, in his experience, in the prison system.

the-texas-muslim-development.title: Jihad means to struggle
the-texas-muslim-development.summary: John Kiriakou's insistence, as a graduate in Islamic theology and an Arabic speaker, that jihad does not mean and has never meant holy war. He traces the American usage to media coverage of the 1979 Iranian revolution and the embassy hostage crisis, and points out that one can declare a jihad against poverty or in favour of education.

the-texas-muslim-development.title: CIA sexpionage
the-texas-muslim-development.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of the CIA''s use of sex in espionage — routine from its founding through the early 1980s, including MK-Ultra and honey-pot operations — and why the agency largely abandoned it: coercion cannot build the trust a long-term source requires. Other services never stopped.

the-texas-muslim-development.title: Olof Palme assassination
the-texas-muslim-development.summary: The 1986 street murder of the Swedish prime minister, which John Kiriakou revisited step by step in Stockholm with researchers who had spent years on it. His conclusion — drawn from dozens of witness reports of two-man cars with walkie-talkies, some identified as police vehicles — is that much of the surveillance that night was carried out by people who believed they were running a practice exercise, until someone walked up and shot Palme dead.

the-texas-muslim-development.title: Ro Khanna
the-texas-muslim-development.summary: Democratic congressman from California, whom John Kiriakou describes as one of the very few selfless people in Congress and grades highly in his case-officer rankings.

the-texas-muslim-development.title: Syrian minorities and the Israeli strikes
the-texas-muslim-development.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of a conflict inside American policy toward post-Assad Syria: Washington wants the country''s Christian, Jewish and Druze communities protected and has recognised the new government and moved to reopen its embassy, while Israel continues to strike Syrian territory despite repeated instructions from Donald Trump to stop.

the-third-term-workaround.title: The National Guard in Washington
the-third-term-workaround.summary: John Kiriakou's response to the August 2025 federalisation of the District of Columbia police — a decision he says was taken without informing the mayor or the police chief, in a city where crime was falling, and which he expected to expire after three days for want of congressional authorisation.

the-third-term-workaround.title: The Lafayette Square tents
the-third-term-workaround.summary: The long-running protest encampment across from the White House that a New Jersey congressman wanted removed by force in 2025, and John Kiriakou's observation that tents have stood on that spot for as long as he has lived in Washington — since 1982.

the-third-term-workaround.title: Cleaning up after Tora Bora
the-third-term-workaround.summary: John Kiriakou was not at Tora Bora. He arrived in Pakistan in January 2002, two months after the bombing, and says he went specifically to clean up what the battle had left behind — scavenging material, detaining the fighters too slow to get away, and mapping the smugglers'' valleys the survivors had used to cross. In his account the clean-up was necessary because the encirclement failed: bin Laden, warned by an al-Qaeda operative working as translator to the commander of Central Command, left in the dark dressed as a woman in the back of a pickup truck, and at dawn there was nobody in Tora Bora to surrender.

the-third-term-workaround.title: Hayden at the National Press Club
the-third-term-workaround.summary: John Kiriakou's account of seeing Michael Hayden, after a series of strokes, at a National Press Club event sponsored by the intelligence centre that bears his name — and the two reactions it produced in him, neither of them satisfaction alone.

the-third-term-workaround.title: Saddam and the journalists
the-third-term-workaround.summary: John Kiriakou's comparison, drawn from fifteen years working the Iraq target at the CIA, between a dictator who hated the press and did not kill it and a government that he says kills journalists deliberately and in numbers.

the-third-term-workaround.title: The balloon test
the-third-term-workaround.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that Israel had warning of the 7 October 2023 attack — that settlers along the Gaza line had reported training for months, that balloons were sent over as a probe in the days beforehand, and that nothing was done.

the-thirty-seven-analysts.title: Suing the CIA
the-thirty-seven-analysts.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer to whether anyone has ever successfully sued the CIA in civil court: not that he knows of. He allows only what he calls small, picky victories — chiefly suing for the right to sue — and applies the same pessimism to the burned officer whose case prompted the question.

the-thirty-seven-analysts.title: The Armitage leak
the-thirty-seven-analysts.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of who actually disclosed Valerie Plame''s identity: Richard Armitage — whom Kiriakou identifies as deputy secretary of defense — who everybody assumed would be charged under the Intelligence Identities Protection Act and who was never charged with any crime at all. Scooter Libby, he stresses, never leaked the name and was never accused of doing so; Libby fell on a perjury count.

the-thirty-seven-analysts.title: Mark Polymeropoulos
the-thirty-seven-analysts.summary: The CIA officer John Kiriakou describes as a friend who was in his first tour when Aldrich Ames blew his identity, was brought in from the cold, and later became station chief in Moscow — an appointment Kiriakou characterises as a deliberate thumb in the Russians'' eye: the officer their spy had burned, put in charge of operations against them.

the-thirty-seven-analysts.title: How the CIA kills
the-thirty-seven-analysts.summary: John Kiriakou''s description of the methods used when the CIA is ordered to kill someone outside a war zone: a team parachuting in miles away, stealing a car, a locks-and-picks specialist opening the door and suppressed weapons inside; a snatch into a van bound for an airport or a boat; or a brush past in a market with something poisoned — a technique he says the Russians used often and taught the Bulgarians into the early 1980s.

the-thirty-seven-analysts.title: Nine recruitments in twenty-five years
the-thirty-seven-analysts.summary: The conversation in which John Kiriakou''s Athens station chief, a twenty-five-year operations officer who had reached senior intelligence service level four with nine recruitments to his name, pointed out that Kiriakou had recruited five in two years — and Kiriakou''s explanation of the knack: that he could hide his disdain for a man completely while talking about whatever interested him.

the-thirty-seven-analysts.title: SEALs on loan to the CIA
the-thirty-seven-analysts.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer to why the CIA did not use its own paramilitary team against Osama bin Laden: it did. The raid was a CIA operation directed by the Counterterrorism Center, and every Navy SEAL involved was temporarily a CIA contractor, on loan to the agency for the duration.

the-thirty-year-old-nominee.title: No declaration of war since 1941
the-thirty-year-old-nominee.summary: John Kiriakou's answer to whether Congress will assert its authority over military action against Venezuela — an unqualified no, resting on the fact that the last declaration of war was on 8 December 1941 and that even the Gulf War was fought on an authorisation to use force rather than a declaration.

the-thirty-year-old-nominee.title: The Bay of Piglets
the-thirty-year-old-nominee.summary: The phrase John Kiriakou wished he had coined for the twice-attempted amphibious landings in Venezuela — and his account of one of the men rounded up coming ashore, who emailed him years later asking to appear on his show as a whistleblower on communism, and was told no.

the-thirty-year-old-nominee.title: Abigail Spanberger
the-thirty-year-old-nominee.summary: Governor of Virginia from 2025 and, before Congress, a CIA officer alongside John Kiriakou in the Counterterrorism Center — whom he calls a perfectly nice person who would have been a middle-of-the-road Republican in the 1970s and 1980s, and whose victory speech, to his surprise, said all the right things.

the-thirty-year-old-nominee.title: Destroying the Dome of the Rock
the-thirty-year-old-nominee.summary: John Kiriakou's agreement with Tucker Carlson that a Zionist extremist plan to demolish the Dome of the Rock and build a third temple would be the event that starts the Third World War — and his additional prediction that it would also be the beginning of the end for the Israeli government and all of its support.

the-thirty-year-old-nominee.title: Jason Miyares
the-thirty-year-old-nominee.summary: The Cuban-born Republican attorney general of Virginia whom John Kiriakou expected to be a right-wing disaster and found instead to be excellent — a judgement he says is hard for him to make about a conservative Republican, and which he repeated on the night Miyares was unceremoniously thrown out of office.

the-thirty-year-old-nominee.title: Joe Rogan
the-thirty-year-old-nominee.summary: The podcast host whose show John Kiriakou finally sat for in October 2025 — an experience that began with signing a non-disclosure agreement and ended with his verdict that Rogan is "a nice guy, very down to earth, very normal." The first thing Rogan asked, walking into the studio ten minutes late: "Hey, do you know my friend Mike Baker?" Kiriakou defends Rogan as unfairly characterized as a right-winger, and had long cited the show as the venue where Zuckerberg admitted Facebook suppressed the Hunter Biden laptop story at the FBI''s behest.

the-threat-to-testify.title: Arabic and Greek
the-threat-to-testify.summary: The qualification John Kiriakou says opened the door to his transfer from CIA analysis to operations: a post in Athens wanted Greek or Arabic, and he had both — by most of his tellings the only officer in the agency who did. The chief who hired him gave the reason in one sentence: it is easier and cheaper to take a linguist and teach him operations than the other way round. The pairing also became a detection tool, since the language nobody speaks in Pakistan is Arabic.

the-threat-to-testify.title: Too much work to be Mrs Kiriakou
the-threat-to-testify.summary: The reason John Kiriakou says his wife gave for leaving in 2017 — that it was simply too much work to be Mrs John Kiriakou — and his statement that he does not blame her.

the-threat-to-testify.title: Eastern District of Virginia
the-threat-to-testify.summary: The U.S. federal district covering northern Virginia — home to Langley, the Pentagon, DHS and much of the intelligence-contractor industry — which John Kiriakou calls 'the espionage court' because the Justice Department files the great majority of its national security prosecutions there and because, in his telling, no national-security defendant has ever won a case in it; Kiriakou, Julian Assange, Edward Snowden and Jeffrey Sterling were all charged there.

the-threat-to-testify.title: Federal plea coercion
the-threat-to-testify.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that the federal justice system coerces guilty pleas by stacking charges and winning 98.2% of its cases — so that even innocent defendants take deals, as he did, told by his own attorney that the system is 'not about justice; it's about mitigating damage.'

the-threat-to-testify.title: Never meet my grandchildren
the-threat-to-testify.summary: The threat John Kiriakou says one of the prosecutors in his case made to him — that he was going to die in prison and would never meet his grandchildren — set against the forty-five years he faced under the original charges.

the-threat-to-testify.title: Failure to accept responsibility
the-threat-to-testify.summary: The federal sentencing enhancement that John Kiriakou says explains why 98 per cent of federal criminal cases end in a plea bargain: a defendant who refuses a deal, goes to trial and loses has time added to the sentence for failing to accept responsibility.

the-three-pro-israel-countries.title: The coffee with the Jordanian intern
the-three-pro-israel-countries.summary: A morning meeting John Kiriakou took with a young intern from the Jordanian embassy who had found him on LinkedIn — and which he credits with reminding him that Palestinians are not a monolith, a point he says pro-Palestinian Westerners in particular tend to get wrong.

the-three-pro-israel-countries.title: Bulldozing the olive orchards
the-three-pro-israel-countries.summary: The sequence John Kiriakou describes preceding Israeli seizures of Palestinian land in the West Bank — olive orchards bulldozed and crops burned to make leaving easier, then the house demolished and a prefabricated one built for a settler family — and the different practice he says applies in East Jerusalem.

the-three-pro-israel-countries.title: Abbas and the three-state problem
the-three-pro-israel-countries.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that no two-state solution is available — because there is already one state, because Mahmoud Abbas is nineteen years into a four-year term and has become a billionaire, and because East Bank, West Bank and Gaza Palestinians are so disconnected that the real arithmetic is three states, which nobody will discuss.

the-three-pro-israel-countries.title: The New Castle News
the-three-pro-israel-countries.summary: The Pennsylvania local paper John Kiriakou says he tries to scan every day and can no longer afford — $250 a year for a sixteen-page paper with no Wednesday or Sunday edition, edited by a 28-year-old, in a region he describes as a news desert.

the-three-pro-israel-countries.title: Elbridge Gerry and the salamander
the-three-pro-israel-countries.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the origin of the word gerrymander — Elbridge Gerry, vice president and former governor of Massachusetts, drawing district boundaries to elect his friends, and Benjamin Franklin saying the shapes looked like salamanders — together with a piece of trivia from his unpublished book on cemeteries.

the-three-pro-israel-countries.title: New Castle, Pennsylvania
the-three-pro-israel-countries.summary: John Kiriakou's home town, an hour north of Pittsburgh on the edge of Amish country — a rust-belt city of roughly 40,000 to 50,000 people when he was growing up and around 18,000 to 20,000 now, whose decline he measures by the arrival of DEA and ATF field offices. It is also where, aged eight or nine and hunting salamanders in Oak Park Cemetery, he found the grave of a Medal of Honor private and acquired the lifelong interest in cemeteries that became a book.

the-thrown-sandwich.title: The seat-belt roadblocks
the-thrown-sandwich.summary: What John Kiriakou reported the federalised National Guard, police, FBI, ATF and DEA were actually doing at roadblocks on Washington's main thoroughfares in August 2025 — writing tickets for unworn seat belts and broken brake lights, in neighbourhoods he says have no street crime to speak of.

the-thrown-sandwich.title: "An actual summit"
the-thrown-sandwich.summary: John Kiriakou's reading of the August 2025 Anchorage meeting between Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin — that the Russian delegation's seniority proved Moscow was serious, that Putin is not the erratic figure American media portray, and that there is never any downside to diplomacy.

the-thrown-sandwich.title: Sergey Lavrov
the-thrown-sandwich.summary: Russian foreign minister, and previously Russian ambassador to the United Nations during John Kiriakou's assignment there, where the two worked the same Security Council. Kiriakou describes him as the most admired diplomat in the building — the most powerful, important and strategic ambassador there despite operating with far smaller resources than his American, British, French and Chinese counterparts, and better than most of the American diplomats Kiriakou worked for. When Lavrov was abruptly sidelined in late 2025, Kiriakou's reading was retirement rather than disgrace.

the-thrown-sandwich.title: The search for a country to take Gaza
the-thrown-sandwich.summary: John Kiriakou's account of Israel approaching one country after another — Albania, Indonesia, Egypt, Saudi Arabia and finally South Sudan — to accept expelled Gazans, a project he calls the literal definition of ethnic cleansing and says cannot be done because it is illegal.

the-thrown-sandwich.title: The Sue Mi Terry case
the-thrown-sandwich.summary: John Kiriakou's reading of the prosecution of analyst Sue Mi Terry — charged not under the Espionage Act but under the Foreign Agents Registration Act, an offence he reduces to failing to fill out a form on the internet, and one whose nominal sentencing range he says means nothing in practice.

the-thrown-sandwich.title: Walking Robert Morgenthau to the hearing room
the-thrown-sandwich.summary: John Kiriakou's recollection of taking the arm of a very elderly Robert Morgenthau in a Senate corridor and walking him to a Foreign Relations Committee hearing — and of telling him he had just read a book about Smyrna, and had not known his father coined the word genocide.

the-tier-one-walk-up.title: The asset recruitment cycle
the-tier-one-walk-up.summary: The four-step professional standard John Kiriakou says governed CIA operations before September 11 — spot, assess, develop, recruit — and without which an officer did not get promoted. He calls it the asset acquisition cycle as often as the recruitment cycle. Spotting looks for access, not rank; assessment looks for a vulnerability, a word he insists is less ugly than it sounds; development is months or years of friendship bought on an unlimited expense account; and the recruitment itself rests not on money, revenge or ideology but on the target believing the officer is his best friend. Threats are forbidden — partly on ethics, partly because the target may come to the next meeting with a gun.

the-tier-one-walk-up.title: Freemasons and Opus Dei at the CIA
the-tier-one-walk-up.summary: John Kiriakou's characterisation of the affinity networks at the top of the CIA — a great many senior officers who are Freemasons, and periods in which most of the leadership belonged to Opus Dei and attended the same church in Great Falls, Virginia. He rejects the idea that these are plots, describing them instead as accidental clusters of men who look out for one another.

the-tier-one-walk-up.title: CIA attention to West Africa
the-tier-one-walk-up.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer on whether the CIA is likely to be operating in Burkina Faso: for all the years he was at the agency it cared very little about Africa and especially West Africa, but the presence of al-Qaeda and Islamic State affiliates plus the drug trade makes CIA and special forces involvement probable — and, he adds, the American public will not hear about it.

the-tier-one-walk-up.title: CIA–FBI incompatible computer systems
the-tier-one-walk-up.summary: John Kiriakou's claim that from the CIA's founding in 1947 until 2009 the computer systems of the CIA and the FBI were not compatible with one another — no message could be sent from one to the other and no intelligence shared — which he offers both as the material substrate of the interagency hatred that helped make September 11 possible, and as the gap through which James Mitchell and Bruce Jessen were able to pass Ali Soufan's FBI debriefings of Abu Zubaydah off as the fruits of torture.

the-tier-one-walk-up.title: Fake CIA résumés
the-tier-one-walk-up.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of being used as a human authenticator in the private sector: at the consulting firm he joined after leaving the CIA, every job applicant claiming agency service was sent to dinner with him, and by his count fully half of them had never set foot inside the CIA.

the-tier-one-walk-up.title: Forcing Iran toward a bomb
the-tier-one-walk-up.summary: John Kiriakou''s argument that Western pressure risks producing the very outcome it claims to prevent: repeated Israeli assassinations of Iranian scientists and generals and strikes on Iranian sites may eventually leave Ayatollah Khamenei with no choice but to permit a defensive weapon — despite the religious prohibition Kiriakou credits him with maintaining, and despite successive American estimates that Iran is not seeking one.

the-tomahawk-red-line.title: Major non-NATO ally status for Ukraine
the-tomahawk-red-line.summary: John Kiriakou''s forecast of how the Russian demand that Ukraine never join NATO can be met without leaving Ukraine unprotected: the designation of major non-NATO ally, already held by Australia, Japan, South Korea, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates, which he says confers essentially the same rights without the membership.

the-tomahawk-red-line.title: Abigail Spanberger
the-tomahawk-red-line.summary: Governor of Virginia from 2025 and, before Congress, a CIA officer alongside John Kiriakou in the Counterterrorism Center — whom he calls a perfectly nice person who would have been a middle-of-the-road Republican in the 1970s and 1980s, and whose victory speech, to his surprise, said all the right things.

the-tomahawk-red-line.title: Destroying the Dome of the Rock
the-tomahawk-red-line.summary: John Kiriakou's agreement with Tucker Carlson that a Zionist extremist plan to demolish the Dome of the Rock and build a third temple would be the event that starts the Third World War — and his additional prediction that it would also be the beginning of the end for the Israeli government and all of its support.

the-tomahawk-red-line.title: Jason Miyares
the-tomahawk-red-line.summary: The Cuban-born Republican attorney general of Virginia whom John Kiriakou expected to be a right-wing disaster and found instead to be excellent — a judgement he says is hard for him to make about a conservative Republican, and which he repeated on the night Miyares was unceremoniously thrown out of office.

the-tomahawk-red-line.title: Joe Rogan
the-tomahawk-red-line.summary: The podcast host whose show John Kiriakou finally sat for in October 2025 — an experience that began with signing a non-disclosure agreement and ended with his verdict that Rogan is "a nice guy, very down to earth, very normal." The first thing Rogan asked, walking into the studio ten minutes late: "Hey, do you know my friend Mike Baker?" Kiriakou defends Rogan as unfairly characterized as a right-winger, and had long cited the show as the venue where Zuckerberg admitted Facebook suppressed the Hunter Biden laptop story at the FBI''s behest.

the-tomahawk-red-line.title: No declaration of war since 1941
the-tomahawk-red-line.summary: John Kiriakou's answer to whether Congress will assert its authority over military action against Venezuela — an unqualified no, resting on the fact that the last declaration of war was on 8 December 1941 and that even the Gulf War was fought on an authorisation to use force rather than a declaration.

the-tomato-patch-surveillance.title: George Washington University
the-tomato-patch-surveillance.summary: The Washington university where John Kiriakou took a bachelor's degree in Middle Eastern studies and began a master's in legislative affairs, and where a professor who was in fact a CIA spotter recruited him into the agency — an institution that recurs throughout his account as the place his intelligence career began, as the venue of his first CIA tests, and later as a classroom he taught in himself.

the-tomato-patch-surveillance.title: The interrupted break-in
the-tomato-patch-surveillance.summary: A break-in in a friendly country nearly failed when the neighbour who was supposed to be at work turned out to have given birth the day before; John Kiriakou talked his way out of it at the door by claiming to be looking for his aunt''s flat in the wrong building.

the-tomato-patch-surveillance.title: The Satan dream
the-tomato-patch-surveillance.summary: Seventeen years after leaving Pakistan, John Kiriakou said he still dreamt about it every night — a recurring dream of Satan hunting him house to house — and described a failed blood pressure drug now used to erase the dreams of PTSD patients.

the-tomato-patch-surveillance.title: No ethics training at the CIA
the-tomato-patch-surveillance.summary: John Kiriakou''s claim that the CIA provides no ethics training of any kind, so that an officer either arrives with a personal moral code or never acquires one — and the classroom hypothetical he uses to show where the line goes undrawn.

the-tomato-patch-surveillance.title: PTSD
the-tomato-patch-surveillance.summary: Post-traumatic stress disorder runs through John Kiriakou''s life and worldview — he had it coming out of Greece after an assassination attempt, brought it home from Pakistan alongside his shock at colleagues'' willingness to kill, and was blindsided by a delayed post-prison version that helped end his marriage. For six months after release he dreamed the same dream nightly: that he was out by mistake and had to get back inside before midnight count. He still takes a repurposed blood-pressure drug that stops the dreams, and he extends the diagnosis outward — to secret-site interrogators who came back crying, to drone pilots, and to prisoners released angry and untreated.

the-tomato-patch-surveillance.title: The booby-trapped Christmas cards
the-tomato-patch-surveillance.summary: Among the devices al-Qaeda left behind in positions it was forced to evacuate in Afghanistan, John Kiriakou describes a detonator laid flat inside a Christmas card, so that opening the card would take the reader''s hands off.

the-toronto-transit-detention.title: FCI Loretto
the-toronto-transit-detention.summary: U.S. Federal Correctional Institution in Loretto, Pennsylvania; the low-medium-security prison at which John Kiriakou served 23 months of a 30-month sentence following his 2013 Espionage Act–era plea deal; the originally ordered "minimum security work camp" placement was countermanded — per Kiriakou, on Brennan's direct intervention — to place him in the actual prison alongside the general population.

the-toronto-transit-detention.title: Kiriakou Greek whistleblower law
the-toronto-transit-detention.summary: A whistleblower protection law John Kiriakou says he was hired by the Greek government to write in 2015, at the invitation of Greece, after which it was passed by both the European Parliament and the Greek Parliament and became law across the European Union. Per Kiriakou, the law's first courtroom use involved a whistleblower who exposed Greece's defense minister for taking bribes from Siemens; the resulting press coverage led a consortium of Greece's four wealthiest families to ask Kiriakou to run a private equity fund for them.

the-toronto-transit-detention.title: Blueprint for Free Speech
the-toronto-transit-detention.summary: The Australian non-governmental organisation that drafts whistleblower protection legislation and markets it to governments around the world, and which hired John Kiriakou in 2015 to help write Greece's law. Its board is mostly academics and transparency activists; Kiriakou credits it with successes in Canada, Zambia, Jamaica and Ukraine, and names its founder and director as Suelette Dreyfus, whom he describes as a co-founder of WikiLeaks with Julian Assange.

the-toronto-transit-detention.title: Eastern District of Virginia
the-toronto-transit-detention.summary: The U.S. federal district covering northern Virginia — home to Langley, the Pentagon, DHS and much of the intelligence-contractor industry — which John Kiriakou calls 'the espionage court' because the Justice Department files the great majority of its national security prosecutions there and because, in his telling, no national-security defendant has ever won a case in it; Kiriakou, Julian Assange, Edward Snowden and Jeffrey Sterling were all charged there.

the-toronto-transit-detention.title: The Greek health care system
the-toronto-transit-detention.summary: John Kiriakou's description of Greek health care as a two-tier system in which the private sector buys nothing but position in the queue — a procedure that takes eleven or twelve months on the public system takes one or two privately, and the care itself is the same.

the-toronto-transit-detention.title: Kiriakou's Greek citizenship
the-toronto-transit-detention.summary: The Greek nationality John Kiriakou acquired in 2010, after his CIA career and before his prosecution — offered, he says, by the Greek ambassador who asked what could be done to help when his troubles began, and granted when he answered "you could give me Greek citizenship." Held by his children too, it made him a Greek national at the moment he became, in Greece, a national hero; it brought him the commission to write the country's whistleblower protection law, and the Athens job that turned out to be a money laundering operation.

the-torture-memo-signature.title: The 1968 waterboarding conviction
the-torture-memo-signature.summary: The precedent John Kiriakou uses to dispose of the argument that waterboarding was legally uncertain after 2002: a January 1968 Washington Post front page showing an American soldier waterboarding a North Vietnamese prisoner, an investigation ordered by Defense Secretary Robert McNamara, and the soldier''s arrest, conviction for torture and imprisonment. The law, Kiriakou points out, never changed in between.

the-torture-memo-signature.title: Abu Zubaydah
the-torture-memo-signature.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

the-torture-memo-signature.title: Bin Laden health rumors
the-torture-memo-signature.summary: John Kiriakou's dismissal of the claim that Osama bin Laden died years before the 2011 raid. He says the CIA received a steady stream of medical rumours about him — kidney failure, dialysis in a cave, a spinal disorder — none of which turned out to be true, and that bin Laden was in fine health apart from arthritis and a hip problem until the day he died.

the-torture-memo-signature.title: SEAL Team Six attrition
the-torture-memo-signature.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer to the claim that the Navy SEALs who killed Osama bin Laden have since been killed off: the dead came from the broader unit rather than the raid party, SEAL Team Six numbers several hundred men rather than the dozen or so people imagine, and losing a high number of them to accidents and combat is, in his phrase, very sadly common.

the-torture-memo-signature.title: The cave myth
the-torture-memo-signature.summary: John Kiriakou's rejection of the popular image of al-Qaeda's leadership living in caves. He says the CIA knew its targets were in major cities, deliberately let them believe the search was concentrated on the tribal areas, and caught them because men who think they are unobserved get sloppy with their phones and email.

the-torture-memo-signature.title: The Taliban lobbyist in Washington
the-torture-memo-signature.summary: A story put to John Kiriakou about a Taliban delegation''s American press conference and the Washington lobbyist who represented them. Kiriakou remembered the episode and the lobbyist''s New Jersey base but not the claim about her parentage, and explained why it caused so little controversy at the time: the United States had no historical quarrel with the Taliban, and had armed and fêted some of its future members during the war against the Soviets.

the-translator-for-the-italian-occupatio.title: George McGovern
the-translator-for-the-italian-occupatio.summary: The 1972 Democratic presidential nominee, whose landslide defeat John Kiriakou identifies as the pretext for creating superdelegates. As a George Washington University sophomore in 1983, Kiriakou wrote to McGovern offering the campus theater for a campaign launch; McGovern telephoned him personally, announced his 1984 candidacy there, and afterwards took him home for tuna sandwiches made by his wife.

the-translator-for-the-italian-occupatio.title: George Washington University
the-translator-for-the-italian-occupatio.summary: The Washington university where John Kiriakou took a bachelor's degree in Middle Eastern studies and began a master's in legislative affairs, and where a professor who was in fact a CIA spotter recruited him into the agency — an institution that recurs throughout his account as the place his intelligence career began, as the venue of his first CIA tests, and later as a classroom he taught in himself.

the-translator-for-the-italian-occupatio.title: Invasion of Grenada
the-translator-for-the-italian-occupatio.summary: The 1983 American invasion of Grenada, which John Kiriakou supported as a nineteen-year-old College Democrat at George Washington University on the grounds that American medical students had to be rescued — an episode he now cites as the clearest example of how completely he once accepted the government's own account of what it was doing.

the-translator-for-the-italian-occupatio.title: John Kiriakou
the-translator-for-the-italian-occupatio.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

the-translator-for-the-italian-occupatio.title: Reza Pahlavi
the-translator-for-the-italian-occupatio.summary: The exiled Iranian crown prince whom John Kiriakou dismisses as an Israeli-backed fantasy candidate to rule Iran — a man who has not lived there since his teens, supported mainly by Beverly Hills exiles, whom Kiriakou says 'wouldn't survive the walk from the plane to the terminal.'

the-translator-for-the-italian-occupatio.title: The draft argument
the-translator-for-the-italian-occupatio.summary: The disagreement John Kiriakou had at eighteen with a fellow College Democrat over Vietnam — that he thought the war immoral and illegal and would have served anyway if drafted, because his country had asked him to — which he identifies as the clearest surviving statement of the belief he later lost.

the-truman-broadcast.title: No prosecution for a dead journalist
the-truman-broadcast.summary: A fact John Kiriakou says he read the day he raised it — that the Israeli government has never prosecuted anyone over the death of any journalist, ever — and the conclusion he draws from it: that killing journalists is state policy, and that Israel should stop pretending otherwise and simply say reporters enter at their own risk.

the-truman-broadcast.title: Truman's regret over Israel
the-truman-broadcast.summary: John Kiriakou's account that Harry Truman called his role in the creation of the state of Israel the act of 'a damn fool' and the biggest regret of his presidency, because the situation spun out of control almost immediately.

the-truman-broadcast.title: Israel-United States relations
the-truman-broadcast.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the U.S.-Israel relationship, including his own first visit to Israel as a tourist in 2022 and his characterization of Israel's willingness to destroy an entire city block to kill a single target, confident that the United States will not object.

the-truman-broadcast.title: The search for a country to take Gaza
the-truman-broadcast.summary: John Kiriakou's account of Israel approaching one country after another — Albania, Indonesia, Egypt, Saudi Arabia and finally South Sudan — to accept expelled Gazans, a project he calls the literal definition of ethnic cleansing and says cannot be done because it is illegal.

the-truman-broadcast.title: Nixon's guarantee of Israeli national security
the-truman-broadcast.summary: John Kiriakou's account that AIPAC, having begun to focus on election fundraising in the late 1960s, succeeded in getting President Nixon to guarantee Israeli national security in 1969 — a commitment he says no American president had made before.

the-truman-broadcast.title: The Damascus consulate strike
the-truman-broadcast.summary: The April 2024 Israeli attack on Iran's consulate in Damascus, which John Kiriakou describes as an unambiguous violation of the Vienna Convention, and whose official Israeli explanation — that it had not occurred to anyone the world would read it as a provocation — he calls disingenuous and intended purely for domestic audiences.

the-trump-appointees-to-the-court.title: Decorum in the Reagan years
the-trump-appointees-to-the-court.summary: John Kiriakou's contrast between the State of the Union addresses he watched as a college student under Ronald Reagan — divided, substantive, but conducted with decorum — and the 2026 address he called a clown show with no decorum on either side.

the-trump-appointees-to-the-court.title: Donald Trump
the-trump-appointees-to-the-court.summary: 45th and 47th U.S. president. Per John Kiriakou, a man genuinely convinced he was doing right by bombing Iran, "duped" by the same Netanyahu nuclear bluff Obama once rejected — and, at the same time, the most blindly pro-Israel president in history, an admirer of autocrats who has never once criticized Vladimir Putin, and prone to gestures — from the Gulf of America to a since-abandoned "Department of War" rename — that test the edges of his actual authority.

the-trump-appointees-to-the-court.title: Get thrown out spicily
the-trump-appointees-to-the-court.summary: John Kiriakou''s criticism of Representative Al Green''s protest at the 2026 State of the Union address: that holding up a banned sign and then walking out quietly accomplished nothing, and that if you are going to be removed you should struggle and fight back.

the-trump-appointees-to-the-court.title: Impeach him again
the-trump-appointees-to-the-court.summary: John Kiriakou's warning that if the Democrats win a House majority in 2026 and immediately move to impeach Donald Trump again, they should never win another race — and his prediction that this is exactly what they will do.

the-trump-appointees-to-the-court.title: Nationalizing the midterms
the-trump-appointees-to-the-court.summary: John Kiriakou's recurring comparison between contemporary party messaging and Newt Gingrich's 1994 Contract with America, including his advice that Speaker Mike Johnson should keep Gingrich on his couch and ask him nightly how the 1994 midterms were nationalised.

the-trump-appointees-to-the-court.title: The six-hour queue for seats
the-trump-appointees-to-the-court.summary: John Kiriakou on learning that members of Congress arrive six hours early with packed meals to hold a seat for the State of the Union, and that in 2026 the absence of 112 Democrats freed those seats for the cabinet, the sub-cabinet and visitors.

the-trump-weave.title: The O'Reilly exclusivity rule
the-trump-weave.summary: The condition Bill O'Reilly's producer attached to booking John Kiriakou — that he appear on no other programme for three days either side — and Kiriakou's refusal to surrender a week of his diary, which meant he never appeared on the show at all.

the-trump-weave.title: The Piers Morgan panel
the-trump-weave.summary: The televised debate John Kiriakou returns to most often — two against two, with Scott Horton and himself on one side and Alan Dershowitz and a senior former Israeli official on the other. Kiriakou set out his position on Hamas, October 7th and Gaza, and Piers Morgan told him at the end that he had come around and agreed. On a second appearance from the same panel he argued that Jeffrey Epstein was an Israeli access agent, provoked Dershowitz — Epstein's own attorney — into an interruption Kiriakou considers self-defeating, and got an unbothered "who knows?" from the Israeli.

the-trump-weave.title: Cleaning up after Tora Bora
the-trump-weave.summary: John Kiriakou was not at Tora Bora. He arrived in Pakistan in January 2002, two months after the bombing, and says he went specifically to clean up what the battle had left behind — scavenging material, detaining the fighters too slow to get away, and mapping the smugglers'' valleys the survivors had used to cross. In his account the clean-up was necessary because the encirclement failed: bin Laden, warned by an al-Qaeda operative working as translator to the commander of Central Command, left in the dark dressed as a woman in the back of a pickup truck, and at dawn there was nobody in Tora Bora to surrender.

the-trump-weave.title: Hayden at the National Press Club
the-trump-weave.summary: John Kiriakou's account of seeing Michael Hayden, after a series of strokes, at a National Press Club event sponsored by the intelligence centre that bears his name — and the two reactions it produced in him, neither of them satisfaction alone.

the-trump-weave.title: Saddam and the journalists
the-trump-weave.summary: John Kiriakou's comparison, drawn from fifteen years working the Iraq target at the CIA, between a dictator who hated the press and did not kill it and a government that he says kills journalists deliberately and in numbers.

the-trump-weave.title: The balloon test
the-trump-weave.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that Israel had warning of the 7 October 2023 attack — that settlers along the Gaza line had reported training for months, that balloons were sent over as a probe in the days beforehand, and that nothing was done.

the-truth-social-announcement.title: The war powers resolution vote
the-truth-social-announcement.summary: John Kiriakou''s assessment of the congressional attempt to take back war powers over the 2026 Iran conflict: a sense-of-the-Congress resolution would have no teeth or authority, and a bill with legal force would simply be vetoed.

the-truth-social-announcement.title: Bahrain's naturalisation policy
the-truth-social-announcement.summary: John Kiriakou's account of how the Bahraini royal family changed the sectarian arithmetic of the country over thirty years — importing Syrians and naturalising Indian and Pakistani Sunni Muslims until a population that had been two-thirds to three-quarters Shia was closer to half and half.

the-truth-social-announcement.title: Bombing the Omanis
the-truth-social-announcement.summary: John Kiriakou's judgement that Iran's strikes on the Gulf states — and above all on Oman, which had been trying to broker peace — made enemies Iran did not need to make, of governments that would otherwise have sat the war out.

the-truth-social-announcement.title: "Iran posed no threat"
the-truth-social-announcement.summary: John Kiriakou''s core objection to the 2026 war, stated as a chain of negatives: Iran had no nuclear weapon, no nuclear weapons programme, no wish for one, a religious ruling against one, and no delivery system if it had had one — findings he says were confirmed twice by the CIA and by the IAEA.

the-truth-social-announcement.title: Marco Rubio and Iran policy
the-truth-social-announcement.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer to who was actually driving American policy toward Iran in 2026: with the Vice President, the Director of National Intelligence and the Chairman of the Joint Chiefs all reported as opposed, and with Marco Rubio holding both the State Department and the National Security Adviser''s job, the policy was Rubio''s.

the-truth-social-announcement.title: THAAD stocks in the Gulf
the-truth-social-announcement.summary: John Kiriakou's report, during the 2026 war, that the United Arab Emirates were seven days from exhausting their THAAD interceptors and Qatar four days — with American resupply unable to keep pace.

the-twenty-five-in-pakistan.title: The Taliban
the-twenty-five-in-pakistan.summary: The Afghan movement John Kiriakou describes as loyal to nobody and, in 2001, genuinely baffled by the American invasion: its leadership held that sheltering al-Qaeda was a cultural obligation to a guest rather than an alliance, that it had never taken up arms against the United States, and that Washington was welcome to fight al-Qaeda on Afghan soil. He supported the Doha peace process but judged the Biden-era power-sharing letter an abandonment, arguing that any deal without guarantees on women, girls'' education and the vote returns the country to the 1990s.

the-twenty-five-in-pakistan.title: Bob Grenier
the-twenty-five-in-pakistan.summary: Career CIA officer who served as station chief in Islamabad before, during, and after 9/11; later associate deputy director of operations for policy support and Iraq Mission Manager; John Kiriakou's boss and, for one year, his supervisor as executive assistant.

the-twenty-five-in-pakistan.title: Jim Pavitt
the-twenty-five-in-pakistan.summary: Long-serving CIA Deputy Director for Operations during the early post-9/11 period; characterized by John Kiriakou as "a legendary officer and a really great guy"; mocked John Brennan openly within the agency for Brennan's recurring stated ambition to head his own intelligence agency.

the-twenty-five-in-pakistan.title: The Grenier counterinsurgency op-ed
the-twenty-five-in-pakistan.summary: The New York Times piece by former CIA officer Robert Grenier arguing that the storming of the Capitol should be treated as an insurgency, and John Kiriakou's published answer to it — that a colleague of thirty years using that word is asking for people to be killed, and that counterinsurgency describes a set of practices the Constitution forbids at home.

the-twenty-five-in-pakistan.title: Bahrain Posting (1994–1996)
the-twenty-five-in-pakistan.summary: John Kiriakou's 1994–1996 assignment to Bahrain under U.S. State Department cover as second secretary for economic affairs — arriving with his wife Joanne and infant son Chris on August 1, 1994, into a tiny Gulf monarchy whose sectarian tensions erupted, two months later, into the first Intifada.

the-twenty-five-in-pakistan.title: Bashar al-Assad
the-twenty-five-in-pakistan.summary: President of Syria; John Kiriakou recounts warning Senator John Kerry to stop publicly calling Assad 'my dear friend' after a speech enraged Washington's Lebanese community, with Kerry citing motorcycle rides they had taken together to the Golan Heights.

the-twenty-seven-cousins.title: Daniel Ellsberg
the-twenty-seven-cousins.summary: The Pentagon Papers whistleblower Kiriakou calls 'the Godfather of all national security whistleblowers' — and one of the great mentors of his life.

the-twenty-seven-cousins.title: Kiriakou's father and grandfather
the-twenty-seven-cousins.summary: The two men John Kiriakou names as the greatest influences on his life: a grandfather with a third-grade education who pushed his children through doctorates and handed his grandson an 11th-century gold coin dug from a Greek garden, and a father, an elementary school principal, who was twice passed over for promotion because he refused to pay the bribe the school board demanded. Kiriakou says that refusal is what made him a whistleblower.

the-twenty-seven-cousins.title: Bill Binney
the-twenty-seven-cousins.summary: Former NSA technical director whom John Kiriakou cites as having debunked the DNC hack. Asked by Veteran Intelligence Professionals for Sanity to examine the science, Binney analyzed the speed of the upload and concluded the emails could only have been copied in person to a thumb drive, not taken remotely by Russia — an argument he later made to Donald Trump in the Oval Office. Kiriakou calls him a friend, the most brilliant person he has met on electronics, and a member of the whistleblower circle he belongs to.

the-twenty-seven-cousins.title: Coffee with a cabinet member
the-twenty-seven-cousins.summary: John Kiriakou's disclosure that he had coffee with a member of the cabinet who told him to be patient about his pardon — and told him to watch what he said. He reports the meeting while stating plainly that there is nothing further he can do to make his case, and that he is not confident the outcome will be decided on justice.

the-twenty-seven-cousins.title: "Do not ever attempt to contact me again"
the-twenty-seven-cousins.summary: The reply John Kiriakou says he received from John Kerry, then Secretary of State, after emailing him privately in the days before reporting to prison to beg that his sentence be commuted. Kiriakou had worked closely with Kerry for two and a half years; the one-line answer, sent after two or three days, was the last he ever heard from him.

the-twenty-seven-cousins.title: Espionage Act
the-twenty-seven-cousins.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

the-twenty-thousand-dollar-tweet.title: The witness letter
the-twenty-thousand-dollar-tweet.summary: A letter John Kiriakou received in August 2025 informing him that he would be called as a witness in Noelle Dunphy's defamation case against Rudy Giuliani — a consequence, he says, of having told the New York Times that Giuliani's people tried to squeeze $2 million out of him for a pardon.

the-twenty-thousand-dollar-tweet.title: Abbas and the three-state problem
the-twenty-thousand-dollar-tweet.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that no two-state solution is available — because there is already one state, because Mahmoud Abbas is nineteen years into a four-year term and has become a billionaire, and because East Bank, West Bank and Gaza Palestinians are so disconnected that the real arithmetic is three states, which nobody will discuss.

the-twenty-thousand-dollar-tweet.title: Bulldozing the olive orchards
the-twenty-thousand-dollar-tweet.summary: The sequence John Kiriakou describes preceding Israeli seizures of Palestinian land in the West Bank — olive orchards bulldozed and crops burned to make leaving easier, then the house demolished and a prefabricated one built for a settler family — and the different practice he says applies in East Jerusalem.

the-twenty-thousand-dollar-tweet.title: Elbridge Gerry and the salamander
the-twenty-thousand-dollar-tweet.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the origin of the word gerrymander — Elbridge Gerry, vice president and former governor of Massachusetts, drawing district boundaries to elect his friends, and Benjamin Franklin saying the shapes looked like salamanders — together with a piece of trivia from his unpublished book on cemeteries.

the-twenty-thousand-dollar-tweet.title: Giuliani Pardon Solicitation
the-twenty-thousand-dollar-tweet.summary: Per John Kiriakou, a meeting at the Trump International Hotel in Washington in which Rudy Giuliani's associate solicited $2 million in exchange for a presidential pardon — a story that subsequently appeared as a front-page New York Times article. Giuliani publicly denied ever meeting Kiriakou; Kiriakou sent the Times the photograph taken at the meeting that morning, and the paper published the story with the note that it had seen documentary proof.

the-twenty-thousand-dollar-tweet.title: New Castle, Pennsylvania
the-twenty-thousand-dollar-tweet.summary: John Kiriakou's home town, an hour north of Pittsburgh on the edge of Amish country — a rust-belt city of roughly 40,000 to 50,000 people when he was growing up and around 18,000 to 20,000 now, whose decline he measures by the arrival of DEA and ATF field offices. It is also where, aged eight or nine and hunting salamanders in Oak Park Cemetery, he found the grave of a Medal of Honor private and acquired the lifelong interest in cemeteries that became a book.

the-twenty-two-month-clearance.title: How the CIA kills
the-twenty-two-month-clearance.summary: John Kiriakou''s description of the methods used when the CIA is ordered to kill someone outside a war zone: a team parachuting in miles away, stealing a car, a locks-and-picks specialist opening the door and suppressed weapons inside; a snatch into a van bound for an airport or a boat; or a brush past in a market with something poisoned — a technique he says the Russians used often and taught the Bulgarians into the early 1980s.

the-twenty-two-month-clearance.title: Mark Polymeropoulos
the-twenty-two-month-clearance.summary: The CIA officer John Kiriakou describes as a friend who was in his first tour when Aldrich Ames blew his identity, was brought in from the cold, and later became station chief in Moscow — an appointment Kiriakou characterises as a deliberate thumb in the Russians'' eye: the officer their spy had burned, put in charge of operations against them.

the-twenty-two-month-clearance.title: Nine recruitments in twenty-five years
the-twenty-two-month-clearance.summary: The conversation in which John Kiriakou''s Athens station chief, a twenty-five-year operations officer who had reached senior intelligence service level four with nine recruitments to his name, pointed out that Kiriakou had recruited five in two years — and Kiriakou''s explanation of the knack: that he could hide his disdain for a man completely while talking about whatever interested him.

the-twenty-two-month-clearance.title: SEALs on loan to the CIA
the-twenty-two-month-clearance.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer to why the CIA did not use its own paramilitary team against Osama bin Laden: it did. The raid was a CIA operation directed by the Counterterrorism Center, and every Navy SEAL involved was temporarily a CIA contractor, on loan to the agency for the duration.

the-twenty-two-month-clearance.title: Suing the CIA
the-twenty-two-month-clearance.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer to whether anyone has ever successfully sued the CIA in civil court: not that he knows of. He allows only what he calls small, picky victories — chiefly suing for the right to sue — and applies the same pessimism to the burned officer whose case prompted the question.

the-twenty-two-month-clearance.title: The Armitage leak
the-twenty-two-month-clearance.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of who actually disclosed Valerie Plame''s identity: Richard Armitage — whom Kiriakou identifies as deputy secretary of defense — who everybody assumed would be charged under the Intelligence Identities Protection Act and who was never charged with any crime at all. Scooter Libby, he stresses, never leaked the name and was never accused of doing so; Libby fell on a perjury count.

the-two-hundred-and-thirty-million-dolla.title: No declaration of war since 1941
the-two-hundred-and-thirty-million-dolla.summary: John Kiriakou's answer to whether Congress will assert its authority over military action against Venezuela — an unqualified no, resting on the fact that the last declaration of war was on 8 December 1941 and that even the Gulf War was fought on an authorisation to use force rather than a declaration.

the-two-hundred-and-thirty-million-dolla.title: Abigail Spanberger
the-two-hundred-and-thirty-million-dolla.summary: Governor of Virginia from 2025 and, before Congress, a CIA officer alongside John Kiriakou in the Counterterrorism Center — whom he calls a perfectly nice person who would have been a middle-of-the-road Republican in the 1970s and 1980s, and whose victory speech, to his surprise, said all the right things.

the-two-hundred-and-thirty-million-dolla.title: Destroying the Dome of the Rock
the-two-hundred-and-thirty-million-dolla.summary: John Kiriakou's agreement with Tucker Carlson that a Zionist extremist plan to demolish the Dome of the Rock and build a third temple would be the event that starts the Third World War — and his additional prediction that it would also be the beginning of the end for the Israeli government and all of its support.

the-two-hundred-and-thirty-million-dolla.title: Jason Miyares
the-two-hundred-and-thirty-million-dolla.summary: The Cuban-born Republican attorney general of Virginia whom John Kiriakou expected to be a right-wing disaster and found instead to be excellent — a judgement he says is hard for him to make about a conservative Republican, and which he repeated on the night Miyares was unceremoniously thrown out of office.

the-two-hundred-and-thirty-million-dolla.title: Joe Rogan
the-two-hundred-and-thirty-million-dolla.summary: The podcast host whose show John Kiriakou finally sat for in October 2025 — an experience that began with signing a non-disclosure agreement and ended with his verdict that Rogan is "a nice guy, very down to earth, very normal." The first thing Rogan asked, walking into the studio ten minutes late: "Hey, do you know my friend Mike Baker?" Kiriakou defends Rogan as unfairly characterized as a right-winger, and had long cited the show as the venue where Zuckerberg admitted Facebook suppressed the Hunter Biden laptop story at the FBI''s behest.

the-two-hundred-and-thirty-million-dolla.title: The Bamiyan precedent
the-two-hundred-and-thirty-million-dolla.summary: John Kiriakou's account of how the Taliban destroyed their own diplomatic position by blowing up the Bamiyan Buddhas — at a moment when Washington was paying Taliban salaries, funding opium eradication, flirting with a trans-Afghanistan pipeline and flying Taliban emissaries to Houston to meet the Bush camp.

the-two-hundred-billion-war-request.title: 2026 Iran war economic shock
the-two-hundred-billion-war-request.summary: John Kiriakou''s running assessment of the economic damage from the 2026 Iran war — an oil shock he says already exceeds both 1970s shocks combined, a natural-gas shock worse than the Nord Stream destruction, and a chokepoint problem that runs through fertilizer as much as fuel, since 65% of the world''s supply must transit the Strait of Hormuz. His summary: "This is an economic slowdown of choice."

the-two-hundred-billion-war-request.title: Advice to an aspiring intelligence analyst
the-two-hundred-billion-war-request.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer to a 21-year-old student asking what to study and what to read: pick a geographic area, become the go-to person on it, and consume everything published in the field — including the journals written by people who have never made policy.

the-two-hundred-billion-war-request.title: Air wars are overrated
the-two-hundred-billion-war-request.summary: John Kiriakou''s summary judgement on the 2026 Iran and Lebanon campaigns, delivered as the meta-headline of the whole war: air power flattened Gaza without destroying Hamas, is bogging down against Hezbollah, and cannot produce the outcome the war requires.

the-two-hundred-billion-war-request.title: Asian fuel reserves, 2026
the-two-hundred-billion-war-request.summary: The effect of the Strait of Hormuz closure on oil-importing Asian economies as John Kiriakou described it — countries counting their remaining fuel in days rather than months, with no substitute supply available, and economies he expects simply to stop.

the-two-hundred-billion-war-request.title: The CIA Insider's Guide to Surveillance and Surveillance Detection
the-two-hundred-billion-war-request.summary: Book by John Kiriakou drawing on his experience as a surveillance detection instructor at the CIA and as a private surveillance training consultant. The book covers the techniques used by intelligence professionals to identify whether they are being followed — including the four-phase surveillance detection route, concealment device placement and retrieval, and counter-surveillance strategy — adapted for use by corporate executives, journalists, and others who want to confirm whether they are being followed.

the-two-hundred-billion-war-request.title: Donald Trump
the-two-hundred-billion-war-request.summary: 45th and 47th U.S. president. Per John Kiriakou, a man genuinely convinced he was doing right by bombing Iran, "duped" by the same Netanyahu nuclear bluff Obama once rejected — and, at the same time, the most blindly pro-Israel president in history, an admirer of autocrats who has never once criticized Vladimir Putin, and prone to gestures — from the Gulf of America to a since-abandoned "Department of War" rename — that test the edges of his actual authority.

the-two-isis.title: The let-them-in strategy
the-two-isis.summary: John Kiriakou has claimed one of the ideas he contributed as CIA counterterrorism chief in Pakistan was to stop trying to intercept al-Qaeda fighters one at a time on the Afghan border, and instead let them cross into Pakistan and take them ten at a time in their safe houses.

the-two-isis.title: Whether anyone is still looking for Zawahiri
the-two-isis.summary: Asked in December 2019 why Ayman al-Zawahiri had never been found, John Kiriakou offered a speculation he was careful to label as an outsider''s: that the United States might simply have stopped looking for him, because al-Qaeda had become largely irrelevant and attention had moved to ISIS.

the-two-isis.title: Fusha and the Gulf dialect
the-two-isis.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of his own Arabic training — a first year in fusha, high standard Arabic, followed by a second year in khaleeji, the Gulf dialect — and what he reports of both: that Yemen is the only place pure fusha is spoken, that Saudis asked him why he spoke Arabic like Shakespeare, that the Gulf dialect is marked by a hard J other Arabs dislike, and that the Maghreb defeats him entirely.

the-two-isis.title: "I only wanted to kill Jews"
the-two-isis.summary: In the hospital room at a Pakistani military base, after telling the wounded Abu Zubaydah that fifty thousand people had been in the towers and that he was not the victim, John Kiriakou says the prisoner answered that he had only wanted to kill Jews and had been overruled.

the-two-isis.title: Abu Zubaydah
the-two-isis.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

the-two-isis.title: The Punjab Elite Force
the-two-isis.summary: The Pakistani provincial counterterrorism unit that supplied part of the assault manpower for the Abu Zubaydah raids of March 2002 — black trousers, black t-shirts stencilled with a pistol, and, in John Kiriakou's telling, a refusal to wear body armour on the grounds that if God called them that night they would go.

the-two-officers-who-changed.title: CIA operational psychologists
the-two-officers-who-changed.summary: The branch of the CIA's psychological staff that John Kiriakou says he worked with directly as a case officer — not the analysts who profile foreign leaders, but the clinicians who vet a prospective recruit for insanity or invention, and advise an officer on exactly how hard a source can be pushed before he breaks.

the-two-officers-who-changed.title: CIA psychological evaluations
the-two-officers-who-changed.summary: The two kinds of psychological work John Kiriakou describes inside the CIA — the recurring psychiatric screening every officer undergoes, before employment, again three years after hiring and every five years thereafter for life; and the long-distance evaluation of foreign leaders carried out by the analytic side. The agency's clinical psychologists are split between the two, with a third group in operations advising case officers on the sources they recruit.

the-two-officers-who-changed.title: Mike Scheuer
the-two-officers-who-changed.summary: Founder and chief of "Alec Station", the CIA unit dedicated to tracking Osama bin Laden in the years before September 11, 2001; per John Kiriakou — alongside his New York FBI counterpart John O'Neill — "100 percent correct" about bin Laden, and uniformly hated for it inside the agency.

the-two-officers-who-changed.title: Osama bin Laden
the-two-officers-who-changed.summary: Founder and leader of al-Qaeda and the central target of the manhunt that shaped John Kiriakou's counterterrorism career. Per Kiriakou, bin Laden came from a billionaire Saudi construction family, was never one of the CIA-funded Afghan mujahideen, overruled subordinates who wanted to attack Israel and insisted the 9/11 attacks hit the United States to crash its economy, escaped Tora Bora dressed as a woman, and spent his final years next to Pakistan's equivalent of West Point — where, Kiriakou says, you would have to be a "mental defective" not to know he was there. Kiriakou believes the United States never intended to capture him alive.

the-two-officers-who-changed.title: The CIA under a left-wing president
the-two-officers-who-changed.summary: John Kiriakou's two-part answer to a hypothetical about a socialist administration — that most of the CIA would carry on as though nothing had happened, because officers serve at the pleasure of the president, while elements of the directorate of operations would actively seek to remove such a president. His supporting example is John F. Kennedy.

the-two-officers-who-changed.title: The NYPD intelligence post
the-two-officers-who-changed.summary: The New York Police Department position — deputy commissioner for intelligence — that John Kiriakou says traditionally goes to someone coming out of the CIA, and which he uses to explain why the agency is indifferent to who wins a New York mayoral election so long as the post and its liaison with the joint terrorism task force survive.

the-two-tunisians.title: The martyrdom bonus
the-two-tunisians.summary: The recruitment offer John Kiriakou says captured al-Qaeda foot soldiers described to him in Pakistan: a monthly wage to go and fight the Americans in Afghanistan, and five hundred dollars paid to the fighter''s parents if he was killed. He uses it to argue that the men he captured had no religious or political motive at all — most had never read the Quran — and that the only way out of the cycle is education and economic development.

the-two-tunisians.title: Pakistan Station (2002)
the-two-tunisians.summary: John Kiriakou's January 2002 arrival in Islamabad to become CIA chief of counterterrorism operations — a journey via London and Kuwait with lost luggage, a warning that steered him away from the soon-to-be-bombed Marriott, a skeleton counterterrorism branch of seven CIA retirees, and the raids that followed.

the-two-tunisians.title: Advanced Counterterrorism Operations
the-two-tunisians.summary: The six-week specialist course John Kiriakou flew back from Athens to attend roughly eighteen months before 9/11 as one of fourteen officers selected worldwide — high-threat operations, technical collection, and a driving syllabus built around crashing through roadblocks that left the class with whiplash. By accident of timing it meant a trained cadre was ready to deploy the moment the attacks came.

the-two-tunisians.title: "You were the first person that ever asked me about my children"
the-two-tunisians.summary: The answer John Kiriakou says he received when he asked a mid-level al-Qaeda member he had recruited in Pakistan why he had allowed the recruitment to happen: that in five years of detention Kiriakou had been the first person to ask about his children.

the-two-tunisians.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
the-two-tunisians.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

the-two-tunisians.title: The Faisalabad cash run
the-two-tunisians.summary: The drive John Kiriakou made to Faisalabad, Pakistan roughly two weeks before the capture of Abu Zubaydah, with two million dollars in cash in two duffel bags in the van, and the exchange with his colleague about why anyone would cheat the CIA out of twenty dollars.

the-unarmed-ship.title: The Iranians only have to survive
