the-unarmed-ship.summary: John Kiriakou's formulation of the asymmetry at the heart of the 2026 Iran war — that winning would require the United States to overthrow the Iranian government and install a pro-American, pro-Israeli replacement in Tehran, while Iran wins simply by continuing to exist. His conclusion is that Washington must either commit to killing half the population of Iran over twenty years or walk away.

the-unarmed-ship.title: 2026 Iran war
the-unarmed-ship.summary: The open-ended American and Israeli war against Iran that John Kiriakou tracked week by week on his own show — a conflict he says was sold as three weeks, ran into its fifth month, achieved every decapitation objective it set, and continued anyway. His grade for it is a D, and his forecast is a Truth Social post declaring victory while nothing changes.

the-unarmed-ship.title: Iran 12-Day War
the-unarmed-ship.summary: 2025 Israeli air campaign against Iran during which Israel killed at least fourteen Iranian nuclear scientists by destroying the apartment buildings they lived in; preceded for each scientist by Farsi-language telephone calls from Iranian-Jewish Mossad and Shin Bet officers offering defection in lieu of certain death; characterized by John Kiriakou as a categorical departure from CIA targeting doctrine in its acceptable-civilian-casualty calculus.

the-unarmed-ship.title: Killing Khamenei
the-unarmed-ship.summary: John Kiriakou's assessment that the killing of Ayatollah Khamenei during the 2026 war would change nothing, because the West had seriously overestimated his authority — an argument he extends to the American habit of expecting a war to end when a leader is removed.

the-unarmed-ship.title: Mojtaba Khamenei
the-unarmed-ship.summary: The successor named as Iran's leader after the assassination of Ali Khamenei, and John Kiriakou's reading of the choice — that the only real objection is the shared surname, which exposes Iran to charges of hereditary succession, but that the appointment was an act of defiance aimed squarely at Donald Trump's declaration that he would choose Iran's next leader.

the-unarmed-ship.title: Assange and the European Court of Human Rights
the-unarmed-ship.summary: The last legal avenue John Kiriakou identified for Julian Assange in 2022 — three precedents in which the Strasbourg court refused to let Britain extradite mentally ill defendants to American solitary confinement — and the procedural trap that made it useless: Britain said the appeal need not halt the extradition.

the-underlying-sadness.title: "Embrace it and keep telling it"
the-underlying-sadness.summary: The advice John Kiriakou says he was given days after his arrest — that he could not hide from the prosecution but had to embrace it, and had to keep telling his side of the story until it became the side of record, because the government would eventually move on to its next target.

the-underlying-sadness.title: Consulting for royal families
the-underlying-sadness.summary: The work John Kiriakou says he was hired to do by members of two different royal families following the 2026 virality of his interviews — advising on ethics in their own intelligence operations — which he offers as evidence of how far the reversal in his standing had gone.

the-underlying-sadness.title: Signing with CAA
the-underlying-sadness.summary: The representation John Kiriakou says followed the 2026 virality of his podcast clips: a contract with the Creative Artists Agency covering books, film, consulting and licensing, and a run of advertising approaches including one from the maker of the spectacle frames he already wore.

the-underlying-sadness.title: Suggested responses
the-underlying-sadness.summary: The second email John Kiriakou says arrived before his first appearance on Fox News — a list of suggested responses to accompany the questions the producers had already sent him — which he ignored, and which he says was never sent again.

the-underlying-sadness.title: The convicted felon introduction
the-underlying-sadness.summary: The MSNBC appearance John Kiriakou says was his last: booked opposite Daniel Ellsberg, having agreed his on-air identification in advance with the producers, he was introduced instead as "convicted felon John Kiriakou", swore on tape, and began removing his microphone.

the-underlying-sadness.title: The NPR walkout
the-underlying-sadness.summary: The Saturday morning interview John Kiriakou says he ended after five minutes of a scheduled half hour, having been attacked on air over an op-ed about Gina Haspel, and which he closed by asking the host where NPR had been while he was blowing the whistle on the torture programme.

the-unexplained-false-statement-charge.title: Espionage Act
the-unexplained-false-statement-charge.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

the-unexplained-false-statement-charge.title: Geneva Conventions
the-unexplained-false-statement-charge.summary: The laws of war at the center of John Kiriakou''s most-told confrontation story: finding hooded prisoners in Pakistan, he demanded of the officer in charge — "Are you seriously telling me that you have never read the Geneva Convention? It is a war crime to put hoods on them. Take the hoods off." The two reported each other to headquarters; Kiriakou got in trouble — "they didn''t give two shits about the Geneva Convention." He indicts the Bush administration''s twin dodges: that al-Qaeda fighters, as non-state actors, fell outside the Conventions'' protections, and that the techniques weren''t torture at all.

the-unexplained-false-statement-charge.title: Intelligence Identities Protection Act
the-unexplained-false-statement-charge.summary: U.S. law enacted in 1982 that makes it a crime to knowingly disclose the identity of a covert intelligence officer; per John Kiriakou, his 2012 prosecution under the act arose from confirming a single surname of a former CIA colleague to a journalist — a confirmation that was never published. The name passed through a chain from journalist to Human Rights Watch to Guantanamo defense attorneys before reaching a judge and ultimately the FBI, which traced it back to Kiriakou.

the-unexplained-false-statement-charge.title: The 1994 women''s class action
the-unexplained-false-statement-charge.summary: A class action brought by female CIA employees who had been passed over for promotion produced, in John Kiriakou''s account, a judicial finding that the Agency had documented its own crime and a remedy of an across-the-board two-level promotion for every woman at the CIA.

the-unexplained-false-statement-charge.title: The Clinton-era asset cull
the-unexplained-false-statement-charge.summary: In the 1990s the CIA reviewed the file of every recruited asset in the world and dismissed any with a history of human rights abuses — roughly a third of its agents, in John Kiriakou''s account, in a reform he says was reversed as though by a switch after 11 September.

the-unexplained-false-statement-charge.title: The new Iraqi flag
the-unexplained-false-statement-charge.summary: Before the invasion of Iraq, John Kiriakou walked into the CIA''s Iraq Operations Group and found its director at his desk with Crayola markers, colouring in a design for a new Iraqi flag.

the-university-of-salamanca-professorshi.title: GeoRisk Solutions
the-university-of-salamanca-professorshi.summary: The political risk consultancy John Kiriakou founded with the dean of the University of Salamanca's intelligence studies programme, staffed with academics and a former assistant secretary of state, with offices in Salamanca and Washington and a stated business of selling cost-effective country and regional risk analysis to banks, funds and companies.

the-university-of-salamanca-professorshi.title: Cofer Black
the-university-of-salamanca-professorshi.summary: Former head of the CIA Counterterrorism Center during and immediately after the September 11 attacks; principal architect of the agency's paramilitary turn on September 12, 2001; later Vice President of Blackwater under Erik Prince.

the-university-of-salamanca-professorshi.title: Brian Ross
the-university-of-salamanca-professorshi.summary: American investigative journalist and seven-time Emmy Award winner who was a prominent reporter at ABC News when, in December 2007, he conducted the on-camera interview with John Kiriakou that produced the first public confirmation by a U.S. official that the CIA waterboarded prisoners. Per Kiriakou, Ross called him out of the blue with the assertion that a source said Kiriakou had personally tortured Abu Zubaydah; Kiriakou's decision to give the interview anyway — driven by the conclusion that 'Brian Ross's source is at the White House and they're going to pin this on me' — became the pivot point of his entire post-CIA life.

the-university-of-salamanca-professorshi.title: The Greek turn toward Israel
the-university-of-salamanca-professorshi.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of why Athens abandoned its traditional pro-Arab alignment and embraced Israel — a 180-degree flip he attributes to the collapse of Turkey''s relationship with Israel and, above all, to money: Israeli property buying that he says has tripled Greek house prices, and Cypriot gas fields Greece hopes to develop with Israeli partners.

the-university-of-salamanca-professorshi.title: Active measures
the-university-of-salamanca-professorshi.summary: The in-house name John Kiriakou gives to the CIA branch responsible for propaganda and for countering hostile propaganda — a division he describes as running twenty-four hours a day, paired with an opposing anti-active-measures branch, and as the ancestor of the political action group that remains the agency's clandestine propaganda arm.

the-university-of-salamanca-professorshi.title: CIA attention to West Africa
the-university-of-salamanca-professorshi.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer on whether the CIA is likely to be operating in Burkina Faso: for all the years he was at the agency it cared very little about Africa and especially West Africa, but the presence of al-Qaeda and Islamic State affiliates plus the drug trade makes CIA and special forces involvement probable — and, he adds, the American public will not hear about it.

the-unredacted-copy-paste.title: The blacked-out grand jury minutes
the-unredacted-copy-paste.summary: John Kiriakou on the 119 pages of grand jury minutes released in the Epstein document tranches with every single word blacked out, despite two federal judges having ordered their release.

the-unredacted-copy-paste.title: The snapshots in the release
the-unredacted-copy-paste.summary: John Kiriakou's summary of what the first Epstein tranches actually contained — investigative documents, grand jury testimony and snapshots taken by Epstein and his friends — and the two photographs that dominated the early coverage.

the-unredacted-copy-paste.title: The letter to Larry Nassar
the-unredacted-copy-paste.summary: The letter from Jeffrey Epstein to the convicted USA Gymnastics doctor Larry Nassar that John Kiriakou singled out from the released documents, in which Epstein wrote that he would have gone home by the time it arrived and blamed everything on Donald Trump.

the-unredacted-copy-paste.title: Clickers and touchers
the-unredacted-copy-paste.summary: The distinction John Kiriakou says prisoners at FCI Loretto drew between convicted sex offenders who had only viewed images of children and those who had travelled across state lines to molest them, and his account of why they are all held at low security.

the-unredacted-copy-paste.title: Prince Andrew
the-unredacted-copy-paste.summary: British royal, now Andrew Mountbatten Windsor, named repeatedly by John Kiriakou as one of the un-recruitable principals whose access made Jeffrey Epstein valuable to a foreign intelligence service. Kiriakou has asked why Andrew was never charged over conduct with minors, reads his alleged provision of classified Ministry of Defence documents to Epstein as evidence of espionage rather than vanity — and expects him to face no criminal consequence at all, because the statute of limitations has run.

the-unredacted-copy-paste.title: The dorm as a reward
the-unredacted-copy-paste.summary: John Kiriakou's explanation that moving a federal prisoner from a cell to a dormitory is a privilege earned over time, and why Ghislaine Maxwell's rapid promotion to dormitory living made no sense to him.

the-unsearched-car-at-mar-a-lago.title: Butler rally shooting
the-unsearched-car-at-mar-a-lago.summary: The July 2024 attempt on Donald Trump's life at a rally in Butler, Pennsylvania, on which John Kiriakou takes no position as to who was responsible but argues the published facts cannot be reconciled with a competent Secret Service — and that the questions it leaves open are owed an answer for the historical record whether or not anyone alive gets one.

the-unsearched-car-at-mar-a-lago.title: Secret Service
the-unsearched-car-at-mar-a-lago.summary: The U.S. agency protecting the president. John Kiriakou, who worked alongside it for 35 years, describes a culture of complacency and poor follow-up — great with guns, weak on training and follow-through — and calls the 2024 Butler rally shooting a colossal historic screw-up in which coverage of the surrounding buildings was outsourced to a county sheriff's department. He has also encountered the Service as an adversary, outside the Venezuelan embassy in Washington in 2019.

the-unsearched-car-at-mar-a-lago.title: Taking the ball and going home
the-unsearched-car-at-mar-a-lago.summary: John Kiriakou''s rule of thumb, offered after the July 2024 Butler shooting, that a failed state-run assassination is not retried: an operation with that many moving parts would not be attempted in front of thousands of people, would not be entrusted to a twenty-year-old, and once blown would be abandoned rather than repeated.

the-unsearched-car-at-mar-a-lago.title: The denials after Dallas
the-unsearched-car-at-mar-a-lago.summary: John Kiriakou''s account, drawn from CIA historical files he read as a junior analyst, of how fast foreign governments moved to clear themselves after the assassination of John F. Kennedy: the Soviets came to the Americans within minutes, the Chinese did the same, and the Cubans asked the Mexicans to pass on that it was not them.

the-unsearched-car-at-mar-a-lago.title: Watergate
the-unsearched-car-at-mar-a-lago.summary: The scandal that ended Nixon''s presidency and the standing benchmark in John Kiriakou''s vocabulary — the CIA spying on the Senate committee investigating its torture program was, to him, "a Watergate-level kind of scandal," except that this time nothing came of it. He draws one lesson from it above all others: Nixon did not fall for the burglary but for the cover-up. Watergate touches his own story directly — his lead defense attorney had been John Mitchell''s lawyer — and its cast overlapped with the agency he joined, from E. Howard Hunt to the tradecraft by which Deep Throat summoned Bob Woodward.

the-unsearched-car-at-mar-a-lago.title: Donald Trump
the-unsearched-car-at-mar-a-lago.summary: 45th and 47th U.S. president. Per John Kiriakou, a man genuinely convinced he was doing right by bombing Iran, "duped" by the same Netanyahu nuclear bluff Obama once rejected — and, at the same time, the most blindly pro-Israel president in history, an admirer of autocrats who has never once criticized Vladimir Putin, and prone to gestures — from the Gulf of America to a since-abandoned "Department of War" rename — that test the edges of his actual authority.

the-unswept-roof.title: The 9/11 truth honorarium
the-unswept-roof.summary: How John Kiriakou came to headline a 9/11 truth event he had not realised was one: a $500 speaking fee from a PR man he had known through better days, a poster that revealed the sponsor, a sister telling him to withdraw, and his decision to honour the commitment anyway — while telling the audience to their faces that he would never believe Building 7 was a controlled demolition or that explosive thermite paint exists.

the-unswept-roof.title: The alternative obituaries
the-unswept-roof.summary: The obituaries John Kiriakou writes for CovertAction Magazine whenever someone associated with the CIA's torture program dies — deliberately mean-spirited pieces arguing the world is better off without them — and the phone call he took from one subject's daughter, who called him a monster, and what he said back to her.

the-unswept-roof.title: Area 58
the-unswept-roof.summary: The claim John Kiriakou says was put to him by a man who presents as entirely serious and is writing a book about it: that beyond Area 51 there is an Area 58 — seven more, and that much more secret — containing an underground bunker where alien craft land, known to those involved as the embassy because it is where the United States liaises with the aliens.

the-unswept-roof.title: Leaks come from the Pentagon
the-unswept-roof.summary: John Kiriakou''s rule of attribution for national security leaks, drawn from his own CIA experience: ninety-nine times out of a hundred the leak came from the Pentagon — which he says leaks constantly, is so gigantic that the source cannot be traced, and does not polygraph anybody. He adds the motive: somebody who opposed the operation and was overruled.

the-unswept-roof.title: Luis Elizondo
the-unswept-roof.summary: Why John Kiriakou never booked the best-known public advocate for unidentified aerial phenomena on his RT programme: viewers kept insisting Elizondo was an expert, so Kiriakou researched him and found chiefly Elizondo saying he was an expert. He says he does not know what the man is an expert on, and that it was not a fit for the show.

the-unswept-roof.title: The Australian pilot
the-unswept-roof.summary: The disappearance John Kiriakou recounts as an argument for declassification rather than as proof of anything: a pilot in his early twenties flying on 10 September 1978 who radioed that a silver cylinder was above his aircraft matching his speed exactly, said it was not an aircraft, was cut off by a loud sound of electronic interference, and was never seen again — along with the plane.

the-uss-gerald-ford-plumbing.title: Hot bunking
the-uss-gerald-ford-plumbing.summary: John Kiriakou''s description of living conditions aboard the overcrowded American warships and submarines he has visited: three men to a bed on eight-hour rotations, a shared pillow, decks raised several inches by the canned food stacked underfoot, and nuclear submarines that surface not because they must but to keep the crew sane.

the-uss-gerald-ford-plumbing.title: The White House tip
the-uss-gerald-ford-plumbing.summary: A week and a half before the 2026 attack on Iran, John Kiriakou said publicly that a friend at the White House had told him the decision to attack had been made and that it would come the following Monday or Tuesday. A podcaster mocked him for it — how could a man twenty years out of the CIA know that? On the morning the strikes began, Kiriakou answered: people with access do call, because they are opposed to the war.

the-uss-gerald-ford-plumbing.title: Frank Snepp
the-uss-gerald-ford-plumbing.summary: The CIA analyst who wrote Decent Interval, and whom John Kiriakou calls a giant — one of the great analysts of his generation, practically the first to say publicly that the United States was losing in Vietnam and committing atrocities there, who paid for it with his career and spent most of the rest of his life fighting the agency's publications review board.

the-uss-gerald-ford-plumbing.title: Israel, Turkey, and NATO Article 5
the-uss-gerald-ford-plumbing.summary: John Kiriakou's scenario in which an Israeli attack on Turkey would oblige every NATO member, the United States included, to come to Turkey's defence — and in which the alliance would sooner dissolve than honour that obligation against Israel.

the-uss-gerald-ford-plumbing.title: John Kiriakou
the-uss-gerald-ford-plumbing.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

the-uss-gerald-ford-plumbing.title: John McCain
the-uss-gerald-ford-plumbing.summary: Late U.S. Senator from Arizona who gave the most consequential Senate-floor defense of John Kiriakou — declaring that 'if it weren't for John Kiriakou, the American people would never have had any idea what the CIA was doing in their name' — and sponsored the McCain–Feinstein amendment banning torture.

the-uyghur-resettlement-trade.title: Brad Birkenfeld
the-uyghur-resettlement-trade.summary: The UBS banking whistleblower, who was prosecuted and imprisoned before winning a $104 million settlement from the Treasury Department and spending it on the legal defence of other whistleblowers. John Kiriakou uses him as the measure of the gap between financial and national-security whistleblowing, and names him among the visitors whose devices he believes were copied at the Ecuadorian embassy in London.

the-uyghur-resettlement-trade.title: Julian Assange
the-uyghur-resettlement-trade.summary: Kiriakou — a 15-year friend and former WikiLeaks board member — on why Assange is a publisher owed a journalist's immunity, and a political prisoner.

the-uyghur-resettlement-trade.title: John Brennan
the-uyghur-resettlement-trade.summary: Former Director of the CIA; characterized in KiriPedia's source corpus as the principal architect of the agency's enhanced interrogation program and as having plotted against an elected President

the-uyghur-resettlement-trade.title: The Senate WikiLeaks ban
the-uyghur-resettlement-trade.summary: The instruction John Kiriakou watched the Senate security officer deliver in person to all one hundred senators and every committee after the WikiLeaks cables were published — that opening the material on a Senate computer would be the crime of unauthorized access to classified information, and that anyone who did so would be prosecuted.

the-uyghur-resettlement-trade.title: Anwar al-Awlaki
the-uyghur-resettlement-trade.summary: American-born al-Qaeda propagandist; in 1993 the imam of the Falls Church, Virginia mosque visited by John Kiriakou's CIA Arabic-language class on a field trip; in 2001 the cleric at whose mosque the 9/11 hijackers prayed the night before the attacks; killed by U.S. drone strike in Yemen in approximately 2011.

the-uyghur-resettlement-trade.title: Daniel Hale
the-uyghur-resettlement-trade.summary: Per John Kiriakou, drone whistleblower Daniel Hale — an NSA contractor and drone targeting analyst who exposed an 80% civilian death rate in the U.S. drone program, was ordered to fire on two young girls his superior called "goats," and was sentenced to 45 months (of which Kiriakou says he actually served about 18) despite prosecutors seeking nine to eleven years.

the-vietnam-speech.title: Frank Snepp
the-vietnam-speech.summary: The CIA analyst who wrote Decent Interval, and whom John Kiriakou calls a giant — one of the great analysts of his generation, practically the first to say publicly that the United States was losing in Vietnam and committing atrocities there, who paid for it with his career and spent most of the rest of his life fighting the agency's publications review board.

the-vietnam-speech.title: Hot bunking
the-vietnam-speech.summary: John Kiriakou''s description of living conditions aboard the overcrowded American warships and submarines he has visited: three men to a bed on eight-hour rotations, a shared pillow, decks raised several inches by the canned food stacked underfoot, and nuclear submarines that surface not because they must but to keep the crew sane.

the-vietnam-speech.title: Israel, Turkey, and NATO Article 5
the-vietnam-speech.summary: John Kiriakou's scenario in which an Israeli attack on Turkey would oblige every NATO member, the United States included, to come to Turkey's defence — and in which the alliance would sooner dissolve than honour that obligation against Israel.

the-vietnam-speech.title: John Kiriakou
the-vietnam-speech.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

the-vietnam-speech.title: John McCain
the-vietnam-speech.summary: Late U.S. Senator from Arizona who gave the most consequential Senate-floor defense of John Kiriakou — declaring that 'if it weren't for John Kiriakou, the American people would never have had any idea what the CIA was doing in their name' — and sponsored the McCain–Feinstein amendment banning torture.

the-vietnam-speech.title: Kiriakou's Greek citizenship
the-vietnam-speech.summary: The Greek nationality John Kiriakou acquired in 2010, after his CIA career and before his prosecution — offered, he says, by the Greek ambassador who asked what could be done to help when his troubles began, and granted when he answered "you could give me Greek citizenship." Held by his children too, it made him a Greek national at the moment he became, in Greece, a national hero; it brought him the commission to write the country's whistleblower protection law, and the Athens job that turned out to be a money laundering operation.

the-visa-reciprocity-rule.title: The Outer Banks seasonal workers
the-visa-reciprocity-rule.summary: John Kiriakou''s observation, from years of family summers on the Outer Banks of North Carolina, that he never encountered an American lifeguard and almost no American shop clerks or waiters — the staff being Bulgarian, Romanian, Moldovan and otherwise Eastern European, working on the cheap, housed eight to twelve to a house and sent home at the end of the season.

the-visa-reciprocity-rule.title: Jesse Jackson
the-visa-reciprocity-rule.summary: American civil rights leader and two-time presidential candidate whose hospitalisation in November 2025 John Kiriakou discussed at length — explaining progressive supranuclear palsy, the condition Jackson was diagnosed with two years after Parkinson''s, from his own family''s experience of the same disease, and giving a poor prognosis.

the-visa-reciprocity-rule.title: Kiriakou's acting career
the-visa-reciprocity-rule.summary: The film role John Kiriakou took in 2025 after Tyrel Ventura wrote a part for him — a former CIA officer running a billionaire's security detail — which he shot in Mexico for a month and which made him, at sixty-odd, a member of the Screen Actors Guild.

the-visa-reciprocity-rule.title: The conscientious objectors book
the-visa-reciprocity-rule.summary: A long out-of-print volume of interviews with American conscientious objectors, published around 1972 and given to John Kiriakou from the personal collection of an objector he was friendly with in prison — a book whose harrowing accounts of objectors sent to real federal prisons rather than to camps convinced him that refusing to serve was often more physically dangerous than serving.

the-visa-reciprocity-rule.title: The Egyptian intelligence chief''s son
the-visa-reciprocity-rule.summary: A coincidence John Kiriakou reported from Oxford, Ohio in November 2025: his own son''s marketing professor turned out to be the son of Muhammad Farag, head of the Egyptian intelligence service some thirty-five years earlier, whom Kiriakou had met in Cairo when the professor was a boy of seven or eight — and the two families went out to dinner together.

the-visa-reciprocity-rule.title: The Giuliani–Epstein emails
the-visa-reciprocity-rule.summary: A cache of correspondence that a former chief of business development for Giuliani Partners told John Kiriakou she holds — thousands of pages of emails between Rudy Giuliani and Jeffrey Epstein, which she says she has offered to news organisations and to congressional committees and which nobody wanted, together with her claim that a second British prince and other former heads of state are implicated.

the-voice-vote-on-the-epstein-files.title: Craig Murray
the-voice-vote-on-the-epstein-files.summary: Former British Ambassador to Uzbekistan whom John Kiriakou cites as a whistleblower of extreme torture: during a meeting at the Uzbek intelligence service, Murray heard screaming, walked in, and saw a man being boiled in oil — reporting it cost him his career.

the-voice-vote-on-the-epstein-files.title: Dumping cash in a Moscow bathroom
the-voice-vote-on-the-epstein-files.summary: John Kiriakou's examples of what covert action has actually meant in practice — American commandos blowing up the Trans-Siberian oil pipeline, Afghan guerrillas hired to cross the Amu Darya and attack a refinery inside the southern USSR, and cash dumped in a Moscow bathroom to undermine the rouble.

the-voice-vote-on-the-epstein-files.title: How Chinese intelligence recruits
the-voice-vote-on-the-epstein-files.summary: John Kiriakou''s assessment of the Ministry of State Security''s tradecraft: very effective with anyone who simply wants money, because the money is limitless, and very bad at cultivating a source who does not yet know who is cultivating him — with the target usually being access to sophisticated technology.

the-voice-vote-on-the-epstein-files.title: MK-ULTRA in Canada
the-voice-vote-on-the-epstein-files.summary: John Kiriakou''s confirmation that many MK-ULTRA experiments took place on Canadian soil, and his explanation of why: the CIA asked the Canadian intelligence service for help with its anti-Soviet, anti-Chinese remote-viewing and LSD work, and the Canadians gladly gave it.

the-voice-vote-on-the-epstein-files.title: Pakistani corruption and democracy
the-voice-vote-on-the-epstein-files.summary: John Kiriakou's assessment that corruption in Pakistan is so deep and so broad that a genuinely functioning democracy is almost impossible there — set against a long history of military coups, a habit of imprisoning former prime ministers, and his insistence that Imran Khan should not be in a cell.

the-voice-vote-on-the-epstein-files.title: Tarpon Springs
the-voice-vote-on-the-epstein-files.summary: The Greek sponge-diving town on the Florida gulf coast that John Kiriakou calls one of his favourite places — settled for a century by divers from Kalymnos, the island immediately north of the one his own family comes from, and, in his verdict, the site of absolutely incredible Greek food.

the-wagner-coverage-asymmetry.title: Rival factions in Libya
the-wagner-coverage-asymmetry.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the CIA and the State Department backing opposing factions inside Libya — proxies funded by two arms of the same government that end up fighting each other, an arrangement he calls insane and treats as characteristic of American intervention in places nobody is reporting on.

the-wagner-coverage-asymmetry.title: The Richard Haass back channel
the-wagner-coverage-asymmetry.summary: The April 2023 Track 2 meeting between Richard Haass, two former National Security Council deputies and Russian foreign minister Sergey Lavrov, which John Kiriakou explained as unofficial diplomacy requiring White House approval to be legal — and which he judged a good thing, because it built a mechanism for talks before the politics allowed them.

the-wagner-coverage-asymmetry.title: The Afghan woman's lesson
the-wagner-coverage-asymmetry.summary: The remark a visiting Afghan intellectual made to the Senate Foreign Relations Committee staff that John Kiriakou says stuck with him for over a decade — that the Taliban did not come down from outer space, that they are Afghanistan's own sons and brothers and husbands, and that if the country had not been secured after ten years of nation-building it was because nobody wanted the Americans there.

the-wagner-coverage-asymmetry.title: The Taiwan blank check
the-wagner-coverage-asymmetry.summary: John Kiriakou''s reading of the Republican revolt against funding Ukraine: that most of the members refusing to write another blank check for Kyiv wanted to write it for Taipei instead, and would rather have a direct confrontation with China than a decade bogged down in Eastern Europe.

the-wagner-coverage-asymmetry.title: The Zaporizhzhia accusations
the-wagner-coverage-asymmetry.summary: John Kiriakou''s inverted reading of the 2023 standoff over Ukraine''s Zaporizhzhia nuclear plant: that Russia and Ukraine publicly accusing each other of planning a false-flag attack on the plant is precisely what prevented one, because ratting each other out forced the whole world to watch.

the-wagner-coverage-asymmetry.title: Elliott Abrams
the-wagner-coverage-asymmetry.summary: The Reagan-era assistant secretary of state whose 2023 appointment to a Biden administration advisory board John Kiriakou treated as proof that neoliberal and neoconservative foreign policy are the same policy with interchangeable players — a man who pleaded guilty over Iran-Contra, was pardoned, helped sell the Iraqi weapons of mass destruction case, and then served Donald Trump on Iran and Venezuela.

the-walk-in-probe.title: Intelligence peddlers
the-walk-in-probe.summary: John Kiriakou''s breakdown of who actually walks into an American embassy offering information: the overwhelming majority are fabricators or probes, a few per cent are peddlers selling the same nugget to five embassies in a month, and about one per cent are the real thing.

the-walk-in-probe.title: The Athens carjacking
the-walk-in-probe.summary: The motorcyclist who followed John Kiriakou''s car through Athens two months into his posting — leading to a gun drawn on a ten-lane intersection, a shot fired, a disabled motorcycle, and a question asked back in Washington: *is John a hothead?*

the-walk-in-probe.title: Walk-in
the-walk-in-probe.summary: In John Kiriakou's telling, someone who walks into an embassy offering information; 95% are lunatics or liars, some are 'intelligence peddlers' or hostile 'probes,' and about 1% are 'the real McCoy' — a framework he used to see through a supposed 'walk-in' tip during the Abu Zubaydah hunt. A genuine walk-in — a witness to a terrorist assassination — was later hypnotized by CIA psychologists in a London hotel room and read back a stolen van's license plate, verifying his account.

the-walk-in-probe.title: Kiriakou on wine
the-walk-in-probe.summary: John Kiriakou's long-standing interest in wine — a subscription to Wine Spectator running a quarter of a century, a climate-controlled cellar built into his house, an eye that has twice caught a host passing off a cheap bottle as something better, and a professional life in which wine served in turn as cover story, surveillance-detection errand, recruitment currency and diplomatic catastrophe.

the-walk-in-probe.title: How Kiriakou went armed in Athens
the-walk-in-probe.summary: The load John Kiriakou carried every day during his Athens tour — a 9mm in a tear-away waist pack with three magazines, a snub-nosed .38 on his ankle, about 47 rounds in total, and a buck knife his boss handed him on his first day *"just in case things go to shit"*.

the-walk-in-probe.title: American shoes
the-walk-in-probe.summary: The detail by which the chief of the Greek intelligence service identified John Kiriakou as an American within minutes of meeting him — not his Greek, which was fluent, but his footwear — and which sent Kiriakou straight to a shoe shop before working the anarchist quarters of Athens.

the-walmart-phone-call.title: Communications management unit
the-walmart-phone-call.summary: The two restricted-contact units inside the American federal prison system, at Terre Haute and Marion; built for "the worst of the worst" but, in John Kiriakou's account, used to silence prisoners whose messages are inconvenient — and a practice he groups with solitary confinement as torture. He served part of his own sentence in a modified one.

the-walmart-phone-call.title: The Kurd from Terre Haute
the-walmart-phone-call.summary: An Iraqi Kurd who reached the modified communications management unit at FCI Loretto after four years inside the CMU at Terre Haute, and who told John Kiriakou that the only way out was to keep your mouth shut for years.

the-walmart-phone-call.title: The mailroom standoff
the-walmart-phone-call.summary: Told at FCI Loretto that he had no right to write to journalists, John Kiriakou printed the Bureau of Prisons regulations in the law library and laid them out in the mailroom until the staff gave up and sent the letter.

the-walmart-phone-call.title: Jared Kushner
the-walmart-phone-call.summary: Donald Trump's son-in-law and senior adviser during the first Trump administration, and the first person inside the White House to open a channel on John Kiriakou's pardon. After Trump saw Kiriakou on Tucker Carlson's show, Kushner's attorney called Kiriakou's attorney Bruce Fein; the meeting that followed produced a request for a one-page paper — three-quarters of it Kiriakou's story, the last quarter an argument for how pardoning him would help Trump get re-elected — after which Kiriakou never heard back.

the-walmart-phone-call.title: The sentencing reform bills that died
the-walmart-phone-call.summary: The bipartisan legislation John Kiriakou watched from prison and campaigned for afterwards — the Recidivism Reduction and Public Safety Act and the Smarter Sentencing Act, alongside a Sentencing Commission move to lower drug guidelines — which would have freed thousands and abolished most mandatory minimums, and which died in the Senate without a vote. Kiriakou blames two majority leaders and two attorneys general, and sets out both the arithmetic behind the bills and the limiting principle he attaches to them.

the-walmart-phone-call.title: Area 58
the-walmart-phone-call.summary: The claim John Kiriakou says was put to him by a man who presents as entirely serious and is writing a book about it: that beyond Area 51 there is an Area 58 — seven more, and that much more secret — containing an underground bunker where alien craft land, known to those involved as the embassy because it is where the United States liaises with the aliens.

the-war-department-renaming.title: Aafia Siddiqui
the-war-department-renaming.summary: Pakistani-American neuroscientist arrested in Afghanistan and convicted in the United States of attempting to shoot FBI agents; per John Kiriakou, who covered the arrest as a terrorism consultant for ABC News and has followed the case since, she never had a gun and never fired, the bullet holes offered as proof predated her capture, and the CIA took her three children — two later recovered, the youngest never found.

the-war-department-renaming.title: The 1991 Saudi plan for Gaza
the-war-department-renaming.summary: A proposal John Kiriakou says he watched Ambassador Chas Freeman float to the Saudis during his first overseas tour in 1991 — that Saudi Arabia fund a port, an airport, a desalination plant and an electrical grid in Gaza. The Saudis agreed; Israel refused outright. Kiriakou raises it because the identical arrangement resurfaced in the Israeli press more than three decades later.

the-war-department-renaming.title: Clive Stafford Smith
the-war-department-renaming.summary: The British human rights lawyer who represents Aafia Siddiqui, described by John Kiriakou as a man who has never charged a client a dollar in his life, lives on donations, holds an OBE for his human rights work, and represented sixty-six Guantanamo detainees — securing the release of every one of them.

the-war-department-renaming.title: Hamid Karzai
the-war-department-renaming.summary: The president installed in Afghanistan after the American invasion, whom John Kiriakou uses as the standing illustration of what occupation actually buys: after twenty years and more than a trillion dollars, Karzai was ''little more than the mayor of Kabul'' — and did not control all of Kabul either. The line began as a joke among Senate Foreign Relations Committee staff, and Kiriakou used it to Senator John Kerry''s face ten years into the war.

the-war-department-renaming.title: Kiriakou on travel
the-war-department-renaming.summary: John Kiriakou''s own ranking of the countries he has visited: Greece his favourite and, he insists, the best food anywhere; Oman the most beautiful landscape; Syria the most extraordinary civilisation; and Chile the cheapest, illustrated by a bottle of a vineyard''s locked-away reserve that cost $8.50 on his honeymoon.

the-war-department-renaming.title: Nigel Farage
the-war-department-renaming.summary: John Kiriakou's assessment that Nigel Farage was a fringe joke five years ago and is no less fascistic now, only accepted — and his prediction that if Farage becomes leader of the Conservative Party it will be the end of that party as a viable political force.

the-war-powers-resolution-vote.title: The Truth Social announcement
the-war-powers-resolution-vote.summary: John Kiriakou''s objection to how the 2026 war was announced: at two o''clock in the morning on Truth Social, with no address from the East Room, and with a president shuttling between Washington and Mar-a-Lago rather than explaining to the country why Americans were being sent to fight.

the-war-powers-resolution-vote.title: The White House tip
the-war-powers-resolution-vote.summary: A week and a half before the 2026 attack on Iran, John Kiriakou said publicly that a friend at the White House had told him the decision to attack had been made and that it would come the following Monday or Tuesday. A podcaster mocked him for it — how could a man twenty years out of the CIA know that? On the morning the strikes began, Kiriakou answered: people with access do call, because they are opposed to the war.

the-war-powers-resolution-vote.title: American missile stockpiles
the-war-powers-resolution-vote.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that the United States has run its interceptor stocks down to the point of strategic vulnerability — that the conventional wisdom in Washington was that a round of the Iran war ended because the Patriots ran out, and that a country which cannot fight a two-front war certainly cannot do it below maximum production.

the-war-powers-resolution-vote.title: The Al Mayadeen debate
the-war-powers-resolution-vote.summary: Two days before the 2026 attack on Iran, John Kiriakou went on the Lebanese network Al Mayadeen expecting the usual point-counterpoint with an academic and found himself opposite Iran's lead nuclear negotiator. His argument to the negotiator — that what the two sides were then negotiating was the JCPOA under another name — was rejected outright before being accepted.

the-war-powers-resolution-vote.title: The indicator he'd be watching
the-war-powers-resolution-vote.summary: Asked what single sign would most alarm him if he were still inside the CIA on the first day of the 2026 Iran war, John Kiriakou named the movement of ground forces: about fifty thousand American troops are in the region, which cannot invade a country of ninety-two million, and it is the arrival of hundreds of thousands more — plus the last uncommitted carrier battle group — that would frighten him.

the-war-powers-resolution-vote.title: "Our job is to break the law"
the-war-powers-resolution-vote.summary: The line John Kiriakou says CIA instructors repeated in training, and the qualification he attached to it at the time: the job is to break the law over there, not here. He describes participating willingly in break-ins abroad while insisting a warrant is required at home.

the-warren-ohio-tail.title: Surveillance detection route
the-warren-ohio-tail.summary: Tradecraft technique used by intelligence officers and assets to determine whether they are being followed before, during, or after an operational meeting

the-warren-ohio-tail.title: The John Kiriakou Task Force
the-warren-ohio-tail.summary: The dedicated FBI unit that John Kiriakou says was created inside the Bureau to investigate him after he blew the whistle on the CIA''s torture program: twelve agents appointed under director Robert Mueller who tapped his phones, intercepted his email and followed him in pairs to work, to church and to the grocery store for three years, trying to catch him committing a crime.

the-warren-ohio-tail.title: Espionage Act
the-warren-ohio-tail.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

the-warren-ohio-tail.title: Japanese diplomat FBI sting
the-warren-ohio-tail.summary: John Kiriakou's account of an FBI entrapment operation in which an agent posing as a Japanese diplomat cold-pitched him for classified information over five lunches, hoping he would commit actual espionage they could charge — a scheme he discovered only in his own case discovery.

the-warren-ohio-tail.title: Planning a surveillance detection route
the-warren-ohio-tail.summary: The hours of paperwork behind every CIA meeting before satellite mapping existed — photocopied road-atlas pages taped into sheets six feet across, legs and stops marked in coloured highlighter, submitted to instructors for approval and then driven in advance to check for no-left-turns and closed roads. John Kiriakou ran routes to and from work every day in Athens against 17 November, taught surveillance detection as an agency instructor, spent four or five hours of a night on the route around a single emergency meeting, and wrote the CIA Insider's Guide to the subject — from which the agency redacted six pages.

the-warren-ohio-tail.title: The business-card espionage charges
the-warren-ohio-tail.summary: Two of the three Espionage Act counts brought against John Kiriakou rested on his having passed a former CIA colleague's business card to two reporters — a man who had left the agency and had never been undercover — and were dropped after an exchange in open court in which the prosecutor's only answer to the judge was that Kiriakou should have been more careful.

the-washed-out-road-to-the-airport.title: Joe Rogan
the-washed-out-road-to-the-airport.summary: The podcast host whose show John Kiriakou finally sat for in October 2025 — an experience that began with signing a non-disclosure agreement and ended with his verdict that Rogan is "a nice guy, very down to earth, very normal." The first thing Rogan asked, walking into the studio ten minutes late: "Hey, do you know my friend Mike Baker?" Kiriakou defends Rogan as unfairly characterized as a right-winger, and had long cited the show as the venue where Zuckerberg admitted Facebook suppressed the Hunter Biden laptop story at the FBI''s behest.

the-washed-out-road-to-the-airport.title: The resort with no air conditioning
the-washed-out-road-to-the-airport.summary: The Baja California resort where John Kiriakou spent a month filming in 2025 — built in the 1960s as a commune by long-haired left-wing Angelenos funded by Thomas Hart Benton's daughter, a dozen buildings on the southernmost tip of the peninsula, no air conditioning, and nothing whatsoever to do unless you dive.

the-washed-out-road-to-the-airport.title: The tarantula on the mini fridge
the-washed-out-road-to-the-airport.summary: The wildlife of the Baja resort as John Kiriakou catalogued it — rattlesnakes everywhere, an emailed instruction never to go barefoot, shoes shaken out before every midnight walk to the mini fridge kept outdoors, a flashlight in hand, and one night at three in the morning a tarantula sitting on the fridge itself.

the-washed-out-road-to-the-airport.title: Abigail Spanberger
the-washed-out-road-to-the-airport.summary: Governor of Virginia from 2025 and, before Congress, a CIA officer alongside John Kiriakou in the Counterterrorism Center — whom he calls a perfectly nice person who would have been a middle-of-the-road Republican in the 1970s and 1980s, and whose victory speech, to his surprise, said all the right things.

the-washed-out-road-to-the-airport.title: Destroying the Dome of the Rock
the-washed-out-road-to-the-airport.summary: John Kiriakou's agreement with Tucker Carlson that a Zionist extremist plan to demolish the Dome of the Rock and build a third temple would be the event that starts the Third World War — and his additional prediction that it would also be the beginning of the end for the Israeli government and all of its support.

the-washed-out-road-to-the-airport.title: Jason Miyares
the-washed-out-road-to-the-airport.summary: The Cuban-born Republican attorney general of Virginia whom John Kiriakou expected to be a right-wing disaster and found instead to be excellent — a judgement he says is hard for him to make about a conservative Republican, and which he repeated on the night Miyares was unceremoniously thrown out of office.

the-washington-post-editorial-on-the-cov.title: The Flynn charges
the-washington-post-editorial-on-the-cov.summary: John Kiriakou supported the appointment of a special counsel in 2017 while rejecting the Russia allegations outright — arguing that the case for an investigation rested not on election interference but on a list of ordinary, provable crimes he believed senior Trump campaign figures, and Michael Flynn in particular, had already committed.

the-washington-post-editorial-on-the-cov.title: The attribution problem in the DNC hack
the-washington-post-editorial-on-the-cov.summary: Asked in 2017 whether he had any confidence in the intelligence community's assessments of Russian interference, John Kiriakou said he had none — objecting that no one had ever defined what was meant by hacking, that the published evidence told the public nothing, and that an agency asking to be taken at its word should not be.

the-washington-post-editorial-on-the-cov.title: Domingo's television
the-washington-post-editorial-on-the-cov.summary: John Kiriakou has used the television rooms at FCI Loretto as his sharpest illustration of prison segregation: sets owned by racial blocs since a riot in the 1990s, a seat in front of one costing fourteen dollars, and one set left tuned to Law & Order every morning because a man named Domingo had paid four hundred dollars for it and had been gone for years.

the-washington-post-editorial-on-the-cov.title: Mental health as a disciplinary problem
the-washington-post-editorial-on-the-cov.summary: John Kiriakou has said that before his own prosecution he never gave five seconds of thought to the American prison system, and that living inside it showed him a broken one — in particular a system in which mental health is treated as a disciplinary problem rather than a medical one.

the-washington-post-editorial-on-the-cov.title: The 2017 European tour
the-washington-post-editorial-on-the-cov.summary: In May 2017 John Kiriakou spent a week speaking about national security whistleblowing in Iceland, Germany, Luxembourg, Belgium and Ireland, addressing the German Parliament and sharing panels with serving European ministers — an audience he contrasted sharply with his reception in the United States, and one he found newly willing to break with Washington because it was, in his word, panic-stricken about Donald Trump.

the-washington-post-editorial-on-the-cov.title: The Ai Weiwei encounter in Berlin
the-washington-post-editorial-on-the-cov.summary: John Kiriakou met the artist Ai Weiwei by pure chance on a Berlin street while dragging a suitcase to the airport after a board meeting — an encounter that led to a tour of Ai Weiwei's studio and a signed iPhone case bearing the Lego portrait the artist had made of him for an exhibition at Alcatraz.

the-washington-post-under-bezos.title: Censorship on the left
the-washington-post-under-bezos.summary: John Kiriakou''s observation that he was censored far less by Forbes and Fortune than by The Nation and Mother Jones, which he offers as an instance of a general rule that a writer''s own side censors them hardest — the counterpart to Ted Rall''s account of being made to fit a particular kind of leftism rather than any kind.

the-washington-post-under-bezos.title: Barrett Brown
the-washington-post-under-bezos.summary: American journalist and former Anonymous associate whom John Kiriakou describes as one of the most intelligent writers and analysts he has ever encountered, with long-standing mental health problems and a two-decade heroin addiction he has now been clear of for at least a year, expelled from the United Kingdom and relocated to Mexico.

the-washington-post-under-bezos.title: Phil Donahue
the-washington-post-under-bezos.summary: American talk-show host who, John Kiriakou discovered seven years after the fact, had been secretly paying his weekly newspaper column fee — $400 a week for nine years, routed through Reader Supported News — because Donahue had learned that Kiriakou came out of prison broke and did not want him sleeping in his car.

the-washington-post-under-bezos.title: The Hall of States
the-washington-post-under-bezos.summary: The Washington office building at 444 North Capitol Street where, in John Kiriakou''s floor-by-floor description, most of the capital''s television news operations share an address — NBC and MSNBC on the ground floor, Fox on the fifth, PBS and Democracy Now on the sixth, and Newsmax in the basement in a single room.

the-washington-post-under-bezos.title: Dr Oz and the Armenian hospices
the-washington-post-under-bezos.summary: John Kiriakou''s reaction to a television segment by Mehmet Oz alleging fraud by Armenian-run hospices in Los Angeles — that a man he identifies as a veteran of the Turkish special forces zeroing in on Armenians in California is not a coincidence, and that each of the administration''s appointees appears to arrive with a racial scandal of their own.

the-washington-post-under-bezos.title: The Iron Dome
the-washington-post-under-bezos.summary: Israel's air-defence system as John Kiriakou reads it — impressive against a wave of slow Iranian drones, but shown by the handful that got through, and later by Iranian ballistic missiles, to be not all it is cracked up to be; each exchange, in his account, buying Iran intelligence about the gaps.

the-waters-edge-doctrine.title: Phil Donahue
the-waters-edge-doctrine.summary: American talk-show host who, John Kiriakou discovered seven years after the fact, had been secretly paying his weekly newspaper column fee — $400 a week for nine years, routed through Reader Supported News — because Donahue had learned that Kiriakou came out of prison broke and did not want him sleeping in his car.

the-waters-edge-doctrine.title: Soviet Union
the-waters-edge-doctrine.summary: The superpower whose collapse framed the start of John Kiriakou's CIA career — it was "literally in the process of collapsing" when he joined in January 1990, ushering in a brief "peace dividend" era when the agency's new threats were environmental degradation and AIDS. Kiriakou cites Brzezinski's "Afghan trap" that lured the Soviets into Afghanistan, argues the U.S. abandoned the radicalized mujahideen the moment the Soviets were beaten, notes America then took "a vacation from history," and recalls that Jonathan Pollard's stolen documents were traded by Israel to the Soviets in exchange for Russian Jews.

the-waters-edge-doctrine.title: The Alaska glacier
the-waters-edge-doctrine.summary: The visitor centre John Kiriakou saw on a 2016 trip to Alaska with Gary Johnson, built at the foot of a glacier close enough to touch from the observation deck and by then a quarter of a mile away from it — an image he uses as the plainest available demonstration of climate change, and one he refuses to let pass as a joke.

the-waters-edge-doctrine.title: The armour at Union Station
the-waters-edge-doctrine.summary: John Kiriakou''s eyewitness account of stepping off an Amtrak train at Washington''s Union Station in August 2025 to find two armoured personnel carriers and a .50 calibre machine gun trained on the entrance — and of tourists posing for photographs with the National Guardsmen deployed in the parts of the city where, he says, there is no crime.

the-waters-edge-doctrine.title: The CIA and Iridium
the-waters-edge-doctrine.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of the Central Intelligence Agency buying the satellite telephone company Iridium when it was unprofitable and about to go out of business, because the agency needed the network — a purchase he places alongside its acquisition of Intelsat, and which he encountered personally when he had to rent the phones for Afghanistan.

the-waters-edge-doctrine.title: The diplomatic stool collection
the-waters-edge-doctrine.summary: John Kiriakou''s confirmation that visiting heads of state routinely carry their own faeces home rather than leave them in an American hotel — because, in his account, entities within the United States government will gladly collect the material for its DNA and health information, and the hotel employee who retrieves it is a CIA officer under cover.

the-weight-of-the-government.title: More money on security in Athens than Beirut
the-weight-of-the-government.summary: John Kiriakou''s measure of how dangerous Athens was for American officials at the turn of the century — that the United States spent more on security there than in Beirut — and the consequence he says followed: no diplomatic plates, because they would make Americans easier to identify and kill.

the-weight-of-the-government.title: "I had no intent"
the-weight-of-the-government.summary: The formula John Kiriakou used in the days around his January 2013 sentencing to describe his own guilty plea — that he had committed the act charged but had neither the intent to commit a crime nor the intent to harm the officer he named, having believed the man was retired and available to be interviewed.

the-weight-of-the-government.title: Counterterrorism Center
the-weight-of-the-government.summary: The CIA's Counterterrorism Center (CTC) — the unit where John Kiriakou spent the defining years of his operational career. He joined in the late 1990s as the only officer in the entire CIA fluent in both Greek and Arabic, served as chief of counterintelligence in the bin Laden unit, watched the Center swell from a few hundred employees to nearly 2,000 by September 12, 2001, and it was to CTC that he walked back down in May 2002 to refuse the torture program — the moment, he says, the CIA began to turn on him.

the-weight-of-the-government.title: Revolutionary Organization 17 November
the-weight-of-the-government.summary: Greek far-left urban guerrilla group active 1975–2002; the deadliest terrorist organization in Greek history

the-weight-of-the-government.title: Stephen Saunders
the-weight-of-the-government.summary: British defense attaché in Athens assassinated by Revolutionary Organization 17 November in March 2000

the-weight-of-the-government.title: "The government is the biggest leaker"
the-weight-of-the-government.summary: John Kiriakou's answer, given on the eve of his imprisonment, to the argument that leaks make clandestine work impossible — that the United States government is itself the largest leaker of classified information in the country, sanctioning disclosure whenever it suits, as with the makers of Zero Dark Thirty and with drone-strike details given to the New York Times during an election campaign.

the-west-africa-cocaine-route.title: Venezuela regime change (2026)
the-west-africa-cocaine-route.summary: John Kiriakou''s assessment of the American operation that removed Venezuela''s president — a clear violation of international law, since none of the three recognised grounds for one state attacking another applied, but not a violation of US law, which since 1985 has expressly permitted special forces to cross borders and seize people for trial. His reluctant conclusion at the time: "as much as I hate admitting it, this regime change seems to be working right now."

the-west-africa-cocaine-route.title: Venezuelan heavy crude and the refining bottleneck
the-west-africa-cocaine-route.summary: John Kiriakou''s economic explanation for American pressure on Venezuela: the country''s oil is unusually high in sulfur and requires specialty refining, which for years could only be done in Houston. He says sanctions pushed India and China to build refineries capable of processing it, and that a Chinese announcement of a Caribbean refinery for Venezuelan crude left Washington with a policy it could not admit had failed.

the-west-africa-cocaine-route.title: Fentanyl and China
the-west-africa-cocaine-route.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that China declines to stop the flow of fentanyl into the United States for the same reason he says the United States tolerated Afghan heroin reaching Iran and Russia — because an addicted society is a weaker one. He distinguishes Chinese-made illicit fentanyl, largely produced in Mexico, from the medical fentanyl that created the addiction pathway.

the-west-africa-cocaine-route.title: Afghan heroin policy
the-west-africa-cocaine-route.summary: The post-2001 U.S. policy in Afghanistan of protecting, and per John Kiriakou actively encouraging, the cultivation of heroin poppy. Under the Taliban in 2000 Afghanistan produced 0% of the world's heroin; by 2009 under American occupation it produced 93%. Per a DEA officer Kiriakou consulted with on the policy paper he was preparing for Senator Kerry, the strategic rationale was that nearly all of the heroin flowed to Iran and Russia, addiction in those countries was considered desirable as a long-run societal weakener, and the same logic now operates in reverse with Chinese fentanyl flowing into the United States.

the-west-africa-cocaine-route.title: The Libyan constitution unveiling
the-west-africa-cocaine-route.summary: A launch event John Kiriakou attended in Washington after the fall of Muammar Gaddafi: a new Libyan constitution, commissioned by wealthy exiles from a lobbying firm, unveiled at the lobbying firm''s offices. He calls the document better than the American one — equal rights for everybody, the oil money shared — and notes that nothing whatever was done with it, because nobody in Washington had heard of the people behind it.

the-west-africa-cocaine-route.title: What we owed Mexico
the-west-africa-cocaine-route.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer to why American and Mexican cooperation against the cartels achieves so little: the federales are incorruptible and outgunned, the government does not control parts of its own territory, and the United States spent a century punishing Mexico instead of helping it develop — allowing four families to own the entire economy.

the-whiskers-rule.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
the-whiskers-rule.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

the-whiskers-rule.title: George W. Bush
the-whiskers-rule.summary: 43rd President of the United States. In John Kiriakou's telling, Bush signed the August 1, 2002 executive order that authorized the CIA torture program, spent years telling the public "we don't torture," and — days after Kiriakou's 2007 ABC interview — blamed torture on "a rogue CIA officer" while walking from the White House South Portico to Marine One, a moment Kiriakou instantly read as the White House preparing to pin the program on him. Bush also ordered the FBI removed from Abu Zubaydah's black site, flew the bin Laden family out of the country after 9/11, and loosened the assassination ban of Executive Order 12333.

the-whiskers-rule.title: The applicant who invented a CIA career
the-whiskers-rule.summary: The job interview John Kiriakou conducted in the private sector at which he took a candidate to lunch, asked two questions any real CIA officer could answer, and was told: "I''m really sorry. I really need this job."

the-whiskers-rule.title: The seventh Espionage Act defendant
the-whiskers-rule.summary: The case John Kiriakou cited two days before his own sentencing to correct the count of Espionage Act prosecutions brought under Barack Obama — a translator at the American naval base in Bahrain who had just been charged, making seven, against three in the whole history of the United States before 2009.

the-whiskers-rule.title: The Afghan National Police poisoning
the-whiskers-rule.summary: An incident John Kiriakou recalls from a 2012 New York Times report and treats as the clearest single illustration of why the American project in Afghanistan failed: at a DynCorp-run training facility that had deliberately mixed recruits from every tribe and region, one recruit poisoned the evening stew and then let four Taliban fighters into the dormitory to stab the survivors in their beds.

the-whiskers-rule.title: Federal Torture Act
the-whiskers-rule.summary: United States statute criminalizing torture; per John Kiriakou, on the books since at least 1946, with concrete enforcement history — after World War II the United States executed Japanese soldiers convicted of waterboarding American prisoners of war, meaning waterboarding was at that time a capital offense under U.S. law. The act was effectively set aside for the CIA's enhanced interrogation program after 2002.

the-white-house-pastry-chef.title: The Libertarian Christmas party
the-white-house-pastry-chef.summary: The party John Kiriakou attended in a townhouse in Old Town Alexandria, held at the end of January because — being Libertarians — the organisers could not get their act together in December, and at which the head of the Libertarian Party of Virginia asked him to run for governor and was refused on the spot.

the-white-house-pastry-chef.title: Donald Trump
the-white-house-pastry-chef.summary: 45th and 47th U.S. president. Per John Kiriakou, a man genuinely convinced he was doing right by bombing Iran, "duped" by the same Netanyahu nuclear bluff Obama once rejected — and, at the same time, the most blindly pro-Israel president in history, an admirer of autocrats who has never once criticized Vladimir Putin, and prone to gestures — from the Gulf of America to a since-abandoned "Department of War" rename — that test the edges of his actual authority.

the-white-house-pastry-chef.title: Lindsey Graham
the-white-house-pastry-chef.summary: Republican senator from South Carolina who died in July 2026, and John Kiriakou's standing shorthand for the permanent war caucus — a "show horse" rather than a workhorse, a "chameleon" who "never saw a war that he didn't want to jump into with both feet," and, on posthumously released documentary footage, a man offering the US Air Force to bomb a country America was not at war with.

the-white-house-pastry-chef.title: Mexico City as an espionage hub
the-white-house-pastry-chef.summary: John Kiriakou''s assessment of Mexico City as one of the world''s principal centres of international espionage, alongside Vienna, London, Paris and Washington — driven by a gargantuan American embassy that Russian services target from next door — and his reading of why Mexico simply ignored a dossier of suspected Russian officers handed over by the Biden administration.

the-white-house-pastry-chef.title: Pakistani prisons
the-white-house-pastry-chef.summary: John Kiriakou''s flat refusal, in a discussion of Imran Khan''s detention, of the idea that a Pakistani prison offers VIP treatment to a former prime minister — grounded in his having visited many of them himself during the period when the CIA was locking people up there.

the-white-house-pastry-chef.title: Savas Kalenderidis
the-white-house-pastry-chef.summary: Greek intelligence officer, national hero and personal friend of John Kiriakou''s, who was involved in the operation to protect the PKK founder Abdullah Öcalan at the Greek embassy in Nairobi in 1999 — an operation that ended when Turkish and Kenyan intelligence diverted part of Öcalan''s motorcade and seized him. Kiriakou flatly denies the claim that the CIA and Turkish intelligence tried to kill Kalenderidis there.

the-white-house-tip.title: American missile stockpiles
the-white-house-tip.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that the United States has run its interceptor stocks down to the point of strategic vulnerability — that the conventional wisdom in Washington was that a round of the Iran war ended because the Patriots ran out, and that a country which cannot fight a two-front war certainly cannot do it below maximum production.

the-white-house-tip.title: Andrew Bustamante
the-white-house-tip.summary: Former CIA officer who sells CIA-style training online; John Kiriakou identifies him as the lone critic of his work hosting a show on a Russian network, and argues Bustamante's training business — open to anyone who pays — is the more problematic of the two.

the-white-house-tip.title: John Kiriakou
the-white-house-tip.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

the-white-house-tip.title: Gulf consultations before the Iran war
the-white-house-tip.summary: John Kiriakou's account of travelling in Kuwait, Abu Dhabi, Dubai and Doha in the weeks before the 2026 strikes on Iran, and finding that the United States had made no diplomatic case to its Gulf partners at all — in sharp contrast to the worldwide campaign that preceded the Iraq war. He told a senior Emirati royal that two carrier strike groups meant an attack was coming.

the-white-house-tip.title: Sarah Adams
the-white-house-tip.summary: A former CIA open-source analyst and frequent television commentator on terrorist threats, whom John Kiriakou dismisses in unusually direct terms: that she never held access to classified information, that she analysed press rather than intelligence, and that she has built a living out of predicting imminent disaster.

the-white-house-tip.title: The USS Gerald Ford plumbing failure
the-white-house-tip.summary: Days before the 2026 war, John Kiriakou raised the possibility that a sewage failure severe enough to send the carrier USS Gerald R. Ford back to Norfolk was sabotage by a crew that did not want to go to war with Iran.

the-witness-letter.title: The twenty-thousand-dollar tweet
the-witness-letter.summary: John Kiriakou's account of asking Jeanine Pirro for help with a pardon and being quoted $20,000 by her assistant — for a tweet. He refused, and says he was never invited back on her programme.

the-witness-letter.title: Noelle Dunphy
the-witness-letter.summary: Former aide to Rudy Giuliani; independently corroborated to the New York Times John Kiriakou's account of Giuliani's 2018 $2 million pardon-extortion attempt, after Giuliani's subsequent sexual harassment of her caused her to come forward.

the-witness-letter.title: Abbas and the three-state problem
the-witness-letter.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that no two-state solution is available — because there is already one state, because Mahmoud Abbas is nineteen years into a four-year term and has become a billionaire, and because East Bank, West Bank and Gaza Palestinians are so disconnected that the real arithmetic is three states, which nobody will discuss.

the-witness-letter.title: Bulldozing the olive orchards
the-witness-letter.summary: The sequence John Kiriakou describes preceding Israeli seizures of Palestinian land in the West Bank — olive orchards bulldozed and crops burned to make leaving easier, then the house demolished and a prefabricated one built for a settler family — and the different practice he says applies in East Jerusalem.

the-witness-letter.title: Elbridge Gerry and the salamander
the-witness-letter.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the origin of the word gerrymander — Elbridge Gerry, vice president and former governor of Massachusetts, drawing district boundaries to elect his friends, and Benjamin Franklin saying the shapes looked like salamanders — together with a piece of trivia from his unpublished book on cemeteries.

the-witness-letter.title: Giuliani Pardon Solicitation
the-witness-letter.summary: Per John Kiriakou, a meeting at the Trump International Hotel in Washington in which Rudy Giuliani's associate solicited $2 million in exchange for a presidential pardon — a story that subsequently appeared as a front-page New York Times article. Giuliani publicly denied ever meeting Kiriakou; Kiriakou sent the Times the photograph taken at the meeting that morning, and the paper published the story with the note that it had seen documentary proof.

the-woman-escorted-from-the-white-house.title: The orange jumpsuits
the-woman-escorted-from-the-white-house.summary: John Kiriakou has argued that the clothing ISIS put on the Western hostages it beheaded was not a coincidence but a citation: the group dressed its prisoners in orange jumpsuits because the United States dressed its own prisoners in orange jumpsuits, and once a government tortures, it has licensed every other government to do the same to its people.

the-woman-escorted-from-the-white-house.title: Brian Ross
the-woman-escorted-from-the-white-house.summary: American investigative journalist and seven-time Emmy Award winner who was a prominent reporter at ABC News when, in December 2007, he conducted the on-camera interview with John Kiriakou that produced the first public confirmation by a U.S. official that the CIA waterboarded prisoners. Per Kiriakou, Ross called him out of the blue with the assertion that a source said Kiriakou had personally tortured Abu Zubaydah; Kiriakou's decision to give the interview anyway — driven by the conclusion that 'Brian Ross's source is at the White House and they're going to pin this on me' — became the pivot point of his entire post-CIA life.

the-woman-escorted-from-the-white-house.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
the-woman-escorted-from-the-white-house.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

the-woman-escorted-from-the-white-house.title: Do what is right or what is easy
the-woman-escorted-from-the-white-house.summary: Asked what he would tell the boy who once told his father he wanted to be a spy, John Kiriakou said he would tell him to always tell the truth and do the right thing — arguing that everyone already knows in their gut the difference between right and wrong, and that the only real question is whether they then do what is right or what is easy.

the-woman-escorted-from-the-white-house.title: National Whistleblower Day
the-woman-escorted-from-the-white-house.summary: John Kiriakou has called National Whistleblower Day an event no whistleblower or supporter should miss — held every year in the Kennedy Caucus Room, which he describes as not merely the biggest room on Capitol Hill but the most historic single room anywhere on it, having hosted every major Senate hearing from the sinking of the Titanic to Watergate and Iran-Contra.

the-woman-escorted-from-the-white-house.title: The Berlin conference list
the-woman-escorted-from-the-white-house.summary: Checking into a Berlin hotel for a conference, John Kiriakou was handed the guest list when the clerk could not find his booking — and discovered that every one of the dozen names on it was a friend of his, and every one of them an outspoken whistleblower.

the-writ-of-coram-nobis.title: Ed Martin and the pardon file
the-writ-of-coram-nobis.summary: The US pardon attorney whose office John Kiriakou directed supporters to write to, and the message a mutual friend brought back from him: that he was the third person that day to call about Kiriakou, that Kiriakou should relax, and that his file was literally on Martin''s desk. Kiriakou''s advice to letter-writers was to send physical mail rather than email.

the-writ-of-coram-nobis.title: Coffee with a cabinet member
the-writ-of-coram-nobis.summary: John Kiriakou's disclosure that he had coffee with a member of the cabinet who told him to be patient about his pardon — and told him to watch what he said. He reports the meeting while stating plainly that there is nothing further he can do to make his case, and that he is not confident the outcome will be decided on justice.

the-writ-of-coram-nobis.title: Pardons nobody asked for
the-writ-of-coram-nobis.summary: Two cases John Kiriakou cites of people pardoned without applying: the Binance founder, who said publicly that he had never met the president, never asked for a pardon and never applied for one; and Darryl Strawberry, a New York Mets great with tax and drug problems behind him. Kiriakou raises both while waiting, unsuccessfully, for a pardon he has actively sought for years.

the-writ-of-coram-nobis.title: Lincoln's candlelight pardons
the-writ-of-coram-nobis.summary: The historical contrast John Kiriakou drew while discussing a mass grant of clemency: stories of Abraham Lincoln staying up late into the night pardoning Civil War deserters by candlelight, on the principle that nobody should be executed for cowardice — set against a modern president who Kiriakou says has pardoned more people than anyone in American history, whenever the mood strikes him.

the-writ-of-coram-nobis.title: Sergey Lavrov
the-writ-of-coram-nobis.summary: Russian foreign minister, and previously Russian ambassador to the United Nations during John Kiriakou's assignment there, where the two worked the same Security Council. Kiriakou describes him as the most admired diplomat in the building — the most powerful, important and strategic ambassador there despite operating with far smaller resources than his American, British, French and Chinese counterparts, and better than most of the American diplomats Kiriakou worked for. When Lavrov was abruptly sidelined in late 2025, Kiriakou's reading was retirement rather than disgrace.

the-writ-of-coram-nobis.title: "Stefanik will not be governor"
the-writ-of-coram-nobis.summary: John Kiriakou's flat, on-the-record prediction about the New York governor's race, made against a friend he describes as irrationally conservative who insisted the contest would turn on a single issue — the right to carry a gun. Kiriakou called it the most ridiculous thing he had heard the man say, and argued that Elise Stefanik's political career is finished.

the-yale-intern-fascist.title: Dick Cheney
the-yale-intern-fascist.summary: U.S. Vice President under George W. Bush. Per John Kiriakou — recounting CIA Director George Tenet's memoir — Cheney intercepted the presidential finding authorizing the CIA's enhanced interrogation program in the Oval Office anteroom and took it from Tenet before Bush could sign it.
