virginia-redistricting-supreme-court-rul.summary: Per John Kiriakou — as chief of counterterrorism operations in Pakistan after September 11, 2001 — the Guantanamo detention facility began as a temporary holding measure intended to last two to three weeks while the CIA and Justice Department determined which federal district court should try each prisoner, not as a long-term detention infrastructure. The Rawalpindi jail had reached capacity, Pakistani intelligence demanded the prisoners be removed, and CIA headquarters directed Kiriakou to load them onto a C-12 cargo plane and fly them to Cuba.

vladimir-putin.title: Ray McGovern
vladimir-putin.summary: Former senior CIA analyst turned antiwar dissident, and one of John Kiriakou's closest friends — "like a brother to me." Kiriakou began working at the CIA on the Monday after the Friday McGovern retired in January 1990, so the two never overlapped inside; they became comrades in the whistleblower world instead. McGovern coined the "MICIMATT" framing Kiriakou often borrows, went into Putin's office with Oliver Stone for a 40-minute meeting, and — per Kiriakou — believes 9/11 was a conspiracy, a view Kiriakou affectionately notes is far from his own.

vladimir-putin.title: Russia-Ukraine war origins
vladimir-putin.summary: John Kiriakou's account that the war began in 2014, not 2022 — rooted in broken U.S. promises that NATO would not expand to Russia's borders, the 2014 removal of a pro-Russian Ukrainian leader, and the seizure of Crimea; he says Russia is now winning and has no reason to negotiate.

vladimir-putin.title: Donald Trump
vladimir-putin.summary: 45th and 47th U.S. president. Per John Kiriakou, a man genuinely convinced he was doing right by bombing Iran, "duped" by the same Netanyahu nuclear bluff Obama once rejected — and, at the same time, the most blindly pro-Israel president in history, an admirer of autocrats who has never once criticized Vladimir Putin, and prone to gestures — from the Gulf of America to a since-abandoned "Department of War" rename — that test the edges of his actual authority.

vladimir-putin.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
vladimir-putin.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

vladimir-putin.title: John Brennan
vladimir-putin.summary: Former Director of the CIA; characterized in KiriPedia's source corpus as the principal architect of the agency's enhanced interrogation program and as having plotted against an elected President

vladimir-putin.title: The Putin call and the China exception
vladimir-putin.summary: In February 2025 John Kiriakou said he was optimistic that relations with Russia would improve, on the strength of a telephone call being arranged between Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin — but drew a sharp exception for China, arguing that nobody in the American government was sincere about improving those relations and that Washington, not Beijing, was instigating talk of war.

volodymyr-zelensky.title: Donald Trump
volodymyr-zelensky.summary: 45th and 47th U.S. president. Per John Kiriakou, a man genuinely convinced he was doing right by bombing Iran, "duped" by the same Netanyahu nuclear bluff Obama once rejected — and, at the same time, the most blindly pro-Israel president in history, an admirer of autocrats who has never once criticized Vladimir Putin, and prone to gestures — from the Gulf of America to a since-abandoned "Department of War" rename — that test the edges of his actual authority.

volodymyr-zelensky.title: Russia-Ukraine war origins
volodymyr-zelensky.summary: John Kiriakou's account that the war began in 2014, not 2022 — rooted in broken U.S. promises that NATO would not expand to Russia's borders, the 2014 removal of a pro-Russian Ukrainian leader, and the seizure of Crimea; he says Russia is now winning and has no reason to negotiate.

volodymyr-zelensky.title: Marco Rubio
volodymyr-zelensky.summary: U.S. official whom John Kiriakou identifies as the real motivator behind pressure on Venezuela; Kiriakou argues Venezuela is not a meaningful drug threat to the U.S. and that Rubio simply wants Maduro gone.

volodymyr-zelensky.title: Lindsey Graham
volodymyr-zelensky.summary: Republican senator from South Carolina who died in July 2026, and John Kiriakou's standing shorthand for the permanent war caucus — a "show horse" rather than a workhorse, a "chameleon" who "never saw a war that he didn't want to jump into with both feet," and, on posthumously released documentary footage, a man offering the US Air Force to bomb a country America was not at war with.

volodymyr-zelensky.title: The Caspian drone strike
volodymyr-zelensky.summary: The July 2026 incident in which Ukrainian drones, unleashed by Volodymyr Zelensky as part of a declared 40-day drone war on June 25 to make the Russian people feel pain, strayed onto an Iranian ship in the Caspian Sea and killed an Iranian sailor. John Kiriakou treats Zelensky's subsequent attempt to spin the mistake into a request that the United States expand its Iran war into the Caspian as a probable Netanyahu suggestion, and Iran's decision to accept an apology and reparations as evidence that Iran no longer needs the mistake to be a war.

volodymyr-zelensky.title: The GUR-SBU gun battle
volodymyr-zelensky.summary: The daylight shootout on Shumsky Street in Kyiv, in which Ukraine's two most senior intelligence services, the GUR (military intelligence) and the SBU (domestic security), fired on each other after the SBU detained a GUR officer. John Kiriakou, asked to react on the Sanchez Effect, said he had tried to think of a precedent and could not; he treats the fight as *"the breakdown of the Ukrainian side."*

waco-siege.title: Ruby Ridge
waco-siege.summary: 1992 federal standoff in Idaho involving Randy Weaver, triggered by an allegation that Weaver had sold a shotgun with a barrel two inches shorter than the legal minimum; per John Kiriakou, FBI sniper Lon Horiuchi shot and killed Weaver's wife while she was holding her baby, and Horiuchi was never punished. Kiriakou describes Ruby Ridge as one of the events that, after his own imprisonment, caused him to fundamentally reassess his earlier acceptance of the official government account.

waco-siege.title: Abu Zubaydah
waco-siege.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

waco-siege.title: Alex Station
waco-siege.summary: CIA unit that tracked Osama bin Laden beginning in 1995; per John Kiriakou, who served as chief of its counterintelligence branch, the unit kept extremely tight security around its files, limited FBI investigators' access to information about future 9/11 hijackers Khaled al-Mihdhar and Nawaf al-Hazmi, and — under a deliberate policy of non-cooperation with the FBI — failed to watchlist participants in the Malaysia summit where al-Qaeda planned the attacks.

waco-siege.title: Allen Dulles
waco-siege.summary: Long-serving CIA director whom John Kiriakou calls a 'monster' and a 'very dark figure in American history' — a United Fruit board member who ran the agency that overthrew Guatemala's Árbenz, who went to Truman's house to talk him out of criticising the CIA, and who stayed in touch with the men Kiriakou believes killed John F. Kennedy.

waco-siege.title: Central Intelligence Agency
waco-siege.summary: U.S. foreign intelligence service; John Kiriakou's employer from 1990 to 2004 and the central institution of KiriPedia

waco-siege.title: Cofer Black
waco-siege.summary: Former head of the CIA Counterterrorism Center during and immediately after the September 11 attacks; principal architect of the agency's paramilitary turn on September 12, 2001; later Vice President of Blackwater under Erik Prince.

walk-in.title: Abu Zubaydah
walk-in.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

walk-in.title: Intelligence peddlers
walk-in.summary: John Kiriakou''s breakdown of who actually walks into an American embassy offering information: the overwhelming majority are fabricators or probes, a few per cent are peddlers selling the same nugget to five embassies in a month, and about one per cent are the real thing.

walk-in.title: John Kiriakou
walk-in.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

walk-in.title: Julian Assange
walk-in.summary: Kiriakou — a 15-year friend and former WikiLeaks board member — on why Assange is a publisher owed a journalist's immunity, and a political prisoner.

walk-in.title: The forged award certificate
walk-in.summary: A recruited source John Kiriakou says he brought to tears twice — first by telling him his reporting had gone directly to the president of the United States, then by presenting him with an award certificate Kiriakou had made himself in Word with clip art, the agency seal, and a forged signature of the director, which he then took back for safekeeping on the grounds that being seen with it would get the man killed.

walk-in.title: The walk-in who was a probe
walk-in.summary: The man who presented himself at the American embassy in Athens claiming to be an Arab with information, and whom John Kiriakou interrogated the next day in a rolling meeting through the city — catching him reversing his own alias, while a hostile embassy's surveillance car followed and Kiriakou's boss ended it by putting a pistol to the man's cheek.

walking-robert-morgenthau-to-the-hearing.title: The search for a country to take Gaza
walking-robert-morgenthau-to-the-hearing.summary: John Kiriakou's account of Israel approaching one country after another — Albania, Indonesia, Egypt, Saudi Arabia and finally South Sudan — to accept expelled Gazans, a project he calls the literal definition of ethnic cleansing and says cannot be done because it is illegal.

walking-robert-morgenthau-to-the-hearing.title: "An actual summit"
walking-robert-morgenthau-to-the-hearing.summary: John Kiriakou's reading of the August 2025 Anchorage meeting between Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin — that the Russian delegation's seniority proved Moscow was serious, that Putin is not the erratic figure American media portray, and that there is never any downside to diplomacy.

walking-robert-morgenthau-to-the-hearing.title: Sergey Lavrov
walking-robert-morgenthau-to-the-hearing.summary: Russian foreign minister, and previously Russian ambassador to the United Nations during John Kiriakou's assignment there, where the two worked the same Security Council. Kiriakou describes him as the most admired diplomat in the building — the most powerful, important and strategic ambassador there despite operating with far smaller resources than his American, British, French and Chinese counterparts, and better than most of the American diplomats Kiriakou worked for. When Lavrov was abruptly sidelined in late 2025, Kiriakou's reading was retirement rather than disgrace.

walking-robert-morgenthau-to-the-hearing.title: The seat-belt roadblocks
walking-robert-morgenthau-to-the-hearing.summary: What John Kiriakou reported the federalised National Guard, police, FBI, ATF and DEA were actually doing at roadblocks on Washington's main thoroughfares in August 2025 — writing tickets for unworn seat belts and broken brake lights, in neighbourhoods he says have no street crime to speak of.

walking-robert-morgenthau-to-the-hearing.title: The Sue Mi Terry case
walking-robert-morgenthau-to-the-hearing.summary: John Kiriakou's reading of the prosecution of analyst Sue Mi Terry — charged not under the Espionage Act but under the Foreign Agents Registration Act, an offence he reduces to failing to fill out a form on the internet, and one whose nominal sentencing range he says means nothing in practice.

walking-robert-morgenthau-to-the-hearing.title: The thrown sandwich
walking-robert-morgenthau-to-the-hearing.summary: The arrest of a man who threw a sandwich at a National Guardsman at 14th and U Street in Washington in August 2025, charged with felony assault on a police officer with a stated demand for ten years — an overcharge John Kiriakou said no Washington jury would ever convict on.

walling.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
walling.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

walling.title: Cold cell
walling.summary: A CIA interrogation technique in which a stripped detainee is chained to a ceiling eyebolt in a cell chilled to 50°F, then doused with a bucket of ice water at hourly intervals; never authorized; documented to have killed at least two prisoners.

walling.title: Sleep deprivation
walling.summary: A CIA interrogation technique used against high-value detainees post-9/11; the agency was authorized to deny prisoners sleep for up to 12 days continuously; people died; at least one detainee was rendered permanently clinically insane.

walling.title: Mitchell and Jessen
walling.summary: The two American psychologists who pitched the CIA's enhanced interrogation program to Director George Tenet at a cocktail party in late October 2001; designers of the program and its theoretical underpinning, "learned helplessness."

walling.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
walling.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

walling.title: Muhammad Atar
walling.summary: Nephew of Khalid Sheikh Mohammed; subjected by the CIA to the walling interrogation technique against a concrete-block wall without protective equipment, producing permanent brain damage that has prevented him from participating in his own defense.

walter-pincus.title: Kill the Messenger (Gary Webb)
walter-pincus.summary: The 2014 film about journalist Gary Webb, on which John Kiriakou served as script advisor; when Kiriakou was arrested in January 2012, the FBI seized his electronics, including a draft of the unclassified Hollywood script, and stamped every page "top secret" despite Kiriakou having no role in writing it.

walter-pincus.title: Dark Alliance
walter-pincus.summary: Gary Webb's seven-part San Jose Mercury News investigation reporting that cocaine reaching Los Angeles and fuelling the crack epidemic had travelled through Nicaragua with the CIA's knowledge. John Kiriakou's account stresses what Webb did and did not claim — that the agency turned a blind eye rather than ran the operation — and that three separate federal investigations later found his reporting correct.

walter-pincus.title: CIA Drug Facilitation
walter-pincus.summary: Per John Kiriakou, the CIA''s reported involvement in facilitating the arrival of cocaine into the United States during the era that became the crack epidemic, and his own firsthand discovery — as a Senate Foreign Relations Committee investigator — that under American military control Afghanistan produced 93% of the world''s heroin. A DEA contact told him the report would never be published because ''we want Iran and Russia to be addicted to heroin. It weakens their societies.'' Kiriakou draws a direct parallel to the current fentanyl crisis: China is doing to the US what the US did to Iran and Russia.

walter-pincus.title: Contra rebels
walter-pincus.summary: The right-wing Nicaraguan insurgency armed by the Reagan administration against the Sandinista government. In John Kiriakou's account they were conservatives, right-wingers, in some cases fascists, and disgruntled military officers; they were split into a northern group the United States armed and a southern group that financed itself by selling cocaine — a distinction that became the pivot of the Gary Webb affair, and that Kiriakou uses to answer the CIA's standing denial that it had anything to do with the drug trade.

walter-pincus.title: Oscar Blandón
walter-pincus.summary: The senior Contra leader whom Gary Webb's reporting identified as running the cocaine operation that moved product from Nicaragua to Los Angeles, and one of two men named in the Dark Alliance series.

walter-pincus.title: Domino theory
walter-pincus.summary: The Cold War doctrine, described by John Kiriakou as Ronald Reagan's organising obsession in Central America, holding that if one country there fell to communism the rest would fall in sequence up to the American border — the stated rationale for backing the Contra rebels against the Sandinistas.

warrenton-training-center.title: Aldrich Ames
warrenton-training-center.summary: Senior CIA officer — a GS-15 who rose to chief of counterintelligence for the Soviet branch — who spied for the KGB for nine years. Per John Kiriakou, Ames walked into the Soviet embassy in Washington in April 1985 and sold the identities of two CIA-recruited double agents for $50,000 to clear a debt run up by his second marriage; both were executed. He went on to identify more than thirty agents, compromise over a hundred clandestine operations, cause at least twelve deaths and take more than $2 million, while being known throughout the agency as a daily drunk and promoted at every turn. The KGB protected him with a decoy mole hunt; analyst Sandy Grimes caught him by matching his handler meetings to his bank deposits.

warrenton-training-center.title: James Jesus Angleton
warrenton-training-center.summary: The CIA counterintelligence chief old-timers were 'genuinely afraid' of — and the wall of illegal files on American citizens kept in his office.

warrenton-training-center.title: Sandy Grimes
warrenton-training-center.summary: CIA analyst who, per John Kiriakou, was the person who actually broke the Aldrich Ames case. After a 27-year-old security officer sat on an Ames file for eighteen months without action, Grimes independently noticed that Ames made $100,000–$150,000 bank deposits within days of every trip to Mexico City — the pattern that identified him as a spy. After Ames's arrest, she submitted a hot-wash paper recommending 27 reprimands across the chain of command that had promoted a known alcoholic into the most sensitive counterintelligence position in the CIA. Director John Deutch responded with strongly worded letters for seven. Grimes resigned in 1993.

warrenton-training-center.title: Dmitry Polyakov
warrenton-training-center.summary: GRU colonel run as a CIA agent by Sandy Grimes, and one of the assets burned by Aldrich Ames. Per John Kiriakou, Polyakov's loss is why Grimes took Ames's treachery personally — the analyst who eventually broke the case had handled one of the men it killed.

warrenton-training-center.title: Kim Philby
warrenton-training-center.summary: The British MI6 deputy director secretly working for the KGB — recruited in college and directed to join the service — and, in John Kiriakou's telling, James Angleton's best man and his child's godfather; his decades of betrayal broke Angleton, and he escaped from Beirut through a bathroom window to Moscow. Kiriakou ranks the Cambridge ring as damage at historic levels, above any modern comparison.

warrenton-training-center.title: Rosario Ames
warrenton-training-center.summary: Colombian cultural attaché recruited to work for the CIA, and the second wife of Aldrich Ames. Per John Kiriakou, Ames began an affair with her in Mexico in 1981 in violation of agency regulations; when he brought her and her mother to America his first marriage collapsed, and their taste for high living put him deep enough in debt that he walked into the Soviet embassy to sell it away. She was arrested alongside him at their Arlington home in 1994 and served four years of a 63-month sentence before returning to Colombia.

washington-dc-home-rule.title: The seat-belt roadblocks
washington-dc-home-rule.summary: What John Kiriakou reported the federalised National Guard, police, FBI, ATF and DEA were actually doing at roadblocks on Washington's main thoroughfares in August 2025 — writing tickets for unworn seat belts and broken brake lights, in neighbourhoods he says have no street crime to speak of.

washington-dc-home-rule.title: Quoted on NPR
washington-dc-home-rule.summary: John Kiriakou's discovery, via a standing Google alert on his own name, that National Public Radio had cited a DeProgram discussion between him and Ted Rall in an article on Palestinians killed while waiting for food — an outlet he had walked out on years earlier.

washington-dc-home-rule.title: The Addis Ababa zoo
washington-dc-home-rule.summary: A visit John Kiriakou made to the zoo in Addis Ababa on a free half-day, where he watched keepers force a screaming donkey into the lion enclosure — and noted the two-tier admission price charged to foreigners.

washington-dc-home-rule.title: The armour at Union Station
washington-dc-home-rule.summary: John Kiriakou''s eyewitness account of stepping off an Amtrak train at Washington''s Union Station in August 2025 to find two armoured personnel carriers and a .50 calibre machine gun trained on the entrance — and of tourists posing for photographs with the National Guardsmen deployed in the parts of the city where, he says, there is no crime.

washington-dc-home-rule.title: The boring cover story
washington-dc-home-rule.summary: The CIA training principle John Kiriakou says governed how officers described their jobs to strangers: pick something so dull that nobody asks a second question. His own standard answer was the foreign service, training work, and some import-export negotiation.

washington-dc-home-rule.title: The election day 1992 poll
washington-dc-home-rule.summary: An informal show of hands taken in a CIA branch office on election day 1992, which John Kiriakou describes as the moment he discovered he had no idea of the politics of the colleagues he sat three feet away from — and that he was not, as he had assumed, the only progressive in the room.

washington-political-culture.title: Butler rally shooting
washington-political-culture.summary: The July 2024 attempt on Donald Trump's life at a rally in Butler, Pennsylvania, on which John Kiriakou takes no position as to who was responsible but argues the published facts cannot be reconciled with a competent Secret Service — and that the questions it leaves open are owed an answer for the historical record whether or not anyone alive gets one.

washington-political-culture.title: Charlie Kirk shooting
washington-political-culture.summary: Kiriakou questions the official account: a court filing says the ATF could not match the autopsy bullet to the rifle tied to the suspect.

washington-political-culture.title: Advanced Counterterrorism Operations
washington-political-culture.summary: The six-week specialist course John Kiriakou flew back from Athens to attend roughly eighteen months before 9/11 as one of fourteen officers selected worldwide — high-threat operations, technical collection, and a driving syllabus built around crashing through roadblocks that left the class with whiplash. By accident of timing it meant a trained cadre was ready to deploy the moment the attacks came.

washington-political-culture.title: Anwar al-Awlaki
washington-political-culture.summary: American-born al-Qaeda propagandist; in 1993 the imam of the Falls Church, Virginia mosque visited by John Kiriakou's CIA Arabic-language class on a field trip; in 2001 the cleric at whose mosque the 9/11 hijackers prayed the night before the attacks; killed by U.S. drone strike in Yemen in approximately 2011.

washington-political-culture.title: CIA directorates
washington-political-culture.summary: The four-part internal division of the CIA as John Kiriakou describes it to lay audiences — the Directorate of Intelligence that analyses, the Directorate of Operations that recruits spies and steals secrets, the administrative arm that makes the trains run on time, and the Directorate of Science and Technology that supplies the scientists, forgers and disguise makers — the structure that determines which training a new officer receives.

washington-political-culture.title: CIA liaison relationships
washington-political-culture.summary: John Kiriakou's critique of CIA intelligence-liaison relationships with foreign governments — sharply expanded after 9/11 — arguing that officers do not consider the long-term risk that disclosing sensitive operations to foreign services hands those governments leverage, including potential blackmail material, over the United States, and that no one left in Congress has the will to provide real oversight of the practice.

washington-rat-city.title: The cats of Athens
washington-rat-city.summary: John Kiriakou's explanation for why there are no rats in Athens — the enormous population of street cats that tourists feed at restaurant tables — offered as a contrast to Washington, where he says the rats are the size of small dogs.

washington-rat-city.title: The Parthenon-view condo
washington-rat-city.summary: The eighth-floor Athens apartment John Kiriakou has been watching on the Greek property app Spitogatos, whose price fell from €600,000 to €250,000 after the city banned new Airbnb conversions — and the golden-visa buying that had emptied the residential market in the first place.

washington-rat-city.title: The Greek brain drain
washington-rat-city.summary: The editorial John Kiriakou read in a Greek newspaper tracking where educated Greeks emigrate — the United States, Britain, Germany, Australia — and the line he took from it: that when fifteen hundred Greeks with master''s degrees, law degrees, MDs and PhDs move to Turkey for better opportunity, you know you are finished.

washington-rat-city.title: Astrology at the CIA
washington-rat-city.summary: John Kiriakou''s confirmation that astrology played a role in CIA work in the 1950s and early 1960s as part of MK-ULTRA, alongside time travel and teleportation — and his explanation for why: officials with unlimited budgets and no obligation to report to the public reasoned that there was probably nothing to it, but that if there were, it would make them a star.

washington-rat-city.title: Carrying passports in Washington
washington-rat-city.summary: John Kiriakou's report in September 2025 that people in Washington had begun carrying their passports for fear of being scooped up by immigration enforcement — alongside the case of an American symphony violinist held for three weeks, and his own belief that ethnic profiling violates the Fourth Amendment.

washington-rat-city.title: "Christians are suckers"
washington-rat-city.summary: John Kiriakou's explanation for how a president who does not go to church, has no spiritual adviser and could not name a line of scripture can push school prayer without cost — that he thinks most Christians are suckers, an assessment Kiriakou says he hates to make and believes anyway.

watching-naval-movements.title: Veteran Intelligence Professionals for Sanity
watching-naval-movements.summary: A group of former U.S. intelligence officials, of which John Kiriakou is a member, that issues the Sam Adams Award for Integrity in Intelligence — which Kiriakou arranged to give to whistleblower-adjacent figure Joe Kent.

watching-naval-movements.title: Bill Clinton
watching-naval-movements.summary: 42nd U.S. president whom John Kiriakou describes as wholly disinterested in intelligence — briefed by the CIA only twice in eight years, with Vice President Al Gore taking the daily briefing instead and relaying anything important.

watching-naval-movements.title: Kharg Island
watching-naval-movements.summary: The island where most of Iran's oil is refined, and in John Kiriakou's assessment a standing target whose destruction would be a crisis for world oil prices. It was bombed in the 1980s, causing a global price shock; Kiriakou considers a repeat by the United States or Israel possible, and expects the Iranians to answer it rather than absorb it.

watching-naval-movements.title: Maduro Capture
watching-naval-movements.summary: CIA-driven nighttime operation in which a team of Delta Force commandos entered Venezuela and removed Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro and his wife from their beds. Per John Kiriakou, the key enabling intelligence — per a New York Times account he cited — came from a CIA asset inside Maduro''s presidential palace who called when Maduro went to sleep: ''He''s sound asleep. If you''re going to do it, do it now.'' At least eighty people were killed in the operation, including approximately thirty-five Cubans. Kiriakou compares it to the 1989 capture of Manuel Noriega, in which US forces blasted death metal at the Vatican Embassy until Noriega was asked to leave.

watching-naval-movements.title: Covert action programs
watching-naval-movements.summary: The most tightly held category of American intelligence activity — so tightly held, John Kiriakou says, that a serving CIA officer may not utter the phrase in public. Which is why he found it extraordinary that a president announced one on television, and doubts the announcement was straightforwardly true.

watching-naval-movements.title: Joe Kent
watching-naval-movements.summary: Kiriakou on the former counterterrorism director he gave an award to, publicly opposed for a nomination, and has never actually spoken to.

waterboarding.title: Cold cell
waterboarding.summary: A CIA interrogation technique in which a stripped detainee is chained to a ceiling eyebolt in a cell chilled to 50°F, then doused with a bucket of ice water at hourly intervals; never authorized; documented to have killed at least two prisoners.

waterboarding.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
waterboarding.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

waterboarding.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
waterboarding.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

waterboarding.title: Music as torture
waterboarding.summary: The use of recorded music played on indefinite loop as a coercive interrogation technique. Per John Kiriakou, the CIA's post-9/11 rotation ran to the Bee Gees and the SpongeBob SquarePants theme song, and the practice was not an invention of the war on terror — he places its use throughout the Vietnam War.

waterboarding.title: Christopher Hitchens
waterboarding.summary: British-American journalist and author who, at John Kiriakou's telling, argued that CIA waterboarding was 'nothing … not a big deal,' underwent a filmed waterboarding in 2008, tapped out after roughly seventeen seconds, and suffered panic attacks thereafter. Kiriakou knew him and corresponded with him — the experiment happened because Hitchens thought Kiriakou was exaggerating — and remained an admirer of the writer and an opponent of his politics on Iraq.

waterboarding.title: The slap approval cable
waterboarding.summary: The cable-by-cable approval chain that governed each escalation of the CIA''s enhanced interrogation techniques, described by John Kiriakou in his December 2007 ABC News interview: permission for even a single open-handed slap of Abu Zubaydah came from Washington after a discussion, was granted by the deputy director for operations, and had to be reported back by cable afterwards.

watergate.title: Kiriakou's transfer to the Directorate of Operations
watergate.summary: John Kiriakou's roughly two-month internal campaign to transfer from the CIA's analytic Directorate of Intelligence to the operational Directorate of Operations, overcoming what he calls a "natural bias in operations against the eggheads on the analytic side," followed by an Athens posting secured because he was the only person in the entire CIA fluent in both Greek and Arabic. Covers his full CIA career arc from 1988/1990 recruitment through analyst years on Iraq, the switch to operations, 9/11, the enhanced-interrogation refusal, executive assistant to the deputy director for operations, and his eventual resignation and post-CIA career.

watergate.title: Dianne Feinstein
watergate.summary: Longtime Democratic U.S. senator from California and chair of the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence. Per John Kiriakou, one of the greatest disappointments on Capitol Hill — an unusually friendly chairwoman who exercised no real oversight, good on torture and a cheerleader for the CIA on everything else. She co-authored the 2015 McCain-Feinstein Amendment that reiterated the federal ban on torture, and she blocked Gina Haspel's promotion in 2013 before publicly warming to her in 2018.

watergate.title: John Kiriakou
watergate.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

watergate.title: Arabic and Greek
watergate.summary: The qualification John Kiriakou says opened the door to his transfer from CIA analysis to operations: a post in Athens wanted Greek or Arabic, and he had both — by most of his tellings the only officer in the agency who did. The chief who hired him gave the reason in one sentence: it is easier and cheaper to take a linguist and teach him operations than the other way round. The pairing also became a detection tool, since the language nobody speaks in Pakistan is Arabic.

watergate.title: Code Pink
watergate.summary: The women-led peace group co-founded by Medea Benjamin. John Kiriakou first met them as a Senate staffer — he was the man who threw them out of a hearing he had produced, and got a lecture from Senator Shaheen for it. When he was arrested they were "right there next to me"; they threw his going-away party on the roof of the Hay-Adams, commissioned a folk group to sing a song rewritten about him, and quietly arranged for Roger Waters to pay off the second mortgage so his family could keep the house. He calls them his angels, and the one institution in American life he still trusts.

watergate.title: Doing Time Like a Spy
watergate.summary: Prison memoir by John Kiriakou, full title Doing Time Like a Spy: How the CIA Taught Me to Survive and Thrive in Prison; winner of two literary awards and reissued in a second edition by Simon and Schuster.

watermark.title: Fort Gordon
watermark.summary: The U.S. Army installation in Georgia where NSA whistleblower Reality Winner, interviewed on Kiriakou's show, worked as a contractor linguist before her arrest.

watermark.title: Miranda Rights
watermark.summary: Reality Winner, interviewed on Kiriakou's show, says she was never read her Miranda rights during her 2017 arrest by the FBI.

watermark.title: Terry Aubry
watermark.summary: Named by Kiriakou both as an FBI whistleblower who exposed racism at the bureau and as one of two Intercept journalists who sent him to prison.

watermark.title: Afghan Languages
watermark.summary: The three major languages of Afghanistan — Pashto, Dari (a form of Persian), and Arabic — as discussed on John Kiriakou's show with NSA whistleblower and former military linguist Reality Winner.

watermark.title: Edward Snowden
watermark.summary: Former NSA contractor who in 2013 disclosed the scope of U.S. [mass surveillance](/wiki/mass-surveillance), including the Section 702 collection program. Per John Kiriakou — who counts Snowden among the small group of national-security whistleblowers prosecuted under the Espionage Act — Snowden was ''stuck between two awful slippery slopes'': breaking his oath and chain of command on one side, and on the other catching something ''cut and dry against the Constitution'' that no one would act on. Kiriakou notes Snowden could not use his chain of command (as Kiriakou could not, his own chain being Jose Rodriguez), and that Judge Leonie Brinkema had reserved the Snowden case for herself before he fled the country.

watermark.title: FBI Arrest Strategies
watermark.summary: Per John Kiriakou, the FBI deliberately times arrests for Thursdays or Friday evenings because no federal arraignments happen on Fridays, forcing detainees to spend the weekend in jail before facing a judge on Monday — a tactic he says he saw applied to January 6 defendants as well as to himself.

we-are-at-war-today.title: The second plane
we-are-at-war-today.summary: John Kiriakou's account of where he was standing when United Airlines Flight 175 struck the South Tower — in Cofer Black's outer office, mid-sentence, explaining to a secretary why a pilot could not possibly fly into the World Trade Center on so clear a day.

we-are-at-war-today.title: The Condoleezza Rice meeting
we-are-at-war-today.summary: The nine o'clock White House appointment John Kiriakou and Cofer Black never kept on the morning of 11 September 2001. The Government Printing Office was about to issue a volume of declassified Greece-Turkey-Cyprus cables in an edition of five or ten copies; three of them named CIA sources who were still alive, and an obscure statute obliges the government to offer citizenship and resettlement to any recruited source it outs. The two men were going to ask the National Security Advisor to quietly pull three cables nobody would miss. The car was at the East entrance at 8.15.

we-are-at-war-today.title: The honey salesman warning
we-are-at-war-today.summary: The al-Qaeda briefing Cofer Black delivered unannounced to a visiting delegation of Middle Eastern intelligence officers at CIA headquarters on 6 July 2001, in which he described intercepted code words — a honey salesman arriving with vast quantities of honey, a great wedding, a great football match — as signals of an imminent attack on a massive scale, and begged the visitors for any source inside al-Qaeda.

we-are-at-war-today.title: Reading in on the Iraq invasion
we-are-at-war-today.summary: John Kiriakou's account of his first day as executive assistant to the CIA's deputy director for operations, when he signed six secrecy agreements and was told that the United States would invade Iraq the following March, and that the agencies opposing the war had already lost the argument.

we-are-at-war-today.title: The seventy-two-year-old contractor
we-are-at-war-today.summary: The hallway conversation John Kiriakou says explained why the CIA had not sent him, an Arabic speaker, to interrogate captured al-Qaeda fighters — a returning contractor's answer that he had been in Afghanistan killing people — and the demand Kiriakou made afterwards that got him sent to Pakistan the next day.

we-are-at-war-today.title: The Tehran slip
we-are-at-war-today.summary: The moment John Kiriakou says he witnessed as note-taker in a secure video teleconference a day or two before the 2003 invasion of Iraq, when a briefing general said that if all went as planned American forces could be in Tehran by August, and CIA Director George Tenet turned off his microphone and asked Kiriakou whether the man had said Tehran or Baghdad.

we-dont-hire-felons.title: "The least I could do"
we-dont-hire-felons.summary: Told that he had kept another whistleblower from slipping, John Kiriakou declined the credit and described the work in the plainest possible terms: getting somebody out of the house for three or four hours, or taking them to dinner, because so many people had done exactly that for him when he was at his lowest.

we-dont-hire-felons.title: Do what is right or what is easy
we-dont-hire-felons.summary: Asked what he would tell the boy who once told his father he wanted to be a spy, John Kiriakou said he would tell him to always tell the truth and do the right thing — arguing that everyone already knows in their gut the difference between right and wrong, and that the only real question is whether they then do what is right or what is easy.

we-dont-hire-felons.title: The Berlin conference list
we-dont-hire-felons.summary: Checking into a Berlin hotel for a conference, John Kiriakou was handed the guest list when the clerk could not find his booking — and discovered that every one of the dozen names on it was a friend of his, and every one of them an outspoken whistleblower.

we-dont-hire-felons.title: National Whistleblower Day
we-dont-hire-felons.summary: John Kiriakou has called National Whistleblower Day an event no whistleblower or supporter should miss — held every year in the Kennedy Caucus Room, which he describes as not merely the biggest room on Capitol Hill but the most historic single room anywhere on it, having hosted every major Senate hearing from the sinking of the Titanic to Watergate and Iran-Contra.

we-dont-hire-felons.title: The cousin who stopped speaking
we-dont-hire-felons.summary: An older first cousin told John Kiriakou after his conviction that he could no longer speak to him because Kiriakou had brought shame on the family; Kiriakou's reply was to point out that the cousin had imported drugs from Colombia, had appeared in the Washington Post as a mayor's cocaine dealer, and had fled to Greece until the statute of limitations expired.

we-dont-hire-felons.title: The orange jumpsuits
we-dont-hire-felons.summary: John Kiriakou has argued that the clothing ISIS put on the Western hostages it beheaded was not a coincidence but a citation: the group dressed its prisoners in orange jumpsuits because the United States dressed its own prisoners in orange jumpsuits, and once a government tortures, it has licensed every other government to do the same to its people.

wealth-concentration.title: CIA intelligence failures
wealth-concentration.summary: John Kiriakou's standing position that the CIA has missed every major world event since its founding in 1947 — the building and the fall of the Berlin Wall, the collapse of the Soviet Union, the Iran hostage crisis, 9/11 — and that the remedy is therefore not more money but fewer overseas bases and actual accountability, of which he says there has been none.

wealth-concentration.title: 2028 presidential field
wealth-concentration.summary: John Kiriakou's assessment of the wide-open 2028 presidential race — the first in his life, he says, where he has no idea who either party will nominate. Predictive markets were listing 44 Democrats and 26 Republicans as possible candidates. His own preferred candidate is Tucker Carlson, whom he says he has repeatedly begged to run; his working assumption about anyone who does want the job is that they are "a narcissist and probably a sociopath on top of it."

wealth-concentration.title: Amaryllis Fox Kennedy
wealth-concentration.summary: Former CIA non-official-cover officer who worked under commercial cover as an international art consultant, later a Trump campaign manager and nominee for deputy CIA director. Per John Kiriakou, Senator Tom Cotton threatened to filibuster her appointment; the president responded by naming her deputy national security adviser instead — a job Kiriakou considers more powerful, since the CIA director reports to the national security adviser.

wealth-concentration.title: Andrew Bustamante
wealth-concentration.summary: Former CIA officer who sells CIA-style training online; John Kiriakou identifies him as the lone critic of his work hosting a show on a Russian network, and argues Bustamante's training business — open to anyone who pays — is the more problematic of the two.

wealth-concentration.title: Angry Birds
wealth-concentration.summary: The mobile game John Kiriakou describes as his only vice besides buying art, played every morning for nine consecutive years and cited by his ex-wife as a grievance in their marriage.

wealth-concentration.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
wealth-concentration.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

weaponization-subcommittee.title: Church Committee
weaponization-subcommittee.summary: U.S. Senate investigative committee operating in 1975–1976 that examined domestic intelligence abuses by the CIA, FBI, and NSA; per John Kiriakou, the Church Committee — alongside the concurrent Pike Committee in the House — was the last genuine moment of legislative oversight over the intelligence community, born of a national consensus that government had gone dangerously off course. Its work led to the creation of the permanent Senate Select Committee on Intelligence, which Kiriakou says ceased to function as real oversight roughly seven years after its founding.

weaponization-subcommittee.title: COINTELPRO
weaponization-subcommittee.summary: The FBI programme of warrantless surveillance and disruption directed at Americans, and one of the four abuses John Kiriakou names when explaining what the Church Committee actually investigated. He treats it as the historical benchmark for what a real congressional inquiry into the security agencies looks like — and, through the campaign against Martin Luther King, as proof that the state will destroy a citizen it considers a threat.

weaponization-subcommittee.title: Jim Jordan
weaponization-subcommittee.summary: Republican congressman from Ohio and chairman of the House Judiciary Committee. John Kiriakou describes a genuinely divided view of him: one of only four members of Congress he names as a friend of whistleblowers, and simultaneously the chairman whose Weaponization subcommittee he says is a partisan counterfeit of the Church Committee — with the whole question settled against Jordan by the Ohio State wrestlers who told him their team doctor was abusing them.

weaponization-subcommittee.title: MK-Ultra
weaponization-subcommittee.summary: The CIA's mid-twentieth-century umbrella program of mind-control, behavioral-modification, and biological-warfare experimentation, encompassing subprojects such as MK-Chickwit and MK-Seesaw; active 1952–1975; documented practices included LSD dosing of unwitting American citizens in CIA-rented brothels and the aerosolized release of pathogens into the San Francisco fog; 80% of the program's documentation was destroyed by the CIA in defiance of a 1975 preservation order from Senator Frank Church.

weaponization-subcommittee.title: Vault 7
weaponization-subcommittee.summary: The 2017 WikiLeaks disclosure of thousands of pages of CIA Directorate of Science and Technology documents — leaked by agency engineer Joshua Schulte — revealing CIA technical capabilities including remote takeover of internet-connected cars, conversion of smart-TV speakers into covert microphones, and the planting of Russian or Persian language fragments in foreign systems to mislead attribution.

weaponization-subcommittee.title: David Petraeus
weaponization-subcommittee.summary: Retired U.S. Army general and director of the CIA who, per John Kiriakou, confirmed the names of ten covert CIA operatives to his biographer and girlfriend and was never criminally charged — a contrast Kiriakou cites repeatedly as proof that his own prosecution under the Intelligence Identities Protection Act was selective. Kiriakou''s explanation for the disparity: Petraeus had not blown the whistle on the torture program and embarrassed the agency.

weapons-cache-map.title: The propane truck ruse
weapons-cache-map.summary: The improvised environmental emergency John Kiriakou staged to empty a Middle Eastern cul-de-sac so a CIA lock-picking team could search a captured Hezbollah organiser's house — after his liaison partners rejected a gas leak on the ground that the country had no underground gas lines.

weapons-cache-map.title: Double-Agent Capture
weapons-cache-map.summary: Clandestine operation in which an intelligence service, having identified a recruited agent as working simultaneously for a hostile service, arranges a controlled final meeting to apprehend the agent before the agent can carry out orders — which may include killing the handler. Per John Kiriakou, he ran one such operation in the Middle East in the early 2000s after an NSA analyst warned him that his agent had just been ordered to shoot him in the next meeting.

weapons-cache-map.title: Training foreign intelligence services
weapons-cache-map.summary: The CIA job John Kiriakou took after returning from Athens — travelling the world to teach foreign services how to carry out counterterrorist raids, break down doors, seize people, conduct interrogations and disrupt cells — and why, he says, those countries asked the Americans rather than the Israelis or the British.

weapons-cache-map.title: The CIA divorce rate
weapons-cache-map.summary: John Kiriakou's account of why marriages fail at the CIA at a rate he says exceeds that of any other part of the U.S. government — the impossibility of explaining a midnight departure to a spouse without a clearance, and the difficulty officers have switching off a professional habit of deception. He gives the figure variously as over 75 percent and upwards of 80 percent, says he was determined not to become a statistic and became one anyway, and dates the end of his first marriage to a sentence spoken in an armoured car on the way to Athens airport. Both his divorces have been costly; of the second he says the agency played an active role he is barred by court order from explaining.

weapons-cache-map.title: Consulting for royal families
weapons-cache-map.summary: The work John Kiriakou says he was hired to do by members of two different royal families following the 2026 virality of his interviews — advising on ethics in their own intelligence operations — which he offers as evidence of how far the reversal in his standing had gone.

weapons-cache-map.title: The Greek community of Warren, Ohio
weapons-cache-map.summary: The Greek-American community John Kiriakou's mother and first wife both came from — overwhelmingly from the island of Chios, closely enough knit that his divorce started a fistfight in a coffee house between men who had never met him.

welch-45.title: Revolutionary Organization 17 November
welch-45.summary: Greek far-left urban guerrilla group active 1975–2002; the deadliest terrorist organization in Greek history

welch-45.title: Stephen Saunders
welch-45.summary: British defense attaché in Athens assassinated by Revolutionary Organization 17 November in March 2000

welch-45.title: Richard Welch
welch-45.summary: CIA Athens station chief assassinated December 23, 1975; the first victim of [Revolutionary Organization 17 November](/wiki/revolutionary-organization-17-november)

welch-45.title: Carlos the Jackal
welch-45.summary: Venezuelan-born militant (Ilich Ramírez Sánchez) active in the 1970s and 1980s; per John Kiriakou, 'the Osama bin Laden of the 70s and 80s.' Kiriakou spent his Athens posting trying to identify the middleman linking Carlos to the Greek terrorist group 17 November, then six months working the lead with MI5 in London; Carlos was finally run down by CIA contractor Billy Waugh in a Khartoum vegetable market and captured in 1994.

welch-45.title: Dimitris Koufodinas
welch-45.summary: The primary assassin of Revolutionary Organization 17 November, known as the Black Hand because everything he touched died — the one member who briefly escaped the collapse of the group, and who was found on a nudist beach on a Greek island.

welch-45.title: Gust Avrakotos
welch-45.summary: CIA case officer, John Kiriakou's operations mentor, and a central figure in Charlie Wilson's War — the prolific, divisive covert-war veteran Kiriakou credits as the greatest teacher of his adult life.

wesley-clark.title: Iraq WMD intelligence
wesley-clark.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of how the case for Iraqi weapons of mass destruction was fabricated: the intelligence community''s consensus was that Iraq had no WMD, but the White House had already decided to invade and sought analysis to fit the policy.

wesley-clark.title: George Tenet
wesley-clark.summary: Director of Central Intelligence from 1997 to 2004, spanning the September 11 attacks and the early enhanced-interrogation program; identified by John Kiriakou as John Brennan's institutional patron at the agency; the figure who ordered the Five Eyes intelligence services to "open the files" to each other in the early 2000s.

wesley-clark.title: Dick Cheney
wesley-clark.summary: U.S. Vice President under George W. Bush. Per John Kiriakou — recounting CIA Director George Tenet's memoir — Cheney intercepted the presidential finding authorizing the CIA's enhanced interrogation program in the Oval Office anteroom and took it from Tenet before Bush could sign it. Tenet later concluded the president probably never actually signed the finding and probably told the truth when he said he had no idea the program was taking place. Kiriakou characterizes Cheney as the one who actually ran foreign policy, intelligence policy, and defense policy during the Bush years.

wesley-clark.title: Principals Committee Meeting (February 2003)
wesley-clark.summary: Senior-most interagency forum of the U.S. national security apparatus, normally chaired by the president. Per John Kiriakou — who served as notetaker for CIA Director George Tenet at the eve-of-Iraq-invasion meeting on February 19–20, 2003 — Vice President Dick Cheney chaired in place of Bush, General Tommy Franks ended his order-of-battle briefing with 'If all goes as planned, we can be in Tehran by August,' and an NSC senior director said 'When we cross that border tomorrow morning, they're going to throw flowers at us.'

wesley-clark.title: Israeli Nuclear Program
wesley-clark.summary: Israel's widely assumed but officially unacknowledged nuclear arsenal; per John Kiriakou, the conventional wisdom within the CIA is that Israel possesses between 120 and 220 nuclear weapons, and the U.S. government's refusal to formally acknowledge this is driven by a specific legal obligation under the Glenn-Symington Act, which would require cutting off all foreign aid to any nuclear-armed country not party to the Non-Proliferation Treaty.

wesley-clark.title: Mary Margaret Graham
wesley-clark.summary: CIA Senior Intelligence Service officer and later Deputy Director of National Intelligence for Collection under John Negroponte — described by John Kiriakou as a career "reports officer" who had never personally recruited a source, and as his difficult chief of station in a later domestic assignment.

what-we-owed-mexico.title: No declaration of war since 1941
what-we-owed-mexico.summary: John Kiriakou's answer to whether Congress will assert its authority over military action against Venezuela — an unqualified no, resting on the fact that the last declaration of war was on 8 December 1941 and that even the Gulf War was fought on an authorisation to use force rather than a declaration.

what-we-owed-mexico.title: The Bay of Piglets
what-we-owed-mexico.summary: The phrase John Kiriakou wished he had coined for the twice-attempted amphibious landings in Venezuela — and his account of one of the men rounded up coming ashore, who emailed him years later asking to appear on his show as a whistleblower on communism, and was told no.

what-we-owed-mexico.title: The West Africa cocaine route
what-we-owed-mexico.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of where cocaine transiting Venezuela actually goes: not north to the United States but east to West Africa, onto camels along an old Tuareg track to Morocco, and by boat to Spain. The drugs, he says, are meant for Western Europe — and are not Venezuelan to begin with, but Colombian and Ecuadorian.

what-we-owed-mexico.title: Abigail Spanberger
what-we-owed-mexico.summary: Governor of Virginia from 2025 and, before Congress, a CIA officer alongside John Kiriakou in the Counterterrorism Center — whom he calls a perfectly nice person who would have been a middle-of-the-road Republican in the 1970s and 1980s, and whose victory speech, to his surprise, said all the right things.

what-we-owed-mexico.title: Destroying the Dome of the Rock
what-we-owed-mexico.summary: John Kiriakou's agreement with Tucker Carlson that a Zionist extremist plan to demolish the Dome of the Rock and build a third temple would be the event that starts the Third World War — and his additional prediction that it would also be the beginning of the end for the Israeli government and all of its support.

what-we-owed-mexico.title: Jason Miyares
what-we-owed-mexico.summary: The Cuban-born Republican attorney general of Virginia whom John Kiriakou expected to be a right-wing disaster and found instead to be excellent — a judgement he says is hard for him to make about a conservative Republican, and which he repeated on the night Miyares was unceremoniously thrown out of office.

whatever-darpa-is-working-on.title: The Hyundai robots
whatever-darpa-is-working-on.summary: The South Korean robots John Kiriakou cites as the answer to a promise the Pentagon has been making for decades — long-life batteries solved by a Hyundai subsidiary, robots ready to go to market that can get into a self-driving car and do the grocery shopping, and his question of why DARPA has not managed it.

whatever-darpa-is-working-on.title: The Pentagon budget reversal
whatever-darpa-is-working-on.summary: The pair of announcements John Kiriakou uses as his cleanest evidence of incoherence in the second Trump administration — a stated intention to cut the Pentagon budget by fifty per cent, celebrated at the time, followed a couple of months later by a stated intention to increase it by fifty per cent.

whatever-darpa-is-working-on.title: "Beyond Your Dreams"
whatever-darpa-is-working-on.summary: The gloss a host gave John Kiriakou on his first trip to China when he asked what the beautiful car with the BYD badge was — and the answer he got when he asked why he had never heard of it, which was that the United States is the only country where they are not sold.

whatever-darpa-is-working-on.title: The ideological circle
whatever-darpa-is-working-on.summary: John Kiriakou's long-held claim that the political spectrum is not a straight line from left to right but a circle, on which the two ends meet — and that in the case of MAGA and the progressive left, the point where they meet is war and peace.

whatever-darpa-is-working-on.title: Carving up Iran
whatever-darpa-is-working-on.summary: The Israeli end goal John Kiriakou says has been discussed with increasingly less discretion — dividing Iran into five small rump countries including Balochistan, Arabistan and Kurdistan, on the reasoning that small states are more easily controlled — and which he expects Israel will eventually try to get Donald Trump to carry out.

whatever-darpa-is-working-on.title: Dumping the treasury bonds
whatever-darpa-is-working-on.summary: The second economic weapon John Kiriakou says China holds against the United States — its position as the second or third largest holder of long-term government treasury bonds, which it could simply dump, and which he says would crash the entire American economy.

where-he-slept-in-afghanistan.title: The fox that ate the scraps
where-he-slept-in-afghanistan.summary: The small grey desert fox that lived on the grounds of the Baja resort, which the cook told John Kiriakou would finish anything left on the plate — and which, every single night, defecated on exactly the spot he crossed to reach his outdoor mini fridge.

where-he-slept-in-afghanistan.title: The resort with no air conditioning
where-he-slept-in-afghanistan.summary: The Baja California resort where John Kiriakou spent a month filming in 2025 — built in the 1960s as a commune by long-haired left-wing Angelenos funded by Thomas Hart Benton's daughter, a dozen buildings on the southernmost tip of the peninsula, no air conditioning, and nothing whatsoever to do unless you dive.

where-he-slept-in-afghanistan.title: The tarantula on the mini fridge
where-he-slept-in-afghanistan.summary: The wildlife of the Baja resort as John Kiriakou catalogued it — rattlesnakes everywhere, an emailed instruction never to go barefoot, shoes shaken out before every midnight walk to the mini fridge kept outdoors, a flashlight in hand, and one night at three in the morning a tarantula sitting on the fridge itself.

where-he-slept-in-afghanistan.title: The Bamiyan precedent
where-he-slept-in-afghanistan.summary: John Kiriakou's account of how the Taliban destroyed their own diplomatic position by blowing up the Bamiyan Buddhas — at a moment when Washington was paying Taliban salaries, funding opium eradication, flirting with a trans-Afghanistan pipeline and flying Taliban emissaries to Houston to meet the Bush camp.

where-he-slept-in-afghanistan.title: Abigail Spanberger
where-he-slept-in-afghanistan.summary: Governor of Virginia from 2025 and, before Congress, a CIA officer alongside John Kiriakou in the Counterterrorism Center — whom he calls a perfectly nice person who would have been a middle-of-the-road Republican in the 1970s and 1980s, and whose victory speech, to his surprise, said all the right things.

where-he-slept-in-afghanistan.title: Destroying the Dome of the Rock
where-he-slept-in-afghanistan.summary: John Kiriakou's agreement with Tucker Carlson that a Zionist extremist plan to demolish the Dome of the Rock and build a third temple would be the event that starts the Third World War — and his additional prediction that it would also be the beginning of the end for the Israeli government and all of its support.

whether-anyone-is-still-looking-for-zawa.title: The two ISIs
whether-anyone-is-still-looking-for-zawa.summary: Asked how much cooperation he got from Pakistan''s intelligence service after 9/11, John Kiriakou answered that the honest answer was two answers: the counterterrorism officers he worked with had all been trained in America and Britain, while the men who gave him the stink eye in the corridors of ISI headquarters were the ones who had created the Taliban.

whether-anyone-is-still-looking-for-zawa.title: The let-them-in strategy
whether-anyone-is-still-looking-for-zawa.summary: John Kiriakou has claimed one of the ideas he contributed as CIA counterterrorism chief in Pakistan was to stop trying to intercept al-Qaeda fighters one at a time on the Afghan border, and instead let them cross into Pakistan and take them ten at a time in their safe houses.

whether-anyone-is-still-looking-for-zawa.title: Fusha and the Gulf dialect
whether-anyone-is-still-looking-for-zawa.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of his own Arabic training — a first year in fusha, high standard Arabic, followed by a second year in khaleeji, the Gulf dialect — and what he reports of both: that Yemen is the only place pure fusha is spoken, that Saudis asked him why he spoke Arabic like Shakespeare, that the Gulf dialect is marked by a hard J other Arabs dislike, and that the Maghreb defeats him entirely.

whether-anyone-is-still-looking-for-zawa.title: "I only wanted to kill Jews"
whether-anyone-is-still-looking-for-zawa.summary: In the hospital room at a Pakistani military base, after telling the wounded Abu Zubaydah that fifty thousand people had been in the towers and that he was not the victim, John Kiriakou says the prisoner answered that he had only wanted to kill Jews and had been overruled.

whether-anyone-is-still-looking-for-zawa.title: Abu Zubaydah
whether-anyone-is-still-looking-for-zawa.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

whether-anyone-is-still-looking-for-zawa.title: Zawahiri assassination
whether-anyone-is-still-looking-for-zawa.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the drone strike that killed al-Qaeda's Ayman al-Zawahiri — using a bladed, warhead-less missile fired as he stepped onto a balcony to smoke, deliberately chosen to avoid killing the women and children inside.

whipping-votes.title: Three Republican congressmen
whipping-votes.summary: John Kiriakou''s arithmetic for why the shutdown fight was not over when the Senate cut its deal: the Senate produced its own agreement rather than voting on the House bill, so the House has to be recalled to vote on the Senate version. Republicans needed seven Democratic senators; the House needs only three Republican congressmen to kill it — which is why he thought attention should shift to the House.

whipping-votes.title: The nineteen-hundred-dollar premium
whipping-votes.summary: John Kiriakou''s own stake in the collapse of the Affordable Care Act subsidies: a monthly health insurance premium going from roughly $900 to $1,900. He says plainly that he cannot do it — that he does not have $1,900 a month for health insurance — and notes that the figure exceeds what the broadcast pays him.

whipping-votes.title: Coffee with a cabinet member
whipping-votes.summary: John Kiriakou's disclosure that he had coffee with a member of the cabinet who told him to be patient about his pardon — and told him to watch what he said. He reports the meeting while stating plainly that there is nothing further he can do to make his case, and that he is not confident the outcome will be decided on justice.

whipping-votes.title: Ed Martin and the pardon file
whipping-votes.summary: The US pardon attorney whose office John Kiriakou directed supporters to write to, and the message a mutual friend brought back from him: that he was the third person that day to call about Kiriakou, that Kiriakou should relax, and that his file was literally on Martin''s desk. Kiriakou''s advice to letter-writers was to send physical mail rather than email.

whipping-votes.title: Lincoln's candlelight pardons
whipping-votes.summary: The historical contrast John Kiriakou drew while discussing a mass grant of clemency: stories of Abraham Lincoln staying up late into the night pardoning Civil War deserters by candlelight, on the principle that nobody should be executed for cowardice — set against a modern president who Kiriakou says has pardoned more people than anyone in American history, whenever the mood strikes him.

whipping-votes.title: Pardons nobody asked for
whipping-votes.summary: Two cases John Kiriakou cites of people pardoned without applying: the Binance founder, who said publicly that he had never met the president, never asked for a pardon and never applied for one; and Darryl Strawberry, a New York Mets great with tax and drug problems behind him. Kiriakou raises both while waiting, unsuccessfully, for a pardon he has actively sought for years.

whispers-in-the-dirt-book.title: Kiriakou's writing process
whispers-in-the-dirt-book.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of how he actually writes — books in waves over roughly nine months, op-eds in forty-five minutes to an hour once an idea has sat for a few days, and a habit of getting up at two in the morning to write one because he cannot sleep. He wrote *Remains of the Day* in six weeks during COVID, losing whole evenings to it: "I look at the clock again, it''s 2:00 in the morning. I''m like, oh my god, what happened?"

whispers-in-the-dirt-book.title: Remains of the Day (book)
whispers-in-the-dirt-book.summary: John Kiriakou's book, announced for publication by Simon and Schuster in March 2026, billed as a definitive guide to the historic cemeteries of Washington DC and the first in a planned series; the second installment will cover the Mafia graves of New York City.

whispers-in-the-dirt-book.title: Greek death rituals
whispers-in-the-dirt-book.summary: The five-year grave rental, exhumation and ossuary practice of rural Greece as John Kiriakou describes it — bones washed in red wine, blessed, boxed, and eventually laid beneath the foundations of a new church, with cremation strictly forbidden. He visits the ossuary in his ancestral Rhodes village, where the records stop in the nineteenth century because the Ottomans burned everything earlier.

whispers-in-the-dirt-book.title: Israel Boyd and the Wonder Bread story
whispers-in-the-dirt-book.summary: John Kiriakou's account of finding the grave of Israel Boyd, one of two brothers forced by their parents into the family bakery business, who went on to invent the first industrial dough mixer and dough-cutting machine, pioneer adding milk to bread dough, and build the largest bakery in America before World War I — before selling the business, whose flagship "Mrs. McGill's Delicious Bread" was renamed Wonder Bread by its buyer.

whispers-in-the-dirt-book.title: John Kiriakou
whispers-in-the-dirt-book.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

whispers-in-the-dirt-book.title: Abraham Accords
whispers-in-the-dirt-book.summary: The Trump-brokered normalization deals between Israel and Gulf Arab states — in John Kiriakou's judgment "a terrible idea in the first place," a great victory for Israel and the Gulf Arabs that was "a punch in the throat to the Palestinians." He argues the Accords are how Trump meant to "solve the Middle East in a day" — by screwing the Palestinians — that Hamas read the abandonment correctly, that October 7 shattered the project, and that reviving the Accords (Saudis in, victory declared, Nobel collected) remains the organizing goal of Trump's regional policy.

whistleblower-protection-act.title: Abu Zubaydah
whistleblower-protection-act.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

whistleblower-protection-act.title: Chuck Grassley
whistleblower-protection-act.summary: The senior senator from Iowa, and in John Kiriakou's assessment the one member of Congress who has taken whistleblower protection seriously as a legislative project — a count he has variously put at one finger, at two names, and at four out of 535. Grassley wrote the whistleblower protection statutes, speaks every year at the National Whistleblower Day luncheon, and is the name Kiriakou gives prospective whistleblowers as the single friendly ear on Capitol Hill. Kiriakou's personal verdict is colder — Grassley, he has said, never did anything for him.

whistleblower-protection-act.title: Espionage Act
whistleblower-protection-act.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

whistleblower-protection-act.title: Mark MacGann
whistleblower-protection-act.summary: The Uber whistleblower whose case John Kiriakou presented on his own programme: a 52-year-old Irishman who ran the company''s lobbying across Europe, the Middle East and Africa from 2014 to 2016, and who later handed 124,000 pages of internal documents covering 2013 to 2017 to the Guardian. Kiriakou''s account turns on one point — that the opportunity Uber marketed to low-income drivers was never what it claimed, and that the company''s leadership knew it from the beginning.

whistleblower-protection-act.title: The order of the whistleblower process
whistleblower-protection-act.summary: John Kiriakou's objection to the 2019 Ukraine complainant — that the Whistleblower Protection Act prescribes a sequence in which the inspector general comes first and the congressional committee last, that this complainant went to the committee first, and that the inversion is a violation of the letter of the law.

whistleblower-protection-act.title: Securedrop
whistleblower-protection-act.summary: The encrypted submission tool pioneered by WikiLeaks to let sources hand over documents without exposing themselves.

whistleblower-psychology.title: Julian Assange
whistleblower-psychology.summary: Kiriakou — a 15-year friend and former WikiLeaks board member — on why Assange is a publisher owed a journalist's immunity, and a political prisoner.

whistleblower-psychology.title: Daniel Ellsberg
whistleblower-psychology.summary: The Pentagon Papers whistleblower Kiriakou calls 'the Godfather of all national security whistleblowers' — and one of the great mentors of his life.

whistleblower-psychology.title: Death threats against Kiriakou
whistleblower-psychology.summary: The threats John Kiriakou has received across two decades — first after going public about the CIA torture program, when FBI advice that at least two were credible sent his family out of the country, and later in waves tied to his opposition to Gina Haspel, his remarks about Pakistan, and his advocacy on Palestine and the Epstein case.

whistleblower-psychology.title: The philosophy class
whistleblower-psychology.summary: The introductory philosophy lecture at Miami University of Ohio in which John Kiriakou's own whistleblowing was set as the ethical dilemma, unknown to the professor with Kiriakou's son sitting in the room — the episode Kiriakou offers when asked how he survived losing his career, his pension and his marriage.

whistleblower-psychology.title: Frank Serpico
whistleblower-psychology.summary: The New York police officer John Kiriakou calls one of the giants of the twentieth century and ranks with Daniel Ellsberg among its greatest whistleblowers — a man shot in the face whose police colleagues did not call an ambulance, and whom Kiriakou counts as a friend.

whistleblower-psychology.title: "There is almost no upside"
whistleblower-psychology.summary: John Kiriakou''s accounting of what blowing the whistle cost him — pension, friends, freedom and finally family — set against the single thing he says is left: knowing he did the right thing. And his timeline, from the whistle in 2007 to a vindication he says took eleven years.

whistleblower-support-network.title: Kevin Shipp
whistleblower-support-network.summary: Former CIA officer and whistleblower whose case John Kiriakou read about in the Washington Post and who, Kiriakou says, believed he was entirely alone until Kiriakou reached out to tell him he was not — an episode Kiriakou uses to illustrate the isolation that follows a national security disclosure.

whistleblower-support-network.title: Bill Binney
whistleblower-support-network.summary: Former NSA technical director whom John Kiriakou cites as having debunked the DNC hack. Asked by Veteran Intelligence Professionals for Sanity to examine the science, Binney analyzed the speed of the upload and concluded the emails could only have been copied in person to a thumb drive, not taken remotely by Russia — an argument he later made to Donald Trump in the Oval Office. Kiriakou calls him a friend, the most brilliant person he has met on electronics, and a member of the whistleblower circle he belongs to.

whistleblower-support-network.title: Veteran Intelligence Professionals for Sanity
whistleblower-support-network.summary: A group of former U.S. intelligence officials, of which John Kiriakou is a member, that issues the Sam Adams Award for Integrity in Intelligence — which Kiriakou arranged to give to whistleblower-adjacent figure Joe Kent.

whistleblower-support-network.title: Communications management unit
whistleblower-support-network.summary: The two restricted-contact units inside the American federal prison system, at Terre Haute and Marion; built for "the worst of the worst" but, in John Kiriakou's account, used to silence prisoners whose messages are inconvenient — and a practice he groups with solitary confinement as torture. He served part of his own sentence in a modified one.

whistleblower-support-network.title: Daniel Hale
whistleblower-support-network.summary: Per John Kiriakou, drone whistleblower Daniel Hale — an NSA contractor and drone targeting analyst who exposed an 80% civilian death rate in the U.S. drone program, was ordered to fire on two young girls his superior called "goats," and was sentenced to 45 months (of which Kiriakou says he actually served about 18) despite prosecutors seeking nine to eleven years.

whistleblower-support-network.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
whistleblower-support-network.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

whistleblowers-and-suicide.title: Thursday arrests
whistleblowers-and-suicide.summary: The scheduling practice John Kiriakou attributes to the FBI — arresting on a Thursday so that a defendant, unable to be arraigned on a Friday, spends four nights in jail before seeing a judge — and the single sentence that he says kept him out of it.

whistleblowers-and-suicide.title: "Whistleblowers die broke"
whistleblowers-and-suicide.summary: The observation John Kiriakou attributes to Daniel Ellsberg — that the one thing all whistleblowers have in common is that they die broke — which Kiriakou applies to his own confiscated federal pension and his expectation of working until the day he dies.

whistleblowers-and-suicide.title: "Embrace it and keep telling it"
whistleblowers-and-suicide.summary: The advice John Kiriakou says he was given days after his arrest — that he could not hide from the prosecution but had to embrace it, and had to keep telling his side of the story until it became the side of record, because the government would eventually move on to its next target.

whistleblowers-and-suicide.title: Assange and solitary confinement
